## Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library

... of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the times of Innocent III; a chronological reprint of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition throughout the first twelve centuries of the Church, based on the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the utmost diligence; continuously illuminated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions published during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or author of significance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; enlarged with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also with works possessing some authority and weight in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which everything that each Father has written on any topic may be surveyed at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is easy for the reader to discover which Fathers, and in what passages of their works, have commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture.

A most accurate edition, easily to be preferred to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the exceedingly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection—single, systematic, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.

### First Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church, from Tertullian to Gregory the Great.

Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

# [Lives of the Fathers]

[Column 0009]

## Notice

To the series of the Fathers extending from Tertullian to Gregory the Great, we append, as it were, a crown: Rosweyde’s *Lives of the Fathers*, a work eagerly desired by everyone and commended with praise. Nor do we seem to depart from our purpose when we place this collection of Lives after the monuments of the first six centuries, since perhaps all its authors belong to that period, and quite a number of them belong to Latin Patrology. Those who wrote in Greek will now present themselves to the learned reader only under the guise of the most ancient translation, having borrowed, as it were, the right of Latin citizenship from this particular form, until they may be read in their proper places in the Greek series, speaking their own language and furnished with a more recent translation. M.

[Column 0009]

## To Antonius de Winghe, Abbot of Liessies of the Order of Saint Benedict, and to His Religious Community

### Preface of Heribert Rosweyde

It is now the fourth year, most reverend Lord, since you entrusted me with the task of revising the *Lives of the Fathers*, yourself repeatedly promising every assistance, both in books and in expense, just as Evagrius once promised Jerome that, in the Syrian desert, he would write the Lives of the holy Fathers no less with his pen than with the experience of his own life. You were spurred on by the abundant harvest which you believed every religious soul could gain from this book. At first I declined, pleading that I was occupied with another work, and suggested that we should seek out the remains of Baronius, whom I knew once to have been disposed to undertake and adorn this task; for that reason, an inquiry ought to be made in Rome to discover whether he had left behind any resources for it.

Accordingly, when I was first considering going to Rome, through the very illustrious and most reverend Lord Moro, abbot of Saint-Michel in France, with the support also of the most illustrious Cardinal du Perron, you asked those familiar with Baronius’s studies whether the outstanding historian of the *Annals* had left anything that might assist in this undertaking. The following reply was received from Rome (*Roman Letter to Cardinal du Perron*):

> “It is indeed true that, at the urging of many pious brothers, the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius had resolved to enlarge and write a book on the *Lives of the Fathers*, and that he promised as much in some of his books; but up to the present he had not applied his hand to the work, because he directed his studies elsewhere. He had indeed instructed the procurator of the Cassinese Order to write to two or three of the principal monasteries of his order and inquire whether printed or manuscript books touching on this subject could be found; and, if I remember correctly, he also asked the most illustrious Cardinal Sappata to write to Spain for a similar inquiry. He believed that he would also find something in the Vatican Library; but, overtaken by death, he could not carry out his pious desire. At home I found only one book of the *Lives of the Fathers*, printed at Lyons in 1522, so corrupt that it can scarcely be understood. This is why I cannot satisfy Your Most Illustrious Lordship as she desires, and as I would gladly do with every respect, if it were within my power. If someone should be willing to apply his hand to this work and devote his labor to making it complete, he would perform a service most pleasing to God almighty and most useful to all religious persons wishing to live piously.”

Having received this answer, and seeing that the entire task you wished me to undertake had been left to me, I set aside all other studies and devoted myself to this single undertaking. I considered that, above all, three things had to be accomplished in this revision.

First, since every book derives its authority from its authors, I had to investigate them thoroughly rather than superficially. The care with which I carried this out will be shown in the following prolegomena, both through the guidance of written books and through the instruction provided by various history.

Second, the text had to emerge genuine, interspersed with no glosses and embellished with no spurious coloring. Gold filings come out purer from their own veins than from the goldsmith’s furnace, where they are repeatedly adulterated by some unknown mixture. For this purpose I summoned manuscript codices from everywhere, not only from Belgium but also from Germany; their catalogue will be found in Prolegomenon 24. I also sought the oldest editions that I could obtain; indeed, I scarcely hesitate to assert that I acquired almost all of them, whether recent or ancient. Certainly I investigated and inspected nineteen different copies, which Prolegomenon 17 will identify by place and date. Relying on these resources, I compared manuscripts especially with printed books, sometimes manuscripts with manuscripts, and sometimes printed editions with printed editions as well.

Third, wherever a difficult word occurred, wherever an unusual rite left the reader in doubt, or wherever a perplexing history disturbed the sense, I had to remove the difficulty by explanation, make the rarity more familiar by adducing similar examples, unravel the perplexity by comparing historians with one another, and finally bring light to all obscure passages, as far as the lamp of my household resources could provide it.

Since I remembered that Baronius had once shown goodwill toward these *Lives of the Fathers* (*Baronius, Notes on the Roman Martyrology*, 17 January), whatever I could gather from his writings to illuminate these Lives I have supplied in the appropriate places in his own words; and for that reason, too, I was pleased to pay my respects to the great man.

You have here, most reverend prelate, the plan of my undertaking; you have the long-desired *Lives of the Fathers*. Posterity will attribute to you and to your community the fact that, through your favor and expense, they now appear in a more elegant dress.

But will you not permit me, in the customary manner of solemn prefaces, to weave here some laurels of praise for you and your community? You do not permit it, being sufficiently glorious in the sight of God and your own conscience. You therefore order me to restrain my pen from praising you and your people: “Your affection for us,” you say, “might carry you beyond the truth of the matter” (*Letter of Abbot Winghe to Heribert*). Though I can testify to my affection and affirm that I think nothing of you or yours beyond the truth, nevertheless, lest I stumble at the threshold—as the saying goes—upon the slippery path of disobedience, I obey your commands.

I shall say nothing of the zeal for religion with which you burn, nothing of the love of poverty in which you rejoice, nothing of the fervor of piety with which you glow toward God, nothing of the distinguished governance of your people, whom you lead more by example than by words; and finally nothing—although I could speak of it at length and you could listen to it most willingly—of your singular affection for our smallest community, an affection which makes you no less one of us in spirit and dress than in your religious observance of the particularly excellent discretion of the Rule (*Gregory, Book II of the Dialogues*, chapter 36), and makes you, as it were, a Benedictine wearing the *maforte*. I shall therefore say nothing of your praises, since you have always regarded these fans of praise as whips.

Nor will it be permitted to me to address you according to your merits, religious community of Liessies, whose discipline presents to us the Thebaid of Pachomius, the Nitrian desert of Ammon, and the Scetis of Macarius. Under Blosius, what sheaves of virtues did Liessies not produce? Under Doulletius, with what rubies of charity did it not shine? Under Le Francquius, with what splendor of religious beauty did it not gleam? Whoever reads the *Lives of the Fathers*, while traversing the deserts of Egypt and visiting Pauls, Antonies, and Paphnutiuses; while crossing the wildernesses of Palestine and visiting Hilarions, Hesychases, and Epiphaniuses; while creeping through the crags and caves of Syria and visiting Ephraems, Aphraateses, and Julians—let that person behold Liessies with the eyes, love Liessies in the heart, and venerate Liessies with the feet. There he will find abbots who are imitators of those great men whose sacred memory lives in the souls of religious persons. Modesty does not allow me to count Winghe among their successors, no less in virtue than in dignity. I therefore leave him to be praised by posterity, not by suspicious censors of the dead.

Meanwhile, most reverend prelate, enjoy with your religious community this volume of the *Lives of the Fathers*, polished through your expense. If another volume should eventually be added, embracing all the ascetic writings of the Fathers in one kind of bundle, you would possess everything that could be required for the ascetic practice of the ancients. For just as this book leads the way in forming morals by examples, the other would guide by teaching. But since I remember that it is written, “Jesus began both to do and to teach” (*Acts* 1), let this book of deeds go before for now.

If you continue to favor my studies in your customary manner, and if lovers of sacred history continue to submit the Lives of the Saints from their several provinces, I shall take care that they too follow, revised in a similar manner.

[Column 0011]

## A New Address

These were my hopes in the year 1615, when, through your patronage, the *Lives of the Fathers* came forth from the shadows into the sunlight in the Moretian press. I was already preparing to undertake the histories of the remaining saints when, behold, an enemy of the Church appeared, one whom it was necessary to confront. Leaving aside the repositories of the saints, I turned to the armories of the holy cause.

After three enemies had been defeated, after I had presented the *Ecclesiastical History* and several other works to my fatherland, when I was already taking up the *Lives of the Saints* again and January was weighing upon my desk so that it might be prepared for the press, I was interrupted by Balthasar Moretus, the most exacting printer and my dearest friend, who maintained that the *Lives of the Fathers* were being requested and requested again. I therefore devoted myself once more to this work and gave these summer months to its correction and publication, aided by your exceptional observations, full of excellent erasures.

Now, as formerly, your distinguished diligence gives me hope that these sheepskin cloaks (*melotae*) of the ancient Fathers, once more cleansed and polished, will enter your household treasury of pious authors; this is the same diligence that you apply to clarifying and adorning Blosius, the excellent father of the people of Liessies, sparing neither labor nor expense, until at last he emerges in a new garment, after these Lives, through the very press of your friend Moretus, for the public benefit of souls. May this happen quickly: we all pray for it.

Meanwhile, most reverend prelate, this book and labor, once again produced through much toil, returns to you and to your crown of Liessies, of which you may rightly be proud. It is wholly your ancient and new possession, yours by money and by purchase, yours by ownership. I ask and earnestly entreat only that, through the prayers which you are able to offer before God almighty, you may obtain that this new-old edition may appear more fruitful throughout the entire world, for the emulation of the virtue of the holy Fathers in every religious community.

[Column 0013]

# Twenty-Six Prolegomena to the Lives of the Fathers

## Greetings to the Benevolent Reader

### [I]

Do not be offended, reader, if the style is sometimes rougher, or if the phrasing in the *Lives of the Fathers* and the sayings of the elders is less polished. Weigh the matter itself, not the words; read the fruit, not the leaves; pluck the flower, and do not long for the fleeting thistle-down. The great lights of the Church, Saint Jerome, speak excellently:

> “The greatness of holiness will excuse simplicity in speech” (*Jerome, Letter 101, to Pammachius*).

Saint Augustine writes:

> “It is a mark of distinguished good minds to love truth in words, not words themselves. For what good is a golden key if it cannot open what we wish? Or what harm is there in a wooden one, if it can, when we seek nothing except that what is closed should be opened?” (*Augustine, Book IV of Christian Doctrine*, chapter 11).

The most illustrious Cardinal Baronius harmonizes admirably with them:

> “Just as excavated gold, shapeless and unworked, is usually more valuable because it appears to contain no admixture of another metal, so outstanding monuments shining with the very marks of their antiquity and simplicity, in which the subject matter rather than the words is usually esteemed, will plainly be more agreeable and pleasant than any writing by a recent author, however adorned with the trappings of eloquence. For whatever is overlaid with cosmetics and pigments becomes suspect, while simplicity shines more beautifully in its own purity; because it does not know how to lie, it recoils from every covering, however carefully arranged for adornment” (*Baronius*, volume III, year 356).

I am accustomed to reason with myself in this way: Those who read these works have either penetrated into the inner sanctuaries of Latin literature, or are still practicing and sighing before its gates. A less Latin style will not harm the former, since they possess at home the means from which they can draw more polished Latin; the latter will sometimes find here their alphabet, nor will they, less ready in the language, blush at truncated words and phrases broken off as though by a stumbling tongue.

For my part, I have always preferred solid gold, even when covered with a muddy crust, to the cheap New Year’s gifts of the date-palm—objects attractive in appearance and falsely promising wealth on their surface, but merely smeared with a thin sprinkling of gold and using that coloring to conceal their domestic poverty.

Nor should you wonder, reader, that the *Lives of the Fathers* have so often been printed, reprinted, and passed through the hands of so many learned men, yet have not until now been restored to their former polish. I want you to consider what Saint Augustine teaches: we are

> “like collectors of public revenues, or like craftsmen in a silversmiths’ quarter, where a single vessel, in order to emerge perfect, passes through many artisans, although it could be completed by one perfect craftsman. But it was thought that the multitude of workers could not otherwise be accommodated except by having each one quickly and easily learn a particular part of the craft, lest everyone be forced to become perfect in one art slowly and with difficulty” (*Augustine, Book VII of the City of God*, chapter 4).

This commonly happens in the revision of books. A single work is often completed not by one person or two, but by many: one investigates the excellence of the antiquarians in order to correct the printers’ errors; another pays greater attention to order and subject matter; another to history. Thus, through the combined labor of many, each guided by his own inclination, something accurate finally emerges.

Although I do not dare guarantee that this is true of this edition, I do not hesitate to invite the reader to compare this edition with the others and to sit in judgment upon the work performed by each.

What resources I have received, both from manuscripts and from printed books, and what others have contributed who traveled this road before me, I shall explain in order—provided that I first discuss, not altogether superficially, the title of these books, their authors, translators, and authority, since these are almost the customary preliminaries.

# First Prolegomenon: The Title of These Books

[Column 0013A]

### [III]

I say first that, just as now generally, so in former times these books—or at least part of them—were entitled *Lives of the Fathers*.

1. Pope Gelasius, at the council held at Rome in the year of Christ 494 with seventy bishops, made a selection of ecclesiastical books and issued a decree preserved in Gratian’s *Decree*, distinction 15, chapter “The Holy Roman Church,” in which he says:

> “We receive with every honor the *Lives of the Fathers*, of Paul, Antony, Hilarion, and all the hermits, which, nevertheless, the blessed man Jerome wrote.”

[Column 0014A]

2. Gennadius, *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 11, under Evagrius the monk:

> “His book too, entitled *Lives of the Fathers*, mentions him as a man of the greatest self-restraint and learning.”

And in chapter 41, concerning Petronius, bishop of Bologna:

> “He is thought to have written the *Lives of the Fathers of the monks of Egypt*.”

3. Paschasius, deacon of the Holy Roman Church, in his prologue to the book which, at the request of Martin, abbot of Dumius, he translated into Latin from the *Lives of the Fathers*:

> “I was ordered by you, most holy Father, to translate into the Latin language the *Lives of the holy Fathers*, carefully composed with the eloquence of the Greeks, as are the other works.”

[Column 0015A]

4. Cassiodorus, *Institutions of Divine and Secular Learning*, chapter 32:

> “Read constantly the *Lives of the Fathers*, the confessions of the faithful, and the sufferings of the martyrs. You will doubtless find them, among other places, in Jerome’s letter to Chromatius and Heliodorus. They flourished throughout the whole world, so that holy imitation, calling you onward, may lead you to the heavenly kingdom.”

5. Saint Benedict, in his Rule, chapter 42:

> “At all times, whether it be a fast or a meal, as soon as they have risen from supper, all the monks shall sit together, and one shall read the *Conferences* or the *Lives of the Fathers*, or something else that edifies those who hear.”

6. Gregory of Tours, Book I of *The Life of the Fathers of His Own Age*, concerning Leobardus the recluse, chapter 12, whom the temptation to leave his cell had beset:

> “I, sighing with no little sorrow, began to rebuke the man, declaring that it was the craft of the devil; and I departed from him after directing to him books, the *Lives of the Fathers*, and the instruction of monks—how those who are recluses ought to be, and with what caution monks ought to live. When these had been read again, he not only drove away the evil thought from himself, but also trained his understanding with such sharpness that we marveled at the eloquence of his speech.”

[Column 0015B]

7. George of Alexandria, in the *Life of Saint John Chrysostom*, chapter 22:

> “In his conversations he expounded the life of the holy Fathers and anchorites, and their conduct and virtue, so that many were moved to compunction by such words and shed a multitude of tears from their eyes; they also desired to pursue the solitary life and to renounce the tumult and confusion of this life.”

The accompanying Latin rendering reads:

> “Moreover, in his familiar conversations he repeatedly made mention of the life of the holy Fathers and anchorites, and of their conduct and virtue, so that no few were moved to compunction by such discourses, abundant tears were drawn forth and flowed from their eyes, and they were seized with a great desire to practice the solitary life and finally to bid farewell to the turbulent confusion of this life.”

8. Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, Letter 79:

> “I am sending you Cyprian, Porphyry, and the *Lives of the Fathers* together with the Psalter, as you requested.”

And at the end of the book, after a hymn on the Nativity of Christ and the Epiphany:

> “In the *Lives of the ancient Fathers* I read something delightful.”

There he recounts rhythmically the little story of John the Little, or John the Short, who wished to act like an angel, doing nothing. It may be found in Rufinus, Book III, no. 56, and in Pelagius, Book X, no. 27.

I say secondly: Some of these books were at times entitled *Sayings of the Elders*.

Thus Bede, in his *Martyrology*, 19 July:

> “In the Thebaid, Saint Arsenius, our Father, concerning whom it is related in the *Sayings of the Elders* that, because of the abundance of tears that had to be wiped away, he always kept a handkerchief in his bosom or in his hand.”

The same account is found in Usuard, Rabanus, Ado, and Notker. It is taken from Rufinus, Book III, no. 163, and Pelagius, Book III, chapter 1.

I believe the origin of this title lies in the frequent mention of a “word” in these books. In Rufinus, Book III of the *Lives of the Fathers*, no. 130:

> “Before I rest, I recount that word late at night in the truth of my heart.”

In Pelagius, Book V of the *Lives of the Fathers*, booklet 3, no. 2:

> “Tell me some word.”

And no. 9:

> “The elders asked him to give a word to the brothers.”

And no. 24:

> “Abba, tell me some word.”

And booklet 5, no. 13:

> “Show charity, Abba, and tell me a word.”

And no. 32:

> “For I heard that Abba Pastor said this saying, and that other brothers did so too.”

Booklet 6, no. 5:

> “Saying a certain word worthy of being committed to memory.”

No. 12:

> “Tell me one word.”

And in John, Book VI of the *Lives of the Fathers*, booklet 3, no. 4:

> “Father, tell the brothers a word of edification.”

And elsewhere throughout.

Certainly, even in ancient secular authors, *word* was used for an axiom or brief maxim, such as these sayings of the Fathers. Terence, *Andria*, act 1, scene 5:

> “What a wretch I am, that I hear such a saying!”

Donatus comments:

> “He used *word* for *axiom* in his customary manner.”

In the same work, act 2, scene 5:

> “That saying is true, the one commonly spoken.”

Donatus comments:

> “That is, a proverb and maxim; and so the ancients used *word* for *maxim*.”

The same author, *Eunuchus*, act 1, scene 2:

> “Would that that saying were true.”

Donatus comments:

> “And that saying, meaning the entire maxim. *Word* for a spoken saying. Properly, however, an *axiom*—that is, a maxim or utterance bound and compressed into a single expression—was called *word* by the ancients.”

In the same passage:

> “Defeated by a single word, how quickly!”

Donatus comments:

> “Understand *word* as a saying expressed in a word, and as the utterance of a completed proposition, which was called an *axiom*.”

The same author, *Eunuchus*, act 4, scene 5:

> “That is a saying, by Hercules.”

Donatus comments:

> “A saying, a proverb.”

The same author, *Adelphoe*, act 5, scene 8:

> “I do not make that saying my own.”

Donatus comments:

> “He used *word* for an *axiom*, which is compressed into one expression. Therefore *word* means a brief maxim; he called it a word because it was a true maxim. For Varro testifies that *words* derive their name from truth.”

What others call *words*, Cassian calls *wise sayings* in Book V of the *Institutes*, chapter 24:

> “When we had gone from the regions of Syria to the province of Egypt, eager to learn the wise sayings of the elders.”

They were also called *maxims*. Pelagius, booklet 11, no. 20:

> “I shall speak of the words and maxims of the elders.”

[Column 0016D]

At times they were called *discourses*. Pelagius, booklet 4, no. 1:

> “Sitting in the boat, they were speaking a discourse of the Fathers.”

And in Cassian, *Conferences* 1, chapter 1, one finds “a discourse of edification.”

Sometimes they were called *responses*. Paschasius, chapter 44, at the end:

> “These are the responses of wise and spiritual Fathers.”

And Sigebert, *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 118:

> “Questions and answers.”

Likewise, they were called *apophthegms*. Petronius, bishop of Bologna, is cited by Alfonso Ciacconius in his treatise on Saint Jerome’s cardinalate, as will be cited below in Prolegomenon 4, section 7. More recently, in the *Library of the Fathers*, volume IX, in the second and third editions, the fifth and sixth books of the *Lives of the Fathers* were published under this name.

Indeed, the prologue to the *Spiritual Meadow*, or *New Paradise*, which was published in Greek at Paris in 1604 from Vatican manuscripts and from the manuscript of the illustrious Francis Olivarius, says that this book contains:

> διηγήματά τε καὶ ἀποφθέγματα ὁσίων καὶ δικαίων καὶ φιλοχρίστων πατέρων τε καὶ ἀδελφῶν

“narratives and wise sayings, or apophthegms, of holy, righteous, and Christ-loving Fathers and brothers.”

Sometimes they were called *deeds of the elders*. John Moschus, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 55:

> “He gave me a book to read in which the deeds of the elders had been written.”

In Greek it is:

> Βίβλιον γεροντικόν

“a book of the elders.”

It is likewise called this by Dorotheus in the *Teachings*.

These books were sometimes called *Paterikon* or *Patrikón*. Thus you will find it below in Prolegomenon 12, concerning the *Paradise* of John Moschus. I have also seen other manuscripts that bear *Paterikon* as their title.

[Column 0017B]

### [VI]

Here some critic may first ask which title is preferable: *Vita* or *Vitae*? I would not raise the question if I had not once read that it had been debated by Gregory of Tours. In the preface to his book *On the Life of the Fathers*, which concerns certain holy men of his own age, he says:

> “Some ask whether we ought to say *the Life of the Saints* or *the Lives*. Aulus Gellius and several other grammarians, however, preferred to say *Lives*. For Pliny the author, in the third book of *The Art of Grammar*, says: ‘The ancients said *Lives* of any one of us; but grammarians do not think that *Life* has a plural.’”

From this it is clearer that *Life of the Fathers* is more correctly said than *Lives*, because although their merits and virtues are diverse, one bodily life alone nourishes them all in the world.

In Gregory’s favor one might cite what Sosipater Charisius has in Book II of the *Institutes of Grammar*, in the chapter on interjections:

> “Life, by the immortal gods! Old Cato.”

Where Statilius Maximus says:

> “An archaic exclamation, like *Popoi*.”

For although Cato was speaking of several persons, he said *Life* rather than *Lives*.

Thus Flavius Vopiscus, in his *Life of Carinus*:

> “Especially since even the *Life* of living emperors is not spoken of without criticism.”

Nevertheless, it prevailed in ancient times, among both secular and ecclesiastical writers, that they should say *Lives*. Virgil, *Georgics* IV:

> “And summon each one for himself, as it is born, tender lives.”

The same author, *Aeneid* VI, concerning Minos:

> “... and he recounts their lives and crimes.”

And in the same book:

> “From there the race of men and beasts, and the lives of winged creatures.”

Again, in the same book:

> “And unless a learned companion, in a slender body, should warn the lives to fly about.”

Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I:

> “The god watches over the welfare and lives of human beings.”

The same author, *On Friendship*:

> “Friendship spreads through the lives of all.”

Terence, *Adelphoe*, act 3, scene 3:

> “I order all people’s lives to be examined as though in a mirror, and each person to take an example for himself from others.”

Capitolinus, in his *Life of Macrinus*:

> “The lives of those emperors—or tyrants, or Caesars—who did not rule for long lie in obscurity.”

And shortly afterward:

> “But the duty of one who begins to write the lives of others is to record what is worthy of knowing.”

Lampridius, in his *Life of Alexander Severus*:

> “He wrote the lives of good emperors in verse.”

Saint Augustine, *City of God* XXII, chapter 29:

> “How do we distinguish bodies from those that are not living, unless we see bodies and lives together?”

Sidonius, Book IV, Letter 14:

> “Because, when Christ is about to heal human affairs and lives, we open the foul ulcer of consciences with a rusty knife.”

To these may be added the authorities supporting the preceding conclusion, where Gregory himself also calls the *Lives of the Fathers* that which we now have before us by this title, because it was exceedingly common under that name.

A second, more religiously minded person may ask whether the name *Fathers* is too presumptuous, and whether it should be used or accepted indiscriminately by religious men and hermits. Jerome, in Book II of his commentary on the Letter to the Galatians, in explaining the passage “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, Abba, Father” (*Galatians* 4), is believed to have disapproved the pious custom of monks who, out of respect, call their superiors abbots and fathers; moreover, he seems there to have deprived Christians of the right to swear an oath. For he says:

> “Since *Abba, Father* is said in the Hebrew and Syriac languages, and since our Lord commands in the Gospel that no one should be called Father except God (*Matthew* 23), I do not know by what license in monasteries we either call others by this name or consent to be called by it ourselves. Certainly the one who had said this also commanded that we should not swear. If we do not swear, then we should not call anyone Father either. If we interpret *Father* in one way, we shall also be compelled to understand swearing in another.”

This is what he says.

But Sixtus of Siena responds in Book VI of the *Holy Library*, annotation 279:

> “I believe,” he says, “that this sentence was written at the head of the page by some petty rebellious monk, and was later transferred into the text by inattentive copyists. Evidence that I am not mistaken is provided by Jerome’s statements, which he wrote in an entirely contrary sense and expressly in Book IV of his commentary on Matthew. There, when investigating how the Savior’s command should be understood—‘Do not be called teachers, and do not call anyone your father on earth,’ etc. (*Matthew* 23:8–9)—he says:

> ‘It is asked why, contrary to this command, the Apostle should have said that he was a teacher of the Gentiles, or how, in ordinary speech—especially in the monasteries of Palestine and Egypt—they call one another fathers. The answer is this: It is one thing to be a father or teacher by nature, and another by courtesy. When we call a man father, we pay honor to his age; we do not present him as the author of our life. A teacher is likewise called so through association with the true Teacher. And not to repeat endlessly: just as the one God by nature and the one Son do not prevent others from being called gods and sons by adoption, so the one Father and Teacher do not prevent others from being called fathers and teachers in an extended sense.’”

Thus far Sixtus cites Saint Jerome.

Saint Augustine is also of the same opinion, in the third Carthaginian Conference, chapter 242:

> “We call those who have preceded us in age or merits fathers as a matter of honor. It is something different when we ask whom we should have as a father in the faith. The former is a matter of honor: every day we say ‘father’ to old men; every day we also say ‘brother’ to certain people who are not with us in the same church or participants in the same sacraments. Lot even called the Sodomites ‘brothers’ (*Genesis* 19), plainly to soften their anger, not to indicate a recognized brotherhood or a shared inheritance as though they possessed one. Let these usages therefore be set aside. Let us distinguish the words owed to human beings on account of honor from the word required on account of salvation.”

[Column 0019A]

Saint Jerome also elsewhere calls the leaders of the anchorites fathers, in Letter 22 to Eustochium:

> “Macarius, Pambo, Isidore, whom they call fathers.”

Cyril of Alexandria likewise jointly entitled the letter which he sent to the presbyters and deacons, preserved in the Acts of the Council of Ephesus, Part I, chapter 2:

> Πατράσι μοναχοῖς

“To the monastic Fathers.”

A third, perhaps overly curious person may ask why, in most printed books, the title *Vitas Patrum* appears almost as though in the nominative or in an indeclinable form. The Venetian edition of 1508 indeed places it on the title page as the heading.

I answer that it may seem to have arisen from certain early editions in which no title page was prefixed to the book, but the beginning of the title was taken from the opening words; or from a prologue which, in the Nuremberg edition of 1478, reads:

> “Here begins the prologue of Saint Jerome the presbyter to the books *Lives of the Fathers*.”

Or it may have arisen from a table of contents, as in the German editions of uncertain place, from 1483 and 1485:

> “Register of the *Lives of the ancient Fathers*, written by the blessed Jerome.”

It appears that later editors then took *Lives of the Fathers* as an indeclinable or uninflected title.

Certainly, the first edition of all, bearing no definite year, place, or printer, has a different form:

> “Here begins the preface of the blessed Jerome the presbyter to the first book concerning the Life of the holy Fathers.”

Thus Galen Westcapellus is not without reason when he asserts in *Catechesis* 225 that he does not know by what grammar this book is entitled *Lives of the Fathers*.

But that the occasion for calling and titling the book *Vitas Patrum* (“Lives of the Fathers”) was not derived from the earliest editions is evident even from the fact that the designation *Vitas Patrum* was already ancient before printing. [Col. 0019D] This is clear from *Vitas Fratrum* (“Lives of the Brothers”), whose authors seem to have drawn and modeled their title from it. Indeed, different books by different authors have been given that title.

Humbert, the fifth master general of the Order of Saint Dominic, is said to have composed the *Vitas Fratrum* of his order, as Brother Theodoric of Apoldia states in the prefatory letter before the *Life of Saint Dominic*, 5 August. I have not yet seen that book published under his authorship. I possess a manuscript copy of the *Vitas Fratrum* of the Order of Saint Dominic, by the Dominican Gerard de Fracheto, who wrote the book at the command of Humbert, the fifth master general, in the year 1260. Anthony of Siena also cites it in his *Library of Writers of His Order*. Since Gerard wrote the book under Humbert’s auspices, and [Col. 0020A] since Humbert himself supplies its preface, Theodoric may perhaps have attributed it to Humbert. Now, as I submit these *Lives* to the press for the second time [IX], that book has appeared at Douai, from the press of Balthasar Bellerus, in 1619.

Jordan of Saxony, likewise, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, composed a book which he titled *Vitas Fratrum*. It was published at Rome in 1587, under the care of Augustine Fivizani, a religious of the same order and sacristan of the Apostolic Palace, with notes by M. Antonio Maffei of Salerno. Joseph Pamphilus, bishop of Segni, in his *Chronicle of the Order of the Hermits of Saint Augustine*, cites from those *Lives* the beginning of *Spiritual Beauty*, but that beginning does not now appear in printed editions. Perhaps a preface once stood before it, beginning with those words, and is now missing.

Furthermore, certain ancient manuscripts have the title [Col. 0020B] *Vitas Patrum*. Thus the Vedastine book, written more than eight hundred years ago in what are called capital letters, bears that title.

But by what grammatical construction, or on what occasion, was that book so titled? D. George Colvenerius, chancellor of the University of Douai, thought that, following the most ancient custom and imitating the Greeks, the book was at first called and titled *Liber Vitas Patrum* (“The Book Lives of the Fathers”), instead of *Liber Vitae Patrum* (“The Book of the Life of the Fathers”); that is, a book containing the Life of the Fathers. On this view, *Vitas* would be a singular genitive, as in *familias* in *paterfamilias*. Later, he thought, *Liber* was omitted, and the title was simply given as *Vitas Patrum*. I do not know, however, whether anyone would admit this form as an antiquity in later centuries. Certainly Johannes Despauterius, in Book II of his *Grammatical Commentaries*, says, under the first declension: [Col. 0020C] “The expression *Liber Vitas Patrum* is not used in this way, but *Vitae Patrum*; I have read *Vitas Patrum*, and so forth.”

Our Hadrian Courten, another Palaemon of our Belgian land in the arena of grammar, thinks that a copyist’s ignorance transformed *Vita S. Patrum* (“Life of the Holy Fathers”) into *Vitas Patrum*—a highly probable and readily available conjecture.

It occurred to me, however, that the origin of this designation may have come from the citations of the ancients, who generally cite this book in that form, although with an additional verb, as is evident here in the first conclusion, where Gelasius says: “We receive the *Lives of the Fathers* with every honor.” Gennadius says: “Petronius is thought to have written the *Lives of the Fathers*.” Paschasius says: “Ordered to translate the *Lives of the Fathers* into the Latin language.” Cassiodorus says: “You will undoubtedly find the *Lives of the Fathers*.” [Col. 0020D] Saint Benedict says: “Let one read the *Lives of the Fathers*.” Gregory of Tours says: “As I was departing from him, I directed the *Lives of the Fathers* to him.”

Thus, because some people repeatedly read *Vitas Patrum* in the works of authors, they gave that designation to the book *technically* (*τεχνικῶς*). It is sufficiently clear, however, from the Gennadius cited above that the book was formerly correctly titled in the nominative, *Vitae Patrum*. For in chapter 11, speaking of Evagrius, he says: “His book, which is titled *Vitae Patrum* [‘The Life of the Fathers’], makes mention of him as a very continent and highly learned man.”

## PROLEGOMENON II. Who Were the Authors of These Books?

[X] Here lies the hinge of the whole matter. For just as the value of a coin comes not only from its weight but also from its image, so the worth of a book is judged not only by its bulk but also by its author. [Col. 0021A]

If the author is sometimes hidden, we shall then endeavor to investigate the translator. If he is ancient, learned, and upright, we shall not be greatly troubled about the author. Why should we not accept, on the translator’s own authority, what a judicious translator judged worthy of his style or pen?

Since there are many books here, written by different authors, and since the matter is extremely perplexing in the case of some of them, I shall investigate each book in its own prolegomenon.

## PROLEGOMENON III. Who Was the Author of the First Book?

I say that the authors of the first book are various: some certain, some doubtful, and some unknown.

[Col. 0021B] The certain authors, each responsible for particular Lives, are these:

1. The divine Jerome, author of several Lives, namely those of Paul the first hermit, Hilarion the anchorite, Malchus the captive monk, Fabiola, Paula, and Marcella, Roman widows.

2. Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, author of the *Life of Saint Antony*.

3. Paphnutius, author of the *Life of Saint Onuphrius the Hermit*.

4. Saint Ephrem the Syrian, author of the *Life of Saint Abraham the Hermit* and of Mary, his niece.

5. Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, author of the *Life of the Divine Basil*, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia.

6. Antony, author of the *Life of Saint Simeon Stylites*.

7. Leontius, bishop of Neapolis on the island of Cyprus, author of the *Life of Saint John the Almsgiver*, patriarch of Alexandria.

8. John Damascene, author of the *Life of Saints Barlaam and Josaphat*.

[Col. 0021C] 9. Jacob the deacon of Edessa, author of the *Life of Saint Pelagia*.

10. Sophronius, patriarch of Jerusalem, author of the *Life of Saint Mary of Egypt*.

[XI] There is one doubtful author: Theophilus, author of the *Life of Macarius the Roman*. For what Baronius says in his note on the Roman Martyrology, 2 January—that the *Life of Macarius the Roman*, which appears in the *Lives of the Fathers*, was written by Theophilus—I do not know whether it should be attributed to him. The name Theophilus does indeed appear at the beginning of the *Life of Macarius*, but the names of two companions, Sergius and Hyginus, are also added. What is narrated is related in the name of all three, so that it is not easy to determine which of them committed this account of Macarius to writing.

Indeed, Gratian, in the *Decree*, 27, question 2, chapter 26, cites Macarius’s flight from the bridal chamber under Jerome’s name, [Col. 0021D] and he seems to have derived it from no other source than this *Life of Macarius*.

That he cited it under Jerome’s name, however, was the result of the common error by which all the *Lives of the Fathers* were generally attributed to Jerome. The occasion and origin of that error may be found below, in Prolegomenon IV, § 8.

The authors of the remaining Lives contained in the first book are unknown.

But D. Constantine Cajetanus interrupts us here. In his *Apology for John Gerson*, he seems determined to assign a certain author to the *Life of Saint Euphrosyne*, and indeed a heretical one. Where he got this, I do not know; certainly he names no author. When that author is identified, his status will be examined. And even if the author were a heretic, what would prevent the Life he recorded from being genuine? It is easy for anyone to “fight battles in the air” (*ἀερομαχεῖν*).

## PROLEGOMENON IV. Who Was the Author of the Second Book?

This question concerns chiefly that book. For it is the one that most of the ancients mean when they cite the *Lives of the Fathers*. This can be gathered both from the divine Jerome, in his letter to Ctesiphon against the Pelagians, where he says that John is placed at the beginning of the very book which you will find here first, and from Gennadius, *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 40, who says that the book “which is titled *Vitae Patrum* makes mention of a very continent and highly learned man”—Evagrius—who appears in chapter 27 of this book.

[Col. 0022B] Opinions concerning the author of this book are so varied and contradictory—unless we wish to suppose that separate books were written or interpolated by each of them—that it is worthwhile to divide them into paragraphs, so that the force of each may become apparent and they may be weighed on the proper scales of judgment. I shall begin with the Greeks.

### § I. The Author Seems to Have Been Timothy, Bishop of Alexandria

[XII] Sozomen, in Book VI, chapter 29 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, after speaking of Apollo, who had lived in the Thebaid, adds:

> “But what his discipline was like, and how many divine and extraordinary deeds he performed, Timothy, who very capably governed the Church of Alexandria, records, having set down in detail the lives not only of him but also of many others whom I have mentioned, as well as of other distinguished monks.”

The Greek reads:

> Ἀλλ᾽ οἵᾳ μὲν ἀγωγῇ ἐχρῆτο, καὶ ἡλίκων ἦν θείων καὶ παραδόξων πραγμάτων ποιητὴς, ἱστορεῖ Τιμόθεος ὁ τῶν Ἀλεξανδρείων ἐκκλησίαν ἐπιτροπεύσας εὖ μάλα, αὐτοῦ καὶ πολλῶν ὧν ἐπεμνήσθην, καὶ ἄλλων δοκίμων μοναχῶν τοὺς βίους διεξελθών.

“But what the character of his discipline was, and how many and how great divine and extraordinary miracles he performed, Timothy, the overseer of the Church of Alexandria, accurately narrates. He has written out in detail not only his Life but also those of many others whom I have mentioned, as well as of other distinguished monks.”

In the preceding chapter, however, mention had been made of the monks John, Or, Ammon, Beni, Theonas, Copres, Helle, Elias, Apelles, Isidore, Serapion, Dioscorus, and Eulogius; the Lives of all of them are found in this second book of the *Lives of the Fathers*.

I have not yet read anyone who made Timothy the author of this book. Nevertheless, it seemed useful to bring forward what Sozomen says about him, so that it might be weighed by the judgment of more learned men. For my part, I find it altogether plausible that most of the Lives in this book were modeled on Timothy. The *Life of Apollo*, which Timothy is said to have written “very accurately” (*εὖ μάλα*), is indeed set down in this book, chapter 7, under the name of Apollonius, with considerable accuracy. It also exists in the same form in Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, chapter 52, but one has entirely drawn from the other—perhaps the later from the earlier—although in age they are rather nearly equal.

### § II. The Author Seems to Have Been Palladius the Galatian, Bishop of Helenopolis

Galenus Westcapellius, in *Catechesis* 215, where he refutes the little story about Macarius who is said to have fled from his wedding, seems to make Palladius the author of this book. For he says:

> “I found nothing at all even in that fictitious book, which is titled—by I do not know what grammatical construction—*Vitas Patrum*, where Palladius, who was personally acquainted with both Macarii, reports something quite different.”

That Palladius—or whoever the author of this book may be—was personally acquainted with both Macarii is not stated in this book, or in the *Lives of the Fathers*. But in Palladius’s own *Lausiac History*, Palladius declares that he lived with Macarius of Alexandria.

But to free Galen from error: the little story is not told about Macarius the Egyptian or Alexandrian, as Galen seems to have thought, but about Macarius the Roman, whose Life you will find here in the first book. The story of Macarius’s flight from the bridal chamber is also found in the *Decree*, 27, question 2, chapter 26, under the heading “He Wrote.”

Since, however, nearly the same things are found both in this book and in the *Lausiac History*, not only concerning both Macarii [XIII] but also concerning most of the others, the suspicion is not entirely groundless that either the author of this book borrowed from Palladius, or Palladius from him, or that both borrowed from some third person, merely changing the order and omitting or adding certain details.

There is some diversity in the narratives, but it is very slight. For in this book, chapter 1, which concerns John, the author says that he approached John with seven brothers; in the *Lausiac History*, however, the author says that he met John alone and afterward informed his fellow brothers about him. They then went to John, and the author reports from their testimony what he relates about John beyond what he himself had seen. See Prolegomenon 14, concerning the translator of Book VIII.

In an extremely old manuscript book of our Bruges college, containing various Lives of saints—including, among others, the *Life of Abraham the Hermit*—a preface to the Life is placed before it, beginning “Blessed be God,” with this title: “Here begins the prologue of Palladius, a most learned man, concerning the Lives of the Egyptian Fathers.” This very preface is placed before this second book.

### § III. The Author Seems to Have Been Heraclides, Bishop of Bithynia

Apart from Gesner, I have found no one who expressly asserted this. For he says in Volume III, Title VII, page 1 of his *Library*: “I think the history of Heraclides is none other than the *Lives of the Fathers*.”

Trithemius, in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, asserts that Heraclides the monk wrote about the life and conduct of the holy Fathers:

> “Heraclides,” he says, “a monk, a man holy in character and distinguished for his knowledge of the divine Scriptures, a most diligent investigator and imitator of the holy Fathers, the anchorites and monks, gathered, like a resourceful bee, the flowers of virtue from each one’s way of life into the honeycomb of his heart and produced honey of spiritual sweetness. Among other works, for the edification of readers he wrote a distinguished work, *On the Life and Conduct of the Holy Fathers Living in the Desert or in Monasteries under a Rule*, whose title is *Paradise*, Book I. He flourished in the time of the emperor Gratian, in the year of the Lord 380.”

This book appeared at Paris from the Bellovisian press of Jean Petit in 1504, under the care of Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples, who says the following about it in his preface to the reader:

> “The work itself makes it possible to recognize that he was an Alexandrian; that, inflamed by love of Christ, he pursued poverty among deserts and the lairs of wild beasts; and that, against his own will and protest, he was made bishop in Bithynia by the suffrage of the entire people.”

See more about him in Peter’s *Catalogue of the Saints*, Book XI, chapter 87.

Baronius, in the year 388 of his *Annals*, identifies Heraclides’ *Paradise* with the *Lausiac History* of Palladius. Certainly, you find the same things in both. [XIV] The same judgment should therefore be made about both regarding the authorship of this book.

Before Baronius, Aloysius Lipomanus, bishop of Verona, had held the same opinion in Volume III of his *Lives of the Saints*. He inserted Heraclides’ work into that volume under Palladius’s name, with some interpolation—concerning which see Prolegomenon 14, where the translator of Book VIII, whose author is Palladius, is discussed.

He also thought it worthwhile to investigate how it happened that this book emerged under the title *Paradise of Heraclides*, with a false author assigned to it, as he himself believed.

“First,” he says, “it occurs to my mind that the Parisian printer was the originator of this fiction. For when he had read that the divine Jerome, in the preface to his *Dialogues against the Pelagians*, had written, ‘Palladius, a man of servile wickedness, is reviving the heresy of Origen,’ and that the divine Epiphanius, in his letter to John, bishop of Jerusalem, had also asserted, ‘Palladius the Galatian, who was formerly dear to me, preaches and teaches the heresy of Origen,’ the good printer feared that, if he published the book under its author’s name, it would immediately be rejected as having been written by a heretic. He therefore devised, in my judgment, that stratagem by which he turned Palladius into ‘Paradise,’ an inversion that seemed very easy, and published the volume as though it had been composed by someone else, so as more readily to encourage learned men to purchase it.” Such is the account of Aloysius.

Just as we praise the diligence and effort of this most learned man in investigating obscure matters, so here we cannot approve the good fortune of his conjecture. For the printer truly found the book marked with Heraclides’ name and bearing the title *Paradise*. Thus the manuscript I examined has it, and Vincent of Beauvais in his *Historical Mirror*, Book XVII, from chapter 64 through chapter 99, as well as Peter de Natalibus in his *Catalogue of the Saints*, Book XI, chapter 87, cite it under that name and title.

Moreover, *Paradise* was known to the ancients. Photius, in Codex 198 of his *Library*, mentions a book titled *Νέον Παραδείσιον*, that is, *The New Paradise*. The following Codex 199 makes clear that this refers to the *Limonarium*, or *Spiritual Meadow*, of John Moschus. From this it is easy to conclude that, if there is a New Paradise, there must also have been an Old one, and that this may reasonably be considered none other than our book.

Heraclides, too, was a certain monk known in the time of the Macarii, as is clear from Nicephorus, Book IX, chapter 14. The synod held at the Oak, moreover, as reported by Photius in Codex 59 concerning the case of John Chrysostom, mentions a certain Heraclides. After examining the first and second charges brought by John the deacon, [Col. 0025A] it adds:

> “Then they began to discuss Heraclides and Palladius, bishops of Helenopolis.”

Heraclides is said to have been an Origenist and to have been ordained bishop of Ephesus by Chrysostom. The two are also joined together in the second article of the document submitted by Acacius to that same synod against Chrysostom. He is discussed at greater length in the *Life of Saint Chrysostom* by George of Alexandria, who says that he lived alone in the desert.

I strongly suspect that Palladius’s work was composed from various authors, since it appeared more extensive in Hervetus’s third translation. For if you inspect Palladius’s first edition, you will scarcely find a third of what appears in the latest edition. From this arose an edition under the title of Heraclides, somewhat fuller than that first edition of Palladius, though less rich than the latest edition.

The basis of my suspicion is the double preface found in Palladius: one by Heraclides and the other by Palladius himself. It could easily have happened that one inserted the other’s book into his own. Certainly, what is found in Book V of the *Lives of the Fathers*, Booklet X, § 67, under Palladius’s name, is also found in the letter of Heraclides, bishop of Cappadocia, to Lausus the prefect, under Heraclides’ own name; that letter is prefixed to the *Lausiac History*. On the varying editions of Palladius, see Prolegomenon 14, where the translator of Book VIII is discussed.

Nor should it seem surprising that the same material should have appeared from different authors, with the order somewhat altered, now abridged and now expanded. For you will find the same practice in the other books attached here. Nearly everything found in Books III and VII is also found in Books V and VI. Nevertheless, I am entirely convinced that each of these books had its own translator and likewise its own author, with the possible exception of Books V and VI, which both seem to have had the same Greek author, as can be inferred from Pothius; in this edition they have been divided only because they have different translators. See the final Prolegomenon, Observation 4.

### § IV. The Author Seems to Have Been Evagrius, Bishop of Antioch

Trithemius, in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, makes Evagrius, bishop of Antioch, the first author of the *Lives of the Fathers*:

> “Evagrius,” he says, “a monk and disciple of Saint Macarius the Egyptian, and afterward bishop of Antioch, a man learned in every field and educated in both secular and divine Scripture, skilled in Greek and Latin eloquence, who even while a bishop maintained the austerity of his former life and practiced such great abstinence that he was regarded as a marvel: he was the first to commend the Life of the holy Fathers in writing.”

Sixtus of Siena repeats the same statement in nearly the same words in Book IV of his *Holy Library*.

I cannot imagine where they got this, since, as far as I know, none of the ancients attributes these Lives to this author. Perhaps they were misled by the name Evagrius prefixed to the *Life of Saint Antony*, which Evagrius of Antioch alone translated from the Greek source of the divine Athanasius into Latin—as we shall say in connection with the *Life of Saint Antony*. Since Evagrius was the translator of this Life, which is joined to the other Lives of the Fathers and perhaps stands before them in some manuscripts, Trithemius and Sixtus may have thought him either the translator or the author of the remaining Lives as well.

Sixtus, moreover, errs along with Trithemius by conflating two Evagrii into one. Evagrius the bishop of Antioch is distinct from Evagrius the monk and disciple of Saint Macarius the Egyptian.

Our Delrio, in the third part of his *Tragic Treasury*, in his notes on Seneca’s *Octavia*, Act IV, p. 552, on the occasion of the *Life of Saint Antony* translated into Latin by this Evagrius of Antioch, in which he restores a certain passage, also discusses another work by him that he thought had not yet been published and that must be examined here:

> “Evagrius,” he says, “lived in the time of the elder Theodosius and wrote three books on the life of the holy monks whom he saw in Egypt. I saw them at Bordeaux in the library of the Jesuit college, written on parchment in extremely ancient characters, in a style sufficiently elegant, though rough. In Book III he writes that he sailed from Narbonne to Egypt and met the divine Jerome at Bethlehem. He is a worthy author to be brought to light someday, distinct from the one to whom some attribute the *Lives of the Fathers*.”

But the title “Evagrius” could easily have misled Delrio into thinking that this was a different book from the published *Lives of the Fathers*, which bear the divine Jerome’s name on their title page. If he had compared those parchments with the printed books, he would immediately have discovered that they contained not different histories but the very *Lives of the Fathers* themselves. He would then not have distinguished author from author any more than book from book.

I first recognized this from Delrio’s own words, when he says: “In Book III he writes that he sailed from Narbonne to Egypt and met the divine Jerome at Bethlehem.” That very narrative is found in the commonly published *Lives of the Fathers*, and you will find it here in Book IV, chapters 1 and 2; it is taken from Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues*, Book I, chapters 2 and 3.

Our Possevinus also adds his testimony in the *Sacred Apparatus*. He says that the Bordeaux manuscript contains everything exactly as it appears in the edition of the *Lives of the Fathers* attributed to the divine Jerome, published at Lyon by Jacob Hugatanus in the year of the Lord 1515. Our fellow Fronto Ducaeus of Bordeaux, an eyewitness (*αὐτόπτης*), wrote the same to me.

### § V. The Author Seems to Have Been Evagrius Ponticus

Gesner, in his *Library*, George Wicelius, in the dedicatory letter before his *History of the Saints*, and John Molanus, chapter 13 of his treatise *On Martyrologies*, as well as frequently in his annotations on Usuard’s Martyrology, judged Evagrius Ponticus to be the author of the *Lives of the Fathers*. Erasmus also seems to have held this opinion when, in his notes on the divine Jerome’s letter to Ctesiphon, he makes Rufinus the translator of this book, asserting that the divine Jerome says Rufinus translated most of Evagrius’s works.

Caesar Baronius, too, in his notes on the Roman Martyrology, 17 January, where he speaks of Saint Antony, after quoting Gelasius’s words from the *Decree*, distinction 15—

> “We receive with every honor the *Lives of the Fathers*, of Paul, Antony, Hilarion, and all the hermits, which the most blessed man Jerome nevertheless recorded”—

adds:

> “Gelasius employed this precaution because Evagrius Ponticus also wrote the *Lives of the Fathers* and mixed in certain Origenists, whom Jerome himself censures in writing to Ctesiphon.”

Baronius repeatedly cites those Lives under Evagrius’s name, both in the Martyrology and in the *Annals*: in the Martyrology, on 15 January, in the note on Isidore; on 17 January, in the note on Saint Antony; and on 27 March, in the note on John the Hermit. In the *Annals*, he does so in the year of Christ 1, in the year 393, in the year 394, and in other places.

Possevinus also says in the *Sacred Apparatus*, under Evagrius, that he is thought to have composed the *Lives of the Fathers*—that is, the first part of them, citing from the extremely widespread edition that I call the second, from the beginning of the prologue, “Blessed be God who wills all,” to the chapter “On the Dangers in the Desert,” which precedes the *Life of Saint Paul*.

Aloysius Lipomanus, too, in the preface before Palladius, whom he presents in Volume III of his *Lives of the Saints*, being led by that passage of the divine Jerome, thought that Evagrius had composed a book concerning monks. He does not, however, expressly say whether he considers him the author of this book; indeed, he seems to think that Evagrius’s book no longer exists.

Let us now see what arguments might support the opinion that makes Evagrius Ponticus the author of this book.

1. Baronius seems to have had no argument for his opinion other than that letter of the divine Jerome to Ctesiphon against the Pelagians, which mentions a certain book *On Monks* or the *Lives of the Fathers*. I reply that Baronius did not properly understand it, as I shall soon show, when I prove with complete clarity from Jerome’s own passage that Rufinus was the author—or at least the translator—of those Lives.

2. Someone might cite Honorius, *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 40, where he says:

> “Evagrius the monk, the familiar disciple of the aforementioned Macarius the Egyptian, distinguished for his knowledge of divine and human literature, wrote many things necessary for monks, namely the *Life of the Fathers* and *Against the Suggestions of the Eight Principal Vices*.”

I reply that I greatly fear this stream has picked up some mud, [XVIII] although it flows more purely from its source. For Gennadius, chapter 11, from whom Honorius usually draws his material, says:

> “Evagrius the monk, disciple of the aforementioned Macarius the Egyptian, distinguished for his knowledge of divine and human literature, whose book, moreover, titled *Vitae Patrum*, makes mention of a very continent and highly learned man, wrote many things necessary for monks, among which are the following: *Against the Suggestions of the Eight Principal Vices*.”

I do not think anyone will easily doubt whether Gennadius or Honorius deserves greater credence, since Gennadius himself states in the same place that he translated most of Evagrius’s Greek works into Latin. See a similar error or corruption by Honorius at the beginning of Book II, in the note on the ancient praises of Rufinus.

I omit the fact that in this second book of the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 27, there is a *Life of Evagrius*, “as of a very continent and highly learned man,” as Gennadius says it is found there. In that book, Evagrius’s “knowledge of spiritual matters and incredible abstinence” are praised; it is scarcely likely that Evagrius himself composed such a history about himself.

3. If certain manuscripts give the name Evagrius, such as the Bordeaux manuscript mentioned above, and another of the kind that I hear is held in Paris by the distinguished man Nicolas Faber, this should not greatly influence us. [Col. 0028B] There are two possible reasons: first, the *Life of Saint Antony*, which is usually placed before the *Lives of the Fathers* and has the title of Evagrius as translator prefixed to it, may have caused that title to adhere to the following works as well; second, it may have resulted from a mistaken understanding of the divine Jerome’s letter to Ctesiphon, which we shall discuss shortly in connection with Rufinus.

4. I find a passage in Socrates, Book IV, chapter 23 in the Greek edition and chapter 18 in the Latin edition, which might be brought forward in support of this opinion. The title of the chapter is framed as follows:

> “Concerning the holy monk Ammon and a catalogue of other holy men, from the work of Evagrius.”

The Greek reads:

> Περὶ τοῦ ἁγίου μονάζοντος Ἀμμοῦ, καὶ ἑτέρων ἁγίων ἀνδρῶν κατάλογος ἐκ τῆς Εὐαγρίου συγγραφῆς.

But in this chapter there is discussion of Ammon, Didymus, Pior, Isidore, Pambo, Petir, the two Macarii, and others, who are also discussed in this second book of the *Lives of the Fathers*. If, therefore, the material in Socrates was taken from Evagrius’s book, as the title of the chapter indicates, then it seems that these passages in the *Lives of the Fathers* were also taken from his book.

I reply that at first I was caught here and did not see how to extricate myself from the snare. But once I had read the entire chapter, I was immediately freed.

For at the beginning of the chapter Socrates does indeed discuss those Fathers, but in the text he makes no mention of where he took the material. After the middle of the chapter he adds certain material about Evagrius’s Life and writings. Among these he does not list any work that expressly included the *Lives of the Fathers*. He then says that it is an appropriate time “to append to this discourse a few things that he recorded about monks.” He proceeds to review certain teachings from a book titled *The Monk*, or *On the Active Life*, and also certain passages from a book called *The Gnostic*, or *The One Possessing Knowledge*. None of these things is found in the book whose author is under dispute here.

Nicephorus, too, in Book XI, chapter 42, enumerates Evagrius’s writings and says nothing about the *Lives of the Fathers*. In chapter 43 he cites certain passages from a book *On Monks and Gnostics*, but none of them appears in this book.

Therefore, the phrase in the chapter title, “from the book of Evagrius,” must be referred not to the whole chapter but to those passages which the text expressly indicates were taken from Evagrius’s book—namely, *The Monk* and *The Gnostic*. The headings of chapters are often not very precise, since they are generally arranged not by the author but by some copyist.

Thus Peter Gilles, in Book II, chapter 10 of his work *On the Thracian Bosporus*, clearly detected that the lists of chapter titles in Sozomen’s history had been made by an ignorant person. For what is clearly stated in the text, in Book II, chapter 3, about Michaelium, that title-maker says is found in Hestiae, in Sosthenium—more than eighteen stadia away from it, as Gilles observes. Instead of *Sosthenium*, Stephanus, in his work *On Cities*, has *Leostheion* under *Gynaecopolis*.

So that no doubt may remain in the reader’s mind because of the authority of Baronius or others who attribute the *Lives of the Fathers* to Evagrius Ponticus, I shall set down here the catalogue of Evagrius’s books as it appears in Socrates, Suidas, Nicephorus, and Gennadius.

Thus Socrates says above:

> “He also composed very serious books. One is entitled *The Monk*, or *On Practical Life*; another is called *The Gnostic*, or *The One Deemed Worthy of Knowledge*”—

the text should be read, according to Suidas, “or *On Those Deemed Worthy of Knowledge*”—

> “and it contains fifty chapters. Another is the *Antirrheticus*, drawn from the divine Scriptures against the demons who tempt us, divided into eight parts according to the number of the eight thoughts. There are also six hundred problems concerning foreknowledge; and, in addition, two books in verse: one addressed to monks living in monasteries or communities, and one addressed to a virgin.”

The Greek reads:

> Τούτῳ καὶ βιβλία ἄγαν σπουδαῖα συγγέγραπται. Ὧν τὸ μὲν Μοναχὸς, ἢ περὶ πρακτικῆς ἐπιγέγραπται, τὸ δὲ Γνωστικὸς ἢ τὸν καταξιωθέντα γνώσεως (lege ex Suida, ἢ περὶ τῶν καταξιωθέντων γνώσεως), κεφάλαια δὲ αὐτοῦ πεντήκοντα. Τὸ δὲ, Ἀντιῤῥητικὸς ἀπὸ τῶν θείων γραφῶν πρὸς τοὺς πειράζοντας δαίμονας, ἐν ὀκτὼ διῃρημένον μέρεσι, κατὰ τὸν ἀριθμὸν τῶν ὀκτὼ λογισμῶν. Καὶ ἑξακόσια προγνωστικὰ προβλήματα· ἔτι μὴν καὶ στιχηρὰ δύο, ἓν πρὸς τοὺς ἐν κοινοβίοις ἢ ἐν συνοδίαις μοναχούς· καὶ ἓν πρὸς τὴν παρθένον.

The same words are found verbatim in Suidas under “Macarius” and in Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 42.

Gennadius, in chapter 11 of *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, says:

> “Evagrius the monk, the familiar disciple of the aforementioned Macarius the Egyptian, distinguished for his knowledge of divine and human literature. His book, moreover, which is titled *Vitae Patrum*, makes mention of a very continent and highly learned man. He wrote many things necessary for monks, among which are the following:

> “He wrote books against the suggestions of the eight principal vices, which he either first perceived or learned among the first, setting against them testimonies from the Holy Scriptures; namely, in imitation of the Lord, who always answered his tempter with testimonies from Scripture, so that each kind of suggestion, whether from the devil or from corrupted nature, might have testimonies directed against it. I translated this work into Latin, as simply as I found it in Greek, at the command of another.

> “He also composed a book of one hundred maxims, arranged by chapters, for anchorites living a simple life.

> “For the learned and studious he composed a book of fifty maxims, which I was the first to translate into Latin. For when I saw that the earlier translation had become corrupted and confused with the passage of time, I restored it to the author’s truth, partly by retranslating it and partly by correcting it.

> “He also composed a teaching suited to the common life for coenobites and members of religious communities.

> “And for virgins consecrated to God, he wrote a little book appropriate to their religious profession and sex.

> “He also published a few very obscure maxims—‘knowable,’ as he himself says in them, ‘only to the hearts of monks.’ I likewise published these in Latin.”

I do not include here what Honorius says about him in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*. As I noted in the second argument, Honorius usually copies Gennadius, and sometimes does so incompletely.

If Evagrius had treated the *Lives of the Fathers* somewhere in one of the books attributed to him by the authors cited above, it is highly probable that he would have done so in his book *On Monks*, since that title is particularly appropriate to the subject. The other titles seem to promise something different from the *Lives of the Fathers*, namely certain teachings and maxims.

But that the book *On Monks* contained no Lives can be inferred from the fragments preserved in Socrates and Nicephorus. They contain only certain moral instructions and maxims, which we shall give in their proper place in Evagrius’s words, where those same maxims, in the translator of the other books of the *Lives of the Fathers*, will identify themselves by the name of Evagrius.

### § VI. The Author Seems to Have Been John, Bishop of Jerusalem

Henry Gravius, in his notes on the divine Jerome’s letter to Ctesiphon, when he says that this book is not by Jerome or John of Jerusalem, seems to imply that some people held the opinion that John of Jerusalem was the author of these Lives.

I have not read anyone who held this view, and therefore cannot guess their reasons. Perhaps they were led to this opinion about John because here, in Book IV, chapter 35, the author says of Abbot Theodore:

> “And calling me by my own name, he said: ‘How many, O John, speak about God?’”

For this reason some may have thought him the author of certain books of the *Lives of the Fathers*. Their understanding “John of Jerusalem” rather than anyone else may have arisen from the fact that a certain ascetic book circulated under the name of John of Jerusalem, which could have suggested to them that it was the same as the book mentioned in that fourth book.

But neither John of Jerusalem nor the author of that fourth book is the author of this second book. For what is found in Book IV, chapter 35, is taken from John Cassian, *Institutes*, Book V, chapter 35; and that entire book is composed from Sulpicius Severus, as I shall show there. Hence the Laetiensis manuscript also places John Cassian at the head of the fourth book.

### § VII. The Author Seems to Have Been Petronius, Bishop of Bologna
Gennadius (not Jerome, as is incorrectly stated in Antoninus, part 2, title 11, chapter 11, § 5), in *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 41, reports that in his own time Petronius, bishop of Bologna, was considered the author of this book [Col. 0031A]:

> “Petronius,” he says, “bishop of the Church of Bologna, a man of holy life and trained from adolescence in the disciplines of the monks, is thought to have written the *Lives of the Fathers, Monks of Egypt*, which the monks embrace as a mirror and standard of their profession.”

Honorius, bishop of Autun, says similar things; as do Vincent of Beauvais in the *Historical Mirror*, book XX, chapter 25; Mombritius in volume II of *The Lives of the Saints*; and Trithemius in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*.

I think that the passage found in the Life of Saint Petronius, 4 October, composed through the efforts of Pietro Galesini, was drawn from no other source than Gennadius, although it appears under the name of Sigonius in Surius, volume V. Galesini himself admits this in his notes to the *Martyrology*:

> “Accordingly, he came to Egypt, where, penetrating into the deepest desert, he did not cease to converse with each of them until he had clearly learned the institutions of their holy life. Returning from there to his homeland, he loved that discipline so ardently that he committed to writing the *Lives of the Monks*, which, devoutly composed and thoroughly approved, the same monks embraced [Col. 0031B] as though they were certain rules in which the entire excellent ordering of their monastic institution shone forth most clearly.”

If, however, this passage was sketched from ancient records rather than from Gennadius, it will provide a second testimony in support of this view.

Since Gennadius says “is thought to have written,” it is not altogether certain that Petronius wrote the *Lives of the Fathers*. And even if he wrote some such lives, it can be firmly established by the evident testimony of Jerome that these were certainly not written by him, since Jerome ascribes them to another, as will become clear in § 10.

Indeed, Alphonsus Ciacconius, in his treatise *On the Cardinal Dignity of Saint Jerome* [XXII], quotes the following from a manuscript treatise by Petronius, *On Selected Sayings of the Holy Fathers*:

> “Jerome, a man most accomplished in every branch of learning, cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church, when accused by his rivals of having transferred innumerable passages from Origen’s volumes into his own works, said: ‘The praise that ought to be offered to Origen is immense; and when I imitated him in my works, I intended to imitate one whom I do not at all fear to be pleasing to us and to all prudent men.’”

Since these words do not appear in this book, it is certain that Saint Petronius wrote some other book concerning the lives and sayings of the Fathers. I have not yet been able to obtain it, although I have summoned it from Italy through various letters.

## § VIII. The View That Saint Jerome Was the Author

Nearly all editions place this title at the head of the work. Nor does it seem that the title lacked either authors or supporters.

1. Pope Gelasius of Rome, in the Roman council mentioned above, in Prolegomenon 1, in the decree concerning authentic books, says:

> “Likewise, we receive with all honor the *Lives of the Fathers*: of Paul, Antony, Hilarion, and all the hermits, which the blessed man Jerome nevertheless wrote.”

By these words Gelasius seems to imply that Jerome also wrote the lives of several other hermits. An old manuscript Life of Saint Jerome likewise says:

> “He frequently wove into historical narratives, with most truthful eloquence, the lives of distinguished hermits and Fathers.”

I reply that Gelasius merely asserts that he receives with all honor the lives of all the hermits which blessed Jerome wrote; it does not necessarily follow from this that he wrote the lives of all the hermits. In addition to those explicitly named—except for the Life of Antony, which is taken from the translation of Evagrius of Antioch, as may be seen in the notes to that Life—he wrote the Life of Malchus, the captive monk, and perhaps the lives of certain others, about which this is not clearly established. Thus that old Life correctly says that he wrote “the lives of distinguished Fathers, such as Paul, Hilarion, Malchus,” and so forth.

Perhaps the editors received from Gelasius the occasion for placing Jerome’s name above all others at the head of the *Lives of the Fathers*. Another circumstance may also have contributed: in certain manuscripts a Life certainly written by Jerome was placed first, and then Jerome’s name was applied to the remaining books that followed, as we said concerning Evagrius of Antioch in this same Prolegomenon 4, § 4. Certainly, in the smaller Laetiensis manuscript, the Life of Hilarion written by Saint Jerome is placed first; then this book, the second, together with the two following books, is appended.

Or, at any rate, it would not be unreasonable to say that Gelasius believed the *Lives of the Fathers* to have been composed by Jerome, since that opinion already seems to have prevailed long before. Certainly, the Greeks brought this second book from Latium into Greece under Jerome’s name. I have recently received a Greek portion of it from Venice; and in the Augsburg Library there is also a certain Greek fragment of a *Narrative*—Διήγησις—of the *Lives of the Fathers*, bearing Jerome’s name. I think this came about for no other reason than that, since the author of the book was uncertain, each person prefixed to it the name of an author according to his own judgment.

2. Cassian, in his preface to the books of the *Institutes*, addressed to Bishop Castor, lists among the other reasons for excusing himself—reasons by which he explains why he undertakes the burden of writing about monastic institutions less readily—and says:
