> “To this is added the fact that men distinguished both in life and in speech and learning have already labored over many little works on this subject. I mean Saint Basil and Jerome, and several others. The former, when the brothers asked him about various institutions or questions, answered not only in eloquent language but also with an abundant discourse furnished with testimonies from the divine Scriptures; the latter not only published books worked out by his own talent, but also translated into Latin works arranged in the Greek language.”

From this testimony it might seem possible to conclude that Jerome wrote about the *Lives of the Fathers*. I reply that Cassian does indeed allow us to conclude that Saint Jerome touched upon certain monastic institutions and lives in his writings, whether he composed them in Latin or translated them from Greek; but it cannot in any way be concluded that he was the author of this book.

3. Cassiodorus, in *Divine Readings*, chapter 32, says:

> “Read constantly the *Lives of the Fathers*, the confessions of the faithful, and the passions of the martyrs, which, among other works, you will undoubtedly find in Jerome’s letter addressed to Chromatius and Heliodorus. They flourished throughout the whole world, so that holy imitation, urging you onward, may lead you to the heavenly kingdoms.”

I reply that a letter bearing Jerome’s name exists at the beginning of Usuard’s *Martyrology*, but there is no mention there of the *Lives of the Fathers*. Thus it is impossible to conclude from that letter that Jerome was the author either of these lives or of any others. The letter refers only to the *Martyrology* which at that time stood after the letter under Jerome’s name. I have recently obtained it from the library of Echternach; it is truly very ancient, written more than nine hundred years ago—that is, in the time of Saint Willibrord. Accordingly, the passage does not refer there to the *Lives of the Fathers*, which are far removed, but only to the two works that follow: the confessions of the faithful and the passions of the martyrs, of which that *Martyrology* contains an extremely brief commemoration, or rather merely a listing of names.

4. Gratian, in the *Decree*, part 2, cause 27, question 2, chapter 26, after quoting the words of Nicholas I to King Charles, in which he decrees “that vows of continence may not be undertaken without the consent of both spouses,” adds the gloss, “They may be undertaken when the parties are merely betrothed.” He proves this as follows:

> “For, as blessed Jerome reports, Macarius, foremost among Christ’s hermits, after the wedding feast had been celebrated, when he was about to enter the bridal chamber in the evening, left the city, sought lands beyond the sea, and chose the solitude of the desert for himself [XXIV].”

This story is found in the Life of Macarius of Rome, which is now included in the first book of the *Lives of the Fathers*, though formerly it may have been appended to the second book, where the other two Macarii are discussed. I reply that Gratian may perhaps have taken the occasion to attribute the Life of Macarius to Jerome because he thought that all the *Lives of the Fathers* had been written by Jerome, led to this conclusion by the two arguments which we gave immediately above under the first heading.

5. Trithemius likewise, in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, attributes the *Lives of the Fathers* to Jerome. And lest anyone think that he is speaking of other lives than those commonly circulated under Jerome’s name, he says that their preface begins with the words, “Blessed be God,” from which the commonly circulated lives also take their beginning. I reply that the common edition misled Trithemius; for in other manuscripts different authors are assigned, as we have partly seen and shall partly see.

6. Jacobus Faber Stapulensis, in the preface to the reader which he prefixed to the Paris edition of the *Paradise of Heraclides*, mentioned above in § 3, asserts that someone among his associates warned him that he had wrongly denied the *Lives of the Fathers* to Jerome in his dedicatory letter, since Jerome himself acknowledged that he had written them. Who, he asks, could we desire as a more reliable witness than Jerome himself? For in the rule for nuns which he wrote to Eustochium and the other virgins, chapter 10, Jerome writes:

> “While, therefore, for seven years I visited the holy Fathers living there on earth in the caverns of the deserts, as though they were angels standing in heaven, traveling with constant labor, through difficult hardships of life and countless other afflictions, I compiled a little book about their life and their remarkable customs, which I myself clearly observed. Let it be for you like a lamp on a lampstand, for meditation upon religion and life.”

This testimony convinced Faber that Jerome had also written a book about the life and customs of the holy Fathers, a book which is now lost. For he could not accept that the book commonly known by the title *Lives of the Fathers* had been written by Jerome. First, because Jerome himself clearly identifies another author for these works, as we shall see later. Second, because from the Life of John, which is placed first, we learn that the person who composed the book was not a priest but only a deacon, and not an old man but a young man. Yet when Jerome sought the desert, no one, perhaps, doubts that he was both a priest and advanced in age. Thus far Faber.

But although Faber is correct to deny that these *Lives* proceeded from Jerome, he allowed himself to be persuaded too incautiously by the cited testimony that Jerome had nevertheless written *Lives of the Fathers* different from the commonly circulated ones. The more discerning authorities have long since banished that Rule for Nuns from the Hieronymian corpus [XXV] and relegated it to the end, as alien to Jerome’s character.

Jerome did indeed write a letter to Eustochium, numbered 22, concerning the preservation of virginity, in which he touches upon certain matters concerning the classes of monks and their rule and institution. But no evidence can be drawn from it that Jerome was either the author of that commonly circulated rule, which has been rejected to the end of his works, or the author of this book.

Indeed, it is proved from Jerome himself, as we shall see in § 10, that Jerome was not the author of this book. For would Jerome have committed to writing and commended as saints those whom he himself had exposed as heretics and asserted had been condemned by a council of bishops?

Nor is Faber’s assertion sufficiently sound when he insists that Jerome was both a priest and an old man when he withdrew into the Syrian desert. In fact, he was then neither old nor a priest. See here at the beginning of the first book Jerome’s journey, and what I argued in the fifth table of the *Law of Talion* on behalf of Baronius against Casaubon.

## § IX. The View That the Monk Postumianus Was the Author

I find that in certain manuscripts—including the Aquicinctine, the larger Laetiensis, and the Camberonensis—this second book, together with the fourth, is attributed to the monk Postumianus. One edition is also said to bear this title. I have read nothing about him that could establish this opinion.

I do not regard the suspicion as entirely groundless if someone says that this title arose from Severus Sulpicius. In his *Dialogues*, Sulpicius introduces Postumianus returning from the East after a three-year pilgrimage and relating many things about the life and institution of monks and hermits:

> “Postumianus,” he says at the beginning of the first dialogue, “having returned from the East, where he had gone three years earlier after leaving his homeland,” and so forth.

For everything contained in the first several chapters of this fourth book has been abridged from the first dialogue of Severus, in which Postumianus is introduced as the narrator.

## § X. The View That the Author Was Rufinus of Aquileia, Priest

The first among the more recent writers, so far as I know, to claim this book for Rufinus, at least as its translator—for he seems also to make Evagrius the author of the book—was Jacobus Faber Stapulensis, in his preface to the *Paradise of Heraclides*. He relied on the authority of Saint Jerome, who, in his letter to Ctesiphon against the Pelagians, writes the following about Evagrius and Rufinus:

> “Evagrius of Pontus, the Hyperborean, who writes to virgins, writes to monks, and writes to her whose name, meaning ‘blackness,’ bears witness to the darkness of perfidy”—he means Melania [XXVI], indicated by the meaning of her name—“published a book and sayings *περὶ ἀπαθείας*, concerning *apatheia*, which we may call ‘freedom from passion’ or ‘imperturbability,’ when the mind is never moved by any fault of disturbance; and, to put it simply, the mind is either a stone or God. His Greek books are read throughout the East, and in the West many read them in Latin, translated by his disciple Rufinus.

> “He also wrote a book ostensibly about monks, and enumerates many persons in it who never existed. Those whom he says did exist were unquestionably Origenists condemned by the bishops: namely Ammonius, Eusebius, Euthymius, Evagrius himself, Or, and Isidore, and many others whom it would be tedious to enumerate. As in that line of Lucretius:

> ‘And just as physicians, when they try to give children  
> bitter wormwood, first touch the edges of the cups  
> with the sweet yellow liquid of honey,’  

> so he placed a single John at the beginning of the book, a man whom there is no doubt was Catholic and holy, so that through him he might introduce into the Church the other heretics whom he had inserted.”

You have heard Saint Jerome, reader. What, then, do you think about the author of this book, in which mention is made of all those who are enumerated?

Consider, therefore, whether others, together with Baronius, have gone astray by thinking that the words “who also wrote a book ostensibly about monks” are to be understood of Evagrius. That they must be understood of Rufinus, whose name immediately precedes, is clear from the following arguments.

1. Saint Jerome adds that the person who wrote the book about monks also enumerates Evagrius himself, namely the man who had already been mentioned. It is not credible, as I said above in § 5, that Evagrius would have adorned himself with such praise and inserted himself into his own *Lives* alongside those of others. Perhaps noticing this, Marianus Victorius, Jerome’s scholiast, thought that in this second passage a different Evagrius, distinct from the Hyperborean, was being mentioned. But everyone will recognize that Jerome must also be understood to mean the Hyperborean in the second passage.

2. Immediately after the words quoted here from Saint Jerome, Saint Jerome himself adds:

> “But who could explain in worthy language that rashness—or rather, his madness—in which he placed at the head of the book of Xystus the Pythagorean, a man without Christ and a pagan, the name of Sixtus the martyr and bishop of the Roman Church, after changing the name?”

This is said not of Evagrius but of Rufinus, who published the book of Xystus the Pythagorean under the title of Sixtus the martyr, as is clear from other passages of Saint Jerome: for example, in chapter 22 of Jeremiah, where he attacks him under the name Grunnius; in chapter 18 of Ezekiel; and also from Augustine, *Retractions*, book II, chapter 40—who, having earlier been misled, had cited the work under the name of Sixtus the Pontiff in *On Nature and Grace* [XXVII], chapter 64—and from Rufinus’s own letter to Apronianus, which he prefixed to his translation of the *Enchiridion* of Sixtus.

3. Saint Jerome adds a similar fraud concerning the forgery attributed to Pamphilus in the defense of Origen:

> “He did the same,” he says, “under the name of Saint Pamphilus the martyr, so that he might title the first book of the six books defending Origen, written by Eusebius of Caesarea—whom everyone knows to have been an Arian—in the name of Pamphilus the martyr.”

That Rufinus stitched together this fraud is exceedingly well known. Saint Jerome mentions the same fraud in *Against Rufinus*, book II; in letter 65, to Pammachius and Oceanus; in chapter 18 of Ezekiel; and in the *Dialogue against the Pelagians*. Saint Jerome had not yet exposed it when he wrote his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, as is evident from chapter 75 of that work, in the entry on Pamphilus.

I judge this one testimony of Saint Jerome sufficient to establish that the book belongs to Rufinus. I omit the support provided by numerous manuscripts, such as the Audomarensis, of excellent quality and written by an ancient hand, which I used especially in reviewing these books, as well as other manuscripts which Henricus Gravius claims to have seen in his notes to Saint Jerome’s letter to Ctesiphon, already discussed.

I do not know whether Rufinus himself may seem to imply that he was the author or translator of this book. For in chapter 29 of this second book, where it discusses Macarius of Alexandria, the text adds:

> “Many other wonders, as we have said, are also reported concerning the deeds of Saint Macarius of Alexandria. Whoever seeks them will find some of them inserted in book XI of the *Ecclesiastical History*.”

In that book XI—that is, the later of the two books added by Rufinus himself to Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*, which he had translated from Greek—chapter 4 contains certain passages concerning Macarius of Alexandria that are absent from this second book of the *Lives of the Fathers*. The first concerns a blind man restored to sight, who wiped dust from Macarius’s cell, steeped it in the water of the well from which Macarius used to drink, and anointed his eyes with it. The second concerns lion cubs whose sight was restored. To these very wonders, in chapter 29 of the second book of the *Lives of the Fathers*, the text seems to refer the reader.

Rufinus himself clearly shows in the chapter just mentioned of book XI that the *Lives of the Fathers* were written after those books of ecclesiastical history—partly translated and partly composed by him. He adds:

> “But if we wished to recount the deeds of each individual wonder, we would be excluded from the brevity we have proposed, especially since they deserve a narrative in a work of their own.”

That he later fulfilled this undertaking by composing this book from a Greek text, we have learned from the testimony of Saint Jerome.

You may ask: Why, even in ancient times, was the author of this book so uncertain? I reply: Because the author suppressed his name, as did the translator [XXVIII], whose name we know only from the evidence of Saint Jerome and a few manuscripts.

As for why Rufinus suppressed his name, I think two reasons may be assigned. First, since, according to Jerome’s letter to Ctesiphon, it is clear that certain Origenists had been inserted here, Rufinus did not dare to put the book forth and sell it under his own name, because he himself was suspected of that heresy. Thus, so that the book might be received without any offense at the outset, he prefixed a preface but concealed his name. He suppressed his name in the same way in the edition of his translation of Origen’s books *On First Principles*, as Jerome indicates in letter 66 to Rufinus:

> “The little preface to the books *On First Principles* was sent to me, and from its style I understood that it was yours.”

Second, Rufinus was not so much the author of this book, as I have already said, as its translator; for this reason he did not wish to claim it for his own name. Since almost everything narrated in this book—with the exception of one chapter concerning Oxyrhynchus—is found in Palladius and Heraclides, it seems likely to me that Palladius, Heraclides, or someone else published these materials in Greek without a name, and that Rufinus translated them. Later Palladius published a fuller version under his own name and entitled it the *Lausiac History*.

Enough has now been said about this perplexing question. The Reverend Father Georgius Garnefelt, a member of the Cologne Charterhouse and its librarian, strongly favoring my studies, diligently investigates the authors of the *Lives of the Fathers* in his appendix to the *Sacred Elucidations of the Images of Hermits*, wishing either to assist me or to lead me back to the road if I am in error. He argues especially that in his letter to Ctesiphon, when Jerome says “who also wrote a book ostensibly about monks,” Evagrius must be understood, not Rufinus.

I add nothing here. Let the judicious reader examine only the text which I gave above and judge. I shall stand secure under anyone’s judgment. And whoever remembers that I have written more than once that Rufinus was rather the translator than the author will see all the missiles deflected by a friendly hand. I do not wish here to raise a shield against a well-disposed friend or to turn weapons back against a friend’s breast. For in the end, after examining everything, he too withdraws the book from Evagrius and declares its author uncertain. This does not conflict with my view, since I have asserted at least that Rufinus was its translator. Certainly, anyone who has carefully read Jerome’s letter to Ctesiphon cannot doubt that Rufinus’s hand was involved here.

## § XI. The View That the Author Was Valerius of Astorga, Archpriest

I had already investigated these proposed authors in this way when, behold, the Reverend Father Christophorus de Castro, professor of Sacred Scripture at the University of Salamanca, sent me from Spain his little treatise on the authors of the *Lives of the Fathers* [XXIX]. Among other things, he writes as follows:

> “It once occurred to me to wonder whether the author of the book might be Valerius, archpriest of Astorga. I happened upon his writings by chance while examining certain manuscripts in the library of the church of Toledo. There I saw a substantial volume written in Gothic letters, whose title was *Lives of the Eastern Fathers*, without an author. Yet I found the preface written by Valerius, archpriest of Astorga, in the year 940 of the era—that is, in the year of the Lord 902. It began with the Life of John, concerning whom Evagrius’s book”—more accurately, Rufinus’s, as I have already proved—“speaks, though this version was much longer. It then contained many lives of Fathers entirely different from those commonly related in the *Lives of the Fathers*. For this reason I abandoned all my suspicion.”

Thus far our Castro.

There was certainly an occasion for suspicion when the preface bore that name. But from Saint Jerome we possess a very certain testimony concerning the author or translator of this second book. Moreover, even if that Toledo book is said to have been written by Valerius, it does not immediately follow that he was the author of the book. Many writers place their names before or after books which they copied, even though they did not compose them; anyone who has examined even a few manuscript books with his own eyes cannot be unaware of this. Since, however, that Toledo book is said to contain “many Lives of Fathers entirely different from these,” Valerius may have established a new collection of the *Lives of the Fathers*.

# PROLEGOMENON V. Who Was the Author of the Third Book?

The printed editions continue weaving the rope of error and make Saint Jerome the author. But the style sufficiently proves that it is not his, although the three final chapters are taken from his letters, which reveal their own author through the elegance of their diction.

I have no assistance here from the manuscript books in investigating the author. For no name is consistently prefixed to this book. Either those who inscribe Evagrius or Postumianus on the preceding and following books allow this middle book to pass without an inscription; or, if they assign the same authors to this book also, they do so incorrectly, as I have already shown concerning the preceding book. If they wish the person whose name is inscribed on the preceding book to be the author of this and the following book as well, there is no better claim for Evagrius and Postumianus than for Rufinus, since Rufinus’s name is also written before the preceding book in certain manuscripts.

What, then? Can no certain author be discovered here? In fact [XXX], what once happened to Saint Jerome in a similar matter has happened to me. When the preface to Origen’s books *On First Principles* was offered to Jerome without any title prefixed, he detected from its style that it belonged to Rufinus, as he himself testifies in letter 66 to that same Rufinus. If I say that the same thing has happened to me today, although my nose is less discerning, I may perhaps not be entirely mistaken. But I shall now present the traces of this investigation, sufficiently certain, unless I am deceived.

When I carefully compared the preface of this book with that of the preceding book, I detected not only similarity of style but also two further features which made me more certain of the author—or at least the translator.

1. Rufinus, in the preface to the preceding book, says the following in praise of the monks:

> “So that there should be no doubt that the world still stands because of their merits.”

Referring to this same passage and responding to it almost as an epiphonema, the author begins the prologue of this second book as follows:

> “Who, indeed, could doubt that the world stands because of the merits of the saints?”

2. In the same preface to the preceding book, Rufinus sketched certain material from Palladius’s preface to the *Lausiac History*. In the prologue of this book, however, he transcribes material from Palladius’s letter to Lausus, which is appended to the preface. You will find these passages compared and marked in their proper places.

Since one preface thus refers to and alludes to the other, and since both arise from the same source and flow along the same channel of style, I think it sufficiently probable that the same author or translator may be assigned to both prefaces and books. Accordingly, I have inscribed this book to Rufinus.

# PROLEGOMENON VI. Who Was the Author of the Fourth Book?

I say: The fourth book was composed from Severus Sulpicius and John Cassian.

It consists merely of certain excerpts from their books, in almost identical words. We have noted for each chapter the individual passages from which they were taken.

I cannot say with certainty who arranged these materials. Let us nevertheless see whether here too, through a fortunate investigation, we may reach the workshop of the compiler. Even if we do not reach it entirely, it will at least be pleasant to follow the pressed tracks.

I know that Gennadius, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 63, reports that Eucherius, priest of the Church of Lyons, condensed certain little works of Cassian, which were extended in a broad manner of expression, into the narrow path of concise wording and gathered them into a single volume.

I know that Cassiodorus, in *Divine Institutes*, chapter 29, asserts that a certain Victor the African, bishop of Martyritana, purified Cassian’s sayings concerning the institution [XXXI] of monks and added what was lacking, not without the highest praise.

But I would not dare to affirm that this book, which we have before us, or some portion of it, should be attributed to either of them. It is preferable, however, to append here the very words of Gennadius and Cassiodorus, so that the reader may see whether anything certain about this compiler can be discerned.

Gennadius says the following about Eucherius:

> “Eucherius likewise gathered certain little works of Saint Cassian, extended in a broad manner of expression, into a single volume, reducing them to the narrow path of concise wording.”

These are the words of Gennadius, says Baronius in *Annals*, year 433, who was of the same Pelagian flour as Cassian. To avoid saying that Eucherius had contracted Cassian’s works by purging them of refuted errors, he pretended that he had merely cut away the broad manner of expression. So much for him.

If Eucherius is the author of the abridgment which we provide in this fourth book, one might rightly say that he used both scalpel and shears: now cutting into the vein and extracting harmful blood, now trimming luxuriant hair. For this Cassian is so healthy and so concise that no vein of Pelagian presumption pulses with excessive heat, nor does tedious eloquence overflow in curls of prolixity. I see no reason why this arrangement from Cassian could not be attributed to Eucherius.

Unless someone should object that this same abridgment travels through the vineyards of Severus, which are themselves cut back by the pruning knife. Thus both the printed editions and the manuscripts present this fourth book as arranged from Severus and Cassian, though their names are omitted. There are nevertheless manuscripts, such as the Camberonensis, which reproduce this fourth book from Cassian alone, omitting the passages taken from Severus that are ordinarily prefixed here and there. In this way the epitome might seem capable of being attributed to Eucherius.

There is also the not entirely dissimilar testimony of Peter Damian, book V, letter 19:

> “But if this seems doubtful to you, at least lend an ear to the testimony of your own side. Read the *Conferences of the Fathers*, which Eucherius, bishop of Lyons, endeavored to abridge in polished language; and if you do not wish to believe us, at least believe his writing.”

There Damian is discussing the clothing of monks, a subject treated in chapter 15 of this abridgment of Severus and Cassian.

Since, however, all the printed editions and most manuscripts represent this book as abridged from both authors, we should consider whether what Cassiodorus says in *Divine Institutes*, chapter 29, concerning a certain Victor the African may apply here:

> “Victor, an African bishop of Martyritana, with the Lord’s help, purified Cassian’s sayings in such a way and added what was lacking, that the palm of these matters may rightly be awarded to him. Among other things, we confidently believe that he will soon be sent to us from the regions of Africa [XXXII].”

Perhaps this addition may be understood as referring to the epitome of Severus appended here to Cassian’s epitome. Or perhaps he added certain things to what he purified—that is, he supplied an antidote against the suggestion of poison which Cassian scattered here and there in his writings.

Baronius above thinks that Cassiodorus was disappointed in his hope and did not receive what he was expecting from Africa. For Ado, bishop of Vienne, in his *Chronicle*, under the year 425, asserts that Cassiodorus himself undertook this work of correcting Cassian, saying:

> “His works must be read with the greatest caution by Catholics, especially those concerning free will and grace; but he also favored the heresy of the Encratites too incautiously. Cassiodorus, the senator of Ravenna, wishing to purge his errors, was not able to do so completely in every respect.”

Whom, then, should we establish as the author of these excerpts? I prefer to leave the matter unresolved rather than assert something rashly.

Petrus Ciacconius, in his preface to Cassian addressed to the reader, reports that in the Vatican Library there are several collections and that the last eight books of the *Institutes* have been translated into Greek, though reduced to an abridgment rather than translated in full. Anyone may read him discussing this matter.

# PROLEGOMENON VII. Who Was the Author of the Fifth Book?

I say: The author of the fifth book is uncertain.

1. Because Sigebertus, in *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Pelagius, chapter 116, calls it a book *On the Life, Teaching, and Perfection of the Holy Fathers*, but does not give the author’s name.

2. Because in Photius’s *Bibliotheca*, Codex 198, it is likewise cited without the author’s name:

> Ἀνεγνώσθη ἀνδρῶν ἁγίων βίβλος — “The book of holy men was read.”

I shall show in that place that this Greek book is the same as the one we possess in Latin.

Margarinus de la Bigne, in the catalogue or chronological index to the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, under the fifth century, considers Evagrius the author of the work which he published in volume IX of the second edition under this title: *Sayings of the Holy Egyptian Anchorites*, which are identical with this fifth book, translated by Pelagius, and with book VI, translated by John. His reason is that Nicephorus, in *Ecclesiastical History*, book XI, chapter 43, cites from the works of Evagrius many sayings of the Fathers which occur in the work just mentioned.

But I fear that Margarinus is mistaken.

1. For although certain things are found in these books which Nicephorus cites from the works [XXXIII] of Evagrius, they are not found in such a way that Evagrius himself appears to relate them as the author of a book; rather, they are cited from Evagrius.

For example, what Nicephorus cites from Evagrius’s *Praktikos* concerning an old man’s saying about a more austere diet is found here in Pelagius’s little book I, number 4:

> “Abba Evagrius said: ‘Because some of the Fathers used to say…’”

If Evagrius were the author of this little book, he would not say, “Abba Evagrius said.”

In the same place, number 5:

> “Again he said”—namely, Evagrius—“A monk was informed of the death of his father…”

Nicephorus also cites this above from Evagrius.

And in little book VI, number 5:

> “Abba Evagrius said that there was a certain brother who possessed nothing in his property except the Gospel.”

Nicephorus likewise cites this above from Evagrius’s *Praktikos*.

2. Certain things which Nicephorus cites from Evagrius’s books are not found here. For example, what he cites from Evagrius’s *Gnostikos* concerning Gregory the Just; the four cardinal virtues; Serapion; the mind imbued with spiritual knowledge; Didymus; providence and judgment; Basil, concerning the increase of knowledge through meditation; Athanasius; and the table of Moses.

3. Because various authors later than Evagrius are cited, such as John Cassian, Cyril of Alexandria, and several others, whom the reader will discover for himself.

It will not be useless here to add what Fr. Joannes Maria Brasichellensis, master of the Apostolic Sacred Palace, himself noted on this subject in the Index of Expurgated Books, under volume IX of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, where the sayings of the anchorites are discussed. He comments as follows:

> “There is considerable uncertainty regarding the author and translator of this work. Some, including Margarinus in the chronological index of the authors of this *Bibliotheca*, believe that its author was Evagrius Ponticus, who is certainly the author of the book *Lives of the Fathers*, to which this collection of sayings is invariably attached. Gennadius, in his catalogue, says the following about Evagrius:
>
> “‘He composed a book of one hundred sayings about anchorites who lived simple lives, which I was the first to render into Latin. For when I saw that the earlier translation had become corrupted and confused through the passage of time, I restored it to the truth of the author, partly by retranslating and partly by emending it.’
>
> “Thus far Gennadius. For my part, even if we should wish to suppose that many sayings in this work were taken from Evagrius’s collection, there are nevertheless more than six hundred here. And since this work mentions Theophilus of Alexandria, John Cassian, and Cyril of Alexandria, who were already dead, it is certain that Evagrius Ponticus—although, according to Gennadius, he lived to an advanced age—could not have survived the holy Cyril. For this reason also it is established that Saint Jerome was not the translator of these sayings. Pelagius, deacon of the Holy Roman Church, and John, subdeacon of the same Holy Roman Church, are named as the translators. Concerning them Sigebert treats in *On Illustrious Men*, chapters 116 and 117.”

Thus, although he rightly assigns these books to Evagrius as author and to Jerome as translator, he is less correct in asserting that the book *Lives of the Fathers* belongs to Evagrius, since it is rather certainly established that it does not. See what was said in Prolegomenon IV, § 5.

## PROLEGOMENON VIII. Who is the author of the sixth book?

I say: The author of the sixth book is uncertain.

First, because Sigebert, in *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 117, calls it *On the Life and Teaching of the Fathers*, but does not give the author’s name.

Second, because Photius, in the *Bibliotheca*, Codex 198—which I cited in the preceding prolegomenon—attaches this book to the preceding one. Consequently, the same judgment must be made concerning this book as concerning the earlier one.

But you may object: John Damascene, in the book entitled *On Those Who Departed from This Life with Faith*, relates a story about Macarius, who questioned a dead man’s skull about that man’s condition, and cites it from Palladius’s *Lausiac History*. Yet this same story is found in this sixth book, booklet three of John, no. 16, so that the author of this sixth book might appear to have been Palladius himself.

I reply: Moved by this argument, Gentianus Hervetus indeed held this opinion in the preface to his translation of Palladius. He says that the story is found in Book IV, entitled *The Teaching of the Fathers*, chapter *On Examples and the Teaching of the Spiritual Life*—for this is how the title and chapter heading are given in the Cologne edition, which combines the sixth and fifth books into a single book—and that this book is identical with the present sixth book.

If that explanation should seem less satisfactory, he supposed that the story had been present in the *Lausiac History* in the time of Damascene, and had later been maliciously removed by some heretic. I believe he said this because, for people of that kind, all these apparitions of spirits are mere fables, and because they resent the existence of even the slightest commemoration of suffrages for the souls of the dead.

Indeed, this is not foreign to a heretical disposition: just as the Philistines stopped up the wells of Israel (Genesis 26), lest any refreshment should come from them to mortals. Certainly, since Palladius appeared in a third edition, and it is evident from the latest edition that the work was first abridged and then published with some interpolations—as will be explained more fully in Prolegomenon XIV, where the translator of the eighth book is discussed—it may be supposed that the third edition too was not published complete. For the account of Macarius that Damascene had formerly read in the *Lausiac History* is not found even in this third edition as it exists today.

I more readily adopt this latter opinion than the former, according to which Palladius is believed to be the author of both the fifth and sixth books—which until now have circulated as a single book—because that account is found in it.

I accept this more readily:

First, because, so far as I know, that fifth and sixth book is called the *Lausiac History* by no one, although Damascene professes that he read the account there.

Second, because in the fifth book, booklet X, no. 67, among the other sayings of the elders there is also a saying of Palladius. From this it may be inferred that the book was arranged not by Palladius but by someone else.

## PROLEGOMENON IX. Who is the author of the seventh book?

I say: The author of the seventh book is uncertain.

Sigebert, in *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 118, calls it *Questions and Answers of the Holy Egyptian Fathers*, but does not mention its author. Paschasius himself, the translator, at the end of chapter 44, states plainly:

> “These are the responses of wise and spiritual Fathers.”

He gives no indication of the author.

## PROLEGOMENON X. Who is the author of the eighth book?

I say: The author of the eighth book is Palladius, bishop of Helenopolis, and it is called the *Lausiac History*.

This is sufficiently clear from Socrates, Book IV, chapter 23, whose words I shall reproduce. See also some additional material in the *Elogia* devoted to that book. He says:

> “If anyone should wish to learn about them—what they did, what they accomplished, what they uttered for the benefit of those who heard them, and how the wild animals obeyed them—a separate book has been composed about them by Palladius the monk, who was a disciple of Evagrius and who set forth everything about them with complete accuracy. In it he has also included an account of women who chose a manner of life equal to that of the men mentioned above.”

The Greek reads:

> Εἰ δέ τις βούλοιτο τὰ περὶ αὐτῶν μανθάνειν ὧν τε ἐποίησαν, ὧν τε ἔπραξαν, καὶ ὧν πρὸς ὠφέλειαν τῶν ἀκουσάντων ἐφθέγξαντο, ὅπως τε αὐτοῖς τὰ θηρία ὑπήκουν, πεπόνηται Παλλαδίῳ τῷ μοναχῷ ἴδιον μονόβιβλον, ὃς Εὐαγρίου μέν τις μαθητὴς, πάντα δὲ ἀκριβῶς περὶ αὐτῶν διεξῆλθεν· ἐν ᾧ καὶ γυναικῶν ἐφάμιλλον τοῖς προειρημένοις ἀνδράσιν ἐπανελομένων βίον, μνήμην πεποίηται.

This passage is also found in the *Tripartite History*, Book VIII, chapter 1, and in Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 44.

Since there are three different editions of Palladius, with different translators, see Prolegomenon XIV, where the translators are discussed, to determine which of them appears to be the more genuine.

## PROLEGOMENON XI. Who is the author of the ninth book?

I say: The author of the ninth book is Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, and it is called *Philotheos* (“God-loving”) or *Theophilēs* (“beloved of God”).

Theodoret himself testifies to this in Letter 82, to Eusebius, bishop of Ancyra:

> “I have also written a mystical book, another work on Providence, another on the Questions of the Magi, and another on the Lives of the Saints, besides many other works.”

He frequently mentions this book by the name *Philotheos* in his *Ecclesiastical History*.

Nicephorus, Book XIV, chapter 54, where he discusses, among other things, the writings of Theodoret, says:

> “Again, *Philotheos*, that is, the History of the Lovers of God, in which he follows the discipline of those who in his own age lived holy lives.”

## PROLEGOMENON XII. Who is the author of the tenth book?

I say: The author of the tenth book is John Moschus, and it is entitled *The Meadow of Sophronius*, or *The Spiritual Meadow*, or *The New Paradise*.

1. He gives his own name in chapter 77:

> “Sophronius said to me: ‘Indeed, Abba John, let us pursue nothing further today.’”

2. Photius, in Codex 199 of his *Bibliotheca*, gives the fuller title and a different title for the book:

> “A book was read containing three hundred and four narratives. This work too is especially useful for the ascetic life, and treats essentially the same subject as the book mentioned earlier, except that it records the deeds and actions worthy of imitation of men who lived later. For, beginning with those who flourished in virtue up to the reign of Heraclius and beyond, it proceeds through their lives. The compiler gives the book the title *Meadow*; some also call it *New Paradise*—certain manuscripts read *Paradise*, and in the margin of Margarinus’s manuscript it is called *Patristic*. The compiler’s name was John, but his surname was Moschus.” He first renounced the world in the monastery of Saint Theodosius, and afterward lived together with those who practiced asceticism in the desert along the Jordan and with those who contended in the New Laura of the great Sabbas. From there he traveled through the regions of Antioch, Alexandria, and the desert around it, as far as the Oasis, gathering the remarkable deeds of many great men—some of which he saw with his own eyes and others of which he learned through fresh reports. For the same reason, having also visited the islands while sailing toward Rome, and having investigated and learned similar things there, he composed this present work and addressed it to Sophronius, or Sophrona, his own disciple. He entrusted it to him, having foreseen the change of life that was soon to come, leading toward better things. Nevertheless, since the sensible and God-loving man gathered the useful material from all these accounts, he would never accuse the compiled work of excessive length.””

The Greek reads:

> Ἀνεγνώσθη βιβλίον, τέσσαρσι καὶ τριακοσίοις διηγήμασι περιειλημένον. Πρὸς τὴν ἀσκητικὴν δὲ καὶ τοῦτο τὰ μάλιστα συντελοῦν ἐστι πολιτείαν, τὰ αὐτά πως πραγματεύομενον τῷ προειρημένῳ, πλὴν ὅτι τῶν μεταγενεστέρων ἀνδρῶν ἔργα τε καὶ πράξεις ἀξιοζηλώτους ἀναγράφει· καὶ γὰρ ἐκεῖθεν τῶν μέχρι τῆς Ἡρακλειου ἀρχῆς καὶ ἐπιπλέον διατρεψάντων ἀρεταῖς, ἐπέρχεται τοὺς βίους. Λειμῶνα δὲ καλεῖσθαι δίδωσιν ὁ συνταξάμενος ὄνομα τὸ βιβλίον· τινὲς δὲ αὐτὸ καὶ Νέον ὀνομάζουσι Παραδείσιον (manuscripti quidam Παραδείσιν, qui ad marginem manuscripti Margunii vocatur Πατερικόν) Ὁ δὲ συντεταχὼς, Ἰωάννης μὲν ὄνομα αὐτῷ, ἐξ ἐπικλήσεως δὲ ἐλέγετο ὁ τοῦ Μοσχοῦ, ὃς ἀπετάξατο μὲν ἐν τῇ τοῦ ἁγίου Θεοδοσίου μονῇ, εἶτα συνδιέτρεψε τοῖς τε κατὰ τὸν Ἰορδάνην ἀνὰ τὴν ἔρημον ἀσκουμένοις, καὶ τοῖς ἐν τῇ νέᾳ Λαύρᾳ τοῦ μεγάλου Σάββα διαθλοῦσιν. Ἐντεῦθεν δὲ τά τε τῆς Ἀντιοχείας κλίματα, καὶ τὴν Ἀλεξάνδρου, καὶ τὴν περὶ αὐτὴν ἔρημον, καὶ μέχρις Ὀάσεως ἐπελθὼν, καὶ πολλῶν καὶ μεγάλων ἀνδρῶν ἀριστείας συναγηοχώς, τοῦτο μὲν ὄψει, τοῦτο δὲ καὶ νεαζούσῃ ἀκοῇ· διὰ τὴν αὐτὴν δὲ αἰτίαν καὶ νήσοις ἱστορησάμενος, ἐν τῷ πρὸς τὴν Ῥώμην διάπλῳ, ἐκεῖσέ τε τὰ παραπλήσια διερευνησάμενος, καὶ μαθὼν, τὸ παρὸν σύνταγμα γράφει, καὶ προσφωνεῖ Σωφρονίῳ ἢ Σωφρονᾷ τῷ οἰκείῳ μαθητῇ, καὶ ἐγχειρίζει αὐτῷ τοῦτο, τὴν τοῦ βίου μέλλουσαν ἐφίστασθαι πρὸς τὰ ἀμείνονα προτεθεαμένος μεταβολήν. Πλὴν ἐξ ἁπάντων τὸ χρήσιμον ὁ συνετὸς καὶ θεοφιλὴς ἀνὴρ δρεπόμενος οὐκ ἂν τῶν συντεταγμένων κόρον καταγνοίη.

This is an abridged extract by Photius from the author’s eulogy, now prefixed to the book in this second Moretian edition from Greek manuscripts.

3. The Second Council of Nicaea, the seventh ecumenical council in order, states in Session 4:

> “From the *Meadow* of our holy father Sophronius. Abba Theodore the Aeliote said that there was a certain recluse on the Mount of Olives, a very great ascetic,” etc.

The Greek reads:

> Τοῦ ἐν ἁγίοις πατρὸς ἡμῶν Σωφρονίου ἐκ τοῦ Λειμωναρίου. Ἔλεγεν ὁ ἀββᾶς Θεόδωρος ὁ Αἰλιώτης, ὅτι ἦν τις ἔγκλειστος εἰς τὸ ὄρος τῶν Ἐλαιῶν, ἀγωνιστὴς πάνυ etc.

There the whole of chapter 45, which is found in this book, is given in Greek. The same passage is repeated in Session 5, where two other examples are also cited from the same *Meadow*.

4. John the Deacon, Book I, chapter 45, of the *Life of Saint Gregory the Great*:

> “Nevertheless, my teacher interpreted from the book which the Greeks call *Leimon* and which the Latins understand as ‘Field’ or ‘Meadow,’ among other miracles already celebrated throughout the world.”

5. John Damascene, at the end of the first book that he wrote concerning images, cites testimony from this book under the following title:

> “From the *Little Meadow* of our holy father Sophronius, archbishop of Jerusalem.”

The Greek reads:

> Ἐκ τοῦ Λειμωναρίου τοῦ ἁγίου πατρὸς ἡμῶν Σωφρονίου ἀρχιεπισκόπου Ἱεροσολύμων.

6. Nicephorus, Book VIII, chapter 41:

> “Sophronius of Jerusalem also left us a long and useful history of these men—the monks—under the title *Meadow* and *New Paradise*, which he gave to his work.”

You may ask: Why is this book now attributed to Sophronius, patriarch of Jerusalem, as in the Second Council of Nicaea and in John Damascene, and now to John Moschus, or Eviratus, and addressed to Sophronius the sophist?

Aloysius Lipomanus, bishop of Verona, gives the answer. He was the first to arrange for the publication of this book, which the Apostolic Library supplied in 1558:

> “The writer of the book was certainly John the anchorite. This will be perfectly clear to you from chapter 77 of the volume itself. Photius likewise asserts that this same author of the book was John Moschus—perhaps by nationality—and that the Latin translator perhaps rendered his surname as ‘Eviratus.’”

Nevertheless, the book is attributed to Sophronius for the following reasons.

Either because it is dedicated to him as its dearest companion, just as Cicero’s *Rhetoric* is called *Ad Herennium*, and his letters are called *Ad Atticum*—so this book is called Sophronius’s because it is addressed to Sophronius. This is especially so because it was written chiefly for his use. For the author himself, in the letter that he places before the book, admits that he wove a crown for Sophronius from this meadow and, through him, offered it afterward to others.

Or because the sayings and deeds of Sophronius himself occupy the greater part of this book. He was the author’s inseparable companion throughout the entire journey, and whatever occurred as the two traveled together, or whatever happened to be reported in response to their inquiries, was recorded with the greatest care. Hence you will also see these words repeated very frequently: “My lord Sophronius the sophist and I came to such-and-such an abbot,” and so forth. For this reason he also consistently uses the plural, saying: “We proceeded,” “we approached,” “we saw,” “the elder, the guide of the monastery, told us.” From all this it can be seen that the writer was never alone in investigating the matters he relates. Just as Plato’s *Phaedrus*, *Timaeus*, *Gorgias*, and *Parmenides*, and Cicero’s book *On Old Age*, entitled *Cato Major*, are named after the persons introduced as conversing and debating in them, what prevents this book from being called Sophronius’s, since he is represented almost everywhere in it as traveling, visiting, acting, questioning, and answering?

Or finally, it is attributed to Sophronius because he may have been, together with the aforementioned John, so to speak, a co-author of the same book. Read chapter 77 of this volume, and at its beginning you will find written:

> “My lord Sophronius and I went to the house of Stephen the philosopher for the sake of instruction,” etc.

Then, at the end of the same chapter, we read:

> “When we had heard these things, my lord Sophronius signaled to me, and we withdrew. He said to me: ‘Indeed, Abba John, let us pursue nothing further today; for we have been sufficiently edified.’ We have therefore written these things so that you too may likewise be edified.”

For one of these reasons—or rather, because all of them converge together—this book reasonably and justly appears to be inscribed under the name of Sophronius.

You may object: In this book Sophronius is not called patriarch of Jerusalem, but sophist.

The same Aloysius replies: This word was formerly not taken in a derogatory sense, as it commonly is today, but in a favorable one; it signified nothing other than a wise and prudent man, such as that Libanius to whom many of Basil the Great’s letters were addressed and in which he is extolled with the highest praises. This man, therefore, could first have been both a monk and called a sophist, and afterward have been raised to the holy see of Jerusalem, from which, as the more distinguished position, he later received his designation.

You may ask: At what time did these men who composed the book flourish?

The same author answers: This is not known with certainty. Nevertheless, since they relate an event involving Gregory the Great, Roman pontiff and the first of that name; since they mention the emperors who were their contemporaries—namely Anastasius, Tiberius, Maurice, and Zeno—and since this book is cited at the Sixth Council, we may infer that it was composed around the year of the Lord 600.

Finally, for the commendation of this book, Aloysius Lipomanus writes in his preface:

> “This book, friendly reader, which we present to you for reading, is called *The Spiritual Meadow*. It was rendered from Greek into Latin by the learned Ambrose, a Camaldolese monk; until now we possessed it in print only in the vernacular, and that in the Italian language.
>
> “It is filled with such a delightful abundance of spiritual flowers that it appears to have sprung up amid the joys of paradise. In it there breathes the splendor of the lives of the ancient monks and of the other Fathers who served God from the depths of their hearts; the observance of regular discipline; the standard of chastity and continence; moderation in food and clothing; unconquered steadfastness against heretics; constant perseverance in fasts, vigils, and prayers; and an exceptional and immeasurable love for the Lord Jesus Christ. It also contains certain marvelous responses, filled with the Holy Spirit, which suffuse the minds of readers with a certain spiritual sweetness. Finally, it contains the unconquered faith, incomparable chastity, and blessed consummation in God of holy women.
>
> “Oh, if only we could now find soldiers serving Christ of such a kind! How illustrious, splendid, and dignified would be the appearance of our Church, which we see so cast down and worn out, and, alas, blackened beyond the skins of Solomon and the Ethiopian woman of Moses!
>
> “Read, therefore, with willing spirit and certain faith, candid reader, this work, a copy of which we received from the Apostolic Library. Order your conduct and your life according to its reading, so that you may prove a worthy imitator of such great men as you will find described here, and afterward may happily be joined to their company in eternal blessedness. May the Lord grant this to you and to me, and to all who love the Lord Jesus in sincerity. Farewell.”

## PROLEGOMENON XIII. In what language were these books written?

I say: Almost all these books were written in Greek.

This will soon become clear when their translators are identified. Since nearly all those Fathers were born and lived in the East, it is not surprising that their deeds were transmitted to posterity by Eastern peoples, especially Greeks, who possessed considerable ability in writing, and who had lived together with the monks.

In the first book, which is a miscellaneous collection, Saint Jerome alone among the various authors is known to have written in Latin.

We have asserted that the second and third books were written by Rufinus, partly from Saint Jerome, partly from manuscripts, and partly on the basis of probable conjecture.

Whether he translated from Greek, however, is uncertain. Saint Jerome seems to imply that Rufinus himself composed the work in the letter cited above. For he says:

> “He also wrote a book, as it were, about monks.”

This must nevertheless be understood of the second book alone, as is clear from the names of the Fathers that Saint Jerome reproduces from that book of Rufinus which circulated in his own time; their lives are found only in the second book.

Since the fourth book has been compiled from Sulpicius Severus and John Cassian, there is little reason to doubt that this compilation was made by a Latin author, especially since the compiler generally uses the authors’ own words.

It is clear from Photius’s *Bibliotheca*, Codex 198, that the Greek author of the fifth and sixth books was Greek, since Photius read them in Greek and praised the clarity of their style.

The fact that the author of the seventh book was Greek is indicated by the translator Paschasius himself.

The author of the eighth book was Palladius, who wrote in Greek, as is clear from Socrates and from Prolegomenon X.

The author of the ninth book was Theodoret, who was Greek, as we have seen above; this is more than sufficiently well known.

The author of the tenth book was John Moschus. Photius testifies that he wrote in Greek in Codex 199 of the *Bibliotheca*, and says the following about his style:

> “The diction of this work inclines toward a humbler and more unlearned style than that of the preceding work”—namely, the fifth and sixth books discussed above.

The Greek reads:

> Ἡ δὲ τοῦ λόγου ἑρμηνεία εἰς τὸ ταπεινότερον τοῦ προτέρου, καὶ ἀμαθέστερον ἀποκλίνει.

## PROLEGOMENON XIV. Who are the translators of these books?

I say: These books have various translators.

The following known translators occur in the first book:

1. Evagrius, bishop of Antioch, translator of the *Life of Saint Antony the Monk*. See the introductory material to that *Life*.

2. Dionysius Exiguus, translator of the *Life of Saint Pachomius*. Consult the introductory material prefixed to that *Life*.

3. Ursus, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, translator of the *Life of Saint Basil, bishop of Caesarea*. Concerning Ursus, see the notes to that *Life*.

4. Gerardus Vossius, translator of the *Life of Saint Ephraem*.

5. Anastasius, librarian of the Holy Roman Church, translator of the *Life of Saint John the Almsgiver, patriarch of Alexandria*. See the introductory material to that *Life*.

6. Jacobus Billius, translator of the *Life of Saints Barlaam and Josaphat*.

7. Eustochius, translator of the *Life of Saint Pelagia*.

8. Paulus, deacon of the Church of Naples, translator of the *Life of Blessed Mary of Egypt*.

Melchior Goldast, in volume I, part 2, of *Alemannic Affairs*, in his notes on Hepidanus, believes that the *Life of Saint Eugenia* was translated by Rufinus. But I do not know where he obtained this information. Possevinus, in the *Sacred Apparatus*, says that the *Life of Saint Eugenia* was written by Ambrose, abbot of Camaldoli. Does he mean that it was translated by him? Certainly, according to the same authority, that author translated several other works concerning the *Lives of the Fathers*.

The second, third, and fourth books were written in Latin, or at least no translation is established. More precisely: the fourth was certainly written in Latin, while there is doubt about the preceding two. See what was said in Prolegomena IV, V, and VI.

The translator of the fifth book is Pelagius, deacon of the Holy Roman Church.

All manuscripts consistently state this. Sigebert, in *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 116, says:

> “Pelagius, deacon of the Roman Church, translated from Greek into Latin sixteen books on the life and teaching and perfection of the holy Fathers, namely: Book I, *On the Progress of Monks*; Book I, *On Solitude*; Book I, *On Compunction*; Book I, *On Continence*; Book I, *Against Fornication*; Book I, *That a Monk Should Possess Nothing*; Book I, *That Nothing Should Be Done for Display*; Book I, *On Patience and Fortitude*; Book I, *That No One Should Be Judged*; Book I, *That One Ought to Live Soberly*; Book I, *That One Ought to Pray Without Ceasing and Soberly*; Book I, *On Humility*; Book I, *On Repentance*; Book I, *On Charity*; Book I, *On Providence, or Contemplation*.”

The translator of the sixth book is John, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church.

All manuscripts state this. Sigebert above, chapter 117, says:

> “John the subdeacon translated from Greek into Latin one book on the life and teaching of the Fathers.”

When Sigebert says that John translated one book from Greek into Latin, although he in fact translated four booklets, this may have happened because he encountered a manuscript in which those booklets were connected indistinctly, without titles. Or he may call it one book because it contains four booklets.

It is worth asking who this Pelagius and who this John were. The Reverend Father Georgius Garnefelt, in the book cited above, believes that this Pelagius, while he was deacon of the Holy Roman Church, when he translated this book, afterward became Roman pontiff, from the year of the Lord 555 to the year 559. He writes:

> “Two considerations impel me to this judgment: first, that he was highly skilled in the Greek language; second, that he undertook various embassies to the Eastern Church. No one who wishes to consult Baronius for the years 538 to 555 will doubt this. I am therefore convinced that during these embassies this Pelagius came upon the Greek book mentioned by Photius in the *Bibliotheca*, Codex 198, brought it with him to Rome, and translated it there. But after he had carried this translation as far as chapter 16 of booklet or part XVIII—as it appears in the first edition—he seems, being hindered by other affairs, or rather burdened with the government of the Roman see, to have entrusted the remainder of the translation to John the subdeacon. I believe that the latter was the same man who succeeded Pelagius in the primacy of the Roman Church. This is my conjecture and opinion; if others should bring forward and prove something more certain, I shall gladly accept it.”

Thus far Garnefelt.

The translator of the seventh book is Paschasius, deacon of the Holy Roman Church, who rendered it into Latin at the request of Martin, abbot of Dume.

The preface prefixed to that book states this explicitly. Sigebert also testifies to it above, chapter 118:

> “Bishop Martin, through the agency of Paschasius the deacon, translated in the monastery of Dume many questions and answers of the holy Egyptian Fathers.”

First observe that there were two deacons named Paschasius at nearly the same time—for Paschasius Ratbertus, who lived two centuries later, cannot be included here—and that both were distinguished for their writings.

The first was Paschasius, deacon of the Holy Roman Church, “whose entirely orthodox and lucid books on the Holy Spirit are extant,” as Saint Gregory says in *Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 40. According to the same testimony, he “died during the time of Symmachus, bishop of the apostolic see.” Symmachus occupied the see from the year 499 to the year 515. Sigebert also mentions this Paschasius in *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 17, as do later writers.

This is the same man to whom Eugippius, a presbyter, sent the *Life of Saint Severinus, Apostle of Noricum*, which he had composed, and submitted it for his judgment. For the name, period, place, and sacred office establish this, says Baronius in volume VI of the *Annals*, under the year 496. The same Paschasius replied to him; Baronius presents that letter in the same place. You will find it here in Prolegomenon XXV.

The second was Paschasius, deacon of the monastery of Dume in Galicia. He dedicated his book on the *Lives of the Fathers*, which is the seventh in this edition, to Martin, presbyter and abbot of Dume. Gregory of Tours places Martin’s death in the fifth year of the younger Childebert, in Book V, chapter 37, of his *History of the Franks*; Baronius assigns it to the year 583 in volume VII of his *Annals*.

Second, observe that there were also two men named Eugippius in the same period.

One was an abbot who wrote “to a certain deacon Paschasius concerning the life of Saint Severinus the monk” and flourished “after the consulship of Importunus the Younger, while Anastasius was emperor,” as Isidore says in *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 13. He therefore flourished after the year 509, the year of the consulship of Importunus, or Opportunus. In his letter prefixed to the *Life of Saint Severinus*, he says that he wrote it two years after the consulship of Importunus.

The other was also an abbot, “who culled extracts from the books of Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo, and lived in the time of the second Pelagius and the emperor Tiberius Constantine,” as Sigebert writes in *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 39. He therefore flourished around the year 580.

From these facts it can now easily be inferred—and the same thought had occurred to our very dear Garnefelt—that the later Paschasius was the translator of the seventh book, since he belongs to the period of Martin of Dume, to whom he dedicates his translation. His style also does not rise to the level of the earlier Paschasius’s style. The translation of the *Paradise of Heraclides* should rather be attributed to the earlier Paschasius. Concerning this, see Prolegomenon XXV. He too was a deacon of the Holy Roman Church, as we have the testimony of Saint Gregory above.

The later Paschasius was also a deacon in the monastery of Dume, but I am uncertain whether he was also a deacon of the Holy Roman Church. I fear that, through confusion between the two Paschasiuses, the title belonging to the first was also attached to the second. It has consequently been printed in this form, and I have not yet dared to alter it.

The translator of the eighth book, which was written in Greek by Palladius, is Gentianus Hervetus, canon of Rheims, who performed excellent work in this kind of translation.

Observe here that there are three different editions of Palladius, with different translators.

The first appeared at the very beginning of printing, in the first edition of the *Lives of the Fathers*, where no certain translator is assigned. This book was omitted from subsequent editions of the *Lives of the Fathers*, but in 1547 Fr. Theodoric Loher of Stratis, a Carthusian, restored it to his edition, which was published at Cologne by Jaspar Gennepaeus.

The second appeared in Paris from the press of Jean Petit in 1504, under the care of Jacobus Faber Stapulensis. It bears a different title—for it is called *The Paradise of Heraclides*—and names a different, likewise uncertain, translator. The same edition later appeared in Venice in 1554, prefixed with the title of Palladius, in volume III of the *Lives of the Saints* collected by Aloysius Lipomanus.

This edition was prepared through the efforts of Franciscus Torres and compared with a manuscript copy of Palladius preserved in Venice in the Library of Cardinal Bessarion. Lipomanus says that, after comparing the entire volume with it “from beginning to end,” Torres “found it to be entirely identical, with only a few changes of very minor importance. The title also differed, as did the dedicatory letter, which in one volume was not by Heraclides of Alexandria but by Palladius, bishop of Cappadocia, although in both volumes it appeared to be addressed to Lausus. After correcting these few passages and bringing it into conformity with the most accurate manuscript”—as Lipomanus believed—he included the book in volume III of the *Lives of the Saints*.

The third is the edition that we present here, which Gentianus Hervetus prepared in his own style from the Greek text under the title *Lausiac History*. Bernard Turrisanus published it in Paris in 1555. It was reissued there by Guillaume Chaudière in 1570, with certain marginal annotations by Fr. Thomas Beauxamis, a Carmelite and doctor of theology. It was further enlarged with the scholia of Laurentius Barrensis and incorporated into the *Christian History of the Ancient Fathers*, published in Paris by Michel Sonnius in 1583, and likewise into volume VII of the *Bibliotheca Sanctorum Patrum*.

If anyone wishes to seek a fourth edition of Palladius, he will not have to work very hard. He will find Rufinus, the most ancient translator of Palladius, if the conjecture that we expressed in Prolegomenon IV, § 2, and X is correct.

You may ask which of these is the genuine history of Palladius.

I answer: It appears to be the one published by Hervetus. For Socrates, Book IV, chapter 18, says that he refrains from describing the lives of the holy Fathers because Palladius had done this sufficiently, and he identifies the work by a definite mark: it treats both women and men. He says:

> “Everything concerning them is accurately set forth in it. It also includes an account of women who practiced a way of life equal to that of the men mentioned above.”

The Greek reads:

> Πάντα δὲ ἀκριβῶς περὶ αὐτῶν διεξῆλθεν· ἐν ᾧ καὶ γυναικῶν ἐφάμιλλον τοῖς προειρημένοις ἐπανελομένων βίον μνήμην πεποίηται.

In the edition of Hervetus, however, you find a fuller treatment of both women and men, whereas the other editions deal very little with women. See above, Prolegomenon IV, § 3.

The translator of the ninth book is the same Gentianus Hervetus, whose translation appears together with that of the preceding book.

Aloysius Lipomanus arranged for this book of Theodoret to be included in volume II of the *Lives of the Saints*, published at Venice in 1553. Its translator was Albericus Longus of Salento; Lipomanus had obtained the book from a learned man at Trent.

The translator of the tenth book is Ambrose, abbot of Camaldoli. Aloysius testifies in his preface to the reader—he was the first to arrange for its publication, in volume VII of the *Lives of the Saints*—that he found this information in the Apostolic Library.

You may object: John the Deacon, later Roman pontiff, while mentioning chapter 63 of this volume in Book IV of the *Life of Blessed Gregory*, where he relates a remarkable deed of that most holy pontiff, professes himself to be the translator. For he says:

> “But lest the humility of so great a prelate be thought to be inculcated by words alone, it remains that the same humility of the Father be demonstrated by living deeds from the Greek accounts recently translated by me. They are reported as follows:
>
> “‘Abba John the Persian, a holy and venerable man, told us about the most blessed Pope Gregory of Rome, saying: “I went to Rome to venerate the shrines of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. One day, as I was standing in the middle of the city, I saw Pope Gregory passing by me, and I considered putting myself before him. When the pope approached me and saw that I was about to place myself before him, I declare before God, brothers, that he was the first to throw himself upon the ground before me, and he did not rise until I had first risen. He embraced me with great humility, gave me three coins by hand, and ordered that a cloak and all my necessities be given to me. I therefore glorified God, who granted him such humility toward everyone, as well as almsgiving and charity.”’”

You will find this same story here in chapter 151.

I reply that it is indeed found there, but in different words, so that it is permissible to recognize two different translators.

Yet this translator was not John the Deacon but his teacher, as he clearly states in Book II, chapter 45, of the *Life of Saint Gregory*. He says:

> “From the book which the Greeks call *Leimon* and which the Latins understand as ‘Field’ or ‘Meadow,’ my teacher interpreted, writing to me, among other miracles already celebrated throughout the world,” etc.

Thus the wording found in most editions is correct: “from the Greek accounts recently translated for me,” not “by me,” as it is incorrectly cited before the *Spiritual Meadow* in the Cologne edition produced by the Birckmann press.

Observe that today this book is read as divided into only 219 chapters, although formerly it consisted of more, as Photius testifies in Codex 199 of his *Bibliotheca*:

> “Nor will you find the same number of narratives preserved in all the books; in some, they extend to three hundred and forty-two.”

The Greek reads:

> Καὶ τὰ διηγήματα δὲ οὐχὶ τὸν ἴσον ἀριθμὸν ἐν πᾶσιν εὑρήσεις τοῖς βιβλίοις διασεσώμενα· ἀλλ᾽ ἔν τισι καὶ εἰς δύο καὶ τεσσαράκοντα, καὶ τριακοσίοις διηπλωμένα.

At the beginning, however, he had said that it consisted of three hundred and four narratives.

He adds two explanations for this variation:

> “This happens either because the number is increased by the division of certain chapters, or because narratives have been inserted.”

The Greek reads:

> Τοῦτὸ μὲν ἐνίων κεφαλαίων ἐπὶ διαιρέσει τοῦ ἀριθμοῦ συναυξομένου, τοῦτο δὲ καὶ διηγημάτων ἐστιν ὡς παρενθήκη.

## PROLEGOMENON XV. What authority do these books possess?

Concerning the authority of these books, I think that those who have read the preceding prolegomena will not easily entertain doubts. In them, several men distinguished for religion, renowned for piety, and eminent for learning either composed portions of these *Lives* themselves or arranged for them to be translated from Greek into Latin, as did Saint Martin, abbot of Dume; or they commended the reading of them to their religious communities, as did Saint Benedict, Cassiodorus, and Gregory of Tours; or they expressly accepted portions of them as authentic writings many centuries ago, as did Pope Gelasius.

Moreover, almost all the authors report matters that they themselves witnessed with their own eyes or learned from trustworthy witnesses. For Jerome, Rufinus, Cassian, Palladius, Postumianus in Severus, Theodoret, and Moschus either lived for several years with those Fathers or visited their holy places on pilgrimage.

[XLVII] Cassiodorus, in *Divine Institutions*, chapter 32—which contains an admonition by Abbot Chalcedonius, Gerontius, and the community of monks—urges them to read the *Lives of the Fathers* diligently:

> “Therefore enter eagerly into the mysteries of the Lord, so that you may be able to point out the way to those who follow, because it is a great burden of shame to possess something to read and [Col. 0053D] not know what to teach. And therefore, mindful of future blessedness, read constantly the *Lives of the Fathers*, the confessions of the faithful, and the sufferings of the martyrs.”

Indeed, although most of these works have been drawn from Greek sources—and although the origin of certain sources is not entirely established—the men who conveyed them into Latin channels were serious and distinguished by ecclesiastical rank: two deacons from the cardinal order of the Fathers, Pelagius and Paschasius, and one subdeacon, John. Since they lived before the eyes of the pontiff, whose alone it is to judge concerning “the fountains of living water and the cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jeremiah 2), I do not see why their authenticity should be doubted.

If, moreover, you desire other serious men who made use of the testimony of the *Lives of the Fathers*, apart from those matters noted in their proper places, the following now come to mind.

1. Gratian, in part 3 of the *Decree*, distinction 3, *On Consecration*, chapter 16, cites certain sayings of Saint Apollonius concerning fasting on the fourth and sixth days of the week; you will find them here verbatim, book II, in Rufinus, chapter 7.

2. Burchard, in book XIX of the *Decretals*, which concerns penance, cites four apophthegms from the *Lives of the Fathers*, or the sayings of the elders. For what he has in chapter 52 is taken from Rufinus, book III, no. 103; what he has in chapter 53 is taken from the same book, no. 131; what is in chapter 54 is taken from the same book, no. 137; and what is in chapter 55 is taken from the same book, no. 141.

3. Abbot Dorotheus cites many passages from these books in the instructions he gave to the brothers. Thus, in the first instruction, he cites certain passages found in Rufinus, book III, no. 144, and in Pelagius’s little book XIV, no. 16. The second instruction cites what is found in Rufinus, the same book, no. 129, and in Pelagius, little book XV, no. 3. The fifth instruction cites what is found in Rufinus, the same book, no. 61; in Pelagius, little book XVIII, no. 9; and in Paschasius, chapter 1, no. 8. In the same place he cites the account of Agathon found in Rufinus, book III, no. 161, and in Pelagius, little book II, no. 2. The sixth instruction cites what is found in Rufinus, book III, no. 137, and in Pelagius, little book IX, no. 3. The seventh instruction brings forward what Rufinus has in book III, no. 51, and Pelagius in little book IV, no. 59. It can also be noted that many other passages in Dorotheus himself and elsewhere are taken from these books.

[Col. 0054C] You will object first: Pope Gelasius, above, in Prolegomenon 1, accepts with full honor only those *Lives of the Hermits* written by blessed Jerome [XLVIII]; yet many others are mixed in with them, and it is certain that blessed Jerome was not their author.

I reply that he expressly receives the *Lives* written by blessed Jerome, but that he does not thereby reject the others. Indeed, Gelasius may seem to have thought that Jerome wrote several more *Lives* besides those of Paul, Antony, and Hilarion, which he expressly mentions and accepts as authentic works written by blessed Jerome. For when he adds, “and of all the hermits,” he appears to be referring to this book of the *Lives of the Fathers*, which at that time was already commonly reported to be Jerome’s. I understand this especially of the second book, which, as I noted above in Prolegomenon 4, § 8, was also circulating among the Greeks under Jerome’s name.

Nor is it surprising that Gelasius considered Saint Jerome the author of the second book—although another author is now recognized for it, Jerome himself bearing witness to this—since he also makes Saint Jerome the author of the *Life of Saint Antony*, which is now certainly known to have been written in Greek by Athanasius and translated into Latin by Evagrius of Antioch. See what will be said about the *Life of Saint Antony* in the preliminary discussions, note.

You will object second, against the authority of the second book as the work of Rufinus: Blessed Jerome, in his letter to Ctesiphon against the Pelagians, attacks Rufinus severely because he inserted certain Origenists into these *Lives*; the passage is quoted above, in Prolegomenon 4, § 10. Theophilus also, writing to Epiphanius while presiding over the Church of Alexandria, boasts in letter 67, preserved by Jerome:

> “The Church of Christ has cut down with the evangelical sword the serpents of Origen emerging from their caves, and has freed the host of monks of Nitria from the contagion of the plague.”

And below:

> “I have learned,” he says, “that the slanderers of the true faith, Ammonius, Eusebius, and Euthymius, raging with a new madness on behalf of heresy, have sailed to Constantinople.”

Jerome makes this matter certain in letter 73 to Epiphanius, as do Theophilus of Alexandria himself in letters 69 and 72; and Jerome congratulates Theophilus on the successful completion of the affair in letters 70 and 71. In letter 61 to Pammachius, against the errors of John of Jerusalem, near its end, while discussing John’s letter, he says:

> “This Isidore, who is exalted to heaven by your praises, is accused at Alexandria of the very thing for which you accuse him at Jerusalem.”

Yet these four—Ammonius, Eusebius, Euthymius, and Isidore—occur in this book.

I reply that the portion in which we shall expose those Origenists on the authority of blessed Jerome is a very small part of these *Lives*. They may indeed have been infected with Origen’s error at a certain time and later have repented—especially since some of them appear in the Greek *Menaea* and have been praised by other holy men.

In fact, in the little book of Acacius, preserved by Photius, *Bibliotheca*, codex 159, presented against Chrysostom to the synod held at the Oak, I find the following article:

> “That blessed Epiphanius, because of the Origenists Ammonius, Euthymius—not properly rendered ‘Eutychius’ by Baronius, through Frederick Metius, from a corrupt manuscript, as appears—Eusebius, Heraclides, and Palladius, refused to communicate with Chrysostom.”

Jerome, in that letter to Ctesiphon, mentions Ammonius and Eusebius, whom he asserts to have been Origenists. Thus, just as we learn from that synod that they were not free from suspicion of Origenian error, so we are likewise taught that the suspicion was not entirely conclusive, since Chrysostom, a man unquestionably most learned and holy, communicated with them.

Nor did I say without authority that monks might first have been Origenists and afterward have repented. Hear Sozomen, book VIII, chapter 17:

> “Then Theophilus assembled there with the others; he said nothing about the books of Origen, but summoned the monks from Scetis to repentance, promising that he would neither remember the injury he had suffered nor do them any harm. When Theophilus’s supporters shouted at them, demanding that they ask forgiveness and pretending that the synod was pleading on their behalf, the monks were thrown into confusion and thought that this truly had to be done. With many bishops presiding, they said what it was customary for them to say, even when they had been wronged: ‘Forgive us.’ When Theophilus readily made peace with them and restored them to communion, the inquiry into the wrongs committed by the Scetians was dissolved. I think this would not have happened if Dioscorus and Ammonius had been present with the other monks. Dioscorus had already died and was buried in the church named after the martyr Mocius. Ammonius, however, when the synod was recently being prepared, became physically weak; after crossing over to the Oak, he was afflicted more severely by the disease, and not long afterward ended his life. The neighboring monks, among whom he lies, granted him a splendid burial. When Theophilus learned of this, he is said to have wept and said to everyone that among all the monks of his time there was no one like Ammonius, although Ammonius had also been the cause of trouble for him.”

[Note: [Col. 0055D] The translation is faulty, as is evident. For the Greek phrase, τοῦτο δὲ . . . ἔφασαν, Valesius translates it most correctly: “what they were accustomed to say, namely, ‘Even if they had been wronged, spare us,’ they said.” EDITOR.]

From this we learn that the affairs of these monks were altogether confused. Certainly George of Alexandria, in his *Life of Chrysostom*, says that Ammonius and Dioscorus died, were honorably buried, and became famous for miracles.

Whatever the case may be, let the testimony of Saint Jerome remain unshaken, and let us receive the sayings of these few men with greater caution in accordance with his warning. Yet nothing occurs in them that sounds objectionable, except perhaps one statement of Evagrius concerning apatheia, to which we have supplied an appropriate antidote in its proper place.

Our own Christophorus Castrius thought that this testimony from Jerome could be satisfactorily answered, and he wrote to me from Spain:

> “First, it must be stated that in the time of Theophilus of Alexandria and Epiphanius of Cyprus a question arose concerning the nature of God: whether God was spiritual or consisted of bodily members. For the simpler people, and especially the monks, believed that God was corporeal. Hence they were called the heretics known as Anthropomorphites. These men opposed Origen because he taught that God is spirit; the wiser, however, like all Catholics, proclaimed that God is spirit. Therefore, because the wiser men agreed with Origen on this point, those simple people hated them as Origenists for this one reason alone.

> “Hence it happened that Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, accused Saint Epiphanius—who was Catholic in all his opinions—of the heresy of the Anthropomorphites, as Socrates reports in book VI, chapter 9; Sozomen in book VIII, chapter 14; and Nicephorus in book XIII, chapter 12. John of Jerusalem likewise accused Epiphanius of this, as Jerome says in letter 61 to Pammachius against the errors of John of Jerusalem. Indeed, Rufinus brought the same charge of heresy against Jerome in book I of the *Invectives*.

> “Conversely, those who were more hostile to Origen accused those who devoted themselves to reading him—though otherwise Catholic—of Origen’s heresies. Thus Epiphanius accused Theophilus, and afterward Chrysostom, as well as the monks who communicated with them. Saint Jerome hints at this matter somewhat in letter 62 to Theophilus against John of Jerusalem, and also in letters 68 and 70 to Theophilus, when he says to him:
