> “‘You have shown that your silence until now was a matter of policy, not agreement; I speak freely to your Reverence. We were distressed that you were too patient, and, ignorant of the helm of leadership, we rejoiced in the destruction of the lost.’

> “Certainly he had given grounds for suspicion by agreeing with Origen and himself being an Origenist. Under this pretext of Origenism, and with the same pretense used against Chrysostom, he attacked the four monks of the Long Mountain of Nitria because they had withdrawn from him and did not approve his conduct. He even assembled an army of Anthropomorphites, among whom was a considerable phalanx of monks inflamed by zeal.

> “John Chrysostom, however, received and defended these fleeing men, after also notifying Pope Innocent I, who rebuked Theophilus. Theophilus, finally moved to repentance, reconciled those Long monks to himself as faithful and upright men. All the Greek historians recount this story at great length: George, archbishop of Alexandria, in his *Life of Saint Chrysostom*; Palladius in his dialogue; Socrates; Sozomen; Symeon Metaphrastes; the emperor Leo in a speech; Cassiodorus; Sulpicius; Isidore of Pelusium; and Nicephorus. There is not space to report their testimonies. All of them commended those monks whom Jerome, deceived by Theophilus, believed to be heretics.”

Thus far our Castrius. For the whole story, see Baronius, volume V, under the year 400.

[Col. 0057D] You will object third, against the authority of the fourth book, as the work of Cassian: In the decree, distinction 15, Cassian’s little works are counted among the apocrypha.

I reply with Aloysius Lipomanus, volume VIII of *The Lives of the Saints*, published at Rome in 1560, in the preface before the excerpts from Cassian:

> “They were prohibited chiefly because of the third conference of Abbot Chaeremon, concerning the protection of God. This may be gathered from blessed Prosper, in his little book against the *Collator*, where he censures this man for holding certain rash opinions concerning the grace of God and free will, contrary to the definitions of the holy Church, and adduces the passage already cited. John Trithemius also appears to hold this opinion.

> “For easier belief in this, one may appeal to the authority of distinguished men, remarkable both for learning and holiness, who read Cassian’s works fearlessly, brought them forward to confirm the authority of their own writings, and even entrusted them to their disciples for reading. Among these were Saint Benedict, Cassiodorus, Climacus, Bernard, blessed Dominic, Saint Thomas Aquinas, and others whom we have honored with eulogies.

> “Moreover, these *Lives of the Saints* do not debate ecclesiastical dogmas, but deal only with the conduct, way of life, and examples of the righteous. Therefore, in the part where he is good, he was admitted; in the part where he is bad—and that is the aforementioned conference concerning the protection of God—he was rejected. The holy mother Church appears to have acted similarly with the books of Origen. For after rejecting *Περὶ Ἀρχῶν* (*On First Principles*) and certain other works of his, we see and hear that the rest may be read without offense; and, what may surprise you even more, we do not hesitate to bring them forward against the madness of heretics.”

Thus Lipomanus.

A similar judgment in a similar matter was made long ago by Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria. Socrates, book VI, chapter 15, reports:

> “His hatred against him increased because he did not afterward refrain from studying the books of Origen. When someone asked him how he could again embrace books that he had condemned, he replied: ‘The books of Origen resemble a meadow filled with every kind of flower. Therefore, if I discover anything good in them, I pluck it; but if anything thorny appears to me, I pass over it as something that pricks.’”

Nor did Saint Jerome judge otherwise when writing to Tranquillus in letter 76:

> “Since you ask the opinion of my humble self, whether Origen should be wholly rejected, as brother Faustinus holds, or partly read, as some think, I judge that Origen should sometimes be read for the sake of his learning, just as Tertullian, Novatian, Arnobius, Apollinarius, and certain other ecclesiastical writers, both Greek and Latin, should be read: so that we may love what is good in them and avoid what is contrary, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: ‘Test everything; hold fast what is good’ (2 Thessalonians 5). But those who are led either into excessive love of him or into hatred through the perversity of their own temperament seem to me subject to the prophetic curse: ‘Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter’ (Isaiah 5). His erroneous doctrines should not be accepted because of his teaching; nor, because of the error of his doctrines, should those who have produced useful commentaries on the Holy Scriptures be entirely rejected.”

At the end he adds:

> “But if his admirers and detractors draw the rope of contention between them, desiring nothing in the middle and observing no measure, but either approving or rejecting everything, I shall more willingly choose pious rusticity than learned blasphemy.”

You will object fourth, against the authority of the eighth book, as the work of Palladius: This Palladius was an Origenist.

Aloysius Lipomanus replies in volume III of *The Lives of the Saints*:

> “Whether he was an Origenist or not has little bearing on the purpose for which this book was written. For it does not present doctrines of faith, but describes the lives of the saints; and, as blessed Pope Gelasius says of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, who was himself also a supporter of Origen, ‘Because of his singular knowledge of matters relevant to instruction, he does not seem to be rejectable’—especially since, as far as the weakness of our intellect has been able to see, nothing is read here that does not breathe piety and Christian purity. We therefore approve the work, but leave the author to God’s judgment, before whom he stands. For to assert doubtful matters as certain seems to us exceedingly rash.”

Thus Aloysius.

You will object fifth, with the same Aloysius, above, against the same book: There is another matter in this work that causes us greater concern. Saint Jerome, whose authority in the Church is as great as we all know, in his letter to Ctesiphon, while reproaching Evagrius Ponticus—indeed, Rufinus, as I showed in Prolegomenon 4, § 10—of Hyperborean origin, who wrote a book apparently about monks, charges him with listing many men who never existed and whom he says were Origenists and condemned by the bishops. To indicate more clearly who they were, he adds:

> “Namely, Ammonius, Eusebius, Euthymius, Evagrius himself, Or, and Isidore, and many others whom it is tedious to enumerate.”

Yet these six whom we have mentioned also appear in this work of Palladius, and their lives are found carefully described in it. What, then, shall we say? Shall we accept men who are asserted to have been condemned for heresy by so great a Father?

The same Aloysius replies:

> “Certainly, most candid reader, we are at a loss here. Although we can answer that it was only the book of Evagrius—indeed, of Rufinus, as I have already said—and not Palladius’s book, that was condemned by Saint Jerome. Or perhaps those mentioned by Evagrius and Palladius are not the same men at all, but entirely different persons. For it happened—as Saint Jerome himself and Gennadius also testify in *On Illustrious Men*—that many holy Fathers, as well as monks and anchorites, bore the same name, as can be seen in the many Macariuses, Pauls, Johns, Isidores, and Evagriuses.

> “But if this answer does not satisfy you, nothing remains for us to say except that, setting aside these six, you should not hesitate to read the others. Far be it from us, who have labored throughout our lives against heretics, to wish now to introduce heretical men into the Church.

> “Yet if some of the six men mentioned above were disciples of Saint Antony, if some were pupils of Saint Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus, if all were endowed with the highest integrity of life and distinguished by divine gifts, if they were renowned for miracles and brought their lives to an excellent end, we can scarcely be persuaded that these are the men whom Saint Jerome asserts were condemned by the Fathers for heresy, rather than entirely different persons.”

To speak frankly of what I think: after I saw this book of Palladius to Lausus so highly commended by John Damascene, a man equally most holy and most learned and a pillar of the Church, in that golden sermon entitled *That the Dead Are Helped by the Benefits of the Living*, I read the whole work two or three times without any scruple of conscience. By that reading I was not only wonderfully delighted but also wholly inflamed with an ardent desire for heavenly things. You, however, should follow whatever seems more probable and safer for you.

Thus far the most learned and serious Aloysius, who presided at the Council of Trent with two other colleagues—as he himself states in the dedicatory letter of the second volume, printed at Venice in 1553, of *The Lives of the Saints*, addressed to Pope Julius III.

You will object sixth, against all the *Lives* in general: Pope Adrian I’s letter to King Charles, in which he refutes those attacking the Second Council of Nicaea, cites the following argument of the opponents in chapter 17, in action 5:

> “Those books, the *Lives of the Fathers*, whose authors are unknown, are not entirely suitable for providing testimony or confirming the matters under dispute.”

Pope Adrian replies:

> “The *Lives of the Fathers* are by no means read in the Church without credible authors. For works entitled and received by orthodox men are both accepted and read. Indeed, the sacred canons have judged the sufferings of the holy martyrs to be more suitable, so that they may also be read in church when their anniversaries are celebrated.”

It is one thing, then, for a work to be so authentic that it is read in the Church, and another for it to be accepted and read by Catholics. Yet the pontiff is perhaps speaking there less of these *Lives of the Hermit Fathers* than of the *Lives* of all the other Fathers, which, without the name of an approved author, were not easily admitted into the Church’s readings.

You will object seventh: Melchior Canus, in book II, chapter 6, *On Theological Places*, a particularly severe critic of books, uses the testimony of Gelasius to silence the insolence of those who have spread the claim that blessed Jerome was the author of these works—works that no one but an uncultivated and inarticulate writer would produce.

I reply: We do not attribute all these *Lives* to blessed Jerome; nor do we deny that most of them are woven in a rougher style, if the many works of Stridon are examined. If Canus intended more than this, the authority of Saint Benedict, Cassiodorus, Gregory of Tours, and others carries greater weight for us.

You will object eighth: Galenus Westcapellius, in *Catechesis* 215, calls the book entitled—he does not know by what grammatical rule—*The Lives of the Fathers*, a forged work.

I reply: Galenus does not mean that this book is fictitious in such a way that it is wholly fabricated; he calls it so only with respect to Saint Jerome, whose name it bears, although it is not his work and is marketed under his fictitious and borrowed name. As for the grammar by which it is called *The Lives of the Fathers*, see Prolegomenon 1.

## PROLEGOMENON XVI. What is the usefulness of these books?

[Col. 0061A]

From these fountains Benedict, Cassiodorus, Martin of Dumio, Dominic, and other leaders of religious communities watered their little gardens. But noteworthy is what Saint Augustine recounts concerning the arrival of Antony’s *Life* in the West, when two agents of public affairs, leaving their betrothed women, chose the solitary life. It will not be useless to read the account here:

> “The conversation turned, as Potitianus himself related it, to Antony, the Egyptian monk, whose name shone with exceptional renown among your servants, though until that hour it had been unknown to us. When he discovered this, he lingered over the subject, making so great a man known to those who did not know him and expressing wonder at our ignorance. We were astonished as we listened to things so recent in memory and so clearly attested, almost in our own time, concerning your miracles in the true and Catholic faith. We were all amazed: we, because these things were so great; he, because they were unknown to us.

> “From there his conversation turned to the communities of monasteries, to the fragrance of your ways, and to the breasts of the desert wilderness, of which we knew nothing. There was also a monastery in Milan, full of good brothers, outside the city walls, nourished under Ambrose as their father; yet we did not know it. He continued speaking, and we listened attentively in silence.

> “Then it happened that he said—I do not know when—that he and three other companions, while the emperor was occupied at Trier with the afternoon circus games, had gone out for a walk in gardens adjoining the walls. There, as they happened to walk in pairs, he and one companion went off separately, while the other two likewise went off separately. Those two wanderers entered a hut where certain servants of yours lived, poor in spirit, ‘for theirs is the kingdom of heaven’ (Matthew 5), and found there a codex in which the *Life of Saint Antony* had been written.

> “One of them began to read it, to marvel, and to be inflamed; while reading, he began to reflect on embracing such a life and, abandoning secular service, serving you. He was one of those called agents of public affairs.

> “Then, suddenly filled with holy love and anger at himself with sober shame, he cast his eyes upon his friend and said to him: ‘Tell me, I beg you: To what do we hope to come through all these labors of ours? What are we seeking? For what purpose do we serve in the army? Can our hope at court be anything greater than becoming friends of the emperor? And even there, what is not fragile and full of dangers? Through how many dangers does one arrive at a greater danger? And how long will this last? If I wish, behold, I now become a friend of God.’

> “He said this, and swollen with the travail of a new life, he returned his eyes to the pages. He read, and he was changed inwardly, where you saw it; his mind was stripped of the world, as soon became evident. For while he read and wrestled with the tumult of his heart, he sometimes groaned, discerned, and resolved upon better things. At last, yours already, he said to his friend: ‘I have now broken away from that hope of ours, and have determined to serve God. From this hour, in this place, I begin. If you are unwilling to imitate me, do not oppose me.’

> “The other replied that he would remain with his companion in so great a reward and so great a service. And now both of them were building your tower, at the cost of abandoning all their possessions and following you.

> “Then Potitianus and those who had been walking with him through other parts of the garden, looking for them, came to the same place. When they found them, they urged them to return, because the day was declining. But after the two had explained their decision and purpose, and how such a will had arisen and become firm in them, they asked the others not to trouble them if they refused to join them.

> “The others, however, unchanged from their former ways, nevertheless—as he said—wept, piously congratulated them, commended themselves to their prayers, and, dragging their hearts along the ground, went away to the palace. The others, fixing their hearts upon heaven, remained in the hut. Both of them had betrothed women. When these women later heard what had happened, they too dedicated their virginity to you.”

Potitianus related this account (*Saint Augustine, Confessions*, book VIII, chapter 6).

This reading benefited the agents of public affairs; likewise, Augustine’s repeated narration of it stimulated his own mind toward better things. He adds:

> “But you, Lord, amid his words, were turning me back upon myself, taking me from behind my own back, where I had placed myself because I did not wish to look at myself, and setting me before my own face so that I might see how ugly I was, how distorted and filthy, stained and ulcerous. I saw and was horrified, and there was nowhere for me to flee from myself. If I tried to turn my gaze away from myself, he continued telling what he was telling, and you again set me before myself and thrust me into my own eyes, so that I might discover my iniquity and hate it. I knew it, but I pretended not to, I closed my eyes, and I forgot it. Then, the more ardently I loved those about whom I heard such wholesome resolutions—that they had given themselves entirely to you to be healed—the more hateful I found myself in comparison with them.” (*Saint Augustine, Confessions*, book VIII, chapter 27.)

But Antony’s *Life* had already become known in the city through Athanasius’s fortunate arrival at Rome. While Antony was still alive, Athanasius made his acquaintance and his splendid sayings and deeds known to the Romans. Women of the highest Roman nobility also began to pursue this way of life, adapted to every element of evangelical perfection. Saint Jerome records the following about them:

> “At that time no woman of noble birth in Rome knew the purpose of the monks; nor, because of the novelty of the matter, did anyone dare to assume among the people a name that was then considered disgraceful and contemptible. Marcella learned from the Alexandrian priests, first from Pope Athanasius and afterward from Peter—who, fleeing the persecution of the Arian heresy, had taken refuge in Rome as though at the safest harbor of their communion—the life of blessed Antony, who was still living at that time, as well as the discipline of Pachomius’s monasteries in the Thebaid and of virgins and widows. She was not ashamed to profess what she had learned was pleasing to Christ.” (Jerome, *To Principia*, letter 16.)

These were the fortunate shoots of the West, propagated even from a single seed brought from the East. Fulgentius, likewise living in the South, read the *Lives of the Fathers* and was inflamed to imitate them, as is recorded in chapter 12 of his *Life*:

> “Blessed Fulgentius, reading the admirable lives of the Egyptian monks and set aflame by spiritual meditation upon their instructions and conferences, resolved to seek those lands by ship, for two reasons: either to lay aside the name of abbot there and live humbly under a rule, or to submit himself to the laws of stricter abstinence.”

Moschus, too, living in the East, reports that a certain old man who had lived near the regions of the Jordan, after reading the example of an old man’s patience—found in Pelagius, little book XVI, no. 13—of one who pursued robbers and even offered them the purse they had failed to take, was moved to imitate the same deed. He adds:

> “That old man took particular delight in this reading of the *Lives of the Fathers*, so that it was always on his lips and in his heart; and from it he acquired the greatest fruit of virtue.” (Mochus, chapter 212.)

Indeed, all Spain long ago valued this book so highly that, when the Latin language was already dying out in those regions, it arranged for the book to be translated into Arabic along with the sacred Scriptures, clearly understanding how great a benefit would flow from it to stimulate souls toward every form of piety. Archbishop Heleca of Zaragoza testifies to this around the year 860, in his additions to the chronicles of Dexter and Maximus:

> “The sacred Scriptures translated into Arabic are held by Catholic priests and circulate with scholia; especially the New Testament, the Letters of Paul, the Apocalypse of Saint John, and the book *The Lives of the Fathers*; also the Latin history of Flavius Lucius Dexter, Marcus Maximus, and others; the *Chronicle* of Eusebius; and the books of Saint Augustine *On the City of God*, because the Latin language was already disappearing.”

More could be brought forward to affirm the merit and usefulness of these books. But for those whom these things do not satisfy, what then?

## PROLEGOMENON XVII. On the various Latin editions of these books

Here we are not discussing the eighth, ninth, and tenth books, which are now added to the *Lives of the Fathers* only in this edition, but the remaining books, nearly all of which have found a place in the commonly circulated *Lives of the Fathers*.

Here is a list of the editions that I have been able to obtain.

The first edition, in folio, without the title of the book, the printer’s name, or the place and year of publication, printed in very crude type; it begins: “The preface begins.”

The second, in folio, without the title of the book, the printer’s name, or the place and year of publication; it begins: “The prologue begins.”

The third, in folio, without the title of the book, the printer’s name, or the place and year of publication; it begins: “A prologue to the fruitful…”

The fourth, the Nuremberg edition, in very large folio, printed by Anton Koberger in 1478.

The fifth, the Nuremberg edition, in smaller folio, printed by Anton Koberger in 1483.

[LVIII] The sixth, apparently German, in folio, with the place and printer uncertain, published in 1483.

The seventh, the Venetian edition, in quarto, printed by Octavianus Scotus of Monza in 1483.

The eighth, apparently German, in folio, with the place and printer uncertain, published in 1485.

The ninth, the Lyons edition, in quarto, printed by Nicolaus Wolff of Lutrea and sold by Jacob Huguetan in 1502.

The tenth, the Lyons edition, in quarto, printed by Jannot de Campis in 1507.

The eleventh, the Venetian edition, in quarto, printed by Bonetus Locatellus in 1508.

The twelfth, the Lyons edition, in quarto, printed by Stephanus Balam in 1509.

The thirteenth, the Lyons edition, in quarto, printed by Jacob Sachon in 1512.

The fourteenth, the Venetian edition, in quarto, printed by Nicolaus of Frankfurt in 1512.

The fifteenth, the Lyons edition, in quarto, printed by Jacob Miit in 1515.

The sixteenth, the Lyons edition, in the same format, printed by Jacob Mareschal in 1520.

The seventeenth, the Lyons edition, in the same format, printed by Antonius Vincentius in 1537.

The eighteenth, the Cologne edition, in folio, printed by Gaspar Gennepaeus in 1547.

The nineteenth, the Cologne edition, in folio, printed by the same man in 1548—unless it is the same as the preceding edition, with only the title and year changed, as I shall indicate in Prolegomenon 20.

The twentieth, the Complutensian edition, in quarto, printed by Juan Gracian in 1596.

[Col. 0064C] Among these editions I find three kinds of variation. I shall set them out before the reader in distinct prolegomena, so that it may be clear what each editor contributed in preparing his own work, and so that no one may be confused when he finds these *Lives* cited differently in different editions.

## PROLEGOMENON XVIII. On the first Latin edition of all, as far as I know

[LIX] The first edition of all, as far as I know, is in folio, without the title of the book, without the printer’s name, and without the place and year of publication; its type is plainly crude. All these features indicate that the book was printed at the very beginning of the printing art, when such preliminary information was generally omitted and more elegant type had not yet come into use.

[Col. 0064D] The book begins as follows:

> “The preface of blessed Jerome the presbyter to the first book on the life of the holy Fathers begins.”

Then:

> “Blessed be God,” etc.

The entire book ends with the monk Marinus. Its beginning is:

> “There was a certain secular man…”

and its ending:

> “Until now Christ has performed many miracles through the prayers of the holy Virgin, to the praise and glory of his name, who with the Father…” etc.

This edition consists entirely of five books.

The first book begins with a prologue—attributed to blessed Jerome, as is the whole book—beginning:

> “Blessed be God,” etc.

It then proceeds to the *Life of Saint John the Abbot*:

> “Therefore, as a true foundation…”

This book ends with the seven dangers of the journey. The chapter begins:

> “In many other places as well…”

and concludes:

> “Who delivered us from such great dangers and displayed such great wonders in us; to him be glory forever and ever. Amen.”

The second book begins with a prologue: “Who could doubt that the world stands by the merits of the saints?” etc. Then follows the first saying: “A certain elder of the holy Fathers, when monks asked him about the reason for abstinence,” etc. It ends with Syncletica’s saying concerning illness: “Because from it health increases in our inner man.”

The third book begins with a prologue by Palladius the bishop: “Many things, both diverse and numerous, have been written at different times by different persons,” etc. Then follows the first chapter: “When I first traveled to Alexandria,” etc.; the second chapter: “Now blessed Isidore,” etc. It ends with the saying of Abba Sisoes: “Forgive me, brother, for I have not yet become a monk” [Col. 0065B]. Immediately afterward is appended a certain account of Saint Macarius, concerning the demon who knocked at night at the door of his cell. It begins: “It has been confirmed to us about him by those who heard from his mouth,” etc. It ends: “And neither the unworthiness nor the merits of those approaching the altar would remain hidden from him.”

The fourth book begins as follows:

> The outline of the fourth book of the words and examples of the holy Fathers, the hermits, begins. Pelagius, deacon of the Holy Roman Church, translated its beginning, while John the subdeacon translated its conclusion from Greek into Latin, for the instruction of monastic life.

Then follows:

> [LX] Since every preface, appropriately preceding the text, etc.,

where it is said that this book is divided into nineteen parts. The first part is *On the Progress of the Monk*. It begins: “A certain brother, wishing to attain progress in the monastic way of life” [Col. 0065C]. The nineteenth and final part is *Examples of Monastic Conduct*. It begins: “Two Fathers asked God.” It ends: “So will it also be with the soul.” The following is added: “The fourth book of the *Lives of the Fathers* ends here.” Immediately afterward comes:

> These are the seven words that Abba Moses sent to Abba Pastor, in which the consummate virtue and perfection of a monk are contained.

The first is:

> A man ought to be as though dead.

The seventh is:

> Again the brother asks him, saying: “Behold, a man is beating his servant.”

It ends:

> For a short time there is labor, and forever there is rest.

The fifth book begins:

> The prologue to the fifth book of the *Lives of the Fathers* begins.

The beginning of the prologue is:

> Although from the beginning of our composition—

Then:

> The fifth book begins, concerning the conduct and instruction of the holy Fathers [Col. 0065D].

The beginning of the text is:

> A certain elder, recounting the benefits shown to us through the humanity of Christ—

The text ends:

> But he recognized that the judgments of God are just.

Immediately afterward comes *On Saint Marinus the Monk*, beginning:

> There was a certain layman.

It ends:

> Where, even to this day, Christ performs many miracles through the prayers of the holy Virgin, to the praise and glory of his name, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

And, to investigate something concerning the date of this edition, I think I can affirm with certainty that this book was published at least before the year 1471. For Dionysius the Carthusian, in *On the Four Last Things*, article 52, recounts the story of Macarius concerning the discovery of the skull of a pagan priest [Col. 0066A], and cites it from Book IV of the *Lives of the Fathers*, where it is found in this first edition. He himself died that very year, according to Trithemius in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*. Indeed, it can be inferred from the manuscript of the monastery of Sion at Courtrai that this edition was prepared even before the year 1469. That book agrees word for word with the printed one, so that it is evident that it was copied from it. At the end of its manuscript, however, it says:

> “Completed in the house of the sisters of blessed Catherine of Mount Sinai, commonly called Sion, at Courtrai, in the year of the Lord 1469, on 17 November, the feast itself of blessed Ninian, bishop and confessor.”

This first edition, in the form and order in which I have described it, was printed three times. The catalogue of editions already given above in Prolegomenon 17 lists all three editions first [Col. 0066B]. The two later editions, however, added and inserted chapter summaries, which are lacking in this first of the three editions.

## PROLEGOMENON XIX. On the second Latin edition, which differs from the first

[LXI] The second edition—whether it was literally the second I do not know, but certainly the one that differs from the first—is the Nuremberg edition of 1478, which has the following statement at the end:

> “In the year of Christ’s nativity 1478, and on the Nones of May, for the advancement of the blessed Fathers who live the life of hermits, the deeds of whom are deservedly to be commended to memory, this distinguished work, called the *Lives of the Fathers*, excerpted from very many manuscripts, adorned by men highly skilled in the sacred Scriptures, has been successfully completed in the town of Nuremberg by Antonius Coburger, an inhabitant of the aforesaid town, and elegantly printed.”

No inscription or title is prefixed to this edition either. Instead, it begins with a preface in which the man who first altered the order of the first edition explains his action. He says:

> “So that none of the readers or hearers may suffer offense because of the style observed in this work, since it does not proceed in every respect as he may previously have seen in copies of this material, he will readily grant pardon once he observes the confused diversity of the many copies.
>
> “For that reason I divided and arranged the work itself into four distinct parts. In the first I gathered historical material into one collection. In the second, little books and doctrinal material [Col. 0066D]. In the third, material concerning regular observance. In the final part, material concerning praise and the efficacy of the virtues. Thus the first part is distinguished by histories, the second by little books and sections (§), the third by rubrics, and the fourth by the chapters of the rubrics.
>
> “And so that the table might provide clearer information about it, I numbered the folios consecutively, adding only four letters, assigning them to the four columns of the folios. Thus, if it is a capital letter, one should look for the reference in the first half of the column; but if it is an ordinary or smaller letter, in the second half.
>
> “It has been sufficient to place these remarks at the beginning of the present work for a general understanding of it. May that wisdom which is the artificer of all things, uncreated and blessed forever and ever, advance me toward its completion” [Col. 0067A]. Amen.”

What the author of this preface says here about his table cannot be understood unless the edition itself is examined. From that table I see that all later editions, although they retain the same order of the book, differ from it.

This editor preserves the following arrangement in his table:

First, after the item that is expressed in alphabetical order in the table, he indicates the folio number with numerical letters.

Second, he uses four large or capital letters—which in the preface he calls *versales*, perhaps because the beginning of a verse is usually written with them?—A, B, C, D, and four lower-case letters, a, b, c, d. He places these after the folio number in the table according to the four columns [Col. 0067B] of which each folio consists. The capital letters serve the first half of each column: A for the first column, B for the second, C for the third, and D for the fourth. The lower-case letters a, b, c, d serve the second half of each column in the same manner, as has already been said concerning the capitals.

These details had to be stated both so that no one could accuse me of having represented the first variation less accurately, and because later editions of this kind either omit this preface—as do the editions of uncertain place printed in 1483 and 1485, which do not use the four capital and lower-case letters in the table, but attach the letters of the entire alphabet after the folio numbers and also print them in the text—or at least abridge the preface, as do the Venetian edition of 1508 and the Lyon edition of 1536 [Col. 0067C]. These omit the words beginning “adding only” and continuing through “it has been sufficient to place these remarks at the beginning,” and arrange their table by folios alone, without any added letters. The remaining editions subsequently retained this practice.

As already stated, this edition consists of four parts.

The first part begins:

> The prologue of Saint Jerome, cardinal priest, to the books of the *Lives of the Holy Fathers of Egypt* begins; also of those who lived in Scythia, the Thebaid, and Mesopotamia—not only those whom he saw with his own eyes and examined with the greatest labor, but also many whom he recorded with notable diligence as reported by trustworthy persons. Finally, he faithfully translated from Greek into Latin the little books of other authoritative writers, and inserted into this work, for the sake of its completeness, works translated by others.

Then follows:

> “Blessed be God,” etc.

Soon afterward:

> “Therefore, first of all, as a true foundation,” etc.,

as above in the first edition, and it ends in the same manner.

This edition, however, additionally contains the following in its first part:

* Life of Saint Paul the First Hermit.
* Life of Saint Antony.
* Life of Saint Hilarion.
* Life of Malchus the Captive.
* Life of Saint Paul the Simple.
* Life of Saint Paula.
* Life of Saint Pelagia.
* Life of Blessed Mary of Egypt.
* Life of Saint Marina the Virgin.
* Life of Saint Euphrosyne.
* Life of Saint Frontonius the Abbot.
* Life of Saint Simeon the Hermit, who stood upon a pillar [Col. 0067].
* Life of Saint Eupraxia the Virgin.
* Life of the Servant of God, Macarius the Roman.
* Life of Saint Posthumius.
* Life of Saint Onuphrius the Hermit [Col. 0068].
* Life of Blessed Abraham the Hermit.
* Life of Blessed Pachomius the Abbot.
* On Christian the Monk.
* Life of Saint John the Almsgiver.
* Life of Saint Eugenia the Virgin.
* Life of Saint Basil the Bishop.
* Life of Saint Ephraem the Father.

Thus the first part comes to an end.

[LXIII] The second part begins with the register of the second book of the holy Fathers. This register is absent from all the other editions at this point, except the Venetian edition of 1508. In the Lyon edition of 1536 it is placed at the beginning of the entire book, after the general index; in the Complutensian edition of 1596, at the end of the entire book, after the general index [Col. 0068B].

Then follows the prologue:

> “Who could doubt that the world stands by the merits of the saints?” etc.

Immediately afterward:

> The exhortations of the holy Fathers and the progress of the monks begin, together with the other following little books, which Saint Jerome, cardinal priest, translated from Greek into Latin.

The Lyon edition has “professions” (*professiones*) instead of “progress” (*profectiones*).

Then follows the first section:

> “A certain elder of the holy Fathers, when monks asked him about the reason for abstinence,” etc.

There follow 207 paragraphs. Then various little books are appended, twenty in number. In the first edition these are called nineteen parts, since one is absent there; here it is the sixteenth, *On Penance*. The first edition, however, has it combined with the seventh little book, *On Patience*, just as this sixteenth book is entitled in the Paris edition [Col. 0068C].

Afterward comes:

> The seven chapters begin which Abba Moses sent to Abba Pimen, and whoever keeps them will be delivered from punishment, etc.,

as in the first edition. But after the seventh, thirty-two sayings of various Fathers follow here, ending in the paragraph or number that begins:

> “There was a certain monk in a coenobium, already an old man of proven virtue.”

It ends:

> “who protects all who serve him in sincerity and truth.”

The third part begins as follows:

> The third part of the book *Lives of the Fathers* begins, namely, concerning the rule or conduct of the Egyptian monks and of those who dwell in Palestine or Mesopotamia.

The prologue is:

> “Often and repeatedly, brothers, you have asked me” [Col. 0068D].

The first chapter is:

> “Three years ago.”

This part consists of fifty-five chapters. The last is:

> “At a certain time, two philosophers, having heard the fame of blessed Antony,” etc.

The fourth part begins in this way:

> The prologue of Saint Paschasius begins, for the exhortation of the holy Fathers, both Greek and Egyptian.

The beginning of the prologue is:

> “To the venerable Lord Father Martin, priest and abbot.”

Then the title of the beginning of the text:

> The book of exhortations begins, first against *gastrimargia*, that is, to avoid the desire of gluttony.

The beginning of the text is:

> “A certain brother, concerning how he ought to live in his own cell.”

This entire part consists of forty-six titles, the last of which is [Col. 0069A]:

> On the meditations of the anchorites.

Immediately afterward is appended the little work *On the Praise and Effect of the Virtues*.

All the subsequent editions—those which I listed above in Prolegomenon 17—followed this edition, or its order, almost word for word, except the Cologne edition, which I shall discuss shortly.

[LXIIII] All the Lyon editions, indeed, place first the dedicatory letter of Celsus Hugo Dissutus, doctor of both laws and canon of Chalon-sur-Saône. In it he explains to the most reverend Father in Christ and lord, Lord John de Ponpet, a most distinguished doctor of laws, bishop of Chalon-sur-Saône, commendatory abbot and perpetual administrator of the monastery of Saint Peter near the walls of Chalon-sur-Saône, the value of his work in preparing this volume:

> “It was so full of errors,” he says, “that scarcely anyone could find in it the traces of the ancient books. For in place of certain words, other and different words had been inserted, perverting the meaning of the holy Jerome. Nor were syllables lacking in place of others, or elements omitted through the carelessness of printers or the inertia of correctors, with the result that the force and meaning of the words were altered. At last, however, this work has been cleansed of such errors, after a copy older than the oldest was consulted.”

I leave it to the reader to judge his effort [Col. 0069B].

## PROLEGOMENON XX. On the third Latin edition, which differs from both earlier editions

The third edition, which differs from the others, is the Cologne edition of 1547. It first appeared under the following title:

> *The Prototype of the Ancient Church*, containing the lives, deeds, and sayings of the holy friends of God of both sexes, authored or compiled partly by Saint Jerome and partly by various others, at Cologne, through Gaspar Gennepaeus [Col. 0069C].

This edition was prepared by Brother Theodoric Loher of Strass, prior of the Carthusian house of Maria in Buxheim and provincial visitor. He dedicated it to the most reverend and illustrious prince Otto, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and bishop of Augsburg. In his dedicatory letter, written at Regensburg in 1546, he informs him of the work he had undertaken in revising this book:

> “I have to some extent revised the *Lives of the Fathers* from eight or ten ancient and trustworthy manuscript copies collated together, with no small labor, and I believe that I have restored it to the integrity in which it was undoubtedly written by Jerome, Athanasius, Leontius, Amphilochius, Antherus, Nicephorus, Evagrius, Petronius, Eutropius, Heraclides, and other holy Fathers of that kind [Col. 0069D].
>
> “Next, insofar as possible, I arranged it in a definite order according to the sequence and reckoning of time, so that the reader might immediately recognize at what time each of the Fathers, through the grace of God, shone in this world—or rather, at what time the grace of God shone in each of them. I established the sequence of this narrative not only concerning men but also concerning distinguished and holy women.”

This same edition was printed a second time, in the same place, by the same printer and in the same type, in 1548 [Col. 0070A], the year following the first, under this title:

> *The Lives of the Holy Fathers*, containing the notable and marvelous sayings and deeds of certain eminent friends of God of both sexes, of the ancient Catholic and Apostolic Church, authored partly by the holy Jerome and partly by various others whom you will be able to learn from the page turned over. Received and approved by the Catholic Church more than 1,050 years ago [LXV].

A new dedicatory letter was prefixed to this edition. He wrote it at Augsburg on 21 January 1548 to the most reverend Father in Christ and lord, Lord Henry, abbot of the distinguished Benedictine monastery at Wiblingen in the diocese of Constance. In it he gives the following account of the work he had performed [Col. 0070B]:

> “We have now cleansed the *Lives of the Fathers* of more than a thousand errors that were scattered throughout it, using copies that were both extremely ancient and diverse. For many things have been restored, most have been added, some have been removed, and finally everything has been examined so exactly that this great treasure, not merely renewed but almost reborn—though not without serious labor—may rightly be welcomed by all devout people. We have also added a certain new order and a new index that will always endure. We spared no labor so that this distinguished work might emerge more purged and polished than ever before.”

I cannot affirm whether this second Cologne edition is entirely new or whether only its title was changed because the name *Prototype* was less well known [Col. 0070C]. Certainly the leaves and type of the second edition correspond exactly with those of the first. Only the paraphrase of Cassian and Climacus, which had been appended at the end of the first edition, has been omitted here; in its place is substituted the *Life of Barlaam and Josaphat*.

Whatever the case may be, I do not doubt that the excellent man expended much labor in correcting the ancient copies.

This edition consists of five books, as does the first edition, but with the order greatly altered and with certain materials added from the second edition and from elsewhere.

The first book consists of three parts. The first concerns holy men; the second, holy women. Both parts are mixed and combined from Book I of Rufinus—which is Book II in our edition [Col. 0070D]—and from other Lives appended after Rufinus’s first book in the second edition. In addition, it inserts the *Life of Epictetus and Astion*, and the Lives of Fabiola and Marcella. The third part contains excerpts from Sulpicius Severus and John Cassian.

The second book contains the Lives, sayings, teachings, and exhortations of the holy Fathers. It is Rufinus’s third book in our edition.

The third book is Palladius’s, taken from the ancient translation, as the first edition has it.

The fourth book is the one translated from Greek by Pelagius, deacon of the Holy Roman Church, and John, subdeacon of the same Church.

[LXVI] The fifth book consists of shorter sayings, as does the fifth book of the first edition [Col. 0071A]. The book of Abbot Paschasius is appended to it, followed by the *Life of Barlaam the Hermit and Josaphat*.

## PROLEGOMENON XXI. On this fourth Latin edition, which partly agrees and partly disagrees with the three preceding editions

After all the editions already listed—which, although I have examined as many as nineteen or twenty on account of their typographical variations, can nevertheless be referred to three kinds, as I noted above—this fourth edition now follows. It is both enlarged by several books and more accurately corrected, with the authors’ style restored according to manuscript copies. It consists chiefly of ten books.

The first book contains various Lives of the Fathers, both men [Col. 0071B] and women, who practiced the ascetic life and whose authors composed their accounts at considerable length. There are sixteen Lives of men:

* Saint Paul the First Hermit.
* Saint Antony the Abbot.
* Saint Hilarion the Monk.
* Saint Malchus, the captive monk.
* Saint Onuphrius the Hermit.
* Saint Pachomius, abbot of Tabennisi.
* Saint Abraham the Hermit [Col. 0071C].
* Saint Basil, archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia.
* Saint Ephraem the Syrian, deacon of Edessa.
* Saint Simeon Stylites.
* Saint John the Almsgiver.
* Saints Epictetus the priest and Astion the monk.
* Saint Macarius the Roman, servant of God, who was found near Paradise.
* Blessed Posthumius, father of five thousand monks.
* Saint Frontonius the Abbot [Col. 0071C].
* Saints Barlaam and Josaphat.

There are eleven Lives of women:

* Saint Eugenia, virgin and martyr.
* Saint Euphrasia, virgin.
* Saint Euphrosyne, virgin.
* Saint Mary the harlot, niece of Abraham the Hermit.
* Saint Thais, the harlot.
* Saint Pelagia, the harlot.
* Saint Mary of Egypt, the harlot.
* Saint Marina, virgin.
* Blessed Fabiola.
* Saint Paula of Rome, widow.
* Saint Marcella, widow.

More Lives of persons of either sex who practiced the same way of life could have been added [Col. 0071D]. But the book would have grown too large, and I would have departed from my purpose, which was to review the popular Lives of the Fathers that were once circulated in the hands of many people and restore them to their former purity.

I dedicated this first book chiefly to the holy priest Jerome, both because Jerome played the principal role in it—he alone composed more Lives of both men and women than anyone else—and so that I might depart as little as possible from the long-standing opinion that had occupied the minds even of many ancient writers, according to which Saint Jerome was believed to be the author of the *Lives of the Fathers* [LXVII]. I therefore included in this first book nearly everything that Jerome produced in this genre.

Nevertheless, so that the title might not deceive anyone, I did not dedicate it to Jerome alone, but also to the various others whose names each Life bears, insofar as we have been able to investigate their authors. Anonymous Lives should remain in the place in which the Fathers of old judged them to belong—those who both read them and drew examples of virtue from them—even though they forbade them to be included among the readings received in the Church [Col. 0072A].

The second book contains the Lives of the Fathers presented in a more concise style. It recognizes Rufinus of Aquileia as its author or translator and is completed in thirty-three chapters.

The third book contains not so much Lives as the sayings of the elders, with the same Rufinus as author or translator. It consists of 220 paragraphs or numbered sections [Col. 0072B].

The fourth book, compiled and arranged from Sulpicius Severus and John Cassian—specifically from the Dialogues of the former and the Institutions and Conferences of the latter—contains various examples and admonitions of the Fathers. It consists of fifty-five chapters.

The fifth book, whose Greek author is uncertain but whose translator is certainly Pelagius, deacon of the Holy Roman Church, contains the sayings of the elders, arranged in eighteen little books:

1. *On the Progress of the Fathers*, consisting of twenty-three paragraphs or numbered sections.
2. *On Quiet*, sixteen sections.
3. *On Compunction*, twenty-seven sections.
4. *On Continence*, seventy sections.
5. *On Fornication*, forty-one sections.
6. *On the Fact that a Monk Ought to Possess Nothing*, twenty-two sections [Col. 0072C].
7. *On Patience or Fortitude*, forty-seven sections.
8. *On the Fact that Nothing Should Be Done for Show*, twenty-four sections.
9. *On the Fact that No One Ought to Be Judged*, twelve sections.
10. *On Discernment*, 115 sections.
11. *On the Fact that One Ought to Live Soberly*, fifty-four sections.
12. *On the Fact that One Ought to Pray Without Ceasing and Soberly*, fifteen sections.
13. *On the Fact that One Ought to Be Hospitable and Merciful with Cheerfulness*, fifteen sections.
14. *On Obedience*, nineteen sections.
15. *On Humility*, eighty-nine sections [LXVIII].
16. *On Patience*, nineteen sections.
17. *On Charity*, twenty-five sections.
18. *On Foresight or Contemplation*, twenty sections [Col. 0072D].

The sixth book, whose Greek author is likewise uncertain but whose translator is certainly John, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, also presents the sayings of the elders in four little books:

1. *On Foresight or Contemplation*, which is part of the final little book of the preceding volume. It consists of seventeen sections.
2. *On Holy Elders Who Performed Miracles*, seventeen sections.
3. *On the Excellent Conduct of Various Saints*, eighteen sections.
4. *The Seven Chapters of Sayings Sent by Abba Moses to Abba Paemen*, “and whoever keeps them will be delivered from punishment,” consisting of thirty-seven sections.

The seventh book has an uncertain Greek author but a certain Latin translator, Paschasius, deacon of the Holy Roman Church [Col. 0073A]. It contains the sayings of the elders arranged under common topics and is completed in forty-four chapters.

The works that we have enumerated thus far appeared in earlier editions scattered in various ways according to the judgment of each compiler; they were included in the commonly circulated book of the *Lives of the Fathers*. The following books are added here.

The eighth book recognizes as its certain author Palladius, bishop of Helenopolis, and as its certain Latin translator Gentianus Hervetus. It contains brief Lives of the Fathers and of certain female ascetics, collected into one volume for the benefit of Lausus the prefect. Hence it acquired the name *Lausiac History*. It is completed in 151 chapters [Col. 0073B].

The ninth book contains a history of the friends of God, both men and women, called *Philotheus*, or *Theophiles*, with the Greek author certainly identified as Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus, and the Latin translator certainly identified as Gentianus Hervetus. It consists of thirty chapters.

The tenth book has John Moschus as its Greek author and Ambrose of Camaldoli as its Latin translator. It acquired the name *Spiritual Meadow*, because it shines with various flowers of the saints. It contains 219 chapters in all.

After these ten books concerning the Lives of the Fathers and the sayings of the elders comes an Appendix. Since it contains almost entirely the same material as that included in the preceding books, I relegated it to the end of the volume and had it printed in smaller type. I decided to append this material because I thought I would be doing something agreeable for antiquarians by producing the ancient translators of Palladius, so that both the variation or agreement of the text and the antiquity of the style might be displayed [Col. 0073C].

The Appendix contains the following:

* Heraclides’ *Paradise*, with an uncertain but ancient translator, in fifty-eight chapters.
* Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, with an uncertain but ancient translator, in twenty chapters.
* The Sayings of the Egyptian Fathers, by an uncertain Greek author and translated by Martin, bishop of Dumio. They consist of 119 numbered sections.

## PROLEGOMENON XXII. What each edition contains that is distinctive and different from the others

To place the matter clearly before the eyes, I decided to compare each edition with the others. To avoid confusion, I shall distinguish the comparisons by paragraphs.

### § I. Comparison of the first and second editions

The first edition, consisting of five books, contains the following features that are peculiar to it and differ from the second edition:

First, the entire third book, or Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, with an uncertain but ancient translator.

Second, in the fourth book it contains a preface lacking from the second edition. So that no one may miss it, here it is:

> “Since every preface, suitably preceding the text, either announces the character of the material that follows or commends its author by defending him, the sequence of the present book also happens to require a prologue for this reason: because, by setting forth particular virtues here and there as though they were precious stones, it proves to the reader’s eyes that its usefulness is offered throughout the whole body of the work. Although divided into nineteen parts, and although it may appear to contain distinct virtues, nevertheless, while on the occasion of one virtue the others are for the most part commended indiscriminately, their bonds are struck together—that is, the virtues are compared with one another—and the immortal brilliance of the spiritual gems, reflecting itself, knows no loss through the light borrowed from one another” [Col. 0074A].

Third, the entire fifth book, which contains shorter sayings *On the Heavenly Conduct of the Egyptian Fathers*. Although these sayings are distributed throughout various books in the second edition, so that nothing is missing from it except the preface alone, I reproduce that preface here:

> “Although from the beginning of our composition it was our intention to include in four books everything that we could learn concerning the conduct of the holy Fathers, afterward, having considered each matter individually, we added a fifth book, lest perhaps either the number of books or the uninterrupted multitude of sayings should displease readers. Since throughout the body of this volume there is such an abundance of brief sayings that the longer sayings can scarcely amount to a tenth of them, after consulting our own judgment we thought that in this way our labor should be commended to the favor of the reader and hearer.
>
> “For if both short and long sayings were placed randomly throughout the preceding four books in order to relieve weariness, whereas a very large number of the little sayings were gathered into one small book—as though they were tiny fragments, or fragments of gems fused into one mass [LXX]—the little sayings are called such with respect to the number of their words. In other respects, some of them are as much stronger in meaning as they are shorter in words, so that if anyone should seek to explain them more fully, he would necessarily need to bring his whole self to the task.
>
> “Indeed, although we had made other arrangements, we believe that it was done by the Lord so that the heavenly conduct of the Egyptian Fathers might be marked by the number of the books of the Law: those whom the Lord himself rescued from the power of Egypt, that is, from darkness, and in whose hearts he inscribed the decrees of the evangelical law with the stylus of the Holy Spirit. Let us therefore contemplate the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith, purpose, and zeal, so that, having become companions in their sufferings, we may also become sharers in their reward” [Col. 0074D].

I found this preface in no manuscript, nor did I find the shorter sayings to which it is prefixed. Therefore I think that the first compiler of the *Lives of the Fathers*, whoever he may have been, excerpted these sayings from the other books, as the preface itself indicates.

The second edition, consisting of four parts, has the following features of its own, which are lacking in the first:

First, the Lives in its first part that I listed individually in Prolegomenon 19, except the Life of Marina, or Marinus, which the first edition has at the end of the fifth book.

Second, the entire third part, which I showed in this fourth edition of ours to have been excerpted from Severus and Cassian [Col. 0075A].

Third, the entire fourth part—that is, the book of Paschasius and the little work *On the Praise and Effect of the Virtues*.

### § II. Comparison of the first and third editions

The first edition contains nothing peculiar that is not also found in the third.

The third edition, however, contains the following features differing from the first in its first book, which consists of three parts. It has the following distinctive materials in its first and second parts:

First, all the Lives that the second edition also has after the Lives written by Rufinus. To these it adds the *Life of Epictetus and Astion*, as well as *On the Woman of Vercelli Who Was Struck Seven Times*, by Saint Jerome, and, at the end of the fifth book, the *Life of Barlaam and Josaphat*. It also has as a distinctive feature the entire third part, which contains excerpts from Severus and Cassian [Col. 0075B].

Second, in the fifth book it has as a distinctive feature the book of Paschasius.

### § III. Comparison of the first and fourth editions

[LXXI] The first edition contains nothing that is not found in this fourth edition of ours, except the preface that it prefixes to its fourth book—which is our fifth book—and which I reproduced above. Also excepted is Book V of the first edition, which consists of shorter sayings. All those sayings, however, occur interspersed in other books of the fourth edition.

The fourth edition has the following features distinct from the first:

1. The entire first book, consisting of various Lives of the saints, except the Life of Saint Marina, which appears at the end of Book V in the first edition.
2. The entire fourth book, compiled from Severus and Cassian.
3. The entire seventh book, translated by Paschasius.
4. The entire eighth book, or Palladius’s *Lausiac History*.
5. The entire ninth book, or Theodoret’s *Philotheus*.
6. The entire tenth book, or John Moschus’s *Spiritual Meadow*.
7. From the Appendix, Heraclides’ *Paradise* and the sayings of the Egyptian Fathers, translated by Martin of Dumio [Col. 0075C].

### § IV. Comparison of the second and third editions

The second edition has at the end the little work *On the Praise and Effect of the Virtues*, which is lacking from the third edition.

The third edition contains the following distinctive materials that are lacking from the second:

First, the *Life of Epictetus and Astion*, the *Life of Barlaam and Josaphat*, and the Lives of Fabiola and Marcella. It also contains the letters of Saint Antony, the letter of Macarius, a certain miracle of Saint Antony translated from German into Latin, and *On the Woman of Vercelli Who Was Struck Seven Times*, by Saint Jerome.

Second, the entire third book, which is Palladius’s *Lausiac History* from the ancient translation.

Third, that part of the fifth book in which the shorter sayings are contained.

### § V. Comparison of the second and fourth editions

The second edition contains nothing peculiar that is not also found in the fourth. I have omitted only from the first part the *Life of Saint Christian of Le Mans*, since it has nothing to do with the *Lives of the Egyptian and Eastern Fathers*, and I do not know how it slipped in among these Lives. Nevertheless, so that no one may miss it, here it is:

[Col. 0076A]

## LIFE OF CHRISTIAN THE MONK.

«A certain man from Le Mans, named Christian, a young convert, entered a certain hermitage in the archbishopric of Tours, [LXXII] called Castinetum. There, when he was being fiercely tempted by his flesh, he afflicted himself during Lent by fasting and abstaining from every drink except on one day of the week. In winter he would stand clothed in cold water up to his neck and discipline himself until the rods were broken. When he was doing this one day and had scourged himself until he bled, he heard a voice from the west saying: “What you are doing profits you nothing. This God whom you invoke will not grant you what you ask; instead, turn to me, and I will help you.” Hearing this, he understood that the voice was the enemy’s. [Col. 0076B] After he had prayed to God for help against the temptations, he resolved to undertake a pilgrimage to various saints, so that he might end his life by wandering on pilgrimage. After considering this for a long time, he took his staff and went out barefoot.

“When he came before a certain church, he knelt and asked God to give him good counsel. He had scarcely risen from prayer when suddenly he perceived a great stench, by which he understood that the devil was standing there and was suggesting to him that he abandon his religious habit and his place. Giving thanks to the Lord for such a sign, he returned to his brothers.

“On one occasion, during the feast of Saint Stephen, he was sleeping through Matins. When the lesson was being read in which it says, ‘And they stoned Stephen,’ he awoke at these words and reproached himself for his drowsiness, [Col. 0076C] saying: ‘Woe to me, because I sleep during the service of God. This holy man did not sleep when he was being stoned, but prayed for his persecutors; and I, wretched man, ought to have asked this holy martyr to pray for me.’ After this he began to keep the most earnest vigils and to ask Saint Stephen to pray for him.

“On the following day, when he was in the refectory, before he had tasted anything, a voice came to him, saying: ‘You are directing your attention to earthly food and are not thinking of the glorious protomartyr who is praying for you.’ Then his eyes were opened, and, raising his eyes to heaven, he saw the martyr praying for him, just as the voice had told him. When he had said this, he immediately rose and asked for a secluded place in which to pray, and said: ‘Saint Stephen, how shall I thank you for so great a benefit? I have nothing of my own [Col. 0076D] to give you; but I do give you this: from now on, for love of you, I will not wear linen garments, but only woolen ones.’ And he did so.

“Later, when he was exhorting the others to persevere in their good purpose, he used to tell this story: ‘Once I was lying at Castinetum on a bed full of straw in an upper room. When I wanted to rest, I felt something—I do not know what—moving beneath my loins. I also told this to my master, but the movement did not cease. One day, however, when the Lord inspired me, I began to overturn the straw of my bed. When I had overturned it and found nothing, I lifted one of the boards of the upper room, beneath which I found a shoe, and in it a large mass of coins. When I found them, I left them there and ran to our master, confessing what I had found. [Col. 0077A] He ordered me to bring them to him. When I had done so, he ordered all the brothers to assemble; and they all excommunicated the man who had done this. When a certain carpenter heard this, he said [LXXIII] that he had done it, and asked forgiveness, humbly promising correction. The master forgave him and imposed a penance upon him. But he was unwilling to retain the ill-gotten coins; rather, he distributed them among the poor and needy.’»

This account is taken from Vincent of Beauvais’s *Speculum Historiale*, book XXIX, chapter 11, where he cites it from Helinand. In chapter 12, the same author relates how this Christian passed over to the Cistercian order. He lived around the year 1160.

The second edition also contains at the end of the book the letter of Macarius [Col. 0077B] and the little work *On the Praise and Effect of the Virtues*. Since these are didactic works and do not properly belong to the *Lives* or *Sayings of the Elders*, they are more appropriately reserved for another ascetic volume that will comprise all the ascetic and didactic writings of the Fathers.

The fourth edition differs from the second as follows: first, in the first book, it contains a Life of Saint Ephraem distinct from that hitherto published, as well as the Life of Epictetus and Astion and the Life of Barlaam and Josaphat; second, the whole of book eight, or Palladius’s *Lausiac History*; third, the whole of book nine, or Theodoret’s *Philotheus*; fourth, the whole of book ten, or John Moschus’s *Spiritual Meadow*; fifth, the whole appendix.

§ VI. Comparison of the third and fourth editions

The third edition contains nothing distinctive that differs from the fourth [Col. 0077C] except the Life of Christian of Le Mans, which, as I have already said, has no place here; *On the Woman Struck Seven Times*, by Saint Jerome, which likewise does not belong here; the shorter sayings, which, as I have also said, occur scattered through other books of the fourth edition; the letters of Saint Antony and the letter of Macarius, which are reserved for another didactic volume of the *Asceticism*. It also contains a certain miracle of Saint Antony translated from German into Latin, but I do not know from where it was obtained or how trustworthy it is.

The fourth edition differs from the third as follows: first, in the first book, it contains a Life of Saint Ephraem distinct from the one found hitherto in the other editions; second, the whole of book eight, or Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, fuller than that contained in the third edition and taken from the recent translation [Col. 0077D] of Gentian Hervet; third, the whole of book nine, or Theodoret’s *Philotheus*; fourth, the whole of book ten, or John Moschus’s *Spiritual Meadow*; fifth, from the appendix, the *Paradise of Heraclides* and the *Sayings of the Egyptian Fathers*, translated by Martin, bishop of Dumium.

In addition, it contains the prolegomena, preliminary materials, notes, onomasticon, and various indexes of various matters, all of which are absent from the other editions.

## PROLEGOMENON XXIII. On the various editions and the various languages

[LXXIV] The Italian edition, in folio, Venice, 1476, printed by Antonio Bartholomaei. This edition [Col. 0078A] consists of six books. The books are thoroughly miscellaneous, with certain Lives inserted that appear in no Latin edition of the *Lives of the Fathers*. The first book names Saint Jerome as its author. Most of it, however, belongs to other authors, especially Rufinus, taken here from the second book. The second book acknowledges the monk Eradius. It is the *Paradise of Heraclides*, whose name, I believe, has been corrupted into “Eradius.” The third book is attributed to John, a monk of Jerusalem. The fourth book is attributed to Leontius, bishop of Neapolis in Cyprus. It is the *Life of John the Almsgiver*, composed by him, to which several others are added. The fifth book is entitled “To Theophilus, Sergius, and Elchinus.” It is the *Life of Macarius the Roman* by those authors, to which certain other material is appended. The sixth book has John Eviratus as its author. It is John Moschus’s *Spiritual Meadow*. [Col. 0078B]

This Italian edition was printed again in quarto with illustrations, with a new translation by Giovanni Mario Verdizotti, Venice, from the press of Guerra, 1589.

The French edition, in folio with illustrations, translated by an anonymous translator, Paris, 1494, printed by Jean du Pré. It was produced from the second Latin edition. Therefore, whatever I said in Prolegomenon 19 that the second Latin edition contains, this French edition also contains. From Prolegomenon 22, where I compared the Latin editions with one another and with this fourth edition, it is consequently easy to discern how this French edition agrees with our fourth Latin edition.

Another French edition, in small folio or large quarto with illustrations, Paris, without indication of year or printer. It agrees entirely with the preceding edition and perhaps is the earlier of the two. [Col. 0078C]

Another French edition, in quarto with illustrations, translated by a later anonymous translator, Paris, printed by Guillaume Chaudière, 1605. This was produced from the third Latin edition and contains only four books, omitting the whole fifth book and Paschasius, which is added after the fourth book in the Latin text.

Another French edition, in octavo, translated by M. Jacques Gaultier, Paris, printed by Guillaume de la Noue, 1606. It contains the first [LXXV] and second books according to the exemplar of the second Latin edition.

The Flemish edition, in small folio, without indication of place, by Peter van Os, 1490. It consists of three parts, variously arranged and mixed together. From our first book it contains only the Lives of Paul, Saint Hilarion, Malchus, [Col. 0078D] Onuphrius, Abraham the hermit, Simeon Stylites, Thais the harlot, and Marina. It also contains the second book. In the third part it contains various examples and sayings excerpted from various books. Although this edition gives no indication of place, I nevertheless believe it was printed at Zwolle, since I have seen a Flemish book *On the Universal Good*, or *The Book of Bees*, printed at Zwolle in 1488 by Peter van Os, who was also the Flemish printer of this book of the *Lives of the Fathers*. The same device was affixed to both books.

Another Flemish edition, in small folio, Delft, printed by Henry Eckert van Homberch, 1498. It consists of three parts, like the preceding edition.

Another Flemish edition, in small folio, Leiden, printed by John Seversoen, 1511. It follows the earlier editions. [Col. 0079A]

The German edition, in folio with illustrations. It agrees for the most part with the Flemish edition.

The English edition, in folio with illustrations, translated by William Caxton of Westminster, Westminster, printed by Wynkyn de Worde, 1495, according to the French exemplar printed at Lyons in 1486. I have not seen that French edition of Lyons, but from the order of the English book I see that it is the same as the other Latin editions of Lyons. Therefore, the English edition contains everything that I said above in Prolegomenon 19 was contained in the second edition. From Prolegomenon 22, where I compared all the Latin editions with our fourth edition, it is consequently easy to see how [Col. 0079B] this English edition agrees with our own. I obtained this book from the Carthusian monastery at Mechelen, supplied most willingly by its very reverend prior.

## PROLEGOMENON XXIV. On the manuscript books used in preparing this fourth edition

My first concern was not to alter anything rashly in the text: I yielded nothing substantial to ingenuity or to conjectures attractive merely in appearance. My first assistance came from manuscripts, including some obtained from Germany, from which our Reverend Father Jacob Gretser sent me five exemplars [LXXVI]. My second assistance came from the oldest printed editions. My third, though very rarely, came from conjecture—not remote conjecture, but conjecture close to the evidence. Since we are presenting ten books of the *Lives of the Fathers*, of which the three later books are now being added for the first time from translations by men who lived in the memory of the Fathers, you should not expect manuscript copies of all the books. Expect manuscript copies, therefore, only of those books that were translated long ago, such as the first seven, which have hitherto been printed under the title *Lives of the Fathers*.

Here is a catalogue of the manuscripts I used, which I give according to the antiquity of their script, insofar as I have been able to determine it either from the year recorded in them or from the script itself. Antiquaries know that some indication of a century can be inferred from the kind of script. I cite them here in reference to this fourth edition.

The Vedastine manuscript, from the celebrated monastery of Saint Vedast, in parchment folio, written in a very ancient hand, since it is composed in capital letters. It had been copied at the request of Abbot Nomedus, who had offered it to the basilica of Saint Medard. I therefore conjecture that this book came from Soissons, where the distinguished basilica of Saint Medard is located. The title of the book was: *Book of the Discourses or Exhortations of the Fathers for the Advancement of Monks*. This manuscript contains only fifteen little books from our fifth book and ends at number 26 of little book XV. It therefore does not contain in full what Pelagius translated. The end of the whole book was: “Here ends the book called *Lives of the Fathers for the Advancement of Monks or Their Imitators*.” I have little doubt that this book was written eight hundred years ago. The matter can be established more securely from the period of Nomedus.

[Col. 0080A] The manuscript of Saint Florian, in folio, on parchment, extremely old, written nearly eight hundred years ago. For at the end it reads: “This book was begun at Hunia, in the army, in the year of the Lord 819, on the fourth day before the Nones of June, and completed at Saint Florian on the second day before the Ides of September, ineha. XVma.” Is this final expression an “indiction XV”? (The reading is uncertain.) You would judge more accurately that it says “in the fifteenth week,” that is, the fifteenth [week]. In this way Aventinus once read it in the passage cited shortly below, when the letters had not yet faded so greatly. It contains from the first book the Lives of Paul, Antony, Hilarion, and Malchus; the second book; and from the fifth book, certain material under this title: “Here begin the exhortations of the holy Fathers, the perfections of monks, which blessed Jerome translated from Greek into Latin.” It also contains the seventh book. From the appendix it contains the *Sayings of the Egyptian Fathers*, under this title: “Questions [Col. 0080B] or Answers of the Egyptian Fathers, which Martin, bishop, translated from Greek [LXXVII] into Latin in the monastery of Dumium.”

Aventinus mentions this book in book IV of his *Annals of Bavaria*, where he discusses the emperor Louis the Pious, who arranged for Lindewit the Slav to be defeated after the emperor had invaded Dalmatia. “During this war,” he says, “a codex was written which, bound from parchment, is displayed in the monastery of monks that stands on the bank of the Ilm, ten thousand paces westward and somewhat toward the winter [i.e. northwest] from my homeland. In that book are written the Lives of the saints translated by Paschasius from the Greek language into the Roman. Also [the Life of] Hilarion by Saint Jerome, in letters so ancient that I had to become a child again and return to my first lessons.” [Col. 0080C] Thus far Aventinus. Hundius, in his *Salisburgian Metropolis*, writes that this book was formerly in the monastery of Munichmunster in Bavaria, on the Danube below Vohburg, but that in 1580 he did not find it there; he nevertheless supposed that it had been transferred to Munich, to the ducal library, together with certain other books. Thus Hundius. An error crept into the *Chronicle of the Benedictine Order* compiled by the very Reverend Father Aubert Miraeus, when the book is said to have been written in the year 918; it must certainly have been 819.

The Ingolstadt manuscript, belonging to our college, in folio, on parchment, very old. It contains the second, third, and fourth books.

The Amandine manuscript, from the celebrated monastery of Saint Amand, written in an old hand. It contained the *Paradise of Heraclides* [Col. 0080D], but in mutilated form; nevertheless I used it to check a few passages in the appendix.

[Col. 0080D] The Audomarian manuscript, from the collegiate church of Saint Omer, old and especially complete, which was of the greatest assistance to me in this revision, both because it contained more books and because it was excellently written. From the first book it contained: the Life of Saint Antony by Saint Athanasius, translated by Evagrius; the Life of Saint Hilarion by Saint Jerome; the Life of Malchus the captive monk by the same author; the Life of Abraham the hermit by Blessed Ephraem; the Life of Blessed Frontonius; the Life of Marina the girl; the second book, beginning: “Here begins Rufinus’s preface concerning the Life of the monks. Blessed…,” [Col. 0081A] and so forth; the third book, in 207 paragraphs or numbered sections; the fourth book, except for the first fourteen chapters, which are excerpts from Sulpicius Severus, for these were lacking; the fifth book, whose title is: “Here begin the exhortations of the holy Fathers and the perfections of monks, which Jerome the presbyter translated from Greek into Latin.” This is manifestly erroneous. For the same manuscript book, at the end of little book XVIII, which is the last in this fifth book, has the following: “Thus far Pelagius, deacon of the Roman Church, translated from Greek into Latin; from this point onward, John the subdeacon.” The sixth book, translated by John, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church.

[Col. 0081B] The Affligem manuscript, from the distinguished abbey of Saint Peter at Aalst, in folio, on parchment, of good quality. It contains from the first book the Lives of Saint Paul, Antony, Hilarion, Malchus, Pachomius, Abraham, Simeon Stylites, Frontonius, Euphrosyne, Mary the niece of Abraham, Pelagia, Mary of Egypt, and Marina; as well as the second, fifth, and sixth books.

The Gembloux manuscript, from the ancient abbey of Saint Peter, of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the town of Gembloux near Namur, in quarto, on parchment, in an old script. It contained from the first book only the Lives of Saint Pachomius, Saint Basil, John the Almsgiver, and Mary of Egypt.

The Crispin manuscript, from the monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict near Valenciennes, in folio, on parchment, written in an old hand. It contained from the first book the Lives of Saint Paul, Saint Antony, Saint Hilarion, Malchus, John [Col. 0081C] the Almsgiver, Frontonius, Paula, and Saint Marina; the whole second book; the whole fourth book; the whole fifth book; and the whole sixth book.

The Anchin manuscript, from the Benedictine monastery near Douai, on parchment, in folio, of good quality. This manuscript presented from the first book the Lives of Saint Paul, Saint Antony, Saint Hilarion, Malchus, Saint John the Almsgiver, Saint Euphrosyne the virgin, Mary the niece of Abraham, Pelagia the harlot, Mary of Egypt, and Paula. It also presented the second book, under this title: “Here begin the acts of the holy Fathers, edited by the monk Posthumianus and sent to Fidus.” The third book, which there consists of 112 paragraphs or numbered sections. The fourth book, beginning: “Here begins Posthumianus’s book on the deeds of the holy Fathers.” From this arose [Col. 0081D] the occasion for some books to be inscribed with the name of Posthumianus. See what was said above in Prolegomenon 4, § 9.

The major Laeti manuscript, from a monastery carefully arranged according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, under the patronage of Saint Lambert, in folio, on parchment, of good quality.
