From the first book it contains the Lives of Saint Paul the first hermit; Saint Antony; Saint Hilarion; Saint Malchus, the captive monk; Saint Simeon Stylites; Saint John the Almsgiver; [LXXIX] Saint Frontonius, which it attributes to Jerome; Saint Euphrosyne; Saint Pelagia the harlot; Saint Mary of Egypt; Saint Marina; and Saint Paula. It contains the second book, which this manuscript attributes to the monk Posthumianus and says was sent to Phydosus. From the third book it contains only [Col. 0082A] number 24, which is likewise attributed to Posthumianus. It contains the fourth book, attributed to John Cassian. It contains the fifth book. Its title is: “Here begin the chapters of Saint Jerome’s book on the Life and deeds of the holy Fathers, the hermits, translated by him from the Greek style into Latin.” In the middle of little book XVI—which is in fact XVIII, since this manuscript omits two little books, XIII, *On Hospitality*, and XIV, *On Obedience*—there is the following: “Up to this point Jerome is said to have translated from Greek into Latin, or, as most maintain, Pelagius, deacon of the Roman Church. From here onward John the subdeacon, dividing the same work into four books.” It contains the sixth book.

The minor Laeti manuscript, in quarto, on parchment, of no lower quality than the preceding one. This book once belonged to Saint Michael in the Marsh. From the first book it contains [Col. 0082B] the Life of Saint Paul the first hermit, by Saint Jerome; the Life of Saint Hilarion, by the same author; the Life or Penance of Thais; and the second, third, and fourth books.

The Good Hope manuscript, from the abbey of that name, of the Premonstratensian Order, near the town of Binche in Hainaut, in quarto, oblong in shape, on parchment, in a good and old script. It contains only various fragments excerpted here and there from various books, from books II and III of Rufinus and also from several little books of Pelagius and John.

The Moret manuscript, in folio, on parchment, not particularly old but containing a great deal, which the sons of Mr. Moret supplied to me. From the first book it contained the Lives of Paul; Antony; Hilarion; Malchus; Pachomius; Abraham; John the Almsgiver; Frontonius, [Col. 0082C] whom it attributes to Jerome; Euphrosyne; Mary the niece of Abraham; Thais the harlot; Pelagia the harlot; Mary of Egypt; Marina; and Paula. It contained the second book, which it attributes to the monk Posthumianus and says was sent to Phydosus. It contained the third book, also attributed to Posthumianus and said to have been sent to Phydosus. It contained the fourth book, which it attributes to John Cassian. It contained the fifth book, which it asserts was translated from Greek into Latin by Jerome the presbyter [LXXX], although at the end of book XVIII it says: “or, as most maintain, Pelagius, deacon of the Holy Roman Church, translated it from Greek into Latin.” It contained the sixth book, which it attributes to John, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church. From the appendix it contained the complete *Paradise of Heraclides*, but attributes it to Paschasius, or to Palladius the deacon. Its title is formulated thus: “Here begins the letter [Col. 0082D] of Paschasius or Palladius the deacon to Eugippius the presbyter in the book called *Paradise*, concerning the miracles and lives of the holy Fathers.” See Prolegomenon 25.

The manuscript of Saint James, the Lord’s brother, on the Island, where there is an abbey of the Order of Saint Benedict at Liège, in folio, on parchment, written in the year of the Lord 1312. From the first book it contains the Lives of Saint Paul the first hermit and Malchus. It also contains the second, fifth, and sixth books.

From the same abbey I obtained a little book in octavo, on paper, containing the Life of Saint Onuphrius, written in a recent hand. Its style was distinct from that of the commonly circulated Life of Onuphrius, but I retained the customary style.

[Col. 0083A] The Cambron manuscript, from the abbey of Saint Mary of Cambron, of the Order of Saint Bernard, near Ath, on parchment, in folio, written in a more recent hand. From the first book it contained the Lives of Saint Paul, Saint Antony, Saint Hilarion, Malchus, John the Almsgiver, and Paula. It contained the second book under this title: “Here begin the acts of the holy Fathers, edited by the monk Posthumianus and sent to Fidus.” It contained the third book, attributed to no definite author there. It contained the fourth book, which is attributed to Posthumianus.

The Clairmarais manuscript, from the abbey of Saint Mary of Clairmarais, near Saint Omer, of the Order of Saint Bernard, in folio, on parchment, in a good but not very old script. From the first book it contained the Lives of Thais the harlot, Mary of Egypt, and Marina the girl. It contained the second book, attributed to no author; [Col. 0083B] the third book, likewise anonymous; and the fourth book, likewise anonymous.

The manuscript of Saint Mary of Bibraich in Germany, on parchment, in folio, in a somewhat old script. From the first book it contained the Lives of Paul, Antony, Hilarion, Malchus, Frontinus, and Thais the harlot. It contained the whole second book and the whole seventh book of Paschasius, as well as certain other mixed materials from various books.

The Rebdorf manuscript, in quarto, on parchment, in a fairly recent script. From the first book it contains the Lives [LXXXI] of Paul, Hilarion, Malchus, Simeon Stylites, and Euphrosyne. It contains the second book, which it attributes to Saint Jerome, and the third and fourth books.

The manuscript of Saint Peter at Münster, in folio, on parchment, in a more recent script. It contains only certain excerpts [Col. 0083C] from the *Lives of the Fathers*: from the first book, the Lives of Paul, Antony, and Hilarion; and certain passages from the second and seventh books.

Two Lille manuscripts, on parchment, belonging to the distinguished and very dear friend of mine, Tussanus Desbarbieux, in folio and not very old. One of them contained from the first book only the Life of Mary of Egypt, Mary the niece of Abraham, Pelagia the harlot, and Thais the harlot. From the appendix it contained only the *Paradise of Heraclides*. The other contained from the first book only the Life of Saint Marina the virgin and Saint Paula the widow. It contained the whole fifth book of Pelagius, deacon of the Holy Roman Church, and the whole sixth book of John, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church.

The major manuscript of the Holy Sepulchre, from the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre at Cambrai, of the Order of Saint Benedict, [Col. 0083D] in folio, on paper, written in a recent hand. From the first book it contains the Lives of Malchus the captive monk, by Saint Jerome; Saint Euphrosyne; Thais the harlot; Mary of Egypt; and Marina the virgin. It contains the second book, which it attributes to Palladius and says was translated from Greek into Latin by Jerome. It contains the third and fourth books. From the fifth book, which consists of eighteen little books, it contains only 240 numbered sections, without any distinction of the little books. These are called “Admonitions of the holy Fathers on various kinds of virtue, which Pelagius, deacon of the Roman Church, translated from Greek into Latin.”

The minor manuscript of the Holy Sepulchre, on parchment, in quarto, also written in a recent hand. It comprises [Col. 0084A] from the first book the Lives of Malchus the captive monk; Frontonius; and Saint Marina. It contains the second book, which it attributes to Saint Jerome. It contains the fifth book, entitled: “Here begin the exhortations of the holy Fathers and the perfections of monks, which Blessed Jerome the presbyter translated from Greek into Latin.” More correctly, at the end of book XVIII: “Up to this point Pelagius, deacon of the Roman Church, translated from Greek into Latin; from this point onward, John the subdeacon.” It contains the sixth book.

The manuscript of the Carthusians of Our Lady of Grace near [LXXXII] Brussels, in folio, written on parchment in the year of Christ 1460, on the Kalends of December, by Brother Peter Weins. From the first book it contains the Lives of Paul the first hermit, by Saint Jerome; Antony, [Col. 0084B] by Athanasius, translated by Evagrius; Saint Hilarion, by Saint Jerome; Malchus the captive monk, by the same author; Saint Pachomius; Abraham the monk and hermit; Simeon Stylites; Macarius the Roman; Frontonius; Saint Euphrosyne the virgin; Thais the harlot; Pelagia the harlot; Mary of Egypt; Marina the virgin; and Paula. It contains the second book. It contains the fifth book. The sixteenth little book, *On Penance*, was absent in its proper place, but was included in the manuscript under the seventh little book, which is *On Patience*; in some manuscripts book XVI is also given this title. It contains the sixth book. The following title was prefixed to books five and six: *On the Sayings of the Elder Holy Fathers*. “Pelagius, deacon of the Roman Church, translated this work from Greek into Latin; John the subdeacon translated the final [Col. 0084C] part.”

The Ruremund manuscript, from our college at Ruremund, on parchment, in folio, written in a recent hand. It consists of five books, like the first edition. Since only a few copies were printed in the infancy of printing, it appears to have been copied from that edition. At the end it also contains the following Lives: Paul the first hermit, Saint Antony, Hilarion, Malchus, Pachomius, Abraham, Frontonius, Barlaam and Josaphat, Thais the harlot, Pelagia the harlot, Mary of Egypt, and Paula.

The Sion manuscript, from the monastery of women religious of Sion, of the Order of Saint Augustine at Kortrijk, in folio, on paper, in a more recent script, written in the year 1469. It agrees completely with the first edition, and I have no doubt that it was copied from it. At the end it adds these Lives of the Fathers: Saint Antony, [Col. 0084D] Saint Pachomius, and Epictetus and Astion.

Let this suffice concerning the manuscript books that contain certain complete books, or a large part of the books we are presenting. For from time to time we also cite other manuscripts that contain only one Life or something similar relevant to this work, such as the Bertinian manuscript at Saint Omer, the Laurentian manuscript at Liège, the Bruges manuscript of our society, and any others of the kind.

Besides these Latin manuscripts, I also obtained several Greek ones from which the Latin texts were produced; but they were few and rather imperfect, and you will occasionally find them cited where they shed light. For certain others came into my hands only later.

## PROLEGOMENON XXV. On the appendix to the *Lives of the Fathers*

[Col. 0085A]

[LXXXIII] It seemed appropriate to join this appendix to the other books concerning the Life of the Fathers, both because of the antiquity of its translators, so that light might occasionally shine upon doubtful passages from the variety of their translations, and also because this appendix contains certain things—though only a few—that cannot be found in the preceding books.

This appendix contains three little works: [Col. 0085A] the *Paradise of Heraclides* and Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, both in the old translation; concerning these, see what was said in Prolegomenon 4, § 3, and Prolegomenon 14.

The *Paradise* that we present here under the name of Heraclides is entitled in the Moret manuscript: [Col. 0085B] “Of Paschasius or Palladius the deacon to Eugippius the presbyter, in the book called *Paradise*, concerning the miracles and lives of the holy Fathers.” This title is followed by the following letter:

> “To his lord and ever most beloved presbyter, Paschasius the deacon.
>
> “Most beloved brother in Christ, while through the eloquence of your learning you … [lacuna] … But it is enlarged to this extent by the success of your wishes [Note: See this letter in *Patrologia*, volume LXII, column 39. Editor].”

[LXXXIV] This was followed by: “The first prologue of Paschasius, or Palladius the deacon, to Lausos the bishop. In this book, etc.” Then: “The second prologue: ‘Many have indeed [written] many things.’” Then the first chapter of the *Paradise*: “When I first came to Alexandria.”

My very dear friend Lucas Holstenius informed me by letter that he had found a similar manuscript, with these titles and prefaces, at Vézelay in the territory of the Aedui, with the most noble [Col. 0085C] abbot of that place, Erard of Rochefort, if it might be useful in preparing this second Moret edition. The distinguished Tussanus Desbarbieux likewise sent me an equal manuscript arranged in the same order; I mentioned him in Prolegomenon 24.

Indeed, this book cannot be attributed as author to this Paschasius, who lived in the time of Eugippius, since the author who speaks in this book certainly lived in the age of Saint Jerome, as did most of the Fathers whose lives he describes. Therefore, the addition “or Palladius” is correct; for Palladius, or Heraclides, or someone else of the same period, is truly the author of this *Paradise*.

Should this Paschasius, then, be called the ancient translator of this [Col. 0085D] *Paradise*? I cannot affirm that either. Certainly, the letter of Paschasius sent to Eugippius suggests nothing of the kind. Indeed, this letter ought rather to be prefixed to the *Life of Saint Severinus*, the apostle of Noricum. Long ago, in 1595, the learned commentator Marcus Welser prefixed it to the *Life of Saint Severinus*. The letter of Eugippius, to which this Paschasius replies, is found in volume six of *Ancient Readings*, page 455 (see *Patrologia*, volume LXII, column 1167). If it can be proved from another source that this Paschasius is the translator of this *Paradise*, let that translation hereafter be inscribed to him. Certainly, the translation is the work of a learned man, and its style differs little from the style of the *Life of Saint Severinus*. Because of this letter, accidentally prefixed here, I did not dare to assert that he was the translator. For more about this Paschasius, see Prolegomenon 14.

[LXXXV] [Col. 0086A] The appendix also contains the sayings of the Egyptian Fathers, translated by Martin, bishop of Dumium. The Reverend Father Christopher de Castro, professor of Sacred Letters at our college in Salamanca, excerpted them from a manuscript in the Library of Toledo and sent them to me from Spain. I also found them in the very old manuscript of Saint Florian that was supplied to me from Germany.

[Col. 0086B] Various authors mention Martin, bishop of Dumium: Isidore, in chapter 22 of *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*; and Sigebert, in his similar catalogue of writers, chapters 19 and 118. He was an abbot and bishop who founded the monastery of Dumium in Galicia and later became bishop of Braga. He is honorably mentioned in the tenth Council of Toledo, chapter 7, from the Council of Valencia, and in the First Synod of Braga, in the year 598 of the Spanish era, and in the second, in the year 610, over which he presided. He arranged for certain works to be translated from Greek by others. Thus Sigebert says above, in chapter 108: “Martin the bishop, through the hands of Paschasius the deacon, translated many questions and answers of the holy Egyptian Fathers in the monastery of Dumium.” What Paschasius translated at his command is found in book seven. Perhaps this same Paschasius also translated these sayings at his request. Yet because I found them under Martin’s name in two manuscripts [Col. 0086C], and because Martin himself states that he corrected the collection of Eastern canons and compared it again with the Greek text—this collection is found in the volumes of the councils after the Second Council of Lugo—he himself may have translated these sayings from Greek. I have therefore placed them in the appendix under his name.

## PROLEGOMENON XXVI. Various admonitions to the reader of this edition

First, note that my primary concern was to reproduce the text of each author with the greatest possible fidelity to the evidence of the ancient manuscripts, preserving even phrases that were less customary and not always very Latin, so that these too might reveal the age of their authors.

Second, note that the orthographic practice judged best by the printer [Col. 0086D] has been maintained. You will nevertheless occasionally find different spellings of certain proper names, but among different translators: now *Scete*, now *Scithi*; now *Poemenius*, now *Pimenius*; and several others of the same kind. For the most part I left these to their translators, since perhaps each found those names written differently in the Greek exemplar.

Third, note that, so as not to have to explain the same difficulties and rare words [LXXXVI] repeatedly when they occurred in various places, I have been content with a brief explanation in the notes and have referred the reader further to the *Onomasticon*, where they are treated more fully. There [Col. 0087A] you will also find some matters for which no indication was given in the notes.

Fourth, it should not be surprising if you find several identical accounts in different books, differing only in style. This happened because different people formerly visited the desert and recorded the Lives and sayings of the Fathers either personally or from the reports of others. Each person placed in writing what he had seen or heard. Moreover, some compiled the notebooks of others and added certain material from their own collections. We have therefore given everything as we found it in the various authors and translators, so that each person’s labor might remain his own and that, through the testimony of several people, greater authority might also accrue to the sayings of the Fathers. See what we said about this agreement in Prolegomenon 4, § 3.

[Col. 0087B] Fifth, observe this: wherever such agreement among authors occurs, I have generally noted the respective locations in the margin [Note: [Col. 0087D] We have brought these notes into the text within square brackets. EDITOR.] so that they might illuminate one another. You will find such agreement in many places among the second book of Rufinus, Hervet’s Palladius, the Paradise of Heraclides, and Palladius from the older translation. I compared Rufinus with Hervet’s Palladius; I illustrated the Paradise of Heraclides with Hervet’s Palladius; and I compared Palladius from the older translation with the Paradise of Heraclides. You will also find much the same material in Book III of Rufinus, in Pelagius, John, and Paschasius, whose agreement you will find noted in the margin.

Sixth, in order to cite that agreement concisely, since in the nine later books, where repeated accounts of the same matter occur most frequently, the author or translator is either known, I cited the author wherever the author is known; where this is less certain, I placed the translator’s name in the margin. For example, when parallel passages occur in Books II and III, which acknowledge Rufinus either as author or translator; in Book IV, which contains excerpts from Sulpicius Severus and John Cassian; in Book VIII, which represents Palladius; in Book IX, which represents Theodoret; and in Book X, which represents John Moschus as authors, I cite only the authors’ names in the margin, together with the chapters or numbers, according as each book is arranged here by chapters or by numbers. Again, when Books V, VI, and VII are to be cited in the margin—books circulated under the names of uncertain Greek authors but having known translators—when Book V is to be cited, I cite Pelagius; when Book VI, [Col. 0087D] John; and when Book VII, Paschasius; each of whom is the translator of his respective book. [Col. 0088A] Since Pelagius and John each have his own book divided into several little books [LXXXVII], whenever I cite them in the margin, I assign both the sequence of the little books and the number of the saying in the margin.

Seventh, for the benefit of students of topography, observe that we have arranged a map of the stations and journeys of the hermits. Since Egypt, Syria, and Palestine were especially cultivated by hermits, you also have a separate delineation of those regions, because a particular distinction of places could not be maintained on the general map. The next leaf will display that map.

Eighth, observe that in this year, 1627, after the first Moretian edition of 1615 had been exhausted, as had the Lyon edition of France, I again revised the Lives of the Fathers at the request of Mr. Balthasar [Col. 0088B] Moret. I especially revised the text of Book VIII through Palladius and of Book IX through John Moschus, which had not previously appeared in Greek. Their Paris Greek edition has now exposed various errors of the translators and shed light on many obscure passages. I have also increased the notes from time to time, and especially the Onomasticon, since this was the wish of many, particularly religious persons who lack an abundance of books and do not have access to lexicographers and critics who deal with antiquarian matters. Three new indexes have also been added: one of Sacred Scripture, another of sermons, and a third of the authors cited in the notes. You will find these inserted among, or appended to, those previously supplied.

Ninth, although some other lives of Eastern hermits have here and there been printed, and more could be recovered from manuscripts, my purpose was not to search out the lives of all hermits and collect them into a single bundle, but only to revise and illuminate the celebrated book of the Lives of the Fathers, which was printed and reprinted so many times during the past hundred years. I therefore refrained from investigating the remainder. Such labor could easily produce another volume. For me, it was enough at present to follow the footsteps of the holy Fathers who once read and commended these lives.

But I ask you, my reader, not merely with my wishes but with my earnest entreaty, to deign to make God favorable to me through your prayers, so that I may be able to express in my character and life, at least in some measure, what is treated in these books, lest I be altogether like sounding brass and a clanging cymbal. Thus may God, through the merits of the hermits interceding, breathe upon you every favor and assistance. Live, and farewell; remember me before God.

# THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS, OR THE EREMETIC HISTORIES. TEN BOOKS.

“The Conferences of the Fathers, their institutions, their lives, and the Rule of our holy father Basil: what else are they but examples and instruments of virtue for monks who live well and obey?” (St. Benedict, final chapter of his Rule.)

“O desert flourishing with the flowers of Christ! O solitude in which those stones are born from which the city of the great King is built in the Apocalypse! O wilderness rejoicing in a more intimate fellowship with God!” (Jerome, Letter 1 to Heliodorus, On the Praise of the Desert.)

## [BOOK I]

# PRELIMINARY MATERIAL TO BOOK I

[Col. 0089]

## To the Reader

3 Since the holy Jerome frequently speaks in this first book, and, inflamed by a desire for the stricter life, once visited the hermits and lived for several years in the desert, I have thought it useful here to place before your eyes, in a brief synopsis, the periods of his journey and life insofar as they concern his travels, to shed some light on what you are about to read. I have compiled these materials from the highly praised Annals of the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius, so that, under the guidance of that great leader, you may follow the footsteps of the holy Jerome.

[Col. 0089]

# THE JOURNEY OF THE HOLY JEROME

[Col. 0089A] **The Beginnings of the Holy Jerome and His Journey to Gaul**

**A.D. 342. Baronius, vol. III, Adam, p. 372.**—He was born at Stridon, a town in Dalmatia, to respectable parents of no mean resources, which he later sold through his brother Paulinianus for the support of a monastery (Jerome, Letter 26). For he does not speak of himself, but of pleasure-loving clerics and monks, though he puts the words in his own person, when he says (Jerome, Letter 2): “Born in a poor household and a rustic cottage, when I could scarcely fill my growling belly with millet and coarse bread, now I disdain fine flour and honey,” and so forth.

He had Bonosus as a foster-brother (Jerome, Letter 41), and grew up with him in the liberal disciplines; Bonosus was a very wealthy young man. From childhood he was entrusted to a teacher to be cultivated in good literature. He himself says of this teacher (Jerome, *Apology against Rufinus*): “I remember that as a boy I used to run about the little cells of the slaves, spend holidays in games, and, dragged captive from my grandmother’s lap, be taken to the savage Orbilius.”

Coming to Rome with his fellow-countryman Bonosus, he heard Donatus [Col. 0090A], whom he himself calls his teacher (Jerome, *Chronicle*, in the twentieth year of Constantius). Then, as he reports himself (Jerome, Book I *Against Pelagius*, and in the *Letter to the Galatians*, chapter II), he played at declaiming controversies in the manner of the schools. There, in mature age, he was initiated into holy baptism (Jerome, Letter 57). After receiving it, he immediately corrected the somewhat looser life he had previously led; for, having lost his former bodily integrity, he preserved intact the second state, which he calls continence after baptism, devoting himself wholly to pious duties together with his companions in the same discipline (Jerome, *Apology for the Book against Jovinianus*). Every Sunday, as he himself reports (Jerome, *Commentary on Ezekiel*, chapter XL), he visited the relics of the holy martyrs in the underground cemeteries; and, leaving himself no leisure on the other days, he was wholly occupied in copying books. Thus he testifies that he prepared a library for himself at Rome with the greatest zeal and labor (Jerome, Letter 22).

## Journey to Gaul; Then to Syria, After Visiting Various Provinces of the World

**A.D. 370. Baronius, under A.D. 372.**—After this it happened that the man who had once begun to travel also resolved to depart for the East, both for the sake of learning and for the sake of religion, as may be seen from what he did. Following the surviving traces of his journey, we say that, returning from Gaul with his companion Bonosus, he reached Aquileia [Note: [Col. 0097D] “He reached Aquileia.”].

“At that time,” says Baronius under A.D. 372, “the Church of Aquileia flourished with the highest renown. After the death of Fortunatianus, a bishop and supporter of the Arian sect, the most holy man Valerian purged it completely of every stain of impiety, since it had been defiled by the pollution of the Arians,” as the same holy Jerome reports (Jerome, Letter 43). After the best and most learned men had been appointed to ecclesiastical offices, it shone so brightly that Jerome himself worthily remembered them in his *Chronicle*: “The clerics of Aquileia are regarded as a choir of the blessed” (Jerome, *Chronicle*, year 11 of Valentinian). Through them, “all the poison of the Arian doctrine of former times was excluded” (Jerome, Letter 43).

But since those who were clerics there were also monks, three above all are praised from among them in the *Chronicle*, where he says: “Florentius [Florentinus], Bonosus, and Rufinus are regarded as distinguished monks. Florentius was so compassionate toward the needy that he was commonly called the father of the poor” (Jerome, *Chronicle*, year 13 of Valentinian). Letters written by Jerome to Heliodorus indicate that Heliodorus, aided by this man, undertook his journey to the East, and that Jerome, at his expense, arranged for numerous books to be copied (Jerome, Letters 5 and 6). These letters again commend the same man’s compassion toward the poor, especially in these words: “I pass over the countless persons whom you sustained, fed, clothed, and visited,” and so forth.] Jerome settled there for some time, intending to enjoy the company of the holiest men—namely, St. Valerian, bishop of that city after Fortunatianus; Heliodorus; Nepotianus; Rufinus; Chromatius; Jovinus; Eusebius; Bonosus; Florentius; Nicaea, the subdeacon; and Chrysogonus, the monk. Letters of Jerome to all of them, witnesses to their intimate friendship, are extant (Jerome, Letters 41–44).

Thus the holy Jerome was detained for some time at Aquileia by the very pleasant companionship of these men. When he was compelled to leave, through some unforeseen turn of events—I do not know what it was—he himself bears witness in these words, writing from the desert to Rufinus: “After a sudden storm tore me away from your side, after an impious separation ripped me away, though I was clinging there by the bond of love” (Jerome, Letter 41), and so forth. Departing from Aquileia, he came to Dalmatia, his native land, where he commended his young sister, who had fallen through the instability of her age, first to the especially pious Julianus, who restored her to a better way of life, and then also by letter to Chromatius (Jerome, Letters 37 and 43).

When, however, he actually adopted the institution of monastic life must be investigated through a careful examination of events and dates. Since we are dealing with a doubtful and uncertain matter, we must rely on conjectures and other arguments, however far-fetched they may appear. This is often how it happens that, through narrow cracks, one catches sight of the truth being diligently sought.

As for this matter, however, we cannot agree with the assertion that Jerome first sought Jerusalem with Rufinus and their companions, his fellow travelers, and that, after they separated from one another there, Rufinus undertook a journey to Egypt, while Jerome traveled through various provinces and then sought the deserts of Syria (Marianus Victorinus, *Life of St. Jerome*). For the facts stated above, as well as those to be stated below, clearly demonstrate that Rufinus withdrew from Rome with Melania and proceeded to Egypt, and from there reached Jerusalem only after the holy Jerome was already living as a monk in Syria.

From Jerome’s own account of his journey we can likewise determine the time of his migration from the West to the East. For, when Rufinus had already arrived in Egypt, Jerome writes to him from the Syrian desert that he first departed for Thrace, then for Pontus and Bithynia, afterward for Galatia and Cappadocia, and finally descended through Cilicia into Syria [Col. 0092A], 5 where he settled as a monk in solitude (Jerome, Letter 4). This is the entire course of his journey, together with his most faithful companions: Evagrius, a presbyter of Antioch [Note: [Col. 0099A] “Evagrius, presbyter of Antioch.”].

But as for what first concerns Evagrius of Antioch, Baronius notes under A.D. 372 that we already mentioned above that this man was exceptionally learned in the time of Julian the Apostate, and that he came to the West together with St. Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli. This is attested by St. Basil, who speaks of him in a letter to Eusebius of Samosata (Basil, Letter 8), saying that, on his return from Italy, he brought letters to him.], Innocentius, Heliodorus, and, as he says, Hylas, the servant of St. Melania.

Since we find that Evagrius was the inseparable companion of St. Jerome, and that Jerome likewise traveled with him from the West to Cappadocia, it is reasonable to believe Jerome’s own statement that he went to Cappadocia with him. The fact that Jerome and Evagrius made the same journey to Cappadocia certainly persuades us to affirm this. That this very Evagrius, whom St. Basil mentions (Basil, Letter 8), is the same as Evagrius, Jerome’s companion and fellow traveler, is demonstrated equally by his name, his office as a presbyter, his homeland—Antioch—and the very place from which he came, namely Italy. He is also the Evagrius who rendered distinguished service at Milan against Auxentius, about whom Jerome had earlier written to one of Innocentius’s companions; we have reported this in its proper place (Jerome, Letter 49).

When Evagrius reached St. Basil in Cappadocia can be understood from the same letter of Basil. Before mentioning Evagrius, Basil speaks of the severe illness into which he had then fallen, saying: “For these fifty days I lay sick in bed, during which our beloved brother and most diligent helper Elpidius attended me assiduously. Wasted greatly by fever, surrounded by this dry flesh, like the papyrus of a lamp, through lack of nourishing substance, I suffered from a withering and prolonged illness. An old wound added to this condition kept me from food, deprived my eyes of sleep, and finally brought me to the border between death and life, permitting me to live only as long as was necessary to feel pain” (Basil, Letter 8).

Basil says this and much more about the same bodily illness. As we stated above, it occurred in the year—A.D. 369 and 370—in which he was made bishop of Caesarea, a year reckoned as A.D. 370. We likewise said that Jerome, with Evagrius and his other companions, arrived in Syria, and from there sought the deserts of that province no earlier, in my judgment, than A.D. 371 [Col. 0092D]. This also seems to be suggested by the letter cited above, written to Rufinus (Jerome, Letter 4). We are therefore led to believe that the present year was the second year of his residence in the desert.

## **A.D. 371. Baronius, under A.D. 372**

When he first came to Syria, he settled at Antioch with Evagrius of Antioch, who had accompanied him on the journey. Evagrius was very wealthy and noble, and lord of an estate called Maronia. Jerome was once staying there with Evagrius when he encountered that most holy monk Malchus and received from him the entire account of his life, which he later wrote down in his old age. Jerome himself bears witness to this when he says:

“Maronia is a small village situated nearly thirty miles east of Antioch, a city of Syria. After many masters or patrons, while I was staying in Syria as a young man, it came into the possession of Pope Evagrius [Note: [Col. 0099A] “Of Pope Evagrius.” Baronius, under A.D. 372. Jerome calls Evagrius “pope” because, by the time he wrote this as an old man, Evagrius had already become— as we shall say in its proper place—bishop of Antioch. Later, in A.D. 389, the eleventh year of Theodosius the Elder, he says that this same Evagrius became bishop of Antioch, citing Theodoretus, Book V, chapter 23; Socrates, Book V, chapter 15; Sozomen, Book VII, chapter 15; and Ambrose, Letter 78. Baronius says that, according to Jerome’s own catalogue, *On Illustrious Men of the Church*, final chapter, he lived at least until the fourteenth year of Theodosius.], my intimate friend. I mention him now for this reason: to show how I know what I am about to write” (Jerome, *Life of Malchus).

After he had admirably described the life of Malchus, he added at the end: “The old Malchus told these things to me as a young man; I, now an old man, have related them to you; and I present the history of chastity to the chaste.”

The example of Malchus, together with that of many other monks by whom Syria was then flourishing, as we have seen, clearly inflamed his heart to pursue the monastic way of life. He also wrote to Theodosius, a man of great renown [Note: [Col. 0100A] “To Theodosius, a man of great renown.” As Baronius notes under A.D. 372, this concerns the anchorite Theodosius, through whose prayers St. Jerome, assisted by him, embraced the arduous discipline of monastic life with an ardent spirit. This is the same man who at that time shone brightly in those regions through his outstanding holiness. Theodoretus wrote an account of his remarkable deeds (Theodoretus, *Philotheus*, chapter 10). He says that Theodosius was an Antiochene by birth and had attained such holiness that sailors, invoking his name, could calm a storm arising at sea. He states that Theodosius died at Antioch and was honorably buried among the saints.], and to other distinguished anchorites, asking that through their prayers he might be released from the bonds of the world. Among other things, he wrote: “Now it is for you that action should follow upon intention; it is for me to desire; it is for your prayers that I may both desire and be able” (Jerome, Letter 38).

During this period, while he was consulting God and the servants of God about what decision should be made concerning his condition, he was staying at Antioch and heard Apollinaris teaching. Concerning him he himself says to Pammachius: “I frequently heard and honored Apollinaris of Laodicea at Antioch. Although he instructed me in the holy Scriptures, I never accepted his contentious doctrine concerning their meaning.” These are his own words. Since, as was said above, Apollinaris was not yet fully known or condemned, he taught openly and was heard even more openly.

[Col. 0093C] Concerning the place in the Syrian desert which St. Jerome chose for his residence, he himself mentions it in a letter to Chromatius as follows: “Your letters, of course, were conveyed to that part which forms the vast frontier between the Syrians and the Saracens.” He says the same in a letter to Florentius. It was a desert in the province of Chalcis, as he himself testifies elsewhere (Jerome, Letters 43 and 6; Preface to Obadiah).

His companions were Innocentius and Hylas, and Heliodorus joined them later. Evagrius of Antioch supplied all their necessities. Indeed, at his expense, copyists were supplied to Jerome for writing books; Jerome testifies that he had an abundance of them there. Through the agency of Evagrius, letters brought to Antioch from various places were delivered to Jerome, and, in turn, Evagrius received from him letters to be sent to others (Jerome, Letters 41, 43, and 6).

But when matters had been properly arranged in this way, the first and most grievous event was that he was deprived of his dearest companion Innocentius, who died, while Heliodorus soon departed, though with the hope of returning. Jerome himself, meanwhile, suffered from frequent bodily illnesses. He often complains of this when writing to various friends (Jerome, Letters 41, 1, 37, 3, 37, and 41).

What assaults of demons he suffered in addition to these things, and what battles of the flesh tormented him, I shall here set out from his letter to Eustochium (Jerome, Letter 22):

“Oh, how often, when I was living in the desert, in that vast solitude which, scorched by the heat of the sun, provides the monks with a dreadful dwelling, did I imagine myself among the pleasures of Rome! I sat alone, filled with bitterness; my deformed limbs were rough beneath the sackcloth, and my squalid skin had taken on the complexion of Ethiopian flesh. Every day there were tears, every day groans; and whenever impending sleep overcame me as I resisted it, I scarcely struck my bones, clinging to the bare earth.

“I say nothing of food and drink, since even monks who are ill use cold water, and to have received anything cooked is considered luxury. Yet I—the very man who, out of fear of hell, had condemned myself to such a prison, companion only of scorpions and wild beasts—often imagined myself among choirs of girls. Faces grew pale from fasting, while my mind burned with desires in my cold body; and in a man already half-dead in his own flesh, the fires of lust alone were boiling [the text reads *sua jam carne praemortuum*; perhaps *suum, jam carne praemortua*, ‘his own body already dead’]. [Col. 0094B]

“Thus, deprived of every means of help, I lay at the feet of Jesus, watered them with my tears, dried them with my hair, and subdued my rebellious flesh by weeks of fasting. I am not ashamed to confess the misery of my unhappiness; rather, I lament that I am not what I once was. I remember that I often cried out, joining day to night, and did not cease beating my breast until, when the Lord rebuked it, tranquility returned.

“I was even afraid of my own cell, as though it were conscious of my thoughts. Angry and severe with myself, I alone penetrated the deserted places. Whenever I saw hollow valleys, rugged mountains, or precipitous cliffs, there was the place of my prayer; there was the prison of my most wretched flesh. And, as the Lord himself is my witness, after many tears, after eyes fixed upon heaven, I sometimes seemed to myself to be present among the ranks of angels; and, joyful and exultant, I would say: ‘We ran after you in the fragrance of your perfumes’ (Song of Songs 1).”

Thus far Jerome himself.

He did not employ fasting and other afflictions alone to restrain the impulses of the flesh, but also constant devotion to study. Therefore, writing to Rusticus, he says (Jerome, Letter 4):

“When I was young, and the deserts of solitude enclosed me, I could not endure the incentives of vice and the heat of nature. Although I broke them by frequent fasts, my mind still seethed with thoughts. To subdue it, I placed myself under the instruction of a certain brother who had converted from the Hebrews, so that, after the refinements of Quintilian, the flowing eloquence of Cicero, the weightiness of Fronto, and the elegance of Pliny, I might learn the alphabet and practice harsh, breathless words. My conscience—mine, who suffered these things, and that of those who shared my life—bears witness to how much labor I spent there, what difficulty I endured, how often I despaired, how often I stopped, and how often, through the struggle to learn, I began again. I give thanks to my God that from the bitter seed of letters I now gather sweet fruits.”

These are his own words.

**Baronius, under A.D. 372 and 378.**—Of the many hardships by which he was severely afflicted there, the following seemed to him the greatest: that, as a man from the West, he was little known to his companions and was regarded by them as suspect in faith. For the very same slander which Paulinus, bishop of Antioch, suffered—as we saw from Epiphanius [Col. 0095A] and Theodoretus—from Vitalis first and then from Flavianus, when they called him a Sabellian, the holy Jerome was forced to endure while living in the desert of Chalcis in Syria. Because he communicated with Paulinus, he was harassed, I think, by the supporters of Meletius; they too called him a Sabellian and tormented him so severely that he was compelled to withdraw.

He himself reports all these things in a letter to Marcus, a presbyter of Chalcis (Jerome, Letter 77) [Note: [Col. 0100A] “Of Chalcis.” The old exemplar reads “of Chalcis,” not “of Celedis”; for he lived, as stated, in the Chalcidian desert of Syria. Thus Baronius under A.D. 378. But other books prefer “of Celedis,” as the same designation occurs in Letter 79. Annianus, pseudo-deacon of Celedis.].

# First Journey to Jerusalem

**A.D. 378. Baronius, under the same year.**—That he had gone to Jerusalem before coming to Rome to Damasus after leaving the Syrian desert is certainly proved by his own statement. In the preface to Paulinus on Didymus’s commentary on the Holy Spirit, written after he had left Rome following the death of Damasus, he says that he had returned to Jerusalem after an absence. In the letter to Asella which he wrote after leaving Rome, when he was about to board ship, he says: “Pray that I may return from Babylon to Jerusalem” (Jerome, Letter 99). From these words we understand that he had already been in Jerusalem before he came to Rome to Damasus. How long he remained in Jerusalem, however, is not sufficiently clear.

# Journey to Constantinople

**A.D. 379. Baronius, under the same year.**—Moved by the fame of Gregory of Nazianzus, the holy Jerome, together with his companion Vincentius, traveled from Syria across so great a distance to Constantinople. Let us investigate more precisely how long Jerome happened to remain with Gregory at Constantinople, using the chronological record of his writings noted above, in which he testifies that he wrote them after Gregory himself had become bishop of Constantinople. That occurred after the following year.

He also testifies that he came to know Gregory of Nyssa there. Gregory of Nyssa happened to travel there with other bishops at the time of the synod held at Constantinople. From these facts, then—if one counts from the present year—you will find that Jerome heard Gregory at Constantinople for approximately three years. Jerome himself says of Gregory of Nyssa: “Gregory, bishop of Nyssa and brother of Basil of Caesarea, read books against Eunomius to me and Gregory of Nazianzus a few years ago” (Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Gregory of Nyssa), and so forth.

# Journey to Rome

**A.D. 382. Baronius, under the same year.**—The year of the Lord 382 is recorded under the second consulship of Syagrius, with Antonius as his colleague. In that year a council was held at Rome, attended by bishops from various provinces, namely from the East and from other regions of the Catholic world.

Writing to Principia, St. Jerome states that he too came to Rome from the East with those same holy bishops. For, speaking of St. Marcella, he says: “Finally, since ecclesiastical necessity had brought me to Rome with the holy bishops Paulinus and Epiphanius” (Jerome, Letter 61), and so forth. Jerome clearly indicates by these words that he was summoned by Damasus.

But when he says that he came to Rome with the bishops named above, I do not think this should be understood to mean that he sailed from Antioch together with Paulinus or from the island of Cyprus together with Epiphanius. Since, as was said above, Jerome himself makes it clear that he remained at Constantinople with Gregory of Nazianzus until the time when Gregory attained the episcopate of that Church, it plainly appears that he did not leave Constantinople before the preceding year. I do not think he returned to Antioch to travel to Rome with Paulinus and Epiphanius. Rather, having been summoned by letters from Damasus to come to Rome, he undertook the journey through Greece and at that time wished to visit Athens.

That he actually visited Athens is confirmed by these words in his commentary on Zechariah: “In the citadel of the Athenians, beside the statue of Minerva, I saw a bronze sphere of very great weight, which I could scarcely move because of the weakness of my little body. When I asked what it meant, the inhabitants of the city replied that the strength of athletes was tested by that mass, and that no one descended into the contest before the lifting of the weight revealed whom he should be compared with” (Jerome, *Commentary on Zechariah*, chapter XII). These are his own words.

Thus Jerome, leaving Constantinople and coming through Greece into Italy, could have encountered the same bishops, who had been summoned at the same time and were coming to Rome. He too is believed to have come at the summons of Pope Damasus, so that Damasus might use him in composing synodal replies.

It also seems that Jerome and the other bishops arrived at Rome in the autumn. For although Jerome says in his letter to Asella that he remained at Rome for nearly three years, though he did not quite complete the period, Jerome’s assertion in his *Apology against Rufinus* makes it certain that he left Rome in August. Therefore he must have come to Rome this year, in autumn—as stated above—or in winter.

# Second Journey to Jerusalem

**A.D. 385. Baronius, under the same year.**—At the beginning of the year 385, specifically on the day before the Ides of January, after the see had been vacant for thirty-one days following the death of Damasus, Siricius, a Roman born to a father from Tibur, was substituted in his place.

Since Pope Siricius, unlike Damasus, did not employ Jerome’s services in composing such letters, nor embrace and support him as Damasus reasonably had, Jerome, deprived of the protection of the Roman pontiff, soon began to suffer the bitterest persecution from those clerics whose wicked conduct he had attacked in his published writings.

Therefore, in order to free himself from the raging storm, he considered a peaceful harbor—namely, a safe residence at Jerusalem—and, intending to sail there, left the city this year and made his way to the Roman port. That this happened in this year is made clear by the fact that Jerome himself testifies that he remained at Rome for almost three years (Jerome, Letter 99), and likewise that he left after the death of Damasus. Since the facts stated above establish that he came to Rome during the consulship of Antonius and Syagrius, in A.D. 382, he must have left the city this year. Accordingly, in August of the present year, he went to the Roman port and boarded a ship, as he clearly demonstrates in his *Apology against Rufinus* (Jerome, Book II *Against Rufinus*).

He describes who Jerome’s companions were on the voyage, and when he sailed from the port, in the same *Apology against Rufinus*, in these words:

“Do you wish to know the order of my departure from the city? I shall tell it briefly. In the month of August, when the Etesian winds were blowing, I boarded a ship safely at the Roman port with the holy presbyter Vincentius, my younger brother, and the other monks [This brother was Paulinianus, whom Jerome, while in Rome, summoned to come to him, since he was the youngest-born.], who now live at Jerusalem, while a great crowd of holy people escorted me.

“I came to Rhegium and stayed for a short time on the shore of Scylla, where I learned the ancient stories: the headlong course of deceitful Ulysses, the songs of the Sirens, and the insatiable whirlpool of Charybdis. When the inhabitants of that place told me many things and advised me to sail not to the pillars of Proteus but to the harbor of Jonah—for the former was the course of those fleeing and in turmoil, while the latter was the course of a secure man—I preferred to travel by Malea and the Cyclades to Cyprus.

“There I was welcomed by the venerable bishop Epiphanius, whose testimony you boast of. I came to Antioch, where I enjoyed communion with the bishop and confessor Paulinus. Led onward by him, I entered Jerusalem in midwinter and in the bitterest cold. I saw many miracles, and whatever rumor had previously brought to me, I confirmed by the judgment of my own eyes.”

Thus far Jerome concerning his arrival at Jerusalem.

# Journey to Egypt

**A.D. 386. Baronius, under the same year.**—Since the holy Jerome had arrived in Jerusalem in midwinter, there is no doubt that he remained there for some time. He later departed for Egypt, drawn by a desire to learn. Although he had become the teacher of almost the entire world, and Pope Damasus had long been accustomed to consult him—writing replies in the name of the pope to the consultations of bishops and instructing nearly all the Churches—he nevertheless sought out Didymus of Alexandria and placed himself under his instruction as a disciple to be trained in the sacred Scriptures.

He himself testifies to this in a letter to Pammachius, where he writes: “My head was already sprinkled with gray hairs, and it was more fitting for me to be a teacher than a disciple; nevertheless I proceeded to Alexandria. I heard Didymus, and I give him thanks in many respects: I learned what I did not know, and through his teaching I did not lose what I knew” (Jerome, Letter 65).

Elsewhere, to the same man, he says: “When I was in Alexandria, I saw Didymus and frequently visited him, the most learned man of his generation. I asked him to complete what Origen had not done and to write commentaries on Hosea. At my request he dictated three books, and five more on Zechariah” (Jerome, preface to Hosea). Thus far his letter to Pammachius.

And to St. Paula: “Finally, only recently and especially for this reason I went to Alexandria, to see Didymus and ask him about all the Scriptures concerning whatever doubts I had” (Jerome, preface to Book IV of the *Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians). These are his words to Paula. Since he makes no mention of having accompanied her when she traveled to Egypt, and since elsewhere, when discussing Paula’s journey to the same province, he does not say that he clung to her as her companion (Jerome, Letter 27), we are clearly led by conjecture to conclude that Jerome did not undertake that journey with her.

Rufinus reproaches Jerome in an invective for having remained in Alexandria only a short time—merely thirty days—to hear Didymus; whether this is true, he himself knows.

Jerome, who had settled in Alexandria for some time in order to hear Didymus, traveled through the monasteries of Egypt before returning to Palestine. Concerning these he himself says: “I hastened to Egypt, visited the monasteries of Nitria, and among the choirs of the saints saw vipers lying hidden” (Jerome, *Apology against Rufinus*).

By “vipers” he himself often declares elsewhere that he meant the Origenists. But we shall discuss them more fully in their proper place.

But what he did afterward he adds immediately: “At once I returned with hurried steps to my Bethlehem, where I worshiped the manger and the cradle of the Savior. I also saw the most famous lake; nor did I surrender myself to idle leisure, but learned many things that I had not known before.” But what were these things? Elsewhere he explains in these words, after recounting his return from Egypt to Palestine: “People thought that, after hearing Didymus, I had finished learning; I came again to Jerusalem and Bethlehem. With what labor, at what price, did I have Barabbas as a nocturnal teacher? For he feared the Jews and presented me with another Nicodemus” (Jerome, Letter 65). These are his own words.

# ON THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS, BOOK ONE, BY THE BLESSED PRESBYTER JEROME AND VARIOUS OTHERS

## [LIFE OF SAINT PAUL]

[Col. 0101]

## PRELIMINARY MATERIAL TO THE LIFE OF SAINT PAUL, THE FIRST HERMIT, OR TESTIMONIES CONCERNING PAUL HIMSELF AND HIS LIFE

[Col. 0101A]

**Gelasius, Distinction 15, chapter “The Holy Roman Church.”**

“We receive with every honor the Lives of the Fathers—of Paul, Antony, Hilarion, and all the hermits—which, nevertheless, the blessed man Jerome wrote.”

**Jerome, in the Chronicle, in the nineteenth year of Constantius the Younger.**

“The monk Antony died in the desert in the one hundred and fifth year of his age. He was accustomed to relate many things to those who came to him concerning a certain Theban, a man of extraordinary blessedness.”

[Note: [Col. 0101B] **Paul.** The birth and death of Paul, the first hermit, since they are assigned to no consuls or years of emperors, must be investigated from Antony’s age, as the illustrious Baronius rightly advised. Antony’s birth and death, however, are expressly recorded in the Chronicle of Eusebius and Jerome under definite imperial years. To these I shall add the years of the Christians from the latest edition of Pontacus and Scaliger, which were supplied by later editors, since they are absent from the ancient manuscripts. I must first point out that Baronius used a defective edition of Eusebius, which places Antony’s death in the twenty-first year of Constantius the Younger. I shall therefore follow the manuscript of Eusebius from Amiens, which I use, written a thousand years ago in capital letters—a sign of its antiquity. In this respect the editions of Pontacus and Scaliger agree with it here. I shall prove at greater length, in the Life of Saint Antony, that the edition used by Baronius is defective. Antony’s birth is therefore assigned there to the first year of the emperor Decius, which Pontacus dates to A.D. 254 and Scaliger to 252; his death, however, is assigned to the nineteenth year of Constantius the Younger, which Pontacus dates to A.D. 359 and Scaliger to 357. Since the Chronicle says at this latter point that Antony died in the 105th year of his age, exactly 105 years intervene between the first year of Decius and the nineteenth year of Constantius the Younger.

[Col. 0101C] Indeed, according to the calculations of Pontacus and Scaliger, the first year of Decius is not counted among Antony’s years of age; otherwise 106 years would be attributed to him. Whether, nevertheless, the first year of Decius ought to be counted, while only 105 years elapsed from it to the nineteenth year of Constantius the Younger, I shall discuss in the Life of Antony.

Now, since the Life of Paul says that Antony was ninety years old when he visited Paul, while at that same time Paul was 113 years old, as the same Life records, and since Antony lived 105 years, as stated above, it follows that Antony survived Paul by fifteen years. Paul’s death must therefore be placed fifteen years before Antony’s death. Since Antony died in the nineteenth year of Constantius, or A.D. 359 according to Pontacus and 357 according to Scaliger, it is clearly deduced that Paul died in the fourth year of Constantius, which is A.D. 344 according to Pontacus’s reckoning or 342 according to Scaliger’s. Paul’s birth must therefore be placed in the seventh year of the emperor Alexander, which is A.D. 231 according to Pontacus or 229 according to Scaliger. Accordingly, in the fifth year of Gordian, which is A.D. 245 according to Pontacus or 243 according to Scaliger, Paul was fifteen years old—the age of approximately fifteen years which Jerome says he had reached when, after the death of his parents, he was left their heir.

But since Jerome says in Paul’s Life that he withdrew “to a more remote estate, when the storm of persecution was thundering,” clearly referring to Decius and Valerian, whom he had mentioned immediately beforehand, if Paul’s flight is assigned to the first year of Decius, which is A.D. 254 according to Pontacus or 252 according to Scaliger, it follows that Paul was then twenty-four years old. Caesar Baronius, certainly, as he explains more fully in his notes on this Life, places Paul’s flight in the first year of Decius, to which he assigns the parallel year A.D. 253; but he places Paul’s death in the seventh year of Constantius, namely A.D. 343. Yet, as I said, he followed an uncorrected copy of Eusebius at the year of Antony’s death, making it the foundation of his whole construction; once that foundation is shaken, the remaining calculations must collapse.

The calculation in the manuscript Florarium of the Saints is remarkable, since it refers Paul’s death to A.D. 355; still more remarkable is that of Theodoric Loher of Strassburg, who prepared the Cologne edition of the Lives of the Fathers. At the end of Paul’s Life he noted that Paul died about A.D. 287, having taken this erroneous calculation from Peter in the Catalogue of the Saints, Book II, chapter 60.]

We have set forth his end in a short treatise.

**The same author, Letter 21 to Paul of Concordia.**

“In the meantime we have sent you to yourself—that is, Paul the elder, Paul the older.”

[Note: [Col. 0103C] **Paul the elder, Paul the older.** Paul of Concordia was only a hundred years old, as the same letter makes explicit: “Behold, the circle of a hundred years of life is already turning.” Paul, however, the first hermit, was 113 years old, as is recorded in his Life. Of Paul of Concordia the blessed Jerome likewise says in *On Illustrious Men of the Church*, chapter 53, in the entry on Tertullian: “I myself saw at Concordia, a town of Italy, a certain old man named Paul, etc.” Jerome may perhaps also be referring to the same man in Letter 6 to Florentius: “A certain old man Paul, from the homeland of the aforesaid brother Rufinus, also wrote to me that Tertullian’s copy was in his possession,” etc.]

In this passage, for the sake of the simpler readers, we labored greatly to lower the style of our speech.

[Note: [Col. 0103D] **“In lowering the style of our speech.”** Baronius, volume III, A.D. 343, the seventh year of the emperors Constantius and Constans: Divine Providence wisely willed that the history of Paul’s life should be written by Saint Jerome, a man utterly remote from every fabrication of fables, who could have consecrated to lasting memory in his writings only matters most fully verified by himself. Especially when writing the events of his own age, he could have been convicted of falsehood by any prudent person and mocked alike by any man from the crowd; and he knew that he had adversaries of keenest scent, seizing every opportunity, however slight, to criticize his writings. Yet—what is lamentable—writings which so many succeeding ages have approved by constant reading and venerated have by no means escaped the Hagiomachian Aristarchuses of our own time. From the Hippocentaur and Faun mentioned in the Acts of his Life, they infer that everything written there is a playful fabrication. Thus far Baronius. Who these Hagiomachi were who judged this Life a playful fabrication because of its mention of the Hippocentaur and Faun, I do not know; indeed, that their argument is itself frivolous will appear in the note on that passage. Erasmus and the Magdeburg Centuriators offer another explanation, maintaining that Saint Jerome was playing in this Life; see below. This view comes from Erasmus and the Magdeburg Centuriators, Century IV, chapter 10. This one passage alone refutes them, for Jerome testifies that he was so far from exercising and elevating his style here in the manner of rhetoricians that he deliberately attempted to lower it for the sake of simpler readers. The learned Alanus Copus connects this argument admirably in Dialogue II, chapter 14: “But these new rhetoricians from Magdeburg,” he says, “play too much with serious matters and wickedly mock the world here. And what a foolish and dull Gelasius, who, in his authority, places this history among the Lives of the Fathers—not as a joke but seriously” (Gelasius, Distinction 15, chapter “The Holy”). Yet this incredible stupidity, if we listen to such acute disputants, has existed not only in Gelasius but until now throughout the Greek and Latin Church. What could be said or imagined more foolish than this? Even if we set aside every authority from elsewhere, the very sequence of the narrative, and especially the clause that concludes it, clearly demonstrates the contrary: “I beg you,” he says, “whoever reads this, to remember Jerome the sinner, who, if the Lord gave him a choice, would much rather choose Paul’s tunic together with his merits than the purple of kings together with their kingdoms.” Do these words sound like those of an orator who is merely playing? These few words inflict no small wounds on the Magdeburg writers, so that they would like, on their account at least, the credibility of the entire history to be undermined. Here we have remembrance and prayers for the dead; here the garment of a monk is held in the highest esteem; here, finally, the merits of monks—whose merits, they most offensively attack, saying that no merits exist either in them or in any saint—are preferred by Jerome to entire kingdoms. If Jerome is doing nothing more than playing, through some dangerous rhetoric, with so great a Father and such serious matters, and if he is so craftily composing a fable under the title of history, then he is no longer worthy of anyone’s remembrance before God, but rather worthy of being cursed by all good people as one who has deceived them in this way. But all is well, and the matter is entirely secure; it does not require our defense. Jerome, as though he had foreseen that these Magdeburg writers would one day arise, defended both himself and his Paul, and Hilarion as well, against their absurdities and slanders: “We despise,” he says, “the voices of slanderers, who once disparaged my Paul and perhaps will now disparage Hilarion as well—slandering the former for his solitude and reproaching the latter for his crowds, so that the one who was always hidden may be thought not to have existed, while the one who was seen by many may be considered worthless. Their predecessors, the Pharisees, once did the same; neither the wilderness and fasting of John nor the crowds, food, and drink of the Lord and Savior pleased them. But I shall lay my hand upon the work I have undertaken and pass the Scyllaean dogs with stopped ears.”]

Yet somehow, even if it is full of water, the flask nevertheless preserves the same odor.

[Note: [Col. 0104C] **“The flask preserves the same odor.”** The blessed Jerome often uses the same phrase and comparison. Thus, in Letter 7 to Laeta: “A new vessel long retains both the taste and the smell with which it was first soaked.” Likewise, in Book I of the *Apology against Rufinus*: “If you had learned letters, your vessel would smell of the quality of your little mind, with which it had once been soaked.” And in chapter 1 of the commentary on Ephesians: “Whatever the liquid was that was poured into the new vessel, the vessel long retains both its smell and its taste.” This is taken from Horace, *Epistle* 1.11:

> What it has once absorbed, the fresh vessel will preserve its odor  
> For a long time . . .

—that is, with which it was soaked while still new.]

**The same author, *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 135.**

“I wrote the Life of Paul the monk.”

**The same author, Letter 22 to Eustochium.**

“The author of this life is Paul, its illuminator is Antony, and, to ascend to earlier times, its founder is John the Baptist.”

**The same author, Letter 27 to Eustochium.**

“Paula alone, if such a thing may be said, and without a companion, longed to go to the desert of the Antonies and the Pauls.”

**Paulinus, in the prologue to the Life of Saint Ambrose, 4 April.**

“You urge me, venerable Father Augustine, just as the blessed men Athanasius, bishop, and Jerome, presbyter, composed in writing the lives of the saints Paul and Antony, who lived in the desert, etc.”

**Sidonius, Eucharistic poem XVI, to Faustus.**

[Col. 0102B]

“Now Antony, naked in that tunic, calls you—that tunic which the kindly hand of his master made from palm leaves.”

[Note: [Col. 0104C] **“Which it made from palm leaves.”** Jerome says in Paul’s Life, chapter 5: “The palm supplied him with food and clothing.” And in chapter 10: “He clothed himself with woven palm leaves.” And in chapter 13: “He had woven it for himself from palm leaves in the form of a basket.” The pious heir Antony later possessed it among the intestate’s goods, as you can see in chapter 13.

Someone may ask here why so few of the ancients remember Paul of Thebes. I answer that he lived almost his entire life in the desert, unknown to everyone and known only to himself and God. Only a few things concerning him became known through Antony’s report: “For how he lived through the middle period of his life, or what ambushes of Satan he endured, is known to no human being,” as Jerome says in the prologue to this Life. Therefore Jerome professes that he will write only briefly about Paul’s beginning and end, since the matter had been neglected down to his own time.

I also think that this was why Jerome’s opponents, as we saw earlier, once doubted this Paul of Thebes, supposing that no such man had existed who had always lived in solitude and whom no one except Jerome had therefore remembered. From this it may also be inferred that the blessed Jerome was the first to commit Paul the hermit’s deeds to writing for the memory of posterity.

Even if there are certain Greek materials in the Bavarian Library that agree with Jerome’s writings, apart from a few details that Jerome has interwoven, I would nevertheless judge that these were later translated from Jerome’s Latin text. If they had existed in Jerome’s time and he had seen them, he would certainly have mentioned them; nor would he have said of Antony that his life had been “carefully handed down to memory in both Greek and Roman style,” while saying of Paul that “the matter had been neglected.”

I think Jerome learned these things about Paul from Amathas and Macarius, Antony’s disciples, who informed him that Paul of Thebes had been the founder of the eremitical way of life. When Jerome committed Paul’s Life to writing, I do not know whether it can be determined from any other source. From the prologue to this Life it may be inferred that it was written while Amathas and Macarius, Antony’s disciples, were still alive. For he says of them: “Even now they affirm it.”

If the reading of the ancient editions and of certain manuscripts is correct, the Life appears to have been written in the Syrian desert, at chapter 5. It reads there: “In that part of the desert which borders Syria and the Saracens, and I both saw and see monks.” However, the words “and I see” are absent from certain manuscripts and more recent editions.]


[Col. 0105]

# JANUARY 10. LIFE OF SAINT PAUL, THE FIRST HERMIT, BY THE BLESSED PRESBYTER JEROME

(See the text of this Life among the works of Saint Jerome, *Patrologia*, volume XXIII, column 17, edited and annotated by Vallarsi and Maffei. Here, however, it is useful to transcribe Rosweyde’s annotations, since they are of the greatest importance, and we believe that we are doing the readers a great service. We mark with an asterisk those places cited at the beginning of the notes where they differ from Vallarsi’s text.)

[Note: [Col. 0105B]

**“Life.”** Erasmus says that there was such great variation among the copies that it appears either that the blessed Jerome treated the same subject more than once in different words, or that someone else did this in order to exercise his verbal abundance. I myself find no such great variation, either in printed or manuscript copies. From time to time I have found certain words changed, whether through the carelessness or boldness of copyists. But I have always reproduced the oldest reading.

**“Of Saint Paul.”** The Roman Martyrology, 10 January: “In the Thebaid, the feast-day of blessed Paul, the first hermit, who remained alone in the desert from the sixteenth year of his age until his one hundred and thirteenth year. Saint Antony saw his soul carried by angels into heaven among the choirs of the apostles and prophets. His feast, however, is celebrated on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February” [15 January]. Nothing concerning him appears in the Menologion. The Menaea contain a brief summary of his life on 15 January.

Bede, Usuard, Rabanus, Ado, and Notker agree with the Roman Martyrology, except for the closing statement that his feast is celebrated on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February. Jerome also mentions Paul in Letter 13 to Paulinus; Cassian in Conferences XVIII, chapters 5 and 6; Saint Aldhelm, *On the Praise of Virgins*, Book I, chapter 31; Isidore, *On the Ecclesiastical Offices*, Book II, chapter 15; Vincent, *Historical Mirror*, Book XI, chapter 86 and the following two chapters; Antoninus, *Chronicle*, Part II, title XV, chapter 3; and Peter of Equilinum, *Catalogue of the Saints*, Book II, chapter 60.

Peter Galesinius, however, in his annotations on the Roman Martyrology for 10 January, says that Cassiodorus remembers this Paul in Book I, chapter 11 of the *Tripartite History*, and that Heraclides mentions him in many places. He is entirely mistaken. In that passage Cassiodorus, following Sozomen, mentions Paul the Simple. Heraclides likewise mentions not Paul the first hermit, but Paul the Simple and other Pauls.

**“The first hermit.”** Rodolphus Hospinianus, *On the Origin of Monasticism*, Book II, chapter 1: “Abba Piamun,” he says, “in Cassian, Conference XVIII, chapter 4, calls those men anchorites—that is, seceders—who, having first been trained in coenobitic communities, chose the solitude of the desert.” He says similar things in Book V of the *Institutes*, chapter 36.

But, continues the heretic, when Piamun writes in Conference XVIII, chapter 6 that the founders of these men were either a certain Paul of Thebes or Antony of Egypt, he is easily convicted of error, since neither of them was first trained in coenobitic communities.

But the heretic is talking nonsense, ever eager to seize an opportunity to disparage holy men. Piamun does not mean that absolutely all anchorites came from coenobitic communities; he means that in his own time, from the most fruitful root of coenobia, flowers and fruits of holy anchorites later came forth—that is, that coenobia were nurseries of anchorites, although Paul and Antony, the founders of this profession, flew to the desert not from coenobia but from their paternal homes, each by his own particular route.

**“By whom, above all, the monks’ desert began to be inhabited.”** There are various opinions concerning the first inhabitant of the desert, which have already been examined by many ascetic writers. See Bellarmine, volume II, *Controversies*, general controversy II; *On Monks*, Book II, chapter 39, which concerns hermits, where he also admirably refutes the heretics’ slanders against this order and state.

What the blessed Jerome adds here concerning John, Paul, and Antony is also found in Letter 22 to Eustochium: “The author of this life is Paul, its illuminator Antony; and, to ascend to earlier times, its founder was John the Baptist.”

**“From blessed Elijah and John.”** This opinion is frequently mentioned by the holy Fathers and historians. Basil, in his Letter to Chilo:

> “Here is the famous mountain, Carmel, on which Elijah, dwelling there, pleased God, etc. Here is the desert in which blessed John, eating locusts, prescribed and proclaimed by his preaching the rule by which human beings are to accomplish repentance.”

Gregory Nazianzen, Oration V, or *Apologetic Oration after His Return from Flight*:

> “I was thinking of Elijah’s Carmel and John’s desert.”

The same author, concerning the same men, Oration XXV.

John Chrysostom, Homily 69 on Matthew, refers the monastic use of clothing to the example of Elijah, Elisha, and John the Baptist.

Theophylact, on Luke 1:

> “John came in the power and spirit of Elijah, because he too was a hermit and lived a frugal life.”

Cassian, Conference XVIII, chapter 6:

> “They should not fear penetrating the vast recesses of the desert, in imitation, of course, of John the Baptist, who remained in the desert throughout his life, and likewise of Elijah and Elisha,” etc.

The Life of Pachomius, chapter 1:

> “Antony, being an emulator of the great Elijah and Elisha, and also of Saint John the Baptist.”

Sozomen, Book I, chapter 12:

> “This excellent way of life was first instituted, as some say, by the prophet Elijah and John the Baptist.”

The same is found in Nicephorus, Book VIII, chapter 39.

Concerning Elijah, Jerome, Letter 13 to Paulinus:

> “Our leader is Elijah, our leader Elisha, and our leaders are the sons of the prophets, who lived in fields and solitudes and made tabernacles for themselves beside the streams of the Jordan” (2 Kings 6).

Concerning John, Chrysostom, Homily 1 on Mark:

> “Just as the apostles are the chief priests among priests, so John the Baptist is the chief among monks.”

And in the same author’s homily on John the Baptist:

> “Consider, monks, your dignity. John is the founder of your way of life; he was a monk from the moment he was born, living in the desert and nourished in the desert.”

And Jerome, Letter 22 to Eustochium, whose words I quoted earlier.

Concerning both men, living a solitary life, the same Jerome writes in chapter 7 of Micah; Isidore likewise, Book II, chapter 15, *On the Divine Offices*.

**“But Amathas and Macarius, Antony’s disciples.”** There were three celebrated disciples of Saint Antony, concerning whom the blessed Jerome says in the Chronicle, in the nineteenth year of Constantius the Younger—A.D. 367 according to Scaliger, or 359 according to Pontacus: “Sarmatas, Amathas, and Macarius are regarded as distinguished disciples of Antony.”

Palladius also mentions Amathas and Macarius in chapter 25 of the *Lausiac History*. This Macarius, Antony’s disciple, appears to have been Macarius of Alexandria, concerning whom Palladius, in chapter 20, relates a remarkable event that occurred in Antony’s presence. He says that this Macarius was also a presbyter of the Cells, just as another Macarius was the Egyptian presbyter of Scetis. More will be said of them in Book II, here. Peter is therefore mistaken in making Macarius the Egyptian a disciple of Antony in the *Catalogue*, Book II, chapters 35 and 81.

**“The elder of whom buried his master’s body.”** I think Jerome means Amathas, for in Jerome’s narrative he is the elder, or predecessor, of Macarius. I am therefore surprised that in the Life of Saint Posthumius, below, chapter 7, we read: “Macarius, of whom we have often spoken, buried his master’s body.” Unless someone wishes to refer the word “elder” to the person immediately preceding, namely Macarius. In that case there will be no disagreement.

Palladius, chapter 25, attributes Antony’s burial to both men: “When I had come to his monastery, which is beside the river, where his disciples Macarius and Amathas were living, they also buried him when he had fallen asleep.”

**“To have been the founder of this undertaking. Which we approve not so much by name as by opinion.”** Here the manuscripts vary remarkably. Some read: “To have been the founder of this undertaking, not so much by opinion as by name.” Others: “To have been the founder of this undertaking, not merely in name. This opinion.” Others: “To have been the founder of this undertaking, but not in name. This opinion.” This variation undoubtedly arose from the difficulty of the meaning. The more widely accepted reading is the one I have reproduced in the text.

There is also disagreement concerning the meaning. Matthew Galenus Westcapellius, in chapter 4 of *On the Origin of Monasticism*, thinks that the blessed Jerome is saying that Paul of Thebes was the founder of the eremitical life, not so much in name—that is, in the opinion of Amathas and Macarius, Antony’s disciples, who made this assertion—as in the judgment that we too approve. It seems to me that the genuine meaning of the blessed Jerome is that, according to his own judgment and opinion, Paul was the founder of the eremitical life, not merely in name; that is, Paul truly was the founder of the eremitical life, and was not merely commonly called so, whether rightly or wrongly.

[Col. 0108A]

**“A long-haired man, down to the heels, in an underground cave.”** Saint Macarius the Roman is described in similar fashion later in his Life, chapter 15: “The hair of his head covered the man’s entire body.” But he was later than Saint Paul of Thebes, since he lived after the reign of Julian, as is recorded in his Life. Nevertheless, since he was then very old, as his hair, white as snow, indicates, he could have been a contemporary of Saint Paul.

Saint Onuphrius also had such hair, below, in his Life, chapter 2: “His hair was so long that his body was covered by its spreading.” He too lived later than Saint Paul, and his life has been approved. Jerome may therefore have been referring here to some other tale concerning a fictitious hermit.

**“Because Antony’s life had been written in both Greek and Roman style.”** Saint Athanasius wrote the Life of Saint Antony in Greek, and Evagrius of Antioch translated it into Latin, as will be discussed fully below.

**“Under the persecutors Decius and Valerian.”** Baronius, A.D. 253, the first year of Decius.
