Since Jerome says that under Decius and Valerian Paul became an exile, Valerian was added for this reason: while Decius was departing for Persia, as we shall explain, Valerian acted as the emperor’s representative at Rome and harassed the Christians by edicts.

**“In the same year.”** In that first year of his reign, Decius assembled an army and undertook war against the Persians, leaving Valerian at Rome. By decree of the Senate, as Trebellius records, he entrusted him with supreme authority; indeed, he granted him the censorship and added the power to draft laws. Hence it happened that the names of Decius and Valerian were jointly inscribed on the edicts. An edict of persecution against the Christians bearing their names survives in the Acts of Saint Mercury the martyr, although Valerian’s name is also read there with the title “Augustus.” We think, however, that this title was added later rather than inscribed at that time.

**“In the same year.”** For this reason the laws were also inscribed in Valerian’s name, and edicts were promulgated against the Christians, to such an extent that the same persecution was regarded as belonging to both men, namely Decius and Valerian, and continued to be called by their names thereafter. Once the persecution of men considered supremely just and holy had been ennobled by the title of their names, and thereby made to appear more religious and just, it proceeded all the more freely against the Church of Christ.

From these points, therefore, many difficulties and confusions are resolved. Many martyrs are said to have suffered together in the persecution of Decius and Valerian, although it is clear that the two emperors did not reign simultaneously but at different times. Some who plainly suffered under Decius are nevertheless said to have completed their martyrdom under Valerian; and those whom Valerian’s persecution destroyed are likewise said to have suffered under Decius and Valerian. Anyone who does not consider these matters will necessarily become entangled in countless and entirely insoluble errors, be driven along byways, and be delayed amid the many twists and turns of the roads. See also Baronius, on the Roman Martyrology, 10 August.

[Col. 0108D]

**“At the time when Cornelius was at Rome and Cyprian at Carthage.”** Baronius, A.D. 253, the first year of Decius. What Jerome says—that Paul then sought the deserts, when Cornelius at Rome and Cyprian at Carthage suffered martyrdom—must be understood in this way: Paul withdrew during the same persecution in which Cornelius and Cyprian were put to death.

Although Decius and Valerian did not reign simultaneously, and although the persecution was interrupted by a brief interval of peace, nevertheless, because it was continued and renewed through the same edicts by which it had been proclaimed, it is regarded as one and the same persecution, and was called by the names of both Decius and Valerian.

**“Cornelius at Rome.”** The memory of Pope Cornelius appears in the Roman Martyrology on 14 September: “At Rome, on the Appian Way, the blessed Cornelius, pope and martyr,” etc. Baronius, in the *Annals*, A.D. 255, the second year of the emperors Gallus and Volusian, asserts that he was crowned with martyrdom.

**“Cyprian at Carthage.”** His celebrated memory also appears in the Roman Martyrology on 14 September: “In Africa, the passion of Saint Cyprian, bishop of Carthage,” etc. Baronius places his martyrdom, crowned with the laurel of martyrdom, in A.D. 261.

**“A savage storm devastated many churches in Egypt and the Thebaid.”** See in Eusebius, Book VI, chapters 33 and 34, the letter of Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, in which he heaps up accounts of this storm’s assaults upon the Alexandrian Church. You will find them explained more fully in Baronius, A.D. 253, the first year of Decius.

**“The Thebaid.”** Jerome’s customary and anachronistic form, *Thebaida*, for *Thebais*. Thus, in the Life of Saint Sebastian, 20 January, *Persida* is used for *Persis*. See the *Onomasticon* below.

**“The crafty enemy, seeking punishments that were slow to bring death.”** Cyprian, Letter 8, concerning this Decian persecution:

> “Tortures came—tortures without an end to the torturer, without a sentence’s conclusion, without the consolation of death; tortures that do not readily release a person to the crown, but torment him until they overthrow him, unless someone, withdrawn by divine favor, makes progress amid the very tortures, attaining glory not through the end of punishment but through the speed of dying.”

The Acts of Saint Gorgonius the martyr, during the time of Diocletian:

> “The grating is not heated suddenly but gradually and little by little, so that the labor of martyrdom would be all the more cruel the longer the delay of the burning.”

**“Those who wished to die were not permitted to be killed.”** Cyprian, Letter 53, to Fortunatus and his companions:

> “We see men who did not fall through weakness of spirit, but who, having entered the battle, were unable, because of the weakness of the flesh, to bear through to the crown of their confession—especially since those who desired to die were not permitted to be killed. Rather, the tortures tore apart the exhausted for as long as they could, until they conquered not the faith, which is fortified, but wearied the flesh, which is weak.”

**“A martyr persevering in the faith.”** The memory of this martyr and of the one who follows appears in the Roman ecclesiastical calendars on 28 July, in words modeled on this passage of Jerome. Baronius, following Jerome, also discusses them under A.D. 253, the first year of Decius.

**“Victorious amid the racks and metal plates.”** Consult the *Onomasticon* concerning these tortures.

**“He ordered him to be smeared with honey.”** An example and vivid description of this punishment may be found in Apuleius, *Milesian Tale* VIII:

> “He seized a little slave, stripped him naked, smeared him entirely with honey, and bound him firmly to a fig tree, whose decaying trunk contained nests of ants; they swarmed in and out in countless streams. As soon as they sensed the sweet, honeyed odor of the body, clinging to it with their small but numerous and continual bites, they consumed him through prolonged torment, eating away his flesh and even his entrails, until, after the man had been devoured, they stripped the limbs bare, while the bones, deprived of their flesh and shining brilliantly white, remained attached to the mournful tree.”

Some refer here to *cyphonismus*, concerning which see the *Onomasticon*.

**“Frying pans set on fire.”** Frying pans are frequently mentioned in the Acts of the Martyrs. The *Onomasticon* will supply many passages from the authors.

**“Another, flourishing in the bloom of youth.”** Nicephorus, Book VII, chapter 13, gives a similar—if not identical—example of a certain ascetic during the persecution of Diocletian. Peter gives another similar account in the *Catalogue of the Saints*, Book VIII, chapter 70, on 12 September, concerning Nicetas, who suffered at Nicomedia during the time of Maximian; he adds many other details about the same man, including some extraordinary matters not easily accepted by everyone.

Marulus took from him the material found in Book V, chapter 5, where the annotator incorrectly added 24 July from Usuard’s Martyrology. For that day does not concern this Nicetas, but another virgin and martyr, the companion of Aquilina, concerning whom see the Acts of Saint Christopher.

[Col. 0110A] **“During the same period, therefore, when such things were taking place.”** Baronius places this in A.D. 253, the first year of the emperor Decius. In accordance with Jerome’s view, however, we must say that Paul became an exile at the very beginning of Decius’s persecution; this can be demonstrated clearly on his authority. For when he says that Paul was 113 years old when he departed this life, as Antony visited him, and that Antony was then ninety years old—whom he likewise says lived 105 years—and when, on Jerome’s testimony in the *Chronicle*, Antony is held to have died in the twenty-first year of Constantius, while Paul survived him by fifteen years, it follows that Paul died after the completion of the sixth year of Constantius and at the beginning of the seventh, which is reckoned as A.D. 343. Since, therefore, as has been said, Paul was 113 years old in the year of his death, it is necessary to affirm that in this very year 253 he was twenty-three years of age.

“Thus,” Baronius continues, “Paul was so far from seeking the desert under Valerian after these events that, if anyone wishes to maintain that he withdrew into the wilderness at the age of fifteen”—as many wrongly interpret the opinion of Saint Jerome—“it must be said that this happened not under Decius and Valerian but under Gordian, at a time when the Church enjoyed complete peace.”

For this reason, Paul’s age of fifteen years must not be referred to the time when he withdrew into solitude, but to the fact that he was then fifteen years old when he was deprived of his parents. Jerome plainly wished to signify this by the words: “After the death of both parents, Paul was left, in possession of a rich inheritance, about fifteen years old.” And what he had said immediately before—“during the period when such things were taking place”—must be referred to what he adds: “when the storm of persecution was thundering.” If these words are understood otherwise, Jerome is made to contradict himself and to lie—which it is impious to say—about the number of years Paul had when he withdrew into the desert.

Thus, according to the opinion of Saint Jerome himself, it is preferable to say that Paul was in his fifteenth year when he was deprived of his parents; and that, in the twenty-third year of his age, driven out by the first onslaught of the persecution, he first fled to his father’s estate and then took refuge in distant mountains. Having found a cave suitable for his purpose and already prepared for him, he remained unknown there for the rest of his life, until the age of 113.

Baronius correctly inferred Paul’s age from Antony’s age, which Jerome expressly recorded in the *Chronicle*. We regret, however, that so outstanding a historian used a corrupt text of the *Chronicle*, as I said earlier. Therefore this entire calculation of Baronius’s years must be measured against what was said above in the preliminary observations to this *Life*.

Those who maintain that Paul became an exile in the sixteenth year of his age—that is, after completing fifteen years—have all the martyrologists cited above as their supporters. With unanimous judgment and one voice, they seem to have understood and explained this passage of Jerome concerning Paul in that way.

[Col. 0110D] **“In the lower Thebaid.”** On the twofold Thebaid, see the *Onomasticon*.

**“He withdrew to a more remote and secluded village.”** In the letter of Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, to Fabius of Antioch, preserved by Eusebius, book VI, chapter 34, concerning the storm of Decian persecution, we read: Ἐξέκλινον δὲ καὶ ὑπανεχώρουν οἱ ἀδελφοί—“The brethren therefore turned aside from the road and withdrew to separated and solitary places.” The same author says there: Τί δεῖ λέγειν τὸ πλῆθος τῶν ἐν ἐρημίαις καὶ ὄρεσι πλανηθέντων, ὑπὸ λιμοῦ καί δίψης, καὶ κρύους καὶ νόσων, καὶ λῃστῶν, καὶ θηρίων διεφθαρμένων—“Why should I enumerate the multitude of those who, wandering and straying through deserts and mountains, were exposed to hunger, thirst, cold, diseases, robbers, and wild beasts?” According to Baronius, this occurred in A.D. 253, the first year of the emperor Decius.

**“Meanwhile, cruelty pressed on, which seemed to imitate piety*.”** Henry Gravius, a diligent reader of Jerome and collector of his phrases, says that some copies read: “It was present; it pressed on; it employed cruelty as though it were piety.” Several manuscripts likewise have this reading. Lucius Florus used the same formula in book III, chapter 5: “It was present; it pressed on; it employed savagery as though it were valor.” See note l, column 20, of the cited volume of *Patrologia*. EDIT.

**24.** As for Jerome’s meaning, he intends to say that Christians were harassed under the charge of impiety, and that violence was inflicted upon them under the pretext of religion, so that they might be recalled to paganism as though to piety. Thus, in book I of the *Life of Saint Sebastian*: “This is what, O most chaste wives of the blessed, under the guise of piety, made you betray the martyrs to impiety of mind.” Gregory of Nyssa, in the *Life of Gregory the Wonderworker*, 17 November, says: Ἄλλοι δὲ πρὸς τὰς κτήσεις τῶν πιστῶν ὁρῶντες, ὡς ἂν ἐγκρατεῖς γένοιντο τῶν πραγμάτων, ἐπὶ τῷ προσχήματι τῆς εὐσεβείας, ἤλαυνον τοὺς ἀντεχομένους τῆς πίστεως—“Others, looking greedily upon the possessions of the faithful so that they might gain control of their property, under the pretext of piety harassed and persecuted those who held fast to the faith.” [Col. 0111B] Paul was harassed in the same way by his brother-in-law. Saint Aldhelm likewise expressed this in book I *On the Praise of Virginity*, chapter 31: “Paul likewise, illustrious and most renowned among the Fathers, was betrayed and exposed against the laws of nature by a deceitful son-in-law, corrupted by the avarice of blind greed.” Thus that passage must be read according to a very ancient manuscript of our Antwerp College. The manuscript *Acts of Saint Gorgonius the Martyr*, from the time of Diocletian, says: “A father betrayed his son, a brother his brother, if he was found to belong to that sect, as an enemy by an open investigation; and therefore each person hid himself as best he could in caves or hiding places.”

How cruel Decius’s edict was is revealed by Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, in Eusebius, book VI, chapter 34: Καὶ δὴ καὶ παρῆν τὸ πρόσταγμα, αὐτὸ σχεδὸν ἐκεῖνο, οἷον τὸ προῤῥηθὲν ὑπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν παρὰ βραχὺ τὸ φοβερώτατον, ὡς, εἰ δυνατὸν, σκανδαλίσαι καὶ τοὺς ἐκλεκτούς—“For Decius’s edict had already been published, and it seemed almost exactly like that which our Lord had foretold, in which that most terrible saying of his was nearly fulfilled: that, if possible, even the elect would be led into error.” Nyssa also reports this in the passage already cited. You have Decius’s edict, breathing both that cruelty and that piety, in the *Life of Saint Mercury the Martyr* by Metaphrastes, 24 November.

**“He turned necessity into willingness.”** Cassian, *Conferences*, XVIII, chapter 6: “We know that the leaders of this way of life—the anchoritic life—were those whom we mentioned shortly before, namely Saint Paul and Antony. They did not, like some, seek the secrets of solitude because of cowardice or the disease of impatience, but from a desire for higher progress and divine contemplation, although the former is said to have entered the desert under the pretext of necessity, while, during the persecution, he avoided the plots of his relatives.”

**“Chisels, also anvils and hammers*.”** Thus the oldest manuscript of Saint Florian. It evidently describes the three principal instruments for striking coins that were found there. [Col. 0111D] On *chisels*, see the *Onomasticon*.

**“A workshop for counterfeit coin*.”** Erasmus says: “I should think that the cave shown today at Cumae was prepared for the same purpose”—namely, as a workshop for counterfeit money.

**“Therefore, having come to love the dwelling, as though* it were offered to him by God.”** In the *Life of Antony*, chapter 24: “Antony embraced this place as though it were offered to him by God.”

**“The palm supplied him with food and clothing.”** That is, food from the fruit of the dates, and clothing from the tree’s hairy leaves.

**“Which borders Syria beside the Saracens.”** This desert is frequently mentioned by Saint Jerome. In letter 6, to Florentius: “While I was staying in that part of the desert which borders Syria beside the Saracens.” In letter 43, to Chromatius, Jovinus, and Eusebius: “For after, through the agency of Saint Evagrius, they had been brought to me in that part of the desert which extends as a vast frontier between the Syrians and the Saracens.” In letter 57, to Damasus: “And because of my sins I have migrated to that solitude which separates Syria from the adjoining frontier of Barbaria.” In letter 58, to the same person: “Having received the garment of Christ in the city of Rome, I am now held by the barbarous frontier of Syria.” In the *Life of Malchus*, chapter 4: “The solitude through which the Saracens, with no fixed dwelling, are always wandering here and there.” See *Desert* in the *Onomasticon*.

**“The Syrians call it *cuba*.”** Gravius reads *guba*. For, he says, in Syriac *guba* means “cistern.” Jerome, on chapter VI of Jeremiah: “The Latin reader should understand this, and it is enough to have said it once: among the Greeks, *lakkos* (λάκκος) means not a pool but a cistern, which in the Syriac and Hebrew language is called *gebe*.” But *g* and *c* easily interchange. See the *Onomasticon*.

**“Five *caricae*.”** Some copies add “that is, dried figs” in the text. Below, in the *Life of Saint Hilarion*, chapter 3: “With the juice of herbs and a few dried figs he sustained his failing soul after three or four days.” [Col. 0112B] Consult the *Onomasticon*.

**“Supporting his weakened limbs by leaning on a staff.”** Jerome, on chapter I of Amos: “Not even people of extreme old age, who support their trembling limbs by the aid of a staff.” Likewise, on chapter VIII of Zechariah: “So that, with no enemy remaining, old age in both sexes may reach the final stage of life, and they may support their trembling limbs by the aid of a staff.”

**“A hippocentaur.”** Jerome himself explains it as a human being mixed with a horse. See the *Onomasticon*.

**“He arms his forehead with the saving imprint of the sign.”** Learn from Antony’s example, heretic, to arm the forehead with the sign of the cross. See *Cross* in the *Onomasticon*.

**“Among mouths bristling with hairs.”** Erasmus says that this passage differs in the copies and that no reading seems satisfactory to him. I see that some books have *senis* (“old man”), others *setis* (“bristles”); the latter is correct. Jerome intends to say that the hippocentaur sought a gentle utterance amid his mouths bristling with hairs—that is, he tried to answer gently, although his mouths bristled with hairs. For this reason it was naturally more apt to utter something barbarous, or to break off words and produce them with a kind of harsh noise. For if the passage referred to the aged Antony, Jerome would have said *address* rather than *utterance*.

**“But whether this was the devil.”** Baronius says, in A.D. 343, that faith is vainly demanded of one who, doubting what it was—whether a phantom or a monster—wished to safeguard his own credibility.

His doubt, however, was neither foolish nor empty: could Egypt, fertile in monsters, have produced an animal of this kind, compounded from two species? Although no one doubts that what poets sang about Ixion and the Centaurs is fiction, and although according to Celsus the promise to produce a centaur is empty—for he says: “If I have stipulated, ‘Present yourself; and, if you do not appear, let a hippocentaur be given’”—and although no one demands centaurs from nature as a species of animal, who would deny that nature has sometimes produced monsters of this kind? Thus Pliny writes: “Claudius Caesar records that a hippocentaur was born in Thessaly and died on the same day; and during his principate we ourselves saw one brought from Egypt to him preserved in honey” (Pliny, book VII, chapter 3). I say, preserved in honey, whose property is such that it does not allow bodies to decay. Alexander ab Alexandro, a highly trustworthy author, likewise testifies that a sea-man was brought in honey from the farthest part of Mauretania to Spain (Alexander ab Alexandro, book III, chapter 8). Anyone who reads him, concerning Tritons seen and captured in various places in his time, presenting a human face and an entirely human body down to the groin, then ending below in a fish, will not doubt that creatures can be found on land such as the sea also produces. For the dwelling of human beings is land rather than sea; and from the mixture of a human being with an animal such monsters might be conceived and generated.

**“Fauns, satyrs, and incubi.”** “There is frequent and certain mention of fauns among ancient historians,” Baronius adds, “in that same year, if we set aside the poets’ tales. Among them Pliny says that, apart from their outward appearance, they possessed nothing of human behavior” (Pliny, book V, chapter 8). All these events reported by Jerome as having happened to Antony must therefore be said to have occurred through a miracle, just as we often read of many other animals lacking reason that, as though endowed with human understanding and rendered almost rational by God’s command, performed services for holy men such as human beings ordinarily perform. To remain with Paul, this happened with the raven, which customarily brought Paul half a loaf of bread every day for so many years, but at Antony’s arrival—something worthy of wonder—brought a whole loaf, so that both men could be refreshed. Anyone wishing to know more about these matters should consult the *Onomasticon*.

**“Constantius.”** This is the reading, not *Constantine*, as many books have. Nicephorus, book IX, chapter 19, discussing the regions of the East and South and the various kinds of animals found in them, says: “The great number of these [apes] that have also been brought to us plainly demonstrates this. Among them is the creature called Pan, resembling a goat in head, face, and horns, and likewise standing below the hips on goat’s feet; but in belly, chest, and hands it is entirely an ape. The king of the Indians sent this creature to Constantius. For some time, while it was being transported in a cage, it lived enclosed because of its wildness. When it died, those transporting it embalmed it after removing its entrails and brought it preserved to Constantinople, so that its unusual form might be displayed. It seems to me that the Greeks of old saw this animal, and, terrified by the strangeness of its appearance, made it a god for themselves, since it was customary among them to deify whatever surpassed belief. They did the same with the satyr, which is itself also an ape.”

**“And after the holy kiss.”** Evidently according to apostolic practice: Romans 16; 1 Corinthians 16; 2 Corinthians 13; 1 Thessalonians 5; 1 Peter 5. See the *Onomasticon*.

[Col. 0113C] **“Rather, return earth to earth.”** Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, book III, from Euripides: “Earth must be returned to earth.” These are the words of Amphiaraus to the grieving mother of Archemorus; they are also found in Plutarch, *Consolation to Apollonius*. Fortunatus, book IV, epitaph 27, for Euphrasia:

“Earth returns to earth, but the spirit has received the stars.”

Thus it should be read, not *dedit* (“gave”) or *edit* (“eats”).

**“Bring the cloak to wrap my little body.”** See *Funeral* in the *Onomasticon*, where this rite of wrapping corpses in linen or a cloak is discussed.

**“But so that, as he was departing from him, his grief at his death might be lightened.”** Baronius, in A.D. 343, thinks that Paul requested the cloak from Antony not only for this reason, but because Antony, who knew Athanasius through prophetic insight and understood that the cloak had been given to Antony, also knew perfectly well of those great labors, exiles, flight, hardships, and countless other troubles that Athanasius had endured for the Catholic faith. Therefore Antony seems to have requested Athanasius’s cloak rather than another man’s garment, so that by this token of communion and inclination of heart toward Athanasius he might at least signify that he held in the highest regard the man whom so many struggles undertaken for the faith had made illustrious. In this way it would become known to all that so great a man approved the faith which Athanasius defended so vigorously and resolutely. This was evidently of no small importance for raising the spirits of those who were wavering and strengthening those who remained firm in the faith. The people are accustomed to value so highly the testimony of illustrious monks concerning the Catholic faith that, perceiving this, the Arians did not hesitate to lie by claiming that Antony agreed with them in their belief about the faith. For this reason Antony had to leave the deepest solitude of the desert, descend to Alexandria, and publicly give an account of the Catholic faith that he professed, lest the people should fall away. Athanasius himself affirms this in his *Life*.

[Col. 0114A] **“Having kissed his eyes and hands.”** Kissing of the hands is frequently encountered, but not so that of the eyes. These kisses were customarily offered both out of reverence and affection; they are discussed more fully in the *Onomasticon*.

**“To the monastery, which was later occupied by the Saracens.”** This occurred in the twentieth year of Constantius, A.D. 358. Jerome, in the *Chronicle*: “The Saracens, invading the monastery of blessed Antony, killed Sarmata.” His memory is recorded in the Roman *Martyrology*, 11 October: “In the Thebaid, Saint Sarmata, disciple of blessed Antony, who was killed by the Saracens for Christ.”

**“He scattered sand over his head.”** It was customary in mourning and grief to sprinkle the head with ashes, dust, or sand. This is frequently mentioned in the Sacred Scriptures. See the *Onomasticon*.

**“He saw him with his knees folded.”** This is the customary posture of those praying, entirely absent from the gatherings of heretics. See the *Onomasticon*.

**“Also singing hymns and psalms according to Christian tradition.”** This too was a customary Christian funeral rite, discussed in the *Onomasticon*.

[Col. 0114B] **“Two lions.”** A similar service by lions is found below in the *Life of Saint Onuphrius*, the final chapter.

**“He prepared the tomb according to custom.”** Jerome, in letter 49, to Innocent: “The clergy, whose duty this was, wrap the bloodstained corpse in linen and, building a pit with stones and earth, prepare the tomb according to custom.” By “clergy” he means the *copiatae*, or laborers, who were responsible for burying the bodies of the dead. Reatinus thinks that clergy are mentioned here because of the psalms being sung; although such psalms were sung at funerals according to ancient custom, the accompanying details suggest that the *copiatae* are intended here, since they once constituted a part of the clergy. See the *Onomasticon*.

**“From the goods of a man who died intestate.”** Cleverly put: for what extremely poor man makes a will, or decides what to leave to whom?

**“Those who do not know their own estates.”** Evidently because, as Ovid says in book XIII of the *Metamorphoses*:

“It is the poor man’s task to count his flock.”

And Horace, book I, letter 6:

“A scanty house is one where many things do not also remain,

elude the owner, and benefit thieves …”

**“Those who sew the prices of estates into a single thread.”** This is taken from Tertullian, *On the Dress of Women*, chapter 9: “Ten million sesterces are woven into a single linen thread; one neck bears estates and islands.”

**“He satisfied nature with hollowed hands.”** Laertius says the same of Diogenes, book VI; and Jerome, book II *Against Jovinianus*, chapter 9: “At one time, having a wooden cup for drinking, he saw a boy drink with his hollowed hand.” Thus it should be read according to an excellent manuscript of our Louvain College, not *cavum* (“hollow”). Therefore Marianus Victorius’s reading κοῖλον ξύλινον (“a hollow wooden vessel”) has no place here. In Laertius, instead of “wooden cup,” the word is κοτύλη (*kotyle*). The word *caucus* also occurs in the *Life of Saint Abraham the Hermit*, chapter 3, which will be discussed later.

[Col. 0114D] **“You wrap them in gilded garments.”** Concerning the clothing of the dead, see our Gretzer, book I *On Christian Funerals*, chapter 5, and Kirchmann, book I, chapter 10, *On Roman Funerals*. Here Jerome reproaches the rich for wrapping their bodies in gilded garments and silk, while such honor and religious observance were paid to holy men and martyrs. Saint Athanasius, in the *Life of Saint Antony*, chapter 56: “It is the custom among the Egyptians to wrap the bodies of nobles, and especially of blessed martyrs, in linen.” See the notes to that *Life*.

**“Of Jerome the sinner.”** Thus the Fathers often used to style and subscribe themselves out of humility. See the *Onomasticon*.

**“Paul’s tunic, together with his merits.”** Recognize, heretic, the merits of the faithful arising from holy works; and you who read and esteem Saint Jerome, imbibe his faith also for the salvation of your soul. Learn to value the relics and garments of the saints. Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration XXV: Καὶ ἡ μηλωτὴ Ἐλισαίου πλείω δυνηθεῖσα ἢ τά σηρῶν νήματα, καὶ ὁ βιασθεὶς εἰς ἐσθῆτα χρυσός—“And the sheepskin mantle of Elisha, which was able to accomplish more than threads of silk, and the gold forcibly sewn into a garment.” John Chrysostom, *Homily 2 to the People of Antioch*, where he says that the rich king needed the poor Elijah: Οὕτω λαμπροτέρα τῆς πορφυρίδος ἡ μηλωτὴ ἦν, καὶ τῶν βασιλικῶν αὐλῶν τὸ σπήλαιον τοῦ δικαίου—“So much more splendid than purple was the sheepskin mantle, and than royal courts was the cave of the righteous man.” Theodosius likewise preferred the sheepskin shoulder-cloak and staff of the monk Senuphius to his own helmet and spear. The *Acts of Cyrus and John*, in Metaphrastes, 31 January, say: “He protects his head with the shoulder-cloak, more safely than with any helmet; he protects his right hand with the staff, far more powerfully than with a spear; and in this way, confident that he would appear more terrifying to his enemies than Hercules once did, as they say, with his club.” Similar examples occur in Glycas, part IV of the *Annals*.

**(61) “Which he preferred to the purple of kings together with their kingdoms*.”** This is the reading of the manuscripts and older editions. More recent editions substituted “together with their punishments”; I do not know on what authority.]

[VITA B. ANTONII.]

[Col. 0115]

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIFE OF BLESSED ANTONY

## EULOGIES OF ILLUSTRIOUS MEN ON BLESSED ANTONY

[Col. 0115B]

### Jerome, *On Illustrious Men of the Church*, chapter 88

Antony the monk, whose life Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, presented in a remarkable volume, sent seven letters in the Egyptian language to various monasteries, filled with apostolic thought and speech; these were translated into Greek, and the most important was addressed to the Arsenoites. He flourished during the reign of Constantine and his sons. He lived 105 years.

### The same author, in the *Chronicle*, year 19

[Note: [Col. 0117C] **“In the nineteenth year of Constantius.”** Thus the Amandine manuscript of Eusebius’s *Chronicle* reads most correctly, as do the editions of Pontacus and Scaliger. Baronius, in volume II, under the first year of Decius—which he assigns to A.D. 253—investigating Paul’s flight into the desert from the date of Antony’s death, asserts from the *Chronicle* of Eusebius and Jerome that Antony died in the twenty-first year of Constantius the Younger. In his *Annals*, volume III, in the chronological sequence, he assigns this year of Constantius to A.D. 357. He repeats this when investigating Hilarion’s age in volume IV, under A.D. 372. Yet in volume III, under A.D. 358, the twenty-second year of Constantius, he places Antony’s death. I shall inquire shortly why he may have done this. I said above, in connection with the *Life of Saint Paul*, that Baronius used a corrupt copy of the *Chronicle*; this will now be demonstrated more fully. The common edition of Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, which Baronius used, places Antony’s birth in the first year of Decius, A.D. 254, and his death in the twenty-first year of Constantius the Younger, A.D. 361. But since the same common *Chronicle* later makes clear that Antony died in the 105th year of his age, it is certain that either Antony’s birth or his death has been incorrectly assigned in that edition. For between A.D. 254, when it places Antony’s birth, and A.D. 361, when it places his death, 107 years intervene. If two years are added—namely, the year in which Antony was born and the year in which he died, although these seem to have to be added because he is said to have died in the 105th year of his age, not after his 105th year—109 years result, whereas only 105 years, the number of years Antony lived, should intervene or result. Therefore, in the Amandine manuscript of Eusebius, as I said regarding the *Life of Paul*, Antony’s birth is correctly assigned to the first year of Decius, and his death to the nineteenth year of Constantius the Younger [Col. 0118C], the emperor; thus the proper 105 years during which Antony lived are obtained. Nor was it read otherwise in Eusebius in the time of Gregory of Tours. For he says in book I, chapter 38, of his *History of the Franks*: “In the nineteenth year of Constantius the Younger, Antony the monk died, in the 105th year of his age.” So reads the manuscript of Trudo, whereas the common editions incorrectly have 100. Vincent likewise, in *Historical Mirror*, book XIV, chapter 14, placing his account in the same *Chronicle* of Eusebius, assigns Antony’s death to the nineteenth year of Constantius the Younger. Therefore, in the common Eusebius, Antony’s death is displaced chronologically by two years if the year of birth and the year of death are excluded from the years of Antony’s life; or by four years if the years of birth and death are included in the number of years of his life. I have indeed wondered at Baronius: although in volume II, under the first year of Decius, when discussing the flight of Paul the hermit, he there asserts from Eusebius’s *Chronicle*—corrupt, as we have said—that Antony died in the twenty-first year of Constantius the Younger, nevertheless in volume III, under the twenty-second year of the same Constantius, he places Antony’s death. As I investigate the reason for this, I find no other explanation than that perhaps Baronius, in volume II, under the first year of Decius, when Antony was born, counted that year among Antony’s years of life. Thus, from the first year of Decius through the twenty-first year of Constantius the Younger, including the first year itself, the correct 105 years result according to Baronius’s calculation, which was Antony’s maximum age. In volume III, however, he seems not to have counted the first year of Decius among Antony’s years of life, but to have begun Antony’s first year of age with the second year of Decius’s reign; hence in that same volume III he extended Antony’s death to the twenty-second year of Constantius the Younger. As for what I said—that in the Amandine manuscript of Eusebius Antony’s birth is most correctly assigned to the first year of Decius and his death to the nineteenth year of Constantius the Younger, and that thus the correct 105 years of Antony’s age result—understand it as follows. The common editions, including the more accurate editions of Pontacus and Scaliger, place two years between the twentieth year of Diocletian and the first year of Constantine and assign them to Galerius; the Amandine manuscript places only one intervening year and omits the paragraph concerning Galerius found in the common text. Even if that paragraph is accepted and two years are assigned to his reign before the first year of Constantine, it will not be necessary to place two intervening years between the twentieth year of Diocletian and the first year of Constantine. Rather, Galerius’s first year can coincide with Diocletian’s twentieth, since Diocletian abdicated the imperial power on 30 April in the twentieth year of his reign, and Galerius could then begin the first year of his own reign. Indeed, that only one year ought to intervene between Diocletian’s twentieth year and Constantine’s first is proved, first, by Eusebius’s own *Chronicle*, which expressly says under Diocletian’s nineteenth year: “In the fourth year of the persecution Constantine began to reign.” Since the persecution began in Diocletian’s nineteenth year, if his twentieth year and one intervening year between Diocletian’s twentieth and Constantine’s first are added, what remains except that Constantine’s first year was the fourth year of the persecution? It is proved, secondly, by the *Politia*, or *Acts of the Holy Fathers Metrophanes and Alexander*, preserved by Photius in the *Bibliotheca*, codex 256, where it is said: Τρίτον δ` ἤδη τὸτε ἦν ἔτος τοῦ καθ` ἡμῶν διωγμοῦ, ἐν ὧ καὶ Κονστάντιος πρὸς τὴν ἄφθαρτον βασιλείαν, τὴν ἐπικήρον ἤμειχε—“It was then already the third year of the persecution raised against us Christians, in which Constantius exchanged his transient kingdom for the eternal kingdom.” But if two intervening years are placed between Diocletian’s twentieth year and Constantine’s first, Constantius would have died not in the third year of the persecution but in the fourth, as is clear from the calculation just made. It is proved, thirdly, by the Olympiads assigned in the Amandine manuscript of Eusebius. The first year of the 271st Olympiad is assigned to Diocletian’s twentieth year; the second to the year intervening between Diocletian’s twentieth and Constantine’s first; and the third to Constantine’s first year. Thus it becomes clear that Eusebius placed only one year between Diocletian’s twentieth and Constantine’s first. [Col. 0119C] Let this suffice for the present regarding the notes that had to be made in order properly to calculate the number of years in Antony’s life.] Constantius.

“Antony the monk died in the 105th year of his age in the desert, etc.”

### Gelasius, distinction 15, chapter “The Holy Roman Church”

We receive with every honor the *Lives of the Fathers*—of Paul, Antony, Hilarion, and all the hermits—which the blessed man Jerome nevertheless wrote.

### Honorius, *On Illustrious Church Writers*, chapter 88

Briefly extracted from Saint Jerome.

**27.** Antony the monk, whose life Athanasius presented in a remarkable volume, sent seven letters to various monasteries, full of apostolic thought and speech.

### Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Antony the monk and abbot, an Egyptian by birth, a most holy man and distinguished inhabitant of the desert, whose praises the whole world resounds, provided many people with a model of a religious and blessed life. Although he had not learned letters, he was nevertheless so learned in the divine Scriptures that none of the learned dared presume to place himself above him. He possessed memory in place of books, understanding and insight in place of letters, and grace in place of the labor of reading. In the Egyptian language he dictated to various monasteries several letters filled with apostolic thought and speech.

[Note: [Col. 0119C] **“Several letters.”** Trithemius himself counts seven here and says that one was written to the Arsenoites; this is correct, and under that title it is the second in the Cologne edition. Jerome likewise mentions only one, as the principal letter, to the Arsenoites. Therefore Possevinus is incorrect in saying that all seven letters were written to the Arsenoites. The titles in the *Library of the Holy Fathers* are likewise wrong in this respect. The translator of these letters from Greek was not Symphorianus Champerius, as Possevinus states, but Valerius Sarrasius, with Symphorianus arranging the edition. As for Possevinus’s citation from Trithemius in the *Sacred Apparatus* under Antony—“He also wrote a celebrated work in two books called *Melissa*, that is, *The Little Bee*”—and his claim that Trithemius was in error: he is indeed in error, if he wrote this. But I do not find those words in Trithemius. I suspect they were added to Trithemius’s words by Margarino de la Bigne in the first edition of the *Library of the Holy Fathers*, who had published those books of Antony’s *Melissa* under the name of Antony the Great. The error was corrected, however, in volume V of the second edition of the *Library of the Holy Fathers*.]

Of these, the notable letter *To the Arsenoites* is one; six are addressed *To Other Monasteries*. The blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, described his life in a remarkable volume written in Greek. He flourished under Constantine the Great and his sons, in the year of the Lord 330, shining forth with many miracles.

# ON SAINT ATHANASIUS

[Note: “Athanasius.”] No one who has read the preceding commendations will be able to doubt that Athanasius was the author of the *Life of Saint Antony*. A Greek edition has recently appeared, in the year 1611 at Augsburg, edited by David Hoeschel, who also added his own translation and certain notes chiefly concerned with the Greek text.

Our Bellarmine ascribes it to Athanasius in volume II, controversy 2, book 2, *On Monks*, chapter 4. First, because it is truly a distinguished volume, as Jerome says that this book was by Athanasius. Second, because it contains those many miracles mentioned by Augustine, *Confessions*, book VIII, chapter 6. Third, because it recounts the story of Ammon’s soul, which Palladius, chapter 8, and Socrates, book IV, chapter 18, report from Athanasius’ book *On the Life of Antony*. Other testimonies no less certain may be added.

First, the most certain testimony is supplied by blessed Ephrem, who quotes verbatim from this Life, under Athanasius’ name, two passages that may be seen in the notes at chapters 23 and 60. Likewise, in his letter to the monk John, in a brief summary of Antony’s Life—whose individual episodes are all contained in this Life—he exhorts monks to the common life.

Second, an equally certain indication is provided by the author of the *Life of Saint Pachomius*, formerly translated by Dionysius Exiguus, who mentions, under Athanasius’ name, Ammon and Theodore, who appear in this Life of Antony.

Third, Damascene, *On Images*, oration I, cites from this Life a passage found here at chapter 57, as does a manuscript catena on Luke compiled from the Greek Fathers, preserved in the Palatine Library, according to Felckmann. What more conclusive evidence, I ask, could be produced for assigning a book to an author?

Nevertheless, there are heretics who do not hesitate to express doubt whether this Life presented here was written by Athanasius. Thus the Magdeburg Centuriators, century IV, chapter 10, page 1306, although they add no reason, conjecture, or authority whatever. Peter Felckmann Coronaeus also expresses doubt, he who recently presided over the Greek-Latin edition of Athanasius. But it is not unusual for heretics to doubt whenever something displeases their palate, as in this splendid Life, where the testimonies to monasticism and to the sign of the cross are especially clear.

Rudolph Hospinian, however, proceeds more stubbornly and shamelessly, *On the Origin of Monasticism*, book III, chapter 1, and with him Abraham Scultetus, *Theological Marrow of the Fathers*, part II. They have dared to assert that this writing, now circulated under Athanasius’ name, deserves absolutely no credence, but is instead the fabrication of a foolish man. They press the following arguments, so closely that one has evidently copied the other.

First: this writing was added to Athanasius’ other works only very recently. It is not found in Greek, neither in the Basel manuscript, nor in the English manuscript, nor in other codices.

I reply that this writing was printed in Latin under Athanasius’ name at the very cradle of printing, in the *Lives of the Fathers*, and that it is found everywhere in manuscript books, including extremely ancient ones. Its Greek text appeared in 1611 at Augsburg, from the library of that city, edited by David Hoeschel, as I have already said. He also added variant readings from the English codex of Henry Savile.

Second: this writing contains none of the rules of monastic life which Nazianzen says Athanasius intended to promulgate under the pretext of his narrative.

I reply: a saint’s Life, as Saint Ambrose says (*On Saint Joseph*, chapter 1), is a rule of life for others. Jerome likewise says, in letter 2 to Nepotianus, concerning the Life of Heliodorus: “Let his manner of life be regarded as a model of virtue.” Again, in letter 15 to Marcella, concerning the Life of Asella: “Let them consider her way of life a rule of perfect living.”

And, not to depart from Antony himself:

> Ἔστι γὰρ μοναχοῖς ἱκανὸς χαρακτὴρ πρὸς ἄσκησιν ὁ Ἀντονίου βίος.

“For monks, Antony’s life is a sufficient pattern for discipline.”

Indeed, knowing who Antony was is a complete way to virtue, as Athanasius says in the preface to this Life. Saint Antony also expresses not a few monastic rules in his exhortations contained in this Life. If Hospinian, Scultetus, or any other Calvinist were to shape his life according to the prescriptions of this Life, he would certainly be said to have obeyed the monastic rules admirably.

Third, when the author of this writing attempts to show that Antony imitated Christ throughout the whole course of his life, he speaks of him so childishly and ridiculously that one may rightly say that he read Athanasius without judgment.

I reply that it is unsurprising for Calvinists to assert this, since it was said long ago even of men of their kind—although they eventually recognize their folly—and of the saints themselves:

> “These are they whom we once held in derision and made a reproachful example of. We foolishly considered their life madness” (*Wisdom* V).

Fourth, this false author says that Antony was unlearned and ignorant of letters, whereas others claim, on the contrary, that he was a lawyer and highly educated.

I reply: Antony was both unlearned and learned. He was unlearned—that is, ignorant of letters—but learned by God’s gift and by the keenness of his mind. This is what you have in the Life by Athanasius. For chapter 1 says that he did not allow himself to be educated in letters; therefore he is rightly called ignorant of letters and unlearned, that is, not learned in literature. Yet in the same author, chapter 38, he is said to have been taught by God, or *Theodidact* (Θεοδίδακτος).

Saint Augustine bears witness to both facts in the prologue to book I of *On Christian Doctrine*:

> “Antony, it is said, without any knowledge of letters, retained the divine Scriptures by hearing them by heart and understood them through prudent reflection.”

As for those who say that Antony was a lawyer: certainly he may have been a lawyer, but one of those who receive eternal life and become lawyers of holiness, as is said of Saint Tiburtius in book I of the *Life of Saint Sebastian*.

It seems truly strange to me that some call Antony a lawyer, as both heretics cite him in the passage already mentioned, without adding any authority. After I had long searched for the source, I finally saw that Hospinian, book II of *On Monasticism*, chapter 3, cited Suidas for this purpose.

Let us therefore turn to him. But Suidas does not refer to our Antony, who was born in Egypt, in the village of Coma near Heraclea, as Sozomen, book I, chapter 13, and Nicephorus, book VIII, chapter 40, report. Rather, he refers to a certain Alexandrian Antony, who pleaded his sister’s case at Alexandria and Byzantium and who lived in Suidas’ own time. For he says:

> Ἔγωγε οὖν καὶ αὐτὸς ὁμολογῶ τῷ ἀνδρὶ μεγίστην ἀτεχνῶς τὴν χάριν, ἣν ἀμείψασθαι αὐτὸν εὔχομαι τοὺς θεοὺς ἐν μακάρων νήσοις ἤδη συζῆν ἠξιώμενον.

“I too openly confess that I owe that man the greatest gratitude, and I pray that the gods may repay him, since he is already deemed worthy to dwell in the Isles of the Blessed.”

Or rather, this may belong to the time of another pagan author, from whom Suidas excerpted the words about him; for praying to the gods is paganism.

Accordingly, when he says elsewhere of him:

> Γάζαν ἀπέφηνεν ἱερατέραν πολλῷ μᾶλλον, ἢ πρότερον ἦν.

“He made Gaza much more august than it had previously been,”

I think he is alluding to the rites of Gaza, or to the idol of Marnas. He had just said that Antony’s mind was shaped

> πρὸς θεοῦ θεραπείαν τήν τε δημοτελῆ καὶ ἀποῤῥητοτέραν,

“for the worship of the god, both public and more secret”—that is, of Marnas or Jupiter Pluvius, who was especially worshiped at Gaza, as is recorded in the *Life of Saint Porphyry* by the Metaphrast, February 26.

You see, reader, what you should expect from that “marrowless marrow” of Scultetus and from Hospinian’s “monasticism,” or rather “adulterous life,” when they bring forward such frivolous arguments against a Life accepted everywhere, against the ancient Fathers, and against antiquity itself.

Apparently the cult of relics displeased him, although it is clearly proved by this Life. Therefore Scultetus, chapter 16 of the *Synthesis of the Doctrine of Blessed Athanasius*, calls this Life of Antony the writing of a fictitious author.

Let it therefore be firmly and immovably established that Athanasius is the author of this Life.

Whether he also appended the conclusion of the Life is disputed. Baronius, in the year of Christ 343, the seventh year of Pope Julius, and the seventh year of the emperors Constantius and Constans, says:

“Since the Life of Antony written by Athanasius makes no mention whatsoever of Antony’s meeting with Paul, this happened because, as Jerome says in the same passage, Athanasius committed Antony’s deeds to writing while Antony was still alive and brought them to Rome two years before, when he was summoned by Pope Julius; at that time these events concerning Paul had not yet occurred” (Baronius, year of Christ 340, citing Jerome, letter 16).

“Later, after many matters had been omitted, his death was added; but whether by the same Athanasius, I would not dare to assert.”

Possevinus holds the same opinion in the *Sacred Apparatus*, under “Antony.”

I, however, find no basis for doubting that Athanasius appended the conclusion of this Life. Nor, I believe, would Baronius and Possevinus have found one, if they had remembered Athanasius’ preface to this Life. For he says to the foreign brothers:

> “Since, then, you asked me to write to you about the way of life of blessed Antony, wishing to learn how he began, who he was before his holy commitment, and what end his life had.”

Why, then, Athanasius did not mention Antony’s meeting with Paul, I find no other reason than that he does not recount all Antony’s deeds. Hence he warns the foreign brothers to consider that they have heard only little concerning great things, since, because of the haste of the bearer of their letter, he was unable to summon monks in order to learn something more fully and send them greater gifts.

When Athanasius wrote the Life of Antony and brought it to Rome, since the matter has now been mentioned, we shall investigate further.

Baronius, in the year of Christ 340, the fourth year of Pope Julius and the fourth imperial year of Constantine, Constantius, and Constans, says:

“How beneficial Athanasius’ journey to Rome was may be understood from the fact that he himself first brought into the city the institution of the Egyptian monks and brought with him the admirable Life of Antony the Great, written by him while Antony was still alive. This way of life, adapted to every dimension of evangelical perfection, noble Roman women also began to follow.”

Saint Jerome gives the following account of them:

> “At that time no noble woman in Rome knew the monastic way of life, nor did anyone dare, because of the novelty of the matter, to assume among the people a name then considered disgraceful and base. Marcella learned this way of life first from the Alexandrian priests and from Pope Athanasius, and afterward from Peter, who, fleeing the persecution of the Arian heresy, had taken refuge in Rome as though in the safest harbor of their communion. She learned the Life of blessed Antony, who was then still living, as well as the discipline of Pachomius’ monasteries in the Thebaid and of virgins and widows; nor was she ashamed to profess what she had learned was pleasing to Christ” (Jerome, letter 16, to Principia).

Thus far Baronius from Jerome.

From these words it is clear that Marcella also learned about the Life of Antony through Athanasius, but not that Athanasius then brought to Rome the Life of Antony written by himself. We have already seen from Athanasius’ own testimony that he wrote it only after Antony’s death, for the foreign brothers.

At Rome, therefore, Athanasius did what the Alexandrian priests had done before him and what Peter of Alexandria did after him—first as a presbyter and afterward as a bishop: he recounted to the Romans what they had seen or heard in person in Egypt and the Thebaid concerning Antony and Pachomius, who were then still alive.

If anyone wishes to suppose that some brief notes were gathered from them at that time so that the matters would not slip from memory, I have no objection, provided that we trust Athanasius himself when he says that he wrote Antony’s Life only after Antony’s death, at the request of the foreign brothers.

Whether Athanasius taught the widow Marcella about Antony in Rome in the year of Christ 340, however, does not seem entirely certain to me. For when Baronius, volume V, places Marcella’s death in the year of Christ 410, she must have been extremely long-lived—indeed ninety years old—if we suppose her to have been twenty when Athanasius first came to Rome in 340.

If this age applies to Marcella, she could have heard about Antony from Athanasius in the year 340. But if Marcella must be assigned a younger age, since Athanasius came to Rome several times—in 340, then 342, and finally 349—Marcella could have learned about Antony from Athanasius in that final year.

On the occasion of Saint Antony and Marcella, Baronius continues with the following against the enemies of monasticism:

> “But by whom, then,” he says (Baronius, year 340), “was Marcella persuaded that this form of life was pleasing to God, unless by the almost innumerable miracles, plainly apostolic signs, and virtues which she knew Antony and others continually performed, with divine approval? In the East, indeed, that supreme way of life, like that of Elijah and John the Baptist, was revered by all people, even pagans and emperors themselves; it was also respected by impious heretics and admired by the citizens of heaven, who rejoiced to have such fellow citizens on earth and associated with them continually and amicably as with their own kindred.
>
> “It happened happily that, once Athanasius had made it known, that exalted way of life was introduced into the city and equally honored—a way of life whose traces had previously been seen only in the mountains and deserts. Nor did the whole Christian world in the West refuse to follow what it knew had been embraced in the Roman Church. This is all credited to Athanasius, although, as was said above, monks had not been lacking during earlier periods of persecution, both in the city and elsewhere—those, I mean, who, like Paul and Antony fleeing persecution, for the same reason hid in crypts, caves, mountain peaks, and the hollow recesses of valleys, worshiping God more earnestly, like Elijah fleeing from the face of Ahab and Jezebel.
>
> “Thus, although the name ‘monk’ seemed new to the city, the reality itself was ancient, though in the great peace of the Church it had been cultivated by certain rules and propagated with more fruitful growth.”

The heretical Donatists, also called Circumcellions, who at this very time were raging against Catholics in Africa, were the first to dare to question and challenge the pious—not about the reality itself, but about the name. Saint Augustine says that they were accustomed to ask:

> “What does the name ‘monks’ mean?”

And later:

> “They say to us: ‘Show us where the name “monks” is written.’”

After other remarks, he himself replied:

> “Why, then, should we not also call them monks, since the Psalm says: ‘Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell together in unity’ (Psalm 132)? For *monos* (μόνος) means ‘one,’ but not merely any kind of one. Even in a crowd a person is one; yet one may be called one together with many, whereas *monos* cannot mean that: it means alone. For one who is alone is *monos*, that is, one alone. Those who live together in such a way as to make one person, so that what is written may truly apply to them—‘one soul and one heart’ (Acts 4)—many bodies but not many souls, are rightly called *monos*, that is, one alone.”

A little later he says:

> “They rightly mock the name of unity who have cut themselves off from unity. They rightly dislike the name ‘monks,’ because they do not wish to dwell together with their brothers; but by following Donatus, they have divided Christ.”

This is Augustine.

You can now clearly see, reader, on whose side stand those who in our most unhappy age so bitterly execrate the name of monks, and whose disciples they profess themselves to be, since they follow their impiety—men plainly twice as impious as those others. The Donatists, as Augustine says, mocked the name of monks because they had fallen away from Catholic unity; these men, however, have defected through a double apostasy, shamefully abandoning both the faith of the Church and monastic observance. Such were plainly those who laid the first foundations of all the heresies that have appeared in this age.

Yet they are not merely twice as wicked as the Donatists in this respect, as we have said, but three times as wicked. For the Donatists did not, like them, raise questions with Catholics merely about the name; they attacked the reality itself with the fiercest hatred. Moreover, while doing so, they acted not only in words but in deeds and in the manner of brigands, attacking and continuing to ravage monasteries of both men and consecrated virgins wherever force permitted. They must therefore be judged four times worse than those others.

As for other matters, however, there is nothing that can be compared between the Sacramentarians and the Donatists, since the latter, apart from a few points, agreed with the Catholic Church in all other respects.]

## THE WRITER OF THIS LIFE

### The Greek *Menaea*, January 17, in the Life of Antony

> Ὁ δὲ βίος αὐτοῦ συνεγράφη ὑπὸ τοῦ μεγάλου Ἀθανασίου ἐπισκόπου Ἀλεξανδρείας.

“But his Life was written by the great Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria.”

[Col. 0116B] “The Life of Antony was written by the great Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria.”

### Gregory Nazianzen, Oration XXI, in Praise of Saint Athanasius

> Πάντα μέν τοι τὰ ἐκείνου (τοῦ Ἀθανασίου) λέγειν τε καὶ θαυμάζειν, μακρότερον ἂν εἴη τυχὸν, ἢ κατὰ τὴν παροῦσαν ὁρμὴν τοῦ λόγου· καὶ ἱστορίας ἔργον, οὐκ εὐφημίας· ἃ καὶ ἰδίᾳ παραδοῦναι γραφῇ παίδευμά τε καὶ ἥδυσμα τοῖς εἰς ὕστερον, εὐχῆς ἔργον ἐμοὶ, ὥσπερ ὃν ἐκεῖνος Ἀντωνίου τοῦ θείου βίον συνέγραψε, τοῦ μοναδικοῦ βίου νομοθεσίαν ἐν πλάσματι διηγήσεως.

“To recount and praise all that belongs to him—that is, to Athanasius—would perhaps take longer than the present purpose of my speech allows; it would be the work of a history, not of a panegyric. I would especially wish to commit such matters to writing for the instruction and delight of posterity, just as he himself composed the Life of the divine Antony, promulgating the laws of the monastic life under the guise of a narrative.”

Ἔφθασε γὰρ Ἀθανασίος, ὁ Ἀλεξανδρείας ἐπίσκοπος, μονόβιβλον εἰς τὸν αὐτοῦ βίον ἐκθέμενος.

“What sort of man and monk Antony was in those same times, in the desert of Egypt; how openly and plainly he fought against demons, discovering their tricks and stratagems and undertaking the contests himself; and how he performed many wonders—it would be superfluous for us to recount, since Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, has already set forth these matters in a separate book on his Life.”

## EVAGRIUS THE PRESBYTER, TRANSLATOR OF THIS LIFE

### Jerome, *Catalogue of Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 125

[Note: “Evagrius.”] Jerome frequently mentions Evagrius, sometimes as a presbyter, sometimes as a man especially dear to him, and sometimes as a saint. See him in letters 5 and 6 to Florentius; letter 41 to Rufinus; letter 49 to Innocentius; letter 43 to Chromatius, Jovinus, and Eusebius; also in the *Life of Malchus the Captive Monk*, chapter 1; and in Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, in the second year of the emperor Aurelian, the year of Christ 273, where he asserts that Evagrius descended from the family of the general Pompeianus, surnamed “the Frank,” who defeated Zenobia.

Blessed Jerome clearly asserts that Evagrius was the translator of this Life, as we saw in the *Eulogy*. All manuscript copies agree, prefixing Evagrius’ name to this Life.

Nevertheless, some have attributed this translation or composition to Jerome. Hilarion Veronese, a Cassinese monk, says in his preface to the *Teaching of Dorotheus*, which he translated into Latin:

> “Jerome translated the Life of Antony the monk in such a way that nothing is missing from its meaning, although much is missing from its words.”

John Grynaeus likewise says in the preface to the *Orthodoxographia*:

> “Jerome described the Life of Antony in a scriptural manner” (*graphikōs*, γραφικῶς).

But Baronius could lead someone to greater doubt, since he appears to offer some reason for his opinion. In his note on the Roman Martyrology, January 17, after discussing Antony’s Acts translated from Athanasius into Latin by Evagrius of Antioch, he says:

> “The same blessed Jerome did this very thing, at the request of Pammachius, as he himself declares when writing to him in letter 101, *On the Best Kind of Translation*. We think that this is the work now in our hands.”

Likewise, in volume III of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 358, he concludes from Jerome’s letter 101 that Jerome translated the Life of Saint Antony from Greek.

I have read and reread the letter cited by Baronius, more than once, and I have found nothing of the sort that he asserts. But, as I see it, Jerome misled a man occupied with many kinds of reading because he had not been read carefully.

After Jerome had defended his own translations—translations in which he expressed meanings by meanings, not words by words, following Cicero—and had stated that he translated Eusebius’ *Chronicle* approximately twenty years earlier, he added, lest he rely only on pagan authority or on his own authority, the testimony of another distinguished man of his age—namely Evagrius, although he does not name him:

> “But, lest the authority of my writings be slight, although I wished only to establish that from my youth I have always translated not words but meanings, learn by reading what sort of preface there is on this subject in the book in which the Life of blessed Antony is described”—namely by Evagrius of Antioch, as Jerome himself testifies in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 125.

He then adds the preface that stands before this very Life:

> “A word-for-word translation from one language into another conceals the meaning and, like luxuriant grass, chokes the planted crops. For while the wording serves grammatical cases and figures, what could have been expressed briefly is scarcely explained after being led around by a long circuit. Avoiding this, therefore, I have rendered blessed Antony at your request in such a way that nothing is missing from the meaning, although something is missing from the words. Let others hunt syllables and letters; seek the sense.”

You see, reader, what led Baronius into error. These words—“Avoiding this, therefore,” and so forth—are not Jerome’s words to Pammachius, but Evagrius’ words to Innocentius, as you have them here in the preface placed before Antony’s Life. Jerome uses its authority to defend his own translations.

For if this preface belonged to Saint Jerome, he would not have said above, “Lest the authority of my writings be slight,” by which he indicates that he is about to invoke the authority of another.

Furthermore, in his prologue to the *Life of Paul the First Hermit*, Jerome says:

> “For Antony has been carefully written about both in Greek and in Roman style.”

As though others had written about him, not Jerome himself.

I have pursued these matters at somewhat greater length so that I might not seem rashly to depart from a great man. Let Evagrius of Antioch, therefore, remain the translator of this Life.

You may say that Gelasius, in the decree *On Authentic and Apocryphal Books*, distinction 15, seems to assert that the Life of Antony was also written by Saint Jerome. For he says:

> “We receive with all honor the Lives of the Fathers—Paul, Antony, Hilarion, and all the hermits—which the most blessed man Jerome wrote.”

Baronius, in his note on the Roman Martyrology, January 17, misunderstood Jerome’s letter 101, as I have already demonstrated. He thought that Gelasius said Jerome had not so much translated as written Antony’s Life because Jerome rendered meanings by meanings rather than words by words. He repeats the same explanation in volume III of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 358.

Possevinus, in the *Sacred Apparatus*, under “Antony,” although he agrees with Baronius that the Life of Antony was also rendered into Latin by Saint Jerome, assigns another reason why Gelasius says that Jerome wrote, rather than translated, the Life of Saint Antony.

He says:

> “Not only because he rendered meanings by meanings, as some—Baronius—have thought, but also because he issued a fuller version. Since Athanasius wrote the Life while Antony the Great of Egypt was still alive, some of what followed was omitted, and it is uncertain whether Antony’s death was later appended by Athanasius. Jerome reports that Athanasius, summoned by Pope Julius, had brought to Rome Antony’s deeds two years before his death”—here Possevinus means Paul’s death—“.
>
> “It is therefore not surprising if Jerome, in the Life of Paul, reports what Athanasius omitted: the demon appearing in the form of a hippocentaur, Antony’s meeting with Paul, the raven bringing bread, the cloak that Athanasius had given to Antony, and other matters of this kind.”

Thus far Possevinus.

I have shown clearly enough, unless my judgment deceives me, that Evagrius translated Antony’s Life. That Jerome also did so has not been proved equally well. Thus someone might think that when Gelasius says that Jerome wrote the Lives of Paul and Antony, he was referring to the Life of Paul, in which nearly as much is said about Antony as about Paul.

Indeed, the Greek title of this Life in the Bavarian Library names both men. It reads:

> Διήγησις τοῦ ἁγίου Πᾳύλου Θηβαίου, καὶ Ἀντωνίου Αἰγυπτίου.

“An account of Saint Paul the Theban and Antony the Egyptian.”

Unless, perhaps, someone wishes to say that Evagrius, a Greek closely associated with Jerome and a patron of his studies, used Jerome’s work in translating Antony’s Life and submitted his own work to Jerome’s editorial correction. Certainly, some features of Jerome’s style appear intermittently.

Someone might nevertheless say that Evagrius, although a man of Antioch, was as familiar with Latin diction as with Greek, since he descended from the general Pompeianus, surnamed “the Frank,” as Jerome says in the *Chronicle* cited above; and it is highly probable that this man was Latin.

Whatever the truth may finally be, I think that many Lives of the Fathers formerly circulated without the name of their author or translator. From this arose such divergent opinions concerning the authors of the *Lives of the Fathers*, as we saw above in the general prolegomena.

Indeed, when Saint Jerome cites this very Life of Antony in that letter 101, chapter 2, and defends himself by means of the translator’s preface, he does not mention the translator’s name. Perhaps this explains why this Life of Antony, formerly copied among the Lives of Paul and Hilarion, gave Gelasius occasion to think that Jerome was also the author of Antony’s Life, although he was the author of the other two.

“Evagrius, bishop of Antioch, was a man of keen and ardent intellect. While he was still a presbyter, he read to me treatises on various hypotheses that he had not yet published. He also translated the Life of blessed Antony from the Greek of Athanasius into our language.”

Honorius says similar things in chapter 125, *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*.

# JANUARY 17

## LIFE OF BLESSED ANTONY THE ABBOT

**By Saint Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria; translated by Evagrius, Presbyter of Antioch**

### Prologue of Evagrius to Innocentius

[Note: “Innocentius.”] The editions add “bishop,” a designation absent from the manuscripts. Correctly so. For Evagrius would not have called Innocentius his “dearest son,” as he does here, if Innocentius had then been a bishop. But who was this Innocentius?

I suspect that he was the man mentioned by Saint Jerome in letter 41 to Rufinus, whom Jerome says was his companion in Syria together with Evagrius:

> “For a sudden fever carried away Innocentius, a part of my soul. Now I enjoy our Evagrius as my one and complete light, to whom I, always weak, have become an added burden for labor.”

I think that the Innocentius mentioned by Jerome in letter 56 to Apronius is another person; Jerome calls him a presbyter there, as also in letter 79 to Alypius and Augustine. There is likewise another Innocentius in Palladius, chapter 103, a resident of the Mount of Olives, also a presbyter.

But this Innocentius, for whose benefit Evagrius the presbyter translated the Life of Saint Antony from Greek into Latin, I think was younger and had not yet been ordained to the presbyterate. Hence Evagrius calls him his “dearest son,” whereas he would have used another title if Innocentius, to whom he was writing, had himself been a presbyter—unless he used the expression on account of their difference in age.

For this same Innocentius, Saint Jerome wrote the story of a woman struck seven times, which you may find in letter 49; there he also calls the same Innocentius “dearest.” It is therefore not correct that the Hieronymian index confuses this Innocentius, whom Jerome mentions in letters 41 and 49, with the one whom he mentions in letter 56.

From this passage of Jerome we learn approximately when Evagrius gave this Life of Antony to the Latin world: namely, when Jerome was living in the Syrian desert together with Innocentius, or shortly before.

Saint Jerome refers to this prologue of Evagrius in letter 101, chapter 2, to Pammachius, and, without naming the translator, quotes certain passages from it, as I have already shown in the introductory material to this Life, where Evagrius’ role as translator of the Life was discussed.

### 35. Evagrius the Presbyter to His Dearest Son Innocentius in the Lord, Greeting

A word-for-word translation from one language into another conceals the meaning and, like luxuriant grass, chokes the planted crops. For while the wording serves grammatical cases and figures, what could have been expressed briefly is scarcely explained after being led around by a long circuit.

Avoiding this, therefore, I have rendered the Life of blessed Antony at your request in such a way that nothing is missing from the meaning, although something is missing from the words. Let others hunt syllables and letters; seek the sense.

## PREFACE OF ATHANASIUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA

### Athanasius the Bishop to the Foreign Brothers

You have undertaken an excellent contest, brothers, striving either to equal the monks of Egypt or to surpass them through your zeal for virtue. For among you there are already many monasteries; the name of monk is also renowned. Everyone will rightly admire this desire of yours, and God will grant the fulfillment you seek as you pray.

Since, then, you asked me to write to you about the way of life of blessed Antony, wishing to learn how he began, who he was before his holy commitment, what end his life had, and whether the things that rumor has spread about him are true, so that you might form yourselves according to his emulation and example, I accepted the command of your charity with great joy.

For it is an immense gain and benefit to me simply to remember Antony [Note: “It is an immense gain to remember Antony.”] the Great, who was always regarded as a holy man, so that even the remembrance of such men was counted as gain and benefit. In the *Life of Saint Pachomius*, chapter 30, Theodore says:

> “I believe that, because I have remembered so great a man, all my sins will be forgiven.”

Knowing that you listen with admiration, I also know that you desire to follow his way of life. Indeed, knowing who Antony was is a complete way to virtue.

Therefore, to put it briefly, believe all that the report of those who speak about him has proclaimed, and consider yourselves to have heard only the least part of the greatest things. For I do not doubt that they were unable to know everything; and although, at your request, I shall indicate as much as I can in this letter, I shall not be narrating things equal to his merits. But all of you who are sailing from here should also make careful inquiries, so that, as each person reports what he knows, a suitable and worthy account of so great a name may be completed.

Accordingly, after reading your letter, I was planning to invite some monks to come to me, especially those who were accustomed to visit him frequently, so that, learning something more fully, I might send you greater gifts. But since the season for sailing was passing and the bearer of the letter was hastening most urgently, I therefore hurried to report to your affection what I myself knew—and I often visited him [Note: [Col. 0169C] “For I often visited him.” Baronius, volume III, in the year of Christ 338, the fifteenth year of Pope Sylvester and the twenty-third of Constantine, supposes that in this year—namely, in the third year of his episcopate—Athanasius visited the churches and monasteries of Egypt, as he says is partly evident from Athanasius’s *Apology 2* and partly from the *Life of Pachomius*, chapter 27. Since, therefore, he visited Pachomius, he should also be believed to have visited the great Anthony, the most renowned of all monks, as older, holier in the excellence of his life, and the founder and leader of all the coenobia. See what is said below, at chapter 58 of this Life.

“Wonderfully,” Baronius says above, “Athanasius’s conspicuous modesty in all things also shines forth in these matters. For when writing Anthony’s deeds, he never says even a word about such a meeting with him; indeed, he left wrapped in silence whatever was done both with him and with other very holy men, though there is no doubt that these things were worthy of remembrance. He did this lest, while composing the illustrious deeds of others, he should appear to become the herald of his own praises, preferring the memory of right actions to be put at risk rather than his modesty.”], and what I learned from the man who had served him for no little time, pouring water over his hands [Note: [Col. 0169D] “What I learned from the man who, after following him for no little time in order to bring him water.” “*Fecit* must certainly be read. The Greek text also agrees: Καὶ ἃ μαθεῖν ἠδυνήθην παρὰ τοῦ ἀκολουθήσαντος αὐτῷ χρόνον οὐκ ὀλίγον, καὶ ἐπιχέαντος ὕδωρ κατὰ χειρὸς αὐτοῦ. ‘And what I was able to learn from the man who followed him for no little time and poured water over his hand.’ What you have here in Latin was rendered by Evagrius. But until now the printed editions have incorrectly read *feci*. This led Baronius, in volume III, in the year of Christ 311, the third year of Pope Eusebius and the sixth of Constantine, and in the year of Christ 328, the fifteenth year of Pope Sylvester and the twenty-third of Constantine, into the error of supposing that Athanasius had served Saint Anthony and diligently ministered to him by carrying him water.

“On the contrary, from childhood Athanasius, after having tasted the study of grammar, began to live with Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, as Rufinus writes in book I, chapter 14 of his *History*: ‘With Alexander,’ he says, ‘he is nourished like a certain Samuel in the temple of the Lord; and when Alexander, advancing in good old age, went to the Fathers, Athanasius was chosen to carry after him the priestly ephod.’ Sozomen also says in book II, chapter 16, that Alexander made Athanasius ὁμοδίαιτον καὶ ὑπογραφέα: ‘his table-companion and secretary.’ And Theodoret, book I, chapter 26: Συνῆν δὲ Ἀλεξάνδρῳ τῷ πανευφήμῳ νέος μὲν ὢν τὴν ἡλικίαν. ‘When he was still young in age, he continually associated with that illustrious Alexander.’

“What is said here, ‘in order to bring him water,’ is in Greek: Καὶ ἐπιχέαντος ὕδωρ κατὰ χειρὸς αὐτοῦ—‘and the one who poured water over his hands while he washed.’ A similar service of Elisha is found in 4 Kings, chapter III: Ὁς ἐπέχεεν ὕδωρ ἐπὶ χεῖρας Ἠλίου, ‘who poured water over the hands of Elijah.’ This was formerly customary. See the *Onomasticon*.”], I hastened to communicate to your affection. In both respects I was concerned for the truth: so that no one, hearing an exaggerated account, would refuse to believe because of an accumulation of miracles, nor, again, knowing only the lesser aspects of his merits, suppose that a man of so great a name was unworthy of miracles.

## Life

### Chapter I

Anthony [Note: [Col. 0170B] “Anthony.” The Roman Martyrology, January 17: “In the Thebaid, Saint Anthony the abbot, who lived most illustriously in life and miracles as the Father of many monks. Athanasius set forth his deeds in a distinguished volume. His sacred body, discovered by divine revelation under the emperor Justinian and brought to Alexandria, was buried in the Church of Saint John the Baptist.”

This day is absent from the Greek Menologion published in Latin from the library of Cardinal Sirletus. But Anthony is remembered under the title “the Great” on this same day in the Greek Menaea. That monks formerly used to celebrate the birthday of Saint Anthony on this day is testified by the monk Cyril in the *Acts of Saint Euthymius* of January 20, written twelve hundred years ago.

The ancient Greek fathers and historians remember Saint Anthony: Chrysostom, *Homily 8 on Matthew*, toward the end; Socrates, book IV, chapter 25; Sozomen, book I, chapter 13; Theodoret, book IV, chapter 27; Nicephorus, book VIII, chapter 40; and others. Among the Latins: Jerome, in the *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 88, and elsewhere; Rufinus, book I of his *History*, chapter 8; Cassiodorus, book I of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 11, and book VIII, chapter 1; Augustine, book I of *On Christian Doctrine*, in the prologue, and book VIII of the *Confessions*, chapters 6 and 12; and others. Vincent also treats Saint Anthony in the *Speculum historiale*, book XIII, chapters 91–93, and book XIV, chapter 14; Antoninus, part II, title 15, chapter 3, through the first five sections; and Peter, in the *Catalogue of the Saints*, book II, chapter 92.”]

He was born of noble and religious parents and was Egyptian by origin [Note: [Col. 0170D] “He was Egyptian by origin.” Sozomen gives his birthplace in book I, chapter 13: Ἐγένετο δὲ οὗτος Αἰγύπτιος, τῷ γένει τῶν εὐπατριδῶν, ἀπὸ Κομᾶ.
