Κώμη δὴ αὕτη ὁμου Ἡρακλείας τοῖς παρ᾽ Αἰγυπτίοις Ἄρκασι. “He was Egyptian, descended from a patrician family, and from Coma. This is a village near Heraclea among the Arcadians who border on Egypt.”

The printed Greek text has ἄκρασι, “mountains,” instead of Ἄρκασι, “Arcadians.” But from the version of Christophorsonus, which I have presented, it appears that he read Ἄρκασι, as did the translator of Nicephorus, as will soon be evident. Heraclea, or the Great City of Hercules, is indeed situated in the Heptanomis of Egypt, which was also called Arcadia. Therefore, when Sozomen calls this Heraclea “of the Arcadians,” he distinguishes it from the other Heracleas, of which there were many in various regions, and even in Egypt itself.

There are three Heracleopolises in Egypt according to Stephanus. The first is πόλις Αἰγυπτία, ἐξ ἧς Θεοφάνης ὁ φυσικός, “an Egyptian city, from which Theophanes the natural philosopher came.” The second is πλησίον Πηλουσίου, “near Pelusium.” The third is κατὰ τὸ Κανωβικὸν στόμα, “toward the Canobic mouth.” Of these, the second is described by Josephus in book V, chapter 14 of *The Jewish War*, and is called “Little Heraclea” by Ptolemy, who places the Great Heraclea on an island of the Nile, from which the Heracleotic Nome was named. I believe this to be Stephanus’s first Heraclea.

Anthony appears to have been born near this place. Scaliger reads Νομοῦ Ἡρακλείου, as if “from the Heracleotic Nome.” But the common reading should be retained, to which Nicephorus’s text also conforms, book VIII, chapter 40: Ὅμορος δ᾽ αὕτη Ἡρακλείᾳ τῶν παρ᾽ Αἰγυπτίοις Ἀρκάδων, “This is adjacent to Heraclea of the Arcadians who are among the Egyptians.”

Epiphanius Scholasticus, in Cassiodorus’s *Tripartite History*, book I, chapter 11, translated this passage from Sozomen as follows: “He was Egyptian by race, born in a distinguished village situated in the region of Heraclea among the Egyptians”—abridged and less clearly expressed. Musculus rendered it more corruptly: “He was an Egyptian of noble birth, born in the village of Apoconia, which among the intemperate Egyptians they call Heraclea.” As you see, he derived Ἀποκονίᾳ from ἀπὸ Κομᾶ, and appears to have read ἀρκάσιοι instead of ἄρκασι.]

He was brought up with such devoted care by his family that he knew nothing except his parents and his home. And when he was already a boy, he did not allow himself to be instructed in letters [Note: [Col. 0171B] “He did not allow himself to be instructed in letters.” Below, chapter 43: “He possessed this remarkable quality: although he had not learned letters, he was most intelligent and prudent.” Sozomen, book I, chapter 13: Γράμματα δὲ οὐδὲ ἠπίστατο, οὐδὲ ἐθαύμαζεν, ἀλλὰ νοῦν ἀγαθὸν ὡς πρεσβύτερον τῶν γραμμάτων, καὶ αὐτὸν τούτων εὑρετὴν ἐπῄνει. “He neither knew letters nor valued them highly, but praised good understanding as older than letters and as their inventor.” See below, on chapter 45.

Augustine, book I of *On Christian Doctrine*, in the prologue, reports that Anthony was θεοδίδακτος, “taught by God”; he adds a similar example: “Nor should he therefore be mocked by Anthony, a holy and perfect man, an Egyptian monk, who is said to have retained the divine Scriptures by hearing them and to have understood them wisely through reflection, although he had no knowledge of letters. Nor should he be mocked by that barbarian Christian slave, about whom we recently heard from men of the greatest seriousness and trustworthiness: without any human teacher, by praying that the letters themselves might be revealed to him, he acquired complete knowledge of them, obtaining through three days of prayer even this—that he should read through an offered book while those present looked on in amazement.”]

But, aflame with desire for God, he did not permit himself to be joined to the foolish stories of children; rather, as it is written in Genesis 25, he lived innocently at home [Note: [Col. 0171C] “He lived innocently at home.” The Greek here is ὡς ἄπλαστος οἰκεῖν ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ αὐτοῦ, “as one guileless, to live in his house.” This is taken from Genesis, chapter 25, verse 27: Ἰακώβ δὲ ἦν ἄπλαστος, οἰκῶν οἰκίαν, “Jacob was a simple—or guileless—man, dwelling in a house.” The Vulgate translator renders it: “But Jacob was a simple man, dwelling in tents.”

For ἄπλαστος, Aquila has ἁπλοῦς, “simple”; Symmachus has ἄμωμος, “blameless.” Evagrius appears to have read ἀπλάστως, since he translates it “innocently.” Saint Augustine discusses the meaning and translation of this word ἄπλαστος in book I of his *Questions on Genesis*, question 74: “What is called ἄπλαστος in Greek, the Latins have translated as ‘simple.’ Properly, however, ἄπλαστος means ‘not fabricated’ or ‘not feigned.’ Hence certain Latin translators rendered it ‘without deceit,’ saying: ‘Jacob was without deceit, dwelling in a house,’ giving rise to a major question, and so forth.” Augustine has the same material in book XVI of *The City of God*, chapter 37.

Surius had noted “Psalm 100” in the margin here, evidently because verse 51 there reads: “I walked in the innocence of my heart, in the midst of my house.” But Athanasius is referring to the passage in Genesis, as I have said.]

Often also going to church with his parents, he did not follow either the frivolities of infants or the negligence of boys; but, listening only to what was read, he preserved the benefit of the teachings by shaping his life accordingly. As is usual at that age, he was never wearied by the lack of various and delicate foods; he did not seek the allurements of more luxurious fare. Content only with what was provided, he asked for nothing more.

### Chapter II

After the death of his parents, when he was about eighteen or twenty years old, he was left with a very small sister and took honorable care both of the household and of his sister. Yet scarcely six months had passed when, hurrying to church as usual, he remembered how the apostles, having rejected everything, had followed the Savior (Matthew 10), and how many, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 4), had sold their possessions, brought the proceeds to their feet, and had them distributed to the needy; he also remembered what and how great a hope had been laid up for them in heaven (Colossians 1).

Turning these things over in his mind, he entered the church, and it happened that the Gospel was then being read [Note: [Col. 0171D] “And it happened that the Gospel was then being read.” Augustine, book VIII of the *Confessions*, chapter 12, while he was caught in the doubtful conflict between flesh and spirit, spurred himself on by Anthony’s example to open a book at random; this proved to be the means of his salvation.

When the mime Babylas heard this verse from the Gospel being read in church—“Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matthew 4)—he passed from a dissolute life to continence (*The Spiritual Meadow* of John Moschus, chapter 32).

Doctor Moneta, when on the feast of Saint Stephen he heard Brother Reginald preaching on the words, “Behold, I see the heavens opened” (Acts 7), devoted himself to the Order of Saint Dominic (*Lives of the Preaching Brothers*, part IV, chapter 10).

When Guerricus heard these words read in church—“All the days that Adam lived were nine hundred and thirty years, and he died. The days of Enoch were nine hundred and five years, and he died” (Genesis 5)—he realized that he too would die and consecrated himself to the same Order (*ibid.*, chapter 12).

A certain scholar in Paris, having heard at the vigils for the dead the responsory, “Woe is me, Lord, for I have sinned greatly in my life; what shall I do, wretch that I am, where shall I flee, except to you, my God?” withdrew into that same religious family (*ibid.*, chapter 10). These three examples from the Dominican Order are also found in the *Speculum exemplorum*, distinction 7, examples 47, 48, and 49.

When Saint Francis heard these words from the Gospel pronounced in the church—“Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money in your belts; no bag for the road, nor two tunics, nor shoes” (Matthew 10)—he resolved to observe them as his rule, as though by God’s command.

When Nicholas of Tolentino happened to hear an Augustinian preacher explaining John’s saying, “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” (1 John 2), he renounced worldly possessions (*His Life*, chapter 3, September 10.”)]

In it the Lord says to the rich man: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have and give to the poor, and come, follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven” (Matthew 19). When he heard this, as though he had conceived such a thought earlier by divine inspiration and as though Scripture were being recited for his sake, he drew the Lord’s command toward himself. Immediately he returned home and sold the possessions he had.

He had three hundred fertile and very fine *arurae* [Note: [Col. 0172B] “He had three hundred fertile and very fine *arurae*.” Someone may wonder at the novelty of this word, which has never before appeared here; but once I have established that this is the true reading, he will cease to wonder.

*Arurae* is found in the Aud. and Camb. manuscripts. In the Greek text: Ἄρουραι δὲ ἦσαν τριακόσιαι εὔφοροι καὶ πανὺ καλαί, “He had three hundred fertile and very fine *arurae*.” The common reading is: “He had three hundred fertile palm trees.” I do not know who first substituted this reading after rejecting the true one; certainly he ought not to have done so.

Evagrius, the ancient translator, wisely retained the Greek word *arurae* here, because it could not conveniently be translated. For ἄρουρα here does not mean a field, as it appeared to the novice interpreter Hoeschel, but a definite kind of measure of land among the Egyptians.

Horapollo, book I, chapter 5: Ἔτος τὸ ἐνιστάμενον γράφοντες, τέταρτον ἀρούρας γράφουσιν. Ἔστι δὲ μέτρον γῆς ἡ ἄρουρα πηχῶν ἑκατόν. “When representing the current year, they draw one fourth of an *arura*. An *arura* is a measure of land comprising one hundred cubits.” See also Eustathius in various places in his notes on Homer. This matter is treated more fully in the *Onomasticon.”]

He gave these to his neighbors, so that they would cause no trouble either to himself or to his sister. He sold all the rest of what he possessed among his movable goods and, collecting a considerable sum, gave it to the needy, reserving only a little for his sister, who seemed weaker because of her sex and age.

### Chapter III

Again entering the church, when he heard the Lord saying in the Gospel, “Do not be anxious about tomorrow” (Matthew 6), he distributed the remaining portion also among the poor. He did not permit himself to remain at home, but entrusted his sister to faithful and well-known virgins, so that she might be nourished by their example. He himself, now free from all the bonds of the world, undertook a harsh and difficult way of life.

At that time monasteries were not yet so numerous in Egypt, nor did anyone at all yet know the deep desert. Whoever wished to benefit himself in the service of Christ was formed in the discipline not far from his own village. There was therefore an old man in a nearby little field who had followed a solitary life from his earliest years. When Anthony saw him, he imitated him for the sake of goodness.

At first, beginning in this way himself, he remained in places somewhat farther removed from the village. From then on, whenever he discovered someone devoting himself earnestly to this pursuit, he went out and questioned him, like a most prudent bee. He did not return to his dwelling until he had enjoyed the sight of the one whom he desired to see; and then he departed to his own place as though he had received a gift of honey.

Having been formed there by such a beginning, he strengthened his spirit day by day, so that he remembered neither his paternal wealth nor his relatives, and devoted every desire and concern to the practice he had begun. He worked with his hands, knowing that it is written: “If anyone does not work, neither let him eat” (2 Thessalonians 3). Yet, after setting aside the price of bread, he distributed the wages of his work to the needy. 37 He prayed frequently, since he had learned that one must pray to the Lord without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5).

He devoted himself so diligently to hearing the Scriptures that nothing slipped from his mind. Observing all the Lord’s commandments, he possessed memory in place of books [Note: [Col. 0172C] “He possessed memory in place of books.” The nature of the things created by God was a book to Anthony.

Socrates, book IV, chapter 18, and from him the *Tripartite History*, book VIII, chapter 1: Τῷ δικαίῳ Ἀντωνίῳ προσῆλθέ τις τῶν σοφῶν, καὶ, Πῶς διακαρτερεῖς, εἶπεν, ὦ πάτερ, τῆς ἐκ τῶν βιβλίων παραμυθίας ἐστερημένος; Τὸ ἐμὸν βιβλίον, ἔφη ὁ Ἀντώνιος, ὦ φιλόσοφε, ἡ φύσις τῶν γεγονότων ἐστι, καὶ πάρεστίν, ὅτε βούλομαι, τοὺς λόγους ἀναγινώσκειν τοὺς τοῦ Θεοῦ. “One of those who at that time were regarded as wise approached the just Anthony and asked: ‘Father, how do you endure, deprived of the consolation that comes from books?’ Anthony replied: ‘My book, philosopher, is the nature of things created by God; and whenever I wish, it is present, supplying me with God’s own books to read.’

“Truly, every creature is an excellent and accessible book, and its use has always been familiar to holy men. For ‘the heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands’ (Psalm 18).”]

Thus ordering his life, he was loved by all the brothers with pure affection. Obedient to all those to whom he went in his eagerness to learn, he drew from each person his particular virtue: from one he imitated continence, from another cheerfulness; he followed the gentleness of one and the vigilance of another; he rivaled another’s diligence in reading. He admired one who fasted and another who rested on the ground; he praised one person’s patience and another’s meekness.

Retaining toward himself the reciprocal affection of all, and watered by every aspect of virtue, he returned to his own place. There he considered everything within himself and strove to reproduce in himself the good qualities of all. He was never moved against his contemporaries; rather, one flame alone grew in the breast of that exceptional man: that he should not be found second to anyone in the works mentioned above. He acted in such a way that, although he surpassed everyone in glory, he was nevertheless dear to everyone.

Neighbors and monks, whom he often visited, seeing Anthony, called him a worshiper of God. And, allowing themselves the natural terms of affection, some loved him as a son and others as a brother [Note: [Col. 0172D] “Some loved him as a son and others as a brother.” Some printed editions read “father” instead of “brother.” But the Greek is ἀδελφόν, “brother,” which fits Anthony’s age better, since he is soon called νεώτερος, “a young man.” They used these natural terms of affection according to his age.

So also in Spartianus, in the life of Didius Julianus: “When dawn first appeared, he admitted the Senate and the equestrian order, coming into the palace; and he addressed each one most graciously, according to his age, as father, son, or kinsman.” Here Heraldus unnecessarily emends *patrem* to *fratrem* in Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 39. I suppose he was misled because he thought that *parens* here meant “father.” But *parens* here means “relative,” as it often does among writers of that period.

Lampridius, in *Alexander Severus*: “The soldiers loved the young emperor himself as a brother, as a son, and as a kinsman.” What he says, “as a kinsman,” means “as a relative,” not “as a father.” For a young emperor could not be regarded by soldiers of equal or greater age as a father. Nerva was rightly regarded as a father, because he was an old man.

Ausonius:

> Closest to the slain tyrant, he governs the scepter—
>
> Nerva, old in years, prince in name, a father in mind.

(Ausonius, *On the Caesars*, Tetrastich 13.) See the *Onomasticon.”]

### Chapter IV

While Anthony was doing these things, by which he won everyone’s affection toward himself, the devil, the enemy of the Christian name, unable to bear such great virtues in a young man, attacked him with his veteran deceits. First, testing whether he could somehow draw him away from the way of life he had undertaken, he brought before him the memory of his possessions, the defense of his sister, the nobility of his family, love of material things, the fleeting glory of the world, the varied pleasure of food, and the other allurements of a more relaxed life. Finally, he suggested the difficult end of virtue and the immense labor required to reach it, as well as the frailty of the body and the long span of life. In short, he raised up within him the greatest darkness of thoughts, wishing to recall him from his right purpose.

But after the devil understood that he was being defeated by Anthony’s prayers to God through faith in the Passion, he took up the weapons customary against all young men and disturbed him with nocturnal temptations. At first he tried to harass him at night with a hostile multitude and terrifying sounds. By day also he rushed upon him with such open attacks that no one could doubt that Anthony was fighting against the devil. The devil tried to insert filthy thoughts, and Anthony drove them away by constant prayer. The devil pricked his senses with the natural heat of the flesh, while Anthony surrounded his whole body with faith, vigils, and fasts. At night the devil transformed himself into the appearance of a beautiful woman, omitting no image of lust; but Anthony, remembering the flames of hell and the pain of the worms, opposed them to the desire imposed upon him.

The devil placed before him the slippery path of youth [Note: [Col. 0173B] “The slippery path of youth.” This is a characteristic epithet for his age. Ambrose, *On the Death of Valentinian*: “For such was the correction of his life during that period of youth, slippery for everyone.” Jerome, Letter 3, to Rusticus: “To climb the step of mature age, but the path by which you proceed is slippery.” The same, Letter 43, to Chromatius: “You yourselves know the slippery path of youth.”], easily leading to ruin; but Anthony, considering the eternal torments of the coming judgment, preserved the purity of his soul unharmed through the temptations.

All these things happened to the devil’s shame. He who had thought that he could become like God was now mocked as a most wretched creature by a young man; and he who raged against flesh and blood was defeated by a human being who bore flesh. The Lord assisted his servant. For having taken flesh for our sake, he granted the body victory over the devil, so that, while each fought in this manner, the apostolic saying might be spoken: “It is not I, but the grace of God which is with me” (1 Corinthians 15).

Finally, when the most dreadful dragon could not destroy Anthony by this means and saw himself continually driven back from his thoughts, he appeared, according to what is written in Mark 9, gnashing his teeth and howling; and his face rightly appeared as he was: a frightful and black boy, falling at Anthony’s knees, wept in a human voice and said: “I have led many astray; I have deceived very many. But now, just as I have been overcome by the other saints, so also I have been overcome by your labor.”

When Anthony asked him who he was who spoke such things, he replied: “I am the friend of fornication. I have taken up against all young men weapons of shame in many forms; hence I am also called the spirit of fornication” [Note: [Col. 0173B] “Hence I am also called the spirit of fornication.” Thus πνεῦμα πορνείας, “the spirit of fornication,” in Hosea 4, as follows.

Palladius, chapter 86: “The demon of fornication once caused him [Evagrius] severe trouble.” In the *Life of Hilarion*, chapter 16: “He had as my companion the demon of love.” The leader of the lustful host is Asmodeus, mentioned in Tobit, chapters 3 and 6. Our Serarius treats the matter at length.

Ascetic authors frequently mention particular demons devoted to particular vices and deriving their names from them. Below, after chapter 15: “Their wickedness is diverse and divided.” Cassian, *Conferences*, VII, chapter 32: “We must not think that these names were given to them by chance or accident.”

For a discussion of the various distinctions and differences among demons, see the French booklet published under the name of our John Maldonatus, where he distinguishes them by name, nature, the places where they operate, the time during which they dominate, the duties of commanding and obeying, and the vices over which they preside.”]

“How many intending to live chastely have I deceived! How many who were beginning only weakly have I persuaded to return to their former filth! I am the one because of whom the prophet rebukes those who have fallen, saying: ‘You have been seduced by the spirit of fornication’ (Hosea 4); and truly, through me, they had been overthrown. I am the one who often tempted you yourself, and was always repulsed.”

When the soldier of Christ heard this, he gave thanks to God and, strengthened by greater boldness against the enemy, said: “You are therefore greatly contemptible and utterly despicable; for both your darkness and your age are signs of weakness. I have no further concern about you. The Lord is my helper, and I shall exult over my enemies” (Psalm 117). Immediately, at the voice of the one singing, the apparition that had appeared vanished.

### Chapter V

This was Anthony’s first victory over the devil—or rather, it was the Savior’s virtue in Anthony: the Savior who condemned sin in the flesh, so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the spirit (Romans 8). Yet this one triumph did not give Anthony security, nor did the devil’s strength fail after being broken once.

The devil, like a roaring lion (1 Peter 5), sought an entrance through which he might burst in. Anthony, instructed in the language of Scripture that there are many traps of demons (Ephesians 6), carefully guarded his purpose through diligent labor, considering that Satan, having been defeated in the conflict of the flesh, might stir up more violently new engines of warfare against him. Therefore he subjected his body more and more, lest, victorious over others, he should himself be conquered in other matters (1 Corinthians 9).

Since he intended to bind himself by a harsher rule of life, and everyone marveled at the young man’s tireless persistence [Note: [Col. 0173C] “When everyone marveled at the young man’s tireless persistence.” Here he uses *instantia* as it is used in sacred Scripture, 2 Corinthians 2: “My daily persistence in contention,” that is, with great care, zeal, and diligence. So earlier, in the preface to this Life: “Or striving to surpass by persistence in virtue.”], he patiently endured the holy labor, because long devotion to voluntary service in God’s work had turned habit into nature.

### Chapter VI

He was so patient in hunger and vigils that he overcame disbelief in his strength. He very often spent the entire night in prayer. He ate once a day, after sunset; sometimes he continued in this way for two or three days and was refreshed only on the fourth day. His food was bread and salt, with very little water to drink. As for meat and wine, I think it better to say nothing than to say anything, since not even among the majority of monks is anything of this kind found.

When he allowed his limbs to rest, he used a mat woven from reeds and a hair shirt. Sometimes he even lay upon the bare ground, entirely rejecting ointments. For he said that the bodies of those who use them, especially young men, cannot be strengthened if they are softened by the gentleness of oil; rather, harsh labors must be imposed upon the flesh, according to the Apostle’s command: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12).

He maintained that the mind’s understanding could thus revive if the body’s force had been wearied. Therefore he did not measure the merit of his labors by the length of time, but always, through love and voluntary service, as though he were just beginning, stirred up his desire to advance in the fear of God. Desiring to increase what had gone before by new achievements, he remembered the words of the aforementioned Teacher, who said: “Forgetting what lies behind and growing strong for what lies ahead” (Philippians 3).

He also remembered the prophet Elijah, who said: “The Lord lives, before whom I stand today” (1 Kings 18). He explained why “today” had been added: Elijah did not reckon the time that had passed, but, as though he were placed daily in the contest, wished to present himself as one whom he knew to be worthy of God’s sight—pure in heart and ready to obey his will.

### Chapter VII

Therefore Saint Anthony, considering within himself that a servant of God ought to take the example of the great Elijah as his rule and ought to conform his life to that mirror, withdrew to tombs situated not far from the village. He instructed one of his acquaintances to bring him food on appointed days. When the brother mentioned above had shut him inside a single tomb [Note: [Col. 0173C] “And when he had shut him inside a single tomb.” The Greek is μνῆμα, “memorial” or “tomb.” Shortly before, he translated the same word as “sepulcher.” Thus Augustine uses *memoria* for the memorials of martyrs, book XXII of *The City of God*, chapter 8, concerning the relics of Saint Stephen: “A great crowd came together and hastened to his memorial,” and frequently elsewhere among sacred writers.”], he remained there alone.

The devil, fearing that with the passage of time Anthony might make the desert inhabited as well, therefore gathered his attendants and tore him apart with such varied slaughter that the magnitude of his pain deprived him both of movement and of speech. He himself later often related that his wounds had been so severe that they surpassed all human tortures. But God’s providence, which never abandons those who hope in him, preserved him.

On another day, the brother mentioned above arrived, bringing the customary food, and found him lying on the ground half-dead, the doors having been broken. He placed him on his shoulders and carried him back to the dwelling of the little village. When this became known, a great crowd of neighbors and relatives gathered and performed the sad rites surrounding the one laid out as though dead.

After half the night had already passed, heavy sleep overcame the eyes of all who were keeping vigil. Then, as his soul returned little by little, Anthony sighed and raised his head. While the others lay prostrate in deep sleep, he saw that the man by whom he had been carried away was awake. Calling him by a sign, he begged him to carry him back to his former dwelling without waking anyone at all.

### Chapter VIII

After he had been carried back, he again remained there alone according to his custom. He could not stand because of his recent wounds, but, prostrate, he prayed; and after the prayer he said in a loud voice:

“Here I am, I, Anthony. I do not flee from your contests. Even if you make them greater, no one will separate me from the love of Christ” (Romans 8).

And he sang, saying: “Though armies encamp against me, my heart will not fear” (Psalm 26).

As he said these things, the devil, the enemy of the good, was astonished that Anthony had dared to return after so many blows. He gathered his dogs and, tearing himself apart in his own fury, said:

“You see that, overcome neither by the spirit of fornication nor by bodily pains, he now attacks us with even greater boldness. Take up all your weapons; he must be assaulted more fiercely by us. Let him feel it—let him feel it. He must learn whom he is provoking.”

He spoke, and at the voice of the exhorter the assembled crowd agreed, for the devil possesses countless arts of causing harm. Then a sudden sound thundered, so that the place was utterly shaken and the walls split open. From there a crowd of demons poured forth in many forms. Taking on the shapes of beasts and serpents, they immediately filled the entire place with phantoms of lions, bulls, wolves, asps, serpents, scorpions, leopards, and bears. Each of these roared according to its own nature.

The lion roared, wishing to kill; the bull threatened with bellowing and horns; the serpent resounded with its hiss; the attacks of wolves were hurled against him; and the leopard, with its variegated coloring [Note: [Col. 0173D] “The leopard, with its variegated coloring.” Thus the manuscripts and the Cologne edition; the latter has *discolor a tergo*, “variegated on the back.” Other copies simply have *discolor*, “variegated.” This description of the leopard is absent from the Greek text.”], displayed the various cunning of its author. All had savage faces, and the sound of their dreadful voices was terrifying.

Anthony, beaten and pierced, felt indeed the harsher pains of his body, but remained undaunted with an ever-watchful mind. Although his wounds forced groans from him, he nevertheless remained unchanged in understanding and spoke as though he were mocking his enemies:

“If you possessed any strength, one of you would be sufficient for battle. But since you are broken because the Lord has weakened you, you try to inflict terror by your multitude. Yet this very thing is an indication of weakness: that you assume the forms of irrational beasts.”

Again, taking courage, he said:

“If you have any power, if the Lord has given you authority over me, behold, I am here; devour what has been granted. But if you cannot, why do you strive in vain? The sign of the cross and faith in the Lord are an impregnable wall for us.”

They threatened many things against Saint Anthony and gnashed their teeth, because none of their temptations achieved any effect; indeed, the opposite result was produced above all: mockery.

## Chapter IX

Jesus did not forget [Note: “Jesus did not forget.” Thyreus, *On the Impersonal Apparitions of Christ*, chapter 6, cites some examples in which Christ was heard but not seen. Such is this passage concerning Antony, when “a voice was made to him, saying: ‘I, Antony, was here.’” Likewise, in chapter 51 below: “And a voice of the Lord was made, saying: ‘My altar shall be abhorred.’” See also 12 August, in the *Life of Saint Clare*, chapter 14, and 7 March, in the *Life of Saint Thomas Aquinas* by John Garzone.] became the protector of his servant in the latter’s struggle. Finally, when he raised his eyes, he saw the roof above him open, and, the darkness being withdrawn, a ray of light stream down upon him. After the arrival of that splendor, none of the demons appeared, and the pain in his body was immediately removed. The building, too, which shortly before had been demolished, was restored.

At once Antony understood that the Lord was present, and, drawing long sighs from the depths of his breast, he spoke to the light that had appeared to him, saying: “Where were you, good Jesus? Where were you? Why were you not present from the beginning, so that you might heal my wounds?” And a voice was made to him, saying: “Antony, I was here, but I was waiting to see your contest. Now, however, because you have not ceased to fight manfully, I will always help you, and I will cause you to be named throughout the whole world.”

When he heard these things, he rose up, so greatly strengthened that he prayed, and understood that he had then received more strength than he had previously lost. Antony was at that time thirty-five years old.

## Chapter X

From that time onward, as he increased in willing devotion through religious merit, he went to the old man mentioned above and entreated him that they might live together in the desert. But when the old man pleaded his advanced age and the novelty of the undertaking, Antony went alone to the mountain and, having cast off fear for his life, attempted to open a path into a wilderness still unknown to monks.

Yet even then the tireless adversary did not cease. For, wishing to hinder his purpose, he threw a silver dish onto the road. When Antony saw it, he recognized the cunning of the skillful artificer. Standing fearlessly and gazing sternly at the dish, he rebuked the author of the trick in the phantom of the silver, reasoning thus with himself:

“Whence is there a dish here in the desert? This is a path for birds; there are no footprints of travelers. If it had fallen from a baggage-load, its great size could not have allowed it to remain hidden. Moreover, if the one who had lost it had returned, he would surely have found what had fallen, despite the solitude of the place. This device is yours, devil. You will not impede my will. May your silver be with you for your destruction.”

When he said this, the dish vanished from his sight like smoke before fire.

## Chapter XI

Afterward, no longer in a phantom as before, he saw a huge mass of gold lying on the road. But whether the devil had fabricated it, or whether heavenly power had displayed it to test Antony, because he would not be ensnared even by genuine riches, is unknown. This much, however, we know: what was seen was gold.

But Antony, astonished at the size of the shining metal, hurried on at a swift pace, as though avoiding some fire, until he reached the mountain. There, after crossing a river, he found a deserted fortress full of venomous creatures because of the passage of time and its solitude. Establishing himself there, he lived as a new inhabitant.

Immediately upon his arrival, a great crowd of serpents, as though they had suffered the arrival of their persecutor, fled. Antony blocked the entrance with stones, stored with him bread for six months, as is the custom among the Thebans [Note: “As is the custom among the Thebans.” I do not doubt that by “bread” here we should understand the loaves that remain unspoiled for a year and that the Thebans store for themselves—*paximates*, or twice-baked bread. Suidas: Παξαμᾶς, ὁ δίπυρος ἄρτος, “paxamas, bread baked twice.” See our *Onomasticon*.], since such bread commonly remains unspoiled throughout the year, and had only a little water. He persisted there alone, never going out and never admitting anyone, to such a degree that, when twice a year bread was brought to him through the roof above, he exchanged no words with those who delivered it.

## Chapter XII

Thus, while many people, desiring and earnestly seeking to see him, spent the night before his door, voices like those of a crowd and a tumult of speakers were heard against Antony:

“Why do you intrude upon our dwellings? What have you to do with the desert? Go away from another’s territory. You cannot live here or withstand our attacks.”

At first those outside thought that some men had entered after setting ladders against the building and were fighting within. But when they looked inside through the openings and saw no one, they understood that demons were contending against him. Terrified by extreme fear, they implored Antony’s help.

He approached the door, however, to console the brothers, asking them not to be afraid and to withdraw from the place. He assured all those who were trembling that the demons were the ones causing the fear:

“Sign yourselves,” he said, “and go away safely. Leave them to deceive themselves.”

When they had returned, Antony remained unharmed and was never wearied in the struggle. The growth in the progress of those who approached him, or the weakness of those who resisted, provided great relief in his contest and instilled steadfastness in his mind.

Again, when crowds came to the desert—people who had already supposed that they would find him dead [Note: “People who had already supposed that they would find him dead.” Thus the manuscripts state it explicitly. But the Cologne edition, Surius, and Suerius read *quidam* (“some”) in place of *quae jam* (“who already”). I believe this was substituted lest the text seem to violate Priscian’s rules, since *reperturos* follows.]—he sang within:

“Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered, and let those who hate him flee from his face. As smoke vanishes, so may they vanish; as wax melts before the fire, so may sinners perish before the face of God” (Psalm 67).

And again:

“All the nations surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I took vengeance upon them” (Psalm 117).

## Chapter XIII

Thus Antony remained for twenty years in solitude, separated from the sight of human beings. When, therefore, a multitude of people who desired to imitate his way of life, together with many acquaintances, hastened to him, and an innumerable crowd of sick people gathered around him [Note: “And an innumerable crowd of sick people gathered around him.” This is absent from the Greek. Below, in chapter 36, concerning a demoniac: “He struggled against the madness of the sick man.” Understand “the sick” either as people suffering from diseases or as those afflicted by demons; for immediately afterward it says: “He freed very many from unclean spirits and various infirmities.” The Greek reads: Πολλοὺς γοῦν τῶν παρόντων τὰ σώματα πάσχοντας ἐθεράπευσεν ὁ Κύριος δι’ αὐτοῦ· καὶ ἄλλους ἀπὸ δαιμόνων ἐκαθάρισε, “Thus the Lord healed through him the bodies of many of those present who were suffering, and cleansed others from demons.”], finally, when the doors had almost already been torn away by force, he appeared as though consecrated from some heavenly entrance [Note: “As though consecrated from some heavenly entrance.” The Greek is: Προῆλθεν ὁ Ἀντώνιος ὥσπερ ἔκ τινος ἀδύτου μεμυσταγωγημένος καὶ θεοφορούμενος, “Antony came forth as though initiated into sacred mysteries and divinely inspired from some sanctuary.” Hence what is *adyton* in Greek is rendered by Evagrius as “heavenly sanctuary.”].

Everyone was astonished at the grace of his face and the dignity of his body: it had not swollen even through rest [Note: “Which had not swollen even through rest.” The Cologne edition has *inquietem*, “through unrest.” The Greek has only μήτε πιανθήν, “neither grown fat.” Bodies swell both through rest, that is, when they are not exercised, and through unrest, that is, sleeplessness.], nor had pallor overwhelmed his face because of fasting and combat with demons. On the contrary, as though he had spent no time at all, the ancient beauty of his limbs remained.

What a great miracle! What purity of mind was in him! He was never dissolved into laughter by excessive cheerfulness; never did sadness contract his face through remembrance of sin; he was not puffed up by the great praises of those who marveled at him. Solitude had contributed nothing indecent to him, nor had his daily battles with the enemies made him harsh; rather, his disciplined mind was carried with equal judgment toward all things.

Thus, by God’s grace, he freed very many through Antony from unclean spirits and various illnesses. His speech, seasoned with salt, comforted the sorrowful, taught the ignorant, reconciled the angry, and urged everyone to prefer nothing to the love of Christ. He set before their eyes the greatness of future blessings and the mercy of God, and he unfolded the benefits that had been granted: God had not spared his own Son but had handed him over for the salvation of us all (Romans 8).

Without delay, this speech persuaded many of his listeners to despise human affairs, and this was the beginning of his establishment of the desert.

## Chapter XIV

I will not pass over in silence what happened in the town of the Arsinoites [Note: “In the town of the Arsinoites.” He means Arsinoe, or the Town of Crocodiles, on the Nile, in the Arsinoite district. He adds here that it contained crocodiles. There is also another Arsinoe in Egypt. See the *Onomasticon*.].

When he wished to visit the brothers, it was necessary for him to cross a stream of the Nile, full of crocodiles and many savage river creatures [Note: “It was necessary to cross a stream of the Nile.” The Greek reads: Χρείας δὲ γενομένης διελθεῖν αὐτὸν τὸν τοῦ Ἀρσενοΐτου διώρυγα, “When necessity arose to cross the canal of the Arsenoite prefecture.” See Strabo, book 17.]. He crossed it unharmed with his companions and returned from there safely.

Again persevering in his former labors, he strengthened many brothers by his instruction, so that within a short time very many monasteries came into being [Note: “Very many monasteries came into being.” Baronius, volume 3, in the year of Christ 328, the fifteenth year of Pope Sylvester and the twenty-third of Constantine, says: “When people of every kind flocked together to visit Antony, and were diligently invited by him to undertake contempt for the world and the pursuit of a perfect life, they adopted the same way and institution of living. He founded numerous monasteries and himself first laid the foundations of the communal life in the desert. Thus he is regarded as the founder—or rather the restorer, if some account should be taken of the Essenes, who flourished in Egypt under Mark, the first bishop of the Alexandrians—of the monks living in community. We have clearly demonstrated elsewhere that they were Christians” (volume 1, in the year of Christ 64). “When more severe storms of persecution arose, during which not only Christians living together and holding public assemblies but also those who were hidden in inner rooms and other hiding places were sought out and dragged away to death, that heavenly way of life had to be interrupted. Saint Antony not only restored it but propagated it widely throughout the Christian world with abundant fruitfulness.”].

There were, indeed, before Antony, people who, through fear of persecution, had abandoned the cities and, hidden either in the countryside or in deserted places, led a life like that of angels. We have said from Eusebius that some of them were crowned with martyrdom. Antony himself also encountered some of these when, in order to avoid the persecution inflicted upon the Church, he withdrew into a deserted place, as has been said, and received from one of them the first rudiments of monastic discipline. He perfected these while concealed in solitude.

Later, inspired by the divine Name, he gathered monks together and distributed them into different places, like swarms of bees in different hives. They had been persuaded under his discipline to renounce the world and embrace the monastic profession. Concerning them, see this *Life*, chapter 21 and following.

Those who came to Antony and submitted themselves to him as disciples—some of them practiced monastic discipline in the same mountains with him; others, cutting branches from that same stock and planting them in distant provinces, soon caused it to happen—indeed, in that very century—that the whole world was filled with such a holy propagation: Palestine, Syria, Asia Minor, Cappadocia, Pontus, Armenia, Mesopotamia, and the northern regions, as far as the robber peoples, the Bessi and Daci.

Saint Paulinus sang the following about them in his *Return of Saint Nicetas*, a most holy man, from whom he received the information he records:

> O changes of fortune! Happily transformed!
>
> Mountains once impassable and bloodstained
>
> Now shelter converted robbers,
>
> Pupils of peace.
>
> Once a land of blood, now it is a land of life;
>
> The pious violence of robbers is turned heavenward,
>
> And Christ favors the one who seizes
>
> The kingdoms above by force.
>
> Where once there had been the ways of wild beasts,
>
> Now the rites of angels flourish;
>
> And the righteous man lies hidden in the caves
>
> Where the robber himself once lived, and so forth.
>
> *(Paulinus, On the Return of Saint Nicetas.)*

Saint Jerome also mentions the Bessi. Writing to Heliodorus, he says:

> “The Indian, Persian, Goth, and Egyptian philosophize; the ferocity of the Bessi and the multitude of fur-clad peoples, who once sacrificed human beings at festivals for the dead, have broken their harsh cry into the sweet melody of the cross” (Jerome, Letter 3).

And to Laeta:

> “Every day we receive troops of monks from India, Persia, and Ethiopia” (Jerome, Letter 7).

That is, those who used to travel out of devotion to visit the holy places.

He governed new and old monks alike, according to age or length of service, with paternal affection.

## Chapter XV

One day, when the holy Antony was asked by the brothers who had gathered together to give them rules of instruction, he raised his voice with prophetic confidence and said that the Scriptures were sufficient for the entire discipline of the commandments [Note: “The Scriptures are sufficient for the entire discipline of the commandments.” Bellarmine discusses how Scripture is called sufficient in volume 1 of *Controversiae Generales*, book 4, chapter 9, “On the unwritten word of God,” under the second argument.]. But he added that it would also be best if the brothers consoled one another through mutual conversation.

“And so,” he said, “report to me as to a father what you know, and I will disclose to you as to sons what I have acquired through long experience.

“Let this be the first command given to all in common: let no one grow weary in the vigor of the undertaking once begun, but, as though always beginning, let him continually increase what he has started—especially since the span of human life, compared with eternity, is very short and small.”

Having begun thus, he was silent for a little while. Then, marveling at God’s excessive generosity, he added:

“In the present life, the exchanges are equal according to the mutual transfer of things; the seller does not receive more from the buyer than he gives. But the promise of eternal life is purchased at a low price.

“For it is written: ‘The days of our life are seventy years; but if [they amount to] more, eighty’ [Note: “And if much.” Thus the manuscripts and the older Cologne editions read here: “But if in powers.” So also our Vulgate translator renders Psalm 89 from the Greek: Ἐὰν δὲ ἐν δυναστείαις, “But if in powers.” Jerome cites “But if much” in Letter 21 to Paul of Concordia, and “But if more” in Letter 34 to Julian. See also Letter 139 to Cyprian, where he likewise has: “But if much.” He quotes from the Septuagint: “But if in powers,” and from Symmachus: “Contrary to expectation.”], ‘eighty; and what exceeds these is labor and sorrow’ (Psalm 89).

“Therefore, when we have lived laboring in God’s work for eighty, or even a hundred years, as much as possible, we shall not reign for an equal period in the future. In exchange for the years mentioned, the kingdoms of all the ages will be given to us. We shall not inherit earth but heaven; and, leaving behind the corruptible body, we shall receive that same body with incorruption.

“Therefore, little sons, let neither weariness fatigue you nor ambition for empty glory delight you. ‘The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the glory that is to come and that will be revealed in us’ (Romans 8).

“No one, when he has despised the world, should suppose that he has abandoned great things, because the whole earth, compared with the infinity of the heavens, is brief and small. Therefore, if even by renouncing the entire world we cannot offer anything worthy in exchange for the heavenly dwelling places, let each person consider himself; and he will immediately understand that, having despised small fields and walls, or a modest portion of gold, he should neither boast as though he had abandoned great things nor grow weary as though he were going to receive little.

“For just as someone despises a single bronze drachma in order to acquire a hundred golden drachmas, so also the person who has abandoned dominion over the whole world will receive a hundredfold better rewards in the heavenly dwelling.

“Above all, we must recognize that, even if we wish to retain our riches, the law of death will tear us unwillingly away from them, as it is written in the book of Ecclesiastes (Ecclesiastes 2) [Note: “As it is written in the book of Ecclesiastes.” The Cologne edition adds in the text: “Because a person does not know what will happen after him in his labor.” This is absent from the manuscripts and older editions. It is certain that the reference is to the sense of Ecclesiastes 2, as the text indicates.]. Why, then, do we not make a virtue of necessity [Note: “Why, then, do we not make a virtue of necessity?” This appears to be a proverbial expression, also common in German. Blessed Jerome uses it in Letter 10 to Furia: “Seize the opportunity, I beg you, and make a virtue of necessity.” And in *Apology 3 against Rufinus*: “Rather, I give thanks that you make a virtue of necessity.”]? Why do we not willingly abandon, in order to gain the heavenly kingdoms, what must be lost when this light comes to an end?

“Christians should care nothing for those things that they cannot take away with them. Rather, we should seek what leads us to heaven: wisdom, chastity, justice, virtue, an alert mind, care for the poor, firm faith in Christ, a spirit victorious over anger, and hospitality. Pursuing these things, we shall prepare for ourselves a dwelling in the land of the peaceful, according to the Gospel (John 14).

“Let us consider that we are servants of the Lord and owe service to him by whom we were created. For just as a servant, because of past service, does not despise a present or future command, nor dare to claim that he ought to have freedom from current work on account of labor already completed, but with unceasing devotion—as it is written in the Gospel (Luke 12)—continually offers the same service, so that he may please his master and not incur fear and blows, so we too must obey the divine commands. We know that the just Requiter will judge each person according to what he finds in him, as the prophetic voice through Ezekiel testifies (Ezekiel 33).

“Even the unhappy Judas, because of the impiety of a single night, was deprived of the labor of all his previous time. Therefore the firmness of the undertaking must be maintained continuously, with God as helper, as it is written: ‘God cooperates with everyone who purposes what is good’ (Romans 8).”

To trample down idleness, let us repeat the Apostle’s teaching, by which he testified that he died daily (1 Corinthians 15). Likewise, as we reconsider the uncertainty of human life, we shall not sin. When we have been roused from sleep, we doubt that we shall reach evening; when we surrender our bodies to rest, we do not rely on the arrival of daylight; and, remembering everywhere the uncertainty of nature and life, we understand that we are governed by God’s providence.

In this way we shall not sin or be carried away by any fragile desire. We shall not even grow angry against anyone, nor seek to gather earthly treasures. Rather, through fear of our daily departure and constant meditation on the separation of the body, we shall trample on all things passing away.

The love of women will cease; the fire of lust will be extinguished; we shall forgive one another the debts owed to us, always keeping before our eyes the arrival of the final retribution. For the greater dread of judgment and the terrible fear of punishments likewise extinguish the incentives of slippery flesh [Note: “The incentives of slippery flesh.” The word *incentive* frequently occurs of the vice of the flesh. Jerome, Letter 4 to the monk Rusticus: “And trampling upon the incentives of youth, indeed of puberty.” The same, on Isaiah 58: “The heat of the body overcame me; the incentives of youth conquered.” Cassian, *Conferences* 2, chapter 13: “Troubled by carnal incentives.” The same noun is also applied to other vices. See the *Onomasticon*.], and sustain a falling soul as though from some cliff [Note: “And sustains the falling soul as though from some cliff.” The Greek has ἀνίστησιν, “raises up.” Evagrius expresses it with what appears to be a proverbial formula: “Sustains as though from some cliff.” Thus Ammianus, book 22, says that Eusebius, “breathing proudly and occupying the highest position with the emperor,” was “driven, resisting Adrastia, headlong as though from some lofty cliff.”].

Therefore I beg you to strive toward the end of the undertaking with every effort (Philippians 3). Let no one imitate Lot’s wife, who looked back (Genesis 19), especially since the Lord said that no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is worthy of the kingdom of heaven (Luke 9). To look back means nothing other than to regret what one has begun and once again to become bound by worldly desires.

Do not, I beg you, fear the name of virtue as though it were impossible, nor let this pursuit seem foreign or far removed from you, since it depends upon our own will [Note: “Since it depends upon our own will.” The editions read: “Since it depends upon our own will, with God’s grace preceding.” Although these middle words are absent from the Latin manuscript and the printed Greek, they are to be understood here according to sound theology.].

The nature for this work has been implanted in human beings [Note: “The nature for this work has been implanted in human beings.” The scholastics explain how the seeds of virtue are implanted in human beings. See the *Onomasticon*.], and this is the kind of matter that awaits only our will. Let the Greeks pursue studies across the sea [Note: “Let the Greeks pursue studies across the sea.” Persius’s sixth satire is relevant here:

> “And Bestius presses
>
> The Greek teachers. Thus it happens, after
>
> Our own ‘wisdom’ came to the city
>
> With pepper and dates, unacquainted with the sea.”

], and, established in a foreign world, seek teachers of empty letters. For us, however, no necessity of crossing the seas [Note: “For us, however, no necessity of crossing the seas.” From this passage Flacius Illyricus, in his *Catalogue of the Witnesses of Truth*—more accurately, of truth and falsehood—book 4, and modern heretics after him, reject pilgrimages. But they distort Antony’s meaning. Antony denies that journeys to the Holy Land or elsewhere are simply necessary for salvation. What Catholic would not deny this together with Antony? We know that the kingdom of heaven exists in every land and that God is present everywhere. But why should we not embrace God’s particular gifts granted in a particular place? Who could demand from him an account of why he grants them in one place rather than another? Augustine speaks excellently in Letter 137: “God is indeed everywhere, and he who created all things is contained or enclosed by no place. He must be worshiped by true worshipers in spirit and truth, so that, hearing in secret, he may also justify and crown in secret. Yet, with regard to those things that are visibly known among human beings, who can search out his purpose—why these miracles occur in some places and not in others?” Antony’s speech here is also addressed to monks, for whom pilgrimages, however holy and praiseworthy, are not especially appropriate.].

There is no necessity for us to cross the waves; the kingdoms of heaven are established in every place on earth. Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17). The virtue that is within us requires only a human mind.

Who can doubt that the natural purity of the soul, if it has not been polluted by any external stain, is the fountain and origin of all virtues? The good Creator must have created it good. If we should perhaps hesitate, let us hear Jesus son of Nun saying to the people: “Make your heart right before the Lord God of Israel” (Joshua 24). John also pronounced no discordant judgment about virtue when he preached: “Make his paths straight” (Luke 3).

For this is what it means for the soul to be straight: its principal integrity is not stained by any blemish of vice. If it changes its nature, it is then called perverse; if its good condition is preserved, it is virtue. The Lord entrusted our soul to us; let us preserve the deposit as we received it.

No one can claim that what is born within him is located outside him. Let the thing made acknowledge its maker; let him who made it find his work as he created it. Natural adornment is enough for us; do not disfigure, human being, what divine generosity has granted you. To wish to alter the works of God is to pollute them.

We must also take careful precautions to overcome the tyrannical madness of anger, because it is written: “The anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God” (James 1). And again: “Lustful desire gives birth to sin; when sin is complete, death is brought forth” (ibid.).

It is a command of the divine voice (Proverbs 4) that we guard our soul with constant vigilance, because we have enemies trained to trip us up—namely, demons—against whom, according to the Apostle’s testimony, we have an uninterrupted struggle. For:

> “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities and powers of this world, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6).

A vast crowd of them traverses this air; a host of enemies moves about not far from us. It is not for my small ability to explain their diversity, but I leave this account to greater men. What is readily apparent, however, and what it is not useful to ignore—their schemes devised against us—I shall briefly set forth.

We must first fix this in our minds: God made nothing that is evil [Note: “God made nothing that is evil.” He rightly adds that demons are evil not by nature but by their own fault. Among the ancient philosophers there was an old question concerning the origin of evil. Arnobius is perplexed by it in book 2 *Against the Nations*. Tertullian briefly explains it in *Against Marcion*, book 2, chapter 14: “Having distinguished between the two forms, and separating the evils of sin from the evils of punishment, the evils of guilt from the evils of penalty, we assign an author to each side: the devil to the evils of sin and guilt, but God the Creator to the evils of punishment and penalty, so that the former kind of evil may be attributed to wickedness and the latter to justice—the judgments of the one who establishes evils against the evils of wrongdoing.” See also Cassian, *Conferences* 8, chapter 6, on the fact that nothing evil was created by God.

The origin of evil as arising from the creature is elegantly explained by a comparison in the *Life of Saint Auxentius*: “Just as the light of the sun is offered commonly to all who possess the power of sight, yet someone can, if he wishes, close his eye and separate himself from the gift of light—not because the sun produced darkness in him, but because, turning away from the brightness of its rays, he voluntarily drew darkness upon himself; and just as someone building a house for himself and providing no entrance for light within makes the house dark, so we too, possessing what is good and honorable in our nature, transform by our own choice what is contrary to nature, freely creating the experience of evils through our rejection of what is good and honorable, by our choice and practice. For evil, considered in itself and outside the intention, has no substance in the nature of things. Whatever was created by God is good, and everything God made is very good” (Genesis 1).].

Nor did the beginnings of demons originate from his institution. This perversity is a fault not of nature but of will. For, though good because they had been created by God, they fell from heaven to earth by their own mental choice. There, rolling in the filth of mud, they established the impious practices of pagan worship. Now they are tormented by envy of us, and they do not cease to stir up every evil, lest we take their former seats.

Their wickedness, however, is diverse and divided [Note: “Their wickedness, however, is diverse and divided.” Cassian, *Conferences* 7, chapter 17: “We must know that not all demons inflict every passion upon human beings, but that particular spirits preside over particular vices, and that some are defiled by filth and the stains of lust,” and so forth. The same *Conference*, chapter 20: “We must also by no means be ignorant that they are not all of the same fierceness and desire, nor even of the same strength and wickedness.” He discusses this more fully in the same *Conference*, chapter 32, where he says: “It is undoubtedly proved that there are as many pursuits among unclean spirits as among human beings.” See Augustine, *City of God*, book 10, chapter 11, concerning the various dispositions of demons, drawing on Porphyry and Iamblichus. Palladius, chapters 19 and 20, on Macarius of Egypt: “There is also an order of demons called fiery. For just as there are differences among human beings, so there are also among demons—not a change of essence, but diversity of mind.” See what was said at chapter 4, section 14.].

Some have reached the highest summit of harmfulness; others, by comparison with the worse, seem lighter. All have undertaken different struggles against different individuals, according to the extent of their powers. Therefore it is necessary to ask the Lord for the gift of discerning spirits (1 Corinthians 12), so that, recognizing both their deceptions and their inclinations, we may raise against unequal combat the single banner of the Lord’s cross.

Having received this gift, Paul taught, saying: “We are not ignorant of his schemes” (2 Corinthians 2). Following his example, we too ought to instruct one another through conversation about the things we have suffered.

They bear a hostile hatred toward all Christians, but especially toward monks and the virgins of Christ. They spread snares along their paths and attempt to overturn their minds with impious and obscene thoughts. But let them inspire no terror in you on this account. They immediately fall before the prayers and fasts of the faithful offered to the Lord. Nevertheless, if they withdraw for a little while, do not suppose that the victory is entirely complete.

They also commonly rise up more fiercely when wounded. Changing their method of fighting, when they have accomplished nothing in thought, they terrify people with apparitions, now assuming the forms of women, now of beasts, now of serpents, and also enormous bodies, with heads extending up to the roof of a house, and countless shapes and hosts of soldiers. All these vanish at the first sign of the cross [Note: “They vanish at the first sign of the cross.” Take note, heretic, of the efficacy of the sign of the cross; you have clear examples of it in this *Life of Antony*, also in chapters 18, 26, and 49. There is more on these matters in the extensive books of our Gretzer on the Cross.

From this passage, too, the falsehood of Flacius Illyricus is refuted. In book 2 of his *Catalogue of the Witnesses of Truth*, he did not hesitate to write: “I read much about Antony’s struggles with Satan, but nowhere about holy water, the cross, wax, or consecrated herbs.” Evidently Illyricus was so sharp-sighted that, although Antony repeatedly praised the efficacy of the cross and raised its banner, he did not notice even one instance of it.].

Once they have recognized these methods of deception, they begin to foresee events and attempt to predict what will happen in future days. And when they have been despised even in these matters, they summon to aid their struggle the very prince of their wickedness and the summit of all evil.

## CHAPTER XVI

Finally, Antony often asserted that the devil had appeared to him in the form which blessed Job, by the Lord’s revelation, had recognized (Job 41): “His eyes are like the appearance of Lucifer; from his mouth burning torches proceed. His hair too is scattered with fires, and smoke comes forth from his nostrils, like the heat of a glowing furnace of coals. His soul is like a burning coal, while flame gathers from his mouth.” When the prince of demons appeared with such terrors, Antony says, and often made vast promises, as I have said, his boastful tongue raged in the impiety of his speech. Concerning him the Lord triumphed, saying to Job (ibid.):

> For he considers iron as straw, bronze as rotten wood, the seas as earth; he reckons the abyss as a captive and the deep as a place for walking.

Through the prophet also he reproves him, saying:

> Pursuing, I shall overtake them (Exodus 15),

and:

> I shall hold the whole earth in my hand like a nest, and, like abandoned eggs, I shall take them away (Isaiah 10).

Thus the wicked one, vomiting funeral-like utterances, frequently ensnares some of those who live well; but we must neither believe his promises nor fear his threats. For he often deceives and promises nothing true. If he did not speak lies in everything, how is it that, while making such vast and countless promises, he has been hooked by the hook of the cross like a dragon and bound by the Lord?

[Note: “By the hook of the cross, like a dragon, he has been hooked by the Lord.” This alludes to Job 40:20: “Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook?” In Greek: Ἄξεις δὲ δράκοντα ἐν ἀγκίστρῳ; “Will you lead the dragon with a hook?” Gregory of Nyssa, in his First Oration on the Resurrection of the Lord, understands the hook as the divinity of Christ by which the devil was captured: “While he eagerly desired the flesh as food,” he says, “he was pierced by the hook of divinity; and thus the dragon was led by the hook, as Job says, who, foretelling what was to come, says: ‘With a hook you will lead the dragon.’” Nor does Gregory the Great speak otherwise: “This Leviathan was captured by a hook because, when in our Redeemer he bit the bait of the body through his agents, the thorn of divinity pierced him. Like a hook, it held the jaws of the one swallowing, since in him the bait of flesh was displayed, which the devourer desired, while the divinity that would destroy him lay hidden at the time of the Passion.” He then teaches that the line of this hook was twisted through the succession of the ancients. See the same author on the hook in the preceding verse of Job. Saint Antony compares the cross to a hook; Olympiodorus, in the Greek Catena, fits nails to it: “For, having offered his flesh as a kind of bait, he caught the fish with his nails as hooks.”]

And, tied with a halter like a beast of burden, and bound like a runaway slave with a chain, and with his lips pierced by a ring (Job 40), how is he permitted to devour any of the faithful at all? Now, wretched like a sparrow, he has been ensnared for sport by Christ.

[Note: “Now, wretched like a sparrow, he has been ensnared for sport by Christ.” Taken from the same chapter of Job: “Will you mock him like a bird, or bind him for your maidservants?” The demons complain of this in The Life of Saint Pachomius, chapter 49: “From the time when the wondrous incarnation of Christ took place on earth, we began to be utterly without strength, so that we are mocked like sparrows by those who believe in his name.” In Clement, Book VIII of the Apostolic Constitutions, chapter 7, in the supplication for the possessed, referring to the power of exorcisms: Ὁ τὴν ἀνθρωποκτόνον ὄφιν δεσμώτην παραδοὺς ἡμῖν, ὡς στρουθίον παιδίοις. “You who delivered the murderous serpent to us bound in chains, like a sparrow to children.” Tertullian, Apology, chapter 23, vigorously presses this power of exorcism against the demons, the gods of the pagans: “Your divinity is subject to Christians.” Cyprian, Against Demetrianus, chapter 6: “You will see us being entreated by those whom you entreat.” Augustine, on Psalm 103, verse 27, applies this verse to the devil, weakened by Christ’s power: “This is the dragon whom you fashioned for mockery. Now mock the dragon; for this is why the dragon was made.” On this mockery consult the Master of the Sentences, Book II, distinction 3, section “Therefore.” The same Augustine, Sermon 197, On Time, which is the second sermon for the First Sunday after the feast of the Most Holy Trinity, explains the devil’s impotence by another comparison, that of a chained dog: “He is tied like a dog bound with chains, and he can bite no one except the one who joins himself to him with deadly security. See now, brothers, how foolish is the man whom a dog placed on a chain bites. Do not join yourself to him through the wills and desires of the world, and he does not dare approach you. He can bark; he can trouble; he absolutely cannot bite unless one wishes it.”]

Now he groans at his companions, as though they were scorpions and serpents, placed beneath the heel of Christians. He who used to boast that he had laid waste to all the seas, he who promised that the whole world was held in his hand—behold, he is defeated by you; behold, he cannot prevent me from arguing against him. His proud boasting, with its empty words, must be utterly despised, my little children. That radiance which pretends to shine is not the true splendor of light, but indicates the flames in which he will burn. For, departing more quickly than a word can be spoken, he carries away with him the images of his own punishments.

[Col. 0139A] Sometimes, too, they appear singing with musical modulation—shame upon it!—and with their impure mouths they even rehearse sacred-scriptural utterances. For while we are frequently reading, they answer like an echo to the final words. They also awaken sleepers to pray, in order to deprive them of the sleep of the entire night. Many, moreover, transforming themselves into the garb of noble monks, rebuke monks and charge them with sins of which they are conscious; but their reproaches must be scorned, as must their exhortations to fast and their fraudulent suggestion of vigils. For this reason they assume forms familiar to us: so that, by appearing akin to virtue, they may more easily insert their poison and overthrow the innocent under the guise of goodness. Afterwards they proclaim this discipline impossible and harsh, so that, when what has been begun seems burdensome, weariness may arise from despair and sluggishness from weariness. Therefore the prophet sent by the Lord, announcing mournful things, said in a lofty voice:

> Woe to him who gives his neighbor drink with turbid subversion (Habakkuk 2).

Such exhortations are perversions of the journey that leads to heaven. Therefore, when the Lord had come to earth and the demons unwillingly proclaimed the truth about him—for they were indeed speaking the truth: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (Luke 4)—he closed the mouths of those who were shouting. He who had loosed the bound tongues of human beings silenced them, lest they mix the poisons of perversity with their proclamation of truth, and so that, following his example, we might give them no assent at all, even if they were advising something useful. For surely it is not fitting that, after the freedom granted by the Lord and the life-giving commands of Scripture, we should take instructions for living from the devil, who abandoned his own order and profaned the sacred dominion of Christ.

For this reason, too, the Lord ordered him to be silent when he was speaking from the Scriptures, since God says to the sinner:

> Why do you recount my justice and take up my covenant in your mouth? (Psalm 49)

The demons imitate everything. They often converse with the brothers; often they raise disorderly noises among the crowd; they seize hands, hiss, and laugh foolishly, so that they may enter the Christian heart, even if only for a moment of sin. When they have been driven back by everyone, at last they testify to their weakness by lamentation.

The Lord, as God and conscious of his own majesty, commanded them to be silent; but we, clinging to the footsteps of the saints, should walk the same path. Perceiving more subtly the deceptions mentioned above, they sang:

> When the sinner stood against me, I was silent and humbled, and I kept silent concerning good things (Psalm 38).

And again:

> But I, like a deaf man, did not hear, and like a mute man who does not open his mouth; and I became like a man who does not hear (Psalm 37).

Christ, as Lord, commanded silence; let us believe nothing of the devil, and we shall conquer. If they compel us to pray, or advise us to fast, let us do these things not because of their admonitions, but according to our own practice. Finally, even if they seem to rush upon us and threaten us with death, they should be laughed at rather than feared, because, though weak, they threaten everything and accomplish nothing. I remember that I have already spoken of these matters in passing; nevertheless, they must now be explained more fully, because repetition provides no small safeguard.

When the Lord came, the enemy was destroyed.

[Note: “When the Lord came, the enemy was destroyed.” Immediately afterward: “because you have been weakened by the Lord.” Below, in The Life of Saint Pachomius, chapter 49: “From the time when the wondrous incarnation of Christ took place on earth, we began to be utterly without strength.” Cassian, Conference 7, chapter 23: “When the power of the cross penetrated even the deserts and its grace shone everywhere, the wickedness of the demons was blunted.” See what was said at the preceding number.]

And all his strength utterly languished. Therefore, mindful of his former power, like a tyrant already growing old, seeing himself collapsing, he rages toward human destruction; yet he cannot corrupt a heart firm in God by the art of thoughts and other deceptions.

For it is clearer than daylight that our adversaries, since they are not enclosed in human flesh and therefore cannot plead that they are unable to overcome us because the inner door is closed, cannot enter.

[Note: “Because the inner door is closed.” Alexander ab Alexandro once held this opinion, as he himself reports in Book 5, chapter 2 of his *Genial Days*: namely, that there is no danger from lemures when the doors are barred. But how greatly his opinion deceived him, he himself relates in the same place. See our Thyraeus, *On Haunted Places*, Part III, chapter 60.]

And indeed, if they had been bound within this fragile body, their access would have been denied when the entrance was guarded. But since, as we have said, they are free from this impediment, penetrate obstructions, and fly freely through every kind of air, it is clear that the body of the Church remains unharmed because their power has been weakened.

Finally, the impious satellites of the devil, together with their prince, whom the Savior declares in the Gospel to have been a murderer and the father of wickedness from the beginning (John 8), would not have ceased from fighting us so strongly if their power had not been taken away. For if I am lying, Satan, why do you spare us, though you roam everywhere? Why can you not, though confined by no place, weaken the steadfastness of those who live and argue well against you?

But perhaps you love us, whom you try every day to overwhelm; or is it credible that you are a teacher of goodness and favor the best people more than you harm them? And what can be so dear to you as to injure, especially those who manfully resist your crimes, according to what is written:

> Piety is an abomination to the sinner (Ecclesiasticus 1).

Who possesses a heart so devoted to wickedness? Who tries so earnestly to fulfill his premeditated ambushes? We know that you are a most filthy corpse. We know that this is why we Christians live, and that our struggle against you is secure, because you have been weakened by the Lord.

Therefore you are pierced by your own arrows, because your threat is not followed by its effect. If we are mistaken, why do you attack our faith with simulated terror? Why with enormous bodies? If ability follows will, let it be enough for you simply to will. For it is the nature of power not to seek external aids for deception, but to accomplish by its own strength what it desires.

But now, while by a theatrical transformation of forms—

[Note: “While by a theatrical transformation of forms.” By an apt comparison he illustrates the various forms and apparitions of the demons. It is a familiar practice of the theater and the stage for someone to put on a different form and sustain a character.]

—you strive to deceive childish inexperience with stage-like pretense, you show your exhausted strength all the more clearly. Was that true angel sent by the Lord against the Assyrians (2 Kings 19) in need of the cooperation of peoples, or did he seek noises and applause? Did he not rather exercise silent power and, in obedience to the command of the Lord who ordered him, strike down 185,000 enemies more swiftly than speech? Therefore, since you are so weak in strength, perpetual destruction pursues you.

## CHAPTER XVII

But someone may say: Why, when the devil went forth, did he cast the whole house of blessed Job into ruin (Job 1)? Why, after completely dispersing his wealth and overturning even the foundations of the walls, did he heap the one offspring of a numerous family into a single grave (ibid., 2)? Why did he finally strike Job himself with the novelty of a dreadful wound?

Let the one who raises this objection hear the answer: it was not the devil who was able to do this, but the Lord, from whom power against us is granted in two ways—either for glory, if we are being tested, or for punishment, if we sin. Rather, let him observe from this that the devil could have done nothing even against one man if he had not received power from the Lord. For no one asks another for what lies within his own authority.

But why do I mention Job, whom the devil could not defeat even when he desired to? He could not exercise his own strength even against Job’s animals or his sheep without God’s permission. Thus it is also written in the Gospel:

> The demons begged him, saying, “If you cast us out from here, send us into the herd of pigs” (Matthew 8).

How, then, can those who seek the death even of pigs, by their own right corrupt a human being, the image of God and an animal so dear to the Creator?

Great weapons against the demons, my beloved, are a sincere life and an unblemished faith in God.

[Note: “Great weapons against the demon are a sincere life and an unblemished faith.” Our Delrio, *Magical Investigations*, vol. III, Book VI, chapter 2, section 3, question 3, treating of supernatural divine or ecclesiastical remedies against sorcery, lists these two remedies. “The first remedy,” he says, “in this category is true and living faith, that is, faith fortified by love of God and neighbor.” Saint Paul offers and presents this shield to us when writing to the Ephesians (Ephesians 6); he urges the Thessalonians to put on this breastplate (1 Thessalonians 5); and that great Antony commends it to his disciples. Thus the demon replied to the magician Cyprian “that he could not harm those fortified by faith in Christ” (Nazianzen, Oration on Cyprian). Thus, in Cassian, two philosophers, unable to disturb Antony by the demons’ illusions, proved “that great power lies in the Christian profession” (Cassian, Conference 8, chapter 18). Thus, in Cornelius Kempensis, Book III of *The Origin and Situation of Frisia*, chapter 31: “The illusions of the white nymphs vanished after the true Gospel of God had been recognized” in Frisia, through a letter of Saint Odulphus on the Trinity that had been written, sent throughout the parishes, and read. The second remedy is a sincere life.
