How effective a remedy observance of God’s commandments and innocence of life are can be shown by Saint Cyprian, *To Fortunatus, On the Exhortation to Martyrdom*; Lactantius, Book II, chapter 16; and Ambrose Ansbertus, Book V on the Apocalypse, chapter 11.]

Believe me, as one who has experienced it: Satan fears the vigils, prayers, fasts, gentleness, voluntary poverty, contempt of empty glory, humility, mercy, mastery of anger, and especially the pure heart’s love for Christ found in those who live rightly. That most dreadful serpent knows that, by the Lord’s command, he lies beneath the feet of the righteous. The Lord said:

> Behold, I have given you power to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy (Luke 10).

But if, while pretending to possess divination, they announce that brothers are about to arrive, and those whom they predicted do arrive, faith must still not be granted to liars. For they went ahead of those who were coming in order to prepare credibility for themselves through the announcement, and then, through credibility, an entrance for deception.

There is nothing marvelous in this for a Christian, since not only can those who travel everywhere with the swiftness of their nature arrive ahead of others, but human beings, too, carried forward with the speed of horses, can announce that others will arrive. They do not report things that have not yet begun to happen, because God alone is aware of the future (Daniel 13); rather, they claim for themselves, like thieves among the ignorant, knowledge of things whose beginning they observe in progress.

How many, do you suppose, could now use childish speed to inform those who are far away about this gathering and our conversations against them, before someone here had reported it? What I am saying can be made clear by examples.

If someone begins to depart from the Thebaid or from a town in some other region, and the demons see him walking on the road, they can use their aforementioned speed to predict his arrival. So also, concerning the customary flooding of the Nile—

[Note: “So also concerning the customary flooding of the Nile.” Below, chapter 20: “How often they foretold the future rises of the Nile River!” On demonic prediction, see the *Onomasticon*.]

when they have seen many rains in Ethiopia, from which the swollen river customarily overflows beyond its bed, they race ahead to Egypt and announce the river’s arrival. Human beings, too, could easily announce this if they possessed such speed by nature.

For example, the watchman of blessed David, climbing to the summit of a higher place (2 Samuel 18), saw those who were coming before those who were on the ground and announced not uncertain things about the future, but things about those who had already begun to come. In the same way, the demons, considering everything with sleepless care, announce it to one another by rapid travel.

But if it should happen that, by God’s will, what has begun does not reach its conclusion—that is, if the traveler turns back midway, or if waters suspended in the clouds are carried upward to the vault of heaven—then the error of the deceivers, together with that of those who believed them, is exposed.

These were the beginnings of paganism. By such deceits of prediction, oracles were once believed at the shrines of demons. But with the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, when silence had been imposed upon them—

[Note: “When silence had been imposed upon them.” As the light of the Gospel shone forth, the oracles of the idols failed. Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, verse 503:

> From the time when that Spirit restrained the mortal womb—  
> that Spirit, God, the Spirit of God—  
> and clothed himself in the body of the Mother  
> and created a human being from virginity,  
> the Delphic caves fell silent, their lots condemned.

See Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book V, chapter 8, where he cites Plutarch’s work *On the Decline of Oracles*. See also Suidas, under “Augustus”; Nicephorus, Book I, chapter 17; and Cedrenus, in his *Compendium of History*. Interpreters apply to this the words of Job, chapter 40, verse 20: “Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook, and bind his tongue with a cord?”]

—they fell silent and lost their captives.

Who, I ask, regards a physician as possessing divine knowledge merely because, by observing illnesses, he investigates the burning condition of a fevered soul through the light touch of his fingers on the veins? Who honors a ship’s pilot with the dignity of a god because he seeks the course of his voyage among the stars of heaven? Who, when a farmer discusses the dry heat of summer, the abundance of winter rains, or the cold, praises him for experience rather than consecrating him under the name of a god?

But, even if we grant for a little while that demons announce true things, answer me: what benefit is there in knowing what is to come? Has anyone ever been praised for knowing these things, or punished for not knowing them? Each person prepares for himself either torments or glory, depending on whether he neglects the commands of Scripture or fulfills them.

None of us took up this life in order to possess foreknowledge of the future, but so that, obeying the Lord’s commands, he might begin to become a friend from a slave. We must take care not to know what is coming, but to fulfill what has been commanded. Nor should we demand this reward for good instruction, since we ought rather to ask the Lord our helper for victory against the devil.

But if someone happens to desire this—that he may know the future—let him have a pure heart. For I believe that a soul serving God, if it perseveres in the integrity in which it was born, can know more than demons.

[Note: “In the integrity in which it was born.” Thus in the manuscript and the Greek text. The printed editions have “reborn.”]

Such was the soul of Elisha, which performed deeds of power unknown to others.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Now I shall explain to you the remaining deceptions of the demons. They commonly come at night pretending to be angels of God; they praise devotion, marvel at perseverance, and promise future rewards. When you see them, arm yourselves and your houses with the sign of the cross, and immediately they will dissolve into nothing, because they fear that trophy in which the Savior stripped the aerial powers and made a spectacle of them.

They also commonly contort their limbs through various pretenses and boldly present themselves to our eyes, so that they may shake the mind with fear and the body with horror. But even in this, faith secure in God drives them away as feeble toys.

The distinction between good and evil spirits is not difficult.

[Note: “The distinction between good and evil spirits.” Our Delrio, *Magical Investigations*, vol. II, Book IV, chapter 1, question 3, section 6, concerning signs derived from the circumstances of revelations, teaches from this doctrine of Antony that one must observe whether what initially caressed the mind with joy later turns into horror and sorrow. Likewise, whether the horror that began at the outset has not gradually been removed, but has remained constant. These are two signs of false revelations. If, however, a person is initially disturbed and feels some horror, but afterward this distress and anxiety of mind are wiped away and he is suffused with a certain inward sweetness, this is a sign of divine consolation. The natural cause of this seems to be the antipathy between a human being and the murderous demon, and the sympathy between a human being and the angels. Yet Antony’s teaching must be understood of a true inward sweetness that produces and increases hunger and desire for the virtues, especially charity and humility. Blessed Catherine of Siena rightly added this limitation; it is confirmed by the testimony of blessed Angela of Foligno, who said that after a vision a stronger desire remained in her soul to endure every torment and injury for God.]

The distinction is disclosed by God’s gift in this way: the appearance of the holy angels is lovable and tranquil. They do not contend or shout, and no one hears their voice. Rather, advancing silently and gently, they pour joy, exultation, and confidence into hearts, since the Lord, who is the source and origin of joy, is with them.

Then our mind is illuminated not by turmoil but by the angels’ gentle and peaceful light. Then the soul, burning with desire for heavenly rewards, hastens to depart to heaven with those whom it sees, as though it could break open the dwelling of the human body and be freed from its mortal limbs.

Their kindness is so great that if someone, because of human weakness, is terrified by their wondrous radiance, they immediately remove all fear from his heart. So Gabriel spoke with Zechariah in the temple (Luke 1); so the angels, when announcing the Virgin’s divine childbirth to the shepherds (Luke 2), and those who kept watch over the Lord’s body, showed themselves to the minds of those who saw them and commanded them not to fear.

Fear is often produced not only by terror of the mind but also by the sight of great things. But the faces of the worst spirits are fierce, their noises horrible, their thoughts filthy, and their applause and movements resemble those of undisciplined youths or robbers. From these arise immediate fear in the soul and dullness in the senses; hatred of Christians, sorrow and weariness among monks, recollection of their own deeds, fear of death, desire for wickedness, weariness of virtue, and dullness of heart.

Therefore, if after fear has been conceived through horror, joy and confidence in God and an ineffable love follow, let us know that help has come, because security of soul is a sign of the majesty present. Thus the patriarch Abraham, seeing God, rejoiced (John 8); and John, sensing that Mary had arrived—she who carried within the lodging of her sacred womb the parent of the universe—leapt for joy while still unborn (Luke 1).

But if the fear that has been inflicted remains, the one who appears is an enemy. For he does not know how to restore comfort, as Gabriel commanded the Virgin, who was afraid, not to fear (Luke 1), and as the shepherds were comforted by the announcement (ibid.). Indeed, he doubles the terror and drives people to prostrate themselves before him, even into the deep pit of impiety.

From this arose the wretched pagan world, ignorant of the Lord’s prohibition, which falsely believed demons to be gods. But the Lord did not permit the peoples of the Christians to be ensnared by these deceptions. In the Gospel he boldly repelled the devil, who presumptuously claimed authority over everything, saying:

> Get behind me, Satan. For it is written: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matthew 4; Deuteronomy 6 and 10).

We, too, have been granted permission to use these words, because he spoke them for this reason: so that the likeness of the temptations might be broken by the words of our Creator.

## CHAPTER XIX

I also admonish you, my dearest ones, that your concern should be more for your life than for signs. Let none of you who perform such things become swollen with pride or despise those who cannot perform them. Rather, examine the conduct of each person. In this life you should imitate what is perfect and complete what is lacking.

For performing signs does not belong to our smallness, but to the Lord’s power. To the disciples who were glorying, he says in the Gospel:

> Do not rejoice because the demons are subject to you, but because your names are written in heaven (Luke 10).

The writing of names in the book of life is testimony to virtue and merit; the expulsion of Satan, however, is the Savior’s gift.

Therefore, when those who exult not in the labors of life but in miracles say:

> Did we not cast out demons in your name, and perform many mighty works in your name? (Matthew 7),

the Lord will answer:

> Truly I say to you, I do not know you. Depart from me, workers of iniquity.

For the Lord does not know the ways of the wicked. Let us therefore earnestly ask that we may deserve to receive the gift of discerning spirits, so that, according to the judgment of Scripture, we may not believe every spirit (1 John 4).

## CHAPTER XX

I had intended to end my discourse already and consign to silence whatever had happened to my humble self. But, lest you think that I have mentioned in vain things that could not happen, I shall therefore—although I may appear foolish, yet the Lord, who observes the secrets of the mind, knows that I do this not for the sake of boasting but for your benefit—repeat a few matters from among many.

How often they tried to exalt me with excessive praises when they received curses from me in the name of the Lord!

[Note: “When they received curses.” Demons were attacked with verbal insults and abuse, as was formerly customary among holy men. Sulpicius, in his letter to Bassula, concerning Saint Martin: “What are you standing here for,” he says, “bloody beast? You will find nothing in me, deadly one.” Abuse was also used in formulas of exorcism. Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, verse 474:

> The Lord’s bishop thunders: “Flee, cunning serpent;  
> strip yourself from the limbs and loosen your hidden coils.  
> You torment Christ’s servant, most corrupt thief.”

See *The Scourge of Demons*, exorcism 4, where there is an abundant harvest of insults. The pagans, too, received demons with dire imprecations and believed that they could drive them away in this manner. Thus Apollonius of Tyana, in Philostratus, Book II, chapter 2, drove away a demonic phantom with abuse while crossing the ridges of Caucasus. On this see our Thyraeus, *On Haunted Places*, Part III, chapter 56.]

How often they foretold future rises of the Nile River, when they heard me say, “What concern of yours is this?” How often, threatening like armed soldiers, they surrounded me with scorpions, horses, beasts, and various serpents, and filled the house in which I was staying, while I sang in response:

> Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we shall magnify the name of the Lord our God (Psalm 19).

And immediately they were put to flight by the mercy of Christ.

Once, when they came in a great light, they said:

> We have come, Antony, to offer you our radiance.

But I closed my eyes, because I disdained to look at the devil’s light, and I prayed. In the blink of an eye the light of the wicked was extinguished.

A few months later, when they were singing in my presence and conversing among themselves about the Scriptures, I, like a deaf man, did not hear them. Once they shook my monastery—

[Note: “Once they shook my monastery.” The Acts of the saints frequently record this kind of demonic assault. Gregory of Nyssa, in the *Life of Gregory the Wonderworker*, speaks of a chamber shaken by an earthquake. See also *The Life of Our Holy Father Ignatius*, Book I, chapter 2, by Ribadineira. On the entire category of demonic infestation, see our Thyraeus, *On Haunted Places*.]

—but I prayed to the Lord with an unshaken mind. Often they produced noises, often dances, often hissing; and when I sang psalms, their sound was changed into mournful voices.

Do you believe, my little children, what I am about to tell you? Once I saw the devil, immense in bodily stature, who dared to call himself the power and providence of God. He said to me:

> What do you want me to give you, Antony?

But I spat—

[Note: “I spat.” Most printed editions have *spectaculum*, “spectacle,” incorrectly. The Greek has: Ἐγὼ δὲ τότε μᾶλλον ἐνεφύσησα κατ᾿ αὐτοῦ, “But I then blew more strongly against him.” Some Greek manuscripts have ἐνεφώνησα, “I shouted at him.” Our translator seems to have read ἐνέπτυσα, “I spat upon him.” Demons are accustomed to being blown upon, driven away by breath, and spat upon. See the *Onomasticon*.]

—repeatedly spitting a great mouthful into his mouth, and, armed entirely against him in the name of Christ, I rushed upon him. Immediately that tall figure faded away between my hands.

When I was fasting, he also appeared to me as a monk. Offering bread, he urged me in these words to eat and to show some indulgence to this little body:

> You too are a human being, he said, and are surrounded by human weakness. Let your labor rest for a little, lest illness creep upon you.

Immediately I recognized the serpent’s livid face. When I fled to the familiar defenses of Christ, he vanished like smoke slipping through a window.

He also frequently laid a trap of gold for me in the desert. He offered it in order either to ensnare me by sight or to defile me by touch.

I do not deny that I was often beaten by demons. But I sang:

> Nothing will separate me from the love of Christ (Romans 8).

At the sound of this voice they rushed upon one another and were driven away—not by my command, but by the Lord’s command, who says (Luke 10):

> I saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning.

Therefore, my little children, remembering the apostolic saying, I transformed these things within myself, so that neither the terror of demons nor any weariness might dissolve your purpose.

But since, by recalling many things for your benefit, I have made myself foolish, and since I wish to impart to you a knowledge of this matter that none of those who hear it can doubt is true, I shall add one more account.

Once a demon knocked at the door of the monastery. When I went out, I saw a man of enormous height, with his head extended all the way to heaven. When I asked him who he was, he said:

> I am Satan.

And I said:

> What are you looking for here?

He replied:

> Why do the monks falsely accuse me? Why do all the Christian peoples curse me?

I answered:

> They do so justly, for they are frequently troubled by your attacks.

But he said:

> I do nothing. They themselves disturb one another. For I have become wretched. I ask you, have you not read: “The swords of the enemies have utterly failed, and you have destroyed their cities” (Psalm 9)? Behold, I have no place now; I possess no city; I have no weapons. Throughout all nations and every province the name of Christ resounds, and even the deserts are filled with choirs of monks. Let them protect themselves, I beg you, and not tear me apart without cause.

Then, marveling with gladness at God’s grace, I spoke to him as follows:

> I do not attribute so novel and unheard-of a statement to your truth, since you have none. For, as you are the head of deception, you have been compelled to confess this without lying. Truly Jesus has utterly overthrown your strength, and, stripped of angelic honor, you roll about in filth.

I had scarcely finished speaking when that lofty figure was cast down at the mention of the Savior.

What hesitation, then, can remain, my little children? What fear can continue any longer? What storm of theirs can shake us loose? Let the souls of each of you be secure. Let no empty thought imagine empty dangers. Let no one fear that he can be seized by the devil and carried away to precipices.

Let every anxiety be driven away. For the Lord, who has cast down our enemies, remains in us as he promised (John 14) and has protected us from Satan’s various attacks. Behold, the devil himself, who practices such cunning with his satellites, admits that he can do nothing against Christians.

Now let Christians and monks take care that, through their negligence, power is not given to demons. For whatever sort of people they find us to be, and whatever sort of thoughts they find in us, they habitually show themselves to us in the same way. And if they find in our hearts any seed of evil-mindedness and fear, like robbers who occupy deserted places, they heap up the fears already begun and, cruelly threatening, punish the unhappy soul.

47 But if we are cheerful in the Lord, and desire for the blessings to come has inflamed us; if we always entrust everything to the hands of God, none of the demons will be able to approach us for battle. Rather, when they see hearts fortified in Christ, they will return in confusion. Thus the devil fled from Job, who was made firm in the Lord; but he bound wretched Judas, stripped of faith, with the chains of captivity.

[Col. 0146A] There is therefore one way of conquering the enemy: spiritual joy and the continual remembrance of a soul always thinking upon the Lord. This, driving away the demons’ games as though they were smoke, will pursue its adversaries rather than fear them. For Satan is not unaware of the future fires, and he knows the abundant flames of the burning Gehenna.

But, that my discourse may now be brought to a close, I recall this at the end: Whenever some apparition presents itself to you, boldly ask who it is and where it has come from. If it is a revelation of the saints, fear will immediately be changed into joy through angelic consolation. But if it is a temptation offered by the devil, it will vanish before the questioning of a faithful soul, because it is the greatest sign of security to ask who it is and where it comes from. Thus Joshua the son of Nave learned who his helper was by questioning him (Joshua V); nor could the enemy remain hidden from Daniel when he questioned him (Daniel X).

[Col. 0146B] When Antony had finished speaking, everyone rejoiced. In some, desire for virtue was kindled; in others, weak faith was strengthened; from the minds of others false opinions were driven out; from the understanding of others the flame of empty terrors was removed. At the same time, when they had come to despise the demons’ snares, all marveled at the great grace Antony possessed for discerning spirits, which he had received through the Lord’s gift.

## CHAPTER XXI

There were therefore monasteries on the mountain, like tabernacles, full of divine choirs singing psalms.

[Note: [Col. 0179C] “Monasteries like tabernacles, full of divine choirs singing psalms.” Above, chapter 20: “The solitudes also are thronged with the choirs of monks.” How greatly the Egyptian desert was illuminated by the ranks of holy monks, Saint John Chrysostom relates in Homily 8 on Matthew, chapter 51:

“And now, if you come to the desert of Egypt, you will see that desert become more excellent than every paradise, and countless choirs of angels shining in human form.”

There he continues by saying that women also excelled in this kind of philosophy. Epiphanius likewise, Book III, Heresy 80, against the Massalians and Martyrianists:

“Just as in every monastery, both in the land of the Egyptians and in all other lands, they labor so toward righteousness that, like the bee, which has in its hands the wax of its work and in its mouth drops of honey, with its own hymn-bearing voice it praises the Master of all according to its own understanding.”

]

[Col. 0146C] Reading and praying. His discourse had breathed such a fervor for fasting and vigils into everyone’s minds that, from eagerness for the hope of the future, they labored continually in mutual love and in showing mercy to the needy. They seemed to inhabit a vast region, a kind of town separated from worldly society and filled with piety and righteousness.

Who, seeing such a multitude of monks, who, beholding that manly fellowship of harmony in which there was no wrongdoer and no whispering slanderer, but a multitude practicing abstinence and a rivalry in acts of service, would not immediately burst forth into this cry:

“How goodly are your houses, Jacob, and your tabernacles, Israel, like groves giving shade, like a paradise beside rivers, like tabernacles established by the Lord, like cedars beside the waters!” (Numbers XXIV)

## CHAPTER XXII

While these things were taking place, and the devotion of those men was increasing day by day toward the blessed life, Antony, remembering the dwellings set in heaven and despising the vanity of the present life—as though everything he had already accomplished were insignificant—was being trained apart from the brothers.

Whenever human condition compelled him to allow his little body food or sleep, or other necessities of nature, he was affected by extraordinary shame that such great freedom of the soul should be confined by the narrow limits of the flesh. Often, while sitting with the brothers, he was drawn away from the food placed before him by the memory of spiritual nourishment. Yet, being human, he did eat—often alone, often with the brothers.

And when he performed these remarkable deeds, as I have said, with a shamefaced soul he strongly urged that diligent care should be given to the body, saying that the body must not be utterly destroyed, lest its operation be dissolved contrary to the Creator’s will; yet neither should all the soul’s attention be devoted to it, lest, overcome by bodily vices, it be thrust into the eternal darkness of hell. Rather, claiming for himself the authority granted over the flesh, he raised his dwelling place, as the apostle Paul did, to the third heaven (II Corinthians XII).

He maintained that this had been commanded by the Savior, who says:

“Do not be anxious about your soul, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will wear, because the nations seek these things. But your Father knows that you need all these things. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew VI).

## CHAPTER XXIII

After these events, when the most impious persecution of Maximian was devastating the Church in its insane fury,

[Note: [Col. 0179D] “When the most impious persecution of Maximian.” Baronius, volume III, in the year of Christ 310, the second of Pope Eusebius and the fifth of Emperor Constantine, says that many Egyptian martyrs suffered in this persecution; yet the precise year in which each suffered is uncertain. Among them was the virgin Potamenia, concerning whom Palladius, in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 1, relates the account of Isidore, who perhaps received it from Antony, an eyewitness, while he was living at Alexandria.]

and holy martyrs were also being brought to Alexandria, Antony himself left the monastery and followed the future victims of Christ, saying:

“Let us go to the glorious triumphs of our brothers; either let us enter the contest ourselves, or let us watch others fighting.”

By love he was already a martyr. But since he could not surrender himself voluntarily or join the confessors confined in mines or prisons, he entered before the judge with great freedom and concern, exhorting them not to deny the Lord after being overcome by the fear of the impious. And when those crowned by the sentence were already rejoicing, Antony, as though he himself had won, followed them to the place of their blessed bloodshed.

For this reason the judge, disturbed by the steadfastness of Antony and his companions, ordered that none of the monks should either attend the proceedings or remain in the city.

[Col. 0147C] On that day all the others decided to hide. Antony, however, fearless and disregarding the persecutor’s command, washed his ependytes.

[Note: [Col. 0180A] “He washed his ependytes.” The editions add, “that is, his scapular,” which is absent from the manuscripts. Nevertheless, the interpretation is sound. See the *Onomasticon*.]

On the following day, standing in a prominent place and girded in a gleaming garment, he challenged the judge by his appearance, burning with desire for martyrdom.

[Note: [Col. 0180A] “Girded in a gleaming garment.” Baronius, volume II, under the year of Christ 256, the first year of Pope Lucius and the third year of the emperors Gallus and Volusianus, discussing the black and white garment, wishes the former to have belonged to other Christians and the latter to the Egyptians. For, he says, Clement of Alexandria, the Christian instructor who took care to imbue the Church in Egypt with the best morals, strongly urges the faithful to use white garments (Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogue*, Book II). We therefore suppose that, through his instruction, Christians in Egypt wore white garments. Hence it happened that Saint Antony, burning with an immense desire to undergo martyrdom, put on white clothing so that he might be recognized as a Christian. Thus far Baronius.

Yet it might perhaps be more accurate to say that Antony put on white clothing not so that he would be recognized as a Christian—for he was already recognizable as such by his monastic habit—but so that he could go more safely to the judge, mingling with Egyptians dressed in white. The monks, who were recognizable by their dark clothing, had been forbidden to remain in the city, as this very chapter shows. It is certain that the monks’ garment was dark. In Metaphrastes, November 5, in the *Life of Galaction and Episteme*, chapter 2, concerning the monk Onuphrius: “Clothed in a white garment, he was truly a monk in spirit.” And in chapter 9: “One choir of them consisted of men honorable in appearance and dressed in black.” These are said to be those who separate themselves from the world, that is, monks. Synesius, Letter 146, to a man undertaking the monastic discipline: “He says that you wear a gray cloak.” Athanasius, *On Virgins*, or *Ascetic Teachings*: “Your ependytes is black.” Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogue*, Book II, chapter 10, and Book III, chapter 11, urges Christians to adopt white clothing and abandon garments of various colors.]

[Col. 0147D] He thus showed us that among Christians the spirit must persevere in contempt of punishments and death, so greatly that he was saddened because martyrdom was not granted to one who desired to suffer for God’s name.

But the Lord, who spared his own flock, preserved Antony as its teacher, so that the institution of the monks might be strengthened not only by his prayer but also by his presence. Nevertheless, he was never separated from the footsteps of the holy confessors. Bound to them by anxious concern and the ties of charity, he suffered imprisonment all the more when he was excluded from it.

After the storm of persecution had subsided, and blessed Bishop Peter had already been crowned with the glory of martyrdom,

[Note: [Col. 0180B–C] “Bishop Peter had already been crowned with the glory of martyrdom.” The annual commemoration of Peter, bishop and martyr of Alexandria, is celebrated in the Latin Church on 26 November and in the Greek Church on the 24th of the same month. On “crown,” that is, martyrdom, see the *Onomasticon*.]

Antony returned to his former monastery and earned the daily martyrdom of faith and conscience. He wore a haircloth garment next to his skin and a sheepskin over it, exhausting himself with harsher fasts and vigils.

[Note: [Col. 0180C] “Exhausting himself with harsher fasts and vigils.” Blessed Ephrem quotes this sentence word for word from this *Life of Antony*, written by Athanasius, in his *Ascetic Sermon* on “Pay attention to yourself,” chapter 10. There, what is found in Athanasius’s Greek and is absent from the Latin text here—“which he also preserved until the end”—namely, the wearing of a haircloth and sheepskin garment, Ephrem also expressed, as is clear from the Latin translation of his interpreter Gerard Vossius.]

He never washed his body and never washed the dirt from his feet, unless necessity compelled him when he had to cross water. In short, no one ever saw Antony’s naked body before he died.

## CHAPTER XXIV

At a certain time, when Antony had withdrawn himself from everyone’s sight and, having closed the monastery, admitted no one at all, Martinianus, commander of the soldiers,

[Note: [Col. 0180C] “Martinianus, commander of the soldiers.” So it appears in Ammianus, Book XXVI: “Petronius, formerly commander of the Martensian soldiers.”]

whose daughter was being tormented by the assaults of an unclean spirit, knocked at the door and begged Antony to help his child and to come out and pray to God for her.

Antony did not wish to open. But looking down from above, he said:

“Man, why do you ask my help? I too am mortal and share your weakness. But if you believe in Christ, whom I serve, go, and according to your faith pray to God, and your daughter will be healed.”

Immediately, believing, the man departed; and after invoking Jesus, he brought his daughter back in good health.

The Lord worked many other miracles through Antony, and rightly so. For he who promised in the Gospel, “Ask, and it will be given to you” (Matthew VII), when he found someone worthy to receive his grace, did not withhold his power. Indeed, many afflicted people slept before Antony’s monastery, whose entrance was closed, and were healed through the prayers that the faithful offered through him to Christ.

This crowd of arrivals, depriving him of the solitude he desired, became burdensome to him.

Fearing, therefore, that the abundance of signs might either inflate his own spirit or compel others to think more highly of him than what they saw in him warranted, he considered going to the upper Thebaid, where no one would recognize him. After receiving loaves from the brothers, he sat on the riverbank, watching for a ship to pass.

While he was thinking about these things, a voice came to him from above, saying:

“Antony, where are you going, and why?”

He replied fearlessly, as though he recognized the familiar voice of the speaker:

“Because the crowds do not allow me to rest, I have thought it best to go to the upper Thebaid, especially since I am being asked to do things that exceed the strength of my weakness.”

And the voice said to him:

“If you go to the Thebaid and proceed, as you are thinking, to the pastoral lands,

[Note: [Col. 0180C] “To the pastoral lands.” In Greek, *boukólia*. Hoeschelius translates it as “herds of cattle,” incorrectly. For Bucola, or Bucolia, is a definite place in Egypt: either near Alexandria by the sea beneath the cliffs, as in the *Life of Saint Mark* after Abdius, by an anonymous author; or elsewhere in the upper Thebaid, as seems to be inferred from this *Life*. See the *Onomasticon*.]

you will endure a greater and double labor. But if you truly wish to rest, go now to the inner desert.”

When Antony said, “Who can show me the place? For I do not know the region,” the speaker immediately indicated to him some Saracens who customarily came to Egypt for purposes of trade. Antony approached them and asked them to take him with them into the desert. No one resisted. Rather, receiving him as a companion sent by God, they embraced his company.

After completing a journey of three days and nights, he found a very high mountain.

[Note: [Col. 0180D] “He found a mountain.” This is the second mountain to which Antony withdrew. A fuller description of it appears in chapter 26 of the *Life of Hilarion*.]

At its foot flowed a spring of fresh water, and a not very large plain surrounded the whole mountain. It was planted with a few palm trees, and even those were neglected. Antony embraced this place as though it had been offered to him by God. It was the very place that the speaker had shown him while he was sitting beside the river.

At first, after receiving loaves from his companions, he remained alone on the mountain, with no one else living with him. He regarded the place as though it were his own home. The Saracens, seeing his confidence and their desired passage accomplished through him, gladly brought him bread; and he also found some relief in the palms, though they were few.

## CHAPTER XXV

From then on, when the brothers had learned the place and, like sons going to their father, carefully sent him provisions, Antony saw that many were being burdened with labor on his account for the sake of his refreshment. Sparing the monks in this matter too, he asked one of those who came to bring him a hoe, double-edged, together with grain.

[Note: [Col. 0180D] “To bring him a hoe, double-edged, together with grain.” This passage should be punctuated as it is in the printed edition. The Cologne edition and Surius have: “to bring him a hoe, double-edged, together with grain.” The manuscript has: “to bring him a hoe with a double-edged iron tool.” In Greek: “a two-pronged hoe, a double axe, and a little grain.” The reading I have presented, with its punctuation, is therefore sound. There is no doubt that “double-edged” is used here absolutely for a double axe. For a double-edged tool, or bipennis, is nothing other than a two-sided axe, or some agricultural implement cutting on both sides. In the *Life of Fronto*, below, chapter 1: “And bringing with them into the desert small seeds of vegetables, and double-edged tools and little hoes.” See the *Onomasticon*.]

When these things had been brought, he went around the mountain and found a small place suitable for cultivation, into which water diverted from above could flow. He sowed it there, and thereafter, laboring for his annual bread, rejoiced that he could live in the desert from the work of his own hands without troubling anyone.

But when some people began to come there again, he pitied their weariness and cultivated vegetables in a small patch of ground, so that those who came after their difficult journey might find some refreshment.

The beasts that gathered there because of the water ate both this refreshment for the brothers and the little crop.

Then, catching one of them, he said to all:

“Why do you harm me, when I have harmed none of you? Go away, and in the name of the Lord do not come here again.”

Who would not believe that, after this warning, the beasts never again approached the place, as though they were afraid?

Thus, while Antony sought the impenetrable recesses of the mountains and the inner desert and devoted himself to prayer, the brothers who came to him could scarcely prevail upon him, by their earnest entreaties, to accept olives, legumes, and oil, which they supplied after several months, and to relax his old age a little.

What an outrage! How many struggles he experienced while living there! Truly, according to what is written, his struggle was not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers (Ephesians VI). We learned this from those who entered to visit him. They reported that the mountain was entirely filled with the tumult and voices of a crowd and the clash of weapons, and swarming with a multitude of demons; they even said that Antony himself openly resisted them as though they were enemies and fought them bravely.

Yet he refreshed those who came by his encouragement, and, falling to his knees, he overthrew the whole army of Satan with the weapons of prayer.

It is truly worthy of wonder that, in such a monstrous solitude, one man neither feared the demons’ daily encounters nor yielded to the savagery of so many beasts, whether four-footed animals or reptiles. David rightly sang:

“Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion; they shall not be moved forever” (Psalm CXXIV).

Maintaining the firmness of his spirit unmoved and tranquil, he drove away demons and made peace with wild beasts, as it is written (Job V). But the devil, as the prophet mentioned above says (Psalm LXIII), watching him, gnashed his teeth; and Antony, safe through the Savior’s help, continued protected from all his snares.

One night, while Antony was keeping vigil and praying to the Lord, the devil gathered such herds of beasts into his monastery that Antony saw around himself all the wild animals of the desert.

[Note: [Col. 0181A] “Wild animals.” In Greek, *hyaenas*. See the *Onomasticon*.]

When they threatened to bite his body with their open jaws, he understood the enemy’s tricks and said:

“If permission has been granted you by the Lord to attack me, then devour what has been given over to you. But if you have come here at the prompting of demons, depart as quickly as possible, because I am a servant of Christ.”

And so it happened. At the voice of the one commanding them, the entire multitude of beasts fled, as though struck by the blow of majesty.

## CHAPTER XXVI

Not many days had passed after this when another contest arose with the same enemy. While Antony was working—for he always labored in order to repay those who came with some small gift for what they had brought him—someone pulled the cord or rope of the basket he was weaving.

[Note: [Col. 0181A] “The cord or rope.” In Greek, “the rope of the work,” that is, the cord used in the work. If I find anything about *tricina*, I will discuss it in the *Onomasticon*. Or is it *trichina*, from *trichos*, “hair,” as though a rope woven from hair? The printed editions have *tritia* or *tricia*, perhaps derived from *trica*, giving *tricina*.]

Rising at its movement, Antony saw a beast that had a human face down to the waist and from there ended in the form of a donkey. After seeing it, he traced the sign of the cross on his forehead and said only this:

“I am a servant of Christ. If you have been sent against me, I do not flee.”

There was no interval. Immediately the shapeless monster fled, faster than words can tell, with its troop of followers, and collapsed dead in the middle of its flight.

This death of the expelled and destroyed monster was the common destruction of the demons, who, striving with every effort, were unable to drive Antony from the desert.

More astonishing things follow upon these astonishing events.

## CHAPTER XXVII

Not much time had elapsed after this when a man who had won so many victories was overcome by the prayers of the brothers. The monks had asked him to visit them, and he set out with them. They loaded a camel with water and loaves, because nowhere along the arid road could drinkable water be found except at the monastery from which they had drawn it.

But in the middle of the journey their supply for drinking ran out. Extreme heat and intolerable blazing threaten everyone with death. They search around and look for at least a pool collected from rain, but no remedy at all appears, nothing at all that might bring safety. The camel, itself almost dying and panting from the heat, is released; the breast of the one suffering from the heat burns, and thirst boils with despair.

The old man was moved by the common danger shared with the brothers and groaned in profound sorrow. Then, having recourse to his accustomed aid of prayer, he withdrew a little from them. There, fixing his knees to the ground, he stretched out his suppliant hands to the Lord.

Immediately, at the first tears of the one praying, a spring burst forth in the place of prayer. Their thirst was quenched, their parched limbs were refreshed, and, with the water-skins filled, they gave drink to the camel when they found it.

It had happened by chance that the camel, wandering through the desert while dragging a rope, had become caught by that rope around a certain stone.

At last, after completing the journey, Antony reached the monks who had invited him. Then they all ran out to meet him as though he were their father, and, greeting him honorably, eagerly rushed to kiss and embrace him.

Antony rejoiced at their fervent purpose. While everyone rejoiced at his arrival, he, as though bringing gifts of hospitality from the mountain, imparted spiritual nourishment.

[Note: [Col. 0181A] “As gifts of hospitality.” In Greek: “And he himself, as though bringing provisions from the mountain, entertained them with spiritual words.” That is: “He himself, bringing as it were provisions from the mountain, enriched them with spiritual gifts.” Some manuscripts have *exenia*, as do the older editions. See the *Onomasticon*. Thus Ambrose, at the beginning of his *Exhortation to Virgins*, uses *apophoreta* for “gifts of holiness.”]

He praised the devotion of the elders and encouraged the newcomers. Seeing also his sister, now an elderly virgin and a teacher of other girls, he was lifted up with extraordinary joy. Then, as though he had been away from the desert for a long time, he hurried back to the mountain.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

By now many people were coming to him, including those afflicted by demons who, compelled by the misery of their necessity, dared to penetrate the deserts. Consoling them and giving common instruction to the monks, Antony said:

“Believe faithfully in Jesus. Keep your mind pure from evil thoughts and your flesh from impurities. In accordance with the divine words, do not allow yourselves to be deceived by the fullness of the belly (Proverbs XXIV). Hate empty glory. Pray very often. Sing psalms in the evening, in the morning, and at midday, and turn over in your minds the commandments of Scripture.

“Remember the deeds performed by each of the saints, so that remembrance of their example may stir the soul to virtue and restrain it from vices. He also urged that the apostle’s saying be retained through constant meditation:

‘Let not the sun go down upon your anger’ (Ephesians IV).

“He interpreted this not merely as meaning that the sun should not go down upon anger, but also that it should not go down upon any human offense, lest the moon at night or the sun by day should ever depart as witnesses to our sins.

“He also urged them to remember the command that says:

‘Judge yourselves and examine yourselves’ (II Corinthians XIII),

so that, taking account of day and night, they might cease to sin if they discovered an offense in themselves. But if no error had deceived them, they should persevere and press on in what they had begun, rather than, puffed up with arrogance, despise others or claim righteousness for themselves, in accordance with the words of the Teacher mentioned above:

‘Do not judge before the time’ (I Corinthians IV).

“Rather, they ought to reserve themselves for the judgment of Christ, to whom alone hidden things are open (Romans II). There are, as it is written, many ways that seem righteous to human beings, but their ends look toward the depths of hell (Proverbs XIV and XVI). Often we cannot understand our own sins; often we are deceived in assessing our actions. The judgment of God, who sees everything, is one thing: he judges not from the outward appearance of bodies but from the secrets of minds.

“It is right for us to have compassion on one another and to bear one another’s burdens (Galatians VI), so that, while leaving judgment to the Savior, we may examine our own consciences and judge ourselves.”

[Col. 0151C] He also said that a great path toward virtue was for each person either to observe what he was doing or to report all the thoughts of his mind to the brothers. For no one could sin when he knew that he would have to report whatever he had done wrong to another and would experience the shame of bringing disgraceful things into public.

In the end, no one dares to sin in the presence of another. Even if he does sin, he avoids the witness of his sin, preferring to lie and deny it, and he increases his old offense by infecting it with a new one.

“Therefore,” he said, “as though under our own eyes, we are ashamed both in thought and in deed if we make everything subject to reporting—and much more if we faithfully write down our sins and arrange them in order. Then the record of the brothers’ offenses will appear before our eyes. If we fear the wax tablets that know our sins,

[Note: [Col. 0181A] “If we fear the wax tablets that know our sins.” This is correctly found in the manuscripts. The Cologne edition, together with the older editions, has “the stains of conscience,” and so forth. Sozomen, Book I, chapter 13, preserves the same admonition of Antony.]

the letters themselves will accuse us. And just as those who join their bodies to prostitutes are ashamed in the presence of others, so we too will be ashamed before the written letters if we do such things.

“Let us walk this path of virtue. Subjugating our bodies to our minds, let us crush the devil’s destructive snares.”

By such speeches and exhortations Antony stirred the monks who came to him to devotion, and he shared the grief of those who were suffering. The Lord freed many of them through Antony.

Yet Antony was never inflated with pride over the recovery of those who were healed, nor did he complain in sorrow about bodies that remained possessed. Rather, always remaining the same in spirit and appearance, he gave thanks to God and urged those who were afflicted to bear more patiently the correction by which they were tormented.

“For this healing,” he said, “belongs not to Antony or to any human being at all, but to God alone, who gives health to whom he wishes and at whatever time he wishes.”

Thus, by his consolation, he taught both those who were tormented to endure their trial with equanimity and those who had been freed to give thanks not to him but to God.

## CHAPTER XXIX

A certain Fronto, a man from Palestine, who was tormented by a most malignant demon—for the demon tore his tongue with his teeth and tried to extinguish the light of his eyes—went to the mountain and asked the blessed old man to pray to the Lord for him.

Antony prayed and said to him:

“Go, and you will be healed.”

When Fronto, not believing him, stubbornly remained there contrary to his command, Antony repeated the same words:

“You cannot be healed here. Go out, and as soon as you have crossed Egypt, the mercy of Christ will reach you.”

At last he believed and departed. When he saw Egypt, the enemy’s assault ceased, in accordance with the old man’s declaration, which the Lord had revealed to him while he was praying.

## CHAPTER XXX

There was also a certain virgin from the city of Busiris in the Tripolitan region.

[Note: [Col. 0181B] “Busiris in the Tripolitan region.” This is a city of Egypt in the Busiritic nome of the Tripolitan region. The final phrase was correctly added for the sake of distinction, because there is also another city called Busiris in Egypt, outside the Tripolitan region, which some identify with Thebes, or Diospolis the Great, in the Theban, or Diospolite, nome.]

She was suffering from unheard-of and pitiable diseases. The discharge from her nostrils, the tears from her eyes, and the putrid fluid from her ears, falling onto the ground, immediately turned into worms. Her misery was increased by a body dissolved by paralysis, and she also had eyes distorted contrary to nature.

When her parents had brought her and learned that monks were going to Antony, they believed in the Lord, who in the Gospel had commanded the persistent flow of blood to stop at the touch of his garment’s fringe (Matthew IX), and they asked the monks to receive their pitiable daughter’s escort.

[Col. 0152C] When the monks refused to take her all the way to Antony, her parents remained outside with their debilitated daughter beside the blessed confessor and monk Paphnutius,

[Note: [Col. 0181B] “Paphnutius.” His memory is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology on September 4. He is mentioned by Rufinus, Book I of his *History*, chapters 4 and 17; Socrates, Book I, chapter 8; Theodoret, Book I, chapter 7; Sozomen, Book I, chapter 22; and Nicephorus, Book VIII, chapters 14 and 19, where he calls him bishop of the upper Thebaid. He mentions him again in chapter 49 of the same book. He is also honorably mentioned in the *Acts of Metrophanes and Alexander* preserved by Photius in the *Bibliotheca*, codex 256. On the various other Paphnutiuses, see the notes here on Rufinus, Book II, chapter 13.

The following words—“who, after his eyes had been gouged out for Christ under the persecutor Maximian, took great pride in such disfigurement of his body”—are absent from the Greek exemplar. The translator Evagrius inserted them to distinguish him more clearly from several other Paphnutiuses.]

who, after his eyes had been gouged out for Christ under the persecutor Maximian, took great pride in such disfigurement of his body.

[Note: [Col. 0181C] “Disfigurement.” A rarer word, although used in that period and also in antiquity. Thus here, chapter 37, *probamentum*. See the *Onomasticon*. The true glory of martyrs is to be adorned with wounds that, in worldly estimation, are disfigurements. There is an illustrious example in Gregory of Nazianzus, *Invective II against Julian*.]

The monks therefore reached Antony. When they were preparing to tell him about the girl’s illness, the old man’s speech anticipated their report. He described the whole cause of her weakness and of their journey as far as the holy Paphnutius, as though he himself had been present.

The monks then asked him to allow the parents and their daughter to enter. He refused and said:

“Go, and you will find the girl healed, if she is not already dead.”

He added:

“No one ought to come to my lowliness, because the granting of healings belongs not to human misery but to the mercy of Jesus Christ, who everywhere habitually grants help to those who believe in him. Therefore the girl for whom you are asking has been freed through her own prayers; and when I prayed to the Lord, I was granted foreknowledge of her healing.”

He spoke, and the girl’s recovery followed his words. For when they went outside to the blessed Paphnutius, they found the daughter safe and the parents rejoicing.

## CHAPTER XXXI

Not many days afterward, two brothers were traveling to Antony when their water ran out on the road. One died of thirst, while the other lay on the ground awaiting death.

Antony, sitting on the mountain, immediately called two monks who happened to be found there and quickly ordered them to take a flask of water and enter upon the road leading to Egypt. He said:

“One of the brothers who were coming here has just departed to the Lord. The other will also be added, unless you hurry to his aid. For this has just been revealed to me while I was praying.”

The monks departed in haste according to his command. They found the dead man’s body, covered it with earth, and joined the other, who had been revived, to their company.

The journey was one day’s distance.

Someone might ask: Why did Antony not say this before the man died? The question is wholly unsuitable for Christians, because the judgment was not Antony’s but God’s. God had made whatever judgment he wished concerning the one who departed, and had deemed it right to reveal the matter concerning the thirsty man.

The only marvelous thing about Antony is that, sitting on a very remote mountain, with his heart ever watchful, he knew everything situated far away because the Lord disclosed it to him.

## CHAPTER XXXII

At another time, while he was sitting on the mountain and had suddenly lifted his eyes toward heaven, he saw some soul—I do not know whose—going up to heaven, with angels rejoicing to meet it.

Amazed by the novelty of the spectacle, he called it a blessed choir of saints and prayed that the knowledge of what had occurred might be disclosed to him.

Immediately a voice came to him, saying that it was the soul of the monk Ammon,

[Note: [Col. 0181C] “The soul of the monk Ammon.” Sozomen also mentions him, Book I, chapter 14, and Socrates, Book IV, chapter 18. The manuscripts almost always have *Amon*, without declension. So also in Greek, Ἀμοῦν.]

who lived at Nitria.

Ammon was an elderly man who had lived in holiness perseveringly from childhood to old age (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 28; Palladius, chapters 7 and 8). Nitria was thirteen days’ journey from the place where Antony was sitting.

[Note: [Col. 0181C] “Thirteen days’ journey.” I believe that Antony’s location is meant here: the second mountain, which was thirteen days’ journey from Nitria and where he lived toward the end. It is described above, chapter 24.]

The monks who had come there saw Antony wondering and begged him to explain the reason for his joy. He told them that Ammon had just rested in peace. They knew him very well because of his frequent journeys to Antony and because of the fame of the signs the Lord had granted him.

Of these matters one further point must be mentioned: once it was necessary for him to ford the river called the Lycus, which had been swollen by a sudden flood (Ruffinus and Palladius, above) [Note: [Col. 0181C] “The river called Lycus.” Palladius, chapter 8, says that the River Lycus is a canal of the great Nile.]. He asked Theodore, who was with him, to withdraw a little from his sight, lest either of them should see the other’s nakedness. Theodore withdrew; nevertheless, when the old man wished to undress, he felt ashamed. As he was considering what to do, divine power transported him to the opposite bank. Theodore, himself also a man devoted to God, crossed afterward and began to marvel that the old man had forded the river so quickly. When he saw no dampness on his feet and no trace of water on his garments, he asked him, as a father might explain something incredible to his son, to tell him about this astonishing transfer. When the old man refused to say what had happened, Theodore embraced his feet and swore that he would not let him go until he had disclosed what he was concealing. Seeing, therefore, that his brother was determined to prevail by persistence, the old man in turn required him not to reveal this to anyone before his death. Then he confessed that he had suddenly been transported to the opposite bank and had not touched the water at all with his footsteps, asserting that this privilege belonged only to the Lord’s body and to those to whom he himself, as to the apostle Peter, had granted that a human body might stand upon the instability of the waters [Col. 0154A] (Matthew XIV). Theodore did not disclose this before the appointed time; he recounted it after the old man’s death.

The monks to whom Antony had spoken about Ammon’s death recorded the day. When brothers from Nitria arrived thirty days later and inquired, they discovered that Ammon had fallen asleep on that very day and at that very hour when the old man had seen his soul being carried away. Thus both groups marveled at Antony’s purity of mind, wondering how knowledge of something that had happened so far away had immediately reached him.

### CHAPTER XXXIII

Archelaus the magistrate also, when he found him on the outer mountain [Note: [Col. 0181D] On the outer mountain.] Below, chapter 56: “Those who were on the outer mountain.” He contrasts the outer mountain with the inner and upper mountain. Chapter 51: “He returned to the inner mountain.” Chapter 44: “He was on the upper mountain.”], asked him to pray for Polycratia [Note: [Col. 0181D] Polycratia.] The Cologne edition and Surius add “daughter of Publius.” I do not know where they obtained this. It is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek text.], who was in Laodicea [Note: [Col. 0181D] Who was in Laodicea.] Since there are several cities called Laodicea, I think this was the Laodicea of Coelesyria, which is nearer Egypt, where Antony was living.], a virgin remarkable for her devotion to Christ. She was suffering severe pains in the stomach and side, which she had brought upon herself through excessive fasting and vigils, and her entire body was utterly weakened [Col. 0154B]. Antony prayed, and Archelaus recorded the day on which the prayer had been offered. He returned to Laodicea and found the virgin well. When he asked on what day she had recovered, he found that the time of her cure coincided with his record. And everyone marveled, recognizing that at the very time when Antony had prayed for her and invoked the goodness of the Savior, she had been freed by the Lord from her pains.

### CHAPTER XXXIV

He also often foretold, days and months in advance, both the reasons why crowds would come to him and the time of their arrival. Some were drawn by the mere desire to see him, others by illness, and still others by bodies possessed by demons. Yet no one ever complained of the hardship or exhaustion of the journey; everyone returned filled with spiritual nourishment [Col. 0154C]. Antony, however, insisted that they ought not to attribute this marvel to his own praise, but to the Lord, who had granted human beings knowledge of him according to the measure of mortal capacity.

### CHAPTER XXXV

Once, when he had gone out to the outer monasteries and the brothers had asked him to pray on a certain boat with the monks who were traveling, he went aboard and alone among them perceived a most dreadful odor. Everyone declared that the stench came from the salted fish and *tarichoi* [Note: [Col. 0181D] *Tarichoi*. This is the reading of the manuscripts and the Greek text. The Cologne edition incorrectly has *carixarum*; the older editions, with Surius, have *caricarum*. Note the ancient *tarichopolia*; see the *Onomasticon*.] placed in the boat. But Antony affirmed that he perceived the stench of something else. While he was still speaking, a young man possessed by a demon, who had fallen down and hidden himself beside the hull of the boat, suddenly cried out. When Antony immediately cured him in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0154D], everyone understood that the odor had been the demon’s.

### CHAPTER XXXVI

Another man, noble among his people and possessed by a demon, was brought to him. He was so overcome by madness that he did not know he was with Antony and even ate his own bodily waste. Therefore, when those who had brought him asked the old man to pray to the Lord for him, he pitied the young man’s misery so deeply that he remained awake with him throughout the night, struggling against the illness of the afflicted man.

But when dawn was already breaking and the possessed man attacked Antony and violently pushed him, those who had brought him began to grow angry, asking why he had insulted the old man. Antony said to them: “Do not attribute another’s guilt to this wretched young man. This frenzy belongs to the one who possesses him, not to the possessed man [Col. 0155A]. The suffering enemy rushed into this audacity because the Lord commanded him to go into a dry region; and this attack against me was a sign that Satan had been expelled.” No sooner had he spoken than the young man recovered his senses, gave thanks to God, recognized the place where he was, and, embracing Antony, kissed him with all affection.

### CHAPTER XXXVII

We have learned of countless other signs of this kind through the unanimous reports of the monks. Yet these things should not cause such great astonishment, because what follows far surpasses the condition of our frailty.

About the ninth hour [Note: [Col. 0181D] About the ninth hour.] The ninth hour was ordinarily the time when the fast was broken; this is now well known. Anyone wishing to learn more may consult the *Onomasticon*.], when he had begun to pray before eating, he felt himself carried away in spirit and borne aloft by angels. When demons obstructed the angels’ passage through the air, the angels began to demand, in opposition to them, what grounds there could be for detaining him, since no accusations existed against Antony. But when the demons attempted to rehearse sins from the beginning of his birth, the angels closed their slanderous mouths, saying that they ought not to recount sins committed from his birth, since these had already been put to rest by Christ’s goodness. If, however, they knew of anything from the time when he had become a monk [Note: [Col. 0182A] When he had become a monk.] From this passage Bellarmine, in volume IV of his *Judgment concerning the Book of Concord of the Lutherans*, error 22, infers that there is some similarity between baptism and the religious life of monks: just as in baptism every penalty due to sins is remitted, so it is credible that the same occurs upon undertaking the monastic life. This is strongly supported both by the testimony of the holy Fathers, by the examples of holy men, and by scholastic teaching.

As for the authority of the Fathers, Jerome writes in letter 25, consoling Paula over the death of her daughter Blesilla: “Indeed, if an untimely death had carried her off while she was thinking of worldly desire and—may God avert it from his own people—the pleasures of this life, she ought to have been mourned. But now, since, with Christ propitious, nearly four months earlier she had in a certain sense washed herself in a second baptism of her purpose, and thereafter had lived in such a way that, having trampled upon the world, she always thought of the monastery, do you not fear that the Savior might say to you: ‘Are you angry, Paula, because your daughter has become my daughter?’”

The same force is found in that exhortation of the same Jerome to Demetrias, letter 8: “Now, because you have abandoned the world and, in a second degree after baptism, have entered into an agreement with your adversary, saying to him, ‘I renounce you, devil, and your world, and your pomp, and your works,’ keep the covenant that you made.”

Saint Bernard, in his book *On Precept and Dispensation*, near the end, not only teaches this but, when asked by some people about the matter, gives two reasons for it: “You also wish to hear from me why, beyond the other institutions of penance, monastic discipline has deserved this privilege, that it should be called a second baptism. First, I think, because of the perfect renunciation of the world and the singular excellence of the spiritual life. By surpassing all forms of human life, this manner of living makes its professors and lovers like angels and unlike human beings; indeed, it restores the divine image in humanity, conforming us to Christ, as baptism does. Finally, we are, as it were, baptized a second time when, by mortifying our members that are upon the earth [Col. 0182C], we put Christ on again, having been planted anew in the likeness of his death.

“Second, just as in baptism we are rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of eternal love, so also, in this second regeneration of our holy purpose, we escape from darkness—not merely from the one original sin, but from many actual offenses—and enter into the light of virtues, applying again to ourselves the Apostle’s words: ‘The night has passed, but the day has drawn near’ (Romans XIII).”

For now, these testimonies from the holy Fathers are sufficient. Nor are examples lacking among the visions of holy men. Below, in John the Subdeacon’s first little book *On Contemplation*, no. 9, we read: “There was a certain great man among those who possess foreknowledge. He declared: ‘The power that I saw standing over baptism I also saw over the monk’s garment when he receives the spiritual habit.’”

Leontius, bishop of Neapolis on the island of Cyprus, in the *Life of Symeon the Fool* preserved by Metaphrastes under July 1, relates how Symeon [Col. 0182D] and John were, as it were, to be regenerated in the holy habit, and how great a glory they themselves saw during the first seven days of their regeneration.

Saint Anselm, in book *On Similitudes*, chapter 191, relates the story of the monk Osbern, and how an angel defended him at the point of death against the devil, who was accusing him of sins committed before he entered the religious life, because those sins had been abolished by his monastic profession. See also the Franciscan *Annals*, concerning the religious Christopher and the angel’s reply.

Among the scholastics, one should consult Saint Thomas, *Summa* II–II, question 189, article 3, reply to objection 3, and in book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 4, question 3, article 3, minor question 3, reply to objection 3. There, the example that he cites from the *Lives of the Fathers* in both places without identifying its location is the very one I have just produced from John the Subdeacon. Thomas of Walden also produces it in volume III, *On the Sacraments*, title 9, chapter 80; see his excellent discussion of this matter. See also Antoninus, *Summa*, part III, title 16, chapter 3, § 3; Paludanus, book IV, distinction 38 [Col. 0183A], question 3; Sylvester, under the word “Religion,” doubt 23; and our own Plato, book I, *On the Good of the Religious State*, chapter 13.

What do the heretics now have to set against the authority of so many Fathers, against histories supported by such clear testimony, and against the universally received teaching of the scholastics? When Philip Melanchthon asserts in the *Book of Concord of the Lutherans* that Catholics teach the monastic life to be better than baptism, this is a substantial lie, as is clear from what has just been said.

If they knew of anything from the time when he had become a monk and consecrated himself to God, it was permissible for the accusations to be brought forward. The demons accused him, brazenly uttering many lies; but when they had no proofs for their falsehoods, a free passage of ascent was opened for Antony. Immediately returning to himself, he found himself again in the place where he had begun to stand, and saw that he was once more as he had been.

Then, forgetting his food, he spent the night from that hour in groaning and lamentation, reflecting upon the multitude of human enemies, the struggle with so great an army, and the arduous journey through the air to heaven. He also reflected upon the Apostle’s saying: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the ruler of the power of this air” (Ephesians VI). Knowing that the powers of the air always attempt, struggle, and contend for this reason—that our passage to heaven might not be free—he exhorted and warned them: “Take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day” (ibid.), so that the enemy, having nothing evil to say about you (Titus II), may be put to shame.

Let us also remember the Apostle’s words: “Whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows” (II Corinthians XII). Paul, indeed, was carried up to the third heaven and, after hearing ineffable words there, descended. Antony, however, was raised only as far as the region of the air and, after the struggle, appeared free.

[Col. 0155D] ### CHAPTER XXXVIII

He also possessed a gift of this kind: if, while sitting on the mountain, he was ignorant of some matter and sought knowledge of it within himself, it was revealed to him by the Lord when he prayed. Thus, according to what is written, he was taught by God (John VI; Isaiah LIV).

Finally, when this subject was being discussed among the brothers and they repeatedly asked him how the soul conducted itself after bearing the burden of the body and what place would be granted to it after its departure, a voice from above called his name during the following night and said: “Antony, rise, go out, and see.” He rose and went out, for he knew whom he ought to answer.

Lifting his eyes toward heaven, he saw a certain tall and terrifying figure [Note: [Col. 0183A] He saw a certain tall and terrifying figure.] Palladius mentions this vision in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 27, as reported by Cronius. A not very dissimilar vision appears in the *Life of Macarius the Roman*, chapter 9: “A man of enormous stature, almost a hundred cubits tall, appeared to us.”], raising its head as far as the clouds [Col. 0156A]. He also saw certain winged beings [Note: [Col. 0183A] He also saw certain winged beings.] The same account is found in Palladius, at the place already cited. In the *Life of Macarius the Roman*, chapter 11: “In those very branches there were many winged creatures, resembling the birds of heaven.”]

As for souls wishing to fly away and escape into heaven, but hindered by Stygian monsters, more than one similar vision is found among the authors [Col. 0183B]. You will find the same story, cited in the name of Athanasius from this Life, in the treatise on the state of those who sleep, which our Raderus recently published after his *Garden of the Saints*, from a manuscript Codex of Bavaria and Augsburg that attributed it to George Hamartolus, or George the Logothete. Thus, on this testimony as well, this Life of Antony is attributed to Athanasius.

In the same treatise John the Confessor relates in his letter to John the Chamberlain: “Everyone attempts to draw and drag toward himself the wretched soul that has already been expelled from the body through the air.” See in the same treatise Cyril the Great and Martyrius of Antioch.]

which were trying to rise toward heaven (Palladius, chapter 27; Paschasius, chapter 19, no. 4), and saw that figure preventing their passage with outstretched hands. Some of them it seized and dashed to the ground; over others it struggled in vain to retain them. It grieved that some were flying past it toward the heavenly realms, while both the victors and the defeated gave rise to immense joy mingled with sorrow.

Immediately a voice came to him, saying: “Pay attention to what you see.” Then, with his heart enlightened, he began to understand that this was the ascent of souls and that the devil was the one preventing them—retaining those subject to him and tormenting himself over the flight of the saints whom he could not deceive. Encouraged by these examples of visions, he grew daily toward better things.

### CHAPTER XXXIX

Nor did he disclose to the brothers what had been revealed to him for the sake of boasting. But because, while praying, he continually praised God’s help, he was compelled to speak when they questioned him. He did not wish to conceal anything from his spiritual sons, whose souls were pure in Christ, especially since the report of such signs both fostered love for their purpose and displayed the fruit of their labor.

He never broke his patience through a sudden burst of anger, nor raised his humility into glory. He compelled all clerics, even down to the lowest rank [Note: [Col. 0183B] “Even down to the lowest rank.”] From this one may perceive the ancient use of ranks within the clerical order. They were called ranks because the ascent to the highest position took place step by step. Pope Siricius, in his letter to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, chapters 9 and 10, and Gratian, distinction 77, chapter “Whoever,” cite the following: “Afterward, let him approach the rank of the diaconate, if, with continence leading the way, he first proves himself worthy.” The First Council of Braga, chapter 38: “Let the layman, instructed through the ranks, come to the priesthood.” Pope Dionysius I, letter 1 to Urbanus the prefect: “For this purpose divine providence established ranks and appointed different orders to be distinct,” and so throughout the sacred authors.] to pray before him. To bishops and presbyters alike, as a disciple of humility, he bowed his head so that they might bless him [Note: [Col. 0183C] He bowed his head so that they might bless him.] Such was the piety of the ancients that they treated the blessing of great priests with reverence and received it with bowed heads. See the *Onomasticon*.]

As for the deacons who came to him for assistance, when he discussed in their presence the help they needed, he placed them before himself in prayer to the Lord, without embarrassment and himself willing to learn. [Col. 0156C] He frequently questioned those who were with him, and if he heard something necessary from them, he admitted that he had been helped.

### CHAPTER XL

He also possessed great grace in his countenance, and had received this remarkable gift from the Savior. If someone unfamiliar with him wished to see him among a crowd of monks, without anyone pointing him out, he would pass over the others and run to Antony. From his face he recognized the purity of his soul and, as though through a bodily mirror, observed the grace of his holy mind.

For he always wore a cheerful expression, clearly showing that he was thinking about heavenly things, just as Scripture says: “When the heart is joyful, the face flourishes; but when one is in sorrow, the face grows sad” (Proverbs XVII). Thus Jacob also recognized that Laban, his father-in-law, was plotting against him when he said to his daughters: “The face of your father is not as it was yesterday and the day before” (Genesis XXXI). So Samuel recognized David: “His eyes were bright with joy, and his teeth were white like milk” (I Samuel XVI).

Antony was recognized in the same way, because he always preserved the same countenance in prosperity and adversity, neither exalted by good fortune nor broken by misfortune. He was lovable in appearance and remarkable in the purity of his faith.

### CHAPTER XLI

He never joined the communion of schismatics, knowing their ancient depravity and transgression. He never offered the Manichaeans [Note: [Col. 0183C] The Manichaeans.] Augustine, in his book *On Heresies to Quodvultdeus*, heresy 46: “In Greece his disciples, avoiding the name of madness as though they were more learned—and thereby more deceitful—called him, by doubling the letter *n*, Mannichaeus, as though he were pouring out manna.” The same author, book XIX, chapter 22, *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, explains the difference in pronunciation: “For you did not add one letter to the first part of the name so that manna might be recognized; rather, you added two syllables to the latter part, not calling him Mannichaeus, but Manichaeus”—that is, as he translates it there, “pourer-out of madness.”] or other heretics even friendly words, except only those words that might recall them from the error of iniquity [Col. 0157A]. He proclaimed that friendship and conversation with such people were the ruin of the soul.

He likewise detested the Arians, telling everyone that one should not even approach them. When certain Ariomaniacs came [Note: [Col. 0183D] “Ariomaniacs.”] This is the reading of the Latin manuscripts and of the printed Greek text. The Cologne edition and Surius have *Arrionitae* or *Arrionianitae*, incorrectly.], he examined their utterly faithless sect and drove them from the mountain, saying that their words were much worse than serpents.

When the Arians were lying [Note: [Col. 0183D] “When the Arians were lying.”] Baronius, volume III, year of Christ 343, under Pope Julius VII, in the sixth year of Constantius and Constans: “The people used to value the testimony of distinguished monks concerning the Catholic faith so highly that, perceiving this, the Arians did not hesitate to lie, claiming that the great Antony shared their belief. For this reason he had to leave the deepest solitude of the desert and descend all the way to Alexandria, publicly to profess the Catholic faith that he honored, lest the people be led astray; and he confirmed it by the signs that followed. When these events occurred is not at all clear. Jerome likewise writes to Castrutius about the same journey of Saint Antony to Alexandria to refute the Arians (Jerome, letter XXXIII). [Col. 0184A] It is also recorded in the *Lives of the Fathers* that Saint Athanasius once summoned to Alexandria the abbot Poemen, a man of tested holiness (Lives of the Fathers, part II). Thus far Baronius.

What Baronius cites here from Jerome is found in book II of Ruffinus, no. 218. As for what he says about Poemen, either his memory deceived him, or he thought Poemen was the same person as Pammōn. Concerning Pammōn, see here in Ruffinus, book II, no. 164. You will conclude that he is the same as Pambōn, not Poemen, from Pelagius’s little book III, no. 14, and little book XVII, no. 2, where the same sayings are related under the name of Pambōn that Ruffinus gives under the name of Pammōn. A different person is Piammon, or Pyaminon, concerning whom see here in Ruffinus, book I, chapter 31; in Palladius, chapter 72, he is Ammonas.]

when some Arians came, claiming to share his belief, Antony marveled at their audacity.
