Moved by righteous indignation, and requested by the bishops and all the brothers, he descended to Alexandria [Note: [Col. 0184A] He descended to Alexandria.] Since there are many cities called Alexandria, the reference here is to Alexandria in Egypt, also called Great Alexandria to distinguish it from the others.]. There he publicly condemned the Ariomaniacs, declaring this to be the final heresy and the forerunner of Antichrist.

He preached to the people that the Son of God was not a work, not made from things that did not exist, but was proper to the Father and of one substance with him. He said that it was impious even to conceive the thought: “There was a time when he was not,” since the Word of God, who is God and always exists, is coeternal with the Father, because he was born from the Father, who always is.

Therefore he said: “You must have no fellowship with the Arians. For what fellowship does light have with darkness? You who believe faithfully are Christians. But they, teaching that the Word—that is, the Son—who is from God the Father is a creature, are separated from the Gentiles by no interval. They serve the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever” (Romans I).

“Believe me, the elements themselves grow angry, and all creation groans against the Arian madness, according to the Apostle’s saying (Romans VIII), because it sees its Lord, through whom all things exist and in whom all things have been made (Romans XI), being reduced to the status of a creature [Col. 0157C].”

### CHAPTER XLII

The preaching of so great a man cannot be adequately expressed in terms of how much it strengthened the people in the faith. They rejoiced that a hostile heresy, inimical to Christ, was being anathematized by a pillar of the Church.

No age or sex remained at home. I say nothing of the Christians: pagans too, and even the priests of the idols, hurried to the Lord’s sovereignty, saying: “We beg you, let us see the man of God,” for this was the name by which Antony was conspicuously known among all people. They also sought at least to touch the fringe of his garment, believing that the touch would greatly benefit them.

How many were then freed from demonic possession and various illnesses! How many spoils were taken from the idols! How many were also recalled from pagan error and joined to our flock! So many, certainly, that within a few days the conversion from the superstition of idols surpassed the entire multitude of believers gained throughout a whole year [Col. 0157D]. Moreover, when his companions drove back the crowd pressing upon him, thinking that the gathering of the people would weary him, he said calmly: “Is this assembly greater than the crowds of demons? Is the multitude of those who obey greater than the companies of our opponents on the mountain?”

### CHAPTER XLIII

It also happened that, as we were accompanying him near the gate on his return, a woman behind us cried out, saying: “Wait, man of God! My daughter is tormented by a most savage demon. Wait, I beg you; wait, lest I too fall and perish.” When he heard this, the remarkable old man, prompted by us, nevertheless wished to stop for a little while.

As the woman approached, the girl lay there in convulsions. Antony silently prayed to the Lord Jesus, and at his command the unclean spirit immediately departed. The girl was safe, the people praised God, and the mother was joyful. Antony himself was happy because he was returning to the solitude he desired.

He was also exceptionally wise. This was remarkable in him: although he had not learned letters, he was extraordinarily intelligent and prudent.

### CHAPTER XLIV

Once two pagan philosophers [Note: [Col. 0184A] Once two philosophers.] Baronius, volume III, year of Christ 328, under Pope Sylvester XV, in the twenty-third year of the emperor Constantine. “Not only those who worshiped Christ,” he says, “but also pagans—and among them especially the philosophers who were accustomed to bark against the Christian religion—wanted to visit Antony and converse with him. They were distressed that an uneducated man should be carried along by such extraordinary praise, as though he had reached the summit of philosophy. If it is pleasant to hear of victories won by the power of the cross against armed enemies, how much more delightful must it be to hear that the unconquerable enemies of Christ were shown to have been overcome entirely by the power of the cross, without weapons? See Cassian, *Conferences* VIII, chapter 18.”] came to him, thinking that they could deceive Antony. He was on the upper mountain. When he saw them, he recognized from their faces that they were pagans. Going out to them through an interpreter [Note: [Col. 0184B] Through an interpreter.] Isaac appears to have been Antony’s regular interpreter. Saint Jerome says of him in the *Life of Saint Hilarion*, chapter 25: “There we found two brothers, Isaac and Pelusianus; Isaac had been Antony’s interpreter.” At times, circumstances required other interpreters, as when Cronius served in this capacity for Antony’s dealings with Saint Eulogius, according to Palladius, chapter 26.], he began to speak as follows:

“Why have wise men troubled themselves by coming such a long distance to a foolish man?”

When they replied that he was not foolish but exceedingly wise, he answered with alertness: “If you have come to a foolish man, your labor is useless. But if you think that I am wise and possess wisdom, it is good that you imitate what you approve, since good things ought to be imitated. If I had come to you, I would imitate you. But because you have come to me as to a wise man, become Christians, as I am.”

The philosophers departed, marveling at both things: the sharpness of his intellect and his expulsion of demons.

### CHAPTER XLV

He similarly bound other wise men of the world [Note: [Col. 0184B] Other wise men of the world likewise.] For how Antony could have been ignorant of letters, see above, at chapter 1, no. 7. I shall append the Greek words of this little story, so that they may be compared with the scholion to Synesius. It will then appear that Synesius suffered a lapse of memory and attributed to Ammon the Egyptian what ought to be attributed to Antony the Egyptian—unless *Ammon* (*Ἀμοῦν*) slipped into his text in place of *Antony* (*Ἀντώνιος*) through a scribal abbreviation.

The Greek passage is as follows:

“Again, when others of this kind met him on the outer mountain and thought to mock him because he had not learned letters, Antony said to them: ‘What do you say? What comes first: the mind or letters? And what is the cause of what? Is the mind the cause of letters, or are letters the cause of the mind?’ When they said that the mind came first and was the inventor of letters, Antony said: ‘Therefore, when the mind is healthy, letters are not necessary.’”

Evagrius translates this as follows: “He also bound other wise men of the world in a similar way. When they wished to mock him because he was ignorant of letters, he ensnared them in this argument, saying: ‘Answer me: which comes first, the mind or letters? And what is the origin of each? Does the mind arise from letters, or do letters arise from the mind?’ When they asserted that the mind was the author and inventor of letters, he said: ‘Therefore, whoever has a sound mind does not need letters.’”

Synesius, in the *Dion*, or *On the Conduct of His Own Life*, while discussing the innate power in certain minds by which they can deal with matters without the assistance of letters and learning, says:

“Such was Ammon the Egyptian: he did not acquire the use of letters, but judged their usefulness. So great was the power of mind within him.”

Our Petavius translates it thus, although the phrase “he did not acquire” (*οὐκ ἐξεῦρεν*) may be rendered more clearly and more in keeping with the sense here as “he did not acquire” or “he did not make use of.” Thus *εὑρίσκω* (“to find”) is used by Demosthenes in the speech against Timocrates, as Ulpian explains it there. Donatus likewise, in his commentary on Terence’s *Eunuch*, act 2, scene 1, explains “to find” as “to acquire.”

A scholion in the margin of the manuscript Medicean Codex clarifies these obscure words of Synesius as follows:

“When someone asked him whether letters were necessary, he said: ‘If the mind is vigorous, what need is there for letters?’ The phrase ‘he did not acquire the use of letters, but judged their usefulness’ means: he himself did not use letters, but declared that those who had not received an abundance of intellect needed letters, so that by means of them they might repair and correct the deficiency of their minds.”

] also came to him, wishing to ridicule him because he was ignorant of letters. He bound them with the following argument:

“Answer me: which comes first, the mind or letters? And what is the origin of each? Does the mind arise from letters, or do letters arise from the mind?”

When they asserted that the mind was the author and inventor of letters, he said: “Therefore, if someone’s mind is sound, he does not need letters.”

Who among those present would not have cried out after this struggle, when even the defeated themselves were astonished and admired such intellectual acuity in a man ignorant of letters?

For although he lived in solitude and the mountains and spent his entire life there, he was not uncultivated or harsh. He was cheerful and approachable, and, in accordance with the Apostle’s commandment, he spoke with conversation seasoned by divine salt (Colossians IV), so that he was free from envy and won everyone’s affection.

### CHAPTER XLVI

Meanwhile, as though it were not enough that the Gentiles had been separated from us twice, men came to him a third time, blinded by the cloud of all secular wisdom and, in their own estimation, highly educated in every philosophical discipline and art.

When they demanded from him an account of the faith that we have in Christ, and tried through pointed sophistical questions to mock him concerning the divine cross, he restrained his voice for a little while and remained silent. First he pitied their error; then, through the interpreter who was accustomed to render his words most carefully into Greek, he began as follows:

“What is more beautiful or more honorable: to honor the cross, or to attribute adultery, parricide, and incest to those whom you worship, when in the one case there is the mark of virtue in despising death, and in the other a shameful religion, a teacher of obscenity [Col. 0159A]?

“What is better: to say that the Word of God, remaining what he was, assumed a human body for our salvation, so that through participation in mortality he might raise us to heaven and make us participants in the heavenly nature; or, as you yourselves assert, to make the draught of the divine mind [Note: [Col. 0185A] “The draught of the divine mind.”] He soon says: “the soul flowing from the most splendid fountain of God.” Baronius, volume III, year of Christ 328, under Pope Sylvester XV, in the fourteenth year of the emperor Constantine, says: “These men appear to have been Platonic philosophers, who said that the soul was an emanation and substance of the divine mind.” See our Coimbra commentators on Aristotle’s books *On the Soul*.], bow its head down toward earthly objects worthy of worship, and enclose the heavenly name in the forms of cattle and serpents?

“With what face do you dare to mock the credulity of Christians [Note: [Col. 0185B] “With what face do you dare to mock the credulity of Christians?”] Baronius, in the same place: “He cleverly turns back their mockery of the incarnation of the Word. For while Christians believe in only one incarnation of God, and that without any alteration or injury to the Word, they were compelled to admit that as many incarnations of God had taken place as there had ever been human beings and beasts, since they said that souls were of divine substance and that the same souls became base, dishonored, and subject to sins.”], who say that Christ, the Son of God, without detriment to himself, both began to be what he was not and remained what he had been; while you, dragging the soul down from heavenly things, habitually bury it in the bodies not only of human beings but also of serpents and cattle [Note: [Col. 0185B] “You habitually bury it in the bodies of cattle.”] He is mocking Pythagorean metempsychosis; concerning it, see our Coimbra commentators on Aristotle’s books *On the Soul*.]?

“Christian credulity testifies that its God came for the salvation of the world; but you, proclaiming an innate soul, transfer it from one body to another. Christian faith, which reveres God’s omnipotence and mercy, consequently declares that the incarnation was possible for God, yet in such a way that his condescension did not empty his dignity. But you, who boast that the soul flowing from the most splendid fountain of God has fallen shamefully, and who dare to assert that, after its diminution, it is mutable and capable of transformation, now assail with impious speech even that nature which is mistress of the ages, through your insults against the soul.

“For the image which, according to you, retains the natural likeness of its author, and which has one and the same substance as the source from which it flowed, consequently refers its own humiliations and injuries back to its origin. Therefore understand that the insults directed against souls rebound, through your blasphemy, upon the father—as you call him—of those souls 55.”

[Col. 0159C] The cross of Christ the Lord, our God, is here thrust upon us. I ask: what obscenity of religion is this? Is it not rather better to endure patiently a cross, or a death of some kind inflicted by wicked men, than to lament Isis after Osiris in aimless and uncertain wanderings?

[Note: [Col. 0185B] Isis.] Isis, the most famous goddess of the Egyptians. I do not wish here to support the well-known tales of antiquity with the authorities of the ancients. Among more recent writers, Lilius Gregorius Giraldus treats these matters most fully in his *History of the Gods of the Gentiles*; see his discussion of Isis in *Syntagma* 12.

[Note: [Col. 0185C] Osiris.] Osiris was Dionysus, or Bacchus, for the Egyptians, the brother and husband of Isis. See Giraldus, *Syntagma* 8.

Shame on you, I beg, for the ambushes of Typhon!

[Note: [Col. 0185C] Typhon.] Typhon was the brother of Osiris, who tore Osiris to pieces. Giraldus, in the same place.

Shame on you for Saturn’s flight and his most cruel devouring of his children!

[Note: [Col. 0185C] Saturn.] This most famous false deity is discussed by Giraldus in *Syntagma* 4.

Blush for Jupiter’s parricide and incest!

[Note: [Col. 0185C] Jupiter.] Poets everywhere speak of Jupiter’s parricide and incest. Giraldus, *Syntagma* 2.

Blush for his rape and intercourse with women and boys. He, as your poets invent, to satisfy the frenzy of his monstrous lust, uttered soft cries of love; he flowed into Danaë’s lap, both lover and payment;

[Note: [Col. 0185C] Danaë.] Arnobius, books V and VII.

he, assuming the form of a bird, sang for Leda’s embraces;

[Note: [Col. 0185C] Leda’s.] Giraldus, *Syntagma* 5, where he discusses Castor and Pollux, or the Dioscuri, born to Leda.

[Col. 0159D] he, raging against his own sex, polluted a royal boy with bird-servants. These are the things you believe, these are the things you worship; these are the ornaments of your temples. I beg you, weigh our words with impartial judgment, for your salvation. Are all things—or is nothing—to be believed in the Christian books? If nothing, then you do not acknowledge even the name of the cross which you disparage. If everything is to be believed, why, when resurrection is joined to the cross in those same books, do you tear apart the divine Passion with foolish speech, and not immediately join to it the restoration of sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, walking to the lame, cleansing of leprosy, the sea serving God as he walked upon it, the expulsion of demons, the resurrection of the dead, and the return of the departed from the underworld? All these things are inserted in the divine Scriptures which you interpolate, and in these same volumes are contained proclamations of majesty and the disgrace of death. Therefore, cast aside the hatred with which you are imbued, and you will immediately discover both that Jesus is the true God and that, for the sake of human salvation, he assumed fragile human nature.

## CHAPTER XLVII

Yet tell us about your religion, if you are not ashamed. But what forms of worship can unhappy error recount amid such filth and madness of affairs? Unless perhaps, as I hear, you assert the tales of your gods—their obscenities, cruelties, vanities, and deaths—while concealing them beneath allegorical coverings.

[Note: [Col. 0185C] Concealing them beneath allegorical coverings.] Baronius, volume III, in the year of Christ 328, the fifteenth of Pope Sylvester and the thirteenth of the emperor Constantine, says: “Antony refuted those arguments which the philosophers might have made concerning the allegories by which they habitually concealed the shameful acts of the gods and referred everything to the heavenly bodies and the various movements of nature. He showed that the Creator is greatly dishonored if human beings offer the honor and glory due to him not to him, but to creatures.” Thus far Baronius. Arnobius discusses the allegorical coverings of the gods in books III and V; Clement, *Recognitions*, book X, chapter 8; Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religion*; Fulgentius, *Mythologies*; Augustine, *City of God*, books IV and VII; and, among more recent authors, Natalis Comes at length in his *Mythologies*.

—the rape of Libera, the earth;

[Note: [Col. 0185D] The rape of Libera, the earth.] Greek: Τὴν ἁρπαγὴν Κόρης εἰς τὴν γῆν, “the rape of Kore, into the earth,” as the Anglican Codex correctly supplies the Augustan text. The Latin editions vary. Some read, “Liber’s rape, the earth of Proserpina”; the Cologne edition, “Liber’s rape, the earth of Proserpina.” But the reference is to the rape of Proserpina, who was also called Libera. Hence the gloss “of Proserpina” entered the text. See Cicero, *Verrine Orations* VI; Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religion*: “calling Proserpina Libera.” See Augustine, *City of God* IV.10 and VII.24, and Giraldus, *Syntagma* 6 and 8.

—crippled Vulcan and feeble fire;

[Note: [Col. 0186A] Vulcan and feeble fire.] The older editions read *Vulcanum et cibilem ignem*, manifestly in error. Greek: Καὶ Ἡφαίστου χωλότητα εἰς τὸ πῦρ ἀλληγορεῖτε, “and you allegorically explain Vulcan’s lameness as fire.” Our author expresses his lameness with a double epithet: “crippled Vulcan and feeble fire.” Minucius Felix, *Octavius*: “Vulcan, a lame and feeble god.” See Augustine, *City of God* VII.16.

—Juno, the air;

[Note: [Col. 0186A] Juno, the air.] Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II; Augustine, *City of God* IV.10 and VII.16.

—Apollo, the sun;

[Note: [Col. 0186A] Apollo, the sun.] Augustine, *City of God* VII.16.

—Diana, the moon;

[Note: [Col. 0186A] Diana, the moon.] Augustine, *City of God* VII.16.

—Neptune, the seas;

[Note: [Col. 0186A] Neptune, the seas.] Augustine, *City of God* IV.10 and VII.16.

—and, interpreting Jupiter, the prince of lusts, as the ether.

[Note: [Col. 0186A] Jupiter, the ether.] Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II; Augustine, *City of God* IV.10 and VII.16.

Even after this insolence of an excuse, you do not embrace God but creatures, despising the Creator. And if the beauty of the elements drew you to venerate them, it was proper to observe moderation; you ought to admire them only, not worship them, lest veneration of the work become an injury to the Creator. For according to this perverse reasoning, which you follow, the honor due to the architect has passed over to the house, the physician’s skill has been transferred to the remedies, and the merits or praises of all craftsmen have been transferred to their works. What do you say to this, so that we may recognize what an absurdly shameful confession of the cross you make?

## CHAPTER XLVIII

While the philosophers were turning their eyes toward one another during this discussion and muttering among themselves, Antony, smiling, said again through the interpreter:

[Col. 0160C]

“Indeed, everything seems exceedingly difficult whenever, after the just order of the whole matter has been trampled underfoot, the merits of labor are attributed more to the works than to their makers.”

[Note: [Col. 0186B] “Exceedingly difficult,” etc.] This entire sentence is absent from the Greek, up to “the elements.”

“The elements, as I have said, prove their servitude simply by being observed. But since, by the dialectical method of inquiry, you gather together whatever you consider necessary, by this same device you compel us also to affirm our religion. Answer me: how is knowledge of God more clearly demonstrated—by an assemblage of words or by the working of faith? And which is more ancient, the working of faith or an argument proceeding by proofs?”

[Note: [Col. 0186B] “Which is more ancient.”] Baronius, volume III, in the year of Christ 328, the fifteenth of Pope Sylvester and the thirteenth of the emperor Constantine, says: “He adduces the proof of true faith and religion from the work and the experience itself, the facts agreeing that deeds are more powerful than words.”

When they replied that action was more reliable than words and that through it clear knowledge of God was obtained, he agreed that they had spoken well. For action, which proceeds from faith, produces the affections of the soul, whereas dialectical disputation derives the beginning of its opposition from the artifice of those who construct it. “Therefore,” he said, “when someone possesses in his soul the working of faith, verbal composition will be superfluous—the composition by which you attempt to uproot the belief conceived in our understanding, although you are often unable to express even your own ideas. Thus the works of the mind are more solid than the fraudulent conclusion of sophistries.”

## CHAPTER XLIX

We Christians do not have the mystery of our life deposited in the wisdom of the world, but in the power of faith, which has been granted to us by God through Christ. The truth of my speech is commended by the order of the things that happen daily; for us, unlearned and ignorant of your literature, his words alone are sufficient for the knowledge of God.

Behold, we who have been drawn away from so many herds of paganism are daily spreading throughout the whole world; whereas, after the Lord’s coming, your knotty sophistries have failed. Behold, while teaching the simple faith of Christ, we have conquered idolatry, and through the preaching of the shameful cross, gilded temples have fallen. Show, if you can, by what weaving of words you have persuaded the nations to prefer paganism to Christ.

Throughout all lands Christ, the true Son of God, has now been acknowledged. Neither the eloquence of sophistries nor philosophical disputation can harm the multitude of believers. We name the Crucified One, and all the demons whom you worship as gods howl and, at the first sign of the Lord’s cross, are driven from the bodies they possess.

Where are those fabled oracles? Where are the incantations of the Egyptians?

[Note: [Col. 0186B] “Where are the incantations of the Egyptians?”] Exodus 7:11: “They also performed them by their Egyptian incantations.” Verse 22: “And the magicians of the Egyptians did likewise with their incantations.”

Where have the songs of the magicians achieved anything?

[Note: [Col. 0186B] “Where have the songs of the magicians achieved anything?”] Ovid, *Fasti* II: “magic song.” Juvenal, *Satire* VI, verse 608: “magical chants.” Columella, book X: “magical songs.” Prudentius, *On the Crowns*, hymn V, verse 23: “magical incantation.”

Certainly everything was laid waste when Christ thundered to the world from his cross. Nevertheless, you attempt to mock the glorious death of Jesus, overlooking the hosts of the afflicted.

What, moreover, is the meaning of this? Paganism, which had never been shaken by royal persecution, indeed which was cherished by the age and supported by the protection of men, has now collapsed. We, Christ’s servants, the more we are oppressed, the more we rise up and flourish. Your images, which once adorned enclosures surrounded by walls, have now collapsed through age. But Christ’s teaching, which seems to you folly and a game, although it has endured the tyrannical assaults of persecuting rulers and has been attacked by various terrors, is confined by no region of the earth and halted by no boundary of barbarian peoples.

When has such splendor of divine knowledge shone forth? When have so many virtues converged together in one place? Continence in marriage,

[Note: [Col. 0186B–C] Continence in marriage.] Several examples of this exist in these books, *Lives of the Fathers*. Other lives of the saints also provide examples, a catalogue of which I shall compile in the *Onomasticon*.

virginity in the Church. The glorious steadfastness of the martyrs for their Lord flourishes, and the cross of Christ is the beginning of them all.

Meanwhile, amid such choirs of virtues, you spread the nets of syllogisms and attempt to envelop the true light of reality in dark arguments. But behold, as our Teacher said, we persuade not by pagan persuasion (1 Corinthians 2), but by the clearest faith, which habitually precedes the affirmation of words.

For here are people suffering, tormented by demons. When he had brought them forward into the midst, he repeated his words, saying: “Now drive out by your collections of arguments, and by whatever magical song you wish, the gods whom you imagine to be yours. But if you cannot, surrender your defeated hands, flee to Christ’s trophies, and immediately the belief in the Crucified One will be followed by the power of his majesty.”

He spoke; and, after invoking the name of Jesus and pressing the life-giving sign upon their foreheads in the sacred number of the Trinity, the empty wisdom of the philosophers present was refuted together with the expelled demons. They were terrified and amazed that, after such intellectual ability, divine generosity in signs should flow through this man.

But he attributed everything to Christ, who heals, and used a conciliatory form of address, saying: “Do not suppose that I have given them health through these things. Christ performs these miracles through his servants. Believe also, and you will see that such signs are merited by devotion to God, not by the empty swelling of eloquence. Flee to the law of the Crucified One, imitate us, his servants, and, content with this limit of knowledge, seek no further arguments of worldly ignorance.”

When Antony had said this, the philosophers, struck by extraordinary amazement, withdrew from him with respectful salutations and acknowledged that his presence had benefited them greatly.

## CHAPTER L

This is truly remarkable: that both the favor of rulers and the whole royal court should honor a man established at the farthest limit of the world. For even the Augustus Constantine,

[Note: [Col. 0186C–D] Constantine Augustus.] Baronius, volume III, in the year of Christ 328, the fifteenth of Pope Sylvester and the twenty-third of the emperor Constantine, says: “At this time the fame of Antony had become so widespread that it had circulated throughout the entire world. Since Alexandria, as we have said from Dio [volume I, under the year of Christ 64], was the marketplace of the whole world, what nation could have been unaware of what had become common knowledge there? His fame also reached Constantinople, and Antony’s name was held in the highest honor in Constantine’s palace. Thus everyone had the fullest opportunity to honor the man, as you find here at the end of the *Life*, chapter 61. Therefore Constantine, the most religious emperor, moved by the powerful fame of Antony’s virtues and convinced of everything, together with his sons the Caesars, sent him letters full of piety, duty, and affection, so that, since they could not see him or speak with him in person because he was so far away, they might visit him through the intermediary of letters and converse with him in this way.”

Baronius also, under the year of Christ 336, the first year of Pope Mark and the thirty-first of the emperor Constantine, notes from Sozomen, book II, chapter 29, that Antony repeatedly wrote to the emperor Constantine on behalf of Athanasius.

—and his sons Constans and Constantius, learning of such things, frequently sent him letters as though to a father, begging him to gladden them with replies. But he remained as he had been before the letters came to him; he was not moved by the rulers’ salutations. As though he had not received the letters, he summoned the monks and said:

“The kings of this world have sent letters to us. What cause for astonishment is there here among Christians? Although their dignity is different, the condition of being born and dying is the same. These are the things that must be honored with every reverence; those are to be held with the whole affection of the soul: that God has written his law for human beings, and that through his Son he has enriched the churches with his own words. What have monks to do with letters from kings? Why should I accept letters to which I do not know how to return the customary courtesies of greeting?”

Therefore, when all the brothers begged him to refresh the Christian kings with a letter, lest they be angered by his silence, he replied suitably to the letters he had received. First he praised them for worshiping Christ; then he offered salutary counsel, warning them not to consider royal power a great thing, not to be puffed up by dominion over present flesh and thus forget that they were human beings and would be judged by Christ. Finally, he reminded them of clemency toward their subjects, justice, and care for the poor, and testified in his letters that Jesus Christ is the one eternal King of all ages.

When the rulers received these letters, they rejoiced exceedingly. Antony’s holy reputation also burned brightly among everyone, so that they desired to be called his sons. His great affability toward those who came to him had indeed turned everyone’s devotion toward him.

## CHAPTER LI

After the pagans had been refuted, the kings admonished, and the brothers strengthened by his consolation, he returned to the inner mountain

[Note: [Col. 0186D] “To the inner mountain.”] Above, chapter 47: “on the higher mountain.” The inner, or higher, mountain is opposed to the outer, or lower, mountain. See above, chapter 33.

and to his customary austerity. There, often walking and sitting with those who entered, he would become amazed, as it is written in Daniel 8; and at intervals of time he would give responses appropriate to what followed, so that it was understood that he had seen some secrets of revelation. While he was on the mountain, he foresaw what was happening far away in Egypt and recounted it to the bishop Serapion, who was stationed there.

[Note: [Col. 0186D] Bishop Serapion.] He was bishop of Thmuis, famous for his confession and his writings. The holy Jerome says of him in *Catalogue of Illustrious Church Writers*, chapter 99: “Serapion, bishop of Thmuis, who earned the surname ‘the Scholastic’ on account of the elegance of his intellect, a friend of the monk Antony, published an excellent book against the Manichaeans, another on the titles of the Psalms, and seventy letters useful for various purposes; under the emperor Constantius he was also illustrious as a confessor.”

A lamentable vision follows.

[Note: [Col. 0187A–C] “A lamentable vision follows.”] Baronius, volume III, in the year of Christ 339, the third of Pope Julius, and the third of the emperors Constantine, Constantius, and Constans, says: “This is the very year in which that holy Antony the Great, the Father of monks, raised by the divine Spirit, foresaw and foretold that dreadful vision of the immense devastation to be inflicted on the Church by the Arians—two years, that is, before it happened. Saint John Chrysostom also remembers this great vision shown to Antony when, at the beginning of his praise, he adorns the man with such words:

Ἐννοείτω τὴν μέχρι νῦν ἐν τοῖς ἁπάντων στόμασιν ὄντα, ὃν μετὰ τοὺς Ἀποστόλους ἡ Αἴγυπτος ἤνεγκε, τὸν μακάριον καὶ μέγαν Ἀντώνιον, καὶ λογιζέσθω ὅτι καὶ οὗτος ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ χώρᾳ γέγονεν, ἐν ᾗ καὶ Φαραώ. Ἀλλ᾽ ὅμως οὐδὲν παρεβλάβη, ἀλλὰ καὶ θείας ὄψεως κατηξιώθη, καὶ τοιοῦτον ἐπεδείξατο βίον, οἷον οἱ τοῦ Χριστοῦ νόμοι ζητοῦσι. Καὶ τοῦτο εἴσεταί τις μετὰ ἀκριβείας ἐντυχὼν τῷ βιβλίῳ τῷ τὴν ἱστορίαν ἔχοντι τῆς ἐκείνου ζωῆς, ἐν ᾧ καὶ πολλὴν ὄψεται τὴν προφητείαν. Καὶ γὰρ περὶ τῶν τὰ Ἀρείου νοσούντων προανεφώνησεν καὶ εἶπε τὴν ἐξ ἐκείνων μέλλουσαν βλάβην γίνεσθαι, τοῦ Θεοῦ δείξαντος αὐτῷ τότε, καὶ περὶ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν τὰ μέλλοντα ὑπογράψαντος ἅπαντα.

‘Let him consider the man whose name has until now been on everyone’s lips, the blessed and great Antony, whom Egypt produced after the Apostles; and let him reflect that he too was born in that land in which Pharaoh was born. Yet he suffered no harm from it. Rather, he was deemed worthy of a divine vision and displayed such a life as the laws of Christ require. Whoever reads with care the book that contains the history of his life will know this precisely; in it he will also see abundant prophecy. For he clearly foretold concerning those who were diseased with the sickness of Arius and declared the harm that would come from them, since God then showed it to him and painted before his eyes everything that was to happen’ (Chrysostom, *Homily 8 on Mark*, chapter 2).

“‘But again,’ Baronius adds, ‘with regard to that vision shown to the great saint Antony, it should also be noted that those are mistaken who suppose that it was shown to him before the heresy of Arius arose. It was not the emerging heresy but the future devastation to be inflicted by the Arians that was shown to him. This occurred long after the heresy of Arius had arisen, when he had already often warned his followers to beware of and avoid the Arians, had previously written to Constantine and his sons, and had withdrawn into the inner solitude of the mountain—all of which occurred long after the Arian heresy had arisen.’”

and worthy of being lamented with every source of tears. While he was working with the brothers seated around him, he fixed his eyes intently upon heaven, groaning and sighing. After some time had passed since the revelation began, he trembled with overwhelming sorrow; and immediately, falling upon his knees before the presence of God, he prayed that God in his mercy would avert the coming crime.

[Col. 0163A] Tears followed his prayer, great fear seized those present, and they begged him to explain the vision of so great a calamity. Sobs possessed his voice, his tongue was hindered by tears, and in the midst of his effort his speech was interrupted by groaning. At last, with mournful cries, he scarcely said:

“It would have been better, my little sons, to gain by a swift death the expiation that threatens.”

Beginning again in this way, he was overcome by tears; and amid painful sighs, finally lending his voice to his breast, he said:

“A great and unheard-of crime, unknown through all the ages, is impending. The Catholic faith will be overthrown by a great storm, and people resembling beasts will plunder the holy things of Christ. For I saw the Lord’s altar surrounded by a multitude of mules, which were scattering everything with repeated kicks.

[Note: [Col. 0187C–D] “The Lord’s altar surrounded by a multitude of mules.”] Sozomen, book VI, chapter 5: “It is said that before those of the Arian heresy seized control of the churches, during the reign of Constantius, Antony saw in a dream mules kicking the altar and overturning the holy table; and he immediately foretold that confusion would seize the Church through adulterated and mixed doctrines, and that an uprising of those holding beliefs foreign to the Church would occur. But that he had truly seen and spoken these things was demonstrated by what had happened before and what happened afterward.

“Tradition records that, before the Arians took possession of the government of the churches, while Constantius was reigning, Antony saw, in a dream, mules standing by and assaulting the sacred table with their hooves and overturning it. He immediately foretold that turmoil arising from adulterated and mixed doctrines, and a rebellion of those holding an opinion alien to the Catholic Church, would afterward take possession of the Church of God. Events both before and after this plainly showed that these things had truly been seen and foretold by him.”

These are the causes of the groans that you have heard.”

And a voice of the Lord came, saying: [Col. 0163B] “My altar will be despised.”

Nor was there delay before the vision was followed by its fulfillment. For two years later,

[Note: [Col. 0187D–188A] “For two years later.”] This was the year of Christ 342, the sixth year of Pope Julius and the sixth of the emperors Constantius and Constans, as Baronius dates it. In that year Gregory the Arian seized the Alexandrian see by military force, with the assistance of the prefect Philagrius. Athanasius describes the disasters then inflicted in his *Letter to the Orthodox*:  Ἡ μὲν ἐκκλησία καὶ τὸ ἅγιον βαπτιστήριον πυρπολεῖται, “The church and the holy baptistery are set on fire.” He adds many other details plainly corresponding to those described in this *Life*. Yet I do not know whether it is altogether certain that Baronius assigns this disaster and the Arian persecution foretold by Antony to the year 342. I shall perhaps discuss this more fully in the *Onomasticon*.

—the savage madness of the Arians broke in. Then the churches were plundered; then the sacred vessels were profaned; then, with the sacred ministry polluted by pagan hands, holy things were defiled; then the support of pagan craftsmen was assembled against Christ, and Christians were compelled to proceed to the church with palm branches in their hands—an emblem of idolatry at Alexandria—so that they might be considered members of the Arian faction.

[Note: [Col. 0188A–C] “With the taking up of palm branches—which is a notable feature of idolatry at Alexandria—they were compelled to proceed to the church, so that they might be considered members of the Arian faction.”] None of this appears in the Greek text, unless we assert that an error has entered the Greek and suppose that, instead of ὅτε καὶ τὰ σκεύη μετὰ βίας ἁρπάσαντες δι᾽ ἐθνικῶν ἐποίουν βαστάζεσθαι, “when they had also seized the vessels by force, they had them carried by pagans,” we should read, with a slight alteration and transposition: ὅτε καὶ τὰ σκεύη ἁρπάσαντες, μετὰ βαΐας δι᾽ ἐθνικῶν ἐποίουν βαστάζεσθαι, “when they had seized the vessels, they had them carried by pagans with palm branches.” Perhaps someone would prefer to leave μετὰ βίας in its proper place and, after ἁρπάσαντες, add μετὰ βαΐας, which one might suspect was omitted by the copyist because of the similarity to μετὰ βίας, which occurs so close before it. It would be better to say that this clause concerning the Christians is missing from the Greek. What is enclosed in parentheses—“which is a notable feature of idolatry at Alexandria”—is very probably a gloss by the translator Evagrius.

That the branches, or palms, were carried by pagans as they entered the temple is evident from Athanasius’s *Letter to Those Living the Solitary Life*: Ἕτερος δὲ μετὰ θάλλων εἰσελθών, καὶ ὡς Ἕλλην κινῶν αὐτὰ τῇ χειρὶ καὶ χλενάζων, εὐθὺς ἐσκοτώθη, καὶ οὐκ ἔβλεπεν.

“Another, entering with branches and moving them in his hand like a pagan in mockery, was immediately struck by darkness and could not see.”

But how were the Arians regarded as palm-bearers, when this is a sign of idolatry? Clearly because the Arians adapted themselves to pagan customs so that they might have the pagans as helpers against the Catholics. Athanasius says above: Τάτε γὰρ εἴδωλα ἑαυτῶν εὐφήμουν, καὶ ἔλεγον· Ἕλλην γέγονε Κωνστάντιος καὶ οἱ Ἀρειανοὶ τὰ ἡμῶν ἐπέγνωσαν.

“Thus they praised their own idols and said: ‘Constantius has become a pagan, and the Arians have acknowledged our gods.’”

Soon afterward, concerning the Arians inclined with the pagans to the sacrifice of a heifer, he says: Τοιαῦτα μὲν οὖν δι᾽ ἀσεβείας οἱ Ἀρειανοὶ, νομίζοντες εἰς ἡμῶν ὕβριν ταῦτα φθάνειν μετὰ τῶν Ἑλλήνων ἔπραττον.

“Such things, then, the irreligious Arians did together with the pagans, believing that they redounded to our disgrace.”

What a crime! The mind shudders to recount what was done: the modesty of virgins and married women was torn away; the blood of Christ’s sheep, shed in Christ’s temple, sprinkled the venerable altars; the baptistery was polluted at the will of the pagans. Nothing was lacking from the truth of the vision, as its fulfillment showed: the impiety of the Arians was the disorder of the many who kicked and trampled.

But he was comforted in this sorrow by the prosperity revealed in the subsequent revelation, and he said:

“Do not give yourselves wholly to grief, my little sons. For just as the Lord has been angry, so again he will have mercy, and his Church will soon recover its adornment. You will see those who preserve the Lord’s faith amid persecutions shining again with their customary splendor. The serpents will return to their holes, and religion will spread farther; only take care that the sincerity of your faith is not stained by the Arian blemish. This doctrine is not of the apostles but of demons and their father, the devil; for this reason their mind has been portrayed as resembling the stupidity of beasts and cattle.”

## CHAPTER LII

Thus far Antony. But we must not at all doubt that so great a miracle could have been foretold through a human being. For it is the promise of the Savior, who says: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will move, and nothing will be impossible for you” (Matthew 17). And again: “Amen, amen, I say to you, whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you. Ask, and you will receive” (John 16).

For he himself, promising his disciples and the entire flock of believers sometimes the subjection of demons and sometimes the healing of various illnesses, said: “You have received freely; give freely” (Matthew 10). Did Antony heal by the command of his own power? Did he consider what he had done to be within his own ability? Demons and diseases yielded to prayers, not commands,

[Note: [Col. 0188C–189A] “To prayers, not commands.”] He rightly teaches that Christ healed not by prayer but by command, or an order, whereas the saints did so by prayer and supplication. Christ did sometimes pray, but not for his own sake, rather for the sake of the people, as Basil of Seleucia teaches admirably in his sermon on the raising of Lazarus, on John 11: “But Jesus, having lifted his eyes upward.” The apostles sometimes used a command, as Peter did in Acts 9: “And turning toward the body, he said, ‘Tabitha, arise.’” But prayers had preceded: “Peter knelt down and prayed.” Or they performed miracles after invoking the name of Jesus, as Basil says in the same place.

Briefly, Arnobius, in book I, says that Christ did all the things he did through the power of his name. He later says: “He accomplished them by his own power”; but he permitted others to do the same through the power of his name, with devotion.

Basil, in his sermon on Elisha and the Shunammite woman, says that Elisha “did not raise the Shunammite’s son to life through prayer, as Peter raised Dorcas, but stretched himself upon the child’s dead body and applied himself to it.”

“Understand that Elisha bore the figure of Christ, who had no need of prayer, even though Elisha employed it, as is clear from 2 Kings 4:33. Basil nevertheless intends that the child was not restored to life by the power of that prayer, but rather by the bodily contact itself, which was a figure of Christ’s incarnation. See Saint Augustine, on Psalm 70, and Bernard, sermon 2 on the *Song of Songs*. Therefore there is no need to resort to an ellipsis and, as though the expression were incomplete, supply μὴ μόνον διὰ προσευχῆς, ‘not only through prayer.’ Basil was not unaware that Elisha used prayer; rather, he denies that the child was restored to life by the power of prayer—as the saints generally performed miracles—but rather through the bodily contact, because by his incarnation Christ was to raise the human race.”

[Col. 0164A] and everything was always accomplished at the naming of Christ, our God. Let no wise person ascribe the wonder of healing to Antony, but to the Lord Jesus, who, displaying his customary benevolence toward his creatures, now also exercised it mercifully through his chosen servant. Antony merely prayed, and because of the merits of his life the Lord granted everything.

## CHAPTER LIII

Often, and against his will, the brothers led him to the outer mountain.

[Note: [Col. 0189A] “To the outer mountain.”] Above, chapter 33: “on the outer mountain”; it is opposed to the inner mountain. See what was said there.

When judges who could not go to the inner *archisterium* because of the harshness of the route, the multitude of those following them, and the rugged solitude had reached the outer place and sought to enjoy Antony’s presence, they could not obtain this, since he endured the disturbance of such journeys with the greatest reluctance. Therefore they sent to him in chains those whom either criminal conduct or public authority had bound, knowing that Antony could not disregard such people.

[Note: [Col. 0189A] “The inner archisterium.”] This means Antony’s inner and principal place, where he himself lived. Just as there was an outer and an inner mountain on which Antony had established his dwelling, as we have already seen, so he also had an outer and an inner *archisterium*. For the meaning of *archisterium*, see the *Onomasticon*.

Overcome by the prisoners’ tears, he was drawn to the outer mountain, recognizing that his labor would be useful to the unfortunate. He urged the judges who had invited him to place the fear of God before hatred and favor when pronouncing judgment. Nor should they be ignorant of what is written: “By whatever judgment you judge, you will be judged” (Matthew 7). Yet amid his conversations he remembered the solitude that was dear to him.

After this compelled presence—which the duke’s requests and, more truly, the tears of the unfortunate had extorted—after his salutary admonitions and his commendation of the accused, and even the acquittal of some, the duke asked him to grant his presence a little more generously. Antony said that he could not remain there any longer, using the familiar example that, just as fish removed from water soon die on dry land (Pelagius, book II, no. 5), so monks who linger with secular people are immediately dissolved in human conversation.

“Therefore,” he said, “just as fish should hasten to the sea, so we should hasten to the mountain, lest, by delaying, we suffer some forgetfulness of our purpose.”

[Note: [Col. 0189A–B] “Lest we suffer some forgetfulness of our purpose.”] Greek: μὴ ἐπιλαθώμεθα τῶν ἔνδον, “lest we forget those who are within.” The word *propositum* is frequently used for steadfastness in the proper institution and vow of life. Above, chapter 28: “Antony rejoices in fervent purpose.” But below, chapter 66: “Lethargy must not creep into the discipline.” The *Acts of Pope Clement the Martyr*, concerning Saint Theodora: “He had persuaded her to profess to God the purpose of chastity.” Jerome, *Letter* 7, to Laeta: “desiring to overcome both the virgin’s purpose and the mother’s desire.” Here *propositum* plainly means a vow, as is evident from the punishment.

The duke, amazed at such wisdom in the man, formed a just and true judgment concerning him and said: “He is truly a servant of God, and such wisdom could never have existed in a peasant unless he were guided by divine love.”

## CHAPTER LIV

Moreover, when Balacius [Note: “Moreover, when Balacius.”]—you have the same story about Balacius briefly recounted in Athanasius’s letter *To Those Leading the Solitary Life*: “When Antony once wrote, he caused the duke Balacius to spit upon the letter and throw it away. But divine justice did not overlook this. For not long afterward, as the so-called duke was sitting on a horse and departing for the first station, the horse turned back, bit him in the thigh, threw him down, and he died three days later.” “Once he handed Antony’s letter to Duke Balacius—who was Gregory the Arian, invader of the Alexandrian Church—to be spat upon and thrown away. But divine vengeance did not leave this unpunished. For not long afterward, as Balacius was traveling to the first station, the horse he was riding turned its neck, bit him in the thigh, threw him from its back, and dashed him to the ground, so that he died within the following three days.” Here you see some difference in the account. In this letter Balacius is said to have been injured by the horse he was riding; in this *Life* of Antony, by the horse on which Nestorius was riding. Perhaps, says Baronius (in the year of Christ 342), this occurred through the fault of copyists. Others, however, might perhaps argue that the letter was not Athanasius’s, since Athanasius himself is repeatedly cited and speaks in it; Baronius nevertheless thinks that this does not prevent the letter from being Athanasius’s.], who under the prefect Nestorius was governor of Egypt at Alexandria, [Col. 0164D] a most zealous supporter of Arian wickedness, persecuted the Church of Christ so fiercely that, in his mad fury, he publicly stripped and beat virgins and monks. Antony sent him a letter, whose substance was this:

“I see the wrath of God coming upon you. Cease persecuting Christians, lest the wrath seize you which now threatens you with imminent destruction.”

The wretched man read the letter, mocked it, spat upon it, and threw it on the ground. He also inflicted many insults upon the bearers and ordered them to report this reply to Antony:

“Since you take such great care of the monks, the discipline of my authority shall also pass over to you.”

But punishment immediately overwhelmed the threatening man, and five days later divine vengeance silenced his unbridled mouth. For he went out to the first station from Alexandria, called Chaereum [Note: “To the first station from Alexandria, which is called Chaereum.”] Gregory of Nazianzus speaks of Chaereum in *Oration* 21, in praise of Athanasius:

“Was it perhaps the poet’s task also to speak of the Nile, truly gold-flowing and rich in grain, which, reversing its course, flows from the city toward Chaereum, a day’s journey, I think, and farther still.”

For “station” the Greek is μονή (*monē*). So also in Athanasius’s *Letter to Those Leading the Solitary Life*; Hoeschel conjectured νόμην (*nomēn*), “prefecture,” though there is no need for it. See the *Onomasticon.], with the aforesaid prefect of Egypt, Nestorius. They rode horses, among which Balacius’s horse was the gentlest of all those he had raised. While the horses were playing together in their customary manner, the gentler one, the horse on which Nestorius was riding, suddenly bit Balacius, threw him to the ground, and, bending over him, tore and gnawed his thighs so violently that, after he had been carried back to the city, he died on the third day. Thus all recognized that the effect of Antony’s predicted threats had swiftly followed, and that the persecutor had met a fitting end.

## CHAPTER LV

Antony admonished the others who came to him with remarkable gentleness, urging them, after forgetting the dignity of the world, to seek the blessedness of a more secluded life. If any were oppressed by greater powers and unable to obtain justice, he defended them so earnestly that he himself seemed to suffer the injury on their behalf.

The speech of the illustrious old man benefited many. Many, abandoning great wealth and a higher military rank, desired to cling to his way of life. And, to encompass an infinite subject in brief speech, Christ had granted Egypt a good physician.

Who did not change sorrow into joy in Antony’s presence? Who did not turn anger into peace? Who did not moderate the grief of bereavement at the sight of him? Who, casting off the sorrow of poverty by which he was oppressed, did not immediately despise the riches of the wealthy and rejoice in his own poverty? What monk, after weariness, was not invigorated by his encouragement? What young man, inflamed by passions, did not become a lover of chastity at his admonition? Who, tormented by the devil, returned without healing? [Col. 0165C] Who, distracted by the enemy’s thoughts, did not return with a serene mind after the blind storm had been calmed?

For he knew what trouble afflicted each person, and, recognizing the discernment of spirits from the merits of their lives, he applied healing to their illnesses according to the wounds they bore. Consequently, after his teaching, all the devil’s snares were exposed.

Many betrothed girls also [Note: “Many betrothed girls.”]—what once happened to Thecla, when she heard Saint Paul preaching, so that she abandoned her earthly bridegroom and dedicated herself to her heavenly Bridegroom, happened likewise to very many virgins at Antony’s exhortations. Above, chapter 49: “Continence in marriage, virginity in the Church.” Virginity afterward flourished so greatly in the Church that one family, the Anician family, gave more virgins to Christ than consuls to the world. Augustine, *Letter* 179, to Proba and Julianus, on the conversion of Demetrias, their granddaughter:

“Who could explain in words, who could celebrate with worthy praise, how incomparably glorious and fruitful Christ has, from your blood, women who are virgins, while the world has men who are consuls? If the passing of time considers it a great and distinguished thing to mark a name by rank, how much greater and more distinguished is it to surpass others in integrity of heart and body? Let the noble girl therefore rejoice more in being noble by birth and nobler by holiness, since through divine fellowship she will attain exceptional exaltation in heaven, than if through human marriage she were to produce illustrious offspring. For the Anician posterity more generously chose to bless so illustrious a family by refusing marriage than to multiply it by childbearing; to imitate the life of angels already in the flesh than still to increase the number of mortals from the flesh. This is the richer and more fruitful happiness: not to grow heavy in the womb, but to grow great in the mind; not to fill the breast with milk, but to bring forth understanding in the heart; not to give birth to earth through the entrails, but to give birth to heaven through prayers.”], leaving their bridegrooms and almost withdrawing from the bridal chamber itself, settled in the bosom of the mother Church.

What more need be said? People from the whole world flocked to him, and the variety of all nations longed to behold the man most warlike against demons. No one complained that he had come there in vain; for all found the exchange for their labor delightful and welcome. The weariness of the journey brought back the profit of the pilgrimage, as the outcome itself proved. For after his passing, as though all had suffered a common bereavement, each mourned him as a personal father.

## CHAPTER LVI

It is fitting that I should also recount what the end of his life was, and that you should hear it eagerly, because this too was something in him worthy of imitation by all. According to his custom, he came to visit the brothers who were on the outer mountain. There, learning through divine providence of his death, he began as follows:

“Listen, my little sons, to your father’s final counsel, for I do not think that we shall see one another again in this world. The condition of nature compels me to depart now that I have passed the age of one hundred by five years.” [Note: “Whom I exceed by five years.”] Greek: Εἰμὶ γὰρ ἐγγὺς ἐτῶν πέντε καὶ ἑκατόν, “For I am nearly one hundred and five years old.” In former times hermits and monks often prolonged their lives for many years; so the heretics foolishly rave against a severe manner of living, as though it diminished longevity.]

Having spoken thus, he saddened the hearts of his hearers. Sighs and tears followed his mournful words. They all embraced him as though he were already about to depart from the world.

But he, as one leaving behind what was alien and departing for his true homeland, urged them with great joy that negligence must not creep into their way of life. Rather, as he had previously taught, they should guard their souls from sordid thoughts as though they were dying every day, direct all rivalry even toward the saints, and not approach schismatics at all.

“You know,” he said, “their ancient perversity. Do not join yourselves in communion with the Arians, for their impiety is already manifest to everyone. Add this also: no Christian should, when he sees the powers of the world fighting on behalf of the Arians and Meletians [Note: “Of the Meletians.” The Meletians were so called from Meletius, a bishop in Egypt. See Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 68; Theodoret, book IV of the *Heretical Compendium*, chapter 10; the *Tripartite History*, book I, chapter 18.], be frightened away from the truth of Christ by their wickedness. That is a defense belonging to mortals, and a deceptive appearance cannot endure for long.

“Therefore the faithful belief in Christ and the religious tradition of the fathers must be guarded” [Note: “The faithful belief in Christ and the religious tradition of the Fathers must be guarded.”] Baronius, volume III, year of Christ 358, seventh year of Pope Liberius and twenty-second of the emperor Constantius:

“Antony, being about to die, had nothing more at heart than to leave his followers a distinguished testimony to the Catholic faith; and he had often previously admonished them to guard that faith. By this commendation, as though entrusting a noble deposit, he commended the faith to his disciples standing around him. But, in addition to faith in Christ, he also urged them to guard the religious tradition of the Fathers.”], “which you have learned from reading the Scriptures and from my frequent, though humble, admonitions.”

## CHAPTER LXVII

When he had finished speaking, the brothers tried with all their strength to detain him, wishing to be adorned by their Father’s glorious end. But for many reasons, which he also indicated by his silence, and especially because of the prevailing Egyptian custom, he opposed them.

For it is the custom of the Egyptians to wrap the bodies of noble persons, especially of blessed martyrs, in linen [Note: “And especially the bodies of blessed martyrs.”] Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* 10, which concerns the dead:

“It is customary to spread before them linen cloths shining with bright whiteness.”

This is also found frequently in the *Acts of the Martyrs*. See the *Onomasticon.], and not to withhold the customary care given to a funeral; but they do not hide them in the earth. Instead, they preserve them after placing them on couches in the home [Note: “To preserve them after placing them on couches in the home.” It was an ancient custom of the pagan Egyptians to keep embalmed corpses in their homes. Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I: “The Egyptians embalm their dead and keep them at home.” Pomponius Mela, book I, chapter 9: “They consider it unlawful either to burn or to bury the dead; instead, after treating them by an art, they place them within their inner chambers.” Sextus Empiricus, book III of the *Pyrrhonian Hypotheses*, chapter 24: “The Egyptians, after removing the intestines, embalm the dead and keep them with themselves above the earth.” They also used their dead as though they were dinner guests. Lucian, *On Mourning*: “The Egyptian embalms; and this man—I speak of something I myself saw—after drying the corpse, made it his fellow-diner and fellow-drinker.” “The Egyptian embalms it.” [Col. 0190D] “And this man, I say, having dried the corpse, used it as a fellow-diner and fellow-drinker.” Silius Italicus, book XIII:

“Egyptian land  
after the funeral encloses the standing bodies  
in fragrant stone,  
and does not separate the bloodless shade from the tables.”

If someone is perplexed about what “fragrant stone” means here, and reads *odorato succo*, “fragrant juice,” Corippus, book III, *On the Funeral of Justinian*:

“and balsams with fragrant juice,  
preserving the sacred body for eternity.”

But I do not rashly disturb Silius’s reading. I therefore understand “fragrant stone” as the ointment itself in which the body is, as it were, enclosed, and which becomes stony and petrified together with the body, making it resemble bronze. The Egyptians call these *gabbaras*, as Saint Augustine, who will be cited shortly, says in *Sermon* 120 *On Various Subjects*, chapter 12. Hence Orientius correctly writes in the *Commonitorium*, “the dust that solidifies”:

“Not only the stones that preserve what has been well embalmed in tombs,  
or the solidifying dust and fragrance of the Arabs hold it.”

Thus our Sirmondus also correctly reads *Arabum* rather than *arvum* in Sidonius, book IX, letter 13. Daniel Heinsius, in his *Silian Cradle-Songs*, suspected that instead of *odorato saxo* one should read *odorata taxo*, that is, “a repository made from fragrant yew,” and, in Herodotus’s words, “a θηκαῖον οἴκημα, a chamber serving as a repository.” Claudius Dausqueius, in his notes on Silius, thinks that “fragrant stone” is so called either because it is such, or because the corpse is stuffed with fragrances.

It is worth noting what Cassian reports in *Conference* XV, chapter 3, from the account of Abbot Nesteros. He gives this origin and reason for why the Egyptians embalmed corpses and placed them in elevated chambers:

“This custom was introduced among the Egyptians by the overflowing of the Nile, because the whole extent of that land, like an immense sea, is covered for a considerable part of the year by the accustomed eruption of the waters, so that at that time no one has any opportunity to travel except by crossing the waters. Therefore the bodies of the dead, preserved with fragrant spices, are stored in higher chambers.”]

This honor paid to the dead was handed down by the vanity of an ancient custom. Antony often begged the bishops to correct the people through ecclesiastical admonition; and he himself rebuked laymen and women more sternly, saying that this was neither lawful nor pleasing to God, since the tombs of the patriarchs and prophets, which have endured down to our own time, proved the contrary.

He also commanded them to contemplate the example of the Lord’s body, which, after being placed in a tomb, was enclosed by a stone until the third day of the resurrection (John XVI; Matthew XXVII).

By these arguments he exposed the Egyptian abuse regarding the dead [Note: “The abuse regarding the dead among the Egyptians.” Damascenus explained the mind of Saints Antony and Athanasius on this passage long ago in *Oration* I, *On Images*:

“We know that blessed Athanasius forbade placing the relics of the saints in coffers, and rather commanded that they be covered beneath the earth, wishing to abolish the absurd custom of the Egyptians, who did not hide their dead beneath the earth but placed them on beds and couches.”

Thus Arsenius, according to Rufinus, book II, no. 163, addressing his disciples under threat of divine judgment, says: “If you give anyone anything from my little body as though it were a relic.” In Pelagius, *Booklet* XV, no. 9, the passage is: “If you allow anyone to do anything with my body.” I shall add the explanation of more recent scholars. Baronius, year of Christ 358, fifteenth year of Pope Liberius and twenty-second of the emperor Constantius:

“For this reason also Antony—so that no equal honor might be bestowed upon him among the saints on earth—detested that ancient Egyptian custom, which had spread to Christians, whereby the bodies of loved ones were not at all committed to burial but, smeared with the substances applied by embalmers, were dried so that they might remain intact without corruption. Once thus treated, they were called by the Egyptians, according to Augustine, *gabbaras*, as though made of bronze. Antony disliked this so greatly that he said this service should not even be performed for the bodies of saints, since, following the example of Christ’s body, the bodies of the saints ought to be placed in a tomb. The Catholic Church has been accustomed to do this, enclosing the bodies of the blessed in tombs, though in the most honorable tombs, namely, sacred altars.” Thus far Baronius.

David Hoeschel, in his notes on this *Life*:

“It is strange,” says this man of great renown and exceptionally learned judgment, “if Antony taught categorically that burial was altogether necessary, when Joseph, in Genesis 50, certainly ordered that he should not be buried in the earth but placed in a coffin, and eventually carried away from Egypt. It is therefore more likely that Antony wished only that the dead should be committed to the earth, which is far more proper, rather than—as the Egyptians did—kept embalmed at home; and that he confirmed this by the example of the patriarchs and of Christ.”

Many writers describe the Egyptian method of embalming: Herodotus, book II, and Diodorus, book I. From them one observes that formerly corpses were kept upright at home, set in a coffin against the wall, whereas in Antony’s time the practice had changed. Athanasius explicitly says that they were accustomed to place them on a couch. I believe this was so that they might more conveniently sit at table. To such absurdities had Egypt descended. Lucian, in *On Mourning*, says that he himself had attended banquets of this kind with the dead as fellow guests and drinking companions, but does not explain whether they were standing or reclining. Silius, somewhat earlier, has them standing:

“Egyptian land  
after the funeral encloses the standing bodies  
in fragrant stone.”

Other examples could be added, but these sufficiently prove that Antony ought not to have tolerated such folly, or rather superstition.

From Saint Augustine, *Sermon* 120 *On Various Subjects*, the earlier treatise *On the Resurrection of the Dead*, chapter 12, we learn the name given to corpses treated in this way:

“Only the Egyptians, then, believe in resurrection, because they carefully preserve the bodies of the dead. For they have the custom of drying the bodies and making them, as it were, bronze; they call them *gabbaras*.”

Immediately afterward, mocking this, he writes:

“Only the Egyptians believe well in the resurrection of their dead; the hope of the other Christians is confined.”

These words show that among Christians also, despite the prohibition, the custom continued even after Antony.

Thus far the great man, “famous by name and most acute in understanding.” [Col. 0192B] And thus far also, from the mouth and pen of the great Hoeschel, whom I have no doubt was Marcus Velser, a man of the second rank among the Augustan Fathers. That man reveals himself everywhere by the rays of his learning. Therefore Antony does not disapprove of the preservation and veneration of relics, but of the Egyptian custom discussed above from Cicero, Mela, Sextus Empiricus, and other authorities. See our Gretzer, *On Christian Funerals*, book I, chapter 7, and *Apology II against Lithus Misenus*, book II, chapter 2.], even when the bodies were holy, saying:

“What greater or holier body can there be than the Lord’s body, which we know was buried in the earth according to the custom of other peoples?”

This sound conviction uprooted the deeply implanted error of many. They placed the corpses in the earth and gave thanks to the Lord for the good instruction. Fearing, therefore, that the aforesaid custom might lead them into the same error concerning him, he quickly took leave of the monks who had gathered and returned to the dwelling of his virtuous friend.

## CHAPTER LVIII

A few months later, when a considerable illness had troubled his aged limbs, he summoned two brothers [Note: “Two brothers.” I think he means Amathas and Macarius, disciples of Antony; one of them also buried Antony. They are discussed in the prologue to the *Life of Saint Paul, the First Hermit*. Unless perhaps Isaac and Pelusianus are intended, who are mentioned in the *Life of Hilarion*, chapter 25, and whom Hilarion found on the mountain immediately after Antony’s death: “There he found two brothers, Isaac and Pelusianus, of whom Isaac had been Antony’s interpreter.”], whom he had instructed there fifteen years earlier, at a short distance from one another, and who had already begun to minister to him in his old age. He said:

“I, my little sons, am following the path of the fathers, according to the sayings of Scripture (Joshua XXIII; 3 Kings II); for the Lord is now inviting me, and I long to see the heavenly things. But you, my inmost hearts, I warn not to lose suddenly the labor of so long a time. Consider that today you have taken up your religious pursuit, and as though the strength of your resolve were only beginning to grow, press on. You know the various snares of the demons; you have seen both their savage assaults and their weakened powers.

“Sigh for Jesus, fix faith in his name firmly in your minds, and all the demons will flee from steadfast faith. Remember my admonitions and the uncertainty of our condition. Consider daily that life is precarious, and the heavenly reward will be granted to you without delay.

“Avoid also the poisons of schismatics and heretics, and imitate my hatred of them, because they are enemies of Christ. You know that I never had even a peaceful conversation with them, because of their perverse will and their obstinate warfare against Christ.

“Be especially concerned that you observe the Lord’s commandments, so that after your death the saints may receive you into the eternal dwellings as friends and acquaintances (Luke XVI). Think on these things, understand these things, recall these things. And if you have any care for me, if you retain any memory of your father, if you offer me a corresponding affection [Note: “If you offer a corresponding affection.” The printed books read *rependatis*, which is an interpolation. The sound and genuine reading is *repraestatis*, an uncommon word. In the Florentine Pandects, book XIX, title 1, *On actions, buying and selling*, law 47, *Lucius*, we read: “So that if he has not restored the materials intact.” The common text has: “So that if he has not furnished them intact.” Likewise, book XXXV, title 1, *On the senatus consultum Trebellianum*, law 22, *Mulier*: “He reports that the divine Marcus decreed that the trust should be restored to them.” In both passages Cujacius, book III of the *Observations*, chapter 15, corrected the reading to *repraesentaverit*. But in book XIII of the *Observations*, chapter 35, he withdrew his correction and retained *repraestat*.], let no one bring my relics to Egypt, lest my body be preserved with empty honor, and lest the practices which, as you know, I have condemned be observed even in my case.

“For this reason above all I have returned here. Therefore cover me with earth yourselves; you yourselves bury your father’s little body. Keep this command of your old man as well: let no one except those whom you love know the place of my tomb. I trust in the Lord that at the necessary time of resurrection this little body will rise incorrupt.”

“As for my garments, let this be their division” [Note: “As for my garments, let this be their division.” Baronius, volume III, year of Christ 358, seventh year of Pope Liberius and twenty-second of the emperor Constantius, says:

“But he who so earnestly commended the Catholic faith also wished to honor its most glorious defenders and confessors with his own garments, when he added such a codicil to his testament of faith.”]:

“Give the melote and the worn cloak on which I lie to Bishop Athanasius, who himself brought me the new one” [Note: “Which he himself brought new.” Baronius, year of Christ 328, fifteenth year of Pope Sylvester and thirty-third of the emperor Constantine, thinks that Athanasius, when he was in the third year of his episcopate, visited the churches of Egypt subject to the Alexandrian Church. He further asserts that at that time he also visited Antony and brought him two cloaks as a blessing. With one of them, as Saint Jerome relates (*Jerome, in the *Life of Paul*), he wrapped the body of Paul, the first hermit, when Paul had departed this life and Antony, at Paul’s request, had hastily brought the garment. The other Antony, dying, finally bequeathed to Athanasius, who had given it to him, with these words: “Give the melote and the worn cloak on which I lie to Bishop Athanasius, who himself brought me the new one.” Since he says that Athanasius brought it to him, rather than sent it, he clearly indicates that Saint Athanasius visited Antony, and not only him but also his monastic disciples, and in his episcopal office visited the churches and monasteries located in the desert.], while Bishop Serapion [Note: “Bishop Serapion.” Namely, of Thmuis in Egypt, as was already said at chapter 51.] is to receive another melote. You yourselves keep the garment of sackcloth. Farewell, my inmost hearts. Antony is departing and will no longer be with you in this present world.”

## CHAPTER LIX

He had finished speaking, and while his disciples kissed him, he stretched out his feet a little and looked joyfully upon death [Note: “He looked joyfully upon death.” Baronius, volume III, year of Christ 358, seventh year of Pope Liberius and twenty-second of the emperor Constantius:

“In this same year,” he says, “that holy man, Antony the Great, renowned throughout the world, migrated from this life to heaven on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February, having lived one hundred and five years. Athanasius and Jerome both affirm this in the *Chronicle*.”

But I have shown in the preliminary remarks to this *Life* that Baronius used an uncorrected *Chronicle*. The corrected *Chronicle* places Antony’s death in the nineteenth year of Constantius, to which different years of Christ are assigned according to different reckonings. See the preliminary remarks just mentioned.], so that his cheerful expression revealed the presence of the holy angels who had descended to carry away his soul.

Looking at them as though he saw friends, he breathed out his soul and was gathered to the fathers according to the order of Scripture. His disciples kept his commands [Note: “His disciples kept his commands.” Baronius, above:

“Antony was buried in an unknown place, for the reason that he himself had commanded this, as Saint Jerome testifies in the *Life of Hilarion* (*Jerome, *Life of Hilarion*, chapter 26*): namely, lest a certain Pergamius, his most devoted admirer and the wealthiest man in those regions, remove the saint’s body to his own estate and construct a shrine. For Antony did not consider himself worthy of receiving equal honor with the saints on earth. Yet, however strongly he urged his disciples that his body should be committed to a hidden tomb, he did not wish to prevent it from sharing in the honor customarily bestowed upon the saints and beloved of God: namely, that the anniversary of his departure should, according to the ancient custom of the Church, be celebrated with a vigil and the other sacred rites. For Jerome writes of Saint Hilarion that, although far away, when he learned of Antony’s death he came there with great labor, specifically so that he might celebrate the anniversary of Antony’s falling asleep at the very place where he had died, preceded by nocturnal vigils. This pious duty has not been neglected to this day by the other Catholics in Egypt or by the universal Catholic Church.” See chapter 26 of the *Life of Saint Hilarion*.], wrapping his body and covering it with earth, as he had commanded. No one to this day, except them, knows where it was buried.

The heir of blessed Antony, who had been deemed worthy by his command to receive the worn cloak together with the melote, embraces Antony in Antony’s gifts; and, as though enriched by a great inheritance, he joyfully remembers through the garment the image of holiness [Note: “He joyfully remembers through the garment the image of holiness.” In the *Life of Saint Paul, the First Hermit*, you find how pleasing Paul’s palm-leaf garment was to Antony—more precious than every Roman *palmata*, or embroidered garment. Now Athanasius, Antony’s heir, embraces Antony in Antony’s cast-off garments.].

## CHAPTER LX

This, then, was the end of Antony’s life and the beginning of his merits. Although I have narrated it, as I said, in relatively restrained language, you can nevertheless perceive from it how the man of God advanced from childhood to old age, and how, having always trampled underfoot every doubt, he never yielded either to weakness or to advanced age.

Rather, preserving the constancy of his resolve [Note: “Preserving the constancy of his resolve.” Everything that follows concerning the integrity of Saint Antony’s body is taken from this writing of Athanasius and is found above in the encomia of blessed Ephraem. Vossius, its translator, seems to have encountered a corrupt manuscript when he translated “or if by chance he touched his feet with water” instead of “nor did he wash his feet.” Ephraem also omits the statement that he preserved the number of his teeth to the very end.], he neither changed his garment nor washed his feet nor pursued more delicate food. He also preserved, for the sake of his merits, the sharpness of his eyes and the number of his teeth, although they seemed slightly worn by age, as well as his manner of walking and the strength of his entire body. Thus, compared with bodies pampered by baths and luxuries, his flesh appeared the more vigorous.

## CHAPTER LXI

This too, brothers: that his love and fame flew through every province, though neither the polished eloquence of widely disseminated books [Note: “Whom neither the polished eloquence of books disseminated abroad.” Peter Damian, book VI, letter 17, to the monk Ariprandus:

“Antony does not practice rhetoric, but, conspicuous throughout the world, is read, so to speak, in letters of life.”

See his excellent treatment of the foolishly learned and the wisely unlearned. Baronius, volume III, year of Christ 358, seventh year of Pope Liberius and twenty-second of the emperor Constantius, says:

“Although Saint Athanasius relates that Antony was by no means distinguished by the memory of written books, it is nevertheless certain that, through divine grace, he wrote many letters in his native language; Saint Jerome testifies that seven of them were translated into Greek (*Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 88*).
