See the preliminary remarks to this *Life*.], nor discourse in worldly wisdom, nor nobility of birth, nor an infinite accumulation of wealth commended him, must be ascribed by every mouth to Christ alone, whose gift it is.

Foreseeing the devotion of his mind toward his own majesty, Christ made known to Africa, Spain, Gaul, Italy, Illyricum, and even to Rome herself, the capital of cities, a man hidden in a region almost of another world and set amid such vast solitudes, as he had promised at the beginning [Note: “Rome, which is the capital of cities.” See Lipsius’s excellent little books *On Roman Grandeur*. These remarks about the *Life of Saint Antony* are sufficient for now. Jerome, in the *Life of Hilarion*, chapter 27, also records that even the elements mourned Antony’s death: “It was already three years that a closed heaven had dried out those lands, so that people commonly said that even the elements were mourning Antony’s death.” In the Cologne edition, after the *Life of Antony*, an account was added of Saint Antony’s invincible chastity, excerpted from a German book. Since I found it in no manuscript, and since it seemed more like a fable, I decided to omit it. The epilogue here under the name of Evagrius the translator was supplied by one manuscript, although I fear that it can scarcely preserve the name of Evagrius, especially when compared with the prologue.].

This is the Creator’s kindness: he habitually ennobles his servants, even against their will, so that the examples of the saints may teach that virtue is possible and is not outside human nature, and so that the best of people may be driven, by the fruit of their labor, to imitate the blessed life.

## CHAPTER LXII

Therefore, brothers, take great care to read this book, so that, having recognized the faithful life of eminent Christians and monks, you may know that our Savior Jesus Christ glorifies those who glorify him; and that to those who serve him and desire to remain hidden even here in the mountain solitudes, he grants not only the kingdoms of heaven but also renown, so that they themselves may enjoy the praise of their merits and others may be stirred by their examples.

If necessary, read it also to the Gentiles, so that at least in this way they may recognize that our Lord Jesus Christ is not only God, the Son of God, but has also given those who diligently worship him and faithfully believe in him the power to trample upon and expel the demons whom they think to be gods—those deceivers of human beings and architects of every corruption.

## EPILOGUE OF EVAGRIUS THE TRANSLATOR

Accordingly, we beg the prudent who wish to read this writing to grant pardon if we have been unable to express the force of the Greek language while transferring it into Latin, although we undertook this contrary to our intention. We did not refuse to do it out of envy, but, knowing sufficiently how great a weakness a Greek expression suffers when translated into Latin, we nevertheless preferred that the Greek expression suffer this rather than that those able to read the Greek discourse, however it may be translated, should suffer the loss of divine profit.

May almighty God, who cooperated with so great a man in accomplishing such things, also cooperate with us in imitating him, even in part, so that his name may be glorified in all things through our teacher, encourager, redeemer, and Savior, Jesus the Lord, with the Holy Spirit, to whom belong glory and everlasting power forever and ever.

## OCTOBER 21. THE LIFE OF SAINT HILARION, MONK, BY THE HOLY PRESBYTER JEROME

(The text of this *Life* may be read in *Patrologia Latina*, volume XXIII, column 29. We therefore refer the reader there and reprint here only Rosweyde’s annotations.) [Note: [Col. 0193D]

### 86. Hilarion

The Roman Martyrology, October 21:

“On Cyprus, the birthday of Saint Hilarion, abbot, whose life, full of virtues and miracles, Saint Jerome wrote.”

The Greek Menologion on the same day:

“The commemoration of our holy Father Hilarion.”

More extensively in the *Menaea* on the same day. There he is called Μέγας, “Great,” apparently to distinguish him from others. For on May 4 there is Hilarion the Wonderworker; on March 28, Hilarion the Younger, abbot of the monastery of Pelecete; and on June 6, Hilarion the Younger, abbot of the Dalmatians.

Of this Hilarion Jerome writes in *Letter* 13, to Paulinus:

“Blessed Hilarion, although he was a Palestinian and lived in Palestine, saw Jerusalem only once, so that he might seem neither to despise the holy places because of their proximity nor, on the other hand, to divide the Lord according to place.”

Sozomen also writes in book V of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 14, that his grandfather Alaphion was freed from a demon by Hilarion after Hilarion invoked the name of Christ. Jerome does not mention either matter here in the *Life*.

Of this same Hilarion, Sozomen speaks in book III, chapter 13, and book V, chapter 9; Nicephorus in book IX, chapter 15, book X, chapter 8, and book XI, chapter 29. Peter Damian mentions him briefly in book VI, letter 17:

“Hilarion casts Plato and Pythagoras aside and, content with the Gospel alone, shuts himself in a sepulchral cave. But behold: he commands demons, although the studies of philosophers do not adorn him.”

This Life of Hilarion was translated from Jerome’s Latin text into Greek by Sophronius, as Jerome himself testifies in chapter 134 of his catalogue of illustrious Church writers. Among the Lives published under the name of Metaphrastes by Lipomanus there is a Life of Hilarion translated from the Greek by Gentianus Hervetus [Col. 0195A]. But it does not bear the name of Sophronius. I received it in Greek at Paris through the kindness of our Sirmond, where no author or translator is identified. Nevertheless, I think it is the work which Sophronius translated from Jerome’s text. For it proceeds in the same order, although it occasionally varies in certain details and even adds some material.

**Nonna [See Patrol. vol. XXIII, col. 29, note b. EDIT.].**] The older editions and some manuscripts place this address or greeting before “I shall write.” On Nonna, see the *Onomasticon*.

**Asella.**] The blessed Jerome has a letter to Asella, volume II, letter 99. On her praises, see the same author, volume I, letter 15, to Marcella. He also mentions her in volume III, letter 114, to Principia.

**For those who performed the deeds, etc.**] There is here a remarkable difference both among editors and among manuscripts. Some have: “For his way of life and abstinence, and the distinguished gifts of miracles which he performed (as Crispus says), are considered so great and so extraordinary as the distinguished talents of anyone could exalt them by means of the few words [Col. 0195B] available.” Others have the version I have printed. Crispus says in his *Catiline*: “The courage of those who performed these deeds is considered as great as the distinguished talents of their writers were able to exalt it in words.” Flavius Vopiscus also imitates him in his *Probus*: “It is certain that Sallustius Crispus, and Marcus Cato and Gellius, have recorded in historical form the principle that all the virtues of all men are as great as the talents of those who describe each man’s deeds have wished them to appear.”

**Alexander the Great.**] This is taken from Flavius Vopiscus’ *Probus*, where he adds to the preceding: “Hence it is that when Alexander the Great of Macedon had come to the tomb of Achilles, he groaned deeply and said, ‘Happy are you, young man, to have found such a herald of your virtues,’ meaning Homer, who fashioned Achilles as great in the pursuit of virtue as his own talent was capable of making him.”

**Whom he called either a bronze [aes] figure or a leopard or a he-goat, etc.**] Rosweydus printed *aes* instead of *arietem* and annotated the passage as follows. EDIT.—“Whom he called either bronze, or a leopard, or a he-goat of the goats.” Do not be surprised, reader, at the novelty of the reading. The reading I present is ancient and has been drawn from manuscripts that have *aes*, not *arietem*. Indeed, that reading agrees both with Sacred Scripture and with Jerome’s meaning.

For what is written in Daniel, chapter II, verse 32, concerning the statue—“Its belly and thighs were of bronze”—and in verse 39—“Another kingdom, a third, of bronze”—Jerome interprets in his commentary as referring to Alexander and the kingdom of the Macedonians.

Again, what is written in Daniel, chapter VII, verse 6—“And behold, another beast, like a leopard”—Jerome likewise interprets as referring to the kingdom of the Macedonians. Concerning this kingdom, he says, we read in the statue: “Its belly and thighs were of bronze.”

But what Daniel has in chapter VIII, verse 5—“And behold, a he-goat of the goats was coming from the West”—the angel Gabriel interprets in verse 21: “The he-goat of the goats is the king of the Greeks.” And Jerome says there: “The he-goat of the goats is Alexander, king of the Greeks.”

The editors, because the leopard and the he-goat followed, thought that a third animal had also to be joined here; therefore they changed *aes* into *arietem*. But Daniel and Jerome understand by the ram not Alexander the Great, but Darius, king of the Persians and Medes.

**Epiphanius.**] His letter in praise of Hilarion, so far as I know, does not exist today. Concerning him, Sozomen, book VI, chapter 32, says:

“Epiphanius, however, practiced the monastic life in the vicinity of the village of Besanducus, where he was from, in the district of Eleutheropolis.”

The same account occurs in Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 39. Concerning Epiphanius and Hilarion visiting one another, see the *Apophthegmata* in Pelagius, booklet IV, no. 15.

**Those who once slandered my Paul.**] See what was said about the *Life of Paul* in the Preliminary Remarks, no. 4.

[Col. 0196A] **Thabatha.**] The older editions have *Thabacha*. The manuscript of Saint Florian has *Thauthac*. In Sozomen, book III, chapter 14, it is Θαβαθά, elsewhere Θανάτα. In Nicephorus, book IX, chapter 15, it is *Thabasa*.

**Gaza.**] A very well-known city of Palestine.

**The rose, as the saying goes, flowered among thorns.**] In Greek: Ῥόδον ἐξ ἀκανθῶν, τὸ τοῦ λόγου, “a rose from thorns, as the saying goes.” This is a proverbial expression. Ammianus, book XVI, says of the eunuch Eutherius: “But roses grow among brambles, and among wild beasts some become gentle.”

**Majuma.**] Jerome calls this the trading port of Gaza. Ptolemy and Sozomen, book V, chapter 3, call it ἐπίνειον Γαζαίων, “the harbor of the Gazans,” in Palestine, twenty stadia distant from Gaza.

**And wearing a leather *ependytes*.**] In the *Life of Antony*, chapter 23: “He washed his *ependytes*.” See there, note 55. Joannes Andreas, the old editor of Jerome’s letters, adds after *ependytes* in the *Life of Hilarion* the word *eraciestem*; in its place, in Adon’s *Martyrology* on 21 October, one finds *tenattem*. We shall investigate these matters in the *Onomasticon*.

**In a vast wilderness between the sea and the marsh.**] Likewise below, chapter 8, concerning the robbers roaming between the sea and the marsh. More concerning deserts and wildernesses is given in the *Onomasticon*.

**Caricas.**] These are *caricae* according to Pliny, book XIII, chapter 5, a kind of fig which he says is peculiar to Syria. Cassian, *Conferences*, VIII, chapter 1, lists *caricae* among the food of hermits. Above, in the *Life of Saint Paul the Hermit*, chapter 5, he was sustained each day by five figs.

**Little baskets.**] Some manuscripts and older editions add, “that is, little baskets.” Let this serve as the interpretation. A *fiscella* is a wicker basket used for various purposes.

**Driver.**] Most printed editions have *gladiator*, “gladiator.” Incorrectly. The error entered because a contest of gladiators had preceded. Cicero, *Academica* IV: “For I, like a skilled driver, shall hold back the horses before I come to the end.”

**Sedge.**] Some printed editions add, “that is, a wild and thorny plant,” which perhaps entered the text from a doubtful marginal gloss [Col. 0196C]. It is a kind of rush, sharp and extremely hard, resembling esparto grass.

**Impetigo.**] Impetigo is an infection and severe roughness of the outer skin accompanied by considerable itching. Lucilius calls it *depetigo* in book XXX of his *Satires*. For remedies against it, see Pliny, book XX, chapter 19; book XXII, chapter 25; and book XXIII, in the preface and chapter 7.

**Eleutheropolitan.**] Eleutheropolis is a city of Palestine, situated between Jerusalem and Ascalon, at approximately a day’s journey from each.

**Aristaeneta, wife of Elpidius, who later became prefect.**] Below, chapter 23: “That Aristaeneta whom we mentioned above, the prefect’s wife.” Concerning Elpidius, Ammianus, book XXI, says: “Amid so many pressing matters, after Hermogenes had died, Elpidius was promoted to the prefecture. He was born in Paphlagonia, insignificant in appearance and speech, but of simple character, bloodless and gentle.”

**Hemitritaean fever.**] The Cologne edition adds “namely, a disease of an incomplete tertian fever,” which is a gloss from the earlier edition. This Greek word is also common among Latin authors. See the *Onomasticon*.

**And let the idol Marnas fall.**] Jerome, letter 7, to Laeta: “Now even the Egyptian Serapis has become Christian. Marnas mourns, shut up in Gaza, and continually trembles at the destruction of his temple.” Likewise, on Isaiah XVII: “The Serapeum of Alexandria and the temple of Marna at Gaza have arisen as churches of the Lord.”

**They kissed the hands of the saints.**] In former times Christians kissed the hands and feet of holy men, martyrs, bishops, and priests as an act of veneration. See the *Onomasticon*.

**Rhinocorura.**] Jerome, *Onomasticon of Hebrew Places*: “Rhinocorura is a city of Egypt mentioned by Isaiah. It should be understood, however, that this name is not found in the Hebrew books, but was added by the translators of the Septuagint because of their knowledge of the place. We have stated this in the book of Hebrew names.” Likewise, on Isaiah XXVII: “For ‘torrent of Egypt,’ the Septuagint translated Rhinocorura, which is a town on the border of Egypt and Palestine, expressing not so much the words of Scripture as the meaning of the words.”

**Aila.**] The old edition has *Achile*. Jerome, *Onomasticon of Hebrew Places*: “Ailat lies at the farthest boundaries of Palestine, adjoining the southern desert and the Red Sea; from there one sails from Egypt to India and from there back to Egypt. A Roman legion called the Tenth is stationed there. Formerly it was called Ailat by the ancients, but now it is called Aila.”

**Against the duumvir of Gaza.**] In municipalities there were duumvirs, equivalent to consuls. The duty of attending the Circus belonged to them; it is listed among personal obligations in book L, title 4, *On Duties and Honors*, law 1, where one finds “the spectacles of the Circus horses.” Gaza, however, was a municipality; hence Jerome calls Italicus a municipal citizen.

**To Consus, as though to the god of counsels.**] Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, chapter 2: “Consus, whom Romulus wished to be worshiped as the god of deceit, or rather as the god of counsels, after treachery had succeeded in the abduction of the Sabine women.” The same author, *On Spectacles*, chapter 4: “Romulus first consecrated the Circus games to Consus, as to the god of counsel, for the purpose of abducting the Sabine women.” These words are taken from Tertullian, *On Spectacles*, chapter 5: “Although they also defend the Consualia on the ground that Romulus dedicated them to Consus, the god—as they wish him to be—of counsel.” Augustine, *City of God* IV, chapter 11: “Let Consus himself also be a god, by providing counsels.” Varro, *On the Latin Language* V: “The Consualia are so called from Consus, because at that time public festivals are held for that god, and in the Circus, at his altar, the priests conduct those games at which the Sabine maidens were abducted.”

**An earthen cup.**] Isaac Casaubon, in his notes to Spartianus’ *Julian*, after discussing certain forms of εἰσοπτρομαντική—ὑδρομαντεία, κυλικομαντεία, and others—says: “I have often been amazed that the very ancient monk Hilarion, a man of renowned virtue, when he was about to perform a miracle in the name of Christ, should have imitated the arts of curious men of this kind.” Jerome relates the story. It is also described at length in the Greek *Martyrologies*. Therefore we have set down here the following brief extract:

“But Hilarion, moved by pity for those present—for they too begged him not to overlook the condition of the Italian, who was a Christian and, having been defeated in the Circus race by the opposing faction not through the horses’ ability but by magical arts, had tearfully sought Hilarion’s help—ordered the cup to be filled with water, the cup from which he himself was accustomed to drink (and it was made of earthenware), and commanded that it be placed in the Italian’s hands. When he had taken it, he clearly saw in the water both the horses and the stable, and even the charioteers themselves with their chariots; for all of them had been bound by the enchantments of the opponents. When he saw this and gave thanks to God and to Hilarion, he immediately returned home. Taking some of that water in which he had seen the horses fettered in the cup, he sprinkled them all with it; then he also sealed them with the venerable sign of the cross. From that time victory passed to the Italian, while the opponents were overwhelmed by the utmost disgrace.”

Who could deny that these words describe that form of κατοπτρομαντεία which was performed with water and a cup? Thus far Casaubon.

Indeed, who would not deny that any form of κατοπτρομαντεία is present here, since that practice is accomplished only by an evil demon, an evil incantation, and a diabolical pact? But the passage which Casaubon gave in Greek I shall first give in Latin from Hervetus’ translation:

“Hilarion, having reverenced those who were present—for they too were asking him not to despise the Italian, who was in such a condition—ordered the cup, from which he himself was accustomed to drink, to be filled with water (it was made of earthenware) and placed in the hands of the Italian. When he had taken it, he saw clearly in the water both the horses and the stable, and even the charioteers themselves with their chariots; but all had been bound by the magic arts of their opponents. When he had seen this and had given thanks to God and to Hilarion, he immediately returned home. Taking that water, he sprinkled all the horses whom he had seen hindered in the cup; then he also marked them with the venerable sign of the cross. From that time victory passed to the Italian, while the opponents were afflicted with the greatest disgrace.”

What demon is invoked here? What evil incantation is sung? What diabolical frauds are employed, so that Hilarion can be said to have imitated the arts of curious men? Perhaps the malicious Casaubon refers the prophecy by Urim and Thummim—which, according to many opinions, was determined from the brightness of the stones—to κατοπτρομαντεία.

What then? Does Hilarion dispel the demons’ magic by magic, when here in the blessed Jerome, chapter 4, he “made the sign of Christ’s cross on his forehead against the demons’ mockeries”? Moreover, the Italian himself protests that with Hilarion it is not proper for a Christian man “to use magical arts,” and for that reason he had fled to him; yet Hilarion uses them? I add that “the saint did not wish, before cleansing the virgin or the young man, to order signs to be sought, lest the demon seem either to have departed through its customary incantations or to have adapted itself to his words and thereby caused him to believe them.” Here too he would be driving out the devil by means of the devil.

True Christians do not act in this way: they are accustomed to drive out demons and dissolve spells by hostile knowledge rather than by shared complicity. Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 57: “The principle of magical deception does not escape Christians alone, who know the spiritual powers of wickedness not through complicity of conscience but through hostile knowledge. We do not deal with the manifold plague of the human mind, the author of every error and likewise the destroyer of salvation and the soul, by inviting activity, but by conquering dominion.” Augustine, *City of God* X, chapter 22: “By true piety the people of God drive out the aerial power, hostile and opposed to piety, by exorcising it, not by appeasing it. They conquer all its temptations and adversities by praying, not to it, but to their God against it.” In chapter 21 he says: “The heroic martyrs conquered Hera and the aerial powers not with supplicatory gifts but with divine virtues.”

Apparently, however, the heretic preferred to see Hilarion as a sorcerer rather than a benefactor, an apostate rather than an apostle, an evil pagan rather than a good Christian. It would be surprising if he did not also make Christ a magician, since Christ used spittle to heal the eyes, because spitting has frequently been associated with the magic practices of ancient superstition.

The water of the earthen cup, then, must have been either marked and blessed by Hilarion with the cross, just as more than one person received bread and oil blessed by him for healing, according to the testimony of the blessed Jerome; or certainly the power belonged to the water from Hilarion’s own cup, which he himself was accustomed to use. There are many examples of such things among the writers of saints’ lives.

Joannes Savaro, in his commentary on Sidonius’ poem XXIII, citing this passage of Jerome concerning Hilarion, notes that the horses were sprinkled with water so that, as horses sacred to Neptune were drenched with water sacred to Neptune, they might run more swiftly in the Circus. I wish such a remark had not escaped this great man. What, then? Did this water stimulate the horses by magical power or by natural power? Not by magic, as I have clearly shown against Casaubon; nor by natural power. For the opponent would not have laughed at it, and the man who consulted the devil concerning the Circus contest would not, I think, have rejected the same natural benefit. Indeed, why was it necessary to sprinkle the stable, the chariot, the starting gates, and the charioteers with the same water, since these contributed nothing to the horses’ speed? It was, it was divine power in the water consecrated by Hilarion and by his cup, and this power kept every spell away from the stable, chariot, starting gates, charioteers, and horses. For this was the purpose for which the Italian sought help. That power did not belong to ordinary water. See the *Onomasticon*, under “Water.”

**Certain monstrous words and monstrous figures engraved on a sheet of Cyprian bronze.**] Sorcerers and magicians sometimes used bronze and sometimes lead for engraving words and figures. Tacitus, *Annals* II: “Human remains dug out of the ground and walls were discovered, together with incantations, curses, and the name of Germanicus engraved on lead tablets, half-burnt ashes smeared with gore, and other magical devices.””

**Who, bound tightly with thread and a thin plate, you hold.**] Ovid, *Amores* I, elegy 8:

“He knows well what grass can do, what the cords  
Stirred by the twisted rhombus can do,  
And what the poison of a mare in love can do.”

By a similar art, in Synesius, letter 121, to Anastasius the water-carrier, Ulysses tries to persuade Polyphemus that he will win Galatea for him:

“But I know incantations, erotic compulsions,  
And love charms against which Galatea cannot resist,  
Not even for a short while.”

Ammianus calls these wicked arts, book XXVIII, where he relates that Marinus, an advocate, employed them: “Because he had dared to seek marriage with a certain Hispanilla by means of wicked arts, after the truth of the proceedings had been examined in passing, he condemned him to a deadly punishment.”

[Col. 0199B] **That I might preserve her.**] See our Serarius on Tobit VI, question 1, at verse 14, where he discusses Asmodeus and how, in the Greek text, he is said to have loved Sarah.

**Who was sending you.**] See our Delrio, *Magical Investigations* II, part I, question 4, section 7, where he discusses whether sorcerers can and are accustomed to curse others and, as it were, hand them over as slaves to a demon. See also our Thyraeus, part I, *Disputation on Demoniacs*, chapter 16.

**The demon of love.**] Particular demons rule over particular vices. Below: “For the old man had this grace, that he knew to which demon or to which vice a person was subject.” *Life of Antony*, chapter 4: “Hence I am also called the spirit of fornication.” See the note there.

**But the saint did not wish, etc.**] Persuaded by this passage, Joannes Hessels of Leuven, in his lectures on book IV of the *Sentences*, judged that it was not lawful to destroy the sign of a magical spell so that the devil might cease to do harm. But the contrary opinion is more widely accepted, and our Delrio proves it at length in *Magical Investigations* III, book VI, chapter 2, section 1, question 3. In response to the example of Saint Hilarion, he says that it proves only that those who resemble Hilarion in holiness and the gift of miracles—or when there is danger of increasing scandal or superstition—ought to do what tends to the greater glory of God, such as driving out a demon by prayer. It does not, however, prove that, when such danger is absent, or when someone is not certain that he possesses the gift of miracles—as no one today is certain in these regions where the faith has been propagated—he may not use a remedy that is at hand and that he knows by frequent experience to be effective.

The blessed Hilarion was afraid not that the demon would depart in this way through its customary incantations, but that the people would think it had departed through them. Indeed, he did not fear even this in an absolute sense, but alternatively: either that, or that he himself might seem to have believed the devil’s words, when the devil claimed that he could not be expelled unless the sign were first removed. [Col. 0199D] This was false, as the blessed Hilarion demonstrated. And because the demon had entered voluntarily, it remained voluntarily; those magical signs had no power to compel it.

**A candidate of the emperor Constantius.**] The word *candidate* has various meanings. Here, I think, it refers to one of the number of attendants who, because of their height, were chosen to protect the emperor. See the *Onomasticon*.

**Provision of transport.**] *Evectio* signifies the furnishing of public transportation. Augustine, letter 55: “Zenobius became master of the archives, and he sent us a transport permit together with provisions.” See the *Onomasticon*.

**Consular governor.**] Jerome speaks precisely. The province of Palestine had a consular governor. Concerning him, see the *Notitia of the East*.

**The decurions.**] In municipalities and colonies, decurions presided over the public council and were, as it were, the senators of their curia. See book X of the *Code*, *On Decurions*, law 32, upon whom serious obligations rested. I think that the candidate of Constantius was commended to the decurions during his journey because they were in charge of the stopping places, book XII of the Theodosian Code, *On Decurions*.

**And blessing them with his hand.**] Below, the Elusites cried out, “Barech,” that is, “Bless, Hilarion.” The saints blessed not only human beings but also inanimate things. Below, here: “Standing on high, he blessed the vineyard.” Elsewhere: “So that they might receive bread or oil blessed by him.” And in another place: “After the oil had been blessed, all the farmers and shepherds, touching their wounds with it, recovered certain health.”

**The desert of Kadesh.**] Psalm XXVIII: “The Lord will shake the desert of Kadesh.” See the blessed Jerome on Ezekiel XLVII and XLVIII.

**Elusa.**] In Greek, Λούσα. Elusa is a town of Idumea according to Ptolemy. Some place it in Palestine II, others in Palestine I. There is another Elusa in Gallia Narbonensis.

**But they worship it because of Lucifer.**] Jerome, on Amos V: “To this day the Saracens venerate Lucifer.”

**That he might draw a line for the future Church.**] “To draw a line” is an expression used proverbially. Some think it was taken from Plautus’ *Mostellaria*. But there it has a very different meaning. A not dissimilar reading appears in the manuscripts and older editions: *limitem mittere*, “to set a boundary,” which is perhaps the more accurate reading, taken from surveyors. Both readings are discussed more fully in the *Onomasticon*.

**As he was crowned.**] This derives from the ancient ritual of sacrificers, in which priests were crowned. Tertullian, *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 10: “Finally, the doors themselves, the victims themselves, the altars themselves, their attendants and priests themselves are crowned.” Pliny, book XVI, chapter 4: “Those who sacrifice in honor of the gods took up the crown, with the victims crowned at the same time.” And book XXI, chapter 2: “Among sacred rites alone and military honors, crowns claim their own name.”

**And would arrange it on a writing tablet.**] Stop, reader, and examine Hervetus’ translation from the Greek of Metaphrastes or Sophronius: “When he had first approached a certain monastery called Scindula.” Hervetus did not err, but reproduced what he found in the Greek: Μονῇ δέ τινι τὰ πρῶτα παραλαβὼν ἣ τοῦ Σκινδουλᾶ λέλεκτο, “when he had first been received into a certain monastery which was called that of Scindula.” From this alone one may infer that Sophronius interpreted Jerome’s Latin text into Greek. From *schedula* he made *Scindula*, the name of a monastery. He makes a similar error below in this same chapter: where Jerome has the monk’s name *Sabas*, Sophronius translates τὴν τοῦ Ἰβᾶ μονήν, “the monastery of Ibas.”

**The prefect’s wife at that time.**] In most manuscripts *tunc*, “at that time,” is absent; the printed editions add it. Nevertheless, it seems possible to infer that it should be understood from what follows, although there is nothing about the prefect’s office; hence she seems to have been the prefect’s wife at that time. Yet if we follow Ammianus, a writer of that period, Elpidius was not then yet prefect. Jerome could therefore have called her the prefect’s wife by anticipation, because Aristaeneta later became the prefect’s wife.

**And a suspension of public business.**] The Cologne edition has this, with the interpretation “that is, a suspension of all affairs and something like public mourning.” This is wrongly read: *justitium* has been printed instead of *exitium*, “destruction.” From this, the gloss explaining the substituted word also entered the text.

**I do not make my Lord deceptive.**] This vision is explained below, in the account of the pagans invading Hilarion’s monastery. Sozomen also relates that the Gazans sought Hilarion, book V, chapter 9. Nazianzen mentions the unrestrained boldness of the Gazans in the time of the emperor Julian in his first invective against Julian, which is the third speech in order; so too Sozomen, book V, chapter 8, and Theodoret, book III, chapter 6. Ambrose, letter 28: “The basilicas at Gaza were burned during the reign of Julian.”

**Bethelia.**] There is variation here between manuscripts and printed books. The reading *Bethelia* is supported by Sozomen, book V, chapter 14, where he speaks of his parents, who “were the first Christians in Bethelia, a village subject to the territory of Gaza.” Likewise, in book VI, chapter 32, speaking of Hilarion’s disciples: “They practiced the monastic life around Bethelea, a village in the district of Gaza.” In the earlier passage Sozomen says that Bethelia is called Πάνθεον, “Pantheon,” by the Greeks and Bethelia by the Syrians.

**Dracontius.**] Athanasius mentions him in his *Apology for His Flight*, saying that he was driven into exile by the Arians together with many other episcopal colleagues. Baronius, under the year of Christ 356, the fifth year of Pope Liberius and the twentieth of the emperor Constantius, thinks that he was the man of this name whom Athanasius himself, after he had long refused, finally compelled to accept the burden of the episcopate, though he had been a monk. Dracontius was bishop of Ἑρμουπόλεως μικρᾶς, “Little Hermopolis,” as Athanasius says in his letter to the Antiochenes.

**Babylon.**] Here Babylon is a city of Egypt, on the Athribitic River, in the district of Letopolis. There is another Babylon in Assyria.

**Philo.**] This man too is mentioned in the *Apology* of Athanasius cited above. Baronius, under the year just mentioned, says that Jerome’s testimony shows that Hilarion visited the confessors of Christ, Dracontius and Philo, in the year following the death of Antony. Antony died after the following year, namely in the year of Christ 358, which is the year to which Baronius assigns his death. Thus, according to Baronius’ calculation, Hilarion would have visited these confessors in the year of Christ 359.

But the chronology must be calculated in an entirely different way. For the Preliminary Remarks to the *Life of Antony* make it clear that he died in the nineteenth year of the emperor Constantius; and from the *Life of Hilarion*, chapter 27, it is clear that almost three years had elapsed before Hilarion went to Antony’s mountain to celebrate his anniversary there. For in that chapter it is said that “it had been three years since the closed sky had dried up the lands, so that people commonly said that even the elements mourned Antony’s death.” Hilarion then immediately returned from Antony’s mountain.

It is also clear from the *Life of Hilarion*, chapter 25, that when he was traveling to Antony’s mountain he visited the confessors Philo and Dracontius, and the number of days spent on the journey is calculated there. Therefore, if Antony died at the beginning of the nineteenth year of Constantius, in the year of Christ 355 and the fourth year of Pope Liberius, Hilarion must be said to have visited those confessors in the twenty-second year of Constantius, the year of Christ 358—at the end of that year, when 15 January, the day he was hastening to celebrate, was already approaching.

The unknown author of the *Life of Athanasius* mentions various men who were driven into exile with Philo and Dracontius after the death of the emperor Constans, when George the pseudo-bishop invaded the Alexandrian Church for the second time:

“For immediately they expelled from Egypt and Libya the bishops Ammonius, Moeus, Gaius, Philo, Hermes, Plenius, Psenosiris, Linamon, Agathon, Agamphus, Marcus, another Ammonius, and Marcus, Dracontius, Adelphius, Agathenodorus, and the presbyters Hierax and Dioscorus. And they drove them out so cruelly that some of them died on the roads and others in exile itself.”

These words are taken from Athanasius’ own *Apology for His Flight*. They are also found in Metaphrastes’ *Life of Athanasius* and in Socrates, book II, chapter 22, although certain names are read differently in different authors. Athanasius has Μούϊον instead of Μώϊον; Πηλάμμωνα instead of Λινάμωνα or Λινάβωνα; Ἀγαθόν and Ἀνάγαμφον instead of Ἀγάθωνα and Ἄγαμφον; and Ἀθηνόδωρον instead of Ἀγαθηνόδωρον.

The places to which each was exiled are given by Athanasius in his letter to those living the solitary life:

“Ammonius to the Upper Oasis; Moeus, Psenosiris, Neilammon, Plenium, Marcus, and Athenodorus to the Ammoniac district; Dracontius the bishop to the deserts around Clysma; Philo to Babylon; Adelphius to Psinabla of the Thebaid; and the presbyters Hierax and Dioscorus to Syene they sent into exile.”

**Aphroditon.**] There were four cities called Aphrodites and Aphroditopolis in Egypt, according to the old map of Egypt in Ortelius: one near Athribis in the Delta; another near the Nile in Heptanomia; a third near the Nile in the Thebaid; and a fourth near Latopolis on the Nile in the Thebaid. Which one is meant here, I shall explain in the *Onomasticon*, under the desert and Antony’s monastery.

**Baisane.**] I have not yet encountered any mention of this person elsewhere.

**With dromedary camels.**] The old edition has “with dromedary camels.” See the *Onomasticon*.

**Isaac and the man of Pelusium.**] I have not yet found anything concerning them.

[Col. 0202B] **Lest Pergamius.**] Antony wished his body to remain hidden out of Christian modesty and humility, not out of contempt for relics, as heretics mockingly claim. It is well known with what devotion he claimed the tunic of Saint Paul, the first hermit.

**A shrine might be built.**] Sacred buildings and martyria were erected both for holy confessors and for martyrs. Here you have an example concerning a confessor. Concerning martyrs, Ammianus, book XXII: “He cast the ashes into the sea, fearing—as he shouted—that after the remains had been collected a building might be constructed for them like those for the others who, compelled to depart from the religion, endured agonizing punishments, advancing with undefiled faith even to a glorious death, and are now called martyrs.”

**To the desert beyond the Oasis.**] Ptolemy mentions a Great Oasis and a Small Oasis in Egypt. But both manuscripts and printed books vary at this passage of Jerome. The manuscript of Saint Florian has: “About to pass to the inner monastery.” The old edition has: “About to pass to the inner monastery of the Oasis.”

[Col. 0202C] **The Gazans with the prefect’s lictors.**] Some printed editions wrongly have *profecti*, “having departed.” Jerome means the prefect of Palestine, in which Gaza was situated, and that prefect’s lictors. What Jerome briefly narrates here is given somewhat more fully by Sophronius the translator, or by Metaphrastes, who identifies the Arians and pagans as the authors of this investigation:

“After Constantius had ended his life together with his empire, while Julian with the greatest ruin had invaded the imperial throne—most impious deeds, O justice and forbearance of God, and laws of true piety, which he wickedly exercised as a tyrant—the Gazans who were Arians and still honored the pagan rites were stirred with great anger and arrogance against the holy man. They sent some of those who shared their views to Bruchium, so that they might subject him to the utmost evils. But when they arrived, they were, as the saying goes, a gaping wolf rushing foolishly, since the holy man had long before foreseen their plot and had already gone to the Oasis, as we have said.

When they could not endure their disgrace, they were inflamed to even greater madness. Returning, they incited the most impious emperor to have his monastery destroyed down to its foundations, to expel the monks after they had first been subjected to many punishments, and to have Hilarion and Hesychius, wherever they might be found, severely punished and then handed over to death. They did not realize, as the saying goes, that they were pursuing an eagle into the clouds, or, as the divine Paul says, beating or shooting at the air.”

Baronius, volume IV, under the year of Christ 362, the eleventh year of Pope Liberius and the second of the emperor Julian, says that the reason the Gazans had sought his death with such determination was principally that the same holy Hilarion, while living among them, had performed remarkable miracles. When one of these miracles had been performed in the theater and made the matter clear, everyone had proclaimed that Marnas, the god of the Gazans, had been overcome by Christ.

Moreover, the persecution of the Christians by the Gazans was so violent that not only was Hilarion forced to flee, but all the others living in the territory of the Gazans were likewise compelled to seek safety by flight and concealment. Sozomen preserved the following account of his ancestors for later generations: “Among the many others of my ancestors, my grandfather also shared in this flight” (Sozomen, book V, chapter 14), and so forth.

**To Paraetonium, a maritime city of Libya.**] This is a city of Egypt. Florus, book IV, chapter 11, calls Paraetonium and Pelusium the two horns of Egypt.

**A certain shield-bearer.**] In Greek, “by name Scutarius.” But I think that *scutarius* here denotes a man by his office. Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 56: “He also attended to his clients, as he did to a certain shield-bearer, once his own recruit.”

**Hesychius.**] Sozomen, book III, chapter 13, calls him *Hesycas*. Likewise in book VI, chapter 32:

“Hesychas, Hilarion’s companion, practiced the monastic life in that very place where his teacher had done so.”

The same account occurs in Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 39.

[Col. 0203C] **Methone.**] Methone is a maritime city of Messenia in the Peloponnese.

**Selling cheap rubbish to the people.**] This is taken from Horace, book I of the *Letters*, letter 7:

“Selling cheap rubbish to the people in tunics.”

**To Epidauros, a town of Dalmatia.**] “Of Dalmatia” has correctly been added, since there are also two other Epidauri in the Peloponnese.

**They call them boas.**] Isidore, *Etymologies* XII, chapter 4: “The boa is a snake of Italy of enormous size. It pursues herds of cattle and oxen, wraps itself around cows with udders flowing with abundant milk, and, sucking them, kills them. From its devastation of cattle it received the name *boa*.” These words are partly adapted from Solinus and partly from Pliny.

Solinus, chapter 8: “Calabria is extremely rich in chelydri and produces the boa, a snake which they say grows to enormous size. At first it attacks herds of cattle, and if there is a cow rich in abundant milk, it coils itself around her udders and, fattened by continual sucking, eventually swells over a long period into such a celebrated mass of fullness that no force can resist its size. Finally, after laying waste to the animals, it drives the regions it has occupied into desolation. During the reign of the emperor Claudius, at the place where the Vatican fields are, a solid infant was found inside the belly of a slain boa.”

Solinus paraphrastically reproduces Pliny, book VIII, chapter 14: “The reports are confirmed by the boas known in Italy, which grow to such a size that, when one was killed during the reign of the emperor Claudius, a whole infant was found inside it in the Vatican. At first they are nourished by the juice of cattle’s milk, from which they derived their name.”

It should be investigated whether the island called Boas in Dalmatia received its name from boa serpents. Certainly here in Jerome you have a boa serpent native to Dalmatia. Concerning the island, Ammianus, book XXII: “Florentius was confined to Boas, an island of Dalmatia.” Likewise, book XXVIII: “He banished him—Hymettius—to Boas, a place in Dalmatia.” Jovianus the heretic was also sent there, book LIII of the Theodosian Code, *On Heretics*.

**Having summoned it, he had given the order.**] The printed editions read: “He had ordered the people to be summoned.” But *people* is absent from the Latin and Greek manuscripts. The meaning is that the serpent itself had been summoned.

At that time, when an earthquake shook the whole world. Jerome, in his *Chronicle*, under the year of Valentinian II: “When an earthquake occurred throughout the entire world, the sea overflowed its shore and overwhelmed the cities of Sicily and of many islands, as well as countless peoples.” The same author, in his commentary on Isaiah, chapter XV: “I heard a certain man from Areopolis—and the whole city bears witness—that, in my childhood, during a great earthquake, when the seas crossed the shores of the entire world, the walls of that city collapsed that same night.” Ammianus, book XXVI: “While this innovator [the tyrant Procopius] was still alive—the many deeds and death of whom we have related—on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, during the consulship of Valentinian for the first time with his brother, dreadful tremors suddenly spread throughout the whole circuit of the world, such as neither fables nor truthful accounts of antiquity report to us.” Ammianus describes the effects of this tremor there in vivid detail.

**In the sand.** Pliny, book XVII, chapter 4: “Conversely, white sand in the territory of Ticinum, and in many places black sand, likewise even red sand mixed with rich soil, is infertile.” It is also called *sabulo*. Columella, book IV, chapter 33, concerning the chestnut: “It does not reject moist sand or crumbled tufa.”

**Of Salona.** Salona is a naval station of the Dalmatians, according to Strabo. Pliny also mentions Salona as a city and river of Dalmatia.

**In a small boat.** Who would not hesitate when reading in Metaphrastes, in Hervet’s translation, “He landed at Berbilimnon, a commercial town of Dalmatia”? I confess that I hesitated, and for that very reason summoned the Greek text from the royal manuscripts at Paris; in them it reads: *Εἰς Βερβήλιμβον ἐμπόριον τῆς Δαλματίας καταίρει*—“He lands at Berbelimbon, a commercial town of Dalmatia.” This does not differ from Hervet’s translation except in having *Berbelimbon* instead of *Berbilimnon*. I fear that anyone who seeks this harbor in Dalmatia will search in vain. I suspect that Sophronius, who rendered this Life from Jerome’s Latin into Greek, made *Berbelimbon*—Βερβήλιμβον—from Jerome’s “small boat.” Nor do I think this conjecture groundless.

**92. In two not-small myoparones.** The Cologne edition adds: “A *myoparon* is a type of vessel equipped for speed and rapid sailing,” which was undoubtedly inserted as a gloss. Here the reading is remarkable: *qua* in the manuscripts, *quae* in the printed editions. One manuscript has the corrupt reading: *myoparonibus desedromonem occurrissent, denuo hinc inde fluctus vehementes, remiges* (“having encountered [them] with myoparones … again, violent waves on either side, rowers”; the syntax is uncertain). An old edition reads: *myoparonibus de se dromone occurrissent, denuo hinc inde fluctus verrente remige* (“having encountered [them] with myoparones, with a dromon of itself … again, with the rower sweeping the waves”; likewise uncertain). Perhaps *dromon* is an interpretation of *myoparon*. A *dromon* is a ship prepared for speed, such as pirate vessels generally are. More about the *myoparon* may be found in the *Onomasticon*. [Col. 0204B–C]

**Paphos.** There are two Paphoses on the island of Cyprus: Old Paphos and New Paphos. The place where Hilarion stayed near Paphos is called *Charbyris* by Sozomen, book V, chapter 9; *Charybdis* by Triparitus, book VI, chapter 12; and *Charybris* by Nicephorus, book X, chapter 8.

**This Salamis, this Curium, this Lapetha.** These are three cities in Cyprus. There is another Salamis, both an island and a city near the Peloponnese. There is also another Curium in Aetolia and among the Sabines. Through Paphos, which he mentioned earlier, and these three cities, he designates the whole island of Cyprus. Salamis lies in the east, Curium in the south, Lapetha in the north, and Paphos in the west. [Col. 0204D]

**Which are called Bucolia.** The older editions have *Bocholia*. Others cite *Bacholia*. But the Greek here is Βουκόλια, as also above, in chapter 24 of the *Life of Saint Antony*, where Evagrius translates it as “Pastoral Places.” See what was said there at no. 60. More may be found in the *Onomasticon*.

**A tunic, a pouch, a hood, and a little cloak.** This was Hilarion’s legacy, and his entire treasure. Shortly afterward he wishes to be buried in a haircloth tunic, a hood, and a rustic cloak. Do not be misled into thinking that, because Hilarion bequeathed some garments and reserved others for burial, he possessed duplicates either for festival use or for cleanliness. He did not. It is established above that he never changed his clothing unless the previous garment had been completely torn. The garments he now bequeaths had recently come to him upon the death of his servant, who had died only a few days earlier, as is stated here. [Col. 0205A]

**And with his whole body intact, as though he were still alive.** On the incorrupt bodies of the saints, see extensively in the *Onomasticon*.

**To assist their prayers.** Learn, heretic, that the prayers of the faithful are assisted by the prayers of the saints. Augustine, book XX, chapter 21, against Faustus the Manichaean, recognizes three benefits in the veneration of martyrs: “The Christian people celebrates the memorials of the martyrs with religious solemnity, both to stir up imitation, and to be joined to their merits, and to be assisted by their prayers.”

Chrysostom, in his book on the martyr Babylas against the pagans, teaches that more than one benefit is drawn from the tombs of the martyrs:

*Ἡ γὰρ ὄψις τῆς λάρνακος εἰς τὴν ψυχὴν ἐμπίπτουσα, καταπλήττει τε αὐτὴν καὶ διανίστησι, καὶ ὡς αὐτοῦ κειμένου συνευχομένου, καὶ παρεστῶτος καὶ ὁρωμένου, οὕτως αὐτὴν διακεῖσθαι ποιεῖ· εἶτα προθυμίας πολλῆς ὁ τοῦτο παθὼν, πληρωθεὶς, ἕτερος ἀνθ᾽ ἑτέρου γενόμενος, οὕτως ἐκεῖθεν ἀπέρχεται.*

“For the sight of the coffin, entering the soul, both strikes and awakens it, and makes it behave as though the one lying there were praying together with us, present and visible. Then the person who experiences this, filled with great eagerness and somehow becoming another person instead of his former self, departs from that place in this state.” [Col. 0205B]

Therefore frequent the tombs of the saints, venerate the relics of the saints, and implore the prayers of the saints.

Baronius, volume IV of the *Annals*, under the year of Christ 372, the sixth year of Pope Damasus and the ninth of the emperors Valentinian and Valens: “In this very year, he says, Hilarion, the most distinguished of monks, after performing innumerable miracles and becoming renowned for holiness, departed this life in the eightieth year of his age, as Saint Jerome testifies. From the same testimony it is also inferred that he departed this life in this very year. For Jerome reports that, at the time of the death of the great Antony—which occurred in the twenty-first year of the emperor Constantius, that is, the year of the Lord 358—Hilarion was sixty-five years old. If fifteen years are added to these in order to reach eighty, the age at which he died, his years are necessarily brought to the present year, 372.”

Thus far Baronius. According to his calculation, Hilarion’s birth must be assigned to the year of Christ 292. For if eighty years are added to that number—the number of years Jerome asserts that he lived—they bring us to the year 372, the year of his death. But I have warned, in the preliminary remarks on Antony, that Antony’s years must be counted differently. [Col. 0205C–0206A]

If you desire a brief chronological summary of Hilarion’s Life, here it is, extracted from this very Life:

- At the beginning of his sixteenth year, he enters the desert and remains there through his twentieth year inclusive.
- From the beginning of his twenty-first year through his twenty-sixth year inclusive, he lives on very little food: for three years, a sextarius of lentils per day; for the next three years, dry bread with salt.
- From the beginning of his twenty-seventh year through his thirtieth year inclusive, he lives on herbs.
- From the beginning of his thirty-first year through his thirty-fifth year inclusive, he takes six ounces of barley bread per day.
- From the beginning of his thirty-sixth year through his sixty-third year inclusive, he adds oil to his diet.
- From the beginning of his sixty-fourth year through his eightieth year inclusive, he abstains from bread, and thus completes the course of his life.

When all these periods are added together, they produce the correct number of eighty years.

Another reckoning of the years can also be derived from the same Life:

- At the beginning of his sixteenth year—or, more precisely, after completing fifteen years—he enters the desert.
- After twenty-two years of solitude, he obtains a child for a barren woman of Eleutheropolis.
- In his sixty-third year, he considers fleeing. Two years later he leaves Palestine.
- Three years after Antony’s death, he visits Antony’s place.
- He remains one year in the Oasis.
- He flees to Sicily, where Hesychius finds him after three years.
- He remains two years at Paphos in Cyprus.
- He remains five years on the mountain.

If one adds the one year he spent in various journeys, the total is eighty years, which Jerome testifies that he lived. [Col. 0206B–C]

[Col. 0205]

## OCTOBER 21. LIFE OF SAINT MALCHUS, THE CAPTIVE MONK, BY SAINT JEROME THE PRESBYTER

(The text of this Life, annotated by Vallarsius and others, may be found in Migne, *Patrologia*, volume XXIII, column 53. Here you receive Rosweyde’s notes.) [Col. 0205D]

**96. Malchus.** The Roman Martyrology, October 21: “At Maronia in Syria, near Antioch, Saint Malchus the monk.” Concerning a certain Malchus, the *Menaea*, November 24:

*Ὁ ἅγιος Μάλχος ἐν εἰρήνῃ τελειοῦται.*

*Οἱ ψυχοπομποὶ συγκατέπτησαν νόες*

*Ψυχὴν ἀπάξαι, Μάλχε, τὴν σὴν Κυρίῳ.*

“Saint Malchus is perfected in peace.

The guides of souls flew down together from heaven

To lead your soul, Malchus, to the Lord.”

Whether this is the same person as our Malchus, I doubt. Theodoret mentions a certain Malchus in book IV, chapter 26 of his *History*, whom Baronius, under the year 370, thinks to be the one about whom Jerome writes. I do not think so, because Theodoret’s Malchus lived on the mountain overlooking Antioch, whereas Jerome’s Malchus lived in the village of Maronia, thirty miles from Antioch.

Here you may see that *Malchus* means “king” in Syriac. See the *Onomasticon*.

**By Jerome.** Jerome truly is the author of this Life. In chapter 135 of his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers* he lists it among his works. Therefore I think that the Life found in volume VII of Metaphrastes, translated from the Greek by Gentianus Hervetus for Aloysius Lipomanus, was first translated from Jerome’s Latin text into Greek.

The Magdeburg Centuriators, century 4, chapter 10, following Erasmus, maintain that Jerome composed the Life of Malchus in an elaborate narrative chiefly to exercise his ingenuity, rather than with the intention of simply presenting the facts. But Alanus Copus rightly catches them in their own words, in dialogue 2, chapter 11: “They marvel,” he says, “that Jerome judged it necessary to recount so many crimes of the man before condemning them.” Jerome. In this complaint they betray themselves and their own cause, and show clearly enough that they understand Jerome to have treated these matters seriously and not as a rhetorical exercise. Otherwise, why that outcry against a rhetorician playing with a fabricated subject?” Thus far Alanus, who then refutes with great skill, in various chapters of that second dialogue, the five crimes that the Magdeburg Centuriators charge against Malchus. [Col. 0206D–0207A]

**Who practices steering in a naval battle.** Ambrose, book I of the *Duties*, chapter 10: “He who strives to guide a ship at sea with the rudders, or to propel it with oars, first practices on a river.” Erasmus goes astray when, from this comparison, he supposes that Jerome is implying that the subject is not serious but chosen merely to exercise his style. As though it were contradictory for something to be serious and nevertheless to be undertaken as an exercise in style. Jerome was seriously contemplating the composition of an ecclesiastical history; so that he might treat it worthily, he preferred first to practice, as he says, in a small work before approaching the larger history. In both cases he was dealing with the matter seriously.

The Audomar manuscript prefixed these words to the beginning of this chapter: “Reader, imitate what you read.”

**Has grown through persecutions.** Jerome, letter 62, to Theophilus, against the errors of John of Jerusalem: “By the shedding of blood, and by suffering rather than inflicting insults, the Church of Christ was founded; it grew through persecutions and was crowned by martyrdoms.” [Col. 0207B]

**And after the Church had come under Christian rulers, it became greater in power and riches, but lesser in virtues.** Modern heretics eagerly seize upon these and similar passages from Jerome and the other Fathers.

First, they use them to condemn the ornamentation of churches and the more precious sacred vessels. Our Bellarmine admirably refutes them in volume II, general controversy IV, book III, *On the Cult of the Saints*, chapter 6, where he discusses the ornamentation of temples; and in volume III, general controversy III, *On the Eucharist*, book II, *On the Mass*, chapter 14, where he discusses sacred vessels.

A timely saying of Saint Boniface also bears on this matter. It is found in *De consecratione*, distinction 1, chapter 44: “When Boniface the martyr and bishop was asked whether it was permissible to consecrate the Sacraments in wooden vessels, he replied: ‘Once golden priests used wooden chalices; now, by contrast, wooden priests use golden chalices.’” This was taken from the Council of Tribur, chapter 18. The holy man plainly wished priests to bring golden minds to the altar as well. [Col. 0207C]

Trithemius expressed the same saying in a kind of imitation in his *Chronicle of Hirsau*: “Formerly, the monks had dark cells, churches, and other dwellings, but their hearts were exceedingly bright in the love of almighty God and in the knowledge of the divine Scriptures. Our people now build churches, cells, houses, and all dwellings exceedingly bright, but their hearts are dark, full of vices and laziness, because they neither love God as they ought nor devote their minds to reading the Scriptures. Likewise, when the chalices were bronze, the priests were golden; today the chalices are golden, and the priests are bronze.”

Second, they attack and condemn the wealth of the clergy. In this they follow the ancient heretics, such as Arnold of Brescia, who lived in the year of Christ 1139, during the reign of Conrad, king of the Romans. According to Otto of Freising, book II, chapter 20 of *The Deeds of Emperor Frederick*, Arnold said: “Neither clerics possessing property, nor bishops possessing royal revenues, nor monks possessing estates can in any way be saved.” [Col. 0207D]

They also follow John Wycliffe, whose following articles were condemned at the Council of Constance, session 8:

“XXXII. Enriching the clergy is contrary to the rule of Christ.

XXXIII. Sylvester and Constantine erred in enriching the Church.

XXXIX. The emperor and secular rulers were deceived by the devil so that they might enrich the Church with temporal goods.”

But Ambrose rightly places the fault not in wealth but in those who misuse it. In book VIII, on chapter XIX of Luke, he writes: “Let the rich learn that guilt does not cling to possessions, but to those who do not know how to use their possessions. For riches are impediments to the wicked, but aids to virtue for the good.”

If someone applies Isaiah’s prophecy to the Church, once abandoned under pagan emperors and later exalted in the time of Christian emperors, he will not be entirely mistaken:

“Instead of your being forsaken and hated, with no one passing through you, I will make you an eternal pride, a joy from generation to generation. You shall suck the milk of nations and be nursed at the breast of kings, and you shall know that I, the Lord, am your savior, and that your redeemer is the Mighty One of Jacob” (Isaiah LX).

And this passage from the same prophet:

“And kings shall be your foster fathers, and their queens your nurses; they shall bow down to you with their faces to the ground and lick the dust of your feet” (Isaiah XLIX).

See the letter of Aeneas Silvius, then a cardinal and later Pope Pius II, entitled *On the Customs of Germany*. In it he refutes various accusations made against the Roman Curia by Martin Meir, who was chancellor to the archbishop of Mainz, and proves by various arguments that Roman prelates ought to be rich and powerful. Above all, he requires wealth for three purposes:

“1. To maintain an honorable condition appropriate to their dignity;

2. To feed the poor and support the churches;

3. To restrain evildoers who obstruct the integrity of the faith.” [Col. 0208A–B]

**Maronia.** Thus read the manuscripts and the old edition. It is commonly written *Maronia*. Ptolemy records a city of Syria called Μαρωνείας. Here it is said to be a village. See the *Onomasticon*.

**To Pope Evagrius.** Evagrius was bishop of Antioch and very close to Jerome. Jerome himself mentions him in chapter 125 of his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*. See what was said in the preliminary remarks on the *Life of Saint Antony*, no. 4. Concerning the title “pope,” see the *Onomasticon*.

**So that he was truly a native of the same place.** Rosweyde has *and, as I thought*, instead of *so that he was truly*, and comments on his reading in what follows.

**EDITOR.** “And, as I thought, a native of the same place.” Thus the manuscript and the old edition. The Cologne edition, with Erasmus, has *and truly, a native*, αὐτόχθων. I do not know whether Erasmus substituted this from his own ingenuity or from a manuscript. H. Gravius says that some books also read “a native of Thebastonis.” One manuscript has *was* instead of *I thought*. But the true reading is the one I have given. Jerome thought that Malchus, who lived at Maronia, was a native of that same place, but Malchus soon informs him that he was from Nisibis. The Magdeburg Centuriators follow Erasmus in error when, century 4, chapter 10, they say that Malchus was born in the village of Maronia. [Col. 0208C]

**My son, a tenant of a little field at Nisibis.** The manuscript of Saint Florian: “My son, a tenant of a little field at Nisivellum.” The Audomar manuscript: “Matheni, a tenant of a little field of Nisibenus,” apparently formed from *my son, of Nisibenus*. Perhaps someone might extract from this the name “Mathe Nisibenus” and invent a place so called in the territory of Nisibis. The common reading has *of Maroniacus* instead of *of Nisibenus*. Metaphrastes has *Sevennia*.

**To the desert of Chalcis.** Chalcis is a city of Syria, in the region of Chalcidice. Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXIV, calls it “the Syrian city of Chalcis.” See the *Onomasticon*.

**Which lies between Immas and Beroea.** Rosweyde reads this from the manuscripts instead of *Beroam*, which is Vallarsius’s reading.

**EDITOR.** Thus it should be read from the manuscripts. Some manuscripts have *Veroea*, following the customary practice of certain ancient writers who put V for B. The old editions read, “which lies between Immas and Beroeas.” The Cologne edition has, “which lies between Imma and Essa.” I would waste my leisure if I reproduced the monstrous readings of certain manuscripts and printed books. There are both Imma and Beroea in Syria, and they suit this passage. See the *Onomasticon*. [Col. 0208D]

**While her mother was still alive.** Vallarsius has “while her mother was still living.”

**EDITOR.** Thus the manuscript of Saint Florian and the printed editions: “And while her mother was still alive.” Tertullian, *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 7: “Moreover, if other women do things for idols, they belong to demons; how much more [do those] who themselves made idols for themselves while they were still alive.” Here Latinius incorrectly restores “while they were still living.”

**For those traveling from Beroea to Edessa.** Thus correctly the manuscripts. The Cologne edition incorrectly has, “for those traveling from Beria to Essa.” Here Beroea is a Syrian city in the region of Cyrrhestica. Edessa also is a city of Syria.

**A solitude near the public road, through which the Saracens …** This vast desert stretches from India all the way to Mauretania and the Atlantic Ocean, as Jerome writes in his commentary on Isaiah XXI. [Col. 0209A]

**The Ishmaelites rush upon them, their heads covered with long, banded hair.** The old editions read “with uncovered heads.” But the manuscript, together with the Cologne edition, correctly has *vittatis*, “banded.” The dress and appearance of peoples vary.

Tertullian, book *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 10: “They too ought to claim for themselves some distinctive marks, whether the feathers of the Garamantes, the topknots of the barbarians, the cicadas of the Athenians, the curls of the Germans, or the tattoos of the Britons.”

Isidore, book XIX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 23: “Some peoples claim for themselves certain distinctive features not only in their clothing but also on their bodies, as we see in the curls of the Germans, the topknots and cinnabar coloring of the Goths, and the tattoos of the Britons. The Jews also circumcise their foreskins; the Arabs pierce their ears; the Getae make their woven hair blond; the Albanians shine with their white hair; the Moors have the grim darkness of their bodies, while the Gauls have bright skin; the Alans are helpless without horses; nor is the name of the Picts absent from their bodies, since an artisan, by means of minute punctures made with a needle, encloses the juices of native plants, so that this spotted nobility bears scars as a mark of its identity on its painted limbs.” [Col. 0209B]

**Dragging cloaks and broad little boots.** Vallarsius reads *caligas*. The manuscript of Saint Florian has this reading. The old editions have *calligulas*. The Cologne edition has *caligas*. Isidore, book XIX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 34: “*Caliculae* are called *ligae*, either from the hardness of the feet or because they are tied. For *socci* are not tied but merely slipped on.” It is well known how often G and C were formerly exchanged. See the *Onomasticon*. [Col. 0209D]

**After a long restoration to his former status.** Festus: “Gallus Aelius, in book I of his *Meanings Pertaining to Law*, says that *postliminium* is the legal status of one who, free, has gone from one state into another and returns to the same state, according to the law established concerning *postliminia*. Likewise, when a slave of ours has fallen into the power of the enemy and afterward returns to us, he returns under the power of the person to whom he previously belonged, by right of *postliminium*.”

Here Jerome uses *postliminium* in its proper sense. He often uses the same word metaphorically elsewhere. See the *Onomasticon*. [Col. 0209C]

**And with sorrow serving as our bridesmaid.** The old edition has *pronubente*, “with sorrow acting as bridesmaid.”

**They carried away the bodies of the dead.** Pliny, book XI, chapter 30, gives an excellent description of the diligence of ants. Among other things he writes: “Among living creatures, only human beings and ants bury their dead.”

**And with continual murmuring.** Elsewhere *susurrio*. In Job, chapter IV, the ancient Fathers read: “And my ear received, as though stealthily, the veins of his whisper.”

**Sitting upon two camels.** Vallarsius has “riding upon two camels.”

The old edition reads “sitting upon two camels.” The Cologne edition reads “riding upon two camels.” But the reading I have given comes from the manuscript of Saint Florian, and is a common expression in the Middle Ages. Jerome himself, above, in chapter 9 of the *Life of Saint Hilarion*, has “sitting upon an ass.” Thus the manuscripts read there. Aelius Spartianus, in his *Life of Hadrian*: “He did not permit horses to be sat upon in the cities.” So also Mark, chapter XI, concerning the colt of an ass: “which no human being had yet sat upon.” Ambrose cites it this way in book IX, at the beginning of his commentary on Luke XX. The Vulgate now reads “upon which no one …” The same author, book IX of his commentary on Luke, at the beginning: “And therefore the colt is sat upon by the she-ass.” [Col. 0209D]

**Enclosed by the consciousness of chastity alone as though by a wall.** Beasts truly respect chastity. They often not only do no harm to the chaste but also protect them. A notable example occurs in the *Life of Chrysanthus and Daria*, October 25, where Daria, thrown into a brothel, was defended by a lion. Likewise, in the case of Thecla, the bravest and most chaste of martyrs, now a lion, now a lioness, not only did no harm but also provided assistance. See her Acts, September 23. “To be as a wall” is a frequent expression in Jerome, in the manner of a proverb. See the *Onomasticon*. [Col. 0210A]

**Having seized the cub in his teeth.** Thus the old edition and the manuscripts. The Cologne edition has “having seized the cubs in their teeth.” Some might think that the singular *cub* was not placed without reason. There are those who maintain that a lioness gives birth only once, and they even offer an explanation. Pliny, book VIII, chapter 16: “I see that the common belief has been that she gives birth only once, because the womb is torn by the sharp edge of the claws during delivery.” But Pliny adds there the contrary opinion of others: “Aristotle gives a different account, and so on. He therefore says that the lioness gives birth to five cubs in her first litter, then one fewer each year, becoming sterile after producing one.” Thus, if the lioness here produced one cub rather than several, it was her final birth.

**The camels that, because of their extraordinary speed, are called dromedaries.** Vopiscus, in his *Life of Aurelian*: “When Zenobia had been defeated, she fled on camels, which they call dromedaries.” [Col. 0210B]

**Refreshed with a new provision of food.** See *Patrologia*, volume XXIII, column 59, note f. [Col. 0210D]

This is the true spelling and reading. Some printed books add an interpretation: “And refreshed with new *sitarcia*, that is, with provisions.” The word occurs in the Bible, but is written differently by different authorities. In 1 Kings IX: “The loaves have failed from our *sitarcia*,” where the Septuagint has ἀγγεῖα, “vessels.” The Royal edition has *sistartiis*; the Louvain edition, *cistarciis*; the Paris edition, *sitarchiis*. But the Roman edition correctly has *sitarciis*, from σῖτος, “grain” or “provisions,” and ἀρκέω, “to suffice,” hence “sufficient provisions.” The word was used in Latin by Apuleius, *Milesian Tales* 2; by Augustine, volume IX, in the treatise *On the New Song*; and by Isidore, book XX, chapter 9 of the *Etymologies*. “The *sitarciae* of sailors are so called because they are sewn together,” but we have given the true etymology from Greek.

**Sabinian, commander of Mesopotamia.** Thus the manuscripts and the old editions. The Cologne edition has *Sabinus*; the Lyons edition, *Sabaudianus*. But *Sabinianus* is correct. Ammianus, book XVIII, does not, however, call him commander of Mesopotamia, but master of the army in the East and in Mesopotamia: “When affairs throughout Mesopotamia had been brought into this condition, and so forth, the decision was made that Sabinianus—an old man, indeed, and rich in money, but unwarlike, cowardly, and far removed by obscurity from obtaining the rank of master—should be appointed and sent to the eastern regions.” [Col. 0210C]

**Yet I did not trust him as I would a sister.** Jerome, letter 2, to Nepotianus: “Let women’s feet seldom or never wear down the threshold of your little dwelling. Ignore all girls and virgins of Christ equally, or love them equally, lest you remain under the same roof with them, and do not trust in your former chastity. You cannot be stronger than Samson, holier than David, or wiser than Solomon. Always remember that a woman expelled the tenant of paradise from his possession.”

In the same author, volume IX, in the rule for nuns entitled *To Eustochium and the Other Virgins*, falsely attributed to Jerome, chapter 18: “Nothing is more dangerous to a man than a woman, nor to a woman than a man; each is straw, each is fire.” [Col. 0210D]

Bernard, sermon 65 on the *Song of Songs*: “To be always with a woman and not know a woman—is that not greater than raising the dead? You cannot do the lesser thing, yet you want me to believe that you can do the greater?”

[Col. 0211]

## JUNE 12. LIFE OF SAINT ONUPHRIUS, THE HERMIT, BY PAPHNUTIUS THE ABBOT, THROUGH AN ANONYMOUS TRANSLATOR

**104. Onuphrius.** Metaphrastes calls him *Honophrius* on June 11. The Roman Martyrology, June 11: “In Egypt, Saint Onuphrius the anchorite, who lived a religious life for sixty years in a vast desert and, renowned for great virtues and merits, migrated to heaven. His distinguished deeds were written down by the abbot Paphnutius.” [Col. 0219A]

The Greek Menologion, on the same day: “Our holy father Onuphrius of Egypt, who, while he was in a coenobium in the city of Hermopolis in the Thebaid and heard about the life of the prophet Elijah and of John the Forerunner, left the coenobium and lived in the desert for sixty years, seeing no human being at all. After his admirable monastic way of life, he migrated to heaven, and the great Paphnutius buried him. His feast is celebrated on June 12 in his most holy oratory, in the monastery of Saint Alypius.” [Col. 0219B]

The same account appears in the *Menaea*, with certain additions that I do not transcribe, lest the notes become too lengthy.

There is another Onuphrius, mentioned by Metaphrastes in the Acts of the martyrs Galation and Episteme, November 5, which Lipomanus presents in volume V and Surius in volume VI. He lived at the time when persecution of Christians by the pagans was raging. The Menologion places their martyrdom under Decius. He lived near Emesa in Phoenicia, which lies by Mount Lebanon. He was not separated from human society as our Onuphrius was. Through his prayers Leucippe, previously barren, obtained a child, Galation. [Col. 0219C]

**Paphnutius.** There were several Paphnutiuses; concerning them, see here at book II of Rufinus, chapter 13. I discussed Paphnutius the confessor in the *Life of Saint Antony*, chapter 30, no. 68. These Acts, with Paphnutius as author—although which Paphnutius this was is not yet clear to me—are also found in Metaphrastes, but with the *Life of Timothy the Anchorite* and certain other material interwoven. Lipomanus presents them in volume VI, and Surius in volume III, June 11, translated by Gentianus Hervetus.

I have also received from the monastery of Saint James at Liège another translation of the Acts of Onuphrius, into which the Life of Timothy the Anchorite is likewise woven. For the present, however, I preferred to retain the version hitherto current in the *Lives of the Fathers*. I possessed no Latin manuscript copy of it, but I did receive the Greek text from the Boiarian Library. [Col. 0219C]

## Prologue of the Anonymous Translator

**99.** Recently I found the Life of blessed Onuphrius written among the Greek narratives, just as I once learned his deeds from a venerable and most prudent man, namely Gregory.

**Gregory.** Who this Gregory was is not yet clear to me. [Col. 0219C]

Paphnutius, also a most holy man, rewrote this Life from the beginning in the Greek language. Following him, I translated it from Greek into Latin, with the Lord’s assistance, so that, once his praiseworthy life had been made known according to my abilities, it might arouse in its readers both admiration and imitation.

Please do not weigh the rusticity of my speech, but consider in your hearts the endurance required for so great a labor—an endurance which the man filled with God patiently maintained when he despised the glory of worldly vanity and, by living with strict discipline, secured the heavenly kingdom as his inheritance.

## LIFE

[Col. 0211A]

Paphnutius, of blessed memory, thus revealed certain secrets of his thoughts and actions, saying:

### CHAPTER I

One day, while I was sitting alone and silently, I thought in my heart that I should seek the deserts, visit all the places of the holy monks and inspect the form of their devout way of life, and consider how they served God.

Accordingly, I silently set out on my journey and hastened with eager speed toward the desert. I carried with me bread and a little water, lest I fail beneath the labor of the journey I had begun.

When the fourth day had passed, the provisions I had brought with me were exhausted, and my limbs, refreshed by no food, lost their strength. Immediately, however, as divine grace shed its light, the death threatening me was taken away. Recovering my strength, I resumed the journey and spent another four days without tasting anything. [Col. 0211B]

When these days had been completed, utterly exhausted, I fell prostrate upon the ground and lay as though dead. At once, comforted by heavenly assistance, I saw standing beside me a man wondrous in glory, terrible in splendor, praiseworthy in beauty, tall in stature, and radiant in appearance. When I saw him, I was exceedingly astonished; but he approached with a calm face and touched first my hands and then my lips, powerfully restoring my strength (John, little book III, no. 12).

Immediately I rose joyfully and, with God’s favor, continued from there through the solitude for seventeen days, until I reached the place that the Lord had provided to show me, his unworthy servant. There I ceased from the labor of the journey. [Col. 0211C]

### CHAPTER II

While I was resting, therefore, and considering how arduous my journey had been—

**Arduous.** The old edition has *peregre*, “abroad” or “far away.” In my opinion, the meaning is “at a distance,” unless perhaps *peraegre* should be read there. Certainly he testifies in the preceding chapter that he had traveled with great difficulty while his strength was failing. [Col. 0219D]

—I saw at a distance a man terrifying in appearance, completely surrounded by hair like a wild beast. His hair was so extraordinarily long that his body was covered by its spreading mass.

**So that his body was covered by the spreading mass of it.** Jerome, in the prologue to the *Life of Saint Paul the First Hermit*: “A hairy man in an underground cave, with hair reaching to his ankles.” In the *Life of Macarius the Roman*, below, chapter 15: “The hair of his head covered the man’s entire body.” [Col. 0219D]

For clothing he used leaves and grasses, with which he covered only the lower parts of his loins.

**The lower parts of his loins.** He means that his private parts alone were covered with leaves and grasses. [Col. 0219D]

When I saw such a man, I was overcome with extraordinary terror, and was afflicted with fear and astonishment beyond belief, since nothing resembling such a form had ever been shown to my eyes in human shape.

I did not know what to do. But as best I could, I fled and swiftly climbed the nearby mountain. There I collapsed trembling and hid myself from his sight beneath a dense covering of foliage, uttering many sighs.

**100.** I was nearly overcome by age and the labor of abstinence. But when he saw me lying on the mountain, he cried out in a loud voice and said: “Man of God, come down from the mountain. Do not be afraid, for I am a suffering human being, like you.” [Col. 0212A]

Comforted by these words, I recovered my senses. I immediately descended and approached the holy man, timidly prostrating myself at his feet. But he prevented me from lying before him and said: “Rise, rise. You are a servant of God, and you are called Paphnutius, friend of the saints.”
