I rose at once. Although exhausted, I nevertheless sat joyfully before him, already burning with the desire to learn who he was and what sort of life he led. I said:

“Behold, the one who led me through this desert has fulfilled my request. See, my failing limbs now feel some consolation, but my thirsting mind has not yet found refreshment.

“Therefore, venerable father, I earnestly beg you, and I adjure you by him for whose love you inhabit the desolate places of this solitude, to tell me plainly from where you come, what your name is, and when you came here.”

And the man of God, recognizing how willingly I would listen to an account of his labor, said to me: [Col. 0212B–C]

## CHAPTER III

Since I see, beloved brother, that with eager mind you wish to know the long hardships of my life, do not hesitate to hear me recount them from the beginning. I, although unworthy, am called Onuphrius. And behold, it is no fewer than seventy years [Note: **Seventy years.** Thus read the old editions together with the Cologne edition. The Roman Martyrology, the Greek Menologion, the Menaea, and Metaphrastes have “sixty years.”] that I have lived laboriously in this desert. I have often associated with wild beasts; for bread I continually ate the fruits of herbs; and in mountains, caves, and valleys I laid down my wretched body.

For all those years I saw no one except you, nor did I receive food from any human being. I was brought up in a monastery called Hermopolis, in the province named Thebaid [Note: **Brought up in a monastery called Hermopolis, in the province of Thebaid.** The Greek reads: “For formerly I lived in an *abage* monastery, in the region of the Thebaid called Eremopolis.” “I formerly lived in the *abage* monastery of the Thebaid region, which is called Eremopolis.” There is no doubt that *eremopolitou* is corrupt for *Hermopolitou*. [Col. 0220B] Likewise, in the Menaea, *in the city of Hermopolis of the Thebans* should be restored in place of *in the city of the desert*. In Metaphrastes it reads: “Previously I lived in the holy monastery called Eriti of Hermopolis, in the region of the Thebans,” plainly corrupt. From Hervetus’s translation, “in the holy monastery,” it appears that he found in the Greek *in a holy monastery*, which may perhaps originally have stood before *in the abage monastery*.], where nearly one hundred monks lived together.

Their manner of life was as follows: in custom and conduct they all lived with equal-mindedness, and with one heart and one spirit they submitted their necks to the yoke and discipline of the holy rule, fearing not at all the waves of this age. Whatever pleased one pleased them all. With holy minds, pure faith, and perfect charity they walked before God, whom day and night they never ceased to serve with all meekness and patience.

Their silence, together with their abstinence, was so great that no one dared utter a word except in response to a proper question or with a fitting answer. There too, from my youth, I received the nourishment of holy teaching; there I learned from the brothers the norm of regular life. They loved me affectionately, and diligently instructed me how I ought to observe the ordinances of God’s commandments.

## CHAPTER IV

Indeed, venerable brothers, I often heard them praise the life of our blessed Father Elijah, who labored in the desert with such abstinence and prayer that he deserved to receive the greatest power from the Lord; and, carried away in a fiery chariot, to impart to his disciple the gifts of the Holy Spirit that he possessed, and, though already advanced in age, not to see the punishment of death.

Moreover, they set before us the example of the blessed Baptist John, who shone most brilliantly in the narrative of the New Testament and, devoted to divine service for many years, mortified his body until he was found worthy to baptize the Redeemer of the world in the waters of the Jordan and to point him out with his finger as the very Lamb of God.

## CHAPTER V

When I heard them recount such things, I said to them: “Why, my elders, do you marvel at their lives and miracles? Or why do you recall their deeds so constantly? Are they stronger than you, because they live in the desert, or are they weaker?”

They replied: “Son, they are stronger than we are, because they live without human assistance. We, on the other hand, are seen by one another, and together we perform the divine office. Whenever we desire food, we find it prepared; whenever illness or some bodily weakness enters upon us, the care of the brothers immediately assists us with every solicitude.

“We live in brightly constructed buildings, where we are sheltered from the heat of the sun, protected from the flooding of rain, and kept safe from the violence of wind and storm. But the monks who are in the desert receive no consolation except from God.

“If they suffer hardships or tribulations, or begin to fight against the devil, the ancient enemy of the human race, who stands by them? By whom are they helped? Yet it is clear that those who lack human consolation possess divine consolation [Note: **Those who lack human consolation clearly possess divine consolation.** Our saint Xaverius experienced this: when he was in Rome, he had human consolation from his companions; but while he lived alone among barbarians and wild beasts, he fled to God, who filled him with wondrous joys.]

“And if they hunger, who will give them bread? If they thirst, who will give them water, where there is neither bread nor water? It is certainly a great labor to be in desert places, where nothing necessary is found.

“Therefore, when they decide to live in solitude, they first strive firmly to stand in the fear of God. In hunger and thirst, in labor and suffering, they afflict their bodies; they fight manfully against the devil’s snares; and, in order to conquer, they battle against the fiery darts of the wicked one with spiritual swords.

“For that ancient enemy, the inventor of every iniquity, strives to overthrow them, entangle them in partnership with his wickedness, and draw them back from the good intention they had begun; and he again ensnares their minds in worldly pleasures, so that they grow weary and fail to persevere in the work they have begun.

“Therefore almighty God, who does not abandon those who hope in him, surrounds them with the armor of his power, so that the assault of Satan cannot overthrow those whom the greatness of divine mercy protects. For this reason God’s angels are continually sent to them, and through their hands whatever necessities they have are frequently supplied.

“They draw water from a rock, which is interpreted as Christ. For it is written: ‘Those who hope in the Lord will gain strength; they will take wings like eagles; they will fly and not grow weary; they will run, and their steps will not falter’ (Isa. 40). And elsewhere: ‘Those who thirst are refreshed from the heavenly spring’ [Note: **Those who thirst are refreshed from the heavenly spring.** I have not yet encountered this passage here in Holy Scripture. Metaphrastes cites it somewhat differently and says that it is taken from Isaiah.], and the leaves of herbs become sweet in their mouths like a honeycomb.

“But if at any time the devil struggles against them, they rise immediately, stretch out their hands to the Lord, and faithfully pour forth prayers before the divine majesty. At once they are raised up by heavenly aid, and the enemy’s deceitful arrows are utterly destroyed.

“Do you not understand, son, how it is written in the Psalm: ‘For the poor shall not be forgotten forever; the patience of the poor shall not perish eternally’ (Ps. 9)? And again: ‘The Lord heard them in the day of tribulation and delivered them from all distress’ (Ps. 106). Indeed, each person will receive his own reward according to his labor (1 Cor. 3).

“Blessed is the man who is always fearful and diligently does the will of God in this present and fragile life (Prov. 28). Know with complete certainty, son, that God’s angels serve holy and righteous men every day, and that by heavenly power their bodies and souls are continually illumined.”

## CHAPTER VI

Thus, instructed with subtle care by the most holy Fathers in my monastery, I, poor Onuphrius, began silently to consider what glorious happiness those enjoy in heaven who have endured arduous struggles on earth for love of the Lord. My heart burned, and my mind fervently desired to reject entirely the joys of the world and to approach the heavenly homeland with all my strength, as the Psalmist teaches, saying: “But it is good for me to cling to God and to place my hope in the Lord God” (Ps. 72).

## CHAPTER VII

While I was anxiously pondering these things, I rose suddenly in the silent night. I took with me a small loaf of bread and a few vegetables, scarcely enough to last until the fourth day. Thus, according to God’s providence and mercy, I set out, so that he might show me the place of my dwelling.

When I had left the monastery and entered the mountains, I came to the desert. As I considered remaining there, I immediately saw a brilliant light before me, as though coming to meet me. When I saw it, I was very frightened. I therefore thought that I ought to return to the monastery from which I had come.

At once a man of exceedingly beautiful appearance came toward me from the ray of the splendid light and said: “Do not be afraid, for I am God’s angel, appointed by divine providence to guard you from your birth [Note: **An angel appointed to guard you from your birth.** Various Fathers mention guardian angels. Jerome, *Commentary on Matthew*, book 3, chapter 18: “The dignity of souls is great, since each one has an angel assigned to guard it from the beginning of its birth.” The same author, on Isaiah 66: “That each one of us has angels is taught by many passages of Scripture. Among them is this: ‘Do not despise one of these little ones, because their angels continually see the face of the Father who is in heaven’ (Matt. 18). And when the girl Rhoda announced Peter the Apostle, some thought that it was his angel (Acts 12). If this is said of the little ones, and of one man, how much more should it be understood of all the saints, and especially of the apostles, whose angels continually see the face of the Father, according to what is written: ‘The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him’ (Ps. 33). And Jacob says of himself: ‘The angel who delivered me’ (Gen. 48). These are the ones who ascend and descend upon the Son of Man.” Augustine, *Soliloquies*, book, chapter 32: “You make your angels spirits for my sake (Ps. 130), commanding them to guard me in all my ways, lest I strike my foot against a stone (Ps. 90). These are the guardians upon the walls of your new city, Jerusalem.”], so that, at God’s command, I might remain with you and lead you into this desert.

“Be perfect; walk humbly before the Lord; labor with joy; guard your heart with every vigilance; live without reproach; persevere in good work. I shall not abandon you until I present your soul before the presence of the supreme Majesty.”

After the angel had said this, he accompanied me on the journey I had begun.

## CHAPTER VIII

We proceeded together for six or seven miles and came to a certain exceedingly beautiful cave. I approached, wishing to ask whether someone might be living inside. According to the custom of monks, I began to call out and humbly asked for a blessing [Note: **I humbly asked for a blessing.** The addition “according to the custom of monks” is appropriate. Nothing occurs more frequently in these *Lives* than that a guest arriving asks a blessing from the host who receives him.], and then I saw the most holy man come out. I prostrated myself before him, adoring him to the ground.

He stretched out his hands to me, raised me from the earth, gave me the kiss of peace [Note: **He gave me the kiss of peace.** In former times those with whom visitors lodged customarily received them with a kiss. See the *Onomasticon*.], and said: “You are my brother, a companion in the eremitical life. Enter, son. May God grant that his fear remain in you and that your work please him.”

Immediately I entered the cave with him and rested there several days, desiring to learn his practices and to investigate more closely his solitary dwelling. When he recognized my desire, he gave me honorable counsel and gladly explained in loving words how I ought to overcome the devil’s snares.

After some days had passed, he admonished me in these words: “Son, rise and come with me. You must enter farther into the desert and live alone in another cave. If you fight bravely there, you will overcome all the temptations of demons. For this reason God wishes to test you in this desert, to see whether you are willing to obey his commandments faithfully.

“‘All his commandments are faithful, established forever and ever, made in truth and uprightness’ (Ps. 110).”

As the holy man said these things, he rose and traveled with me into the interior of the desert for four days. On the fifth day we came to a place called Calidiomea, where palm trees stood nearby [Note: **Calidiomea.** I do not doubt that the translator encountered a corrupt Greek text and that *Calidiomea* arose from *Kalybe nea* or something similar. The Greek here is certainly *in a little hut*. Likewise, in chapter 9: “And beside Calidiomea I committed his remains to the earth,” where the Greek reads: “And I laid his remains near my hut.” “And I placed his remains beside my *kalybe*, or little hut.” In chapter 12: “We came to Calidiomea, a spiritual place pleasantly adorned with palm trees.” The Greek reads: “We reached a most venerable hut, with a palm tree standing nearby.” “We came to a most religious hut, which had a palm tree standing beside it.”]

Then the man of God said: “Behold, son, see the place that the Lord has prepared for you to dwell in.”

He remained with me for thirty days, teaching me to observe God’s commandments with watchful diligence [Note: **Canta diligentia.** The old edition reads *cautem dignitatem* (“cautious dignity”); the printed *canta diligentia* is materially uncertain.]. When this had been completed, he commended me to the Lord with his holy prayer and, separating from me, returned to his own place. Every year he was accustomed to visit me and never ceased to admonish me, through divine exhortations, with what diligence and simplicity I ought to live.

## CHAPTER IX

Once, when he came to me according to his custom, he suddenly fell to the ground amid words of greeting. Giving his soul back to the Lord, he fell asleep. When I saw this, I was deeply saddened; and, throwing myself upon the ground, I wept profusely, with tears pouring forth. I immediately took his body and committed it to the earth beside Calidiomea.

## CHAPTER X

While I, Paphnutius, was hearing this account from the most holy man Onuphrius, I said to him: “Holy Father, I now perceive that the labor you endured in this wilderness for the name of Christ was no small one.”

The holy man replied: “Believe me, dearest brother: in the desert I endured such things that I often thought myself overcome by death. I was also without hope [Note: **I was without hope (*abspes eram*).** Thus correctly in the manuscripts and the old edition; the Cologne edition reads *ab spe eram*. *Abspes* is formed like *exspes*.] of life many times, scarcely feeling any breath remain in my body.

“By day I was burned by the heat and fire of the blazing sun; by night I was drenched with dew and frost; I was weakened by hunger and thirst. Oh, how great and terrible were the things I suffered! It is neither sufficient nor fitting for anyone to recount the wounds and labors that a dying man must endure for love of the living God.

“The Lord will repay the labors of his saints (Wis. 10). As his riches are not increased, so they will in no way be diminished. He through whom I endured hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and sufferings of many kinds is powerful to console me with heavenly riches among the hosts of angels. I rejected bodily nourishment so that I might be found worthy to receive spiritual nourishment.

“For a holy angel brought me bread every day and supplied water in measured quantity, so that my body might be strengthened, might not fail, and might continually persevere in the praise of God.

“Palm trees stood there, producing the fruit of dates twelve times a year [Note: **Producing the fruit of dates twelve times a year.** Below, in John’s third book, section 2, the same matter is presented somewhat more clearly under an anonymous name: “I found this palm tree bringing me twelve clusters of dates. Each month it brings me one cluster, which is sufficient for me for thirty days; and after that another ripens.”]

“Gathering them each day, I ate them instead of bread, mixed with leaves of herbs; and they were in my mouth like a honeycomb. For it is written in the Gospel: ‘Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God’ (Matt. 4).

“Brother Paphnutius, if you strive to fulfill God’s will, everything necessary for you will be prepared by him. Therefore Truth itself admonishes us, saying: ‘Do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will wear. For your Father knows that you need all these things. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you’ (Matt. 6).”

## CHAPTER XI

As I listened more intently to these words of the blessed man Onuphrius, marveling at his speech, deeds, and labors, I said: “Kind Father, did you receive Communion on Sunday or Saturday from someone? [Note: **Did you receive Communion on Sunday or Saturday?** Some books have “and Saturday.” The Greek reads: “From where do you receive Communion? On Saturday or Sunday?”]

He replied: “Every Sunday or Saturday I find an angel of the Lord waiting, carrying with him the most holy body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. From his hand I receive the most precious gifts and the perpetual salvation of my life.

“Indeed, all the monks who lead a spiritual life in the desert share in such joy. If these holy hermits who inhabit this solitude ever desire to see a human being, they are immediately carried by an angel into heaven. There they contemplate the vision of the souls of the righteous, shining like the sun in the kingdom of their Father; there they behold the multitude of angels and their own souls mingled with the assemblies of the blessed.

“Therefore all who contend in the struggle burn with their whole mind, whole heart, and all their strength in good work, so that they may deserve to possess the glory of the heavenly homeland with Christ and with the saints.”

I learned all these things as the venerable Onuphrius narrated them, near the summit of the little mountain where he had met me [Note: **Near the summit of the little mountain.** The Greek reads: “Below the wing of the mountain.” Here alone I have found *little mountain* for *mountain* rather than *hill*.]. My joy was thus fulfilled, so that I consigned to oblivion every hardship I had endured on the journey.

## CHAPTER XII

“I believe, Father,” I said, “that I may be counted among the fortunate, because I have been found worthy to see you and your outstanding works. Your words are exceedingly beautiful, sweetened with every sweetness; they penetrate the innermost parts of my heart so deeply that I can say with the Psalmist: ‘How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth’ (Ps. 118)!”

He said: “Son, come with me; behold the place of my dwelling. Let us spare words for a little while.”

He immediately rose, and I followed him. He led me on a journey of about three miles. We came to Calidiomea, a spiritual place pleasantly adorned with palm trees. There we poured out prayers to the Lord. When they were completed, we sat upon the ground, conversing about divine words.

As the sun was already turning toward sunset, I saw bread set out with a little water. For the man of God, perceiving that I was weary, said to me: “Indeed, son, I see that you are in danger unless you take food. Rise, therefore, and eat.”

I replied: “The Lord lives” (3 Kings 17), “and blessed is the Lord my God, in whose presence we shall be. I shall neither eat nor drink until, in pure charity, we take food together.”

Thus I scarcely compelled him to do what I wished. When he recognized my desire, however, he broke the bread and gave it to me. We ate and were satisfied, and fragments remained for us after we had eaten. We spent that night almost without sleep, remaining occupied with divine praises.

## CHAPTER XIII

When morning came, after an hour of prayer, I saw that his face had changed so greatly in pallor that I asked him what had happened. He said:

“Do not be afraid, brother Paphnutius, for almighty God has directed you by a straight path to this solitude so that you might bury me honorably and commit my body to the earth. For at this hour the soul is released from the bonds of the flesh and carried into the heavenly kingdom to its Creator.

“Most beloved brother—for I know your desire—when you return to Egypt, remember me in the presence of your brothers and before all who worship Christ.

“This is my request [Note: **This is my request.** An entirely singular privilege and grace before God is here attributed to Onuphrius. In the manuscript *Florarium of the Saints* there is a brief summary of this privilege: “He departed from the world in the year of salvation 370. For he asked and obtained from the Lord that, if anyone should make remembrance of him or offer offerings, feed the poor in his name, or write a book in memory of him, all his sins would be forgiven. And when his soul departed from the body, it would be clean from sins, like an infant newly born.” Such privileges, because the wording varies in certain books, must always be understood with sound judgment.], which I obtained from the Lord God.

“If anyone offers an offering before the sight of our Lord Jesus Christ for love of my name and to his praise [Note: **And to his praise.** Thus in the Cologne edition; the old editions omit it.], he will be freed from every temptation of the devil and from the bondage of human wickedness, and he will become capable of an eternal inheritance with the holy angels in the kingdom of heaven.

“But if anyone is unable to offer an offering or to redeem one because of poverty, let him give alms to a poor person in the name of the Lord and to his honor [Note: **Let him give alms in the name of the Lord and to his honor, etc.** Thus the Cologne edition. The old edition reads: “Let him, for love of me, give alms in the name of the Lord.”], and I shall pray for him before God, so that he may be found worthy to enjoy the heavenly life above.

“If anyone can offer neither an offering nor alms, let him burn incense to our Lord God as a sweet fragrance for love of me, and I shall pray for him to possess everlasting joy.”

I said to him: “My Father, do not be angry if I speak. If someone has neither incense nor any means by which he can appease God [Note: **By which he can appease God.** Thus the Cologne edition. The old edition reads: “By which he can appease you.”], how may he invoke you in any tribulation and yet not lack your blessing?”

Then he replied: “If some poor person in the desert or in any other place has no offering, alms, or incense to sacrifice, let him rise, stretch out his hands to the Lord, and recite the Lord’s Prayer—that is, the *Our Father*—three times for me with attentive mind, singing it in the name of the Holy Trinity. I shall intercede with the Lord for him, so that he may deserve to become a participant in heavenly life with all the saints of God.”

## CHAPTER XIV

Again I said to him: “Lord, if I were worthy, or if the gifts of your grace permitted it, I would most willingly take possession of this place after your death.”

But he said: “It is not granted to you, son, nor did God send you on the pilgrimage of this solitude so that you might take possession of a dwelling here. Rather, he sent you so that you might rejoice with the righteous who are in the desert and strive to make known to the world what you have learned in the wilderness.

“Go to Egypt. Remain there until the end of your life. Complete the good work, and you will receive the crown of everlasting glory.”

## CHAPTER XV

While the man of God was saying these things, I threw myself at his feet and said: “Dear Father, I know that whatever you ask of God, the Lord will grant you, because of the immense labor of your long struggle, by which you afflicted your body for seventy years for the name of the Lord. Therefore give me the gifts of your holy blessing, so that I may become like you in virtue, that my spirit may be directed through your intercession, and that in the future I may deserve to share with you.”

He immediately replied: “Paphnutius, do not be saddened. By the Lord’s gift, your request will stand firm. Stand fast in faith; act manfully; lift your eyes and mind to God; grow strong in the commandments; strive eagerly to do good; and take hold of eternal life (1 Cor. 16).

“May God’s angels protect you and preserve you from every counsel of wickedness, so that you may be found pure and without stain before God on the day of his judgment.”

After this he rose and prayed to the Lord with tears, bending his knees. Suddenly he said: “Into your hands, God, I commend my spirit.”

When he had said this, a splendid light overshadowed his body, and in the brightness of that light his holy soul was released from the flesh.

## CHAPTER XVI

Suddenly I heard the voice of many angels praising God. At the departure of the most holy soul of Saint Onuphrius, the heavens resounded with angelic songs and brought ineffable joy to the stars [Note: **The heavens resounding with angelic songs.** *Aether* is generally listed among the anomalous masculine nouns lacking a plural; here, however, its neuter plural occurs, as elsewhere you will find *aethere* and *aere*. See the *Onomasticon.*]. Through them the heavenly armies carried the soul of the renowned soldier into heaven.

At once my eyes poured forth tears, my inner being gave birth to groans, streams of tears flowed, and the lamentation of wretched Paphnutius overflowed. I mourned him grievously because, having scarcely found him, I could not keep him with me longer.

Then I tore my tunic [Note: **Tunic.** The Greek has *lebitonárion*. It undoubtedly means *lebitonarium*, as in Metaphrastes; the word also occurs elsewhere here. See the *Onomasticon.*] in half. I clothed myself with one part, placed the blessed body in the other, and buried it in a tomb cut from the rock.

When I saw that I remained alone, I began to mourn again. Grieving, I rose and wished to enter the cave where he had lived. But while I stood there, the cave itself collapsed with a great crash, and the palm trees were uprooted and fell together.

Thus I, Paphnutius, understood that it was not the Lord’s will for me to live in that place. I withdrew from it, returned to Egypt, and there reported to the Church what I had seen and heard.

Saint Onuphrius therefore died in the month of June, on the eleventh day [Note: **On the eleventh day.** Thus all editions and the manuscript *Florarium of the Saints*. The Greek, however, has “on the twelfth,” and so do the Roman Martyrology, the Greek Menologion, and the Menaea. Metaphrastes reads: “It was the sixteenth day of Pauni, but the ninth of the month of June according to the Romans.” For how this is to be understood, see the table of months in the *Onomasticon*. The manuscript *Florarium of the Saints* assigns Onuphrius’s death to the year 370; I do not know from where it derived this. The manuscript of Saint James at Liège, in its final chapter, says that lions dug out the tomb for Onuphrius with their claws; I mentioned this in the *Life of Saint Paul the First Hermit*, chapter 13, section 50. This is absent from the present *Life* and from Metaphrastes.], that is, on the third day before the Ides of that month.

There his benefits are granted even to the present day, to the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and power for ever and ever. Amen.

# LIFE OF SAINT PACHOMIUS

## PRELIMINARY MATERIAL

### Eulogies of Distinguished Men concerning Saint Pachomius

The Roman Martyrology, May 14:

“In Egypt, Saint Pachomius, abbot, who established many monasteries in that region and wrote a rule for monks, which he learned at the dictation of an angel.”

The Greek Menologion, May 15:

“Of our holy Father Pachomius of Tabenna. Saint Pachomius was from the Thebaid of Lower Egypt, in the time of Constantine the Great. His parents were worshipers of idols; but after converting to the faith of Christ, he received baptism and embraced the monastic life. He hastened to the desert, where, having attained perfection of life and become famous for virtues and miracles, he acquired many followers, so that before he departed this life the number of monks formed by him had reached one thousand four hundred.”

The Menaea likewise, on May 15, give a more precise brief account of his life.

Bede, Usuard, Rabanus, Ado, and Notker also speak of him; they drew their accounts from Gennadius, whose eulogies are given below.

Of this same Pachomius, see Palladius, chapter 38; Sozomen, book 3, chapter 13; Nicephorus, book 9, chapter 14; Vincentius, *Historical Mirror*, book 17, chapter 82, and book 18, chapter 47; Antoninus, part 2, title 15, chapter 11, section 1; and Peter Equilinus, bishop, in the *Catalogue of the Saints*, book 4, chapter 171.

Athanasius was the first to bring to Rome the name of Pachomius and the discipline of the monks whom he had instituted, as Saint Jerome states in letter 16, to Principia.

Concerning the date of his death, Sigebertus of Miraeus, in his *Chronicle*, places it in the eighth year of Arcadius and Honorius, which he reckons as the year 405 of Christ, while other editions place it in the following year: “Pachomius the abbot, at the age of 110, was brought to completion in virtues.”

There was another Pachomius, a confessor, mentioned by Heraclides in the *Paradise*, chapter 11, who lived in Scetis and is called Pachon by Palladius in chapter 29 of the *Lausiac History*. Peter speaks of this Pachomius above, book 4, chapter 172.

There was also another Pachomius, a bishop and martyr, mentioned by Eusebius, book 8 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 14; Peter speaks of him above, book 11, chapter 32.

### Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 3, chapter 13

“Pachomius became the leader of those called the Tabennesiotes. Their habit and manner of life differed in certain respects from the discipline of the other monks, yet it was directed toward virtue and stirred up the soul to despise earthly things and to look upward, so that it might easily proceed toward heavenly things when it had been released from the body,” and so forth.

The printed Latin rendering reads: “Pachomius was the leader of those called Tabennesiotes. Their dress and way of life differed in certain respects from the discipline of the other monks, yet fixed the mind’s gaze upon the contemplation of virtue, stirring the soul both to despise earthly things and to seek heavenly things, so that, when it departed from the body’s custody, it might have a very easy entrance into heaven,” and so forth.

### Gennadius, *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 7

Pachomius was a monk, a man endowed with apostolic grace both in teaching and in performing signs, and the founder of the Egyptian coenobia. He wrote:

**A Rule** [Note: **A rule.** A brief summary of this rule is found here in the *Life of Pachomius*, chapter 22. The first person, so far as I know, to publish it in full was Achilles Statius of Portugal, at Rome from the press of the heirs of Antonio Blado, in the year of the Lord 1575; then again in 1588. Peter Ciaccon also published a more accurate version from the Roman presses and added it to his edition of Cassian. Saint Jerome translated Pachomius’s rule, written in Egyptian, into Greek and rendered it into Latin at the request of the monk Silvanus, at the time when Saint Paula departed this life, in the consulship of Honorius VI and Aristenetus, in the year of the Lord, according to the *Fasti* of Onuphrius, 404.] suitable for both kinds of monks, which he had received at the dictation of an angel.

He also wrote:

**Letters to the fellow-superiors of his office** [Note: **Letters.** None of these letters, so far as I know, survives today except the preliminary ones placed before his other works.], in which he enclosed an alphabet veiled in mystical sacraments, as though surpassing the understanding of ordinary human custom, and, I believe, revealed only to those who possessed the corresponding grace or merits.

One to Abbot Syrus; one to Abbot Cornelius.

To the superiors of all the monasteries, so that, gathered together in one older monastery called *Baum* in the Egyptian language, they might celebrate the day of Easter as though according to an eternal law: one letter.

Likewise, concerning the day of remission, which is observed in the month of August, so that the superiors might gather together: one letter.

And to the brothers who had been sent outside the monastery to work: one letter.

### Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Pachomius was an abbot, a very great organizer of the monks of his time, founder of many coenobia, and a man of most holy conduct, shining with many miracles during his life and after his death. Since he was learned and instructed in the divine Scriptures, he wrote many letters for the edification of the brothers, of which the following are reported:

To Cornelius, abbot, one letter; to Syrus, abbot, one letter; to the superiors of the coenobia, one letter; to the working brothers, one letter; and also one book containing the rule of the monks.

He flourished under the emperors Valentinian and Theodosius, in the year 390.

## Concerning Dionysius Exiguus, the Translator of This Life

### Cassiodorus, *Institutions of Divine and Secular Learning*, chapter 23

Dionysius was a monk, Scythian by nation but thoroughly Roman in character, highly learned in both languages, and by his actions rendering the justice he had read in the Lord’s books. He had examined and understood the divine Scriptures with such diligence that, whatever question he was asked, he had a suitable answer ready without any delay. He studied dialectic with me and, by the Lord’s favor, spent many years of his life gloriously, as an example of a splendid mastery. I am ashamed to say of a companion what I cannot find in myself.

For in him great simplicity existed together with wisdom, humility together with learning, and restraint in speech together with eloquence; so that he never placed himself before even the lowest servants, yet was unquestionably worthy of conversation with kings.

May he intercede for us, who was accustomed to pray with us, so that, supported here by his prayer, we may now be aided by his merits.

Requested by Stephen, bishop of Salona, he composed from Greek exemplars the *Ecclesiastical Canons* [Note: [Col. 0225D] *Ecclesiastical Canons.* These canons were formerly published at Mainz in folio in 1525; afterward at Paris in octavo in 1609. In the latter edition, from the library of Nicolas Fabri, one finds Dionysius’s own letter to Stephen, bishop of Salona, in which he briefly states what canons he translated and published: “First of all, the 110 Canons of the Apostles from Greek; then the rules of the Council of Nicaea; and thereafter those of all the councils, both those held previously and those held subsequently, [Col. 0226A] up to the council of the 150 bishops who assembled at Constantinople, arranged in numerical order—that is, from the first chapter through 162, as they are found in the Greek authority. Then, adding the decrees of the holy Council of Chalcedon, we declare that in these the series of Greek canons ends. So that we may not appear to withhold anything further from your knowledge, the decrees of the Council of Sardica and of the African Council, which have been published in Latin, are likewise shown to be distinguished by numbers assigned by us.”] according to his character, being straightforward and eloquent, he arranged them with the light of great eloquence. Today the Roman Church embraces them in its highly celebrated practice. You too ought to read them continually, lest you appear culpably ignorant of rules of the Church so beneficial.

He also translated many other works from Greek into Latin [Note: [Col. 0226A] *He translated many works from Greek into Latin.* Since Cassiodorus does not specify what these were, you have them here partly in Sigebert and partly in Trithemius.], which may serve the benefit of the Church. He possessed such mastery of Latin and Greek that, whenever he took Greek books into his hands, he could run through them in Latin without difficulty, and then reread Latin works in Attic speech, so that one would believe that what his mouth poured forth with effortless speed had actually been written in that language.

It would be lengthy to recount everything about that man, who is shown to have possessed this outstanding virtue among his other virtues: although he had given himself wholly to God, he did not disdain to take part in the company of secular people. He was exceedingly chaste, although he saw other men’s wives every day; gentle, although he was almost continually assailed by the mad turmoil of the nations. He shed tears, moved by compunction, when he heard the chattering words of merriment. He fasted without reproaching those who were dining, and for that reason gladly took part in banquets, so that, when questioned amid bodily feasts, he might always display spiritual riches. [Col. 0223D] Yet if he sometimes ate, he used little food, but food of the ordinary kind. 188 Hence I judge it the highest kind of patience to remain amid human delicacies while preserving the measure of abstinence. But, to report the goodness of his mind without affected praise, he was wholly Catholic, wholly and steadfastly devoted to the rules of the Fathers; and whatever readers can seek out in various places was recognized as shining in his knowledge. Certain wicked men maliciously attempt to heap accusations upon his name, so that their own errors may appear to be excused to some extent. But he, having now abandoned the perversity of the world, and by the Lord’s favor buried in the peace of the Church, must be believed to have fellowship among the servants of God.

[Col. 0224A] Venerable Bede, *On the Reckoning of Time*, chapter 45.

The order of the times is prefixed by the course of the first nineteen-year cycle, which Greek calculators observed from the years of the emperor Diocletian. But Dionysius, the venerable abbot of the city of Rome, endowed with no mean knowledge of both languages, namely Greek and Latin, when writing Paschal cycles, did not wish—as he himself testifies—to attach to them the memory of the impious persecutor; rather, he chose to mark the times from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that the beginning of our hope might be clearer to us, and the cause of the restoration of humankind—that is, the passion of our Redeemer—might shine forth more evidently.

Sigebert, *Catalogue of Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 27.

Dionysius, Roman abbot, surnamed Exiguus, [Col. 0224B] distinguished by twofold learning in Greek and Latin, translated from Greek into Latin the writings of Proterius [Note: [Col. 0226B] *Proterius.* These writings, or letters to Pope Leo, no longer exist. The following authors explain more clearly how many there were and what they contained. Sigebert, in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 26: “Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, also wrote to Pope Leo, who was uncertain about celebrating Easter in that year; since it was an embolismic year, some thought it was an ordinary year.” That year was 455, as Sigebert states here in his notice of Dionysius Exiguus. Isidore likewise speaks of the same Proterius, in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 10: “Proterius, bishop of the Alexandrian Church, wrote letters to Leo, bishop of the Roman see, concerning the feast of Easter. During the reign of Leo Augustus, the successors of the heretic Dioscorus, under the leadership of Timothy, stirred up a revolt and most cruelly killed him; they installed Timothy himself in his place as bishop of Alexandria.” Trithemius, in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*: [Col. 0226C] “Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, a man most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular literature, an outstanding theologian and computist, whom, during the reign of Leo Augustus, the successors of the heretic Dioscorus, after fomenting a revolt under the leadership of Timothy, cruelly killed, and in whose place they set up Timothy as an idol for the bishopric of Alexandria. Among other works he wrote: Three letters to holy Pope Leo concerning the celebration of Easter; one letter to Hilary on the same subject, beginning *Quoniam sanctitas vestra orta* (‘Since your Holiness has arisen’); several letters to various persons; and certain other works.” He flourished under the emperor Leo, in the year of the Lord 460.”] of Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, to Pope Leo concerning the celebration of Easter in the year of the Lord 455.

He also translated from Greek into Latin Gregory of Nyssa’s book *On the Making of Man* [Note: [Col. 0226C] *Gregory of Nyssa’s Book On the Making of Man.* This book, with Dionysius Exiguus as translator, was published among the works of Nyssa from the press of Episcopius in 1562. The letter of John Conon, in which he admits that he corrected this translation somewhat in certain places, was not prefixed to it; according to Lewenclavius, this was because of a Greek fragment. For that letter was prefixed there to another book of Nyssa. Later Lewenclavius published this same book of Nyssa in Greek and Latin from his own version, in octavo, at Basel, from the press of John Oporinus, in 1567. Trithemius is incorrect in reading *Emissenus* instead of *Nyssenus*.], and the *Life of Abbot Pachomius* [Note: [Col. 0226D] *The Life of Abbot Pachomius.* This is the work that has hitherto circulated among the *Lives of the Fathers*. Gentianus Hervetus translated it from Greek as well; it may be found in Aloysius Lipomanus, volume VI of *The Lives of the Saints*, and in Laurentius Surius, volume III. His version is much fuller than ours. See below, after number 2.]. He himself also wrote, after Cyril, a cycle of five cycles, beginning with the year of the birth of Jesus Christ 532, which is the final year of the great cycle, consisting of 532 years once completed from the birth of Christ, and so forth.

Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

Dionysius, Roman abbot, surnamed Exiguus, as is said, a man certainly great and most distinguished in talent and learning, learned in the sacred Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular literature, renowned in Greek and Latin eloquence, and an excellent computist and calculator of times. He wrote in Latin several short works, of which I have found only the following:

The great Paschal cycle of 532 years, one book;

*On the Reckoning of the Feast of Easter*, one book; *The Reckoning of the Feast of Easter*.

As for the rest [Note: [Col. 0226D] *As for the rest.* In our Louvain library there is a manuscript letter of Dionysius Exiguus to the monk Eugyppius. [Col. 0227A] His letter to Bishop Petronius is also cited by Petavius, in *The Epoch of Years*.], I have found nothing. He translated from Greek into Latin the *Life of Saint Pachomius the Abbot*, as well as Gregory of Emesa’s book *On the Making of Man*, and the writings of Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, to Pope Leo [Note: [Col. 0227A] *To Pope Leo.* From this passage of Trithemius, Genebrard, in book III of his *Chronology*, thought that this Dionysius lived in the time of Pope Leo I. Because he did not properly understand Trithemius, he believed that Dionysius had dedicated to Pope Leo his book, which he had translated from Proterius. Trithemius does not mean this; rather, he means that Dionysius translated Proterius’s book, which Proterius himself had sent to Pope Leo. For Trithemius says both here and more clearly in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Proterius: “Among other works he wrote three letters to holy Pope Leo concerning the celebration of Easter.” Lewenclavius errs more seriously, believing that Dionysius, the translator of Nyssa’s *On the Making of Man*, lived four hundred years ago.]. And certain other works [Note: [Col. 0227A] *And certain other works.* Besides those already cited, I find Proclus of Constantinople in Greek and Latin, with a preliminary letter by Dionysius Exiguus to Felicianus and Pastor. It was published by John Sichardus in the *Antidote against Heresies*, in folio, at Basel, by Henry Petri, in 1528; Margarinus de la Bigne afterward included it, in Latin only, in volume III of the *Library of the Fathers*. In the same *Antidote* there are two letters of Cyril of Alexandria to Successus, bishop of Diocaesarea in Isauria, [Col. 0227B] translated by Dionysius Exiguus, together with his preface to John and Leontius. The authors cited here, who compiled the *Catalogue of Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, do not mention these letters. In our college at Louvain there is also a manuscript translation by Dionysius of Nyssa’s work *On the Nature of Man*. 111 Thus far, then, concerning both Pachomius himself and the translator of his Life. But who was the author of his Life? Aloysius Lipomanus, in volume VI of *The Lives of the Saints*, and Laurentius Surius, in volume III, assign the *Life of Pachomius* to the author Metaphrastes. Yet the author of this Life, who was far more ancient, must be sought. For Metaphrastes lived around the year 930, whereas Dionysius, the translator of this Life, lived around the year 530. Whoever the Greek author was, he was contemporary with Pachomius himself. For in chapter 10 of this Life he says that he received what he writes from those who lived with Pachomius. Although Metaphrastes expresses the Life word for word as it was composed by the first author, he nevertheless includes many chapters [Col. 0228B] that do not appear in Dionysius, the ancient translator: among them all the chapters from 40 through 57 inclusive; likewise those from 73 through 78 inclusive; again chapters 85 and 86; and finally chapter 90. Hence Metaphrastes seems to have encountered more complete copies.].

He began his cycle in the year of the Lord 532, which was the final year of the great Paschal cycle, which, once completed, always returns to the same point.

He therefore flourished under the great emperor Justinian, in the year of the Lord [Col. 0224D] 540.

The same author, *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, book II, chapter 4.

Dionysius, Roman abbot, surnamed Exiguus, a man highly learned in the divine Scriptures and most skilled in secular literature, an outstanding calculator and geometrician, instructed in Greek and Latin eloquence. Having acquired great authority for his learning among the ancients, he published works not unworthy of notice, of which only a few have come to my knowledge.

A book *On the Reckoning of Easter*. 109 Also the great cycle of 532 years. He composed several letters as well.

From Greek into Latin he translated the writings of Proterius of Alexandria to Pope Leo concerning the celebration of Easter; [Col. 0225A] also Gregory of Emesa’s book *On the Making of Man*; and he rendered the *Life of Saint Pachomius* into Latin.

He flourished in the year of the Lord 570.

Baronius, *Notes on the Roman Martyrology*, 14 May.

Dionysius, Roman abbot, surnamed Exiguus, translated into Latin, more than a thousand years ago, the remarkable deeds of Pachomius, written in Greek. [Col. 0226A] His preface stands before the *Life of Saint Pachomius*; you have it in the first part of the *Lives of the Holy Fathers*, chapter 54. We are surprised that Lipomanus and Surius omitted it; as a monument to the talent of so great and highly praised a man, it ought not to have been passed over. For what sort of man he was, and how great in holiness and learning, consult Cassiodorus, his contemporary, in book I of the *Institutions for Divine Reading*.

[Col. 0227]

## MAY 14: THE LIFE OF SAINT PACHOMIUS, ABBOT OF TABENNA, BY AN UNCERTAIN GREEK AUTHOR, TRANSLATED BY DIONYSIUS EXIGUUS, ROMAN ABBOT

## PROLOGUE OF DIONYSIUS EXIGUUS, THE TRANSLATOR

[Col. 0227] To the venerable and in Christ also most magnificent lady, Dionysius Exiguus.

[Note: [Col. 0271C] *To the lady.* This entire prologue of the translator is absent from the Cologne edition. It is found in manuscripts and older editions. In the editions the reading is incorrectly *Domine* (“lord”), as though this Life were addressed to some prominent man. Rather, both the dedication itself and its grammatical construction recommend reading *Dominae* (“lady”), as the manuscripts of Saint Lawrence at Liège and of Gembloux have it. [Col. 0271D] But who is this lady? It is difficult to determine. I nevertheless suspect that Galla is meant, the daughter of the consul and patrician Symmachus, born of a distinguished family and eminent in religion. She lived at Rome in a monastery beside the church of Saint Peter during the time of this Dionysius Exiguus. I am led to this by the subject matter of the following two sections, in which the informers of Symmachus and his glorious martyrdom for Christ are indicated. This famous Galla is commemorated in the Roman Martyrology on October 5: “At Rome, Saint Galla, widow, daughter of Symmachus the consul, who, after the death of her husband, remained for many years at the church of blessed Peter, devoted to prayer, almsgiving, fasting, and other holy works; Saint Pope Gregory described her most blessed passing.” Arnoldus Wion, however, disputes the day of Saint Galla’s death in part II, book III of *The Tree of Life*, under April 6, on which day he proves from Saint Gregory that her death occurred. He insists that October 5 is rather the day of her Translation or Commemoration. Saint Gregory says of her in book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 13: “For in the time of the Goths, Galla, a girl of the highest nobility of this city, daughter of the consul and patrician Symmachus, was given in marriage during her adolescence; within the space of one year she was widowed by his death, and she devoted herself in a monastery to the church of the apostle Peter,” and so forth. From this the later authors drew their accounts: Peter in book IX, chapter 25 of his *Catalogue of the Saints*; Trithemius in book III, chapter 13 of *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*. Fulgentius also wrote an excellent letter to Galla on consolation over her husband’s death and on the condition of widows, in which, among other things, he says: “Learn, then, that you too should attribute nothing to nobility of birth. Although formerly, among secular people, you were distinguished by a grandfather, father, father-in-law, and husband who had been consuls, recognize that you are now to become distinguished in that in which the virtue of humility increases within you.” In the same letter he states that he would write to her sister Proba, since they evidently lived as sisters in the same monastery: “We have also decided, if the Lord wills and if we live, to write something about fasting and prayer to your sister, the holy virgin of Christ Proba, whom the Lord has now deigned to give to the city of Rome as an exceptional example of virginity and humility.” At about the same time Eugyppius wrote to the virgin Proba the book *Treasures*, compiled from Augustine, as Cassiodorus testifies in *Divine Reading*, chapter 23. In my opinion there was another, older Galla, the granddaughter of Quintus Aurelius Symmachus the elder, ordinary consul and prefect of the city, whom he himself mentions in book VI, letter 32, and whom he calls his little granddaughter. There was also another Galla, the wife of Eucherius, later bishop of Lyon, whom Ado mentions in his *Martyrology* under November 16 when discussing Eucherius, as does Peter in book X, chapter 67 of his *Catalogue of the Saints*. There is another Galla whose tomb Gregory of Tours discusses in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 36; she was buried in the church of Saint Venerandus in Auvergne, and Baronius in the *Martyrology* thought her to be the same as the first. But the former was enclosed at Lyon, whereas this woman was buried in Auvergne. [Col. 0273B] There was likewise another widow named Galla, with her daughter Simpliciola, whom Saint Augustine praises in letter 103; they lived in Africa.]

I have responded to the pious purpose of your devotion with whatever ability I possessed, fulfilling as a translator my duty concerning the Life of Saint Pachomius, just as it was found in Greek. Since your authority had compelled me to delay over this work for a long time, it was not proper for me, who had already become bound by my promise, to postpone what I had promised—especially to you, who are accustomed to consider the will rather than the strength of those who make promises. For, by Christ’s grace, you undertake many things both to be read and to be imitated, and with eager desire you wish to learn the institutions of the blessed Fathers, so that, combining their achievements with your own efforts, you may offer to future ages a singular testimony to the divine gift. You openly acknowledge that you devote the greatest care to the virtues that you love in the conduct of the saints, with whom you are also joined by the quality of your distinguished works. For no one loves virtue except the one who follows it, and similarity of character provides a great indication of union. Conversely, a differing way of life is a great source of discord even among those related by blood. Thus wicked hatreds frequently arise among relatives; thus hostile quarrels are born; thus insatiable and blind malice rages even to the shedding of blood, while the wicked envy the good, the greedy the generous, the turbulent the most peaceable, the sluggish the diligent, the implacable the mild, the savage the tranquil, the rash the modest, the foolish the wise, the cunning the simple, and the frenzied even the most gentle.

But the apostolic trumpet rebukes such conduct more effectively. For when the Teacher of the Gentiles was describing the dangers of the last times, he continued, saying: “For people will be lovers of themselves, greedy, boastful, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, without peace, slanderers, incontinent, savage, without kindness, traitors, reckless, swollen with pride, lovers of pleasures rather than of God” (2 Tim. 3). Here blessed Paul gathered together with marvelous brevity what he had set forth at greater length above, showing that they would be such because they would be lovers of pleasures and because they would subject themselves to the most vicious desires. From this all evils arise: God is despised, while pleasures are loved. Through these the devil entices in order to deceive, delights in order to mislead, and flatters in order to destroy. And lest future things be preferred to present things, heavenly things to earthly, and eternal things to what is brief, he presses the point: “Lovers of pleasures rather than of God, having the appearance indeed of piety, but denying its power” (ibid.). That is, they appear to be Christians in name only, not in deed. Like internal enemies, they rage even more wickedly than external enemies; established within the Church, they tear apart the Church’s pious members. The Apostle immediately commands us to avoid them, so that we may be separated from their company not so much by difference of place as by difference of character.

Nor should anyone find it surprising that such plagues [Note: [Col. 0273B] *That such plagues.* He immediately adds: “Such things were experienced by your blessed and glorious father, my lord.” He means, I think, the informers against Symmachus and Boethius, concerning whom Procopius writes as follows in book I of *The Gothic War*: “Symmachus and Boethius, his son-in-law, had from their ancestors the nobility of their family. They were foremost among the Roman Senate and had both held the consulship. Both practiced philosophy and cared for justice no less than anyone; by relieving the poverty of many citizens and foreigners with their wealth, they brought them aid. Having attained great glory, they aroused against themselves the bitterest men, who were driven by envy. Theodoric, persuaded by these slanderers that the two men were attempting revolutionary measures, had them killed and entered their possessions into the public treasury.”] should oppose just men, since, full of deceit and full of trickery, they do not spare even themselves and often disagree with one another.

“Such things were experienced by your blessed and glorious father” [Note: [Col. 0273C] *Your father.* This was Quintus Aurelius Memmius Symmachus, former ordinary consul and patrician, to whom there survives a letter of Ennodius, book VII, letter 25; the same man is also mentioned in book VIII, letter 28. King Theodoric likewise wrote to him, in Cassiodorus, book II, letter 14, and book IV, letters 6 and 51. He is also mentioned by the same author among the senators to whom the investigation of Praetextatus and Basilius, who were accused of magic, was entrusted, book IV, letter 22. Pope Hormisdas also mentions Symmachus in letters 37 and 66, which are found among the decretal letters of the popes. It seems, however, that Dionysius means here Symmachus, the father of Galla, who endured martyrdom for Christ; this may be inferred from the words that follow: “He not only patiently and courageously endured their attacks for justice, but also, by a blessed end, steadfastly and sublimely overcame all the adversities of the world for the truth—which is Christ.”] my lord, who not only patiently and courageously endured their attacks for justice, but also, by a blessed end, steadfastly and sublimely overcame all the adversities of the world for the truth—which is Christ.

I earnestly desire that the perfect rule of his life, almost consonant with the merits of the saints, be set down in learned and eloquent discourse by accomplished men, so that the great distinction of your family and its great honor may be recognized in some degree, and so that the admirable virtue of a man scarcely expressible even by the ancients—virtue which, with Christ’s favor, you fulfill by hereditary right—may be made known to posterity through the service of reading.

## Prologue of the Author

[Col. 0229]

Our Lord Jesus Christ, the fountain of wisdom and the true light of knowledge, the true Word of God the Father, through whom all things were made, knowing that our weakness is inclined and prone to sins, displayed many remedies of his mercy toward us. For our father Abraham, when he obeyed the divine commands and offered his son in sacrifice, pleased God and, on account of his faith, immediately received both an heir and a reward (Gen. 22). God also swore to him by himself, saying: “Surely I will bless you, and surely I will multiply you, like the stars of heaven in multitude and like the innumerable sand at the shore of the sea. And again: In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed” (ibid.). Concerning this seed the Apostle clearly instructs us, saying: “He does not say ‘and to seeds,’ as though referring to many, but as to one, ‘and to your seed,’ which is Christ” (Gal. 3).

All the holy prophets also, foreseeing this mystery of such great salvation as the Holy Spirit revealed it, and knowing that God could in no way lie, announced that the heavenly physician would come to heal our sicknesses, and they sought by continual supplication that he would hasten his coming for the sake of the human race. But the merciful God, who always anticipates pious prayers and never abandons those who seek him with their whole heart, fulfilled his promises in the last days, sending his Son, born of a woman, made subject to the law, 113 who would suffer in the flesh in the likeness of our mortality and by his death destroy him who held the power of death (Heb. 2). Finally, remaining impassible in his divinity, he redeemed us from corruption and destruction and released us from the unbreakable bonds of hell. Having completed the dispensation of our redemption, he bestowed forgiveness of sins upon all nations through the washing of regeneration, and embraced all who came together in true faith through apostolic teaching, according to what he says in the Gospel: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28).

Therefore, when the proclamation of the Gospel shone throughout the whole earth and many came by the grace of Christ into adoption as sons, the enemy of the human race burned fiercely and attempted to stir up battles of temptation far more severe than those he had previously raised against the servants of God, unhappy in his suspicion that he might be able to block the path of heavenly mercy for us. But by this very intention he was deceived and overthrown. For, by the help of the divine gift, the snares of his power are trampled down by faithful and watchful people, so that shame may come upon him, while everlasting glory is granted to the servants of Christ.

For, by the Lord’s permission, when pagan emperors existed as a test of the patience and faith of those who wisely waged spiritual battles, and the storm of persecution raged everywhere against Christians, many holy martyrs in Egypt persevered in the name of Christ through various tortures even unto death. Together with Peter, bishop of the city of Alexandria, they obtained everlasting crowns and immortal rewards.

The multitude of the faithful increased day by day and was wonderfully enlarged in every place. Many churches and memorials of the martyrs were also built with ever greater zeal. Monasteries too became extremely numerous; those who devoted themselves to continence and renounced the world adorned the solitude itself. For those who had believed in Christ from among the nations, considering the sufferings of the martyrs and their sincere devotion in confessing Christ, began themselves, through the Lord’s grace, to follow the life and conduct of the saints and to adopt this discipline, so that the Apostle’s words might also apply to them: “They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, in want, oppressed, afflicted—of whom the world was not worthy—wandering in deserts and mountains, in caves and caverns of the earth” (Heb. 11).

Finally, desiring the repose of solitude, they obtained, by the divine gift, the joys of their own salvation and faith, and soon provided others with examples of a higher and more sacred life. Stripped of all earthly concerns, while still dwelling in the body they imitated the holiness of angels. By climbing through it to the highest summits of virtue, they shone beyond the wonder of mortals, so that they were in no respect inferior to the most ancient Fathers. They even equaled the merits of those who fought unto blood for the name of Christ Jesus our Lord, destroying the assaults of invisible enemies, concerning whom the Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in heavenly places” (Eph. 6).

Guarding against their manifold attacks and bravely crushing the head of the ancient serpent, they obtained everlasting rewards, concerning which it is written: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (Isa. 64; 1 Cor. 2).

## LIFE

[Col. 0231]

### CHAPTER ONE

At that time the Life of blessed Antony had been splendidly set before everyone for imitation. He was an emulator of the great Elijah and Elisha, as well as of Saint John the Baptist; with singular zeal he pursued the secrets of the inner desert and lived on earth the life of heavenly beings through his love of virtue. Saint Athanasius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, bore witness to him in his own style: truly a worthy narrator of Antony’s way of life, who, at the request of the brothers, wrote his Life for the benefit of many and presented him for imitation by spiritual men.

In this work the same pontiff also mentioned Saint Ammon [Note: [Col. 0273D] *Ammon.* You may read about him and Theodore in Athanasius’s *Life of Antony*, chapter 32. In the older editions the entire line after “foundations” is missing, namely, “of the conduct of those brothers who now dwell on Mount Nitria.”], by whose grace-filled agency the foundations of the way of life of those brothers who now dwell on Mount Nitria were first laid, and also Theodore, a most holy man, who had been with the old man mentioned above. He reported that Theodore, devoted to God with a singular and perfect purpose and with undeceitful faith, had overcome the devil’s many machinations.

Thus, with divine grace abundantly diffused everywhere, it showed that what is sung as written in the Psalms had been fulfilled: “You visited the earth and watered it; you multiplied it and enriched it” (Ps. 64). For joy and gladness arose in place of sadness and groaning; happiness and security succeeded anxiety and misery.

From this point onward, therefore, remarkable Fathers of monks arose in almost every region, whose names are shown to have been inscribed in the book of the living. At that time very few monks were still reported throughout Egypt [Col. 0231C] and the Thebaid. For after the persecution of the cruel emperors Diocletian and Maximian, a multitude of nations entered in (Rom. 11), as had been divinely ordained, and the fruitfulness of the Church began to produce abundant harvests, as holy bishops, according to the apostolic teaching of that time, displayed the way of faith also by sincere conduct.

### CHAPTER TWO

At that time a certain Pachomius, living in the Thebaid as a pagan according to the rite and tradition of his parents, became a Christian under the guidance of divine grace. From his adolescence, he is said to have taken up the eminent virtue of frugality. Therefore, for the glory of Christ, who called us from darkness to light, and for the benefit of those who will read this account, I shall briefly recount what his conduct was like from childhood, because even his beginnings do not differ from such perfection as his.

### CHAPTER THREE

When he was still a boy, he came with his parents to a certain idol placed on the bank of the Nile, as though to offer sacrifices. When the most impure priest wished to perform the sacrilegious rites as usual, the presence of Pachomius caused the demon’s illusions to vanish completely. Then the same priest, hesitating for a long time, remained motionless in the likeness of the idol he worshiped, greatly wondering why the demons did not give their customary responses. At last, when an unclean spirit revealed the matter, he learned that the unusual silence had occurred because of the boy Pachomius, and, astonished, burst out with these words: “Why has the enemy of the gods come here? Drive him far away from here—far away—and remove him as quickly as possible.”

When his parents heard this and saw him separated from their company, they were filled with great sorrow, especially because he had been declared the enemy of the gods by such a testimony. His parents were therefore uncertain what would become of him, since earlier, when he had tasted a little of the demons’ libation wine, he had immediately vomited it up. Since they saw that they could not determine the matter, they remained silent. They nevertheless insisted that he be instructed in Egyptian letters and trained in the studies of the ancients.

### CHAPTER FOUR

At the same time, while Constantine continued in imperial power after the persecution [Note: [Col. 0273D] *While Constantine continued in power after the persecution.* This is the reading of the manuscripts and older editions. In the Cologne edition, “after the persecution” is missing, and *properante* appears there incorrectly instead of *perdurante*. Understand this as referring to the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian, which lasted ten years, as stated by Eusebius in book VIII, chapter 37 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, and in the *Chronicle*. That persecution began in the nineteenth year of Diocletian and lasted until the sixth year of Constantine—thus producing the exact ten-year period—when Maxentius was killed, as stated by the uncorrupted manuscript of the Amandine *Chronicle of Eusebius*, and by the editions of Pontacus and Scaliger. Therefore “after the persecution,” namely that of Diocletian and Maximian, is correct.

Although they had laid down the purple in the second year of the persecution, according to Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, persecution nevertheless continued in their name under the emperors and Caesars who followed, all of whom were destroyed within that decade. Severus Caesar was killed in the first year of Constantine; Galerius Maximianus and Maximinus died in the third and fourth years of Constantine respectively; and Maxentius was defeated and killed in Constantine’s sixth year. The emperor Maximianus Herculius himself was killed in Constantine’s second year. Thus the Amandine manuscript of Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, into which Jerome inserted much, as he admits in the preface, arranges these years. It is therefore not surprising if the *Chronicle* differs from Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History* concerning the death of Maximinus, for in book IX, chapter 8, Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History* places Maximinus’s death after the death of Maxentius. “But the ruler of the East, having survived him [Maxentius] for not a long time.” Baronius likewise assigns the death of Maximinus to the year of Constantine. Whatever the case, persecution ceased after the death of Maxentius. For even if, with Eusebius in his *Ecclesiastical History*, we suppose that Maximinus lived after Maxentius, Eusebius nevertheless testifies in the same passage that Maximinus issued an edict on behalf of the Christians. And although Diocletian lived until Constantine’s tenth year, he lived deprived of imperial power; therefore, as I have said, persecution ceased in Constantine’s sixth year. See Baronius, volume III, under Constantine’s seventh year.], and was waging war against the tyrant Maxentius [Note: [Col. 0274B] *The tyrant Maxentius.* No books thus far published have expressed the word “tyrant.” It is expressed by the manuscript of Saint Lawrence. Even with the word “tyrant” standing without qualification, Prudentius, in book I *Against Symmachus*, verse 483, understood Maxentius:

> The tyrant captured and cast into the Tiber’s waters—

<sup>1</sup>
Precipitately [lacuna] Baronius, in the year of Christ 316, the third year of Pope Sylvester and the eleventh of the emperor Constantine, because the name “tyrant” had until then been absent from the printed editions, referred this passage to Licinius. But that Maxentius is intended, as the manuscript already cited prefers, is proved by the fact that it is subsequently said that Constantine ordered the recruits to be discharged. The war in which the recruits served therefore did not last a full year, if they were released from military service while they were still recruits, since the period of recruit training lasts only one year, as I shall say shortly. But the war against Maxentius did not last one year; the war against Licinius, on the other hand, lasted several years.

That Pachomius served in the war against Maxentius, not in that against Licinius, is clearly established from the Life of Pachomius itself and from the Chronicon of Eusebius and Sigebert. For since chapter 4 of the Life of Pachomius says that Pachomius was twenty years old when he was enrolled among the recruits, and Sigebert’s Chronicon says that Pachomius, having reached the age of 110, completed his course of virtue, that is, died, assigning the year 405 of Christ as the year of his death, while the war against Maxentius is noted in Eusebius’s Chronicon under the year of Christ 315, you will rightly infer that ninety years elapsed between the year of Christ 315 (when Pachomius, then a twenty-year-old recruit, served in the war against Maxentius) and the year of Christ 405 (when he died). If you then add the twenty years of his age when he was enrolled among the recruits, you will correctly conclude that he died at the age of 110. Consequently, his birth may be assigned to the year of Christ 295, which was the eighth year of Diocletian’s reign.]

While he was engaged in battle, royal decrees went forth [Note: [Col. 0274D] “Royal decrees went forth.”]

Baronius, under the year of Christ 316, the third year of Pope Sylvester and the eleventh of the emperor Constantine, says: “This appears plainly to be that year in which, while Licinius was ordering a levy to be held everywhere for the ensuing battle and recruits to be enrolled, that great Pachomius, then still a pagan, was enrolled in the army in Egypt among the others.”

According to Baron’s view, since he wishes Pachomius to have served in the year 140 of the era under Licinius, this passage could be referred to what Zosimus says in book II of his History, where he discusses Licinius’s preparations for war: Διέπεμπεν ἀγγέλους κατὰ τὰ ἔθνη, “He sent messengers here and there among the nations.” But that Baronius draws the wrong conclusion is demonstrated by the text itself, which plainly indicates that Constantine’s royal decrees went forth and that he ordered a levy of recruits to be held. For it reads as follows:

“Accordingly, while Constantine continued in imperial power after the persecution and was waging war against the tyrant, royal decrees went forth, so that everywhere the most distinguished of the young men might be retained for military recruit training.”

Nor could Licinius here be designated by the title “tyrant,” while his decrees would at the same time be called “royal.” [Col. 0275B] I scarcely doubt that the reason Baronius referred this levy of recruits to Licinius was that Egypt obeyed Licinius, as Sozomen indicates in book I, chapter 11, and Zosimus in book II. For how could Constantine have ordered a levy in the province of his adversary? Baronius would indeed have drawn the correct conclusion, had the passage concerned the war of Licinius against Constantine. But since we have already established that the reference is to the war against Maxentius, and since the words just cited concerning the levy of recruits clearly indicate that it was ordered by Constantine, even though Egypt had fallen to Licinius and obeyed him, nevertheless, because Licinius was allied with Constantine in the war against Maxentius, the levy could have been proclaimed in Egypt in the name of both.

so that everywhere the most distinguished of the young men might be retained for military recruit training [Note: [Col. 0275B] “Might be retained everywhere for military recruit training.”]

At times it was necessary for soldiers and recruits to be held and seized in an emergency levy, lest they evade service. Livy, book III: “Whomever the lictor had seized at the consul’s command, the tribune ordered to be released.” See Lipsius, *De militia Romana*, book I, dialogue 4.]

Among them Pachomius, twenty years old, was detained, as he later related himself. When he had been transported with the others by ship to foreign parts, they were brought to a certain city [Note: [Col. 0275C] “To a certain city.”]

Metaphrastes has “a certain town of Thebes.” Baronius, under the year of Christ 316, the third year of Pope Sylvester and the eleventh of the emperor Constantine, says:

“It will not be irrelevant to investigate the place in which Pachomius, having admired the charity and piety shown there by the Christians toward the pagans also, conceived an affection for the Christian religion, which, like a seed carefully cultivated, grew into a great tree. Since the author [Metaphrastes] writes that it was a city of Thebes, I recall to mind that one city of Thebes and suppose it to have been the city called Oxyrhynchus, which abounded in various classes of holy men and women according to the condition of each (Evagrius, *Lives of the Holy Fathers*, chapter 5); it was a refuge of the holiest men and an assembly of blessed citizens. Their outstanding virtues, while shining forth in all their actions, gleamed especially in receiving guests, like the rays of the sun, so brightly that they brought even pagans to the height of their admiration and stirred their hearts to embrace the Christian faith.”

Thus Baronius, who considers the city of Thebes to be the same as the city of the Thebaid. I do not know whether this can be admitted here without qualification. In any event, that Oxyrhynchus was not the city to which Pachomius came and through which he passed may be demonstrated as follows.

First, it is said that, as evening approached, he was brought by ship to the city. But Oxyrhynchus is far from both the sea and the Nile; and Ptolemy calls it, in the nome of Oxyrhynchus, “the inland metropolis” (*μέσον μητρόπολις*, that is, an inland metropolis).

Second, it is said that, after being transported to foreign parts, he arrived at a city of Thebes. But Oxyrhynchus lies in the Thebaid, and Pachomius himself originated from that province and was enrolled in the army there.

Baronius had two reasons for thinking of Oxyrhynchus and considering it the city at which Pachomius arrived. First, Metaphrastes says that it was a certain town of Thebes. But, as I have already said, Oxyrhynchus cannot be inferred from this. Second, Evagrius—or rather Rufinus (Rufinus, here, book II, chapter 5, *On the Lives of the Fathers*)—in the *Lives of the Holy Fathers*, chapter 5, as I explained in the prolegomena, has a similar account of the kindness and hospitality of the Christians, which he says he experienced in his own time at Oxyrhynchus, corresponding to what Pachomius once said he had found in a certain city of Thebes. But Eusebius, in book IX, chapter 7, relates that Christians performed no lesser acts of benevolence in other places as well, and indeed in Pachomius’s own time; therefore there is no stronger reason for thinking of Oxyrhynchus than of some other city.

Accordingly, I think that, since there are many cities called Thebes, Pachomius arrived at one city of Thebes after setting out from the Thebaid and Egypt with the other recruits and hastening toward Constantine, and that there he experienced the charity of the Christians.]

As evening approached, they were brought there by ship. The citizens of that place, seeing that the recruits were being kept under especially strict guard [Note: [Col. 0276B] “Seeing that the recruits were being kept under especially strict guard.”]
