Metaphrastes: “When the citizens had seen that they were being kept in a sufficiently secure custody”—in accordance with the ancient Roman custom by which guards were assigned to recruits. Servius, on book VII of the *Aeneid*: “Before the city, Roman boys served for a year at the age of seventeen; during that same period they lived under guard.” Cicero, in the *Caeliana*: “For us, in former times, one year was appointed for restraining the arm beneath the toga, so that we might wear the tunic in exercises and field games; and the same arrangement was maintained in the camp and in military service if we immediately began to receive pay.” Plautus, *Mostellaria*, act 1, scene 2:

> When they go to the legion, they give them assistance—  
> Then some relative of theirs.  
> Thus they depart from the craftsmen.  
> Once one year of service has been completed, then  
> It becomes clear what kind of building will result.]

And when they had learned what had happened to them, they were moved by compassion and, in accordance with Christ’s command, brought comfort to those placed in the greatest sorrow and supplied them with the necessities of the body.

Then Pachomius, observing what they had done and greatly wondering at it, asked those who were present who these men were, so ready and willing to show mercy and humility. He heard that they were Christians, who extended the spontaneous services of their generosity toward everyone, and especially toward travelers.

He asked what the designation “Christian” itself meant. He was told that they were pious men and worshipers of the true religion, believing in the name of Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, doing good to all as far as they were able, and hoping to receive from God in the life to come a reward for their good works.

Hearing this, Pachomius was pierced in heart. Enlightened by divine light, he admired the faith of the Christians and, inflamed by the fire of divine fear, withdrew for a little while from the sight of those present. Raising his hands toward heaven, he said:

“Almighty God, who made heaven and earth, if you will look down and regard my prayer, and grant me the true and perfect rule of your holy name, and release me from this fetter of sorrow, I will devote myself to your service all the days of my life, and, having rejected the world, I will cling to you continually.”

After praying these words, he returned to his companions. The next day they departed from that city. As they sailed around various places, whenever bodily pleasure or worldly allurements tempted Pachomius, he turned away from them with the greatest aversion, remembering his pledge in which he had vowed that he would serve the Lord. For, with divine grace assisting him, [Col. 0233A] he had already become a lover of chastity from his earliest years.

## Chapter V

Accordingly, the emperor Constantine, having obtained victory over his enemies through the piety and faith by which he believed in Christ, ordered the recruits to be discharged. Thus, when Pachomius had been granted the freedom he desired, he immediately returned to the farther parts of the Thebaid and entered a church located in a village called Chenoboscium [Note: [Col. 0276B] “Chenoboscium.”]

The old edition incorrectly has *Cynobostium*. In chapter 53 it has *Thynobostium*. Below, in chapter 40: “A certain brother from the monastery of the Chenoboscia.” And in chapter 53: “Because he had learned that he himself was ill in the monastery called Chenoboscia.” Χηνοβοσκία, *Chenoboscia*, is a city of the Thebaid, perhaps so called because geese were pastured there. See the *Onomasticon*.]

There he immediately became a catechumen, and shortly afterward obtained the grace of the life-giving washing. On the very night when he had been instructed in the sacred mysteries, he dreamed that dew, as if descending from heaven, had filled his right hand and had grown into the richness of honey [Note: [Col. 0276C] “And into the richness of honey.”]

Thus, in the primitive Church, those who had been baptized tasted the sweetness of honey and milk. Tertullian, *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 3, discussing the ceremonies of baptism after he has already discussed baptism itself: “Then, after we have been received, we taste beforehand the fellowship of milk and honey.” The same author, book I *Against Marcion*, chapter 14, speaking of Marcion’s god, who, although otherwise rejecting God’s creation, nevertheless did not reject it in his own sacraments but imitated the rites of the Church: “Yet even now he has not rejected the water of the Creator, with which he washes his own people; nor the oil, with which he anoints his own; nor the fellowship of honey and milk, with which he makes his own infants.”

Blessed Agnes, according to Ambrose, sermon 90, used to say: “I received milk and honey from his mouth.” [Col. 0276D] Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*, chapter 4, teaches from Tradition that this practice was observed in the Churches and explains its meaning, namely, that those recently baptized should remember that they are like infants:

“For many other things also which are observed in the Churches by tradition have claimed for themselves the authority of written law, such as immersing the head three times in the washing, and then, after coming out, tasting the fellowship of milk and honey as a sign of infancy.”

Innocence belongs especially to infants. Hence Clement of Alexandria, book I of the *Paedagogus*, chapter 6, notes that Homer calls innocent and righteous men γαλακτοφάγους, “milk-eaters,” that is, those who feed on milk.

I think the origin of this practice came from that passage of Exodus III: “I will bring them out of that land into a good and spacious land, into a land flowing with milk and honey.” Clement of Alexandria, above, applies this to perfect catechesis.

Jerome also notes another custom, not greatly different, in the Churches of the West: that those newly reborn in Christ tasted wine and milk, so that they might learn to desire rational milk and wisdom. This custom derived its origin from Isaiah LV: “Come, buy without money, and without any exchange, wine and milk.”

Jerome writes as follows on this passage:

“Wisdom mixed wine in her cup, calling all the foolish of the world, who do not possess the wisdom of the world, to drink. And let us buy not only wine but also milk, which signifies the innocence of little ones. This custom and type is preserved to this day in the Churches of the West, so that those reborn in Christ are given wine and milk. Concerning this milk Paul also said: ‘I gave you milk to drink, not solid food’ (1 Cor. III). And Peter: ‘Like newborn infants, desire rational milk’ (1 Pet. II). Hence Moses too, understanding wine and milk in relation to the passion of Christ, bears witness in mystical language: ‘His eyes are more pleasing than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk’ (Gen. XLIX).”

Indeed, since those reborn through baptism are like infants, Tertullian rightly said above that the Church makes its children infants through the fellowship of milk and honey. Paulinus, epistle 12, calls those washed in the sacred font infants:

> From there the priest, the parent, leads infants from the sacred font,  
> Infants in body, in heart, and in dress as white as snow.

Hence even today in the Catholic Church, on the Sunday *in albis*, when those baptized formerly removed their white garment, the following is sung: “Like newborn infants, desire rational milk without deceit.”

He also heard a voice saying to him: “Consider, Pachomius, what is taking place. This is a sign of the grace that has been bestowed upon you by Christ.” From that moment, inflamed by divine affection and wounded with a salutary wound by the arrow of love, he subjected his whole self to divine disciplines and instructions.

## Chapter VI

He heard of a certain anchorite named Palaemon [Note: [Col. 0277B] “Palaemon.”]

His memory is preserved in the Roman Martyrology on 11 January: “In the Thebaid, Saint Palaemon, abbot and teacher of Saint Pachomius.”]

He was serving the Lord in the seclusion of the desert. Pachomius immediately went to him, desiring to live with him, and, knocking at the door of his cell, begged admission.

The old man opened the entrance slightly and said: “What do you want? Or whom are you seeking?” He had a stern appearance, because he had spent a long time living alone in a rigorous manner.

Pachomius answered: “God has sent me to you so that I may become a monk.”

The elder replied: “You cannot become a monk here. For it is no small matter to assess the chaste conduct of a true monk; many who have come here in the past, overcome by weariness, have not maintained the virtue of perseverance.”

Pachomius said: “The character of all people is not the same. Therefore I beg you to deign to receive me; in time you will more fully test both my willingness and my ability.”

The elder said: “I have already told you that you cannot become a monk here in any way. Go instead to another monastery, and after you have practiced self-restraint there for a while, return to me; I will receive you without delay. Nevertheless, heed what I say. Here, my son, I live very frugally. I discipline myself with an exceedingly demanding and harsh way of life, using no food except bread and salt. I abstain altogether from oil and wine. I keep vigil for half the night, spending that time either in solemn prayer or in meditation on divine reading; sometimes I remain awake for the entire night.”

Hearing this, Pachomius was afraid, as children are accustomed to fear the presence of their teachers. But strengthened by the Lord’s grace, he resolved to endure all this labor and replied to the old man:

“I believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, who will grant me strength and patience, so that, aided by your prayers, I may become worthy to remain in holy conduct throughout all the course of my life.”

## Chapter VII

Then Saint Palaemon, perceiving Pachomius’s faith with spiritual eyes, at last opened the entrance. Receiving him, he consecrated him in the monastic habit [Note: [Col. 0277B] “He consecrated him in the monastic habit.”]

Take note, heretic, of how great was formerly the reverence for the sacred garment of monks, since laymen were consecrated to religion through it. See Dionysius the Areopagite, *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 6, on the initiation and consecration of a monk, where, among other things, he discusses the change of clothing when someone is consecrated as a monk. Tertullian, *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 3: “O sacrilegious hands, which have been able to strip off a garment dedicated to God.” Jerome, epistle 15, to Marcella: “Having put on a darker tunic, she suddenly consecrated herself to the Lord.”]

Thus they lived together, devoting themselves to abstinence and prayers. They also wove haircloth garments and worked with their hands, in accordance with the blessed Apostle, not merely for their own nourishment or rest, but so that they might have something from which to give to those suffering need (Eph. IV).

During the vigils, when they were celebrating the nighttime prayers, if the elder ever saw Pachomius overcome by sleep, he would lead him outside and order him to carry sand from one place to another. By such an exercise he lifted his mind, weighed down by the burden of sleep, and trained and formed him to be attentive in prayer, saying to him:

“Work, Pachomius, and keep watch, lest at some time—which God forbid—the tempter remove you from the purpose you have now begun, and our labor become fruitless.”

Pachomius accepted all this obediently and diligently. Growing from day to day in the progress of holy self-restraint, he made the venerable old man exceedingly cheerful and happy, so that Palaemon always gave thanks to Christ for his way of life.

## Chapter VIII

At that time the most sacred day of Easter arrived, and the elder said to Pachomius: “Since this is the universal festival of all Christians, prepare for us what is appropriate for our use.”

Ready to obey, Pachomius fulfilled what had been commanded him. Taking a little more oil than usual, he mixed it with ground salt. They were accustomed to eat *lapsana*, that is, wild vegetables [Note: [Col. 0277C] “For *lapsana*, that is, wild vegetables.”]

Thus all the printed editions and manuscripts. Authors sometimes append explanations of difficult words even within the text itself, which seems to have happened here. Cassian, book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 11: “Likewise omitting that difficult and sublime form of self-restraint in which the greatest delicacies are reckoned to consist when an herb seasoned with salt, which they call *lapsanium*, diluted with water, is served to the brothers for refreshment.” The same author, book IV, chapter 22: “Among them, the leaves of leeks, *lapsana*, fried salt, olives, and small salted fish, which they call *maenidia*, are the greatest pleasure each month.” See the proverb *Lapsana vivere*, “to live on *lapsana*,” referring to a meager and poor diet. Dioscorides, book II, chapter 142, calls it λαμψάνη.]

Besides oil, they were accustomed to eat herbs and other greens. When Pachomius had prepared the meal, he said to the elder: “I have done what your fatherhood commanded.”

After the prayers, blessed Palaemon came to the table. When he saw the oil prepared with the salt, he rubbed his forehead with his hands and shed abundant tears, saying: “My Lord has been crucified, and I am now going to eat oil?”

When Pachomius asked him to take a little of it, he absolutely refused. Then they brought salt and bread as usual and sat down together to eat. The old man blessed the food with the sign of Christ’s cross, as he was accustomed to do, and both of them took the meal, humbly offering thanks to the Lord, as was fitting.

## Chapter IX

One day, while Palaemon and Pachomius were keeping vigil together and kindling a fire, a certain brother arrived and wished to remain with them. After he had been received, he suddenly blurted out, as often happens in conversation:

“If any one of you is faithful, let him stand upon these burning coals and slowly and quietly recite the Lord’s Prayer.”

Blessed Palaemon recognized that he had been deceived by the swelling of pride and admonished him, saying: “Stop, brother, this madness, and do not say anything of the kind again.”

The old man’s correction did not improve him; rather, inflated still more by mental arrogance, he boldly began to stand upon the fire, with no one compelling him in the least. It was a spectacle to behold how, with the enemy of the human race cooperating and the Lord permitting it, he was not burned at all by contact with the fire.

The fact that he had done this with impunity increased his madness, according to what is written: “The Lord sends the perverse to perverse ways” (Prov. XXVIII; Sir. II). After this had happened, the same brother departed early the next day and, as though reproaching them, said: “Where is your faith?”

Not long afterward, the devil saw that he was wholly enslaved to him and that he could easily compel him to whatever crimes he wished. He therefore transformed himself into a beautiful woman dressed in splendid garments and began to pound violently on the door of the brother’s cell.

When the brother opened it, the devil, changed into the appearance of a woman, said to him: “I beg you, because I am being pressed very hard by creditors and fear that some dangers may overtake me, receive me into your cell, since I cannot repay my debt. Then, having been saved through you, I will give thanks; for God has directed me to you.”

The wretched man, completely darkened by blindness of mind and unable to discern who was speaking such things to him, received the devil into his own destruction. Then the enemy of our substance, seeing that he was inclined to every crime, stirred up in him a shameful lust.

He immediately yielded to the enemy’s suggestions and sought what he thought were the woman’s embraces. The unclean spirit attacked him and struck him down violently. He rolled upon the floor and remained there for a long time, as though dead.

After several days he finally came to himself, and, repenting too late of his madness, went to Saint Palaemon. With great weeping he explained what had happened to him, crying out:

“I recognize it, Father, I recognize that I am the cause of my own destruction. You graciously admonished me, but I was wretched and scorned to listen to you. Therefore I beg you to deign to assist me with your holy prayers, lest the enemy, finding me placed in such great danger, tear me apart and destroy me.”

While he continued speaking amid lamentations and tears, and Saint Palaemon and blessed Pachomius shed tears for him out of compassion, he was suddenly seized by the unclean spirit, sprang from their sight, and ran through the wilderness, driven on without restraint.

He reached the city called Panos [Note: [Col. 0277C] “To the city of Panos.”]

Panos is a city of Egypt in the Thebaid, called Πανόπολις, *Panopolis*, by Ptolemy. Some wish it also to have been called Chemnis.]

Then, in his madness, he threw himself into a bathhouse furnace and immediately perished in the fire.

## Chapter X

When Pachomius heard and saw this, he applied himself more and more to maintaining the measure of abstinence and, in everything, but especially in prayer, to keeping his mind constantly vigilant, in accordance with what is written: “Guard your heart with all vigilance” (Prov. IV).

He did this to such an extent that the elder was astonished at him: Pachomius not only energetically practiced the customary rule of abstinence outwardly, but also inwardly endeavored to make his conscience utterly pure according to the pattern of heavenly things, as the blessed Apostle says: “Our glory is this, the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. I), confident that by this he was preparing for himself a great reward in heaven.

When he read the divine Scriptures and committed them to memory, he did not do so carelessly or negligently. Rather, examining each command attentively and considering it with a devout mind, he strove each day to fulfill in action what he had retained in memory.

Above all, he excelled many others in the gift of humility and patience and in the purest love toward God and neighbor.

We learned these and many other things about him from holy men of God who had lived with him for a long time. He had also given them examples of the spiritual life, carefully explaining, after the reading of the divine law, those things that contribute to the edification of souls.

Because these matters are numerous and exceed the abilities of our small capacity, we have not committed them all to writing in the present work. We are not capable of expressing in words worthy of so great a man the merits of his life.

## Chapter XI

Near the mountain where the holy men lived there was a desert completely covered with thorns. Pachomius often went there to gather wood, walking barefoot over the thorns. When many of them pierced him, he rejoiced, patiently and bravely enduring the pain and remembering that our Lord had graciously been fastened to the cross with nails.

He greatly loved the anchorite life and frequently sought solitude. There, remaining for a long time in prayer, he begged the Lord mercifully to free him from so many snares.

## Chapter XII

At a certain time Pachomius went some distance from his cell and came to a village called Tabennese [Note: [Col. 0277D] “Tabennese.”]

Cassian, book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 1: “Some things, namely, from the rules of the Egyptians and some from those of the Tabennesiots were combined; the latter have a coenobium in the Thebaid which, while more populous than all others in number, is more strict than all others in the rigor of its way of life. Indeed, more than five thousand brothers are governed there under one abbot.”]

At that time it had absolutely no inhabitant. While he remained there for a long time in prayer, as was his custom, a voice came to him from heaven, saying:

“Remain here, Pachomius, and build a monastery. For very many will come to you, desiring to advance through your instruction. You will guide them according to the rule that I shall show you.”

Immediately an angel of the Lord appeared, carrying a tablet on which the entire pattern of their instruction had been written—the instruction by which all who came to study under his teaching were to be taught.

The Tabennesiots still observe this rule today, always using the same food and clothing and carefully maintaining the discipline itself. For the monks who live there differ greatly from others not only in custom but also in bodily strength and in the character of the place; consequently, they must also observe a different rule.

Pachomius discerned this voice by the sincerity of mind that divine grace and the merits of his life had bestowed on him, recognized that it had been brought to him from heaven, and approved the exceedingly wondrous rules.

Then he returned to the venerable elder Palaemon and reported how he had been admonished by a divine voice, begging him to come with him to the place where they could fulfill the Lord’s commands together.

Palaemon, unwilling to cause him any distress, since he loved him as a dearest son, immediately complied with his prayers. They reached the aforementioned village together and, building a small cell there, rejoiced in the Lord while awaiting the benefits of his promises.

After some time Palaemon said to Pachomius: “Since I see that a grace has been bestowed upon you by God and that you intend henceforth to remain here, come, let us establish a covenant between us, so that we may not be separated from each other but, for as long as we remain in this life, may console one another by constant visits.”

This agreement pleased them both, and throughout their lives both the blessed old man and blessed Pachomius carefully fulfilled it.

## Chapter XIII

Meanwhile, the same venerable Palaemon began to suffer throughout his body from a serious illness caused by pain in the spleen, which had arisen from excessive self-restraint.

He would take food while often abstaining from drink; then again he would drink only, taking no food at all.

Some brothers who had come to visit him urged him not to break his weakened body completely but to allow a little comfort to be provided for it. At last he yielded to their pleas, so that he might restore his weakened limbs with suitable nourishment.

But he did not endure this for long. When he experienced pains in the spleen more severe than usual, he abandoned this unfamiliar food and immediately returned to his former diet, saying:

“If some martyrs of Christ were torn apart limb by limb, others beheaded, and still others burned in the fire, yet all endured bravely for the faith to the end, why should I, yielding to small pains, impatiently throw away the rewards of patience and needlessly fear momentary afflictions because of a desire for the present life?

“Indeed, I yielded to those who urged me to take unfamiliar foods, and they increased my pains rather than providing me with any relief. I shall therefore return to the former remedies and shall not abandon the supports of self-restraint, in which, as I am certain, there is, after God, all rest and true joy.

“For I did not take up these weapons on account of human beings; rather, out of love for Christ I resolved to fight with them.”

Thus acting manfully, he was consumed within a month by severe illness.

Pachomius came to him and cherished him as a father, kissing his feet and embracing him. As though bidding him farewell, he seemed to address him in these words.

The venerable old man, filled with every grace of virtue and full of days, rested in peace, as it is written (Job XLII). Then Saint Pachomius buried his body; his soul was received into the angelic choirs and carried up to heaven.

When this had been done, Pachomius returned to his own dwelling.

## Chapter XIV

Not long afterward, his brother, named John, learned everything about him and came to him. When Pachomius saw him, he rejoiced greatly. For ever since he had been baptized into Christ, believed, and chosen the solitary life, he had seen none of his relatives.

John, truly a brother of Pachomius, became his imitator and remained with him. They shared the same purpose and the same affection of love toward God.

Because they meditated on the law of God by day and by night, their minds were not weighed down by any concerns over earthly affairs. If anything remained to them from the things they made with their hands, they immediately distributed it to the needy, so that, in accordance with the command of the Lord Jesus Christ, they might not worry about the following day (Matt. VI).

They had reduced themselves to such poverty of clothing that they never used another *lebiton*, except when necessity compelled them to wash the dirt from their garment.

A *lebiton* [Note: [Col. 0277D] “Lebiton.”]

He explains here what a *lebiton* is: “A *lebiton* was a linen garment, like a sleeveless tunic, which monks still wear throughout the Thebaid and Egypt.”

Below, in chapter 22, in Pachomius’s rule: “At night they shall put on linen *lebitons*.”

Jerome, in the preface to the rule of Saint Pachomius, calls it a *lebitonarium*: “They have nothing in their cells except a mat and two *lebitonaria* (which among the Egyptian monks is a kind of sleeveless garment).”

Isidore, book XIX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 22: “A *lebitonarium* is a sleeveless tunic, such as the Egyptian monks use.” [Col. 0278A] See the *Onomasticon*.

Concerning the sleeveless tunic, Cassian, book I of the *Institutes*, chapter 5: “They are also dressed in linen sleeveless tunics, which scarcely reach to the lower part of the elbows.”

For what the differing clothing of the monks who lived under Pachomius’s rule signifies, see Sozomen, book III, chapter 14, and below in the *Onomasticon.]

A *lebiton* was a linen garment, like a sleeveless tunic, which monks still wear throughout the Thebaid and Egypt. [Col. 0238A] But blessed Pachomius, in order to humble his own body, generally dressed himself in sackcloth.

For fifteen years, after those immense labors and outstanding exertions of vigils and abstinence, he did not lie down to sleep at night. Instead, he sat in the middle of his cell, so that he did not even lean his back against the wall for support.

Although this afflicted him greatly, he nevertheless endured the labor with equanimity, tasting in some way beforehand the rest that was being prepared for him in heaven.

Considering the practices of many of the Fathers, he always took care, together with his own brother, to rise to greater increases of virtue. They also made seats, and each lived as he was able, with the greatest humility and patience and with sincere faith.

[Col. 0238B] **CHAPTER XV.**—Amid these events Pachomius was once again divinely warned concerning the rules by which those who were to entrust themselves to the Lord through him ought to be instructed. He therefore began, together with his brother, to make the dwelling in which they lived more spacious and to enlarge it with very many buildings, for the sake, as we have said, of those who, renouncing the world, were certainly going to come to serve Christ, so that there might be spaces suitable for the members [Note: [Col. 0278A] “So that there might be spaces suitable for the members.”] Shortly afterward: “And he enlarged the members of the monastery.” The word is familiar, but not all its meaning is equally well known. The ancients used *membrum* for a part of a building or a room. Pliny, Book II, Letter 17: “A sleeping-room adjoins the bedchamber, with a passage lying between.” The same author, Book V, Letter 6: “There are many rooms in this house.” Columella, Book I, chapter 6, divides the “rooms of a villa” into three parts: “urban, rustic, and productive.” Sidonius, Book II, Letter 2: “He made a very cool room.” Cassiodorus, in his commentary on Psalm 148: “We say that there is one palace, which is surrounded by many rooms, many spaces.” The term also occurs several times among the ancient jurists.], in which their multitude could be received.

When holy Pachomius was enlarging, as has been said, the circuit of the place and extending the rooms of the monastery, his brother, thinking about solitude and the eremitical life, preferred the narrowness of their dwelling. Taking this very badly—for he was the elder—he said to blessed Pachomius:

“Give up this purpose of yours. What are you doing, striving uselessly to enlarge yourself in vain?”

When he heard this, Pachomius was deeply distressed that he had heard an insult so unusual; nevertheless, he answered him nothing at all but, enduring it meekly, restrained himself.

The following night he went down to the lower part of the house, some portion of which he himself had built, and prostrated himself in prayer. He began to weep bitterly and say:

“Woe is me, because the wisdom of the flesh still claims a place for itself in me. For I still walk according to the flesh, as I have recently discovered. Since I have undertaken the discipline of so great a way of life, it is not right that now impatience should cast me down, now grief harass me, now anger provoke me, although I may seem to have reason and justification for being angry. Have mercy on me, Lord, lest I perish, lest, deceived by the devil’s fraud, I succumb.

[Col. 0238D] “For if your grace abandons me, and the enemy finds in me any part of his own works, I shall be subjected to his harshest slavery, because it is written: ‘By whatever a person is overcome, by this he is enslaved’ (2 Peter 2). And again it is written: ‘If anyone fulfills the whole law but stumbles in one point, he has become guilty of all’ (James 2).

“I believe, Lord, that your mercies are many. They have helped me, though supported by no merits of my own, and, enlightened by you, I shall enter the way of your saints; ever stretching myself toward what lies ahead, I shall forget what is behind (Philippians 3). For in this way the choir of your servants, which pleased you from the beginning of the world, protected by your help, avoided the devil’s attacks and, for the salvation of many, shone far and wide with wondrous beauty.

[Col. 0239A] “But how shall I, Lord, attempt to teach others, whom you will deign to call through me to the monastic vocation, when I have neither conquered the passions of the flesh that wage war against the soul nor kept your law with an undefiled mind? Yet I trust, Christ, that your power will always assist me in everything, and that I shall do what pleases your sight. Forgive, most merciful God, forgive, I beg you, all my sins, and continually purify my heart by your scrutiny.”

Thus he confessed these things to the Lord with tears and weeping. Remaining awake in prayer throughout the entire night, and because of the abundance of sweat and tears—for it was summertime—he so moistened the floor where he had prayed that one would have thought water had been poured there.

[Col. 0239B] He was accustomed, while standing in prayer, to stretch out his hands, and for several hours scarcely to draw them together; but through this prolonged extension he held his body motionless, as though it had been fastened to a cross, and thus stirred his spirit to remain watchful in prayer.

Although he was exceedingly powerful in every kind of virtue, nevertheless, while living with his brother, he supported him in everything with extraordinary humility and remarkable gentleness. Not long afterward, his brother completed the course of the present life. Pachomius arranged his funeral with due honor. He remained awake over his corpse the whole night, occupied with psalms and hymns, commended his soul to the Lord in whom he himself had believed, and carefully consigned his body to burial.

**CHAPTER XVI.**—Then the tireless Pachomius, afflicting himself through a strict and singular discipline, strove to show himself whole and undefiled in every respect. For whenever an unlawful thought assailed him, he immediately drove it away by divine favor and remained steadfast in the fear of the Lord, mindful of eternal punishments and of the sufferings that endure without end—namely, that unquenchable fire and the worm that never wholly dies.

By these means Pachomius both abstained from unlawful things and advanced toward better ones. He also devoted himself intensely to enlarging the monasteries for the reception of many people. The devil began vehemently to oppose him and, gnashing his teeth at him like a solitary wild beast [Note: [Col. 0278B] “Like a solitary wild beast.”] The expression *solitary wild beast* occurs in Psalm 79, where the Greek has **μονιὸς ἄγριος** (*monios agrios*). It is understood to refer to a particular animal of the boar species. See the *Onomasticon*.], stirred up various temptations against him, in case he might find some opening for his deceit.

But Pachomius, protected by the shield of faith, watchfully avoided the enemy’s snares, retaining the holy Scriptures in his memory and chanting them.

**CHAPTER XVII.**—One day, while Pachomius was entreating the Lord and wished to bend his knees in prayer, a lake appeared before him through the magical illusions of demons. The enemy of the human race was always eager to display such empty and pointless forms, so that, by some theft or deception, the mind of the person praying might be drawn away from its proper purpose and be unable to offer the Lord prayers in perfect purity.

Pachomius therefore recognized the demons’ devices through Christ’s revelation and, despising them at the same time, gained great increases of faith. He steadfastly reproved them, while blessing God with his customary thanksgiving.

The holy man was also accustomed, for the sake of prayer, to go down to more remote places some distance from his monastery. When he returned from there, unclean spirits frequently appeared to precede him in a kind of procession, encouraging one another as though their ranks had been sent before a judge, and saying:

“Make way for the man of God.”

Pachomius, armed with hope in Christ the Redeemer, scorned their ridiculous fabrications and considered them no more than the most senseless barking of dogs.

When they saw the man’s great perseverance—that he was in no way broken by such mighty struggles—they rushed upon him in a great mass. Surrounding his dwelling, they seemed to tear it up from its foundations, so that the saint thought the place had collapsed completely.

Remaining undaunted, he played his customary spiritual lyre with the melody of his plectrum, singing in a loud voice:

“God is our refuge and strength, a helper in the tribulations that have found us exceedingly; therefore we shall not fear when the earth is shaken” (Psalm 45).

As he sang the psalm, tranquility immediately came about, and the enemy’s attack vanished like smoke. They withdrew for a little while, like dogs that, when exhausted, seem to depart for the moment but later return more shamelessly.

For when the same saint had finished praying and sat down to his customary work, the enemy appeared before him in the form of a rooster of extraordinary size, repeatedly uttering loud and disorderly cries. Then, leaping upon him, he tore him viciously as though with claws.

Pachomius fortified his forehead with the sign of the cross and blew upon him [Note: [Col. 0278B] “He blew upon him.”] Below, chapter 48: “And, blowing upon him, he said.” Demons were accustomed to be blown upon from the time of the primitive Church down to this age. See the *Onomasticon*.], and he was immediately put to flight.

Pachomius understood all the enemy’s cunning. Endowed with divine fear, he counted his illusions as nothing. Thus, though frequently provoked by him, he could not be provoked into any response; but, like an impregnable tower, he endured every conflict with the greatest patience.

Again, at another time, companies of demons attempted to tempt the holy servant of God with this kind of apparition. For when many of them had gathered together, they seemed to tie a leaf of a tree before him with great ropes and to pull it with all their strength, their lines drawn out to right and left. Encouraging one another, they tried to persist as though they were moving the immense weight of a great stone.

The most wicked spirits did this so that, if they could, they might dissolve his mind into laughter and find something with which to reproach him.

When Pachomius saw their shamelessness, he groaned and hastened to the Lord with his customary prayers. Immediately, by the power of Christ, their entire band was reduced to nothing.

For frequently, when he was sitting at table and giving thanks to God, they appeared to him in the guise of extremely beautiful women, differing in appearance and conspicuous for their brazen and shameful nakedness. They seemed to stand beside him and to wish to touch the food that had been set before him.

But the strongest of athletes, although he felt distress from this, closed his outward eyes and opened his inward eyes to the Lord, overcoming their attempts. For the merciful Lord was present, who even now deigns to be present to all who are contrite and upright in heart, and says:

“Do not be afraid; I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28).

Thus he preserved his faithful servant in every respect.

**CHAPTER XVIII.**—On another occasion, when the same saint was being pressed by severe assaults of the devil, he was beaten so cruelly by him that from evening until morning his whole body was marked with many blows.

Although he was tormented by immense pains, he was not at all broken by despair; rather, he remembered the Lord, who does not abandon his servants in temptation.

Then a certain monk named Apollo came to visit him [Note: [Col. 0278B] “Apollo.”] There were various monks named Apollos, Apollines, or Apollonii. It is difficult to determine precisely which one this was.]

Pachomius spoke to him about matters pertaining to salvation. Declaring that the devil’s attacks were manifold, he also began to explain what was happening to him and to recount how many blows had been inflicted upon him through the demons’ cruelty.

The monk said to him:

“Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, venerable Father. For the devil knows that if he defeats you by seeing you yield to his conflicts, he will consequently overcome us also with the greatest ease—we who, to the extent of our strength, are followers of your struggles and who receive through you the greatest examples of virtue. For this reason he does not cease to attack you violently.

“But you, fortified by the Lord’s protection, receive his assault bravely, lest, God forbid, you be compelled to give an account on our behalf as well. For if you, who by divine grace have been placed over us, yield through any negligence, you will provide many with an occasion and a cause for ruin.”

When Pachomius heard this, he received great strength against the demons’ snares. Glorifying God for his brother’s presence, he begged him not to abandon him.

From then on the aforementioned Apollo often came to the old man. After some time, while visiting Pachomius as usual and remaining with him for a few days, he was seized by a serious illness and departed from human affairs, completing his days in a perfect discipline according to the old man’s desire.

He was buried by the saint’s hands, with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs customarily sung by Pachomius.

**CHAPTER XIX.**—After these events blessed Pachomius had acquired such confidence before the Lord and was regarded as so mighty through divine hope that he frequently trampled upon serpents and scorpions and remained unharmed in every respect. Even crocodiles, whenever necessity compelled him to cross a river, carried him with complete submission, setting him down wherever he ordered.

Giving thanks to God for these things, because he was preserved unharmed from all the enemy’s deceits, he prayed:

“Blessed are you, Lord God of our fathers, who have not despised my humility nor allowed me, so weak, to be deceived or mocked by the devil’s fraud; rather, mercifully dispersing the darkness of my ignorance, you have taught me to do your will.

“For when I was small and despised, and utterly ignorant of my own life, you bestowed upon me a sense of your fear, so that, avoiding outer darkness and eternal punishments, I might recognize you as the true light and everlasting joy.”

**CHAPTER XX.**—Seeing himself continually assaulted by the devil, Pachomius fought with great eagerness for the holiness of his life, like a most valiant athlete. He asked the Lord that, if it were possible, he might overcome the need for sleep beyond the measure of human weakness (Rufinus, Book III, no. 35), so that, keeping watch day and night, he might destroy the enemy’s devices, as it is written:

“I will pursue my enemies and overtake them; and I will not turn back until they fail. I will afflict them, and they will not be able to stand; they will fall beneath my feet. And you have girded me with strength for battle” (Psalm 17).

After this request had been fulfilled insofar as human condition permitted, he endured the invisible enemy as though seeing him, continually exercising himself in heavenly words. His prayers were unceasing, so that the Lord’s will might be fulfilled in everything.

[Col. 0242B] **CHAPTER XXI.**—At a certain time, while Pachomius was keeping vigil in prayer, an angel of the Lord appeared to him and said:

“It is the Lord’s will, Pachomius, that, serving him with a pure mind, you gather a multitude of monks, instruct them all according to the form that has been shown to you, and strive to present them to God.”

For some time earlier he had received a tablet [Note: [Col. 0278B] “For some time earlier he had received a tablet.”] Concerning that rule, which he received from the angel written on a tablet, see above, chapter 12, in the text. On the same rule, see the prefaces to this Life, no. 2. Pachomius thus received, like another Moses, divine laws in the desert, by which he might teach his followers to lead a perfect and blessed life on earth.], on which the following had been written:

**CHAPTER XXII.**—Allow each person to eat and drink according to his strength, and compel him to work in proportion to what he eats. Do not forbid either eating moderately or fasting. Assign stronger work to the stronger and well-fed; impose lighter work on the weaker and those who abstain.

You shall make separate cells, and establish three persons in each cell. The food of all shall be prepared and consumed in one place.

At night they shall put on linen *lebitons* [Note: [Col. 0278C] “Linen lebitons.”] See above, at chapter 14, no. 18.], girding their loins, and each shall have a *melote* [Note: [Col. 0278C] “And a melote.”] Here again an explanation of the obscure word in the text is supplied: namely, a goatskin. Jerome, in the preface to the Rule of Saint Pachomius: “And the goatskin which they call a *melote*.” Cassian, Book I of the *Institutes*, chapter 5: “Their final garment is a goatskin, which is called a *melote* or *pera*.], that is, a finished white goatskin, without which they shall neither eat nor sleep.

When, however, they approach the communion of Christ’s sacraments, they shall loosen their belts and lay aside the *melote*, using only their cowls.

It was also commanded that, according to the number of the elements and of the Greek letters, companies of twenty-four monks should be formed, so that each company would be assigned the name of one letter, beginning with α and continuing through ω. Thus, whenever the superior asked about someone among so great a multitude, he could learn the answer easily.

For example, when he said how α or ζ, and again λ or ρ or σ, was doing [Note: [Col. 0278C] “And again λ or ρ or σ.”] Thus consistently in the Cologne edition. The Cologne edition has: “And again: Greet ρ or σ.” So also in Palladius, chapter 38: “Greet ρ.” Some manuscripts spell out all the names in full: “And again, labda, ro, or simma.” Thus the Gembloux manuscript. In the manuscript of Saint Lawrence it reads: “And again, lauta, ro, or simma.” Sozomen, Book III of *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 13, says that in the tablet of Pachomius, which he received from the angel, it was written:

**Πᾶσαν δὲ τὴν συνοικίαν εἰς εἰκοσιτέσσαρα τάγματα διελεῖν, καὶ ἐπονομάσαι ταῦτα τοῖς Ἑλλήνων στοιχείοις, καὶ ὅπως ἔχει βίου καὶ ἤθους ἑκάστῳ τάγματι τὴν προσηγορίαν ἐφαρμόσαι, οἷον ἁπλουστέρους α ἢ ι ἀποκαλοῦντας, σκολίους δε ζ ἢ ξ, καὶ ἄλλους ἄλλως, καθὼς ἐκλαμβάνειν εὔστοχόν ἐστι πρὸς τὸ σχῆμα τοῦ γράμματος τὴν προαίρεσιν τοῦ τάγματος.**

“That the whole community should finally be divided into twenty-four classes, and that each should be called by one of the Greek letters; for example, that the simpler ones should be called α or ι, the crafty ones ζ or ξ, and others by the names of other letters, according as it seemed fitting to infer from the shape of the letter the character of the class’s way of life.”

Each company’s customs were expressed by a particular sign bearing the name of a letter. He appropriately assigned ι as the name for the simpler and more innocent, and ξ for those who were more difficult and crooked, so that, according to the manner of their conduct and purpose, the elements of the letters might correspond to each company, with only those spiritually minded enough to understand knowing what these signs meant.

It was also written on that tablet that, if a visitor from another monastery came wearing a different habit, no one should eat with him, except someone who, while traveling, could not observe this rule.

Whoever entered this monastery with the intention of remaining there permanently was to be excluded from the more sacred studies for three years. He was to perform only his ordinary work in a simple manner, and after three years he was to enter the course of the struggle.

When they ate, they were to cover their heads with their cowls [Note: [Col. 0278D] “When they ate, they were to cover their heads with their cowls.”] Cassian, Book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 17, concerning the Egyptian monks, especially the Tabennesiots: “Such a discipline of silence is maintained among them while they eat that, with their cowls lowered below their eyelids, so that their unrestrained gaze may not have freer opportunity to wander curiously, they look at nothing more than the table and the food placed upon it or contained in it.”], lest one brother see another eating. No one who was eating was to speak, nor was anyone to let his eyes wander elsewhere from the table.

It was also established by the angel who spoke with Pachomius that there should be twelve prayers during the day [Note: [Col. 0279A] “It was also established by the angel, etc., that there should be twelve prayers during the day, etc.”] Cassian, Book II of the *Institutes*, chapter 4, mentions the number twelve of the psalms, preserved both in the evening and in the nocturnal offices: “This,” he says, “has remained unbroken down to the present, because the elders affirm that it was not established by human invention but delivered to the fathers from heaven through the instruction of an angel.” See Palladius below, chapter 38.], twelve in the evening, and twelve at night.

When Pachomius said that these were few prayers, the angel replied:

“I established these as prayers that the weaker might complete without difficulty. Those who are perfect, however, do not need this rule. Remaining in their own cells, they do not cease to pray; they are nourished by purity of mind and divine contemplation.”

When he had said this, the heavenly messenger departed. Pachomius, giving thanks to God as usual, was assured of the vision, which he had recognized through a threefold revelation.

He began to receive all who, through repentance, offered themselves to God’s mercies. After a long experience of the discipline, he also incorporated them into the communities of monks, teaching them to flee the allurements of the world and always to adhere to holy instructions. First he warned them that, in general, a monk must renounce the entire world; then, according to the evangelical commandment (Luke 24), his parents; and finally himself, so that he might take up his cross and follow the venerable footsteps of Christ.

[Col. 0243C] Formed by this instruction of the blessed old man, they bore most worthy fruits of repentance, especially when they considered that, already weary with age, he preserved his commitment to the spiritual life with tireless zeal.

For he had not only subjected himself to a stricter rule, but also carried the concern and care of the entire monastery, striving to serve everyone beyond his strength. At the hour of the meal he himself prepared the table for the brothers and performed his customary duties. He also planted vegetables in the little gardens and watered them with his own hands.

If anyone knocked at the monastery door, he promptly went to meet him and gave an immediate answer. He served the sick by day and by night, and in all these things he offered himself as a great example to his disciples.

Therefore those who had recently come to the Lord’s service became more eager for every work of piety. Yet because the blessed old man saw that they were not yet able to undertake the burden of such responsibilities, he urged them to remain free from every distraction, saying:

“Brothers, remain manfully in that to which you have been called. Recite the psalms; commit other books, and especially the holy Gospel, to memory. For by serving the Lord in this way and loving one another according to his commandments, you will be perfect; and you will refresh my spirit in every respect, especially if you carefully carry out the heavenly commands.”

**CHAPTER XXIII.**—There were three men who had first come to Pachomius. Their names were Psenthessus, Suris, and Obsis. Pachomius frequently impressed the word of God upon them, greatly helping them and urging them to emulate spiritual work.

As they contemplated that the old man’s life was an example of virtue, they marveled greatly and said:

“They are profoundly mistaken who think that people are blessed from the very birth of their parents by some privilege, so that freedom of choice is taken away and sinners cannot devote themselves to virtue through repentance.

“For here, in this venerable father Pachomius, we plainly see the Lord’s generosity. Although he was born of pagan and profane parents, he advanced in the worship of God to such great blessedness that he fulfilled all Christ’s commandments.

“Therefore it is certain that anyone among us who wishes may, with God’s grace assisting, follow the pattern of this holy man, just as he himself imitated the holiness of the most perfect fathers.

“Indeed, what else is written in the Gospel when Christ says, ‘Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you’ (Matthew 11), except that, casting away the unrighteous burdens that weigh down the human race, we should join ourselves without hesitation to the unchanging good?

“Therefore let us persevere to the end with this old man, so that we may deserve to be glorified with him in that everlasting blessedness. For he rightly instructs us in everything, not only by word but also, more effectively, by wondrously shaping us through his own example.”

Then they approached holy Pachomius and said to him:

“Venerable Father, why do you alone bear the care of the monastery?”

He answered them:

“No one suddenly places a yoke upon beasts and compels them to work, burdening them with so great a load that they collapse beneath the weight. Rather, he gradually accustoms them, first exercising them with lighter burdens, until they become able and appropriately capable of rising to heavier tasks.

“In the same way, it is fitting for us also to deal with you according to the measure by which Christ has measured us, so that we may rejoice in your strength in every respect.

“May the most merciful God, who never despises the prayers of my humility, strengthen your hearts in his discipline, so that you may be able to complete every good work with patience and perseverance, following in the footsteps of the holy Fathers. Then, when others see your sincere conduct, pleasing to God, they too will come to Christ’s service and sustain the care of the monastery of the father with equal labor.”

**CHAPTER XXIV.**—Accordingly, he handed over to them the rules that he had received: that they should have moderate food, extremely humble clothing, and sufficient sleep.

As a result, in accordance with the Lord’s will—who calls all people to salvation and grants every increase of good—very many flocked to the old man, wishing to remain with him. Among them were Pecusius, Cornelius, Paul, another Pachomius, and John. All of them gladly embraced the blessed Father’s undefiled faith and salutary teaching.

He appointed those who were able to undertake the care of the monastery, and thus the number of monks quickly multiplied.

[Col. 0245A] When custom required them to participate in the heavenly mysteries, they summoned priests from the neighboring villages to fill them with the joy of spiritual celebration. The same old man did not permit anyone among them to perform the office of a cleric.

For he said that it was much better and more advantageous for monks not only to seek no primacy of honor or glory whatsoever, but also to cut off such opportunities from the monasteries, since contentions and useless rivalries frequently arose among the brothers from such causes.

Just as a spark of fire, when it falls upon a harvest, is not quickly extinguished and sometimes burns up the produce of an entire year, so the destructive thought of ambition, if it enters the minds of monks, making them desire either to be first or to become clerics, will immediately destroy the self-control acquired through many labors unless they quickly drive the heat of this suggestion from their hearts.

Therefore, with all gentleness and purity, monks ought to venerate the clergy who serve in Christ’s churches, because this is beneficial for monks, but they should seek no ecclesiastical dignities.

If, however, we find that some of the monks were previously ordained clerics by bishops, we should embrace their ministry. For even in the Old Testament the entire people did not presume to undertake sacred office; only those born from the tribe of Levi were appointed to such service.

If an outside brother should arrive who is known to exercise the priestly office, let us not reproach him as though he had seized sacred rights and arrogantly thrust himself into these ministries. How could we suspect this of someone whom we ourselves earnestly ask to celebrate the heavenly sacraments?

Rather, we ought to honor him even more as a father and as one who is obedient to us in this matter, since he follows the footsteps of the saints and does not cease to offer God an undefiled gift—especially if his conduct is awaited and approved by everyone.

If, God forbid, he is thought to have fallen into some fault, we cannot judge him. For God, the just judge, has appointed bishops as judges over such matters. They are successors and imitators of the blessed apostles, and they can examine the affairs of individuals through spiritual judgment and pronounce an equitable decision concerning them.

We, however, should sympathize with such people from the depths of our hearts, since the Lord also admonishes us to be merciful (Matthew 6). We ought continually to entreat him not to allow us to be led into any temptation.

These things were not merely spoken forcefully by the Father just mentioned; they were also observed with the greatest care.

Finally, whenever a cleric came to him wishing to live under his rule, Pachomius gave his dignity the honor due to the Church. The cleric, however, serving according to the institutions of the monks, humbly submitted himself to Pachomius as to a father.

**CHAPTER XXV.**—Blessed Pachomius loved all Christ’s servants so greatly that he always sympathized with them in fatherly affection. To the elderly, the sick, and also the little ones, he personally supplied works of mercy, strengthening their minds with spiritual protection above all else.

As many advanced in faith and works, and the number of brothers increased greatly, almost all strove to be imitators of virtue.

Accordingly, he appointed some of them as superiors [Note: [Col. 0279A] “Superiors.”] Jerome, in the preface to the Rule of Saint Pachomius: “They—the Tabennesiot monks—have in each monastery fathers and stewards, weekly officers, ministers, and superiors of the individual houses.”], so that they might be his assistants in winning the souls who flocked to him each day.

Since, as has been said, very many came to him and advanced in spiritual work in various ways, there appeared to be considerable diversity in their manner of life. Guided in every respect by Christ’s grace and by the rule divinely given to him, the old man therefore judged that the measures and forms of work should be adapted to the abilities and dispositions of each person.

Some were to earn their livelihood through manual labor; others were to occupy themselves with serving the brothers. They were not all to eat at the same times, but each was to preserve the restraints of moderation according to his labor or discipline.

He entrusted the entire administration and care of the brothers and visitors to those who followed him in rank.

[Col. 0246B] He admonished all the monks to be ready for obedience, so that by this shortcut they might easily reach the lofty heights of perfection and carefully cultivate their hearts in the fear of Christ. In this way they would live for God rather than for themselves, offering him the humble fruits of obedience.

Although this venerable father was occupied with spiritual activities, whenever the person to whom he had entrusted the care of the monastery happened to be absent, he carried out everything alone, as though he were the servant of all.

He did this without any display or boasting, which commonly empties spiritual men of their great virtues. With the utmost humility of mind he edified everyone in the Lord, managing everything beneficially.

He also went carefully through all the monasteries, until he returned again to those same sons of his with fatherly affection. When he found them diligently keeping watch over the work of God, he rejoiced and took great pleasure in the increase of their progress.

**CHAPTER XXVI.**—At a certain time, seeing some ordinary people in the neighboring places abstaining from communion in Christ’s sacraments while tending their flocks, and not enjoying the reading of the divine books that are solemnly recited everywhere every Saturday and Sunday, Pachomius took counsel with Saint Aprion, bishop of Tentyris [Note: [Col. 0279A] “Aprion, bishop of Tentyris.”] The Cologne edition has *Pycerius* instead of *Aprion*. The name Aprion occurs in ancient inscriptions in Gruter, p. 695:

**“For Publius Livius Articulus Aprius; [his] father [erected this]; the burial-plot was granted by the heirs” (abbreviations expanded with some uncertainty).**

[Col. 0279B] The name *Aprius* also occurs in these inscriptions. In Athanasius, *Apology 2 for His Flight*, p. 618, there is Bishop Saprion. In the same work, p. 596, there is Aprianus among the bishops who signed the Council of Sardica.], so that a church might be built in their nearly deserted village, to which they could gather and receive the divine mysteries.

When this had been done, and no clerics had yet been ordained to conduct the solemn services for the people, Pachomius himself came with the monks at the hour when the congregation gathered in the church, rereading the pages of salvation to the people. For, as I have said, no readers had yet been appointed there, nor any other clerics to celebrate the sacred offices.

Thus, as long as the priest and the rest of the clerical order were absent, Pachomius came and cheerfully and without embarrassment performed the office of reader. He kept the eyes of his mind and body so intent that, when the people saw him, they believed him to be not a man but an angel of God.

As a result, many were converted from error through his instruction and became Christians. For he was exceedingly perfect in his love for his neighbors and so merciful that, whenever he saw people deceived by the devil’s fraud—worshiping not the true God but serving empty idols—he groaned bitterly over their destruction and poured out abundant tears for their salvation.

## CHAPTER XXVII

At that time the holy bishop Athanasius presided over the Alexandrian Church, a man remarkable in every virtue. As he was making his solemn circuit of the churches of Upper Thebaid and instructing the people in the saving doctrine of the faith in Christ, it happened that he arrived by boat at the territory of the Tabennisians. When Pachomius learned this, he immediately hastened with all the monks to meet him. All, rejoicing and exulting, received the supreme pontiff of Christ with psalms and hymns; and there was a great multitude of brothers who rejoiced in the Lord at his arrival.

Pachomius, however, did not present himself to the aforementioned bishop. Deliberately withdrawing, he concealed himself among the ranks of the monks [Col. 0247B], for this reason: the aforementioned bishop of Tentyris had often pleaded with Saint Athanasius on his behalf, saying that he was a remarkable man and truly a servant of God, whom Athanasius should most worthily promote to priestly honor. Knowing this, Pachomius did not show himself openly to him, but remained hidden among the throngs of monks until the bishop had passed by. He venerated him so greatly that he said no one in those times was superior to him.

For he had learned of Athanasius’s holy life and the countless persecutions that he had endured from the Arians for his confession of Christ. He also admired, with attentive devotion, the charity that Athanasius showed toward everyone, and especially toward monks, and he venerated him with the whole affection of his heart. Nor did he love only this man more ardently; he also esteemed above all others, with the greatest zeal, all men of orthodox faith.

He detested heretics exceedingly, and especially abhorred Origen as blasphemous and faithless. Origen, having been declared a precursor of Arius and Meletius, was expelled from the Church under Heraclas, the venerable bishop of the city of Alexandria.

> **Note: Heraclas.**  
> This man was bishop of the city of Alexandria. Eusebius mentions him in the *Chronicle*, in the eighth year of the emperor Alexander: “Heraclas is ordained the twelfth bishop of the Church of Alexandria and holds office for sixteen years.” Eusebius also mentions him in Book VI, chapters 12, 14, 24, and 28 of the *Ecclesiastical History*. His memory is preserved in the Roman Martyrology on 14 July: “At Alexandria, Saint Heraclas, bishop, whose celebrated reputation led the historiographer Africanus to say that he hastened to Alexandria to visit him.”

Origen had mixed into his interpretations teachings hateful and detestable to the doctrines of Sacred Scripture, teachings that subverted the hearts of certain people. Just as those who prepare poisons conceal their bitterness with honey, so he, coating the poison of his own error with the sweetness of heavenly words, administered deadly doctrines to the inexperienced.

Therefore he warned all the brothers most earnestly not only that they themselves should not read Origen’s writings,

> **Note: Origen’s writings.**  
> Below, chapter 45: “But if you wish to heed me and please God in all things, [Col. 0280A] plunge all the books of Origen into the river, lest you yourselves be plunged beneath them.”  
> Baronius, under the year of Christ 402, the fifth year of Pope Anastasius, and the eighth year of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, says concerning this same matter: “I think that Origen’s *On First Principles* (*περὶ ἀρχῶν*), the fountainhead of errors, is what is meant in the Acts of blessed Pachomius, where he is said to have condemned monks who read Origen’s books.” For those books, *On First Principles* (*περὶ ἀρχῶν*), were circulating through the monasteries of Egypt; and, because Didymus had adorned them with notes, they were held in high esteem by some. Hence it also happened that Pachomius, as he was departing this life, left Origen’s errors condemned, as though in a testament. You will find this later in this *Life*, chapter 53.

but that they should not even lend a receptive ear to those who read them. It is therefore reported that on one occasion he found a volume of Origen’s and immediately threw it into the water, declaring in these words:

> “If I did not know that the name of God was written in it, I would have burned all his babblings of blasphemies in the fire.”

He was so much a lover of the orthodox faith and a champion of truth. Just as he opposed the enemies of the Church with hostile hatred, so he was known to rejoice in the progress of Catholics, and he testified that he saw Christ himself, the redeemer of all, in his priests upon the throne of the Church.

If he ever learned that a brother was slandering someone over any matter, he not only did not believe him, but immediately turned away and withdrew from him as swiftly as from the face of a serpent. He frequently impressed upon them the words of the Psalmist:

> “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I pursued” (Psalm 100).

“No good man,” he used to say, “brings anything evil from his mouth, nor does he speak abusively with a poisonous tongue against the holy fathers.” Concerning this matter he demonstrated from many passages of Scripture the offense provoked against the indignant God. Above all, however, he produced the example of Miriam, who, as soon as she poured out complaints of slander against Moses, could not escape divine judgment, but was covered with leprosy. By teaching these things, he conferred the greatest benefit upon his hearers (Numbers 12).

## CHAPTER XXVIII

His own sister learned of the old man’s renowned and sublime instruction (Rufinus, Book III, no. 34). Desiring to see him, she came to his monastery. When Pachomius learned this, he sent her the following reply through the doorkeeper:

> “Behold, sister, you have heard that I am alive and well; go, therefore, in peace, and do not grieve because I do not see you with bodily eyes. But if you wish to follow this way of life that I maintain, so that you may find mercy with the Lord, think carefully and deliberate within yourself. If I learn that this holy purpose has taken root in your heart, I shall order my brothers to build you a dwelling at a distance, where you may persevere with discipline and modesty. Nor do I doubt that the Lord will call others through your example, so that they may remain with you and through you deserve to find the help of eternal salvation. For no one can have true rest in this body of death unless he has pleased God by good works.”

When his sister heard this, she wept bitterly. Divinely moved and persuaded by this most salutary exhortation, she immediately inclined her mind to it and professed that she would serve Christ [Col. 0248C]. Recognizing this disposition of his sister, Pachomius gave thanks to God, who had granted her a ready will, and at once ordered the more religious brothers to build her a monastery at a distance from his own.

When this had been done and she was leading her life according to the fear of God, many other women gathered to her, and within a short time she became the mother of a great multitude. Instructing and teaching them to withdraw their hearts from carnal desires and raise them toward heavenly things that endure forever, she showed them the paths of salvation both by her life and by her words.

Saint Pachomius ordered a certain Peter, already advanced in years and distinguished by venerable old age, to visit the women servants of God from time to time and raise them up by holy exhortation. Along with the mortification of every passion, he also possessed speech that was, as it is written, seasoned with salt. He was exceedingly chaste in the eyes of both mind and body, and he often spoke to the virgins of Christ from the Holy Scriptures (Colossians 4), explaining what pertained to salvation.

Pachomius also wrote rules for them, by which they were to direct the moments of their way of life continually. Except for the *melotes*, which women do not wear, the whole form of their discipline was judged to be similar to that of the monks.

If one of the brothers had a female relative or sister in the women’s monastery and wished to visit her, one of the elders of approved life was sent with him. First he would see the woman who presided over the sisters; then, in her presence and in that of the other women who were more advanced in age, the brother would see his sister or other female relative with complete modesty and the grace of holiness. He neither gave anything to her nor accepted anything at all from her. They possessed nothing of their own that they could give one another; it was enough for both merely to perform the duty of visitation and to remember future things with the hope of eternal happiness.

If the women ever needed the monks for construction or any other matter, men of exemplary conduct were selected to carry out the requested duties on behalf of the brothers. Working in the fear of the Lord, they returned to the monastery at the hour of the meal, taking care not to receive from the women any food or drink.

One rule for both men and women still endures today, except that women do not use *melotes*, as we have said (Palladius, chapter 39).

If a virgin died, the women who remained took care of her funeral and completed everything belonging to her burial. They carried her as far as the bank of the river that divided the two monasteries, singing psalms according to custom. Then the monks crossed over with branches of palms and olive leaves, carried her across while singing psalms, and buried her joyfully in their own tombs.

## CHAPTER XXIX

This way of life, so great and so admirable, spread far and wide, and the name of holy Pachomius reached everywhere, stirring everyone to give thanks to God. Not a few, moreover, despised the affairs of this world and loved the singular way of life of the monks and their spiritual pursuits. Among them was also Theodore.

> **Note: Theodore.**  
> Concerning him Gennadius writes in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men of the Church*, chapter 8: “Theodore the presbyter, successor to the grace and governance of the aforementioned abbot Pachomius, wrote to other monasteries works arranged in the form of discourses on the Holy Scriptures. In them he frequently mentions his master and teacher Pachomius and sets forth examples of his doctrine and life, which Pachomius had learned through the ministry of an angel in order to teach them. He also urges perseverance in the purpose of heart and in zeal, and calls back to concord and unity those who, after the abbot’s death, had separated themselves from the assembly by withdrawing from unity. There are three letters of this exhortation.”  
> The memory of this Theodore is celebrated in the Greek Church on 15 May, as the Greek Menologion records: “On the same day, Theodore who was sanctified. This blessed Theodore, after meditating upon the law of God, became wholly pure through a most chaste mind and was shown to be a useful and sanctified vessel. Surpassing the perception of visible things, he was joined to Saint Pachomius in companionship and character, and truly worthy to be called sanctified, since he became rich in the working of miracles. Having therefore lived his life so well, he departed to the Lord in extreme old age.”  
> You also find this account, with certain additions, in the Greek *Menaea*, where his feast day is marked on 16 May [Col. 0280C]. Thus it appears that an error entered the *Menologion*, where 16 May is omitted; that date should be marked and assigned to Theodore. He is also mentioned in the *Menaea*, in the *Life of Saint Pachomius* on 15 May, where he is likewise called “the sanctified” (*ὁ ἡγιασμένος*).

Theodore was about fourteen years old, born to Christian parents who were also very distinguished according to the world. He was converted in the following manner.

On the eleventh day of the month Tybi—that is, the eighth day before the Ides of January—

> **Note: The eleventh day of the month Tybi, that is, the eighth day before the Ides of January.**  
> Do not be surprised that the eleventh day of the Egyptian month Tybi corresponds to the sixth day of the Roman month of January, or the eighth day before the Ides of January. For the Egyptians began their month Tybi on the sixth day before the Kalends of January, that is, on 27 December. From 27 December to 6 January there are eleven days. See the table in the *Onomasticon of the Months*.

a certain festival was customarily celebrated in Egypt. Seeing that his house was exceedingly spacious and splendid and abounding in every good thing, Theodore, by the grace of God pierced in heart, began to reason with himself as follows:

> “What will it profit you, wretched Theodore, if you gain the whole world (Matthew 16), and, enjoying temporal pleasures to the full, are excluded from those eternal and immortal goods? No one can both enjoy present pleasures and earn the rewards of everlasting glory.”

Groaning deeply over these things, he entered the inner rooms of his house. Falling on his face, he said with tears:

> “Almighty God, knower of hidden things, you know that I place none of the things belonging to this world above your love. Therefore I beseech you, merciful one, to direct me in your will, enlightening my wretched soul, lest, darkened by sins, it fall asleep in eternal death; but, redeemed by your gift, may it praise and glorify you in all things.”

While he was praying in this way, his mother came and found his eyes full of tears. She said:

> “Who has saddened you, dearest son, so that you withdraw from us? We were anxiously and sorrowfully looking for you everywhere, so that you might dine with us.”

He replied:

> “Please go, mother, and eat, because I cannot eat now.”

He did not yield to her entreaties that he eat with her. And when he walked to school to learn his letters, [Col. 0250A] he fasted until evening. Frequently he also completed two-day fasts. For two years he abstained from all costly and delicate foods, extending himself toward perfect continence as far as his age allowed.

He then began to consider how he might seek a monastery and devote himself to a holy rule. Abandoning everything he possessed, he found certain religious men living according to excellent discipline. He dwelt with them, making progress in the fear of the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXX

At a certain time, after evening prayer, when the monks had sat down and were customarily meditating on the divine words, one of them, speaking in the hearing of Theodore, interpreted the tabernacle of the Old Testament and the Holy of Holies with reference to the new peoples—that is, to circumcision and uncircumcision.

He said that the outer tabernacle represented the former people of the Jews, while the inner one, which is the Holy of Holies, foreshadowed the calling of all the nations, which had been granted access to the more sacred entrance and had become participants in greater mysteries.

In place of the animal sacrifices, and in place of the ark containing the manna, Aaron’s budding staff, and the tablets of the covenant; in place also of the censer, the table, the lampstand, and the mercy seat, God the Word mercifully appeared to us in his incarnation and enlightened us with the light of his presence. He became the propitiation for our sins and gave his own body to be eaten in place of the manna.

While this brother was devoutly discussing these things with the monks who were present, he added:

> “I learned this interpretation from our holy father Pachomius, who first gathered monks together in the monastery at Tabennisi. With them, by the Lord’s help, I have progressed day by day.”

“And I believe that, because I have remembered so great a man,

> **Note: “And I believe that, because I have remembered so great a man.”**  
> Athanasius attributes great importance to the memory of Saint Antony. Above, in the preface to his *Life*: “For it is a great gain and benefit to me that I remember Antony.” Bernard recognizes in himself a threefold desire arising from the memory of the saints, sermon 5 on the feast of All Saints: “Clearly, that we venerate their memory benefits us, not them. Do you wish to know how much it benefits us? In myself, I confess, I feel that from this remembrance a vehement desire is kindled, and a threefold desire.” See the rest in his work.

all my sins will be forgiven.”

Hearing this, Theodore was inflamed in spirit. He prayed within himself, saying:

> “Lord God, if such a righteous man exists on earth, make me worthy to see him, and, following in his footsteps, to fulfill all his commandments. Having also been saved, may I deserve to obtain the good things you promised to those who love you.”

Saying these things with tears, he was overcome, having been powerfully wounded by divine love.

After several days, a venerable man named Pecusius, adorned with long old age, came to visit the brothers and at the same time wishing to learn how they were faring. Theodore earnestly begged him to receive him as a companion and to deign to lead him to Saint Pachomius. Without delay, Pecusius gladly took him with him.

When they had arrived at the place, Theodore adored the Lord, saying:

> “Blessed are you, Lord, who so quickly heard the prayer of a sinner; and, as I had asked of you, you have deigned to fulfill my desire.”

As he approached the monastery door, he saw Pachomius and immediately began to weep for joy. The venerable father said to him:

> “Do not weep, my son, because I too am a sinful man, although I have undertaken the work of God.”

Saying this, he brought him into the monastery. When Theodore saw the multitude of brothers, his mind was enlightened, and he burned intensely with devout zeal for divine worship. As time went on, he made great progress in the virtues.

He was endowed with an abundance of divine gifts and was very prudent in good works and words. He was exceedingly remarkable for humility and contrition of heart; diligent in fasts, attentive in vigils, earnest in prayer, and never at all ceasing to pursue greater gifts of spiritual grace.

He consoled many who were weighed down by sorrow, and corrected those who had gone astray through some sin with humble and kindly admonition.

## CHAPTER XXXI

Finally, when Pachomius saw Theodore’s conduct so distinguished and radiant, he loved him greatly and treasured him in his heart.

When Theodore’s mother learned that he was staying with blessed Pachomius, she immediately hastened to him, bringing with her letters from the bishops ordering that her son be returned to her. The virgins received her in the monastery, which, as stated above, was not far from that of the men.
