She immediately sent letters to Saint Pachomius, likewise begging that he permit her to see her own son (Rufinus, Book III, no. 34).

Then Pachomius summoned Theodore and said to him:

> “I have learned, my son, that your mother has come here and wishes to see you. Behold, she has also brought us letters from the bishops. Go, therefore, and satisfy your mother, especially on account of the holy bishops who have deigned to send us letters through her.”

Theodore replied:

> “First assure me, venerable father, that after such knowledge of spiritual things, if I see her I will not have to give an account of it to the Lord on the day of judgment; and then I shall do what you command. For, in accordance with Christ’s command, I abandoned her along with the whole world. How would I now dare to see her, to the offense of the brothers? For if previously, before the manifestation of such great grace, the sons of Levi ignored their own parents in order to fulfill the justifications of the law (Exodus 32; Deuteronomy 33; Leviticus 21), how much more ought I, who have become a participant in so great a gift, not place parents before divine love, since the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me’ (Matthew 10)?”

Pachomius said to him:

> “If you judge that this is not expedient for you, my son, I do not compel you. This is the conduct of those who renounce this world perfectly and utterly deny themselves. Monks ought to flee useless and worldly greetings and empty conversations, and to associate with those who are members of Christ with devout minds. But if someone, captivated by some passion of the world, says, ‘My parents are my flesh; I ought to love them,’ let him hear the blessed apostle Peter proclaiming: ‘By whatever anyone is overcome, by that he is also enslaved’ (2 Peter 2). Whoever is overcome by love of the flesh is without doubt a slave of the flesh.”

Since Theodore did not agree to present himself to his mother, she decided to remain in that same monastery with the virgins of Christ, reasoning within herself:

> “If it is the Lord’s will, at least among the other monks I shall see him; and through this opportunity I shall also gain my own soul, while I persevere in this holy way of life.”

It is therefore evident that those who preserve strictness for the name of Christ, not for empty praise, apply many virtues to the benefit of others, although they may appear for a short time to offend some people.

## CHAPTER XXXII

Just as we have set forth this man’s zeal for the imitation of those who desire to follow what is better, so we consider it right to make known the negligence of certain others, for the warning of those who will read these things.

Certain monks, living according to the flesh (Colossians 3) and taking no care to strip off the old man, afflicted Saint Pachomius severely. He often addressed them with salutary admonitions, but perceived absolutely no progress in them.

Therefore, sad and anxious, he prayed to the Lord for them with greater earnestness, saying:

> “Lord and Ruler, you commanded us to love our neighbors as ourselves (Leviticus 19; Matthew 19). Since you know the secrets of my heart, I beseech you not to disregard me as I cry out to you for their salvation. Rather, have mercy on them and give them your fear, so that, recognizing your divine power, they may serve you in truth, strengthened in all things by hope in your promises. For my soul is exceedingly distressed on their account, and all my senses are utterly troubled.”

Saying this, he fell silent.

After several days, seeing that they had not been made better even by prayer, he again stood for prayer and supplicated the Lord for them. He gave them certain private and particular rules for prayer and conduct, so that, at least as servants fulfilling established regulations, they might gradually become accustomed, through diligent affection, to attaining the role of sons.

When they saw that they could no longer follow their desires and feared the presence of Saint Pachomius, they were deceived by a spirit of fear—not the chaste fear—and went back after Satan, unable to endure his remarkable way of life.

When they had departed, the whole flock remained in the integrity of its condition, rising more and more toward an increase of virtues, just as the finest grain in the fields usually blossoms more luxuriantly when the weeds have been uprooted from it completely.

I have related these things to show that, just as it does no harm to people devoted to the world if they surrender themselves to the discipline of monks, so the venerable profession of monks brings no benefit to monks if they are negligent. Neither paternal prayer nor condescension will be able to help those who remain sluggish.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

Meanwhile, the confessor Dionysius, presbyter and steward—that is, administrator—of the Church of Tentyris, a very close friend of Saint Pachomius, learned from certain people that Pachomius did not allow those who came to him from other monasteries to eat with his own brothers, but received them in a separate place beside the monastery gates.

Greatly distressed by this, Dionysius came to him. Taking on more the attitude of one reproving than of one offering advice, he said:

> “You are not acting rightly, abba, by not showing the charity owed to the brothers equally to all.”

Pachomius accepted his correction with great forbearance and patience and replied:

> “The Lord knows my purpose, and your fatherly affection knows that I never wish to sadden anyone’s soul, nor do I mean to despise anyone. How, then, would I dare to do this and provoke my Lord against me, offending him who openly testifies in the Gospel, saying: ‘As long as you did it to one of the least of my brothers, you did it to me’ (Matthew 25)?

> “Accept, therefore, my explanation, venerable father. I do not do what you allege as though I were avoiding or despising those who come here. Rather, because I have received a congregation into a coenobium, I know that many who have recently been converted have varied customs. I also know that some are so ignorant of this way of life that they do not even know the habit of monks. Among them are little ones who live with such simplicity that they cannot distinguish the right hand from the left.

> “For this reason I have judged it more beneficial that the brothers who arrive should be received separately and treated with the greatest honor. Therefore I do not think that any insult is done to the fathers or brothers who visit us; rather, due reverence is shown to them—especially since they gather with us at the appointed hours to offer their vows to God, and afterward each returns to his assigned place, attending to rest, while I, according to God, carefully provide what is necessary for their needs.”

Hearing this, the aforementioned presbyter declared him most worthy of all praise, recognizing with certainty that he did everything according to God. Greatly relieved by Saint Pachomius’s explanation, he happily returned home.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

A certain woman in the same city of Tentyris suffered from an issue of blood and had already endured this illness for a long time. When she heard that Pachomius was a worshiper of God and remarkable for his holy way of life, and moreover that the presbyter Dionysius was his dearest friend, she asked Dionysius to take pity on her and, under the pretext of some necessary matter, summon Pachomius to him.

Moved by the woman’s entreaties, Dionysius did not delay in doing this. When Pachomius came to the church and, after prayer, had greeted Dionysius, he immediately sat down beside him.

While they were speaking with one another, the woman, strengthened by the confidence of faith and believing Christ’s words, “Take courage, daughter; your faith has saved you” (Matthew 9), secretly approached from behind. Trembling, she touched the hood that covered his head, and she was immediately healed.

Falling on her face, she adored the Lord and glorified his mercy, because he had bestowed such great benefits upon believers through his servants.

Then the holy man Dionysius, sensing what had happened, blessed the woman, and he immediately returned home.

## CHAPTER XXXV

At one time necessity required that the monastery be enclosed with a fence for protection. While the brothers were laboring at this work, Pachomius himself gladly provided the greatest assistance.

Several days later, a certain monk who was a presbyter and father of many brothers, and who was accustomed to visit Saint Pachomius frequently, came to him with one of the brothers, because a dispute had arisen in the monastery.

The brother who had come with him was causing him great difficulty, desiring clerical rank. Knowing him to be unworthy of such an office, the presbyter had delayed the matter in various ways so that it would not come about. When he could no longer endure the man’s importunity, he came to Saint Pachomius and disclosed to him everything concerning the matter, certain that Pachomius alone could resolve disputes of this kind.

When Pachomius had fully understood the case, he said to the presbyter:

> “Did you not come for this purpose, to learn the Lord’s will through me? Listen to me, then, and give him what he asks, despairing of nothing in this matter. Perhaps through this office his soul will be freed from captivity to the devil. It often happens that a bad man, being treated with benefits, turns to good conduct. For the desire for better things is known to generate a devout purpose in those souls that have not fallen so deeply through the sluggishness of negligence that they are unable to strive after the virtues.

> “Therefore, brother, we ought to do what pleases God. His love will be shown to exist in us if we sympathize with one another.”

Having received this reply, the elder did what he had been ordered to do.

But the brother, having obtained what he desired, returned to blessed Pachomius, now sober and contrite in mind. Falling on his face, he confessed, saying:

> “Man of God, you have been greatly exalted by God, because, discerning what pertains to salvation, you have conquered evil with good. If you had not been gentle and patient toward me, but had shown me some severity, I would have departed from this habit and become utterly alienated from God. But now, blessed are you in the Lord, through whom my soul has been saved.”

Then the venerable old man raised him from the ground and earnestly exhorted him to adopt a life suited to his dignity, lest, if he were ever negligent, he should suffer everlasting torments in the future. He kissed him and dismissed him in peace, accompanying him even to the monastery gates.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

While Saint Pachomius was still standing there, behold, a man came hurrying from far away and threw himself at his feet. He begged that Pachomius, through the grace of Christ, deign to cure his daughter, who was tormented by a demon.

Leaving the man outside, Pachomius entered and sent him this reply through the doorkeeper:

> “It is not our custom to speak with women. But if you have anything from her clothing, send it to us. We shall bless it in the name of the Lord and immediately send it back to you. We believe in Christ that in this way your daughter will be freed from the assault of the enemy.”

When the girl’s tunic had been brought to the holy man, he examined it very carefully and said:

> “This is not her garment.”

When the father affirmed that it was hers, he replied:

> “I also know that it is hers. But although she dedicated her virginity to God, she did not preserve the purity of her holiness. For this reason, examining her tunic and understanding that she had not guarded her chastity, I declared that it was not hers. Let her therefore promise you, in the presence of the Lord, that henceforth she will live continently, and Christ will be propitiated toward her and restore her health.”

The father, indignant and sorrowful, questioned his daughter and learned from the girl’s confession that it was as Saint Pachomius had said.

After she had promised under oath never again to do such things, the blessed man prayed to the Lord for her. He blessed oil and sent it. When she had been anointed with it, she was cured without delay. She continually glorified the Lord because she had been freed not only from the demon but also from her detestable conduct, and through Christ’s help had devoted herself thereafter to the pursuit of continence.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

As such a reputation for the holy man spread everywhere, another man who continually lamented that his son was possessed by a demon, and who could not bring him to the monastery, knelt and begged Pachomius to pray for him to the omnipotence of Christ.

After praying, Pachomius gave the father some blessed bread, carefully instructing him always to give a little of it to the possessed boy before food.

When the boy became hungry, the father offered him a small piece of that bread. But the unclean spirit did not allow him to taste it at all. From the other loaves that had been set out, however, the boy filled his hands and began to eat.

The father therefore broke the blessed bread into pieces and, removing the bones from his palms, placed the pieces inside them. He then offered the boy only those palms, so that, without knowing what had been done, he might deserve to receive the blessing.

When the boy opened his hands, he threw away the pieces that had been placed there. Cursing his own palms, he absolutely refused to take any food.

After the father had compelled him to remain without food for many days, hunger forced him to receive some of the blessed bread. Immediately he was overcome by sleep and was freed from the evil spirit.

The father brought him with him to the feet of Saint Pachomius, praising and glorifying God, who works great and glorious deeds through his servants, deeds whose number cannot be counted.

The most blessed man also performed many other healings through the power of the Holy Spirit, but he was not elated, nor was his heart ever lifted up. He had received this grace from the Lord: he was always the same and equal in all things, and he kept his mind earnestly disciplined according to the Lord.

Whenever he asked something of the Lord and did not obtain the result of his petition, he was not at all saddened. Rather, he endured it with the greatest patience, knowing that whatever the divine mercy had determined was beneficial either for himself or for everyone. For often, with sincere intention, we seem to ask for things that are contrary to our good; and when the Lord does not grant them, he graciously grants what is truly beneficial. He hears us more mercifully when he does not fulfill the desires veiled in the darkness of our ignorance.

CAP. XXXVIII.—A certain young man, Silvanus by name, converted from the stage, came to Saint Pachomius, wishing to remain in his monastery. When he had been received, however, being infected with the perverse habits of the world, he could be restrained by no rules of discipline. Neglecting his own salvation, he occupied his days with his former vanities and absurdities, to such an extent that he led some of the brothers astray and stirred them toward a similar way of life. Many of them, unable to endure this, reported to Saint Pachomius that he should order the young man expelled from the monastery. He did not agree to this request; rather, bearing with him patiently, he admonished the aforesaid brother to correct himself and renounce his former way of life. For him he also continually entreated the Lord, asking that, in the accustomed abundance of His mercy, He might grant him compunction of heart.

[Col. 0256A] When the young man persisted in his depravity and offered others an example of ruin, it finally seemed to everyone that he should be excluded from the holy community as utterly unworthy. But blessed Pachomius believed that this should still be delayed. Meeting with him through an exceedingly gentle and wise correction, and instructing him in heavenly principles, he so kindled him with the fear of God, and his soul was so pierced by faith in things to come, that thereafter he could not restrain himself from tears.

Thus corrected in every respect, he offered the others a great example of conversion. In every place and in every task he wept continually; even when he was eating with the brothers, he did not cease lamenting. This moved many of the monks, who said: “At last restrain yourself from mourning, and, we beg you, do not cast yourself down by such great affliction.” He replied: “I do try, as you command, to restrain my tears, but I cannot. My breast, burning as though with a kind of flame, does not allow me to be at peace.”

Again they said to him: “Weep in private, in your own solitude, or at least during your prayers; but when we come together at table, you ought to take food and abstain from weeping. For it is possible for the soul to remain continually in compunction even without these outward tears. Indeed, when many of the brothers see you weeping, they cannot eat.” They compelled him to explain why he thus washed himself in his own tears.

Then he said to them: “You do not want me to weep when I see myself being cherished with so many services by the holy brothers, whose feet-dust is venerable to me, and to whom I consider myself wholly unworthy to be compared. Shall I not weep, when I, a man from the stage and burdened with many sins, receive such attentions? I greatly fear that, like Dathan and Abiram, the earth may swallow me too, profane as I am, in its chasm (Num. 16). They attempted, in their impious boldness and with polluted hands, to usurp holy things for themselves; but I, after receiving such knowledge of the divine gift, neglected the salvation of my soul through a negligent way of life. Therefore, recalling these things, I am not ashamed to weep before everyone, because I know that my crimes are many and that I ought to expiate them through continual fountains of tears. [Col. 0256C] And if I were to pour out my wretched soul itself through lamentation, I would be doing nothing great, since I can find no punishment in the present life proportionate to my deeds.”

When this brother advanced daily toward better things and surpassed almost everyone in humility, Saint Pachomius began to speak of him publicly to all in this way:

“I call you to witness, brothers and sons, before God and His holy angels, that since this coenobium was founded, I know of no brother who is or has been with me who has followed my humility, except one alone.”

When they heard this, some thought that this one was Theodore, others Petronius, and others Orsesius. When Theodore asked him to reveal who this person was, and the holy man delayed identifying him, Theodore pressed him again and again. Other senior brothers also earnestly begged him to say whom he honored with such a testimony.

Then Pachomius replied:

[Col. 0257A] “If I knew that the person of whom I am about to speak would be stirred by the goads of vainglory, I would never point him out. But because I firmly believe that, by Christ’s grace, the more praise comes to him, the more he will acquire the gift of humility, I do not cease openly to call him blessed without fear, so that you may be able to imitate him.

“You, Theodore, and all who resemble you, fighting bravely in the monastery, have bound the devil like a sparrow [Note: [Col. 0280D] ‘You have bound the devil like a sparrow.’ The devil himself, below, in chapter 49, acknowledges his weakness and captivity: ‘Since Christ’s wondrous incarnation took place on earth, we have begun to exist utterly without strength, so that by those who believe in His name we are mocked like sparrows.’ Athanasius has something similar above, in chapter 16 of the Life of Saint Antony. Edinerus, in Book II of the Life of Saint Anselm, whose feast falls on 21 April, also has another and contrary little story and comparison concerning the sport with a sparrow, by which the devil keeps sinners bound by an evil habit and mocks them:

‘On another occasion he saw a boy playing in the road with a little bird. The bird had one foot tied with a thread and, whenever it was allowed to go farther out, tried to fly away to save itself. But the boy, holding the thread in his hand, pulled it back and threw it down again at his side, and this gave him great pleasure. This happened repeatedly. When the father saw it, he pitied the wretched bird and wished that, once the thread was broken, it might be restored to freedom. And behold, the thread breaks, the bird flies away, the boy weeps, and the father rejoices. Then, calling us, he said: “Did you observe the boy’s game?” When we confessed that we had, he said: “By a similar game the devil plays with many people whom he has entangled in his snares and drags at will into various vices. There are some—for example, those inflamed by greed, lust, and similar passions and enslaved to them through long habit—who sometimes come to reflect on their deeds, grieve over them, and promise themselves that they will henceforth cease from such things. Behold, like the bird, they think themselves free to fly away. But because, entangled in evil practice, they are held by the enemy even while flying, they are thrown back into the same vices. This happens repeatedly, and they are not completely freed unless, through a great effort and by consideration of God’s grace, the thread of evil habit is broken.”’

You also have this in Anselm’s Book On Similitudes, chapter 189, and in Antoninus, volume II of the Chronicle, title XVI, chapter 11, section 2, somewhat more fully.] You have trampled him beneath your feet, by God’s grace crushing him like dust. But if—which God forbid—you neglect anything, he who lies beneath your footprints will rise up and rage against you with savage fury.

“But the young man Silvanus, whom a short while ago you wished to expel from the monastery because of his negligence, so overthrew the enemy and banished him from his thoughts [Col. 0257B] that he never appears before him again; and by profound humility he surpassed him in every respect. You, indeed, possess works of righteousness and confidently glory in what you have done. But the more vigorously he fights, the worse he judges himself than everyone else, declaring with his whole mind and all his strength that he is useless and rejected.

“For this reason he always has tears ready, because he humbles and bows himself down excessively and considers nothing that he has done to be of any importance. Nothing makes the devil so powerless as humility from a pure heart, provided that works of correction accompany it.

“Thus this young man Silvanus served God manfully through the course of eight years and ended his life in peace. Blessed Pachomius testified concerning his departure that a multitude of holy angels, taking his soul with great joy, offered it before the presence of Christ like a chosen sacrifice.”

CAP. XXXIV.—At that same time, the bishop of the city of Panos, named Varus [Note: ‘The bishop of the city of Panos, named Varus.’ In Metaphrastes, chapter 62, he is called Panuarius, bishop of the city by name; this is undoubtedly corruptly derived from Panos and Varus.], a man venerable in every respect, devoted to God, and an exceedingly fervent lover of the true faith, heard about Pachomius’s manner of life. He summoned him by letters, earnestly begging him to establish the desired monasteries also near his city.

When, for many reasons, Pachomius had yielded to the bishop’s requests, and was hastening to him, he considered it right to visit along the way all the monasteries under his care. When he had approached one of these monasteries, he encountered the funeral of a certain brother who had spent his life negligently. The brothers of that monastery were escorting the funeral honorably, singing the customary psalms, while the dead man’s parents and relatives were also present.

When they saw Pachomius, they immediately set down the bier so that he might pray to the Lord both for the dead man and for themselves. As soon as he had offered the required prayer to God, he turned to the brothers and said: “Stop singing psalms.” He ordered the splendid garments in which the dead man had been dressed to be removed; he had them burned in the sight of everyone, ordered the corpse to be carried out, and commanded that it be buried without any psalmody.

The brothers, therefore, together with his parents and all who were present at the time, watched this strange spectacle, greatly astonished, and begged the old man to permit the customary psalmody to be performed over him. When he did not consent, the dead man’s parents began to blame him, saying:

“What is this new spectacle? Who does not pity a dead man, even if he is an enemy? The calamity itself is sufficient. We beg you, do not inflict upon the dead what not even beasts would do, and what is wholly unworthy of your holiness. We too are marked here by the greatest disgrace, and many other insulting suspicions are arising. Would that we had never come to this place! Would that this man had never become a monk! He would not then inflict this eternal grief upon us. We therefore beg you to restore the customary psalmody to the dead.”

He replied:

“Truly, brothers and sons, I pity the present dead man more than you do—so much so that while you are concerned with what is visible and temporal, I am anxious about his invisible substance. For this reason I have decided that these things should be done to him.

“You acquire greater pains for him through this honor which you imagine you are showing; but I prepare for him whatever small measure of rest or satisfaction I can through this injury [Note: ‘But I prepare for him whatever small measure of rest or satisfaction I can.’ In the fourth book of the Dialogues, chapter 50, Saint Gregory has Peter ask whether it benefits the souls of the dead if their bodies are buried in a church. Saint Gregory replies:

‘Those whom grave sins do not weigh down are helped by being buried in a church, because their relatives, whenever they gather in those sacred places and see the tombs of their own people, remember them and pour out prayers to the Lord for them. But those whom grave sins weigh down have their bodies placed in churches not for release, but rather for a greater accumulation of condemnation.’

He proves the latter part by examples in the three following chapters. You have the whole passage quoted in the response of Pope Nicholas I to the inquiries of the Bulgarians, chapter 99. How sacred burial harms the wicked is explained by Gregory himself in chapter 53, where he says:

‘From this, Peter, understand that, if those whom grave sins weigh down arrange to be buried in a sacred place, it remains for them also to be judged for their presumption, so that sacred places do not free them but rather their fault of rashness accuses them.’

Saint Thomas likewise, in the Supplement, question 71, article 11, response to objection 5, answering Gregory’s earlier passage, says:

‘Burial in a sacred place does not harm an impious dead person, except insofar as he procured this burial, unworthy of himself, for the sake of human glory.’

See him disputing admirably in that question whether the rites of burial benefit the dead. In accordance with the mind of these holy doctors, Pachomius’s judgment too must be understood. To this may also be referred what John has below in Book I, which concerns Providence, no. 13: at Nikiopolis a rich man condemned to punishment is buried honorably, so that, having done little good while living in this world, he might also receive little good in this world. Conversely, a holy hermit is eaten by wild beasts, because he had incurred little guilt in this life, and this was thus expiated.], not for this lifeless little body, but I am concerned for his immortal soul, which will receive this flesh again in the resurrection, incorrupt and whole.

“If I agree to what you wish, I shall be judged to be pleasing people; and, merely to appear to satisfy you for the moment, I shall disregard what may benefit him in the future. For our God, being the fountain of goodness, seeks opportunities through which He may pour out upon us the abundance of His mercy and forgive us our sins, not only in this world but also in the world to come.

“When the Gospel says that whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this world nor in the world to come, it undoubtedly indicates that there are certain offenses which may be forgiven even after this life, if prayers are offered for them (Matt. 12). We, whom divine power has judged worthy to exercise the medicine of Christ’s dispensation, will certainly be considered contemptuous if we do not offer each person the help suited to him; and we shall hear what is written in the prophecy: ‘Behold, you despisers, wonder and perish’ (Acts 13; Hab. 1).

“Therefore, I beg you, allow the dead man to be stripped, to some extent, of his own evils and to obtain whatever small measure of rest he may merit at that future judgment. Bury him, then, without psalms, as I have said. For the kind and merciful God, who is greatly compassionate, is able, in response to the prayer of our insignificance, to place him in His eternal rest.”

When he had said this, they departed and, according to what the venerable Father had commanded, took care to bury him on the mountain where the tombs had been prepared.

CAP. XL.—Saint Pachomius remained there with the monks for two days, teaching each of them first the fear of the Lord, and then how they ought to fight against the devil and, through Christ’s grace, avoid his snares.

Then it was announced to him that a certain brother from the monastery of Chinoboscus, held by a serious illness, was asking for the final blessing of his prayer. Hearing this, the man of God immediately followed those who had brought him the report.

As he hurried on, when he was two or three miles from the monastery to which he was going, he heard a very sweet voice resounding in the air. Looking upward, he saw the soul of that brother being swiftly carried up by angels of the Lord, who praised it, to blessed and everlasting life.

Pachomius’s companions, however, heard no voice and perceived nothing at all. They merely saw him gazing toward the east for a long time, and said to him: “Why have you stopped, Father? Let us hurry so that we may meet him.”

He replied: “We are already running in vain. This is what I have been observing for so long: how the brother himself is being led to perpetual joys.”

When they begged him to explain how he had seen the soul, he related to them, as far as they were able to hear, what he himself had witnessed.

Some of them, therefore, went to the monastery mentioned above and carefully inquired at what hour the brother had fallen asleep. They discovered that everything they had learned from the holy man was true.

We have related this for two reasons: first, because we wished to show that the blessed old man was exceedingly perceptive, possessed prophetic grace, and foresaw distant events with the eyes of the intellect; and second, so that, always imitating such men, we might diligently avoid the company of the wicked. Let what has been said about these matters suffice for now.

CAP. XLI.—Saint Pachomius, therefore, came with his monks to the aforesaid bishop and was received by him with the highest honor. The bishop celebrated a great festival at his arrival and gave him places where he might establish the monasteries he had requested in writing some time before. The venerable man constructed them eagerly.

As he was building a surrounding wall for protection, so that no one could easily break in, certain wicked men, blinded by the devil’s envy, came by night and destroyed what had been built. But the punishment of their wickedness was not long delayed. When the old man was exhorting his disciples to endurance, and those most wicked men had gathered according to their custom to complete what they had begun, they were immediately burned by an angel of the Lord and reduced to nothing, like wax before fire.

The brothers therefore quickly completed the entire building. In it blessed Pachomius established monks, devout men, over whom he appointed Samuel, a cheerful man and outstanding in the gift of frugality. Since the monasteries mentioned above had been founded in the suburb, the same saint wished to remain there longer, until those whom he had appointed were strengthened by Christ’s gift.

CAP. XLII.—Meanwhile, a certain philosopher of that city, having heard the reputation of the servants of God, came to them, wishing to learn who they were and what they professed. Seeing some of the monks, he said to them: “Call your Father to me, because I intend to debate necessary matters with him.”

When the holy man learned that he was a philosopher, he sent Cornelius and Theodore to him, instructing them to answer prudently whatever he asked.

The philosopher came out to meet them and said: “Much has been reported to us about you: that you devote yourselves to wisdom, that, in accordance with your religion, you especially love quiet, and that you also seem able prudently to answer those who propose questions. Therefore I have decided to question you about what you have read.”

Theodore said to him: “Put forward whatever you wish.”

The philosopher said: “Will you undertake a disputation with me, so that you may resolve whatever questions are asked?”

Theodore replied: “State now what you intend.”

Then the philosopher said: “Who, though not born, died? Who, though born, was taken away from death? And who, though dead, was not corrupted by stench?”

Theodore said: “Your proposition is not difficult, philosopher, for I can easily solve what you ask. The one who was not born yet died is Adam the first-formed man. The one who was born yet did not die is Enoch, who pleased God and was translated. The one who died yet was not corrupted by any stench is Lot’s wife, who was changed into a pillar of salt (Gen. 19) and has remained in that form to this day as an example for unbelievers.

“Therefore I advise you, philosopher, to abandon these foolish propositions and empty questions and turn without delay to the true God whom we worship, receiving the forgiveness of your sins for eternal salvation.”

At this the philosopher was utterly astonished and asked nothing further. He departed, marveling at the man’s acumen and at his answer, so swift and ready.

CAP. XLIII.—Pachomius accordingly remained for many days in the same newly built monasteries. From there he departed and arrived at another monastery under his authority.

When all the brothers hurried to meet him and received him with the highest reverence, a small child from that community, who had come out among the others, began to cry out and say: “Truly, Father, ever since you went away from here, no one has cooked vegetables or any legume for us.”

The holy man replied kindly: “Do not be distressed, my son; I shall cook now.”

Entering the monastery, he went after prayer to the kitchen. There he found the brother in charge of the kitchen making *psiathoi*—that is, mats, which the common people call rush-mats—and said to him:

“Tell me, brother, how long has it been since you cooked vegetables or legumes for the brothers?”

He replied: “Nearly two months.”

Saint Pachomius said: “Why did you wish to act against the commandment, so that such a great benefit for the brothers might be neglected?”

The brother replied with humble submission:

“I had indeed wished, venerable Father, to fulfill my ministry every day. But whatever I cooked was not consumed by the brothers, because they all abstain—only the boys receive some cooked food. I therefore did not cook a stew, lest food prepared with so much labor be thrown away. But, so that I would not be idle, I chose *psiathoi* [Note: ‘*Psiathoi*.’ Below, in chapter 47: ‘He came to the brothers who were making *psiathioi*.’ And in chapter 52: ‘He was always making *psiathioi*.’ The forms are *psiathi*, *psiathii*, and *psiathia*, meaning mats. Some editions ridiculously read *ciathoi*. This word occurs frequently in these Lives of the Fathers. See the *Onomasticon*.] and wove them with the brothers, knowing that one of those assigned to me for such work would be sufficient to prepare small foods—namely, olives and greens—for the brothers’ refreshment.”

Hearing this, Pachomius said: “And how many *psiathoi* did you say you had made?”

He replied: “Five hundred.”

“Bring them all here,” he said, “so that I may see them.”

When they had been brought, he immediately ordered a fire to be placed beneath them and had them burned. Then he said to them:

“Just as you have despised the rule handed down to you concerning the administration of the brothers’ affairs, so I have burned your labors indiscriminately, so that you may understand how harmful it is to tear down the institutions of the Fathers, which have been devised for the salvation of souls.

“Do you not know that it is glorious always to abstain from things that are present? If someone restrains himself, through divine consideration, from something that lies within his power, he receives a great reward from the Lord. But if he is restrained by some necessity from something he has no permission to use, he is recognized as being held back by compulsion; therefore he seems to await a reward in vain for a forced and fruitless abstinence.

“When many foods have been set before them, if the brothers use them sparingly for God’s sake, then they place their greatest hope in God. But with regard to foods they do not see, and which they have no ability to receive, how is a reward granted for frugality? Therefore, for the sake of a small expense, such a great benefit to the brothers ought not to have been neglected.”

CAP. XLIV.—While he was speaking these things to them and sufficiently reproving their offense, the doorkeeper hurried in to him, announcing that important men and distinguished anchorites had arrived who wished to see him.

He immediately ordered them to enter. Greeting them with due reverence, he led them after prayer through the brothers’ cells and showed them all the places of the monastery.

They asked the old man to speak with him privately about whatever matters they wished. He then led them aside and sat with them.

While they were discussing hidden and secret matters at length, Saint Pachomius began to perceive an exceedingly foul odor. He saw that they spoke with considerable polish and were well prepared in the sacred Scriptures, and he could neither imagine nor mention anything concerning the intolerable stench.

After they had discussed divine teachings for a long time, and the ninth hour was already indicating the time for refreshment, they rose and immediately wished to depart. The holy man earnestly begged them to take food with him. They absolutely refused, saying that they were hurrying to return to their own homes before sunset. They bade him farewell and departed without delay.

Then Saint Pachomius, wishing to learn the cause of the stench more certainly, prostrated himself in prayer, asking the Lord to reveal to him what sort of men they were. He immediately understood that the impious doctrines with which they had been shown to be imbued were exhaling such destruction from their hearts.

Without delay he pursued the men, caught up with them, and said: “I wish to ask you one question.”

They said: “Ask.”

“Have you read Origen’s commentaries?” he asked.

They denied it, saying: “Not at all.”

He said to them:

“Behold, I testify before the Lord that every person who reads Origen and agrees with the things he wickedly taught will descend into the depths of hell, and his inheritance will be worms and outer darkness, in which the souls of the wicked will be punished without end.

“Behold, I have carefully announced to you what the Lord has revealed to me. From this point I shall be innocent; you must decide for yourselves if you reject what is right. But if you wish to heed me and please God in all things, drown all of Origen’s books in the river, lest you yourselves be drowned by them.”

Having said this, he departed from them. Returning to the exercise of his customary virtue, he found the brothers standing in prayer, and with them he joyfully completed hymns of spiritual song.

CAP. XLV.—When the monks had gathered to eat, the venerable old man withdrew into the cell where he was accustomed to entreat the Lord. Closing the door, he prayed intently, remembering a vision he had once seen. He begged the Lord to reveal to him the future condition of the monks and what would happen after his death in so great a community.

From the ninth hour until the time when the brother in charge of the nocturnal prayers would raise his voice and summon them to the customary prayers, he extended the urgency of his supplication.

As he prayed more earnestly, suddenly, around midnight, he saw a vision that instructed him more fully, in accordance with his request, concerning the condition of his successors. For he learned that, while his monasteries would be greatly expanded, some would live piously and continently, while many others would neglect their duties and utterly lose their salvation.

He saw, as he himself related, a multitude of monks standing in a very deep and dark valley. Some wished to climb out but could not, because others came toward them from the opposite direction; they could not recognize one another, nor could they emerge at all from that deep and gloomy place. Others, having tried in vain, fell from exhaustion and reached the lower regions. Others lay there, lamenting in a pitiable and tearful voice. But some climbed up with the greatest labor; as they ascended, light immediately met them, and, standing in it, they gave thanks to God that they had been able to escape.

Thus Pachomius understood what would happen in the last times. He grieved deeply over the blindness of mind, the error of heart, and the lack of goodness among those who would come afterward. Above all, he grieved that the superiors of that time would be negligent and idle, would not trust in God, but would employ concord discordantly, pleasing the foolish multitude and displaying the monastic habit while exhibiting no good works.

Once the worst men held positions of leadership, and themselves knew nothing of the name of the holy way of life, rivalries and quarrels would necessarily arise, and they would contend in ambitious strife over who should preside and who should be greater. The good would be rejected and the wicked chosen. Each person would wish to be preferred to the others not because of moral excellence, but because of seniority or rank.

As a result, good men would have no confidence to speak for the common benefit. They would remain in silence and quiet, or else, under the guise of respectability, would be afflicted by great persecutions. And why enumerate each detail, when almost everything founded upon divine rules would then be exchanged for human enticements?

Then Pachomius cried out to the Lord with tears, saying:

“Almighty God, if this is how it will be, why have You permitted these coenobia to be established? For if, at the end of time, all who rule over the brothers are to be perverse, what will those who live under their government be like? If the blind leads the blind, both fall into a pit (Matt. 15). Woe is me, for I have labored in vain and to no purpose.

“Remember, Lord, my efforts, which You have accomplished by Your gift. Remember Your servants, who serve You with their whole mind. Remember Your covenant, which You promised Your worshipers would preserve until the consummation of the age.

“You know, Lord, that from the time I received this monastic habit, I have been exceedingly humbled in Your sight. I have never been satisfied with bread, water, or any other creature that You made.”

As he was saying this, a voice came to him, saying:

“Do not glory, Pachomius, since you are a human being and need mercy, because all that I created subsists through My compassion.”

He immediately prostrated himself on the ground and sought the Lord’s mercy, saying:

“Almighty God, let Your mercies come to me, and I shall live” (Ps. 118); “and do not take Your mercies from me, for Your mercy and truth have always received me” (Ps. 32).

“For I know, Lord, that everything falters and limps without the help of Your protection.”

When he had said this, angels of light stood over him. In their midst was a young man shining with ineffable beauty and brightness, emitting rays of splendor from himself like the sun and wearing a crown of thorns upon his head.

The angels lifted Pachomius from the ground and said to him:

“Because you have asked mercy from the Lord, behold, your mercy has come to you: Jesus Christ, the God of glory, the only-begotten Son of God the Father, who was sent into this world and crucified for the salvation of the human race, bearing a crown of thorns upon His head.”

Pachomius said: “I ask, Lord, was it I who crucified You?”

The Lord, in a gentler manner, replied to him:

“You did not crucify Me, but your parents did. Nevertheless, be more at peace, and let your heart be strengthened, because your posterity will remain forever and will not fail until the end of the world. Those who come after you will be freed from that deep darkness—those, that is, who live abstinently and take care of their own salvation.

“Those who now restrain themselves in your presence, following the examples of your virtues, shine with the greatest light of grace. But after you there will be those who remain in the darkness of this world. Because they will wisely understand what should be sought and what should be avoided, and because, of their own free will, without any human example, they will leap forth from such great darkness, preserve every form of righteousness, and love eternal life with their whole heart, I tell you truly that they will be with those who are now distinguished with you by the highest continence and holiness, and they will share the same salvation and rest.”

Having said this, the Lord ascended into heaven. The air was so illuminated that the splendor of that light cannot be expressed in human words.

## Chapter XLVI

Then Saint Pachomius, greatly astonished at the things that had been shown him, assembled with the entire brotherhood for the nocturnal synaxis. When the sacred office had been solemnly completed, all the monks, according to custom, stood before the old man to hear the word of God. Opening his mouth, he taught them, saying:

“My little sons, with whatever strength and ability you possess, contend valiantly for your salvation, and fight manfully against the armed enemy—before the time comes when, if we have been sluggish and negligent, we shall lamentably mourn over ourselves. Let us not waste the days that the Lord has granted us; rather, let us work virtue in them with complete eagerness.

“For I tell you that, if you knew what great blessings are prepared for the saints in heaven, and what torments await those who have strayed from the path of virtue and, having recognized the truth, have not lived worthily according to it, you would hasten with all your strength to avoid eternal punishments and to obtain that blessed inheritance promised to God’s servants. No one flees or neglects it except an evil and ruined person, because he has no understanding at all of what he is losing. Such a one ought immediately to come to his senses and be released from earthly desires, so that by continually mourning his past evils he may obtain the Lord’s forgiveness; and thus, turning toward better things, he may direct his journey, so that at the end of life he may arrive joyfully, with great praise, before the heavenly King.

“This is when the soul, leaving this earthly dwelling, hastens toward knowledge of its own substance; when, joined to the heavenly virtues, it hastens to reach the Father of lights. Why is man lifted up by empty glory? Why does dust exalt itself? Why does earth and ashes grow proud? (Ecclesiasticus 10.) Let us rather mourn for ourselves while we have time, lest, when the appointed respite has been completed for each person, we are then found asking for a time of repentance, when we no longer deserve to receive it.

“For in this life we are permitted to mourn our sins; but in hell, as we have learned from the holy prophet David, ‘Who will confess to God?’ (Psalm 6.) That soul is proved exceedingly unhappy, and deserving of mourning with every fountain of tears, which, after renouncing the world, becomes entangled again in the world’s activities and, having once been stripped of useless cares, returns again to the service of harsh slavery.

“And therefore, dearest brothers, let us not allow perpetual and blessed life to be taken from us by this unstable world, which will shortly pass away. Yet I fear, and I tremble inwardly with my whole being, lest the parents of our flesh, occupied with worldly affairs and absorbed in the business of the present life, who thought that we had abandoned the evils of the world and were already enjoying perpetual life, condemn us by their judgment, saying to us: ‘How have you grown weary in your paths?’ (Wisdom 5), overwhelmed by such great miseries? For from your great sorrow grief has also come upon us, and your fire has been added to our punishments.

“Indeed, our branches have become useless, and they have not produced the fruits they displayed in blossom. I am also afraid that they may bring against us that prophetic saying: ‘Therefore the beloved have fallen into plunder; they have become abominable, and the crown of their heads has been taken away. The cities situated toward the South have been closed, and there is no one to open them’ (Jeremiah 13). ‘Let the impious be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of God’ (Isaiah 26, according to the Septuagint).

“Considering these things, my brothers, let us contend with all our strength, lest we be overcome by the enemy. He is always intent on destroying; let us keep vigilant watch, lest—God forbid—we be destroyed by his deception.

“Above all, let us keep the final day before our eyes, and at every moment let us fear the punishments of eternal sorrows. For by such considerations the soul learns to recognize itself; and, subduing its own body with fasts and vigils, it remains in continual sorrow and mourning until, kindled by the warmth of the Holy Spirit, it becomes worthy of the help of heavenly contemplation. Released from earthly contagions, it is continually satisfied with divine discourse.

“Moreover, whoever constantly considers these things obtains purity of mind and acquires humility of heart; he rejects empty glory and strives to be free from all worldly prudence. Let the spiritual soul therefore philosophize daily, dearest brothers, against the gross substance of its flesh; and let it deal with it so carefully that it may consent to better things.

“When evening comes and one reaches the bed, let the soul say to each of its bodily members: ‘While we are together, obey me as I urge what is right, and serve the Lord with me eagerly.’ Let it say also to its hands: ‘The time will come when your boasting will cease, when the fist that administers anger will no longer exist, and when the palms stretched out for acts of plunder will come to rest.’ Let it say to its feet: ‘There will come a time when you will no longer be able to run toward iniquity, when you will not be able to enter the paths of wickedness.’

“Let it address all its members in the same way and say to them: ‘Before death separates us from one another, and the separation that came about through the sin of the first man is fulfilled, let us contend bravely, stand perseveringly, fight manfully, and serve the Lord without sluggishness or laziness, until he comes again and, wiping away our temporal sweat, leads us to the everlasting kingdoms.

“‘Pour forth tears, O eyes. Show, O flesh, your noble servitude. Work together with me in the prayers by which I confess to God, lest, when you wish to rest and sleep, you procure everlasting torments for us. Therefore keep watch always in your works, because if you conduct yourself soberly, abundant recompense for good things will come to you. But if you neglect this, pitiable kinds of torment will cut you down; and then the wailing of the soul lamenting to the body will be heard: “Woe is me, because I am bound to you, and on account of you I am suffering the punishment of everlasting condemnation.”’

“If we constantly reconsider these matters within ourselves, we shall truly become the temple of the Lord, and the Holy Spirit will dwell in us; nor will any trickery of Satan be able thereafter to deceive us (1 Corinthians 4). More than ten thousand teachers and tutors, the fear of the Lord will instruct us through thoughts of this kind and will preserve us in prudence. Whatever we perhaps cannot grasp by human understanding, the Holy Spirit will inspire in us. For, as the blessed Apostle says, ‘We do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself pleads for us with unspeakable groanings’ (Romans 8).

“There were indeed many other things that we could say, but lest we cause you too much labor, we bring our discourse to an end here. May the God of peace and grace confirm you and strengthen you in his fear, brothers. Amen.”

Having said this, he immediately rose, commended them to the Lord, and departed.

## Chapter XLVII

As he was proceeding to the monastery called Tabennese, with Theodore and Cornelius and very many other brothers, he stopped briefly on the road, as though asking someone about a secret matter; and in spirit he learned that one of the commands he had established in the monastery had been neglected.

For he had ordered the brothers who worked in the bakery that, whenever they made offerings, they should say nothing superfluous but should meditate inwardly on words that brought salvation. He therefore summoned Theodore, who was in charge of that monastery, and said to him:

“Go secretly and inquire carefully what the brothers said in the evening while they were making the offerings; and whatever you discover, report it to me.”

Theodore went, investigated everything carefully, and reported to Saint Pachomius what he had learned. Pachomius said:

“Do the brothers suppose that the traditions we have given them to observe are merely human, and do they not know that, for contempt even of the smallest commandment, great dangers await the negligent? Did not Israel maintain silence unanimously around the city of Jericho for seven days, and then, at the appointed time, did not the entire people shout and immediately capture the city? Thus it did not disregard God’s command, although it had been given through a human being.

“Therefore now and henceforth let the monks observe our commands, so that this sin of negligence may be forgiven them, since we ourselves carefully observe the things we prescribe to others.”

Then he entered the monastery. After prayer, he went to the brothers who were making *psiathoi*—woven mats—and, sitting with them, began to weave himself.

As a little boy passed by, who had been assigned to serve the one performing the weekly duty [Note: “Who was performing the weekly duty.” He was called the weekly assistant, or hebdomadary, to whom a servant was assigned, as here. Jerome, in the preface to the Rule of Saint Pachomius: “In each monastery there are 144 fathers, stewards, weekly assistants, and servants.”], watched the blessed Pachomius weaving and said to him:

“You are not working correctly, Father; Abbot Theodore wove it in another way.”

Immediately Pachomius rose and said to the boy:

“Show me, son, how I ought to weave.”

When he had learned from him, he sat down again to his work, tranquil in mind, and by this act suppressed the spirit of pride. For if he had possessed even a little worldly wisdom according to the flesh, he would certainly not have accepted the boy’s instruction; rather, he would have rebuked him for presuming to speak beyond his years.

## Chapter XLVIII

At another time, when Pachomius had withdrawn from everyone’s sight and was staying in his solitude, the devil came to him in a disguised form and, standing opposite him, said:

“Hail, Pachomius. I am Christ [Note: “I am Christ.” He appeared to Saint Martin by a similar deception, as reported by Sulpicius Severus, *Life of Saint Martin*, chapter 25], and I have come to you, my faithful friend.”

Then Pachomius, with the Holy Spirit revealing the truth to him, rejected the enemy’s vision and thought within himself, saying:

“The coming of Christ is peaceful, and his appearance is free from every fear and full of joy. At once human thoughts depart and eternal desires take their place. But I am now troubled and seething with various thoughts.”

Immediately he rose, fortified himself with the sign of Christ, and stretched out his hands to seize him. Blowing upon him, he said:

“Depart from me, devil, for you are accursed, as are your vision and the devices of your ambushes. You have no place among God’s servants.”

Then, becoming like dust, the devil filled his cell with an exceedingly foul stench, so that he corrupted the air itself, loudly proclaiming:

“Just now I would have won you and brought you under my power, but the power of Christ is exalted; therefore I am mocked by you in everything. Nevertheless, as far as I can, I shall not cease attacking you. For I must complete my work without interruption.”

Pachomius, strengthened by the Holy Spirit, confessed to the Lord, giving him thanks for the wondrous benefits and gifts he had bestowed upon him.

## Chapter XLIX

One night in this same monastery, while Pachomius was walking with Theodore, he suddenly saw at a distance a great apparition, elaborately fashioned for deception. It was in the form of a woman, surpassing all human beauty, so that neither a description nor a view of its form could be adequately conveyed.

When Theodore also saw it, he was greatly disturbed, and his face changed. The venerable old man, seeing him excessively afraid, said:

“Take courage in the Lord, Theodore, and do not be frightened in any way.”

Having said this, he stood in prayer, imploring the Lord that the terrifying apparition might be dissolved by the presence of the divine majesty. As they prayed together, it began to draw near, preceded by a great multitude of demons.

When Pachomius had finished his prayers, it came and said to them:

“Why do you labor uselessly, when you can do nothing against me? For I have received power from the Lord to test whomever I wish.”

Pachomius questioned it, saying:

“What do you wish to be? From where do you come? Whom are you seeking to test?”

It replied:

“I am the power of the devil, and the entire multitude of demons is subject to me. I am the one who casts the holy lights down to earth and wraps them in the deadly darkness of pleasure. I also deceived Judas and cast him down from the height of the apostolate.

“And so, Pachomius, I asked the Lord for you, and I do not cease attacking you. I can no longer endure the reproaches of the demons, because you have shown yourself superior to all my attacks and battles. No one has rendered me powerless as you have. For your teaching has made me subject to both young and old, and even children, and has caused me to be completely trampled under their feet.

“You have gathered such an army of monks against me and surrounded it with the impregnable wall of the fear of God, so that my servants cannot seduce any of you by their manifold deception. All this has happened to us because of the Word of God made human, who has granted you power to trample down our strength.”

Pachomius said:

“What then? Have you come, as you said, to test me alone, or others as well?”

“You also,” it replied, “and those who are like you.”

Again the holy man asked it:

“Then Theodore also?”

It answered:

“I sought Theodore as well, and I received power to test you, but I am utterly unable to approach you.”

When they asked why it could not do this, it replied:

“If I fight with you, I shall provide you with no small benefit, especially you, Pachomius, who have reached such greatness that you have been deemed worthy to behold the glory of the Lord with bodily eyes. But will you live forever with your monks, whom you now protect by your prayers and strengthen by your exhortation?

“There will be a time after your death when I shall rage among them as I please and do with them whatever I wish. You are the reason I am now trampled down by such a great congregation of monks.”

The holy man said:

“Do you not know, unhappy one, that perhaps after us there will be better men who, serving Christ with sincere devotion, will teach those who flee to the discipline of the Lord with spiritual instruction and build them up by holy examples?”

“I know,” it replied, “that you have just lied concerning your own head.”

Pachomius then said:

“You possess the primacy of lying, for you have no power whatsoever to know beforehand. To foresee all things belongs solely to God and is proper to his majesty and power.”

It answered:

“As you say, I know nothing at all by foreknowledge; nevertheless, I learn many things by conjecture.”

When Saint Pachomius asked how it made conjectures, it said:

“I consider what is to come from what has preceded.”

The holy man said to it:

“Explain how you can conjecture.”

It replied:

“The beginning of every matter tends, with the passage of time, toward its established growth; thereafter it turns toward decline. Thus I also conjecture concerning this divine vocation, which in its beginnings, strengthened by heavenly protection, grew through signs, wonders, and various virtues.

“When it begins to grow old, it will be diminished by its own increase, either becoming weary through the long passage of time or failing through the torpor of negligence. Then I shall be able to prevail against such a condition.

“Even now it is my work to trip up those whom I can, and I do not cease testing great men.”

Pachomius said:

“If, as you say, you do not cease testing great men, and if you confess that your particular work is the destruction of souls—for you surpass all demons in wickedness—tell me why you cannot now prevail against God’s servants.”

It replied:

“I already told you that, from the time when the wondrous incarnation of Christ took place on earth, we began to become utterly powerless, so that we are mocked like sparrows by those who believe in his name [Note: “We are mocked like sparrows.” See the remarks above on the *Life of Saint Antony*, chapter 16, no. 41].

“Nevertheless, although we have been weakened, we are not so idle that we do not attempt to deceive those whom we can. We never cease opposing your race, sowing evil thoughts in the souls of those who strive to fight against us.

“And if we perceive that they yield in some measure to our tickling enticements, then we introduce even more wicked thoughts and kindle the fires of various pleasures. Fighting with the utmost ferocity, we enter them and subject them more completely to our power.

“But if we see that they not only do not accept the things we suggest, but do not even willingly attend to them, and that they vigilantly and soberly fortify themselves with the faith that is in Christ, then we are driven and expelled from their hearts as smoke is scattered in the air.

“We are not permitted to engage every person with all our forces, because not everyone can withstand our assaults. If we were allowed to fight openly against all with our full strength, we could deceive many who are now sustained by your labor.

“But what can we do? They are aided by your prayers and fortified by the virtue and power of the Crucified One.”

Then Saint Pachomius said to it in a loud voice, with a groan:

“O your sleepless wickedness, which never ceases to rage against the human race, until divine power—that is, the Son of God—comes again from heaven and utterly consumes and destroys you!”

Having said this, he rebuked the multitude of demons in the name of Christ. It immediately dispersed and was dissolved into nothing.

When morning came, Pachomius summoned all the brothers who excelled either in holiness of life or in length of time, and recounted to them everything he had seen and heard from the evil spirits. Through letters he also informed those who were absent, fortifying them with discipline and the fear of the Lord, and prudently instructing them not to yield in any way to demonic apparitions or fear the tricks of their manifold ambushes.

When these men saw and heard of the miracles performed through divine grace by Pachomius, they were strengthened and firmly established in faith, and endured the labor of self-restraint with complete eagerness.

## Chapter L

Meanwhile, as a certain brother who rivaled and imitated the old man’s patience was standing in prayer, a scorpion struck his foot and injected so much poison that the pain reached his heart, and he almost breathed out his spirit.

Although he was afflicted with the extremity of suffering, he did not move from his place until the prayer had ended. Pachomius immediately poured out prayers to Christ on his behalf, and the brother was restored to his former health.

## Chapter LI

Theodore was also afflicted with a severe disorder of the head, which caused the sharpest pains. When he asked Pachomius to relieve him by his prayers, Pachomius said to him:

“Do you think, my son, that any pain, illness, or anything of this kind happens to anyone without God’s permission? Therefore endure in your pain, and maintain patience in your humility. When the Lord wills, he will grant you health.

“If he is pleased to test you for a longer time, be grateful, as was the most perfect and patient Job, who, enduring many trials of tribulations and sufferings, blessed the Lord. Like him, you too will receive from Christ greater rest in return for your pains.

“Abstinence is indeed good, as is perseverance in prayer; yet the sick person receives a greater reward when he is found to be long-suffering and patient.

“And since our discourse has proceeded to magnanimous men, I think it necessary, for the benefit of many, to bring forward the endurance of one more man—an endurance that surpasses all human praise.”

## Chapter LII

A certain monk named Zacchaeus, after long periods of self-restraint, was struck by jaundice (the “royal disease”). He kept a cell apart from the brothers and was content throughout his life with bread and salt alone.

He was always making *psiathoi* [woven mats], and endured such great hardship for the Lord that, twisting cords again and again, his hands were pierced and drops of blood flowed from them. Thus the man’s great endurance was displayed through the work itself.

Though established in such bodily infirmity, he never left the brothers’ assembly. He hastened diligently to complete all the daily prayers, so much so that he never slept during the day.

Every night, before he went to sleep, he was accustomed to meditate on certain passages from the holy Scriptures. Fortifying all his limbs with the sign of Christ, he continually glorified the Lord and then rested for a little while. Around midnight he rose and remained alert until the morning prayers.

Once a brother examined his hands, which were severely wounded and covered with blood from the excess and violence of his work, and said to him:

“Why, Father, do you torture yourself with such arduous labor, especially when you are weighed down by such an illness? Do you perhaps fear that you will incur offense before God or be charged with the crime of idleness if you do not work diligently?

“The Lord knows what you suffer, and that no one afflicted by such great tribulations can perform any work—especially you, who are compelled by no necessity. If, after God, we give sufficient support to foreigners and to the poor, how much more should we serve you, such a great Father, with the utmost devotion?”

He replied:

“It is impossible for me not to work.”

The brother said:

“If this pleases you, at least rub your hands with oil, so that, bleeding so profusely during your labor, they may not fail.”

Zacchaeus accepted his advice and did what the brother had urged him to do. But his wounded hands became so burdened that he could no longer bear the suffering.

The blessed Pachomius came to visit him, learned what had happened, and said:

“Did you think, brother, that oil could help you? Who compelled you to work so assiduously that, under the pretext of labor, you placed your hope more in this visible oil than in God?

“Is it impossible for God to heal you? Does he not know the illnesses of individuals and need our reminders? Or does he despise us, although he is merciful by nature?

“Yet, considering the benefit of our souls, he permits us to suffer sadness for a moment, so that he may grant us everlasting rewards for our endurance. Let us therefore cast all our care and anxiety upon him; and whenever he wills, or in whatever way he judges, he himself, in his kindness, will bring an end to our pains.”

Zacchaeus replied:

“Forgive me, venerable Father, and pray to the Lord for me, that in his mercy he may deign to forgive me this sin as well.”

Many also affirmed concerning this old man that for an entire year he wept for himself, taking only a little food after a two-day fast. Saint Pachomius proposed him to the monks as an example of good works and a foundation of virtue. He also sent those who were in sorrow to him, because he possessed a consoling word as no one else did.

After contending bravely to the end in holy old age, he passed into the heavenly kingdoms, destined to receive eternal consolations for such great sufferings.

## Chapter LIII

Pachomius was certain that he had never hidden away the talent entrusted to him, but had dispensed it to everyone and sent both this man and many others of perfect conduct ahead to Christ. He therefore celebrated the feast with a joyful mind over such great and excellent fruits granted to him by the Lord, fruits about which this discourse of ours has been long extended, giving thanks to God.

After the most blessed day of the Paschal feast, when many brothers had already been sent ahead to the Lord, Saint Pachomius himself finally fell ill. Theodore, whom we have often mentioned, ministered to him.

Although his whole body was exceedingly wasted and weak, his face was cheerful and radiant, so that even in this he displayed to those who saw him the signs of his devout mind and most sincere conscience.

Two days before his holy repose, he summoned all the brothers and said to them:

“I, dearest ones, am entering the way of the fathers without fear, for I see that I am immediately being summoned by the Lord. Therefore remember the words you have often heard from me, and be vigilant in prayer and sober in your works.

“Have no association with the followers of Meletius, Arius, Origen, or the others who oppose the commands of Christ. Associate instead with those who fear the Lord and who can benefit you by holy conduct and provide spiritual consolations for your souls.

“For I am already being poured out, and the time of my release is at hand (2 Timothy 4). Choose from among yourselves, while I am present, a brother who, after God, may preside over everyone and care for your souls.

“As far as I can judge with my discretion, I consider Petronius suitable for this task; but it is your responsibility to choose what is beneficial for you.”

The obedient sons therefore accepted their father’s counsel in this matter as well. Petronius was strong in faith, humble in conduct, most prudent in understanding, of good character, and perfect in discernment.

Saint Pachomius poured out a prayer to the Lord for him, because he had learned that Petronius himself was ill in the monastery called Chinoboscion. Although absent, he commended the entire brotherhood to him in the Lord and immediately sent word that he should come.

Then, fortifying himself with the sign of Christ and looking with a joyful expression upon the angel of light who had been sent to him, he surrendered his holy soul on the fourteenth day of the month Pachon according to the Egyptians, which according to the Romans is the seventh day before the Ides of May [Note: “On the fourteenth day of the month Pachon according to the Egyptians, which according to the Romans is the seventh day before the Ides of May.” In the old edition, *Chon* appears instead of *Pachon*. But *Pachon* is correct, as it is found in the manuscripts; it is a known Egyptian month. The Egyptian date assigned here correctly corresponds to the Roman date given. For the first day of Pachon begins, according to the Romans, on April 26; therefore the fourteenth day of Pachon corresponds to the seventh day before the Ides of May, that is, May 9, since from April 25 to May 9 there are fourteen days. See the table of months in the *Onomasticon*.]

His disciples, caring for his venerable little body as custom required, kept vigil over it throughout the entire night, singing psalms and hymns. On the following day they buried him on the mountain where the monastery had been established.

Those who had been sent to Saint Petronius brought him back, although he was still suffering from that illness. After governing the entire brotherhood for a few days, he too died in peace, leaving behind a just man acceptable to God, named Orsesius [Note: “Named Orsesius.” Concerning him, Gennadius writes in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Men of the Church*, chapter 9, calling him Oriesies: “Oriesies the monk, companion of both Pachomius and Theodore, a man perfectly instructed in the holy Scriptures, composed a book seasoned with divine salt and constructed with the instruments of the entire monastic discipline. To put it simply, in it almost the whole of the Old and New Testament is explained in concise discussions according solely to the needs of monks. He presented it to the brothers in place of a testament shortly before the day of his death.” In the Rule of Pachomius edited by Achilleus Statius he is called Orsiesius; he appears in Pelagius below, in little book 11, no. 37, and little book 15, no. 51, as Orsisius. Oriesis’s rules concerning monastic institutions are found in volume 5 of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*.]

## Chapter LIV

We have drawn these few things from the many merits of these men and arranged small matters from great ones—not to bestow any honor upon them, for it is not right that those should need praise for whom eternal praise and unfailing glory are sufficient, which they have attained before Christ and his holy angels and will obtain more fully with their bodies at the resurrection of all.

“For they will shine like the sun in the kingdom of God” (Matthew 13), and he has testified that he glorifies those who glorify him (1 Samuel 2). May we also become imitators of them according to our strength, as, recognizing their most excellent lives, we strive, with Christ’s gift, to imitate them, always assisted by the prayers of the blessed fathers, patriarchs, prophets, apostles, martyrs, and all the saints.

Through them our almighty and merciful God—the blessed, coeternal, consubstantial, and inseparable Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is continually glorified and praised, because to him belong all praise and glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: “During that same period.” Baronius, volume 3, in the year of Christ 328, the fifteenth year of Pope Sylvester and the twenty-third year of the emperor Constantine:

“‘In this year Athanasius, who had been made bishop of Alexandria before the preceding year, was soon harassed by the accusations of the Meletians. When the Eusebians assembled, and after the previous year had elapsed—as we have seen—while they were laboring to restore Arius to Alexandria, he was grievously persecuted up to the present year. After they had been repelled and Constantine had been persuaded, he finally found peace. Now at last he obtained those long-awaited days of tranquility, like halcyon days, so that he might undertake his episcopal office as he ought. He began a work that seemed all the more necessary to him: a very difficult task, namely, to travel throughout the entire and very extensive diocese subject to the Alexandrian Church and, with the utmost vigilance, restore what heresy, schism, and corrupt morals had damaged in the Church, restoring faith and peace, which had been driven into exile, and reforming corrupt morals through ecclesiastical discipline, and so forth. He himself mentions this journey undertaken as part of his episcopal office, and so forth.

“‘When, therefore, Saint Athanasius (Athanasius, *Apology* 2) visited all the churches as part of his office—not only those situated in cities, towns, and villages, but also those that existed in deserts and deserted places among the holy monks—he likewise visited the monastery of Saint Pachomius.

“‘Pachomius, who had been twenty years old in the first year of the Licinian war, that is, in the year of the Lord 316, as was stated above, was therefore thirty-two years old in this year and had twelve years of monastic formation. Consequently, the fact that he is called an old man in those Acts appears to be due to veneration rather than age, since he had become the father of many monks, who themselves flourished in outstanding holiness.’”

Thus far Baronius. But Pachomius’s years must be corrected according to what was said above, chapter 4, no. 6, where we proved that Pachomius served in the army during the war against Maxentius, which took place in the year of Christ 312. Therefore, in this year 328—in which Baronius believes Athanasius visited him—he would have been thirty-six years old.]

[Col. 0281]

# March 16. Life of Saint Abraham the Hermit, by Saint Ephraem

[Note: “Of Abraham.” His memory is recorded in ecclesiastical calendars. Thus the Roman Martyrology for March 16 reads: “In Syria, Saint Abraham the hermit, whose deeds were written by the blessed deacon Ephraem.” The Greek Menologion for October 29 reads: “The feast of our holy father Abraham.” His life is recounted more fully on the same day in the *Menaea*, where his niece Maria is also associated with him.]

[Note: “Ephraem.” This author of the Acts of Saint Abraham is preferred by the manuscripts and by the Cologne edition. These Acts also appear under this author in Lipomanus, volume 2, who took them from the Cologne edition of the *Lives of the Fathers*. For in other editions they are abridged at the end. Three final chapters are missing after the Life of Maria, Abraham’s niece, which is joined to this work there. The same Ephraem mentions him in the little book entitled *The Testament of Ephraem*. Metaphrastes also narrated his deeds at greater length; they may be found in Lipomanus, volume 6, and Surius, volume 2. Sozomen, book 3, chapter 15, and Nicephorus, book 9, chapter 16, mention Abraham, the disciple of Saint Ephraem.]

Deacon, translated by an anonymous interpreter

[Note: “Translated by an anonymous interpreter.” These same Acts were recently published from a new translation by Gerard Vossius, among the works of blessed Ephraem, volume 3.]

### Author’s Prologue
