My brothers, I wish to recount to you the good conduct of the perfect and admirable man Abraham, which he began in such a way that at its completion he deserved everlasting glory.

But I am afraid to compose an admirable and brilliant history about him when I consider the image of his virtues. For behold, the man’s conduct is indeed perfectly excellent, while I am weak and rustic. His virtue is an admirable and splendid image, but the colors of the words with which it must be painted are exceedingly dull and gloomy.

Nevertheless, although inexperienced, I shall attempt it at least in part. Though I cannot comprehend it perfectly, I shall nevertheless recount as much as I am able to say about this man, since the one who deserved to be called a second Abraham cannot easily be described by a human mouth.

For he lived in our own times, leading an angelic life on earth. He acquired patience, like an exceedingly strong diamond, and through it deserved to attain heavenly glory. And because from his youth he preserved the chastity of purity, he became a temple of the Holy Spirit, like a sanctified vessel. He presented himself to God in such a way that he had God as a dweller in the lodging of his mind.

## Life

[Col. 0283]

## [Col. 0283A] CHAPTER ONE

This blessed Abraham had very wealthy parents, who held him dear and loved him beyond measure, so that their affection surpassed even ordinary human love. They betrothed him to a girl while he was still a child [Note: “They betrothed him to a girl while he was still a child.”] They had to be at least seven years old in order to contract a betrothal, as Barnabas Brissonius notes in his work on the rite of marriage. Modestinus, the jurist, Book IV of the *Differentiae*, under “On Betrothals,” in “On the Rite of Marriage,” writes:

> “In contracting betrothals, the age of the parties is not defined as it is in marriages. Therefore betrothals may be made from the beginning of life, provided that it is understood that this is done by both persons—that is, provided that they are not younger than seven years.”

These words indicate that no definite age had been expressly prescribed for contracting betrothals. Nevertheless, with regard to the rewards established by the Papian Law, Augustus decreed that only those betrothals were to be approved and admitted to which a just and lawful marriage could be added after two years. Thus girls younger than ten years were vainly regarded as brides. The reason for establishing this rule was that he had observed that the law was being defrauded under cover of betrothals which, because of the brides’ immaturity, could not soon be brought to completion and fulfillment.

Dio, Book LIV, in the record of the year 736:

> “Since some people, betrothing infant girls, enjoyed the privileges of married persons but did not provide the actual result or function of marriage, he ordered that no betrothal should have legal force after which no one could marry the betrothed girl once two years had passed; that is, that a girl should in every case be ten years old when betrothed, if the betrothed man was to obtain some benefit from her. For girls are considered to have completed twelve full years by the time of marriage, as I have said.”

Brissonius rendered these words as follows, since the translator Xylander had translated them less accurately and less clearly:

> “Since certain persons, betrothing infant girls, enjoyed indeed the privileges of husbands but did not provide the actual result or function of marriage, he decreed that such betrothals should have no force after which the bride could not be taken in marriage once two years had passed; that is, that a girl of ten years should be betrothed, if the betrothed man wished to derive some advantage from her. For in her twelfth year a girl is considered mature for a man and marriageable, as I said earlier.”

Zonaras also adduces this passage in almost the same words, and clearly sets forth Dio’s meaning. Suetonius briefly touches upon the same matter in *Augustus*, chapter 34:

> “And when he perceived that the force of the law was also being evaded through the immaturity of brides and the frequent changing of marriages, he restricted the period during which betrothals could be maintained.”

To this belongs the passage of Gaius, under “Penalties,” in “On Betrothals,” which the compilers of the *Digest* excerpted from Book I of his commentary on the Julian and Papian Laws:

> “Often just and necessary causes prolong betrothals not merely for one or two years, but even for three or four years and longer—for example, the illness of the betrothed man or woman, the deaths of parents, capital crimes, or longer journeys undertaken out of necessity.”

See also Cujacius, Book XVI of the *Observationes*, chapter 35.

His parents awaited and desired that he should advance to some secular dignity. But he, thinking very differently, regularly attended the gatherings of the churches from the very first stage of adolescence. Whatever was read there from the divine Scriptures, he listened to eagerly and stored it in the memory of his heart, so that even when he was absent he would mentally chew over, with the deepest concentration, what he had learned.

When his parents thought that the time for marriage was approaching [Note: *Propinquabile*, “approaching.” Elsewhere, *propinqui habile*. Then *memorati parentes* (“the aforesaid parents”) should be deleted.], they compelled him to be bound by the bonds of marriage. At first he resisted, but afterward, unable to endure their constant and persistent pressure, overcome by modest shame, he was driven to consent.

When the wedding had been celebrated and the bride was sitting in the bridal chamber on the seventh day [Note: “On the seventh day.” This is found in the Audomarian manuscript and in Metaphrastes; it is absent from the printed editions. Here the custom of certain peoples who celebrated weddings for seven days is expressed. Genesis 29:27, concerning Jacob’s marriage to Leah: “Complete the week of this union.” Judges 14:12: “If you solve it for me within the seven days of the feast.” And verse 17: “For seven days of the feast she wept before him.” Tobit 8:23: “Raguel adjured Tobias to remain with him for two weeks.” Our Serarius says that the wedding feast continued to the fourteenth day, because of the doubled joy occasioned by the wedding and by the expulsion of the demon. Augustine, *Question 89 on Genesis*: “What he says, ‘Complete the week of this one,’ refers to the celebration of marriage, which is customarily celebrated for seven days.” Jerome, *Traditions on Genesis*: “His father-in-law Laban tells him to complete seven days for the marriage of his elder sister.” This custom prevailed among Eastern peoples and is still observed among the Jews. It may also be inferred from this *Life* that it was practiced among the Egyptians.], suddenly, as though a certain light, divine grace shone in his heart. Finding in it a guide for his resolve, he immediately leapt up, followed it, and departed from the city.

## CHAPTER II

About two thousand paces from his home he found an unoccupied cell. Settling himself there, he remained in great joy, glorifying God; but he had caused the greatest astonishment both to his parents and to his neighbors by this action. They went out, dispersed in different directions, and searched everywhere for the man of God.

After seventeen days they found him praying in the aforementioned cell. When the blessed man saw them struck with astonishment, he said:

“Why do you look at me in amazement? Rather, glorify the most merciful God, who has rescued me from the mire of my sins; and pray for me, that I may be able to carry to the end this most gentle yoke, under which the Lord has deigned that I, unworthy as I am, should serve, and that I may be able in all things to conform my way of life acceptably to his will.”

When all of them had heard him and replied, “Amen,” he begged them not to trouble him frequently under the pretext of visiting him. When they had departed, he blocked the entrance to his cell, shut himself inside, and left only a very small opening in the window through which he could receive his daily food.

## [Col. 0284A]

Thus divine grace illumined his mind, withdrawn from turbulent interruptions. Advancing daily in the best way of life, he made self-restraint the first foundation of his life; he also devoted himself to vigils and prayers, with weeping, humility, and charity.

When a holy reputation concerning him had spread throughout the entire region, everyone who heard of him flocked from all directions to see him and to be edified by him. A discourse of wisdom, knowledge, and consolation was also abundantly granted him by God; it shone in the minds of his hearers like a most brilliant lamp.

## CHAPTER III

In the twelfth year after his renunciation, his parents departed this life and left him abundant gold and large estates. He summoned a certain friend who was especially dear to him and entrusted him with the religious duty of distributing everything to the needy and to orphans, lest this matter create an impediment to his prayers.

When this had been done, he remained secure in spirit and tranquil in mind. For this was the holy man’s greatest concern: that his heart should not be bound by any earthly affairs. Therefore he possessed nothing else on earth except a single cloak and likewise one cilicium tunic, which he wore, as well as a very small cup [Note: *Caucum*. This is how the Audomarian manuscript reads, as also below, chapter 15; the editions have *catinum*, “bowl.” The word is used by both Greeks and Latins. The Greek-Latin Glosses: καῦκα, “a shallow cup.” Suidas: “Among us, a *kaukion*; among learned people, a cup.” What is commonly called a *caucium* is called a cup by more learned writers. Marcellus Empiricus, chapter 25: “An earthworm is dug out and placed in a wooden *caucus*, if possible one that is split and bound with iron.” Jerome, Book II against Jovinianus, chapter IX: “At one time, having a wooden *caucus* for drinking, he saw a boy drinking from his cupped hand.” I noted above, from a manuscript, that it should be read this way, in the *Life of Saint Paul the First Hermit*, chapter 14, no. 55. See also the *Onomasticon*.], from which he was accustomed to eat or drink; and one *psiathium* [Note: *Psiathium*. This word frequently occurs among ascetic writers for the bed or mat of ascetics. In this same *Life*, chapter 14, another edition has *mattula* instead of *psiathium*. See what is said in the *Life of Pachomius*, chapter 43, no. 40.], on which he was accustomed to lie.

With all these things he possessed humility beyond measure and equal charity toward everyone. He did not prefer the rich to the poor, the ruler to the subject, or the nobleman to the obscure; loving everyone alike, he honored all without respect of persons. He never reproved anyone insolently, but his speech was seasoned with charity and gentleness.

Who could ever hear his eloquence and be satisfied with what was continually brought forth from the sweetness of his speech? Or who, looking upon his face, which displayed the image of holiness, would not acquire an even greater desire to see him more often?

At all times he did not alter the rule of abstinence that he had once undertaken [Note: “He did not alter the rule of his abstinence.” Ephraim, in his ascetic discourse, or *On the Monastic Life*: “The most approved and holy Fathers of old, having firmly laid the foundations of a single rule, retained to the end of their lives the canon they had once undertaken. For some did so for fifty years, others for more,” and so forth. The same author, in his paraenetic discourse on the Advent of the Lord: “Keep one canon, as the holy Fathers also did, who for fifty years and more did not alter their canon or rule.”]; he completed his chosen discipline for fifty years with complete eagerness. Because of the great love and longing he had for Christ, he regarded the whole span of that time as only a few days, and the entire severity of his rigorous way of life seemed to him as nothing.

## CHAPTER IV

Not far from that city there was a very broad and large village in which all the inhabitants, from the least to the greatest, were exceedingly cruel pagans. No one at all was able to turn them away from the worship of idols.

Certain priests and deacons, ordained and sent there for this very purpose by the bishop, departed without producing any fruit of salvation among them, unable to endure the labor of their affliction. Their fierce spirit could not be persuaded or bent to agreement; indeed, they stirred up the most violent persecutions and disturbances against those who admonished them.

A crowd of monks, nevertheless, tried once and again to visit them, but they were wholly unable to accomplish anything for their conversion.

One day the bishop was sitting with his clergy and mentioned this most blessed man. He said to them:

“I have not been able in my time to see such a man, so perfect in every good work and so adorned with every virtue, in whom God chose to dwell, as the most holy Abraham now is.”

The clergy replied that it was true: he was a servant of God and a perfect monk.

The bishop then said:

“I wish to ordain him priest in that village of gentiles. Through patience and immense charity he can convert them to God.”

He immediately rose and proceeded with his clergy to the holy man’s cell. After greeting him, he at once told him about the gentiles of that village and begged him to go to them for their salvation.

When Abraham heard this, he became exceedingly sad and said to the bishop:

“I beg you, most holy Father, permit me to weep over my sins, and do not impose such a task upon me, who am weak and insignificant.”

The bishop replied:

“By God’s grace you are capable; therefore do not hesitate in this good obedience.”

The blessed man answered again:

“I beseech your holiness to permit me to mourn my sins.”

The bishop said to him:

“Behold, you have abandoned the whole world and everything in it, and embraced a crucified life. Yet, though you have accomplished all these things, understand that you do not possess the obedience that surpasses all virtues.”

When he heard this, Abraham began to weep bitterly and said:

“What am I, a dead dog (1 Samuel 24)? And what is my life, that you have judged such things concerning me, most holy Father?”

The bishop said to him:

“Here, while you remain seated, you are acquiring only your own salvation; there, through you and by the working of divine grace, many will be saved—namely, all whom you convert to the Lord God. Consider, therefore, where you will have the greater reward: whether if you save only yourself, or if you bring many to salvation with you.”

Then the holy man of God, weeping, said:

“Let the Lord’s will be done. Nevertheless, for the sake of obedience, I will go wherever you command.”

## CHAPTER VI

The bishop therefore led him out of the cell and immediately brought him into the city. There, through the laying on of hands, he was ordained a priest [Note: “He was ordained a priest through the laying on of hands.” Thus, even in the time of the apostles, the ordination of priests was performed by the laying on of hands, or χειροθεσία (*cheirothesia*; 1 Timothy 4:14; 5:22). See the *Onomasticon*.], and without delay he was sent to the village of pagans.

As Saint Abraham was going there, he prayed to the Lord:

“Most merciful and kindest God, look upon my weakness and send your heavenly grace for my protection, that your holy name may be glorified.”

When he reached the village and saw that all its inhabitants were violently maddened by the frenzy of idolatry, he groaned from the depths of his heart and wept bitterly. Raising his eyes to heaven, he said:

“You alone, God, who are without sin, do not despise the work of your hands.”

He quickly sent a messenger to the city to his most beloved friend, asking him to bring money from the remains of his inheritance. When he received it, he built a church within a few days and adorned it, like a splendid bride, with rich and wondrous decoration.

While it was being built, however, the man of God passed daily through the midst of the pagans’ idols. He said nothing at all, but prayed only in his heart and sent groans, accompanied by tears, to the Lord.

When the church had been completed, he offered it to God as a kind of gift, with many tears. There, kneeling, he poured out this prayer in humble supplication:

“You, almighty Son of the living God, who through your presence led the whole world, sunk in the darkness of error, to knowledge of your light: gather this people of yours, scattered as they are, into the bosom of your Church; enlighten the eyes of their minds, so that, rejecting the worship of images, they may recognize you alone as the lover of humanity and the merciful God.”

When he had finished this prayer, he immediately left the church and went to the temple of the pagans. With his own hands he overturned and destroyed their altars and images.

When the pagan crowd saw what had happened, they rushed upon him like wild beasts, tore him apart with many blows, and drove him away. At night he secretly remained in the church. He paid no attention to the wounds caused by his beatings but prayed to the Lord with tears and groans that they might be saved.

At dawn the pagans came and found the man of God praying. Struck with immense astonishment, they became, as it were, speechless [Note: *Enei*. Thus it should be written and read. The printed editions have hitherto had *aenei*. Although that could be understood as meaning that they became rigid with astonishment, the author does not write that way. The Greek is ἐνεοί. In Greek, ἐνεός means “struck speechless.” Hesychius: ἐνεοί, ἔκπληκτοι, “astonished.” See the *Onomasticon*.].

For this reason they came to the church every day—not for the sake of prayer, but so that, looking upon the church’s decoration and beauty with their own eyes, they might take pleasure in it.

One day the blessed man Abraham began to urge them to acknowledge God. But they became even more savage, beat him with clubs as though he were a stone or a lifeless object, and then, tying his feet with a rope, dragged him outside the village and covered him with stones. Thinking him dead, they left him half-alive.

In the middle of the night he recovered consciousness, began to weep most bitterly, and said:

“Why, Lord, have you despised my humility, and why have you turned your face away from me? Why do you reject my soul, and why have you despised, Lord, the work of your hands? And now, Lord, look upon your servant, hear my prayer, and strengthen me. Release your servants from the bonds of the devil, and grant them to know you, because you alone are God and besides you there is no other.”

Then, rising from prayer, he entered the village. He went into the church and sang psalms to the Lord.

At daybreak they came again and saw him. Astonished and driven to madness, without any compassion in their hearts, they subjected him to the harshest tortures and cruelly tormented him. Then, binding him as usual with ropes, they dragged him outside the village.

## CHAPTER VI

For three years he endured these things. Like true adamant, he persisted with steadfast endurance and did not yield to so many and such great tribulations of persecution. When he was beaten, dragged, persecuted, stoned, and afflicted by hunger and thirst, he was never provoked to anger by anything that happened to him, never stirred to indignation, never weakened through faintheartedness, and never exhausted by weariness.

Rather, while he suffered every hardship, his love and charity toward them increased more and more. At one moment he admonished them, at another he coaxed them, and at another he smoothed them with the sweetness of his gentle speech. He begged the elders as fathers, the young men as brothers, and the adolescents as sons, while they, in return, mocked and ridiculed him and heaped upon him a thousand insults.

## CHAPTER VII

One day the inhabitants of that village gathered together. Greatly astonished and terrified, they spoke among themselves:

“Do you see this man’s extraordinary patience and his indescribable charity toward us? How, amid all the tribulations we have inflicted upon him, has he not departed from this place, spoken an evil word to any one of us, or turned away from us, but endured everything with great joy?

“If there were not—as he asserts—a true God whom he preaches, a kingdom and paradise, and also punishment for evil deeds, he would not endure this tribulation pointlessly.

“Consider also that, when he was alone, he overturned our gods, and they were in no way able to harm him. Truly this man is a servant of God, and everything that rumor has spread about him is true. Come, therefore, let us believe in the God whom he preaches.”

While saying these things to one another, they all went together to the church, crying out:

“Glory to the heavenly God, who sent his servant to save us from error!”

## CHAPTER VIII

When the holy man of God saw this, he was filled with immense joy, and his face was changed like the morning dew.

Opening his mouth, he said to them:

“My fathers, brothers, and sons, come, let us give glory to God, who has deigned to enlighten the eyes of your minds so that you may recognize him. Receive the seal of life, so that you may be purified from the uncleanness of idols. Believe with all your heart and soul that there is one God of heaven and earth and of all that is in them, without beginning, indescribable and incomprehensible, giver of light, lover and redeemer of humanity, terrible and gentle.

“Believe also in his only-begotten Son, who is his Wisdom, and in the Holy Spirit, who gives life to all things, so that, having been made heavenly from earthly beings, you may attain heavenly life.”

They all replied:

“Yes, our father; yes, guide of our life. As you announce and teach us, so we believe and shall do.”

Immediately Saint Abraham took up the sacred baptism and baptized them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, from the least to the greatest. They numbered as many as a thousand persons.

Afterward, day by day, he read the divine Scriptures to them and taught them about the kingdom of God, the delights of paradise, the punishments of Gehenna, justice, faith, and charity.

As good earth receives good seed and produces fruit—some a hundredfold, some sixtyfold, and some thirtyfold (Matthew 13)—so they, listening most eagerly to his words and advancing in the fear of the Lord, produced abundant fruits.

In their sight he appeared like an angel of God and like a kind of bond holding a building together. Such was their love for him because of the teaching of his most gentle speech that they seemed, through this, to believe in God.

## CHAPTER IX

When a year had been completed after their conversion, the blessed Abraham did not cease preaching the word of the Lord to them every day.

When he saw their devotion to God, their most steadfast faith, their intense attachment to him, and the great honor they showed him, he feared that, on their account, he might be forced to violate his rule of abstinence or that his mind might in some way be bound by earthly concerns.

He rose in the middle of the night and is said to have poured out this prayer to the Lord:

“You alone are without sin, God, who, although holy, rest in the holy; you alone are the lover of humanity and the merciful Lord. You have enlightened the eyes of the minds of this multitude; you have released them from the bonds of the Adversary; you have converted them, entangled as they were in the errors of images; and you have granted them knowledge of you.

“I beg you, Lord, to deign to govern and preserve them to the end, and mercifully to grant continual and abundant assistance to this excellent flock, which you chose to possess. Surround them, as with a strongest wall, with the grace of your goodness, and always enlighten their hearts, so that, accomplishing what pleases you, they may deserve to receive eternal life.

“Grant support also to me, who am most weak, and do not reckon it as sin that I hasten to depart from them. For you, knower of all things, know that I desire you alone and acknowledge you as my Lord.”

When he had completed his prayer, he departed and marked the village three times with the sign of Christ. Then he secretly went away to another place and concealed himself in whatever hiding places he could find.

## CHAPTER X

In the morning the crowds gathered at the church as usual. When they did not find him at all, they were struck with the greatest astonishment and, like wandering sheep, searched in different places for their own shepherd, crying out his name with tears.

When they could not find him despite searching for a very long time, they were cast down by overwhelming grief. They immediately went and reported what had happened to the bishop.

When he learned this, he too became very sad and immediately sent many people to search for the man of God, especially to console his flock, since he saw them grieving bitterly.

When everyone was searching for him as for a most precious stone, and he could nowhere be found, the bishop, after consulting with his clergy, entered the aforementioned village. He began to offer them words of consolation and, by gentle preaching, to ease the great sorrow they had conceived over the departure of the man of God.

Seeing that they were most steadfast in the faith of Christ, he chose worthy men from among them and appointed them priests, deacons, and readers.

When the most holy Abraham heard this, he rejoiced exceedingly and, glorifying God, said:

“What shall I render to you, Lord my God, most gracious Father and sweetest lover of humanity, for all that you have rendered to me? I honor and glorify your dispensation.”

Then he immediately returned to his former cell. He built another cell outside it and shut himself away with great joy in the inner one.

O miracle, dearest brothers, full of praise and everlasting glory! Amid such great afflictions as he had suffered in the oft-mentioned village, he never broke the rule of his abstinence, nor turned aside from it to the right or to the left.

Glory and magnificence be to God, who granted him such endurance that he could both convert others and preserve the grace of his own purpose.

## CHAPTER XI

The devil, envious of good men, saw that although he had stirred up so many troublesome tribulations against Abraham, he had not been able to draw the man of God into negligence or separate the mind of the man of God from the Lord in any way. What was more, like gold in a furnace, Abraham became brighter through his trials and advanced into still greater patience and eagerness of charity.

The devil, therefore, became violently irritated and fiercely enraged. He came against him with a great display [Note: “With a great display,” that is, with pomp or apparatus. Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 18, concerning the emperor Valens: “When the festival day of the Epiphanies arrived, he came into the church with all the display that he had around him, and with empty and splendid pomp.” The Greek is σὺν τῇ περὶ αὐτὸν φαντασίᾳ, “with the display surrounding him.”], so that, at least in this way, he might instill fear in him and deceive and trick him.

## CHAPTER XII

While Abraham was standing in the middle of the night and singing psalms, suddenly a great light, like that of the sun, shone in his cell. A voice, as though belonging to a multitude, was heard saying:

“Blessed are you, Abraham; truly blessed and faithful are you. No one like you has been found in the whole of life, for you have fulfilled all my will.”

Immediately the holy man recognized the evil one’s deceit. He raised his voice and said:

“May your darkness be for your destruction, you who are full of deceit and falsehood. I am a sinful man, yet I have the defenses of hope; through the grace of God I fear none of your snares. Nor do very many apparitions instill fear in me. The name of my Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, whom I have loved and do love, is a most powerful wall to me. In that name I rebuke you, filthy dog, thrice to be pitied.”

As he said these things, the apparition immediately vanished from his sight like smoke. The holy servant of God, with great eagerness and a tranquil spirit, blessed the Lord as though he had seen no apparition at all.

## CHAPTER XIII

Again, a few days later, while Abraham was praying at night, the devil, holding an axe, attempted to overturn his cell. When he thought that he had already pierced it, he cried out in a loud voice:

“Hurry, my friends, hurry quickly; enter and violently take away his life!”

The blessed Abraham answered him:

“All the nations surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I shall take vengeance upon them” (Psalm 117).

As soon as Satan heard this voice, he vanished, while the blessed man’s cell remained intact and unharmed.

## CHAPTER XIV

Again, a few days later, while he was singing psalms at midnight, a violent flame began to burn the *psiathium* on which he was standing.

Then, fearless, he stamped upon the fire and said:

“Upon the asp and the basilisk I shall walk; I shall trample the lion and the dragon” (Psalm 90). “And, in the name of my Lord Jesus Christ, who gives me assistance, I shall overcome all the power of the enemy.”

Satan fled and cried out in a loud voice:

“I shall overcome you by an evil death, and I shall find ways by which to crush you, since you now regard me as contemptible.”

## CHAPTER XV

One day, while Abraham was taking food, the demon, transformed into the appearance of a young man, entered his cell. Approaching, he tried to overturn Abraham’s cup.

But the man of God held it with his hand and ate without fear.

Then the devil leapt up and suddenly devised another apparition. Behold, he set what appeared to be a candlestick before Abraham, with a burning lamp above it, and, with his filthy and foul-smelling mouth, sang psalms in a loud voice:

“Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Psalm 116).

After he had sung many words from that psalm, the holy man gave him no answer until he had received his customary food.

When he had risen from the table, he said to him with complete firmness:

“Unclean dog, thrice to be pitied, most weak and most deceitful: if you know that they are blessed, why do you trouble them? For truly blessed are all who love God with their whole heart.”

The devil replied:

“For this reason I am hostile to them: to overcome them, so that, hindered from every good work, they may be joined to my crimes.”

The blessed man answered him:

“May it go ill with you, accursed one, so that you may have power to overcome or hinder anyone who fears God—unless perhaps those who are like you and depart from God of their own will. You conquer and deceive them because God is not in them. But from those who love God you evaporate and perish like smoke before the wind. Their one prayer pursues and casts you down in the same way that dust, chased by the wind, is scattered.

“My God lives, and he is blessed forever; he is my glory. I shall not fear you, even if you remain here for all time. I shall despise you as nothing, just as someone might disregard a single crushed puppy.”

When he had said these things, the devil immediately vanished, as he was accustomed to do.

## CHAPTER XVI

Again, five days later, after he had completed his nighttime psalmody, the enemy devised another form of apparition.

For behold, what appeared to be a very large crowd was seen to have arrived. As though pulling one another along, they encouraged one another with shouts to throw the man of God into a pit.

The blessed man looked around at them and said:

“They surrounded me like bees; they blazed like fire among thorns; and in the name of the Lord I shall take vengeance upon them” (Psalm 117).

Then Satan cried out:

“Alas! Alas for me! I do not know what else I can do to you. Behold, I understand that I have been defeated and overcome in everything, that all my powers have been despised, and that I have been trampled on from every side. Nevertheless, even so I shall never depart from you until I overcome you and make you abject and subject to me.”

The man of God said to him:

“Anathema to you and to all your power, most filthy demon! Glory and honor belong to the Lord alone, the holy and wise God, who has handed you over to be trampled upon by us, his lovers. Therefore we mock and despise your tricks. Know, then, most weak and most wretched demon, that we fear neither you nor your apparitions.”

## [Col. 0291B] CHAPTER XVII

For a long time the devil fought against this most courageous man with various devices and machinations, but he could not, even while striving to do so, instill fear in his steadfast thoughts.

Rather, by fighting, he aroused in Abraham ever greater eagerness and charity toward God. Since Abraham loved God with his whole soul and ordered his life according to God’s will, he abundantly merited divine grace; and for that reason the devil could not harm him.

For Abraham had perseveringly knocked, so that the treasures of divine grace might be opened to him. When the entrance had been opened, he took from it three most precious stones: faith, hope, and charity. By these the remaining virtues were perfectly and firmly adorned in him.

He also wove a most precious crown from good works and offered it to the King of kings, the Lord from whom he had received the gift.

For who loved God and his neighbor as himself with such a whole heart (Luke 10)? Or who showed such compassion and mercy toward those who labored?

Whenever he heard that some monk was living well, did he not pray to the Lord for him, that he might be preserved free from all the devil’s snares and complete the course of his life without blame?

Or whenever he heard of someone sinful or wicked, did he not ask the Lord with tears, day and night, that the person might be saved?

Throughout the whole period of his discipline, no day passed without tears. He did not easily release his lips into laughter. Oil never approached his little body; from the day of his conversion, he never washed his face or even his feet.

He presented himself as though he were dying every day.

## CHAPTER XVIII

O truly, brothers, what a glorious miracle: amid such great abstinence, continual vigils mingled with tears, sleeping on the ground (*chameuniae*) [Note: *Chameuniis*. Thus it should be read. This word is also frequently corrupted in manuscripts. The old edition has *Cammeniis*; the Cologne edition, *Caumeniis*. The latter arose from a transposition of letters, which was very common in certain words.], and bodily mortification, he was never at all wearied; he never became ill or was numbed by sluggishness; he was never exhausted by tedium.

Rather, just as a hungry or thirsty person endures everything with a certain appetite, so Abraham, sustaining all things with eager desire, could never have his mind satisfied by the sweetness of his purpose.

His appearance was like an unfading flower, and the purity of his soul was recognized in his face. His whole little body also appeared strong and vigorous, as though he had done nothing strenuous, since he enjoyed divine grace in all things and possessed the delight of spiritual joy.

At the hour of his sleep he appeared so radiant in countenance that one would have thought he had never spent the time of his life in abstinence.

Another miracle also occurred in him through divine providence. Throughout all fifty years of his abstinence, he never changed the cilicium garment with which he had been clothed.

The remainder concerning the life of Abraham and his niece is found below, among the lives of women.

## [Col. 0293]

# JANUARY 1. THE LIFE OF SAINT BASIL

[Note: “Of Basil.”] The Roman Martyrology, January 1: “At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the deposition of Saint Basil, bishop, whose feast is chiefly commemorated on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July, the day on which he was ordained bishop.” Concerning his ordination as bishop, it says under June 14: “At Caesarea in Cappadocia, the ordination of Saint Basil, bishop, who in the time of the emperor Valens shone forth remarkably in teaching and wisdom, adorned with every virtue, and defended the Church against the Arians and Macedonians with extraordinary steadfastness.” The Greek Menologion, January 1: “On the same day, the commemoration of our holy father Basil.” In the Menaia, on the same day, he is treated at greater length. His memory is also celebrated there with Gregory Nazianzen the theologian and John Chrysostom on January 30, and in both places he is honored with the epithet “the Great” (μεγάλου). Evagrius, in the *Gnostic*, calls Basil “the pillar of truth.” Nicephorus reports this in Book XI, chapter 43. Gregory of Nyssa, in his *Encomium of Ephraem*, says that Basil was “the mouth of the Church,” “the golden nightingale of doctrine.” Ephraem himself calls him in his encomium, ἡ βάσις τῶν ἀρετῶν, βίβλος τῶν ἐπαίνων, “the foundation of virtues, the book of praises.” There too he adorns him with other splendid eulogies. Theodoret, Book IV, chapter 19, calls him ὁ τῆς οἰκουμένης φωστήρ, “the radiant light of the whole world.” See various eulogies of him at the beginning of his works. Cardinal Baronius inserted accounts of his illustrious deeds into his highly praised *Annals*. Here Amphilochius himself declares who among the ancients wrote Basil’s encomium in the Prologue.]

## ARCHBISHOP OF CAESAREA IN CAPPADOCIA

## BY AMPHILOCHIUS

[Note: “By Amphilochius.”] The Roman Martyrology, November 23: “At Iconium in Lycaonia, Saint Amphilochius, bishop, companion in the desert of the saints Basil and Gregory Nazianzen, and their colleague in the episcopate, who, after undertaking many struggles for the Catholic faith, renowned for holiness and learning, rested in peace.” The Greek Menologion on the same day: “The feast of our holy father Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, under the emperor Theodosius the Great, a man distinguished by knowledge of the divine Scriptures, holiness of life, and sincerity in the true and catholic faith, commended by his friendship with and testimony concerning Basil the Great. He wrote books containing the orthodox faith and, having reached an advanced old age, rested in peace.” He is treated at greater length in the Menaia on the same day.

That Amphilochius was the author of this Life was believed long ago, more than eight hundred years ago, by Ursus, cardinal and subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, who at that time rendered it into Latin. More about him appears below, at no. 3. Sigebert, in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 7, says: “Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, wrote the life of Basil, bishop of Caesarea.” Sixtus of Siena likewise attributes it to Amphilochius in Book IV of his *Holy Library*. As the work of Amphilochius, Vincent of Beauvais cites it in the *Historical Speculum*, Book XIV, chapters 78–80; Antonius, Part II, title IX, chapter 4, sections 1 and 2; and Peter, bishop of Equilio, in his *Catalogue of the Saints*, Book II, chapter 28.

I received in Paris, from the royal library, a Greek copy bearing the name of Amphilochius. Baronius, however, says in the Roman Martyrology, under January 1: “There exists a Life of Basil written under the name of Amphilochius, yet, in the judgment of all more prudent scholars, it is thought to belong rather to someone else than to Amphilochius, Basil’s contemporary, since certain matters occur there that seem less suitable to him.” In the *Annals*, volume IV, he likewise points out various blemishes in this Life; I shall indicate each of them in its proper place, so that, with this great critic as guide, you may distinguish what is genuine from what has been interpolated.

Long ago Glycas, seeing this Life circulate under the name of Amphilochius, denied its authorship to Amphilochius, chiefly on the following grounds:

“Although,” he says (*Glyc.*, Part IV of the *Annals*), “we find written in the book concerning the miracles of Saint Basil—said to have been committed to writing by that great man Amphilochius—that, at the command of the perpetual Virgin and Mother of God, through Saint Mercury, and at the prayers of Basil the Great, this deserter was struck down, the account nevertheless does not deserve immediate belief. Why is that? Because in the same writing we read that Basil the Great was bishop of Caesarea at the time when the most wicked emperor, having undertaken an expedition against the Persians, was traversing those regions. But the outstanding Gregory, surnamed the Theologian, handed down the matter differently. For if, according to this account, Basil was living in Pontus at the beginning of the reign of Valens, who came to the throne somewhat later, while Eusebius was bishop of Caesarea, then Basil was even less likely to have held the episcopal office under Julian. It is plainly evident that when Julian traveled through Cappadocia he found neither Basil serving there as bishop nor any threat made by him against the church itself. Likewise, Basil the bishop did not pray to God for this purpose, nor was that Mercury, Christ’s witness, sent to remove the deserter from the world. For if the matter had happened in this way, it would not remain unknown to the present day by whose weapon Julian was struck down. It is agreed that he was pierced by a spear, but the perpetrator of the deed is entirely unknown.”

Although Baronius agrees with this judgment in volume IV, under the year of Christ 363—“Yet Glycas himself,” he says, “cannot be approved by us in this matter, since, merely because these writings were composed under the fictitious name of Amphilochius, he wholly withdraws his confidence from a history that is splendidly confirmed by the authority of Helladius, cited by Damascenus (*On Images*, Oration 1), who, although Glycas did not see him, nevertheless recounts the event differently”—whatever may be the case concerning the disagreement between the account established by Helladius and that of Amphilochius, if indeed the accounts belong to different authors, and Amphilochius did not instead reproduce Helladius in full, whom Damascenus cites in abbreviated form, certainly that history does not appear in this translation of Ursus, so that we are not at all compelled to explain it.

Although a more reliable and substantial Life of Basil could be compiled from Basil’s own writings, those of Gregory Nazianzen, and other contemporary authors—as Baronius largely does in his *Annals*, and as our Peter Halloix has already done in several Lives of the Doctors of the Church and others—nevertheless, since our present purpose was not to set forth whatever might be investigated about each saint from every possible source, but rather to review the Lives of the Fathers, so often printed, found in the hands of many, and cited by learned men, explaining doubtful points in them and marking the apocryphal, I have allowed this Life also to retain its place among the others. I preface it, however, with the warning of Baronius, which he gives in volume IV, under the year of Christ 378, the twelfth year of Pope Damasus, the fifteenth of Valens, the twelfth of Gratian, and the third of the emperor Valentinian:

“The Life of Basil circulated under the false name of Amphilochius is not considered sufficiently worthy to be placed before the ears of the learned, unless they are so perceptive that they can investigate and separate what is true from what is false. For no one will deny that many things in it are true, especially those known to have been taken from both Gregorys, Nazianzen and Nyssen, as well as from Ephraem, or borrowed by the author from Helladius.”

Thus far Baronius.]

## BISHOP OF ICONIUM, TRANSLATED BY URSUS

[Note: “By Ursus.”] Baronius, under January 1 in the Roman Martyrology, says:

“He rendered into Latin”—speaking of the Life of Basil believed to have been written by Amphilochius—“Ursus, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church. We read his preface, which is lacking in the other copies, in an old manuscript codex of our library, which we possess through the pious generosity of the memory of the excellent and most learned man, Achilles Statius of Portugal.

“Moreover, certain miracles of the same Basil, written by Helladius and translated into Latin by Anastasius the Librarian in the time of Nicholas I, Roman pontiff, are found there; the preface addressed to the aforementioned Ursus and composed by Anastasius is also preserved there.”

Thus far Baronius. From this we infer the date of Ursus, the translator of this Life, since Anastasius flourished around the year of the Lord 860.

Having learned from this statement of Baronius that a preface by Ursus to the Life of Basil existed in Rome, though it had not yet seen the light of day, I wrote to Rome to the Reverend Father Andrea Zazzara, a distinguished ornament of the Oratorian Congregation. He immediately had it copied from manuscript codices and sent it to me. After receiving it, I found its style somewhat better than that of the text of Basil’s Life as it has until now appeared in the commonly circulated Lives of the Fathers. Therefore I also summoned the text of Basil’s Life, by the same translator, from the index, and present it here.

Do not be misled, however: only the first eight chapters, together with the preface bearing the name of Ursus, were sent to me from Rome. I received the remaining three from manuscripts of the Oratorian Congregation, but they did not bear the name of Ursus, so that I doubt whether they came from his workshop. Certainly Ursus himself appears to have translated at least chapter 10 as well, as he indicates in this preface, no. 5. But whether these chapters derive from his translation, I cannot affirm.]

### SUBDEACON OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

## PREFACE OF THE TRANSLATOR

Know that I have translated into Latin the Life of blessed Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, at your request. For I ought not to disobey you, since I am indebted to all my brothers and neighbors. Would that I had carried out what you requested as well as I undertook it promptly, and as usefully as successfully—especially since you necessarily urged me to undertake this task, and rightly took pains that so great a man should be celebrated among the Latins as he is among the Greeks.

Finally, although the Latin language possesses some of his salutary writings, how admirable his life was has until now remained unknown. Certainly it is sufficiently incongruous that what he taught should be known while what he accomplished should be unknown, since the holy man, as an imitator of the one about whom Luke writes, “Jesus began both to do and to teach” (Acts 1), not only taught people the words of God but, in order to be called great in the kingdom of heaven, first practiced them.

Enjoy his teachings, then, all the more profitably; and lest you perhaps say that he taught but did not practice, you will now learn that he did what he taught, and henceforth you will have something to imitate.

Although before this work I had not dared to undertake it, thinking—as you yourself know—that it had already been translated by someone else, in this I rightly reproved myself. Is it the case that, because certain people have interpreted Sacred Scripture, later interpreters therefore interpreted it less? If that were so, the Latin Church would not have received the same Sacred Scripture from the Hebrew source through the blessed Jerome, priest of the Roman Church.

[Note: “Jerome, priest of the Roman Church.”] You see that, already long ago—even in the time of this translator Ursus—the opinion had become widespread that Jerome was a Roman presbyter. The manuscript Life of Jerome that I possess also reports this. Jerome himself, however, contradicts it, saying that he was ordained at Antioch, though in such a way that he was not compelled to bind himself to any particular church. Thus he says in Letter 61, to Pammachius, against the errors of John of Jerusalem, speaking of Paulinus, bishop of Antioch:

“Did I ask you to ordain me? If you confer the presbyterate in such a way as not to take the monk away from us, you must answer for your own judgment. But if, under the name of presbyter, you take from me that for which I abandoned the world, I possess what I have always possessed and have suffered no loss in my ordination.”

If someone should wish to call Jerome a Roman presbyter because he served Pope Damasus as a secretary for letters, I would not strongly object.]

Yet after careful investigation I found nothing written among the Latins about the Life of this saint except two of his miracles.

[Note: “Except two of his miracles.”] Thus, in the time of Ursus, nothing in Latin concerning the Life and miracles of Basil by Amphilochius had come into his hands apart from those two miracles found here, in chapters 8 and 10. Because they were marred by the roughness of their style, he attempted to express them somewhat more elegantly.]

That is, the story of a boy delivered from denial of Christ and of a woman rescued from sins. Yet I found them so corrupted that I preferred to translate them anew rather than correct them.

It should certainly be noted that some people, when they read in these Acts what Saint Amphilochius wrote, assert that they differ from what Saint Gregory Nazianzen commemorates in the epitaph of this great man.

[Note: “In the epitaph.”] The epitaph, or funeral oration, composed by Gregory Nazianzen, is found in volume I of Nazianzen’s works, Oration 20. He also composed another epitaph or funeral poem about him, found in volume II of Nazianzen’s works, poem 14.]

Yet one may have passed over in silence what the other mentioned, just as we find the same thing among the Evangelists. Especially since Amphilochius himself, who wrote about the life of so great a man, appropriately indicates this when he proceeds to explain it—

## PROLOGUE OF THE AUTHOR

[Col. 0295]

Most beloved, it was neither improper nor unjust for devoted sons to grieve over the death of their father and to offer him the gift of tears, which we have until now performed in sympathy. But after, as Scripture says, we had laid aside the whirlwind of mourning, we were moved to offer a grateful supplication to Christ our God and Lord on behalf of all. I judged it worthwhile to commit to writing so memorable a Life, together with the true miracles of our shepherd and teacher Basil, lest, through the long passage of time, they be consigned to deep oblivion.

Since three most holy and distinguished men—Gregory, namely, who excelled in theology,

[Note: “Gregory, namely, who excelled in theology.”] Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 19: “Gregory, whom the ancients called Nazianzen and we call Theologian, because he is worthy of such a surname.”—and Gregory, the memorable bishop of Nyssa,

[Note: “Gregory, the memorable bishop of Nyssa.”] You may find the oration of Gregory of Nyssa, in which he celebrates the praises and memory of his brother, among his works, translated by Lorenzo Sifano. In it he compares Basil with Moses, Samuel, Elijah, John the Baptist, and Paul, on account of the distinctive virtues and deeds of each.—as well as blessed Ephraem,

[Note: “Blessed Ephraem.”] You may find the encomium of Basil written by Ephraem among Ephraem’s works, volume III, translated into Latin by Gerard Vossius. Ephraem himself mentions this encomium in his oration on the Forty Martyrs.—have presented such a great man in different ways and in funeral discourses, it seemed fitting that I too, as an abortive child, if I may speak with the Apostle, having received into my hands the accounts published by both those admirable men, should supply what seemed lacking in them. I have done so in the manner of a devoted son presenting to his father what is owed, reaching upward, as one may suppose, to certain things and receiving reliable knowledge of them. For he knows—yes, he knows—that clouds conceal the sun, and that the tedious passage of good accounts easily introduces oblivion.

Great, therefore, was our shepherd Basil, famous throughout the world, a speaker of heavenly virtues, fellow-minister of the angelic orders, praiseworthy teacher of the Church, incorruptible pillar of orthodox doctrines. He explained with exceptional clarity the nature of existing things; he overthrew Julian, that worst apostate of the Trinity;

[Note: “The apostate Julian.”] I believe this refers to the account of Julian’s death, said to have been obtained through Basil’s prayers, as reported by Helladius in Damascenus, Oration 1, *On Images*. It is told somewhat differently in the commonly circulated Amphilochius. But it is absent from this translation of Cardinal Ursus. For an exact investigation of Julian’s death, see Baronius, volume IV, under the year of Christ 363, the twelfth year of Pope Liberius and the second year of the emperor Julian.]

he closed the blasphemous mouth of Valens;

[Note: “He closed the mouth of Valens.”] Gregory Nazianzen describes how firmly Basil stood against Valens in his funeral oration in praise of Basil; Ephraem, in his oration on Basil’s praises; Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 15; Socrates, Book IV, chapter 21; Theodoret, Book IV, chapter 17; Gildas the Wise, in his oration *On Ecclesiastical Order*; and Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 18. See Baronius, volume IV, under the year of Christ 370.]

he utterly destroyed the most wicked error of the Arians; he clearly established the right belief of Christians. He was an acceptable shepherd of the people of the Church, a partner in the royal priesthood, clothed round about with the truth of Christ, a ram among the sheep, a renowned teacher of the divine faith. Both while alive and after death he shone with great miracles. By his prayer he brought about the destruction of Julian, hated by God, who, as has been said, exalted his horn on high and spoke wickedness against God.

Meanwhile Valens, indignant at receiving the imperial purple and offering patronage to the wicked doctrine of the Arians, came to the illustrious city of Caesarea, which is ours. But how or for what reason this occurred is not a matter for the present account. Let us return to our subject and narrate his virtues, which he possessed from the womb to the end of his life.

# THE LIFE

[Col. 0295]

## CHAPTER ONE

Basil alone upon earth displayed perfection: a life adorned with deeds and illumined by words of divine wisdom; giving everything—soul and body—to Christ; offering the palms of words.

[Note: “The palms of words.”] The Vulgate editions have “the hands of discourse.” The Greek is λόγον, παλάμας, “word, palms.” Both interpreters read λόγων παλάμας. Chrysostom, Homily 2 on the Maccabees, which is number 49 in volume I of the Frontonian edition: Ἀλλὰ καθάπερ χερσὶ τῇ παρακλήσει των λόγῶν, “But as though with hands, by the exhortation of words.” The same author, Homily 1 on the Maccabees, number 44 in the same edition: Ἐνῆκεν ἀντὶ χειρῶν τῇ τῶν λόγων πρὸς αὐτὸν χρησαμένη παρακλήσει καὶ συμβουλῇ, “Instead of hands, she impelled him by using exhortation and counsel toward him through words.”]

For this reason he tore apart pagan error like spiders’ webs.

When he was seven years old, his parents entrusted him to the study of letters. Devoting five years to mathematics, he produced abundant fruit in philosophical discipline through the gentleness of his nature. Then, leaving his homeland—for he was Cappadocian by birth—he came to the mother of discourse, that is, Athens.

[Note: “Athens.”] Gregory Nazianzen, in his funeral oration for Basil, from which Nicephorus draws in Book XI, chapter 17. Before this, however, he had studied literature at Caesarea and Constantinople, as the same Gregory testifies. Just as Athens is here called “the mother of words,” so Gregory, in the passage cited immediately above, calls it τῶν λόγων ἔδαφος, “the seat or dwelling-place of letters.” Libanius, declamation 29, calls it Τῶν λόγων ἐργαστήριον, “the workshop of discourse.”]

Adorned with chastity, or with great continence and self-control, he attached himself to Eubulus, a teacher of Greek wisdom.

[Note: “Eubulus.”] Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 17, assigns other teachers to Basil and Gregory Nazianzen:

Ἄμφω νέοι ὄντες, Ἱμερίῷ καὶ Προαιρεσίῳ τοῖς τότε δοκιμωτάτοις σοφισταῖς ἐν Ἀθήναις ἐφοίτησαν, μετὰ ταῦτα ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ Λιβανίῳ τῳ Σύρῳ.

“While both were still young, they studied at Athens under Himerius and Proaeresius, at that time easily the most distinguished sophists; afterward, at Antioch, under Libanius the Syrian.”

Baronius, volume III, under the year of Christ 354, through a lapse of memory or pen, says from Sozomen that Libanius taught at Athens together with Himerius.]

He devoted himself so completely to his studies that both teachers and fellow students imitated him. His companions included the great bishop Gregory Nazianzen, who governed the reins of the Apostolic throne for twelve years;

[Note: “Who governed the reins of the Apostolic throne for twelve years.”] The opinion that Gregory Nazianzen presided over the Church of Constantinople for twelve years was not peculiar to Amphilochius alone. The Menaia likewise say so on January 30, in the commemoration of the three Doctors of the Church:

Προέστη δὲ καὶ Κωνσταντινουπόλεως ἐκκλησίας χρόνους δώδεκα.

“He presided over the Church of Constantinople for twelve years.”

This means the years he spent there defending that church against the Arians.]

Julian, who was a Christian for a short time, and Libanius.

[Note: “Libanius.”] Sozomen, cited above at no. 14, asserts that Libanius was Basil’s teacher.]

This admirable man resolved above all in his heart not to partake of bread or wine until, by the provision of heavenly wisdom, he had penetrated its mysteries. After spending fifteen years in learning and passing through the whole of pagan philosophy, finally reading astronomy, geometry, and everything excellent, he was unable by these means to discover the Creator of all things. One night, while he was keeping vigil, a certain divine splendor began [uncertain reading] to urge him to pass through the Scripture of our religion.

He therefore arose and hurried to Egypt.

[Note: “He therefore arose and hurried to Egypt.”] It is established from the funeral oration of Nazianzen already cited that Basil undertook certain journeys:

Ἔπειτα ἐκδημίαι τινὲς, ἐπειδήγε ἡμᾶς οὐκ εἶχε, τῶν ἀναλκαίων ὑπολαμβάνουσι καὶ οὐκ ἀπὸ σκοποῦ τῆς προκειμένης φιλοσοφίας.

“And afterward, since he did not have me with him, he undertook certain necessary journeys, by no means foreign to the aim of the philosophy he had adopted.”

Nicetas, Gregory’s commentator, thinks that Basil went to Seleucia, to the temple of Thecla, either for prayer or in pursuit of a quiet and peaceful life. But Basil himself mentions his journey to Egypt in two letters. First, in Letter 165, to Eustathius the philosopher, Basil, not yet properly instructed, nearly attributed to fortune’s displeasure the fact that he had not found Eustathius during his long journey, neither in his homeland, nor in Syria, nor in Egypt.

He expresses more clearly his inward ardor and the journeys undertaken in search of truth in Letter 79, to Eustathius, bishop of Sebaste:

Ἐγὼ πογὺν χρόνον προσαναλώσας τῇ ματαιότητι, καὶ πᾶσαν σχεδὸν τὴν ἐμαυτοῦ νεότητα ἐναφανίσας τῇ ματαιοπονίᾳ ἣν εἶχον προσδιατρίβων τῇ ἀναλήψει τῶν μαθημάτων τῆς παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ μαρανθείσης σοφίας, ἐπειδή ποτε ὥσπερ ἐξ ὕπνου βαθέος διαναστὰς, ἀπέβλεψα μὲν πρὸς τὸ θαυμαστὸν φῶς τῆς ἀληθείας τοῦ εὐαγγελίου, κατεῖδον δὲ τὸ ἄχρηστον τῆς σοφίας τῶν ἀρχόντων τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου τῶν καταργουμένων, πολλὰ τὴν ἐλεινήν μου ζωὴν ἀποκλαύσας ηὐχόμην δοθῆναί μοι χειραγωγὸν πρὸς τὴν εἰσαγωγὴν τῶν δογμάτων τῆς εὐσεβείας, καὶ πρό γε πάντων ἐπιμελὲς ἦν μοι, διόρθωσίν τινα τοῦ ἤθους ποιήσασθαι, πολὺν χρόνον ἐκ τῆς πρὸς τοὺς φαύλους ὁμιλίας διασφραθέντος. Καὶ τοίνυν ἀναγνοὺς τὸ εὐαγγέλιον, καὶ θεασάμενος ἐκεῖ μεγίστην ἀφορμὴν εἰς τελείωσιν τὴν διάπρασιν τῶν ὑπαρχόντων, καὶ τὴν πρὸς τοὺς ἐνδεεῖς τῶν ἀδελφῶν κοινωνίαν, καὶ ὅλως τὸ ἀφροντίστως ἔχειν τοῦ βίου τούτου, καὶ ὑπὸ μηδεμίας συμπαθείας πρὸς τὰ ὧδε τὴν ψυχὴν ἐπιστρέφεσθαι, ηὐχόμην εὑρεῖν τινα τῶν ἀδελφῶν, ταύτην ἐλόμενον τὴν ὁδὸν τοῦ βίου, ὥς τε αὐτῷ συνδιαπεραιωθῆναι τὸν βαθὺν τοῦτον τοῦ βίου κλύδονα· καὶ δὲ πολλοὺς μὲν εὗρον κατὰ τὴν Ἀλεξάνδρειαν, πολλοὺς δὲ κατὰ τὴν λοιπὴν Αἴγυπτον, καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς Παλαιστίνης ἑτέρους, καὶ τῆς κοίλης Συρίας καὶ Μεσοποταμίας, ὧν ἐθαύμαζον μὲν τὸ περὶ τὴν δίαιταν ἐγκρατές, ἐθαύμαζον δὲ τὸ καρτερικὸν ἐν πόνοις.

“I, after spending a long time on vanity and consuming nearly all my youth in the futile labor to which I had devoted myself while occupied with acquiring the disciplines of the wisdom that had been made foolish by God, at last, when I had awakened as though from a deep sleep, looked toward the wondrous light of the truth of the Gospel and saw the uselessness of the wisdom of the rulers of this age, who are being brought to nothing. After shedding many tears over my miserable life, I prayed that a guide might be given me to lead me into the doctrines of godliness. Above all, I was concerned to make some correction of character, which had been corrupted through long association with the wicked.

“Accordingly, after reading the Gospel and seeing there that the greatest means toward perfection was the selling of one’s possessions, sharing them with needy brothers, living altogether without concern for this life, and allowing the soul to be turned toward earthly things by no attachment whatever, I prayed that I might find one of the brethren who had chosen this way of life, so that I might cross with him this deep surge of life. I found many in Alexandria, many also throughout the rest of Egypt, and others in Palestine, Coele-Syria, and Mesopotamia. I admired in them both their self-control in diet and their endurance in labors.”]

He approached a certain archimandrite named Porphyrius and asked that sacred books be given to him for the understanding of divine doctrines.

[Note: “Porphyrius.”] Various saints named Porphyrius may be found in the Greek Menaia, but I do not know whether any of them fits this story.]

After receiving them, he remained there, devoting himself to meditation on the divine utterances and being nourished on water and vegetables. After remaining there for a full year and considering the account of truth by faith, he persevered in searching the word of truth. Then he asked to be dismissed to Jerusalem for the sake of prayer.

[Note: “To Jerusalem for the sake of prayer.”] This pilgrimage had long been famous, dating perhaps from Christ’s own ascension into heaven. Jerome, Letter 17, to Marcella:

“It would take too long now to pass through every age from the Lord’s Ascension to the present day and list which bishops, which martyrs, and which men eloquent in ecclesiastical teaching have come to Jerusalem, thinking that they possessed less religion, less knowledge, and had not received, as the saying goes, the finishing touch of virtue unless they had adored Christ in those places from which the Gospel first shone forth from the cross.”

For various examples of those who traveled to Jerusalem for prayer, see our Gretzer, Book I of *On Pilgrimage*, chapter 4 and several following chapters.]

When he had been entreated, the archimandrite dismissed him, and Basil went there to see the miracles.

[Note: [Col. 0297D] This note appears at the foot of column 297, but the callout letter (a) has not been printed in the text. This chapter is absent from the *Lives of the Fathers*.]

## CHAPTER II

When he returned to the place where he had been instructed in Greek philosophy, he began to persuade many philosophers and to show Christ to the multitude of pagans, demonstrating to them the way of salvation. He also sought out his teacher Eubulus, who was a leader in discourse, in return for the studies in which Eubulus had instructed him, in order to draw him over and incline him toward the undefiled faith, since Basil himself was running well toward it.

He taught all who had been imbued with philosophy to follow him as a teacher. Seeking him in all the schools, he found him in a suburb among philosophers.

[Note: “In a suburb.”] Another version has “in the suburbs.” Medieval translators often retain the Greek word. Below, in Rufinus, Book III, no. 19. See the *Onomasticon*.]

For they had no pursuit among them except saying and hearing something new. While Eubulus was disputing, Basil, who was standing nearby, reproved him. One of those who were with them said: “Who is reproving you, philosopher?” He replied: “Either God or Basil.”

Recognizing him, Eubulus dismissed those who were with him and remained with Basil. They continued fasting for three days and put questions to one another.

Eubulus then asked Basil: “What is the definition of philosophy, Basil?”

He replied: “The first definition of philosophy is meditation on death.”

Eubulus, marveling, said: “What is the world?”

Basil answered: “That which is above the world. The world’s words are indeed sweet, but the world itself is exceedingly bitter if someone holds it wickedly.”

“There is one pleasure of the body and another of incorporeal nature, and it is clearly impossible for both to exist in anyone at the same time. For no one can serve two masters (Matthew 6).

“Yet insofar as virtue supplies strength, we break the bread of knowledge for the hungry, and through virtue we lead under shelter those who, through the wickedness of certain people, are without a roof. If we see someone naked, we cover him with clothing, and we do not despise those of our own seed.”

Having said this, he imaginatively represented, in a parable, the mercy of our Savior that he works in us through repentance, and gradually set before Eubulus three tablets.

[Note: “Three tablets.”] Another version has “three dishes.” The Greek is τρεῖς πίνακας. In Greek, πίναξ means both “tablet” and “dish” or “basin.” Our translator correctly renders it here as “tablet.” The passage is modeled on the *Tablet of Cebes*, where there are three περίβολοι, or enclosures, just as there are three tablets here. There too you find virtues and vices, as here.]

He gradually set out these three tablets in the forecourts of the mind: one in the upper part of the gates, bearing the virtues—prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice. On the left side he placed seduction; and on either side, intemperance, profanation, loquacity, persuasion, and every such array of evils.

Repentance stood nobly nearby, fearless, cheerful, and gentle, opposing the contrary things but invoking every good upon the people. Beside it were abstinence, shrewdness, mercy, chastity, modesty, humanity, and a multitude of other good things.

The meaning of this story is admonition to those who see it and an occasion for greater zeal to those who hear it.

“Seeing this myself, I was delighted, Eubulus, and was led to this conclusion. For among us there are not images or riddles, but the truth itself, clearly leading us to salvation.

“For we shall all rise again: some to eternal life, others to reproach and everlasting confusion. We shall stand before the tribunal of Christ (2 Corinthians 5), as the great-speaking prophets Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel, King David, and the distinguished Paul teach us.

“After them comes the Lord himself, the giver of repentance and the one who rewards it. He sought the lost sheep (Matthew 18). When the boy who had departed from his father’s embrace with great wealth, squandered it in dissipation, and afterward returned emaciated with hunger, he embraced him as a true son. He adorned him with a shining robe, a ring, and costly garments, and teaches us, in the case of the sinful son, not to rage but to grant forgiveness as to a brother (Luke 14).

“In the same way, without envy, the Lord, outstanding in goodness, gives an equal reward to those who came at the eleventh hour (Matthew 20). To us also, when we repent and recover our senses, he will grant regeneration from water and the Holy Spirit, because eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what the Lord has prepared for those who love him (1 Corinthians 2).”

When Eubulus understood these things, he said:

“O Basil, defender of the heavenly Trinity, through you I believe in one God, the almighty Father, and so forth; I await the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Amen.

“In practice I shall show you the faith that is in me. I shall place everything I possess in your hands and, for the remainder of my life, if it is pleasing in the sight of God, I shall remain with you, having received regeneration from holy water, that is, from the Spirit.”

Basil replied:

“Blessed is the Lord our God, from this time forth and forever, O Eubulus, who has illumined the true light in your mind and transferred you from the error of many gods to knowledge of his mercy.

“Since, as you have confessed, you wish to remain with me, I shall show you how we may provide for our salvation and be freed from the bonds of this age. Let us sell everything we possess and give it to the needy. Then at last let us go to the holy city, to become observers for ourselves of the miracles performed there and to acquire confidence before God.”

Accordingly, after both of them had piously distributed their possessions, they bought only those garments normally prepared for holy baptism and set out for Jerusalem, converting a great multitude of pagans to the Lord.

## CHAPTER III

When they arrived at the city of Antioch, they turned aside to a certain lodging. The host’s son, named Philoxenus, was sitting before the door, deeply engaged in study. He was a disciple of the sophist Libanius, from whom he had received Homeric verses to transfer into rhetorical form.

Since he was undergoing great distress and was becoming exhausted through his labor, Basil looked at him and said: “Why are you so sad, young man?”

He replied: “What benefit will I gain if I tell you?”

Basil persisted and promised to help him. Then the young man told him about the sophist, the verses, and the fact that he was laboring because of them.

Basil took the verses and began to give their interpretation. The young man, astonished and delighted at once, asked him to set it down in writing. Basil wrote out the solution of the verses in three editions. The boy joyfully received them, and at daybreak went to Libanius and gave him the elucidation of the verses.

Libanius received it and, astonished at the translation, said: “By divine Providence, none of the learned men here could interpret anything like this. Where, then, is the one who has produced this new interpretation?”

The boy replied: “A certain traveler came to my lodging and explained their solution to me with great ease.”

Libanius, neglecting nothing, hurried to the lodging. When he saw Basil together with Eubulus and recognized them, he was astonished at the unexpected arrival of both men.

He asked them to come to his house. Having obtained this, he also asked them to take some sweet or seasoned food. But after they had moderately taken bread and water, according to the discipline they observed, they gave thanks to God, the giver of every good thing.

Libanius then began very readily to question them and to display rhetorical verbosity. They, however, put before him a discourse concerning the faith.

When Libanius understood what was being said, he replied: “The time for this undertaking has not yet come. But when heavenly Providence commands it, no one can resist. Since you have benefited me greatly, O Basil, do not disdain also to dispute with my beginners.”

He quickly gathered the young men, and Basil taught them purity of soul; freedom from bodily passions; a gentle step; a restrained voice; orderly speech; undisturbed moderation in food and drink; silence in the presence of elders; attentive listening before the wiser; submission toward those set over them; sincere love toward equals and inferiors; saying little but understanding more; not being provoked by speech; not exceeding in talk; not being quick to laughter; being adorned with modesty; not conversing with immodest women; keeping the eyes cast down and the soul raised upward; fleeing disputes; not pursuing the dignity of a teacher; and considering honors bestowed by anyone to be nothing.

“If any of you can also benefit others, let him expect his reward from God and from Christ Jesus our Lord the return of eternal blessings.”

After saying these things to the disciples of Libanius, Basil, greatly praised by all, set out with Eubulus.

## CHAPTER IV

When they had reached Jerusalem and had visited every most holy place with faith and love [Col. 0299D], and had worshiped there the God who is above all, they became known to the bishop of the city, named Maximinus.[^c0030-1] Falling down before him, they asked to attain divine regeneration in the river Jordan.[^c0030-2]

[^c0030-1]: **Maximinus.** Jerome, in his *Chronicle*, calls him Maximus, in the eleventh year of Constantius and Constans, to which they assign the year of Christ 349: “Maximus, the fortieth bishop of Jerusalem after Macarius, dies.” Baronius, in volume III, under the year of Christ 331, the eighteenth year of Pope Sylvester and the twenty-sixth year of the emperor Constantine, places the appointment of Maximus to the see of Jerusalem. Sozomen also speaks of him in Book II, chapter 19. [Col. 0315D–0316A]

[^c0030-2]: **In the Jordan.** There were formerly some who, because the waters of the Jordan had been consecrated by Christ’s baptism, desired to be baptized in the Jordan as well. Eusebius relates in Book IV, chapter 62, of his *Life of Constantine* that Constantine the Great burned with such a desire. [Col. 0316A]

When this holy man of God, full of grace, saw them, he fulfilled their request and went with the faithful men to the Jordan. When Basil had approached the bank, he threw himself upon the ground and, with tears and a loud cry, asked that the sign of his faith be revealed. Then, rising at once with trembling, he removed his garments and, undoubtedly laying aside with them the old man, descended into the water. He prayed there, and the priest approached and baptized him.

And behold, a flash of fire shone before them, and a dove came forth from it and descended into the water; when the water was disturbed, it flew up into heaven. Those who were standing there, terrified, glorified God, while Basil, after being baptized, came out of the water.

**And a dove.** Thus the Holy Spirit had already appeared when Christ was baptized by John. Nicephorus, Book I, chapter 18, assigns this explanation: “This happened both because of the bird’s purity and because it once joyfully foretold the end of the Flood.” As here to Basil, so not infrequently a dove appeared to other saints at baptism. Formerly, too, it was customary in certain Churches to suspend a dove above the baptisteries, as is recorded in the Constantinopolitan synod held under Menna, bishop of Constantinople, session 5; see the passage cited below at no. 34. [Col. 0316A–B]

Maximinus, marveling at Basil’s love for God and having poured out a prayer over him, clothed him in the garments of Christ’s resurrection. He also baptized Eubulus, anointing him with the holy chrism,[^c0030-3] and gave him the life-giving Communion. After prayer, the priest of God asked Basil to eat, and he did so, saying:

> “Lord Jesus Christ, our God, I thus believe your evangelical word and hope in your kindness. As I eat and drink, I shall, through the cooperation of your Holy Spirit, conquer the devil who resists us.”

[^c0030-3]: **And anointing him also with the holy chrism.** The use of this sacred chrism in baptism and after baptism continues in the Catholic Church even now, from the very beginnings of the Church. On this, consult Bellarmine, volume III, *Controversies*, General Controversy II, Book II. [Col. 0316B]

The priest of God, astonished at his faith, returned with them to the holy city. After they had remained there for a year, they came by common agreement to Antioch. Basil was advanced by Meletius, bishop of that city, to the order of deacon,[^c0030-4] and, having interpreted the discourse on Proverbs,[^c0030-5] he advanced greatly in renown. [Col. 0300A–B]

[^c0030-4]: **By Meletius.** Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 17: “Basil was made deacon by Meletius, bishop of Antioch; afterward he became bishop of his native Caesarea in Cappadocia, and governed the Churches with care and faith.” [Col. 0316B]

[^c0030-5]: **Of Proverbs.** Among Basil’s works there is a treatise on the beginning of Proverbs. [Col. 0316B]

## CHAPTER V

Not long afterward, he hastened with Eubulus toward the region of Cappadocia. When they were just about to enter the city of Caesarea, the arrival of these men, and the fact that Basil would be his successor, was revealed in a nocturnal vision to the bishop of that city, whose name was Eusebius.[^c0030-6] When he awoke, he summoned the chief administrator of the Church and some venerable clerics, and sent them to the eastern gate of the city, telling them of the vision. When they went to the gate, they encountered them as they were entering. [Col. 0300B–C]

[^c0030-6]: **Eusebius.** Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 18: “Eusebius, who governed the Church of Caesarea before Basil, had some disagreement with Basil while he was still a deacon.” He later relates that Basil was reconciled with Eusebius and succeeded him in the episcopal chair. [Col. 0316B–C]

When they saw and recognized them, they asked that they be brought up to the bishop. When they entered, the most holy bishop looked at them and, astonished at the likeness to his vision, gave thanks to God. He asked where they had come from, where they were going, and what their names were. After learning this, he told the deacons to provide whatever was suitable for their rest. They led them to a distinguished lodging,[^c0030-7] and supplied everything for their comfort.

[^c0030-7]: **To a distinguished lodging.** Another edition reads, “to a distinguished *zoeta*.” The Greek is ἐν ἐπισήμῳ διαίτῃ, “in a distinguished dwelling,” which another translator altered into *zoeta*, as *dia* sometimes changes into *za*. See the *Onomasticon*. [Col. 0316C]

At that very hour the most holy man summoned the choicest clergy and citizens and recounted to them what had been revealed to him by God. They all said with one voice:

> “Truly, your pure life is worthy of this also: that the one who is to adorn the pontifical throne after you should be revealed from heaven by God. Therefore, without hesitation, do what seems good to you.” [Col. 0300C–D]

The bishop summoned Basil together with Eubulus and began to examine the sacred Scriptures with them. Admiring the sea of wisdom that was in them, and finding them suitable assistants, he died not long afterward.

The bishops therefore assembled in synod,[^c0030-8] and, through the working of the Holy Spirit, elected Basil to the episcopal throne. When he had been consecrated, he governed the Church of God by divine providence.

[^c0030-8]: **Synod.** I do not yet know which synod this was. Perhaps the author means merely this assembly of bishops, who came together for Basil’s election as bishop. [Col. 0316C]

## CHAPTER VI
