After some time, he asked God to grant him the grace of wisdom and understanding, so that he might offer to God, in his own words, the unbloody sacrifice and come into the presence of the Holy Spirit. After six days, when the coming of the Holy Spirit had taken place, as it were, in an ecstasy of mind, he began on the seventh day to minister to God each day. After some time, with much faith and prayer, he began to write the mysteries of the Mass with his own hand.

One night the Lord appeared to him in a vision with the apostles, setting forth the bread upon the holy altar. He raised Basil up and said to him:

> “According to your request, let your mouth be filled with praise, so that through your own words you may offer the unbloody sacrifice.”

Unable to endure the vision with his eyes, Basil rose trembling, approached the holy altar, and began to say and write upon a sheet of paper as follows:

> “Fill my mouth with praise, so that I may praise your glory, Lord God, who created us and brought us to this life.”[^c0030-9]

[^c0030-9]: **“Fill my mouth with praise.”** These first words cited here from Basil’s Liturgy are not found in the Greek edition of Basil’s Liturgy published in Paris by the royal press in 1560. But this is not surprising, since over so long a period something in the liturgies may have been altered, added, or removed. Indeed, different Greek copies of the same liturgy are often found. Certainly Morellus’s Greek edition of Chrysostom’s Liturgy differs greatly from Erasmus’s Latin version.

The words that follow, cited here from Basil’s Greek Liturgy, are found almost identically in Morellus’s edition. The words cited in this *Life* are given in Greek as follows:

> Πρόςχες Κύριε Ἰησοῦ Χριστὲ ὁ Θεός ἡμῶν ἐξ ἀξίου κατοικητηρίου σου, καὶ ἐλθὲ εἰς τὸ ἁγιάσαι ἡμᾶς ὁ ἄνω τῷ Πατρὶ συγκαθήμενος, καὶ ὧδε ἡμῖν ἀόρατος συνών, καὶ καταξίωσον τῇ κραταιᾷ σου χειρὶ μεταδοῦναι ἡμῖν καὶ δι’ ἡμῶν παντὶ τῷ λαῷ, τὰ ἅγια τοῖς ἁγίοις. Ὁ λαός, Εἷς ἅγιος, εἷς κύριος Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς εἰς δόξαν Θεοῦ Πατρός, ἀμήν.

> “Attend, Lord Jesus Christ, our God, from your worthy dwelling place, and come to sanctify us—you who sit above with the Father and are invisibly present here with us. Deign, with your mighty hand, to grant to us and through us to all the people the holy things to the holy.  
>   
> The people: ‘One is holy, one is Lord Jesus Christ, to the glory of God the Father. Amen.’”

Ursus rendered these words into Latin as follows:

> “Attend, Lord Jesus Christ, our God, from your holy dwelling place, and come to sanctify us—you who sit above with the Father and are invisibly present here with us. Deign, with your mighty hand, to give us and through us to all the people the holy things to the holy.  
>   
> The people responded: ‘One is holy, one is Lord Jesus Christ with the Holy Spirit, to the glory of God the Father. Amen.’”

The Greek of Basil’s edition by Morellus differs scarcely at all from the foregoing:

> Πρόσχες Κύριε Ἰησοῦ Χριστὲ ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν ἐξ ἁγίου κατοικητηρίου σου, καὶ ἀπὸ θρόνου δόξης τῆς βασιλείας σου, καὶ ἐλθὲ εἰς τὸ ἁγιάσαι ἡμᾶς ὁ ἄνω τῷ Πατρὶ συγκαθήμενος, καὶ ὧδε ἡμῖν ἀοράτως συνών· καὶ καταξίωσον τῇ κραταιᾷ σου χειρὶ μεταδοῦναι ἡμῖν τοῦ ἀχράντου σώματός σου καὶ τοῦ τιμίου αἵματος, καὶ δι’ ἡμῶν παντὶ τῷ λαῷ.

> “Attend, Lord Jesus Christ, our God, from your holy dwelling place and from the throne of the glory of your kingdom, and come to sanctify us—you who sit above with the Father and are invisibly present here with us. Deign, with your mighty hand, to grant us your undefiled body and precious blood, and through us to all the people.”

Together with these he wrote the remaining prayers of the holy Mass. [Col. 0301A; 165]

After the prayers had ended, he elevated the bread,[^c0030-10] praying at length and saying:

> “Attend, Lord Jesus Christ, our God, from your holy dwelling place, and come to sanctify us—you who sit above with the Father and are invisibly present here with us. Deign, with your mighty hand, to give us and through us to all the people the holy things to the holy.”

[^c0030-10]: **He elevated the bread.** On the elevation of the bread, or Eucharist, in the Mass, see Claudius Sainctes, *On the Eucharist*, Repetition IX, which concerns the Adoration of the Eucharist, chapter 7. [Col. 0317A]

The people responded:

> “One is holy, one is Lord Jesus Christ with the Holy Spirit, to the glory of God the Father. Amen.”

Dividing the bread into three portions, he received one with great fear, kept another to be buried with him,[^c0030-11] and placed the third upon a golden dove,[^c0030-12] which he suspended above the altar.

[^c0030-11]: **To be buried with him.** It was once the custom of certain people to place the Eucharist in the mouths of the dead and bury it with them. The Third Council of Carthage abolished this practice in canon 6:

> “It has seemed good that the Eucharist not be given to the bodies of the dead; for it was said by the Lord: ‘Take and eat’ (Matthew 26). But corpses can neither receive nor eat. Care must also be taken lest the weakness of the brethren suppose that the dead can be baptized, when it observes that the Eucharist is not given to the dead.”

Saint Augustine subscribed to this council. The same canon is repeated in the Council of Hippo, canon 5; in the Council of Auxerre, held in the year 540, canon 12; and in the Sixth Ecumenical Council, that is, the Third Council of Constantinople, held at Trullo in the year of Christ 680, in the third year of Pope Agatho and the thirteenth year of Constantine Pogonatus, when he was sole ruler. Canon 83 there reads:

> Μηδεὶς τοῖς σώμασι τῶν τελευτώντων τῆς εὐχαριστίας μεταδιδότω· γέγραπται γὰρ· Λάβετε, φάγετε· τὰ δὲ τῶν νεκρῶν σώματα οὐδὲ λαβεῖν δύνανται, οὐδὲ φαγεῖν.

> “Let no one give the Eucharist to the bodies of the dead, for it is written: ‘Take and eat.’ The bodies of the dead can neither receive nor eat.”

Peter Crespetius is therefore mistaken in the *Summa Catholica* when he thought that Cyprian dealt with this matter in Book I, Letter 2, and Book IV, Letter 6. When Cyprian says, “Communion is to be given by us not to the dying but to the living,” he is speaking there of the lapsed. He wishes communion to be given not so much to those who are dying as to those who are living—that is, when they had already repented and were preparing themselves for the martyrdoms that daily threatened them. [Col. 0317A–C]

[^c0030-12]: **Upon the dove.** Doves were once hung both over altars and over baptisteries in memory of the Holy Spirit. Thus, in a letter of the clergy of Antioch to John, bishop of Constantinople, against their heretical bishop Severus, they wrote:

> Τὰς γὰρ εἰς τύπον τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος χρυσᾶς τε καὶ ἀργυρᾶς περιστερὰς, κρεμαμένας ὑπεράνω τῶν θείων κολυμβηθρῶν, καὶ θυσιαστηρίων, μετὰ τῶν ἄλλων ἐσφετερίσατο, λέγων, οὐ χρῆναι ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς ὀνομάζεσθαι τὸ ἅγιον Πνεῦμα.

> “For he appropriated to himself, along with the other things, the golden and silver doves hung above the divine baptisteries and altars as figures of the Holy Spirit, saying that the Holy Spirit ought not to be named in the form of a dove.”

This letter was read in the Constantinopolitan synod, session 5. That synod was held at Constantinople after the death of Agapetus, during the papal interregnum, under Menna, bishop of Constantinople, in the year of Christ 536. The same words are cited in the Seventh Ecumenical Council, that is, the Second Council of Nicaea, session 5. [Col. 0317C–D]

Eubulus and the chief of the clergy, standing together before the doors of the church, saw an intelligible light in the church, men clothed in brilliant garments, the voice of the people glorifying the Lord, and Basil standing at the altar. Overcome by the vision, they fell on their faces and glorified the Lord with tears.

When Basil came out, they fell at his feet. He asked them the reason for their adoration and their coming. They told him of the glorious miracle they had seen in the church. Then Basil gave extensive thanks to the Lord and recounted the glorious events.

He summoned a goldsmith and had a dove made of the purest gold. In it he placed the portion, suspending it above the holy table in imitation of that holy dove which had appeared in the Jordan when the Lord was baptized.

After this had been done, he promised to deliver a speech of exhortation to the people. An immense crowd gathered in the church, among whom was a great man and worshiper of God, Ephraem,[^c0030-13] concerning whom we shall later relate how, through a divine apparition, he became a witness to the memorable Basil. [Col. 0301B–D; 156]

[^c0030-13]: **Ephraem.** The account promised here concerning Saint Ephraem is found below, chapter 11. [Col. 0317D]

## CHAPTER VII

When the divine service was being celebrated, a certain Jew,[^c0030-14] wishing to mingle with the people as though he were a Christian and to examine the order of the service and the gift of Communion, saw a little child being cut limb by limb in Basil’s hands. When everyone was receiving Communion, he too came forward, and in truth flesh was given to him. Then he approached the chalice, which was full of blood, and became a participant in it.

[^c0030-14]: **A Jew.** This example, in which Christ is shown in the Eucharist in the form of a child, is cited from this *Life* by Saint Thomas in his *Opusculum* 58, chapter 11. Paschasius gives a similar vision in his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, chapter 14. It was granted to the priest Plegus, who saw Christ in the form of a child on the altar and embraced him: “So that,” Paschasius says, “the truth might be revealed in what was shown, the priest’s desire might be fulfilled through the miracle, and our faith might be strengthened through the account.” Saint Thomas cites this example from Paschasius above, where Aegidius is incorrectly read instead of Plegus. [Col. 0317D]

Taking from both the bread and the chalice what remained, he went home and showed it to his wife, confirming what had been said and recounting what he had seen with his own eyes. Convinced that the mystery of the Christians was truly fearful and glorious, he went to Basil the next day and begged him to receive without delay the seal of Christ.

Basil, neglecting nothing and giving the customary thanks to him who desires all to be saved, baptized him and his whole household, which believed in the Lord. [Col. 0302A]

## CHAPTER VIII

Helladius,[^c0030-15] who was a witness and minister of the miracles performed by Basil, and who after the death of Basil, whose apostolic memory is revered, deserved to receive his see, was a man renowned for miracles and adorned with every virtue. He told me that when a certain faithful senator named Proterius[^c0030-16] was going to the holy places in order to venerate them, and wished to cut the hair of his daughter there,[^c0030-17] send her to one of the venerable monasteries, and offer a sacrifice to God, the devil—who was a murderer from the beginning—envying her religious purpose, stirred one of the senator’s servants and inflamed him with love for the girl. [Col. 0318A; Col. 0302A–B]

[^c0030-15]: **Helladius.** John of Damascus testifies in his first oration *On Images* that the *Life of Saint Basil* was written by Helladius, his disciple and successor. From it he cites the following short narrative:

> “That the institution of images is not a new invention but ancient, and known and customary among the holy and eminent Fathers, learn from what was written in the *Life of blessed Basil* by Helladius, his disciple and successor in his hierarchy. The holy man, as he himself relates, stood before an image of our Lady, in which the likeness of the renowned martyr Mercurius was also depicted. He stood there praying that Julian, the most godless apostate and tyrant, might be destroyed. From this image he learned what was going to happen. For a short time he saw the martyr disappear from his sight, but not long afterward he saw him holding a bloodstained spear.”

The Greek text is:

> Ὅτι δὲ οὐ καινὸν ἐφεύρημα τὸ τῶν εἰκόνων, ἀλλὰ ἀρχαῖον, καὶ τοῖς ἁγίοις καὶ ἐκκρίτοις πατράσιν ἐγνωσμένον τε καὶ εἰθισμένον, ἄκουε· γέγραπται ἐν τῷ βίῳ Βασιλείου τοῦ μακάριος, τῷ δι’ Ἑλλαδίου τοῦ αὐτοῦ μαθητοῦ καὶ διαδόχου τῆς αὐτοῦ ἱεραρχίας, ὡς παρειστήκει ὁ ὅσιος τῇ τῆς Δεσποίνης εἰκόνι, ἐν ᾗ καὶ ὁ χαρακτὴρ ἐγέγραπτο Μερκουρίου τοῦ ἀοιδίμου μάρτυρος· παρειστήκει δὲ ἐξαιτῶν Ἰουλιανοῦ τοῦ ἀθεωτάτου, καὶ ἀποστάτου τυράννου ἀναίρεσιν· ἐξ ἧς εἰκόνος ἐμυήθη ταύτην τὴν ἀποκάλυψιν· ἑώρα γὰρ πρὸς μὲν βραχὺ ἀφανῆ τὸν μάρτυρα, μετ’ οὐ πολὺ δὲ τὸ δόρυ ᾑμαγμένον κατέχοντα.

[^c0030-16]: **Proterius.** This narrative is found only in Amphilochius. [Col. 0318B]

[^c0030-17]: **To cut her hair.** Another edition reads, “to consecrate her.” The Greek is ἀποθρίξαι, “to cut the hair.” Since the maiden was to be consecrated to God through tonsure, the other translator rendered it “to consecrate.” [Col. 0318B]

Since he was unworthy of so great a vow and did not dare even to approach the girl’s purpose, he addressed one of the detestable sorcerers, promising him a large quantity of gold if by his art he could somehow move her.

The sorcerer said to him:

> “I am powerless for this; but, if you wish, I will send you to my patron, the devil. He will accomplish your desire, provided that you do his will.”

The servant replied:

> “Whatever he tells me, I shall do.”

The sorcerer said:

> “Do you renounce Christ in writing?”

He answered:

> “I do.”

Then the worker of iniquity said:

> “If you are prepared for this, I shall become your accomplice.”

The servant replied:

> “I am prepared, so long as I obtain what I desire.”

A letter was therefore written, and the minister of the evil operation sent it to the devil. It was dictated in these terms:

> “Since I ought to serve my lord and patron so that people may depart from the religion of the Christians and come over to your fellowship, so that your portion may be fulfilled, I have sent you this man, who bears my little letter and is wounded by desire for the girl. I beg that he may obtain what he desires, so that I may glory in this matter and gather your lovers with greater eagerness.”

After giving him the letter, he said:

> “Go at such-and-such an hour of the night, stand upon the tomb of some pagan, and raise the paper into the air. Those who are to lead you to the devil will then stand beside you.”

He did this eagerly, uttered that wretched cry invoking the devil’s aid, and immediately the princes of the power of darkness, the spirits of wickedness (Ephesians 6), stood beside him. They took the deceived man and, with great joy, led him to where the devil was. They showed him the devil sitting upon a lofty throne, with spirits of wickedness surrounding him.

After receiving the sorcerer’s letter, the devil said to the unfortunate man:

> “Do you believe in me?”

He answered:

> “I believe.”

The devil said to him:

> “You Christians are fickle. Whenever you need me, you come to me; but when you have obtained your purpose, you deny me and go over to your Christ, who, because he is good and merciful, receives you. But write for me a voluntary renunciation of your Christ and of holy baptism, together with a spontaneous promise that you will belong to me forever, and that on the day of judgment you will share with me in the eternal punishments prepared for me.”

The man presented the writing in his own hand, just as he had been asked. Then that corrupter of souls, the dragon, sent demons appointed over fornication,[^c0030-18] and caused the girl to burn with love for the young man. She threw herself upon the pavement and began to cry out to her father:

> “Have mercy on me, have mercy! I am cruelly tormented because of this young man, our servant. Have compassion on your own flesh; show me your fatherly affection for your only child, and unite me to the young man whom I have chosen. If you refuse to do this, you will soon see me dead an agonizing death, and you will give an account of me to God on the day of judgment.”

[^c0030-18]: **Demons appointed over fornication.** See the remarks above on the *Life of Saint Hilarion*, chapter 16, number 35. [Col. 0318B]

Her father said with tears:

> “Woe is me, a sinner! What has happened to my wretched daughter? Who has stolen my treasure? Who has wronged my daughter? Who has extinguished the sweet light of my eyes? I always advised you to be betrothed to Christ, the heavenly Bridegroom, to become the companion of the angels, and to hasten to sing to God in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. But you have gone mad with wanton lust. Leave me to make the covenant I desire with God, lest you drag my old age sorrowfully into hell and cover the nobility of your parents with shame.”

She paid no attention to anything her father said and continued to cry:

> “My father, either fulfill my desire, or you will soon see me dead.”

Her father, therefore, overcome by great madness, absorbed both by the enormity of his grief and by the counsels of his friends, who advised him that it was better to fulfill the girl’s wish than to let her kill herself, consented. He ordered her desire to be fulfilled rather than deliver her to a deadly end.

At once he brought forth the young man she sought, together with his own daughter, and, giving them all his possessions, said:

> “Farewell, truly wretched daughter. You will lament greatly and repent at the end, when nothing will benefit you.”

After the impious marriage had been contracted, the devil’s deed accomplished, and a short time had passed, some people noticed that the young man did not enter the church or touch the immortal and life-giving sacraments. They said to his pitiable wife:

> “Know that your husband, whom you chose, is not a Christian. He is an outsider and entirely alien to the faith.”

Filled with darkness and a dreadful wound, she threw herself upon the pavement, tore herself with her fingernails, struck her breast, and cried:

> “No one who has ever been disobedient to his parents has been saved. Who will announce my disgrace to my father? Woe to me, unhappy woman! Into what depth of perdition have I descended? Why was I born? Or why, when I was born, was I not immediately snatched away?”[^c0030-19]

[^c0030-19]: The Greek is ἀνάρπαστος, “snatched away.” [Col. 0303D]

Her deceived husband, recognizing her lamentation, came to her and insisted that the matter was not as she believed. When she had been brought some relief by his persuasive words, she said to him:

> “If you wish to satisfy me and assure my unhappy soul, tomorrow you and I shall go together to the church. Receive the undefiled mysteries in my presence; then you will be able to satisfy me.”

Then, compelled, he told her the terms of the agreement.[^c0030-20]

[^c0030-20]: That is, he disclosed to her the truth of the matter. [Col. 0304A]

Immediately the girl, laying aside womanly weakness and accepting good counsel, ran to the shepherd and disciple of Christ, Basil, crying out against such great impiety:

> “Show mercy to me, miserable woman, holy man of God; have mercy on me, disciple of the Lord, for I have made a covenant with demons. Have mercy on me, for I have become disobedient to my own father.”

After learning what had happened, Basil called the young man and asked whether these things were true. With tears, he said to the saint:

> “They are, holy man of God. Even if I were silent, my deeds would cry out.”

He too recounted to Basil the devil’s wicked work, explaining how he had followed it from beginning to end.

Then Basil said to him:

> “Do you wish to turn to the Lord our God?”

He replied:

> “I do, but I cannot.”

Basil asked:

> “Why?”

He answered:

> “I renounced Christ in writing and made a covenant with the devil.”

The saint said to him:

> “Do not be concerned. Our God is merciful, and he will receive you when you repent. He is kind beyond all our wickedness.”

The girl threw herself at Basil’s feet and begged him in evangelical words:

> “Disciple of Christ our God, if you can do anything, help us.”

The saint said to the young man:

> “Do you believe that you can be saved?”

He replied:

> “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” (Mark 9).

Immediately Basil took him by the hand, made over him the sign of Christ, prayed, and shut him up in a place where the sacred vestments were kept.[^c0030-21] He gave him a rule of life and also prayed for him for three days.

[^c0030-21]: **In the place where the sacred vestments were kept.** Another version reads, “in an inner place within the sacred enclosure.” The Greek is Ἐν ἐνὶ τόπῳ ἔσω τῶν ἱερῶν περιβόλων, “in one place within the sacred enclosures.” One translator retained the Greek term, while the other explained the matter. [Col. 0318B]

Afterward he visited him and said:

> “How are you, my son?”

The young man answered:

> “I am in great distress, lord. Holy man of God, I cannot endure their cries, terrors, darts, and stones. For, holding the writing in my own hand, they reproach me, saying: ‘You came to us; we did not come to you.’”

The saint said to him:

> “Do not be afraid, my son; only believe.”

He gave him a little food, again made over him the sign of Christ, prayed, and shut him in. After a few days he visited him and said:

> “How are you, my son?”

He answered:

> “Holy father, I hear their cries and threats from far away, but I do not see them.”

Again Basil gave him food, closed the door after pouring out a prayer, and departed.

On the fortieth day he went to him and said:

> “How are you, brother?”

He answered:

> “I am well, holy man of God. Today I saw you in a dream fighting on my behalf and conquering the devil.”

Then, after praying according to his custom, Basil led him out and brought him to his own chamber. [Col. 0304B–D; 157]

When morning came, he summoned the venerable clergy, the monasteries, and all the people who loved Christ, and said to them:

> “My beloved children, let us all give thanks to the Lord. For behold, the good shepherd is about to place the lost sheep upon his shoulders and bring it back to the Church (Luke 15). We must keep vigil through the night and beseech his will, lest the corrupter of souls prevail.”

This was immediately done. The people gathered most readily and, throughout the entire night, prayed to God with the good shepherd, crying out with tears on the young man’s behalf:

> “Kyrie eleison”—“Lord, have mercy.”

At dawn, the saint took the young man with the entire multitude of the people. Holding his right hand, he led him into the holy church of God with psalms and hymns.

And behold, the devil, who always envies our life, came with all his destructive power, unwilling to see this occur without sorrow. Invisibly seizing the young man, he tried to snatch him from the saint’s hand. The young man began to cry out:

> “Holy man of God, help me!”

The devil attacked him with such shameless force that he pushed down and overthrew the great Basil together with the young man.

The saint turned toward the devil and said:

> “Most shameless one, violator of souls, father of darkness and perdition, is your own destruction not enough—the destruction you have acquired for yourself and for those under you? Do you still not cease, but continue to tempt the creature of my God?”

The devil answered him:

> “You prejudice me, Basil,”

so that many of those present heard his voice.

The holy man of God said to him:

> “The Lord rebukes you, devil” (Jude).

The devil replied:

> “You prejudice me, Basil. I did not go to him; he came to me. He renounced Christ and entered into a pledge with me. Behold, I have the writing, and on the day of judgment I shall bring it before the common Judge.”

The saint of the Lord said:

> “Blessed be the Lord my God. This people shall not lower their hands from heaven above until you return the writing.”

Then he turned to the people and said:

> “Raise your hands to heaven, all of you, crying out with tears, ‘Kyrie eleison.’”

While the people stood for many hours with their hands extended toward heaven, behold, the young man’s written confession was carried through the air. It was seen by everyone, came down, and was placed in the hands of our eminent father and shepherd Basil.

After receiving it, Basil gave thanks to God and rejoiced greatly with all the people. He said to the young man:

> “Do you recognize this writing, brother?”

He answered:

> “I do, holy man of God; it is the writing of my own hand.”

Basil tore up the writing, brought him into the church, and judged him worthy to attend the sacred offices of the Mass, to participate in the sacred mysteries, and to receive the gifts of Christ.

After this reception, he restored the whole people to joy. He took the young man, instructed him, gave him a proper rule of life, and handed him over to his wife, while he continually glorified and praised God. Amen. [Col. 0305A–D; 158]

## CHAPTER IX

The noble Helladius mentioned above also related this story: One day, when the sun was shining brightly, the holy father and great Basil set out from our city without telling anyone where he was going. After entering before us, he said:

> “My children, follow me, so that you may see with me the glory of God, and so that we disciples may marvel at the master.”

As our common father set out from the city, Anastasius the presbyter recognized him through the power of the Holy Spirit.[^c0030-22] He said by name to his wife—although in practice she was his sister[^c0030-23]—[Col. 0305D; Col. 0318B]

[^c0030-22]: **Anastasius.** This narrative is found in only one copy of Amphilochius. [Col. 0318B]

[^c0030-23]: **Although in practice she was his sister.** This is a remarkable example of conjugal chastity, confirmed by a miracle, when Theognia carried live coals in her unharmed bosom. Just as here the coals were taken from the censer and placed in Theognia’s bosom as testimony to her chastity, so in the *Life of John the Almsgiver*, chapter 46, there is a similar example and miracle of continence involving an abbot who converted Porphyria the prostitute. Those women were wives before their husbands entered the sacred orders, but afterward they were and were called sisters. Idacius, in his manuscript *Chronicle*, preserved by our Sirmond, says of the wife of Paulinus, bishop of Nola: “Therasia, from wife made sister.” Fortunatus, Book I, poem 15, says of Placidina, wife of Leontius, bishop of Bordeaux:

[The supplied source ends here, with the sentence incomplete.]

What is now your wife is now your dear sister.]: “I shall go to cultivate the field, my lady [Col. 0306A] sister; but rise and arrange your house, and around the ninth hour take the censer and candles [Note: [Col. 0318C] “Take the censer and candles.”] As in the worship of the gods incense, lamps, and torches were once used, so they were also employed in the veneration of emperors. Herodian, in his account of Commodus, says of his sister Lucilla: “And fire preceded her” (Καὶ τὸ πῦρ προεπόμπευεν αὐτῆς). He likewise reports that this honor was denied to Marcia, Commodus’s concubine, and that Pertinax, too, did not permit this emblem of sovereignty to be carried before him. M. Antoninus likewise places λαμπάδες, “lamps” or “torches,” among the insignia of imperial power in his books of his own life. Xenophon teaches, in Book VIII, that fire was carried before the king of the Persians. Ammianus also hints at this with regard to the peoples of Asia, Book XXIII. See Lipsius on Book I of Tacitus’s *Annals*. Thus lamps were carried before the emperor and empress of Constantinople, as Codinus relates in *On the Offices of the Palatine Court*, and as Theodorus Balsamo, to be cited shortly, also relates. From there this practice passed to leading men, especially patriarchs and chief bishops. Theodorus Balsamo, *On the Privileges of Patriarchs*, Book VII of the *Greek-Roman Law*:

“Since some say that it is not permitted to the Alexandrian or Antiochian patriarch, for example, to travel with a patriarchal lamp or torch to the imperial city or to another diocese, except for those provinces assigned to them by the canons—for, they say, the torch belongs to the office of a teacher, whereas it is not permitted for a bishop to teach outside his own province, according to Canon 20 of the holy and universal Sixth Council held at Trullo.”

[Note: [Col. 0319A] “Since some say that it is not permitted to the Alexandrian or Antiochian, for example, to travel with a patriarchal lamp to the imperial city or to another diocese, beyond the provinces assigned to them by the canons; for the lamp, they say, belongs to the office of a teacher, but a bishop is not permitted to teach outside his own province, according to Canon 20 of the holy and universal Sixth Council held at Trullo.”]

In that author see more concerning the carrying of these lamps, and who may use them.]: “Go to meet the holy Basil, the archbishop, for he has come to lodge at our house.”

She, trembling at so glorious a declaration, did as she had been instructed. She was a virgin living chastely and was passing her fortieth year, preserving her secret with her husband while pretending to people that she was barren. When she met us with due modesty and offered the appropriate greeting, she was first blessed by our holy Father. Then he said to her: “How are you, lady Theognia [Note: [Col. 0319A] Theognia.] Another version has *Theogenia*. In Greek it is Θεογνία.”?

She, astonished that he had called her by name, said to him: “Well, holy man of God.”

Our holy Father said to her: “Where is the presbyter Anastasius, your brother?”

She replied: “He is my husband, lord, and [Col. 0306B] has gone to cultivate the land.”

He said: “He is in your house; do not tire yourself.”

The modest woman was ashamed not only because of this word and the calling of her name, but also because our God-bearing Father had said that she was a woman in name but a sister in practice. Astonished and shaken with trembling, she fell to the ground, crying out: “Holy man of God, pray for me, a sinner, because I behold great and wondrous works.”

After blessing her, he said to her in the presence of everyone: “Stretch out the cloth between your arms.” When she had stretched it out, he ordered coals to be poured from the censer onto the cloth, placing incense upon them. He went ahead of everyone, and when we came to the presbyter’s house, she met us there. He himself kissed his honorable feet, offered him a greeting in the Lord, and said to him:

“From where has this come to me, that the holy man of God should come to me?”

Our Father said to him: “I have found you well, disciple of Christ. Let us go and celebrate the holy liturgy of God.”

The presbyter of God fasted every day, except Saturday and Sunday, taking nothing but bread and water. As we proceeded to the church, he instructed the presbyter to chant the liturgy. The presbyter said to him:

“Holy man of God, as you teach, the inferior is blessed by the superior.”

Our holy Father said to him: “With all your zeal, hold obedience.”

The presbyter consented and stood for the holy liturgy. At the time of the elevation of the life-giving body of our Lord Jesus Christ, the holy man of God, and certain other worthy persons, saw the Holy Spirit descending in the form of fire and surrounding the presbyter and the holy altar.

After receiving Communion and giving thanks to the Lord, we went to the presbyter’s house. While we were taking food, the holy man of God said to him:

“Tell me, where did you get this treasure, and what is your way of life?”

The presbyter said to him:

“I, holy man of God, am a sinner, subject to public taxes. I have two yokes of oxen: I drive one myself [Note: [Col. 0319A] “I drive one myself.” Another version has “I lead one.” The Greek is Τὸ μὲν ἓν ἐγὼ ἐλαύνω.] and my hired man the other. One is assigned to the administration of hospitality, and the other to the administration of tax collection. This woman is my fellow servant, ministering to guests and to me.”

He said to him: “Call her ‘sister,’ as she truly is, and tell me your deeds.”

The presbyter said to him: “I possess no good upon earth; I am a stranger to every virtue.”

Our common Father said to him: “Rise, and let us go together.” And he led him to a small chamber in his house and said to him: “Open the door.”

He replied: “Holy man of God, do not order me to enter, for the house is necessary [Note: [Col. 0319A] “For the house is necessary.” Another version has, “Because the house’s necessities…” The Greek is Ὅτι χρεία ἐστι τοῦ οἴκου.]”

The saint said to him: “I have come for this very work.”

When the presbyter was unwilling to open with the key, our distinguished Father opened it by his word. He entered and found there a man covered with ulcers, from whose body many members had fallen away. No one knew that he was there except the presbyter and his sister.

The holy Father said to him: “Why did you wish to hide this treasure?”

The presbyter said to him: “He is insane, lord, and abusive, and I was afraid that perhaps he might fall into speech.”

The Father said to him: “You have fought well on his behalf. But let me minister to him tonight, so that through you I too may obtain a reward.”

We left the holy man alone with the ulcerous man, who could not speak because of the weakness caused by his illness, and, closing the door, departed. The physician of wounds prayed over him and entreated God throughout the whole night, healing every illness and every infirmity. Thus he cured him.

The presbyter said with us: “Glory to you, God, who work wonders for those who fear you and hear their prayers. Behold, the physician has made the sick man well.”

Immediately the holy man of God called out that we should open the door. He then brought out the ulcerous man completely healed, without a scar on his body, speaking clearly and glorifying God.

After this great miracle had occurred, we returned to our city with joy, praising and blessing God, to whom are honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## Chapter X

A certain woman [Note: [Col. 0319B] “A certain woman.” A not dissimilar story occurs below in the *Life of Saint John the Almsgiver*, chapter 51.] noble by birth, [Col. 0307C] born of wealthy worldly parents, adorned with the vanities of this world, exalted above all others, and having become a widow, indecently devoured her money. Living luxuriously and subjecting herself to fornication, she did nothing pleasing to God, but, like a pig, wallowed in a dung heap.

By God’s direction she eventually came to herself. Her mind enlightened concerning the immeasurable crimes she had committed, she silently recalled the multitude of her sins and wept bitterly, saying:

“Woe is me, a sinner! How shall I give an account of the multitude of my sins? I have corrupted the spiritual temple and defiled the soul dwelling in the body. Woe is me, woe is me! What have I been doing? What has happened to me? Shall I say that I have sinned like that prostitute or like that tax collector?”

[Col. 0307D] [Another interpreter adds: “But no one has sinned as I have, especially after holy baptism. How, then, can I be certain that God will receive me when I repent?”]

While she was considering all these things within herself, he who desires to save everyone, to restore them to the judgment of truth, and does not wish anyone to perish, deigned to bring back to her memory the sins she had committed from her youth. Sitting down, she wrote on a sheet of paper the offenses she had committed from adolescence to old age. Finally she wrote the great and worst sin she had committed and sealed [Note: [Col. 0319B] “Sealed.” Another version has “stamped,” and the Greek is ἐβούλλωσεν. *Bullare*, in place of *sigillare*, “to seal,” is a common expression of the Middle Ages. In the *Life of John the Almsgiver*, below, chapter 51: “You cannot write, seal, and bring it to me?” And afterward: “He gives him his own sealed note.”] that sheet with lead.

When she foresaw a suitable time, when Saint Basil was accustomed to go to church for the sake of prayer, she suddenly ran ahead and threw the sheet before his feet [Col. 0308A]. Prostrating herself before him, she said:

“Have mercy, have mercy on me, a sinner, holy man of God, for all my sins.”

The most blessed man stood there and carefully asked her what her moaning and wailing meant.

She said: “Behold, holy man of God, I have written all my sins and offenses on this sheet and sealed it. But you, holy man of God, do not disturb this seal; only erase all these things through your holy prayers.”

The great Saint Basil lifted the sheet, looked toward heaven, and said:

“To you alone, Lord, are this woman’s deeds manifest. You have taken away the sins of the world, and you can more easily erase them from this one soul. All our crimes are numbered before you; for you are of boundless and inscrutable mercy.”

And saying this, [Col. 0308B] he entered the holy church, holding the aforesaid sheet in his hands. Prostrating himself before the altar, he entreated God throughout the whole night and on the following day during all the solemnities of the liturgy.

Then he summoned the woman, handed her the sheet, and said to her:

“Have you heard, woman, that no one can forgive sins except God alone?”

She said: “I have heard, Father, and for that reason I brought you, Father, to intercede with the most merciful God for me.”

As she said this, she unsealed the sheet and found it completely erased. Only that great sin she had committed remained written.

When she saw that this sin had not been erased, she struck her breast, began to be distressed, and fell before his feet, crying and saying:

“Have mercy on me, servant of the Most High God. Just as you contended on behalf of all my sins, and were heard, so you can intercede with God concerning this one alone, that this sin also may be erased.”

Saint Basil wept out of compassion and said:

“Rise, woman. I too am a sinful man and in need of forgiveness. He who erased and forgave you the sins he wished to forgive is able also to take this one sin away from you—the one who took away the sins of the world. If from now on you keep watch and walk in the ways of the Lord, you will have not only forgiveness but also be worthy of glory. Go into the desert; there you will find a holy man renowned among all the holy Fathers, named Ephraem. Give this sheet to him. He will intercede and obtain your request before the Lord.”

Then the woman commended herself to the holy bishop of God [Col. 0308D] and ran into the desert, traveling a long distance. She reached the great and wondrous hermit named Ephraem and, knocking at the door, cried out:

“Have mercy on me, have mercy, holy man of God!”

He, discerning in spirit for what request she had come, said to her:

“Go, woman, for I am a sinful man and I too need assistance.”

She threw down the sheet, saying:

“The archbishop Saint Basil sent me to you, so that you might entreat God to erase the sin written on this sheet. Saint Basil erased the many other sins by his prayer; do not be reluctant, holy man of God, to intercede with God for this one offense also, because I have been sent to you.”

Then that confessor said:

“No, daughter. Could he who was able to obtain from God the forgiveness of the multitude of those crimes not intercede and obtain forgiveness for this one? Go, then, and do not delay, so that you may meet him before his soul departs from his body.”

Then the woman commended herself to the holy confessor Ephraem and returned to Caesarea. When she entered the city, she met those carrying the body of Saint Basil. Seeing this, she prostrated herself on the ground and began to cry out against the holy man of God:

“Woe is me, a sinner! Woe is me, who am consumed! Woe is me, holy man of God! For this reason you sent me into the desert, so that you might depart from me without trouble; and behold, I have returned without accomplishing anything, having uselessly devoured the road across so vast a sea. Let the Lord God see and judge between you and me, since you could have interceded and obtained forgiveness with God, unless you had sent me to another.”

Saying this, she threw the aforesaid sheet upon the bier on which the body of Saint Basil was being carried. She related the events in detail before all the people.

One of the clergy, wishing to discover what that sin was, lifted the sheet and unsealed it. He found it completely erased and clean, and cried out loudly to the woman:

“O woman, this sheet contains no writing! Why are you wasting yourself in such labor and distress, unaware of the great things God has done in you and of his inscrutable mercy?”

The multitude of the people, seeing so glorious and great a miracle, glorified God, who has such power that he forgives the sins of all upon earth, and who gives grace to his servants so that after their departure they heal every illness [Col. 0309C] and every infirmity. He granted them the power to forgive the offenses of all who preserve right faith in the Lord, strive in good works, and glorify God and our Lord Jesus Christ.

## Chapter XI

Brothers [Note: [Col. 0319B] “Brothers.” A Greek manuscript used by Gerard Vossius attributes this chapter to Amphilochius and calls it “A Comparison and Likeness of the Holy Fathers Basil and Ephraem the Syrian.” Vossius places it before the works of Ephraem. Ephraem himself also describes certain contents of this chapter in his encomium of Saint Basil.] I wish to tell a story about Basil, who was noble, and Ephraem the Syrian. Some things I heard from our Father, and some from the truthful mouth of the holy and wondrous Ephraem. It is as follows:

Ephraem, being noble and dwelling in the desert, saw some things through an illumination of the Holy Spirit, while others he learned through desire and inquiry. He continually asked that it be revealed to him [Note: [Col. 0319B] “He asked that it be revealed to him.” See our Delrio, volume II of *Magical Investigations*, Book IV, chapter 1, question 3, section 1, where he discusses whether revelation may be requested from God.] what the great Basil was like. [Col. 0309D] Being in ecstasy, he saw a column of fire whose top reached to heaven, and a voice from above said:

“Ephraem, Ephraem, just as you have seen this column of fire, so is the great Basil.”

Immediately he took an interpreter, since he did not know how to speak Greek, and came to the great church of the renowned city of Caesarea. He arrived during the holy feast of the Theophany and, entering secretly, saw the great Basil processing into the church. He said to those following him:

“We have labored in vain. For I think that this brother, being in such a position, is not like the one I saw.”

Basil was surrounded by a white robe, and around him was a venerable clergy, clothed in white and attending him. Standing in a hidden place in the church, Ephraem observed the procession and said to himself:

“We who have borne the burden of the day and the heat have accomplished nothing, while this man, amid such attendance and human honor, has become a column of fire! I am amazed.”

As he was saying this, the saint sent his archdeacon, saying:

“Go toward the western door. In the corner of the church you will find an abbot with another man wearing a hood, scant-bearded, small in stature, and with the rest of his features as described. Say to him: ‘Enter the sacristy [Note: [Col. 0319B] “Sacristy.” Another version has “presbytery.” The Greek is ἱερατεῖον.] Your father the archbishop invites you.’”

When the message had been conveyed through the interpreter, Ephraem replied:

“You are mistaken, brother; we are guests.”

The archdeacon went and reported this to great Basil, who was reciting the sacred books. The holy Ephraem saw a fiery tongue speaking through Basil’s mouth. Basil said to the deacon:

“Go and tell the lord Ephraem: ‘The archbishop calls you to enter the holy sanctuary [Note: [Col. 0319C] “Into the holy sanctuary.” The Greek is εἰς τὸ ἅγιον βῆμα. The *bēma* was a definite place in the temples of the ancients beside the altar. See the *Onomasticon*.]. Enter the holy sanctuary.’”

The saint was astonished at these things, glorifying God and making a *metanoia* [Note: [Col. 0319C] “And making a *metanoia*.” The Greek is καὶ ποιήσας μετάνοιαν. Another version has “and kneeling.” It correctly renders the Greek expression of that period, when βαλεῖν μετάνοιαν meant “to kneel, to cast oneself at someone’s feet as an act of honor, to prostrate oneself reverently, and to ask for a blessing.” It occurs in the *Life of Saint Chrysostom*, cited by John of Damascus, *Oration I, On Images*: βαλὼν μετάνοιαν τῷ Ἰωάννῃ, “falling reverently at John’s feet.” Francis Zinus translated this incorrectly as “instilling desire in John.” See James Billius on the passage of Damascenus cited.] He replied to him:

“Truly Basil is great; truly Basil is a column of fire; truly the Holy Spirit speaks through his mouth.”

He asked the archdeacon to report that after the liturgy [Note: [Col. 0319C] “After the liturgy.” Another version has “after the service.” The Greek is μετὰ τὴν λειτουργίαν.] he would greet him in the sacristy.

After the dismissal of the liturgy, he entered the sacristy, summoned the holy Ephraem, and gave him the kiss [Note: [Col. 0319C] “The kiss.” Another version has “the greeting.” Both were true, for they greeted one another with a kiss. Ephraem himself, in his *Panegyric in Praise of Basil*, says of this very matter: “And when he had embraced me, he greeted me with his holy kiss.”] of the Lord.

He said to him:

“You have come well, for you have multiplied Christ’s disciples in the Church and have driven out demons through Christ, in whom your labor lies. Father, you have come to see a sinful man. May God give you a reward according to your labor.”

The honorable Ephraem replied, saying everything that was moving in his heart. Together with the abbot who was with him, he received Communion from Basil’s holy hands. When Basil had shown them charity, Saint Ephraem said:

“Honorable Father, I ask one favor of you; grant that this be given to me.”

He said to him:

“Command me; tell me what you wish. I owe you much, especially because of your labor and your coming.”

Ephraem said to him:

“I know, holy Father, that whatever you ask from God he will grant you. I want you to entreat God so that I may speak Greek [Note: [Col. 0319D] “Greek.” Baronius, volume IV, under the fourth year of Pope Damasus, the seventh year of the emperors Valentinian and Valens, says: “Some add that at that time Saint Basil granted Ephraem this grace, that he understood what was said in Greek and likewise spoke in Greek. But since Ephraem himself says nothing of this and testifies that Basil spoke to him through an interpreter, we prefer to omit the matter, being content to report fewer things supported by complete faith and entirely worthy of acceptance rather than to introduce more things uncertain in their truth.” Thus far Baronius. Nevertheless, this history, which is circulated here under the name of Amphilochius as author, is also found in the Greek manuscript *Menologion* belonging to the Cardinal of Cremona, among the Lives collected by the Emperor Basil—whom the Eighth Council praises—with their icons. There it reads: “And so that he might be still more beneficial to mortals, when Ephraem had come to Caesarea, he was made a presbyter by Basil the Great and suddenly began to master the Greek language, of which, as a man born in central Syria, he had been completely ignorant and unacquainted.” This passage, cited from the manuscript, may be found in Gerard Vossius at the beginning of volume I of the works of Saint Ephraem.].”

He said to him:

“You have asked for something beyond my power. But because you have asked faithfully, come, Father and teacher of the desert; let us entreat the Lord. For he is able to fulfill your desire. It is written: ‘He will do the will of those who fear him, he will hear their prayers, and he will save them’ (Psalm XLIV).”

After they had prayed for many hours, great Basil rose and said:

“Why, lord Ephraem, do you not receive priestly ordination, since it is fitting for you?”

Through the interpreter Ephraem replied:

“Because I am a sinner.”

Basil answered him:

“Would that I had your sins!”

Then he said:

“Let us make the genuflection.”

When they had lain upon the pavement, the great priest placed his hand upon the holy Ephraem and recited the prayer of the diaconate. Then he said to him:

“Command us; raise us up.”

His tongue was filled, and the holy Ephraem said in Greek:

“Save, have mercy, receive, and preserve us, O God, by your grace.”

Thus was fulfilled what is written:

“Then the lame man shall leap like a stag, and the tongue of the stammerers shall be opened” (Isaiah XXXV).

When he spoke in Greek, at that very hour they glorified the Lord, who can do all things and hears the prayers of those who fear him. Rejoicing spiritually for three days, Basil ordained his interpreter a deacon and Ephraem himself a presbyter [Note: [Col. 0320B] “A presbyter.” The Menologion cited immediately above bears witness to the same. Sozomen, however, in Book III, chapter 5, relates that Ephraem was raised in the clerical order only to the diaconate.]

Thus far the *Life of Saint Basil*, which I received at Rome from the congregation of the Oratory, translated by Urso, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church. It agrees entirely with the version that has hitherto been circulated in the *Lives of the Fathers* in a barbarous and rough style by an uncertain translator. The only difference is that in that version, at the end, there is added or inserted a story about Joseph the Hebrew physician and the death of Basil, which is absent here.

In this version, by contrast, there is Chapter 3, “How Basil reached Antioch and instructed the disciples of Libanius,” [167] a chapter absent from the *Lives of the Fathers*. This shows that the Life was once written and translated in various fragments.

I received at Paris from the Royal Library the complete Life of Basil written in Greek and bearing the name of Amphilochius. It was translated long ago by someone unknown, and I possess his translation from a very ancient Marcian manuscript. Its style agrees with that found in the *Lives of the Fathers*: entirely rough and unpolished.

In the Greek exemplar, however, there is one chapter, “On Basil’s miracle concerning his brother Peter and Peter’s wife,” which is also absent from that translation. This Greek Life, and the old Latin version by an unnamed translator, contains the following additional chapters, which are absent both from this Life of Basil translated by Urso and from the version hitherto found in the *Lives of the Fathers*: “On the mystical revelation and death of the apostate Julian”; “On the writing made for the little woman”; “How he saw the coming of the Holy Spirit, and concerning a certain deacon and Libanius the Sophist”; “On certain pagans and the interpretation of the *Hexaemeron*”; “How he was led to Antioch and concerning the son of Valens”; and finally, “On Valens, hateful to God, or the opening of the church at Nicaea.”

Surius, offended by the inelegance of the old version, which he possessed complete in manuscript except for the aforementioned chapter on Peter, revised it in a more Latin style and inserted it in the first volume of his *Lives of the Saints* under January 1. But because he lacked the Greek exemplar, while following the rugged tracks of the old translation he could not avoid stumbling from time to time. I shall discuss this matter more carefully elsewhere.]

He dismissed them in peace, glorifying God for all they had heard (Luke II), according to what had been said to them.

[Col. 0321]

# February 1

## Life of Saint Ephraem the Syrian, Deacon of Edessa

[Note: [Col. 0323C] Ephraem.] The Roman Martyrology, February 1: “Saint Ephraem, deacon of the Church of Edessa, who, after undertaking many labors for the faith of Christ, remarkable for holiness and doctrine under the emperor Valens, rested in the Lord.”

The Greek *Menologion*, January 18: “The nativity of the most reverend holy Father Ephraem the Syrian, from the city of Edessa, in whose praise there is a sermon by Saint Gregory of Nyssa.” A brief eulogy of him on the same day may also be found in the *Menaea*.

[Note: [Col. 0323C] “Deacon of Edessa.”] Thus Jerome says in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Church Writers*, chapter 115:

“Ephraem, deacon of the Church of Edessa, composed many works in the Syrian language and attained holy renown, so that after the reading of Scripture his writings were publicly recited in certain churches. I read his Greek volume on the Holy Spirit, which someone had translated from the Syriac language, and I recognized even in the translation the keenness of his lofty intellect. He died under the emperor Valens.”

Palladius, too, calls him a deacon of the Church of Edessa in chapter 101 of his *Lausiac History*.

## By an Unknown Greek Author

[Note: [Col. 0323D] “By an unknown Greek author.”] This Life was found anonymously in Rome among the most ancient Greek Vatican manuscripts and others. Only in a very ancient Greek manuscript, Codex Bibliothecae Cryptae Fer., under the letter XX, does an inscription of this kind occur:

Περὶ τοῦ Κυροῦ Ἔφραιμ. ἴσ. τοῦ Ἀμφιλοχίου ἐπισκόπου.

“Concerning Lord Ephraem, perhaps by Bishop Amphilochius.”

You have an excellent encomium of Ephraem written in Greek by Gregory of Nyssa, translated by Gerard Vossius, among the works of Ephraem and in the latest edition of Nyssa’s works. Gregory testifies that he composed Ephraem’s Life from various writings and, like a diligent bee, made a spiritual honeycomb from many flowers.

Metaphrastes also wrote a Life of Ephraem, found in Lipomanus, volume V of the *Lives of the Saints*, and in Surius, volume I. Vincent also discusses Ephraem in the *Historical Mirror*, Book XIV, chapter 86; Antoninus, Part II, title IX, chapter 4, sections 1 and 2; and Peter, bishop of Equilinum, in his *Catalogue of the Saints*, Book III, chapter 70. They derived their material from the Life of Saint Basil by Amphilochius, which you have in the preceding Life, chapter 11.

## Translated by Gerard Vossius

[Note: [Col. 0324C] Gerard Vossius.] He was a theological scholar, provost of Tongeren, born at Borlo in the county of Loon, in the diocese of Liège. He lived in Rome for many years and translated various works of the Fathers from Greek into Latin. Anyone who wishes may find a catalogue of them at the end of volume III of the works of our holy Father Ephraem.]

[Col. 0321A] ## Chapter I

This holy Father of ours, Ephraem, was from the East, Syrian by race, and born of pious parents in Edessa [Note: [Col. 0324C] “Born in Edessa.”] Thus also says Metaphrastes. Sozomen, however, says in Book III, chapter 15, that he was born at Nisibis: Ὃς ἐκ Νισίβῆς ὢν, τῶν τῇδε ἐπιχωρίων τὸ γένος εἶχεν, “Who, being from Nisibis, derived his lineage from the natives of that city.”

He lived during the time of King Constantine the Great and of the others who ruled after him. From childhood he abstained from every evil thing. While his parents were still alive and he was yet a child, they saw in a dream a vision: a vine rose from the mouth of Ephraem [Note: [Col. 0324C] “A vine rose.”]—the same vision is affirmed by Gregory of Nyssa in his encomium of Saint Ephraem, by Metaphrastes in his Life, and by the Greek manuscript *Menologion* of the Cardinal of Cremona, cited in the final chapter of the preceding Life—which was exceedingly fruitful, grew high, and filled the whole region beneath heaven. All the birds of heaven came and ate from the fruit of the vine, and, beyond what they ate, fruit still remained.

From his youth he inhabited the desert, claiming for himself an abyss of compunction, through which he also received the divine grace of the Holy Spirit.

## Chapter II

Concerning him, a certain man inspired by the divine Spirit [Col. 0321B] saw in a dream a terrifying man holding a scroll of paper. He asked:

“Who, do you think, will be able to receive and preserve it?”

A voice came to him:

“No one else except Ephraem, my servant.”

While Ephraem stood there, opened his mouth, and swallowed the scroll, immediately a fountain of words proceeding from God sprang forth from him, full of compunction and repentance, recalling the fear of judgment and the second coming in majesty of the universal King and Lord Jesus Christ, our true God, so that he might repay each person according to his works (Matthew XVI; Romans II). Moreover, he committed the rectitude and truth of the divine doctrines to writing in books.

## Chapter III

Another of the holy elders, again in a vision, saw bands of angels [Note: [Col. 0324D] “Bands of angels.”] descending from heaven at the divine command and holding in their hands a scroll, that is, a volume written inside and out. This vision is also affirmed by the Nyssen previously cited and by Metaphrastes.

They said among themselves:

“To whom should this book be entrusted?”

One named one person, and others named others. But others replied:

“These men are truly holy and just; nevertheless, this volume can be entrusted to no one except Ephraem, who is gentle and humble in heart.”

The elder saw that they had handed the scroll to Saint Ephraem. In the morning, when he rose, he heard from Ephraem’s mouth perfectly suitable discourses for the instruction of others, flowing forth as though from some fountain, all filled with compunction and divine fear. The elder recognized that what flowed from Ephraem’s mouth had been suggested by the Holy Spirit.

## Chapter IV

This holy Father of ours Ephraem was seized by the desire to see the city of the Edessenes [Note: [Col. 0324D] “To see the city of the Edessenes.”] Not from mere novelty, but from the desire to visit holy places, draw some benefit from associating with wise men, and impart that benefit to others. Nyssa says above: “For these reasons he went there, so that he might visit the holy places there and meet some wise man, either receiving the fruit of knowledge himself or providing it to others.” Metaphrastes also relates that Ephraem hastened to Edessa with this intention.]

He prayed to God, saying:

“Lord Jesus Christ, grant that I may see that city, and, when I enter it, that I may be worthy to meet a person who will begin a conversation with me from Scripture.”

When he was already entering the place and passing through the city gate, a woman met him [Note: [Col. 0324D] “A woman met him.”] who was a prostitute in the city. When the servant of God Ephraem looked at her, he was grieved and spoke to himself:

“Lord Jesus Christ, you have despised the prayers of your servant Ephraem. How could this woman discuss Scripture with me?”

The prostitute stopped and gazed at him.

The saint said to her:

“Tell me, girl, why have you stopped and why do you look at me with such intent eyes?”

The prostitute replied:

“I look at you because I am a woman taken from you, a man. But you must not look at me; look instead at the earth from which you, the man, were taken.”

When the servant of God Ephraem heard this, he looked upward and glorified God, who had given her such wisdom that he received such an answer from her. He recognized that his prayer had by no means been rejected by God [Col. 0322B]. He entered the city and stayed there.

## Chapter V

By chance another prostitute [Note: [Col. 0324D] “Another prostitute.”] lived near his lodging. Gregory of Nyssa seems to refer to this story in his encomium of Saint Ephraem when he says: “From the immodest he made her modest, from the wanton serious, from the defiled pure and chaste.” The whole story is found in Metaphrastes, where what is here “in your enclosure” appears there as “in your food.]

While he was staying in the city for several days, she said to him:

“Bless me, lord abbot.”

With his eyes fixed upon the window, he saw her looking out and said to her:

“May God bless you.”

She said to him:

“What is lacking from your enclosure and dwelling?”

The saint replied:

“Three stones and a little clay, so that the window through which you look may be blocked.”

She answered:

“When I first address you, you reject me. I want to sleep with you, and you exclude me even from conversation?”

The servant of God Ephraem replied:

“If you wish to sleep with me, come where I shall tell you, so that we may sleep together there.”

The prostitute said:

“Tell me the place, and I shall come.”

The saint said to her:

“If you wish to sleep with me, you will be unable to do so anywhere except in the middle of the city.”

She replied:

“Would we not be ashamed before the eyes of the people?”

The great Ephraem answered:

“If we are ashamed before human beings, we ought to be much more ashamed before God and fear him, since he knows even the hidden things of human beings. For he is the one who will come to judge the world and repay each person according to his works (Romans II).”

When the prostitute heard this, she was pierced with compunction by his words. Approaching him, she fell at his feet, weeping and saying:

“Servant of God, lead me onto the road of salvation, so that I may be freed from my many evil deeds and wicked works.”

The holy elder admonished her at length from Sacred Scripture and strengthened her repentance. He sent her to a monastery and saved her soul from the mire of her shameful deeds.

## CHAPTER VI

And departing from that city, he came to Caesarea of Cappadocia. When he entered the church, he found Saint Basil, archbishop, preaching to the people, and the most blessed Ephraem began loudly to praise him. Some from the crowd were saying: “Who is this foreigner, who praises the bishop in this way? Surely he is flattering him so that he may give him something.”

When the sermon had been completed, Basil said: “Bring to me the man who was persistently praising me.” When he had been brought, he said to him: “Why, Lord Ephraem, were you crying out so insistently in praising me?”

The holy old man replied: “I persisted in shouting and praising you because I saw an immaculate dove [Note: [Col. 0325A] “An immaculate dove.” The same is related by Gregory of Nyssa in his encomium of Ephraem; it is also found in Metaphrastes. A similar account appears in the Life of Saint Gregory by John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 69, where Peter the Deacon, who was Saint Gregory’s closest associate, relates that “he had very frequently seen the Holy Spirit himself, in the likeness of a dove, moving about above [Gregory’s] head.” In the following chapter John the Deacon adds: “For this reason the Holy Spirit is customarily depicted in the form of a dove above the head of the writing Gregory.”] standing upon your right shoulder and whispering into your ears what you were preaching to the people.”

The great Basil, filled with the Holy Spirit, recognized him and said to him: “Are you not Ephraem the Syrian? Truly, just as I understood, so I have found you to be: a lover of quiet. It is written in the prophet David: ‘Ephraem is the strength of my head’ (Ps. LIX, CVII). For your gentleness and mercy, and your evident simplicity, are like a light appearing to everyone.”

## CHAPTER VII

Elsewhere, as Saint Ephraem was passing by, a prostitute approached him deceitfully [Note: [Col. 0326A] “A prostitute.” The same account is found below, Book V, On the Lives of the Fathers; and in Pelagius, little book X, no. 21.]. She was trying by flattering him to draw him into shameful intercourse; or, failing that, at least to provoke him to anger, since no one had ever seen him angry.

He said to her: “Follow me.”

When he had already drawn near to a place frequented by a great crowd of the city, he said to her: “Come here; let us do what you wish” (Pelagius, little book X, no. 21).

But when she saw the crowd, she said to him: “How could we do this here, in the presence of so many people? Are we not ashamed?”

He said to her: “If you are ashamed before human beings, how much more ought you to be ashamed before God, who reproves the hidden things of darkness” (1 Cor. IV).

Confounded, she departed without accomplishing anything, unable either to do anything with him or even to provoke him to anger.

## CHAPTER VIII

169 These, then, are the struggles of the great Ephraem. He was a gentle and patient man, meek, pure, and simple; in divine knowledge he was as free from every embellishment as Scripture says (Job I); subdued and modest, humble and filled with compunction beyond belief. Even when he was silent, or merely from looking at him [Note: [Col. 0326A] “Or merely from looking at him.” Nyssenus, above: “His appearance was angelic, and by itself it was sufficient, without any speech, to move those who looked upon him to compassion.”], he seemed to instruct those who saw him.

He was wholly intent upon pouring out prayers to God. Thus this holy father of ours, after living a good and blessed life, having displayed himself as an example of divine virtue and expounded many sermons of holy teaching, foreseeing his death, composed a testament for his disciples and for all the monks, warning them about the future. Then, after a brief illness, he fell asleep in the Lord and was given burial by the monks of the desert.

Therefore, through the prayers and intercession of Saint Ephraem, may Christ our God deem us sinners worthy to become imitators of his divine life, through which we may attain mercy and the forgiveness of our sins into which we have fallen. For to Christ our God belongs all honor and worship, with the Father and the holy and life-giving Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0325]

## JANUARY 5

## LIFE OF SAINT SIMEON THE STYLITE, BY ANTONY, HIS DISCIPLE

[Note: [Col. 0333C] “Of Simeon the Stylite.” The Roman Martyrology, January 5: “At Antioch, Saint Simeon the monk, who lived for many years standing upon a column; hence he received the name Stylite. His life and conduct were admirable.”

The Greek Menologion, September 1: “Commemoration of our holy Father Simeon the Stylite, who lived under the emperor Leo the Great and under Martyrius, bishop of the city of Antioch; he was from the province of Cilicia, from the village of Sesan. Having entered the monastic life, he climbed onto a column, upon which he stood for forty-seven years, and, having performed many miracles through him, he fell asleep in peace.” These words appear verbatim in the Menaea, where Sesan is written Σισᾶν.

There were three Simeons the Stylites, whom learned men sometimes incorrectly confuse. The Triodion mentions all three together, p. 32:

Οὐρανὸς τετραφώστηρος ἐφάνη ἐν γῇ, ἡ δὶς δύο αὕτη Συμεώνιος ὁμωνυμία, οἱ ἐν τοῖς στύλοις τρεῖς εἰσι, καὶ εἷς ὁ Σάλος.

“Fourfold heaven appeared upon earth: this twice-two namesake group of Simeons—three are upon columns, and one is the Fool.”

The Menaea likewise mention three Stylites. The one with whom we are concerned here is the elder, whom Theodoret mentions in the Philotheus, chapter 26. He calls him a Cilician from the village of Sesa and a shepherd of sheep. Evagrius also speaks of him, Book I of Ecclesiastical History, chapters 13 and 14; as does Theodore the Reader, Book I of the Collection; and Nicephorus, Book XIV, chapter 51, who reports that his Life was written by Theodoret in the Philotheus and by Simeon Metaphrastes. The former survives among Theodoret’s works; the latter does not, unless this work, which has Antony as its author, once bore the title of Metaphrastes.

He is also mentioned by Eulogius, archbishop of Alexandria, in Oration 9, in Photius, Codex 230; by Metaphrastes in the Life of Theodosius the Coenobiarch, January 11, and in the Life of Daniel the Stylite, December 11; by Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Confessors, chapter 26; by Suidas, under Συμεὼν; by Cedrenus, in his Summary of History, in the twenty-fifth year of Theodosius the Younger; and by Glycas, Part IV of the Annals.

This one is called simply “the Stylite,” although Suidas also calls him Θαυμαστὸν, “the wondrous one”; others add some qualification. Thus the second is called in the Menaea, May 24: Ὁ ἐν θαυμαστῷ ὄρει, “the one on the wondrous mountain.” He lived under Justin the Elder, as is noted there; in the Menologion of May 24 he is called “the wondrous Stylite.” In the Fifth Synod, which is the Second Council of Nicaea, session V, he is called:

Συμεὼν Στυλίτης, ὁ εἰς τὸ θαυμαστὸν ὄρος

“Simeon the Stylite, who was on the wondrous mountain.”

There, too, John of Damascus says that he lived under Justin the Younger, Oration 3, On Images:

Συμεὼν τοῦ θαυμαστοῦ ὄρους

“Simeon of the wondrous mountain.”

As Evagrius writes, Book VI of Ecclesiastical History, chapter 22, who knew him, he was:

Ἐν κίονι ἑστὼς ἀνωτάτω τοῦ ὄρους ἀκρωρείας

“Standing upon a column placed at the very summit of the mountain.”

Nicephorus also speaks of him, Book XVIII, chapter 24.

The third, in the Menaea on July 26, is designated πρεσβυτέρου καὶ ἀρχιμανδρίτου, “presbyter, or elder, and archimandrite.” Whether this is the same as one of the two preceding men, or as the one whom John Moschus mentions in the Spiritual Meadow, chapter 57—who lived forty miles from the Cilician city of Aegeae and died after being struck by lightning—I do not know. If he is a different man, then there was a fourth Simeon the Stylite in Moschus, whose memory is found neither in the Menaea nor in the Menologion.

There is a serious error in the Menologion of May 24. Since it concerns the younger Simeon the Stylite, who lived in the time of Justin, it wrongly says that Theodoret is speaking about him, whereas Theodoret speaks about the elder. This may also have led Baronius into error when, in his note on the Roman Martyrology for January 5, he says that the elder Stylite is treated in the Menologion on May 24 and the younger on September 1. The opposite should have been asserted.

The outstanding holiness of this man became known throughout the world. His image was placed in Rome in the entrances of workshops for protection, as Theodoret relates above. Genoveva in Gaul likewise came to know him divinely as though he were present, as her Acts record, January 3. A letter of Theodosius the Younger to him is preserved in the Acts of the Council of Ephesus, volume V, chapter 15, edited by Pelt. The emperor Leo the Great also wrote to him, according to Evagrius, Book II of Ecclesiastical History, chapter 9.

176 Regarding the time in which he lived, Baronius says that his beginnings can be inferred from Theodoret, who says that he was already inhabiting the column during the time of Meletius, bishop of Antioch, who lived under the emperor Valens and died in the year in which the great synod of Constantinople was celebrated, with Siagrius and Eucharius as consuls. According to the more reliable chronographers, that year was 381 after Christ.

Simeon survived until the fourth year of the emperor Leo the Great, as Cedrenus says; this is also inferred from the Acts of Daniel the Stylite. That year was 460 after Christ, so it is clear that Simeon fell asleep when he was more than a hundred years old. In the margin of Nicephorus he is said to have lived 103 years, but nothing of the sort appears in the text.

Evagrius summarizes the length of his austere life in this way, Book I, chapter 13:

Διέτριψε τοίνυν ἐν σαρκὶ τόνδε τὸν βίον διαβλέπων ἔτη ἓξ καὶ πεντήκοντα. Ἐν μὲν τῷ πρώτῳ φροντιστηρίῳ, ἔνθα τὰ θεῖα κατηχήθη, ἔτη ἐννέα· ἐν δὲ αὐτῇ καλουμένῃ Μάνδρα, ἑπτὰ καὶ τεσσαράκοντα· ἤν τινι μὲν στενωπῷ ἔτεσι δέκα τὸν ἀγῶνα διανύσας· ἐν δὲ κίοσι βραχυτέροις ἑπτά· καὶ ἐν τεσσαρακονταπήχει, ἔτη τριάκοντα.

“This Simeon, carrying out this austere way of life in the flesh, passed through this life for fifty-six years. In the first monastery, where he was instructed in divine teachings, he lived nine years; in the place called the Mandra, forty-seven years, of which he spent ten in a very narrow passage; seven on shorter columns; and thirty on a column forty cubits high.”

Nicephorus gives the same account in Book XIV, chapter 51, but a numerical error has entered the text. For twenty-nine, thirty should be written. If this calculation is correct, he could not have reached his hundredth year. Otherwise one would have to assert that he first entered the monastery when he was forty-four years old. That does not agree with the Life written here by Antony, who says that he entered the monastery immediately after adolescence.

From this Life the following summary is obtained: When he was thirteen years old, he was tending sheep. From there he appears to have entered the monastery, where he lived for one year; then three years in enclosure; afterward four years on a four-cubit column; again twelve years on a twelve-cubit column; again twelve years on a twenty-cubit column; then four years on a thirty-cubit column; finally sixteen years on a forty-cubit column. Thus the years of his discipline amount to fifty-two, not greatly differing from Evagrius’s number.

Theodoret says that he remained two years in the first monastery; ten years in the monastery of Heliodorus; three years in the village of Telanessus; and twenty-eight years on the column, up to the time when Theodoret wrote his Life. This gives only forty-three years of discipline, but he was still alive at that time.

Cedrenus, in his Summary of History, says that in the twenty-fifth year of Theodosius the Younger he climbed the column, and that he died in the fourth year of Leo. From this interval, according to Baronius’s chronological calculation, only twenty-eight years result.

Against the Magdeburgian slanderers, the illustrious Cardinal Bellarmine ably defended this Stylite, volume II of the General Controversies, Book II, On Monks, chapter 39; as did Alanus Copus, Dialogue II, chapter 18.]

[Note: [Col. 0335D] “Stylite.” Grammarians derive both στῦλος and στήλη from the same origin, ἵστημι, “I stand.” Suidas: Στυλίτης, ὁ ἐπὶ κίονος ἱστάμενος, “A Stylite is one who stands upon a column.”

Asconius teaches us who first built a chamber above a column among the Romans, in his commentary on Cicero’s speech Against Quintus Caecilius, called the Divination against Verres: “When Maenius sold his house to Cato and Flaccus, the censors, so that a basilica might be built there, he reserved for himself the right to one column, over which he could project a roof from projecting beams, so that he and his descendants could watch the gladiatorial show, which was still being held in the forum.” Hence such structures were called Maeniana, after that same Maenius.

Festus: “Maeniana buildings were named after Maenius; for he was the first to extend beams beyond the columns, so that the upper stories might be enlarged.”

Glosses: Maenianum, ἕξώστρα, “a balcony”; Menianus, ἐκθέτης, “a projecting structure.”]

[Note: [Col. 0336A] “Antony.” The author of this Life is not unknown, as Baronius thought, but is Antony, who declares his own name in chapter 7: “A certain young man named Antony stood beside him; he saw and wrote these things.” And in the final chapter: “I, the humble and sinful Antony, have briefly set forth this account as far as I was able.”

I think Evagrius is referring to him in Book I of Ecclesiastical History, chapter 13:

Τούτου τὰς θεοσημείας γέγραφε μὲν καί τις τῶν αὐτόπτων γενομένων, γέγραφε δὲ, καὶ λογίως ἀπέθετο καὶ Θεοδώριτος ὁ τὴν Κυρεστῶν ἐπισκοπήσας

“His divine signs were recorded by someone who had been an eyewitness; and Theodoret, who governed the church of Cyrrhus, also recorded and presented them intelligently.”]

## CHAPTER I

170 Saint Simeon was chosen by the Lord from his mother’s womb, and he meditated on obeying and pleasing Him. His father was Susocion [Note: [Col. 0336A] “His father was Susocion.” The old edition reads: “He was the son of Susocion.” No other writer gives the name of his father. It is merely said that he came from the village of Sesan or Sisan, which Theodoret says was near his own region and in Cilicia. Theodore the Reader also mentions the village of Sisan in Book I of the Collection. The manuscript of Saint Laurence at Liège varies in the father’s name and also gives the mother’s name: “He was the son of a certain man named Isicius, and his mother was called Mathana.”] and he was brought up by his parents.

When he had reached the age of thirteen, he was tending his father’s sheep. Seeing a church [Note: [Col. 0336B] “Church.” Theodoret says that it was the church of the holy Martyrs.], he left the flock and entered. There he heard the Apostle being read. He asked an elder: “Sir, what is this that is being read?”

The elder answered him: “It concerns the nourishment of the soul, so that a person may learn to fear God with all his heart and with all his mind” (Luke X).

Blessed Simeon said: “What does it mean to fear God?”

The elder said to him: “Why do you question me so insistently, son?”

And he replied: “I am questioning you as though you were God. I wish to learn these things that I hear from you, because I am ignorant and foolish.”

The elder answered him: “If someone fasts continually, makes supplications at every moment, humbles himself before everyone, does not love gold, parents, clothing, or possessions, honors father and mother, and follows after the priests of God, he will inherit the eternal kingdom. But whoever does not keep these things, on the contrary, will inherit the outer darkness, which God prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXII, XXV).

“All these things, son, are intensified in the monastery.”

When blessed Simeon heard this, he fell at his feet and said: “You are my father and my mother, the teacher of good works, and the guide to the heavenly kingdoms. You have won my soul, which was already sinking into destruction. May the Lord repay you in return for my soul. These are the things that build up.

“Now I shall go, as you have taught me, to a monastery, wherever God wills; and may His will be done in me.”

The elder said to him: “Son, before you enter the monastery, listen to what I say. You will have tribulation, for you must serve and keep vigil in nakedness and endure hardships without ceasing. Yet you will again be strengthened, a precious vessel for God.”

## CHAPTER II

And immediately blessed Simeon left the church and went to the monastery of Saint Timothy [Note: [Col. 0336B] “To the monastery of Saint Timothy.” In Theodoret the name of this man is not given. The monasteries of other men are named, such as those of Ammianus and Eusebius, Eusebona and Abiton, and likewise that of Heliodorus. Some details mentioned here concerning Timothy’s monastery agree with the latter.], a magnificent man [Note: [Col. 0336B] “A magnificent man.” Here “magnificent” means one who performs great signs and miracles. See the Onomasticon.]. Falling before the monastery gate, he lay there for five days without eating or drinking.

On the fifth day Abbot Timothy came out and asked him: “Where are you from, son? Or who are your parents, that you are so afflicted? What is your name? Perhaps you have done some evil, or perhaps you are a slave and have fled from your master?”

Then blessed Simeon said with tears: “Not at all, sir; rather, I desire to be a servant of God, if He Himself wills it, because I wish to save my lost soul. Therefore command me to enter the monastery and serve everyone. Do not leave me outside any longer.”

Then the abbot took him by the hand and brought him into the monastery, saying to the brothers: “My little sons, behold, I hand this brother over to you. Teach him the rules of the monastery.”
