He remained in the monastery for about four months, serving everyone without complaint. During that time he committed the entire Psalter to memory [Col. 0326C], receiving the divine food each day. But the food that he received together with the brothers he secretly distributed to the poor, without concern for the following day.

Thus the brothers ate in the evening, but he took food on the seventh day.

## CHAPTER III

One day he entered the well to draw water. He took the rope from the bucket, by which the brothers drew water, and wrapped it around his entire naked body from the waist to the neck. Then he came in and said to the brothers: “I went out to draw water, but I did not find the rope in the bucket.”

They said to him: “Be quiet, brother, lest the abbot discover it before some time has passed.”

His body became rotten from the binding and roughness of the rope, because it cut into him as far as the bones. For it had entered his flesh so deeply that it could scarcely be seen.

171 One day some of the brothers went out and found him giving his food to the poor. When they returned, they said to the abbot: “Where did you bring this man from? We cannot fast as he does. From Sunday to Sunday he fasts, and he gives the food he receives to the poor. Moreover, an exceedingly foul stench comes from his body, so that no one can stand near him. When he walks, worms fall from his body, and his bed is full of worms.”

Then the abbot went out and found things as they had said. He said to him: “Son, what is this that the brothers say about you? Is it not enough for you to fast as we do? Have you not heard the Gospel speaking about teachers, that ‘the disciple is not above his master,’ but that everyone will be perfect if he is like his teacher” (Matt. X)? Tell me, son, where does this stench come from?”

Blessed Simeon stood there and made no reply.

The abbot became angry and ordered that he be stripped. They found the rope around his body, so that nothing of it showed except its very top. Then the abbot cried out in a loud voice: “Where has this man come from among us, wishing to destroy the rule of the monastery? I beg you, leave here and go wherever you wish.”

With great pain and difficulty they removed from his body the rope with which he had been wrapped, together with the rotten flesh. They took care of him for many days and healed him.

## CHAPTER IV

After he had been healed, he left the monastery without anyone knowing. He entered a deserted well, where there was no water, not far from the monastery, and where unclean spirits dwelt.

That same night it was revealed to the abbot that a multitude of people were surrounding his monastery with clubs and swords, saying: “Give us Simeon, the servant of God, Timothy. Otherwise we will burn you together with your monastery, because you have provoked the just man.”

When he awoke, he said to the brothers: “My little sons, I have seen a vision and am greatly troubled by it.”

On another night he saw a multitude of powerful men standing before him and saying: “Give us Simeon, the servant of God. He is beloved by God and by the angels. Why have you troubled him? He is greater than you before God; all the angels are grieving because of him. God intends to set him over the world, so that through him many signs may be performed such as no one has performed.”

Then the abbot arose and said to the brothers in great fear: “Search for that man and bring him here, lest we all die because of him. Truly he is a saint of God, for I have seen and heard great wonders about him.”

Then all the monks went out to search for him. After examining everywhere and not finding him, they reported to the abbot: “We have left no place where we did not search for him, except only the deserted well.”

The abbot replied: “I beg you, brothers, go and search for him; I too will go with you. Truly he is a saint and servant of God.”

Taking five of them with him, he came to the well. After praying, he descended with the brothers into the well.

When blessed Simeon saw him, he began to plead, saying: “I beg you, servants of God, leave me for one hour, so that I may give up my spirit. It is already failing a little. My soul is greatly wearied, because I have provoked the Lord.”

The abbot said to him: “Come, servant of God, so that we may lead you to the monastery. I have learned that you are a servant of God.”

But when he refused, they brought him by force to the monastery. All prostrated themselves at his feet, weeping and saying: “We have sinned against you, servant of God; forgive us.”

Blessed Simeon groaned and said: “Why do you burden an unhappy and sinful man? You are the servants of God and fathers.”

He remained there for about one year.

## CHAPTER V

After this he secretly went out and proceeded a short distance from the monastery. There he remained for a long time and built himself an enclosure of dry stone [Note: [Col. 0336B] “An enclosure of dry stone.” In the Menaea, February 22, in the Life of Thalassius and Limnaeus, the term is ξηρόλιθος. Longus and Hervetus translate it simply as “stone” in Theodoret’s Philotheus, chapter 22, if ξηρόλιθος was indeed present in the Greek text.

Suidas: Ξυρὸς λίθος, ὁ ἄνευ πηλοῦ κτιζόμενος· ἦν γὰρ λίθῳ ξηρῷ διεσκευασμένον τὸ φρούριον, ἐκ μεγάλων λίθων συνηρμοσμένον.

“Dry stone: that which is used in building without mud. The fortress had been constructed of dry stone, joined together from great rocks.”

In Theodoret, Philotheus, chapter 18, concerning Eusebius: “With stones joined together without even mud.” On the other hand, in the same Theodoret, chapter 29: “With mud and stones,” corresponding in the Menaea to πηλῷ καὶ λίθοις, “with mud and stones.”]

He remained there for three years, and many came to him for prayer. Then he made a small column four cubits high and stood upon it for four years.

His holy reputation grew throughout the world, and they made for him a column twelve cubits high; he stood upon it for twelve years. Again they made a column twenty cubits high, and he stood upon it for twelve years.

Then all the inhabitants of that place assembled and built two basilicas beside the column, as well as a column thirty cubits high. He stood upon it for four years and began to perform miracles.

Many sick people came to him, as did those possessed by demons, and he healed them. The blind received their sight, the hands of the disabled were restored, the deaf received their hearing, and lepers were cleansed.

He brought many peoples to the Christian faith: Saracens, Persians, Armacenians [Note: [Col. 0336C] “Armacenians.” Armaca is a city of Cappadocia according to Antoninus. But I think that Armenians are intended here, as Theodoret has it.], and Laoti [Note: [Col. 0336C] “Laoti.” I find this people nowhere. The word sounds in Greek like “the people with ears.” Are they perhaps the same as the Panotii? Isidore, Book XI of the Etymologies, chapter 3: “They say that the Panotii live near Scythia, with ears so broad that they cover their entire bodies. For πᾶν in Greek means ‘all,’ and ὦτα means ‘ears.’”

The peoples listed in this Life are Saracens, Persians, Armacenians, Laoti, and Allophyles. In their place Theodoret has Ishmaelites, Persians, Armenians, Iberians, and Homerites. Cedrenus has the same peoples except for the Homerites, unless someone wishes to suspect that his ὁσημέρας, “daily,” has been corrupted from Homerites, or conversely in Theodoret. More likely, Cedrenus expressed himself from a later passage of Theodoret, where the Homerites are omitted, although in the earlier passage he joins them to the others.], and likewise Allophyles.

When they heard of him and of his miracles, they gathered together and worshiped him.

## CHAPTER VI

Then the envious devil transformed himself into the appearance of an angel, shining with brilliance, with fiery horses. A fiery chariot appeared beside the column where blessed Simeon was standing. It shone with brightness and splendor, gleaming as though it were an angel.

The devil said in flattering words: “Simeon, hear my words, which the Lord has commanded you. He has sent me, His angel, with a fiery chariot and fiery horses, to snatch you away, just as I snatched Elijah away” (4 Kings II). Your time has now come. Therefore climb with me into the chariot, since the Lord of heaven and earth has sent it here. Let us ascend together into heaven, so that the angels and archangels, Mary the Lord’s mother, the apostles, martyrs, confessors, and prophets may see you. They rejoice to see you, so that you may pray to the Lord who made you in His image. I have spoken to you; do not delay in ascending.”

When Simeon had completed his prayer, he said: “Lord, do you wish to snatch me, a sinner, into heaven?”

He raised his right foot to climb into the chariot, lifted his right hand, and made the sign of Christ. When he had made the sign of the cross, the devil immediately disappeared completely, vanishing with his contrivance like dust before the face of the wind.

Then Simeon understood that it was a work of the devil.

## CHAPTER VII

Coming to his senses, he said to his foot: “You shall not turn back from here, but shall stand here until my death, until the Lord summons me, a sinner.”

Meanwhile the devil inflicted a wound upon his thigh in the cold. It became rotten, so that a multitude of worms swarmed from it and descended from his body; they ran down from his feet onto the column, and from the column to the ground.

For an entire year he stood upon the column on one foot.

A certain young man named Antony stood beside him; he saw and wrote these things. At Simeon’s command, he gathered the worms that fell to the ground and handed them back up to him. Simeon placed them upon the wound itself, in imitation of the just Job, saying: “Eat what the Lord has given you.”

## CHAPTER VIII

When Basilicus, king of the Saracens, heard of his fame [Note: [Col. 0336D] “Basilicus, king of the Saracens.” This should be investigated in the histories. Theodoret says that a certain prefect, or tribal chief, of the Saracens approached Simeon, but gives no name and relates a different matter.], he came to him.

When he saw him standing above and praying, suddenly a worm fell from his body. Basilicus ran, took it up in faith, and placed it upon his eyes [Note: [Col. 0336D] “And placed it upon his eyes.” This is a rite of veneration, by which they indicated that they held the object precious to their eyes. Thus, in chapter 17: “I placed his hands upon my eyes, saying: ‘Bless me, I beg you, my lord.’”].

When Simeon saw this, he said: “Why have you done this, illustrious man, and burdened me? It is a worm from my rotten body.”

When King Basilicus heard this, he opened his hand and found a most precious pearl.

He said to blessed Simeon: “It is not a rotten worm, but a most precious pearl.”

Simeon replied: “Man, according to your faith it has been given to you, and it is blessed in your hands all the days of your life.”

Thus that man entered, full of faith.

## CHAPTER IX

After a long time, his mother heard of his fame [Note: [Col. 0336D] “Mother.” Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Confessors, chapter 26: “It is read in the book of his Life that after his conversion he never looked closely upon any woman. Afterward, when his holiness burned more ardently and he had mounted the higher column, he allowed neither a strange woman nor even his own mother to see him.”] and came to see him. But she was forbidden to see him, because a woman was not permitted to enter that place [Note: [Col. 0337A] “Because a woman was not permitted to enter that place.” Theodoret has the same account. Likewise Evagrius, Book I, chapter 14; Nicephorus, Book XIV, chapter 51; and Gregory of Tours, above, who relates a remarkable story about the boldness of a certain woman:

“They say,” he writes, “that a certain woman put on men’s clothing and wished to enter the basilica of the column. The wretched woman reckoned that she could conceal her deed from the Most High by means of her clothing, not knowing the Apostle’s saying: ‘God is not mocked’ (Gal. VI). Although she came to the temple and raised her foot to enter the holy threshold, she immediately fell backward and died. This was enough to prevent any woman thereafter from attempting such a thing, when the people saw this punishment inflicted so terribly.”]

When blessed Simeon heard his mother’s voice, he said to her: “Wait, mother, for a short time, and we shall see each other, if God wills.”

When she heard this, she began to weep and beg to see him. With her hair loosened, she rebuked him, saying: “Son, why have you done this? In return for the womb in which I carried you, you have filled me with grief; in return for the nursing with which I nursed you, you have given me tears; in return for the kiss with which I kissed you, you have given me bitter anguish of heart; in return for the pain and labor that I endured, you have imposed upon me the most savage wounds.”

She spoke at such length that she made us all weep.

When blessed Simeon heard the voice of his mother, he placed his face in his hands and wept bitterly. He sent word to her, saying: “Lady mother, be quiet for a little while, and we shall see each other in eternal rest.”

But she began to say: “By Christ who formed you, if it is possible for me to see you, after you have been separated from me for so long, permit me to see you. Or, if that is not possible, let me at least hear your voice, and then I shall die immediately, because your father died in sorrow on your account. And now, son, do not destroy me in this bitterness.”

As she said this, she fell asleep from grief and lamentation. For three days and three nights she did not cease begging him.

Then blessed Simeon prayed to the Lord for her, and immediately she gave up her spirit.

They gathered her little body and brought it before him. Weeping, he said: “May the Lord receive you in joy, because you were afflicted on my account, carried me in your womb for nine months, nursed me, and also nourished me with labor.”

As he said this, his mother’s face began to sweat, and her body moved, while we all looked on.

Then he raised his eyes to heaven and said:

“Lord God of hosts, who sit upon the Cherubim and search the foundations of the abyss; who knew Adam before he existed; who promised the riches of the kingdom of heaven to those who love you; who spoke with Moses in the burning bush (Exod. III); who blessed Abraham our father (Gen. XXII); who lead the souls of the righteous into paradise and plunge the souls of the wicked into destruction; who subdued the two lions and calmed the mighty fires of the Chaldeans for your servants (Dan. VI); who fed Elijah through ravens carrying food (3 Kings XVII): receive her soul in peace and place her in the dwelling of the holy fathers, for power belongs to you forever and ever.”

## CHAPTER X

After these days, they again made for him a column forty cubits high, and 173 he stood upon it for sixteen years, until his death.

At that time an enormous dragon lived near him in the northern regions. No grass grew there. A piece of wood had also entered its right eye.

One day that blind dragon came, dragging itself along until it reached the dwelling where the man of God lived. It curled itself completely around, as though asking forgiveness, and lay there with its head bowed.

When blessed Simeon looked at it, a piece of wood one cubit long immediately came out of its eye.

When everyone saw this, they glorified God, but they fled from the beast out of fear. The beast itself coiled up and remained motionless in one place while all the people passed by.

Then it rose and worshiped the monastery door for nearly two hours. Afterward it returned to its lair and harmed no one.

## CHAPTER XI

A certain thirsty woman came by night to a jar to drink water. There was a small snake in it. As she drank, she swallowed it, and it grew in her womb.

Many physicians, enchanters, and magicians applied their efforts, but accomplished nothing.

After some time she was brought to Saint Simeon. He ordered her to be laid upon the ground and water from the monastery to be poured into her mouth.

Then she cried out loudly, and immediately a snake came out of her mouth. It was three cubits long.

At that very hour the snake burst, and, as a testimony to many, it was hung there for seven days.

From that moment the woman was made well.

## CHAPTER XII

Although anyone’s eloquence could scarcely enumerate his miracles, nevertheless, insofar as my strength allows, I will not permit them to be entirely covered by silence.

It happened that water could not be found in the region. The whole population was in danger, and all the animals suffered from the lack of water.

When Saint Simeon saw their distress, he stood in prayer.

About the tenth hour of the day, the earth suddenly split open, and a great chasm appeared on the eastern side of the monastery. A cavern was discovered containing an immeasurably abundant supply of water.

Then he ordered that they dig seven cubits. From that time onward, water abounded in that place until the present day.

At that time, certain people who had come from far away seeking his prayer and works turned aside around midday to a little shelter beneath a tree, because of the heat, in order to rest. While they were sitting, behold, a pregnant doe suddenly passed beside them, and they said to her: “By the prayer of Saint Simeon we adjure you: stop for a little while, so that we may catch you.” She stopped at that very moment. They seized and killed her, and ate some portion of her. Immediately they became speechless, and so they came to be, just like that doe. Running, however, they came to Saint Simeon, carrying her hide, and remained there for two years; only with difficulty were they ever able to recover their health. For it is wicked to recount their sin. They hung the doe’s hide there as a testimony to many.

## CHAPTER XIII

But there was also an enormous leopard in those places, which killed both people and animals and laid waste to everything around it. The people of that region came to Saint Simeon and reported to him that the leopard was committing such great and grievous evils. Then Saint Simeon ordered earth or water from the monastery to be sprinkled over those places. And it was done. When they later made inquiry, they found the leopard itself lying dead, and everyone glorified the God of Simeon.

## CHAPTER XIV

Whenever he healed anyone, he ordered him, saying: “Go to your house and honor the God who healed you; and do not dare to say that Simeon cured you, lest something suddenly worse happen to you. Do not presume to swear by the name of the Lord, because it is a grave sin; but swear by me, humble and sinful, whether justly or unjustly.”

**[Note: “Swear by me, humble and sinful, whether justly or unjustly.”]** This must be understood correctly; for one must not swear unjustly. He merely wishes to abolish the rashness of swearing perversely by God, offering his own name to the man instead. This is relevant to the punishment of a certain man mentioned by Theodoret, who had violated a vow made in the presence of Simeon: flesh like that of a bird became stone in his mouth and breast.

For this reason all the peoples of the East and the barbarian nations living in those regions swear by him.

## CHAPTER XV

A certain robber from Antioch, named Jonathan,

**[Note: “Jonathan.”]** I do not remember having read of this man; perhaps no one else has either. In Greek the name is Ἀγόνατος, “without knees,” which may have become the robber’s nickname as a result of what happened to him. Hence they first wrote the corrupted form Gonathas, and from that Jonathan.

committing many evils and being pursued by many people, so that he could no longer hide himself from them, suddenly entered the monastery, fleeing like a lion from the faces of his many pursuers. He embraced Saint Simeon’s column and began to weep most bitterly. But Simeon said to him: “Who are you? Or where have you come from, man, and why have you entered here?” He replied: “I am Jonathan the robber, who have committed every evil. I have come here to repent.”

Then Saint Simeon said: “The kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (Matthew 19). “But do not try to test me, lest you again be found in the very crimes that you have abandoned.”

While he was saying this, behold, officials were coming from Antioch, saying: “Hand over to us Jonathan, our enemy and evildoer, lest the city suddenly be stirred into revolt. The beasts are ready to devour him.”

Blessed Simeon answered them: “My sons, I did not bring him here; for the one who brought him here is greater than we are, and he assists such men—for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these. If you can enter, seize him from here. I cannot, because I fear the one who sent him to me.”

**[Note: “Officials.”]** This was what they called public ministers. Thus *officium* is frequently used by the authors.

When those men heard this, they returned in great fear and reported everything in Antioch. But Jonathan the robber, after embracing and holding the column for seven days, said to blessed Simeon: “Lord, if you command it, I wish to depart.”

The righteous man answered him: “Are you hastening again toward those same evils?”

Jonathan said to him: “No, lord, but my time has been fulfilled.”

And while he was speaking with him, he gave up his spirit.

When they wished to bury him beside the monastery, behold, other officials came from Antioch because of him and began to shout and say: “Give us our enemy; for the whole city has been thrown into turmoil because of him.”

Blessed Simeon answered them: “The one who brought him came with a multitude of the heavenly host. He is powerful enough to cast your city, with its inhabitants, into Tartarus; and he has also reconciled this man to himself. I was afraid that he might suddenly kill me. Therefore, do not trouble me any further, humble and poor as I am.”

And so they returned in fear, reporting everything they had seen and heard.

## CHAPTER XVI

After a few years, one day—that is, on the sixth day of the week—he bowed himself in prayer and remained so for three days: Friday, Saturday, and Sunday.

Then, terrified, I went up to him and stood in his presence, saying to him: “Rise, lord, and bless us, for the people have spent three days and three nights awaiting a blessing from you.” He did not answer me.

Again I said to him: “Why do you grieve me, lord? Or in what have I offended? I beg you, extend your hand to me; or perhaps you have already departed from us?”

When I perceived that he was not speaking to me, I resolved to tell no one, because I was afraid to touch him. After standing there for about half an hour, I bent down and placed my ear near him to listen. There was no breath, except that something like the fragrance of many spices seemed to rise from his body. Thus I understood that he had fallen asleep in the Lord.

Stupefied, I wept most bitterly. Bending down, I kissed his eyes

**[Note: “I kissed his eyes.”]** This was a rite of veneration in which the most excellent members and parts of the body were lightly touched with a kiss. Saint Jerome, in *The Life of Saint Paul the First Hermit*, chapter 11: “When his eyes and hands had been kissed.” Soon afterward, out of humility: “And I kissed his footprints.”

and embraced his beard and the hair of his head. Rebuking him, I said: “To whom, lord, do you leave me? Or where shall I seek your angelic teaching? What answer shall I give on your behalf? Or whose soul will look upon the column without you and not mourn? What answer shall I give to the sick when they come and seek you here and do not find you? What shall I say, or what shall I, humble as I am, speak? Today I see you, but tomorrow I look to the right or to the left and do not find you. Or with what covering shall I cover your column? Woe is me, when people come from far away seeking you and do not find you!”

Because of my great sorrow I fell asleep.

Immediately he appeared to me, saying: “I shall not abandon this column, nor this place and this blessed mountain in which I was illumined. But go down, satisfy the people, and secretly announce in Antioch what has happened to me, lest an uproar arise among the people. I have indeed fallen asleep, as the Lord willed. You, however, do not cease ministering in this place, and the Lord will give you your reward in heaven.”

Awakening from sleep, I said in fear: “Lord, remember me in your holy rest.”

Lifting his garments, I fell at his feet and kissed his footprints. Taking his great toe, I placed it upon my eyes, saying: “Bless me, I beg you, my lord.”

Again I wept and said: “What relics shall I take from you as a memorial?”

As I said this, his body moved. But I was afraid to touch him.

## CHAPTER XVII

So that no one would know, I quickly went down and sent a faithful brother to the bishop of Antioch.

**[Note: “To the bishop.”]** At that time it was Martyrius, as is clear from Evagrius and Nicephorus above.

He immediately came with three bishops, and with them Ardaburius, the military commander,

**[Note: “Ardaburius, the military commander.”]** In Evagrius, book 1, chapter 13: Ἀρδαβουρίου δὲ αὐτῶν ἑῴων στρατηγοῦντος ταγμάτων, “while Ardaburius was commander of the troops in the East.” The same appears in Nicephorus above.

together with his men. They stretched curtains around his column and removed his garments. These were embroidered with gold. After laying him down beside the altar before the column and gathering around him, they saw birds flying over the column, crying out and seeming to mourn, so that everyone could see them.

The lamentation of the people and the beasts of burden also resounded for seven miles. The mountains, fields, and trees around those places were likewise sorrowful; for everywhere a dark mist arose all around.

I observed an angel

**[Note: “An angel.”]** Daniel the Stylite, although far away, recognized the solemn procession displayed by the heavenly beings on the very day when Simeon, in triumph, ascended into heaven, as recorded in his Life written by Simeon Metaphrastes on 11 December. The same vision of Simeon’s triumph was also shown to Saint Auxentius while he was in Bithynia, as his Acts in Metaphrastes state, 4 February.

who came to visit him. Around the seventh hour, seven elders were speaking with the angel, whose face was like lightning and whose garments were like snow. In fear and trembling I watched him and listened to his voice for as long as I was able to hear it; what he said, however, I do not know.

## CHAPTER XVIII

When Saint Simeon was lying in the coffin, the pope of Antioch wished to touch something of his beard as a blessing. He extended his hand, and it immediately dried up. Many entreaties and prayers were offered to God on his behalf, and thus his hand was restored.

## CHAPTER XIX

They placed the body in a coffin and carried it to Antioch with psalms and hymns.

**[Note: “With psalms and hymns.”]** Immediately afterward, chapter 22: “They carried him into the principal church with psalms and hymns and with many lamps.” Saint Jerome, in *The Life of Saint Paul the First Hermit*, chapter 13: “Also chanting hymns and psalms according to Christian tradition.” This occurs frequently in the rites of the earliest Christians described in these Lives.

All the people who lived throughout that region mourned because the protection of such relics was being taken away from them, and because the bishop of Antioch had sworn that no one should touch his body.

## CHAPTER XX

When they had reached the fifth mile from Antioch, at a village called Meroe,

**[Note: “Meroe.”]** A village said here to be five miles distant from Antioch. Stephanus says of it: Ἔστι δὲ Μερόη κατὰ ἀνατολὰς τῆς περὶ Δάφνην Ἀντιοχείας· τὸ ἐθνικὸν Μεροαῖος, ἢ Μερούσιος, κατὰ τὸ τῆς ἑορτῆς ὄνομα· καὶ τὸ κτητικὸν, Μερουσιακός, “It is Meroe, to the east of Antioch near Daphne; its ethnic name is Meroaeus or Merusius, according to the name of the festival; its possessive form is Merusiacus.”

no one could move him.

Then a certain man who had been deaf and mute for forty years suddenly fell before the coffin and began to cry out, saying: “You have come well, servant of God; for your arrival will save me. And if I am found worthy to live, I shall serve you all the days of my life.”

Raising himself, he seized one of the pack animals that were carrying the coffin,

**[Note: “One of the pack animals that were carrying the coffin.”]** Although *burdo* is an ambiguous word, here it clearly refers to an animal, because the Greek has μοῦλαι. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 12, chapter 1: “A *burdo* is produced from a horse and a she-ass.” The Glossary: “A *burdo*, ἡμίονος, is produced from a stallion and a female donkey”; likewise, “A mule, ἡμίονος, is produced from a female horse and a donkey,” which is found in Varro, *On Agriculture*, book 2, chapter 8: “From a mare and an ass comes a mule; conversely, from a stallion and a she-ass comes a hinny.” *Burdones* are mentioned in book 3 of *Digest* 30, *De legatis*, law 49.

and immediately it moved from that place. Thus the man was healed from that hour.

The man’s sin was as follows: he loved another man’s wife and, wishing to commit adultery with her, was unable to do so. She died and was placed in a tomb. He went and violated her grave; immediately he became mute and deaf, and he was bound to that place for forty years.

## CHAPTER XXI

Then everyone went out from the city of Antioch. They carried the body of Saint Simeon upon silver and gold, with psalms and hymns, and with many lamps,

**[Note: “With many lamps.”]** Funerals were once solemnly celebrated with lamps, candles, torches, and *scolaces*. The Acts of Saint Cyprian: “With candles and *scolaces*.” The word *scholaribus* has wrongly prevailed here until now, as I have shown from ancient books in my notes to Ado’s *Martyrology*, 14 September, in the martyrdom of Saint Cyprian.

The author omitted here, as did Theodoret, the account of Simeon’s obedience toward the monks of Egypt, about which Suidas writes as follows:

Συμεὼν, ὁ θαυμαστὸς, περὶ οὗ οἱ ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ μοναχοὶ μαθόντες ὅτι ἐπὶ κίονος ἵσταται, μεμψάμενοι τῷ ξένῳ πρῶτος γὰρ αὐτὸς τοῦτο ἐποίησεν, ἀκοινωνησίαν αὐτῷ ἔπεμψαν, εἶτα ἐγνωκότες τὸν βίον τοῦ ἀνδρὸς καὶ τὸ ἄτυφον, πάλιν αὐτῷ ἐκοινώνησαν· ὁ δὲ Μαρκιανὸς ὁ βασιλεὺς ἐν σχήματι ἰδιώτου πρὸς αὐτὸν ἀφανῶς παρεγένετο.

“Simeon, that wondrous man, concerning whom the monks in Egypt, after learning that he stood upon a column, took offense at the unusual thing—for he had been the first to attempt it—and sent him exclusion from their communion. Later, having learned the man’s way of life and his freedom from pride, they again received him into communion. The emperor Marcian, however, secretly came to him disguised as a private person.”

For a fuller account, see Evagrius, book 1, chapter 13, and Nicephorus, book 14, chapter 51.

They carried him into the principal church, and from there into another church called Repentance. Many miracles also occur at his tomb, more than during his lifetime. The man who had been healed served there until the day of his death.

Many, in faith, offered treasures to the bishop of Antioch, asking for relics from his body; but because of his oath he did not grant them any.

I, the humble and sinful Antony, have briefly explained this reading as far as I was able. Blessed is the one who has it written in a book and reads it in church and in the house of God; and when he commemorates him, he will receive a reward from the Most High—to whom belong honor, power, and might for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0337]

# JANUARY 23. THE LIFE OF SAINT JOHN THE ALMSGIVER, BY LEONTIUS

**[Note: “John.”]** The Roman Martyrology, 23 January: “At Alexandria, Saint John the Almsgiver, bishop of that city, most renowned for his mercy toward the poor.” The Greek Menologion, 12 November: “Commemoration of our holy father John, archbishop of Alexandria, surnamed the Merciful. He was a Cypriot by birth, the son of Epiphanius, commander of that region. Having devoted every diligence and effort to the pursuit of virtue and the gaining of God’s favor, he became archbishop of Alexandria at the request of the emperor Heraclius, because of the splendor of his life. Thus he shone like a lamp placed on a lampstand. After spending many years in the priesthood and performing many miracles, he supplied the necessities of life abundantly to the poor and needy. Hence he received the surname Merciful, and, venerated by all, even by unbelievers, he departed to the Lord.” The same things are found on the same day in the *Menaea*, with a few additions. I do not know where Baronius obtained the statement under 23 January that the Greeks also commemorate him on that day, although his natal day is 3 February. We have already seen from the *Menaea* and the Menologion that the Greeks celebrate his memory on 12 November. Below, in the *Life*, chapter 52, it is said that John died on the day of Saint Menas; Menas the Great Martyr is found in the *Menaea* and Menologion on 11 November, in the same month as John and scarcely differing in date. Baronius adds there: “I think that this very day, 23 January, is the day of his ordination, which also came to be called his natal day and was solemnly celebrated, as we said above when we dealt with the chair of Saint Peter.” Yet in the *Annals*, volume 8, in the year of Christ 620, under the third year of Pope Boniface V and the eleventh of the emperor Heraclius, he says that the anniversary of John’s death was 23 January.

**[Note: “Leontius.”]** Sigebertus, *Catalogue of Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 57: “Leontius, bishop of Neapolis on the island of Cyprus, wrote the Life of John, bishop of Alexandria, who because of his exceptional mercy toward the poor was surnamed the Almsgiver.” Trithemius also discusses him in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, and cites no work of his other than this Life. The Seventh General Council lists more of Leontius’s works in its fourth session.

Οὗτος ὁ ἀναγνωσθεὶς πατὴρ, ἐν μιᾷ τῶν πόλεων Κύπρου ἱεροπρεπῶς διέτρεψε· καὶ πολλὰ ἐγκώμια καὶ πανηγυρικοὺς λόγους αὐτοῦ ἔχομεν· μεθ’ ὧν καὶ εἰς τὴν μεταμόρφωσιν τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν· συνεγράψατο δὲ καὶ τὸν βίον τοῦ ἁγίου Ἰωάννου ἀρχιεπισκόπου Ἀλεξανδρείας, τοῦ Ἐλεήμονος, ἔτι μὴν καὶ τοῦ ὁσίου Συμεῶν τοῦ Σαλοῦ, καὶ ἕτερά τινα· καὶ ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς λόγοις αὐτοῦ ὀρθόδοξος γνωρίζεται. Ἤκμαζε δὲ κατὰ τοὺς χρόνους Μαυρικίου τοῦ βασιλέως.

“This father who has been read aloud flourished in one of the cities of Cyprus in a manner worthy of his sacred office. We possess many encomia and festal sermons of his, including one on the Transfiguration of our Savior. He also composed the Life of Saint John, archbishop of Alexandria, the Merciful, as well as that of the holy Simeon the Fool, and several other works. In all his sermons he is recognized as orthodox. He flourished during the reign of the emperor Maurice.”

Anastasius the Librarian, in his version of the Seventh Council, adds after Simeon that Leontius wrote about “the disturbances that occurred in the Church around those times because of Christ,” which is absent here from the Greek. Therefore, either Anastasius obtained a more complete Greek copy, or else he explains in a paraphrase τοῦ Σαλοῦ, which is Simeon’s epithet and by which the Syrians designate a simple or foolish person. It comes from the Greek τοῦ σάλος. For among the Greeks σάλος means agitation or disturbance. Perhaps, therefore, nothing is missing from the Greek text, but Anastasius was misled by the ambiguity of σαλοῦ and σάλου. This may have given Baronius an opportunity, in volume 8, under the years 594 and 620, to err by supposing that this Leontius had written the history of his own time, beginning with Maurice and recounting the disturbances that had occurred in the Church. Our Possevinus says the same in the *Sacred Apparatus*. Thus that book may not have perished or be hidden somewhere, because perhaps it was never written. Nor is Leontius correctly called bishop of Constantia in the earlier passage of Baronius and in Possevinus; rather, he was bishop of Neapolis. See the *Onomasticon* under “Neapolis.”

In the same council and session, several books of Leontius against the Jews, written in defense of Christians, are cited; John of Damascus also draws certain passages from them in Orations 1 and 3 *On Images*. In his note to the Roman Martyrology, 23 January, Baronius believes that there were two editions and translations of Leontius’s work, differing from one another, with some material present in one and absent from the other. There are indeed two editions and translations of the Life of John the Almsgiver, but by different authors. One has Leontius as its author; it survives in the *Lives of the Fathers* and is found in volume 2 of Lipomanus. The other has Metaphrastes as its author; it is found in Lipomanus, volume 5, and in Surius, volume 1.

**BISHOP OF NEAPOLIS IN CYPRUS, TRANSLATED BY ANASTASIUS, LIBRARIAN OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH.**

**[Note: “Anastasius.”]** Sigebertus, above, chapter 104: “Anastasius, at the command of Pope Nicholas, translated into Latin the Life of John the Almsgiver, written in Greek by Bishop Leontius.” Trithemius says the same about him above, where he lists several other works translated by Anastasius from Greek.

## PREFACE OF ANASTASIUS THE TRANSLATOR TO LORD POPE NICHOLAS

**[Note: “Lord.”]** Thus the Gembloux and Aquicinctus manuscripts read; this heading is absent from the printed editions. *Domnus* was formerly used of human beings instead of *Dominus*, which they reserved for Christ alone as a title of reverence.

While I was thinking and for a long time silently and anxiously considering with myself what useful and worthy work I might perform in the house of God—so that I might not presume to undertake duties that had not been entrusted to me, nor seize upon tasks exceeding the powers of my little intellect—according to Solomon’s saying, “You have found honey; eat what is sufficient for you, lest, when you are satisfied, you vomit it up” (Proverbs 25), and elsewhere, “Do not seek what is above you, and do not investigate what is too difficult for you” (Ecclesiasticus 3), behold, certain energetic and learned men suddenly wished to exhort me to translate into Latin Leontius’s account of the remaining parts of the Life

**[Note: “Leontius’s account of the remaining parts of the Life.”]** Leontius deals with the remaining portions of the Life of John the Almsgiver, which had been omitted by John and Sophronius, the earlier writers of that Life, as Leontius himself asserts in the following prologue.

of John, bishop of Alexandria, whom the Greeks, because of the manifold compassion that he possessed toward all people, rightly and without qualification call Ἐλεήμων, that is, “the Merciful,” so that so great a man might be useful and beneficial not only to those who speak Greek but also to those who possess Latin eloquence.

Therefore, since I did not consider myself worthy or suitable for so great a work, I lifted my eyes to the mountains, from which help would come to me (Psalm 120); and, applying the consolations and prayers of the fathers, I could not bear to conceal so beneficial a man from the Latins. Although I had cut the parchment and prepared the sheets, I did not dare to compile this book until I had obtained permission from Your Lordship, O thrice-blessed one.

For it is not lawful for anything to be completed or published without the vicar of God,

**[Note: “Without the vicar of God.”]** Here the pontiff is given remarkable titles: “vicar of God, keeper of heaven’s keys, charioteer of spiritual Israel, universal pontiff, unique pope, singular shepherd, special Father, judge of all.”

without the keeper of heaven’s keys, without the chariot and charioteer of spiritual Israel, without the universal pontiff, without the one pope, without the singular shepherd, without the special Father, without you, the judge of all.

For you hold the keys of David (Luke 11); you have also received the keys of knowledge. In the ark of your breast rest the tablets of the covenant and the manna of heavenly flavor. For what you bind, no one looses; what you loose, no one binds; when you open, no one shuts, and when you shut, no one opens (Matthew 16). You possess on earth the place of God.

When I translated this blessed man into Latin, I could neither follow, nor ought to follow, the idioms of the Greeks or the order of their words. For I did not extract word from word, but sense from sense. Nor did I take care to observe Latin rules everywhere, so long as my intention was directed toward producing benefit for the readers.

Therefore, O lord, angelic companion, do not regard the insignificance of my person, nor investigate my cleverness, nor demand verbal ornament; rather, foresee with the pious eye of your heart the benefit of the readers. By your apostolic authority, confirm this translation if it pleases your judgment; if it displeases you, correct it—provided that the Latin language does not lament being deprived of the salt with which Greece rejoices that it has been excellently seasoned.

Receive, then, a saint translated by a sinner, and do not consider by whom he was translated, but who has been translated. For you do not despise the clearest water because it flows through a leaden pipe,

**[Note: “Because of the leaden pipe.”]** Saint Augustine offers a similar comparison in book 4 of *On Christian Doctrine*: “It is a mark of outstanding intelligence in good minds to love the truth in words, not the words themselves. For what good is a golden key if it cannot open what we wish? Or what harm is there in a wooden one if it can? For we seek nothing except that what is closed may be opened.”

nor do you reject the rose that is produced because of the thorns that produce it.

Finally, your guardian and lover, whenever he wished, showed dreams to Pharaoh (Genesis 41) and to Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 4), wicked kings, by which they might foresee future events; and he brought forth through Caiaphas the wicked man what was expedient (John 11). Indeed, whenever he wished, he permitted a she-ass to speak with articulate voice (Numbers 22).

Hail, beloved bishop, beloved of God, through the ages;

Blessed pope of the whole world, fare well.

## Author’s Prologue

Our purpose is one and the same as that of the learned men and holy men who came before us in narrating the Life of this notable man: namely, that from it all may receive pious imitation and benefit, while glory and magnificence are returned to the holy and adorable Trinity. And in this, as in all things, it continually displays its own lights from generation to generation, to illumine those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death (Luke 1) and of sin.

Because we are friends of Christ, we do not greatly marvel at the men who lived before our generation and conducted their lives in a manner pleasing to God. But, speaking of the devil’s activity, we always say to one another that in the time of the men who lived before us human iniquity had not multiplied as it has now, as divine Scripture foretold: “Because iniquity has abounded, the love of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24). For this reason we are unable to rise to their merit. Therefore we have come in part to the narration of this holy Life in order to show that even in our own days there have been men who, willingly and by constraining themselves to their purpose, have proved superior to us; that it is possible to walk the narrow and difficult way (Matthew 7), to stop the mouths of those who speak wicked things (Psalm 62), and to thwart thoughts harmful to the soul.

Others before us have already philosophized in the best and most excellent manner about this admirable man and supreme priest, John, being powerful in deed and word. I mean John and Sophronius,

**[Note: “John and Sophronius.”]** I have not yet had the opportunity to see what these men wrote about John the Almsgiver. They are also mentioned below, chapter 31.

worshipers of God, lovers of virtue, and champions of piety. Yet although they were such men, they too omitted something concerning the dignity and merit of this man’s zeal and suffered the same fate as certain diligent farmers who harvest a rich and fruitful vineyard. They leave behind, even unwillingly, a blessing from the fruit for the needy who follow after them and choose from the vineyard; we are among the least of these.

All these saints, although with all their strength they sought to harvest this fruitful olive tree planted in the house of God, as the Psalmist says (Psalm 51), because of the many olives truly present in it, nevertheless many of the tree’s fruits remained hidden from them, by the Lord’s dispensation.

Receive, therefore, our wretched and cold eagerness as the widow’s two small coins (Luke 21). We have not hastened to commit the deeds of the righteous to writing by detracting from those men, nor because we might be able to imitate the wisdom given them by God. Rather, first, we have done so because it would not be right to conceal in silence what we understand and what may benefit those who hear it, lest we too fall under the judgment of that servant (Matthew 25) who hid his talent in the earth.

Second, we have done so so that, in this account, a more corrected and pleasing history may be written concerning matters not written by the best men in praise of the truly most holy and blessed John.

Finally, because those men were wise and powerful in speech and lovers of history, they depicted their subject wisely and sublimely. This especially and most fully encouraged us to undertake the present labor, so that with the pedestrian, ungainly, and humble style we possess we might narrate these matters in a way that even the uneducated and illiterate could profit from what is said.

## THE LIFE

[Col. 0341]

### CHAPTER ONE

When I, unworthy as I am, had arrived in Alexandria to embrace the holy and victorious martyrs Cyrus and John

**[Note: “Cyrus and John.”]** Below, chapter 30: “To the temple of the holy victorious martyrs Cyrus and John.” The Roman Martyrology, 31 January: “At Rome, on the Portuensian Way, the holy martyrs Cyrus and John, who, after many torments, were beheaded for confessing Christ.”

and to enjoy their pleasant banquets and refreshment, certain venerable and Christ-loving men had gathered there and were conversing with one another.

**[Note: “Christ-loving.”]** The printed editions have hitherto read *philosophers*. Likewise below, chapter 12: “and received mutually from many Christ-lovers.” Chapter 22: “O Christ-lovers.” And chapter 25: “The aforesaid Christ-loving man saw in a dream.” For *philochristus* means “a lover of Christ,” as is explained here in chapter 14: “We have already mentioned this, O lovers of Christ.”

We were discussing the Scriptures and the formation of the soul when a stranger came to us asking for alms. He said that he had recently been rescued from Persian captivity.

It happened that none of those seated there was found to possess either money or a coin. One of them, however, had a hired servant standing there, a shrewd giver who received only three coins per year and had a wife and two sons.

When the beggar had departed, this man cleverly followed him, took from himself the little silver cross he wore,

**[Note: “The little silver cross.”]** Here we see the Christian custom of wearing small crosses around the neck. See the *Onomasticon*.

and gave it to him, saying that he had nothing else in his lifetime, not even a single *siliqua*.

**[Note: “Not even a single *siliqua*.”]** Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 16, chapter 24: “A *siliqua* is the twenty-fourth part of a solidus, taking its name from the seed of a tree.”

Considering by the grace of God what had happened—or rather, what I had seen being done—and feeling compunction, I immediately related it to a man sitting nearby, named Mennas, an industrious and God-fearing man who was also administering the affairs of the most holy church under the noble and blessed patriarch John.

When he saw me admiring and praising the man who had given the alms, he said to me: “Do not marvel, because he became an agent of such an action through this man’s tradition and teaching.”

When I said to him, “How so? For charity’s sake, help me to understand,” he replied:

“He remained in service to our thrice-holy and blessed patriarch John, and, like a true son, took up his father’s industry. The saint said to him: ‘Humble Zacharias, be merciful; and you have a word from God through my misfortune: God will not be lacking to you either during my life or after my death.’ He keeps this promise to the present day.

“For God sends him many blessings, but he does not keep anything without immediately giving it to the poor, almost constricting and reducing his own household to nothing. Many times people found him in a state of exultation, saying to God: ‘So then—either you send, or I distribute; we shall see which of us prevails. For it is clear that you, Lord, are rich and the provider of our life.’

“Sometimes, however, as circumstances require, he has nothing at hand for the person asking him. Then, saddened, he says to a shopkeeper or merchant: ‘Lend me one *tremissis*,

**[Note: “A *tremissis*.”]** The printed books add, “that is, a third part of a gold solidus.” This explanatory gloss entered the text in place of a translation. Isidore, as above: “They called a third part [of a solidus] a *tremissis* because, when sent three times, it makes a solidus.” Below, chapter 37, *tremissia*.

and I will serve you for one or two months, as you wish and wherever you wish, because those in my house are very hungry.’

“Taking it, he gives it to the needy person, asking him to tell no one.

“When that same worshiper of God, Mennas,

**[Note: “Mennas.”]** He related to Leontius the entire history of John the Almsgiver, which is contained in chapters 2 through 48, as the text says there.

saw that I was listening to him as though to the Gospel, he said to me with compunction: ‘Do you marvel at this, lord? What if you had encountered the holy patriarch himself?’

“I said to him: ‘What more could I have seen?’

“Then he said to me: ‘Believe through God’s mercy. He made me a priest and steward

**[Note: “Steward.”]** That is, the church’s administrator or dispenser. Shortly before, concerning the same man: “who was administering the affairs of the most holy church.” See the *Onomasticon*.

of the most holy church, and I saw in him works exceeding almost the whole of nature. If you would be gracious enough to come today to your servants and sanctify us, I shall recount to you deeds that I myself witnessed and observed.’

“When he had said this, I took his hand and raised him up. He seized me and led me to his house, preserved by God.

“When he wished to set a table before us, I said to him: ‘It is not right, O lord, while leaving aside food for the soul, to refresh the body before the soul. Rather, let us take food that does not perish, and afterward provide what the body requires.’

“When he had begun to recount the saint’s life without falsehood, he said: ‘His first and chief virtue was that he never swore in any way.’

“I then asked for paper and an inkpot, and I recorded in order what was said.”

## Chapter II

Having therefore been advanced and seated upon the throne in Alexandria, the great city beloved of Christ, by a truly divine decree—and not from human beings or through human beings—he at once demonstrated this first and extraordinary deed, and a reward for all. For he immediately sent the stewards and the man called the “superintendent of peace” [Note: *Superintendent of peace.* He means the deacon who formerly proclaimed before the sacred offering the *εἰρηνικά*, “peace-prayers,” which were fixed formulas found in the *Euchologion*. See the *Onomasticon*.], and said publicly to them in the honorable secret chamber 207 [Note: *In the honorable secret chamber.* Metaphrastes has *τῶν ἀπὸ τοῦ σεκρέτου*, “those who were from the secret chamber.”]:

“It is not right, brothers, for us to concern ourselves with anyone else’s affairs before those of Christ.”

When the entire multitude that had gathered heard this saying, they were moved to compunction and remained silent. Then that blessed man said again:

“Go, therefore, throughout the whole city, and write down for me, without exception, all my masters.”

They did not understand who these persons were, but asked him to explain and wondered who the patriarch’s masters could be. That angelic mouth answered again and said:

“Those whom you call the poor and beggars, I proclaim to be my masters and helpers. For they truly will be able both to help us and to grant us the kingdom of heaven.”

When the imitator of Christ saw that this had been carried out with great speed, he ordered stipends to be distributed to them day by day, providing them with sufficient necessities through his own steward. They numbered more than seven thousand five hundred.

Then, like a true shepherd and not a hireling, he went with his sacred flock and with the holy bishops who had assembled to the holy church, and was consecrated by divine judgment [Note: *Was consecrated by divine judgment.* Baronius, volume VIII, in the year of Christ 610, the fourth year of Pope Boniface IV and the first of the emperor Heraclius, places the consecration of John as patriarch of Alexandria.].

## Chapter III

It is right not to pass over this good deed among his actions. For on the following day he again sent throughout the whole city those same friends of God, the stewards and chancellors [Note: *Chancellors.* Below, chapter 5, “of the chancellors and defenders of the church.” And in chapter 23: “He summoned him through his chancellor, a monk.” It appears here to have been an ecclesiastical office. See the *Onomasticon*.], and the others to whom the administration of the city had been entrusted. He did not permit any measure, nor any weight, large or small, anywhere in the city; rather, he ordered buying and selling to be conducted entirely according to one Campanian balance [Note: *According to one Campanian balance.* The editions read: “on one balance,” that is, with a just and equal balance. Isidore, *Etymologies*, XVI.24: “The Campanian balance received its name from the region of Italy where its use was first discovered. It does not have two pans, but is a rod marked with pounds and ounces and measured by a movable weight. Each weight has its fixed measure, designated by its proper names.”], by the modius and the artaba [Note: *By the modius and the artaba.* The editions read *modo* and *artaba*, that is, a measure containing three modii and a third part of a modius; this explains the artaba. The manuscript of Aquicinctius had this explanation in the margin. Isidore, *Etymologies*, XVI.25: “The artaba is a measure among the Egyptians, of seventy-two sextarii, composed according to the number of the seventy-two peoples or languages that filled the world.”].

He wrote in his subscription the following regulation for the whole region:

“John, humble and insignificant servant of the servants of our Lord Jesus Christ, to all who live under our poverty and who have been entrusted by that same Lord and our God with administration:

“To the distinguished and blessed Paul, through him who spoke in him, Christ gave the command and established the law for all: ‘Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they keep watch as those who must give an account for your souls’ (Hebrews XIII).

“My insignificance believes that, obeying the divine word, you will receive our requests as coming from God and not from a human being. Therefore, knowing this, I admonish your charity that no such transgression should appear in any one of you. For, as divine Scripture says, ‘God hates a large balance and a small one’ (Proverbs XI).

“But if, after the present regulation of our subscription, anyone should be found to have fallen into such a crime, he shall, unwillingly and without compensation, place all his possessions at the disposal of the needy.”

Therefore, as something worthy of remembrance, we have hastened to set down here this public order itself.

## Chapter IV

It was once reported to this man, who had obtained wisdom from God, that the administrators were being bribed by the church’s gifts of hospitality [*xenia*] and showing favoritism in matters concerning the distribution of captives. Neglecting nothing, he summoned them and, without angering anyone at all, increased the payments previously given to them, adding this instruction: they were absolutely not to accept gifts from anyone.

“For,” he said, “fire will consume the houses of those who accept gifts.”

From that time onward, by the grace of God, their households prospered so greatly that some of them gave up the amount of the additional payment granted to them.

## Chapter V

That thrice-rich man later learned that certain people were suffering injustice at the hands of their adversaries. When they wished to approach him, they were prevented by fear of the chancellors and defenders of the church [Note: *Defenders of the church.* Below, chapter 23: “The defenders of the church struck him down.” This too was an ecclesiastical office. See the *Onomasticon*.], as well as of those attending him.

He considered such a matter pleasing to God. On Wednesdays and Fridays he publicly set out a chair and two benches and sat before the church, conversing with certain capable men or holding the holy Gospels in his hands. He allowed no one to approach him in the exercise of such great service, except for one defender of the church, whom he hastened to authorize and encourage to admit those wishing to approach him. Through the defenders of the church he immediately did for them whatever was appropriate. He ordered that none of them should taste food until they had arranged the matter.

He said in the hearing of all:

“If we, being human beings, always have permission, whenever we make our petitions, to enter the house of God and make our requests known to him—who is inaccessible and exalted above every creature—and if we take pains that our prayers may be fulfilled, and also ask him not to delay, but immediately cry out the saying of the Prophet, ‘Let your mercy, Lord, quickly go before us’ (Psalm LXXVIII), how, do you think, ought we to carry out the petitions of our fellow servants with all haste, remembering what the Lord says: ‘In the measure with which you measure, it will be measured to you’ (Matthew VII)? And the Prophet again testifies: ‘As you have acted, so shall it be done to you.’”

One day, therefore, this remarkable man proceeded in the same manner and sat in his usual place until the fifth hour. No one approached him, and he withdrew sorrowful and weeping. No one dared to ask him the cause of his grief. Saint Sophronius, who was then present, said to him privately:

“What is the reason, guardian of God, that your holy spirit is held by sorrow? It has suddenly troubled us all.”

He answered him in a gentle voice [Note: *Today.* Such was once the saying of Emperor Titus in Suetonius, *Titus*, ch. 8; in Metaphrastes it is: *Τὸ μὴ βασιλεῦσαι σήμερον ἐπεὶ μηδένα εὐεργετήσαμεν*, “Not to have reigned today, since we have benefited no one.”]:

“Today humble John received no sort of payment from anyone, nor did he offer anything to Christ for his innumerable sins—as has never happened before.”

Saint Sophronius, inspired by God—for he immediately understood the reason why the patriarch was grieving—answered him:

“Today you ought to rejoice and be glad, most blessed one; truly you are supremely blessed. For you have so pacified the flock entrusted to you by Christ that it has no dispute or uncertainty against its neighbor. You have made human beings like angels, without litigation and without judgment.”

That truly gentle shepherd, believing what had been said to be true, raised his eyes toward heaven and said:

“I give you thanks, God, because you have deigned both to allow my undeserved weakness to serve as a priest, and to have me, insignificant and sinful, called your priest, and to feed your rational flock.”

Immediately, therefore, having laid aside all weakness, he experienced great joy in his humility. Some say that Constantine, who became emperor after Heraclius and was his son, imitated him in this.

## Chapter VI

During the time of this holy patriarch, the Persians invaded and plundered Syria [Note: *The Persians.* This Persian invasion and devastation occurred in the year of Christ 614, the fourth year of Pope Boniface IV and the fifth of the emperor Heraclius, as Paulus Diaconus relates in his *Miscella Historia*, drawing on Theophanes, book XVIII: “In the fifth year of the reign of Heraclius, the Persians conquered the Jordan in war, as well as Palestine and the holy city, and killed many there at the hands of the Jews—that is, as some say, ninety thousand. For these men, buying Christians according to what each person could afford, killed them. They seized Zacharias, bishop of Jerusalem, and carried him away into Persia, together with the precious and life-giving wood of the holy cross and much booty.” The monk Antiochus of Palestine mourns the misery of this calamity in various homilies. See Baronius under that year of Christ, and Ado in the *Martyrology*, September 14.].

Therefore almost all who escaped the hands of the Persians hurried to this thrice-blessed man as to a harbor without waves, asking that they too might enjoy his assistance and hospitality. This blessed man received them as guests and comforted them, not as captives but as genuine brothers by nature.

At once, therefore, he had the wounded and sick laid in hospices [*xenodochia*] and hospitals [*nosocomia*], ordering that care and medicine be provided for them free of charge, and that they depart whenever each wished of his own accord.

To those who came while healthy but needy and requested a daily allowance [Note: *Daily allowance.* Thus correctly in the Aquicinctine manuscript and the old editions, together with the Cologne manuscript. The Gembloux manuscript has *rogandum*, incorrectly. Shortly afterward: “to whom the allowance had been entrusted.”], he gave one *siliqua* to each male, but to women and girls, as weaker members, two.

Some people came wearing golden ornaments and bracelets and asked for alms. Those entrusted with the allowance reported this to the patriarch. Then that blessed man, although gentle and cheerful in appearance, addressed them with a stern look and severe voice:

“If you wish to be stewards of humble John—or rather of Christ—obey the divine command without deceit: ‘Give to everyone who asks of you’ (Luke VI). But if, when they come, you investigate them inquisitively, God does not need inquisitive servants, nor does humble John.

“For if what is given were mine and had been born together with me, perhaps I would rightly be stingy with my own possessions. But if what is given belongs to God, surely he wishes his command to be observed among his own things.

“If you fear, because of unbelief or little faith, that the number of those who receive may exceed the income of the funds, I will not allow myself to share your little faith. For if it was God’s good pleasure that I, unworthy, should be the steward of his gifts, even if the whole world were gathered at Alexandria in need of alms, they would not diminish God’s immeasurable treasures or the holy church.”

## Chapter VII

When he had dismissed these men and cut through all the defection and lack of faith that had surrounded them, he spoke to those seated beside him, who were astonished at the compassion given him by God:

“When I was still a young man in Cyprus, about fifteen years old, I saw one night in a dream a certain maiden whose appearance shone more brightly than the sun. She was adorned beyond all human understanding. She came and stood before my bed and struck me on the side.

“When I awoke, I saw her standing there in reality and thought she was a woman. Having therefore made the sign of the cross, I said to her: ‘Who are you, and how have you dared to enter upon me while I was sleeping?’

“She also had a crown of olive branches upon her head. Then, with a cheerful face and smiling lips, she said to me: ‘I am the first of the king’s daughters.’

“When I heard this, I immediately worshiped her. Then she said to me: ‘If you make me your friend, I will lead you into the presence of the emperor. For no one has power with him as I do. Indeed, I caused him to become human on earth and to save human beings.’

“When she had said this, she disappeared. Coming back to myself, I understood the vision and said: ‘I believe that she is Compassion and Almsgiving, and that is why she wears a crown of olive leaves upon her head. For truly compassion and kindness toward human beings caused God to clothe himself in flesh.’

“Immediately I dressed myself and, without waking anyone in my house, went to the church. It was already dawn. As I went, I met a brother suffering from cold [Note: *Suffering.* So the Aquicinctine manuscript; the editions have *suffering as one who had been afflicted*. Writers of this age commonly use such forms in similar ways. Thus, frequently in the books that follow, they use ‘those afflicting’ for ‘those afflicted.’]. I removed my goatskin garment and gave it to him, saying within myself: ‘By this I shall know whether the vision I saw was true or demonic.’

“Before I had even reached the church, someone suddenly came toward me, dressed in white, and gave me a band [Note: *Band.* In Greek, Metaphrastes has *ἀπόδεσμον*. Below, chapter 25, a band of gold.] containing one hundred coins, saying: ‘Take these, brother, and distribute them as you wish.’

“Overjoyed, I immediately accepted them. Then I turned back, wishing to return the band to him, since I needed nothing, but I no longer saw anyone.

“Then I said to myself: ‘Truly it was not a phantom.’

“From that hour onward I often gave something to the brothers and said: ‘I shall see whether God will send me, as he said, a hundredfold.’ When I had tested the Lord—doing wrong—and had been satisfied in various ways through those things, I said: ‘Stop, wretched soul, testing the One who cannot be tested.’

“My humble soul, therefore, having received so many certainties from God, perhaps these unbelievers have come today and were urging me to fall with them into distrust.”

## Chapter VIII

While the same multitude of people was still in the city [Note: *Still.* The editions read *Adrione*, whose origin I do not know.], one of the foreigners, seeing such compassion in him, wished to test him. He put on old clothing and approached him as he went to visit those lying in the hospital. For he went there twice or three times each week.

The man said to him:

“Have pity on me, for I am a captive.”

He said to the dispenser:

“Give him six coins.”

After receiving them, the man went away, changed his clothing, approached him from another direction, and fell before him, saying:

“Have pity on me, because I am in distress.”

The patriarch again said to the dispenser:

“Give him six gold coins.”

When he had gone, the distributor whispered in the patriarch’s ear:

“By your prayers, lord, this is the very man who received them a second time.”

The patriarch pretended not to know. The man came a third time to receive something; the dispenser, who was carrying the gold, touched the patriarch, indicating that he was the same person.

Then that friend of God, truly compassionate, answered:

“Give him twelve coins, lest he perhaps be my Christ and be testing me.”

## Chapter IX

A foreign sailor suffered losses. He approached this blessed man and begged him with many tears to have compassion on him, as he did on everyone else. The patriarch ordered five pounds of gold to be given to him.

After receiving them, he departed, bought a chest [Note: *Chest.* The old edition and the Cologne edition have *antheca*, that is, a chest. *Entheca* is noted among the jurists and writers of a later age. Cassian, *Institutes* IV.14: “Although he regards the entire *entheca* of the monastery as his own substance.” Below, chapter 27: “The total was a great amount of his chests.”], and put it on his ship.

Soon afterward he suffered shipwreck outside the Pharos [Note: *Pharos.* So both manuscripts and Metaphrastes in Greek, *φάρον*. The editions incorrectly have *forum*. The well-known place near Alexandria is meant. The same appears below, chapter 25.]. He did not, however, lose the ship.

He approached the patriarch again, presuming upon his good will, and said:

“Have pity on me, as God has had pity on the world.”

The patriarch said to him:

“Believe me, brother: if you had not mixed the church’s money with the money that remained to you, you would not have suffered shipwreck at all. You obtained it from wickedness, and the money that came from good was lost together with it.”

Nevertheless, he again ordered ten pounds of gold to be given to him, warning him not to mix other money with it.

After buying another chest and sailing for one day, while a strong wind was blowing, he was thrown onto the shore. He lost everything, the ship itself as well, and nothing was saved except the people.

The sailor, therefore, in shame and anguish, wished to kill himself. But God, who always provides for the salvation of human beings, revealed this to the blessed patriarch. When he heard what had happened, he sent word that the sailor should come to him, without any hesitation.

The sailor then sprinkled himself with dust, tore his tunic, and approached him indecently. When the saint saw him in such a condition, he rebuked him and said:

“May the Lord, the blessed God, have mercy on you. I believe him that from this day onward you will never suffer shipwreck until you die. This has happened to you because your ship itself had been acquired through injustice.”

Immediately he ordered that a large ship be given him, filled with twenty thousand modii of grain, from those ships subject to and serving the most holy church.

After receiving it, the sailor left Alexandria. He himself affirmed and maintained:

“For twenty days and nights we sailed with a violent wind, entirely unable to know where we were going, neither by the stars nor by the landmarks. The only exception was that the helmsman saw the patriarch holding the rudder with him and saying: ‘Do not be afraid; you are sailing well.’

“Thus, after the twentieth day, we appeared at the islands of Britain. When we went ashore, we found a great famine there. When we first told the ruler of the city that we were carrying grain in the ship, he said: ‘God has brought you here well. Choose whatever you wish: either one coin for each modius, or tin of the same weight.’

“We therefore chose half one way and half the other.”

What follows is incredible and unbelievable to those without experience of God’s gifts, but credible and acceptable to those who have experienced his miracle.

When the ship had returned joyfully to Alexandria, we rested in Pentapolis [Note: *Pentapolis.* Metaphrastes has Decapolis.]. The sailor carried some of that tin away to sell. He had an old business associate there who wanted tin of the same kind. He gave him almost fifty pounds in a sack.

The other man, wishing to test whether the material was good, melted it in a fire and found pure silver. Thinking that he himself had been tested, he returned the sack to the sailor, saying:

“May God forgive you. Did you find me dishonest toward you, that you gave me silver instead of tin as a test?”

The sailor, terrified at these words, said:

“Believe me, I regard it as tin. But if the one who made wine from water (John II), through the patriarch’s prayers, also made tin into silver, there is nothing astonishing in it. And, to convince you, come to the ship, and you will see the rest of this metal, of the same kind as what you received.”

They went aboard and found that the tin had become excellent silver.

“Do not regard this miracle as strange, friends of Christ. The one who multiplied the five loaves (John VI), and again transformed the water of Egypt into blood (Exodus VII), transformed the staff into a serpent, and changed flame into dew (Daniel III), more easily performed this glorious miracle as well, so that he might enrich his servant and show mercy to the sailor.”

## Chapter X

One Sunday, when this most holy man was going down to the church, a man approached him who had possessed extensive property. Thieves had entered his house and stripped it down to the bedding. After a thorough investigation had been made and those who had committed the deed could not be found, he was compelled by extreme poverty to appeal with great reverence to the most holy patriarch, telling him of his misfortune.

The patriarch had great compassion on him—for he had been one of the most distinguished and powerful nobles—and said into the ear of the man entrusted with the gold that he should give him fifteen pounds of gold.

As the man went to deliver this amount, the logothete [Note: *Logothete.* The old editions have *logothetae*, that is, “accountant”; the Cologne edition has “reckoner.” The Aquicinctine manuscript wrote above it: “that is, one who sets down causes and accounts.” There was a definite office of logothetes among ecclesiastical officials; more about it is found in the *Onomasticon*.] and the steward intervened. Out of diabolical influence and envy, they gave him only five pounds.

When the most honorable archbishop returned from the distribution [Note: *Distribution.* The Aquicinctine manuscript explains: “that is, distributions to the poor.”], a widow who had one son gave him in writing a certificate of a gift [Note: *Certificate of the gift.* Here *notitia* means a small written slip, as follows. Metaphrastes has the Greek *χάρτην*, “document.”] of five hundredweights of gold.

When he had received it and dismissed the honorable secret chamber, he summoned the stewards and said to them:

“How many pounds did you give to the man who approached me?”

They said:

“Lord, as your most sacred holiness ordered, fifteen pounds.”

When, through the grace dwelling within him, he realized that they were lying, he brought in the man who had received the money and asked him what he had received.

When the man said five pounds, the saint brought forth from his honorable hand the little written slip [Note: *Little written slip.* This word occurs frequently here. It means a small sheet of paper. See the *Onomasticon*.] that had been delivered to him and said to them:

“May God demand from you those other ten hundredweights as well. For if you had given fifteen pounds, as my humility instructed, the woman who brought five hundredweights would have given fifteen. And, so that I may make you certain, I shall send for the woman who brought these things.”

He sent two venerable men to summon the reverend woman who had handed him the written slip in the baptistery. He sent her this message:

“Carry with you the blessing which God sent into your heart to be offered to him, and come to my humility.”

She quickly rose and, together with the quantity of gold, seized the holy man’s feet.

When the patriarch had received the offering, prayed sufficiently over it and over her son, he said:

“I ask you, mother [Note: *I ask you, mother.* So correctly in both manuscripts and the old edition. The Cologne edition incorrectly has *nonne*. Here *nonna* means “lady.” The same word occurs elsewhere in these books; below, chapter 46, “Mother Pelagia.”], did you intend to give only this much to Christ, or something else as well?”

When she realized that the God-bearing man had recognized what she had done, she was overcome with trembling and said:

“By the holy prayers of my lord and by my holy Menna [Note: *And by my holy Menna.* I think he means Menna, the church’s steward in the time of our John, as stated above, chapter 1. Another well-known Menna was the holy martyr.], I had written fifteen hundredweights on the slip. But an hour ago, when I was standing in the assembly to give this to you, my lord, I unfolded it and read it unwillingly. I, your unworthy handmaid, had written this with my own hand, and found that ten had been erased by itself.”

Then, astonished within herself, she said:

“Clearly it is not God’s will that I give more than five.”

When the patriarch dismissed the reverend woman, the stewards who had transgressed his will fell at his feet, asking forgiveness and affirming that they would never again do anything of the kind.

## Chapter XI

The patrician Nicetas [Note: *The patrician Nicetas.* Evidently the son of Gregora, patrician of Alexandria and Pentapolis, as related in the *Miscella Historia* from Theophanes, in the first year of Heraclius, book XVIII, in Paulus Diaconus. Baronius thinks that Nicetas’ statement that the empire was under pressure refers to the following, in volume VIII, in the year of Christ 610, the third year of Pope Boniface V and the eleventh year of the emperor Heraclius. Paulus Diaconus records it in the *Miscella Historia*, book XVIII:

“ In the twelfth year of Heraclius’ reign, in April, on the fourth day, in the tenth indiction, the emperor Heraclius, after celebrating the Paschal solemnity, set out against Persia on Monday evening. Since he was pressed by financial difficulty, he borrowed money from the venerable households and also took from the great church many vessels bearing candles, together with other liturgical vessels. After melting these down, he ordered many gold and silver coins to be struck from them.”

Baronius adds that such a collection of money was not made only in Constantinople but also in other cities throughout the empire wherever anything valuable could be found. The emperor sent distinguished men as collectors into the eastern region; Nicetas the patrician was sent to Alexandria and throughout Egypt.

When he attempted to bring the money of the Alexandrian church into the treasury, he encountered opposition from John, bishop of Alexandria, who habitually distributed everything to the poor and refused to give what did not belong to him but to the poor.

Yet, with due respect to Baronius, these facts do not accord with the chronology and history of John. Paulus Diaconus places this exaction of money in the twelfth year of Heraclius, whereas Baronius places it in the eleventh year of the same emperor. But, as Baronius himself testifies in the same place, John died in the eleventh year of Heraclius.

Furthermore, both Leontius and Metaphrastes state in the Life of John that, after this dispute between John and Nicetas over money, they lived as friends, so much so that John later became the patrician’s *compater*—perhaps receiving his children from the sacred font as their sponsor. The account of Leontius and Metaphrastes itself sufficiently indicates that this dispute occurred not in John’s final year but long before.] observed the greatness of this man, filled with virtues, his openhandedness without restraint, and the way he continually provided for everyone as from a fountain.

At the instigation of certain people who imitated the devil, he approached the saint and said:

“The empire is under pressure and needs money. Since the money brought to you is distributed without restraint, give it to the empire; give it to the public treasury.”
