The patriarch remained untroubled by what had been said and answered:

“I do not think it is right, lord patrician, to give to an earthly king what has been offered to the heavenly King. But if you have judged that such a thing must be done, believe me: humble John will not give you a single coin from it. Yet behold, beneath my humble bed is Christ’s treasury; do whatever you wish.”

The patrician immediately rose, summoned his men who were to carry the money, and loaded all of it upon them, leaving only one hundredweight.

As those carrying this money went down, others came up carrying small flasks containing money sent to the patriarch from Africa. Some bore the inscription “THE BEST HONEY,” others “HONEY WITHOUT SMOKE.”

When the patrician, coming down, read the inscriptions on the flasks, he sent word to the patriarch asking him to send him some of that honey for his own use. For he knew that the patriarch did not remember evil.

The man entrusted with the little flasks went up, gave the response, and explained that the vessels contained money sent for the honey. Immediately the truly gentle shepherd sent him one small flask bearing the inscription “THE BEST HONEY,” and also gave him a written slip containing this:

“The Lord who said, ‘I will not leave you nor forsake you’ (Hebrews XIII; Joshua I) is truthful, and he is the true God. Therefore a corruptible human being cannot constrain God, who provides food and life for all. Farewell.”

He ordered those departing with the flask to tell the patrician to have it opened in his presence and to say that all the flasks he had seen being carried away had been filled with money instead of honey.

It happened, therefore, while he was sitting at table, that he was informed that the men carrying the flask and the patriarch’s written slip had arrived. When they came up and he saw only one flask, the patrician said to them:

“Tell him: ‘I believe, lord, that you retain great anger against me, since you would not send me only one.’”

When the same written slip and the seal [Note: *Seal.* The Aquicinctine manuscript explains above it: “that is, a seal.” Below, chapter 51, *to seal*; likewise, “a sealed written slip.” The word frequently occurs in various authors in this meaning, as also in the *Life of Saint Basil*, above, chapter 10. See the *Onomasticon*.] had been opened, and the money emptied out in the presence of everyone, he recognized that the other flasks he had seen were likewise full.

When he read that a corruptible human being could not constrain God, he was moved to compunction and said:

“And the Lord lives: neither will Nicetas constrain him, for he too is a sinful and corruptible human being.”

He immediately left his meal, took with him all the money he had removed from the honorable Father, the flask sent by him, and three hundredweights from his own resources. He seized the patriarch’s honorable feet, taking no one with him for his own service. Ascending in great humility, he asked him to seek forgiveness from God, as though he had been moved by the accusations of others, assuring him that even if the patriarch imposed penance upon him, he would readily accept and observe it.

The archbishop marveled at the man’s swift conversion. He made no complaint about the offense, but comforted him still more with words of consolation.

From that time onward, the love of God between the two was so firmly established that John became the patrician’s *compater*.

## Chapter XII

Just as Abraham was tested in what was expedient, so that the whole world, learning what was known to God alone—his faith—might imitate it (Gen. 22), so this memorable John was also tested. The manner of that testing became an example of benefit for his holy churches.

The matter was as follows. An immeasurable multitude of refugees from the Persians, as has already been said (above, chap. 6), arrived in Alexandria. A severe scarcity of food arose because the river Nile did not rise according to its custom. After all the gold that the patriarch possessed had been distributed, he sent and borrowed from many lovers of Christ about ten centenaria. When these too had been exhausted, while the famine still continued, and no one thereafter was willing to lend him anything—everyone fearing the persistence of the famine—and when the people whom he fed were being oppressed by necessity, while the blessed man persevered in great concern and prayer, a certain inhabitant of the city perceived the destitution and utter poverty that had surrounded that most holy man.

This man was a bigamist and desired to become a deacon of the holy Church. Because of the necessity that pressed upon the saint from every side, he wished to persuade him to consecrate him. He therefore sent him a petition containing the following—for he did not dare say such a thing to his face:

> “To the most holy and thrice-blessed Father of fathers, John, vicar of Christ: a petition and request from Cosmas [Note: [Col. 0387C] Cosmas.] The vice of simony had already become prevalent in the Alexandrian Church before John’s time. To eradicate it, Pope Gregory urges Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria, in Book XI, Letter 49, indiction 6.] the unworthy servant of the servants of your holiness.
>
> “Having learned, most holy lord, of the food shortage that has overtaken your honorable head by God’s permission—or rather, on account of our sins—I, your servant, did not consider it right to live in abundance while my lord remained in poverty [Note: [Col. 0387C] Poverty.] The printed editions have subtilitate, meaning ‘thinness’ and ‘poverty.’ The same meaning occurs below, chap. 38.].
>
> “Your unworthy servant therefore possesses two hundred thousand measures of grain and one hundred eighty pounds of gold. I ask that they be given to Christ through you, my lord, provided only that I, unworthy as I am, may deserve to enjoy your diaconate in the ministry, so that through such service with you, the lord of the holy altar, he may cleanse me from the wantonness of my sins. For the holy Apostle, the true preacher of God, says: ‘For of necessity there is also a change of the law’ (Heb. 7).”

The divinely wise man received this petition and summoned the man. He said to him:

“Are you the one who sent us these prayers through your notary and son?”

When he replied, “Yes, lord,” the blessed and most merciful man sent everyone else out, unwilling to shame him before them, and began to say:

“Your offering is indeed very just and necessary for the present time, but it is blemished. You know that under the Law no sheep, whether small or large, was offered as a sacrifice unless it was unblemished (Lev. 22); and therefore God did not regard Cain’s sacrifice (Gen. 4).

“But since you said, brother, that ‘of necessity there is also a change of the law,’ the Apostle says this concerning the Old Law. For how does the brother of the Lord, James, say that whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all of it (Jas. 2)?

“As for my needy brothers and the holy Church, God, who nourished them before either you or I were born, will himself nourish them now as well—provided only that we preserve his words unharmed. For he who then multiplied the five loaves (John 6) can also bless the ten measures of my granary [Col. 0350D].

“Therefore I say to you, son, what was said in the Acts of the Apostles: ‘You have neither part nor inheritance in this matter’ (Acts 8).”

After he had dismissed the man sorrowful and without result, it was announced to him that two great Church ships had been sent to land. He had dispatched them to Sicily for grain.

When the blessed man heard this, he fell to the ground and gave thanks to almighty God, saying:

“I give you thanks, Lord, because you did not permit your servant to sell your grace for money. Truly, those who seek you, Lord, and keep the regulations of your holy Church, will not lack any good thing (Ps. 33).”

## Chapter XIII

When two clerics fell into fault—that is, when they laid hands on one another—the patriarch excommunicated them canonically for several days. One of them willingly accepted the reprimand and acknowledged his fault; the other, being malicious, accepted the sentence with joy. The wretch was looking for an excuse not to enter the church, so that he might have permission to persist in his wicked deeds. He was angry with the holy patriarch and threatened, insofar as he was able, to harm him.

Some said that he himself was the man who had betrayed the Church’s money to the patrician Nicetas (above, chap. 11), money which he had also seized with his own hand, as has been related.

It was therefore reported that this man, mindful of his evil, was preserving his malice and did not have a right disposition toward the blessed patriarch. But the patriarch, truly a shepherd, remembering the saying, “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. 11), and again, “You who are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak” (Gal. 6; Rom. 15), wished to summon him, admonish him appropriately, and release him from excommunication. For he saw the wolf trying to snatch away the sheep.

By God’s providence, however, it became known to everyone that the patriarch bore no resentment. He forgot to summon the man and release him from excommunication.

When the holy Sunday arrived and he had taken his place at the holy altar [Note: [Col. 0387C] “And had taken his place at the holy altar.” In Greek, in Metaphrastes: Αὐτὸς δὲ τῷ βήματι παραστάς. Hervetus translated this: “But when he himself was standing in the tribunal, or rather at the altar”; for in Greek sacred usage βῆμα is understood in this way.], in order to offer the unbloody sacrifice, and the deacon was nearly finished with the general prayer and was about to raise the holy veil [Note: [Col. 0387C] “Was about to raise the holy veil.” Metaphrastes is clearer: Κατ᾽ αὐτὴν τὴν ὥραν, ἐν ᾗ τὸ ἱερὸν καταπέτασμα τῶν θειων ἀφαιρεῖται δώρων: “At that very hour when the sacred veil is removed from the holy gifts.” Thus also in William the Librarian, *Lives of the Popes*, chap. 112, concerning Stephen VI, one finds *velothera* around the altar: “In that same basilica of the apostles James and Philip he presented one linen curtain and three silk *velothera* around the altar.” The same work frequently mentions veils around altars.], he remembered his forgotten malice. Immediately recalling the divine command that says, “If you bring your gift to the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there,” and so forth (Matt. 5), he signaled to the deacon who was saying the prayer customarily said by the deacon that he should begin again from the beginning [Note: [Col. 0387D] “He signaled to the deacon who was saying the prayer customarily said by the deacon that he should begin again from the beginning.” Metaphrastes has: Δηλοῖ τῷ διακόνῳ τὴν συναπτὴν αἴτησιν ἐπαναλαβεῖν: “He signifies to the deacon that he should resume the connected petition.” Anastasius the translator seems to have read συνήθην, “customary,” instead of συναπτήν. Unless he was rather acting as a paraphrast. For συναπτή was the prayer customarily said by the deacon, which was also called διακονικά; perhaps this was the Greek reading here. See the *Euchologium* concerning both terms.]; and, when it had been completed, to recapitulate it again, until he reached the sanctification.

He pretended that he had been compelled by a need of the stomach. He went into the honorable *cimiliarchium* [Note: [Col. 0387D] *Cimiliarchium.* It occurs again below, chap. 46. The printed editions have *cimiliarcium*, meaning “the principal secretariat,” and this was likewise written above the word in the Aquicinctine manuscript. Properly, Greek κειμηλιαρχεῖον, *cimeliarchium*, is a wardrobe or archive of treasures, where the ornaments and gifts of the Church were stored. Anastasius the Librarian, *Lives of the Popes*, chap. 72, concerning Severinus: “They sealed the entire wardrobe of the church, or the treasures of the bishopric, which various most Christian emperors, patricians, and consuls had left to the blessed apostle Peter for the redemption of their souls.” William the Librarian calls these treasures of the wardrobes “the wealth of the wardrobes” in *Lives of the Popes*, chap. 112, concerning Stephen VI: “What wonder if he found the wealth of the wardrobes removed, when, searching the sanctuaries, he found almost nothing of the many gifts and ornaments of the churches?”], and immediately sent nearly twenty attendants to look for the aforementioned ill-behaved cleric [Note: [Col. 0388A] “Ill-behaved cleric.” The Aquicinctine manuscript explains this by writing above it: “that is, one who has bad manners.” The Greek may have been κακότροπον.].

The shepherd’s intention was to lead the sheep out of the lion’s mouth. But God, who fulfills the will of those who fear him, caused the cleric to be found immediately at hand.

When he came and bore witness to the truth, the patriarch first bent his knee and said:

“Forgive me, brother.”

The cleric, fearing the honorable pontiff and the presence of those who were there, but more especially fearing God’s judgment and dreading lest fire should perhaps descend from heaven at that very hour and consume him, saw that venerable gray head lying on the ground. He too bent his knee, asking pardon and mercy.

When the patriarch said, “May God forgive us all,” they rose and entered the church together. Then the cleric stood beside the holy altar with great joy and gladness, possessing a clean conscience and able to say to God: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6).

From that time onward the reader became so sound and contrite in mind that he deserved to obtain ordination to the priesthood.

## Chapter XIV

Certain God-bearing holy Fathers [Note: [Col. 0388A] “Certain holy Fathers who bore God.” I have not yet discovered whose saying this is.] said:

“It belongs to angels never to quarrel, but to remain in complete and perpetual peace; it belongs to human beings to quarrel, but immediately to be reconciled; it belongs to demons to quarrel and to pass the entire day unreconciled.”

We have prefaced the present account with this saying, lovers of Christ.

On one occasion this noble man became involved in a dispute with the aforementioned patrician Nicetas over a public matter. The dispute was conducted as follows; since the matter is useful for the soul, it must be related.

The patrician wished to arrange the marketplace for the sake of public profits, whereas the patriarch would not permit it, seeking thereby to protect the welfare of the poor. After contending much and privately against each other [Note: [Col. 0388B] “After contending much and privately against each other.” The printed editions have: “contending before the secretary.” The Gemblac manuscript has: “contending sharply against each other.” The Aquicinctine manuscript has: “contending before the secret council.”], and remaining inflexible, they both withdrew from one another angry and unreconciled.

It was the fifth hour. The patriarch’s opposition and bitterness were on account of God’s command, whereas the patrician’s were on account of financial profits. Nevertheless, the just man said:

“A person ought to become angry neither for a reasonable nor for an unreasonable cause.”

When the eleventh hour arrived, the patriarch sent the patrician, through the archpriest and the clergy, this memorable word:

“Lord, the sun is setting.”

When the patrician heard this, he could not endure the burning of his heart. As though inflamed by divine fire, he was pierced by the saint’s words, and immediately became completely covered with tears. He rose and came to the blessed patriarch.

When he saw him, the patriarch said:

“You have come well, son of the Church, obeying its voice” (Eph. 4).

Both then performed *metanoia* [Note: [Col. 0388B] “Both performing *metanoia*.” The printed editions add: “that is, repentance or acknowledgment.” I have already explained what βάλλειν μετάνοιαν means in the *Life of Saint Basil*, chap. 11, no. 54. Below, chap. 35: “And making prostrations.”], and, embracing one another, sat down.

The patriarch opened his mouth and said:

“Believe me, lord: if I had not seen you greatly troubled by this matter, I would not have been slow to come to your dignity. For the Lord and our God himself went around cities, villages, and houses, visiting people.”

When everyone had been edified and filled with admiration by the humility of the high priest, the patrician replied:

“Believe me, Father, henceforth my ears will no longer receive the words of those who bring me contentious matters.”

Then the wise teacher said to him:

“Believe me, son and brother: if we choose to believe all such people, we shall become responsible for many sins, especially at this time, when many people have become haters of one another.

“Many times those who brought me reports about the administration of affairs also tried to persuade me. When I had often brought a matter to an end because I had been misled, afterward others would tell me that I had been deceived in the matter. When I had suffered this a second and a third time, I set a rule for myself: I would take neither side, lest I issue a judgment concerning the matter.

“If those who brought me the reports were lying, they themselves would pay the penalty that the accused would have borne if the accusation against him had truly been made.

“From that same day no one has dared to bring me an ill-considered report against anyone, and I ask and admonish your great dignity, son, to act similarly. For those who hold entrusted authority often inflict unjust killings if they are moved by persuasive words and rashly cut off those who come before them.”

The patrician, as though commanded by God, promised that he would preserve the patriarch’s command unharmed at all times.

## Chapter XV

This memorable man had a nephew named George [Note: [Col. 0388B] “George.” Both manuscripts read this, and so does Metaphrastes. The Cologne edition has “Gregory.” Baronius, vol. 8, year of Christ 620, the third year of Pope Boniface V and the eleventh of the emperor Heraclius, because in Nicephorus’s *Chronicle* John George follows in the Alexandrian episcopate, supposes that this was the same John’s cousin, of whom we are speaking here. He adds the reason for his conjecture: that formerly it had been customary in the Alexandrian Church for a relative of bishops who had been more distinguished and had adorned that Church to be elected as successor after their death, as we saw in the case of Cyril, nephew of Theophilus, who was appointed in his place (Baronius, chap. 4, year 412). Thus far Baronius. I very much doubt that George could at that time have been John’s nephew and have been able to serve as bishop of Alexandria, since in this chapter we find him weeping like a boy or adolescent.].

One day, while this man was quarreling with a certain shopkeeper of the city, the shopkeeper severely abused him. George was deeply grieved, not only because the insult had been public, and not only because he had been dishonored by an inferior, but especially because he was the patriarch’s nephew. He went to the patriarch in his private chamber while the patriarch was alone, weeping bitterly.

When the gentlest patriarch saw him so agitated and tearful, he asked the cause of the anxiety that was holding him, wishing to know it. Since George could not utter a word because of the bitterness that surrounded him, those who had been present when the shopkeeper dishonored him began to relate the matter to the archbishop:

“Your holiness ought not to have been treated with such contempt,” they said, “as to allow your own relatives and kin to be dishonored by contemptible men.”

But the true physician, wishing first to treat his nephew’s fury as though with a poultice, yet also wishing, like a surgeon’s knife, to bring incision and release from the affliction through his most wise mouth, began to extinguish the disease with such words:

“Did anyone actually dare to open his mouth and contradict you? Believe me, my son: today I shall do something to him that all Alexandria will marvel at.”

When he saw that George had received the remedy and cast off all his sadness—thinking, of course, that the patriarch would act against the man who had insulted him, have him flogged by the official appointed over the marketplace, and dishonor him with various public humiliations—the patriarch kissed his breast and said:

“My son, if you are truly my nephew by reason of the humility I possess, prepare yourself both to be flogged and to suffer abuse from everyone. True kinship is recognized not from blood and flesh but from the virtue of the mind.”

He immediately summoned the official appointed over the tavernkeepers and ordered him to accept from that tavernkeeper neither his customary dues, nor public dues, nor the rent of his workshop. For he himself belonged to the most holy Church.

Everyone was astonished at the patriarch’s immovable patience and understood the meaning of his words, “I shall do something to him that all Alexandria will marvel at”: he not only failed to return the insult but even provided assistance in place of vengeance.

## Chapter XVI

It was once reported to this blessed man that a certain cleric was preserving malice in his heart against another and remained unreconciled to him. The patriarch asked to know the man’s name and rank.

On the following day, a Sunday, he learned that the man’s name was Damian and that his office was that of deacon. He therefore ordered the archdeacon to point Damian out to him when he came to the church.

When the Sunday station was held on the following day, the deacon also came to the station. The archdeacon saw him and pointed him out to the patriarch. The pontiff was standing at the holy altar solely because of this dispute; he had confided to no one what he intended to do.

When the deacon Damian came to receive holy Communion from him according to his rank, the saint took hold of his hand and said:

“Go first and be reconciled to your brother; then return and worthily receive the immaculate mysteries of Christ, forgetting the malice.”

Out of reverence, and unwilling to contradict him before such a great multitude of clerics, especially in such a place and at such a dreadful hour, Damian promised to do this. The patriarch then gave him the holy mysteries.

From that time onward all the clerics and laypeople guarded themselves against retaining malice among themselves, fearing that the patriarch might expose them and triumph over them as he had over that deacon.

## Chapter XVII

This most holy man possessed knowledge of the divine Scriptures, but he did not recite them from memory as though through empty eloquence and vainglory. Rather, he embodied them through the very practice of good works and observance of the commandments.

In the privacy of his daily counsel no idle speech was heard, unless perhaps the administration of a civic matter required it. Otherwise there were reports about the holy Fathers, questions from Scripture, or doctrinal problems, because of the multitude of heretics—too numerous even to name—who surrounded the region.

If anyone began to slander another, the patriarch, as a wise man, cleverly removed him through another conversation. If the man persisted, he said nothing to him, but marked him down and ordered the weekly attendant not to allow him to enter again with those who brought reports, so that through him he might restrain and instruct the others.

## Chapter XVIII

Another determination that this saint desired must not rightly be omitted.

He had heard that after an emperor had been crowned [Note: [Col. 0388C] “After an emperor had been crowned.” I do not remember reading this expression elsewhere as a customary thing said when an emperor was crowned. John the Almsgiver deliberately imitated it, and after him others devised something not unlike it. The emperor Maximilian I furnished a notable example. When he disliked the palace being built at Innsbruck, he declared that he would build another house that would please him more. On that day he secretly ordered a sarcophagus prepared with all funeral furnishings, carried it with him on all his journeys, and ordered it to be preserved most carefully every night. Most courtiers thought that some treasure was being kept there; others thought it contained books relating ancient history. The emperor, smiling, said that he carried it for the use of something he held most dear. Thus reports Reinhard Lorichius Hadamarius. In former times, however, the priest Philoromus of Galatia is said to have lived for six years in the tombs of the dead in order to overcome his fear of death. Palladius, chap. 113; Heraclides, chap. 32.]

When no one from the entire senate or among the attending armies announced any ancient memorial, but those called builders of monuments immediately took four or five tiny pieces of marble of different colors, entered the emperor’s presence, and said, “Lord, of what material does your empire command that your monument be made?”—thereby suggesting that, since he was a corruptible and transitory human being, he should care for his own soul and govern the kingdom piously—this blessed man truly imitated that praiseworthy tradition.

He ordered a monument to be built for himself where his predecessors, the patriarchs, also lay. He ordered it to remain unfinished until his death, so that, while it was incomplete, during a solemn festival and in the presence of the clergy, those who were called the *studiosi* [Note: [Col. 0388D] *Studiosi.* I cannot determine what the Greek reading was here. Σπουδαῖοι corresponds to the Latin word. But who were these *studiosi*? Metaphrastes has: “Those who were appointed over the work.”] would enter and say to him:

“Lord, your monument is unfinished. Therefore command that it be completed, since you do not know at what hour the thief will come” (Matt. 24).

The holy man did this so that he might leave behind a good example for the patriarchs who would come after him.

## Chapter XIX

When the Lord permitted, on account of our many sins, the temples at Jerusalem to be burned by the Persians whom God was allowing to strike them, this most holy patriarch learned that the holy Modestus, patriarch of Jerusalem, was in great poverty [Note: [Col. 0388D] “The holy Modestus, patriarch of Jerusalem.” This should be read according to the Aquicinctine manuscript. The old and Cologne editions have “the holy and modest [man].” Antiochus the monk, of the Laura of Sabbas the Abbot, who lived at this time, frequently mentions this Modestus in his letter to Eustathius, provost of the monastery of Datalena in the city of Ancyra in Galatia, found in Antiochus’s *Pandect*. The following passage is relevant:

> “Modestus, a man of outstanding holiness—of whom mention has been made more than once—not only takes vigilant care of the monasteries scattered and dispersed throughout this vast wilderness, but also diligently oversees the administration of this city and the entire surrounding region, God cooperating with him in all things. For he vividly presents to us the image of a new Bezalel, or certainly a Zerubbabel. Full of the grace of the Holy Spirit, he raises up the temples of our Savior Jesus Christ, which were consumed by barbarian fire, to a height worthy of all reverence: the churches of holy Calvary and the holy Resurrection, as well as the house worthy of every honor, the venerable Cross, which is the mother of the churches. He also rebuilt from its foundations the church of the holy Assumption, so that from these joyful beginnings we may conceive the greatest hopes for the future—especially because of those expected to come here from foreign regions to worship these holy places—and so that together we may all glorify God.”

Baronius and other authors place Modestus as presiding over the Church of Jerusalem. The *Acts of Anastasius the Persian*, January 22, says: “He reports this to Modestus, who presided over the apostolic see.” Suidas, under “Heraclius,” says:

> Ηἰς τὰ Ἱεροσόλυμα ἀφίκετο, καὶ Μοδέστῳ ἀρχιερεῖ καὶ τῷ αὐτοῦ κλήρῳ ταῦτα ὑπέδειξεν.
>
> “He went to Jerusalem and showed these things to Modestus the pontiff and his clergy.”

The Greek *Menaea* assign his feast day to November 16 and call him Ἱεροσολύμων ἀρχιεπίσκοπον, “archbishop of Jerusalem.”

Baronius, vol. 8, year of Christ 616, the second year of Pope Deusdedit and the seventh of the emperor Heraclius, says that because Zacharias was still alive no other bishop of Jerusalem was admitted, since it was not permitted for two bishops to be in the same place. Yet, on account of the episcopal administration, Modestus was called prefect of Jerusalem while Zacharias was still alive, as in the *Acts of the holy martyr Anastasius*, where his baptism after Zacharias’s return is said to have been administered at Jerusalem by Modestus.

In truth, even if he was not a bishop, Modestus administered that church in the place of a bishop until Zacharias returned, restoring everything. Paul the Deacon mentions this disaster at Jerusalem, during which the pontiff Zacharias was also carried away, in Book XVIII of his *History*:

> “In the fifth year of the reign of Heraclius, the Persians conquered the Jordan in war, as well as Palestine and the holy city, and killed many there at the hands of the Jews—ninety thousand, as some say. For these men, buying Christians according to what each person could afford, killed them. They captured Zacharias, bishop of Jerusalem, and carried him into Persia together with the precious and life-giving wood and much booty.”]

To relieve and rebuild these places, he sent him one thousand coins, one thousand sacks full of grain, one thousand [units] of legumes, one thousand pounds of iron, one thousand strings of dried fish called *menomenae* [Note: [Col. 0389C] “One thousand strings of dried fish, called *menomenae*.” [Col. 0389D] From this word for a string on which dried fish and garlic are fastened, I think that even today the vernacular has *een rist* or *rest buckingh*, “a string of herring,” and *een rist aiupn*, “a string of onions.” I think *menomenae* are what Pliny, Book 32, chap. 11, calls *maenae*.], one thousand vessels of wine, and one thousand Egyptian laborers. He sent him a letter saying:

> “Forgive me, true laborer for Christ, for I am sending nothing worthy of Christ’s temples. Believe me, I wish—if it were fitting—to come there myself and work myself on the house of the holy Resurrection of Christ.
>
> “Nevertheless, I ask your honorable head not to attribute this in any way to the insignificance of my poverty, but rather to ask Christ to enroll me there where the blessed enrollment truly exists.”

## Chapter XX

The saint also took this upon himself—I mean the good practice of lying on the lowest bedding and using cheap coverings in his cell.

When a certain wealthy citizen heard of this, he went up to him. Seeing that he was covered with a worn woolen blanket, he sent him a covering worth thirty-six coins and earnestly asked him to cover himself with it, “in memory,” he said, “of the one who sent it.”

The patriarch accepted it because of the man’s great entreaty and covered himself with it for one night. For nearly the whole night, as his chamberlains reported, he kept saying to himself:

“Who will say that humble John”—for he always had this word in his mouth—“is covered with a cloak worth thirty-six coins while the brothers of Christ are dying from the cold? How many are now chattering their teeth from frost? How many now have half a mat beneath them and half above them, and cannot stretch out their feet, but sleep trembling like a ball [Note: [Col. 0389D] “Trembling like a ball.” This is how both the printed editions and the Gemblac manuscript read; but the Aquicinctine manuscript has “like a ball, dragging themselves along.”]?

“How many have slept on the mountain without food and without a lamp, suffering a double torment from both cold and fasting? How many desire to be filled with the leaves of vegetables thrown out from my kitchen? How many would like to dip their bread into the *zemate* [Note: [Col. 0389D] *Zemate.* The Aquicinctine manuscript has this reading and writes above it: “that is, the wastewater in which meats are boiled, or yeast or dregs.” The Gemblac manuscript has *zimate*. The printed editions have *schemate*, incorrectly. See the *Onomasticon*.] that my cooks throw away?

“How many long even to smell the wine that is poured out in my wine cellar? How many strangers are in this city at this hour, having nowhere to lodge, lying in the marketplace, perhaps soaked by rain? How many, do you think, go an entire month, or even two, without tasting oil?

“How many do not have one garment for summer and another for winter, and are thus tormented by misery? Yet you, while expecting to attain eternal joy, drink wine, devour enormous fish, and linger in your chambers; and now, together with all your other evils, you warm yourself beneath a covering worth thirty-six coins?

“Living truly in this way and behaving with such indulgence, you will not expect to enjoy the joys prepared there. Rather, you will certainly hear what that rich man heard: ‘You received your good things during your life, and the poor received evil things; now they are comforted, but you are tormented’ (Luke 16).”

Blessed God! Humble John would not cover himself with that covering the next night. For it is just and pleasing to God that one hundred forty-four brothers and your lords should be covered rather than you, wretched man.

Four *rachanellae* were being sold for one coin [Note: [Col. 0389D] *Rachanellae.* Both manuscripts have this reading, and the Aquicinctine manuscript writes above it: “that is, little pieces of cloth.” The printed editions have *recunellae*, incorrectly. *Rachanellae* is formed from *rachanae*, as they are called below, chap. 26. I think both words are ῥάκη. See the *Onomasticon*.]. He therefore immediately sent the covering away the next day to be sold.

The man who had offered it, seeing it, bought it for thirty-six coins and again offered it to the patriarch. When he saw it on the following day, he likewise bought it and again offered it to the patriarch, asking that he cover himself with it.

When the man had done this a third time, the saint said to him cheerfully:

“We shall see who gives out first—you or I.”

The man was extremely wealthy, and the saint was gently harvesting him, gradually taking much from him. He always said that someone could strip the rich by the intention of giving to the poor without sinning, especially if the rich were merciless and greedy.

Such a person gains two things: first, he saves their souls; second, he himself receives no small reward from it.

He brought forward as confirmation of his statement the true testimony of what happened concerning Saint Epiphanius and John, who became bishop of Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0390A] “What happened concerning Saint Epiphanius and John.” See the *Life of Saint Epiphanius*, January 10.]: Saint Epiphanius, by a stratagem, took money from the patriarch—namely, that same John—and gave it to the needy.

## CHAPTER XXI

The following account, appropriate and fitting for the chapter just mentioned, this holy man once related before everyone:

“I had,” he said, “a certain servant in my warehouse in Cyprus, a man of great fidelity and a virgin until his death. He told me that, while I was in Africa, the following incident occurred.

“‘I was staying with a tax collector who was exceedingly wealthy and merciless. Once, in winter, some poor people were sitting in the sun and warming themselves. One by one they began praising the houses of those who gave alms and praying for each of them; likewise, they condemned the houses of those who gave no alms. In the midst of this conversation the name of my master, the tax collector, was mentioned. Each began asking his neighbor: “Really, brother, have you ever received a blessing from that house?” As they questioned one another, no one was found who had ever received anything from his house.

“‘Then one of them said: “What will you give me if I obtain a blessing from him today?” They made an agreement with him, and he went and stood outside the door of the house, waiting for the man to return home. By God’s providence they arrived at the same time: the tax collector was entering the gate with a pack animal carrying rye loaves from a bakery [Note: **From a bakery.** That is, from a bread oven. This is known to only a few. See the *Onomasticon*.], for his meal.

“‘When he saw the poor man, and finding no stone, in his fury he seized a rye loaf from the pack saddle and threw it into the man’s face. The poor man received it and went away to satisfy his fellow brothers that he had received a gift from those very hands.

“‘Two days later the tax collector fell ill with a fatal sickness. In a dream he saw himself giving an account and weighing all his deeds on a balance. On one side [Note: **On one side.** Does this mean the pan of a balance? Or did the Greek have *phalanx* (φάλαγξ), an ambiguous word that signifies both a balance and a battle line? See the *Onomasticon*.] were gathered certain misshapen Ethiopians; on the other side stood others, white-robed and terrifying in appearance. Since they found nothing good to place on the opposite side against the evil deeds that the Ethiopians were collecting on their side, they were greatly troubled and saddened, and were dismayed among themselves. They said: “So then, do we have nothing here?”

“‘One of them replied: “Indeed, we have nothing except one rye loaf, which he gave to Christ two days ago—and even that unwillingly.”

“‘When they placed the flour on the balance, equilibrium was established. Then those who had appeared to him in white garments said to the tax collector: “Go and add to this rye loaf, for these Ethiopians will certainly seize you.”

“‘Wailing, he recognized that what he had seen was not false but true. All the deeds he had committed from his youth, and of which he himself had forgotten, he saw those Ethiopians gather and carry to the scales. He said: “Alas!” [Note: **Alas!** Older printed editions have *ve ve*; the Cologne edition has *Papae!* (“Good heavens!”).] “If one portion of flour that I threw in anger was of such benefit, from how many evils does the person free himself who sincerely gives his possessions to the needy?”

“‘From that time onward he became so moderate, prudent, and outstandingly charitable that he did not even spare his own body.

“It once happened that, according to custom, he went early in the morning to the customs house. A sailor met him who had escaped naked, as he was born, from a shipwreck. He fell before him and begged him to obtain protection for him. Thinking that the man was needy, the tax collector removed his own *esophorium* [Note: **Esophorium.** The Aquicinctus manuscript explains it as an inner garment, called an *interula*, or a garment fastened at the neck. See the *Onomasticon*.], which was the better garment, and gave it to him, asking him to wear it himself.

“But the man went away, ashamed to wear it, and gave it to a merchant to sell. As the tax collector was leaving, he saw the garment hanging there and was exceedingly saddened. He went up to his house and would not taste anything. Closing the door of his room, he sat weeping and thinking: “I was not worthy,” he said, “that the poor man should remember me.”

“As he was distressed, he fell asleep. Then he saw someone beautiful, like the sun, carrying a cross above his head and wearing the *esophorium* that he had given to the sailor. The figure stood beside him and said: “Why are you weeping, Lord Peter?” For that was his name.

“He replied, as though arguing with God: “Because, Lord, from what you lavish upon us we give to others, and those who receive it turn it into shameful profit.”

“The figure then said to him: “Do you recognize this?” He showed him that he was clothed beneath with Peter’s *esophorium*. He said to him: “Look, I am wearing the garment with which you clothed me when you gave it to me; and I give thanks for your good will, because I was suffering from the cold and you covered me.”

“Returning to himself, Peter was astonished. He began to call the poor blessed and to say: “The Lord lives! If my Christ is among the needy, I shall not die; I shall become like one of them.”

“He summoned his notary, whom he had also purchased, and said to him: “I wish to entrust a secret to you. Believe me: if you reveal me, I shall sell you to the barbarians—or, if you do not obey me, I shall do so.”

“He gave him ten pounds of gold and said: “Go and purchase a business for yourself. Then take me and lead me to the holy city, sell me to any Christian, and give the price to the poor.”

“When the notary refused, he said to him again: “If you do not sell me, I shall sell you to the barbarians, as I told you.”

“The notary obeyed him. When they reached the holy places, the notary found a dear friend of his, a silversmith who had suffered losses. When the two came together to speak, the notary said to him: “Listen to me, Zoilus, and buy a slave. I have one so good that people would say he was a patrician.”

“When the silversmith heard that he had a slave, he was astonished and said: “Believe me, I have no means with which to buy one.”

“The notary replied: “Borrow the money and buy him. He is exceedingly good, and God will bless you through him.”

“He agreed, and bought Peter, dressed in filthy clothing, for thirty coins. The notary then left him and went to Constantinople, fulfilling his promise not to reveal the matter to anyone and not to retain or defraud himself of any part of the price, but to give it all to the poor.

“Peter sometimes cooked for his master and sometimes washed his clothes, although he had never been accustomed to any such work. He also afflicted himself with much fasting. When his master saw that he was being blessed beyond all blessing, he said to him, ashamed before his immense virtue and humility: “I wish, humble Peter, to set you free, so that henceforth you may be my brother.”

“But Peter refused. His master often saw him endure insults and be beaten by his fellow servants. They regarded him as mad, so much so that they gave him the name ‘The Madman.’

“Whenever his fellow servants troubled him and he fell asleep amid his tribulation, the man who had appeared to him in Africa appeared to him again, clothed in his *esophorium* and holding the thirty coins in his hand. He said to him: “Do not be sad, brother Peter. I have received both you and your price; endure until you are recognized.”

“After some time, certain silver merchants from his homeland came to pray at the holy places. Peter’s master invited them to dinner. While Peter was serving them, he immediately recognized them. As they were dining, they began looking closely at him and whispering to one another: “How much this boy resembles the tax collector Peter!”

“He concealed his face as much as he could. Again, while they were eating, they began saying to their host: “We think, Lord Zoilus, that something great has happened to you. Unless we are mistaken, you have a distinguished person serving you.” They did not know for certain, since his face had been altered by kitchen work and fasting.

“After studying him for a long time, one of them said: “It really is Lord Peter. I shall rise and seize him. The emperor is very displeased when he hears of him, because he has not appeared for a long time.”

“Peter, standing outside, heard this. He set down the dish and did not go inside, but ran directly to the gate. The doorkeeper of the house where he was staying had been mute and deaf from birth, though he opened and closed the door by signs.

“As the servant of God hurried out, he said to the deaf and mute man: “I speak to you in the name of Christ.”

“The man immediately heard and said: “Yes, my lord.”

“Peter said to him again: “Open.”

“The deaf and mute man answered a second time: “I, my lord.”

“He immediately rose and opened the door for him. When Peter had gone out, the doorkeeper went inside and cried out before everyone, rejoicing and exulting because he had heard and spoken: “Lord, Lord!”

“All who were in the house were terrified, because they heard him speaking. Then the man who had formerly been mute said again: “The one who cooked in the kitchen has run out, but see to it that he has not escaped by flight. He is a great servant of God.

“When he was leaving, he said to me: “I speak to you in the name of the Lord.” At once I saw a flame come out of his mouth and touch my ears; immediately I heard and spoke.”

Then all rushed out and followed him, but they did not see him again. Everyone in that house repented, including the master who had purchased Peter, because they had humiliated him so greatly—especially those who called him “The Madman.”

These are the accounts of the most blessed John, patriarch honored by God. He was not content merely to edify those who wished to advance through his own life; he also did so through the true accounts he had received from God. He always said to those who heard them:

“If some people did not spare their own blood, but gave it into the hands of their brothers—indeed, of Christ—how do you think that we ought, with eagerness and humility, to give our possessions to Christ and to the needy and poor, so that we may receive recompense from God, the just giver and rewarder, on that fearful and dreadful day of reckoning?

“Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly; and whoever sows with blessings—that is, generously and magnanimously—will also reap abundantly (II Cor. IX). That is, he will inherit those good things that surpass every mind.”

## CHAPTER XXII

This holy man was adorned with every upright virtue, and he also possessed the following quality: he greatly loved speaking about the deeds of the holy Fathers and of those who practiced almsgiving.

One day, therefore, while he was reading about the life of Saint Serapion, who was called “the Linen-Clad,” he found that Serapion, as the story tells, had given his cloak to a poor man (Palladius, chapter 83). After proceeding a little farther, he met another man suffering from cold and gave him his tunic. Since Serapion was sitting naked, holding the holy Gospel, someone asked him: “Abba, who stripped you?”

Pointing to the holy Gospel, he replied: “This one.”

On another occasion he sold that same Gospel and gave the proceeds as alms. When his disciple said to him: “Abba, where is the Gospel?” he answered: “Believe me, son, the one who said to me, ‘Sell what you have and give to the poor’ (Matt. XIII), I sold it and gave the proceeds to them, so that on the day of judgment we may have greater confidence before God.”

On yet another occasion, a widow came to the same Saint Serapion and asked him for alms, because her children were hungry. Since he had absolutely nothing, he surrendered himself to her, so that she might sell him to Greek actors. He converted them to Christianity within a few days.

When the holy man read this about Saint Serapion, he was astonished and amazed at the saint’s resourcefulness. Entirely covered in tears, he summoned all his stewards, read the whole account of Saint Serapion to them, and said:

“Alas, lovers of Christ! What benefit is there for a person in speaking about the deeds of the holy Fathers? Believe me: until today I thought that I was doing at least something by giving whatever money I could possess. I did not know, however, that they even sold themselves, overcome by a certain compassion.”

## CHAPTER XXIII

This holy man always honored, revered, and pitied the monastic habit, especially when he saw a monk distressed by bodily necessities. He also possessed this outstanding quality above many others: he would not accept any accusation against anyone clothed in the monastic habit, whether the accusation was true or false.

Once, however, through the instigation of certain accusers, something of the following kind occurred. A monk was going about the city with a young girl and asking for alms for several days. Some people who had seen this were scandalized and supposed that the woman was his wife. They brought complaints against him to the patriarch, saying:

“Why, O one honored by God, does such a man dishonor the angelic form of monastic life by having a girl as his wife?”

The servant of God immediately thought that he was preventing sins committed against God, as though he had been promoted by God for this purpose. He ordered the woman to be beaten with lashes and separated from the monk, and ordered the monk himself to be scourged and shut up in a secret prison.

While the holy man’s command was being carried out with all speed, a monk appeared to him at night in a vision. He showed him his back, which was covered with wounds and festering—for the defenders of the Church had not spared him—and said:

“Does this please you, lord patriarch? On this one occasion you have erred as a human being. Believe me, life and death are near at hand.”

Having said this, he departed from him.

When morning came, the blessed patriarch remembered the vision of the night and sat sorrowfully on his bed. He immediately sent his chancellor to summon the monk from the place where he was confined. The blessed patriarch was thinking within himself whether the monk was like the one who had appeared to him during the night.

When the monk arrived after much difficulty—for he could not move because of the wounds—and the patriarch saw his face, he remained speechless and motionless, unable to speak. With his hand alone he indicated that the monk should sit near him on his little bed.

Coming to himself and making the sign of the cross, he asked the monk, who was girded with a linen cloth, to undress without embarrassment, so that he could see whether his back was as he had seen it in the dream.

The monk was scarcely persuaded to do this, but he undressed. When he was undressing in order to show his back to the holy man, by God’s wondrous providence the garment he was wearing came undone and fell to the ground. Everyone saw that he was a eunuch. Since this had only recently occurred, no one had known it.

When everyone, and especially the holy bishop, saw the grievous wounds on his back, the patriarch immediately sent for those who had treated him so recklessly and separated them from the monk. He spoke at length with the most venerable monk, acknowledging in his ignorance that he had sinned both against him and against the true God.

The holy man then admonished him:

“No, son. Those who are clothed in your holy angelic garment ought not to live so carelessly in the cities, especially by leading a woman about and becoming a scandal to those who see them.”

Then the monk humbly gave the holy man an account, saying:

“Believe me, lord, I am not lying. A few days ago I was in Gaza. When I was leaving the city to go and greet the holy abbot Cyrus [Note: **And to greet the holy abbot Cyrus.** Metaphrastes gives a fuller account: “to worship the saints Cyrus and John.” Their memory was celebrated in Alexandria, and a church was also dedicated to them. See above, chapter 1, note 9.], this well-looking girl met me outside the gate as evening was approaching. She ran to my feet and begged to travel with me. She said that she was a Hebrew and wished to become a Christian. She began telling me the matter in dreadful words, so that I might not allow her to perish.

“Fearing, therefore, the judgment of God, I took her with me, thinking that Satan would not cast temptation upon eunuchs. I did not know that he spares no one.

“When we arrived, most holy Father, and had completed our prayer, I baptized her at the shrine of the holy abbot Cyrus. I traveled about with her in simplicity of heart, seeking a small amount of money with which I might place her in a monastery.”

When the patriarch heard this, he said:

“Good heavens! How many hidden servants God has, while we humble people do not know it!”

He related to those present the vision he had seen concerning the monk during the night. Then the patriarch took one hundred coins from his hand to give him. But that truly God-loving monk would not accept any of them. Instead, he spoke to the patriarch a memorable word:

“I am not asking for this, lord. If a monk has faith, he does not need these things. If he needs them, he does not have faith.”

This greatly satisfied everyone who heard that this monk was a servant of God. He knelt before the patriarch and departed in peace.

From that time onward the patriarch honored monks more greatly and received them as guests, whether they were considered good or bad. He immediately built a separate hospice and called it “The Refuge of All Monks.”

## CHAPTER XXIV

When an epidemic once afflicted the city, this holy man himself went out to observe the funeral rites. He said that this was greatly beneficial, as was consideration of the tombs. He often sat beside those who, as they were dying, suffered anguish in the departure of the soul. He himself closed their eyes with his own hands, wishing thereby to preserve an everlasting remembrance and to reflect upon his own departure.

He also ordered that collections for the dead be made diligently [Note: **Diligently.** This is correctly read in the manuscripts. The old edition has *impingere*; the Cologne edition has *injungere*.] and completed without fail.

He said that, a short time earlier, a certain man had been taken captive by the Persians. When he entered Persia, he was shut up in a prison called Lethe, that is, “Oblivion.” Some people escaped from there and came to Cyprus. When his relatives asked them whether they had perhaps seen him, they replied: “We buried him with our own hands.”

But the man they were asking about was not the one they had seen; it was someone else who closely resembled him. They also told them the month and day of his death. The relatives, supposing him dead, made three memorial collections for him each year.

After four years the man came to Cyprus, having escaped from the Persians. His relatives said to him:

“Indeed, brother, we heard that you were dead, and we made memorial observances for you three times each year.”

When he heard that they had commemorated him three times a year, he asked them on what day and in what month they held these observances. When they told him that they did so at the holy Epiphany, Holy Sunday, and holy Pentecost [Note: **At the holy Epiphany, Holy Sunday, and holy Pentecost.** Collections were made for the man who was believed dead at these three seasons. Gregory gives a similar example of a captive being released from his chains while a sacred service was being celebrated for him as though he were dead (*Homily* 37 on the Gospels).], he said:

“On these three occasions each year, someone like the sun, clothed in white, came and released me from my iron chains and confinement. I would walk about all day, and no one recognized me; the next day I would be found again carrying iron chains.”

The holy bishop therefore said that from this we learn that the departed have rest when we make collections for them.

## CHAPTER XXV

What we heard happened in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts IV) frequently happened also to this most compassionate man. Many people, seeing his tireless and unfathomable compassion toward the nations, were often moved to sell much of their property. They brought the proceeds and placed them before the servant devoted to God.

One day a certain man came and offered him seven and a half pounds of gold, assuring the holy man that he possessed nothing else in gold. With many genuflections he begged him to pray that the Lord God would save his son. He had only one son, about fifteen years old, who had gone to Africa to bring back his ship with a favorable cargo.

The high priest took the quantity of gold from his hand and was astonished that he was so generous as to offer the entire amount of gold he possessed. He prayed for him [Note: **He prayed for him.** I think this means “he prayed on his behalf.” Below, chapter 37: “Go, pray for my thefts.”] at length and in his presence, and then dismissed him.

Nevertheless, because of the man’s great faith, the patriarch placed the quantity of gold beneath the holy table in the oratory of his chamber and immediately celebrated a complete synaxis over it for the man who had offered it, entreating God fully and abundantly both to save his son and to bring the ship back safely, as the man had requested.

Before thirty days had passed, the son of the man who had offered the seven and a half pounds to the patriarch died. On the third day after the boy’s death, the father received his ship back from Africa. The man’s own brother was also aboard; he was a creditor of that same man.

When the ship came near the Pharos, the uncle reported that it had suffered shipwreck and lost everything with which it was laden, and that only the lives of the men and one empty boat had been saved.

When the ship’s owner and the boy’s father learned that this calamity had befallen him, then, according to the prophet’s word, “his soul dwelt almost in hell” (Ps. XCIII). For before the tribulation caused by the death of his son had subsided, the shipwreck also overtook him. Everything that had happened was reported to the patriarch, and he remained almost more sorrowful than the man who had suffered these things, especially because of his only son.

Not knowing what to do, he asked the most merciful God to console the man through his immense compassion. The holy patriarch was ashamed to summon him and console him in person, but he sent him word that he should by no means despair. God did nothing without just judgment, he said, but did everything for what was beneficial, although we do not know what that is.

So that he would not lose the reward he had earned through the seven and a half pounds of gold, nor the faith he had placed in the holy patriarch—and so that we too may remain undisturbed and thankful to God amid the trials that come upon us after we have done something good—the aforementioned lover of Christ saw the following dream on the next night.

He saw someone resembling the most holy patriarch in appearance saying to him:

“Why are you troubled, brother, and dissolved in grief? Did you not ask me to pray to God that your son might be saved? Look: he has been saved. Believe me, if he had lived, he would have become a wicked and impure man.

“As for your ship, truly, unless God had been appeased because of the good you did for my lowliness, sentence had been passed that the whole ship, with all the men aboard it, should descend into the depths and that you should lose your brother.

“Therefore rise and glorify God, who has given him back to you and has saved your son, still pure, from this vain world.””

The man awoke and found his heart consoled and all his sorrow removed. He put on his clothes and hurried to the most honorable patriarch. He threw himself at his feet, giving thanks to God and to the patriarch and relating the vision he had seen.

When the most righteous man heard it, he said:

“Glory to you, good and merciful God, who hear even the prayers of sinners.”

Then he said to the man:

“By no means, son, attribute this grace to my prayer, but to God and to your faith; for your faith was able to obtain all these things.”

The holy man was exceedingly humble in his thoughts, as was evident in both his words and his wisdom.

## CHAPTER XXVI

This blessed man once went to visit the poor in a place called the Caesarium. There he had built for them certain spacious domed shelters [Note: **Domed shelters.** See the *Onomasticon* concerning this type of building.], with a floor laid with wooden boards for their rest, together with mats and *rachanae* [Note: **Together with mats and *rachanae*.** The Aquicinctus manuscript reads *cum toris et rachanis*; the Gemblacensis manuscript, *cum storis et rachanis*; the old edition, *cum storis et raconis*; the Cologne edition, *cum storeis et racis*. The *rachanae* mentioned here are presumably the same as the *rachanellae* mentioned above, chapter 20.], for the whole winter.

A certain bishop who accompanied him was a lover of money and was oppressed in a manner that revealed his weakness. The blessed patriarch said to him:

“Love and honor the brothers of Christ, brother Troilus.” For that was his name.

Some people informed the patriarch that, at that very hour, the domestic servant of Bishop Troilus was carrying thirty pounds of gold to purchase a piece of embossed silverware for his master’s table.

The bishop, as though afraid of the patriarch’s words—or rather, warmed by them for the moment—ordered the man carrying the thirty pounds to distribute the entire amount to all the brothers.

The quantity of gold was quickly spent in this way. When the two men departed—the patriarch, and Bishop Troilus, who had made the alms unwillingly, so to speak—Troilus returned to his own episcopal residence. There, as though he were deranged, a thought dangerous to his soul fell upon him because of the gift of the money. The horror, love of money, cruelty, and negligence that followed him were mixed with an unnatural fever, and against his will he fell sick and took to his bed.

The patriarch’s weekly attendant came to him and invited him to the patriarch’s table, but Troilus refused, saying that he was suffering from chills and fever for some reason.

When the patriarch heard this, he immediately understood the cause: Troilus had fallen ill because of the loss of the twenty pounds, since he was, as has been said, exceedingly merciless and a lover of money.

The blessed patriarch could not bear to refresh himself at table while Troilus was suffering severely on his bed. He therefore hurried to him without any arrogance and said to him with a cheerful face:

“Do me this kindness, son Troilus. Do you think I truly told you to give this money to the brothers? Believe me, I was joking when I told you to give it. I had intended to provide each of them with one coin for the holy festival; but since my distributor did not have a sufficient amount with him, you lent it to me for this purpose. Look, I have brought you those thirty pounds.”

When the bishop saw the amount of gold in the honorable hand of the wise physician and shepherd, his fever immediately disappeared, the chills departed, and the strength and bodily warmth returned to him. Thus it could not remain hidden that this was the reason for the sudden change that had overtaken him.

He received the gold from the patriarch’s venerable hands without offering any objection. The patriarch then waited for him to write a document renouncing any claim to the reward for the thirty pounds of gold that had been given.

Bishop Troilus did this gladly, writing with his own hand:

“God, grant my lord John, most blessed patriarch of this great city of Alexandria, the reward for the thirty pounds that were given to you, since I have received my own.”

The holy man took this document and brought the same bishop with him to dinner; for, as has already been said, Troilus had immediately been restored to health.

But God, the giver of rewards, wished both to rebuke him and to raise him to pity and compassion for those in distress. That same day, after dining with the patriarch, while Troilus was asleep, God showed him in a dream what reward he had lost.

He saw, as he said, a house whose beauty and greatness no human art could imitate. Its door was entirely of gold, and above the door was written:

**ETERNAL DWELLING AND REST OF BISHOP TROILUS**

When he had read this, he rejoiced, for he knew that the emperor would grant him such a house as a place of feasting.

Before he had finished reading the inscription, a royal chamberlain appeared, accompanied by others engaged in divine service. When he reached the shining door of the house, he said to his officials:

“Remove the inscription for me.”

When they had removed it, he said again:

“Change it and put up the one sent by the king of the whole world.”

They brought and affixed another inscription while I watched. It read:

**ETERNAL DWELLING AND REST OF JOHN, ARCHBISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA, PURCHASED FOR THIRTY POUNDS**

When he saw this, he awoke from sleep and related what he had seen to the great and supreme shepherd. Bishop Troilus advanced because of this and from that time became a magnificent giver of alms.

## CHAPTER XXVII

The Lord, who once took away Job’s riches, did the same to this holy patriarch John, who was full of every virtue.

When the ships of the most holy church encountered a violent storm at a place called Adria [Note: **Adria.** The Cologne edition has *Adhira*, but both manuscripts agree with the printed reading.], they threw overboard everything the ships were carrying. All the ships were together.

The total amount of their cargo was extremely large. They had clothing, silver, and other valuable goods, so that the weight of what was lost was reckoned at thirty-four hundredweights. There were more than thirteen ships, each capable of carrying ten thousand *modii*.

When they reached Alexandria and proceeded inland, the other creditors and the senior sailors immediately fled to the church. When the saint heard this and learned the reason for their flight, he sent them a message written in his own hand:

“‘The Lord gave, brothers; the Lord has taken away, as he wished. As it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord’ (Job I).

“Come out, my sons, fearing nothing because of this. The Lord will take care of tomorrow.”

Almost half the city then went up to the patriarch’s private quarters. On the following day, those who wished to console this noble man [Note: **Those who wished.** Both manuscripts have *volentes*; the printed editions have *volebant*, but changed it out of fear of a barbarism. Likewise below, at the beginning of chapter 33, *audiens* is printed for *audivi*.] came to him. But he anticipated them and began saying to everyone:

“By no means, sons and brothers, be saddened because of the misfortune of the ships. Believe me, humble John has been found guilty. If I had not been proud, I would never have endured this. But because I was proud of what belonged to God and thought that I was doing great deeds by giving away what belonged to human beings, this happened to me. God allowed it so that I might understand this.

“Almsgiving often raises one who is not watchful into pride; but an unwelcome fall humbles the one who endures it.

“For divine Scripture says: ‘Poverty humbles a man.’ And David, knowing this, said: ‘It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I may learn your ordinances’ (Ps. CXVIII).

“Since I had become liable to evils, because I was wasting my giving through vainglory, and because such great sums of money were lost through my fault, I now have the judgment of souls that are in distress.

“Nevertheless, beloved, the God who was with that righteous man Job then is the same now. He will not abandon us because of my poverty, but for the sake of the need of the needy. For he himself said: ‘I will not leave you, nor will I forsake you’ (Heb. XIII).

“And again: ‘Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you’ (Matt. VI).”

Thus the inhabitants of the city had wished to console him, as has been said, but they themselves were found instead to have received consolation from his blessedness.

A very short time passed, and God restored the resources of our new Job twofold. He again became generous in mercy, and perhaps even more devout than he had been before.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

When one of his household servants had fallen into extreme poverty, this holy man secretly gave him two pounds of gold with his own hand, so that no one would know.

The recipient said to him: “After receiving this, lord, I no longer have the face to look upon your honorable and angelic countenance.”

The wise man spoke a truly praiseworthy word:

“Not yet, brother, have I shed my blood for you, as my Lord and the Christ God of all commanded me (John X).”

### CHAPTER XXIX

A certain man, pressed by those who demanded the tax, had nothing to give—for the region was in great difficulty, since the river Nile, contrary to its custom, was not irrigating the land with its waters. He went and entreated one of the leading officials to lend him fifty pounds of gold, saying that he would provide double the amount in pledges if he wished. The official promised to give it to him, but postponed doing so for the moment.

When the tax collectors were pressing him, he went—to the harbor that receives everyone—to the most gentle and admirable patriarch. He had scarcely begun to tell him of his need when the saint said to him: “I will give it, my son, if you wish, and also the garment in which I am clothed.” For, together with his other admirable virtues, he possessed this quality also: he could not see anyone weeping because of his needs without immediately watering himself with his own tears. Thus he at once fulfilled the request of the man who wished to borrow from him.

On the following night the official saw in a dream someone standing above an altar, to whom many people were offering gifts; for each one that they placed there, they received a hundred from the altar. The patriarch was also behind him. One offering was lying before them on a bench, and someone said to the official: “Go, sir, take that offering, present it at the altar, and receive a hundred offerings in return.”

When the official hesitated, the patriarch—although he was standing behind him—ran forward, took the offering before him, presented it, and received, like everyone else, a hundred from the altar.

When he awoke, he could not interpret the dream. He sent for and brought to him the man who wished to borrow the money, in order to lend it to him. When the man arrived, the official said to him: “Take what you requested as a loan.”

The man replied: “The patriarch has already received your reward. For when you, sir, delayed giving it to me, I was compelled to flee to him as to a harbor, since the pressure of the tax collectors’ demands was very great.”

When he heard this, the official immediately remembered the dream and said: “You have spoken truly: ‘He has already received your reward.’ He received it beforehand. Woe to the man who wishes to do good and delays!”

He then recounted to him and to everyone the dream he had seen.

### CHAPTER XXX

Once, when the saint was going to the church of the victorious holy martyrs Cyrus and John to pray at their glorious shrine, a woman met him as he was leaving the city gate. She fell before him and said: “Vindicate me, for I am suffering injustice at the hands of my son-in-law.”

Some of those in his service who enjoyed his confidence said: “When you return, you will take up her case.”

The most wise man replied: “How will God receive our prayer if I put this woman off? Who has promised me that I shall live until tomorrow? Shall I go to Christ having to give an account for her?”

He did not leave that place until he had done for her what was sufficient.

### CHAPTER XXXI

Accordingly, in response to the will of this memorable man, whose whole will was centered in God, God sent him the wise and ever-memorable men John and Sophronius.

They were truly good counselors. He obeyed them without reserve as though they were fathers, and he gave them thanks as to steadfast and manly soldiers laboring for the sake of true religion. Relying on the power of the Holy Spirit, they engaged in battle and conflict through their wisdom and disputations with the Severians [Note: [Col. 0390C] “Severians.” He means, I think, the Acephalous heretics who arose shortly before the time of John the Almsgiver, around the year 513, from Severus, bishop of Antioch. Concerning him, see Evagrius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapters [Col. 0390D] 33 and 34.] and the other unclean heretics living in that region. Like good shepherds, they strove to snatch many fortresses, numerous churches, and likewise monasteries from the mouths of such beasts. For this reason that truly most holy man honored these saints exceedingly.

### CHAPTER XXXII

Whenever that blessed man perceived someone to be harsh, inhuman, and prone to striking his own servants, he first summoned him and gently entreated him, saying:

“My son, it has reached my sinful ears that, through the enemy’s activity, you behave somewhat too harshly toward your own servants. But I ask you: give place to anger. God did not give us these people so that we might strike them, but so that they might serve. Perhaps not even for that reason, but so that they might be sustained by us, from the resources God has granted us.

“Tell me: what has a man given, and what has he purchased, when the person created and honored in the image and likeness of God is concerned? Do you, his master, possess anything more in your own body—a hand, a foot, hearing, or a soul? Is he not in every respect like you?

“Hear the glorious light, Paul, saying: ‘All who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ’ (Gal. III). ‘There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free; for you are all one in Christ.’

“If, then, we are equal before Christ, let us also become equal with one another. For Christ assumed the form of a slave, teaching us not to be proud toward our servants. There is one Lord of all, dwelling in heaven and looking upon the lowly; he did not say ‘the lofty,’ but ‘the lowly’ (Ps. CXII).

“How much gold have we given in order to subject to slavery one who has been honored and purchased together with us by the divine and Lordly blood? For his sake there are heaven and earth, for his sake the stars, for his sake the sun, for his sake the sea and everything in it. Indeed, the angels also minister to him. For his sake Christ washed the feet of servants; for his sake he was crucified; and for his sake he suffered all the rest.

“But you dishonor the one honored by God, and, as though he were not of the same nature, you do not spare him when you beat him. Tell me, I beg you: would you wish God to repay you immediately whenever you committed a fault? Certainly not. Tell me, then, how do you pray every day, saying: ‘Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors’ (Matt. VI)?”

With these and similar words, reminding him of the treasure dwelling within him, he dismissed the man. But if he did not learn that the man had reformed, he prepared and instructed the afflicted servant to flee and request to be sold. Then the just man purchased him and immediately declared him free.

### CHAPTER XXXIII

Once he heard of a boy, the orphaned son of a certain benefactor, who had been left behind after his parents’ death and was living in great poverty. Those who had been found as witnesses to his father’s will said:

“His father, lord, when he died, did not leave him even a single coin. Rather, although he possessed ten pounds of gold, he brought the boy in at the very time when he was writing his will and said to him: ‘Take these ten pounds, my son. What do you wish? Shall I leave these to you, or shall I appoint my Lady, the Mother of God, as your guardian and provider?’

“When the boy chose the holy Mother of God, he ordered that everything be given to the poor. And behold, most holy one, he is now in great poverty, never leaving our Lady’s house by night or by day.”

When this saint heard this from those who knew the facts, he said nothing to anyone but summoned a notary. He explained the matter to him and made him promise not to disclose to anyone the task he ordered him to perform. He said:

“Go and write, on old documents, the will of a certain man named Theopentus. In that same document make me and the boy’s father first cousins. Then go and say to the young man: ‘Do you know, brother, that, being related to the patriarch, you should not be living in such poverty?’ Show him the document and say: ‘If you are ashamed, I shall arrange your case with the patriarch; then see what he will tell you.’”

When the notary had done everything the patriarch had ordered him, he came back and said: “The boy has entrusted me with speaking on his behalf to the lord, and he gave me many thanks.”

The saint then said: “Go and tell him: ‘I have spoken to the patriarch. I said: “I also know that my cousin had a son, but I do not recognize him by his appearance. You are therefore doing well to bring him to me.”’ When you bring him, bring the document with you.”

When they arrived, the just man took the boy aside, began to kiss him, and said: “Welcome, son of my cousin.”

He then enriched him, married him to a woman in Alexandria, and gave him a house and everything he needed, hastening to demonstrate that “the Lord does not forsake those who hope in him” (Judith VI).

### CHAPTER XXXIV

This admirable man also cared for this commandment without interruption: “Do not refuse one who wishes to borrow from you” (Deut. XV; Luke VI). He did not prevent anyone who sought such assistance from him.

A certain wicked impostor, knowing this, asked him to lend him twenty pounds of gold. He was one of those called *Gallodromi* [Note: [Col. 0390D] “Gallodromi.” The Aquicinctine manuscript writes above the word: “roaming hucksters who deceive by fraud.” Thus also the text of the old and Cologne editions. In Palladius, chapters 15 and 16, the corresponding term is σπανοδρόμος, which they translate as “a merchant trading in Spain.”].

He despised the saint, as he did many others, and said: “He gave me nothing.”

The shepherds and administrators of the Church therefore sought to have him imprisoned and his property confiscated. But the saint, who imitated the one who said, “Be merciful, as your Father also is merciful” (Luke VI)—the one who makes his sun rise over the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust—would not consent to their harming him.

When they were angry with him because he had mocked the patriarch and said to the same saint: “It is not right, lord, that what the poor would receive should be given to this luxurious man,” that thrice-blessed man replied:

“Believe me, brothers: if you were to take anything from him against his will, you would transgress two commandments, while you would fulfill one when such an amount had been given to the poor.

“One commandment would be transgressed because you would appear impatient regarding loss and would become a bad example to others. The second would be transgressed because you would not obey the Lord God, who says: ‘From the one who takes what is yours, do not demand it back’ (Luke VI).

“It is better, then, my sons, that we become an example of patience to everyone. For the Apostle says: ‘Why do you not rather suffer injustice? Why do you not rather submit to being defrauded?’ (1 Cor. VI).

“It is truly good, brothers, to give to everyone who asks; but it is higher and more honorable to give even to one who does not ask. To give both one’s garment and one’s tunic to the person who takes them from us without permission is truly an imitation of the angelic nature—or rather, of the divine nature.
