“For from what we possess the Lord has commanded us to do good to our neighbor: ‘You shall do good,’ he says, ‘to your brother according to what your hand possesses—not from what is taken through quarrel and contention from one who has suffered injustice.’”

### CHAPTER XXXV

A certain great old man, about sixty years of age, heard of the blessed man’s deeds and wished to test him—to see whether he could be persuaded by words, easily moved to take offense, and, as might happen, induced to condemn someone.

He had formerly lived in the monastery of Abba Seridon [Note: [Col. 0390D] “Seridon.” Below in this chapter: “He entered the monastery of Abba Seridon in Gaza.” The holy Seridon, or Siridon, bishop, appears in the Roman Martyrology on 2 January.]. He left it and came to Alexandria, adopting a way of life blameworthy in human eyes but pleasing to God, who, as David says, gives each person according to his heart (Ps. XIX).

When he entered the city, he wrote down the names of all the prostitutes known there. He began to perform small jobs and receive one *siliqua* each day. When the sun went down, he ate lupins worth one bronze coin [Note: [Col. 0390D] “Lupins worth one bronze coin.” Thus the Aquicinctine manuscript supplies what is lacking in the printed editions. The Gembloux manuscript has: “the price of one bronze coin.”]. Then he entered one of the prostitutes’ houses, gave her bronze coins, and said: “Give me this night, and do not commit fornication.”

He remained beside her that night, watching her so that she would not commit fornication. From evening he stood in a corner of the little room where the woman slept, singing psalms and praying for her, making prostrations until dawn. When he left, he obtained from her a promise that she would tell no one what he had done.

He always acted in this way, until one of the women revealed his manner of life, explaining that he did not enter them in order to commit fornication but to save them. The old man prayed, and the woman began to be tormented by a demon, so that the others would fear and would not expose him during the whole of his life.

Some people said to the woman who was tormented by the demon: “What is this? God has repaid you because you lied. This worst of men enters you in order to commit fornication; there is nothing else to it.”

Saint Vitalius—for that was his name—wished to avoid human glory and bring souls back from darkness. While laboring at his work and finishing in the evening, he would say within everyone’s hearing: “Come now; such-and-such a lady is waiting for us.”

What was his practice? Although many accused and mocked him, he said: “Do I not clothe my body like everyone else? Or is God angry only with monks? They too are human beings, like everyone else.”

Someone said to him: “Take one woman for yourself, abba, and change your clothing, so that God may not be blasphemed through you. You will then be accountable for those whose souls are scandalized.”

But he answered them again, pretending to be angry, and said: “Truly I will not obey you. Go away from me. I shall do nothing else now to keep you from being scandalized except take a woman, so that I may manage a household and make bad days. Let whoever wishes to be scandalized be scandalized and strike his forehead against the wall. What do you want from me? Have you been appointed judges over me by God? Go, take care of yourselves; you will not give an account to God on my behalf. There is one Judge and one holy day of judgment, and he will repay each person according to his works.”

He said these things while shouting.

Some of the church officials, having often heard such words from him, reported to the patriarch what was happening. But God, knowing that the saint did not wish to offend Abba Vitalius, hardened the patriarch’s heart so that he would not believe them. He remembered the eunuch mentioned earlier, but he sternly rebuked those who brought accusations against Abba Vitalius, saying:

“Stop accusing monks. Do you not know what happened concerning the emperor Constantine of holy memory [Note: [Col. 0390D] “Constantine.” The story is found in Sozomen, Book I, chapter 16, and Theodoret, Book I, chapter 11.]? The records written about him contain the following:

“Certain people who did not fear God, when the Second Council was being celebrated at Nicaea [Note: [Col. 0390D] “The Second Council at Nicaea.” Rather, the First General Council at Nicaea—unless perhaps some local council had previously been held there. Alternatively, understand ‘the second council at Nicaea’ in relation to the council of the apostles, which was the first general council of all.], began to circulate written, disgraceful reports against that blessed emperor. Some were clerics and some monks.

“Saint Constantine the servant of God brought the accuser and the accused face to face and heard both of them. When he found that many of these accusations were true, he brought a burning candle, set fire to all the evil reports that had been written, and said:

“‘Truly, if I had seen with my own eyes a priest of God, or any of those clothed in the monastic habit, sinning, I would have spread out my purple cloak and covered him, so that no one would see him. You thought the same concerning that servant of God, the eunuch; you led me astray, and I committed a great sin against my soul.’

“After greatly shaming them, he dismissed them.”

The servant of God, Vitalius, did not cease his work. He prayed that, after his death, God would reveal to some people in dreams that those who had been scandalized by him should not be charged with sin because they had judged his conduct to be scandalous, and that no one should be condemned for whatever he had said on that account.

His conduct therefore brought many of these women to compunction, especially when they saw him stretching out his hands by night and praying for each one of them. As a result, some of them ceased from fornication; some took husbands and lived chastely; and some, abandoning the world in every respect, adopted the solitary life.

Yet no one knew until his repose that, through his exhortation and prayer, these immoral women had ceased from fornication.

One day, as he was leaving the first of these women’s houses at dawn, a certain impure man met him, entering to commit fornication with her. When he saw Saint Vitalius coming out, he slapped him in the face and said: “How long will you continue, worst deceiver of Christ, without reforming yourself from these wicked practices?”

He replied: “Believe me, you will receive a slap from me, the humble man, such that all Alexandria will gather at your cries.”

Not long afterward, Saint Vitalius fell asleep peacefully in his cell, with no one knowing at all. His cell was extremely small, above the place called the Gate of the Sun [Note: [Col. 0391A] “Gate of the Sun.” A place in Alexandria, near which stood the church of Saint Metras, as follows.].

Often, when an assembly was being held near his cell in the church of Metras [Note: [Col. 0391A] “In the church of Metras.” The Cologne edition: “in the church metre.” The old edition: “in the church metre.” The Aquicinctine manuscript: “in the church of Metras.” The Gembloux manuscript: “in the church of the little prostitute.” Metras, or Metranus, was a martyr of Alexandria, commemorated on 31 January. The Roman Martyrology, 31 January, says: “At Alexandria, the birthday of Saint Metranus the martyr, who, under the emperor Decius, refused at the command of the pagans to utter impious words. They beat his whole body with clubs, pierced his face and eyes with sharp reeds, and drove him outside the city amid torments; there they killed him by crushing him with stones.”], some of these women would gather and say to one another: “Come, come; Abba Vitalius is holding an assembly again.”

When they came, he cared for them.

As has been said, while he was sleeping in his own cell and no one knew it, a demon in the form of a hideous Ethiopian suddenly appeared to the man who had slapped Abba Vitalius. It slapped him and said: “Receive the slap that Abba Vitalius sent you.”

The man fell down and immediately began to foam at the mouth. In accordance with Vitalius’s prophecy, almost the whole of Alexandria gathered around the affliction that the man was suffering from the demon—especially because some people heard the sound of the slap, as though it had been thrown from the distance of a single arrow-shot.

After several hours, when the afflicted man came to himself, he tore the clothing from his chest, ran to the cell, and cried out: “I have wronged you, servant of God Vitalius; have mercy on me.”

Everyone who heard him ran with him. When he reached the saint’s cell, the demon again came out, throwing him down before all who were watching. Those who had run with him entered and found the saint standing on his knees and praying, as he surrendered his soul to the Lord. On the floor was written the following:

“Men of Alexandria, do not judge anything before the proper time, until the Lord comes” (1 Cor. IV).

The man who had been tormented by the demon also confessed what he had done to the saint and what the saint had said to him.

Everything that had happened concerning Saint Vitalius was reported to the most blessed patriarch John. He came down with the clergy and went to the body of Saint Vitalius. When he saw the inscription, he said:

“Truly this humble John escaped it through God, for I would have received the slap that the sufferer received.”

Then all the prostitutes, including those who had renounced their former life and taken husbands, went before him with candles and lamps, weeping and saying: “We have lost our salvation and our teacher.”

They now explained his way of life to everyone, saying: “He did not enter us for any shameful purpose,” and: “We never once saw him sleeping on his side or holding one of us by the hand.”

Some people reproached them, saying: “Why did you not say these things to everyone? The whole city was being scandalized by him.”

They then recounted the incident involving the woman who had suffered demonic possession, and explained that they had remained silent out of fear.

After he had been buried with great honor, the man whom he had corrected and healed continued to commemorate him. Later he renounced the world, entered the monastery of Abba Seridon in Gaza, and, according to his faith, received Abba Vitalius’s cell. He remained there until his death.

The most holy patriarch gave many thanks to God because he had not allowed him to sin against his servant Vitalius.

From that time many people in Alexandria greatly benefited themselves and received monks as guests; they were warned not to condemn anyone, as had happened in this case.

After his death, the honorable name of Saint Vitalius also performed healings through divine grace. Through his prayers may the Lord grant us a good manner of life and mercy on the day when he will reveal what is hidden in human beings and lay bare the thoughts of their hearts (1 Cor. IV).

### CHAPTER XXXVI

Once, when he had ordered that only ten bronze coins be given as alms to a certain petitioner, that blessed man endured savage abuse from him to his face because he had not given him as much as he wanted.

When those who were in his service asked permission to beat the man who was abusing him, the patriarch sternly rebuked them, saying:

“Leave him alone, brothers. I am sixty years old, blaspheming Christ through my deeds, and I cannot endure one insult from this man?”

He ordered the giver to loosen the moneybag, so that the poor man might take as much money as he wished.

### CHAPTER XXXVII

Whenever the most wise man heard that someone was a benefactor, he would cheerfully take him aside and say:

“How did you become a benefactor? By nature, or by forcing yourself against your inclination?”

Some of those whom he questioned were ashamed and concealed the truth; others told him.

One man whom the saint questioned answered:

“Believe me, lord, I neither give nor do anything good. Yet I have become accustomed to doing and providing what I do, from the resources which God and your prayers bestow.

“Formerly I was very unmerciful and cruel. Once I suffered losses and fell into straits. Then my thought began to say to me: ‘Truly, if you were a benefactor, God would not abandon you.’

“So I decided to give five bronze coins each day to the poor. When I began to give, Satan immediately prevented me, saying: ‘Surely these five coins are enough for the household to buy vegetables or obtain a bath.’ Immediately I gave nothing, as though I were depriving my children of food.

“When I saw that I was being overcome by the vice, I said to my boy: ‘Every day, without my knowing it, steal five coins and give them as alms. For I am a money-changer, lord.’

“But although I had told him to steal five, he began to steal ten [Note: [Col. 0391A] “Ten.” Thus both manuscripts; the printed editions have *denarii*. The master ordered him to steal five coins, but he stole ten.]. Sometimes they were even *siliquae*.

“When I saw that we were being blessed and abounding in wealth, he began to steal and give even *tremisses*. Once, marveling at God’s blessings, I said to him: ‘Truly those five coins have benefited us greatly, my son. I therefore want you to give ten.’

“Then the boy said to me with a smile: ‘Go and pray over my thefts. For truly today we would have no bread to eat. But if there is an upright thief, I am he.’

“Then he told me that, since the boy gave *tremisses* and even *siliquae*, I became accustomed, on the basis of his faith, to giving from the heart, lord.”

The saint was greatly edified and said to him: “Believe me, I have read many accounts of the lives of the Fathers, but I have never heard anything like this.”

### CHAPTER XXXVIII

The great John heard that a certain prominent man was harboring malice against another ruler. He often admonished him and urged him toward reconciliation, but could not turn him to peace.

Once the saint sent for and brought him, supposedly on public business. He celebrated Masses in his oratory, having no one present except his own attendant [Note: [Col. 0391B] “He celebrates Masses in his oratory, having no one present except his own attendant.” Here is evidence of the practice in the Church of celebrating Mass privately.].

When the patriarch had blessed the holy things and had begun the Lord’s Prayer, only the three of them began to say: “Our Father.” When they reached the words, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,” the patriarch signaled to his attendant to be silent.

The patriarch therefore fell silent, and the ruler alone continued to say the verse: “Forgive us, as we also forgive.”

The saint immediately turned to him and said in a gentle voice:

“Consider what a terrible hour it is in which you are saying to God: ‘As I forgive, so forgive me.’”

As though he had at once felt the torment of fire, the ruler fell on his face at the saint’s feet and said: “Whatever you command, lord, your servant will do.”

From that time he was fully reconciled with his enemy.

### CHAPTER XXXIX

Whenever the blessed man saw someone who was proud, he did not rebuke him to his face. But when he saw him sitting in private, he introduced reflections on humility, so that through this instruction he might gradually strike the proud man and make him modest. He would say:

“I marvel, my lords, that my wretched soul does not remember the humility which the Son of God showed us by appearing on earth, but swells up and exalts itself over my brother if I am slightly more handsome than he, or richer, or more honored, or if I hold some position of authority. I do not understand the divine voice which says: ‘Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls’ (Matt. XI).

“Nor do I consider the words of the saints: some called themselves earth (Gen. XVIII), some ashes, some a worm and not a man (Ps. XXI), and some one impeded and slow of speech (Exod. IV). Isaiah, when he was granted the privilege of seeing God—as far as a human being can—declared that he had unclean lips (Isa. VI).

“What am I, even if I am humble? Was I not fashioned from clay, from which bricks are also made? Does not all the glory that I think I possess wither like the flower of grass (Isa. XL)?”

With these words, words like them, and many others, the most wise man, speaking as though of himself, cauterized the soul of the man who possessed the swelling and disease of pride and thereby benefited him. The man who had the ulcer understood that the patriarch was speaking these things about him.

### CHAPTER XL

This man, honored by God, also frequently brought forward the following as an argument for humility:

“If we had considered and reflected upon God’s mercy and goodness toward us, we would not even lift our eyes toward heaven, but would always live in humble conduct and understanding.

“To pass over how the Creator brought us into existence when we did not exist, and how, after we were deceived by sin and disobedience, he gave us life again, redeemed us from death by his own blood, and subjected the whole earth and heaven itself to human service: consider also how, even now, that immovable nature and patient eye does not destroy us when we sin, but rather waits for us with great patience.

“Although we often blaspheme, he himself consoles and caresses us through his mercy, sending rains from above for the sake of our life. How many evil laborers, going out to kill or steal, does he shelter and not hand over, so that they may not be caught and punished? How many people in ships at sea, intending to plunder vessels that meet them and kill those aboard, does he not permit to sink into the depths, but commands the sea not to swallow them, awaiting their conversion from wickedness?

“How many swear falsely by his most holy body and blood [Note: [Col. 0391B] “Swear falsely by his body.” Thus both manuscripts. The old edition has “have asked for his body”; the Cologne edition, “unworthily receive the body.”], and he endures them and acts with long-suffering, not repaying them here with anything harsh? How many robbers on the road does he not hand over as food to the beasts that meet them? How many who go into the hollows of the earth and cause disturbances along the roads does he protect, so that they are not destroyed by the dogs or even by human guards?

“And while I sometimes lie with a prostitute, or associate with those who get drunk, or converse with those who speak shamefully, or am entangled in any other sin of this world, the bee flies about, goes through valleys and honeycombs, seeking to gather fruit so that it may make sweet the throat which speaks foully and wickedly; the grape hastens to ripen in the heat, so that it may fill the mouth and gladden the heart which has transgressed against its Maker. The flowers vie with one another to be first, so that they may delight the eyes which beckon toward fornication and foreign women for pleasure. The fig is agitated [Note: [Col. 0391B] “The fig is agitated.” Thus the old and Cologne editions and the Aquicinctine manuscript. The Gembloux manuscript has: “the fig is beaten.”], so that it may grow large enough to fill the hand and sweet enough to fill the mouth which holds and kisses another man’s wife.

“Since, then, brothers, we perform such deeds and receive such rewards from the benevolent God, what kind of understanding ought we to possess as we consider our final and dreadful hour?”

That blessed man always spoke at length about the remembrance of death and the departure of the soul. As a result, people would often enter him with an arrogant manner, a smiling face, and a heedless eye, but leave in a humble manner, with a contrite face and tearful eyes.

For this reason he also said:

“As I, humble as I am, judge it, it is sufficient for salvation continually and sorrowfully to think about death and to be concerned about it, since no one will sympathize with us or accompany us from this life at that hour except our good works.

“How the soul is then troubled when the angels come and hasten toward it, if it is found unprepared! How it begs that a little time of life be added to it, and hears: ‘What? Have you used well the time in which you lived?’

“Again he would say, as though speaking of himself: ‘How will I, humble John, pass by the beasts of the reeds (Ps. LXVII) when the tax collectors meet me? Alas, what fear and trembling then seize the soul giving an account to such numerous examiners, so bitter and unmerciful!

“For this saint always kept in mind what was revealed to Saint Simeon who stood upon columns [Note: [Col. 0391B] “Simeon who stood upon columns.” This vision is absent from the *Life of Simeon the Stylite* printed above. It says that he stood upon columns because that same Simeon stood upon various columns. See above, in his Life, chapter 5.]. As he said:

“‘When the soul departs from the body and rises from earth to heaven, choirs of demons meet it, each in its own order. The choir of the spirits of pride meets it and searches whether it possesses their works. The choir of the spirits of slander meets it and examines whether it has ever spoken against anyone without repenting. Again, higher up, the demons of fornication meet it and scrutinize it to see whether they recognize their own pleasures in it.

“‘And when the wretched soul, having traveled from earth to heaven, has reached the point where it must give an account, the holy angels will stand apart from it and will not help it except for the good deeds it has performed.’

“Considering these things, this noble man was terrified and became anxious concerning that hour. He also kept in mind the saying of Saint Hilarion (*Life of Hilarion*, chapter 38): when he was about to depart from life, he was afraid and said to his soul:

“‘For eighty years, humble soul, you have served Christ, and you are afraid to depart? Go out, for he is merciful.’

“The patriarch would say to himself:

“‘If the man who served Christ for eighty years, raised the dead, and performed signs feared that bitter hour, what will you, humble John, have to say or do when those cruel and unmerciful tax collectors and inquisitors meet you face to face?

“‘To how many will you be able to give an account—to those who inquire about lying, to those who inquire about slander, to those who inquire about cruelty, to those who inquire about greed, to those who inquire about remembrance of evil, to those who inquire about hatred, and to those who inquire about perjury?’”

In his bewilderment he would say:

“God, rebuke them, for no human strength is sufficient to resist them.

“You, Lord, give us holy angelic guides to guard and direct us. Their madness against us is great, their trembling great, their fear great, and great the danger of this aerial sea.

“If, while walking on earth from city to city, we beg those who guide us not to let us fall down precipices, or into places inhabited by wild beasts, or into impassable rivers, or inaccessible and trackless mountains, or into the hands of robbers, or into an immeasurable and waterless wilderness where we might perish—how many strong guides and divine guardians do we need as we travel this long and eternal road, namely, the departure from the body and the ascent to heaven?”

These were the blessed man’s wisdom-filled teachings to himself and to everyone; these were his daily cares and meditations.

### CHAPTER XLI

He was also very greatly concerned about the sacred service and showed his solicitude for it. One day, wishing to cut short the stay of many people, so that after the dismissal of the holy Gospel they would not leave the church and spend the time intended for prayer in idle conversation, what did he do? As soon as the holy Gospel had been read, he left the church; he himself went out and sat down with the crowd. When everyone was astonished, the just man said to them:

“My little children, where the sheep are, there is also the shepherd. Either go inside, and we shall go in; or remain here, and I shall remain here. For your sake I go down into the holy church, since I could celebrate the Masses for myself in the episcopal residence.”

Thus that blessed man enacted this same device once and twice. In this way he magnificently instructed and corrected the people, for they were afraid that the man who must always be remembered would enact the same device against them again.

### CHAPTER XLII

He absolutely did not allow anyone to speak in the sanctuary; instead, in the sight of everyone, he sent the person outside, saying:

“If you have come here to pray, desire that your mind and mouth be free for this purpose. But if you have come for conversation, it is written: ‘The house of God shall be called a house of prayer’ (Matthew XXI). Therefore do not make it a den of robbers.”

### CHAPTER XLIII

What was even more admirable in this most holy patriarch was that, although he had neither led the monastic life nor remained in the clergy at the church, but had long before been lawfully joined to a woman,

[Note: [Col. 0391B] “Long before lawfully joined to a woman.” He does not say “joined to a woman while he was patriarch,” but “long before,” that is, in former times. Metaphrastes makes this clear at the beginning of his Life.]

nevertheless, from the very beginning when he was consecrated patriarch, he maintained the vigor of the Church and was exalted to such a height that he surpassed many hermits and those living under an austere discipline.

### CHAPTER XLIV

But wishing not to be deprived even of this good—namely, of being numbered among those living the monastic life—he devised the following arrangement. Gathering two orders of holy monks, he decreed that they should receive every kind of provision from his estates in his city. He built cells for them in two oratories, one of our holy Lady, the Mother of God, and the other of Saint John, which he himself had built from their foundations. He said to the monks who loved God:

“After God, I shall provide for your bodily needs; but you must care for my spiritual salvation. Let the evening and nightly vigil be counted to me before God; whatever service you perform in your cells, let it be for your souls.”

He did this in order to make the monks, God’s friends, more diligent. Thus an arrangement of communities pleasing to God continued; and, in the likeness of a monastery, the city almost lives by means of them, offering God unceasing hymns of praise in various places.

### CHAPTER XLV

This blessed man also taught and solemnly charged everyone as follows:

“Under no circumstances should you ever become participants in the communion—or rather, in the defilement—of heretics, even if throughout your entire life, because of some pressure or necessity, you remain without communion, unable to find communion with the Catholic Church.

“For if,” he said, “when we lawfully possess a wife according to the flesh and remain for a long time in some distant region without her, we are forbidden by God and by the laws to abandon her and join ourselves to another woman—and if we do this, we are punished—how do you think that we, joined to God through right faith and the Catholic Church, as the Apostle says, ‘I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ’ (II Corinthians XI), will escape becoming participants in the torment awaiting heretics in the age to come if you adulterate the orthodox and holy faith through communion with heretics?

“For this reason,” he said, “communion is so called, because it makes the communicant share in and become bound to those with whom he communicates. Therefore, I beg you, my children, do not attach yourselves to such oratories.”

### CHAPTER XLVI

Among all his other virtues, this blessed man also possessed the quality that, as has been said, he neither condemned his neighbor nor received those who condemned others. I shall also relate his teaching on this matter, profitable to everyone.

A certain young man, having abducted a nun, fled to Constantinople. When the just man heard this, he became sorrowful even unto death. Some time later, as he was one day sitting in the honorable treasury with certain clerics and initiating a spiritually useful conversation, the young man who had abducted the servant of God was mentioned. Those sitting with the holy man began to anathematize such a young man, as one who had destroyed two souls—his own and that of the holy woman.

The blessed man therefore restrained and stopped them, saying:

“Not so, my children, not so. For I shall show you that you too are committing two sins: first, because you transgress the command of the one who says, ‘Do not judge, so that you may not be judged’ (Matthew VII); and second, because you do not know with certainty whether they are still sinning to this day and have not repented.”

For I have read something of this kind in the Life of a Father:

Two monks in a certain city went out to perform a service. As one of them was passing through a particular place, a prostitute called out to him, saying, “Save me, Father, as Christ saved the prostitute.” Without paying any attention whatsoever to human shame, he said to her, “Follow me.” Taking her by the hand, he left the city publicly, while everyone looked on.

It then became known that the abbot had taken a woman named Porphyria—for that was the woman’s name. As they went on in order to place her in a monastery, the woman found a child lying on the ground in a church and picked him up to raise him. After a year, some people came to the district where the abbot and Porphyria, who had formerly been a prostitute, were living. Seeing that she had a little child, they said to her, “Truly, you have borne the abbot a fine little boy.”

She had not yet received the holy monastic habit. Those who had seen her went to Tyre—for the abbot had taken her from there—and spread the report that Porphyria had borne the child by the abbot, saying, “We saw with our own eyes a little boy resembling him.”

When the abbot learned from God that his death was approaching, he said to the nun Pelagia—for that was the name he gave her when he bestowed the holy habit upon her:

“Let us go to Tyre, because I have a revelation there, and I want you to come with me.”

Since she could not oppose him, she followed him. They both arrived, bringing with them the child, who was seven years old.

When the abbot fell ill with a sickness unto death, as many as a hundred people came up from the city to visit him. He said, “Bring coals.” When a censer filled with coals had arrived,

[Note: [Col. 0391B] “Censer.” A similar example of chastity appears above, in the Life of Saint Basil, chapter 9.]

he took the coals, emptied them into his garment, and said:

“Believe me, brothers: just as God preserved the bush unburned by fire, and just as these coals have not burned this tunic of mine, so I have not known the woman’s sin from the time I was born.”

Everyone was amazed that the garment did not burn from the fire, and they glorified God, who has hidden servants.

Because of the example of the former prostitute, the nun Pelagia, other prostitutes followed her, renounced the world, and went with her to her monastery. The servant of God, the monk who had tonsured her, after satisfying everyone, surrendered his spirit to God in peace.

“That is why,” he said, “I tell you, my children: do not be rash in condemning and judging another person. Many times we have seen the sin of fornication, but we have not seen the repentance that the sinner made secretly. We have seen someone committing theft, but we do not know the sighs and tears he poured out before God. We regard him as he appeared to us—as a thief, or fornicator, or perjurer—but before God his hidden confession and repentance have been accepted, and he is precious to Him.”

Everyone therefore marveled at the teaching of this capable shepherd and teacher.

[Col. 0378B]

### CHAPTER XLVII

Two clerics made shoes and worked beside one another. One of them had many children, a wife, a father, and a mother; nevertheless, he devoted himself without interruption to the church and supported them all, after God, by his craft. The other, although more learned than he was, because he did not remain in the church but worked even on Sundays, was unable to support even himself.

This man therefore envied his neighbor. On one occasion, unable to endure his envy any longer, he said to him angrily:

“How have you become so rich? I, who devote myself to my craft more than you do, have fallen into poverty.”

The other, wishing to make him devote himself to the church, said:

“I find money on the ground, and by this I have gradually become rich. But if you wish, I shall always call you, and you may come with me; whatever we find, you shall receive half.”

When the other agreed and followed him as he went to the church, God blessed him without interruption and made him rich.

Then that good counselor said to him:

“Do you see, brother, how much one lie told for God’s sake has benefited your soul and your possessions?”

[Note: [Col. 0391C] “One lie told for God’s sake.” One must not understand this as permission to lie in any circumstance. He explains how he understood this pious deception, even though the other believed that he had found actual money on the ground.]

“Believe me, I never found any money on the ground, as you supposed. But because the Lord said, ‘Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you’ (Matthew VI), I devised this pretext solely to deceive you. And behold, I did not labor without purpose: you found, and you found more than you expected.”

When the holy patriarch learned this, he made him a presbyter, as one worthy to be a good counselor; for he had been a reader.

### CHAPTER XLVIII

Thus far the aforementioned worshiper of God, Mennas, who had been steward of the most holy church of the Alexandrians in the great city, has related the account to us. What follows has been set down by my unworthiness; some matters I also heard from persons who deserve to be believed.

When, in the preceding discussion in a certain chapter (above, chapter 11), we stated that the patriarch and the patrician Nicetas were bound to one another by great spiritual affection, the present chapter provides a fitting indication of such a relationship.

When, by God’s permission,

[Note: [Col. 0391C] “When, by God’s permission.” Baronius, volume VIII, in the year of Christ 620, the third year of Pope Boniface V and the eleventh of the emperor Heraclius, says:

“Moreover, we do not deny that Metaphrastes, who copied from the original, added something paraphrastically to the Acts of Leontius, since the words which he subsequently added, and which do not stand securely upon truth, are these: ‘This truly good shepherd, the divine patriarch, I mean, trusting in Christ, the Prince of Shepherds, who commands, “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matthew X), when Alexandria was about to be delivered into the hands of the Persians, withdrew from there by divine providence and migrated to his own homeland, Cyprus, in order to give it his body, since it had nourished him; for he had already foreseen that his death was approaching.’”

“I have no doubt that these words were added by him. For it is certain from what was said above that the Persian invasion of Egypt had occurred long before; at that time he by no means abandoned his own church, although he may have sought hiding places so as not to be taken captive. The reason for this departure from Alexandria was entirely different. When the patrician Nicetas had recognized the virtue of so great a man, he wished to take him to the emperor at Constantinople, so that, having received his blessing, the emperor might set out more securely for the Persian war. This is demonstrated by the words of Leontius himself that follow.”

Thus far Baronius.

I could wish that Baronius had remembered what he wrote in the Roman Martyrology on January 23, where he says that there is a double edition and translation of the Acts of John, and that this passage—supposedly inserted by Metaphrastes—had not occurred to him. For Leontius, whom we publish here, also has the same passage, so that I have no doubt that Metaphrastes likewise drew it from Leontius.

Although, in the sixth year of Heraclius—which Baronius assigns to the year of Christ 615—Paul the Deacon, in the Miscellaneous History, book XVIII, records that the Persians devastated Egypt, he says that they immediately returned to their own territory. Later, however, a grave storm was impending, in which not only the wealth but also the lives of Christians were endangered. Concerning this same event Paul writes:

“In the eleventh year of the reign of Heraclius, harsh Chosroes imposed his yoke upon all men through the shedding of blood and the imposition of tribute.”

Our John fled from this storm. Seizing this opportunity, as Leontius and Metaphrastes relate, the patrician Nicetas wished to bring him to the emperor, who was already preparing himself for war against the Persians, so that the patriarch might bestow his blessing upon him.]

it was destined, on account of our sins, that Alexandria should be handed over without God’s protection to the Persians, the shepherd, remembering the words of the one who said, “When they persecute you in this city, flee into another” (Matthew X), took flight to his native country, namely Cyprus, to his own city.

Taking this as an opportunity, the aforementioned patrician Nicetas said to the holy man:

“I beg you, if I have found favor before you, do not disdain to travel as far as the imperial city, and to offer your well-received prayers to the most devout emperors.”

The man of great faith consented. He became obedient to God and to His will, while God wished through him to demonstrate the honor bestowed by the patrician upon the blessed man.

The ship on which the holy man and the patrician were traveling was repeatedly battered by the force of the winds and was about to be cast into the depths. During one night, when the storm arose, the aforementioned patrician and the leading men who were with him repeatedly saw the patriarch: at one moment he was running about everywhere on the ship with the poor; at another, he was extending his hands with them toward heaven and drawing help down from above.

When they had reached Rhodes,

[Note: [Col. 0392A] “To Rhodes.” Both manuscripts have this reading; the printed editions have “in the interval.” Rhodes is the well-known island.]

and had gone ashore, the patrician, awakened by God, saw a certain eunuch shining in appearance, holding a golden scepter in his right hand, standing beside him and saying:

“Come; command. The King of kings seeks you.”

[Note: [Col. 0392A] “Come; command.” So the Aquicinctine and Gemblacensis manuscripts; the printed editions have “you are commanded to come.” The word *jube* (“command”) was used in various ways by writers of a later age.

Aurelius Victor writes, “He commands Maximian to be emperor,” and likewise, “He commands him Caesar,” as Casaubon explains in his notes on Aelius. In Spartianus, however, it means “appoint.” Thus *non jubere* is noted in the Life of Alexander Severus by Spartianus as meaning “to prohibit.”]

Immediately neglecting nothing, he summoned the patrician Nicetas and said to him with many tears:

“You, my lord, called me to an earthly emperor; but the heavenly one, arriving first, has already called my littleness.”

He related to him the vision of the eunuch—or rather, of the angel—that had appeared to him.

That most glorious man was both joyful and saddened, but he was unable to detain the holy man. Having therefore been abundantly filled with his holy prayers, and carrying them to the emperors, he ordered him to return to Cyprus with great honor.

### CHAPTER XLIX

When he had arrived in his native city, which was called Amathunta,

[Note: [Col. 0392B] “Amathunta.” This is how names were formed in that period. In Ptolemy, Amathus is a town of Cyprus. Just as *Persida* was formed from *Persis* in the accusative, so from *Amathus* they formed *Amathunta*, even in the nominative.]

he quickly ordered his attendants to write his testament. When they promptly and without delay presented paper and pen, he ordered that holy mouth to write as follows:

“John, a servant, but on account of the priestly dignity imposed upon me, free by the grace of God. I give thanks to You, God, because You have heard my misery when I begged Your goodness that, when I died, I might not be found to possess even one tremissis.

“When I found myself in the honorable episcopal residence of the most holy Church of the Alexandrians in the great city, which I received by God’s indulgence when I was consecrated bishop there, I found approximately eighty hundredweights of gold; and the gifts that came to me from Christ’s friends almost exceed the measure of a man. Gathering my mind into itself and recognizing that all these things belong to the Lord of all, I hastened to give to God what belonged to God. Therefore, what remains to me—this tremissis, which also belongs to God—I order to be given to those who belong to God.”

O glorious deed! O devotion of the holy man! He did not think, as he ought to have done, of his own family, as do many who possess wealth, who hoard God’s gifts—or things gathered through injustice—as though they were their own and as though they could carry them away with them, instead of giving generously to the needy. He sought those things that remain forever and are never diminished.

Thus he was not defrauded of the promises that had been made to him in God’s name: “Those who honor me, I will honor” (I Samuel II). Indeed, He magnificently honored this holy man, through whom the Lord was always honored in his good works.

For this noble man could not bear to let his holy and praiseworthy deeds come to an end with his temporal life. What did he do? He built hospitals for strangers, homes for the aged, and monasteries from their foundations, and established choirs of holy monks. Through the good works celebrated in them, he possesses an unceasing memorial of true righteousness.

Concerning those who do evil and leave behind in this life successors to their own evils after death, the Apostle, filled with the Lord, says: “The sins of some people are manifest, going before them to judgment; but the sins of others follow after” (I Timothy V).

Conversely, this must be said concerning this blessed man:

“The righteousness of some is manifest, going before them into the kingdom of heaven; but the righteousness of others follows after.”

[Note: [Col. 0392B] “Conversely.” This entire clause, though contrary to the preceding one, is necessary to the sense and is absent from all the printed editions. I have supplied it from both manuscripts.]

He was one of these. And since what has been said is not a fable or a statement made merely to please, let the miracle that occurred immediately at his precious death bear clear witness to us.

When he entrusted and commended his soul into the hand of the Lord, as Holy Scripture says somewhere, “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God” (Wisdom III), and offered it to Him as a sacrificed offering, his honorable body was to be buried with honor and with the fitting rite of the priests in an oratory of the holy wonder-worker Tychon.

[Note: [Col. 0392B] “Tychon.” The Aquicinctine manuscript has *Thiconis*; the Gemblacensis manuscript, *Tichonis*; the printed editions, *Tyronis*. The reading must certainly be *Tychonis*, for his memory is found in the ecclesiastical calendars. The Roman Martyrology, June 16, reads: “At Amathus in Cyprus, Saint Tychon, bishop, in the time of Theodosius the Younger.” He is also mentioned in the Greek Menologion and the Menaea on June 16.]

Then a certain glorious sign occurred.

### CHAPTER L

In a certain tomb, where this just man was also to be placed, there lay the truly holy bodies of two former bishops who had fallen asleep before him. Although they were meanwhile lying in lifeless condition, they granted him equal honor, as though they were genuinely alive.

When the body of the blessed man was to be placed between the two, the shepherds honoring the chief shepherd, revering his great confidence before God, and at the same time marveling, by God’s command separated their bodies as though they were alive and received this holy man in their midst.

[Note: [Col. 0392C] “Separating their bodies.” Something similar occurred in the primitive Church. Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 51, writes: “There is also another account among our people: when body was placed beside body in the cemetery, space was made by their drawing apart. If such a thing is also reported among the pagans, God certainly displays signs of his power—among his own people for consolation, and among outsiders for testimony.” I seem to have read similar examples in other Lives of the saints. See Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 32, concerning two lovers, where tombs separated from one another opened and joined together.]

They offered him honor as one honored by God, by God’s command, and immediately showed everyone the glory and sublimity that had been granted to him by God.

This greatest and most glorious miracle was seen not by one person, nor by ten, nor by a hundred, but by the entire crowd that had gathered for his precious burial.

[Col. 0380D]

### CHAPTER LI

Another miracle of his, more glorious still, which began while he was yet living in the flesh but was completed after he had departed to God, this narrative will now attempt to recount.

A certain woman from the city that had produced the holy man, having heard that he had come from Rhodes

[Note: [Col. 0392C] “From Rhodes.” Both manuscripts have this reading; the printed editions have *Arbodo*, a very bad reading.]

and that an angel had appeared to him there and announced his summons to the common Lord, recognized within herself a very grave sin, which, she declared, could not enter human ears. Taking up unwavering faith, she hurried to the holy man. Seizing his feet, she cried out with many tears, saying secretly to the saint:

“I, miserable woman, possess a sin, thrice-blessed one, which cannot reach human ears. I know that, if you are willing, you can forgive it for me. For the Lord said to you: ‘Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven’ (Matthew XVIII); and, ‘Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained’ (John XX).”

When the holy man heard these words from the woman, he was afraid that, if he rejected her request, he would become guilty of her punishment, since she could be freed from her own sin through the faith she had in him. He therefore said to her humbly:

“If, woman, you truly believe in God that the crime you mention can be forgiven through my unworthiness, confess it to me.”

She replied:

“I cannot tell it, lord; human hearing cannot bear it.”

The holy man said to her again:

“If you are ashamed, go and write it down, if you know how to write, and bring it to me.”

She answered again:

“Truly, lord, I cannot.”

After waiting silently for a little while, he said to her:

“Can you not write it, seal it, and bring it to me?”

Then she said to him:

“I can, lord. I shall do this. But I beg your honorable, angel-like soul not to undo it, and not to allow this written document to be found by anyone at any time.”

[Note: [Col. 0392C] “Written document.” Both manuscripts have this reading; the printed editions have “sin.” The following context suggests that *pittacium* is correct. It is usually written *pyctacium* or *pictacium*. Greek *πύκτις* means a little book, letter, or tablet. See the *Onomasticon*. A similar example occurs above in the Life of Basil, chapter 10.]

Having received from God the honorable assurance that no human being would open or read her document, she went away, wrote the sin with her own hand, sealed it, and brought it to the blessed man.

The holy man received the document. Five days later he departed to the Lord, without either arranging anything concerning such a document or telling anyone about it.

By chance—or rather, by God’s providence—the woman was not in the city on the day when the patriarch was transferred in peace from this world to the next, God wishing also through this to show how great a confidence he possessed before Him as His own servant.

But arriving one day after the burial of his precious relics,

[Note: [Col. 0392D] “Relics.” Both manuscripts correctly have *lipsani*. The old edition has *lipsam*, from which the Cologne edition produced *ipsa*. The Aquicinctine manuscript glosses the word: “that is, body or relics.”]

and hearing of his death, she became almost crazed and delirious. She supposed that the document she had given him had been left in the episcopal residence and that it would make her guilt manifest to everyone.

Quickly recovering herself, however, and taking up again her former unwavering faith in his soul, she grasped the coffin of the man honored by God and, as though he were truly still alive, she declared in her agitation:

“Man of God, I could not tell you this sin, because it was exceedingly grave; and now, perhaps, it has become manifest and known to everyone. Would that I had not revealed my matter to you! Alas, alas for me! Hoping to find release from shame, I have become a source of shame to everyone. Instead of healing, I have received blasphemy. Why did I need to reveal the secret of my soul to you?

“Yet I shall neither fail nor lose hope, nor shall I remove my tears from your tomb, until I receive satisfaction concerning my request. For you are not dead, holy man of God, but alive. For it is written that ‘the righteous live forever’ (Wisdom V).

“Taking up the same words again, she said: ‘I ask nothing of you, man of God, except that you make my heart certain about what happened to the document I gave you.’”

The God who once said to the Canaanite woman, “Your faith has saved you” (Matthew XV), also made this woman certain.

For she persevered for three days at the saint’s tomb, tasting neither food nor drink. On the third night, while once again amid tears she was speaking the same harsh yet faithful words to the most blessed man, behold, God’s servant came forth from his tomb, visibly appearing with the two bishops who lay there with him, one standing on this side and the other on that.

[Note: [Col. 0392D] “One on this side and the other on that, looking.” Thus the Aquicinctine manuscript. The printed editions read: “with one standing on this side and the other on that side beside him.” From the reading of the Aquicinctine codex, someone might perhaps conjecture that the correct reading is *astantibus* or *aspectantibus*. I have reproduced the old reading, if it should prove sound and should be found elsewhere as well. In the Glosses of Isidore I find: *Aspita*, “a ruin.” The same appears in the manuscript Glossary of Camberon.]

He said to her:

“How long will you disturb those who are here and not allow them to rest? For your tears have soaked our robes.”

As he spoke, he gave her her own sealed document, saying:

“Take this. Do you recognize it? Open it and look.”

Coming to herself after the vision, she saw the saints entering again into their own place. When she opened the document, she found that her writing had been erased, with the following subscription beneath it:

“For the sake of my servant John, your sin has been erased.”

Who can proclaim the mighty acts of the Lord, O friends and brothers? How merciful and loving toward humanity He is—fulfilling the will of those who fear Him, glorifying those who glorify Him, and magnifying them through the working of miracles!

The grace he possessed before God was not revealed only in this place, where his precious death occurred; it shone far and wide everywhere.

### CHAPTER LII

On the very day when this blessed man departed from this life to God, one of those who possessed the angelic life and monastic habit—a remarkable and capable man named Sabinus, who lived in Alexandria—saw, as though in an ecstatic vision, John, honored by God, coming out of his episcopal residence with all the clergy carrying wax candles and going to the emperor.

A certain eunuch—so Sabinus himself said—was calling him as a chamberlain. After John had left the door of the episcopal residence, signifying the separation from his own body, a young girl like the sun received him, took him by the hand, and had a crown of olive branches wrapped around her head.

At once the holy Sabinus recognized that the patriarch’s departure to the Lord had taken place at that very hour.

They noted the month and day, which was a celebrated one—namely, the day of Saint Mennas the martyr.

[Note: [Col. 0392D] “Of Saint Mennas the martyr.” His feast occurs in the Menologion and the Menaea on November 11. Yet in those same books John’s feast is placed on November 12. Did this result from a transfer of the feast because Mennas was a most celebrated martyr, known throughout the East, so that they gave John the following day?]

Some people who lived in Alexandria questioned others who had come from Cyprus about the holy patriarch’s death, and they learned that the vision had been true, since it occurred at the same hour at which the blessed man died—especially as regards the example of the young girl who was holding him by the hand.

For, as we said in the preceding words of the Life (above, chapter 7), the saint had received promises from her:

“If you regard me as your friend, I shall introduce you before the emperor.”

And this she truly did.

### CHAPTER LIII

Nor did everyone find assurance only from the fact that the almsgiving and mercy he had shown toward the needy led him into the kingdom of heaven. Another God-fearing man, one of those who lived in the city of Alexandria, saw that same night—the night on which the holy Sabinus had his vision—all the poor, orphans, and widows carrying olive branches, going in attendance upon the patriarch and proceeding to the church.

There are not merely two, or ten, or a hundred assurances by which we clearly know that this memorable man deserved a place among the saints. Behold, there are also others, which the following account displays.

[Col. 0383A]

### CHAPTER LIV

After a considerable time had passed since the saint’s death, an annual hymn-service was celebrated in the temple of the aforementioned Saint Tychon (above, chapter 49), where the precious relic of the most blessed patriarch John had been deposited. The sacred vigil being celebrated was the annual hymn-service in memory of the wonder-worker Saint Tychon.

The Lord of miracles, wishing to show everyone with what honor He had deemed His holy servant John worthy to be honored, caused a healing fragrance of ointment to flow from his honorable relic. All were filled with joy and returned glory to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—to our true God, who glorifies His own saints with infinite glory.

### CHAPTER LV

Let no one, O friends of Christ, be an unbeliever concerning so great a miracle. For even to this day, in the Christ-loving island of Cyprus, such divine grace is seen working through various saints, and sweetness like that flowing from springs of perfume pours forth from their precious relics, to the glory of that same goodness, to the honor of His saints, and to the encouragement and good zeal of those who will come afterward.

Thus, living according to their imitation, may we also be made worthy of the same honors by God, the just giver of rewards.

Let us therefore, beloved, also become fulfillers of the rectitude prescribed above by this most holy Father of ours, John. Like inhabitants and pilgrims in this present life, let us lay up an eternal treasure through the generous gift distributed to those in need (I Corinthians IX).

For, according to the divinely inspired Apostle, “the one who sows with blessings will also reap from blessings” (II Corinthians IX); and, in place of corruptible things, incorruptible things; in place of temporal things, eternal things—things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the human heart,” which God has prepared for those who love Him.

May we all obtain these things through the grace and mercy of Jesus Christ our Lord, with whom, together with the Holy Spirit, there is glory, honor, and dominion to the Father, now and always, forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0393]

## JULY 8. LIFE OF THE SAINTS EPICTETUS THE PRESBYTER AND ASTION THE MONK

[Note: [Col. 0413C] “Of Epictetus the presbyter and Astion the monk.” I find no mention of these saints anywhere in the ecclesiastical calendars, except in the manuscript *Florarium of the Saints*, where the following appears under July 8:

“On this day in the East, the holy martyrs Epictetus and Astion, slain for Christ under the emperor Diocletian; their wondrous deeds and sufferings are recounted. They suffered in the year of salvation 290.”

The same day is assigned in the Martyrology of Usuard as expanded by the Carthusian monks of Cologne in 1521.

The *Speculum exemplorum* cites an example from this Life, distinction 8, which derives from the *Lives of the Saints*, example 21; it is found here in chapter 11.

I possessed no manuscript copy of this Life except one from the church of Saint Salvator at Utrecht, written by a recent hand. Nor did I possess any printed copy except one from Cologne in the *Lives of the Fathers*. The remaining editions lack this Life.]

BY AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR

[Col. 0393A]

## CHAPTER ONE

In the time of the most profane emperor Diocletian,

[Note: [Col. 0413D] “Of the most profane emperor Diocletian.” The printed edition adds: “who reigned around the year of the Lord 190,” which is absent from the manuscript and is plainly an erroneous date.]

there was a certain presbyter in the regions of the East named Epictetus, leading a religious life and remaining chaste in all his conduct.

From early childhood he had been brought up in the service of the Lord and was exercised in all the ordinances of Jesus Christ (Psalm CXVIII). When he reached mature age, he earned the privilege, like Samuel of old, of wearing the priestly ephod (I Samuel II), because through him divine grace worked many signs and wonders in every place.

Indeed, he often enlightened the eyes of the blind through his prayers. He also cleansed lepers who came to him, healed the paralyzed, and drove demons from bodies possessed by them.

## CHAPTER II

Accordingly, one day, while he was sitting alone in his cell and offering his customary prayers to Christ, a certain girl, the daughter of a count, who was entirely dead in all her limbs except her tongue, was brought to him. When her father had placed his daughter before his door, he himself entered and, suddenly falling at the holy man’s knees, cried out and said:

“Have mercy on me, O man of the Most High God, since your God is proclaimed by his servants to be wholly merciful and compassionate. Please do not cast me away from your presence, since he gladly receives all who flee to him. For I have one only daughter, about fifteen years of age, but for three years she has been paralyzed and deprived of the use of her limbs. Therefore I do not doubt that he who restrained the flow of blood lasting twelve years (Matt. 9) can, if he wills, through you grant my daughter complete recovery, since we have vowed ourselves to his faith and are members of the holy Church, and have been baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.”

Hearing this, the priest of the Lord ordered that the girl be brought inside to him. When her father had placed her at his feet, the man of God poured out prayers to the Lord God on her behalf, saying:

“Eternal God, driver of the cherubim, who descended from heaven in order to restore the exile of Paradise to its ancient possession; who, through the dispensation of your humanity, took upon yourself our weakness, so that we might deserve to possess you in our earthen vessels: I ask you, Lord, I ask you, deign to look upon the faith of your servant. And just as you recalled the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue from the gates of death to life (Mark 5), so now, by your grace, deign to restore this only child [Col. 0394A] to her former condition, so that this faithless and perverse generation may learn to honor your holy and fearful name and to proclaim your wonders at all times.”

When he had finished praying, he anointed all the girl’s limbs with consecrated oil. Having received this health and cure, she blessed the Lord together with her parents.

Then Saint Epictetus instructed the girl’s father, saying:

“If you wish, my dearest friend, that no illness or affliction thereafter prevail in your household, hasten each week, together with your entire family, to receive the Lord’s sacraments with deepest devotion and a pure heart.”

After saying this, he ordered him to depart joyfully and in good spirits with all his household to their own home.

## CHAPTER III

Again, at another time, a certain demoniac was brought to him. When the man of God had arranged for him to live with him, the devil began for three days to cry out to him in the following manner:

“O cross! O torments that I suffer without cause! How well things always went for me in the regions of Phrygia! How every day I persuaded human beings to offer my sacrifice and observe my rite! In what great honors, wretched that I am, I lived there. Yet until now I did not understand this, because in a kind of rashness I departed from there and came here. For I am the one who, through Montanus, uttered many words full of blasphemy. Through Maximilla I committed various crimes. I dragged that entire region into my worship and filth. Through Arius I invaded the city of Alexandria and persuaded him to call the Son of the living God a creature. Through Mani I instituted the Manichaean heresy and taught them to consecrate fasts to me. Through Donatus I devastated the whole of Africa. And behold, now I am held bound by one of your servants like a fugitive slave, O Christ.”

**[Note: [Col. 0413D] “I.” What follows until “And behold” was lacking in the printed edition. Some of the stories related here do indeed correspond to the time of Diocletian and earlier; others, however, seem to be later than Diocletian. Hence it may be inferred that some addition has been made here.]**

While the demon was crying out these and many other things, he was rebuked by the blessed man and, on the third day, departed from his dwelling. The man who had been cleansed gave thanks to Christ the Lord.

## CHAPTER IV

At another time a blind woman was brought to him. Standing before him, she lamented in these words:

“I recognize who you are, and I also believe how powerful you are with God. Therefore do not despise my weeping or disregard my supplication. The physicians of this entire province have exercised their knowledge and skill upon me, but they have been unable to help me in any way. Rather, the more they demonstrated their art upon me, the more miserably I was weakened by pain. Therefore I beseech your holiness to deign merely to place your right hand upon my eyes in the name of your Christ; and I believe that through you the sight of my eyes will immediately be granted to me.”

Then Saint Epictetus, admiring the woman’s faith, placed his right hand upon her eyes, glorifying the goodness of the Lord and saying to her:

“Let it be done for you, daughter, according to what you have believed.”

The words were still forming in the mouth of Christ’s priest when, suddenly opening her eyes, the woman saw the light and cried out:

“Glory to you, God of the Christians, who do not despise sinners placed in error, but, because of your great mercy, receive and save those who turn to you.”

After saying this, she immediately believed in God the Savior together with her entire household.

Since it would be quite lengthy to set forth for the diligent reader all the wonders that the Lord worked through him, it is enough for the present to have briefly touched in passing upon these few among the many. Now let us return to the work at hand.

## CHAPTER V

One day, then, a certain young man, exceedingly handsome in face and beautiful to behold, named Astion, came to him for a visit. The blessed presbyter asked him to sit beside him, placed his hand upon his head, and began to exhort him to the faith of the Lord with gentle words, saying:

“Who are you, my sweetest son,” he said, “and where do you come from, or where are you going? Tell me whose son you are and of what family.”

He replied:

“How shall I explain my origin or family to your blessedness, most blessed father, I do not know. I shall therefore tell you briefly and in passing only what I know. My father is regarded as the chief man of this city and is exceedingly wealthy. My mother belongs to an illustrious family and was the daughter of the senator Julian. They look upon me every day as their only child and most precious pearl.”

The holy man answered:

“You have spoken well, my son, in saying that they look upon you as a pearl; for they no longer possess you, but only look upon you, since your blessed soul is considered more precious than every pearl and every metal. Christ himself, as I see, has already chosen it for his service and for serving him. Come, therefore, my son, and reject the things that are valued in this world, so that together with all the saints you may receive in the future those things that are not seen here.

“For all these things that they behold here are transitory and destined to perish. But those things that God has prepared for those who serve him remain forever, just as he himself remains forever. For this gold, my son, which is seen, is not real, but a certain vanity of appearance, by which the souls of the righteous are deceived in this world. Likewise, the silver seen by these eyes bears a false name: it is fashioned and polished by everyone merely to deceive the greedy and persuade the foolish.

“Come, then, and listen to me, sweetest son, and I shall show you what gold you ought to choose and what silver you ought to desire—namely, that which our Lord and Savior grants to those who believe in him, saying: ‘I advise you to buy from me gold refined by fire, so that you may become rich and be clothed in white garments, so that the shame of your nakedness may not appear’ (Rev. 3).

“This refined gold tested by fire is Christ our Lord. And, my son, whoever wishes to have him enthroned in his heart will immediately deserve heavenly riches and will be clothed in white garments—that is, in faith, hope, and charity—through which thereafter you will be able to overcome not only this visible world but also the devil, whom you worship as lord, together with all his angels.

“For this father of yours whom you see, my son, is not the true father. Rather, God the Almighty is called your Father; and for that reason one is called ‘that one’ and another is pronounced ‘this one.’ The former is invisible and indescribable; the latter is visible and corruptible. The former remains incomprehensible and immortal; the latter exists in all things as corruptible and mortal.

“By the dispensation of the former, therefore, all things endure; by the ordering of the latter, nothing remains established. He commanded, and you were made; he ordered, and you were formed in your mother’s womb; he decreed, and you came forth; he commanded, and you were brought to this youthful age.

“Your visible father is indeed to be honored, my son, but not as that other Father is honored, since he made and created us in his own image and likeness, granted us understanding and prudence, gave us alert perception and the memory of good things, and established us as rulers over all his works. By his grace he adopted us from servants as sons, brothers, and friends. Therefore it is always fitting, my son, to acknowledge and worship this true Father, who has bestowed such great blessings upon us.

“Honor is also to be given to this visible father for this reason alone: that he often performed a servant’s ministry toward us when we were little; frequently he fed us; often he was concerned for the necessities of our infancy; he cherished the flesh that belongs to flesh; and he cared for his own offspring. Behold, for such reasons honor is to be given him.

“But we have another mother as well, my son. She is not this visible mother, but remains immortal; she is rightly betrothed to our Savior and adorned by angels, embellished by prophets, glorified by apostles, exalted by martyrs and confessors, and raised in Christ, and through Christ, into the heavenly bridal chamber. Human beings call her the holy mother Church.

“Her voice is like that of a turtledove; from her lips distill perfumes, namely, the teaching of the apostles. Her eyes are the two lights of heaven. Her teeth are white, like those ascending from a washing. This mystical meaning is represented in the twenty-four most sacred books.

**[Note: [Col. 0414C] “The twenty-four books.” The number assigned to the sacred books was formerly various. This passage should be understood in light of that variation.]**

“From her hands drips myrrh, which is righteousness and true faith. Her ten fingers contain the power and mystery of the Decalogue. Her two breasts are the two Testaments, namely, the Mosaic Law and the grace of the Gospel. Her feet are like bronze. Her womb and innermost parts signify the most sacred font of Baptism and the regeneration of all nations.

“Come, therefore, my sweetest son, and suck the breasts of this most true mother of yours. Heed her admonitions and reject the things seen in this age, so that you may deserve to enjoy those things that God has promised to grant to his children in the life to come.

“But listen also to our true Father saying: ‘Go out from your land and from your kindred, and come into the land that I shall show you’ (Gen. 12)—that is, into the land of the living and the region of the saints; into a land flowing with milk and honey, that is, into the teaching of the apostles and prophets.

“When you have fulfilled everything that he has commanded you, he will then hand over to you the possessions of Paradise, disclose to you the heavenly mysteries, grant you the glory of the kingdom of heaven, show you the immeasurable joy of the apostles, and repeatedly reveal to you the choirs of martyrs and the multitude of angels and archangels. Above all these things, he will adopt you by grace as a son and brother to himself.”

Hearing this, the exceedingly wise young man fell at the old man’s knees and began to beg that he himself might instead offer himself to the one whom he would serve from his earliest age, who alone was held to possess such power and greatness.

And because of the servants or ministers who were at his service, lest any of them report these matters to his father, Astion said nothing further to the man of God on that day.

## CHAPTER VI

On the following day, rising at first light like a most prudent bee, he hurried to the same place from which he had fed upon heavenly flowers the day before. Entering the dwelling of the Lord’s priest, he greeted him in these words:

“Hail, O apostle of Christ and minister of the New Testament.”

The holy man replied:

“And hail to you, young man, who bear upon your head the robe of martyrdom and a crown woven with many gems.”

When he had made him sit beside him, he spoke to him as follows:

“What is it, my son? Has the seed of the Lord, which yesterday by divine grace we sowed in the soil of your heart, risen to fruit, or is it still held back by the fault of unbelief?”

Astion answered:

“As your blessedness knows, most holy father, I am the only son of my father and exceedingly dear to him. I fear greatly that, if I become a Christian, he may, in utter despair, either violently deprive himself of life or throw himself into the depths of the sea, or—God forbid—become deranged because of me; and that from the very source from which I hope salvation will come to me, I may prepare perpetual death and the fires of hell for him.

“Therefore, if you deign to accept my counsel, do for the present what I say. Order me to become a catechumen today, impose upon me a fast for as many days as you wish, and after the appointed days grant me the sacrament of Baptism. When I have fulfilled everything pertaining to the Christian religion, I beg you that we both leave this city together and hasten to a distant region, wherever the Holy Spirit may lead us, lest my father pollute my unstained conscience with his tears.”

When everything the prudent young man had planned had been accomplished, a few days later, after prayer had been offered to Christ, they both departed from the city. They boarded a ship and entered the territory of the Scythians, reaching the city of the Almiridenses.

**[Note: [Col. 0414D] “The city of the Almiridenses.” This Life indicates that it was a city of Scythia. See the Onomasticon.]**

There, no one could recognize either them or their homeland.

## CHAPTER VII

After the blessed men had undertaken this holy flight, the parents of Saint Astion began to search for him through various places and, running here and there, to call out his name with immense sorrow.

His father cried out:

“My sweetest son and my only treasure, dearest Astion, what has happened to you? What wild beast suddenly devoured you, so that I could not find even the smallest remnant of you? O staff of my old age and light of my inward being, I no longer know where to seek you, nor into what region I should send my servants because of you.

“You were the most precious pearl of this city; among your fellow citizens you walked like the most beautiful dove; like a ray of the sun you shone among them all; like the most splendid moon you gleamed amid the common people; among the wise you were wiser than all. And why say more? Through your honey-sweet words you provoked everyone to desire your love.”

This was the father’s lament.

But the mother, tearing her clothing and beating her breast with her hands, mourned in the following manner:

“Who separated you from me, or who deceived you? What mad bird snatched you from my lap, sweetest son Astion? I do not know. But, as I suspect, perhaps the God of the Christians sent one of his own, perverted your heart, and alienated you from us.

“And now woe to me, miserable and alone, because infinite sadness and unbearable grief have seized me, and the labor of so many years has proved vain. The crown of my head has fallen. The fruit of my womb has withered, and I sit like a desolate city.

“Until today, through you, my son, I was a mother and a queen; but now, having lost you, I possess neither the glory of a queen nor the joy of a mother.

“But you too, sweetest son, were a tree, and you have been cut down; a pearl, and you have been stolen by the Galilaeans; a precious gem, and you have been placed in darkness; a lamp, and you have been extinguished; a pillar, and you have been thrown down; a royal statue, and you have been overturned.

**[Note: [Col. 0414D] “The Galilaeans.” Christians were formerly called by this name. Lucian, *Philopatris*. See the *Onomasticon*.]**

“And why say more? You were a human being, and, as I suspect, in a moment’s time you suddenly died. And now, because of you, my son, I have become deranged, so that I no longer understand either my life or my name.”

As his father and mother uttered these and similar words, they could in no way relieve themselves of their overwhelming grief.

## CHAPTER VIII

When the holy men of God had found suitable dwellings for themselves in the aforementioned city, they offered thanksgiving in it to God alone. And because it is written, “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5), nor can divine grace remain concealed under a bushel, heavenly power again began to work through Saint Epictetus in the region of the Scythians more signs and wonders than it had worked in the eastern regions.

One day a woman came to him and brought her son, about fifteen years old, who was mute and deaf and withered. Throwing him at the feet of Saint Epictetus, she spoke to him as follows:

“I do not know where you come from, nor do I know from what region you originate. But I believe only this: that if you wish, you can grant healing to the sick, since your appearance and religious observance declare that you are a disciple of that Nazarene. For we have heard how many signs and wonders others of your number have worked in his name.

“Therefore, since you are regarded as one of his disciples, help our infirmities. Preach to us about his wonders; explain to us his origin and the mystery of his divinity, so that we too may deserve through you to become his servants.”

Hearing this, the priest of the Lord spoke to the woman in these words:

“If you wish to believe in him whom I proclaim as God, woman, and if no fault of unbelief thereafter remains in your heart, but you believe with all your heart that he is himself the creator of heaven and earth, of the sea and the fountains of waters, and of all that is in them, then what you have requested will be done. For he is not far from each one of us, since ‘in him we are, and live, and move’ (Acts 17).”

Saying this, he ordered the disabled boy to be raised. Then, lifting his eyes toward heaven, he prayed to the Lord on his behalf:

“Almighty God, who are boundless and invisible, indescribable and incomprehensible as well; salvation of Christians, physician of the sick, pilot of those at sea, harbor of those in danger, light of the blind, foot of the lame, way of those who wander: look, I beseech you, Lord, upon this servant of yours, and loosen the bond of his tongue for the praise of your name.

“Open his ears also, so that he may hear your heavenly mysteries. Heal all his crushed limbs, both soul and body, just as your venerable coming granted complete health to that paralytic who had lain for thirty-eight years (John 5), so that those who have not known you may acknowledge your name and believe that you alone are the true God, who reign and remain with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever.”

When he had completed the prayer, he spat three times into the child’s mouth. Then he questioned him, saying:

“Son, in which God ought we to believe: in the idols made by human beings, or in Jesus Christ crucified, who today has deigned to heal you?”

The boy cried out in a loud voice:

“We ought to believe in Jesus Christ, most blessed man, who always and even to the present day works such benefits in human beings.”

When the people of Almiridenses witnessed this miracle, they glorified God, and more than a thousand souls believed in the Lord Savior on that day.

## CHAPTER IX

Not only Saint Epictetus, but also the most blessed Astion, worked many miracles in the Lord’s name. Indeed, abundant grace was granted to them against all illnesses, and they were also given the greatest power against demons.

One day, as he was going to the Danube to draw water, a man who was tormented by a demon met him. Approaching him and praying sufficiently on his behalf, he made the saving sign upon his forehead and traced it over all his limbs. At that very hour the demon departed from him.
