As the devil fled, he said:

“Your faith, O Astion, and purity of mind have received great power from the Savior against our race.”

After saying this, he disappeared completely.

## CHAPTER X

Again, at another time, he saw a man who had fallen from a great height and was being carried home by his parents, half dead. When he saw them lamenting greatly over this sudden event, he was moved by compassionate pity and withdrew to a certain secluded place. Standing there, he prayed to our Lord on the man’s behalf:

“Christ God, who through the blessed apostle Paul recalled Eutychus, who fell from a window, from the gates of death to life (Acts 20); who through Saint Peter granted strength of limb to Aeneas, who had lain on a bed for eighty years; and who bestowed complete health upon the man lame from his mother’s womb (Acts 3): now, I beseech you, Lord, look upon this man, who through the devil’s working has fallen from so great a height. Grant him complete health and make him one of the number of your flocks, because you are our shepherd, the true Lord, who spoke in your holy Gospel, saying (John 10): ‘I am the good shepherd, and I know my sheep, and my sheep know me. Just as the Father knows me, I also know the Father, and I lay down my life for my sheep.’”

When the prayer was finished, he approached the man and spoke to him:

“In the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk.”

Taking his right hand, he raised him up. Immediately his legs and feet were strengthened, and he sprang up and walked.

Coming with his parents to the dwelling of the holy men, he cried out in a loud voice:

“The God of Epictetus and Astion is one God, truly the one God of the Christians. Therefore I shall not leave this place unless today I become a Christian together with my parents.”

Then the priest of the Lord took the man and, together with all who were present, made them catechumens at that very hour. A few days later he gave them the sacrament of Baptism.

## CHAPTER XI

At another time, when the most blessed Astion had gone to draw water from the river without the old man’s permission or blessing, a shameful thought suddenly invaded his mind as he was walking along the road.

For three days this great and holy man was unable to drive it from his breast. He became exceedingly sad, and his face remained deeply troubled because of it.

When the venerable elder saw him, he said:

“What is this, my son? Why do I see you so sad and observe that you are worn down by unusual grief? This sadness, which now seems to hold you, is not the kind that the saints ordinarily bear upon their faces, nor that which penitents bear for the common salvation of all. Rather, I think it is that deadly sadness which killed either the apostate Judas (Matt. 27) or Ahithophel, the counselor of Absalom (2 Sam. 17).”

Then Astion replied:

“Three days ago, when your venerability was speaking with those men about the heavenly mystery, I, prevented by shame, went to the river to draw water without your knowledge. As I was walking along the road, a shameful and exceedingly filthy thought—one that, I think, was sent by the devil—rose in my mind.

“And now, behold, for three days I have been striving as much as I can, with tears and prayer from the Scriptures, to drive it out, but I am in no way able to overcome it.”

Then Saint Epictetus, displaying a terrible expression toward him and in a certain way showing indignation against the demon, spoke to him:

“Why did you leave the door of your cell without my permission, or go to the river without the prayer of Christ’s priest? Do you not know that the superior’s blessing is always an impregnable wall and a breastplate of faith for the young in overcoming the devil?”

After saying this, he ordered him to prostrate himself with him in prayer before the Lord.

When they had long and earnestly prayed for the Savior’s mercy, and after the prayer had ended they rose from the ground, the blessed Astion saw a certain black boy emerging from his bosom with a fiery torch, saying to him:

“Your confession, Astion, has today shattered my great strength, and your one prayer has made me powerless and wholly desolate. Therefore I shall leave this place, enter the heart of the duke Latronianus, and quickly stir him up against you. He will punish you through various kinds of torment, because you have entered his province like robbers or sorcerers and, turning many people away from the worship of his gods through your magic arts, are joining them to your God.”

**[Note: [Col. 0414D] “The duke Latronianus.” At this time Latronianus was the duke or governor of Scythia. Further investigation is required concerning him.]**

After saying this, the demon disappeared and was seen no more.

## CHAPTER XII

While the holy servants of God were engaged in such spiritual exercises and were serving our Savior Jesus Christ with one accord in psalms and prayers—and while divine grace was working many wonders through them not only among human beings but also among animals—suddenly the duke Latronianus arrived in the city of Almiridenses.

After spending three days inspecting the public works and imperial services that were there, on the fourth day certain men from his staff reported to him concerning the blessed men, saying that they were sorcerers and magicians and that through their magic arts they were already turning many people away from the sacrifices to the gods.

When he heard this, he immediately ordered certain officials of the interrogations, after sunset, to go to the dwelling of the holy men, seize them, bind them in irons, and bring them into prison custody.

When the blessed men had been seized and were being led to the prison, they sang:

**[Note: [Col. 0414D] “Vinculatorium.” This means a prison. The Greeks call it δεσμωτήριον (*desmōtērion*), because there is there an abundance of δεσμῶν (*desmōn*), “bonds” or “chains.”]**

“God is our refuge and strength, a helper in the tribulations that have found us exceedingly” (Ps. 45).

And again:

“The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our protector” (ibid.).

And once more:

“Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and not of the wicked; yet from all these the Lord will deliver them. The Lord guards all their bones; not one of them will be broken” (Ps. 33).

When they had entered the prison, they spent the entire night, as was their custom, in psalms and prayers.

After the solemn vigil had been completed, Saint Epictetus spoke to the blessed Astion as follows:

“If tomorrow the judge interrogates us, saying, ‘What is your origin, what are your names, from what province are you, and from where have you come here?’ let us answer him nothing at all. Let us not tell him our origin or our names, nor confess to him the homeland from which we were born. Let us say only this: ‘We are Christians, and this name is our identity, this is our origin, this is our homeland. We are nothing other than worshipers of the true God.’

“And again: if after this confession he orders punishments to be inflicted upon us, let us say nothing else while placed under torture except: ‘Lord Jesus, may your will always be done in us.’”

## CHAPTER XIII

The next day, at first light, the duke Latronianus ordered a tribunal to be prepared in the middle of the city. He commanded the heralds, with very loud cries, to invite a multitude of people to such a wicked and dreadful spectacle.

When the third hour of the day had arrived, Latronianus came forth like a raging beast. With the people waiting on every side, he sat at the tribunal and ordered the saints to be brought before him.

When they had been presented and stood before him, as soon as he saw them he stiffened entirely from excessive fear. He could not look directly at the saints, because their faces shone like the sun on account of the extraordinary grace they bore.

Saint Epictetus was about sixty years old, tall in stature, with a long beard and adorned by the splendor of his white hair. Likewise, the most blessed Astion the monk was tall in stature; he was also exceedingly handsome and delicate-looking, and appeared to be about thirty-five years of age.

After an hour had passed, the duke Latronianus questioned them:

“Explain before this crowd what your names are, what your origin is, and from what province you come.”

The saints replied:

“We are Christians, born of Christian parents, and we come from a Christian homeland.”

The duke Latronianus said:

“For now I wished to hear your names. As for the fact that you belong to that accursed superstition, I know it, and so do all those standing around.”

The holy martyrs answered:

“We are Christians, and we acknowledge and worship Jesus Christ our Lord, in whose power all things are held. We detest all your idols, as Scripture says: ‘Let those who make them and all who trust in them become like them’ (Ps. 113).”

When the duke heard this, he became exceedingly angry and ordered that, after being stripped, they be beaten forcefully.

While the martyrs of Christ were being beaten by the officials, they raised their eyes toward heaven and said:

“Lord Jesus, our teacher, may your will be done in us.”

But when they had been beaten long and hard, and his brutality had accomplished nothing against the worshipers of God, Latronianus spoke to them in anger:

“Where is that marvelous defender of yours whom you continually invoke to come to your aid? Let him come now and, if he can, rescue you from my hands.”

The holy martyrs replied:

“We are Christians, O tyrant; may the will of our God be done in us.”

When Latronianus heard this, he ordered them to be lifted onto the rack and cruelly scraped with iron claws.

While they were being scraped, they again said:

“We are Christians, O tyrant Latronianus; may the will of our God be done in us.”

Then the tyrant ordered that burning lamps be placed against their sides while they still hung upon the rack.

As they endured this form of torture with courage, they said:

“We are Christians, O tyrant; may the will of our God be done in us.”

When the seventh hour had arrived, Latronianus ordered them taken down from the rack and led into prison custody.

## CHAPTER XIV

One of the interrogators, named Vigilantius, heard the holy martyrs repeatedly and often saying under torture, “We are Christians, O tyrant Latronianus; may the will of our God be done in us.” He supposed that the words possessed some power of magnificent incantation, since they said that those who meditated upon them could in no way feel pain.

He therefore began to repeat this same formula incessantly, musing upon it inside the house and in the streets, while sleeping and rising, and chanting it at every moment.

After he had continued without interruption for three days, on the fourth day he began to proclaim publicly:

“I am a Christian, O tyrant Latronianus; may the will of our God be done in us.”

Coming to the most blessed martyrs in the prison, he deserved to receive from them the seal of life. Believing in God the Savior together with his entire household, he later buried the holy bodies of the blessed men with the greatest honor.

### Chapter XV [Cols. 0403C–0404A]

After the fifth day had finally passed, the governor Latronianus again sat in judgment and ordered the holy priest Epictetus and the monk Astion to be brought before him. As the servants of the demons were leading them, they sang, saying:

> “In you, Lord, we shall scatter our enemies, and in your name we shall despise those who rise up against us. For we do not trust in our bow, and no human sword will be able to save us; but your right hand, your arm, and the illumination of your face, because you have been pleased with us” (Psalm 43).

When the martyrs of Christ had stood before the bench of the utterly profane governor, Governor Latronianus said to them: “Do you submit to me and sacrifice to the gods, or do you still persist in your madness?”

The holy Epictetus replied: “You have questioned us repeatedly, often flattered us, and many times promised us very many gifts and the greatest honors; yet you have been able to hear absolutely nothing else from us except that we are Christians. And behold, even now we do not cease repeating the same thing.”

When Latronianus had heard all these words, he roared like a lion. Crying out in a loud voice, he spoke thus to his soldiers:

“Quickly, servants of this most splendid eminence, bring salt and vinegar here and rub them into their previous wounds. At the same time, put pitch and fat into a bronze cauldron, and when it begins to boil violently, throw them into it.”

When the saints heard this, they said: “We are Christians, O tyrant; may the will of God be done in us.”

After they had courageously endured this form of torture for Christ’s name and had been utterly unharmed, the most savage tyrant ordered them to be thrown out from there and taken again into the custody of the prison. “Lest,” he said, “their steadfastness should seem to bring us disgrace and boldness to the Christians.”

And so he ordered that for thirty days no one should enter to see them, nor should food or drink be brought to them by anyone. But the athletes of Christ were daily refreshed by the fullness of the divine word and by that bread which descended from heaven. They sang without ceasing, saying:

> “May God have mercy on us and bless us; may he illumine his face upon us and have mercy on us, so that we may know your way on earth, your salvation among all nations.”

### Chapter XVI [Cols. 0404A–0404C]

While the holy martyrs were enduring these tortures for Christ’s name in the city of the Almiridenses, a certain foreigner, seeing the most blessed Astion standing before the judge’s tribunal one day and learning who he was and of what family he was thought to be, hastily sailed toward the regions of the East. When he arrived in the city from which Astion originated, he announced to his father and mother everything that had happened to him, saying that he was undergoing martyrdom with a certain old Christian named Epictetus. He also carefully informed them of the name of the city in which they were.

When they heard this, they immediately fell at the feet of the man who had reported these things and began earnestly to beg him to tell them what was true. He affirmed under oath that these things were true.

Then his father began to say: “If I, unhappy man, should be found worthy to see the face of my son, whatever it may be that he commands and teaches me, I shall do it without any delay.”

His mother likewise said: “I, wretched and humbled in every respect, if I should still be found worthy to behold him in this body, shall abandon my home and all my possessions and cling to him alone, since, above all else, he alone is dearer and sweeter to me. And if he commands me to become a Christian, I shall not refuse to do that either; and afterward, if he wishes, I am ready to endure tortures with him and gladly accept death.”

As they said these things, they left all their possessions and wealth in the hands of agents and stewards. They went out from their house with three boys, immediately boarded a ship, and began to sail so that they might reach the land of the Scythians and the city of the Almiridenses.

At that time the bishop and superior of the holy churches of God in that province was the most blessed Evangelicus.

[Note: [Col. 0414D] “Evangelicus.” A very diverse Scythian nation. Some were converted before the time of Diocletian, others afterward. Some Scythians had already been converted to Christ in Tertullian’s time, as is clear from his book *Against the Jews*, chapters 7 and 8. Indeed, Saint Philip is said to have brought the faith to Scythia, as the Roman Breviary states under 1 May; thus it is not surprising that Evangelicus was bishop of Scythia during the reign of Diocletian.]

### Chapter XVII [Cols. 0404D–0405B]

When the thirty days had been completed, the tyrant ordered the holy martyrs to be brought before him. When they had stood before him with cheerful spirit and radiant countenance, Governor Latronianus spoke to them as follows:

“I have often questioned you about the designation of your names, your ancestry, and the place from which you originated, yet you have never told me the truth. Now, since I know neither your homeland nor your lineage, and have not even been able to learn your names, I have considered the matter within myself, saying: Since you seem to be nothing other than bodily demons, who are known to exist without name or lineage, I shall now call you by the designation you deserve.”

He continued speaking to them: “Tell me, bodily demons, if you do not sacrifice to the immortal gods, I shall have your heads cut off today.”

The martyrs of Christ said: “We are Christians, and in the name of Christ we drive out from possessed bodies the demons whom you worship and honor as gods. Would that the most evil demon did not dwell in you!”

When that mad and dreadful man heard this, he became exceedingly enraged and ordered his servants to crush the mouths of the saints with stones. Then he commanded them to bring ash rods and to beat them with them until they breathed out their spirit.

But the most blessed athletes of Christ, suffering in this way, said nothing else except: “Lord our God, may your will be done in us.”

When they had been beaten for a long time and continued always cheerful and courageous in their confession of the Lord, that servant of the devil saw that his madness had in no way prevailed against their steadfastness. He ordered his wicked servants to lead them outside the city and cut off their heads with a sword.

As they were being led away, they sang, saying:

> “Praise the name of the Lord; praise him, servants; praise the Lord” (Psalm 134),  
> “for the will of our God has been done in us in every respect.”

### Chapter XVIII [Cols. 0405B–0406A]

When they had reached the place where they were to be struck down, they stood facing east, with their hands extended and their eyes raised toward heaven. They prayed to the Lord as follows:

“Blessed are you, Lord God of our fathers, worthy of praise and exalted above all forever, because it was not a human will but your will that was done in every respect in us.

“For you are the one who teaches those who believe in you to do your will and to proclaim your wonders at all times, because your Holy Spirit guides each person toward what is good according to the purpose of his heart and according to his own will.

“For you are the one who always guided Abraham according to your will, sanctified Isaac, and wrestled with Jacob, giving him the new name Israel; who kept Joseph chaste from the enticements and flatteries of the Egyptian woman, and likewise preserved Susanna undefiled from the pollution of her plotters; who purified the hearts of your holy prophets and illumined the minds of your most blessed apostles through the gift of the Holy Spirit, saying to them: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John 20);

“who crowned your athletes by your grace and always granted victory to those fighting for your name; who brought us, your most humble and sinful servants, to this land so that we might announce and preach in it the teaching of your Gospel to those who dwell here; who have been our guide, teacher, and good provider in all things; who have always guided us according to your will up to this hour.

“We ask you, Lord, to deem it worthy to send us your holy angels, who may free and defend us from the power of our adversaries and, by your grace, lead us as victors and triumphators to the throne of your majesty.

“Preserve also the men of this region and city in your fear; protect them in your mercy; guard them in your goodness; guide them according to your will. Bless their little ones together with their great ones, and, in return for the honor they have shown us because of your holy name, display to them their reward in eternal blessedness.

“Grant us also confidence, so that whenever we entreat your divine majesty, you may fulfill our petitions for what is good.

“And now, we ask you, Lord, receive us into your everlasting hands and lead us into the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of all the saints, whose light, bridegroom, founder, and builder you yourself are, so that together with the angels and archangels, fathers, patriarchs, prophets, apostles, martyrs, and confessors, we may continually praise and glorify the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit forever and ever.”

### Chapter XIX [Cols. 0406A–0406D]

When those standing around had answered, “Amen,” the holy Epictetus began to ask the executioners to strike the blessed Astion before him.

But when Astion said, “Because it is fitting that you first, most blessed Father, should merit this life-giving and personal propitiation,” the holy Epictetus replied:

“Son, the ancient cunning of the serpent is sufficiently subtle and deceitful; and therefore what I now command to be done is for your salvation and my repose. For by divine grace I have preserved you chaste and undefiled for seventeen years, and now do you wish me to lose in a single hour the labor of so many years? No. What I desire to do, my son, I do through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

“For thus Abraham offered his son Isaac as a burnt offering; Jephthah presented his daughter to the Lord as a sacrifice; and Peter sent Stephen before him into the heavens.

“Although I cannot doubt God’s goodness, since he is able to preserve you in all things even without my presence, just as he has kept you undefiled up to this day, nevertheless you must recognize that the good shepherd always lays down his life for his sheep (John 10). Therefore what I am doing, my son, I am doing for both you and me. Do not henceforth doubt my companionship.

“For I believe that holy Michael with the angels, Abel with the prophets, Peter with the apostles, Stephen with the martyrs, and Daniel with the confessors have already come to meet you, my son. May they now receive you into their embrace and lead you with hymns and spiritual songs to the throne of Christ our Savior.”

When the most blessed Astion heard these and even greater things, he replied: “May the will of God and your will be done, priest of God and venerable father.”

Making the sign of the cross on his forehead, he prayed to the Lord as follows:

> “For you are my protector, Lord; into your hands I commend my spirit” (Psalm 30).

As he said this, the executioner immediately cut off his head.

When this had been done, the holy Epictetus gave glory to God. Throwing himself upon Astion’s little body, he began to ask the executioners that, just as he was lying upon the corpse of the holy martyr, they should strike him also.

When this had been carried out, all the Christians and pagans who were present looked on and, with tears, gave thanks to God for the good teacher Epictetus and the disciple’s perfect obedience.

### Chapter XX [Cols. 0406D–0407B]

While they were giving glory and honor to God, suddenly the bodies of the holy martyrs appeared white like snow; and because of the immense brilliance, they seemed to be like rays of the sun.

All who appeared to be afflicted by any illness, as soon as they touched their corpses in faith or reverently kissed them, were immediately freed from every anxiety and pain.

Around sunset, Vigilantius, together with all his household and other Christians, secretly took away the bodies of the holy martyrs. Pouring myrrh and the most precious spices over them, he buried them in a suitable and most fitting place, with hymns and psalms and great devotion.

Many signs and wonders are celebrated at that place to the praise of Christ’s name down to the present day.

During the night, Latronianus was attacked by a most evil demon. Rising at first light, he came to the headquarters, where he began to utter many senseless and insane words. Then, seizing a sword, he pursued and wounded those who held the foremost offices. Against others he leapt like a rabid dog, tearing the clothing of some and running about here and there.

When they saw and understood that he had become mad and insane, they stripped him and began to beat him violently with fists and blows. Then, binding his hands and feet, they threw him into a very small room. After two days, suffocated by the demon, he violently breathed out his spirit.

### Chapter XXI [Cols. 0407B–0409B]

When the third day since the passion of the holy martyrs had dawned, and Vigilantius had come to their tomb for the sake of prayer, the blessed Astion suddenly appeared to him and said:

“My parents are coming here today from our homeland to seek me. Therefore I ask you, dearest brother, hasten down to the harbor and receive them into your house. Console them in every respect, since they are being worn down by intense grief on my account. Finally, make them hear instruction concerning the faith of our Savior and his various mighty works.”

When Vigilantius heard these and many further things, he gave glory to God and immediately hurried down to the river.

And behold, around the third hour he saw a small boat suddenly arrive at the harbor. When the *epibatae* had disembarked from the ship—

[Note: [Col. 0415A] “Epibatae.” Hirtius uses this term for those who earn bronze through naval work. Here sailors are meant.]

—they began carefully asking the men standing there whether any of them had ever heard of or seen there a young man named Astion.

While many were saying various things about him, Vigilantius arrived and said: “I truly saw him and know him. But meanwhile, come to my house and rest a little, since you are very tired from the voyage. Later, if you wish, I shall take you to him without any delay when the proper time comes.”

But they fell at his knees and began earnestly clinging to his feet, kissing them and begging that, if it were possible, he take them to him before they ate anything.

Vigilantius replied: “First do what I ask, so that I too may fulfill your request and desire.”

When they had entered his house and sat down at table, Astion’s mother began to speak to Vigilantius as follows:

“If you show me, dearest brother, the place where my only son Astion now dwells, today I shall place a golden crown upon your head.”

His father likewise said: “If through you, young man, I should be found worthy to see him today, I shall cover you with garments woven with gold and grant you half of my possessions.”

Vigilantius replied: “Three days ago he departed from here and went into a distant region. He entrusted half of his possessions, together with his house, to me with a little document, saying: ‘If anyone comes sent by my father to seek me, bring him into this little house of mine and tell him: “This is what the monk Astion says: Wait here for me until I return to you in safety.” And if you wish to be heir to my possessions, hasten to fulfill everything written in this book, and be happy, doubting nothing.’”

The mother said: “What is that region called, to which my sweetest and only Astion has gone?”

Vigilantius replied: “The region of strong and courageous men.”

The mother said: “Are there any people dwelling there?”

Vigilantius replied: “There are many, and they are very noble. Their dwelling is called paradise; their tabernacles are constructed of light; their life is God, and their way of life is immortal. Their garments are spattered with blood, and upon their heads are crowns made of the purest gold and adorned with various gems.

“There is also a most powerful and fearsome King in that region, whose name is called God of gods and Lord of lords. His messengers are called angels of justice; they all have one garment, and their touch resembles burning fire.

“The senate of this emperor is also held in great renown. One part is called prophets, while the others are designated apostles.

“The city of this King is also exceedingly glorious. Among those devoted to Christ its name is proclaimed. Its wall is constructed of the purest gold, having twelve gates, and from each of them hangs a single pearl; at each gate one of the senators sits continually (Revelation 21).

“The first gate is called Peter’s, the second Paul’s, the third Andrew’s, the fourth John’s, the fifth James’s, the sixth Philip’s, the seventh Bartholomew’s, the eighth Thomas’s, the ninth Matthew’s, the tenth Thaddeus’s, the eleventh Simon’s, and the twelfth Matthias’s.

“There is also a marvelous temple in it, containing the Holy of Holies and a golden altar. Before it stands a certain marvelous man, holding a ten-stringed psaltery, and continually urging those who dwell there to praise that King, saying:

> ‘Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his powers’ (Psalm 148).

“His name is proclaimed to be David, son of Jesse.

“The streets of this city are paved with the purest gold. Its river pours forth eternal life; its fruit-bearing trees produce their fruits each month, and their leaves serve as medicine for souls. Its light is indescribable, and its gates are never closed, because there will never be night there, nor are there any darknesses. Rather, joy and perpetual gladness continually dwell there.”

The woman replied: “Did you not understand, dearest brother, by whom my Astion was summoned and went there? Perhaps he was found guilty of some offense; or perhaps someone from among the companions or senators who dwell there summoned him and, because of his extraordinary beauty, adopted him as a son?”

Vigilantius replied: “He was summoned by the prince of that region himself and went there with great honor and an escort. At that time I could not see the attendants themselves; nevertheless, as he reported to me, they had exceedingly beautiful and radiant faces and wore golden armor and hyacinth-colored garments.

“And because he had faithfully fulfilled with all his heart in this region of ours everything that had been commanded him, he said that for this reason he had been summoned there by the prince’s attendants, so that he might be granted authority over ten cities.”

The mother said: “Do you suppose, then, that now, placed in such glory, he remembers us?”

Vigilantius replied: “He certainly keeps you very much in his mind and greatly desires always to have you near him—provided that you are willing to fulfill what is written in that book which he left with me.”

The mother replied: “Come, then, and quickly present to us the deposit.”

As they said these things, they rose together from the table.

### Chapter XXII [Cols. 0409B–0410D]

Then Vigilantius took them and led them into the cell of the holy martyrs. Showing them the Lord’s cross and the most holy Gospel of Christ, he said to them:

“These are the things that Astion, your son, left with me. Therefore, if you perform the mystery of this divine power and the things written in this book, you will certainly see him and will be with him forever in that region.”

When his father heard this, he took the Gospel of Christ in his hands and, opening it, came to the place where the Lord Jesus spoke to his disciples, saying:

> “Amen, amen, I say to you, you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. And everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields, for my name’s sake, will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life. But many who are first will be last, and the last first” (Matthew 19).

The father said: “Who is this Lord Jesus, and who are those who followed him? And who are those commanded to leave father or mother, wife and children, for his name’s sake, whom he says will receive eternal life in the blessedness to come? We ask you, dearest brother, if you know anything true about these matters, do not hesitate to explain it to us.”

Vigilantius opened his mouth and, beginning from this Scripture, evangelized them concerning the Lord Jesus Christ: how, from the beginning of the world, all things were made through him; how he made humanity in his own image and likeness and placed it in the paradise of delights; how he took one rib from its side and fashioned it into a woman; how, because of the serpent, he expelled Adam from the paradise of delights into this land of mortals; how Eve, because she preferred to obey the serpent rather than the Lord her God, was condemned to anxieties and pains in childbirth; how the holy prophets, coming before the first advent of the Son of God, proclaimed that he would come but were not received; and how the Lord our God Jesus Christ, who is the Father’s only-begotten Son, the Word and Wisdom, that is, the power and radiance of glory, deigned in the last days to be born into the world from the Holy Spirit and Mary ever-virgin.

He also explained how he made those who followed him his disciples, sending them to preach the word of salvation to the nations and giving them the name apostles; and how he made them participants in his kingdom because they despised the vanity of this age and loved him alone more than their relatives.

When Vigilantius had wisely explained these and many greater things to them, they came again to the place where it is written:

> “And Jesus said to his disciples: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you, everyone who confesses me before human beings, I also will confess before my Father who is in heaven; but whoever denies me before human beings, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven. Do not think that I have come to bring peace upon the earth; I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. For I have come to separate a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies will be those of his own household. Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me. And whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me. Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake and for my Gospel will find it’” (Matthew 10).

And again:

> “When they hand you over to kings and governors, do not consider how or what you should speak. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you. Brother will hand brother over to death, and father his son; and children will rise against their parents and put them to death. You will be hated by all because of my name. But whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.”

Then, reaching the final part of the holy Gospel, he began again to read according to John, saying:

> “Father, those whom you have given me, I will that where I am, they also may be with me, so that they may see my glory, which you have given me, because you loved me before the foundation of the world” (John 17).

And again:

> “That all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I in you, so that they also may be one in us, so that the world may believe that you sent me. And the glory that you gave me, I have given them, so that they may be one, just as we are one. I in them and you in me, so that they may be perfected into one, and the world may know that you sent me and loved them just as you loved me.”

### Chapter XXIII [Cols. 0410D–0411C]

When the father had read these and many greater things, he said to Vigilantius:

“I beg you, dearest brother, explain to us again more carefully the things we have just read, because we understand absolutely nothing in these words.”

Vigilantius replied:

“Those of whom our Lord Jesus says, ‘Whoever confesses me before human beings, I also will confess before my Father who is in heaven; but whoever denies me before human beings, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven’—we are those who believe in him and place our hope in his holy name.

“If the time of persecution should come, and the rulers of this age say to us, ‘Deny your God and worship with us the idols that are our great gods, who made everything,’ and if we do not agree with them or do what they command, but endure the threats and tortures of tyrants for his name, then he himself, in that blessed region of his, before the Father and before his holy angels, will confess us—that is, he will establish us as friends and exceedingly dear to him.

“Your only and most holy Astion has now become one of their number. For a few days ago, when the governor of this province, Latronianus, was compelling him to deny Jesus Christ—the true one whom we call the heavenly emperor—and to consent to his will and serve the demons, Astion in no way submitted to obey his commands. Strong in faith and exceedingly courageous against the evils inflicted upon him, he remained steadfast to the end in his holy confession together with another venerable Christian old man named Epictetus.

“When that heavenly emperor saw this and greatly admired his goodwill and sincere love toward him, he sent his attendants—that is, his saving angels—and took him with immense honor to the city where he himself dwells, so that he might grant him eternal rewards because he had fought manfully against the emperor’s adversaries.

“And therefore the mysteries you have read are applied both to your Astion and to those like him:

> ‘That all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I in you; and they also may be one in us, so that the world may believe that you sent me. And the glory that you gave me, I have given them, so that they may be one, just as we are one.’

“Therefore all who are found worthy to belong to the number of your Astion, honorable father, are called martyrs of our Savior.”

### Chapter XXIV [Cols. 0411C–0412A]

The mother said: “Do you mean that he is dead and do not wish to make it clear to us?”

Vigilantius replied:

“We are the dead, who dwell in this mortal flesh and seem to exist in this vain age without knowledge of our Creator. For true life is there, and true food and drink are found there, together with endless dignity, for those who have been found worthy to receive it. It is there that immortality always reigns and perpetual joys dwell.”

Then the mother said: “I wanted just now to see him standing in that glory. Do you think he will recognize me, since I was once his mother? Or perhaps, placed in such great honor there, as you say, he will now disdain to look upon me because I have lost the beauty of my face by mourning him?”

Vigilantius replied:

“If you do what is written in this book, which the holy Epictetus and Astion left with me, and if you believe with all your heart in Jesus Christ, his king, in whom Astion also believed, you will be able to see him. But if you do not wish to believe, it is impossible for you to see him or for him ever to call you his mother, since you were unbelieving regarding the commands of his Father.”

The mother said: “Behold, this man is his father.”

Vigilantius replied:

“His true Father is the one who is also Lord, with whom he now dwells, and who has granted him such great blessings in the blessedness to come. This man, however, is mortal and has mortal children; while he is thought to stand, suddenly he falls; while he says that he lives, he suddenly dies, because he does not even recognize as the true Father the one whom Astion recognized, of whom it is written: ‘Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name.’”

### Chapter XXV [Cols. 0412A–0412D]

After they had spent a whole week discussing among themselves, recounting Christ’s wonders to one another and listening willingly, Sunday arrived, and both of them believed in Christ.

Vigilantius took them to a certain holy priest named Bonosus, who, avoiding the ferocity of the persecution, lived secretly in a secluded place. After praying sufficiently for them and catechizing them, he made them catechumens at that very hour.

When they had left from there, they began to say to Vigilantius:

“Behold, we have fulfilled the things contained in the book that you gave us. Come now and show us that treasure which, as you affirmed, our Astion entrusted to you.”

Vigilantius replied: “Follow me; I shall show it to you without any delay. But meanwhile I have it hidden, and I do not know whether I can now bring it out from there. Therefore, if it pleases you, let us go by night to the place and remain there working until daylight. Perhaps we shall be able to find it, since I hid it quite deeply.”

When the sun had declined, Vigilantius took them and went out of the city with them. When they reached the tomb of the saints, he urged them to keep vigil with him there all night in prayer.

When dawn had already risen and daylight had begun, suddenly they saw an immense light shining around them and an exceedingly sweet fragrance spreading. They also saw the holy martyrs, who had already fallen asleep, standing bodily beside them and praising the Lord with them.

Then the holy Astion rushed into the embrace of his mother and began to kiss her, saying:

“Well have you arrived from the regions of the East, disciple of Christ and my mother, Marcellina.”

Likewise, the most blessed Epictetus took her husband by the head and kissed him, saying:

“Rejoice in the Lord, dearest brother Alexander, because you have been found worthy to be numbered among the faithful and to merit everlasting blessedness.”

They also said to Vigilantius:

“And you too, dearest brother Vigilantius, rejoice in the Lord, because you have been found worthy that what is written might be fulfilled in you:

> ‘Whoever converts a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins.’”

### Chapter XXVI [Cols. 0412D–0413C]

Then the holy Astion began to speak to his mother in this way:

“O my sweetest and blessed lady mother, all the things written in the most holy Gospel of Christ our Lord are true and firm. Therefore hasten to fulfill them without any delay, so that you may be found worthy to attain what is written there.

“Divide and distribute among the poor the portion of your possessions that falls to me, for my repose—

[Note: [Cols. 0415A, 0416A] “For my repose.” Understand this properly as referring to a greater, namely an additional, glory. For the well-known saying from Augustine, *Sermon* 22, *On the Words of the Apostle*: “He does an injury to the martyr who prays for the martyr.”]

—and for your salvation, so that you may merit to come to us adorned with the crown of righteousness and good works.”

The mother said: “Are you well received by your King, or by his companions, my sweetest son?”

Astion replied:

“I dwell in such well-being that I do not know how to explain it to you. The Lord and our God has adopted me, formerly a servant, as his son through his grace; he has granted me a dwelling in his city; he has made me serve in his palace; he has bestowed upon me the greatest dignity among the senators; he has given me the delights of paradise for my enjoyment.

“His attendants have also deigned to regard me as one of their own and love me. For each day I go with them to visit the sick, raise up the fallen, illumine the blind, save those endangered at sea, conquer the barbarian peoples fighting on land, console the sorrowful, defend the helpless, and drive demons out of possessed bodies in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

“Every day they also give me instructions concerning you, saying: ‘Warn your father and mother to come to these places.’”

The mother said: “Do they recognize us, then, my son?”

The holy Astion replied:

“They love and recognize you exceedingly, lady mother—provided only that you wish to recognize them, so that you may reach that blessedness without any doubt.”

The mother, striking her breast because of her overwhelming joy, said: “Do you think that I, unhappy and wretched, shall ever reach that place?”

The most blessed Astion replied:

“If you believe perfectly in Jesus Christ, our Lord and God, just as Vigilantius believed, and distribute all your goods to those in need, then without a doubt you will both live and rejoice with me in that eternal blessedness in which I dwell.”

When the athletes of Christ had been instructed by these and similar words, they withdrew from them.

## Chapter XXVII

When, therefore, the fortieth day since their dormition had dawned, and the evangelical bishop of Christ had arrived in the city of the Almiridenses, Vigilantius, together with the holy presbyter Bonosus [Col. 0414A], brought them to him. They explained to him in order everything that had taken place and asked him to consecrate them to Christ among the number of the faithful. He, greatly rejoicing in the Lord, took them in, prayed sufficiently for them, and administered the sacrament of baptism. After celebrating with them for eight days, he returned to another city, which was nearby.

When the priest of the Lord had departed from there, Alexander and Marcellina began to say to Vigilantius:

“Many are the benefits we owe you, dearest brother and one exceedingly beloved by us, because through your saving instruction we have been able to escape the yoke of the devil and arrive at knowledge of Christ our Savior. Indeed, you are exceedingly glorious in wisdom within the holy Church, distinguished by the grace of teaching; you possess perfect love for the religion of the holy Gospel [Col. 0414B], and immense affection in receiving strangers, indescribable benevolence in defending the helpless and visiting the sick; you burn with the warmth of faith for the destruction of idols and the love of the holy martyrs; and, in accordance with the mystery of your name, you are vigilant in every good work for the love of God. Therefore nothing else should be declared about you except that you are counted among the most intimate friends of God.”

Having said these things, they took him and the holy and venerable presbyter Bonosus with them to their own city. They returned cheerful in spirit and perfected in the Lord; distributing all their possessions to the needy, they glorified God the almighty Father, who had graciously led them from darkness into the light of the knowledge [Col. 0414C] of himself.

The holy athletes of Christ, the presbyter Epictetus and the monk Astion, suffered martyrdom in the city of the Almiridenses on the eighth day of July, during the reign of the tyrant Diocletian, under the governor Latronianus. According to us, however, Jesus Christ our Savior reigns in heaven, to whom be glory and dominion, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0415]

## October 23. The Life of Saint Macarius the Roman

[Note: [Col. 0425D] Macarius the Roman.]

There is no mention of him in the Roman Martyrology. The Greek Menologion, October 23: “On the same day, the commemoration of our holy father Macarius the Roman.” The Menaea give a full account of his Acts on the same day, and they agree perfectly with this account of ours. In the Menaea, however, the pilgrimage and the difficulties of the journeys undertaken by the three travelers, the authors of this Life, are omitted.

I had a single manuscript copy of this Life from the abbey of Einham, written in an entirely recent hand. [Col. 0426D] Baronius, in the Roman Martyrology under January 11, thinks that Palladius is speaking of this Macarius the Roman when, in chapter 123, he lists those who visited Pinianus, the husband of the younger Melania, who was at one time active in the fields of Sicily and at another in those of Campania: “Likewise,” he says, “a certain man named Macarius from the vicariate.” Here Baronius correctly understands the prefecture of the vicariate, since Macarius embraced the monastic life from that position.

[Col. 0427A] I do not, however, think that this Macarius of ours, the Roman, is the same as Palladius’s Macarius; rather, I believe Palladius’s Macarius to be the man mentioned by Rufinus in his Apology. See what will be said concerning Palladius.

Baronius says that these Acts, whose author is Theophilus, are not especially credible; but he does not specify what in the Acts is objectionable. I have allowed them to appear in this edition because they have been published in all editions up to the present. Indeed, the Greek Menaea also include them in their office, and Gratian, XXVII, question 2, chapter 26, cites testimony from them. I have therefore compared these Acts with the Menaea, so that it may be evident in what respects the Greeks agree with the Latins. Perhaps there will be some who judge that at least those portions should be accepted in which both agree.

Our Raderus translated them from the Menaea and inserted them into his *Viridarium of the Saints*, part I. If Saint Jerome, in the *Life of Paul the First Hermit*, is referring to this story—which in chapter 15 says “that his beard and hair covered his entire body”—when, in the prologue, inquiring about the first inhabitant of the desert, he says:

“Some people, according to their fancy, loudly proclaim this and other things, inventing a man covered with hair down to his heels in an underground cave, and many incredible tales which it would be tedious to pursue. Since their lie was shameless, the account does not even seem to require refutation”—

if, I say, Jerome is referring to this story, then it is certainly an ancient tale, rejected by his judgment.

], Servant of God, Who Was Found Near Paradise, by Theophilus, Sergius, and Hyginus

[Note: [Col. 0427B] Theophilus, Sergius, and Hyginus.]

The Menaea give these names as the authors. The printed Latin texts have *Thimus* in place of Hyginus; the manuscript has *Gunnus.

## Chapter I

Glory and majesty belong to God alone, the most benevolent, who through innumerable examples of miracles daily invites us, sluggish and unworthy as we are, to the joys of blessed heavenly life.

We therefore, the wretched and humble monks Theophilus, Sergius, and Hyginus, beg all of you, most holy fathers and brothers, to lend your ears to what we are about to tell you concerning the life and conduct of the most holy Macarius the Roman, who appeared to us near paradise, twenty miles away. We ask this so that you may give credence to what is said; for we believe that it would have been much better for us to remain innocent in the harbor of silence than to be punished as guilty of falsehood.

## Chapter II

We, the brothers named above—Theophilus, Sergius, and Hyginus—renouncing the world through the favor of the Divinity [Col. 0415C], came to a monastery in Mesopotamia of Syria, midway between the two rivers, the Tigris and the Euphrates. There the illustrious Asclepion was abbot.

[Note: [Col. 0427B] Asclepion the Abbot.]

The Menaea read: Ἐκ τῆς μονῆς τοῦ ἁγίου Ἀσκληπιοῦ, “from the monastery of Saint Asclepius.” Theodoret, in his *Philotheus*, chapter 25, mentions Asclepius, an admirable monk, ten stadia from the village of Cittica, where Zebinas was buried; Polychronius, his disciple, seems to have lived there. But since those men lived in Theodoret’s time, I think there was an earlier Asclepius who presided over this monastery situated in Mesopotamia [Col. 0427C], from whom it also received its name.

He was the father of many monks. Joining them there, we were gladly received by the aforementioned Father and the entire community of brothers. We submitted our necks to the yoke of the rule and lived together in the common life.

## Chapter III

[Note: [Col. 0415] What follows is absent from the Menaea and is considered apocryphal by certain learned men.]

After a long time had passed, one day, when the ninth hour’s synaxis had been completed—

[Note: [Col. 0427C] When the ninth hour’s synaxis had been completed.]

Concerning the ninth hour, at which the synaxis is customarily concluded and the fast broken, see the *Onomasticon*. All the following chapters, which I have marked with little crescents, contain astonishing journeys and are absent from the Menaea. I nevertheless think that they existed in the original exemplar from which the Menaea drew their account of Macarius, but were omitted from the Menaea because they did not concern Macarius’s Life.

Certainly the Menaea hint at the subsequent journeys of these three men in the following words:

Καὶ τῆς πορείας ἀρξάμενοι ἀλλεπάλληλα, ηὕρισκον δεινά, πὴ μὲν ἐξ ἀνθρώπων, πὴ δὲ ἐκ θηρίων θλιβόμενοι κακοχούμενοι (sic), καὶ αὐτοὶ ἐστὶν ὅτε τῆς ἐκ τῶν ἀγρίων βοτάνων τροφῆς στερούμενοι.

“Having begun the journey, they encountered one misfortune after another, suffering affliction and hardship sometimes from human beings, sometimes from wild beasts, and at times themselves being deprived of food from wild plants.”

From this it is apparent that the Menaea express only briefly the hardships of these travelers that are narrated in several following chapters.]

We came to the bank of the Euphrates and sat down there. For a while we discussed among ourselves the endurance, conduct, and labor of the servants of God. Then a thought came into my mind, wretched Theophilus; and I answered my brothers Sergius and Hyginus:

“I desire, beloved brothers, to walk all the days of my life and to go to the place where heaven joins the earth.”

[Note: [Col. 0427D] Where heaven is joined to earth.]

Many of the ancients held that the earth was flat and that there were no antipodes; thus heaven would be joined to earth somewhere else. Indeed, many located paradise in a particular region of the earth, at a higher place where heaven joins the earth. Alcimus Avitus, book I of *Genesis*:

“Therefore, where, once the Indies have been crossed, the world’s head begins,

where they say the earth’s boundaries join heaven,

a grove inaccessible to all mortals remains upon a lofty height . . . . . .”

But they said to me:

“Brother Theophilus, we have always regarded you as a spiritual brother, and as one who goes before us; from now on we will not be separated from you in any way. Your words please us. Therefore, go wherever you have conceived in your heart; in life and in death we shall be with you.”

So we rose from that place and entered the monastery. When evening came, and all the prayers of the daily office had been completed, while the others were sleeping we secretly left the monastery.

Afterward, walking for seventeen days, we reached Jerusalem.

[Note: [Col. 0427D] We reached Jerusalem.]

This is the expression of that period. Earlier, in chapter 2, it similarly says *there joining them*. Later: “At last we reached,” that is, “we arrived.” How common pilgrimage to Jerusalem once was is evident from various passages in these books. See the *Onomasticon*.]

We adored the holy Resurrection of Jesus Christ and the Cross. [Col. 0416B] Then, leaving for Bethlehem, we saw and venerated the holy manger where Christ deigned to be born and where the star led the Magi, bringing gifts to Christ. We also saw the marvelous place where the angel, together with a multitude of the heavenly host, sang, “Glory to God in the highest”; that place lies two miles from Bethlehem.

We also climbed the Mount of Olives and worshiped at the holy place where Christ stood with his feet when he was lifted up, received by a cloud, and ascended into heaven. From there we returned to Jerusalem, worshiped God, marked ourselves with the sign of the Cross, and commended ourselves to Christ and his saints.

[Note: [Col. 0427D] Marking ourselves and commending ourselves to Christ and his saints.]

It was the devout custom of the ancient fathers, when beginning a journey, to mark themselves with the sign of the Cross and commend their journey to God and the saints.]

We departed, no longer having our heart and mind in this world.

## Chapter IV

“With the grace of Christ accompanying us, [Col. 0416C] we immediately set out on the road; and on the fiftieth day, crossing the channel of the Tigris River, we entered the land of the Persians. We came to a great and level plain called Assia, where the martyr of Christ Mercurius is said to have killed the apostate Julian.

[Note: [Col. 0428A] Asia, where the martyr of Christ Mercurius.]

It is certain that Julian was killed in Persia. See Baronius, volume IV, under the year of Christ 363, the twelfth year of Pope Liberius and the second of the emperor Julian, where he investigates in various ways the identity of Julian’s attacker.]

Then, entering a Persian city called Kitissefodo—

[Note: [Col. 0428A] Kitissefodo.]

I think that this means Ctesiphon, a city of Persia. As for the statement that Ananias, Azarias, and Misael rest there, I do not know where he got it. The Roman Martyrology, December 16: “The three boys Ananias, Azarias, and Misael, whose bodies are placed in a certain cave near Babylon.” Certainly Ctesiphon is not far from Babylon, as is also said here in Macarius’s Life.]

—we worshiped there, because the three boys Ananias, Azarias, and Misael rest there, not far from Babylon. Eating in the same place and offering a hymn of praise to the Lord, we remained for several days.

After departing from there, four months later we crossed the region of Persia and entered the land of India. Entering a certain house and finding no inhabitant there, we stayed two days.

Behold, on the third day afterward, two armed people appeared approaching, a man and a woman. We, terrified by overwhelming fear, rose and decided to go toward them. But when they saw us, believing at the same time that we were scouts, they quickly turned back by the road they had come. Shortly afterward, having gathered together, about three thousand Ethiopians from their people arrived.

They hurriedly surrounded the house in which we were praying with a rampart; and as they all watched us, they set a great fire at the four corners of the house, intending to burn us alive. When we saw this, terrified by great fear, we invoked Christ, the Savior of all, and sprang into their midst.

Then they murmured loudly to one another in their language and for a long time snarled against us. Since we could not understand them, nor they us in any way, they seized us and shut us in a dark prison.

As we sat in darkness, there was no one to give us bread or water. We nevertheless did not cease invoking with tears the mercy of almighty God, the Creator of all. After we had spent several days there, they gathered again, believing that we had been exhausted by hunger and thirst, and surrounded the prison.

But when they saw us praying, they opened the door and led us out. After speaking at length among themselves with much muttering, they finally beat us severely with rough wooden clubs—

[Note: [Col. 0428A] Rough pieces of wood.]

I think he means crude and unworked timber. Or does he mean Pliny’s *phalanges*, book VII, chapter 56, with which the Africans once fought battles?]

—and expelled us from their territory. We completed eighty days without food, as God is our witness.

## Chapter V

“Thus expelled from that territory, we traveled for many days toward the East and reached a marvelous place, a glorious plain full of very tall trees and abounding in honey-sweet fruits. Finally, glorifying and praising God, we ate the sweet-flowing fruits and were greatly satisfied.

Leaving from there, we entered the land of the Canaanites—

[Note: [Col. 0428A] The Canaanites.]

This is strange, and I have not read it elsewhere: that these same Canaanites were the Cynocephali.]

—who are called by others Cynocephali. When we saw them, we were greatly astonished at their appearance. They lived beneath the rocks with their women and little ones, but they did not touch us at all, because the grace of Christ protected us.

## Chapter VI

“From there we departed toward the East. After traveling for one hundred and ten days across their territory, we entered the land of a people called the Pichiti.

[Note: [Col. 0428A] Pichiti.]

The manuscript has *Pytici*. Perhaps someone might derive *Pythecos* from this, and from it *Cercopitheci*. But the ancient editions have *Pichiti*, and the manuscript adds: “and by another name they are called Pygmies.”]

This people, in bodily stature and height, was no more than the measure of one cubit. When they saw us, they were struck with fear and fled. We, praising God together because he had delivered us from their hands, hastened our journey every day.

## Chapter VII

“After this we came to exceedingly high and terrifying mountains, where the sun does not enter and neither tree nor grass grows. There we saw countless serpents, dragons, and asps, as well as many basilisks, vipers, unicorns, and buffaloes; also many other deadly beasts and venomous animals whose names and nature we entirely do not know.

[Col. 0417D] With the right hand of God protecting us, we passed through them unharmed. For twenty consecutive days we heard the hissing of dragons and serpents in our ears, and we could endure it only by blocking our ears.

## Chapter VIII

“Meanwhile we came upon a terrifying place, with extremely rugged cliffs rising upward and descending into the depths. We remained there seven days, unable to go farther.

On the seventh day afterward, a stag appeared walking before us and bellowing. We rose and followed it. As we traveled, we found cliffs before us that were much larger. With the greatest labor and distress we escaped from there and came to a broad, level plain [Col. 0418A], where a great multitude of elephants stood. We passed unharmed through their midst.

After this, no road appeared to us at all. Then, invoking the Lord’s mercy with tears and traveling for nine days through trackless places without food, we finally reached a broad, level place that abounded in many fruits.

By then the thickest darkness had filled all those regions. Nothing shone, but there were the darkest mists. Greatly troubled and afflicted, we fell to the ground and cried out to God in prayer with loud lamentation. We remained in that same place for seven days, eating nothing, drinking nothing, and seeing no light of heaven.

While we were greatly afflicted and persisting in prayer, after seven days a dove appeared. Approaching us, flying around us for a long time, and beating its little wings strongly, it seemed to encourage us to walk.

Then, giving thanks to God, we rose; with the dove going before us, we traveled through trackless places. Behold, before us we found a huge arch, inscribed all around.

[Note: [Col. 0428B] An arch.]

The manuscript adds, “that is, an arch.” In ancient usage both *absis* and *absida* were equally current. See the *Onomasticon*.]

When we saw the inscription, we rejoiced and praised the Lord together. The inscription read:

“Alexander, son of Philip, the Macedonian emperor, made this arch when he pursued Darius, king of the Persians. Whoever wishes to enter this land should go to the left; for on the right the land is impassable and full of cliffs and narrow defiles.”

## Chapter IX

“We entered on the left and walked for many days. After forty days had passed while we were traveling, an exceedingly foul and intolerable stench came upon us. We became almost lifeless and fell to the ground, praying the Lord to command that our souls be mercifully received.

A little later, rising from the ground, we saw a large lake and a multitude of fiery serpents in it. From the lake came voices, and we heard great howling and lamentation, as though from an innumerable multitude. A voice sounded from heaven, saying:

‘This place is a place of judgment and punishment, where those who denied Christ are tormented.’

Hearing this voice, beating our breasts with tears and extreme fear, we crossed the lake and came between two exceedingly high mountains. In their midst a man of enormous stature appeared to us, about one hundred cubits tall.

[Note: [Col. 0428B] A man of enormous stature.]

It is not unprecedented for monstrous beings to appear in places of punishment or places afflicted by the devil. In the *Life of Antony*, chapter 38: “He saw a certain tall and terrible being raising its head up to the clouds.”]

He was bound with bronze chains and fastened over his entire body. Two chains from one side of his body were fixed to one mountain, and two to the other. A huge fire surrounded him on every side.

The sound of his shouting could be heard as far as forty miles. When he saw us, he cried out most cruelly, weeping and wailing, for he was being savagely burned by the fire.

## Chapter X

“When we saw such things, we were greatly terrified. Covering our faces, we passed the mountains from a distance. Immediately we came to another place, where there were many cliffs and a great depth.

There too we saw a woman standing with her hair loose, her entire body entwined by a huge and terrifying dragon. Whenever she wished to open her mouth to speak, the dragon immediately thrust its head into her mouth and bit her tongue. The woman’s hair descended all the way to the ground.

As we gazed at her in amazement and fear, suddenly from the depth of the valley we heard pitiable voices saying:

‘Have mercy on us, have mercy, Christ, Son of the Most High God.’

We were exceedingly terrified. Falling on our knees, we prayed with tears:

‘Lord, who created us, take our souls, for our eyes have seen your judgments upon the earth.’

## Chapter XI

“We rose and, in great grief, sorrow, and fear, came to another place. There we saw many very large trees resembling fig trees. On their branches were many flying creatures resembling the birds of heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0428B] Many flying creatures resembling the birds of heaven.]

In the *Life of Saint Antony*, chapter 38: “He also saw certain winged creatures attempting to rise toward heaven.” Paschasius, chapter 19, section 4: “Antony saw flying souls, like restless birds.”]

They cried out loudly in human voices, saying:

‘Spare us, Lord, who formed us; spare us, merciful one, because we have sinned before you throughout the whole earth.’

We prayed, saying:

‘Most merciful Lord, show us these miracles we have seen, for we do not know what they are.’

Then a voice came, saying:

‘It is not yours to know the mysteries you have seen. Continue on your way.’

## Chapter XII

“From there we departed in great fear and came to a more honorable and most beautiful place. Four men stood there, with venerable forms, adorned with such wondrous beauty that it can scarcely be believed or expressed.

They wore golden crowns upon their heads, honorably set with gems and stones, and carried golden palms in their hands. A great and terrifying fire stood before them, and they held extremely sharp swords before themselves.

When we saw these things and were struck by powerful fear, we cried out to them:

‘Lords and servants of the Most High God, have mercy on us, so that the swords and this fire may not prevail against us and harm us.’

They answered us:

‘Do not be afraid. Go confidently along the way God has shown you. The Lord has placed us in this place to preserve and guard this road until the day of judgment, when he will come to judge the world.’

## Chapter XIII

“Hearing this from those holy men, and saluting them from a distance, we crossed that place. For forty continuous days we traveled, taking no food at all, but drinking only water.

As we walked, we suddenly heard the voices of an innumerable multitude of people.

[Note: [Col. 0428B] Suddenly we heard the voices of an innumerable multitude.]

Many people believed that certain souls inhabit a most pleasant meadow. So Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, book V, chapter 13; Dionysius Carthusianus, *Dialogue on Particular Judgment*, article 31; and Ludovicus Blosius, *Spiritual Necklace*, chapter 13. See Bellarmine, volume II, *On the Controversies of the Christian Faith*, third general controversy, concerning Purgatory, book II, chapter 7; Suarez, on the third part, disputation 46.]

We heard them singing psalms, and an exceedingly sweet fragrance, like the finest and most precious balsam, came to us. It sweetened our mouths as though from the sweetest honeycomb.

From the nectar of that most delightful fragrance and the song of heavenly melody, sleep seized us. After a short while we rose from sleep and saw before us a church adorned with marvelous and most precious decoration. It appeared entirely crystalline.

In the middle of the church was an honored altar, and from the altar water flowed, having the color of the whitest milk. We truly thought that the water itself was milk.

Around that fountain stood holy and honorable men, [Col. 0420A] singing a heavenly song, namely the voices of cherubim. When we looked upon these things, we were very afraid.

The church itself, on the southern side, resembled precious green stone; on the southern side it displayed the color of the purest blood; on the western side it was entirely white, as bright as milk and spotless snow.

The stars above the church shone more brightly than the stars of this world. The sun there shone and gave heat seven times more intensely than in the region of this earth. All the mountains and trees were taller, and their leaves and fruits more numerous and sweeter, than those of the trees of this world. The birds of heaven also sounded differently from the birds of this earth.

The whole land had two colors: one surface was white like snow, and the other was of the brightest red. We were astonished, worshiped in that place, and saluted those men. Then, leaving in fear, we hurried to resume the journey we had begun.

## Chapter XIV

“After this one hundred days had been completed—as the Lord is our witness—we had received no food, refreshing ourselves frequently with water. Suddenly, as we traveled, an innumerable multitude of men and women came toward us, gathered together.

Among them we saw no one taller than one cubit. When we saw them, we were greatly terrified.

Then I, the wretched sinner Theophilus, said to my brothers Sergius and Hyginus:

‘Let us loosen our hair and go against them. Perhaps they will flee from us, and the Lord will deliver us from their hands.’

When this seemed good to them, we loosened our belts and our hair and suddenly rushed upon them. When they saw this, they immediately seized their children and all fled as quickly as possible, gnashing their teeth.

We praised the Lord together, who had rescued us. Crossing a river, we found white and pale grasses, like milk, sweet as honey, and a cubit high.

We ate of the honey-sweet grasses and satisfied ourselves with them, offering thanksgiving to the Creator of all, who had preserved us through so many dangers and nourished us by his gratuitous grace.

As we traveled through trackless places, we suddenly found a beautiful path. Falling to the ground, we worshiped and praised together the merciful Lord, who had shown it to us.”

[Col. 0420D]

## Chapter XV

After following that road for many days, we finally reached a venerable cave. Having fortified our limbs on every side with the sign of the holy Cross, we entered the same cavern. Finding no inhabitant there, we said among ourselves:

“This cleanliness can only come from the hand of a human being. Let us remain here until evening, and we shall see the inhabitant of this place.”

After saying this, we sat down for an hour, being tired, and suddenly fell asleep, overcome by an exceedingly sweet fragrance. After a short interval we were again awakened from sleep, went outside the cave, and looked toward the East.

Behold, suddenly we saw from a distance the figure of a man hurrying toward us. The hair of his head, white as the purest milk [Col. 0421A] or snow, seemed to fly in the air and covered the man’s entire body.

As soon as he saw us from afar, he immediately threw himself to the ground. Then, rising again, he began to call out to us:

“If you are from God, fortify yourselves with the sign of the holy Cross and hurry toward me; but if you are from the devil, flee from me, the servant of God.”

When he said this, we addressed him in these words:

“Bless us, holy Father, and do not be troubled, for we too are servants of Jesus Christ, our Lord and Savior. We have renounced this vain world and have become monks.”

As soon as he heard this, he came to us. Raising his hands to heaven, he prayed for a long time. Rising from prayer, he removed the hair from his mouth and face, blessed us, and spoke with us.

His head hair and beard—

[Note: [Col. 0428C] His head hair and beard.]

The description of Macarius here is word for word the same in the Greek Menaea:

“His hairs were white as snow; his body was like the shell of a tortoise; and, because of his extreme old age, his eyebrows had drooped over his eyes, while the nails of his hands and feet were more than a span long; and the hairs of his beard reached down to his feet.”]

—were white as milk, and his face was like the countenance of an angel. For he was like a tree planted beside streams of water (Psalm 1). Because of his extreme old age, his eyes could not open, since his eyebrows covered them. The nails of his hands and feet were exceedingly long; his beard and hair covered his entire body. His speech was faint, as though issuing from a depth; and the skin of his face was like tortoise skin.

## Chapter XVI

Then he began to speak to us with tears:

“My blessed brothers, where are you from, and from where have you come here? Tell us how the human race is faring, how the faith of Christians is doing, and whether Saracens or pagans are still inflicting persecution upon the people of Christ.”

When questioned, we answered him in order. We told him of the hardships and dangers we had suffered throughout the entire journey and explained that our will and desire had been to go to the place where heaven joins the earth.

He answered:

“My dearest sons, listen to me. From this place no human being clothed in flesh can go farther toward the regions of paradise. I, a small and sinful man, struggled greatly even with this desire, wishing to proceed farther so that I might see the end of the earth and of the sky.

But one night the angel of the Lord appeared to me in a vision and said: ‘Do not go farther, and do not presume to tempt the Lord.’

I answered him: ‘For what reason, my lord, is it not permitted to go farther?’

He said: ‘From this place it is twenty miles to paradise, where Adam and Eve lived in delights. The Lord placed before that same paradise a cherub with a fiery, whirling rhomphaia to guard the tree of life (Genesis 3). It has the appearance of a man from its feet to its navel, a chest like the chest of a lion, and a hand like crystal; it holds a sword to protect paradise, so that no one may approach it.’

[Note: [Col. 0428C] A cherub with a fiery sword.]

There are various opinions concerning the cherubim who guard paradise. “It should not be believed,” says Theodoret, “that by ‘cherubim’ invisible powers are meant, as some think, since an invisible nature would have contributed nothing there, given that the vision was to be sensible, so that it might terrify Adam himself. Therefore that flaming sword was not naturally fiery, but appeared so to the sight; nor were the cherubim animals, but they appeared to be such.”

He further adds: “‘And he stationed the cherubim,’ as Genesis 3 says, indicates a powerful and terrifying vision and form, as if he had placed certain animals at the entrance of paradise, by which Adam would be kept away.”

Theodore, bishop of Heraclea, held the same opinion, as did Procopius of Gaza. See our Pererius on Genesis, chapter 3.]

“Having heard these things from the angel, I gave no further answer and did not attempt to proceed any farther.

“Therefore I, Theophilus, and my companions and brothers on the journey, hearing these things from the holy man, prostrated our entire bodies, praised the Lord together, and saluted this servant of Christ.

## Chapter XVII

“When evening came, he said to us:

‘My beloved brothers, go outside the cell and wait a little while. I have two lions, who walk outside during the day [Col. 0422A] and return to me late in the day; lest, if they come suddenly, you suffer some harm from them.’

[Note: [Col. 0428D] Who walk outside during the day.]

This is contrary to the custom of others. “The lion,” says Jerome on Nahum 2, “always prowls at night.” And Psalm 103: “At night all the beasts of the forest pass through it.”]

When we had gone outside for a short while in fear, the lions immediately came roaring and worshiped the holy man of God.

He placed his hands upon them, stroked their necks, and said:

‘My sons, three good brothers have come to us from the world. Do not harm them.’

Then he called us at once and said:

‘Brothers, come, and do not be afraid now.’

We entered with great fear, saluted him, celebrated the evening synaxis, and sat down. We took acorns and the roots of herbs as food and drank water in silence.

When morning came, we spoke to the holy man:

‘Holy Father and lord, we beseech your blessedness to tell us about your way of life: how you came here, where you came from, and what your name is.’

## CHAPTER XVIII

But the saint gave us this answer:

“I am called Macarius, my most beloved brothers and sons,” he said. “I was born and raised in the royal city, the son of a Roman man who was illustrious and powerful in the imperial city. When I had passed beyond childhood, my father, against my wishes and unwillingness, betrothed me to a wife and appointed the day of the wedding.

“In the meantime, when the bridal chamber had been decorated, the crowd had already been invited, and the bride was seated, my father, becoming increasingly cheerful, urged all the guests to enjoy the banquet. While everyone present was occupied with jokes and dancing, I slipped away secretly, entered the house of a certain familiar widow, and remained hidden with her for seven days. [Col. 0422C]

“Each day she entered my father’s house and listened to what they were saying about searching for me. Then she came and repeated everything to me. But when my father could not find me, although he searched everywhere, he wept most bitterly, as did my mother and the entire household.

“On the eighth day thereafter—that is, on the Lord’s night—I took leave of that woman, went out onto the public road, and found a certain man, venerable with gray hair, standing as if prepared to walk. I worshiped him and said: ‘Where are you going, holy elder?’

“He turned toward me with a cheerful face and said: ‘Wherever you desire to go, I intend to go with you, because those roads are very well known to me.’

“Then, strengthened, I began to follow the man. Entering the neighboring houses along the way, we asked for bread and received it. After walking for many days, we finally reached the place of torments and entered all the narrow roads from which you said you had come.

“When we had come to within about thirty miles of this place, we were sitting one day and conversing with each other when suddenly my companion disappeared. I was exceedingly troubled, not knowing where to turn; I fell to the ground and mourned most bitterly. And behold, without delay, the one who had disappeared earlier appeared with great brightness and addressed me:

“‘Do not be troubled, beloved one. I am the angel Raphael,

[Note: [Col. 0428D] Raphael. He was Macarius’s guide here, as once he was Tobias’s.]

[Col. 0422D] sent to help you. I have brought you here at the command of the Most High. The Lord has made your journey prosperous. You have passed through places of darkness, places of torments, and places of punishment; you have come into the light and have seen a fountain of living water and the places of the righteous. Therefore do not fear; rise and continue your journey.’

“Having said this, the one who had appeared disappeared again.”

## CHAPTER XIX
