Meanwhile, having recovered my strength, I rose and began to walk. From a distance I saw a wild ass, and I called out to it, saying: “Hail, by Christ who created you! Show me the road on which I should walk.”

It came toward me swiftly, entered a small and narrow path ahead of me, and I followed it. Thus we completed two days walking together.

On the third day we saw from a distance a stag of extraordinary size. When the wild ass saw it, it became afraid and turned away from me. Once again I was left alone and distressed, having no road at all.

Then, calling out to the stag, I said: “Because you have brought me help, I adjure you by God: show me a path.”

At these words it turned toward me like a domesticated animal, entered a narrow track, and continually looked back at me. Thus we walked together for three days.

Then, on the fourth day, behold, we encountered an immense and terrifying dragon stretched across the middle of the road. When the stag saw it, it suddenly fled. Meanwhile I was struck with great fear and fell to the ground. Then, strengthened in the Lord, I arose, armed myself with the sign of the holy cross, and said to the dragon: “Fear God almighty, and do not harm me.”

Then it raised itself terrifyingly from the ground and addressed me in a human voice, saying:

“Come, blessed lord, for you are Macarius, servant of the Most High God. The holy angel Raphael, showing me your form and appearance, urgently commanded me to meet you and lead you to the place prepared for you by God. I have awaited you here for four days, eating absolutely nothing. Last night, in a very bright cloud, I saw you sitting, and at the same time I heard a voice from above saying to me: ‘Hurry, so that you may rescue Macarius, the servant of God, who is here, as I foretold to you.’

“Therefore rise and follow me; do not hesitate. Come, and I shall show you the place where you must praise the Lord.”

After saying these things, he appeared like a young man and came with me as far as this cave. When we had entered it, he suddenly vanished. [Col. 0423D]

## CHAPTER XX

Then I, a sinner, looked toward the other side and saw two lion cubs lying there; their mother lay dead beside them. I threw her outside and buried her, praising and glorifying the Lord, who had performed such great wonders in me and freed me from such grievous straits.

I plucked tree-fronds and offered them to the lion cubs, raising them as my own sons. Thus we completed two years living peacefully together.

But behold, after this the devil’s snare appeared—for his envy never ceases against the servants of God. One day, at about the seventh hour, I went out of the cave and sat down while the sun was burning hot. Suddenly I saw a delicate little cloth, pleasing to the eyes, lying on the ground beside me.

[Note: [Col. 0428D] A small band. *Menaea*, σουδάριον, “cloth,” “sweat-cloth.”]

Thinking within myself, I said: “Where could a little cloth come from in this solitude?” Nevertheless, supposing that it really was a cloth, and forgetting, most wretchedly, to arm myself with the sign of the cross—for the sign of the most holy cross weakens every fantasy of the enemy—I stretched out my hand, lifted the cloth, and carried it back into the cave.

The next day, when I went out, I found women’s shoes lying on the ground.

[Note: [Col. 0428D] Shoes. The manuscript has *caligas*, “boots.” Indeed, *caligae* were once used in place of shoes. Thus Acts XII: “Put on your *caligae*.”]

But even then, miserable as I was, I did not perceive the devil’s ambush or protect myself with the banner of the cross. I lifted the shoes, carried them into the cave, and joined them to the little cloth.

On the third day, when I went out again, I found the devil standing in the beauty and appearance of a woman dressed in costly garments. Miserable as I was, I still did not remember the enemy’s snares, nor did I sign myself in any way; instead, believing that she truly was a woman, I said to her:

“Where have you come from? Or who brought you into this wilderness?”

Immediately she began to weep most bitterly. Then I, wretched man, wept greatly with her as if sharing her grief.

Afterward she answered:

“I am a most miserable woman, holy father. I am the daughter of a Roman man. When he had betrothed me, against my will and unwillingness, to a certain most noble Roman youth, and the wedding day had arrived and they had prepared the bridal chamber and banquet, my bridegroom disappeared during the wedding itself.

“When everyone was thrown into confusion and searched for him here and there, I became joyful, slipped away secretly, and set out that same night. Having no guide for my journey, I wandered through the narrow mountain passes and valleys until I reached this place.”

When I heard this and believed that everything was as she said—and also hoped that she was my bride—I took her by the hand and brought her into this cave. Tears did not cease flowing from her eyes.

Pitying her misery and tears, and grieving deeply for her, I made her sit beside me. I likewise offered her acorns to eat. For I did not understand the devil’s ambush, nor did I arm myself in any way with the sign of the cross. We sat together and conversed for a long time.

Then I began to become heavy with sleep, as though from great weariness. She stroked and touched all my limbs with her hands, and I became even more burdened with sleep.

Why delay? I, wretched man, who previously had never consented to sin with a woman, realized in my sleep that I had committed sin. For, suddenly awakening from sleep, I found myself lying on the ground uncovered, as though with a woman; but she herself had now disappeared. [Col. 0424D]

## CHAPTER XXI

Then I, unhappy man, recognizing the devil’s ambush too late, quickly went out of the cave and, beating my breast, shed copious tears.

Meanwhile the lions who were with me, understanding my offense, immediately fled from me. When I saw this—namely, that the lions had fled—I began, with immense grief and sorrow, devoutly to invoke Christ’s mercy, asking that he show me a pattern of repentance and command the lions to return.

Without delay, the most merciful Father, who had preserved me for repentance, immediately caused the lions to return. They entered this cave with me and heaped up the earth with their feet to the height of a man.

Understanding this, I entered the pit up to my neck, commanding the lions to bury me in that same place. When this had been done, I spent three years buried in that pit.

Meanwhile, when a great rain descended, the cave above my head, where I was standing, was broken open. I saw light, and, extending my hands outside, I plucked and ate the grasses that were around me above my head.

After three years had passed, the lions came and, seeing light around me, dug away the earth in which they had buried me. I emerged with my entire body sound, feeling my former strength within me.

Then, glorifying my Lord Jesus Christ, I left the cave, placed my knees upon the ground, and remained immobile in that same place for forty days and forty nights, praising and beseeching God and offering thanksgiving to him, who continually grants such great gifts of mercy to us sinners. [Col. 0425B]

## CHAPTER XXII

When these days had been completed, I looked into the cave, and behold, its four corners shone brightly with heavenly light. I saw Christ the Savior in the form of a man, holding what seemed to be a golden rod in his hands and producing a wonderful song in a sweet-sounding voice. His voice was heard as powerful and strong, as though it were the voice of a thousand men.

When the melody of the heavenly song had come to an end, suddenly the voice sounded three times, saying: “Amen, and amen forever.”

At that very hour the Savior emerged from the cave and ascended toward the ether. Immediately, behold, a huge column of fire, like a powerful cloud, entered the cave; thunderclaps and immense flashes of lightning occurred; and I heard all the birds of heaven singing in their own voices, saying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God.”

When I saw and heard these things, I was greatly terrified because of the magnitude of the vision and was seized in ecstasy. I fell to the ground and remained there for eight days. Then I understood that Christ the Lord, Savior of the world, had entered this cave, blessed it, and sanctified it.

Then I entered it and began to make satisfaction for my ignorance and negligence, praising and glorifying Christ our Savior and Redeemer and Creator of all, who had endured me with such patience, led me to repentance, and again shown me such clemency.

When these things occurred, I had been in this cave for seven [years?], and I was forty years old.

Behold, now, as to dearly beloved sons, I have truthfully recounted my entire life to you. [Col. 0426A]

Therefore, if you can endure the struggles and snares of the wicked enemy, consider them and remain here with us. Otherwise, return to the monastery from which you came, and may the Lord be with you on your journey.

## CHAPTER XXIII

When we had heard these things from the holy man of God, we fell to the ground and glorified the Lord, who alone performs wonders. Then we spoke to Macarius, the holy servant of Christ, saying:

“Most blessed Father Macarius, pray to the Lord for us, that we may return to our monastery and recount your holy way of life throughout all the churches of Christ. For we believe that the Lord brought us to you for this purpose.”

Then the elder prayed over us for a long time. When he had finished praying, he blessed and kissed us all and commended us to Christ, asking that he direct our journey in peace. Then he entrusted us to those lions, commanding them to lead us until we had passed through the places of darkness where previously we had lain in darkness for seven days and as many nights.

Thus dismissed by the holy servant of Christ Macarius, we arrived safely at Alexander’s apse, where the lions, after greeting us, quickly returned to the servant of God. [Col. 0426B]

## CHAPTER XXIV

Therefore, with Christ God’s favor, we traveled our road without any distress. Entering the land of the Persians, we came to a marvelous plain called Assia, where Saint Mercurius killed the apostate Julian. We entered again the city of Kitissefodo, in which three children rest, not far from Babylon.

After crossing the river Tigris, on the fifteenth day we entered Jerusalem. At the tomb of our Lord Jesus Christ, praying throughout all the holy places of the saints, we offered thanksgiving to Christ, the Savior of all, who by his grace had preserved us unharmed both on our outward journey and on our return.

From there we departed and by a swift journey reached our monastery. Finding our abbot and all our brothers in peace and good health, we recounted to them in order the wonders and mercies of the Lord that we had seen and heard, as well as the life and way of life of the most blessed Macarius.

All who heard these things praised and glorified God and sang a hymn to God the almighty Father, and to his only-begotten Son, our Lord and Savior, and also to the life-giving Spirit who enlightens our souls. He is named the blessed and praiseworthy God, three in persons and one in divinity; he lives and reigns everywhere, now and forever, throughout the immortal ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0429]

# LIFE OF THE BLESSED POSTHUMIUS, FATHER OF FIVE THOUSAND MONKS, BY AN UNCERTAIN AUTHOR

[Note: [Col. 0437B] Posthumius. Other editions have *Pasthumius*. I have found nothing about him either in ecclesiastical records or among historians. Much here resembles Pachomius and his rule. Since Pachomius is called Pachumius by some, I fear that *Pasthumius* may have arisen from *Pachumius*.]

## Prologue

[Col. 0429]

Since you have always greatly desired to hear what is holy, and we ought to take care that time not pass in silence, we therefore cannot be silent about the works of the Lord, which he continually displays in his servants.

First, it should be known concerning the holy servant of God Posthumius by what order the Lord deigned to call him to his grace, as the account of those who knew the order of his conversion has proclaimed. I have taken care to communicate these matters in writing to your love: how, through country people, the Lord revealed the mystery of his kingdom to those who believe in him.

## LIFE

[Col. 0429]

### CHAPTER I

[Col. 0429A] Posthumius was a Memphite by birth, born a pagan, innocent from infancy, ignorant of letters, and alien to all Egyptian learning. He was always a stranger to the shrines of the pagan Egyptians.

He had been a maker of palm-fiber ropes.

[Note: [Col. 0437B] *Spatarius*. All editions have this word. Shortly afterward, he braided a *plectam* from *spatha*. The notes mention palm-leaf strips, Leviticus XXIII. Hermits used to make their ropes and braids chiefly from palms. I had formerly thought that *spartarius* should be read, meaning one who braids a rope from *spartum*, who is called by Pollux, Book VII, chapter 33, **σπαρτοπλόκος** (“one who braids spartum”).]

He never mingled with groups of young men, never learned the stories of public life, and his foot was never moved to dance. In his life no shameful speech ever came from his mouth, nor did greed ever enter his heart. While he was still in the world, he did not raise his eyes toward a woman. He avoided falsehood with all his strength. He knew neither discord nor hatred toward his neighbor or toward a stranger; he guarded peace in his heart at all times.

### CHAPTER II

While he was conducting himself in this way and was thirty-seven years old, it pleased God to rescue him from the corruption of sins and call him to the incorruptibility of eternal life.

Accordingly, it is said that an angel of the Lord entered to him while he was braiding a rope from palm fiber.

[Note: [Col. 0437B] *Plectam*. Shortly afterward, *funis plectacius*, “a braided rope,” from the Greek **πλεκτόν**, that is, “braided” or “twisted.” This word occurs not infrequently in these books.]

The angel said to him: “Posthumius.”

He answered: “What is it?”

And the angel of the Lord said to him: “What is in your hand?”

He answered: “A braided rope.”

And the angel of the Lord said to him: “Do you know the Most High God, who dwells in heaven?”

Posthumius said: “Lord, I do not know whether there is a God in heaven. I am a rustic, and I have no wisdom. From my infancy I have served my craft, and I have heard nothing from city-dwellers that I could learn; moreover, I have always avoided public gatherings.”

The angel said to him: “Pray to God, and wisdom and understanding will be given to you.”

Posthumius said: “I do not know how to pray to God, for I do not know what to say.”

Then the angel took a laurel leaf, wrote on it the words of a prayer, and gave it to Posthumius, saying: “Eat it. It will be bitter in your mouth like gall; it will fill your belly with petitions for wisdom and give you the form of prayer and sound teaching.”

Posthumius took it and ate it, and his mouth became bitter. But his belly was filled with sweetness, and he greatly magnified the Lord. Indeed, we believe that in him was fulfilled what was written by the prophet Ezekiel (Ezekiel III), or by the apostle John (Revelation X): they received a book from the hands of angels, ate it, and were filled with wisdom for prophesying. [Col. 0430A]

### CHAPTER III

Again the angel of the Lord touched Posthumius’ lips. The bitterness was removed, and his tongue spoke great things about God.

The angel said to him: “Posthumius, fix your knees upon the ground and turn your face toward the East; then God will give you the ability to pray.”

Posthumius placed his knees upon the ground and also turned his face toward the East. Prayer was poured into him, and he said:

“I will bless you, Lord God almighty, heavenly King, who causes your name to become known to those who do not know you, through our Lord Jesus Christ your Son, making your name manifest, so that he might gather for you an adopted people from all nations.

“For when you wished to aid the world, laboring under its burden, for the salvation of the human race you did not spare your only Son. Through him, therefore, I beseech you and your mercy: show me, blind and placed in darkness, the true light.

“For you know, Lord, that I knew no speech at all, and you deigned to grant me what I should say to you; you taught me by what words I should ask you. From my own experience I know, my Lord God, that truly the blind see, the deaf hear, the tongues of the mute are loosened, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the poor are evangelized, and sinners are called (Matthew XI).

“What was I, that you remembered me? In what way does my weakness prevail with you, that you sought me? Why, then, do I now ask you to wash me from the filth of my sins and of my natural misery, which has weighed upon me for so long? For I lived, instructed by unbelieving parents in the pagan manner, like a companion of beasts.

“You sent me your angel, struck my thigh, and opened my stony breast. Woe to the one who is silent about you, for he is slaughtered forever by the burning of fire.

“Behold, in a short time I have learned that there is no joy for the wicked with you, nor will gladness come to sinners after death; unless they turn to you, they cannot be saved.

“And since it has not seemed right to you to destroy me, Lord, redeemer of my humility, show me the better way, so that I may fully know the Lord and Savior Jesus, and that there is no other besides you, who are blessed forever.”

This was the first prayer of Saint Posthumius, through which the angel of the Lord introduced him to the way of seeking faith.

### CHAPTER IV

From then on blessed Posthumius was attentive, waiting for the angel of the Lord to return to him. He trusted and hoped that the Lord would always visit him.

When a few days had passed, behold, Posthumius was, as usual, twisting a rope from rushes. The angel of the Lord entered to him and said: “Hail, Posthumius.”

Posthumius immediately rose in terror.

The angel said to him: “Do you wish me to lead you to a priest of God who will baptize you in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit?”

Posthumius answered: “My holy lord of God, it is exceedingly desirable and joyful for me that you should fully teach me the way of God and what the perfect salvation of heavenly works is.”

The angel of the Lord took him by the crown of the hair on his head and led him to a certain man named Priscus, a holy man who feared God.

[Note: [Col. 0437B] Priscus. He is called a priest here; in the following chapter, a bishop.]

The angel said to him: “Teach him the way of the Lord, wisdom and understanding, and baptize him in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.”

When the Lord’s priest heard this, he rejoiced greatly. But the priest did not understand that it was God’s angel who had brought him to him.

Immediately the angel, transformed into a splendid figure, shone before the priest’s face in white garments and with a beautiful appearance. Then Christ’s priest, terrified by fear, fell prostrate upon the ground.

Again the angel raised him and said: “Do not fear, for I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of all your brothers” (Revelation XXII). “For it was necessary to reveal to you the glory of our God, so that you may know how to teach this man the word of the Lord, instructing him according to his salvation, so that he may live forever before the Lord.”

After saying this, he departed from them.

### CHAPTER V

Bishop Priscus took Posthumius with him and taught him to fast. Laying his hand upon him, he made him a catechumen and then baptized him immediately, teaching him the Creed of the Sacrament.

As soon as he had been baptized, he was filled with the Holy Spirit and said this prayer:

“I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, who through the Holy Spirit have deigned to reconcile me to God the Father and have redeemed me from death and eternal punishment, which those who do not believe in you suffer, weighed down by the burden of their sins.

“Yet sins are heavier than lead. I rejoice that I have been drawn out from them and freed from all iniquities and necessities. I exult.

“For truly there is no partiality with God (Acts X), but abundant mercy. How, then, could I, unworthy as I am, approach the abodes of your creation, unless you touched me with your heavenly finger—me, badly withered grass, whom you had commanded to dwell in bodily matter? You wished to come swiftly to my aid, overthrowing the enemy of your law who ruled over me in the flesh; by water, through the regeneration of the Holy Spirit, you cleansed me.

“A renewed soul speaks in me, a soul that for a long time lay cast aside among lost sheep. Having received the sign, I rejoiced as though I were enrolled under a great name: the imperial census is restored to favor when it is impressed upon a soldier.

[Note: [Col. 0437B] The imperial census. This sentence appears to be a fragment of a more polished style, perhaps sketched from some elegant Father. It alludes to military service, when the emperor’s name was inscribed upon a soldier. Here the imagery concerns a sheep and a soldier. Compare Augustine, Letter 50: “Thus error must be corrected in the sheep, so that the Redeemer’s mark is not corrupted in it. For if someone is marked with a royal character by a deserter who had been marked, receives pardon, and returns to military service, while another begins to serve in the army in which he had not previously been enrolled, is that character erased in either of them? Rather, is it not recognized in both and, because it is royal, approved with the honor it deserves?”]

“As one who was mute, I have received a voice. I desire to speak to your sons and proclaim a hymn in confession, because you have released a captive who was wandering.

“You sought the foolish through wisdom; you gave life; you enriched the needy; you raised the dead; you brought one who was far away near to your majesty; you wished one alien to the fellowship of Israel to become, through Christ’s grace, a companion of your saints.

“Therefore I confess you and will sing a psalm to your name when you have taught me the order. I will sing to you and bless your name forever and throughout the ages of ages.”

### CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0432B] Thus, after receiving baptism, Posthumius did not know letters; nevertheless, through the increase and strength of faith, his knowledge of the Lord grew from day to day.

He was inflamed by zeal for brotherly love and bound to all the brothers by the bond of humility. He loved the yoke of charity intensely and diligently sought out all the brothers who were present and lived in the places near the church.

He recited psalms zealously. He afflicted his body with fasts and spent every night in prayer to God. He ate wild herbs and drank cold water. He tormented his body by covering it with sackcloth and running through the wilderness, so as to break his wretched body, asserting that it was sinful ever to be free from work.

He avoided excessive speech, lent his ear to the divine books, and utterly detested swearing. He showed himself pure in all his prayer and never ceased weeping. For when he frequently suffered the temptations of demons in his body, he fled to the familiar safeguards of prayer.

And lest he seem to indulge sleep any longer to cherish his mortal limbs, he rested briefly upon rocks, so that the hardness of the bed might subject his body to pain and he might rise immediately for God’s work.

He also received his bread by measure and drank water by measure. He never left a meal with a full stomach, nor did he ever satisfy his thirst, saying that it was not proper for the desire of the flesh to be fulfilled.

He practiced obedience and taught it. By patience he gently calmed proud and angry people. But whenever Satan wished by his suggestions to impede his purpose, he raised his eyes to heaven and immediately felt that holy help was present to him.

Such was his life until old age, just as it had been from the beginning: in all these things he utterly despised his body to the very end.

And whenever an illness of fever or stomach pains afflicted him with severe torment, he did not indulge the disease of infirmity, did not use warm remedies, and did not lessen his fasts, believing that if the body were aided with warm food, redemption of the soul would not be given by the Lord.

For if severe illness sometimes wearied his weakened knees so that Posthumius could not rise for the vigils, he did not cease praying and singing psalms on his bed. If his tongue dried from thirst, the depths of his heart cried out, lest the devil, the enemy of his soul, rejoice in his silence, or lest the holy man be found negligent in God’s work.

While Posthumius continued in such a strict life, he went to his baptizer, asked him for a commendatory prayer, and sought from him the secrets of the wilderness without any provision of food. Remaining there for a long time, he endured countless snares of demons.

But the Lord, who had converted this venerable man from the world, daily armed his heart to withstand the demons’ deceptions.

### CHAPTER VII

The way of life of Posthumius became known to Saint Macarius, the disciple of blessed Antony, and his name became famous. It seemed right to Macarius to go to him in the wilderness.

For Macarius had received from the illustrious man Antony the governance of nearly fifty thousand monks. The departure of that same Macarius from the world was approaching, and inquiry was being made as to who should be appointed to the Lord’s flock as master after his death.

When holy Macarius came to holy Posthumius, he welcomed him gladly, especially since he had already heard his reputation from the angel. He had not come merely as a guest, however, but to examine his purpose carefully.

Posthumius’ way of life pleased Macarius, and he began to persuade him not to disdain visiting the relics of Saint Antony, the prince of the anchorites. But when Posthumius resisted with every effort and absolutely refused to go, he was commanded in a dream to go without any hesitation and could not oppose the divine majesty.

Thus he set out on the journey with Macarius and entered the multitude of the monastic congregation, which Macarius alone governed—the same Macarius of whom we have often said that he buried the body of his master when that master’s spirit was called from the world.

[Note: [Col. 0438B] “Where we have often said.” This shows that the author of this Life patched together this and other Lives of the saints. Concerning Macarius, who is said to have buried Antony, see above, the prologue to the Life of Saint Paul the First Hermit, no. 6.]

When Macarius saw himself at the end of this temporal life, he summoned Saint Posthumius and began to address him:

“Behold, brother, the time of my dissolution is near. Therefore, having heard good testimony about you, I have brought the last strength of my weakened old age to my feet in order to reach you.

“You have done well to come with me. Receive, therefore, with fatherly love, the flock of God to govern. Do not seek what is useful to you, but what is useful to many, so that they may be saved (1 Corinthians X). Do not, then, refuse to accept the grace of this office; you will receive your reward from the Lord at the proper time.”

Then Saint Posthumius fell at his feet and said:

“Most beloved Father, how can you impose the care of so great a multitude upon me, a rustic who does not know letters? Therefore choose from among them a worthy man who can govern so many souls of the peoples with care.”

Then Macarius said to Posthumius:

“I hear no excuses and accept no arguments. All these people will remain under your authority, and there is no other man of such great abstinence who can govern the souls of this people and care for them diligently.

“And to speak more certainly, most beloved brother: the Lord has designated you by his own choice to receive this place of ministry. Therefore you will in no way be able to oppose the heavenly command.”

Posthumius said nothing further to Macarius. But while he turned Macarius’ words over in his mind, Macarius gave up his spirit. Immediately a vast crowd of the people hurried attentively to the funeral.

There the multitude of those singing psalms, with different hymn voices as though with one mouth, sang praises to God until the body was led to the tomb for burial. No one, however, grieved excessively that Saint Macarius was so quickly leaving the monastery, because the Lord had provided his flock with a similar master in Posthumius.

### CHAPTER VIII

For three days after Saint Macarius’ death, Posthumius prayed that he might receive from heaven, through Jesus in the Holy Spirit, a fountain of teaching, so that he could teach prudence to so great a host of peoples.

On the third day, the angel who had converted him came to him according to his custom and spoke to him. He appointed him teacher and prince of the monasteries, in the place from which Macarius had withdrawn. He gave him the form of spiritual commandments and departed.

Then Posthumius gathered all the brothers. Opening his mouth, he spoke to them, saying:

“Listen, little sons, to the word that the Lord has spoken to you, wishing to pour into our minds the splendid justice of his commandments and the rule of charity.

“For I speak to you with a father’s voice in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the Spirit of our God. I have received a form from the hand of the angel, so that I may speak for your edification of everything that has entered my understanding.

“Therefore lend your ears attentively: God himself has commanded what proceeds from my mouth.”

[Col. 0434C] “The first union of the commandment is that you obey your superiors in everything.

“The second commandment is submission, so that in chaste fear you may serve the Lord.

“The third ordinance is that you live temperately, devoutly, and justly in this world (Titus II).

“The fourth rule of the commandment is that you afflict your bodies in every way, so that you may obtain the salvation of souls, subduing them by fasts and putting the flesh to death, because this is the delight of good works.

“The fifth constitution is to devote yourselves frequently to prayer, just as the Apostle also commands us to pray without ceasing (1 Thessalonians V). For by always praying and fasting, we shall keep the gifts of faith fixed in the memory of our minds, so that we may overcome the nature of the demons that pour forth.

[Col. 0434D] “Another kind of error follows, in which the soul suffers greater harm: the evil of pride must be avoided in every way. It cast the angel down from heaven at the beginning of the world, and we know that pride is the original sin.

“To exclude it from our thoughts, let us always beseech God that the form of humility may be granted to us.

“Another assault of death also arises in the body if anyone should trouble a monk because of the worldly cause of vices.”

Maintain among yourselves above all the bond of charity, remaining steadfast in faith and hope, since you are hastening toward the kingdom of God’s eternity. Therefore the complete care of monastic discipline is love. These bonds of charity and peace adorn you without avarice. Thus, in sincere love, a sufficient measure is present in what you now possess; and those who love one another will be called sons of the kingdom. Those who love one another more perfectly are the ones who eat bread without blemish in the kingdom of God (Luke XIV). You will therefore be perfect if charity kindles the pure sacrifice in you as an odor of sweetness. For the Lord Jesus will rejoice in you, because you have faithfully done what he himself commanded. For this was the first ordinance of the law given to Moses on Mount Sinai: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deut. VI; Luke X; Lev. XIX). The second is: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” For love of God is fruitless unless love of one’s neighbor is joined to it. The commandment of truth is therefore complete, so that the undivided rule of charity may remain in the heart. Then love will be blessed in its fullness, if you place your necks beneath the yoke of obedience to your undertaking.

Obedience, too, is praised within the congregation. It will profit you nothing, little sons, if you love one another but do not wish to obey one another. Love without obedience will make a man guilty and his conscience sick. For just as the grass of the seedbed hinders fruit, so the disobedient man fasts in vain and receives no fruit from prayer. Therefore those who desire to be one and have resolved to live with one mind should serve the counsels of their superiors. Whatever proceeds from the counsels of the Fathers, let him who is still far from perfection do. Whenever a brother carries some burden upon his neck and, if the abbot is present, cannot even endure the burden’s remaining upon his shoulder, and comes upon springing or bubbling water

[Note: [Col. 0438B] “Springing or bubbling water.” He explains what *scativa* water is, namely water that gushes forth and bubbles. Or is the expression derived from its origin? Unless perhaps he means corrupted water, teeming with worms. Or one may read *stativa*, as I restored it from the manuscript in the *Martyrologium* of Ado, 30 July, where the water is almost muddy. Thus another man drinks muddy water in the *Life of Paul the First Hermit*, chapter 5.]

and turns aside to drink without the abbot’s advice, or that of another brother accompanying him, even if he is younger, you have sinned: you drank water without a blessing. And if the heat of the sun has blazed forth and you wish to drink, but the abbot has forbidden you to do so in order to discipline you, if you murmur even inwardly, you have sinned. Furthermore, if you step on a thorn while traveling, it must not be removed until the abbot has ordered it.

Lay the vines woven together far apart from one another.

When you withdraw for sleep, let there be a space of one cubit between you, lest, while your bodies draw near to one another, the sparks of lust be nourished.

Moreover, the business of the night, because of the demons that flee the light and prowl by night, should be carried out in spiritual labor. When you awake, no worldly matter is to be introduced until, at cockcrow, the common hour of the brothers’ prayers arrives. Let the singing of one not awaken another to prayer; rather, when the first to awaken begins to beat his breast, let the sleeping brother also be summoned to rise. For Satan often wraps a soul seized by sleep in the darkness of night, so that, while the devil—the companion of darkness—is at work, it may be separated from the protection of prayer. Therefore I say to you, little sons: keep watch, because you do not know at what hour the thief of souls will come (Matt. XXIV).

Strive, therefore, to please God, maintaining a spiritual way of life. Let the divine commandments in the love of God, together with the precepts of the law, be inscribed on the tablets of your hearts; and do not be wiser than the simplicity confirmed by the Scriptures of God. Many, however, by thinking differently about God, have fallen away from love of him and of their neighbors. But those who are such should hear the prophet Baruch saying: “Peace of justice and honor of piety” (Baruch V). For when he sees that the love of brotherhood among his people is uncorrupted, he makes them all companions in friendship with God. For those who love God, according to the glory of good works, make the life of this world worthless among themselves through good deeds, profaning whatever in the hearts of God’s servants comes from the devil—from evil thoughts. For they desire to enjoy the life of the anchorites; if they renounce the body while still placed on earth, let them already delight in heavenly things and seek nothing earthly at all, so that they may now trample down and overthrow the causes of worldly darkness.

But since it is fitting that you, suited for the heavenly regions, should please the Creator sufficiently, remaining virgins in mind and body, preserving as fully as possible the fruits of faith and the refinement of speech—for it is sacrilegious for anyone to reproach a monk in either a small or a great matter—the Apostle teaches that we must be irreproachable (Col. IV), and that our speech should always be seasoned with grace and salt, namely with the seasoning with which the Evangelist seasoned us when he said: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matt. V). I ask that this salt not lose its savor in you, lest, when it has lost its savor, it be thrown outside the congregation of the multitude, to be trampled daily by the tongues of enemies.

This, little sons, I beg of you according to the form given me by the hand of an angel: flee the tongue of unjust slanderers,

who hasten, with biting tooth, to insult the Church of Christ even without cause.

Cast away from one another the dissensions that exist among you, knowing that our Lord is not of dissension but of peace (I Cor. XIV). Therefore, if a brother has any scandals against another brother at the prompting of the enemy, let him put them aside for the sake of obedience, with faith standing firm; for I do not speak from myself but from God, who taught me through the hand of his messenger.

And if you offer obedience to your superior and hospitality to a traveler, you do so at the Lord’s command.

If it can be done, a soldier of God ought not to become angry for any reason, not only with his companions but even with strangers.

In no matter whatsoever should any worldly person dare to judge a servant of God, because there is a difference between him and that servant. Do not allow a married man to contend with you in judgment; for it is better for a monk to endure fraud and injuries than for the voice of Christ’s soldier to be heard amid shouting.

It is not fitting for a monk to be a merchant on account of money, but to trade in the profit of heavenly goods. Let him preach the word of salvation, invite souls to heaven, and reduce the desire for the world to nothing. Rejoice, Christian heart—especially you, servant of God—for through prayer of divine power you defeat the tyrant who defrauds souls.

If they inflict any terrors, let him run to the aid of the cross; at once the enemy will withdraw. His cunning is overcome by frequent prayers and fasts. Little sons, what concern is it to you if the armies of demons assemble against you?

You too can be assisted by many battalions of angels. But when the bands of demons begin to increase, lift your eyes to heaven, saying: “Lord Jesus Christ, help my weakness.” Then the word of the prophet Elisha will apply to you against those who had come from Samaria to seize him. When his servant was terrified, he answered him: “Open, Lord, the eyes of your servant, and let him see that there are more with us than with them.” At once legions of God’s angels will come to help you and provide assistance to your faith.

### Chapter IX

These, little sons, are the commandments which, when I perceived the faintheartedness of your hearts, I explained to you concerning the contests with the devil. I do not wish to pass over in silence the things that happened to us when he himself sent them upon us, so that you too may be able to resist his wickedness.

One day, as I was sitting on a mountain, an immense troop, seemingly of soldiers, appeared. When I saw them approaching from afar, I immediately recognized them as angels of Satan. But, laying aside all fear, I fell on my knees upon the ground and prayed that they withdraw, invoking the Lord our Redeemer. Then the troop that had come disappeared completely, like straw carried away by the wind. I therefore gave thanks to the Lord through Jesus Christ our Lord, because he quickly brought my contest to an end and immediately heard my prayer. I have suffered many ambushes, and the Lord delivered me from them all. Therefore you too, little sons, stand firm, because the Lord is gentle in delivering us. Love the Lord, hate the evil one, and the God of mercy will be with you, so that you may escape his snares.

Amen.

---

## April 14. Life of Saint Frontonius, Abbot, by an Unknown Author

[Note: [Col. 0441D] Fronto.] He is called Fronto by others. The Roman Martyrology, April 14: “At Alexandria, Saint Fronto the abbot, whose life shone with holiness and miracles.” The same is found in Usuard and Ado. Bede adds: “He became the father of nearly seventy monks.” Rabanus and Notker relate the matter at somewhat greater length, evidently drawing it from this passage. I wonder where the manuscript *Florarium Sanctorum* obtained the statement: “He died in the year of salvation 174.” Concerning him, Peter writes in the *Catalogue of the Saints*, book XI, last chapter, no. 120. Peter’s error in book IX, chapter 109, and that of Antoninus in the *Chronicle*, part I, title VI, chapter 26, §1, must be avoided: they confuse the acts of this Fronto with the acts of Fronto, the disciple of Saint Peter, bishop of Périgueux. They must be distinguished, and the life of one must be separated from that of the other. Our Peter Maturus, the commentator on Antoninus, rightly observes that what is narrated here about camels does not suit the regions of Gaul, unless, he says, the author of this Life—whoever he may have been—used “camels” for any pack animals. But, as I have said, these two Frontos must be distinguished: one flourished in Gaul, the other in Egypt, where camels are used. The memory of the Gallic Fronto is celebrated on October 25 in the Roman Martyrology. There was also another Fronto, one of the eighteen martyrs of Zaragoza, concerning whom see the Roman Martyrology, April 16, and Prudentius, hymn 4, *On the Crown* (*περὶ στεφάνων*). Peter, *Catalogue of the Saints*, book IV, chapter 56.]

### Prologue

Since you have often desired to hear things that are holy, and I have calmly resolved to undertake the work, I have now decided to build the temple of God—not with goat skins, but with gold, silver, and most precious gems—so that we too may be built, like living stones, into a spiritual house, advancing from the works of the better sort in Christ Jesus our Lord (I Pet. II). I shall relate what happened at Nitria, and I shall in no way pass over the truth, since this little work is sufficiently edifying for monks.

## Life

### Chapter I

Fronto, then, the true servant of God, advancing day by day in devotion to the fear of God, shrinking from the public and communal life and desiring the remote solitude, summoned the brothers to him and said—for there were about seventy men with him:

“Behold what have we to do with the condemnable world, whose works it is altogether fitting for us to renounce, so that we may attain heavenly life? Therefore let us go into the desert, taking nothing with us, in order to acquire heavenly glory; and let us seek the higher discipline through virtues.”

When he had said this, everyone agreed. Taking with them into the desert a few seeds of vegetables, and double-edged little hoes,

[Note: [Col. 0443A] “Double-edged little hoes.” Here *bisacuta* or *bisacutus* is a particular tool, as also in the *Life of Saint Anthony*, chapter 25, no. 62. The manuscript *Glossary of Camberon*: “*Bisacuta*, a certain iron tool cutting on both sides.” It is plainly named in the same manner as a double axe, as though “twice-edged” or “twice-sharp.”]

with which they could dig the soil, they departed and came into the desert. Again Fronto said:

“The Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Do not consider what you shall eat, or what you shall drink, or with what you shall be clothed; for all these things the nations of the world seek. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you’ (Matt. VI). Let us hold fast to the promise, and we shall find the Lord’s work preserved within us.”

Thus they all lived in the desert, continually laboring in the Lord’s work and advancing in spiritual combat; for the Lord assisted his servants. Fronto himself prayed not only for himself but for all, knowing that it is written: “Not seeking what is useful to me, but what is useful to many, so that they may be saved” (I Cor. X).

### Chapter II

When they had remained for a long time in the same desert, the adversary of Christians began to tempt them, so that they would think in their hearts that they ought to remain in the world, because the life of anchorites is extremely harsh and no one can endure it. They therefore murmured in their hearts, saying:

“Why did our father Fronto wish us to live in the desert? Can those who live in cities and towns not see God, while those who live in the desert see him alone? Do not good deeds commend them? Who could live on the food of angels? Behold, we are dying of hunger. The exhaustion caused by vigils does not allow us to work, but harsher fasts are breaking us, and our knees are becoming weak, so that none of us can stand.”

### Chapter III

Hearing their murmuring, before they came to him to say anything, Fronto anticipated them and said:

“How long will you provoke God by murmuring in your hearts and saying: ‘Are those who inhabit the desert the only servants of God? And who can live on the food of angels? Let us go to the abbot and speak to him, so that we may live in the city; for if anyone sees us there, they will suitably provide us with food according to God’s will, as the Lord may have granted each person the ability to do.’ But know this: the Lord will not kill the soul of the righteous by hunger. ‘Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him, to feed them in famine’ (Ps. XXXII). Do you not remember what the Apostle wrote: ‘In hunger and thirst’ (II Cor. XI)? Yet even in the desert you have never lacked roots of plants, nor have you ever remained fasting.

“Remember also that I previously said to you: ‘Do not consider what you shall eat, or what you shall drink, or with what you shall be clothed; for all these things the nations of the world seek’ (Matt. VI). The Lord knows how to give food to those who fear him. ‘Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you.’ For if the Lord feeds the birds and does not abandon the ravens, how could he abandon us, who continually keep him in mind and pray to him without ceasing?

“Certainly, if we should fail from hunger in the desert, let us accuse the Lord and reproach him when we come before him, saying: ‘We believed your Gospel, where you said that you would feed all who believe in you with the nourishment of heaven. We did everything you commanded; we hoped in you, and you despised us. But since you tested us there, now restore what you promised all the more, to prove the truth.’

“Do not therefore murmur against God, lest, by murmuring, you perish from serpents like our fathers in this desert. But if you wait for the Lord, he will give good things to those who fear him, whenever he wills.”

At these words they all fell silent for a little while, ceasing their murmuring; nevertheless, they remained in sorrow.

### Chapter IV

I have decided to set forth everything briefly and to comprise all things in rustic speech, as it is proper to treat them under their title, and to let the sentences and syllogisms of this little book flow in sweet expression, insofar as each reader is able to understand. Let us return to the order of the work begun, so that we may not appear to assert things of our own.

### Chapter V

An angel sent by the Lord therefore went by night to a certain rich man and said to him:

“You feast splendidly amid your riches, while my servants in the desert lack bread. Rise therefore at dawn and send my servants food from everything I have given you, because I have appointed you steward of my flock. I have continually nourished you with heaven’s milk and have never abandoned you. Thus it has pleased me to refresh my poor, who live spiritually in the desert and have entrusted themselves to me, their Lord, through your almsgiving. Therefore do what I now command you, sent by the Lord. Unless you do so, you have broken the peaceful covenant of the Lord your God.”

### Chapter VI

Overcome by such terror, the man awoke from that sleep. Rising in the morning, he summoned his necessary friends and his faithful servants and spoke to them:

“While I was lying in bed at night, I had begun to fall asleep; and suddenly a messenger stood before me saying: ‘Behold, you feast splendidly in your riches, while my servants in the desert lack bread. Rise therefore at dawn and send my servants food from everything I have given you, because I have appointed you steward of my flock.’

“Behold, I wish to send it, but I do not know where the servants of God are staying. I desire to fulfill the command I have received, but who will show me the place to which I should send it? An angel came to me, and God gave the command. But you, who are older, show me the place.”

No one was able to indicate the place to him, because they lived in a hidden part of the mountain, and no one knew where they were staying.

### Chapter VII

The following night, overcome by a harsher threat and pierced by blows, that rich man was seized and pressed to send food to the servants of God. Again he rose at dawn and sought advice from his former friends, asking them to tell him—or at least to inquire of others—where the servants of God were staying. He said these things with the greatest weeping, showing the wounds with which the angel’s hand had struck him during the night.

But when no one could show him the place where the servants of God lived, one who was more distinguished than the others for wisdom answered:

“If you are willing to accept my advice, dearest friend, perhaps it will be beneficial to you. There are seventy camels. Load them with all the goods by which you understand that the servants of God could be nourished, and send the camels along the road without anyone leading them. If this command has come from God, your animals will return safely to you; but if loss threatens you from the devil, willingly endure the scourges of this present time, lest you be struck by some harsher slaughter. If this advice displeases you, seek another who can give a better answer.”

Having said this, he fell silent, but the rich man himself and those who were with him approved this advice. He therefore loaded sixty-five camels

[Note: [Col. 0444A] “Sixty-five camels.” Thus in the manuscript of Saint-Omer and in the old edition. Rabanus and Notker omit the five. They are required to make up the number seventy, since five others follow shortly afterward.]

with those things that the servants of God could eat. But he placed fodder for the five camels among them, food for all the animals, saying in great distress:

“If anyone finds them and unloads their burdens, when he sees the fodder he will pity them and give them something to eat.”

With great weeping, he tied them together in a single line with ropes and sent them along the road, commending them to the Lord, so that, if the command had come from God, they might return swiftly and safely. No driver went with the animals.

[Note: [Col. 0444A] “Driver.” Thus they used *ducator* for *ductor*. Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, chapter 13: “When his driver had to suffer in that place.”]

### Chapter VIII

When they had gone out through the gate, the servant released the first camel, holding its driving rope,

[Note: [Col. 0444A] “Driving rope.” The same form occurs as in *ducator*. Thus *ducatio* in Tertullian, *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 11: “Or perhaps I myself have laid these foundations, and the other grounds for the crowns of officials, to which this driving of necessity is most familiar.”]

and the others followed it. They went along the road beside the mountain’s enclosure,

[Note: [Col. 0444A] “Beside the enclosure of the mountain.” Thus the manuscript. The old edition has “beside the enclosure of the mountain.” The Cologne manuscript has “beside the aforesaid road of the mountain.”]

traveling alone. But I do not know whether camels could proceed by themselves; rather, with the Lord’s messenger going before them, they traveled by a direct route, as was later understood. On the fourth day, when the journey had been completed, at the ninth hour, while the brothers were engaged in the work of God, as someone later reported to us, behold, the first camel lay before the doors. But the sound of the bell could not be heard,

[Note: [Col. 0444A] “The sound of the bell.” From this it appears that bells were already attached to herds in ancient times. See *Onomasticon*.]

because the sound of the hymns was resounding. The abbot, however, because he was near the entrance, saw it first and rejoiced greatly. The entrance of the monastery was narrow, and the abbot alone blocked the doorway with his body; with the other brothers interposed, he remained silent and said nothing until the hymns had been completed.

When the order of hymns was finished, he summoned the brothers and said, almost reproaching them:

“Where are your murmurings? Behold, the Lord has sent us food from above, with a mighty rebuke, commanding a prudent man as he wished; he has brought us loaded camels. Come, let us unload the burdens, so that the exhausted animals may be refreshed.”

Then, all rejoicing with wondrous gratitude, they collectively gave thanks to God and joyfully unloaded the camels’ burdens. When they opened the packs on the five camels, they found fodder. They washed the animals’ feet and made mangers from their bedding; they placed before them the food they had brought for themselves, and they themselves also ran through all the hollows of the mountain, seeking familiar plants, so that the laboring animals might be refreshed with a greater abundance of food.

### Chapter IX

When morning came, the abbot, choosing a useful plan and utterly rejecting avarice, took half of the provisions. Dividing the other half among all the camels, so that some might not seem to carry more and the others be wronged, he placed an equal load on each, assigning it as *eulogies* to the Lord of all things,

[Note: [Col. 0444A] *Eulogies*. This Greek word is common among Latin writers for blessings or a gift of blessing. See *Onomasticon*.]

so that he might break the law of avarice and return half the offering to the camels’ own master.

The friends mentioned above were with the owner of the camels, consoling him over the danger to so many animals and at the same time praying the Lord that such a loss might not befall an innocent man. On the eighth day, when they had all gathered together fasting, one whose ears were sensitive and quick to hear caught, through the currents of the winds, the sound of a little bell and was silent for a while. At last, when he clearly recognized the sound, he said:

“I think the movement of a ringing bell can be heard from the heights of the mountains.”

Then they all went out and perceived the arrival of the camels. A marvelous joy arose amid their rejoicing, and consolation brought forth abundance of happiness for the man. For he had already been mourning the animals as dead or lost; now, rejoicing over their return, he was glad. They all arrived unharmed, neither sad in appearance nor bearing the emaciation of want.

That man therefore received his camels with great thanksgiving. When he saw their burdens, he was even more restored and rejoiced. Then he invited those friends and many poor people to a splendid meal, and distributed to the needy the same *eulogies* that he had received. He also gave some of them to the friends who were present; and he too, receiving the blessing of holy joy, rejoiced in the Lord.

### Chapter X

From that year until Fronto’s death, at the appointed time when he had first sent the food, that rich man continued to send the necessities to the brothers. The Lord likewise commanded other rich men, so that, nourished from all their provisions, the servants of God with holy Fronto might lack nothing. The sons labored in the works of God with the Father, and he filled them daily with heavenly speech, admonishing them with spiritual food. He rejoiced and exulted in the Lord, who had given him such understanding that he had sought worthy places in the remote solitude.

### Chapter XI

Hand this reading on for the edification of many monks. For the one who will be better in God’s sight is not simply whoever reads it, but whoever, by believing, does likewise for God’s servants. He will receive his reward from Christ Jesus our Lord, if he has not despised the alms of the poor and has looked upon God’s servants with an upright heart, in the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory forever and ever.

Amen.

These events took place under the emperor Antoninus

[Note: [Col. 0444B] “Under Antoninus.” Thus the manuscript and the Cologne edition. In the old edition, incorrectly, “under Antonius.”]

in the thirteenth year of his reign.

---

## November 27. Life of Saints Barlaam the Hermit and Josaphat, King of India, by Saint John Damascene; translated by Jacobus Billius Prunaeus

[Note: [Col. 0603C] 339. *Life*.] On this history I approve the judgment of the most illustrious Cardinal Bellarmine, who, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under John Damascene, investigates the matter as follows:

“There is a doubt whether this narrative is a true history or rather something composed for the instruction of noble youths, such as the *Life of Cyrus* by Xenophon. Nevertheless, it is clear that it is a true history from the fact that Saint John Damascene invokes Saint Barlaam and Josaphat at the end of the history, whose deeds he had written, and that the Catholic Church honors these same saints Barlaam and Josaphat, listed in the Martyrology, on November 27.”

The translator Billius reasons as follows:

“As regards the truth of the history itself, for certain reasons that need not be mentioned here, it might perhaps have seemed to some that this work was not so much a true history as a hidden commendation, under the appearance of history, of the monastic life and of a life directed toward Christian perfection, unless the author testified near the end that he had received it from men entirely removed from the charge of falsehood. To distrust him, especially when he insists upon the matter, would seem to me characteristic of one who attributes more to his own suspicions than to Christian charity, which believes all things. I scarcely doubt that the foundation of the entire history is true. Perhaps certain discussions of certain mysteries of faith were added or expanded by the author. For how could Josaphat, newly converted to the faith, have fortified himself with so many passages of Scripture when he had never read them?

“You have this entire Life and history in Vincent, in the *Speculum historiale*, book XV, divided into sixty-four chapters; he slightly abridged the old version. Peter abridged it more in the *Catalogue of the Saints*, book X, chapter 114. You have the complete work from the old version in the *Lives of the Fathers* of the Cologne edition, and in Lipomanus, volume V.”]

### Life of Saint Barlaam the Hermit and Josaphat, King of India, by Saint John Damascene

[Note: [Col. 0604C] Barlaam, etc. The Roman Martyrology, November 27: “Among the Indians bordering on Persia, Saints Barlaam and Josaphat, whose wondrous acts Saint John Damascene wrote.” The manuscript *Florarium Sanctorum*, September 29: “Josaphat, king and confessor.” And December 27: “Josaphat, king and hermit, in the year of salvation 383.” I do not know where the *Florarium* obtained this date. The *Menaea* also mention Josaphat alone, August 26: “Of the holy Josaphat, son of Abenner the king.”]

The title identifies the work as the *Life of Saint Barlaam the Hermit and Josaphat, King of India*, with John Damascene as author and Jacobus Billius as translator.

[Note: [Col. 0604C] John Damascene.] Billius defends the view that John Damascene is the author of this Life or history on the following grounds:

“First, because the Greek-born man of Trebizond, a man of great renown not only among his own people but also among us, named no other author of it than Damascene. Second, the very phraseology, extremely similar to that of his other works, testifies that Damascene is the author. Third, to confirm this opinion, it seems to me highly significant that, just as in the books *On the Orthodox Faith* and almost all his other works Damascene freely borrows much from Basil, Gregory Nazianzen, and other Fathers of the same rank, often borrowing whole verses and even entire periods from them, so in this history also I have noticed that much is brought forward from the same authors without their names being given, especially from Nazianzen, as in chapters 7, 8, 10, 11, 15, 17, 20, and 24, and in many other places.

“Fourth, he not only freely borrows from them but also presents many passages transcribed word for word from the books *On the Orthodox Faith*, such as everything he discusses in chapter 15 concerning freedom of the will. In my judgment he would not have done this so openly unless, as though by his own right, he treated those writings as his own. Fifth, in chapter 19, the discussion of images—which was flourishing in Damascene’s age—confirms me considerably in the same opinion.

“But while all these points support Damascene, they most clearly prove that this history is not by John of Sinai. First, since John of Sinai lived in the time of the elder Theodosius, as is clear from book XIII of Paul the Deacon’s *Miscellaneous History*, how could he have cited Nazianzen in this history, which the author testifies had been brought over from India, when Nazianzen’s writings had scarcely yet circulated among men? And how could he also have cited Basil, an even earlier bishop who died during the time of Valens, even though he suppressed his name—in chapter 19, where he discusses images, and in chapter 34, where Josaphat offers to God the prayer that he plainly took from Basil’s *Constitutions*, chapter 1?

“Second, how could he have introduced Barlaam as discussing images with the king’s son when that question had not yet arisen in his time?”

Thus far Billius.

Bellarminus, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under John Damascene, raises and resolves an objection concerning Damascene as author:

“The history of Barlaam and Josaphat is remarkable and useful. But because Barlaam, while instructing his disciple Josaphat, commands him to believe in the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son, a doubt arose whether this work could have been by John Damascene, who, in book I of *The Orthodox Faith*, chapter 11, teaches that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son but through the Son. It may be answered that in the history the phrase ‘from the Son’ appears to have been added by someone. For in the new edition corrected by Billius, ‘from the Son’ is not found.”

Thus far Bellarmine.

Nevertheless, this history is found in various Greek manuscript libraries under the name of John of Sinai. Thus it is in the Sfortian Library, no. 63, as Baronius notes under November 27; and Billius himself found it under that name in the Greek codex of the distinguished Fumaeus.

### Translated by Jacobus Billius

[Note: [Col. 0605C] Jacobus Billius.] This well-known man produced various translations from Greek into Latin. He was a truly Catholic man, a noble Frenchman, and abbot of Saint Michael in the Hermitage, in Brittany. There is also another ancient version, which some claim was prepared by George of Trebizond. It is published under his name in the 1548 edition of Damascene, printed at Basel in the workshop of Heinrich Petri.

It seems to me that the old translation is much earlier than Trebizond. For it is found in parchment manuscripts, and Vincent was already using that translation three hundred years ago in the *Speculum historiale* cited above. Trebizond, however, lived within the memory of our fathers, with not yet one hundred years having elapsed.

Whoever the old translator may be, Billius says of his version:

“As for Trebizond’s translation, I shall say nothing except that it had always seemed to me exceedingly rough and unpolished; but afterward, when through John of Saint Andrew—a man as excellent and learned as he was abundantly supplied with the best and most learned books—I was given access to a Greek exemplar, I found it faulty in innumerable places. I would certainly prefer to attribute this to excessive haste rather than ignorance of the Greek language, unless there were too many passages in which the translator can scarcely avoid the mark of ignorance under the excuse of haste.

“This matter would give me some suspicion that Trebizond was perhaps not the parent of this translation, unless I had also found in certain other matters that he very often failed to understand the Greek adequately. Whatever the truth may be, here you have a new translation which, if it offers nothing else, is certainly, unless I am mistaken, somewhat clearer and more faithful than the preceding one.”

By Prunaeus.

### Prologue of the Author

“Those who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God,” as the Apostle says (Rom. VIII). To be given the Holy Spirit and to become sons of God is the highest of all desirable things (Nazianzen, Oration on Athanasius); and when one has arrived there, all contemplation comes to rest, as the divine Scriptures declare.

All the saints who have existed since the foundation of the world have therefore attained this excellent and supreme blessedness, the highest of all desirable things, through the cultivation and pursuit of virtues and by divine favor. Some of them underwent martyrdom and stood in battle against sin even to the shedding of blood; others endured the contest of a religious and God-devoted life, followed the appointed path, and became martyrs through the determination of their minds.

Christ’s Church received from the divine apostles and blessed Fathers the practice of commending their shining virtues and glorious deeds—both those who completed their course through martyrdom and those who, through religious discipline, imitated and expressed the angelic manner of life—in written records and transmitting them to later generations as examples of virtue. They proclaimed this, as it were, by a universal law for the salvation of our race.

For the road that leads to virtue is rough, steep, and exceedingly difficult, especially for those who have not yet transferred themselves wholly to God but are still struggling under the tyranny of vices and disturbances of the soul. Consequently, we need many incentives to draw us toward it: counsels and exhortations, certainly, but also the examples of those who entered upon this road before us.

This draws us toward it with less difficulty and ensures that we are not broken in spirit or overcome by despair because of the hardship of life. For when someone must undertake a steep and difficult road, another person will not persuade him equally well to enter it merely by advising and exhorting him. But when he shows him many who have completed it and at last found a very comfortable lodging, he will then move him much more effectively to take up that same road.

Insisting, therefore, on these very principles, and moreover fearing the danger threatening that slothful servant who buried in the ground the talent he had received from his Lord, concealing the money given him for the purpose of making a profit so that he gained nothing from it (Matt. 25), I shall by no means pass over in silence a story useful to souls, which has come down to me and which certain devout men of inner Ethiopia—whom they call Indians—recounted to me as translated from reliable records. It runs as follows.

# LIFE

[Col. 0445]

## CHAPTER ONE

India, which is a vast and densely populated region, lies far from Egypt; on every side it is washed by the sea on the Egyptian side, while on the mainland it approaches the borders of Persia. In former times it was covered by the black darkness of idolatry, teeming with the utmost barbarism and devoted to abominable crimes. But after the only-begotten Son of God, who is in the bosom of the Father (John 1), saw with compassion that his own creation was oppressed by slavery to sin and, moved by mercy toward it, appeared in our likeness except for sin, leaving the throne of the Father for the sake of our salvation—that is, so that we might dwell in heaven, be raised up from our former fall, and, freed from sin, receive again our former adoption—and dwelt in the Virgin’s body; after he had fulfilled all the functions of the flesh he had assumed for our sake, accepted the cross and death, wondrously joined earthly things with heavenly, returned from death to life, ascended into heaven with glory, and magnificently sat at the Father’s right hand; then he sent the Spirit, the Paraclete, in the form of tongues of fire to the disciples who had seen him, as he had promised, and commissioned them to all the nations, so that they might enlighten those who sat in the darkness of ignorance (Luke 1) and baptize them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Thus, thereafter, some travelled around the eastern regions and others the western lands allotted to them, traversing the northern and southern climates in order to carry out their appointed task. Among them, the most holy Thomas, one of Christ’s twelve apostles, was sent to India to preach there the doctrine that brings salvation.

[Note: “Thomas.” Dorotheus testifies in his *Synopsis* that Thomas proclaimed the faith to India, and writes that his body rests at Calamine, a city of India.]

With the Lord cooperating and confirming the message through the signs that followed (Mark 16), the darkness of pagan superstition was driven away. The people were freed from the sacrifices and worship of idols and joined themselves to the true faith. Thus, as though remade by apostolic hands and reconciled to Christ through baptism, they increased by silent growth in the faith, advanced while keeping themselves free from every stain, and built churches throughout the entire region.

When monasteries also began to be built in Egypt, and enormous multitudes of monks began to gather, and the fame of their virtue and manner of life—approaching the imitation of the angels—had spread to the ends of the world and reached even the Indians, this too stirred them to pursue the same way of life. Many of them consequently abandoned everything, withdrew into the deserts, and undertook, in mortal bodies, the manner of life of those who are without bodies.

When matters were in this splendid condition, and, as the saying goes, most people were flying up to heaven on golden wings—

[Note: “And on golden wings.” This proverb is rarer and not easily encountered.]

—in that region there arose a certain king named Abenner.

[Note: “Abenner.” He is mentioned in the Greek *Menaea* on 26 August, in the account of Josaphat, his son, where the name is written Ἀβενήρ.]

He was distinguished by wealth and power, by victories and military courage, and by the stature of his body; he was also renowned for the elegance of his appearance and, because of worldly successes—swiftly withering as they are—he arrogantly exalted himself. Yet as far as his soul was concerned, he suffered the utmost poverty and was bound and worn down by many evils, since he adhered to the pagan party and was deeply devoted to the superstitious error of idols.

While the king lived amid great luxuries, entertainments, and pleasures, and nothing failed to turn out according to his will and desire, there was one thing that interrupted his joy and struck his mind with cares: the evil of childlessness. Since he had no children, this anxiety troubled him, and he wondered how he might be released from these bonds and, having children, obtain the name of father—which, for most people, is plainly the thing they desire above all else. Such was this king, and such were his mind and convictions.

But the most illustrious nation of the Christians, and the companies of monks, regarded the king’s worship and veneration as nothing and were not afraid of his threats. By God’s grace they made the greatest progress, increasing into a multitude too large to be counted, paying the king very little heed, and devoting themselves in a singular manner to matters belonging to the worship of God. For this reason, very many of those who had entered the monastic order utterly despised everything pleasant in this life, being held only by love of piety, thirsting to undergo death for Christ, and burning with desire for future blessedness.

Accordingly, with a spirit neither timid nor hesitant but exceedingly confident and free, they proclaimed the saving name of Christ. Christ alone was ever on their lips, and they openly and appropriately demonstrated to all the transitory and fleeting nature of present things and the permanence and immortality of the life to come. They offered them, as it were, certain supports and seeds, by whose aid they might turn themselves toward God and attain the life hidden in Christ (Col. 3). As a result, many, having received that most delightful teaching, withdrew from the bitter darkness of error and joined themselves to the sweet light of truth. Some distinguished men and senators even cast off the burdens of this life and enrolled themselves among the monks.

When the king learned of this, he was moved by immense anger and, burning with indignation, immediately decreed that all Christians should be compelled to renounce their piety. Thereafter he devised new kinds of torture and threatened unprecedented forms of death. He sent letters to every part of the region subject to his rule, ordering the governors and commanders to attack religious people with tortures and unjust slaughter. Above all, he raged against the most eminent members of the monastic order and stirred up an implacable war against them.

For this reason, most of the former wavered in spirit; others, because they were unequal to enduring the tortures, obeyed his wicked command. But the leaders and superiors of the monastic host, some of them condemning and refuting his injustice, ended their lives in martyrdom and reached everlasting blessedness; others hid themselves in deserts and mountains—not from fear of the tortures threatened against them, but because of some more divine counsel and providence.

## CHAPTER TWO

When such darkness had invaded the land of the Indians, and devout and holy men were being persecuted everywhere, while the champions of impiety flourished in wealth and power, and even the air was polluted by bloodshed and the stench of sacrifices, one of the leading satraps of the royal court surpassed all the others in courage of spirit, bodily size and beauty, and in all the other qualities by which physical elegance and nobility of character are usually expressed as though by certain signs.

When, therefore, he heard that wicked decree, he dismissed this empty glory and these pleasures that crawl upon the ground, joined himself to the company of monks, and, living as an exile in solitary places, cleansed his senses thoroughly through fasts, vigils, and diligent meditation on the divine oracles. His mind, freed and withdrawn from every vicious affection, was illuminated by that light which tranquility produces when the passions have been removed.

The king, however, loved and esteemed him exceedingly. When he heard this, he felt grief at the loss of his friend and burned even more fiercely against the monks. He sent men in every direction to search for him and, as the common saying goes, “moved every stone” in order to find him.

[Note: “Nullum non lapidem novisset” (“he had known every stone”; the reading is uncertain and may be *movisset*, “had moved every stone”). This proverb occurs again below, in chapter 26. It is found in various authors. Euripides says in the *Heraclidae*: Πάντα κινῆσαι πέτρον, “to move every stone.”]

Eventually, when those sent to investigate learned that he was staying in the desert, they searched so thoroughly that at last they seized him and brought him before the king’s tribunal.

When the king saw the man who had once worn splendid garments and lived amid great luxury now clothed so meanly and humbly, afflicted by the severity of religious discipline and openly bearing the marks of a solitary life, he was filled at once with grief and anger. Tempering the two emotions in his speech, he addressed him as follows:

“Madman and fool, what has brought you to exchange honor for disgrace, and illustrious glory for this shameful and utterly dishonorable appearance? You who once presided over my kingdom and held military command over my armies—have you made yourself the plaything of children? Not only have you cast the memory of my friendship far from your mind, but you have also attacked nature itself. Without pity even for your own children, you have regarded both wealth and all the splendor of life as worthless, and have considered such immense disgrace preferable and more desirable than such conspicuous glory?

“What has driven you to this? What hope of gain has led you to prefer the one called Jesus to all gods and human beings, and to place this harsh and superstitious way of life above the most delightful pleasures of this life?”

After hearing this speech, that man of God replied in a voice at once witty, calm, and even:

“If you intend to engage me in conversation, O king, remove your enemies from the middle of the tribunal. Then I shall answer you about the matters you wish to understand. While they are present, I shall have no conversation with you. Apart from conversation, torture me, cut me down, and do whatever you please. For, as my teacher says, the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world (Gal. 6).”

When the king said, “Who, then, are these enemies of mine whom you order me to remove from here?” he replied:

“Anger and desire. In the beginning they were produced by the parent and architect of all things so that they might assist nature, and even now they provide the same service to those who live in accordance not with the flesh but with the spirit. But in you, who are wholly carnal and possess no part of the spirit, they have become hostile and perform the actions proper to enemies and adversaries.

“For desire, when you give it employment, arouses pleasure; when it is abolished, it arouses anger. Let them therefore depart from you today. Let prudence and justice preside over the hearing and judgment of what I shall say. For if you remove anger and desire and introduce prudence and justice in their place, I shall tell you everything truthfully.”

The king replied:

“See, I have yielded to your request. I shall expel desire and anger from the council and will take care that prudence and justice be brought in.”

“Now, therefore, explain to me without any fear where this error arose in you: that you prefer things based on empty hope to things held in the hands and seen by the eyes.”

The hermit replied:

“If you wish to understand, O king, how it first entered my mind that I should despise perishable things and entrust myself wholly to hope in eternal things, listen.
