“Long ago, when I was still of youthful age, I heard a good and saving word whose power carried me away completely. Its memory remained implanted in my heart like a divine seed and could never be torn from me. It put down roots, produced a shoot, and in due season bore fruit in me.

“The force of that word was this: ‘Senseless and foolish people are so disposed that they despise things that exist as though they did not exist, but embrace and cling tenaciously to things that do not exist as though they did. Whoever has not tasted the sweetness of things that exist cannot possess a perfect understanding of the nature of things that do not exist. Unless he has investigated the former, how will he despise the latter and regard them as nothing?’

“By ‘things that exist,’ this speech meant eternal things, free from display; by ‘things that do not exist,’ it meant this life, its pleasures, and its deceptive prosperity—things to which, O king, alas, your heart is badly attached, and which I too once embraced.

“Yet the power of this discourse, continually pricking my mind, stirred the intellect that rules me to choose what was better. But the law of sin, warring against the law of my mind and binding me as though with fetters, held me captive through my affection for present things.

“When it pleased the kindness and goodness of our Savior to rescue me from this bitter captivity, and he himself strengthened my mind to overcome the law of sin and opened my eyes so that I might distinguish good from evil, then—then, I say—I perceived and saw that all present things are vanity and affliction of spirit (Ecclus. 1), as the wisest Solomon also said in a certain passage.

“Then the veil of sin was removed from my heart, the darkness cast upon my mind by the grossness of the body was dispersed and scattered, and I recognized for what purpose I had been created. I understood that I must ascend, through observance of the commandments, to that supreme maker of all things.

“Therefore, leaving everything, I followed him. I give thanks to God through Jesus Christ our Lord, because he delivered me from the clay and brickmaking labor, and from the cruel and pestilential ruler of the darkness of this age; and because he showed me a short and easy road by which, in this body of clay, I might embrace an angelic way of life.

“Desiring to attain this, I judged that I must enter this narrow and confined way (Matt. 7). I was thus resolved in mind: to condemn intensely the vanity of present things and their unstable display and change, and to refuse to be persuaded that anything besides what is truly good ought to be called good. From this, O king, you have wretchedly torn and separated yourself.

“For this reason we too are separated and divided from you, since you are rushing headlong toward clear and unquestionable destruction and are compelling us to be carried precipitously into the same danger. For as long as we were enrolled only in the service of the world, we neglected no part of our duty. You yourself will also be our best witness that we were never marked or reproached for negligence or laziness.

“But after you attempted to extort from us that which is the head of all good things—namely, piety—and to inflict upon us the loss of God, which is the ultimate and gravest of all losses; and while you recall to our minds the honors bestowed upon us and the greatest benefits conferred for that reason, how can I fail, with the fullest justification, to say that you suffer from ignorance of the true good, since you altogether set these things alongside one another—piety toward God, that is, alongside human friendship and glory, which flow away like water?

“How, then, shall we be your companions in this matter, rather than despise friendship, honor, love of children, and anything else that might be greater, when we see you acting wickedly toward God? He is the one who gave you being and breath; he is Christ Jesus, Lord of all. Though he has no beginning and shares eternity with the Father, and though by his word he created heaven and earth, he nevertheless fashioned the human being with his own hands, adorned him with immortality, and appointed him king of all things on earth. He assigned him what was most excellent of all things, namely paradise, as a kind of royal palace.

“But that man, deceived by envy, led into fraud, and softened by the allurements of pleasure (Gen. 3; Wis. 3), was wretchedly cast down from all these things. He who had previously been considered blessed became a pitiable spectacle and was worthy of tears because of the calamity he had received.

“Yet the one who had fashioned and created us, looking again with kindly eyes upon the work of his hands, without undergoing any change in his divinity, became for the sake of our salvation what we are, except for sin. Voluntarily submitting to the cross and death, he cast down the enemy who had envied our race from the beginning. Having freed us from that bitter captivity, he restored us, in his goodness toward us, to our former freedom; through his love for humankind he brought us back to the place from which disobedience had expelled us, and he honored us with greater honor than before.

“This, then, is the one who endured so many torments for our sake and again bestowed such great benefits upon us. Yet you reject him, attack his cross with insults, and, wholly fastened to bodily pleasures and destructive passions, call shameful and disgraceful images gods.

“You have not merely torn yourself away from fellowship with heavenly goods; you also remove from it all who obey your commands and cast them into danger of soul. Therefore, know that I shall never agree to obey you and share with you in the same ingratitude toward God, nor shall I renounce the one who has deserved so greatly of me and brought me salvation—even if you hand me over to be torn apart and devoured by wild beasts, or consign me to the sword or the fire. These things are indeed within your power.

“For I do not fear death, nor do I desire present things, since I have learned that they are exceedingly weak and vain. What benefit is there in them? What is stable or lasting? Nor is that all: even when they are present, immense misery accompanies them—immense grief and immense, perpetual anxiety—since nothing connected with their enjoyment and apprehension is free from sorrow and pain. Their riches are poverty; their exaltation is utter abasement. Who could enumerate all their evils and reach the end?

“My theologian demonstrated these things to me in a few words.”

[Note: “My theologian.” Thus John the Evangelist is called κατ’ ἐξοχήν, “par excellence.” See Suidas.]

“He used these words: ‘The whole world lies in the evil one’ (1 John 5; 2). And again: ‘Do not love the world or the things in the world. For everything that is in the world is either the desire of the flesh, or the desire of the eyes, or the pride of life. And the world is passing away, and its desire. But whoever does the will of God remains forever.’

“Seeking this good will of God, I regarded everything as abandoned and joined myself to those who are held by the same desire and seek the same God. Among them there is no hostility, no envy, no grief, and no anxiety; rather, all run the same course, so that they may reach those eternal dwellings which the Father of lights has prepared for those who love him (James 1; 1 Cor. 2).

“I regard these as parents, these as brothers, these as friends and companions. From those who were once my friends and brothers I withdrew and fled, and I remained in the desert, awaiting God, who saved me from faintheartedness of spirit and from the storm (Ps. 62).”

When the man of God had spoken these things so appropriately and pleasantly, the king was indeed driven by anger and desired to torture the holy man with harsh punishments; yet he restrained himself and hesitated to undertake the deed, fearing the man’s venerable dignity and splendor.

Receiving his speech, he addressed him in these words:

“Wretch, you have sought your own destruction from every direction. It seems that fortune has driven you to sharpen both your mind and your tongue for this very purpose, and that you have consequently poured forth a certain obscure and empty dirge of words. If I had not promised you at the beginning of our conversation that I would drive anger from the council, I would now have thrown your flesh into the fire.

“But since you forestalled me and, taking precautions against yourself, bound me with such words, I endure your boldness for the sake of my former friendship toward you. Therefore rise and flee from my sight. I shall no longer see you—but I shall slaughter you cruelly.”

So the man of God departed and withdrew into the desert, grieving because he had not undergone martyrdom, but nevertheless suffering martyrdom every day as far as conscience was concerned, and fighting, as blessed Paul says, against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this age, against spiritual forces of wickedness (Eph. 6).

When he had gone, the king, stirred by even greater anger, began to conduct a fiercer persecution against the monastic host and at the same time to honor the worshipers and priests of idols more greatly.

## CHAPTER THREE

While the king was living in such grave error and deception, a son of exceptionally beautiful form was born to him. The beauty poured upon the child foreshadowed what he was destined to become. For it was commonly said throughout that land that nowhere had a child of equal beauty and loveliness appeared.

The king, filled with the greatest joy at the child’s birth, named him Josaphat. In his madness he went to the temples of the idols to offer sacrifices to the more foolish beings and to sing praises in order to express his gratitude, not knowing who was truly the author of all good things and to whom a spiritual sacrifice ought to be offered.

Attributing the birth of his son to lifeless and deaf objects, he sent messengers in every direction and took care to compel the people to celebrate the child’s birthday. It was possible to see everyone streaming together through fear of the king, bringing with them whatever was suitable for a sacrifice, according to each person’s means and goodwill toward him.

The king himself especially urged them toward generosity, offering a great many and very large oxen to be slaughtered. After the splendid festival had been completed in this manner, he bestowed the most generous gifts upon all: those of senatorial rank and those who held office, the soldiers, and even the common and low-born people.

On the solemn day of the son’s birthday, about fifty chosen men who devoted their study and effort to that Chaldaean wisdom concerned with observing and recording the stars came to the king. When the king ordered them to approach him more closely, he questioned each one about what the boy would become after his birth.

After prolonged consideration, they said that he would flourish in wealth and power and surpass all who had held the kingdom before him. But one astrologer, who surpassed all his companions in learning, spoke as follows:

“As far as I can learn from the course of the stars, O king, the greatness and advancement of the son now born to you will not be in your kingdom but in another, more distinguished and incomparably superior. I also think that he will embrace the religion of the Christians, which you persecute, and that he will not deviate from this goal and hope.”

The astrologer spoke in this way, like Balaam of old (Num. 23)—not because astrology rests upon truth, but because God, in order to cut off every excuse from the impious, revealed the truth through the very adversaries themselves.

When the king understood this, he received the message heavily and with distress, and felt his pleasure interrupted by grief. Nevertheless, in a certain private city he had a most beautiful palace built and an elegant house prepared, and placed his son there. He ordered that, once the child had passed his earliest years, no one should have access to him.

He appointed as his tutors and attendants men in the prime of life and endowed with exceptional beauty, and instructed them to ensure that the child learned nothing of the unpleasant things in this life—not death, not old age, not illness, not poverty, nor anything else distressing or capable of interrupting his enjoyment. Instead, they were to place before him everything pleasant and connected with sweet gratification, so that his mind, occupied with pleasure and luxury, might be unable to entertain any thought of future things and might not even hear a word about the Christian religion or its doctrines.

For this above all things the king intended to conceal from him, fearing the astrologer’s prophecy. If any attendant happened to fall ill, he ordered him to be expelled immediately and replaced by another who was clean, healthy, and in excellent condition, so that nothing rough or bitter might at all meet the eyes of his son.

Thus the king conducted himself; thus he thought and acted. He saw but did not see, and heard but did not understand.

When he was informed that some monks still survived—though he believed that not even a trace of them remained—he seethed with anger and attacked them with the greatest violence. He ordered heralds to run throughout the city and the region, proclaiming that after three days no member of the monastic order was to be found anywhere. If one were found, he would be consigned to the flames.

“For these,” he said, “are the men whose authority persuades the people to worship as God the one who was fastened to the cross.”

Meanwhile, something occurred that provoked his indignation still further and made him more hostile to the monks.

## CHAPTER FOUR

Among the men distinguished by rank there was one who held first place at court. He was a man of honorable life and devout faith, and he devoted himself with the greatest diligence to his salvation—though secretly, because of fear of the king.

For this reason, some who envied the authority he possessed with the king sought to accuse him and exerted themselves with all their strength to do so. On one occasion the king had gone hunting, as was his custom, surrounded by a company of guards, and that upright man was among the hunters.

As he was walking alone—for, as I think, divine providence had arranged it so—he came upon a man lying prostrate on the ground among dense trees, with one foot badly crushed by a wild beast. When the man saw him passing, he begged him not to pass him by but to pity his misfortune and arrange to have him carried to his house. At the same time, he added that his service would not be entirely useless or empty to him.

The distinguished man replied:

“I shall indeed take you in for the sake and love of virtue and will care for you as much as I can. But what, precisely, is this benefit that you say will come from you to me?”

The poor and infirm man replied:

“I heal wounds caused by words. For whenever some wound or affliction is found in words or conversations, I treat it with appropriate remedies and prevent the evil from spreading further.”

Although the devout man considered what he had said to be of no importance, nevertheless, for the sake of the divine command, he ordered that the man be carried to his house and given the care appropriate to him.

But those envious men, inflamed by spite, of whom we spoke earlier, now brought to light the wickedness they had long been plotting. They accused him before the king on the ground that he had not only forgotten the king’s friendship, neglected the worship of the gods, and turned his mind toward the Christian religion, but was also plotting serious things against the king’s majesty—corrupting the common people and gaining everyone’s goodwill for himself.

“If you wish to know for certain,” they said, “that we are not fabricating and inventing anything, privately test him. Tell him that you have abandoned the religion of your homeland and the glory of your kingdom, that you wish to embrace the Christian faith, and that you intend to put on the monastic habit, which you once persecuted as dishonorable.

“For those who wickedly fabricated these charges against the man knew that his character was especially inclined toward repentance. They had no doubt that, if he heard such words from the king, he would immediately advise him to choose what was better and urge him not to delay doing what had been rightly resolved. In this way, they thought, what they were saying would be found true.”

The king, who was well aware of the man’s goodwill toward him, judged that these accusations lacked all plausibility and were false. He did not think he should accept them rashly; rather, he wished to investigate both the matter itself and the charge brought against him.

Accordingly, he summoned him when no witnesses were present and, in order to test him, addressed him as follows:

“You know, my friend, how I have recently acted against those called monks and indeed against all Christians. Now, however, regretting this and weary of present things, I wish to turn toward those hopes that I have heard them mention—namely, a certain immortal kingdom that will exist in another life, since the present kingdom is wholly interrupted by death.

“I believe that I cannot attain this in any other way or fulfill my desire unless I become a Christian, bid a final farewell to the glory of my kingdom and the other pleasures and delights of this life, seek out those practitioners of the religious life and those monks whom I wickedly and criminally expelled, wherever they may be, and join myself to them.

“What do you say to this? What do you think I should do? Please tell me—I adjure you by truth itself. For I know that, above all mortals, you are devoted to truth and endowed with integrity of character.”

When the good man heard this, he recognized the hidden deception in no way. Moved by repentance and overflowing with tears, he replied with a simple heart:

“May you live forever, O king. You have formed a good and saving resolution. For although the kingdom of heaven is difficult to find, it must nevertheless be sought with all one’s strength. ‘For whoever seeks will find it,’ he says (Luke 11).

“The fruit of present things, though it seems pleasant and brings delight outwardly, is nevertheless best driven away and rejected. Indeed, it is ours only while it exists; and those whom it delights, it torments again all the more. For both its sweetness and its distress are weaker than their shadow, and vanish as swiftly as the wake of a ship moving across the sea or the trail of a bird traversing the air (Wis. 5).

“By contrast, the hope of future things preached by Christians is firm and completely secure, even though they experience affliction in the world (John 16). The pleasures we enjoy now are brief; there, however, they summon nothing but punishment and tortures that never end. The sweetness of these things is fleeting and temporary, but their bitterness is eternal. For Christians, on the contrary, hardship is temporary, while pleasure and benefit are immortal.

“Therefore, may your good resolution prosper happily. It is beautiful—indeed, exceedingly beautiful—to exchange things subject to destruction for things everlasting.”

When the king heard these words, he was exceedingly indignant. Nevertheless, he restrained his anger and said nothing to him at that time.

But the other man, being prudent and perceptive, noticed that the king had received his words seriously and with displeasure, and recognized that the king had acted with a crafty mind solely to test his disposition. When he returned home, he remained in grief and weakness, wondering how he might appease the king’s mind and escape the danger threatening him.

As he spent the entire night sleepless, he remembered the man suffering from the crushed foot. He summoned him and addressed him as follows:

“I remember that you told me you heal injuries caused by harmful words.”

The other replied:

“It is true. If necessary, I shall give you a demonstration of my skill.”

The senator then related to him the longstanding goodwill he had shown the king and the authority he possessed with him. He also described the recent conversation in which the king had craftily tested him, explaining how he himself had answered properly, while the king, receiving his speech with displeasure, had revealed through changes in his expression the anger concealed deep within his heart.

That poor and sick man, having considered the matter carefully in his heart, said: “You must understand, most illustrious sir, that the king has formed a bad and hostile opinion [Col. 0455C] of you, namely, that you are trying to seize his kingdom, and that he said what he did merely to test you. Therefore rise, have your head shaved, cast off these splendid garments, put on sackcloth, and, as soon as daylight appears, go to the king. When he asks what this attire means, answer: ‘O king, concerning those matters about which you spoke with me yesterday, here I am, ready to follow you on this path which you have decided to enter. For although luxuries and pleasures are delightful, far be it from me to retain them after you. But the path of virtue, which you are preparing to enter, although difficult and rough, will nevertheless be easy, smooth, and pleasant, provided I am with you. Just as you had me as your companion in the pleasures of this life, so you will also have me as your companion in its hardships, so that I may come with you into the fellowship of the future [Col. 0455D] blessings.’”

That excellent man, therefore, approving the sick man’s words, did as he had advised. When the king saw and heard him, he was indeed delighted by this, marveling at the man’s devotion to him; and, recognizing that the reports brought against him were false, he honored him more highly and granted him greater influence and intimacy at court. Nevertheless, his anger against the monks flared up again, since he declared that these were their teachings: that people should abstain from the pleasures of this life and allow themselves to be deceived, as if in a dream, by an uncertain hope.

[Col. 0456A] When he went out hunting again, he saw two monks traveling through the desert. He immediately ordered them to be seized and brought to his chariot. Looking at them with angry eyes and, as the saying goes, breathing fire [Note: [Col. 0606B] “Breathing fire,” as the saying goes. This too has the appearance of a proverb.], he said: “Have you not heard, you impostors and deceivers, my heralds publicly proclaiming that none of your diabolical institution was to be found after three days in the city or in any region of my kingdom, or else was to be burned completely in the fire?”

The monks replied: “Here we are, departing from your cities and regions, as you commanded. But since we have a long journey before us in order to go to our brothers, and are without food, we are traveling by this road so that we may obtain provisions for the journey and not perish from hunger.”

The king said: “One who fears death has no time to procure food.”

[Col. 0456B] The monks replied: “You have spoken rightly, O king: those who fear death concern themselves with how they may escape it. But who are these people except those who waste away over fleeting things and admire them to the point of stupefaction? Since they despair of obtaining anything good in the other life, they cannot be torn away from present things, and for that reason they fear death. But we, who have long hated the world and the things in the world, and are entering the narrow and constricted way for Christ’s sake, are moved neither by fear of death nor by desire for present things; we are held only by longing for future things. Since, therefore, the death which you inflict upon us becomes a passage to eternal and more excellent life, it is for us rather an object of desire than of terror.”

[Col. 0456C] Then the king, cunningly seeking to trap the monks, said: “What? Did you not say a little earlier that you were withdrawing in order to obey my command? If you do not fear death, why are you fleeing? Here again you have spoken vainly and emptily and have lied.”

The monks answered: “We are not fleeing because we fear the death you have announced to us. Rather, moved by compassion for you, and lest we bring upon you a heavier condemnation, we have resolved to withdraw.^250 Otherwise, so far as we are concerned, we are in no way frightened by your threats.”

At this the king, provoked to anger, ordered them to be burned. Thus the servants of God, having completed the final day of their lives, obtained the crown of martyrdom through fire. Immediately an edict was issued that if any monk could be found, he was to be slaughtered without investigation. And so no one of this order remained in that region, except those who had hidden themselves in the mountains, caves, and hollows of the earth. But enough of this for now.

## CHAPTER V

Now the king’s son, about whom our account began at the outset, remained in the palace built for him, in such a way that no one could approach him. At last he reached adolescence, having meanwhile absorbed all the learning both of the Ethiopians and of the Persians. He was prudent and intelligent, distinguished by every endowment of virtue. He even posed natural-philosophical questions to his teachers, so that they too marveled at the young man’s intellect and sharpness of mind, while the king himself was astonished by the beauty of his countenance and the disposition of his spirit.

[Col. 0457A] The king instructed those who attended him to take every care that he should learn nothing at all of the hardships of this life, and should not know that death follows present pleasures. He was nevertheless relying on an empty hope and, as the proverb says, was trying to shoot arrows into heaven [Note: [Col. 0606B] “To shoot arrows into heaven.” It is found in Suidas and Zenodotus: Εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν τοξεύεις, “You shoot arrows into heaven.”]. For how could death be unknown to human nature? Thus it did not escape even the boy’s awareness.

Since he possessed a mind adorned and equipped with the greatest intelligence, he considered within himself what had induced his father to bar everyone’s access to him and permit no one to approach him. He understood by himself that this could not be done without his father’s command. Yet he was afraid to ask, partly because he thought it wholly contrary to reason that his father should fail to recognize what was advantageous for him, and partly because he reflected that, if this was being done by his father’s will, then no matter how much he questioned him, he still would not discover the truth of the matter. Therefore he resolved to learn these things from someone other than his father.

[Col. 0457B] Since he had one of his tutors dearer and more familiar to him than the others, and had bound him to himself by still greater affection and bestowed upon him very generous gifts, he asked him what had moved the king to keep him enclosed in this enclosure. He added: “If you explain this openly to me, I will put you before everyone else and make with you a covenant of perpetual friendship.”

The tutor, being himself prudent and intelligent, and having tested the boy’s keen intelligence and fully accomplished wisdom, did not think that he would incur any danger from him, and explained everything to him in detail: the persecution proclaimed against the Christians, especially against those who had wholly devoted themselves to the practice of piety; how they had been expelled and driven out from all the neighboring places; and likewise what the astrologers had foretold when he was born.

[Col. 0457C] “Therefore,” he said, “so that you would not hear their teaching and prefer it to our religion, the king deliberately arranged that you should have dealings with very few people, indeed with scarcely anyone at all. He also commanded us repeatedly to take care that you should learn nothing through us of the hardships of this life.”

When the young man heard this, he added no other word. But the saving message touched his heart, and the grace of the Paraclete began to open his spiritual eyes, leading him by the hand, as it were, to the true God, as we shall show in the progress of our narrative.

[Col. 0457D] When the king, his father, frequently visited him—for his love for him was extraordinary—the son addressed him one day as follows: “O lord and king, I wish to learn something from you, because of which perpetual grief and an anxiety that never relents gnaw at and consume my mind.”

The father, deeply distressed by these words, said: “Tell me, dearest son, what this grief is that besieges you, and I shall immediately endeavor to turn it into joy.”

Then the boy said: “Explain why I am kept here and shut away by you between walls and doors, in such a condition that no one may approach or see me.”

[Col. 0458A] “Because, my son,” said the king, “I do not want you to see anything that might trouble your heart or interrupt your pleasure. For this is my aim and concern: that you spend your whole life in perpetual luxury, in complete joy, and in every delight of the mind.”

“But I want you to know, O lord,” the son said to his father, “that by living in this manner I am not living in joy and delight of mind, but rather in affliction and great distress, so much so that even food and drink are distasteful and bitter to me. My spirit longs to see what lies beyond these doors. Therefore, if you wish me to live happily and pleasantly, order me to go outside at my own discretion and delight my mind with the spectacle of those things whose sight is denied me.”

[Col. 0458B] When the king heard this, he was overcome with sadness,^251 and reflected that, if he denied him what he requested, he would cause him even greater grief and anxiety. Accordingly, he said that he would do what pleased him. Immediately he ordered splendid horses and a retinue of attendants suitable to royal dignity to be prepared, and gave him permission to go out whenever he wished.

He strictly instructed those who accompanied him to ensure that nothing unpleasant should meet his eyes, but that they should show him whatever was beautiful, agreeable, and delightful; that they should perform dances along the roads, provide the accompaniment of the sweetest songs, and arrange various spectacles, so that he might occupy and entertain his mind with these things.

[Col. 0458C] When the king’s son frequently went out in this manner, it happened one day through the servants’ forgetfulness that he saw two men, one suffering from leprosy and the other from blindness. When he saw them and was saddened in spirit, he asked those who were with him who they were and what this dreadful spectacle might be. Since they could not conceal what had come before his eyes, they replied that these were human calamities, which commonly befall mortals because of corrupted matter and a body filled with unhealthy humors.

Then he said: “Are these things accustomed to happen to all human beings?”

“Not to all,” they replied, “but only to those whose health has been corrupted by diseased humors.”

[Col. 0458D] The young man continued to inquire: “If not all people are accustomed to fall into these calamities, but only some, is it known who will be seized by the severity of such evils? Or, on the contrary, do they come upon people without distinction and unexpectedly?”

“And which human being,” they answered, “can foresee the future and understand it perfectly? This exceeds the capacity of human nature and has been assigned only to the immortal gods.”

At that point the king’s son ended his questioning, but he took grief into his heart from such a spectacle. He was so affected by the novelty of the matter that the appearance of his face changed.

[Col. 0459A] As he went out again, he encountered a very old man, his face wrinkled, his legs broken down and weakened, his body bent, his head completely white, and, in addition, without teeth; he spoke in a chopped and interrupted manner. Struck with astonishment, he ordered the man to be brought closer to him and asked those who were present what this extraordinary spectacle might be.

They said: “This man, having advanced very far in age, as his strength gradually declined and his limbs contracted weakness, has reached the misery that you see.”

“And what is his end?” he asked.

“Nothing other than death will receive him,” they replied.

“Is this fate appointed for all human beings,” he asked, “or does it happen only to some?”

[Col. 0459B] They answered: “Unless death overtakes and carries someone away beforehand, it is impossible for anyone, as time advances, not to run the risk of reaching this condition.”

Then the young man said: “At what age does this happen to a person? Is it absolutely necessary to die, and is there no art by which we may escape death and avoid falling into this misery?”

They told him: “People reach this old age in their eightieth or hundredth year, and then they die; it cannot happen otherwise. Death is a natural debt imposed upon human beings from the beginning, and its arrival cannot be avoided by any means.”

[Col. 0459C] When that keen and prudent young man heard and understood all these things, he groaned from the depths of his heart and said: “This is a bitter life, full of every pain and sadness, if matters are truly as they say. How can anyone be tranquil while awaiting an uncertain death, whose arrival not only cannot be avoided but is also, as you have said, uncertain?”

He went away turning these things over in his mind and considering them continually, repeatedly recalling the thought of death, and thereafter living in pain and mental consternation, dwelling in perpetual grief. He said to himself: “Will death one day seize me as well? And who will remember me after my death, when time has crushed everything into oblivion? Moreover, when I have died, shall I dissolve into nothingness, or is there instead another life and another world?”

[Col. 0459D] Thinking about these and similar things continually, he was consumed by pallor. Yet whenever his father was present and came to him, he displayed a cheerful spirit free from grief, because he did not want what he was thinking to come to his father’s knowledge. He longed beyond belief to find someone who could establish a firm conviction in his heart and pour a good message into his ears.

Therefore he again asked that tutor whom we mentioned earlier whether he knew anyone who could help him in the matter for which he was burning with desire, and strengthen his mind, which was seething with grave thoughts and unable to cast off such anxiety.

[Col. 0460A] The tutor,^252 recalling to him what had previously been said, replied: “I have already explained to you how your father partly slaughtered those wise men devoted to the practice of piety who discuss such matters, and partly drove them out in anger and hostility. Nor do I know anyone of this kind in this entire surrounding region.”

At this he was filled with great distress and suffered a grievous wound of the spirit, like someone who has lost an immense treasure and has his entire mind occupied and fixed upon searching for it. Accordingly, he remained in continual languor and anxiety, and all the world’s joys and pleasures seemed in his eyes like some offense and abomination.

While he was in this state of mind and desired with many a sigh to find the good, that sleepless eye which sees all things and desires that all should be saved and come to a knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. II) looked upon him and, displaying its customary benevolence toward him, showed him in this manner what path he should follow.

[Col. 0460B] At that time there was a certain monk skilled in divine matters, adorned in life and speech, and exceedingly practiced in every form of monastic living. I cannot say where he was born or from what family, but he lived in a certain solitude in the land of Sennaar and held the dignity of the priesthood. This old man’s name was Barlaam.

When he had learned through a divine prompting what condition the king’s son was in, he left the solitude and went to a cultivated and inhabited land. Changing his own dress and putting on worldly clothing, he boarded a ship and made his way to the kingdom of the Indians. Pretending to be a merchant, he entered the city in which the king’s son had his palace.

[Col. 0460C] After remaining there for many days, he carefully investigated the circumstances of the prince’s life and who were accustomed to approach him more closely. When he learned that the tutor whom we mentioned above was the prince’s most intimate associate, he met with him privately and spoke as follows:

“I want you to know, my lord, that I am a merchant and have come from a distant region. I possess a gemstone of exceptional value, the like of which has never been found, and which I have not yet shown to anyone. I disclose this to you because I see that you are a prudent and intelligent man: introduce me to the king’s son, and I will give it to him as a gift. It surpasses all good things incomparably. It brings the light of wisdom to those whose eyes of the heart are blind; it opens the ears of the deaf; it grants speech to the mute; it restores the sick to health; it gives wisdom to fools; it drives out demons; and, finally, it supplies its master most abundantly with whatever is beautiful and desirable.”

[Col. 0460D] The tutor replied: “I see that you are a man of grave and steadfast character; but your words display a certain excessive boasting. Since I have seen precious stones and pearls of outstanding and immense value, how could I list and recount them all? Yet I have never seen or heard of any possessing the powers you have mentioned. Nevertheless, show it to me, and if it is such as you say, I shall introduce you without hesitation to the king’s son, who will honor you with the greatest distinctions and benefits.

“But before your words are confirmed by the very sight of eyes that cannot be deceived, it is impossible for me to report to my master and king such extravagant and presumptuous claims about something uncertain and unknown.”

[Col. 0461A] Barlaam said: “You have spoken rightly in saying that you have never seen or heard of such powers and capacities. For my speech to you concerns not an ordinary matter but something immense and marvelous. Since you have asked to see it, hear what I have to say.

“This stone of supreme value possesses, besides the powers and capacities I mentioned, this further property: no one who lacks a sound and healthy eye and a pure body free from every impurity can look upon it readily and without difficulty. If anyone, being deficient in these two respects, rashly and arrogantly directs his eyes toward this precious stone, he will also be deprived of the very power of sight and understanding with which he himself is endowed.

[Col. 0461B] “Now, since I am by no means ignorant or inexperienced in medicine, I perceive that your eyes are not very healthy. I therefore fear that you may lose even the power of sight that you now possess. But I have heard that the king’s son is both endowed with purity of life and possessed of beautiful and clear-sighted eyes. For that reason I shall not hesitate to show him this treasure. So do not neglect this matter and deprive your master of something so important.”

The tutor replied: “If this is so, do not show me the stone, since my life is stained by many sins and, besides, I do not even have sufficiently healthy eyes. But I shall not hesitate to inform my master the king about it.”

[Col. 0461C] After this conversation, he entered the presence of the king’s son,^253 and explained everything to him in detail. When the prince heard his tutor’s words, he felt his heart breathed upon by a certain spiritual joy and delight; and, as if seized by divine inspiration, he ordered the man to be brought in quickly.

When Barlaam entered, gave him the greeting of peace appropriate to him, and was ordered to sit, the tutor withdrew. Josaphat then said to the old man: “I would like you to show me that precious stone about which my tutor has told me, recounting the great and marvelous things you have said of it.”

[Col. 0461D] Barlaam began his discourse with him as follows:

“It would in no way be right, O king, for me to say anything false or rash to your illustrious excellence. Everything that has been reported to you about me is true and beyond all doubt. But unless I first test your prudence, it would be wrong for me to disclose this mystery to you.

“For my Lord says: ‘The sower went out to sow. And as he sowed, some seed fell beside the road, and the birds of heaven ate it. Other seed fell on rocky ground, where it had little soil, and immediately sprang up because it had no depth of soil. But when the sun rose, it was scorched, and because it had no root, it withered. Other seed fell among thorns, and the thorns sprang up and choked it. Finally, other seed fell on good soil and produced fruit a hundredfold’ (Matt. XIII).

[Col. 0462A] “Therefore, if I find in your heart fruitful and good soil, I shall not hesitate to cast the divine seed into you and disclose a great mystery to you. But if it is rocky and thorny, and a road trodden by everyone, it will be better not to sow this saving seed at all, but to throw it as prey to birds and wild beasts, before whom I am utterly forbidden to cast pearls.

“Nevertheless, I have better hopes of you, and trust that you are nearer to salvation: namely, that you will both see the stone which surpasses all value and, through the radiance of its light, attain this—that you yourself will become light and bear fruit a hundredfold. For your sake I have undertaken a long journey, so that I might show you what you have never seen and teach you what you have never heard.”

[Col. 0462B] Josaphat said to him: “Indeed, venerable old man, I am held by an extraordinary desire—one that cannot in any way be restrained—to hear some new and good message. A fire has been kindled in my breast, and it inflames me intensely to understand certain necessary questions. Until now, however, I have not been able to find anyone who could give me firm assurance about this matter.

“If I find a wise and learned man and hear a saving message, I shall not, as I think, hand it over to the birds or the wild beasts; nor shall I be, to use your words, rocky and thorny. Rather, I shall receive it with a pure and sincere heart and preserve it intelligently and diligently. Therefore, if you know anything of this kind, please do not conceal it, but tell me.

[Col. 0462C] “As soon as I heard that you had come from a distant region, I was filled with joy of spirit and began to entertain the good hope that through your efforts I might attain what I desired. For that reason I immediately had you brought to me and received you courteously, as one of my companions and equals. Would that my hope not prove false!”

Barlaam replied: “You have acted splendidly and in a manner worthy of royal magnificence, since you did not direct your attention to outward lowliness, but entrusted yourself to a hidden hope.

[Col. 0462D] “There was once a great and illustrious king who, while traveling in a golden chariot surrounded by a retinue worthy of royal majesty, happened to encounter two men in torn and filthy garments, their faces wasted by emaciation and exceedingly pale. The king knew that through bodily affliction and the labors of a life consecrated to God they had so wasted away their flesh.

“When he saw them, he immediately leapt from his chariot, prostrated himself on the ground, and did obeisance to them. Then he rose, embraced them most warmly, and greeted them.

“His nobles and governors were displeased by this, believing that he had committed an act unworthy of royal glory. Since they did not dare rebuke him openly to his face, they approached his brother and urged him to admonish the king not to disgrace and dishonor the greatness and sublimity of his diadem in this way.

[Col. 0463A] “When his brother had said these things to him and accused him of untimely and misplaced humility, the king gave him an answer which he did not understand.

“It was the king’s custom, whenever he sentenced someone to death, to send a herald with a trumpet—called the trumpet of death for this reason—to the condemned man’s door; and from the sound of that trumpet everyone understood that he must die. Accordingly, as evening fell, the king sent the deadly trumpet to sound at his brother’s door.

“When the man heard this trumpet, despairing of safety, he spent the whole ^254 night attending to his household affairs. In the morning, dressed in black and mournful clothing, he went with his wife and children to the palace gates, weeping and lamenting.

[Col. 0463B] “When the king had admitted him and saw him thus wailing, he said: ‘O fool and madman, if you were so terrified by the herald of your brother, with whom you share the same lineage and equal rank, and against whom you know yourself guilty of no crime whatsoever, how could you brand me with reproach because I humbly and submissively greeted the heralds of my God—those who announce to me, more loudly and clearly than any trumpet, the approach of death and of the Lord whom I know myself to have offended by many grave crimes?

“‘Thus, to expose your madness, I have used this method; and I shall immediately demonstrate that those who persuaded you to rebuke me are fools and madmen as well.’”

In this way he sent his brother home, corrected and usefully instructed.

[Col. 0463C] He then ordered four chests to be made of wood. After covering two of them entirely with gold and placing foul corpses’ bones inside, he secured them with golden bolts. He smeared the other two with pitch and bitumen, filled them with precious stones, exquisite pearls, and every fragrant perfume, and bound them tightly with rough ropes.

Then he summoned the nobles who had rebuked him for the encounter with the two men and set the four chests before them, asking them to estimate the value of these and of those. They declared that the two gilded chests were of the greatest value, saying that otherwise they could not but contain the royal crowns and belts. The chests smeared with pitch and bitumen, by contrast, they called altogether cheap and worthless.

[Col. 0463D] The king said to them: “I was not unaware that you would say this, since with your physical eyes you see what falls within the senses. But that is not how one ought to proceed. Rather, one must look with the inner eyes at the value, usefulness, and ugliness contained within.”

He immediately ordered the gilded chests to be opened. When they were opened, a heavy and foul odor escaped, and a most unpleasant spectacle was presented to the eyes.

The king therefore said: “This is the likeness of those who wear splendid and illustrious garments and exalt themselves insolently because of their immense glory and power, yet are inwardly full of foul corpses and crimes.”

[Col. 0464A] Afterward, when he had ordered the chests smeared with pitch and bitumen to be opened, he delighted all who were present with the splendor and sweetness of the fragrance stored within them. He said to them: “Do you know what these chests resemble? They resemble those humble and despised men dressed in poor garments, whose outward appearance you observed and on account of whom you considered it an insult and disgrace that I had cast myself upon the ground before them.

“‘But when I considered their dignity and the beauty of their souls with spiritual eyes, I gained glory from contact with them and judged them superior to every crown and every royal purple garment.’

“In this manner he made them ashamed and taught them not to go astray by judging matters that fall within the field of sight, but to direct their minds toward those things perceived by the intellect.

[Col. 0464B] “Thus you too have approached the likeness of that pious and wise king, since you received me relying on a good hope—which, as I think, will certainly not deceive you.”

Josaphat said to him: “You have spoken all this beautifully and appropriately. But I desire to know who your Lord is, whom you said at the beginning of your discourse had spoken about that sower.”

## CHAPTER VII

Barlaam therefore took up his discourse again and said:

“If you wish to know who my Lord is, he is the Lord Jesus Christ—the only-begotten Son of God, I say; the blessed one and the only powerful one; the King of kings and Lord of lords; who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light; who is glorified with the Father and the Holy Spirit (1 Tim. VI).

“For I am not one of those who worship many wanton gods and venerate these soulless and deaf images. Rather, I acknowledge and confess one God, who is glorified in three persons—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—and in one nature and essence, in one undivided glory and kingdom.

[Col. 0464C] “This one God in three persons, without beginning or end (Nazianzen, Oration 2, On Easter), eternal, uncreated, immutable, without body, invisible, without limitation, beyond the comprehension of the mind, alone good and just, brought all things into being from nothing, both those seen by the eyes and those beyond the sight of the eyes.

[Col. 0464D] “First, he created an innumerable multitude of invisible and heavenly powers, separated from matter and body—that is, spirits serving the divine majesty. Then he created this visible world: heaven, earth, and sea. He also adorned it with joyous light: heaven with the sun, moon, and stars; earth with plants of every kind ^255 and various living creatures; and the sea with countless species of fish.

“He spoke all these things, and they came to be; he commanded, and they were created (Ps. CXLVIII).

[Col. 0465A] “Afterward he fashioned the human being with his own hands, taking from the earth the clay for the composition of the body, while granting the soul, which participates in reason and understanding, through his own breath. This soul, Scripture says, was made according to the image and likeness of God (Gen. I): according to the image, because of the power of understanding and freedom of choice; according to the likeness, because of the imitation of his virtue, insofar as this is possible.

“He endowed this human being with freedom of choice and immortality, appointed him king of the things on earth, and from him fashioned a woman like him to be his helper.

[Col. 0465B] “Having planted a paradise in Eden toward the east, full of every pleasure and delight, he placed in it the human being whom he had fashioned. His goodness allowed him to partake freely of all the trees that were there, but forbade him to taste one alone, which was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, saying: ‘On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die.’

“Now one of the angelic hosts mentioned above, who presided over one order, had received not the slightest trace of natural defect from the Creator, but had been created for the sake of goodness. Yet, by a free movement of the mind, he turned from good to evil, and, lifted up by arrogance, desired to rebel against the Lord and God.

“Therefore he was expelled from his order and dignity and, in place of that blessed glory and angelic name, received the name of devil and Satan. For God, judging him unworthy even of heavenly glory, cast him headlong from heaven.

“With him a great multitude of angels under his authority was torn away and expelled. Having become evil through a movement of the mind and followed the defection of their leader instead of goodness, they received the name of demons, as impostors and deceivers.

[Col. 0465C] “Thus the devil, having wholly renounced goodness and assumed an evil nature, conceived envy against the human being (Wis. II), because he saw himself expelled from such glory while the human being had been raised to such honor. He sought to cast him down from that blessed manner of life.

“Therefore, having made the serpent the workshop of his deception, he approached the woman through it. After leading her, by the hope of divinity, to taste the forbidden tree, he then through her also deceived Adam—for this was the name of the first man.

[Col. 0465D] “When the first man had tasted the forbidden plant in defiance of the divine command, he was expelled by the supreme Father and architect from the paradise of delights and fell from that blessed life, immune from destruction, into this—alas!—wretched life, and was finally condemned to death.

“From this the devil gained strength and, elated by victory, as the human race increased, implanted every kind of wickedness in their minds. Consequently, wishing to restrain and suppress the immense onrush of sin, God brought a flood upon the earth and destroyed every living creature (Gen. VII).

“But when he found only one righteous man in that generation, he preserved him alone on the earth, together with his wife and children, in an ark. Afterward, when human beings again began to increase in number, they were seized by forgetfulness of God and broke out into greater impiety, enslaving themselves to various sins and scattering themselves among many kinds of error.”

[Col. 0466A] For some judged that everything came about by chance and accident and was devoid of providence, as though there were no Lord who governed and directed it. Others introduced fate and committed everything to the stars under which people were born. Others worshiped many evil gods, afflicted by many vicious passions, so that they might have them as defenders and patrons of their own passions and grave crimes. Representing their forms in paintings, they set up deaf statues and senseless images on high, enclosed them in temples, and worshiped and adored them, serving the creature rather than the Creator.

Some worshiped the sun, the moon, and the stars, which God established to bring light to this earthly world. These things, however, are without soul and sense; they are illuminated and preserved by the Creator’s providence and possess no power of their own. Others worshiped fire, water, and the remaining elements of the earth, in which there is neither soul nor sense. Nor were they ashamed to render worship to such things, although they themselves possessed soul and reason.

Others bestowed veneration upon wild beasts, reptiles, cattle, and four-footed animals, thereby showing themselves more devoid of reason than the very creatures they worshiped. Others painted the forms of certain disgraceful and worthless men and called them gods, some male and some female. They themselves even handed down that these beings were adulterers, murderers, hot-tempered, envious, frenzied, parricides, fratricides, thieves, 256 robbers, lame, weak, sorcerers, and insane. They also related that some of them had died, some had been struck by lightning, some had served human beings and lived in exile, some had received wounds and uttered laments, and some had changed themselves into animals because of their wicked and shameful crimes. Thus it came about that human beings, taking occasion from the gods themselves, polluted themselves with every kind of impurity. At that time a dreadful darkness indeed held our race; there was no one who understood, and no one who sought God (Ps. XIII).

At that time Abraham alone was found to possess a firm and vigorous understanding and, from contemplating created things, to recognize the Creator. For when he had considered heaven, earth, and the sea, as well as the sun, moon, and the rest, he admired an order so full of harmony. And when he had observed the world and the things within it, he did not think that they had come into being and were preserved by chance and accident. Nor did he attribute the cause of such an ordered arrangement to the elements of the earth or to lifeless images; rather, through these things he recognized the true God and understood him to be the maker and preserver of the universe.

God, approving the goodness and purity of his soul and his sound judgment, revealed himself to him—not indeed as he is by nature, for it is impossible for created nature to behold God, but through certain manifestations of God’s dispensation, in the manner known to him—and, implanting in his soul a fuller knowledge of himself, honored him and adopted him as his servant. Through the piety transmitted successively to those who descended from him, Abraham instructed them in the knowledge of the true God.

For this reason the Lord willed that his offspring should grow into an innumerable multitude and called them his own special people (Gen. XV; 1 Pet. II). When they were oppressed by the slavery of the Egyptian nation and the tyrant Pharaoh, he led them out through Moses and Aaron, holy men endowed with the gift of prophecy, by means of terrible and wondrous signs and miracles (Exod. XV). Through them he also afflicted the Egyptians as their wickedness deserved; and the Israelites—for thus the people descended from Abraham were called—he led across the Red Sea on dry feet, the waters having been divided and made like walls on both the right and the left.

When Pharaoh and the Egyptians pursued them from behind, the waters returned and utterly destroyed them. Later, having led the people through the desert for forty years by means of the greatest miracles and divine manifestations, and having fed them with heavenly bread, he gave them the law—which was a type and foreshadowing of future things—inscribed by God on tablets of stone, and bestowed it upon Moses on the mountain (Exod. XXXI). It drew them away from all images and shameful deeds and taught them to venerate the one true God.

Thus, through mighty miracles, he brought them into a good land, which he had formerly promised to the patriarch Abraham that he would give to him and his descendants. It would be a long task to recount how many and how great, wondrous, illustrious, and extraordinary benefits—exceeding all number—he bestowed upon them. Through all these things he was working to draw the human race away from every impious worship and crime and to restore it to its former condition. Nevertheless, our nature still remained enslaved to the freedom of error, and through the tyranny of the devil death continued to reign over human beings, sending all who had been condemned by the divine sentence into hell.

When, therefore, we had fallen into such calamity and misery, the one by whom we had been fashioned and brought into being did not despise us, nor did he allow the work of his hands to perish utterly. Rather, by the gracious will of God the Father, the only-begotten Son and Word of God, who is in the bosom of the Father—I mean the one of the same substance as the Father and the Holy Spirit, the one older than every age, without beginning, who was in the beginning, who was with God the Father and was God—kindly humbled himself to his servants. Indeed, this humiliation is such that it can be declared neither in words nor comprehended by the mind.

For while he was perfect God, he became perfect man from the Holy Spirit and the holy Virgin Mary, the Mother of God—not from the seed, will, or intercourse of a man (John I). Conceived in the womb of the Virgin, who was free from every stain, he was conceived from the Holy Spirit, just as, before the conception, one of the archangels was sent to announce to the Virgin that new and wondrous conception. The Son of God was conceived without seed, from the Holy Spirit; and, having united to himself in the Virgin’s womb flesh animated by a rational and intellectual soul, he came forth as one person in two natures, perfect God and perfect man, preserving his mother’s virginity free from every stain even after childbirth.

He became subject to the very same passions as we are, except for sin (Heb. IV); he took upon himself our infirmities and bore our diseases (Isa. LIII). Since death had entered the world through sin (Rom. V), it was necessary that the one who was to accomplish the work of redemption should be free from every sin and in no way subject to the death of sin.

After living among human beings for thirty years, he was baptized in the waters of the Jordan by John, a holy man and the greatest of all the prophets. When he had been baptized, a voice of this kind came from heaven from God the Father: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” [Luke III]; and the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove.

Afterward he began to perform great and wondrous signs: restoring the dead to life, bringing light to the blind, putting demons to flight, healing the deaf and lame, cleansing lepers, renewing our long-corrupted nature in every way, teaching through his works, instructing us in the way of virtue, drawing us away from corruption, and showing us the path to eternal life. Therefore he also chose twelve disciples (Matt. XIX), whom he called apostles, and entrusted to them the task of preaching the heavenly manner of life for which he had come: to display it on earth and, through his incarnation, to make us humble and earthly beings heavenly.

But the Jewish priests and rulers, among whom he dwelt and for whose benefit he had performed such wondrous signs and miracles, were moved by envy and fury against his admirable life, consistent with his divinity. Forgetful of all his benefits, they condemned him to death, taking one of his disciples to betray him and handing him over, once he had been seized, to the Gentiles. I mean the one who was the life of all and who willingly endured these things.

For this reason he came: to suffer everything for our sake, so that he might redeem us from vicious passions into freedom. After they had inflicted many kinds of punishment upon him, they finally condemned him to the cross. He endured all these things in the nature of the flesh that he had assumed from us, while his divine nature remained free from every suffering. For although he possessed two natures—divine, and human, the nature he had assumed from us—the human nature suffered, while the divinity was incapable of suffering and immortal.

Thus our innocent Lord Jesus Christ was fastened to the cross in the flesh. “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (Isa. LIII; Rom. V); therefore he was not subject to death. For, as I have already said, death entered the world through sin. Yet for our sake he suffered death in the flesh, so that he might redeem us from the tyranny of death. He descended into hell and, having crushed it, freed the souls that had been confined there from the foundation of the world.

Placed in the tomb, he rose on the third day, having conquered death and granted us victory over it, and having reconciled immortality to the flesh as the giver of immortality. He appeared to his disciples and granted them peace (John XX; Acts I), and through them to the entire human race.

After forty days he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father. He will come again to judge the living and the dead and to repay each person according to his works (Ps. LXI). After his glorious ascent into heaven, he sent the most holy Spirit to his holy disciples in the form of fire. Through the Spirit’s inspiration they began to speak in foreign languages, as he enabled them to speak.

Thus, by his grace, they were scattered among all the nations and preached the orthodox faith, baptizing them [Col. 0469B] in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to observe all the Savior’s commandments (Matt. XXVIII). In this way they enlightened the nations that had strayed from the right path and removed from their midst the superstitious error of idolatry.

Although the enemy, bearing his defeat with the utmost indignation, even now stirs up war against the godly, persuading foolish and senseless people to retain the worship of idols, his power has nevertheless become feeble, and through Christ’s power his sword has finally failed. Behold, in a few words I have declared to you my Lord and God and the author of salvation. You will know him more fully if you receive his grace in your soul and, by divine favor, it should be granted to you to become his servant.

[Col. 0469C] **CHAPTER VIII.**—When the king’s son heard these words, his soul was struck by the light. Rising from his throne out of joy and embracing Barlaam, he said:

“Perhaps, unless conjecture deceives me, most excellent man, this is that priceless stone which you rightly keep hidden and do not show indiscriminately to everyone, but only to those endowed with sound and healthy faculties of soul. For as soon as I received these words with my ears, a most delightful light entered my breast, and that heavy veil of sorrow which had long pressed upon my soul from every side was immediately lifted. If, then, I judge rightly, please let me know. But if you know anything more excellent than what you have related, do not hesitate to reveal that to me also.”

Barlaam replied again:

“Indeed, my lord and king, this is that great mystery which was hidden from ages and generations but was revealed to the human race in the last times (Col. I). Its disclosure was formerly foretold by many prophets and righteous men through the grace of the divine Spirit, instructed in many ways and by many means (Heb. XI), and announcing it with a loud voice. Although they foresaw that salvation would certainly come and longed to behold it, they did not see it; but this last generation, by divine favor, received the author of salvation. Therefore, whoever believes and is baptized will be saved (Mark XVI).”

Josaphat said:

“I believe without any doubt everything that you have said, and I glorify as God the one whom you proclaim. This one thing I ask: declare everything to me without error, and teach me exactly what I must do. Also make me understand what baptism is, which you say is received by those who possess faith.”

He replied:

“The grace of divine baptism is the root and sure foundation, as it were, of this holy and undefiled Christian faith. It cleanses all the sins contracted from birth and completely purifies those defilements formed through vice. For the Savior commanded that we be regenerated through water and the Spirit and restored to our former dignity: namely, that the Holy Spirit should approach the water through prayer and a saving invocation.

We are therefore baptized, according to the Savior’s words, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. XXVIII). Thus the grace of the Spirit dwells in the soul of the one who is baptized, enlightening it, making it divine, and restoring in it that image and likeness of God according to which it was created.

Thereafter, casting aside all the former works of vice, we enter into a covenant of new life with God (Nazianzen, Oration on Holy Baptism) and begin a purer manner of life. In this way we also become fellow heirs of those who have been regenerated for immortality and have attained eternal salvation. Without baptism, however, no one can obtain good hope, even if he has surpassed all the godly in piety.

For the Word of God, who assumed humanity in order to bring salvation to our race, said: ‘Truly I say to you, unless someone is regenerated from water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven’ (John III). Therefore, before all else, I ask you to receive faith in your soul and immediately approach baptism with the most ardent desire, without making any delay at all. Delay is dangerous, since the day appointed for death is uncertain.”

Josaphat said to him:

“And what is that good hope which you said no one can obtain without baptism? What also is that which you call the kingdom of heaven? From where, moreover, did you hear the words of God clothed in humanity? And again, what is this uncertain day appointed for death, about which such great anxiety entering my breast consumes my flesh with sorrows and pains, and even eats away the strength of my bones? Finally, do we who die dissolve into nothingness, or does another life remain after this present pilgrimage? I wished to learn these things and others like them from you.”

Barlaam gave this answer:

“The good hope of which I spoke is hope of the kingdom of heaven. It is of such a kind that no human tongue can explain it at all. For Scripture says: ‘What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him’ (Isa. LXIV; 1 Cor. II).

When, by divine favor, we have cast off this gross flesh and attained that blessedness, then he whose favor has not allowed our hope to deceive us will teach us and enable us to know the glory of those good things, surpassing every capacity of the mind; that light which no speech can express; that life which death does not interrupt; and, finally, that fellowship of life with the angels.

For if we obtain by divine gift to have fellowship with God, insofar as this is permitted to human nature, we shall learn from him everything that is now unknown to us. Instructed by the divinely inspired Scriptures, I regard this above all as the kingdom of heaven: to approach the contemplation of the holy Trinity, which gave life its beginning, to be more purely illuminated by its incomparable light, and, with unveiled face (2 Cor. III), to behold its glory, which surpasses every power of speech.

Nor is it surprising that that glory, that light, and those hidden blessings cannot be declared in words. They would not be great and extraordinary if we, being earthly and mortal and carrying this flesh, weighed down by passions, could both grasp them in knowledge and express them in words.

Since these things are now certain to you, accept them by faith alone and without any doubt, and shun every form of deception. Strive to seize that immortal glory through good works. When it is granted to you to possess it, you will understand these things more perfectly.”

259 “As for what you asked me—how we have heard the words of the incarnate God—know this: through the sacred Gospels we have learned the matters belonging to the theandric dispensation, that is, to God joined with man. That sacred book is so called because it announces good news to us, who are mortal, subject to destruction, and earthly, concerning immortality, a state free from corruption, eternal life, the remission of sins, and the kingdom of heaven.

The men who wrote it were spectators and ministers of the Word. I said earlier that our Savior Christ chose disciples and apostles. After the glorious ascent of God into heaven, they committed to written records his manner of life on earth, his teaching, and his miracles, insofar as human beings were able to do so.

Thus that distinguished one among the divine evangelists said at the end of his book: ‘There are also many other things that Jesus did; if they were written down one by one, I do not think that the world itself could contain the books that would be written’ (John XXI).

In this divine Gospel, therefore, there is contained a history, written by the Spirit of God, of his incarnation, manifestation, miracles, and commandments. It also mentions that punishment free from every stain which the Lord endured for our sake; his holy resurrection on the third day; his ascension into heaven; and, finally, his glorious and fearful second coming.

For again the Son of God will come to earth with glory, with a multitude of the heavenly host greater than any speech can describe, to pass judgment upon the race of mortals and repay each according to what he has done [Col. 0472A] (Luke XXI).

For when God fashioned man in the beginning—as I have already explained to you—he breathed into him the breath of life (Gen. II), which is called a soul endowed with reason and understanding. Since we have been condemned to death, it is necessary for all of us to die; no human being can escape this cup. Death is nothing other than the separation of the soul from the body.

The body, fashioned from earth, after it has been separated from the soul, returns to the earth from which it had been taken and dissolves in corruption (Gen. III; Ecclesiasticus III). But the soul, being immortal, goes where the supreme Maker commands—or, more correctly, where it itself prepared a dwelling for itself while it was still in the flesh. For according to the life each person has lived here, that person will receive there.

Finally, after long periods of time have passed, our God will come to judge the world with fearful glory surpassing the power of speech. At his fear the powers of heaven will be shaken, and the entire army of angels, seized with trembling, will stand before him (Luke XXI). This will occur when, at the voice of the archangel and the divine trumpet, the dead return to life and are set before his dread throne (1 Thess. IV).

Resurrection is the reunion of the soul with the body. Therefore this very body, which perishes and dissolves, will rise in such a way that thereafter it cannot perish (1 Cor. XV). Do not let it occur to you in any way to refuse belief in this. For it is not impossible for the one who first fashioned it from earth, after it returned to the earth from which it was taken, to raise it again to life according to the Creator’s decree.

If you consider with me that God the King brought into being from nothing what he produced, this will be a sufficiently strong proof for you. For earth, which previously did not exist, was taken and produced a human being (Gen. II). How, then, was a human being made from earth? How was earth itself produced from nothing? Upon what foundation does it rest? And finally, how were from it produced the countless kinds both of brute animals, seeds, and plants?

Moreover, in our own birth I would have you consider this. Is not a very small seed emitted into the earth—that is, into the womb that receives it? From where, then, does this great formation of a living creature arise?

Therefore, for the one who produced everything from nothing and continues even now to produce it, it is in no way impossible to restore to life from the earth those bodily things that have been extinguished and corrupted by death, so that each person may receive a reward corresponding to his works (2 Cor. V; Ps. LXI). ‘The present time,’ he says, ‘is a time of labor; the future, however, is a time of recompense.’

Otherwise, where would God’s justice be, if there were no resurrection? Many virtuous men, after enduring many calamities and punishments in this life, have finally been violently removed from it. Conversely, some impious and criminal people have spent their present life amid pleasures and prosperous circumstances. But God, who excels equally in goodness and justice, appointed a day of resurrection and reckoning, so that when each soul has received back its body, the wicked and criminal person who enjoyed every favorable and happy circumstance here may there suffer the punishment of his crimes; while the virtuous person, having paid in this life the penalties for whatever wrongs he committed, may there obtain the inheritance of good things.

“For,” says the Lord, “those who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God. And they will come forth: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment” (John V).

At that time thrones also will be set up, and the Ancient of Days (Dan. VII), the father and maker of all things, will preside. Books will be opened, in which the deeds, words, and thoughts of all of us are recorded. A river of fire will roll along in rapid course, and everything concealed in secret will be revealed.

There no advocate, persuasive eloquence, false excuse, power of wealth, arrogance of rank, or the most abundant gifts and bribes will be able to suppress righteous judgment. Rather, that incorruptible and true judge will weigh everything for the vindication of justice: deed, word, and thought.

Those who devoted themselves to virtue will depart to eternal life and to a light surpassing every power of speech, so that they may rejoice with the angels, enjoy hidden blessings, and stand in purity before the holy Trinity. But those who have bound themselves to shameful crimes, and all the impious and sinners, will go to eternal punishment, which is called Gehenna, outer darkness, the sleepless worm, the gnashing of teeth, and countless other torments.

Of all these, none is equally grievous and bitter as being alienated from God, cast away from his most sweet presence, deprived of that glory which no words can explain, exposed before the eyes of the whole world, and marked with an everlasting disgrace.

After that dreadful sentence has been pronounced, everything will thereafter remain unchangeable and incapable of alteration: the joyous life of the righteous will have no end, nor will affliction and punishment for sinners receive a limit. For there is no higher judge after him, no purification through subsequent works, no appointed term of correction, and no other method or means for those who are suffering punishment, since the penalty will endure eternally together with them.

Since these things are so, what sort of people ought we to be in holy conduct and pious actions, so that we may be judged worthy to escape the coming threats and to stand at the right hand of the Son of God (2 Pet. III)? For this is the station of the righteous, just as the most wretched portion on the left has been assigned to sinners.

Then the Lord, calling the righteous blessed of his Father (Matt. XXV), will bring them into the eternal kingdom. But the sinners, cast away with anger and execration from his sweet and peaceful presence—which nothing more grievous and bitter can be imagined—he will send away to eternal punishment.

**CHAPTER IX.**—Josaphat addressed him in these words:

“You tell me of great and wondrous things, worthy of great fear and trembling, O man, if these things are indeed so—if, after we have yielded to fate and been dissolved into ashes and dust, there will be a resurrection and regeneration, and an examination and recompense for the deeds performed in life. But by what argument do you prove these things? And how have you acquired such firm and unquestioning faith in something not yet seen with the eyes, heard, or understood?

What has already happened and been made evident in reality you have heard from those who saw it and recorded it, even if you did not see it yourselves. But how, while proclaiming such great and exalted things about the future, have you obtained certainty concerning them?”

Barlaam replied:

“From what has already occurred I have also gained certain faith concerning the future. Those who proclaimed these things never departed from the truth in any matter; through signs and miracles and various powers they gave strength to their words, and they likewise instructed us concerning the future.

Just as they taught nothing disordered or fabricated here, but everything they said and did shone more brightly than the sun, so likewise there they truly handed down all things. Our Lord and Master Jesus Christ himself confirmed these matters both by word and by deed.

For he says: ‘Truly I say to you, the hour is coming when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live’ (John XII).
