And again: ‘The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God. And those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment’ (Luke XX).

Again he says: ‘Concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was spoken to you by God, who said: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob”? He is not the God of the dead but of the living. As the weeds are gathered and burned, so will it be at the consummation of this age (Matt. XXIV). The Son of God will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all causes of stumbling and those who commit iniquity. And they will cast them into the furnace of fire; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.’”

[Col. 0474D] Having said this, he added: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke II).

In these and many other words the Lord declared the resurrection of bodies. In reality he also confirmed his words when he restored the dead to life. At the close of his earthly life, he called a certain friend of his, Lazarus, who had already been dead for four days and was putrefying, out of the tomb, and showed alive the one who had breathed out his soul (John XI).

Indeed, the Lord himself also inaugurated a perfect resurrection, no longer subject to death. Having tasted death in the flesh, he returned to life after three days and became the firstborn of the dead (1 Cor. XVI). Although others also had been raised from death to life, they died again and could not provide an image of the true resurrection to come. He alone, however, became the author and prince of that resurrection, having returned to life through an immortal resurrection.

These things were also proclaimed by those who from the beginning were spectators and ministers of the Word. For blessed Paul, who was called not by human beings but from heaven (Gal. I), says:

“I make known to you, brothers, the Gospel that I preached to you. For I delivered to you first of all what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he rose again according to the Scriptures” (Rom. IV).

“But if Christ is preached as having risen from the dead, how do some say that there is no resurrection of the dead? For if the dead do not rise, neither has Christ risen. But if Christ has not risen, your faith is vain; you are still in your sins. If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are more pitiable than all human beings. But now Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep. For since death came through a human being, through a human being also comes the resurrection of the dead. For just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Cor. XV).

And a little later:

“For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality. But when this mortal has put on immortality, then the saying that is written will come to pass: ‘Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death?’”

The power of death will be utterly destroyed and abolished, so that it may no longer exercise its force; instead, immortality and everlasting incorruptibility will thereafter be granted to human beings.

There will, then, there will indeed be, I say, without any doubt, a resurrection of the dead, and we believe this most certainly. Moreover, we know that there will be an examination of the deeds performed in life, rewards, and punishments, on the fearful day of Christ’s coming (1 Pet. II), when the heavens will be dissolved by fire and the elements will melt with heat, to use the words of a certain theologian. We await new heavens and a new earth according to his promise.

That there will be rewards and punishments for deeds there, and that nothing whatsoever, whether good or evil, will be neglected, but that the recompense for actions, words, and thoughts is stored up, is established by these words of Christ:

“Whoever gives one of these least ones a cup of cold water, only in the name of a disciple, will not lose his reward” (Matt. X).

And again by these words:

“When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty. All the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. He will set the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left.

“Then the King will say to those at his right hand: ‘Come, blessed of my Father; inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; I was naked, and you clothed me; I was sick, and you visited me; I was in prison, and you came to me’” (Matt. XXV).

Why does he use these words, unless it is because he attributes to himself the benefits that we confer upon the needy? And elsewhere he says:

“Everyone who acknowledges me before human beings, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven” (Luke XII).

Behold, through all these things and many others he declared that the rewards of good works are firm and certain. Conversely, he also announced that the punishments for wicked deeds are stored up there, through the wondrous and extraordinary parables which that wholly wise fountain of wisdom explained with complete wisdom.

For he introduces a certain rich man (Luke XVI), clothed in purple and fine linen and feasting splendidly every day. He was miserly and far removed from mercy, so much so that he despised a certain poor man named Lazarus, lying at his gates, and did not even give him the crumbs from his table.

When both had reached the end of their lives, the poor man, covered with sores, was carried into Abraham’s bosom—the term by which he indicated the dwelling of righteous men—whereas the rich man was condemned in hell to the most bitter punishment of flame. Abraham addressed him in these words:

“During your life you received good things, and Lazarus likewise bad things. But now he is comforted, while you are tormented.”

262 Again, elsewhere he says that the kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding feast for his son (Matt. XXII). By the wedding feast, future joy and glory are signified. For when speaking to humble people imbued with earthly passions, he drew his parables from things familiar and customary to them—not because he was showing that there would be weddings and tables in that age, but because he accommodated himself to their dullness and used these terms to make future things clear to them.

“Therefore,” he says, “that king invited everyone to the wedding feast with a lofty proclamation, so that they might enjoy those good things to the full.”

Many of those who had been invited, however, neglected to go. Instead, occupying themselves—some with fields, some with business, and some with wives whom they had recently taken—they were deprived of the splendor of the bridal chamber. When those men had of their own accord excluded themselves from that most delightful joy, others were invited, and the feast was filled with those reclining at table. But when the king entered to see those reclining at table, he saw there a man not clothed in a wedding garment. And he said to him: “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?” But he was speechless. Then the king said to his attendants: “Bind his feet and hands, take him away, and cast him into the outer darkness. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

By those who refused to attend the wedding and in no way obeyed the one by whom they were summoned are signified those who did not hasten at all to the faith of Christ, but persisted either in the worship of idols or in some heresy. By the one who lacked a garment appropriate to the wedding is understood the man who indeed possessed faith, but defiled his spiritual garment with impure sins and was therefore deservedly removed from the joy of the bridal chamber.

He also brought forward another parable of the same kind, pertaining to the same matter, namely, the parable of ten virgins, five of whom were wise and five foolish (Matt. XXV). The foolish ones, after taking their lamps, did not take oil with them, whereas the wise ones did. In this passage, by “oil” he signified the possession of good works.

“At midnight,” he says, “a cry was made: Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him.” By “midnight” he indicated the uncertainty of that day. Then all those virgins arose; and those who were ready went out to meet the bridegroom, entered with him into the wedding, and the door was shut. But the unprepared ones—whom he therefore not without reason called foolish—when they saw their lamps being extinguished, went to buy oil. Afterward, when the doors had already been closed, they approached and cried out, saying: “Lord, Lord, open to us.” But he answered them: “Amen I say to you, I do not know you.”

From all this it is plainly evident that a recompense has been appointed for evil actions, and even for words and thoughts themselves.

For the Savior said: “I say to you that for every idle word which men have spoken, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matt. XII). And again: “But even the hairs of your head are all numbered” (Matt. X). In this passage, clearly, by “hairs” he signified even the most minute considerations and the thoughts of the mind.

The blessed Paul also teaches things consistent with this: “The word of God,” he says, “is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and body, and of spirit and joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. And there is no creature invisible in his sight, but all things are naked and open before his eyes, to whom our account is given” (Hebr. IV).

The prophets also, enlightened long ago by the grace of the Holy Spirit, announced these things most openly. Isaiah says:

“I know their works, and I will repay them. Behold, I am coming to gather all nations and tongues; and they will come and see my glory. And there will be a new heaven and a new earth, which I will make to remain before me. And all flesh will come and worship before me, says the Lord; and they will go out and see the corpses of the men who transgressed against me. For their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished. And they will be an object of loathing to all flesh” (Isa. LXVI).

And again, concerning that day, he says:

“And heaven will be rolled up like a book; all the stars will fall like a leaf from the vine. For behold, the day of the Lord comes, full of fury and wrath, to make the earth desolate and to destroy its sinners from it. For the stars of heaven and their splendor will not spread their light. The sun will be darkened at its rising, and the moon will not shine with its light. And I will bring to rest the pride of the unbelieving, and I will humble the arrogance of the strong” (Isa. XIII).

And again he says:

“Woe to those who drag iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as though with a wagon-rope. Woe to those who call evil good, placing bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter. Woe to those who are mighty to drink wine and strong men to mix drunkenness; who justify the ungodly for gifts and take away the justice of the just from him; who turn aside the judgment of the poor and plunder the substance of the needy, so that the orphan may be your prey. And what will you do on the day of visitation? To whom will you flee for help? And where will you leave your glory, lest you fall under visitation? Therefore, just as a tongue of fire devours straw and the heat of a flame consumes it, so their root will be like embers and their shoot like dust. For they have rejected the law of the Lord of hosts and blasphemed the word of the Holy One of Israel” (Isa. V).

To this may be added what another prophet says:

“The great day of the Lord is near, and exceedingly swift. The sound of the day of the Lord is bitter; the mighty man will be troubled. That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and storm, a day of trumpet and blast against fortified cities and against the lofty corners. And I will trouble the wicked, and they will walk as blind men, because they have sinned against the Lord; and their blood will be poured out like earth, and their bodies like dung. Neither their silver nor their gold will be able to deliver them on the day of the Lord’s fury. In the fire of his zeal the whole earth will be devoured, for he will make a swift end of all the inhabitants of the earth” (Zeph. I).

Moreover, King and prophet David cries out in this manner:

“God will manifestly come, our God, and he will not be silent. Fire will burn before him, and around him there will be a mighty tempest. He will summon heaven above and the earth, to judge his people” (Ps. XLIX).

And again:

“Arise, O God,” he says, “and judge the earth, for the thought of man will confess to you” (Ps. LXXVII).

And again:

“You will repay each according to his works.”

The Psalmist and all the prophets, taught by the divine Spirit, proclaimed many other things of this kind concerning the future judgment and its recompense. The Savior also, most certainly confirming their words, taught us to believe in the resurrection of the dead, the recompense for the things done in life, and the immortal life of the age to come.

## CAP. X

Josaphat, filled with great contrition of heart because of these words, was bathed in tears and addressed the old man as follows:

“You have made everything perfectly clear to me and, in eloquent speech, have set forth this dreadful and wondrous account in its entirety. Since these things have therefore been placed before us, what must finally be done so that we may escape the punishments prepared for wicked men and attain the joy of the righteous?”

Barlaam replied:

“It is recorded in the sacred writings (Acts II) that when Peter, who is called the chief of the apostles, was instructing the people in doctrine, they were pierced in their hearts, just as you too have been today. And when they said, ‘What shall we do?’ Peter said to them: ‘Repent, and let each one of you be baptized for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is for you, and for your children, and for all who are far away, whomever the Lord our God shall call.’

“Behold, then, he himself has poured out upon you the riches of his mercy and has summoned you, who in mind and will were far removed from him and were worshiping not foreign gods, I will not say, but destructive demons and deaf, senseless statues. Therefore, above all, approach him who has called you. From him you will receive true knowledge both of the things seen by the eyes and of those removed from the perception of the eyes.

“But if, after you have been called, you refuse to approach or weave delays, you will be disinherited by God’s just judgment and rejected, because you yourself rejected him. In this manner the apostle Peter himself also spoke to a certain disciple:

[Note: [Col. 0479] This appears to have been taken from some apocryphal book.]

“‘But I believe that you have obeyed the call and that, obeying still more sincerely, you will take up the cross and follow God and the Lord who calls you, who invites you from death to life and from darkness to light. For ignorance of God is darkness and death of the soul; and to worship images is a madness exceeding every limit, leading to the destruction of nature.’”

To what, then, shall I compare such men? By what image shall I place their folly before your eyes? Nevertheless, I will offer you an example that was related to me by a man endowed with supreme wisdom.

He said that the worshipers of images were like a bird-catcher who, having caught a nightingale, a very small bird, and seized a sword in order to slaughter and eat it, heard the bird, having been granted articulate speech, say to the bird-catcher:

“Why, man, will any benefit from my death accrue to you? You will not be able to fill your stomach through me. But if you free me from my bonds, I will give you three precepts. If you obey them, you will enjoy great benefits throughout your life.”

Moved with wonder by its speech, the man promised that he would do so: if he heard anything new from it, he would immediately grant it freedom and let it go.

The nightingale then turned to the man and said:

“Never undertake something you cannot attain. Never regret a past matter. Never put faith in an incredible thing. Keep these three commands, and all will go splendidly for you.”

Admiring the intelligence and wisdom of these words, the man released it from its bonds into the air. The nightingale, wishing to test whether he had understood the force of the words he had heard and derived any benefit from them, flew through the air and said to him:

“Alas! How little judgment you possess, man! What a treasure you have lost today! For there is a pearl in my entrails larger than an ostrich egg.”

When he heard this, the man was distressed with grief and regretted that the nightingale had escaped from his hands. Trying to seize it again, he said:

“Come, please, into my house; and after you have been received by me splendidly and courteously, I will release you with honor.”

But the nightingale said to him:

“Now I know plainly that you are foolish and senseless. For although you received with willing mind and gladly heard what was said to you, you obtained no benefit from it. I warned you not to be troubled by regret for a past matter; and behold, you are distressed with grief because I escaped from your hands, being afflicted with regret over a past matter. I commanded you not to undertake what you could not attain, yet you try to seize me when you cannot catch up with my flight. In addition, I told you not to put faith in an incredible statement, yet you believed that there was in my entrails a pearl exceeding the size of my body; nor did you have enough prudence to understand that I do not even approach the size of an ostrich egg. How, then, could this little body contain so large a pearl?”

In this manner, then, those too who trust in images are engaged in the utmost folly. For they made them with their own hands and worship the work of their fingers, saying: “These are our craftsmen.” How, then, can they consider those whom they themselves made and fashioned to be their craftsmen? Moreover, although they guard them with great care so that they may not be stolen by thieves, they nevertheless call them the guardians of their salvation.

What folly is this—to fail to understand that those who cannot help or protect themselves cannot protect and save others? Besides, they squander their wealth while erecting statues and images for demons, and foolishly assert that these demons are givers of good things, claiming to receive from them things which they themselves have never possessed and never will possess.

For this reason it is written:

“Let those who make them and all who trust in them become like them” (Ps. CXIII).

They hired a goldsmith for a fee, who made an image with his hands, and they worshiped it with their bodies bent low. They lift it upon their shoulders and depart; but if they set it down anywhere, it remains there and cannot be moved. However loudly anyone may cry out to it, it will not hear, nor will it rescue him from calamities.

Therefore, let those who trust in carved images be put to shame, and those who say to cast images, “You are our gods.” For they sacrificed to demons and not to God, to gods whom they did not know—new and recently arrived ones whom their fathers did not worship. For the generation is perverse, and there is no longer faith in them (Deut. XXXII).

From this perverse and unbelieving generation the Lord calls you, using these words:

“Come out from their midst and separate yourselves, and do not touch what is unclean; rather, rescue yourself from this perverse generation” (Num. XVI). “Arise and walk, for you have no rest here” (Mic. II).

For the multitude of gods worshiped by you is a disorderly dominion, joined with discord, and of such a kind that it cannot in any way endure. But among us there are not many gods, nor many lords, but one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we for him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him (I Cor. VIII). He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation and of all the ages, because in him all things were created, both those in the heavens and those on earth, both visible and invisible, whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers (Col. I).

“All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made” (John I).

And there is one Holy Spirit, in whom are all things, who is Lord and gives life, who is God and bestows divinity: the good Spirit, the right Spirit, the Paraclete Spirit, the Spirit of adoption as sons.

Each of these is God when considered separately: as the Father is, so is the Son; as the Son is, so is the Holy Spirit. Yet there is one God in three persons, one nature, one kingdom, one power, one glory, one substance. This is divided with respect to the persons, but is one with respect to the Godhead.

For there is one Father, whose distinctive property is that he is not begotten. There is likewise one only-begotten Son, whose distinctive property is that he is begotten. Finally, there is one Holy Spirit, whose distinctive property is that he has proceeded.

Thus, contemplating from the light—that is, from the Father—light, namely the Son, in the light (Ps. XXXV), that is, in the Holy Spirit, we honor one divinity with praise and glory in three persons. He himself is the true and only God, who is recognized in the Trinity, because from him, through him, and in him are all things (Rom. XI).”

By his favor and grace, once he had learned more accurately about your condition, I too was sent to teach you the things I learned and preserved from the beginning of my youth until this gray hair.

Therefore, if you believe and are baptized, you will be saved; but if you do not believe, you will be condemned (Mark XVI). For the things you see today and in which you glory—that is, glory, pleasures, riches, and every deception of this life—will very shortly pass away and will drive you from here, even unwilling and resisting.

Your body will be enclosed in a very small tomb, left alone and deprived of every gathering of friends and relatives. The pleasures of the world will depart, while a great unpleasantness and foul corruption will be poured upon you from every side in place of the present beauty and fragrance. Your soul, however, delivered over to hell, will be cast into the lower regions of the earth until the final resurrection. At that time, after the soul has received its body again, it will be thrown from the presence of the Lord and handed over to Gehenna, whose flame is everlasting. These things, and things far more grievous than these, will happen to you if you persist in unbelief.

But if you obey with willing mind the one who invites you to salvation, and hasten to him with eager and joyful spirit, and are marked with his light (Ps. IV), and follow him in such a way that you do not look back at all, and, casting away and despising all other things, cling to him alone, hear what confidence and joy you will obtain from this:

“If you sit, you will be secure; if you sleep, you will rest pleasantly. You will not fear sudden terror or the attacks of wicked demons” (Prov. III), but you will walk confidently like a lion (Prov. XXVIII), and live with joy and everlasting exultation. For exultation, praise, and joy will seize you upon your head. Pain, sorrow, and groaning will flee.

“Then your light will break forth like the morning, and your health will quickly arise. Your justice will go before your face, and the glory of the Lord will gather you. Then you will call, and the Lord will hear; you will cry out, and he will say: Behold, I am here” (Isa. LVIII).

“For I am he who blots out your iniquities, and I will not remember them. But you remember, and let us be judged. Declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified” (Isa. XLIII).

“If your sins are like scarlet, they will be made white as snow. And if they are red like crimson, they will become like white wool. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken” (Isa. I).

## CAP. XI

Josaphat said to him:

“Your words are excellent and wondrous, and I have believed them and do believe them. I hate and detest every worship of idols from my heart. Even before you approached me, my mind was already, in a certain obscure and hesitant way, disposed against them. But now, after I have learned from you their vanity and the folly of those who worship them, I persecute them with perfect hatred and desire to submit myself to the true God, provided only that he does not utterly reject me, an unworthy man because of my iniquities, but, in accordance with his goodness, as you teach, forgives me everything and deigns to receive me as his servant.

“I am therefore ready to receive baptism and to observe everything you prescribe. But what must I do after baptism? Is it enough for salvation to believe and be baptized, or is it also necessary to add something else?”

Barlaam said to him:

“Hear what you must do after baptism: namely, abstain from every sin and every vicious inclination, and build the practice of virtues upon the foundation of orthodox faith. For faith without works is dead (James I), just as works are dead when separated from faith.

“The Apostle says (Gal. V): ‘Walk by the Spirit, and do not fulfill the desires of the flesh.’ The works of the flesh are manifest: adultery, fornication, uncleanness, wantonness, service of idols, sorcery, enmities, quarrels, rivalries, angers, disputes, dissensions, factions, envy, murders, greed, curses, love of pleasures, drunkenness, carousing, and things like these. I warn you of them, as I warned you before, because those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God.

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control, sanctification of soul and body, affliction and contrition of heart, almsgiving, forgetfulness of injuries, humanity, watchfulness, sincere repentance for all the preceding sins, tears of contrition, mourning both for one’s own sins and for the sins of others, and other things of the same kind. These, joined together like steps and a ladder, each supported by the others, raise the mind toward heaven.

“These, then, are the things which we are commanded to embrace after baptism, and from the other things which oppose them we must abstain.

“But if, after receiving knowledge of the truth, we again take up our former dead works and, like a dog, return to our own vomit (II Pet. II), what the Lord said will happen to us (Luke XI):

“‘When the unclean spirit has gone out from a man’—namely, through the grace of baptism—‘it passes through waterless places, seeking rest, and does not find it. And being greatly distressed that it has been without shelter and a dwelling for so long, it says: I will return to my house from which I came. And when it comes, it finds it swept with brooms and adorned, but empty and vacant, since it has not received the cultivation and operation of grace, nor filled itself with the riches of virtues. Then it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and entering, they dwell there. And the last state of that man becomes worse than the first.’

“Baptism, indeed, buries the contracts of all former sins in water and completely erases and obliterates them. Thereafter it is for us a most firm wall and tower, and a powerful weapon with which to engage the enemy in battle. Yet it does not remove freedom of choice, nor does it forgive the sins contracted after baptism, nor does it contain a second immersion in the pool. For we confess one baptism. Therefore, with the greatest diligence we must take care not to fall into new defilements, but to embrace the commandments of the Lord.

“For when he had said to the apostles: ‘Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,’ he did not stop there, but added: ‘Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you’ (Mark XVI).

“He commanded us to be poor in spirit (Matt. V), for he declares such people blessed and worthy of the heavenly kingdom. Then he commands us to mourn in the present age, so that in the future we may receive consolation. Next, he commands us to be meek and to hunger and thirst for righteousness. Then we must be merciful and generous, inclined to compassion; pure in heart, abstaining from every defilement of flesh and spirit; and peaceable both toward others and within our own souls—subjecting what is worse to what is better and restraining the internal and perpetual war by right judgment.

“Finally, we must endure every persecution, affliction, and reproach inflicted upon us for the sake of righteousness and for his name, so that we may attain everlasting joy in that glorious distribution of rewards.

“Moreover, while he was still living in the world, he exhorted his own in this manner: ‘Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in the heavens’ (Matt. V).

“For the law of Moses, given anciently to the Israelites, said: ‘You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness.’ But Christ says: ‘Everyone who is angry with his brother without cause will be liable to judgment. Whoever says, “Fool,” will be liable to the fire of Gehenna.’

“And again: ‘If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother. And whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart’—calling the uncleanness of the soul and the consent of lust adultery.

“Furthermore, although the law prohibits perjury, Christ entirely forbids swearing and permits nothing other than ‘Yes, yes; No, no.’ ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth’ there; here, however: ‘Whoever strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also. And to anyone who wishes to contend with you in judgment and take your tunic, give him your cloak also. And whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two. Give to him who asks you. And do not turn away from him who wishes to borrow from you.’

“You have heard that it was said: ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you: ‘Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust’ (Luke VI).

“Do not judge, so that you may not be judged. Forgive, and you will be forgiven. Do not lay up treasures for yourselves on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and thieves break in and steal. But lay up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart is also.

“Do not be anxious about your soul—what you shall eat—or about your body—what you shall wear. For your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things. Therefore, he who gave soul and body will certainly also give food and clothing: he who feeds the birds of heaven and adorns the lilies of the field with such beauty. But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. Do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself” (Matt. VI).

“Whatever you wish men to do to you, do the same to them” (Luke XVIII). “Enter through the narrow gate, for the gate is wide and the way spacious that leads to destruction, and there are many who enter through it. For the gate is narrow and the way constricted that leads to life, and there are few who find it” (Matt. VII; Luke XIII).

“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. VII). “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me. And whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me. And whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Matt. X).

Behold, the Savior commanded all these things, and things like them, to the apostles, so that they might teach those endowed with faith. We must observe all these things if we truly desire to attain perfection and receive crowns of righteousness untouched by corruption, which the Lord, the just judge, will bestow on that day upon all who have loved his coming (II Tim. IV).

Josaphat said to him:

“Since such perfect teaching demands a most pure life, tell me, please: if I should happen to stray from one or two commandments, will I therefore have missed the whole aim, and will all my hope prove vain?”

Barlaam replied:

“You must not think so. For God the Word, who assumed humanity for the sake of our salvation, fully aware of the great weakness and misery of our nature, did not permit us to suffer from an incurable disease in this respect either. Rather, like a most wise physician, he mixed the medicine of repentance into our slippery will, which is eager to sin, proclaiming repentance for the forgiveness of sins.

“After we have received recognition of the truth, and have been sanctified through water and the Spirit and cleansed without effort from every sin and impurity, if we should happen to fall into some sins, there is no longer another regeneration through baptism (Hebr. VI), which is obtained through the water of the pool by the Spirit and perfectly restores us—for this benefit is granted only once. But through harsh repentance, burning tears, labors, and sweat, because of the tender mercies of our God, we obtain cleansing and forgiveness of sins.

“Indeed, through the Lord’s grace the fountain of tears is called baptism, although it otherwise requires labor and time. It has rescued many from many sins, because there is no sin that can overcome God’s goodness, provided that we first come to our senses and wash away the stains of our offenses with tears, lest death overtake us and cast us from here polluted by the stains of our crimes. For in hell there is neither repentance nor confession (Ps. VI).

“As long as we enjoy the use of life, provided that the foundation of orthodox faith remains firm, even if some beam or upright support has been shaken—whatever has been corrupted by sins—it is possible to repair and renew it through the help of repentance. For the multitude of God’s compassions cannot be counted, nor can the greatness of his mercy be measured (Ps. CXLIV). Sins, on the other hand, whatever they may be, are subject to measure and number. Thus, since they fall within measure and number, they cannot overcome the boundless mercy of God and his countless compassions.

“Accordingly, we are not commanded to despair because of the multitude of our sins, but to recognize God’s goodness and condemn our sins, whose forgiveness has been offered because of the kindness of Christ, who poured out his blood for our offenses.

“From many passages of Scripture we learn the power of repentance, but especially from the actions and parables of our Lord Jesus Christ. ‘From that time,’ he says, ‘Jesus began to teach and to say: Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near’ (Matt. III).

“He also introduces, in a parable (Luke XV), a certain son who, after receiving his father’s wealth, departed into a distant region and squandered it in every kind of luxury and excess. Later, when that region was suffering from famine, he departed and attached himself to one of the citizens of that region. The man sent him into his field to feed pigs—that is, the most harsh and detestable sin.

“When he had suffered many calamities and had fallen into such misery that he was not even permitted to fill his stomach with the pods of the pigs, at last, recognizing such grievous disgrace and mourning his life, he said:

“‘How many hired servants in my father’s house abound in bread, while I perish here from hunger! I will arise and go to my father and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants.’

“And he arose and went to his father. But while he was still far away, his father saw him, was moved with compassion, ran and fell upon his neck, kissed him, restored him to his former place of honor, and, rejoicing greatly at his recovery, celebrated a magnificent feast, slaughtering the fattened calf.

“Behold, he recalled this parable for us concerning those who recoil from sins and hasten to repentance.

“Again he introduces a good shepherd (Luke XV) who, having one hundred sheep and losing one, left the ninety-nine and went to search for the one that had strayed until he found it. He then carried it upon his shoulders and reunited it with those that had not strayed. For this reason he also invited his friends and neighbors to a feast to celebrate its recovery.

“‘Thus,’ says the Savior, ‘there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance.’”

Moreover, Peter, the chief of the disciples—that rock of faith—was, during the very time of the saving Passion, by a certain deliberate purpose temporarily abandoned by God, namely so that he might understand clearly the worthlessness and misery of human weakness. He fell into such sin that he denied the Lord (Luke XXII).

But afterward, he says, immediately remembering the Lord’s words, he went outside and wept bitterly; through those burning tears he repaired the damage he had suffered and turned the victory to the other side. For although he was experienced in warfare, even though he fell, he was not broken in spirit and did not abandon hope of his salvation. Rather, recovering himself, he poured out the most bitter tears from his oppressed breast; and as soon as the enemy saw them, as though his eyes had been scorched by the heat of a most violent flame, he drew back and fled far away, howling horribly.

He, on the other hand, again held the place of primacy. Just as he had been appointed teacher of the whole world, so he also became an example of repentance. After the resurrection, when Christ had said to him for the third time, “Peter, do you love me?” he corrected the threefold denial by answering: “Yes, Lord, you know that I love you.”

From all these examples, and from countless others—indeed, more than can be numbered—we understand the power of tears and repentance. Let care be taken that repentance be made in a manner consistent with reason: arising from an affection that execrates the sin, pursues it with hatred, condemns it, and sheds tears, as the prophet David says:

“I have labored in my groaning; every night I will wash my bed; I will water my couch with my tears” (Ps. VI).

Then the cleansing of sins will come through Christ’s blood, in the greatness of his mercy and the multitude of his compassions. For these are his own words:

“If your sins are like scarlet, they will be made white as snow; but if they are like crimson, they will become like white wool.”

It is therefore worthwhile, after we have received knowledge of the truth, attained regeneration and adoption as children, and received the divine mysteries, to take every care and apply every diligence lest we fall. For it is not fitting that an athlete should fall, since many, once they had fallen, were quite unable to raise themselves up. Indeed, some, after opening the doors to vicious passions and becoming fastened to them by the closest bonds, could no longer turn themselves toward repentance. Others were seized by death before they had wiped away through repentance [Col. 0487B] the stains of vice they had contracted, and were condemned. Therefore it is dangerous to slip into any vice whatsoever. But if it should happen that we fall, we must immediately strive to spring back and once again stand ready to undertake the glorious contest. And whenever it happens that we fall, each time we must immediately, right up to the final day of life, take care to rise again and stand prepared. “Turn to me, and I will turn to you,” says the Lord (Zech. I).

## CHAPTER XII

At this Josaphat said: “How, then, can a person preserve himself pure from every stain of sin after baptism? For although, as you yourself say, repentance is open to sinners, it nevertheless requires labor and exertion, weeping and mourning; and these things seem to me to be of such a kind that many cannot easily attain them. Therefore I would rather find a way [Col. 0487C] by which I might sincerely and exactly observe God’s commandments, neither depart from them nor, after obtaining forgiveness for my former sins, provoke that most gracious Lord and God to anger.”

Barlaam replied: “You have spoken rightly, my lord and king, and this is very pleasing to me. Yet it is difficult, not to say impossible, for someone to be in fire and nevertheless not be enveloped in smoke. In the same way, it is difficult and exceedingly hard for one who is held fast by the affairs of this life as by certain bonds, distracted by its cares and commotions, and living amid riches and pleasures, to travel the way of God’s commandments without swerving and to preserve himself pure and unharmed from them. For the Lord says [Col. 0487D] (Matt. VI): ‘No one can serve two masters. For either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will adhere to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and mammon.’

“Moreover, his beloved disciple, John the Evangelist and Theologian, says in his epistle: ‘Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. For everything that is in the world is either the desire of the flesh, or the desire of the eyes, or the pride of life, which is not from the Father but is from the world. And the world is passing away, and its desire. But whoever does the will of God remains forever’ (1 John II).

“When our divine and divinely inspired fathers observed these things and heard the apostle’s statement [Col. 0488A] that ‘through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of heaven’ (Acts XIV), they devoted all the strength of their souls to preserving after baptism the spotless garment of incorruption, free from every stain. Accordingly, some of them undertook yet another baptism in addition—the baptism consisting in the outpouring [269] of blood and martyrdom. This too was called baptism, and indeed the most excellent and most worthy of supreme veneration; for it is not defiled by later stains of sin. My Lord also received this baptism and rightly called it so.

“Then, becoming his imitators—first his beholders, disciples, and apostles, and afterward the entire chorus of the holy martyrs—they offered themselves for Christ’s name to worshipers of idols [Col. 0488B], kings, and tyrants, and endured every kind of punishment: they were thrown to wild beasts, burned in fire, and slaughtered by swords. After making their noble confession, completing their course, and keeping the faith, they obtained the palm of righteousness, became companions of the angels and coheirs of Christ. Their virtue shone forth so greatly that their sound went out into all the earth, and their radiance to the ends of the world (Ps. XVIII); the things they rightly accomplished in virtue gleamed forth. Not only their words and deeds, but their very blood and bones, are filled with all holiness. For they put demons to flight by force and drive away incurable diseases from those who approach them in faith. Even their garments, and anything else [Col. 0488C] that has come near their precious bodies, are objects of universal veneration.

“I would need a long discourse about them if I wished to set out their glorious deeds one by one. But after those cruel and beastlike tyrants had perished miserably, as their wickedness deserved, and persecution had come to an end, and pious emperors had gained rule over the whole world, others succeeded them, setting before themselves that zeal and divine longing as something to imitate, and bearing in their souls the wound of the same fear. They carefully considered and contemplated how they might present soul and body pure of every defilement to God. They prepared themselves in such a way as to cut off every activity of vicious passions and cleanse themselves from every pollution of flesh and spirit [Col. 0488D].

“Since they understood that this could be accomplished by them in no other way than through observance of Christ’s commandments, and since they perceived that amid the tumult of the world they could scarcely attain observance of the commandments and cultivation of the virtues, they established for themselves a new and different manner of life. In accordance with the divine word, they abandoned everything—that is, parents, children, friends, relatives, riches, pleasures, and every convenience of the world—and withdrew into solitudes like exiles, needy, distressed, and afflicted, ‘of whom the world was not worthy’ (Heb. XI). They wandered in deserts, mountains, caves, and caverns of the earth, removing themselves far from all earthly delights [Col. 0489A] and pleasures, and suffering such severe poverty of even bread and clothing that they were greatly afflicted.

“Two motives impelled them to do this. The first was that, by no longer seeing the sources of vicious passions, they might tear their desires up by the roots from their souls, erase their memory, and implant within themselves love and longing for divine and heavenly things. The second was that, by afflicting the body, they might wear it down and, having become martyrs in mind and will, not be deprived of the glory obtained by those who had undergone martyrdom; rather, since they too had imitated Christ’s passion as far as they were able, they might also share in his kingdom. In this way, after applying the most careful reflection, they pursued the monastic and solitary life.

“Some of them lived in the open air [Col. 0489B], afflicted by the heat of the sun, the harshest cold and rains, and violent storms. Others lived in huts they had built, or concealed themselves in caves and caverns. Thus, cultivating virtue, they rejected every carnal consolation and comfort to the very end, sustaining life on uncooked vegetables and herbs, fruits, or even dry and exceedingly hard bread. They did not merely bid farewell to the quality of pleasant foods; through an extraordinary degree of self-control they extended the greatness of their spirit even to the quantity of food. From the foods that were especially cheap and necessary, they took only so much [Col. 0489C] as was sufficient to endure hunger.

“Some of them spent an entire week in fasting and admitted food only on the Lord’s Day. Some remembered food only twice each week; others ate on alternate days toward evening, and then only tasted their food. By contending almost even with the angels through prayers and vigils, and by entirely dismissing the possession of gold and silver, as well as buying and selling, they forgot altogether that they were among human beings.

“Among them there was no place for envy or arrogance of spirit, which are usually the chief companions of good works. The one who held a lower place in the exercises of monastic life did not admit into his mind a thought of jealousy [Col. 0489D] against one whose virtue was more illustrious. Nor did the one who excelled in virtues allow arrogance [270] and conceit to raise him up against the weaker and drive him into the snare of despising his neighbor or boasting about his religious discipline, or to think highly and arrogantly of himself because of the things he had accomplished with praise.

“For the one who surpassed another in virtue, attributing the whole matter not to his own labors but to God’s power, humbly persuaded himself that he had accomplished absolutely nothing and that much more remained for him to do, in accordance with what the Lord says: ‘When you have done everything that was commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were bound to do’ (Luke XVII). Some even persuaded themselves that they had not [Col. 0490A] in any way done the things God had commanded them, but that there were far more things lacking in them than those they had already accomplished.

“Again, the one who was inferior in religious discipline, perhaps because of bodily weakness, thought nothing of himself and called himself miserable, attributing his deficiency to the cowardice of his spirit rather than to weakness of nature. Thus each showed himself more modest than the others, and all more modest than everyone else.

“How could the desire for empty glory, or the ambition to please human beings, have existed among them? For they had abandoned the world and lived in deserts for precisely this reason: that they might display their virtues not to human beings but to God, from whom they also hoped to receive the rewards of virtue. They knew very well that religious exercises undertaken for the sake of empty glory remain without reward, since they are performed for the sake not of God’s praise but of human praise. Such people therefore suffer a double loss: they wear out the body and yet receive no reward [Col. 0490B]. But those who burn with desire for heavenly glory and hasten toward it with all speed despise everything earthly and human.

“Among such people, some live in retreat and solitude, carrying on the contest of piety and withdrawing from human society for the whole of life, drawing near to God. Others, living far apart from one another in buildings they have constructed, go on the Lord’s Days to one and the same church and receive the divine mysteries—that is, the unbloody sacrifice of Christ’s pure body and precious blood—which [Col. 0490C] the Lord has given to the devout for the remission of sins and for the illumination and sanctification of both soul and body.

“Feeding one another through the practice of the divine oracles and through wonderful counsels and exhortations, and revealing the secret battles of the enemies—so that no one still ignorant of the struggle might be overcome by them—they return home individually, carefully storing the honey of virtue in the combs of their breasts and cultivating a most delightful fruit worthy of the heavenly table. Others, however, pursue the coenobitic life.

“These, gathered together in very large numbers, submit themselves to the authority of one superior and leader, who surpasses all in virtue. Cutting off their own will completely with the sword of obedience, and willingly regarding themselves [Col. 0490D] as purchased slaves, they no longer live for themselves but for him to whom they have submitted themselves for the love of Christ—or, to speak more aptly, they no longer live for themselves, but Christ lives in them (Gal. II), the Christ whom they followed after renouncing everything.

“For this, finally, is what withdrawal from the world consists in: that, because of desire for things naturally higher, a person conceives a voluntary hatred of himself and renounces his nature. These men therefore live like angels, singing psalms and hymns to the Lord with harmonious minds and earning the name of confessors through their contests of obedience. In them that saying of the Lord is also fulfilled: ‘Wherever two or three have been gathered in my name, I am there in their midst [Col. 0491A]’ (Matt. XVIII). By these words he did not restrict those gathered in his name to that particular number, but signified an indefinite number by ‘two or three.’ For whether few or many come together because of his holy name and worship him with ardent love, we have no doubt that he is there in the midst of his servants.

“Through these examples, and through such gatherings and practices, earthly people have imitated the life of the heavenly: they have completed the course of the present life in fasting, prayers, and vigils; in burning tears and mourning free from every distraction of mind; in pilgrimage and remembrance of death; in gentleness and a disposition of spirit removed from anger; in silence of the lips; in poverty and want; in chastity and modesty [Col. 0491B]; in humility and quiet; and finally in perfect love toward God and neighbor. In character they have reproduced the angels.

“For this reason God adorned them with miracles, signs, and various powers, and caused even the ends of the earth to resound with the report of their admirable way of life. If I were to set before you in detail the life of one of them—namely, Antony, who is said to have been the guide and founder of the monastic life—you would surely understand from one tree the sweetness of fruits of the same kind and species; you would learn what foundation of religious discipline he laid, what summit he built, and how many thanks he received from the Savior. Many others also, after him, having completed the same contest [Col. 0491C], reached the same crowns and the same rewards.”

Blessed, truly blessed three times over, were those who burned with love for God and considered everything worthless for his sake. They poured out tears and remained in mourning day and night so that they might obtain everlasting consolation. They voluntarily humbled themselves so that there they might be raised on high. They exhausted their flesh with hunger, thirst, and vigils so that there the delights and exultation of paradise might receive them. Through purity of heart they became a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, as it is written: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (2 Cor. VI). They crucified themselves to the world (Eph. VI), so that they might stand at Christ’s right hand. They girded their loins with truth and always kept their lamps [Col. 0491D] ready, awaiting the coming of the immortal bridegroom (Matt. XXV).

For, possessing the eyes of the mind, they always looked toward that dreadful day. They carried contemplation both of future blessings and of future punishment so fixed within their bodies that they were never torn away from it. They strove to labor here so that they might share in eternal glory. Free from disturbances, like the angels, they lived; and now they dance with those whose life they imitated.

Blessed, truly blessed three times over, were those who saw with firm eyes of the mind the vanity of present things and the uncertainty and instability of human prosperity. Rejecting these, they built up eternal goods for themselves and seized the life [Col. 0492A] that never perishes and is not interrupted by death.

We too, unworthy and contemptible as we are, strive to imitate these admirable and holy men. Yet we do not attain the summit of their heavenly life; rather, according to the measure of our weakness and miserable capacity, we reproduce their life. We wear their habit, even if we do not equal their deeds. For we have recognized that this divine profession repels sin and is the companion and helper of the incorruption granted to us through divine baptism.

Moved by the words of those blessed men, we strongly condemn the transient things of this life, subject to decay—things in which nothing firm or even, nothing that always preserves the same condition, can be found [Col. 0492B]. Everything is vanity and affliction of spirit (Eccl. II), undergoing many changes in a moment of time. Indeed, they are weaker than dreams, shadows, and winds passing through the air.

Their pleasure is small and brief—or rather, it is not pleasure but a kind of deception and imposture belonging to the perversity of the world, which we are taught not to love in any way, but rather to hate and pursue with all our heart (1 John II). And truly it is worthy of hatred and detestation. For whatever it gives its friends as a gift, it later snatches away again in anger; after stripping them of every good and clothing them in disgrace and burdening them with heavy loads, it sends them to everlasting calamity. Those whom it raises to a lofty position it quickly renders subject to extreme humiliation and affliction, exposing them to the mockery of their enemies. Such are its benefits [Col. 0492C]; such are its gifts.

It is the enemy of its friends and lays ambushes for all who obey its wishes. In a dreadful manner it agitates those who lean upon it and destroys every strength of those who place their confidence in it. It makes a covenant with fools and enters into false promises, with the sole intention of drawing them to itself. But to those who sincerely join themselves to it, it proves to be wicked and deceitful, fulfilling none of the agreements it had made.

For today, when it has soothed their throats with pleasant foods, tomorrow it casts them before their enemies to be devoured. Today it makes someone a king, and tomorrow subjects that same person to wretched slavery. Today it makes him flourish with innumerable goods, and tomorrow makes him a beggar and the slave of slaves. Today [Col. 0492D] it places a distinguished crown upon his head, and tomorrow dashes his face against the earth. Today it adorns his neck with the splendid honors of dignities, and tomorrow throws him down bound in iron chains.

For a short time it wins him the love and goodwill of everyone; shortly afterward it brings upon him everyone’s hatred and cursing. Today it gives him pleasure, and tomorrow exhausts him with griefs and lamentations. But hear what end it also brings upon them: it makes those by whom it was loved into pitiable inhabitants of gehenna. This is always its mind and intention; this is its design. It neither mourns those who have passed away nor feels pity for those who remain. After punishing the former with severe loss and enclosing them in its nets [Col. 0493A], it tries once again to apply its craft to the latter, desiring that no one escape its dangerous snares.

Therefore I consider those who serve so pestilent and cruel a master, who, removing themselves from the good and kindly one through utter madness, gape after and waste away over present things without considering the future in any way, and who continually devote themselves to bodily pleasures while allowing their souls to perish from hunger and suffer countless evils, to resemble a man fleeing from the face of a raging unicorn. Unable to endure the sound of its shouting and dreadful bellowing, he flees with great force lest he become its prey.

As he runs swiftly, he falls into a vast pit [Col. 0493B]. In falling, he stretches out his hands, seizes a tree, and clings to it as tightly as possible. Fixing his feet upon a kind of foothold, he then supposes that everything is calm and free from danger. But when he looks down, he sees two mice—one white, the other black—continually gnawing at the root of the tree he has seized and already almost cutting it through.

Moreover, when he casts his eyes into the bottom of the pit, he sees a dreadful dragon, breathing fire by its very appearance, staring at him with fierce eyes and eagerly awaiting his devouring. Again, fixing his eyes upon the foothold on which his feet rest, he sees the heads of four asps projecting from the wall upon which he is standing. But when he turns his eyes upward, he perceives a little honey dripping from the branches [Col. 0493C] of that tree.

Accordingly, setting aside consideration of the calamities that surrounded and pressed upon him from every side—how, outside, the unicorn, driven by violent fury, sought to devour him; how, below, the savage dragon ardently desired to swallow him; how the tree he had seized was already on the point of being cut through; and how his feet rested upon a slippery and treacherous foothold—forgetting, I say, all these immense dangers, he occupied himself with tasting the sweetness of that little drop of honey.

This is the figure of those who waste away amid the deceptions of the present life. I shall immediately explain it to you. The unicorn represents death, which continually pursues the human race and strives [Col. 0493D] to seize it. The pit is the world, teeming with evils of every kind and deadly snares. The tree that we hold with clasped hands, which the two mice ceaselessly gnaw, is the course of every human life. It is consumed and worn away through the hours of day and night and gradually approaches its cutting down.

The four asps signify the constitution of the human body upon four slippery and unstable elements. When these are disordered and behave immoderately, the structure of the body is dissolved. Furthermore, that fiery and savage dragon represents the dreadful maw of hell, which longs to receive those who prefer present pleasures to future goods. The drop of honey that drips [Col. 0494A] signifies the world’s pleasure and sweetness, by which it deceives its friends and prevents them from looking after their salvation.

## CHAPTER XIII

Josaphat, expressing his complete approval of this parable, said: “How true this discourse is, and how full of every kind of elegance! Therefore, I beg you, do not tire of continually showing me figures of this kind, so that I may clearly understand what our life is like and what sort of things the world procures for its friends.”

The old man said: “Those who are captivated by love of the pleasures of this life and lulled by their sweetness, and who have preferred fleeting and feeble things to those that are future and free from instability, are likewise like a man who had three friends. He cherished and loved two of them with immense affection, so much so [Col. 0494B] that he never refused to fight for them to the death or face any danger on their behalf. But he greatly despised the third, never granting him honor or the goodwill that was his due, but showing him only a little friendship—and that friendship false and feigned.

“Then one day savage and dreadful soldiers came and dragged him in great haste before the king, so that he might render an account of the ten thousand talents he owed. Reduced to the greatest distress, he sought someone who might help him in that fearful rendering of accounts before the king.

“Running, therefore, to his first and dearest of all his other friends, he said to him: ‘You are not unaware, my friend, how I have always placed my life in danger [Col. 0494C] for your sake. But today, with necessity pressing upon me, I need your aid and assistance. Can you perhaps promise me some help? What hope, dearest man, may I place in you?’

“The man replied: ‘I am not your friend, my fellow, nor do I know who you are. I have other friends with whom I must enjoy myself today and whom I shall regard as friends in the future. Therefore I offer you only two hair shirts, so that you may have them on the road you are traveling; even these will bring you no benefit. You should expect nothing from me.’

“On hearing this, and abandoning all hope of the assistance he had expected from him, he went to his second friend and said: ‘Remember, my friend, how much honor and how many benefits you have received from me. Today [Col. 0494D], having fallen into the greatest calamity and affliction, I need someone to help me. Tell me, then, what assistance you can now bring me.’

“But the man said: ‘Today I cannot undertake this struggle with you, because of my affairs. I am pressed on every side by cares and anxieties and am in distress. Nevertheless, I shall go a little way with you, although no advantage will return to you from this; afterward I shall immediately return home and attend to my own business.’

“Thus the man returned empty-handed and deprived of help in every respect. He lamented himself over the vain hope he had placed in his faithless and ungrateful friends, and over the useless labors he had undertaken out of his love for them.

“Then he went [Col. 0495A] also to the third friend, whom he had never valued in any way or invited to share his joy. With shame and his face cast down toward the earth, he addressed him in these words: ‘My mouth scarcely permits me to speak to you. For I am fully aware that I have never treated you kindly or been a friend to you. But since I have been overwhelmed by the gravest calamity and have found no hope of safety in my other friends, I come to you and beg and beseech you: if you can bring me even a little assistance, do not refuse to do so out of remembrance of my ingratitude.’

“The man, however, said with a cheerful and pleasant face: ‘I openly acknowledge that you are my most sincere friend, and, remembering your slight kindness toward me, I shall repay it to you today with interest. Therefore do not fear or be terrified. For I shall go before you and plead with the king on your behalf [Col. 0495B], so that he may not hand you over to the power of your enemies. So take heart, dearest friend, and do not torment yourself with sorrow.’

“Then, moved by remorse and covered with tears, the man said: ‘Alas, miserable me! What shall I lament and mourn first? Shall I condemn my vain goodwill toward those false friends, forgetful and ungrateful as they were? Or shall I rather attack that mad ingratitude with which I treated this true and sincere friend?’”

Josaphat received this discourse with no little wonder and asked for its explanation. Barlaam therefore said:

“The first friend is the abundance of possessions and love of riches, on account of which a person falls into six hundred dangers and endures many hardships. But when the final [Col. 0495C] day of life has closed, he takes nothing at all away with him from all those riches except certain useless rags, which are used for his funeral.

“The second friend is wife and children, and the other relatives and members of one’s household. We are bound to them by affection and goodwill, so that we can scarcely be separated from them and, out of love for them, even neglect our body and soul. Yet none of them provides any benefit at the hour of death, except that they accompany the corpse only as far as the grave; then they immediately return home and attend to their own cares and affairs, abandoning the memory of the one who was once dear to them to forgetfulness no less than they leave his body to the tomb.

“But the third friend, who was despised and distasteful, whose approach we dread and shun, is the chorus of excellent [Col. 0495D] works: faith, hope, love, mercy, kindness, and the remaining company of virtues. These can go before us when we depart from the body, bend God through prayers on our behalf, and deliver us from our enemies and dreadful exactors, who wage a bitter lawsuit against us over the accounts that must be rendered and strive cruelly to seize us. This is that bright, upright, and pleasing friend who remembers even our smallest good work and repays it to us with interest.”

## CHAPTER XIV

Josaphat said again: “May everything fortunate and joyful be yours from the Lord your God, wisest of men. For you have gladdened my soul with your excellent [Col. 0496A] and appropriate words. Therefore portray for me again an image of the vanity of this world, and tell me how I may pass through this life in peace and security.”

He then continued his discourse, saying: “Hear also the likeness relating to this question. I have learned that there once existed a great city in which the citizens had established the following custom and practice: they would take some foreign and unknown man, completely inexperienced and ignorant of the city’s laws and customs, and make him their king. He would possess power over everything for the course of one year and could freely and without hindrance do whatever he wished.

“Afterward, while he lived wholly free from care, dwelling in luxury and pleasures [Col. 0496B] without any fear, and supposing that his kingdom would last forever, they would suddenly rise up against him, strip him of his royal garment, and lead him naked through the entire city as though in a triumph. Then they would banish him to a certain very large and distant island, where, with neither food nor clothing available, he was miserably oppressed by hunger and nakedness. The pleasure and cheerfulness that had been granted to him beyond all hope were thus changed, again beyond all hope and expectation, into sorrow.

“Now it happened that, according to the ancient custom and practice of those citizens, a man endowed with great intelligence was chosen for the kingship. Immediately, however, he was not carried away headlong [Col. 0496C] by the sudden prosperity that had befallen him. Nor did he imitate the carelessness of those who had possessed royal dignity before him and had been miserably expelled. Instead, with an anxious and concerned mind, he considered how he might best provide for his affairs.

“While he turned these matters over within himself through frequent reflection, he was informed by a certain very wise counselor about the citizens’ custom and the place of perpetual exile. He understood how he ought to guard himself without any error. Once he had learned this, and since the day when he would be sent to that island was approaching, and he would leave his temporary and foreign kingdom to others, he opened his treasures, which at that time he could use freely and readily. He entrusted a great mass of gold and silver and precious stones to certain servants whom he considered utterly faithful and sent them in advance to the island [Col. 0496D] to which he was to be taken.

“When the year had passed, the citizens raised a rebellion and sent him naked into exile, just as they had sent the earlier kings. The others, foolish and kings for a brief time, suffered the severest hunger. But he who had sent his wealth in advance, living amid perpetual abundance and enjoying infinite pleasure, having entirely cast off fear of the treacherous and criminal citizens, proclaimed himself blessed on account of his most wise counsel.”

Understand by this city, then, this vain and deceitful world. By the citizens, understand the demonic principalities and powers, the rulers of the darkness of this age, who entice us through the softness of pleasure [Col. 0497A] and induce us to think about perishable and transitory things as though they were immortal, as if their enjoyment were going to be perpetual and everlasting for us.

When, therefore, we have been deceived and led astray in this manner, and have never formed any plan concerning those certain and everlasting things, nor stored anything up for ourselves for the age to come, sudden death overtakes us (Prov. I). Then at last those wicked and savage citizens of darkness receive us naked and stripped of all the things of this life—us who have spent all our time for them—and lead us away into a dark and gloomy land, into a land of everlasting shadow, where there is no light and where it is not permitted to behold the life of mortals (Job X).

By the upright counsellor, however, who truly disclosed everything to that prudent and exceedingly wise king and presented him with the advice he needed, understand me, a vile and humble little man, who have come here for this reason: to show you a good path, free from every error, and to lead you toward everlasting and never-ending gifts; to advise you to store all your possessions there, and to lead you away from this deceitful world.

I myself once loved that world miserably and embraced its pleasures and delights. But when I had observed with the sound eyes of my mind how the whole of human life is consumed in these things—some continually arriving, others departing, and nothing at all established in a firm and stable place; neither the rich and prosperous in their wealth, nor the powerful in their power, nor the wise in their wisdom, nor those whose affairs prosper in their prosperity, nor those devoted to luxury in their luxury and delicacies, nor those who seem to live securely in their weak and fragile security, nor anyone in any other of the things that are praised to the skies [Col. 0497C]—I understood that all these things are like the passage of torrents of water rushing into the depths of the sea. For everything present is equally fleeting and fragile.

Thus I understood that all these things are vain and possess no usefulness. Indeed, just as all former things have been buried in oblivion—whether you call them glory, kingship, the splendor of rank, the greatness of power, the boldness of tyrants, or anything else of the same kind—so old age will eventually obscure the things of the present as well. Since I too belong among these things, I am wholly subject to their customary transformation. For just as those who existed before me were not permitted to enjoy the pleasures of present things forever, neither shall I be permitted to do so.

I observed how this tyrannical and turbulent world treats human beings: turning some this way and others that, leading some from wealth to poverty and others again from the deepest poverty to glory; taking some from life and bringing others into life in their place; rejecting and casting aside certain wise and ingenious men, and making those who were in honor and splendor despised and contemptible; while, on the contrary, placing other foolish and senseless people upon the throne of glory, and elevating those who were rejected and obscure [Col. 0498A] so that all honor is paid to them.

It can be seen that the human race is so constituted that, before this cruel tyranny of the world, it possesses nothing whatever that is firm or stable. For just as a dove fleeing an eagle or hawk repeatedly changes its place—now in this tree, now in that shrub, then in the caves of the rocks, fastening its feet among various thorns, and never finding a secure refuge—so that it remains in perpetual agitation and distress, so it is with those who admire present things to the point of stupefaction. They are miserably tormented by a certain heedless impulse; they possess nothing whatever that is firm or stable; they do not understand to what end they are going to arrive, nor where the vain life to which they have subjected themselves will lead them—a life in which, with great misery and misfortune, they prefer evil to good and pursue vice instead of virtue [Col. 0498B]. Nor do they know who will inherit the cold fruits of their many and wretched labors: a relative or a stranger, perhaps not even a friend or acquaintance, but rather an enemy and adversary.

When, I say, I had debated all these things and others agreeing with them in the marketplace of my soul, I was seized by hatred for my entire life, which I had spent consuming myself in vain things and devoting myself to earthly labors. When I had shaken their love from my soul and cast it out, those things that are truly good presented themselves to my eyes: namely, to be endowed with fear of God and to obey his will. For I discovered that this is the head and beginning of all good things. It is called the beginning of wisdom—and indeed, perfect wisdom.

For those who embrace it and rely upon it as upon a lord have a life free from sorrow and protected from every offense, secure and immune from every danger. When, therefore, I had directed my mind toward the path of the Lord’s commandments, free from every error, and had clearly discovered that there was nothing crooked or winding in them, nothing filled with chasms, rocks, thorns, and briars, but that the path was altogether level and even—delighting the eyes of those who enter it through the most brilliant contemplations, conferring beauty upon their feet, and equipping them with the preparation of the gospel of peace—I judged myself wretched because of my former deceit and foolish delusion [Col. 0498D], and began to walk along that straight path. I rightly preferred it to all things and began to restore the fallen and ruined house of my soul.

As I was thus caring for my affairs and striving to correct the slipperiness of my mind, I heard the voice of a certain wise teacher, who cried out to me:

“Come out,” he said, “all you who desire salvation, and withdraw yourselves from the vanity of the world, for its outward form is passing away (I Cor. VII). Soon—indeed, very soon—it will no longer exist. Depart with unflinching eyes; yet do not depart empty and destitute, but carrying provisions for everlasting life. For you must undertake a long journey, one requiring a great supply of provisions for this present life; and you will arrive at an everlasting place containing two regions in which there are many dwellings (I Cor. II).

“God has prepared one of these for those who burn with love for him and obey his commandments. It flourishes and overflows with every good thing. Those who, by divine favor, are admitted there (Isa. XXXV) dwell in everlasting incorruption, enjoying immortality untouched by any destruction; from there pain, sadness, and groaning have fled.

“The other region, filled with darkness, calamity, and sorrow, has been prepared for the devil and his angels. Those who have earned it for themselves through disgraceful actions will also be cast into it. They have exchanged the everlasting goods that are free from destruction for present things and have made themselves wholly fuel for the eternal fire.”

When I had heard this voice and understood its truth, I devoted myself to this one task: to reach that dwelling which is free from every pain and sorrow and abounds in such security and such great blessings. At present, however, my knowledge of these things is only partial, since in spiritual age I am still a child, and I perceive the realities of the future life only as through mirrors and riddles. But when that which is perfect has come, and I know face to face, then that which is partial will be brought to an end (I Cor. XIII).

Therefore I give thanks to God through Jesus Christ our Lord. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death, and has opened my eyes so that I may clearly perceive that the inclination of the flesh is death, but the inclination of the Spirit is life and peace (Rom. VIII).

Just as, therefore, after recognizing the vanity of present things I held them in perfect hatred, so I urge you to think of them in the same way and to regard them as though they were foreign and were about to dissolve as quickly as possible. Having thus withdrawn all your resources from them, store up for yourself in the immortal age, to which you must depart without delay, a treasure that cannot be plundered by theft and riches that cannot in any way be exhausted (Luke XII; Matt. VI). Then, when you arrive there, you will suffer no poverty but will abound in riches, just as I earlier set before you a most fitting image.

## CHAPTER XV

Josaphat said to the old man: “By what means, then, can I send the treasures of my money there in advance, so that when I have departed from here I may obtain their fruit, free from every theft and destruction?
