And by what means may I demonstrate my hatred of present things and attain everlasting things? Please explain this openly to me.”

Barlaam therefore said: “Riches are sent ahead to the everlasting region through the hands of the poor. For a certain exceedingly wise prophet named Daniel said to the king of Babylon: ‘Therefore, O king, let my counsel please you, and redeem your sins with almsgiving and your injustices through compassion toward the poor’ (Daniel IV).

“The Savior also uses these words: ‘Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into everlasting dwellings’ (Luke XVI). He repeatedly teaches much about almsgiving and generosity toward the poor in the Gospel book [Col. 0500A] (Matt. XXV).

“In this way, therefore, you will send all your possessions there most securely through the hands of the needy. For whatever benefit you confer upon them, the Lord will take as his own and repay you with great interest. He always surpasses in the rewards of his benefits those who are endowed with love for him.

“In this way, having secretly taken away the treasures of this age, which you have served for so long and not without great suffering, you will acquire excellent provisions for yourself in the future. By rescuing them from another, you will first store them up for yourself, purchasing firm and stable things with these fleeting and perishable goods.

“Then, with God lending you his aid, you will perceive the uncertainty and instability of this world. After bidding farewell to all things, you will transfer yourself to the future; passing beyond the things that pass away, and devoting yourself to those things that are founded upon hope and are firm; abandoning darkness and the shadow of death; pursuing with hatred both the world and the ruler of the world; and considering the flesh, subject as it is to destruction, your enemy. You will hasten toward the inaccessible light (I Tim. VI), and, with the cross lifted upon your shoulders, you will follow Christ with unflinching eyes, so that you may also be glorified with him and become an heir—not of a fleeting and deceptive life, but of life itself.”

Josaphat then said to him: “Is this very teaching—to consider everything as nothing and to undertake so harsh a way of life, as you described above—an ancient institution derived from the teaching of the apostles, or is it a recent invention devised by your own intellectual skill, as though you had judged it better and more excellent and therefore chosen to embrace it?”

The old man replied: “I bring you no recently introduced law—far from it—but one handed down to us from ancient times. For the Lord said to a certain rich man who asked him what he had to do to inherit eternal life, and who boasted that he had observed everything written in the Law: ‘One thing is lacking to you. Go, sell everything you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, take up the cross, and follow me.’

“But when he heard this, he became sorrowful, for he was exceedingly rich. When Jesus saw that he was saddened, he said: ‘How difficult it is for those who have money to enter the kingdom of God! For it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God’ [Col. 0500D] (Mark X; Luke XVIII).

“When all the saints heard this commandment, they strove to withdraw themselves from the difficulty presented by such riches. By generosity toward the poor, distributing all their possessions and storing up everlasting riches for themselves, they took up the cross and followed Christ. Thus, as I have already said, some endured martyrdom, while others contended through the discipline of the religious life; and, insofar as the practice of this true philosophy is concerned, they were in no way inferior to the martyrs.

“Therefore I want you to know that this is the commandment of our King and God, through which human beings are made participants in everlasting goods.”

Josaphat said: “If this philosophy is so ancient and necessary, what is the reason that today so few people imitate this life?”

The old man replied: “Many have imitated it and still imitate it. But far more hesitate and delay. For, as the Lord says, few are those who walk along the narrow and constricted way, while very many take the easy and broad way (Matt. VII; Luke XXIII).

“Those who have once been seized by the desire for money, by love of the vices that arise from pleasures, and by devotion to vain and empty glory can scarcely be torn away from these things. They have enslaved themselves to another master, who commands everything contrary to God and holds them bound as though by chains, so that they have surrendered themselves beyond their own control [Col. 0501B].

“For once the soul has abandoned hope of its salvation and handed over its reins to desires turned away from reason, it is carried wherever they take it. Therefore the Prophet, lamenting the madness that has darkened such souls and mourning the thickness of the gloom pressing upon them, used these words: ‘Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?’

“Likewise, one of the wise teachers among us, a man most skilled in divine matters, singing the same song as the Prophet and adding something from himself, cried out to everyone as though from a high and exceedingly lofty watchtower:

“‘Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?’ (Ps. XLIV)—thinking, of course, that this life, its pleasures, its little glory, and its deceptive prosperity are something great (Nazianzen, *Oration on His Own Affairs and to Julian the Apostate*).

“Yet these things belong no more to those who enjoy them than to those who have held them in hope; and again they belong no more to the latter than to those who have never even expected them. They are blown from one person to another like dust before a whirlwind, tossed about in turn, or drift away like smoke; they mock human beings like a dream and cannot be held like a shadow. Their nature is such that, when they are absent, people do not despair of possessing them, while, when they are present, they are not certain or stable for those who possess them.

“When the Savior thus commands, the prophets and apostles proclaim, and all holy men urge us, both by their deeds and their words, toward the path of virtue, which is most free from every error—even though few hold to it, while many choose for themselves the broad path that leads to destruction—the institution of this divine philosophy must not for that reason be esteemed less highly.

“For just as the sun, rising in order to give light, sends forth its rays abundantly and invites everyone to receive its brightness, if some people refuse to look upon its splendor with their eyes closed, it does not thereby deserve blame, nor should it be neglected by the rest; nor is the glory of its radiance held in contempt because of their foolishness. Rather, they deprive themselves of the light and, like blind people, feel their way along walls, fall headlong into many pits, and have their eyes pierced by many thorns. The sun, meanwhile, retaining its brilliance, illuminates those who gaze upon its light with unveiled faces [Col. 0502A].

“In the same way, the light of Christ shines upon everyone and freely imparts its splendor to us all; but each person receives it according to his own desire and eagerness of mind. For the Sun of justice neither deprives any of those who wish to fix the sight of their eyes upon him of this benefit, nor does he compel those who willingly choose darkness. Rather, as long as each person is in this life, he is left to his own free will and choice.”

When Josaphat asked what freedom of will and choice were, the old man replied:

“Freedom of will is the will of a rational soul, impelled without any impediment toward whatever it desires—whether virtue or vice—and fashioned in this way by that supreme parent and architect.

“Again, freedom of will is the self-directed activity of an intellectual soul. Choice, however, is the appetitive impulse, joined with deliberation, toward those things that lie within our power. We desire the thing that, after deliberation, has been judged better.

“Deliberation is an investigative desire concerning actions that lie within our power. A person deliberates whether it is expedient to do something or not. Then he judges which option is superior, and the judgment is formed. Next he is affected by it, loves what has been judged as the result of deliberation, and this is called a decision. For if someone judges in this way but is not at all affected toward what has been judged—that is, does not love it—it is not called a decision.

“After affection comes choice. For choice is nothing other than embracing and selecting one of two proposed things in preference to the other. This is also clear from the etymology itself: choice is deliberation joined with discrimination. The Greek word προαιρετόν means ‘chosen in preference to another.’

“No one prefers one thing to another after applying judgment unless he has first deliberated; nor does anyone choose unless he has first judged. For since we do not endeavor to put into practice everything that seems right and excellent to us, choice—and the thing to be chosen—comes into being only when what has been proposed as the result of deliberation has acquired desire as its companion.

“From this it follows that choice is desire joined with deliberation concerning things that lie within our power. For we desire the thing that has been set before us as the result of deliberation. Every deliberation is undertaken for the sake of action and on account of action. Thus deliberation precedes choice, and choice precedes every action.

“Therefore not only actions but also the things that are entertained in the mind—which indeed give rise to choices—bring either crowns or punishments. For choice, operating in matters that lie within our power, is the source both of sin and of righteous action. Since the capacities for those things lie within our power, the actions corresponding to those capacities also lie within our power. Therefore, since capacities corresponding to virtue are within our power, virtues themselves must likewise be within our power. Properly speaking, everything that touches the soul and about which we deliberate lies within our power [Col. 0503A].

“In this way, then, as human beings deliberate freely and also choose with free will, to the extent that a person chooses, to that same extent he perceives the divine light and makes progress in the pursuit of philosophy.

“For the kinds of choices are various. Just as certain springs of water gush forth from the depths of the earth—some arising near the earth’s surface, others somewhat deeper, and others at the greatest depth; some of these waters flowing nearby and being sweet to the taste, others emerging from below and being salty or sulphurous, while some pour forth abundantly and others drip little by little—so you should understand that choices too are of different kinds. Some are swift and exceedingly fervent, others sluggish and cold; some are wholly inclined toward virtue, others incline with all their strength toward vice. The impulses to action that follow are accordingly shaped by the affections of each choice.”

## CHAPTER XVI

Josaphat said to the old man: “Are there also others who proclaim the same things as you, or are you alone today in teaching these doctrines and warning that the present life must be so utterly rejected and pursued with hatred?”

He replied as follows: “In this most wretched region of yours I know no one. For the tyranny of your father has punished people with countless forms of death and has taken care that the proclamation of divine knowledge should not be heard among you at all.

“Among the other nations, however, these things are sung and celebrated—by some in the most upright manner, but by others perversely, since the enemy of our souls has driven them across the straight road and divided them into alien opinions, teaching them to interpret certain passages of divine Scripture differently from what their true meaning requires [Col. 0503C].

“Nevertheless, there is one truth, proclaimed by the illustrious apostles and divine fathers, and shining more brightly than the sun in the Catholic Church, spread from the farthest ends of the world to its opposite extremities. I have been sent to you in order to proclaim and hand this truth on to you.”

Josaphat said to him: “Did my father never learn any of these things?”

The old man replied: “Clearly—and as was fitting—he learned nothing. For with his senses closed, he deliberately rejects the good and freely inclines his mind toward evil.”

“But I wish,” said Josaphat, “that he too might be imbued with this teaching.”

The old man replied: “Among human beings these things are impossible, but with God nothing is impossible (Matt. XIX). Do you know whether it may happen that you bring salvation to your father and eventually come to be called, in an astonishing manner, the father of your own father?

“I was told of a certain king who administered his royal dignity with great excellence and treated the people subject to his authority and rule gently and peacefully. Yet he failed in one respect: he lacked the light of divine knowledge and remained bound by the worship of idols [Col. 0504A].

“He had a certain upright counsellor, adorned both with piety toward God and with every other virtue. The counsellor was distressed by the king’s error and took it very badly. Although he intended to rebuke the king for it, he restrained himself for this reason: he feared that he would bring destruction upon himself and his companions and cut off the benefit that flowed from him to others. Nevertheless, he sought an opportunity by which he might conveniently draw the king toward the good.

“One night the king said to him: ‘Come, let us go out and walk around the city, to see whether we may discover something that will be useful.’ As they walked through the city, they saw the brightness of a light shining through an opening. When they directed their eyes toward it, they saw an underground, cavernous dwelling in which a man afflicted by extreme poverty was seated, dressed in certain cheap and tattered rags.

“His wife stood beside him, mixing wine for him. When he had taken the cup in his hands, she brought him pleasure by singing a sweet song, dancing, and soothing her husband with praise.

“The king observed these things for some time and wondered that, although they were oppressed by such poverty that they had neither a house nor clothing sufficient for them, they nevertheless lived such a happy and cheerful life. He then addressed his principal counsellor in these words:

“‘What a strange thing, my friend! Neither you nor I have ever found our life so pleasing—even though it otherwise shines on every side with such glory, luxury, and pleasure—as this vile and wretched life pleases and delights these senseless people. Although it is otherwise harsh and repellent, it appears easy and agreeable to them.’

“The chief counsellor, having found an opportune moment, said: ‘But you, O king, what sort of life do you suppose theirs to be?’

“‘The most unpleasant and miserable of all that I have ever seen,’ he replied, ‘worthy of curses and to be rejected.’

“Then the chief counsellor said to him: ‘Believe me, O king, our life appears in the same way—and even much more bitter—to those who contemplate and understand that everlasting glory and those goods that surpass every capacity of the mind. These buildings gleaming with gold, these splendid garments, and all the other delights of life appear to those who behold the heavenly dwellings not made with hands, the garment woven by God, and the crowns free from every corruption that the architect and Lord of all things has prepared for those who love him, to be more foul-smelling than dung and mud [Col. 0504D] (I Cor. II).

“‘For just as these people are foolish in our judgment and estimation, so we—and even more so—who wander about in the world and take pleasure in this deceptive glory and foolish luxury are, in the eyes of those who have tasted the sweetness of those goods, worthy of mourning and tears.’

“Struck by these words, the king said: ‘Who, then, are those who live a better life than we do?’

“‘All who have preferred everlasting things to perishable and fragile things,’ he replied.

“When the king again asked what those everlasting things were, he answered: ‘A kingdom free from succession, a life not subject to death, riches that fear no poverty, joy and delight separated from every sadness and pain, and perpetual peace free from every hostility and conflict.

“‘Those to whom it is granted by divine providence to enjoy these goods are blessed—indeed, blessed many times over. They will lead a life free from every labor and sorrow for all eternity, enjoying without effort all the delights and pleasures of the kingdom of God and reigning forever with Christ.’

“When the king said, ‘Who, then, will be worthy to attain these things?’ he replied: ‘Everyone who takes hold of the path leading there; no one is denied entry, provided only that he wishes to enter.’

“Then the king asked: ‘And what is the way by which one goes there?’

“That man of noble spirit replied: ‘To know the one true God, and Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, and the holy, life-giving Spirit’ (John XVII).”

The king, endowed with truly royal prudence, then said to him: “What has prevented you until now from explaining these things to me? For if they are true, they do not seem to me to deserve hesitation or delay. But if they are uncertain, they must be investigated carefully and accurately until we discover them without any ambiguity or doubt.”

“It was not negligence or indifference,” he replied, “that made me hesitate to explain these things to you, since they are true and free from every doubt. Rather, I feared the greatness of your splendid glory and was afraid that I might be burdensome and troublesome to you. Therefore, if you command me, your servant, to remind you of these matters hereafter, I shall obey your command.”

“Certainly,” said the king, “renew the memory of these things for me not only during the day but at any hour. For we must direct our minds toward these matters not carelessly and superficially, but with the greatest zeal and fervor.”

“After this,” Barlaam said, “I heard that this king ordered his life thereafter piously and religiously, and, having completed the course of the present life peacefully and calmly, attained everlasting blessedness.

“Therefore, if someone reminds your father of these matters at the proper time, perhaps he will understand and recognize what great evils entangle him; turning away from them, he may embrace what is good (II Pet. I). At present he is blind, feeling his way with his hand, because he has deprived himself of the true light and fled into the darkness of impiety.”

Josaphat said to him: “As for my father, let what the Lord commands be done. For, as you yourself have said, all things that seem impossible among human beings are possible for him. As for me, through your exceptional and extraordinary discourses I have grown weary of the vanity of present things. I have therefore determined to withdraw my mind from them altogether and to spend with you whatever life remains to me, lest, through fleeting and fragile things, I fall short of the enjoyment of everlasting goods that are free from every destruction.”

The old man replied: “If you do this, you will show yourself like a certain exceedingly wise young man whom I learned to have been born of wealthy and illustrious parents.

“His noble and exceedingly wealthy father had betrothed him to a girl of remarkable beauty, the daughter of a certain distinguished and very rich man. When the father discussed this marriage with his son and explained what he had in mind, the young man, upon hearing it, considered the matter absurd and improper. He examined it carefully, left his father, and fled.

“As he traveled, he turned aside to the house of a certain poor old man in order to refresh himself from the heat of the day.

“The old man had a daughter, his only child, who was a virgin. She sat before the door, working with her hands, while with her mouth she praised God without interruption, giving him thanks from the depths of her heart.

“When the young man heard her praising him, he said: ‘What is your way of life, girl? And why, when you live in such degradation and poverty, do you praise the author of these things as though you had received enormous benefits?’

“She replied: ‘Do you not know that, just as a small medicine usually rescues a person from great diseases, so giving thanks to God for small things brings about great blessings? I, the daughter of a poor old man, give thanks for these small things and praise the Lord, assured of this: that he who has given these things can also give greater ones.

“‘These matters concern external things, things that are in no way truly ours. From them no benefit arises even for those who possess much; indeed, they often bring harm. Nor does any disadvantage or loss arise for those who have received fewer things, since both groups travel the same road and strive toward the same end.

“‘But in matters that are more necessary and of greater importance, I have been granted many, very great, and indeed innumerable benefits by God. I was created in the image of God, imbued with knowledge of him, adorned with reason beyond all other living creatures, recalled from death to life through the compassion of our God, and given the ability to receive his mysteries.

“‘Finally, the gate of paradise has been opened, offering me free access if I should wish to enter. For all these many and great benefits, of which the poor share equally with the rich, I am utterly unable to give God thanks worthy of them. If I do not offer even this small praise to him who has heaped so many gifts upon me, what excuse shall I have?’”

The young man, admiring this great wisdom, summoned her father and said: “Give me your daughter, since I have fallen in love with her prudence and piety.”

The old man replied: “You, who were born of rich and prosperous parents, may not take this daughter of a poor man.”

The young man replied again: “I shall certainly take her unless you prevent me. A noble and wealthy girl had been betrothed to me, but after rejecting and abandoning her I fled. Now, captivated by love for your daughter because of her piety and wisdom toward God, I am ready to marry her.”

The old man said to him: “I cannot give her to you to take her away to your father’s house and remove her from my arms, for she is my only child.”

“But I,” said the young man, “will remain with you and adopt your way of life.”

Afterward he put aside his splendid clothing, asked for the old man’s garments, and dressed himself in them. The old man tested him for a long time and examined his mind in various ways. When he recognized that the young man possessed seriousness of mind and was not asking to marry his daughter because of some foolish infatuation, but was embracing a poor life out of devotion to piety and preferring it to his own glory and nobility, he took him by the hand, led him into his chamber, and showed him the great riches stored there, an immeasurable mass of money such as the young man had never seen [Col. 0507B].

He said to him: “My son, I give all these things to you as a gift, because you have resolved in your mind to be the heir of my riches.”

Having received this inheritance, the young man surpassed all the rich and distinguished men of the earth.

## CHAPTER XVII

Josaphat said to Barlaam: “This story also aptly expresses the condition of my affairs, and therefore I think that what you have said has been spoken about me as well. But what is the test by which you wish to ascertain the steadfastness of my mind?”

The old man replied: “I myself have also made trial, and have understood how great are the prudence and steadfastness of your mind, and how upright and whole your spirit is; but the outcome of your conduct will confirm this. For this reason I bend my knees to our God [Col. 0507C] (Eph. III), who is celebrated in the Trinity—to him, I say, who brought into being all things, both those perceived by the senses and those that escape the sight of the eyes; who truly and eternally is, and who has never had, nor will ever have, either a beginning or an end to his glorious state—to him, I say, who is awesome, all-powerful over all things, good, and inclined to mercy, that he may enlighten the eyes of your heart and give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation for the knowledge of him, so that you may know what is the hope of your calling, what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the saints, and what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who have believed; so that you may no longer be a stranger and foreigner, but a fellow citizen with the saints and a member of God’s household (Eph. I), built upon the foundation of the apostles and [Col. 0507D] prophets, with Jesus Christ himself as the chief cornerstone, in whom the whole structure, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord (Eph. II).”

Josaphat, deeply pierced in spirit, said: “Since I too eagerly desire to know all these things, I ask you to declare to me both the riches of the divine glory and the excellence of his power.”

Barlaam then said to him: “I beseech God that he may teach you these things and implant in your mind the knowledge of matters of this kind. For among human beings his glory and power cannot in any way be adequately expressed, even if all the tongues of all human beings, both those now living and those who have ever lived, were to unite. For, as the Evangelist [Col. 0508A] and theologian says (John I), ‘No one has ever seen God. The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has made him known.’ Who, then, among those formed from earth could comprehend the glory and majesty of him who escapes the sight of the eyes and is immeasurable, unless he himself should reveal it according to his own will, just as he revealed it to his prophets and apostles? We learn as much of it as we are able to attain, both from their preaching and from the very nature of things. For Scripture says: ‘The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands’ (Ps. XVIII). And again: ‘His invisible attributes are clearly perceived from the creation of the world through the things that have been made, and so are his eternal power and divinity’ (Rom. I).

[Col. 0508B] “For just as someone who sees a house constructed splendidly and with the greatest skill, or a vessel elegantly fashioned, immediately brings its architect or craftsman to mind, so I too, fashioned from nothing and brought into being, although I cannot see my maker and producer, nevertheless arrive at knowledge of his wisdom from the exceedingly well-ordered and most admirable structure of myself—not as he is in himself, but insofar as I am able to understand. For I was not brought forth by chance or accident, nor did I come into existence from myself; rather, he fashioned me according to his own will. He established me as the head of all created things, made me lower than certain others, and, when by his divine command he brings me out of this life, even after I have been crushed, he transfers me to another life without end and everlasting. [Col. 0508C] In all these matters I cannot struggle against the power of his providence. I can neither add nor subtract anything from myself, whether concerning my stature or the shape of my form; I cannot renew what has been worn out in me by age, nor restore to wholeness what has been weakened and corrupted. For no mortal has ever been able to accomplish any of these things—not a king, not a wise man, not a rich man, not a powerful man, nor anyone else pursuing human endeavors. For, as he says, ‘None of the kings, or of those in high position, had any other beginning of birth. For there is one entrance into life for all, and the exit is the same’ (Wis. VII).

“Therefore, from the things that concern me, I am led, as though by an outstretched hand, to knowledge of the magnificence of that supreme architect. [Col. 0508D] Moreover, I have considered the exceedingly well-ordered structure and preservation of all created things: namely, that by their own nature all things are subject to change and alteration—those endowed with mind, through the reasoning of the will and through progress in or retreat from the good; and those that fall within the senses, through coming into being and passing away, increase and diminution, change in quality, and finally local movement. Through these things they proclaim, in a kind of silent speech, that they were brought forth by God the creator, who is free from every change and alteration; that they are held together and preserved by him, and are always governed by him. For in what other way could natures opposed to one another have come together for the completion in every respect of the adornment of one [Col. 0509A] world, and have remained free from dissolution, unless some omnipotent power had both joined them together and continually preserved them from dissolution? How could anything have remained unless his will had so ordained? Or how could that which, to use the words of Scripture, was not called forth by him have been preserved?

“For when a ship cannot remain in place after its helmsman has withdrawn, but immediately founders, and when no house, however small, can stand unless someone takes care of it, how could the world—a work so vast, so splendid, and so admirable—have remained established for so long a period without some extraordinary, immense, and wondrous governance and most wise providence? For see [Col. 0509B] how much time has already passed since the heavens came into being: yet they have not grown dark; the strength of the earth, which has been bearing offspring for so long, has not weakened; the springs have not ceased to gush forth from the places where they arose; the sea, receiving so many rivers, has not exceeded its measure; the courses of the sun and moon have undergone no alteration; and the sequences of day and night have not been reversed. Through all these things the power and magnificence of God, which surpasses every capacity of speech, are plainly revealed to us and confirmed by the testimony of the prophets and apostles. Yet no one will ever be able to conceive or praise his glory worthily. For the divine Apostle—he, I say, who had Christ speaking in him (II Cor. XI)—when he had considered in his mind all things, both those perceived by the understanding [Col. 0509C] and those subject to the senses, said: ‘We know in part, and we prophesy in part; but when the perfect comes, the partial will be brought to an end’ (I Cor. XIII). And therefore, struck with wonder and astonishment at the immeasurable riches of his wisdom, he openly exclaimed: ‘O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and inscrutable his ways!’ (Rom. XI).

“Now if he who had ascended as far as the third heaven and heard secret words (II Cor. XII) uttered such words, who among those like me could turn his eyes toward the abyss of such great mysteries and, not merely speak anything worthy of them, but not even think anything worthy of them, unless he himself, the dispenser of wisdom [Col. 0509D] and corrector of the ignorant, should grant it?” For in his hand are we and our words, and all prudence and knowledge of skill. Through his kindness we possess true knowledge of the things that exist, and understand the structure of the world, the powers of the elements, the beginning, middle, and end of times, the changes of the seasons, and the alterations of the weather, because he has established all things according to measure and proportion. For power is always at his disposal; and who can resist the strength of his arm? Indeed, before him the whole world is like a grain on a balance, and like a drop of morning dew that descends upon the earth. Yet he overlooks human sins for the sake of [Col. 0510A] repentance. For he has mercy on all, because he can do all things. For he detests none of those who hasten to him, nor does that one good Lord, who loves souls, turn away from anyone (Wis. XI). Blessed be the name of his glory, holy, praiseworthy, and exalted above all forever. Amen (Dan. III).”

## CHAPTER XVIII

Josaphat then said to him: “If you had spent a long time considering, most wise man, how you might make the solution of the questions proposed to you clear to me, in my judgment you could not have done better than by recalling to me what you have now set forth. For you have taught that God is the maker and preserver of all things, and have demonstrated by the clearest arguments that the glory of his majesty exceeds the capacity of every human mind, and that no one can attain it by any other means [Col. 0510B] except the one to whom he himself, according to his own will, reveals it. In this respect I greatly admire your most eloquent wisdom.

“But I wish you to tell me, most blessed man, what your age is, in what places you dwell, and what companions in philosophy you have, since my soul clings most closely to yours, and throughout the whole of life I desire not to depart from you even by a finger’s breadth.”

The old man replied: “If I am not mistaken, I am forty-five years old, and I live in the deserts of the land of Sennaar. As for my fellow soldiers, I have those who labor and strive with me along the course of the journey toward heaven.”

“What do you say?” Josaphat exclaimed. “You appear to me to be more than seventy [Col. 0510C] years old. Why, then, do you say that you are only forty-five? For you do not appear to me to be speaking the truth in this matter.”

Barlaam replied: “If you ask to know my years from the very beginning of life, you have rightly judged that they are more than seventy. But I do not count among the years of life, in any way at all, those spent in the vanity of this world. For when, enslaved to sins, I lived for the flesh, I was dead as far as the inner person was concerned. Therefore I would never call the years of death years of life. But from the time when the world was crucified to me, and I to the world (Gal. VI), and when I stripped off the old person, who is corrupted according to the desires of error, I no longer live for the flesh, but Christ lives in me; and the life I now [Col. 0510D] live, I live in faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me (Eph. IV): these years of life and days of salvation I may rightly call so. Asserting that these are forty-five, I have told you their number consistently and without absurdity.

“I wish that you too might always hold this thought and judgment: namely, that you should in no way regard as living those who are dead to every good work but live in sins, who obey the ruler of those who lie prostrate on the earth, and who consume their lives in pleasures and destructive desires. Rather, persuade yourself that they are extinguished and dead to the function of life.” For a certain wise man rightly declared sin to be the death of the immortal soul. The Apostle also [Col. 0511A] uses these words: ‘When you were slaves of sin, you were free with respect to righteousness. What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. But now, having been freed from sin and made slaves of righteousness, you have your fruit in sanctification, and the end is eternal life. For the wages of sin is death, but the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord’ (Rom. VI).

Josaphat then said to him: “Since you do not regard the life lived in the flesh as life, it follows that you should not regard this death, which everyone undergoes, as death either.”

The old man replied: “I hold this view of these matters also, without any doubt, since I do not fear this temporary [Col. 0511B] death at all. Indeed, I do not call it death at all, if it should seize me while I am walking along the path of the divine commandments. Rather, I call it a passage from death to a superior and more perfect life, hidden in Christ (Col. III). The best men, burning with desire to attain this life, found the present life burdensome. Hence the Apostle also says: ‘For we know that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. For in this we groan, desiring to put on over it our dwelling that is from heaven, if indeed, when clothed, we shall not be found naked’ (II Cor. V).

[Col. 0511C] “For we who are in this tent also groan under our burden, because we do not wish to be stripped, but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. And again he says: ‘Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?’ (Rom. VI). And elsewhere: ‘I desire to depart and to be with Christ’ (Phil. I). And the prophet David says: ‘When shall I come and appear before the face of God?’ (Ps. XLI).

“That I too, the weakest of all, in no way fear bodily death, you can easily understand from this: although I disregarded and counted as nothing the threats of your father, I came fearlessly to you in order to expound the doctrine that brings salvation, even though I knew with absolute certainty that, if he learned of this, he would inflict six hundred deaths upon me, if that were possible. But since I place the word of God above all things and desire to enjoy it, I neither dread this temporary [Col. 0511D] death nor consider that it should be called by such a name, obeying the command of the Lord, who says: ‘Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna’ (Matt. X).”

Josaphat said: “These splendid deeds of your true philosophy greatly and far surpass the nature of earthly people, who can scarcely be torn away from this present life. Blessed are you, endowed with such vigorous minds. But tell me truthfully what food you and your companions have in this kind of solitude, and likewise from where and of what kind your clothing comes.”

Barlaam replied: “[Col. 0512A] Our food is supplied by fruits and plants, which the solitude, watered by heavenly dew and obedient to the command of the Creator, nourishes for us. Because of this, no one fights or contends against us, or tries to seize the greater share, as the law of greed prescribes. Rather, food in great abundance, requiring no labor, and an improvised table are set before us. If sometimes one of the devout brothers who live near us brings the blessing of bread, we receive it as though it had been sent by divine providence as a blessing for those who offered it with faith.

“Our clothes are made from rough haircloths and sheepskins, all old and sewn together from various scraps, chafing our feeble flesh. We have the same clothing in summer and winter. Once we have put it on, we are not permitted afterward to remove it [Col. 0512B] until it has been completely destroyed by age. In this way, by afflicting the body with the discomforts of cold and heat, we prepare for ourselves the clothing of future immortality.”

When Josaphat asked where he had obtained the garment he was wearing, the old man replied: “I borrowed it from one of the devout brothers when I was setting out to come to you. It was not fitting for me to approach wearing the garment I ordinarily wear. For just as someone who wishes to rescue a beloved relative carried away captive into a foreign land puts aside his own clothing, assumes the appearance of the enemy, and goes to their country, freeing his kinsman from bitter tyranny by various stratagems, so I too, having learned of your situation, came in this attire in order to sow divine preaching in your heart and rescue you from the slavery of the world’s savage ruler.

“Now [Col. 0512C], through divine power, I have completed my ministry, insofar as it lay within me. For I have announced to you knowledge of him, expounded the preaching of the prophets and apostles, and truly and without error demonstrated the vanity of present things and the evils with which this world teems, deceiving those who obey it and ensnaring them in various ways. Therefore I must return to the place from which I came, and, laying aside this borrowed attire, put on my own.”

Josaphat begged the old man to show himself to him in his customary clothing. When Barlaam had taken off the garment [Col. 0512D] he was wearing, a dreadful spectacle presented itself to Josaphat. For all the fullness of his flesh [πιότης perhaps to be read, that is, “fatness”] had been consumed, and the skin was stretched around his bones by the heat and burning of the sun, just as if someone had stretched a hide over slender reeds. He was girded from the loins to the knees with patched and exceedingly rough haircloth, and he wore the same kind of cloak over his shoulders.

Josaphat, astonished at the harshness and severity of this life and struck with wonder at such great and singular endurance, groaned and, with tears pouring forth, said to the old man: “Since this was the reason you came here—to draw me out of the bitter slavery of the devil—complete your work by your kindness, [Col. 0513A] and bring my soul out of confinement (Ps. CXLI). Take me as your companion on your journey, so that, entirely freed from the deception of the world, I may at last receive the seal of saving baptism and become your companion in this admirable philosophy and extraordinary discipline.”

Barlaam replied: “A certain rich man once raised a kid of a she-goat. When it had grown, however, it was drawn by natural affection toward the wilderness. One day it went out and found a herd of she-goats engaged in grazing. Joining itself to them, it wandered through fields and plains, returning home late in the day; but in the morning, through the negligence of the servants, it went outside and joined the wild goats. When they went [Col. 0513B] farther afield to feed, it accompanied them as well.

“When the servants of that rich man learned what had happened, they mounted horses and pursued them from behind. They captured their own goat alive, brought it home, and thereafter kept it so that no one could gain access to it. They slaughtered part of the remaining herd and severely punished the rest. I fear that the same may happen to us if you join yourself to me as a companion: namely, that I should both lose your companionship and bring great calamities upon my companions, as well as everlasting condemnation upon your father. Therefore the Lord now wills that you be marked with the seal of divine baptism, remain here, devote yourself to every kind of piety, and apply yourself to his commandments. But when an opportunity presents itself through the gift of that giver of all good things, then [Col. 0513C] you will come to us and spend the rest of this life with us. Trusting in the Lord’s goodness, I have no doubt that in the life to come we shall be joined together in such a way that we can never be separated.”

Josaphat, again covered with tears, said to him: “If this pleases the Lord, let his will be done. Therefore, when you have initiated me through divine baptism, and have received from me money and clothing both for your own food and clothing and for that of your companions, depart to the place of religious discipline, surrounded by the protection of divine peace. Pray to God for me without ceasing, so that I may not disappoint your hope, but may reach you at the earliest opportunity and receive from you the benefit of deep quiet.”

Barlaam replied: “There is nothing to prevent you from receiving the seal of Christ [Col. 0513D]. Therefore prepare yourself, and, with God’s help, you will be initiated into the sacred rites of the Christian faith.

“But as for the money you said you would give both to me and to my companions, how could you, being poor, bestow alms upon the rich? It is the part of the rich to do good to the poor, not, conversely, the part of the poor to do good to the wealthy and prosperous. For the last of all my companions surpasses you entirely in wealth. Yet, trusting in the divine mercies, I persuade myself that you will soon be exceedingly rich. When that happens, you will not be at all ready or inclined to give generously.”

Josaphat replied: “Please explain to me how the last of your companions surpasses me [Col. 0514A] in wealth, when a little earlier you said that they live in great want and struggle with extreme poverty. And why do you now call me poor, when you say that, once I possess the greatest wealth, I will not be generous, although I am now ready and inclined to give?”

Barlaam replied: “I did not say that they struggle with poverty, but rather that they flourish in inexhaustible riches. To add wealth continually to wealth, to refuse to restrain desire as with a bridle, and to seek more without any satisfaction is the mark of extreme poverty. On the other hand, those who despise all present things out of desire for eternal things, and regard them as refuse in order to gain Christ alone (Phil. III), and who, having dismissed every care for food and clothing and cast it [Col. 0514B] upon God, derive more pleasure from want than any of those inflamed with love of the world derives from an abundance of wealth and money—those who have accumulated for themselves the greatest riches of virtues and nourish themselves with hope of immortal goods—I would rightly call richer than you, and indeed richer than any earthly king.

“If, with God’s favor, you too seize such spiritual riches, you will preserve them with the utmost zeal and diligence, and will always, and rightly, desire to increase them, nor will you endure to pour out any portion of them. For true riches are located precisely in this. But the mass of riches that fall within the senses will have affected their possessors’ friends more by harm than by advantage. Therefore I did not call them extreme poverty without reason: the lovers of heavenly [Col. 0514C] goods flee from them, having dismissed all other things, just as someone flees from a serpent.

“But if I bring back alive to my companions—that enemy whom the companions and fellow soldiers of my pious discipline have already struck down and trampled beneath their feet—after receiving him again from you, I shall become a fatal messenger to them, bringing them the cause of wars and disturbances.” May it be far from me to do this.”

285 [Col. 0514D] “I wish you to understand the same concerning clothing as well. For how could I once again clothe those who have stripped off the stain and corruption of old age, and, insofar as it lay within them, laid aside the garment of disobedience, but have put on Christ as a garment of salvation and a cloak of joy? How could I put leather tunics upon them again and place a garment of disgrace upon them? Rather, since I know that my companions, content with the pious and religious discipline of solitude and regarding it as the truest delight, have no need whatsoever of such things, distribute the money and clothing that you said you would give them among the poor, and store up for yourself a treasure of this kind for the future, which cannot in any way be stolen, joining God himself to you as your helper through their prayers. In this way you will achieve that your riches serve you for every good purpose.

“Then, when you have received the armor of the Spirit, girded your loins with truth, put on the breastplate of righteousness, placed the helmet of salvation upon your head, shod your feet with the preparation of the gospel of peace, and taken up in your hands the shield of faith and the [Col. 0515A] sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph. VI), and when you have equipped and fortified yourself on every side with the finest weapons, then go forth with confident spirit to wage war against ungodliness, so that, when it has been put to flight and its leader, the devil, has been struck down upon the earth, you may receive the victorious crown from the right hand of the Lord, which bestows the beginning of life.”

## CHAPTER XIX

When Barlaam had imbued the king’s son with teachings of this kind and with words bringing salvation, and had prepared him for divine baptism, instructing him, as custom requires, to fast for several days and devote himself to prayers, he did not cease coming to him frequently. He taught him all the doctrines of the orthodox faith, expounded the divine Gospel, [Col. 0515B] and also explained the apostolic exhortations and passages of the prophets. For, being endowed with divinely handed-down teaching, that man recited the whole of both the Old and the New Testament from memory. And, carried along by the divine Spirit, he illumined the young man with the light of the true knowledge of God.

On the day when he was to be baptized, he addressed him for the purpose of instruction in these words: “Behold, you are about to receive the seal of Christ and to be marked with the light of the Lord’s countenance (Ps. IV), and to become a son of God and a temple of the life-giving Spirit.

“Therefore believe in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit—the holy Trinity, I say, from which life has its beginning, celebrated in three persons and one divinity. With respect to persons and personal [Col. 0515C] properties it is distinct, but with respect to essence it is joined and united. Acknowledge one unbegotten God and one only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, light from light, true God from true God, begotten before all ages. For from the good Father the good Son was begotten, from the only-begotten light eternal light shone forth, from true life the life-giving fountain proceeded, and from that very power the Son’s power flashed forth. He is the radiance of glory [Heb. I] and the truly subsisting Word, who was in the beginning, was with God, and was God [John I], without beginning and eternal; through him all things were made, both those seen by the eyes and those that cannot be seen.

[Col. 0515D] “Acknowledge also one Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father, perfect God, bringing life and granting holiness, possessing one will, almighty, having the same eternity, truly subsisting. In this way, therefore, adore the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in three persons or properties, and in one divinity. The divinity is common to these three, and their nature is one, their substance one, their glory one, their kingdom one, their power one, and their authority one. It is common to the Son and the Holy Spirit that they are from the Father; but it is proper to the Father to be unbegotten, to the Son to be begotten, and to the Spirit to proceed.

[Col. 0516A] “Believe these things in this way, but do not attempt to comprehend the manner of generation or procession—for it cannot be comprehended. Rather, hold with an undivided heart and without any superfluous investigation that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are in every respect one, except for the property of being unbegotten, generation, and procession. Hold also that the only-begotten Son and Word of God, who is God, descended to earth for the sake of our salvation at the command of the Father and with the cooperation of the Holy Spirit; that without seed he was conceived in the womb of the holy Virgin and Mother of God, Mary, through the Holy Spirit; that he was born without corruption and became a perfect human being; and that he is himself perfect God and perfect human being, from two natures—that is, divinity and humanity—and endowed in both natures with intellect, will, operation, and freedom [Col. 0516B] of choice, perfect in every respect according to the rule and character proper to each nature, divine and human, yet one composite person.

“Receive these things simply and without any curious investigation. Do not try to understand how the Son of God emptied himself and became a human being from virgin blood without seed or corruption, or how the two natures came together in one person. For we are taught to hold by faith these things divinely spoken to us by Holy Scripture; but we do not know the manner, nor can we explain it.

[Col. 0516C] “Believe that the Son of God, who became human through the bowels of his mercy, assumed all the human affections that are natural and are not counted as faults. As far as his human nature was concerned, he suffered hunger and thirst, slept, was in anguish, was led to death for our iniquities, fastened to the cross, and, having tasted death, was buried, while his divine nature remained free from all suffering and change. We attribute no suffering whatever to that nature which is free from all suffering. Rather, we acknowledge that he suffered and was buried in the nature he assumed, that he was raised by divine glory from death to life and immortality, that he ascended into heaven, and that he will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead and repay each person according to his merit (Matt. XVI; Rev. XXII).

[Col. 0516D] “For the dead will rise, and those who are in the tombs will be raised. Those who have observed Christ’s commandments and departed this life in the right faith will possess eternal life as an inheritance; but those who have corrupted themselves in sins and turned away from the right faith will go away to eternal punishment (John V).

“Believe that there is neither any essence of evil nor any kingdom of evil. Do not suppose that it is without beginning, that it exists in itself, or that it originated from God—far from you be such absurdity. Rather, this is the work of us and of the devil, which enters through our carelessness and negligence because we possess free choice and voluntarily choose both good and evil.

“Further, confess one baptism from water [Col. 0517A] and the Holy Spirit for the remission of sins.

“Moreover, receive the mysteries of Christ, pure from every stain, believing with complete certainty that they are the body and blood of our God, which he has given as a gift to human beings endowed with faith for the forgiveness of sins. For on the night when he was betrayed, Christ established the new covenant with his disciples and apostles, and through them with all who would believe in him (I Cor. XI), in these words: ‘Take and eat; this is my body, which is broken for you for the remission of sins.’ Likewise, taking the cup, he handed it to them, saying: ‘This is my blood of the new covenant, which is poured out for you for the remission of sins. Do this in remembrance of me.’

“Therefore the living and effective Word of God [Col. 0517B] (Heb. IV), accomplishing everything through his own power, through the divine and most holy word and the coming of the Holy Spirit, makes and changes the bread and wine of the offering into his body and blood, and brings holiness and light to those who receive them with eager devotion.

“Adore the venerable image of the Lord’s character—that is, of the Word of God who assumed our humanity for our sake—kissing it with faith and believing that in the image you behold the Creator himself. For the honor shown to an image, as has been handed down by a holy man (Basil, *On the Holy Spirit*, ch. 18), is referred to the exemplar. The exemplar is that of which the image is made and from which it is derived.

[Col. 0517C] “For when we see the painting in an image, we pass with the eyes of the mind to the true form of which it is the image, piously adoring him who took flesh for our sake. We do not attribute divinity to the painting itself; rather, we embrace it as the image of the incarnate God, out of our love and goodwill toward him who for our sake emptied himself even to the form of a servant.

“In the same way, embrace also the images of his pure Mother and of all the saints, and likewise kiss and adore in faith the representation of the life-giving and venerable cross, for the sake of Christ, God, and Savior of the world, who for our salvation was hung in the flesh upon it and gave us this sign by which to obtain victory over the devil. For he shudders and trembles, unable to endure the sight of its power.

[Col. 0517D] “In these doctrines and in this faith you shall be baptized, preserving it, free from every change and pure from every heresy, until your final breath. But abominate every teaching and all doctrines that oppose this faith, which is free from reproach, and regard them as an alienation from God. For the Apostle says: ‘Even if an angel from heaven should preach to you something other than what we preached to you, let him be accursed’ (Gal. I). For there is no other Gospel or other faith besides that which was preached by the apostles and confirmed by the divine Fathers in various councils.”

When Barlaam had said these things and explained to the king’s son the creed composed at the Council of Nicaea, he baptized him in the name of the Father, Son, and [Col. 0518A] Holy Spirit in the pool that was in his garden, and the grace of the Holy Spirit came upon him. When he had returned to his chamber and celebrated the sacred rite of the unbloody sacrifice, he imparted to him the immaculate mysteries of Christ. Afterward the young man rejoiced in spirit, honoring Christ God with praise and glory.

Barlaam said to him:

“Blessed is God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who, in his great mercy, has regenerated in you a living hope unto an inheritance incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven in Christ Jesus our Lord through the Holy Spirit (1 Peter 1). For today you have been freed from sin, dedicated to God after receiving the pledge of eternal life; and, having abandoned the darkness, you have put on the light, adopted into the freedom of the glory of the children of God. ‘For as many as received him,’ he says, ‘to them he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name’ (John 1). Therefore you are no longer a slave, but a son and heir of God through Christ in the Holy Spirit (Galatians 4).

“Accordingly, dearest one, make it your endeavor to be found pure and undefiled before him, building proven works upon the foundation of faith. For faith without works is dead, just as works are dead without faith (2 Peter 3; James 2).

“And, as I remember having said to you before, now that you have laid aside all malice and the old self, which is corrupted according to the desires of error (Ephesians 4), and have come to hate all its works, long, like a newborn child, to suck the rational and guileless milk of the virtues (1 Peter 2), so that you may grow in it and attain to the knowledge of God’s commandments, to a perfect man, to the measure of the fullness of Christ (Ephesians 4). Thus you will no longer be a child in understanding, tossed and driven about by the waves and storm of vicious passions; rather, you will be a child in malice, but possess a firm and steadfast mind for what is good. You will conduct yourself, as is fitting, according to the calling with which you were called, observing the Lord’s commandments, having shaken off and removed from yourself the vanity of your former life, just as the Gentiles walk in the vanity of their understanding, having their intellect darkened, alienated from the glory of God, and subjected to their desires and to impulses turned away from reason.

“But you, just as you have approached the living and true God, so also walk as a child of light. For the fruit of the Spirit consists in all goodness, righteousness, and truth (Galatians 5). Take care not afterward to weaken through the oldness of your former life the new man whom you have put on today; rather, be renewed every day in righteousness, holiness, and truth. No one is unable to do this, if he wishes, as you have heard: he has given power to become children of God to those who believe in his name (John 1). Therefore we can no longer say that we are altogether unable to attain the virtues. The way is easy and accessible; and even though, because of the affliction of the body, it is said to be somewhat narrow and constricted (Matthew 11), it is nevertheless straight and bright, on account of the hope of the things to come, for those who do not walk foolishly but understand God’s will exactly, put on his armor to fight against the cunning devices of the enemy, the devil, and remain vigilant in prayer and supplication, with patience and hope, for this very purpose (Ephesians 6).

“Accordingly, just as you have heard and been instructed by me, and have laid a firm foundation, make progress in it, growing and advancing, and fulfilling the duty of a good soldier, holding faith and a good conscience confirmed by the testimony of honorable works (1 Timothy 6). Cultivate righteousness, piety, faith, love, patience, and gentleness; lay hold of eternal life, to which you were called; and remove far from yourself every desire for pleasure and vicious passion, not only in action but also in thought, so that you may present your soul to God pure from every defilement. For not our actions alone but also our thoughts are accounted before God, and they procure for us either crowns or punishments. We know that Christ, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, dwells in pure hearts. And we likewise know that, just as smoke drives away bees, so evil thoughts drive from us the grace of the divine Spirit.

“Therefore strive with the utmost zeal to extinguish and erase every vicious thought from your mind, and plant in it the finest thoughts, making yourself a temple of the Holy Spirit. For through thoughts we come to actions themselves; and every deed, proceeding from thought and the mind’s movement, begins at first from a small starting point, then grows through silent increments, and finally becomes immense. For this reason, do not allow a wicked habit to rule you in any way. Rather, while it is still fresh, tear up its small root from your breast, lest, when it has sprouted and driven its roots deep, it afterward be possible to eradicate it only with much time and great labor.

“For this reason greater sins gain daily access to us and obtain authority over our souls: because no proper correction is applied to what appear to be lesser faults—that is, wicked thoughts, shameful speech, and evil conversations. Just as those who neglect small wounds in the body commonly bring upon themselves suppuration and death, so the same thing happens in souls: those who regard the smallest vices and sins as nothing bring more serious ones upon themselves. As graver sins arise in them, the soul gradually acquires a settled habit and falls into contempt. ‘When the ungodly comes into the depth,’ he says, ‘he despises’ (Proverbs 8). Thereafter, just as a pig delights in wallowing in the mud (2 Peter 2), so that soul, immersed in an evil habit, no longer even senses the stench of its sins; rather, it rejoices and delights in them, clinging most tightly to vice as though it were some good thing. And even if, after recovering a better mind, it comes to feel its crimes, it is nevertheless not freed without great labor and sweat from the evil habit to which it willingly and voluntarily enslaved itself.

“Therefore remove yourself with all your strength from every evil thought and every vicious habit. Instead, become accustomed to the virtues, and cultivate and exercise them in such a way that you acquire a settled disposition toward them. For if you undertake a little labor in them and acquire their habit, afterward, with God’s help, you will advance without any labor. The habit of virtue, implanted in the soul—as it has a natural kinship with it and is aided by God—scarcely undergoes any change at all; above all, it is firm. Thus you see that courage, prudence, temperance, and justice scarcely admit any change, because dispositions, qualities, and activities of the soul penetrate it completely.

“For if the affections of vice, which are not natural to us but adventitious, can scarcely be removed once they have become habitual, what can be said against the conclusion that virtue—which has been implanted in us naturally by that supreme Father and Maker, and rests upon his aid and assistance—can much less be changed, if, after some labor on our part, it has taken root in the soul through habit?”

**Chapter XX**

A certain devotee of his also related the following to me:

“When,” he said, “I had acquired a most firmly established habit of divine contemplation, and my soul had been imbued with its meditation, I once wished to test the matter. I restrained my mind so firmly that I did not allow it, as was its custom, to join itself to meditation. I realized that it bore this very painfully and unwillingly, and that it hastened toward it with a kind of unbridled desire, unable in any way to turn toward an opposing thought.

“But when I had loosened the reins for it somewhat, it was immediately carried with the swiftest course toward its customary study and activity. There was fulfilled what the Prophet says:

> ‘As the deer longs for the springs of water,  
> so my soul longs for you, O God.  
> My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain’ (Psalm 41).

“From all this, then, it has been demonstrated that it lies within us to attain virtue, and that it is subject to our free choice and power whether we wish to embrace it or instead prefer sin to it. Those who have enslaved themselves to vice can indeed be drawn away from it only with difficulty, as I said above.

“But you, who have been freed through the tender mercies of our God and have put on Christ through the grace of the divine Spirit, transfer yourself wholly to the Lord. Do not open the door in any way to vicious passions. Rather, adorn your soul with the sweet fragrance and radiance of the virtues, make it a temple of the holy Trinity, and occupy all the faculties of your mind in contemplation of him.

“For if one who lives with and converses with an earthly king is proclaimed blessed by everyone, there can be no doubt that the one to whom it has been granted by divine favor to converse mentally with God and to enjoy fellowship with him is filled with every blessedness. Since this is so, always set him before your eyes and converse with him.

“But in what way will you converse with God? By approaching God through prayer and supplication. For the one who prays with the most ardent desire and a purified breast, withdrawing his mind from all material and earthly things and standing as though before God, and who offers his prayers to him with fear and trembling—this person truly enjoys fellowship with him and converses with him face to face.

“For our good God and Lord is present everywhere, hearing those who pray to him with a sincere and pure heart, as the Prophet says:

> ‘The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous,  
> and his ears are toward their prayers’ (Psalm 33).

“For this reason the Fathers define prayer as the union of man with God, and call it the work of angels and the prelude to future joy. They hold that the kingdom of heaven consists chiefly in this rather than in anything else: that one should approach the holy Trinity and contemplate it. Since constant prayer leads the mind to this as though by the hand, it has rightly been called a prelude, and as it were an image, of that blessedness.

“But not every prayer is of this kind. That name belongs finally only to prayer which has as its teacher God, who supplies its subject; which rises above all earthly things; and which lives with the Lord Christ without any intermediary.

“I wish you to acquire this prayer and strive to advance in it. For it has the power to lift you from earth into heaven. You will not progress in it rashly or without preparation; you will do so only after first purifying your soul from all vicious passions, wiping it clean from every evil thought and making it like a pure and newly polished mirror. You must also remove yourself far from every recollection of injuries and from anger—which is a greater hindrance than all the rest to the lifting of our prayers up to God—and forgive from your heart all who have wronged you. Then, by almsgiving and compassion toward the poor, add wings, as it were, to your prayer, and offer it to God with burning tears.

“Praying in this manner, you may use the same words as that blessed David, who was a king and was distracted by six hundred cares, yet nevertheless purified his soul from vicious passions and addressed God thus:

> ‘I have hated iniquity and abhorred it,  
> but I have loved your law.  
> Seven times a day I have praised you  
> because of the judgments of your righteousness.  
> My soul has kept your testimonies  
> and loved them exceedingly.  
> Let my supplication draw near before you, O Lord;  
> according to your word give me understanding’ (Psalm 118).

“When you cry out in this way, God will hear you, and while you are still speaking he will say: ‘Behold, I am here’ (Isaiah 85). Therefore, if you acquire such prayer, you will be blessed. For it is impossible that the one who prays and supplicates God with such eagerness of soul should not make daily progress in virtue and overcome all the snares of the enemy.

“For the one who, to use the words of a certain holy man, has warmed his mind, raised his soul, and transported himself into heaven, and thus invokes his Lord, recalls his crimes, converses with God about their forgiveness, and beseeches him with the hottest tears to show himself gracious and readily merciful according to his goodness—such a person, through the practice and habit of these words and thoughts, achieves this: that he lays aside all concern for this present life, rises above human passions, and is deemed worthy to be called God’s companion.

“What could happen that is more blessed or sublime than this? May you therefore, by God’s favor, become the possessor of this blessedness!

“Behold, I have shown you the way of the Lord’s commandments, and I have withheld nothing that would prevent me from declaring to you the whole counsel of God. I have now completed my ministry (Acts 20). It remains for you, with the loins of your mind girded, to make yourself holy in every aspect of your life, like that holy one who called you. ‘Be holy, for I am holy,’ says the Lord (Leviticus 19).

“The foremost of the apostles also speaks in this way:

> ‘If you call upon the Father, who judges each person’s work without partiality, conduct yourselves in fear during the time of your sojourn, knowing that you were redeemed from your futile way of life handed down by your ancestors, not with perishable gold or silver, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a spotless and undefiled lamb’ (1 Peter 1).

“Store all these things in your mind and recall them without interruption: the fear of God and his dreadful tribunal; the splendor that the righteous will receive in the age to come; and, in contrast, the sorrow of sinners in the most horrible darkness. Keep always before your eyes the weakness and vanity of present things and the eternity of those to come; and remember also that all flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass. ‘The grass withers, and its flower falls; but the word of the Lord remains forever’ (Isaiah 40).

“Always meditate on these things (1 Timothy 4), and may the peace of God be with you (Philippians 4)—the peace that will illumine you, instruct you in wisdom, lead you along the way of salvation, drive wicked willing far from your mind, and imprint the sign of the cross upon your soul, so that no stumbling-block of the perverse spirit may come near you. Thus, by divine favor, may you attain the future kingdom, perfect in every virtue, without end, termination, or succession, and may you be illumined by the light of the blessed Trinity, which is glorified in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.”

**Chapter XXI**

When the most excellent old man had instructed the king’s son with teachings suited to the formation of character, he withdrew to his lodging. The young man’s servants and tutors, seeing him frequently enter the palace, were astonished. One of them, who held the first place among them and whom the king had appointed over his son’s palace as one especially faithful and devoted to him, was named Zardan. He addressed the king’s son in these words:

“You are not unaware, my lord, of how greatly I fear your father, or of my loyalty toward him. For this reason he has ordered me, as his most faithful servant, to attend you. But now, seeing this foreigner conversing with you so frequently, I fear that he may be a follower of the Christian religion, which your father persecutes with immense hatred, and that I may consequently be found liable to capital punishment.

“Therefore either inform your father about him, or cease conversing with him hereafter; or, at least, lest I incur blame, send me away from your presence and ask your father to appoint another in my place.”

The king’s son said to him:

“Let us do this first, Zardan. Stand concealed behind a curtain, listen to his words to me, and then I will explain to you what you should do.”

When Barlaam was about to approach him, Zardan having been brought inside the curtain, he said to the old man:

“Repeat your divine teaching to me in summary, so that it may be more firmly implanted in my breast.”

Barlaam therefore, taking up the subject, delivered a long discourse about God and piety toward him: that he alone ought to be loved with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole mind, and that his commandments ought to be observed with fear and desire (Matthew 22); and that he himself had created all things, both those perceptible to the senses and those removed from the sight of the eyes.

He then recalled the creation of the first man, the commandment given to him, and the sentence imposed upon him by the Creator because he had violated the command. Next he recounted the good things from which we excluded ourselves by rejecting God’s command. Then he mentioned the troubles that miserably overwhelmed us after we had fallen from those good things.

Thereafter he added what concerned God’s kindness and love toward the human race: how that supreme Maker, caring for our salvation, sent teachers and prophets to proclaim the incarnation of the Only-Begotten. He then spoke of Christ’s descent, incarnation, benefits, miracles, the punishments he endured for us who were afflicted by the vice of ingratitude, his cross, the spear, his voluntary death, and finally our restoration and return to our former condition, and our return to the first good.

After this he spoke of the kingdom of heaven, which awaits those worthy of it; of the hidden and unquenchable fire of torment prepared for the wicked; of perpetual darkness, the immortal worm, and all the other punishments that those who have bound themselves in slavery to sin have heaped upon themselves.

When he had pursued these matters in his discourse and, toward the end, had turned to teaching suited to the formation of character, speaking at length about purity of life, condemning the vanity of present things, and exposing the misery of those who devote themselves wholly to them, he finally concluded his discourse with a prayer. He asked God to grant him a firm and steadfast confession of the orthodox faith, a life free from every reproach, and the purest administration of his office. After bringing the prayer to an end, he returned again to his lodging.

The king’s son summoned Zardan and, testing what he thought, said:

“You heard what this man told me—namely, that he is trying to lead me astray by the empty charm of his words, deprive me of this pleasant delight and enjoyment, and convert me to the worship of a foreign god?”

Zardan replied:

“What did you think you were doing, my king, by testing your servant? I plainly see that the man’s words have penetrated deeply into your breast. For if that were not so, you would not converse with him so willingly and continually.

“Indeed, we are by no means ignorant of this kind of preaching. But ever since your father raised up the most savage persecution against the Christians, they were expelled from here and their preaching fell silent. If this doctrine pleases you, and you are able to endure its harshness and labor, then may what has taken root in your mind be fortunate and blessed.

“But what am I to do? I cannot even look upon such harshness without aversion, and through fear of the king I have my mind torn apart by anguish and bitterness. What excuse shall I use before him, since I have neglected his commands and allowed this man access to you?”

The king’s son said to him:

“Recognizing nothing else that could adequately repay your great goodwill toward me, I have found no greater service from you than this: to make that good which surpasses nature clear to you—that is, to make you understand for what end you were created, recognize your Creator, abandon the darkness, and hasten toward the light. I was hoping that as soon as you heard something of it, you would follow it with a most ardent desire.

“But, as I see, I have been deceived in my hope, since I observe that you are lukewarm toward what has been said. If you report these matters to the king, my father, you will gain nothing from it except to fill his mind with cares and sorrows. But if you are well-disposed and sincere toward him, take care that he learn nothing of this from you before a favorable opportunity presents itself.”

After he had addressed him in this way, it seemed that he was “sowing upon water.”

[Note: “To sow upon water.” Theognis:

> “It is equal to sowing seeds in the gray sea’s waters.”

It seemed, that is, like entrusting seed to the waters of the sea.]

For access to wisdom will never be opened to a foolish mind.

The next day Barlaam approached him and began to speak of his departure. The young man, unable to bear being separated from him, was tortured in spirit and wholly drenched in tears. The old man spoke with him at length, urged him to remain steadfast in goodness, and strengthened his heart with words suited to encouragement. Then he begged him in prayer to allow him to depart with a cheerful and joyful spirit. He added that the brief separation between them would soon be followed by a renewed union free from all division.

But the king’s son, unable either to trouble the old man any longer or to prevent him from undertaking the journey he desired, and moreover fearing that Zardan might inform the king about him and subject him to punishment, addressed him in these words:

“Since this has so firmly taken root in your mind, spiritual Father, excellent teacher, and author of every good for me—since you are determined to abandon me, who am entangled in the vanity of the world, and depart for the place of spiritual rest—I no longer dare to detain you or stand in your way. Go, then, surrounded by the peace of God; and do not cease to remember my misery in your splendid prayers to the Lord, so that at last I may come to you and behold your face.

“I ask one thing of you: since you refused to accept anything for your companions in the religious life, at least accept from me a small amount of money for food and clothing.”

The old man replied:
