“Since I accepted nothing from you for my brothers—for they have no need to receive anything from the things of this world, from which they have voluntarily withdrawn themselves—how could I acquire for myself what I forbade them? If possession of money were good, I would certainly have bestowed it upon them before myself. But since I know that possessing it is destructive, do not entangle either them or me in such snares.”

[Note: Understand this as referring to riches that someone misuses.]

When he could not persuade him of this either, he turned again to a second request. Humbly he begged him not to disregard his prayers entirely or overwhelm him with every kind of sorrow, but to leave him that worn and rough cloak, weathered by age—both to renew the memory of his teacher’s religious life and to serve as protection against all Satan’s assaults—and to accept another garment in its place. “Then,” he said, “when you see what I have given you, you will retain the memory of my humility.”

The old man said:

“It is not permitted me to give you my old and worn cloak and receive another garment, lest divine judgment declare that I have received here the reward for my small labor. Nevertheless, so that I may not blunt your eagerness, let the garments you give me be old and no different from my own.”

The king’s son therefore searched out some rough and old rags and gave them to the old man. Receiving his clothing in exchange, he experienced great joy, considering it incomparably better than any purple robe or royal ornament.

The most divine Barlaam, eager to depart at once, spoke of the matters relating to his departure and gave him this final instruction:

“My dearest brother and sweetest son, whom I have begotten through the Gospel (1 Corinthians 4), you know to which King you have given your name and with whom you have entered into a covenant. Therefore you must keep that covenant firmly and fulfill with cheerful spirit all the duties of warfare that you promised in the document of such a covenant, in the presence and testimony of the entire heavenly army, which also committed the covenant itself to writing.

“If you fulfill these things, you will be blessed. Accordingly, you must take care not to prefer any present thing to God and to his blessings. For what terror can present things bring that compares with the torment of eternal fire, which burns in such a way that it is entirely without light and never comes to an end of burning?

“And again, what good does this world possess that can fill the soul with such delight that it compares with God’s giving himself to those who love him? His beauty surpasses every word, his power is unconquerable, his glory eternal, and the good things awaiting his friends surpass incomparably everything that the eyes see:

> ‘What eye has not seen, nor ear heard,  
> nor has entered into the heart of man’ (1 Corinthians 2).

“May it be granted you to become an heir of these things, enclosed and fortified by the mighty hand of God!”

The king’s son, drenched in tears, was distressed and afflicted with the greatest anguish, unable to endure being abandoned by his most loving father and excellent teacher.

“And who,” he exclaimed, “Father, will fulfill your role? Whom shall I finally obtain as such a shepherd and guide? By what consolation shall I ease my longing for you? Behold, you have brought me, an evil and rebellious servant, to God, placed me among the ranks of sons and heirs, sought out me, who was lost and exposed as prey to every beast, and joined me to those sheep of God who had not gone astray (Luke 15). You have shown me the short path of truth (Psalm 85), led me out of darkness and the shadow of death (Luke 1), and drawn my feet away from the slippery, destructive, perverse, and crooked path.

“Great and wonderful benefits have arisen for me from you—benefits whose extraordinary greatness no speech could ever express. May you therefore also become, on behalf of me, a little man, a participant in his great benefits; and may the Lord supply what is lacking in my thanksgiving, he who alone surpasses in requiting benefits those endowed with love for him.”

Barlaam cut short his lamentations, rose, and prepared himself to pray. Raising his hands toward heaven, he spoke these words:

“God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, you who have flooded with light the things that were previously covered in darkness, and brought forth from nothing all created things, both those perceived by sight and those removed from the sight of the eyes; you who have turned back your creature and did not permit us, after our folly, to depart; we give thanks to you and to your power and wisdom—that is, to our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom you also made the ages (Hebrews 1). You raised us, who had fallen and lay prostrate; you forgave the sins of those who offended; you brought back those wandering in error; you redeemed captives; and, through the precious blood of your Son and our Lord, you restored to life those extinguished by death.

“I therefore call upon you, and upon your only-begotten Son, and upon your most holy Spirit. Look upon this rational sheep, which through me, an unworthy man, approaches your altar, and sanctify its soul by your power and grace. Visit this vineyard (Psalm 79), which was planted by your Holy Spirit, and grant it to bear the fruit of righteousness. Strengthen him, confirming your covenant in him; and by the wisdom of your good Spirit rescue him from the devil’s deceit and imposture. Teach him to do your will (Psalm 142), and do not withdraw your help from him (Psalm 50).

“May it be granted by your favor that both he and I, your useless servant, may inherit your blessings, which know no end. For you are blessed and glorified forever. Amen” (Daniel 3).

When he had finished the prayer, he turned and kissed him, now the son of the heavenly Father. After praying for peace and eternal salvation for him, he left the palace and departed joyfully, giving thanks to God, by whose favor his journey had succeeded according to his heart’s desire.

**Chapter XXII**

After Barlaam had departed, Josaphat devoted himself to prayer. Pouring forth the hottest tears, he spoke in this manner:

“God, attend to my help; Lord, hasten to help me (Psalm 69). For the poor man is abandoned to you; you will be the helper of the orphan (Psalm 9). Look upon me and have mercy on me (Psalm 85), who wish all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (2 Timothy 1). Preserve me, although I am an unworthy little man, I beg you, and strengthen me, so that I may walk in the way of your holy commandments. For I am weak and wretched, and I do not possess the strength to do anything good. But you can bring salvation to me, you who contain and preserve all things, both those seen by the eyes and those that cannot be seen.

“Do not permit me to go after the wicked desires of my flesh; rather, teach me to do your will (Psalm 142), and preserve me for eternal and blessed life. O Father, Son, and divine Spirit, consubstantial and undivided Godhead, I call upon you; I glorify you. For everything created praises you, and the intellectual and bodiless powers glorify you forever. Amen.”

Thereafter he guarded himself with the greatest diligence and prepared himself in such a way as to acquire purity of soul and body. He lived in continence, and extended his prayers and supplications throughout the entire course of the night.

Since during the day he often found himself interrupted—both by the companionship of those who lived with him and sometimes by the king’s visits to him or by being summoned by the king—the night made up for what the day lacked. He remained in prayer and tears until dawn, imploring God’s help. Thus that prophetic saying was also fulfilled in him:

> “By night lift up your hands in the holy places,  
> and bless the Lord” (Psalm 113).

But when that Zardan learned of this manner of life, and was deeply saddened and tormented by grave anxieties, not knowing what to do, he was finally overcome by sorrow and withdrew to his own house, pretending to be ill.

When the king learned of this, he sent another of those whom he considered most faithful to serve his son in Zardan’s place. He himself, concerned for Zardan’s health, sent him the most famous physician and asked the physician to devote the greatest care to his treatment.

The physician, perceiving that Zardan was valued and favored by the king, visited him diligently. After examining his condition carefully, he immediately informed the king that he had been unable to discover anything in him that could have caused illness. He therefore judged that Zardan had fallen ill because he was suffering from some sorrow of the mind.

When the king heard this, he supposed that Zardan had been treated harshly by his son and had withdrawn in grief for that reason. Wishing to learn what had happened, he announced that he would visit Zardan the next day to discover the cause of the illness.

When Zardan was informed of this promise, he set out for the king as soon as day broke, having put on suitable clothing. As soon as he entered, he prostrated himself and worshiped him on the ground.

The king said:

“What force drove you to come to me? I myself intended to go to you and declare my affection for you to everyone.”

Zardan replied:

“My illness, O king, is not of the kind from which people ordinarily suffer. Rather, because of sorrow of mind, my heart fell into anguish, and my body also suffered with it. It would be madness for me, in such a condition, not to come to you in the manner proper to a servant, but instead to wait for your royal majesty to come to me, your servant, and weary itself.

When the king asked what had plunged him into this sorrow, Zardan replied:

“A great danger threatens me, and I recognize myself as deserving great punishments and many forms of death, because, by obeying your commands negligently, I have already brought upon you an immense sorrow.”

Again, when the king asked him what this negligence was into which he had fallen, and what the danger was in which he found himself, he replied: “While in the custody of my master, your son, I proved negligent. For a certain wicked impostor entered and spoke to him about the teaching of the Christian religion. Afterwards he related to the king in detail what conversations the old man had held with his son, how much pleasure the latter had taken in them, and that he had wholly devoted himself to Christ. He even told him the old man’s name, saying that he was called Barlaam. For the king had already heard much about Barlaam and the extreme severity of his religious life. But when these things reached the king’s ears, such grief arose in him that he was utterly shaken, seethed with anger, and was almost deprived of life by the news. At once he summoned a certain Araches, who held the second rank of dignity after him, was first in all secret counsels, and moreover possessed knowledge of astrology. With great grief and consternation of spirit he related to him what had happened. But when Araches saw his agitation and confusion of mind, he said: ‘Cease, O king, to be sorrowful and disturbed in spirit. I do not doubt that I shall myself dissuade him from his present opinion; indeed, I am fully convinced that shortly he will renounce that impostor’s teaching and comply with your will.’”

When Araches had turned the king’s mind toward cheerfulness by these words, he applied himself to considering the matter. “First, O king,” he said, “let us do this: let us make every effort to seize that pestilential Barlaam. If we succeed, believe me, we shall not miss our mark or be deceived in our hope. For he himself, either by words suited to persuasion or compelled by various instruments of torture, even against his will and in resistance, will confess that his words are false and full of error; he will turn my master, your son, from his opinion and bring him to adhere to his father’s doctrines. But if we cannot seize him, I know another hermit, an old man named Nachor, so exactly like Barlaam that he can scarcely be distinguished from him. He professes the same doctrine as we do, and I had him as my teacher in mathematics. I shall therefore go to him by night, explain everything to him in detail, and then, after spreading the report that Barlaam has been arrested, we shall present him in Barlaam’s place. He too, taking the name of Barlaam, will pretend to honor the Christian rites and will profess to regard and defend them. Afterwards, after a long debate, he will finally be defeated and yield. When your son sees this—that is, when he sees that Barlaam has been overcome and that our doctrine has carried the day—there is no doubt that he will join the side of the victors. This consideration is also of great importance: he fears your majesty and earnestly desires to obey you. Add that the man who assumes Barlaam’s role will also come to his senses and declare that he had been in error.”

The king was delighted by this speech and judged the man’s plan excellent, relying, of course, on an empty hope. Accordingly, when he learned that Barlaam had recently departed, he hastened to seize him. He sent soldiers and centurions to occupy the various exits of the roads; but he himself mounted his horse and pursued Barlaam with all speed along the route he considered most suspect, intending by every means to overtake him. After exhausting himself in this futile labor for six full days, he remained in a certain royal palace situated in the countryside. But he sent Araches with a considerable number of horsemen as far as the Sennaarite desert to search for Barlaam.

When Araches reached that place, he threw all its inhabitants into confusion. When they denied having seen the man, he entered the desert to hunt for the holy men. After traversing much of the desert, encircling the mountains, and crossing on foot, with the men he had brought with him, certain valleys that were entirely unfrequented and difficult to approach, he proceeded toward a hill. At its summit he saw a company of hermits walking about. Without delay he ordered them to be brought before him.

The soldiers therefore hurried toward the hill at the greatest speed, each striving to outstrip the others. When they arrived there, they surrounded the hermits like many dogs (Psalm XXI), or like certain pestilential and savage beasts. They seized them—men worthy of veneration both in appearance and in dress, bearing on their faces the marks of solitary discipline—and dragged them before Araches. They were so disposed in spirit that they were neither disturbed in any way nor displayed or uttered anything cowardly or sorrowful. The man who led all the others, like their superior, carried a sack woven of haircloth, filled with relics of certain holy Fathers who had departed this life.

When Araches saw them and did not see Barlaam—for he knew him—he was troubled with grief and said to them: “Where is that impostor who led the king’s son into error?”

The man carrying the sack replied: “He is not among us—far from it. Driven away by the grace of Christ, he fled from us. Rather, he has his dwelling among you.”

“Then you know him?” the commander asked.

“Certainly,” replied the hermit. “I know him who is called the impostor: the devil, who dwells in your midst and is worshiped and honored by you.”

“I am asking about Barlaam,” said the commander. “I was asking where he was.”

“Why, then,” said the monk, “did you speak so perversely about the man who committed an imposture against the king’s son when you questioned me? For if you were looking for Barlaam, you ought to have said: ‘Where is the man who brought the king’s son back from error to the true path and granted him salvation?’ He is our brother and a companion in religious discipline. It has already been many days since we saw him.”

“Show me his dwelling,” said Araches.

The monk replied: “If he wished to see you, he himself would have come out to meet you. But it is not permitted us to point out his dwelling.”

At this the commander, inflamed with indignation and glaring at him with an angry and furious face, said: “I shall now slaughter you by new and unheard-of forms of death unless you immediately produce Barlaam for me.”

“And what,” said the monk, “do you see in us that we should reluctantly be torn from this life because of our attachment to it, or fear the death you would bring upon us? Rather, we shall be grateful to you for leading us out of life while we cling to the pursuit of virtue. The uncertain hazard of our departure does not cause us much fear—namely, that we do not know in what condition death will seize us, lest perhaps some lapse of will or some assault of the devil bend the steadfastness of our discipline and persuade us to think or do something contrary to the agreements we have made with God. Therefore, since you have now entirely abandoned hope of attaining what you promised yourselves, do without hesitation whatever you please. We shall neither point out the dwelling of our holy brother, although we know it, nor reveal any other monasteries unknown to you merely to escape death shamefully. Rather, we shall meet death nobly, having first offered the sweat of virtue and now offering to God the blood of courageous resolve.”

The wicked man could not endure this freedom of speech. Moved instead to the fiercest anger by such greatness of spirit, he inflicted on them many blows and tortures. Yet they endured them in such a way that even the tyrant himself was filled with admiration for the strength and courage of their spirits. When he could not bend them even after imposing many punishments, and no one among them could be found willing to point out Barlaam, he ordered them to be seized and taken to the king, beaten on the way, and subjected to insults, while they continued to carry the sack of relics.

### CHAPTER XXIII

After a considerable number of days had passed, Araches brought them before the king and informed him of their condition. Then, when the king had been inflamed with the bitterest anger, he presented them to him. On seeing them, the king seethed with indignation and displayed the appearance of a raging man. He ordered them to be beaten most cruelly; and when he saw that they had been mangled by the blows in a dreadful fashion, he scarcely emerged from his immense fury and ordered the executioners to stop beating them. Then he said to them:

“Why do you carry these bones of the dead? If you carry them out of longing for those to whom they belong, I shall place you with them this very hour, so that, having obtained what you desire, you may be grateful to me.”

The leader and superior of that divine company, regarding the king’s threats as nothing—as though nothing adverse had happened to him—replied in a free voice and with a radiant face that showed the grace dwelling in his soul:

“We carry these pure and holy bones about for this reason: that we may in some measure assuage our longing for the admirable men to whom they belong, recall to ourselves their religious discipline and life dear to God, and stir ourselves to pursue that same life. Setting before our eyes the rest and delights in which they now dwell, we proclaim them blessed and encourage one another to follow in their footsteps. We also acquire from them the remembrance of death, which brings immense benefit and makes us ready, as though winged, for the struggles of religious life; and through contact with them we draw sanctity.”

The king asked again: “If, as you say, the remembrance of death produces benefit, why do you employ this remembrance upon the bones of others, which are alien and decayed, rather than upon the bones of your own bodies, which belong to you and will soon perish?”

The monk replied: “I have given five reasons why we carry the relics, yet you answer only one of them and use sophistry against us. But believe me: the bones of those who have already died represent the remembrance of death more clearly than do the bones of those who still enjoy the use of this life. Since you hold that the bones in your own flesh place death before your eyes, why is it that, mindful of the death that is already approaching, you do not take proper care of your affairs? Instead, you surrender your soul to every kind of wickedness and seek to destroy, with savage cruelty, the worshipers of God and those devoted to piety—men who have neither harmed you nor any share in present affairs with you, nor seek to take anything from you?”

The king said: “I punish you as pestilential men and seducers of the people, because you drive everyone into deception and call them away from the pleasures of life. In place of a sweet life and the most pleasant desires, you compel them to embrace this harsh, filthy, and miserable way of life, and you proclaim that the honor due to the gods ought to be given to Jesus. Therefore, lest the people, following your imposture, abandon the land, cease to honor their ancestral gods, and worship a stranger, I have judged you worthy of punishment and death.”

The monk replied: “If you wish everyone to share in the goods of this life, why do you not distribute your pleasures and wealth equally among all? Instead, very many are afflicted by poverty, while you add their possessions, seized by force, to your own. From this it is clear that you are not at all concerned for the people’s salvation; rather, you fatten your flesh, preparing material for worms to gnaw. For this reason, having renounced the God of all, you have called those who are nothing and who invented every kind of wickedness ‘gods,’ so that while you live lustfully and wickedly in imitation of them, you may attain the reputation of being an imitator of the gods. For what can be said against the proposition that human beings who set their minds upon your gods do the same things that your gods have done?

“You are therefore certainly sunk in great error, O king. You fear that we may persuade some of your subjects to assent to our decrees, defect from your rule, and join the side of him who contains and preserves all things. For you desire to have many servants of your greed, so that they may undergo hardships while your profits increase through their labor—just as someone who raises dogs or birds trained for the hunt first caresses them before the prey, but after they have seized something, snatches the prey from their mouths.

“In the same way, because you desire to have many people bringing you tribute and taxes, some from the land and some from the sea, you say that you are concerned for their welfare; yet you bring them everlasting ruin before you yourself summon destruction upon yourself. You are satisfied merely that riches, more worthless than any dung or mud, should flow to you, and you do not perceive that you are embracing darkness instead of light. But emerge, I beg you, from this heavy sleep, open your closed eyes, and behold the glory of our God, shining upon everything from every side. At last return to yourself. ‘Understand, you foolish among the people; and you fools, become wise at last’ (Psalm XXXIX). Know this: there is no other God besides our God (Psalm XVII), nor is there salvation anywhere except in him.”

The king replied: “Put an end to these foolish trifles of yours, and immediately show me Barlaam; otherwise you will experience instruments of punishment of a kind you have never yet tested.”

But that most courageous monk, a lover of heavenly philosophy and endowed with exceptional greatness of spirit, was in no way moved from his conviction by the king’s threats. Standing with fearless courage, he said:

“It has not been commanded us, O king, to do what you order, but what has been commanded by our Lord, who teaches us to pursue temperance, to keep every pleasure and desire under control, to cultivate courage, and to endure every labor and affliction for the sake of justice. Therefore, the more grievous evils you inflict upon us for the sake of piety, the more nobly you will have served us. Do whatever you please; we shall not commit anything contrary to what is right or devote ourselves to sin. Do not think it a slight crime if we hand over to you our fellow combatant and fellow soldier. Yet you will not mock us on this account, even if you inflict six hundred deaths upon us. We are not so cowardly that, out of fear of your tortures, we would betray our philosophy or commit anything unworthy of the divine law. Bring forth, then, whatever instruments of torture you know against us. For to us ‘to live is Christ, and to die is gain’ (Philippians I).”

Inflamed with fury at these words, the king ordered that their God-speaking tongues be cut out, their eyes torn out, and their hands and feet cut off. After this sentence had been pronounced, the executioners and attendants surrounding them mutilated them inhumanely and cruelly. With a kind of bestial ferocity they drew out their tongues from their mouths with hooks and cut them off; they tore out their eyes with iron claws; and finally, using instruments with which they mangled their hands and feet, they severed them. But those blessed, venerable, and noble men, as though invited to a banquet, advanced steadfastly and courageously to their torments, strengthening one another with mutual exhortations and proceeding with brave and fearless spirit to undergo death for Christ.

Amid such varied punishments, the seventeen most holy monks [Note: [Col. 0606B] “The most holy monks.” Concerning these, I think, see the Roman Martyrology, 3 August: “Among the Indians neighboring Persia, the passion of the holy monks and other faithful, whom King Abenner persecuted and ordered to be beaten after subjecting them to various punishments.” Unless the Martyrology is referring to those mentioned above in this Life, chapter 1.] commended their courageous and steadfast souls to the Lord. From this it is plainly evident that a soul endowed with piety rules over vicious passions, just as Josephus, a man outside our doctrines, related when he commemorated the struggles of the aged priest and his seven sons, who fought together with their mother, possessing exactly the same conviction, in defense of the law of their country. These distinguished Fathers, citizens of the Jerusalem above, were in no way inferior to them in endurance and greatness of spirit.

### CHAPTER XXIV

After they had met their holy death, the king said to his chief counselor Araches: “Since the first plan has failed completely, turn your attention to the second and arrange for Nachor to be summoned.”

Araches therefore went in the dead of night to his cave, for Nachor lived in the desert and practiced divination. After Araches had explained to him the entire plan they had devised, he returned to the king as soon as day broke. Then, having again obtained horses, he pretended to set out to search for Barlaam. When he had departed and was examining the solitary places, he saw a man emerging from a certain ravine. He ordered his companions to pursue him, and they hastened so swiftly that they seized the man and brought him before Araches.

When Araches asked who he was, what religion he followed, and by what name he was called, the man declared that he was a Christian and was named Barlaam—as he had been instructed by them. Delighted at hearing this name, Araches, as he outwardly appeared, accepted him and returned as quickly as possible to the king, presenting the man to him. In the hearing of those standing nearby, the king said:

“Then you are that servant of the demon, Barlaam?”

The man replied: “I am a servant of God, not of demons; therefore do not assail me with insults. You ought to give me very great thanks, for I have freed your son from error and imposture, taught him the worship of God, restored him to favor with the true God, and trained him in every virtue.”

Again the king assumed an angry expression and said: “It would have been fitting for me to deprive you of every power of speech and defense and to put you to death without questioning you. But in my humanity I shall spare you until I have examined your case on a fixed day. If you decide to obey me, you will obtain pardon; if not, you will suffer the worst of deaths.”

Having said this, he handed him over to Araches and instructed him to guard him with the greatest care.

The following day he returned from there to his palace. Suddenly the report spread that Barlaam had been captured, so much so that the king’s son himself, on hearing it, was afflicted with the deepest grief and could not restrain his tears in any way. Instead, amid groans and lamentations, he entreated God and implored him to aid the old man.

Nor did that good God despise him in his mourning. He is kind to those who await his help in the day of tribulation, and he recognizes those who fear him. Therefore, in a nocturnal vision, he made everything known to the young man, strengthened him, and confirmed him for the struggle of piety. When he awoke, he found that his heart, which shortly before had been crushed by sorrow and grief, was filled with joy, confidence, and the sweetest light.

The king, having carried out these actions and formed this plan, rejoiced, thinking that he had employed an excellent strategy, and showing Araches the greatest gratitude. But, to use the words of the divine David, “iniquity lied to itself” (Psalm XXIX), and justice carried off the victory against iniquity, utterly overthrowing and casting it down; “its memory perished with a sound” (Psalm IX), as will be shown by the continuation of the narrative.

Two days later the king went to his son’s palace. When the son came out to meet him, the father did not kiss him in his customary manner. Instead, appearing indignant and angry, he entered the royal chamber and sat down with a sorrowful face. Then he summoned his son and addressed him as follows:

“My son, what is this report that has reached my ears and is filling my mind with grief? I do not think that any man was ever filled with as much joy at the birth of a son as I experienced because of you; nor do I believe that anyone ever received such grief from a son as I have now received from you. You have disgraced my gray hairs, taken away the light of my eyes, and cut off the strength of my limbs. The fear I feared on your account has come upon me; what I dreaded has happened to me. I have become a mockery to my enemies and a laughingstock to my adversaries (Job III).

“With a foolish mind and childish judgment you have believed the words of impostors, preferring the counsel of wicked and malevolent men to my counsel. You have abandoned the worship of our gods and turned to the worship of a foreign God. What came into your mind, my son, that you should do these things? You, whom I had hoped to raise in complete security, whom I thought would be the staff and strength of my old age and whom I intended to leave as the best successor to my kingdom—you have not hesitated to display toward me the evidence of an enemy’s and hostile spirit.

“Was it not fitting that you should obey me and follow my secrets rather than yield to the trifles and foolish speeches of that deceitful and filthy old man, who put this into your mind: that in place of a sweet life you should undertake a bitter one, and in place of the most pleasant delights enter upon that hard and rugged path which the son of Mary urges you to follow?

“Do you not also fear the anger of the greatest gods, lest they strike you with lightning or destroy you with thunder because, having rejected and counted as nothing those who have bestowed so many and such great benefits upon us, adorned us with the royal diadem, subjected innumerable nations to our authority and rule, and finally brought it about—through the effect of my prayers and supplications—that you should be born and become a participant in this sweetest light, you have bound yourself most closely to him who was crucified? You have been deceived by the empty promises of his worshipers, who invent new ages, babble about the resurrection of dead bodies, and introduce six hundred other absurdities in order to deceive foolish men.

“But now at least, dearest son, if you think that you ought to obey me, bid these lengthy follies a long farewell and sacrifice, I beg you, to the benevolent gods. Let us strive to appease them with very many victims and sacrifices, so that you may obtain pardon from them for your error, since they possess the power both to bestow benefits and to inflict punishments.

“We ourselves are an example to you of what we have said. By their favor we have attained this empire, and we repay them for their benefaction by honoring their worshipers and torturing with punishments those who cannot be induced to sacrifice to them.”

As the king continued to recount such absurdities, disparaging and condemning our doctrines while praising and extolling the worship of idols, the most divine young man, seeing that the matter had reached the point where he no longer desired a corner and hiding place but rather a lampstand and a mirror (Matthew V), spoke with complete freedom and confidence as follows:

“What I have done, O lord, I shall by no means deny. Abandoning darkness, I hastened toward the light; leaving error behind, I joined myself to the truth. I sent my farewell to the demons and joined the ranks of Christ, who is the Son and Word of God the Father. By his word all things were brought into being from nothing, and after forming man from the earth, he breathed into him the breath of life and placed him in the paradise of delight, so that he might dwell there.

“When man violated his command and thereby made himself subject to death and subjected himself to the power of the dreadful ruler of the world, Christ nevertheless did not cease to do everything necessary to restore him to his former dignity. Therefore he who brought all created things into being, the architect of our race, became man for our sake. Coming to earth and being born of the holy Virgin, he lived among human beings (Baruch III). For us ungrateful servants the Lord underwent death—indeed, death on a cross (Philippians II)—so that the tyranny of sin might be abolished, the former condemnation erased, and the gates of heaven opened to us once more. For he lifted our nature there and placed it upon the throne of glory, and he granted an endless kingdom to those who love him, together with goods surpassing all speech and hearing (1 Corinthians II).

“He is the strong one, the only one who is powerful, the King of kings and Lord of lords (Revelation XIX), whose strength is unconquerable and whose power exceeds every conjecture of the human mind; he alone is holy and rests among the holy; he is glorified with the Father and the Holy Spirit. In their name I was baptized, and them I confess, celebrate, and adore: one God in three persons, consubstantial and free from confusion, uncreated, immortal, eternal, infinite, removed from every limitation, without a body, alien to disturbance, change, and alteration, lacking every boundary, the source of goodness, justice, and eternal light, the maker of all created things, both those that can be seen and those that escape the eyes’ perception, containing and preserving all things, providing for all things, and holding dominion and authority over all.

“For without him nothing was made, nor can anything be formed or endure without his providence. He is the life of all things, the bond of all things, the illumination of all things, wholly sweetness, and wholly desirable without satiety (Song of Songs V); he is the highest summit of everything that ought to be desired.

“Why, then, O father, would it be the act of anything but folly and madness to abandon this God, endowed with such goodness and power, and to worship impure demons, the architects of every vice? Why give worship and veneration to deaf and mute statues that neither are nor will be anything? When have they ever been heard to speak? When have they given even the smallest thing to those who offered prayers to them? When have they walked or received any sensation? Those who stood have never remembered sitting, nor have those who sat ever been seen standing.

“When I had learned from a holy man of their shamefulness, stench, and stupidity, as well as the weakness and feebleness of the demons working in them and using them to deceive you; when I had rejected their wickedness and pursued it with perfect hatred, I joined myself to the living and true God and shall serve him to my last breath, so that my spirit may at the end pass into his hands.

“When such great blessings, incapable of being explained by any speech, had come before me, I rejoiced that I had been freed from the slavery of wicked demons, recalled from dreadful captivity, and illumined by the light of the Lord’s countenance (Psalm IV). But this distressed me and tore my mind apart: that you, my lord and father, did not share in such benefits. Yet fearing the stubbornness of your mind in your opinion, I kept my grief pressed within my breast, since I did not wish to provoke your anger. Nevertheless, I did not cease praying and entreating God to recall you from the distant exile you had brought upon yourself, when you became a fugitive from piety and a servant of every vice and impiety.

“But since you yourself, O father, have brought my affairs into the open, hear what my settled judgment is. I shall not break the covenant I have made with my God—no, by him who redeemed me from slavery with his precious blood. Since you now know what I have in mind, cease troubling yourself by trying to draw me away from my noble confession. Just as your attempt would be futile and useless if you resolved to seize the heavens with your hand or dry up the entire sea, so you may be convinced that this attempt too will be futile. Therefore either obey my counsel and join yourself to Christ, so that you may receive those goods that surpass all thought and so that we may be companions not only in nature but also in faith; or, believe me, I shall withdraw from your sonship and worship my God with a pure conscience.”

When the king heard all this, he was immediately seized by uncontrollable fury and spoke angrily to him, gnashing his teeth like a madman:

“Who else is responsible for such evils as these, except you? I myself embraced you with such love and did such things for your sake as no father ever did. It was this very indulgence of mine that gave your perverse and stubborn mind the strength to rage against me. It was not without reason, then, that the astrologers said at your birth that you would be a wicked, depraved, arrogant, and disobedient man toward your parents. But if you now also cause my plan to fail, I shall regard you as an enemy and punish you in such a way that no one would display such cruelty even toward his enemies.”

He replied again: “Why, O king, are you inflamed with anger and tormented for this reason—that I have obtained such great blessings from God? When has any father ever been seen to grieve and be distressed at his son’s happiness? And how should such a man be called a father rather than an enemy? Therefore I shall no longer call you father, but shall withdraw from you as one flees from a serpent, if I see clearly that you begrudge my salvation and seek to drive me forcibly into destruction.

“For if you wish to use force against me and deal tyrannically with me, as you have said, believe me, you will gain nothing else by this except to be called, in place of father, a tyrant and executioner. It would be easier for you to follow the tracks of an eagle and fly through the air itself than to draw me away from my faith in Christ and from the noble covenant I have made with him.

“But understand, O father; dispel this dimness and cataract of the mind’s eyes; look upward and behold the light of my God, shining upon all things from every side, and at last allow yourself to be illumined by his sweetest radiance. Why have you surrendered yourself entirely to the affections and desires of the flesh and cannot in any way rise above them? Understand this: ‘All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass withered, and its flower fell; but the word of my Lord, which has been proclaimed to all, remains forever’ (1 Peter II).

“Why, then, do you cling so desperately and insanely to a glory that withers and is destroyed like fresh flowers? Why embrace accursed and filthy pleasures, and the appetites of the belly and of the parts below the belly—pleasures that delight the senses of fools for a time but are later digested more bitterly than gall, when these shadows and the empty dreams of this life have passed away and their lovers, together with those who practice wickedness, are hurled into the perpetual, dark torment of an unquenchable fire? Among them—you dreadful thought—you too will be confined. For your criminal counsels you will suffer heavy remorse, long for these days, and remember my words. But you will derive no benefit from such remorse, since in hell there is no place for repentance or confession (Psalm VI).”

For the present time has been appointed for labor, but the future for reward. And indeed, even if present pleasures were not subject to decay and destruction, but endured forever with their possessors, ought they therefore to have been preferred to Christ’s benefits and to blessings superior to every thought? For just as the sun is brighter and more splendid than deep night, so—and much more so—the blessings promised to those endowed with love of God are more illustrious and magnificent than any earthly kingdom. It was therefore altogether fitting to regard the greater and more excellent things as prior to those that are inferior and more worthless.

But since all the affairs of this life are subject to corruption (Job XIV), and pass away and are destroyed like a dream and a shadow (Psalm CXLIII), so that one should place confidence rather in unstable winds and in the tracks of a ship running across the sea than in human prosperity, what sort of simplicity—or, more accurately, folly and madness—is this: to consider things that are transient, weak, and subject to corruption—indeed, things that are absolutely nothing—better than those that are free from corruption and eternal, and, for the sake of the fruits of transient things, to be deprived of the fruits of those blessings that are beyond all succession? [Col. 0538D]

Will you not understand this, father? Will you not let passing things pass away and direct your mind toward what is firm and certain? Will you not prefer your homeland to exile, light to darkness, spirit to flesh, eternal life to the shadow of death, and things that do not dissolve to those that are fleeting and fragile? Will you not withdraw yourself from the atrocious slavery of the horrible ruler of this world—that is, of the perverse Devil—and betake yourself to the Lord, most inclined toward goodness and mercy? [Col. 0539A] Will you not withdraw yourself from the worship of the many fictitious gods and offer worship to the one living and true God?

For although you have sinned against God, when you poured forth many blasphemies against Him and killed His servants after subjecting them to grievous torments, I nevertheless do not doubt that He will receive you when you return to a better mind and will cast all your offenses from His memory. For He does not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live (Ezekiel XVIII)—He who, in order to seek us when we were straying from the right path, descended from that height which no words can describe, endured the cross and death for our sake, and redeemed us, who were sold under sin, with His precious blood. To Him be praise and glory forever and ever. Amen (Romans VII). [Col. 0539B]

The king, however, was seized simultaneously by amazement and anger: by amazement because of his son’s prudence and because of such arguments, which could in no way be refuted; by anger because he did not cease to disparage and accuse his gods and was attacking and assailing his entire way of life. Because of the dense inward darkness within him, he did not admit the brilliance of this speech. Yet, since the affection implanted by nature prevented him from punishing his son or inflicting any harm upon him, and since he utterly despaired of being able to move him from his conviction, he feared that, if he provoked him with further arguments while the young man continued to speak freely and confidently, deriding and mocking the gods, he himself might be inflamed with greater anger and plot something hostile against him. Accordingly, he rose in anger and withdrew, using only these words: [Col. 0539C]

“Would that you had never been born or come into the light, if you were destined to be so impious and insulting toward the gods and to abandon your father’s friendship and admonition! But the adversaries of the gods, whose strength is invincible, will not mock them forever, nor will they rejoice for long, nor will their deceptions retain their power. For unless you show yourself obedient to my command and grateful toward the gods, I will first subject you to many and various torments and then remove you from the world by the most bitter death. I will deal with you not as with a son, but as with some enemy and rebel.” [Col. 0539D]

## CHAPTER XXV

When his father had addressed these threats to him and had withdrawn in anger, the son entered his chamber and, lifting his eyes toward the arbiter of his contest, cried out from the depths of his heart:

“My Lord and God, sweet hope and wholly truthful promise, firm refuge of those who have wholly devoted themselves to You, look with a gracious and kindly eye upon the contrition of my heart. Do not abandon me, and do not depart from me (Psalm XXXVII); rather, according to Your promise, which is wholly free from falsehood, be with me—that is, with an unworthy and despised little man. For I acknowledge and confess You as the author and governor of all created things. Therefore, in this noble confession, strengthen me, so that I may remain in it to my final breath. [Col. 0540A]

“Look upon me and have mercy on me (Psalm XXIV); stand by me, preserving me unharmed and safe from every operation of Satan. Look upon me, O King, since my soul burns with vehement longing for You and is inflamed as though by the heat of thirst in a waterless land, desiring You, the fountain of immortality (Psalm LXII). Do not hand over to beasts the soul that confesses You, and do not forget forever the soul of Your poor servant (Psalm LXXIII). [Col. 0540B]

“Grant me, by Your goodness, to endure everything throughout the whole course of my life for Your name and for my confession, and to offer my entire self to You. For when You supply strength, even the weak are powerful, since You alone are the unconquered defender and the merciful God, whom everything created blesses and celebrates forever and ever. Amen.”

After completing this prayer, he felt divine consolation enter his breast; and, filled with confidence, he spent the entire night in prayer. The king, meanwhile, having spoken with Arache about his son’s condition and having explained to him the rigidity of his freedom and his obstinacy in his conviction, adopted this plan: to converse with him as amicably and submissively as possible, hoping by means of flattery to draw him over to his side. [Col. 0540C]

Accordingly, on the following day he went to his son. Sitting down nearer to him, he summoned him, embraced and kissed him, and gently and calmly insinuated:

“O dearest and most loving son, honor your father’s gray hairs. Listen to my entreaties, come over to my side, and offer sacrifice to the gods. In this way you will have them favorable and gracious toward you, and from them you will receive length of days, every kind of glory, an undisturbed kingdom, and blessings of every sort. You will also remain dear to me, your father, throughout your life. Finally, you will achieve this: that all people will hold you in honor and exalt you with praises. For obedience to one’s father is of the greatest importance in attaining praise, especially in matters relating to one’s welfare and to the goodwill of the gods. [Col. 0540D]

“But what do you think, my son? Do you suppose that I deliberately and intentionally turned away from the good path and preferred to enter the opposite one, or that through ignorance and lack of understanding I surrendered myself to destructive doctrines? Certainly, if you think that I voluntarily and deliberately prefer evil to good, contrary to what is useful, and regard death as better than life, you seem, my son, to be seriously mistaken in your judgment. [Col. 0541A]

“Do you not see how often I surrender myself to hardships and afflictions, both when I occupy myself with expeditions against enemies and when I attend to public affairs, so that, whenever necessity requires, I endure even hunger and thirst, walk on foot, and sleep upon the ground? As for wealth and money, my contempt and disregard for them are so great that at times I lavishly empty the treasures of my palace in order to build magnificent temples to the gods and adorn them with every ornament, or distribute heaps of money most generously among the soldiers.

“If, then, I have such contempt for pleasures and such endurance in dangers, if I recognized the religion of the Galileans as superior to the one we hold in our hands, would I not exert the greatest effort to obtain salvation for myself after despising everything else? But if you blame me for ignorance and lack of understanding, consider with me how many sleepless nights I have spent after proposing some question—sometimes not even a particularly necessary one—allowing myself no rest until I had found a clear and most appropriate solution to it. [Col. 0541B]

“Therefore, since I do not regard even the least of these transient matters as beneath contempt, but examine and resolve them altogether for practical advantage and the common benefit—for I believe that it is universally acknowledged that no one beneath the sun has ever investigated the knowledge of hidden things more carefully than I have—how could I have considered divine matters, and those things that ought to be revered and honored as divine, contemptible? Why would I not rather have devoted my time and labor to investigating them with every effort, all my strength, and finally with my whole soul and mind, so that I might discover what is true and most coherent? [Col. 0541C]

“For I sought these things with great labor: I spent many nights and many days upon them, consulted many wise and learned men, and even conversed with many of those who are called Christians. Through tireless inquiry and ardent investigation, I discovered the way of truth, confirmed by the testimony of wise men endowed both with learning and with intelligence. Their judgment is this: that there is no other way than the one we hold today—honoring the supreme gods, and embracing with the greatest devotion the sweet life joined with pleasure that they have granted to all human beings, a life suffused with delight and the enjoyment of the mind. The leaders and bishops of the Galileans foolishly rejected this, so that with ready minds they cast away this pleasant light and all the pleasures that the gods granted us to enjoy, in hope of another and uncertain life, evidently knowing neither what they say nor about what they make assertions (1 Timothy I). [Col. 0541D]

“But you, my dearest son, obey your father, who through careful and most truthful investigation has discovered what is truly good. For it has been demonstrated that I have not departed from the good either voluntarily or through ignorance, but have both discovered and embraced it. I want you also not to remain in foolish error, but to cling to my footsteps. Therefore, see that you fear your father. Do you not know how great a good it is to obey one’s father and submit to him in all things, just as it is destructive and accursed to provoke a father’s spirit and regard his commands as nothing? For all who have done such things have perished by a deadly form of death. May you not, my son, be counted among them! Rather, by doing what is pleasing to your parent, may you become the possessor of every good and heir to my kingdom.” [Col. 0542A]

But the magnanimous and truly noble young man, after hearing his father’s superfluous speech and foolish counsel and recognizing the arts of the winding serpent—namely, that he had laid a snare at his feet on the right, working and contriving to bend his divine soul and hinder him from attaining the palm set before him—placed before his eyes the Lord’s command:

“I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. For I have come to separate a son from his father and a daughter from her mother,” and what follows (Matthew X). [Col. 0542B]

And likewise:

“Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me.”

And again:

“Whoever denies me before human beings, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven.”

When he had considered these things within himself and bound his soul with divine fear, he most opportunely employed Solomon’s saying:

“A time for loving and a time for hating; a time for war and a time for peace” (Ecclesiastes III). [Col. 0542C]

First, he prayed in his mind in this manner:

“Have mercy on me, God; have mercy on me, for in You my soul trusts, and in the shadow of Your wings I will hope until iniquity passes away. I will cry out to God Most High, to God who has dealt well with me” (Psalm LVI);

and the rest that follows in the psalm.

Then he addressed his father in these words:

“Our common teacher instructs us to honor our father, obey his commands, and serve him with a friendly and benevolent spirit (Exodus XX), since he implanted this natural affection in our souls. But when love for parents and benevolence toward them endanger the soul itself and remove it far from that supreme Creator, we are commanded to cut off this affection entirely and in no way yield or submit to those who draw us away from God, but to hate and shun them—even if the one giving accursed commands is a father, even if a mother, even if a king, even if, finally, the power of our life lies with him. [Col. 0542D]

“Since this is so, I absolutely cannot suffer the loss of God for the sake of paternal affection. Therefore, cease causing trouble both for yourself and for me. Rather, grant me this favor, and let us both worship the living and true God. For those whom you now worship are images made by human hands, without spirit and deaf, bringing upon their worshipers nothing at all except destruction and everlasting torment. [Col. 0543A]

“But if you refuse this, inflict upon me whatever you wish, for I am a servant of Christ. Neither by flatteries nor by torments will I abandon His love, just as I told you yesterday, invoking the name of my Lord and confirming my speech by an oath.

“As for your statement that you do not act wrongly either voluntarily or, again, depart from the good through ignorance, but have learned this through immense and laborious investigation—namely, that it is good to worship images and to be attached to the pleasures of lust—I certainly cannot say that you act wrongly voluntarily. But I know with complete certainty, and I want you, my father, to understand this too, that you are surrounded by a great cloud of ignorance and, as though walking in palpable darkness, do not perceive even the slightest gleam of light. Because you have lost the right path, you wander into precipices and abysses. [Col. 0543B]

“Therefore, while holding darkness in place of light and embracing death as though it were life, you imagine that you have formed useful counsels and adopted fruitful thoughts. But it is not so—no, it is not so. For those whom you worship are not gods, but statues of demons, containing within them all their accursed activity. Nor does the life that you call sweet and pleasurable, and consider full of every delight and cheerfulness, possess such a nature. If one must stand by the judgment of truth, it is accursed and to be shunned in every way. For although it may soothe the throat for a time, afterward, as my teacher said, it is digested more bitterly than gall and is sharper than a two-edged sword.

“And by what means could I finally recount its evils to you? I shall number them, and they will multiply beyond the sand (Psalm CXXXVIII). For it is the Devil’s hook, covered with accursed pleasure like a lure, by which he drags those who are deceived down to the deepest gulf of hell. [Col. 0543C]

“But the blessings promised by my Lord—which you now call the hope of an uncertain life—are free from every falsehood and change. They know no end and are not subject to corruption. In short, no speech can express the greatness of that glory and delight, that indescribable joy and perpetual gladness.

“For, as you yourself see, we all die, and there is no human being who lives and will not see death (2 Kings XIV; Psalm LXXXVIII). But we will return to life again, when the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, comes in glory that no words can describe and in dreadful power (Matthew XXV)—He, I say, the King of kings and Lord of lords (Revelation XIX), before whom every knee will bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Philippians II), and who will arouse such terror in everyone that even the heavenly powers themselves will be astonished (Luke XXI). [Col. 0543D]

“Thousands upon thousands and ten times one hundred thousand angels and archangels will stand before Him in fear, and everything will be full of dread and trembling (Daniel VII). For one of the archangels will sound the trumpet; immediately heaven will be rolled up like a book, while the shattered earth will send upward the bodies of all human beings who have ever lived from the origin of the first man Adam until that day. Then all who have died since the creation of the world will in the twinkling of an eye stand before the Lord’s tribunal, and each person will give an account of the deeds performed in life (1 Corinthians XV). [Col. 0544A]

“Then the righteous, who have believed in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit and have completed the course of their present life in upright actions, will shine like the sun (Matthew XIII). But how can I recount to you the glory that awaits them? Even if I compared their splendor and beauty to the sun’s light or even to the brightest flash, I would still say nothing equal to that radiance. For eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered the human heart what God has prepared in the kingdom of heaven, in incomparable light, in hidden and endless glory, for those endowed with love of Him (1 Corinthians II). Such blessings and such blessedness will belong to the righteous. [Col. 0544B]

“But those who have denied the true God, ignored the Maker and Creator, worshiped impure demons, offered veneration to deaf images, burned with desire for the pleasures of this vain life, rolled about like pigs in the mire of vicious passions, and made their souls a workshop of every vice will stand naked and exposed, covered with disgrace, sorrowful, and pitiable both in appearance and in reality.

“All their words, actions, and thoughts will come before their faces. Then, after the gravest disgrace and that intolerable shame, they will be consigned to the fire of Gehenna, which is never extinguished and is deprived of all light, to the outer darkness, the gnashing of teeth, and the poisonous worm. This will be their portion; this their inheritance. Throughout everlasting ages they will remain in these things, paying the penalties for their crimes, because, for the sake of brief pleasure, they rejected and cast aside those good things stored up in the promise and brought eternal punishment upon themselves. [Col. 0544C]

“For these things, then—that is, so that we may attain that joy superior to every utterance, enjoy that hidden glory, equal the angels in splendor, stand with confident hearts before the good and most gracious Lord, and escape the most atrocious and never-ending punishments and that most bitter disgrace—what sums of money, what bodies, indeed, what very souls would it not be fitting to pour out?

“Who is so sluggish in spirit, who so senseless, that he would not resolve to undergo six hundred temporary deaths in order to be freed from everlasting death, which knows no end, to possess by inheritance a blessed life removed from all destruction, and to be illumined by the light of the holy Trinity, which gives life its beginning?” [Col. 0544D]

## CHAPTER XXVI

When the king heard these words and perceived his son’s firmness and constancy—how he yielded neither to flatteries, nor to the enticement of speeches, nor finally to threats of punishment—he admired the plausibility of his speech and the answers that could not be refuted. He was also convicted by his own conscience, which showed him that his son was speaking what was true and just. Nevertheless, he was drawn in the opposite direction by his perverse habit and by the vicious passions whose pattern he had acquired and which restrained him as though with bit and bridle, preventing him from seeing the light of truth. [Col. 0545A]

Accordingly, moving every stone, as the saying goes, he clung to the plan he had previously formed, wishing to carry into effect the design he had made with Arache. Thus he said to his son:

“You ought, my son, to obey my commands simply in every matter. But since, through your hardness and obstinacy, you have resisted me so vehemently, insisting only that your own opinion should carry more weight and authority with you than everything else, come now: let us dismiss this empty contention and proceed by arguments suited to persuasion.

“Since Barlaam, by whom you have been deceived, is held bound by me, let a most extensive assembly be convened, all our people and all the Galileans gathered together, and let eloquent heralds proclaim in clear words that no Christian should fear any danger, but that all should assemble without fear through their associations and kinships. Let us consider the matter by common counsel. Either you and your Barlaam will bring us over to your opinion and obtain what you desire, or, brought over to our opinion, you will obey my commands voluntarily and willingly.” [Col. 0545B]

But the truly prudent and sensible young man, having learned the king’s deception through the vision divinely granted to him, said:

“Let the Lord’s will be done, and let it be as you have commanded. May the good and divine God grant us this also: that we do not depart from the right path. For in Him my soul trusts, and He will have mercy on me.” [Col. 0545C]

Then the king ordered all the worshipers of idols and the Christians to assemble in one place. Letters were sent in every direction, and heralds proclaimed throughout all the towns that no Christian should be afraid, as though about to suffer something unexpected, but that all should gather through their associations and kinships, since an inquiry devoted to the truth and neither coerced nor violent was to take place together with their leader and standard-bearer, Barlaam.

In the same way he summoned the worshipers and priests of idols, as well as the Chaldean and Indian sages throughout his entire empire, and also certain diviners, magicians, and prophets, so that they might obtain victory over the Christians. [Col. 0545D]

A vast multitude of the king’s accursed religion indeed flocked to him. But only one Christian, named Barachias, was found to assist Barlaam—as was believed. Some of the devout men had met the final day of their lives, slaughtered by the furious governors of the cities; some hid in the mountains and caves out of fear of the dangers hanging over them; and others, terrified by the king’s threats, did not dare to come into the light, but were worshipers of piety by night, worshiping Christ only in secret and not openly professing His faith. He alone, being endowed with a noble spirit, came forward to defend the truth. [Col. 0546A]

When the king had taken his seat upon a high and elevated throne, he ordered his son to sit beside him. But the son, out of honor and reverence toward his father, refused to do so and sat on the ground not far from him.

There stood men skilled in the wisdom that has been made foolish by God, to use the Apostle’s words: “Their foolish heart went astray” (1 Corinthians I). For, “claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of corruptible human beings, and four-footed animals, and serpents” (Romans I). They had assembled in order to engage in discussion with the king’s son and with those who stood on his side. In them the proverb was fulfilled:

> “A doe has entered into battle with a lion.”

**[Note: [Col. 0606C] “A doe has entered into battle with a lion.” In Suidas, an iambic senarius: Μὴ πρὸς λέοντα δορκὰς ἅψωμαι μάχης — “May I not, a doe, engage in battle with a lion.”]

For he himself had made the Most High his refuge and hoped in the shadow of His wings (Psalm XC). But they placed their confidence in the rulers of this age, who are being destroyed, and in the ruler of the darkness of the world, to whom they had miserably subjected themselves (Psalm LVI; Ephesians VI). [Col. 0546B]

Nachor was then brought forward, pretending to be Barlaam. The king had indeed intended this, but the wise providence of God was directing something else from heaven.

While all these people stood present, the king said to his orators and philosophers—or rather, to the deceivers of the people and men possessed of foolish hearts:

“Behold, a contest—indeed, a very great one—has been placed before you. One of two things will happen to you: either, with our doctrine confirmed and Barlaam and his associates convicted of error, you will receive the greatest glory and honor from us and from the senate, and be adorned with crowns of victory; or, defeated and overcome, you will suffer the most grievous death amid complete disgrace, and all your possessions will be handed over to the people, so that your memory may be utterly erased from the earth. For I will also throw your bodies to the beasts to be devoured and punish your children with perpetual slavery.” [Col. 0546C]

After the king had delivered this speech, his son spoke as follows:

“Today you have pronounced a just judgment, O king, and I pray that God may confirm it. I say the same to my teacher.”

Then, turning to Nachor, who was thought to be Barlaam, he said:

“You are not unaware, O Barlaam, amid what glory and what pleasures you found me. Yet by many speeches you led me to abandon my ancestral laws and institutions and worship an unknown God, drawing my mind toward the pursuit of your doctrines and toward angering my father and lord by the hope of certain hidden and eternal blessings.

“Therefore, imagine that you now stand as though upon a balance. If you emerge victorious from the proposed contest—demonstrating that the doctrine you delivered to me is true and showing that those who oppose us today are in error—you will receive greater glory than anyone has ever received and will be called the herald of truth. I, for my part, will persevere in your doctrine and worship Christ, as you have proclaimed, to my final breath.

“But if, whether by deceit or in earnest and truth, you are defeated and bring disgrace upon me, I will immediately avenge my humiliation. With my own hands I will tear out your heart and tongue and give them, together with the rest of your body, as prey to the dogs, so that by your example all may learn never to deceive the sons of kings.” [Col. 0546D]

When Nachor heard these words, he conceived immense sadness and grief, seeing that he had fallen into the pit he had dug, become entangled in the snare he had hidden, and pierced himself with his own sword.

After considering the matter, he decided, in order to escape the danger threatening his life, to join the side of the king’s son and confirm his doctrines, since the young man would have every right to punish him if he had offended his spirit. But all this was the work of divine providence, which wisely confirmed the decrees of our religion through its adversaries. [Col. 0547A]

For when the priests of the idols and Nachor began to engage in debate, just as that Barlaam, when he had once resolved under Balaak to curse Israel and devote it to imprecations, nevertheless showered it with many and various blessings (Numbers XXII), so Nachor also vehemently resisted the foolish and senseless sages.

The king was seated on his throne, and his son—as we have already said—was seated beside him. Foolish rhetoricians also stood nearby, having sharpened their tongues like a sword in order to crush and overthrow the truth (Psalm LXIII), and who, to speak with Isaiah, “conceive labor and give birth to iniquity” (Isaiah LIX). An innumerable crowd of the people had also gathered to watch the contest, so that it might learn which side would gain the victory. [Col. 0547B]

One of the rhetoricians, who surpassed all the others in learning, said to Nachor:

“Are you that exceedingly bold and insulting Barlaam, who led the king’s dearest son into such error and taught him to worship one who was crucified?”

Nachor replied:

“Indeed, I am Barlaam, who, as you have said, regard your gods as nothing, and who did not lead the king’s son into error but freed him from error and brought him to the true God.”

Then the rhetorician spoke in this manner:

“Since great and eminent men, from whom all wisdom and knowledge have arisen, call them sublime and immortal gods, and since all the kings and distinguished men of the world worship and honor them, how do you sharpen your tongue against them and proceed to such a degree of boldness as to utter these things? By what argument do you prove that they are not gods, but that the one who was fastened to the cross is?” [Col. 0547C]

Nachor took up the speech but did not deem the rhetorician worthy of any response. Instead, after imposing silence upon the people with his hand and opening his mouth like Balaam’s ass, he spoke what he had not at all intended to say and addressed the king:

“I, O king, came into the world by the providence of God. When I looked upon heaven, earth, sea, sun, moon, and the other things of this kind, I marveled at their order. Seeing that the world and all that it contains are necessarily moved, I understood that the one by whom they are moved and preserved is God. For whatever moves is stronger than that which is moved, and whatever contains and preserves is stronger than that which is contained and preserved.

“Therefore I say that God is the one who brought all things into being and preserves them, who is without beginning, eternal and immortal, needing nothing, and exalted above every disturbance and deficiency—that is, above anger, forgetfulness, ignorance, and all other things of the same kind. Through Him all things have been joined and compacted together (Psalm XV). Nor does He need sacrifices, libations, or anything else perceptible to the senses (Acts XVII); rather, everything has need of Him.” [Col. 0547D]

## CHAPTER XXVII

Having spoken thus about God, insofar as by His favor I have been permitted to speak about Him, let us come to the human race, so that we may see which of them share in truth and which in error.

For this is agreed among us, O king: that there are three classes of human beings in the world—those who among you are called worshipers of the gods, the Jews, and the Christians. Again, among those who worship many gods there are three groups: the Chaldeans, the Greeks, and the Egyptians. For these were leaders and teachers to the other nations in the worship and adoration of many gods. [Col. 0548A]

Let us therefore examine which of them are in the truth and which in error.

The Chaldeans, being ignorant of God, went astray after the elements and began to worship created things in place of the Creator. After they had also fashioned certain forms of them, they called these forms representations of heaven, earth, sea, sun, moon, and the other elements and heavenly bodies; they enclose them in temples, worship them, and call them gods. They even guard them carefully and diligently so that thieves may not steal them.

Nor does it occur to them that whatever guards something is greater than that which is guarded, and that the one who makes something is superior to what is made. For if their gods are so weak that they cannot provide for their own safety, how could they possibly bring safety to others? Thus the Chaldeans have fallen into great error, venerating dead statues incapable of usefulness. [Col. 0548B]

I am also moved to wonder, O king, how those among them who bear the name of philosophers have not noticed that the elements themselves are subject to destruction. But if the elements are altogether subject and liable to destruction, how can they be gods? And if the elements are not gods, how will statues constructed in their name be gods? [Col. 0548C]

Let us therefore approach the elements themselves, O king, and demonstrate that they are not gods but subject to corruption and change, and that they were brought forth from nothing into being at the command of the true God. He is free from corruption and change and is invisible, while He Himself sees all things and changes and transforms them according to His will.

What, then, do I say about the elements? [Col. 0548D]

Those who suppose that heaven is a god are in error. For we see that it revolves, moves of necessity, and consists of many things; for this reason it is called *kosmos* (κόσμος), that is, “world.” The world, moreover, is the construction of some craftsman. Whatever is constructed has a beginning and an end. [Col. 0549A]

Heaven, however, together with its heavenly bodies, moves of necessity. The stars, driven along according to a fixed order and interval, move from point to point; some set and others rise, and at fixed intervals of time complete their course, producing summers and winters, just as God has commanded them. Nor do they violate the laws established for themselves according to the unavoidable necessity of nature, together with the heavenly order. From this it is clear that heaven is not a god but the work of God.

Those who consider the earth a goddess are in error. For we see it suffering violence at the hands of human beings and being subject to their power; it is also dug up and contaminated and becomes useless. If it is scorched by fire, it dies, since nothing can grow from baked clay. Moreover, if it is drenched with excessive rains, both it and its fruits are spoiled. It is trampled underfoot by human beings and the other living creatures, polluted with the blood of the slain, dug up, filled in, and made into a container for corpses. Since these things are so, the earth cannot be a goddess, but is a thing made by God for human use. [Col. 0549B]

In the same way, those who think that water is a goddess are mistaken. For water too was created for human use and is subject to human control. It is also polluted and weakened, and when it is constrained by fire it is changed: it continually takes on different colors, since it freezes through cold, contracts filth from blood, [Col. 0549C] and is used for washing away every kind of impurity. From this it is plainly evident that water cannot be a goddess, but is the work of God.

Now those who consider fire a god are likewise mistaken. For fire was created for human use, is subject to human control, and is carried by human beings from place to place for every kind of meat—partly to boil it, partly to roast it—and also for burning dead bodies. Moreover, it is corrupted in many ways and extinguished by human beings. Therefore fire cannot be a god, but is the work of God.

In the same way, those who think that the blowing of the winds is a god are mistaken. For it is evident that the wind serves another and was created by God for the sake of human beings, to carry ships, transport grain, and serve their other [Col. 0549D] needs. In addition, it increases and diminishes according to God’s command and authority. Therefore the wind cannot be a god, but is the work of God.

Furthermore, those who think that the sun is a god are likewise mistaken. For we see that it moves necessarily, travels and changes from point to point, sets and rises, so that, for the benefit of human beings, it may warm trees and plants. We also see that it shares its division with the other heavenly bodies, is much smaller than the heavens, is sometimes deprived of its light, and possesses no authority or sovereignty. From this it is clear that the sun cannot be a god, but is the work of God.

[Col. 0550A] In a similar way, those who suppose that the moon is a goddess are mistaken. For we see that it moves and changes necessarily, travels from point to point, rises and sets in turn for the benefit of human beings, and is smaller than the sun. It also waxes and wanes and sometimes undergoes eclipses. Therefore the moon cannot be a goddess, but is the work of God.

Finally, those who think that a human being is a god are mistaken. For we see that a human being moves necessarily, must be nourished, grows old against his will, is sometimes delighted and sometimes afflicted with grief, and needs food, drink, and clothing. He is also prone to anger and envy, driven by lust, led by remorse, and afflicted with many deficiencies. Moreover, he is corrupted in many ways—by the elements, by living creatures, and finally [Col. 0550B] by death, which threatens him. Hence it follows that a human being cannot be a god, but is the work of God. Consequently, the Chaldaeans have fallen into enormous error while following the inventions of their opinions. For they worship the elements, upon which destruction falls, and dead statues, and they do not realize that they are counting such things among the gods.

Let us now turn to the Greeks, to see whether they have any correct understanding of God. The Greeks, then, arrogating to themselves the praise of wisdom, showed themselves even more foolish than the Chaldaeans by introducing numerous gods, some male and some female, makers of every kind of vicious passion and crime. For, O king, the Greeks introduced ridiculous, foolish, and impious ideas, calling those who do not exist gods according to their own perverse desires, so that, having them as patrons and [Col. 0550C] defenders of vice, they might commit adultery, rape, murder, and every kind of atrocious crime. For since their gods have perpetrated such outrages, how could the Greeks themselves not perpetrate the same things? From these pursuits and institutions of error it has repeatedly happened that human beings have experienced wars, slaughter, and bitter captivity. Indeed, if we wished to speak of their gods one by one, you would perceive an immense absurdity.

For they introduce Saturn above all as a god, and sacrifice their own children to him. He had many children by Rhea, and, seized by madness, he himself used to devour them. They say that Jupiter cut off the genital member and threw it into the sea, from which, they invent, Venus arose. [Col. 0550D] Jupiter bound his father in chains and cast him headlong into Tartarus. You see the error and lust which they attribute to their god. For can it be that a god is bound in chains and that his genitals are cut off? O extraordinary madness!
