Who endowed with a mind could say such things?

A second Jupiter is introduced, whom they say rules over all their gods and changes himself into various forms of living creatures in order to violate mortal women. For they relate that he changed himself into a bull so that he might possess Europa; into gold, so that he might possess Danaë; into a swan, so that he might possess Leda; into a satyr, so that he might possess Antiope; and into lightning, so that he might possess Semele. Later, they say, many children were born from these women: Bacchus, Zethus, Amphion, Hercules, [Col. 0551A] Apollo, Diana, Perseus, Castor and Pollux, Helen, Minos, Rhadamanthus, Sarpedon, and also nine daughters, whom they call the Muses.

Finally, they introduce the story of Ganymede. Thus, O king, human beings came to imitate all these things in imitation of their god: they became adulterers, were seized by insane love for males, and perpetrated other horrible crimes. How, then, can it be that God is an adulterer, a sodomite, or a parricide?

They also claim that there is a certain god named Vulcan, and represent him as lame, holding a hammer and tongs, and practicing the smith’s craft to earn his livelihood. Thus he was suffering from poverty. Yet it is contrary to the nature of God to be lame and to need human assistance.

[Col. 0551B] Moreover, they introduce Mercury to us as a god who is greedy, a thief, avaricious, a magician, devious, and an interpreter of speech. Such qualities in no way belong to the nature of God.

They also count Asclepius among the gods. He was a physician and prepared medicines and poultices in order to earn his livelihood—for he lived in poverty. Later, they say, he died after being struck by Jupiter’s thunderbolt because of the son of the Lacedaemonian Tyndareus. But if Asclepius, though he was a god, was struck by a thunderbolt and could not help himself, how will he ever be able to help others?

[Col. 0551C] They also introduce Mars as a god devoted to war and prone to anger, desirous of sheep and other possessions. They say that later, when he had committed adultery with Venus, he was bound in chains by the boy Cupid and by Vulcan. How, then, can he be a god who burns with desire, delights in wars, commits adultery, and is bound in chains?

Again, they count Bacchus among the gods: he celebrates nocturnal festivals, is the master of drunkenness, carries off the wives of others, rages with madness, flees, and is finally slaughtered by the Titans. If Bacchus, when he was being killed, could not help himself, but was driven headlong by madness, devoted himself to drunkenness, and fled, how can he be a god?

[Col. 0551D] Then they introduce Hercules, who overwhelms himself with wine, plunges into madness, slaughters his own sons, and afterward perishes, consumed by flames. How can he be a god who overwhelms himself with wine, kills his children, and is consumed by the heat of fire? Or how can he help others, when he could not bring help to himself?

Furthermore, they introduce Apollo as afflicted with envy, holding a bow and quiver, and sometimes also a lyre and flute, and uttering prophecies to human beings in order to make money. He was therefore in need. Yet it is impossible for God to be needy, envious, or a lyre-player.

In the same way, they introduce Diana, his sister, as devoted to hunting, carrying a bow and quivers, [Col. 0552A] and wandering alone with dogs in order to capture a stag or boar. How, then, can a woman be a goddess who hunts and roams about with dogs?

Finally, they say that Venus too is a goddess and an adulteress. For at one time she slept with Mars, at another with Anchises, and at another with Adonis, whose death she also mourns while searching for her beloved. They even say that she descended to the underworld to ransom Adonis from Proserpina. Have you ever seen, O king, madness greater than this—to introduce a goddess who binds herself by the crime of adultery and weeps and laments?

They also introduce Adonis as a hunter-god, saying that he was struck by a boar and died a violent death [Col. 0552B], and that he could not help himself in such a calamity. How, then, will an adulterer and hunter who died a violent death care for human beings?

All these things and many others of the same kind—still more shameful and criminal—are introduced by the Greeks concerning their gods, things which it is not lawful either to speak or in any way to recall. Hence human beings, seizing upon an opportunity from their gods, have perpetrated every kind of crime, lust, and impiety, polluting the earth and the air with their horrible outrages.

The Egyptians, surpassing them in folly and stupidity, went astray more grievously than any other nation. For they were not content merely to worship the gods of the Greeks; in addition, they counted among the gods irrational animals, both those that live on land [Col. 0552C] and those that live in the waters, as well as trees and plants, and they defiled themselves with every kind of madness and lust more grievously than any nation on earth. In ancient times they worshiped Isis, who had Osiris as both her husband and her brother; he was slaughtered by his brother Typhon. For this reason Isis fled with her son Horus to Byblos in Syria, searching for Osiris and lamenting bitterly until Horus had grown up and removed Typhon from the world. Thus Isis could not help her brother and husband; Osiris, when he was being murdered by Typhon, could not help himself; and finally Typhon, the fratricide, when Horus and Isis brought destruction upon him, could not save himself from death. Yet when these figures had come to human notice because of such calamities, the foolish Egyptians regarded them as gods.

Nor were they content with these or the deities of the other nations; they introduced irrational animals as well. Some of them worshiped a sheep, others a goat, others a calf and a pig, others a raven and a hawk, others a vulture and an eagle, and others a crocodile. Some worshiped a cat, a dog, a wolf, a monkey, a dragon, and an asp; others [Col. 0552D] onions, garlic, thorns, and other created things. Yet these wretched human beings do not perceive that there is absolutely no power in any of these objects. For although they see their gods being eaten by other human beings, burned by fire, slaughtered, and corrupted, they nevertheless have not understood that they are therefore not gods.

Consequently, the Egyptians, the Chaldaeans, and the Greeks alike have fallen into great error by introducing such gods, [Col. 0553A] making statues of them, and regarding deaf and senseless images as gods. I am astonished that, when they saw their gods being cut, carved, and mutilated by craftsmen, growing old and changing through the passage of time, and being melted by fire, they did not recognize from this that they were not gods. For those who have no power over their own salvation—how will they ever provide for the salvation of human beings? But their poets and philosophers, both Chaldaean and Egyptian, while striving to adorn their gods in verse and written records, have instead exposed their disgrace more fully and displayed it naked before everyone’s eyes. For although the human body consists of many [Col. 0553B] parts, it does not cast away any of its limbs; rather, maintaining the firmest union with all of them, it agrees with itself. How, then, could such conflict and discord exist in the nature of God? For if there were one divine nature, one god ought not to pursue, slaughter, or punish another god with some evil. But if gods have been harassed, killed, stripped, and struck by thunderbolts by other gods, then their nature is not one; rather, their wills are distinct, and all are destructive and pestilential.

From this it must be concluded that none of them is a god. It is therefore clear, O king, that all their discussion of the nature of the gods is full of error. How, then, did those who flourished among the Greeks [Col. 0553C] for their reputation in wisdom and learning fail to understand that those who made the laws are judged by their own laws? For if the laws are just, their gods are altogether unjust, since they have murdered one another contrary to the prescriptions of the laws and have rushed into poisoning, adultery, theft, and unnatural lusts. But if the gods acted rightly, then the laws are certainly unjust, since they were established against the gods. Yet the laws are excellent and just, since they praise virtues and prohibit vices, whereas the deeds of the gods whom the Greeks worship are unjust. Therefore their gods too are unjust, and all who introduce such gods are impious and deserving of death. For if the things handed down concerning them in written records are fabricated and legendary, they are nothing more than mere stories; but if they are natural realities, then those who did and suffered these things are not gods; and if they are spoken in an allegorical sense, they are fables and nothing more.

[Col. 0553D] It has therefore been demonstrated, O king, that all these forms of worship, which are assigned to many gods, are works of error and destruction. For it is not fitting to call gods those who see and do not see; rather, God is the one who, although he himself cannot be seen, sees all things. The God who created all things must be worshiped.

Let us therefore also turn, O king, to the Jews, to see what they too think about God. They are descended from Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and lived in Egypt. From there God led them out by a mighty hand and an exalted arm through Moses, their lawgiver, and by many wonders and signs declared his power to them. [Col. 0554A] But they too showed themselves faithless and ungrateful: they repeatedly worshiped the gods of the nations and put to death the prophets and righteous men sent to them. Then, after God’s will had determined that his Son should come to earth, they treated him with contempt, handed him over to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor, and condemned him to the punishment of the cross, taking no account of his benefits or of the innumerable miracles that he had performed among them; and by their crime they perished. For even now they worship only the omnipotent God, but not according to knowledge, since they deny Christ, the Son of God (Romans 10). They are like the Gentiles, although they may seem to approach somewhat more closely the truth from which they have removed themselves. Thus far concerning the Jews.

[Col. 0554B] But the Christians derive the origin of their teaching from our Lord Jesus Christ. He is believed to be the Son of the Most High God in the Holy Spirit. For the sake of human salvation he descended from heaven, was born of a holy Virgin, assumed flesh without seed and without corruption, and appeared to human beings in order to turn them back from the worship of many false gods. Having accomplished the wondrous dispensation of his incarnation, he willingly and by a great design tasted death through the cross. On the third day he rose again and ascended into the heavens. If you should resolve to read the Scripture that they call the Gospel, O king, you can perceive from it the glory of his presence.

He had twelve disciples, who, after his ascent into heaven, went out into the provinces of the world and proclaimed his august greatness. [Col. 0554C] One of them also traveled through our regions to preach the doctrines of the truth (above, ch. 1). Hence those who now devote themselves to administering the justice of their preaching are called Christians. These are the people who have found the truth above all the nations of the earth. For they acknowledge the God and creator of all things in his only-begotten Son and the Holy Spirit, and they worship no other God besides him.

They have the commandments of the Lord Jesus Christ engraved upon their hearts, and they keep them, awaiting the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. [Col. 0554D] They do not bind themselves by the crime of adultery or fornication; they do not bear false witness; they do not covet what belongs to others; they honor father and mother; they love their neighbors; they render just judgment; and what they do not want done to themselves, they do not do to others. They plead with those by whom they are wronged and win their friendship. They strive to benefit their enemies; they show themselves gentle and accommodating; they abstain from every unlawful sexual union and from every impurity; they do not despise a widow; they do not cause an orphan grief; whoever has supplies generously for whoever does not have.

If they see a stranger, they admit him under their roof and rejoice at his arrival as though he were a true and genuine brother. For they call one another brothers not according to the flesh but according to the spirit. They are ready to pour out their lives for Christ, for they firmly observe his commandments, living in holiness and righteousness, just as the Lord God commanded them. [Col. 0555A] At every hour they give him thanks for every food and drink and for all other good things (Ephesians 5). For this truly is the way of truth, which leads those who enter upon it by the hand, as it were, to the eternal kingdom promised by Christ in the life to come.

And so that you may understand, O king, that I am not inventing these things from my own mind, if you turn your eyes to the Scriptures of the Christians, you will find that I say nothing alien to the truth. Therefore your son understood admirably and learned, with the greatest justice, to render worship to the living God, so that he might obtain salvation in the age to come. For the things both said and done by the Christians are great and wondrous. They proclaim not human words but the words of God; the other nations, however, [Col. 0555B] are in error and deceive themselves, since, walking in darkness, they stumble against themselves like drunkards.

Let this, O king, be the end of my address to you, which truth has dictated in my mind. Let your foolish wise men cease their babbling against the Lord. For it is advantageous for you to worship God the creator and to lend your ear to his words, so that, escaping condemnation and punishment, you may inherit life free from destruction.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

After these things had been recounted by Nachor, the king was seething with anger, while his rhetoricians and priests stood mute, since they could bring forward nothing against him except some feeble and worthless little speeches. But the king’s son was exultant in spirit and, with a joyful face, praised the Lord, [Col. 0555C] who gives those whose confidence is placed in him a way out of difficult and perplexing circumstances, who also confirmed the truth through an enemy and adversary, and caused the leader of error to present himself as a defender of sound doctrine.

Although the king was otherwise fiercely angry with Nachor, he could inflict no harm upon him, because, by a law previously proclaimed before everyone, he had permitted him to speak freely on behalf of the Christians. Nevertheless, the king often opposed him in words and, by certain gestures, warned him to lessen the sharpness of his attack and yield to the disputation of the rhetoricians. But Nachor grew still more forceful, refuting all their propositions and arguments [Col. 0555D] and exposing the deceit and fraud of the error by which they were held.

When the debate had continued almost until evening, the king ordered the assembly dismissed, evidently intending to discuss the matter again on the following day.

Josaphat then addressed the king: “Just as you first ordered everything to be conducted fairly, O king, so also bring justice to its conclusion by doing one of two things: either permit my teacher to remain with me this night, so that together we may consider the matters about which we must speak tomorrow with those who challenge us to battle, while you likewise take your own men and deliberate with them at your discretion on whatever seems likely to be useful; or, if you grant me your men for this night, accept mine in return. But if both parties remain with you—mine in distress and [Col. 0556A] fear, while yours are in joy and relaxation—this judgment does not seem fair to me, but rather an exercise of princely license and a violation of agreements.”

The king, overcome by the charm of this speech, took his wise men and priests and granted Nachor to his son, relying on the hope that he would fulfill what he had promised.

The king’s son therefore proceeded to his palace like some Olympic victor, having overcome his opponents and taking Nachor with him. When he had summoned him after dismissing the attendants, he addressed him as follows:

“Do not suppose that I am unaware of who you are. I am completely certain that you are not the most divine Barlaam at all, but Nachor the astrologer. I am astonished at what came into your minds, that you should fabricate such a [Col. 0556B] story and persuade yourselves that in broad daylight you would cast darkness before my eyes, so that I would take a wolf for a sheep. But the proverb rightly says, ‘The heart of a fool thinks vain thoughts.’ This thought and plan of yours was truly stale and utterly foolish, but the work that you yourself performed is full of every kind of prudence and shrewdness. Therefore rejoice and exult, Nachor.

“For this reason I give you many thanks: today you undertook the defense of the truth and did not contaminate your lips with criminal words and cunning pretense. Rather, you cleansed them of many stains by refuting the error of false gods and confirming the truth of Christian doctrines.

“I brought you with me for two reasons. First, so that the king, if he detained you privately, would not punish you because you had not said what pleased him. [Col. 0556C] Second, so that I might repay you today for the favor you have done me. But how can I do this? By warning you to turn aside from this crooked and dangerous path, which you have followed until this day, and to enter the straight and saving path. Although you knew it, you fled from it by willingly embracing evil and driving yourself into the abysses and precipices of iniquity.

“Understand, then, O Nachor: since you are prudent and shrewd, strive to gain Christ alone and the life hidden with him, despising and regarding as nothing these fleeting and perishable things. For you will not live forever. Since you are mortal, you will soon depart from here, as did all those who existed before [Col. 0556D] you. And, O wretched man, if you depart carrying with you the heavy burden of sin, without first casting it off—although it is easy to cast it off—what will you do when there is a just judgment and a just recompense for deeds?”

Nachor, pierced in heart by these words, replied:

“You have spoken rightly, O king—rightly, I say. For I too know the true God, free from every falsehood, through whom all things were made, and I also know that there will be a future judgment, having been taught this by many words of Holy Scripture. But evil habit and the cunning of the ancient deceiver have blinded the eyes of my heart and poured thick darkness over my mind. Now, at your word, I shall cast away the dark veil and hasten toward the light of the Lord’s countenance. [Col. 0557A] Perhaps he will take pity on me and open the door of repentance to me, a wicked and rebellious servant.

“Although it seems impossible to me that I can obtain forgiveness for my sins, which are heavier than sand, and for the things I have committed both knowingly and unknowingly.”

After hearing this speech, the king’s son immediately rose, grew fervent in spirit, and began to recover and lift Nachor’s mind, which was inclining toward despair.

“Let no doubt whatsoever about this matter enter your heart, O Nachor,” he said. “For it is written (John 8) that God can raise up children for Abraham even from these stones. As Father Barlaam used to say, what else does this mean except that people whose wickedness has been despaired of and who have been polluted by every kind of iniquity can [Col. 0557B] attain salvation and become children of Christ? Because of his supreme and incredible humanity, Christ has opened the gates of heaven to all who reform their lives.

“For he has closed the way to salvation to no one at all; rather, he receives with a merciful heart those who repent of their crimes. For this reason an equal reward is given to those who came to the vineyard at the first, third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours, as the Gospel writings relate (Matthew 20). Therefore, even if you have grown old in sins up to this very day, if you approach with a fervent heart, you will receive the same rewards as those who entered the contest from their youth.”

When the divinely inspired young man had spoken these and many other words to Nachor, who was hardened in his evils, promised him forgiveness, and assured him that Christ would be gracious and favorable toward him—affirming with certainty that, in his goodness, Christ is always ready to receive the sinner’s repentance—[Col. 0557C] he softened his ailing soul as though with medicines and restored him completely to health.

Immediately Nachor said to him:

“You are nobler in spirit than in body, and have been splendidly instructed in these wondrous mysteries. I ask you to remain to the very end in this excellent confession, and let neither time nor any circumstance tear it from your heart. I, however, shall depart this very hour to seek my salvation and, through repentance, make the God whom I provoked to anger gracious and favorable toward me. [Col. 0557D] From now on, unless you think otherwise, I shall not look upon the king’s face again.”

The king’s son was filled with immense joy and gladly received these words. He embraced and kissed Nachor, and, after pouring out attentive prayers to God, sent him from the palace.

After leaving, Nachor, pierced in heart, sprang into the deepest solitude like a stag and went to the cave of a certain monk who was adorned with priestly dignity and was hiding there because of the imminent danger. Before him Nachor fell prostrate on the ground with a fervent heart, drenched his feet with his tears, like that harlot of old (Luke 7), and asked for [Col. 0558A] divine baptism.

The priest, being filled with divine grace, experienced immense joy in his heart. He immediately instructed Nachor, according to custom, for many days in the rudiments of the Christian faith and completed him through divine baptism in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Mark, last chapter). Nachor remained with him, continually moved to repentance for the sins he had committed and blessing God, who wishes no one to perish but awaits the repentance of all and receives those who repent with humanity and kindness (2 Peter 3; Ezekiel 18).

When the king learned in the morning what had happened to Nachor, had lost his hope, and moreover saw that his wise men and foolish orators had been defeated without difficulty, [Col. 0558B] he was in great anguish of mind. After previously inflicting severe insults and disgraces upon them, and even tearing some of them cruelly with ox-hide whips and smearing their eyes with soot, he dismissed them from his presence.

He himself began to condemn the weakness of the false gods, although he had not yet decided to turn his eyes fully and completely toward the light of Christ. For a dense cloud of darkness spread around him still held the eyes of his heart. Nevertheless, he no longer honored his priests or performed festivals and libations for his images. Rather, his mind wavered between two alternatives: on the one hand, he condemned the weakness of his gods; on the other, he feared the sincerity of the Gospel life and was so bound by evil habit that he could scarcely be torn away from it. For he was exceedingly addicted to the service of bodily pleasures and devoted himself entirely to vicious passions, led like a captive and, to use the words of Isaiah, drunk without wine (Isaiah 51), and pulled back from his evil habit as though by a bridle.

[Col. 0558C] While the king was struggling in this way with his double-mindedness, his most noble son, truly endowed with a royal spirit, lived quietly in his palace, declaring to everyone by his deeds the nobility, modesty, and steadfastness of his nature. For he considered theaters, horse races, hunting exercises, all the empty pursuits of youth, and the deceptions by which foolish minds are soothed and enticed to be utterly worthless. Rather, he depended entirely upon Christ’s [Col. 0558D] commandments and, wounded by divine love, sought him who is truly worthy to be sought, wholly sweet and wholly desirable (Song of Songs 5), and such that he is awaited without any satiety.

When he recalled his teacher Barlaam and set his life before his eyes, he felt his heart being soothed by love for him, and he devoted himself earnestly to finding a way to see him. Carrying his teacher’s words continually in his heart, he was like a tree planted beside streams of water, perpetually irrigated and bearing timely fruit for its lord.

For he rescued many souls from the devil’s snares and presented them, preserved, to Christ. [Col. 0559A] Many came to him and enjoyed his saving words. Among these, not a few abandoned error and hastened to the saving doctrine. Others, bidding a long farewell to the affairs of this life, undertook the monastic contest.

He devoted himself to prayers and fasts and repeatedly sent this voice to God:

“O my Lord, O my Lord and King, in whom I have believed, to whom I have fled, and by whom I have been freed from error, repay your servant Barlaam with a worthy reward, because he showed me you, who are the way, the life, and the truth (John 14), when I was wandering. Grant me also this: that I may once again see in the flesh that angel, unworthy of the world (Hebrews 11), and complete with him what remains of my life, so that, following in his footsteps, I may please you, God and Lord.”

[Col. 0559B] ## CHAPTER XXIX

At that time there was a public festival of the false gods in that city. The king was expected to attend this festival and adorn it with the most abundant sacrifices. But when the priests saw that he was sluggish and lukewarm in the worship of the gods, they feared that he might neglect to come to the temple and that they themselves would thus be deprived of the gifts they were accustomed to receive from the king and of their other revenues.

So they rose and went to a certain cave situated in the vastest solitude. There lived a man devoted to magical arts and a fierce champion of the false worship of idols, named Theudas, whom the king also embraced with singular honor and regarded as a dear teacher. He claimed that through Theudas’s [Col. 0559C] prophecies his kingdom flourished in abundance of all things and increased day by day.

When the priestly devotees had come to him, they implored his aid and assistance and explained to him the disapproval of the gods into which the king had fallen, what the king’s son had done, and how Nachor had addressed the assembly according to the son’s will and judgment.

“Unless you yourself come,” they said, “and offer us assistance, all hope is extinguished, and all worship and veneration of the gods has perished. For you alone have been left to us as a consolation in our calamity, and in you alone we have placed all our hopes.”

Theudas therefore set out on campaign with that satanic army which he had with him and prepared weapons against the truth. He summoned many wicked spirits, [Col. 0559D], whom he knew readily and willingly to lend an assisting hand for evil deeds and whom he had always employed as servants. Accompanied by them, he approached the king.

When the king was informed of his arrival, and Theudas entered holding a palm branch in his hand and dressed in a sheep’s skin, the king leapt from his throne and came out to meet him. He kissed him, ordered a chair to be brought, and seated him beside himself.

Then Theudas addressed the king as follows:

“May you live forever, O king, surrounded by the favor and goodwill of the greatest gods. For it has been reported to me that you have entered into a mighty contest against the Galilaeans and have carried away a splendid victory. For this reason I have come [Col. 0560A] here, so that, as a display of gratitude, we may celebrate the festival together, sacrifice to the immortal gods young men of elegant appearance and beautiful girls, and offer them a hundred bulls and many other animals, so that we may also have them thereafter as unconquerable helpers, making the whole course of our life smooth and even.”

To this the king replied: “Not at all,” he said, “old man; we have not won—no, I say, we have not won. Rather, we have been defeated with scarcely any difficulty. For those who were on our side suddenly rose up against us; and, finding our army as though stricken with madness and insanity, and weakened, they utterly broke and overthrew it. Now, if you possess any ability or power by which you can assist our religion lying prostrate on the ground and raise it up again, I would have you explain it.” [Col. 0560B]

Theudas answered the king in this manner: “Do not fear in the least, O king, the arguments and empty speeches of the Galileans. For what are the things they bring forward, at least so far as men endowed with reason and prudence are concerned? In my judgment, they will be cast down more easily than a leaf shaken by the wind. They will not even endure my presence, much less engage in argument and set foot against me in debate.

“Moreover, so that both this proposed contest and whatever else we may have in mind may proceed on a straight course, and matters may turn out for us according to our desire, see that you adorn this public festival and clothe yourself in the benevolence of the gods as though in the strongest weapons; then you will have every good fortune.” [Col. 0560C]

When he had made these boasts—he who, to speak with David, was powerful in wickedness and meditated injustice all day long (Psalm 51)—and who, to use Isaiah’s words, was offering his friend a turbid overturning [Note: [Col. 0559D] He has suffered a lapse of memory.] (Habakkuk 2), he accomplished, through the assistance and aid of the wicked spirits whom he himself had as companions, that the king completely cast from his memory those thoughts that were reminding him of salvation and diligently clung once more to the pursuits to which he was accustomed. Accordingly, when royal letters had passed in every direction, ordering everyone to assemble for the accursed festival of the gods, one could see an enormous multitude of people streaming together and bringing with them sheep, oxen, and various animals.

When everyone had assembled, the king rose and, together with the impostor Theudas, went to the temple so that they might sacrifice bulls and very many animals. Thus they celebrated a wicked festival, worthy of execration, so that the whole city resounded with the bellowing of the brute animals and even the air itself was polluted by the stench of the victims. [Col. 0560D]

When these things had been completed, and the wicked spirits were boasting exceedingly of Theudas’s victory, while the priests had given him thanks, the king withdrew once more to the palace and said to Theudas:

“See: as you commanded, I have neglected no effort whatever that concerned the splendor of the festival and the magnificence of the sacrifices. Now, therefore, it is time for you to fulfill what you promised me: rescue my son, who has defected from our religion, from the error of the Christians, and reconcile him again with the kindly gods.

“For although I have employed every art and moved every stone, I have nevertheless found no cure for his illness; rather, I have perceived that his mind is superior to everything. For when I undertook to deal with him gently and mildly, I discovered that even then I could in no way win his affection. But when I treated him harshly and bitterly, I saw that this only drove him further into stubbornness.

“Therefore I entrust to your wisdom the calamity that has befallen me. If, freed through your aid and assistance, I see my son once more worshiping my gods with me and enjoying the pleasures of this luxurious life and the delights of the kingdom, I shall erect a golden statue to you and ensure that henceforth, forever, the same honor as that given to the gods is bestowed upon you by all.” [Col. 0561A]

Theudas, therefore, lending an attentive ear to the devil, and having learned from him a wicked and deadly plan, devoting his tongue and mouth to the devil’s service, said to the king:

“If you wish to bring your son under your control and render his stubbornness in fighting ineffectual, I have devised a method which he will in no way be able to resist. His hard spirit will be softened more easily than wax brought near a great fire.” [Col. 0561B]

The king, seeing the empty man puffed up with hollow pride, immediately turned to pleasure and gladness of heart, hoping, of course, that this impudent and audacious tongue, instructed by divine wisdom and filled with philosophy, would overcome his son. When he asked what this method was, Theudas, like a sharp razor, wove his deception (Psalm 72) and craftily prepared his drugs. [Col. 0561C]

“Consider, I ask, the wicked scheme and the devil’s plan. O king,” he said, “order that all who stand by and serve your son be kept far away from him, and that women of beautiful and exceedingly elegant appearance, adorned to attract the mind, remain constantly with him, minister to him, and share his life and companionship. I shall then send one of the spirits whom I have procured for such purposes to him and kindle a fiercer fire of pleasure.

“As soon as he has had intercourse with even one such little woman, if everything does not proceed for you according to your desire, you will have cause to despise me and regard me as a man of no use, deserving not honors but the greatest punishments. For nothing attracts and soothes the minds of males as much as the sight of women.

“And, so that you may put faith in my words, I would have you hear this story.” [Col. 0561D]

### Chapter XXX

A certain king was deeply distressed because he had no male offspring, and considered this a great misfortune. While he was in this condition, a son was born to him, and he was filled with the greatest joy on that account.

Some learned physicians told him that if the boy saw the sun or fire before the age of twelve, he would be completely deprived of his sight, for this was indicated by the position of his eyes. When the father heard this, he is said to have built a dark chamber inside a certain rock and shut his son up there with his nurses, showing him no brightness of light at all before the completion of twelve years. [Col. 0562A]

When this period had been completed, he brought his son out of the chamber—the boy, who up to that day had seen nothing whatever of the things of the world—and ordered everything to be displayed and explained to him according to its kind: men in one place, women in another; gold from one direction, silver from another; pearls and precious stones of exceptional value; splendid and elegant garments; chariots of remarkable beauty, together with royal horses equipped with golden bridles, purple curtains, and armed riders; herds of oxen and flocks of sheep; and, to sum it up, he showed the boy everything in a fixed order. [Col. 0562B]

When the boy asked by what name each thing was called, the king’s attendants and guards explained the name of each. When he wished to know the name of the women, one of the king’s armor-bearers, jokingly and playfully, said that they were called demons, by whom the minds of human beings were led into error.

The boy’s heart was enticed and soothed by love and desire for them more powerfully than by longing for anything else. When, after he had been led through all the objects, they brought him to the king, and the king asked him which of all the things he had seen pleased him most, he replied:

“What else but those demons who lead human beings into deception? For my mind has been inflamed by love for them more than by love for any of the other things I saw today.”

The king marveled at the boy’s words and judged from them how violent and tyrannical the love of women was. Therefore you too should think that you will bring your son under your control by no other means than this.”

The king accepted this advice, and immediately selected girls of outstanding and exceptional beauty were brought to him. After adorning them in elegant clothing and equipping them entirely to attract the young man’s mind, he expelled all his servants and attendants from the palace and substituted the girls in their place. [Col. 0562C]

They therefore clung to him on every side, embraced him, and incited him to wicked intercourse, provoking him to pleasure through all their gestures and words. He had no one else to look at, no one else with whom to converse or dine; for they were everything to him.

This was what the king was doing. Theudas, however, returned once more to his deadly cavern, took into his hands books capable of producing such effects, and sent one of the wicked spirits he had summoned to challenge Christ’s soldier in battle. The wretched man did not know how much laughter he was about to provoke, nor how great a mark of disgrace he and his entire diabolical cohort would incur.

The wicked spirit, taking additional and even more evil spirits with him, went to the chamber of the noble young man and attacked him, kindling an exceedingly fierce furnace of the flesh. The devil applied inward flames to him, while the girls, as distinguished in bodily beauty as they were deformed in spirit, supplied wicked fuel from without. [Col. 0562D]

But that pure soul recognized the attack of the deadly spirit and saw the perverse battle of thoughts that was coming against him with a great and violent assault. He was troubled and wished to be delivered from so great an evil and to present himself pure to Christ, not to defile with the filth of lust that holy robe with which baptismal grace had clothed him.

Therefore he immediately opposed love to love—that is, divine love to impure love—and recalled to mind that beauty and glory surpassing every word, which pure souls will possess at the marriage feast of Christ the Bridegroom, from which those who have defiled their wedding garment will be cast out and, with hands and feet bound, dragged into the outer darkness (Matthew 22).

As he considered these things in his heart and poured out tears, he beat his breast, driving those wicked thoughts to flight like drones. Then he rose, lifted up his hands, and with warm tears and groans implored God’s aid and assistance, using these words:

“Almighty Lord, who alone possess power and are inclined to mercy—Lord, I say, hope of the despairing and of those who lack help, remember now, I beg you, me, your useless servant; look upon me with an easy and favorable eye; rescue my soul from the devil’s sword and my only one from the hand of the dog, and do not permit me to fall into the hands of my enemies (Psalm 22).

“Let those who hate me unjustly not rejoice over me (Psalm 35); do not permit me to be corrupted by iniquities, nor allow my body, which I promised to present to you chaste, to suffer disgrace and insult. For you I desire, and you I adore, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, forever.” [Col. 0563A]

When he had added “Amen,” he felt divine consolation coming to him from heaven, and the wicked thoughts withdrew. He continued in prayer until morning. Having understood the tricks and devices of his deceitful enemy, he began to afflict his body both through lack of food and through thirst and other forms of hardship. He spent the night standing upright in prayer, recalling to himself the promises he had made with God, envisioning in his mind both the future splendor of those who practice righteousness and the Gehenna announced for the wicked.

He did this so that, if the enemy found his soul idle and relaxed, he might not easily insert perverse thoughts into it and disturb and pollute its purity. When the enemy had completely lost heart and utterly despaired of overthrowing the steadfast young man, he turned to another and more cunning deception—as one who is always evil and never ceases either to devise something or to inflict injury and harm—devoting all his effort to carrying out what Theudas had ordered him to do. Thus he prepared drugs of this kind once more. [Col. 0563B]

A girl, the most beautiful of all those women, entered the young man’s presence. She was also the daughter of a certain king, carried away captive from her homeland and presented to King Abenner as a gift of exceptional value. The father had sent her, since she possessed extraordinary beauty, to weaken and overthrow his son’s mind.

That impostor whispered to her and suggested such words as would clearly reveal her prudence and wisdom—if indeed the devil readily and skillfully practices every art suited to vice. Then, approaching the king’s son on his right side, he implanted love for the girl in him, on account, he claimed, of her prudence and dignity, and also because she was of noble birth and had come from royal stock, though at the same time deprived of her homeland and glory. [Col. 0563C]

He also insinuated thoughts of this sort: that he should free her from the mad worship of idols and make her a Christian.

All this, however, was the stratagem of the crafty dragon. For since the king’s son was disposed and established in mind so that he perceived in himself no obscene thought or lustful love for the wavering girl, but felt himself moved only by her misfortune and the ruin of her soul, he did not notice at all that the matter was a diabolical contrivance. For that being was truly darkness, and he made himself resemble light.

When the king’s son began to address the girl and explain to her the oracles of divine knowledge, he said:

“Recognize, woman, the God who lives forever, and do not allow yourself to be held by the error of idols. Understand that the Lord is the maker of all things, and you will be blessed, joined to an immortal bridegroom.” [Col. 0563D]

When he had said many things of this kind, the wicked spirit immediately put it into the woman’s mind to spread out the snares of deception and drag that soul, dear to God, headlong into the pit of lust—just as once, through Eve’s agency, he had wretchedly expelled the author of the human race from paradise and from God, condemning him to death instead of blessed and immortal life.

When the girl had heard those words filled with all wisdom, she did not understand them because of her stupidity. Instead, she gave the reply appropriate to one who was the tongue and mouth of the devil. She said:

“If you care about my salvation, O lord, and strive to reconcile me to your God and bring salvation to my abandoned soul, grant one request of mine, and immediately, rejecting all the gods of my ancestors, I shall join myself to your God and worship him to my final breath. In this way you will receive a reward for my salvation and conversion to God.” [Col. 0564A]

When he asked what this request was, she prepared herself in dress, appearance, speech, and finally in every respect to attract his mind, and said:

“Join yourself to me in marriage, and I shall willingly obey your commands.”

But he replied:

“You have proposed a difficult request to me in vain, woman. For although I am deeply concerned for your salvation and wish to draw you out of the pit of death and destruction, it is nevertheless exceedingly grievous—indeed wholly impossible—for me to defile my body through shameful intercourse.”

But she, clearing a smooth path for the crime, said:

“Why do you use such language, you who possess every kind of wisdom? Why, I ask, have you called this matter impurity and shameful intercourse? I too am not ignorant of or deprived of the books of the Christians. I have read many books in my homeland and have often conversed with Christians.

“What then? Is it not written in one of your books: ‘Marriage is honorable, and the bed undefiled’ (Hebrews 13)? And again: ‘It is better to marry than to burn’ (1 Corinthians 7)? And again: ‘What God has joined, let no man separate’ (Matthew 16)? Do not your Scriptures teach that all the ancient righteous men—the patriarchs as well as the prophets—were joined in lawful marriage? Is it not written that Peter, whom you proclaim to have been the chief of the apostles, had a wife (Luke 4)?

“What, then, has led you to call such a matter impurity? You seem to me to be greatly departing from the truth of your doctrines.” [Col. 0564B]

He replied to her:

“Indeed, woman, these things are as you have said. Anyone may be joined in marriage, except those who have once promised virginity to Christ. From the day on which, through the washing of divine baptism, I was cleansed from the sins of my youth and ignorance, I promised to present myself pure to Christ. How, then, would I dare dissolve and violate the promises I made with God?”

The woman spoke to him again:

“Let this matter be as you yourself wish. But if you truly care about bringing salvation to my soul, satisfy this other small desire of mine, one of no importance. Have intercourse with me on this one night, and arrange that I too may enjoy your beauty and that you in turn may be satisfied by the elegance of my form. If you do this, I promise you that as soon as day dawns I shall embrace the Christian religion and abandon the worship of all my gods.

“For such a course you will obtain from your God not only forgiveness but also benefits, on account of my salvation. For, as your Scripture says, ‘There is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents’ (Luke 19). If joy is stirred in heaven over the repentance of a wicked person, what could be offered so that the author of this repentance would not deserve a great reward? [Col. 0564C]

“This is certainly how matters stand, and you have no reason to doubt. What of it? Did not the apostles also, the leaders of your religion, often do many things with deliberate purpose, occasionally violating a divine command for the sake of a greater command? Is it not said that Paul circumcised Timothy for the sake of a superior purpose (Acts 16)? Yet circumcision is regarded as a crime among Christians; nevertheless, he did not hesitate to do this. You will find many other things of this kind in your Scriptures.

“Therefore, if you seriously wish to bring salvation to my soul, satisfy this small desire of mine. Although otherwise I wish to be joined with you in the perfect bond of marriage, since that is not at all pleasing to you, I shall no longer force you but will henceforth do whatever you wish. Only do not utterly reject and execrate me; comply with me in this one matter, bring me salvation, and free me from superstitious error. Afterward you may do throughout your life whatever seems good to you.” [Col. 0564D]

As she used these words—for she had someone to suggest them to her, to whom she secretly lent her ears, and that craftsman of vice, the devil, was skilled in the Scriptures—she soothed him and began to weaken the tower of his mind, to slacken the sinews of his resolve, and to soften his will and purpose, weaving nets and snares around him on every side, both right and left.

The sower of vice and enemy of good men, seeing that his mind was wavering and filled with the greatest joy at this, immediately called the wicked spirits who were present with him:

“See,” he said, “how this girl is attempting to accomplish what we were unable to accomplish. Come, then; let us now attack him fiercely. We shall never find another time so suitable for fulfilling the will of the one who sent us.”

When the deceiver had spoken thus to his companions, they leapt upon Christ’s soldier, disturbing all the powers of his mind, implanting in his breast the most intense love for the girl, and kindling within him the fiercest fire of lust. [Col. 0565A]

But when he perceived that he was burning violently and being dragged captive toward sin, and that his thoughts—while proposing to him the girl’s salvation and conversion to God—were concealing the crime like bait beneath a hook, and that, at the enemy’s instigation, they were troubling him as though it were scarcely a crime to have intercourse once with a woman for the sake of saving her soul, he groaned from the depths of his heart in such anxiety and lack of counsel. Immediately he turned to prayer and, pouring abundant streams of tears from his eyes, cried out to him who can bring salvation to those who trust in him:

“In you, Lord, I have hoped; I shall not be put to shame forever (Psalm 31). Let not my enemies mock me as I cling to your right hand; rather, at this hour stand by me according to your will, directing my paths, so that your holy, glorious, and fearful name may be glorified in me, your servant, for blessed are you forever. Amen (Psalm 25).” [Col. 0565B]

After he had poured out prayers with tears for several hours and had frequently bent his knees, he threw himself upon the ground. Falling asleep for a short time, he saw himself seized by certain terrifying men. After traveling through regions he had never seen, he was brought to a vast plain, endowed with beautiful flowers and immense sweetness. There he saw plants of every kind, overflowing with certain unusual and marvelous fruits, delightful to behold and most pleasant to taste.

The leaves of the trees produced a sweet sound when stirred by a very gentle breeze, and as they moved they emitted an inexhaustible fragrance. There were also seats set up there, constructed of gold and stones of immense value, giving off a brilliant splendor; and splendid couches, adorned with marvelous coverings whose elegance surpassed every power of speech. [Col. 0565C]

In addition, exceptionally clear waters flowed there, delighting the eyes themselves. Then those terrifying men led him through this immense and wondrous plain into a city glowing with indescribable splendor. Its walls were made of translucent gold, while its towers and battlements were constructed of stones never seen by anyone.

Who could possibly describe in words the beauty and splendor of that city? A light flashing repeatedly from above filled all its streets with rays, and bright winged armies dwelt throughout it, producing a song such as no mortal ear had ever heard.

He heard a voice saying:

“This is the rest of those who have practiced righteousness; this is the delight of those who have proved the account of their lives to the Lord.”

The terrifying men said that they wished to lead him back out of that place. But he, completely carried away by that delight and joy, said:

“Do not, I beg you, deprive me of this joy, which cannot be expressed in words. Rather, grant me this: that I may dwell in one corner of this most spacious city.”

They answered him:

“It is not now possible for you to be here. But you will attain this at last through many labors and sweats, if only you do violence to yourself.” [Col. 0565D]

When this had been said, and they had once more crossed the great plain, they led him into dark places full of every sorrow, directly opposed both to the splendor he had previously seen and to that joy. It was a completely obscure and dark gloom, and the whole place overflowed with affliction and tumult.

There a furnace of fire was kindled, and a kind of torturing worm crawled about; avenging powers hovered over the furnace. Some were burning miserably in the fire, and a voice of this kind was heard:

“This is the place of sinners; here is the torment of those who have defiled themselves with shameful crimes.”

Afterward he was led out of that place by those who had brought him there. Immediately returning to himself, he trembled throughout his body, and tears flowed from his eyes like rivers. The beauty of that shameless girl and of all the others appeared to him more foul-smelling than any filth or putrefaction. Recalling what he had seen, seized both by longing for those good things and by fear of those torments, he lay in bed in such a condition that he had no ability to rise. [Col. 0566A]

When word reached the king concerning his son’s adverse condition, he immediately went to him and asked what had happened. The young man explained what he had seen and said:

“Why have you prepared a snare for my feet and bent down my soul (Psalm 57)? For if the Lord had not helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell (Psalm 39). But how good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart! He also rescued my humility from the midst of lion cubs; I slept while troubled (Psalm 72). But God, my Savior, visited me and showed me how greatly those who provoke him to anger deprive themselves of good things, and how many torments they make themselves liable to suffer.

“But now, O father, since you have closed your ears so that you would not hear my voice singing good and useful things to you, at least do not prevent me from taking the right path. This is what I desire and seek: that, freed from everything, I may hasten to those places where Barlaam, the servant of Christ, dwells, and complete what remains of my life with him.

“If you resolve to retain me by force, you will soon see me extinguished by sorrow and disgust. Thus you will no longer be called my father, nor will you have me as your son.” [Col. 0566B]

### Chapter XXXI

Again, therefore, great sorrow seized the king. Again he began to abandon all hope for his life, and, turning bitter thoughts over in his mind, he went into his palace.

But the wicked spirits who had been sent by Theudas against the divine young man returned to him covered with shame. Although they otherwise delight in lying, they nevertheless confessed the defeat they had suffered. Indeed, they bore clear signs of their defeat on their wicked faces.

He said to them:

“Are you so weak and wretched that you were utterly unable to overcome one young man?”

Then the wicked spirits, tortured by divine power, unwillingly brought the truth to light, using these words:

“We cannot resist even in the slightest the power of Christ and the sign of his Passion, which they call the Cross. For as soon as it is formed, all of us who are princes of the air and rulers of the darkness of this world (Ephesians 6) flee as quickly as possible, and we are driven away even before it has been fully and perfectly traced.

“Therefore, when we attacked this young man, we greatly disturbed him. But when he invoked Christ’s aid and fortified himself with the sign of the Cross, he drove us away in anger and secured for himself the strongest protection.

“Accordingly, without delay we seized that instrument by whose agency our own prince first attacked the first human being and subjected him to his power. We certainly considered the young man’s hope vain; but when Christ was again summoned to his aid, he turned us to flight, consumed by the fire of heavenly wrath.

“Therefore we have resolved not to approach him again.” [Col. 0566C]

In this manner Theudas’s wicked spirits clearly explained what had happened.

The king, completely perplexed in mind and deprived of counsel, summoned Theudas once more and said to him:

“Although everything you taught has been completed and carried out, we have nevertheless gained no advantage. Now, therefore, if you have any other advice remaining, let us try it. Perhaps we may find some means of driving away this evil.”

When Theudas asked to come into conversation with the king’s son, the king set out in the morning with him to visit his son. When he had sat down beside him, he began to address him, attack him with reproaches, and accuse him of stubbornness and hardness of spirit.

But when the young man once more affirmed the true doctrines and declared that nothing ought to be valued above love for Christ, Theudas came forward and said:

“What fault have you found, O Josaphat, in our immortal gods, so that you have departed from their worship and, by offending the mind of the king your father, have brought upon yourself the hatred of the entire people? Did you not receive life from them? Did they not give you to your father as a gift, having heard his prayers and released him from the bonds of barrenness?” [Col. 0566D]

When that man of long-established wickedness had raised many empty arguments and many useless questions and had woven arguments concerning the preaching of the Gospel—with the intention of attacking it and strengthening the worship of idols—the son of the heavenly King and citizen of that city which was built not by man but by God (Hebrews 8), after restraining himself for a short while, finally said to Theudas:

“Listen, abyss of imposture, darker than palpable darkness; Babylonian seed, and descendant of the builders of the Chaldean tower, because of whom the world was thrown into confusion (Genesis 11); vain and wretched old man, who have bound yourself with crimes heavier than those of the five cities consumed by divine fire.

“Do you attempt to attack with mockery the preaching of salvation, through which those things surrounded by darkness received light, through which those who were wandering found the way, and through which those who had perished and were oppressed by miserable servitude were restored to their former condition?

“Tell me, then, which of these two is superior: to worship and honor the almighty God together with his only-begotten Son and the Holy Spirit—the uncreated and immortal God, the fountain of every good thing, whose dominion and power cannot be grasped by conjecture, nor his glory comprehended by the mind; before whom thousands upon thousands and ten-thousands upon ten-thousands of angelic and heavenly orders stand; whose glory heaven and earth are full of; through whom all things were brought forth from nothing; through whom the world is held together and preserved and governed by his providence—or to worship pestilential demons and lifeless images, whose praise and glory consist in adultery, the defilement of boys, and the other crimes written about your gods in the volumes of your superstition? [Col. 0567A]

“Are you not ashamed, wretches and food for everlasting fire, bearing the likeness of the Chaldean race? Are you not ashamed, I ask, to worship dead statues constructed by human hands? You call carved stone or wood, polished by a craftsman’s art, a god. Then you take an exceptional bull, or perhaps another of the most beautiful animals of its kind, and in your madness sacrifice it to the dead divinity.

“Yet the victim is superior to your god. Man fashioned the god, but God created the animal. For that reason the brute animal surpasses you, who possess reason, in prudence and understanding. It knows the one who feeds it; you, on the other hand, suffer from ignorance of the one by whom you were brought forth from nothing and by whose beneficence you live and are preserved.

“You call him a god whom you had just seen being beaten with iron, melted by fire, and struck with hammers; whom you covered with silver and gold and raised up from the earth. Then, when he has been thrown down upon the ground, you, a worshiper more contemptible than the rejected stone, adore him—not God, but the dead and lifeless works of your hands. [Col. 0567B]

“Indeed, it is not even right to call the image dead. Rather, one should invent some new name worthy of such madness. The stone image is crushed; the clay image is broken; the wooden image decays; the bronze image is stained by rust; the golden and silver images are melted by fire. Moreover, some of your gods are sold for a small and cheap price, others for the highest price. It is not divinity that gives them their value, but their material.

“Yet who could buy or sell God? And how can one call a being a god who is incapable of movement? Do you not see that the one who stands never sits, and the one who sits never stands?

“Be ashamed, senseless man. Put your hand over your mouth, you fool, who praise such things. Turned away from the truth, you are deceived and led into error by false representations, fashioning statues and assigning the name of God to things made by your own hand.

“Come to your senses, wretched man, and understand that you are older than the god made by you. What madness is this? Have you persuaded yourself that, although you are a human being, you can make a god? How could such a thing ever happen?

“Therefore you do not make a human being, but merely the form of a human being or of some animal, without a tongue, throat, brain, or any internal part. Consequently, it is not even a likeness of a human being or an animal, but altogether a useless thing filled with vanity.

“Why, then, do you flatter things devoid of sensation? Why do you sit beside things without mind and without use? If the art of the stonecutter, architect, or hammer-smith were absent, you would have no god. If guards were not present, you would lose your god. For the city, often filled with a vast multitude of foolish people, entreats that object as a god, asking to be protected by it, while only a few guards remain with the object itself so that it may not be stolen.

“If it is made of silver or gold, it is carefully guarded; but if it is made of stone, clay, or some other cheaper material, it guards itself. Thus, according to your own judgment, the one made of clay is stronger than the one cast from gold.” [Col. 0567C]

The source ends here, incomplete.

Can we not, then, with the greatest justification, mock—or rather mourn over—you foolish, blind, and senseless men? For your works breathe madness rather than piety. The man devoted to military affairs gives the name Mars to a statue fashioned in the likeness of a military figure and set up in a particular place. Another, burning with love for women to the point of insanity, gives form in a painting to the desire of his soul and makes his vice into a god, calling it by the name Venus. Yet another, because of his drunkenness, fashions an image and calls it Bacchus himself. In the same way, those who are devoted to other vices set up images of them and impose the name of gods upon their vices.

For this reason, lascivious dances, meretricious songs, and frenzied impulses take place before their altars. Who, then, could go on to recount their abominable depravity? Or who could endure defiling his mouth by embracing in speech their utterly foul lust? Yet these things are clear to everyone, even if we remain silent. These are your gods, Theudas, more stupid than your statues. You urge me to worship them and to venerate them. That counsel is certainly consistent with your wickedness and foolish opinion; but may you become like them, and all who trust in them (Ps. CXIII).

I, however, shall worship my God and consecrate my whole self to him—to God, I say, the creator and governor of all things—through our Lord Jesus [Col. 0571B] Christ, our hope, through whom we have also gained access to the Father of lights in the Holy Spirit, and through whom we have been freed by his blood from bitter bondage (Eph. II). For unless he had also humbled himself even to the form of a servant (Phil. II), we could by no means have attained adoption as sons. For our sake he humbled himself; he did not regard his divinity as something to be seized, but remained what he was and assumed what he was not. He lived among human beings (Baruch III); in his flesh he ascended the cross; he was laid in the tomb for three days; he descended to the underworld; and from there he led out those whom the dreadful ruler of the world held bound, sold under sin.

What harm, then, did he suffer from this, that you appear to attack him with taunts on that account? Do you not perceive into how many foul and indecent places the sun sends his rays, and how many stinking corpses he looks upon? Does he thereby contract any stain? Or does he not rather dry up and harden whatever is filthy and rotten, illuminate whatever is dark, and meanwhile himself remain wholly unharmed and free from every stain? Likewise, when fire takes up iron, which by its nature is black and cold, does it not set it completely aflame and make it glow white-hot, without meanwhile taking on any of the properties of iron? For when iron is struck with hammers, the fire suffers nothing and receives no harm.

Therefore, if these created things, whose nature is such that they will at some time perish, suffer no disadvantage from contact with things lower and worse than themselves, by what reasoning, O senseless man with a heart of stone [Col. 0571D], do you dare mock me because I say that the Son, God the Word, in no way departed from the glory of the Father, but, although he was God, assumed a human body for the salvation of humankind, so that he might make human beings partakers of the divine and spiritual nature, adorn our substance—brought up from the subterranean regions of hell—with heavenly glory, and also overcome the ruler of this age of darkness, having lured him by the assumed flesh as by a kind of bait, and free our race from his bondage and tyranny?

For this reason he also underwent the torment of the cross without suffering, thereby declaring his two natures. As man, he is led to the cross; as God, he casts darkness over the sun, shakes the earth, and raises many bodies that had died from their tombs [Col. 0572A] (Luke XXIII). Again, as man, he dies; but as God, after hell has been despoiled, he returns to life. Therefore the Prophet also cried out:

> Hell was in bitterness, meeting you below.

For it was in bitterness and was deceived: thinking that it had received a naked man, it encountered God and suddenly became empty and captive. Thus he rises as God; and he ascends into heaven, from which he had in no way departed, and makes our contemptible nature, lower than all others, higher than all, placing it, radiant with immortal glory, upon the throne of glory.

What harm, then, was inflicted upon God the Word by this, that you do not blush to pursue him with curses and insults? Which of these two, I ask, is more excellent: to confess these things and venerate this good and human-loving God—who commands justice, enjoins self-control, prescribes purity, teaches that one should be inclined toward mercy, grants faith, proclaims peace, and is himself named and is truth itself and love itself—or, on the contrary, to venerate your wicked gods, bound by countless offenses and foul and obscene both in their deeds and in their names?

Woe to you, harder than stones, more senseless than brute animals, sons of destruction and heirs of darkness! But blessed am I, and blessed are all Christians, who have a good and gracious God. For those who render him worship, even if for a short time in this life they are harassed by adversity, will nevertheless receive the immortal fruit of their reward in the kingdom of everlasting and divine blessedness [Col. 0572C].

Then Theudas said to him:

“Here is an obvious point: many great and wise men and interpreters, admirable both for virtue and for learning, established our religion, and all the kings and rulers of the world accepted it as distinguished and free from every danger. But, on the other hand, the doctrine of the Galileans was proclaimed by certain rustic, poor, and despised men—very few of them, no more than twelve. Should, then, the preaching of obscure and rustic men be regarded as superior to the laws and institutions of many great men who flourished with such renown for wisdom? What basis do you have for demonstrating that these men spoke the truth and those others lied?”

Again the king’s son replied:

“You are an ass, Theudas, as the saying goes, listening to a lyre [Note: [Col. 0606C] ‘You are an ass listening to a lyre.’ A well-known proverb: Ὄνος λύρας, namely ἀκροατής, ‘an ass listening to a lyre.’ See the paroemiographers.], and you remain without understanding—or, to speak more accurately, you are an asp, stopping your ears lest you hear the voice of those who chant excellently (Ps. LVII). Rightly, then, the prophet said of you:

> If an Ethiopian can change his skin and a leopard his spots, then you also, foolish and blind man, will be able to do good after learning evil.

Why does this not affect you with a sense of the truth? For this very claim of yours—that your impious worship is praised by many men endowed with admirable wisdom and confirmed by many kings, whereas the evangelical preaching is proclaimed by only a few, and those obscure men—demonstrates both the power of our religion and the weakness and ruinous character of your wicked doctrines [Col. 0573A]. Your doctrine, although it has learned advocates and strong supporters, is nevertheless weakened and extinguished; whereas our religion, though it lacks every human resource, shines more brightly than the sun and has occupied the whole world. For if it had been produced by orators and philosophers, and had kings and rulers as its supporters, you might perhaps have said, wicked man, that human power had accomplished the whole thing.

“But now, when you see the holy Gospel written by lowly fishermen and harassed by every tyrant, yet nevertheless possessing the whole world—for, as he says [Ps. XVIII; Rom. X], ‘Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world’—what else can you say except that it is divine and unconquerable power confirming its worship for the sake of human salvation? What stronger argument than those already offered do you, foolish man, seek by which I may prove that your people lie and ours speak the truth? For unless all your claims were trifles and fabrications, they would certainly not be weakened and brought low, supported as they are by such great human forces.

“For I saw,” he says, “the wicked man highly exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon; then I passed by, and behold, he was not there; I sought him, and his place was not found” (Ps. XXXVI). Concerning you, who are mad defenders of idol worship, the Prophet said:

> Soon, very soon, his place will not be found; but as smoke disappears, so he will disappear, and as wax melts before the fire, so you will perish (Ps. LXVII).

“Against the knowledge of God proclaimed in the Gospel, the Lord said:

> Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away (Luke XXI).

“And again the Prophet uses these words:

> In the beginning you, Lord, founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain, and they will all grow old like a garment. Like a covering you will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years will not fail (Ps. CI).

“The divine heralds of Christ’s coming, the wise fishermen of the world, who drew everyone out of the abyss of error and fraud—whom you, though you are truly a slave of sin, despise and count as nothing—shone in the world like the sun through signs and wonders, giving light to the blind, hearing to the deaf, the power to walk to the lame, and finally life to the dead. Indeed, even their shadows alone drove away every disease of human beings (Acts V) [Col. 0573D].

“The demons whom you fear as gods they not only drove from human bodies but also put to flight from the whole earth by the sign of the cross. By its power and aid they destroyed all magic and rendered every enchantment ineffective. They were healed in this manner of human weakness through the power of Christ, and, when all created things had been renewed, they were praised and admired by all who possessed wisdom as heralds of the truth.

“What, then, do you have to bring forward concerning your wise men and orators, whose wisdom God made foolish—those, I mean, the devil’s advocates? Explain what worthy of remembrance they left to the world. What do you have to proclaim about them except madness and disgrace, and an empty art concealing the filth of their foul religion beneath the elegance of words?”

Moreover, even among your poets, those who managed to emerge even slightly from immense frenzy and madness spoke what was more truthful: namely, that those who are called gods were human beings, and that, because some of them ruled cities and regions while others accomplished some other thing of scarcely any importance during their lives, human beings, deceived by error, called them gods.

In the beginning, Seruch [Note: [Col. 0606C] Seruch. Is Sarug, the son of Reu, intended, as in Genesis XI? Certainly Epiphanius, at the beginning of the Panarion, traces the origin of idolatry to Terah and Seruch. In the Latin biblical text Terah had Sarug as his grandfather. Moreover, the figure who is Sarug in the Latin text is Σερούχ in the Greek, so that there can be no doubt that Damascene is referring to that passage of the Bible and to Epiphanius.] is reported in written records as having discovered statues. For it is said that those who in ancient times had accomplished something worthy of remembrance through courage, friendship, or some other virtue were honored with statues. But later generations, ignorant of the intention of their ancestors—namely, that statues and pillars had been erected merely for the sake of memory to those who had accomplished something worthy of praise—gradually went astray through the work of the demon, the author of vice. They worshiped as immortal gods men subject to the same passions and corruption, and devised sacrifices and libations for them: for the demons dwelling in the statues drew such honor and sacrifices to themselves.

Thus they lead those who do not approve of having God in their knowledge (Rom. I) to believe that they themselves are gods for two reasons. First, so that they themselves may be celebrated by this name; for, being full of pride and arrogance, they rejoice when honor is given to them as gods. Second, so that they may drag those whom they have deceived into the everlasting fire prepared for them. For this reason they instructed them in every kind of depravity and disgrace, with the result that people once devoted to their fraud and imposture, surrounded by the darkness of the mind and approaching the culmination of evils, each set up a statue of his own vice and desire and called it a god.

In this matter they are to be execrated both because of their error and, even more, because of the absurdity of the things they worship. This continued until the Lord, through the depths of his mercy, freed us who possess faith in him from such wicked and destructive error and filled us with the true knowledge of God [Col. 0574D]. For salvation is found in no other, and besides him alone who made the world and bears all things by the word of his power (Heb. I), there is no other god either in heaven or on earth. For, as he says:

> By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host (Ps. XXXII);

and:

> All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made (John I).

When Theudas had heard these words and perceived that this speech was full of divinely infused wisdom, he remained silent, as though struck by the sound of thunder. At last, recognizing his misery—for saving doctrine had touched the darkened eyes of his heart—he was overwhelmed by profound remorse for his former life [Col. 0575A]. Condemning the error of idolatry, he hastened toward the light of piety and thereafter withdrew so completely from his wicked and accursed way of life, and waged such a great war against his shameful affections and magical arts, as the bond of love he had previously made with them had been strong.

For then, standing in the midst of the assembly, with the king presiding, he cried out in a loud voice:

“Truly, O king, the Spirit of God dwells in your son; truly, we have been broken and defeated. We have no defense, nor can we even turn our eyes toward the things he has mentioned. Great, then, is truly the God of the Christians; great is his faith; great are his mysteries.”

Then, turning toward the king’s son, he said:

“Tell me, I ask you, O man endowed with a noble and illustrious spirit: will God receive me if I withdraw from wicked actions and turn to him?”

“Certainly,” replied the herald of truth, “certainly, I say, he will receive you, and likewise all who turn to him. Nor will he receive you in an ordinary manner; rather, as a father goes out to meet a son returning from a distant land (Luke XV)—that is, one turning from a wicked way of life to a better course—so will he go out to meet you, embrace you, and kiss you. Removing the filth of sin, he will immediately place upon you the garment of salvation, clothe you in the most beloved robe of glory, and prepare a mystical banquet with the powers above, celebrating a festival for the recovered lost sheep (ibid.).

“For the Lord himself said that there is great joy in heaven over one sinner who repents. And again:

> I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance (Luke V).

“And through the prophet he says:

> As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he turn from his way and live. Turn from your evil way; and why will you die, house of Israel? The wickedness of the wicked will not harm him on whatever day he turns from his wickedness, practices justice, and walks in the commandment of life: he will live and will not die. None of all the sins he committed will be remembered, because he practiced judgment and justice; in these he will live (Ezek. XXXIII).

“And again, through another prophet, he cries out:

> Wash yourselves; be clean. Remove the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes. Cease to act wickedly; learn to do good. If your sins are like scarlet, they will be made white as snow; and if they are red like crimson, they will become white like wool (Isa. I) [Col. 0575D].

“Since these promises have been set forth by God for those who return to a better course, do not delay, O man, and do not defer; instead, approach Christ our gracious God, and you will be enlightened, and your face will not be put to shame (Ps. XXXII). For as soon as you have been immersed in the pool of divine baptism, all the filth of the old person and the entire burden of crimes will be buried in the water and will dissolve into nothing. You will come up from it new and fresh, pure from every stain, carrying with you no mark or wrinkle of sin. Thereafter it will depend on you to guard and preserve the cleansing which you have received here through the deep compassion of our God.”

Theudas, instructed by these words, immediately left the palace and went to his wicked cave. There he shook out his magical books as the first fruits of every crime and the treasures of diabolical secrets. Then he went to the cave of that most holy man to whom Nachor too had gone, explained to him the whole condition of his affairs, sprinkled dust upon his head, uttered deep groans, drenched himself with tears, and recounted to the old man, one by one, all his impious crimes.

But the old man, being highly skilled in bringing salvation to the soul and rescuing it from the jaws of the wily dragon, soothed him with saving words [Col. 0576A], as though casting a spell over him; he promised forgiveness and assured him that God would be a favorable and merciful judge.
