Afterwards, when he had instructed him in the rudiments of the Christian faith and prescribed a fast of many days, he cleansed him through divine baptism. From then on, throughout his life, Theudas sincerely repented of the crimes he had committed and strove to appease God with tears and groans.

### CHAPTER XXXIII

When matters had come to this point, the king, utterly bereft of counsel, was plunged into profound grief and greatly tormented in mind. After the senate had again been convened, he considered what he should do with his son. When many men had offered many opinions, Araches—the man whom we mentioned above, who was both the most distinguished of all the commanders and held the foremost place in the senate—addressed the king as follows:

“What ought we to have done to your son, O king, that we have not done, in order to induce him to follow our doctrines and worship our gods? But, as I see, we are attempting the impossible, since obstinacy and hardness of spirit have been implanted in him by nature, or perhaps even by fortune. Therefore, if you decide to afflict him with punishments and tortures, you will both show yourself an enemy of nature and lose the name of father; and you will suffer his loss, since he is prepared to seek death for Christ.

“It remains, then, for you to adopt this course: divide the kingdom with him and entrust him with the administration of the royal office in that part which belongs to him. If the nature of affairs and the concern for worldly matters draw him toward embracing our way of life and our institutions, matters will turn out according to our wishes. For habits deeply strengthened in the soul are difficult to erase and obliterate, and are changed more readily by the blandishments of words than by force. But if he persists in the religion of the Christians, then at least the fact that you have not been deprived of your son will mitigate your grief to some extent.”

When Araches had delivered this speech, everyone approved his opinion, and the king agreed to act accordingly.

Accordingly, when day had dawned on the following day, he summoned his son and addressed him thus:

“This is my final speech to you, my son. Unless you obey it at once and at least in this matter ease the pain of my heart, believe me, I will no longer deal indulgently with you.”

When his son asked what he meant by these words, he replied:

“I have found you, after many efforts, utterly unyielding and obstinate toward everything, since you have never thought that you ought to obey any of my words. Come, then: by dividing my empire, I shall arrange for you to live separately and rule a kingdom. Thus you will now be able safely to enter the path you desire so greatly.”

That divine soul, although he understood that the king was proposing this as a means of undermining his purpose, nevertheless decided that he ought to obey, intending thereby to slip from his father’s hands and enter the path he desired. He therefore answered the king:

“I myself was eager to seek that holy man who showed me the way of salvation and, bidding farewell to all other things, to spend whatever remains of my life with him. But since, through you, O Father, I cannot at all do what lies nearest my heart, I shall comply with you in this matter, since in affairs where manifest destruction and estrangement from God are not at stake, it is honorable to obey one’s father.”

The king, therefore, filled with the greatest joy, divided the entire region subject to his rule and authority into two parts, made his son king, adorned him with a diadem, and, marked with every royal glory, sent him into the portion of the kingdom assigned to him with a splendid retinue of attendants. He also granted the nobles, commanders, military prefects, and satraps permission to depart with his son and king, if they were so disposed. He assigned him a large and populous city in which he could establish his royal residence and bestowed upon him everything appropriate to kings [Col. 0577C].

When Josaphat had thus obtained royal authority and power, and had arrived at the city where everything necessary for governing the kingdom had been prepared, he placed the sign of the Lord’s Passion—that is, the venerable cross of Christ—on each of the city’s towers. He demolished the shrines and altars of the idols and tore them up from their very foundations, leaving no remnant of impiety.

In the middle of the city he raised a great and splendid temple to Christ the Lord and commanded the people to come frequently to that place and render worship to God through the adoration of the cross. Then he himself came forward before all the others and offered prayers with the deepest devotion. He admonished and entreated all who were under his power and authority, omitting nothing that might draw them away from superstitious error and attach them to Christ: he exposed the fraud and imposture of idol worship, explained the preaching of the Gospel, recalled the wholly gracious condescension of God the Word [Col. 0577D], proclaimed the miracles of his coming, declared the punishment of the cross by which we attained salvation, recounted the power of the resurrection and the ascension into heaven, and finally announced that dreadful day of his second and terrifying coming, together with the blessings reserved for the pious and the torments awaiting the impious and wicked.

He expressed all these things in exceedingly gentle and persuasive words. For he wished to inspire veneration and awe in them less through the greatness of his power and royal magnificence than through modesty [Col. 0578A] and gentleness. This also drew everyone more strongly to him: just as he was admirable in life and conduct, so he was approachable and modest in spirit. The result was that his power, having received great support from modesty and mildness, brought everyone to obey his words.

Indeed, in so short a period of time, all the people subject to him—both the townspeople and those living nearby—were instructed in the Christian religion by his divine discourses. They renounced the worship of many false gods, broke away from the sacrifices to idols and from their accursed worship, turned to a faith free from error, and, renewed by his teaching, were joined to Christ.

All the priests and monks, and some bishops as well, who through fear of his father had hidden themselves in the mountains and caves, came out of their hiding places and went to him with joyful hearts. He came forth to meet those who had suffered such great hardships, bitterness, and calamities for Christ’s sake, received them honorably, and brought them into his palace. He washed their feet, wiped away their unkempt hair, and embraced them with every form of service.

Afterwards he arranged for the newly constructed church to be dedicated, and appointed as its bishop a certain man who had endured many afflictions for the sake of the Christian faith and had lost the throne of his bishopric—a holy man, I say, skilled in the ecclesiastical canons and wholly aflame with divine zeal [Col. 0578C]. Then, having quickly constructed a pool, he ordered those who had converted to Christ to be baptized. The rulers and magistrates were baptized first, then those of military rank, and afterwards the rest of the populace.

Those who received baptism obtained not only healing of their souls; all who suffered from bodily illnesses and fevers also returned from the pool, every adverse condition having been cast off, with pure minds and sound bodies—that is, having received health both of soul and of body.

For this reason an immense multitude of people from every direction flocked to King Josaphat, asking to be instructed by him in the teaching of piety. All the temples of the idols were destroyed, and all the wealth and money stored in the shrines were removed. In their place, holy temples were built for God, and King Josaphat assigned to them those riches, garments of immense value, and treasures, thus making that worthless and superfluous material useful and productive [Col. 0578D].

The accursed demons who dwelt in those shrines and altars were tormented and driven away with the utmost violence, and they cried aloud to many who heard them about the calamity that had overtaken them. The whole neighboring region was freed from their dark fraud and imposture and illuminated by the Christian faith, free from every stain and reproach.

The king himself was also an example of every virtue [Col. 0579A], and he aroused and inflamed many to the same will and conviction. Such is the nature of kingship and rule: subjects always model themselves upon the one who holds power and ordinarily love and pursue whatever they perceive pleases their ruler.

Thus, with God’s help, piety increased among them and made daily progress. The king devoted himself entirely to observing Christ’s commandments and depended upon his love. He was a dispenser of the Word and a governor of many souls, bringing them into the harbor of God. For he clearly understood that the foremost and highest of all royal duties is to instruct people in the fear of God and the worship of justice. This too he himself practiced, preparing himself to keep the passions of his soul under control, admonishing his subjects, and diligently holding the rudder of justice like an excellent helmsman.

For this is truly the law and rule of a genuine kingdom: to command pleasures and exercise mastery over them, just as he himself did. He did not in any way exalt himself on account of the nobility of his ancestors or the royal glory in which he lived—for we all have clay as the author of our race, and rich and poor alike are made of the same earth—but continually cast his mind into the abyss of humility. Holding future blessedness in his mind and thoughts, he regarded himself here as a tenant, and considered those things his own which he would enjoy after the pilgrimage of this life.

After he had accomplished these things splendidly, freed all those under his rule from the ancient error handed down by their fathers, and made them servants of him who redeemed us from evil bondage with his precious blood, he began to consider cultivating the virtue of benevolence and generosity. He had already perfected temperance and justice in every respect, being crowned with temperance and clothed in the purple of justice.

He therefore observed that the uncertainty of earthly riches resembles the flow of running water. Accordingly, he hastened to store them where neither moth nor rust destroys them, and where thieves do not break in and steal. He began, therefore, to distribute all his money to the poor without any restraint.

For he clearly understood that a person who has attained immense power must strive, as far as possible, to imitate the one through whose favor he attained that power. He would approach imitation of God in this way, if he considered nothing more important or more ancient than mercy. Therefore he amassed for himself the riches of piety, which both delight the soul here with the hope of future joy and gladden it there with the fruit of the blessedness hoped for, valuing them above gold and precious stone.

Afterwards, inspecting his prisons, he supplied abundantly both those condemned to the mines and those being strangled by creditors, and finally everyone with whatever they needed. He was the father of all orphans, widows, and poor people—a compassionate and gracious father—and he was so disposed that he considered himself benefited when he conferred some benefit upon them [Col. 0580A].

For, being endowed with a most generous and truly royal spirit, he gave abundantly to all who were in need, since he hoped for a reward infinitely greater than these gifts when the time should come for deeds to receive their recompense.

When his reputation of this kind had quickly spread everywhere, everyone came flocking to him daily, drawn as though by the fragrance of some perfume, so that they might shake off both bodily and spiritual poverty. He was on everyone’s lips. For it was not fear or tyrannical force that drew the people to him, but desire and sincere love for him—love divinely implanted in everyone’s heart through the excellence of his life.

At that time—even, I say, those who were under the rule of his father joined themselves to him instead, abandoned all error, and proclaimed the truth. The house of Josaphat grew and became strong, while the house of Abenner declined and weakened, just as it is recorded in the Book of Kings concerning David and Saul (II Kings II).

### CHAPTER XXIV

When King Abenner saw these things, at last recovering his senses, he condemned the weakness of his false gods and their empty imposture. After again assembling the leading men of the senate, he brought into the light what he had in mind.

When everyone confirmed the same course—for “the Dawn from on high had visited them” (Luke I), that is, the Savior, having heard the prayer of his servant Josaphat—the king decided that his son should be informed of these matters. Accordingly, on the following day he wrote him a letter in the following form:

> “King Abenner sends greetings to his dearest son Josaphat.
>
> “Many thoughts, dearest son, entering my mind, disturb it most grievously. For as I see all our possessions failing and vanishing like smoke, while your religion shines more brightly than the sun, I have recognized that what you told me is true. Dense darkness of crimes and impiety so overwhelmed us that we could not cast our eyes toward the truth or acknowledge the parent and maker of all things. Indeed, we deliberately refused to perceive the light, so brilliantly demonstrated to us by you, with our eyes closed on purpose; we afflicted you with many evils; and—O wretched me!—we slaughtered not a few Christians with cruel savagery. They, strengthened by unconquerable power assisting them, fought against our brutality to their final breath.
>
> “Now that this thick darkness has been removed from our eyes, we perceive a small ray of truth, and remorse for our former vices enters our mind. But another cloud of dreadful despair is rising and attempting to overwhelm and extinguish even this brightness: it places before my eyes the multitude of my sins and the fact that I am already hateful and accursed to Christ, so that I cannot now be received by him, since I rebelled against him and declared war upon him.
>
> “What hope, then, O most beloved son, can you offer concerning these matters? Let me know as soon as possible, teach me what I, your father, ought to do, and lead me by the hand, as it were, to an understanding of what will be for my benefit. Farewell.”

When Josaphat had received this letter and, in reading it, had gone through all that it contained [Col. 0581A], his spirit was filled at once with joy and wonder. He immediately entered his chamber, cast himself face down upon the ground before the image of the Lord, and drenched the earth with tears, giving thanks to the Lord while moving his lips in exultation to praise him, and using these words:

I will exalt you, my God and King, and bless your name forever and ever. Great are you, Lord, and greatly to be praised, and there is no end to your greatness (Psalm 144). And who can speak of your mighty deeds, or make all your praises heard (Psalm 105)? You who turned the rock into pools of water, and the crag into springs of water (Psalm 113). For behold, even this crag—and my father’s breast, harder than a crag—has by your will been softened like wax. For you can also raise up children for Abraham from stones (Matthew 3).

I give you thanks, gracious Lord and God of mercy, because you have dealt—and still deal—with our sins in gentleness, and have left us unpunished even to this day (Basil, *Book of the Constitutions*, chapter 1). For we had long since deserved to be cast away from your presence and branded in this life with public infamy, like those wicked men of Pentapolis who were consumed by fire and brimstone (Genesis 19). But your patience and incomparable gentleness dealt kindly with us. I, unworthy and contemptible as I am, give you thanks, even though I am unequal to praising and celebrating your kindness.

And I appeal to you, Lord Jesus Christ, Son and Word of the invisible Father, who brought all things into being by your word and by your will sustain and protect them; you who were stretched out upon the wood and bound the strong one (Matthew 12), and brought everlasting freedom to those whom he held bound: I entreat you, through your mercies, now also to stretch out your invisible, all-creating hand and completely free your servant and my father from that grievous captivity of the devil. Show him plainly that you, endowed with eternal life, are the true God and the only immortal and eternal King [Col. 0581D]. Look with a merciful and gracious eye, I beg you, upon the contrition of my heart; and, in accordance with that promise of yours into which falsehood cannot enter, stand on my side, for I confess and acknowledge you as the maker, creator, and governor of all things.

May your water flow into me as a spring (John 4), and may speech be given me when I open my mouth (Ephesians 6); and may my mind be firmly fixed upon you, the cornerstone, so that I, your useless servant, may properly explain to my father the mystery of your incarnation, lead him away by your power from the vain and deadly error of demons, and reconcile him to you, God and Lord, who do not desire the death of sinners but await their conversion and repentance (Ezekiel 18) [Col. 0582A]. For you are glorious forever and ever. Amen.

When he had prayed in this manner and had persuaded himself that he would obtain what he desired, relying upon Christ’s mercy, he departed from there with the royal retinue and made his way to his father’s palace. As soon as his father learned of his son’s arrival, he immediately went out to meet him, embraced and kissed him, and was filled with the greatest joy at his arrival; and he celebrated a public and solemn festival. What happened next? Once the witnesses had been dismissed, they sat down together. And who could encompass in any speech the conversations that the son then held with the king, or the wisdom with which he argued?

For what else did he speak of than what was instilled in him by the divine Spirit, through whom the fishermen ensnared the whole world for Christ and, though unacquainted with letters, surpassed learned men in teaching? Instructed and equipped by his grace, he too addressed the king, illuminating him with the light of knowledge.

Earlier, indeed, when he had labored long and hard to draw his father away from superstitious error, saying and doing everything possible to attract his mind to himself, he nevertheless seemed to be singing to the deaf and speaking to one who could not hear. But when the Lord looked upon the affliction of his servant Josaphat, and, having heard his prayers, opened the closed doors of his father’s heart—for, as the psalm says, “He will fulfill the desire of those who fear him, and he will hear their prayer”—then at last the king easily understood what was being said. Thus the son, having found an opportune moment, through Christ’s grace gained victory over the wicked spirits that ruled his father’s mind, freed him entirely from their error and deception, clearly delivered saving instruction to him, and reconciled him to the heavenly and living God.

At the outset, therefore, beginning from a higher level, he announced to him great and wondrous matters that he had previously neither understood nor grasped with the ears of his heart. For he delivered to him a lengthy discourse about God and showed him pious teaching—namely, that there is no other god above except the one God, who is acknowledged in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and he also disclosed many mysteries of theology.

Afterward he explained matters concerning the creation of created things, both invisible and visible: namely, how that supreme Father and maker, having brought all things forth from nothing, fashioned man in his own image and likeness; how, after granting him freedom of choice, he made him a participant in the beautiful things that were in paradise, forbidding him only the taste of one tree, that is, the tree of knowledge. When this command had been violated, he expelled him from paradise. Hence both he and his wife, having fallen through the union they had with one another, fell into these many errors, being enslaved to sin and made subject to death through the tyranny of the devil. After he had once brought human beings under his power, the devil caused them to be wholly seized by forgetfulness of God and the Lord, and persuaded them to worship him through the accursed worship of idols [Col. 0583A].

But God our creator, moved by compassion, and with the good will of the Father and the cooperating work of the Holy Spirit, willed to be born from a holy Virgin in our likeness. He who was immune to suffering nevertheless underwent torment, and three days later was raised from death to life; he freed us from the former curse and condemnation and bestowed upon us a more excellent glory. For when he ascended into heaven, he raised us with him to the place from which he had descended.

We also believe that he will come again, to restore his creation to life and render to each person according to his works. After this he spoke of that kingdom of heaven which awaits those who deserve it, and he set before him those hidden blessings, as well as the punishment reserved for the wicked: the unquenchable fire, the outer darkness, the immortal worm, and the other forms of torment that the slaves of sin have stored up for themselves [Col. 0583B].

Having pursued all these matters at great length, in words that testified that the grace of the Holy Spirit dwelt abundantly within him, he finally described the unfathomable ocean of divine kindness: how gladly God awaits the repentance of those who turn to him, and how no crime surpasses his mercy, provided that we resolve to return to a better way of life. When he had made this clear through many examples and testimonies from Scripture, he brought his discourse to an end.

### CHAPTER XXXV

The king, pierced by this wisdom given by God, confessed Christ the Savior with a mighty voice and the most fervent spirit, and withdrew from every superstitious error. In the sight of all he worshiped the sign of the life-giving cross, and before all who heard him proclaimed the true God and our Lord Jesus Christ. Recalling his former impiety and condemning his cruelty and savagery toward Christians, he became greatly devoted to piety. The saying of Paul was fulfilled: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5).

When the most wise Josaphat spoke at length about God and devotion toward him to the commanders and satraps of the army, and finally to the entire people, singing as though with a fiery and melodious tongue some splendid song, the grace of the Holy Spirit came upon them and stirred them all to celebrate God’s glory. Thus the entire multitude cried out with one voice: “Great is the God of the Christians, and there is no other God besides our Lord Jesus Christ, who is glorified with the Father and the Holy Spirit” [Col. 0583D].

Then King Abenner, filled with divine zeal, attacked the golden and silver idols that stood in his palace with fierce determination, threw them all down, and afterward broke them into small pieces and distributed them to the poor—thus making useful what previously had been entirely without usefulness or benefit. Moreover, together with his son, he besieged all the temples and altars of the idols, tore them up from their foundations, and built temples to God in their place [Col. 0584A]. Nor did they carry out this work only in the city; they diligently performed it throughout the whole region.

The evil spirits that had dwelt in the altars were driven out with howling, and with trembling cries bore witness to the unconquerable power of our God. The whole neighboring region, and many peoples of the surrounding lands as well, turned to the devout faith.

Then, when that most divine bishop whom we mentioned earlier had arrived, King Abenner was instructed in the elements of the Christian faith and completed by divine baptism in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Josaphat received him from the divine pool—a truly extraordinary event. He became the father of his own father and obtained spiritual regeneration for the one from whom he had been carnally begotten. For he was a son of the heavenly Father and, truly, the most divine fruit of the divine root—the root, I mean, that cries out: “I am the vine; you are the branches” (John 15).

Thus regenerated through water and the Spirit, the king was filled with a joy that no speech can explain. At the same time, the whole city and the neighboring region were also granted divine baptism, and those who had previously lived in darkness became children of light. Every sickness and every calamity inflicted by demons was driven far away from those who possessed the faith, and all were sound and unharmed in both soul and body.

Many other miracles were also performed to confirm the faith. Churches were built, and bishops who had been hiding in fear came into the light and resumed possession of their churches [Col. 0584C]. Others as well, from both the order of priests and that of monks, were appointed to feed Christ’s flock.

King Abenner, having thus withdrawn from his wicked and shameful way of life and repented of the crimes he had committed, handed over the entire royal power to his son. He himself lived in solitude, continually sprinkling his head with ashes, uttering deep groans, and washing himself with tears. Alone with the One who is present everywhere, he conversed with him, asking forgiveness for his offenses.

Indeed, he plunged himself into such an abyss of contrition and humility that he refused even to utter the name of God with his lips, and only after being admonished by his son did he at last dare to pronounce it. So great and so remarkable was the change in his life, and so honorably did he pursue the path of virtue, that the greatness of his piety surpassed the former ignorance of his iniquities.

After he had spent four years in this manner in repentance, tears, and every kind of virtue, he fell into a fatal illness. As the end of his life drew near, he began to live in fear and anxiety of mind, recalling the evil deeds he had committed. But Josaphat lightened the burden of sorrow that had arisen in him with a consoling discourse, saying:

“Why are you sad, O father, and why do you trouble yourself? (Psalm 41). Hope in God and confess to him, who is the hope of all the ends of the earth and of the distant seas (Psalm 65), who cried out through the prophet: ‘Wash yourselves; make yourselves clean; remove the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes; learn to do good. And if your sins are like scarlet, they shall be made white as snow; and if they are red like crimson, they shall become white like wool’ (Isaiah 1).

“Therefore do not be afraid, father, and do not be of doubtful mind; for the sins of those who turn to God do not overcome his immeasurable goodness. However great their number may be, they fall within measure; but no one can measure or number his goodness. Therefore it is impossible for what is subject to measure to overcome what cannot be encompassed by any measure.”

With words of this kind, suited to consolation, he soothed his father’s mind and, as if by an incantation, recalled him to good hope. Then his father, stretching out his hands, gave him thanks and blessed him, and praised the day on which he himself had been born, saying:

“My sweetest son—son, I say, who are not so much mine as the son of the heavenly Father—what thanks shall I render to you? With what blessings shall I bless you? What thanks shall I give God on your account? I had perished, and through your work I was found; I was dead through sin, and I came back to life (Luke 15); I was an enemy and rebel against God, and I have been received back into favor. What, then, shall I repay you for all this (Psalm 30)? It is God who can reward you with sufficiently great recompense.”

After this speech, having kissed his beloved son repeatedly and then poured out his prayers, he said, “Into your hands, O gracious God, I commend my spirit,” and in repentance he surrendered his soul to the Lord.

[Col. 0585C] Josaphat, the son, mourned his dead father with tears, performed the rites due to him, and buried his body in the tombs of pious men. Yet he did not wrap his body in royal clothing; rather, he adorned it with garments of repentance. Then, standing at the tomb, stretching his hands toward heaven, and pouring tears from his eyes like rivers, he cried out to God:

“I give you thanks, God, King of glory, who alone are mighty and immortal, because you did not disregard my prayer, nor count my tears as nothing. Instead, you willed to draw your servant and my father away from his wicked way of life and bring him to you, the Savior of all—leading him away from the error of idols and granting him to understand that you are the true and gracious God [Col. 0585D].

“And now, O Lord God, whose ocean of goodness cannot be fathomed, place him in a place of pasture, in a place of refreshment, where the light of your face shines. Do not remember his former iniquities, but, in accordance with your great mercy, erase the record of his sins and tear up the documents of his debts. Reconcile him with your saints, whom he destroyed with fire and sword (Psalm 78), and command them not to show themselves hostile and angry toward him.

“For all things are possible for you, Lord of all, except this one thing: you cannot fail to have mercy on those who turn to you. For your mercy is poured out upon all, and you bring salvation to those who call upon you, Lord Jesus Christ, for glory is fitting for you forever. Amen.”

He offered such prayers and supplications to God, remaining at the tomb for seven full days. He took neither food nor drink, nor did he refresh his body with sleep; instead, he watered it only with tears (Psalm 142) and persisted in prayer with lamentations that surpassed every capacity for prayer [Col. 0586A].

On the eighth day, at last, he returned to the palace and distributed all his possessions and money to the poor, so that no one who was burdened by want remained. After spending a few days in this service, he exhausted all the treasures, doing this so that, as he prepared to enter through the narrow gate, the mass of his money might not hinder him.

[Col. 0586B] ### CHAPTER XXXVI

On the fortieth day after his father’s death, while celebrating his memory, he summoned all the magistrates, the military establishment, and many members of the common people. Sitting on the royal throne, he delivered this speech before them all:

“Behold, as you yourselves see, Abenner, the king and my father, died no differently from any poor man. Neither riches, nor wealth, nor royal glory, nor I, his most loving son, nor any of his other friends and relatives could bring him aid or assistance or rescue him from the inevitable judgment. Instead, he goes to that tribunal to render an account of his life in this world, taking with him no one at all to help him except—whatever they may be—the deeds he himself performed.

“This too has been established by nature for all who have received mortal nature, and it cannot happen otherwise. Now therefore listen to me, sons and brothers, people of the Lord and holy inheritance, whom Christ our God redeemed with his precious blood and reclaimed for freedom from ancient error and the slavery of the adversary.

“You know how I have lived among you: namely, that from the time when I attained knowledge of Christ and by divine favor became his servant, despising and hating all other things, I burned only with desire for him. This alone was my wish: to leave the storm and empty confusion and turmoil of this life, to dwell alone with him alone, and to serve my God and Lord in the greatest tranquility of soul.

“But the will of my father, who strove in the opposite direction, held me back, as did that commandment which orders honor to be shown to parents (Deuteronomy 5). Therefore, by God’s grace and assistance, I did not labor in vain, nor did I spend these days fruitlessly. Rather, I reconciled both him and all of you to God, and taught him to recognize him alone as the true God and Lord of all—not that I did this myself, but God’s grace with me, which also rescued me from superstitious error and the worship of idols and freed you, my people, from grievous and bitter captivity.

“Now therefore it is time for me to fulfill what I promised to God. It is time, I say, for me to depart wherever he leads me and to pay the vows by which I bound myself to him. Therefore consider among yourselves whom you wish to rule over you and possess the kingdom. For you have now been perfected in the will of the Lord, and nothing of his commandments is hidden from you. Walk in them; do not turn aside either to the right or to the left. And may the God of peace, I pray, be with you all.”

When the people heard this, tumult and uproar immediately arose, together with a great cry and confusion. Everyone wept and lamented their bereavement. Indeed, amid their mourning and wailing they also declared under oath that they would not let him go but would retain him, and would in no way allow him to depart.

While the people and all the magistrates were crying out, the king restrained the populace and ordered them to be silent. Declaring that he would yield and submit to their contention, he sent them home, although they were otherwise sorrowful and bore signs of wailing upon their faces.

But he took aside one of the leading men, whom he esteemed above all others and admired both for piety and for holiness of life: Barachias, of whom we also spoke earlier, when Nachor, pretending to be Barlaam, debated with the philosophers. We said that Barachias alone, burning wholly with divine zeal, had stood on Josaphat’s side and had been prepared to enter into debate against them.

Taking him aside, he addressed him gently and kindly, and with urgent prayers begged him to accept the kingdom and govern his people in the fear of God, so that Josaphat might set out upon the journey he desired.

When he saw that Barachias refused and utterly rejected this, saying:

“O king, how unjust is this judgment of yours; how little does your speech agree with the divine command! For since you are taught to love your neighbor as yourself, by what reasoning do you hasten to lay upon me the burden that you are striving to cast off? If it is good to perform the royal office, retain for yourself what is good; but if it is a stumbling block and scandal to the soul, why do you cast it upon me and wish to lead me into deception?”

When he saw him speaking and insisting in this manner, he ceased conversing with him. At dead of night, however, he composed for his people a letter full of great wisdom and urging every form of piety. In it he prescribed what opinion they ought to hold concerning God, what life they should lead, what praises and finally what thanksgivings they should offer [Col. 0587D]. He afterward forbade them to admit anyone other than Barachias to royal dignity.

Leaving this letter in his chamber, he went out without anyone’s knowledge. Yet he could not make his departure remain unknown to the very end. For as soon as day broke, news of it brought disturbance and grief to the people, and everyone set out with the utmost speed to search for him, intending by every means to intercept his flight.

Thus his purpose did not fail entirely. For when they had occupied all the roads, blockaded every mountain, and traversed the trackless valleys, they found him in a certain torrent, stretching his hands toward heaven and completing the prayer of the sixth hour.

When they caught sight of him, they immediately surrounded him and begged him with tears, reproaching him for his departure. But he said: “Why are you undertaking a useless labor? You have no reason to hope that you will continue to have me as king.” Nevertheless, yielding to their vehement insistence, he returned to the palace. After gathering everyone together, he declared what he had in mind and then confirmed his speech with an oath, namely, that from then on he would not remain with them even for a single day.

“For I have completed my ministry among you,” he said, “and have neither omitted nor evaded anything that would prevent me from announcing to you (Acts 20) and teaching you, bearing witness to all concerning faith in our Lord Jesus Christ and showing you the way of repentance [Col. 0588B]. Now I am entering upon this way, which I have long desired, and none of you will see my face again.

“Therefore, to use the words of the divine Apostle, I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of you all. For I did not shrink from announcing to you the whole counsel of God.”

When they heard this and recognized the firmness of his resolve—that they could not call him back from the plan he had undertaken—they lamented their bereavement, but could not in any way turn him from his decision.

Then the king took Barachias, of whom we spoke above, by the hand and said: “This man, O brothers—this man I appoint as your king.”

When Barachias strongly resisted such a thing, the king placed him, unwilling and struggling, upon the royal throne, set the diadem upon his head, and placed the royal ring in his hand. Then, standing toward the East, he offered prayers for the king, asking God that Barachias might steadfastly hold to the faith of God and find the path of Christ’s commandments free from every deviation.

He also prayed for the clergy and the whole flock, asking God to give them aid, assistance, and salvation, and that he might regulate whatever they asked for their benefit.

After this prayer, he turned to Barachias and said:

“Behold, brother, I give you this command which the Apostle testified: ‘Pay attention to yourself and to the whole flock in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as ruler, so that you may govern the people of Christ, whom he acquired with his own blood’ (Acts 20).

“And just as you previously knew God and worshiped him with a pure heart and conscience, so now apply yourself with greater zeal to proving yourself worthy of him in the conduct of your life. For the greater authority you have received from God, the greater repayment you must make to him.

“Therefore pay him the debt of gratitude, since you have been enriched by his gifts, keeping his holy commandments and turning away from every road that leads to destruction. For just as among sailors, when some sailor errs, he causes only a small loss to those sailing with him, but when the helmsman errs, he brings destruction upon the whole ship, so also in a kingdom: when one of those subject to it sins, he harms not so much another as himself; but when the king himself sins, he shakes and injures the entire kingdom [Col. 0589A].

“Therefore, since you will have to render a great account, if you neglect any of the things that are required, guard yourself in goodness with great zeal and care. Pursue with hatred every pleasure that draws you into sin. For the Apostle says: ‘Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, without which no one will see God’ (Hebrews 12).

“Consider the wheel of human affairs, how it turns in a circle, carrying and twisting them now in one way and now in another. Strive to retain a devout mind steadfastly amid their various changes. For to change along with circumstances is evidence of a doubtful and unstable mind. But see to it that you are firm and wholly established in virtue.

“Do not become arrogant through empty swelling on account of temporary and fleeting glory. Rather, purify your mind and consider the lowliness of your nature, as well as the brevity of this life and the death joined to the flesh. If you consider these things, you will not fall into pride, but will fear the true and heavenly King, God, and thus all will go well and happily with you.

“For, he says, ‘Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways’ (Psalm 128). And again: ‘Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he will greatly delight in his commandments’ (Psalm 112).

“But hear what commandments above all others you must keep: ‘Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy’ (Luke 6). And again: ‘Be merciful, just as your heavenly Father is merciful.’ This commandment is especially demanded of those who are placed in supreme authority.

“Indeed, whoever has obtained great power ought, as far as possible, to imitate the one from whom he received such power. He will imitate God above all in this matter if he considers nothing more important or more valuable than mercy.

“Moreover, nothing draws subjects equally toward goodwill as a benefit granted to those in need. Obedience that arises from fear is disguised flattery, mocking and deceiving under a fictitious name of honor those who attach themselves to the ruler. The one who obeys unwillingly raises rebellion when the opportunity arises; but the one held fast by bonds of goodwill offers firm obedience to the one who holds power.

“Since this is so, take care that access to you be easy for the needy and that your ears be open to those afflicted by want, so that you too may find God’s ears open. For whatever we show ourselves to be toward our fellow servants, such will we find the Lord toward us; as we hear, so shall we be heard; and as we see, so shall we be seen by the divine eye that beholds all things. Therefore let us show mercy before we need mercy, so that we may receive like for like.

“Hear also another commandment joined to and related to the preceding one: ‘Forgive, and you will be forgiven.’ But if you do not forgive people their offenses, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins.

“Therefore do not show yourself mindful of injuries inflicted by those who have offended you. Rather, when you ask forgiveness for your own sins, forgive those who sin against you. Forgiveness is repaid with forgiveness; and if we are reconciled with our fellow servants, the Lord will also restrain his anger toward us. On the other hand, our cruelty toward those who have done something against us causes no forgiveness to be granted to our sins (Matthew 18).

“You hear what happened to the man who owed ten thousand talents: because of his cruelty toward his fellow servant, he renewed against himself the exaction of so great a debt. We must therefore take great care lest this also happen to us. Rather, let us forgive every debt and cast all anger from our hearts, so that our own many debts may also be forgiven us.

“Above all these things, guard the good deposit: the devout teaching of the faith in which you were instructed and educated (2 Timothy 1). Take care that no weed of heresy spring up among you. Preserve instead the pure and guileless divine seed, so that you may present a rich and abundant harvest to the Lord when he comes to demand an account of what each person has done in life and to render a reward corresponding to our deeds.

“At that time the righteous will shine like the sun, but darkness and everlasting disgrace will overwhelm the wicked (Matthew 13). And now, brothers, I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and give you an inheritance among all the sanctified (Acts 20).”

[Col. 0590C] When he had said this, he knelt down, as it is written, and prayed again with tears. Then he turned to Barachias, whom he had designated as king, and kissed him and all those who held public office.

Then a truly tearful scene took place. All those standing around him—as though they lived only for the purpose of being with him, and would lose their lives as soon as they were separated from him—said everything that might arouse compassion and left nothing undone that could increase their grief. They kissed and embraced him and were beside themselves with sorrow.

“Woe to us,” they cried, “what grievous calamity overwhelms us!” They called him lord, father, author of their salvation, and benefactor. “Through you,” they said, “we have received knowledge of God; we have been freed from error; we have found rest from every evil. What will become of us after your departure? What evils will seize us?”

As they said these things, they beat their breasts and lamented the calamity that had overtaken them. But he restrained their immense wailing with words of consolation and promised that, since he could no longer be with them in body, he would be with them in spirit.

After delivering this speech, he left the palace while all looked on. Immediately everyone followed him, despairing of his return, and fled from the city that they could no longer bear to see.

After they had left the city, only with difficulty and reluctance—when he admonished them more sternly and sometimes added harsher reproaches—were they separated from him and forced to return against their will. Again and again they turned their eyes back toward him, stumbling with their feet as they walked. Some of those who possessed more fervent spirits followed him from a distance in mourning until night came and separated them from one another [Col. 0591A].

### CHAPTER XXXVII

That noble man therefore left the court as joyful and cheerful as someone returning to his homeland from a long and distant exile. Externally he wore the clothing to which he was accustomed; internally, however, he wore the hair shirt that Barlaam had given him.

That night, entering the little house of a certain poor man, he removed the clothing he was wearing and gave this final gift to the needy man. Having thus called upon himself the help and aid of God through the prayers of that man and of many other poor people, and having clothed himself in God’s grace and protection as in a garment of salvation and a cloak of joy, he went out into the solitary life. He took with him neither bread nor water nor anything else necessary for nourishment, and wore no other garment except that rough hair shirt of which I spoke shortly before.

For he was wounded by an extraordinary desire and by divine love for Christ, the immortal King. With his whole mind he devoted himself to what he loved, wholly carried beyond himself and transformed by God, entirely seized by the love of God. “For love,” says the psalm, “is strong as death” (Song of Songs 8).

He had been made drunk, as it were, with such divine love and burned with such thirst, like the one who said: “As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God. My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain” (Psalm 42). And as that soul which had been wounded by such love says in the Song of Songs: “I am wounded by love” (Song of Songs 2). And again: “Show me your face, and let me hear your voice; for your voice is sweet and your face is beautiful.”

Struck in his breast by the desire for Christ’s beauty, superior to every form of speech, the choir of the apostles and the ranks of the martyrs despised everything visible to the eyes, and preferred countless kinds of torment and death to this whole fleeting and perishable life. They burned with love for divine beauty and considered within their souls the immense love of God’s Word toward us [Col. 0591D].

When this fire had also been kindled within a distinguished man—noble in body, but endowed with a spirit far nobler and more kingly—he utterly despised all earthly things, trampled upon every bodily pleasure, and regarded wealth, glory, and human honors as nothing. He cast aside diadem and purple, judging them more worthless than spiders’ webs, and willingly devoted himself to every harsh and bitter discipline of the monastic life, crying out with the Psalmist:

“My soul clings to you, O Christ; may your right hand receive me” (Psalm 63).

As he had proceeded in this manner, turning his eyes not at all backward, he withdrew into the deepest solitude and shook off the confusion of fleeting things as though it were some exceedingly burdensome load and chain. He rejoiced in spirit and, fixing his eyes upon Christ, for whose sake he burned with longing, called out to him as though he were present and hearing his voice, addressing him in these words:

> “I beg you now, O Lord, let my eyes no longer see the goods of this life; nor let the vanity of the present world draw my mind away from the journey I have undertaken. Rather, my Lord, fill my eyes with spiritual tears, direct my steps, and show me your servant Barlaam. Show me, I say, him through whom salvation has been secured for me, so that through him I may learn the sincerity of the solitary and monastic life and not be led astray through ignorance of the enemy’s warfare. Grant me, Lord, to attain my way—the way by which I may reach you—for my soul is wounded by longing for you and ardently thirsts for you, the fountain of salvation.”

He continually revolved these thoughts within himself and spoke to God, joining himself to him through prayer and the loftiest contemplation. Thus he pursued the journey he had begun with determined steps, striving to reach the place where Barlaam lived. He was sustained by the herbs that grew in the desert. For, as I have already mentioned, he carried nothing else with him besides his body and the rags with which he was clothed.

Since he obtained from the herbs only a meager sustenance of no consequence whatsoever, he suffered greatly from lack of water, because that solitude was without water. As he traveled while the sun was already burning fiercely toward midday, his thirst blazed even more intensely because of the heat in that arid region, and he was tormented by the most extreme and grievous hardship. Yet longing overcame nature, and the divine thirst with which he was afflicted diminished the flame of his thirst for water.

But that enemy and jealous foe of the good, the devil, seeing with the greatest indignation such a purpose of soul and his love for God burning so intensely, stirred up many temptations against him in the solitude. He revived the memory of his royal glory and of the most splendid company of attendants by whom his side had once been surrounded, as well as of his friends and peers. He also placed before his mind the thought that the souls of all depended upon his soul, and finally set before him the other pleasures of this life. Then he presented the harshness of virtue, his immense labors, the weakness of his body, hardships unknown and unaccustomed to him, the length of time involved, and the present oppression of thirst, insisting that no consolation could be expected from any quarter and that there would be no end to such labor and fatigue. Finally, as is related in a certain passage concerning the great Antony, he stirred up in his mind a great dust of thoughts.

When that enemy saw himself too weak to shake his purpose—for Josaphat kept Christ before his mind, was inflamed by longing for him, strengthened by excellent hope, and supported by faith, counting the devil’s impulses and counsels as nothing—he was covered with shame, having been overthrown, as the saying goes, at the first assault. Therefore he began to take another path, for he has many roads of vice, and tried to overthrow him and cast him into fear by means of various apparitions.

Sometimes he appeared to him black, as he is; at other times he attacked him holding a drawn sword and threatened to strike him unless he immediately abandoned his purpose. Again, he assumed the form of various beasts, roaring at him and producing a most terrifying bellowing and din. At times he even changed himself into the form of a dragon, an asp, or a basilisk.

But that illustrious and most courageous champion stood firm with a tranquil spirit, having made the Most High his refuge (Psalm 90). Keeping watch in his mind and mocking the destructive spirit, he said:

> “I am not unaware, impostor, of who you are, you who stir these things up against me: plainly, you are the one who has plotted destruction for the human race from the beginning and never cease to pursue wickedness and inflict harm. And how well this appearance suits you! For by imitating beasts and reptiles you display the savagery and perversity of your mind and the readiness of your will to bring about injury and destruction. Why, then, wretch, do you undertake what you cannot accomplish? Since I have learned that these devices and apparitions proceed from your wickedness, I am no longer troubled by any anxiety. ‘The Lord is my helper, and I will look down upon my enemies’ (Psalm 117). I shall tread upon the asp and the basilisk, whose likeness you have assumed, and, strengthened by Christ’s power, I shall trample upon the lion and the dragon (Psalm 90). ‘Let all my enemies be put to shame and confounded; let them be put to shame and confounded very quickly’ (Psalm 6).”

Using this prayer and arming himself with the sign of the cross—that is, with invincible weapons—he rendered all the devil’s apparitions powerless. Immediately the beasts and reptiles vanished like smoke, “and as wax melts before the fire” (Psalm 67). Strengthened by Christ’s power, he proceeded with a joyful spirit and gave thanks to God.

Yet many beasts of various kinds, and serpents and dragons of different sorts, which that solitude nourished, came to meet him. He now saw them not as an empty apparition but in reality. The road was therefore full of fear and labor, but he overcame both in spirit and thought. For love, to use the words of Scripture, “cast out fear” (1 John 4), and longing lightened his labor.

After struggling for many days against many and varied calamities and hardships, he reached that solitude of Sennaar in which Barlaam lived. There he found water and quenched the flame of his thirst.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII

Josaphat remained for a full two years in this vast solitude, wandering here and there without finding Barlaam, while here too God was testing the steadfastness and courage of his spirit. Living under the open sky, he was at one time scorched by heat and at another stiffened by cold, never ceasing to seek that excellent old man as though he were a treasure of immense value.

He endured many temptations from destructive spirits, many battles, and likewise many hardships because of the scarcity of the herbs on which he ordinarily lived; for that solitude, suffering from dryness, produced even these only very sparingly. Yet his spirit, adamantine and unconquered, burning with love and longing, endured such troubles more easily than others ordinarily endure pleasures. Therefore he was not deprived of divine assistance. In proportion to the multitude of his sorrows and labors (Psalm 34), the consolations brought by Christ, for whom he burned with longing, gladdened his spirit both by night and by day.

When the two-year period had been completed, Josaphat continued constantly to wander about, seeking the one he desired, and pouring out tears like a river before God. He meditated, crying out:

> “Show me, Lord—show me, I say—the one who brought me to know your name and obtained for me such great blessings. Do not deprive me of so great a good because of the multitude of my sins. Rather, grant that I may enjoy his presence and undertake with him the same contest of religious discipline.”

By God’s favor he found a cave, having traced the path of those who went there. He encountered a solitary monk devoted to this manner of life. Embracing and kissing him with the greatest fervor of spirit, he asked where Barlaam lived, and at the same time explained to him the circumstances of his own life.

When he had learned from him where the dwelling of the man he sought was, he went there as quickly as possible, like a highly skilled hunter who has found his quarry. At the direction of another old man, he traveled several thousand paces and proceeded joyfully, strengthened by hope, just like a boy who hopes soon to see a father whom he has not seen for a long time. For once divine love has taken possession of the soul, it is usually far sharper and more ardent than the love that proceeds from nature.

He therefore stood at the entrance of the cave and, knocking, said: “Bless me, father; bless me, I say.” When Barlaam heard this voice and came out of the cavern, he recognized him through the spirit. Because of the remarkable transformation by which he had departed from his former appearance and the beauty of his flourishing youth, he could scarcely be recognized by his outward aspect: he had grown dark from the sun’s heat, was covered with hair, had cheeks wasted by emaciation, eyes deeply sunken, and eyelids worn all around by streams of tears and scorched by the great affliction of hunger.

Josaphat, however, immediately recognized his spiritual father, since he still possessed the same features of countenance. At once the old man, standing toward the East, offered God a prayer joined with thanksgiving. When he had said “Amen,” they immediately rushed into one another’s arms, satisfying their long-standing desire without any satiety.

After they had embraced one another fully and had taken counsel together, they sat and conversed. Barlaam began the conversation in these words:

> “You have done excellently by coming here, beloved son—son, I say, of God and heir of the heavenly kingdom through our Lord Jesus Christ. You loved him and rightly valued him more dearly than fleeting and fragile goods. Like a prudent and wise merchant, you sold all your possessions and bought a pearl surpassing every price. Having found the treasure that cannot be stolen, hidden in the field of the Lord’s commandments (Matthew 15), you gave everything and spared nothing among the things that are already about to pass away, in order to purchase that field for yourself. May the Lord grant you eternal things in place of the fleeting and perishable, and things upon which neither destruction nor age can fall in place of those subject to ruin.

> “But I would like you to tell me, dearest one, by what means you came here, what became of your affairs after my departure, and whether your father knows God—or whether, even now, seized by the same madness as before, he is being led captive by the deception and imposture of demons.”

When Barlaam questioned him, Josaphat, beginning again from the start, explained point by point what had happened to him after Barlaam’s departure and how prosperous a course the Lord had granted to his affairs up to the time when they had met again.

When the old man heard these things, he was filled at once with joy and wonder. Shedding warm tears, he said:

> “Glory to you, our God, who are always present to those who possess love for you and assist them. Glory to you, Christ, King of all and most excellent God, because your benevolent will ordained that the seed you cast into the heart of your servant Josaphat should bear fruit a hundredfold—you, the husbandman of our souls and one worthy of the Lord. Glory to you, good and most holy Paraclete Spirit, because you deemed it right to bestow upon this man also the grace that you granted to your holy apostles. Through his agency you freed a great multitude of people from superstitious error and enlightened them with the true knowledge of God.”

In this manner both of them gave thanks to God. While they were conversing with one another and rejoicing in God’s grace, evening arrived. Accordingly, they rose for prayer and completed their customary office of prayer.

Afterward, when the body needed to be restored with food, Barlaam set out a splendid table, filled with spiritual fare but participating as little as possible in the consolation perceived by the senses. There were only raw vegetables, planted and cultivated by his own hands, a few dates found in that solitude, and finally wild herbs.

When they had given thanks to God, restored their bodies with the food that had been set out, and drunk water from a nearby spring, they again gave thanks to him “who opens his hand and fills every living thing with blessing” (Psalm 144). Then, after rising and completing the nocturnal prayers, they began a spiritual conversation, weaving together discourses filled with salvation and heavenly wisdom throughout the night, until the rising of dawn recalled them once more to their customary prayers.

Josaphat remained with Barlaam in this manner for a long time, practicing this admirable life, superior to human nature, and following him as a father and teacher with complete obedience and humility. He was trained in every pursuit of virtue and taught how to struggle against spiritual and invisible spirits.

As a result, he extinguished every vicious affection and subjected the inclination of the flesh to the spirit, as a slave to his master. He became oblivious to every pleasure and relaxation of the mind and commanded sleep as though it were a wicked slave. In short, he devoted himself so earnestly to the contest of the solitary life that even Barlaam, who had spent a very long time in it, marveled and yielded to his intensity.

Josaphat admitted so little of that harsh food, deprived of consolation, that he merely sustained life and did not deprive himself through deliberately summoned death of the rewards bestowed upon the cultivation and pursuit of virtues. He subjected nature to nightly vigils as though he consisted in no part of flesh or body. Prayer was his continual occupation, and the whole time of his life was spent in spiritual and heavenly contemplation, so that from the time he dwelt in that solitude he did not squander even one hour—or, indeed, any single moment of time.

For this truly is the duty of the monastic order: never to be found empty of spiritual work. That noble and unencumbered runner of the heavenly road fulfilled it excellently. From the beginning to the very end he continually preserved the ardor of his spirit, “always arranging ascents in his heart” (Psalm 83), leaping from virtue to a loftier virtue, and unceasingly joining longing to longing and effort to effort, until at last he reached the blessedness he hoped for and desired.

### CHAPTER XXIX

While Barlaam and Josaphat were living together in this manner and competing with each other in a noble contest, free from every care and disturbance of this life and possessing minds pure and separated from all confusion, the old man one day summoned his spiritual son—whom he had begotten through the Gospel—and, after the many labors they had undertaken for the sake of piety, began the following spiritual discourse:

> “For a long time, my friend Josaphat, you ought to have been living in this solitude, and Christ had promised me, when I prayed, that I would see you before the end of my life. I have therefore seen you as I wished; I have seen you torn away from the world and the things of the world, joined to Christ with an unwavering and undoubting spirit, and advancing toward the perfect measure of his fullness.

> “Now, since the time of my death is at hand and that long-standing desire, equal in age to myself, which has always held me—that I might be with Christ—is now being fulfilled, you must bury my body in the earth and return dust to dust. Afterward remain here, pursuing the manner of spiritual life you have undertaken and preserving the memory of my lowliness. For I fear that, because of the multitude of my ignorance, the dark host of demons may place an obstacle before my soul.

> “But you, my son, must not fear the labor of religious discipline or grow faint because of the length of time and the plots of demons. Rather, strengthened by Christ’s power, boldly mock their weakness. Prepare your mind for the harshness of labor and the length of time as though you were expecting departure from this life every day, and regard that same day as both the beginning and the end of your monastic life.

> “Thus, always forgetting what lies behind and stretching yourself toward what lies ahead, pursue the goal, toward the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus (Philippians 3), as the holy Apostle urges in these words: ‘Let us not grow weary. Although our outer person is being corrupted, yet the inner person is renewed day by day. For our momentary and light affliction is producing for us, beyond all measure, an eternal weight of glory, while we look not at what is seen but at what is unseen. For what is seen is temporal, but what is unseen is eternal’ (2 Corinthians 4).

> “Keeping these things in mind, dearest one, act manfully and be strengthened (Psalm 26). Like an excellent soldier, take care to please the one who enlisted you as a soldier (2 Timothy 2). Even if that wicked spirit sends you thoughts of weakness and languor and endeavors to break and weaken the sinews of your purpose, do not fear his plots. Consider the Lord’s command: ‘In the world you will have tribulation; but take courage, I have overcome the world’ (John 16).

> “Therefore rejoice always in the Lord, because he has chosen you and set you apart from the world before his face. He who called you with his holy calling is always near. Be anxious about nothing, but in every prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God (Philippians 4). For he himself said: ‘I will not abandon you, nor forsake you.’

> “Keeping these things in mind amid the hardship of life and the lowliness of religious discipline, dwell in spiritual joy, retaining the remembrance of the Lord our God. ‘I remembered God,’ he says, ‘and I rejoiced’ (Psalm 76).

> “When your adversary again devises another kind of warfare against you—placing before you lofty and arrogant thoughts, setting before your eyes the glory of the earthly kingdom you abandoned and the other things that are in the world—hold out, like a shield, the saving teaching that says: ‘When you have done all that is commanded you, say: We are useless servants, because we have done what we were obliged to do’ (Luke 17).

> “And who among us can repay that debt by which we are bound to the Lord, because, although he was rich, he became poor for our sake, so that through his poverty we might become rich, and because, though exempt from suffering, he endured torments in order to free us from vicious affections (2 Corinthians 8)? For what merit is it for a servant to undergo the same things as his master? Yet we remain very far from his sufferings.

> “Reflect upon these things, destroying thoughts and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and taking every thought captive into obedience to Christ (2 Corinthians 10). And may the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your heart and your thoughts in Christ Jesus (Philippians 4).”

When Barlaam had delivered this discourse, Josaphat poured forth an immeasurable flood of tears, streaming as though from a most abundant spring and thoroughly washing both him and the earth on which he sat. Lamenting this separation, he pleaded with great fervor that Barlaam allow him to be his companion on that final journey and not remain in the world after his departure. He said:

> “What, father, do you care only for yourself and not for your neighbor? How can you fulfill in this matter the duty of perfect love—as Christ commanded, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’—when you go to rest while leaving me in oppression and hardship, and expose me to solitary combat with the enemy before I have been properly trained in the contests of the religious life and learned the various snares of our foes?

> “What else can result from this except that I shall be overthrown by their deceitful arts and, as happens to inexperienced and timid gladiators, suffer eternal death of soul? Beg and entreat the Lord, I implore you, to admit me also as your companion in departing from this life. I adjure you to do this by the very hope you have of receiving the reward of your labor. Plead this with God in your prayers: let me not wander for even a single day after your departure in this life or roam through this exceedingly dense solitude.”

As Josaphat said these things while weeping, the old man gently and calmly restrained him, saying:

> “We must not resist the judgments of God, which surpass the understanding of the human mind. For when I had poured out many prayers to God concerning this matter and had tried to compel him, as though by force, though no force can be brought against him, so that we might not be separated, I learned from his goodness that it is not now beneficial for you to cast off the burden of the flesh. Rather, you must remain in religious discipline until you have woven a more splendid crown for yourself.

> “You have not yet contended sufficiently for the reward prepared for you. You must labor a little longer, so that you may enter joyfully into the joy of your Lord. I am now nearly a hundred years old and have spent seventy-five years in this solitude. Although you will not have so long a period of time, you must nevertheless approach that span, as the Lord commands, so that you may be in no respect inferior to those who bore the burden of the day and the heat (Matthew 20).

> “Therefore, my friend, receive with a ready and willing spirit what has been decreed by God. Who among mortals can undo what he has decreed? Preserved by his grace, practice endurance.

> “Take care also to keep watch in your mind against hostile thoughts and to preserve the purity of your mind safe and unharmed, as though it were a treasure of immense value. Raise yourself day by day to loftier action and contemplation, so that what the Lord promised to his friends may be fulfilled in you, in these words: ‘If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him’ (John 14).”

After the holy old man had spoken these and many other words worthy of a sanctified soul and theological speech, he eased Josaphat’s grieving spirit. Then he sent him to certain brothers living a long distance away, instructing him to bring what was needed for the celebration of the most holy sacrifice.

Josaphat, girding his garments, carried out this service as quickly as possible. For he feared that Barlaam might, in his absence, pay the due of nature and surrender his spirit to the Lord, and that he himself would suffer serious loss if deprived of Barlaam’s words, final instructions, and prayers.

When he had completed that distant journey with the greatest courage and brought back what was needed for the most holy sacrifice, the most divine Barlaam offered the bloodless sacrifice to God. After receiving Christ’s mysteries, pure from every stain, and giving them also to Josaphat, he rejoiced in spirit. Then, having taken food according to custom, he began again to nourish Josaphat’s soul with salutary discourses, saying:

> “No longer, dearest son, will the same house and table unite us in this life, for I am now entering upon the final journey of my fathers. Therefore you must show the proof of your love for me by observing the divine commandments and remaining in this place until the last day of your life. Order your life according to what you have learned, and never cease to remember my lowly and feeble soul.

> “Farewell, then, and rejoice and exult in Christ, because you have exchanged earthly things subject to destruction for eternal goods free from destruction. The reward of your works is near, and the one who brings the reward is already at hand. He will come to inspect the vineyard you have cultivated and will grant you an exceedingly great reward for its cultivation.

> “For the word is faithful, as the divine Apostle Paul proclaims (1 Timothy 1), and worthy of all acceptance: ‘If we remain with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him,’ illumined by incomparable light in that eternal kingdom without end and granted the illumination of the truly blessed and sovereign Trinity.”

Barlaam spoke these words to Josaphat until evening and throughout the entire night, while Josaphat wept profusely and endured their separation with the greatest anguish. When daylight had come, Barlaam raised his hands and eyes toward heaven and, giving thanks to God, spoke as follows:

> “Lord my God, who are present everywhere and fill all things, I give you thanks because you have regarded my lowliness (Psalm 50) and granted me to complete the course of this pilgrimage in your orthodox faith and in the way of your commandments.

> “Now, most excellent Lord, most inclined to mercy, receive me into your eternal tabernacles, and do not remember the sins I have committed against you, whether knowingly or unknowingly. Preserve also this faithful servant of yours, whom you willed to place under the authority of your useless servant. Deliver him from every vanity and from the harassment of the adversary. Grant that he may rise above those most intricate snares which the devil spreads for the offense of all who care for salvation.

> “Erase, almighty God, all the power of the impostor from before your servant’s face, and grant him strength to trample underfoot the destructive head of the enemy of our souls. Send down upon him from above the grace of your Holy Spirit and add strength to him for invisible conflicts, so that he may receive from you the crown of victory and so that your name, O Father, and the name of your Son and of the Holy Spirit may be celebrated in him; for to you belong praise and glory forever. Amen.”

After offering this prayer, he embraced Josaphat with fatherly affection, kissed him with a holy kiss, fortified himself with the sign of the cross, and stretched out his feet. Filled with immense joy, as though certain friends had come to him, he departed upon the blessed journey and to receive the rewards of that blessed life—an old man indeed, and full of spiritual days.

### CHAPTER XL

Josaphat embraced his father with the utmost veneration and lamentation. After washing his body with tears and wrapping it in the coarse hair shirt that he had received from him in the palace, he recited the customary psalms, singing throughout the entire day and night and watering the precious body of the blessed man with his tears.

The following day he dug a grave beside the cave and, carrying the sacred body with the greatest reverence, buried his spiritual father. Then, inflamed more ardently in spirit and striving with all his might toward prayer, he said:

> “Lord my God, hear my prayer with which I have cried out to you; have mercy on me and hear me, for I seek you from my heart. My soul has sought you; do not turn your face away from me, and do not turn away in anger from your servant. Be my helper; do not abandon me or despise me, O God my Savior. For my father and my mother have abandoned me, but you, Lord, have taken me up. Set your law before me, Lord, in your way, and guide me upon a straight path because of my enemies. Do not hand me over to the souls of those who afflict me (Psalm 26), for I have been cast upon you from the womb. From my mother’s womb you have been my God; do not depart from me (Psalm 21). For apart from you I have no helper.

> “Behold, I have fixed the hope of my soul in the abyss of your mercies. Govern my life, you who rule all created things by the providence of your wisdom, by a word superior to every word. Make your way known to me, the way in which I should walk. As a good and merciful God, preserve me through the prayers and supplications of your servant Barlaam, for you are my God, and I glorify you, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, forever. Amen.”

After completing this prayer, he sat weeping beside the grave and, while sitting, fell asleep. He seemed to see those terrifying men whom he had previously observed coming toward him, leading him to that great and wondrous plain, and introducing him into that illustrious and most splendid city.

When he was entering the gate, others came to meet him, radiant with immense light and holding in their hands crowns shining with such beauty that no words could express it—crowns such as mortal eyes had never seen.

When Josaphat asked whose the splendid crowns he saw were, they answered:

> “One of them is yours, made for you on account of the many souls to whom you brought salvation; now it has been fashioned more diligently and carefully because of the religious discipline you are practicing, provided that you traverse it with a courageous spirit to the very end.

> “The other is also yours, but you must give it to your father, who through your efforts turned away from his wicked manner of life, sincerely repented, and converted to the Lord.”

Josaphat seemed troubled by this and said:

> “How can it be that my father, merely because of one act of repentance, should obtain benefits equal to mine, when I have endured so many and such great labors?”

As soon as he had said this, he seemed to see Barlaam before him, reproving him and saying:

> “These are my words to you, Josaphat, which I once spoke: that when you had attained immense wealth, you would no longer be liberal and generous, and that because of this word you were of divided mind. But now, how could you have been troubled that your father received equal honor, rather than rejoicing in your spirit for this very reason, because the many prayers you poured out for him have been heard?”

Josaphat then said to him, as he was accustomed to do:

> “Forgive me, father, forgive me. But make me understand where you dwell.”

Barlaam replied:

> “I have obtained a dwelling in this beautiful and immense city, in the middle of a street shining with immeasurable light.”

Again Josaphat seemed to be dealing with him, asking to be led by him into his tabernacle and received hospitably. But Barlaam replied that the time had not yet come for him to enter those tabernacles, since he was still weighed down by the burden of the body.

> “But if you persevere courageously,” he said, “in the holy manner of life as I instructed you, you will come somewhat later and attain the same tabernacles, the same joy and glory, and you will be with me forever.”

When Josaphat awoke, his spirit was still filled with that light and with a glory more exalted than any power of speech could express. With great wonder, he praised God in thanksgiving.

He continued to lead an entirely angelic life on earth until the very end, adopting a harsher form of religious discipline after the old man’s departure. When he had left the earthly kingdom in the twenty-fifth year of his life and entered the contest of monastic life, he lived for thirty-five years in that vast solitude, as though he consisted in no part of flesh, leading a life superior to human nature.

In this way he had first drawn many human souls away from the destructive serpent and preserved them whole and unharmed for God, thereby attaining apostolic grace. In the disposition of his soul he also became a martyr and confessed Christ with courageous spirit before the eyes and presence of kings and tyrants. He showed himself a most eloquent herald of Christ’s majesty.

Again, he routed many evil spirits in the solitude and overcame them all by the power and might of Christ. He became most abundantly a participant in heavenly blessing and grace. Therefore he kept the eye of his soul pure from every earthly darkness and saw future things as though they were present.
