Christ was everything to him: he longed for Christ, saw Christ as though he were present, and never ceased to behold Christ’s beauty, according to the Prophet’s words:

> “I kept the Lord always before me, because he is at my right hand, so that I may not be moved” (Psalm 15).

And again:

> “My soul clung to you; your right hand received me” (Psalm 26).

For in truth his soul clung to Christ, joined to him by an unbreakable bond. He did not turn away from that admirable practice or alter the rule of his religious discipline. Rather, from beginning to end, and from the dawn of youth to such advanced age, he preserved the same eagerness of spirit—or, to speak more accurately, he advanced daily toward loftier virtue and, by divine favor, attained a purer contemplation.

Finally, when he had lived in this manner and had rendered to the One by whom he had been called an effort so worthy of his calling, and had crucified the world to himself and himself to the world, he departed in peace to the God of peace and journeyed to the Lord, whose perpetual desire had held him fast. He appeared before the Lord’s face, pure and without any intervening thing, and was adorned with the crown of glory already prepared for him. By divine gift he attained this: that he might behold Christ, be with Christ, and rejoice forever in Christ’s beauty. His soul, commended into Christ’s hands, passed into the dwelling of the living, where there is the sound of those who feast and the habitation of those who rejoice (Ps. XLI).

A certain holy man who lived not far from him, and who had earlier shown him the way to Barlaam, was divinely warned and arrived at the very hour of Josaphat’s death. After adorning his body with sacred hymns, pouring forth tears as signs of his love for Josaphat, and completing all the other rites customary and prescribed among Christians, he buried him in the monument of his father Barlaam. It was fitting, indeed, that the bodies of those whose souls were destined to be together forever should also be joined together.

Obeying the command of a certain fearsome man who seriously ordered this in a dream, the monk who had carried Josaphat out for burial went to the kingdom of India, approached King Barachias, and informed him of everything concerning Josaphat. Without delay, Barachias set out with a great multitude of people. At last he reached the cave and looked upon the tomb. There, after pouring forth the hottest tears, he removed the covering and saw Barlaam and Josaphat lying with their limbs arranged in proper order; their bodies had not changed at all from their former color but were whole and entirely unharmed, together with their garments. The king therefore transferred these tabernacles of the most holy souls, emitting a most pleasing fragrance and displaying nothing repulsive, into splendid reliquaries and carried them back to his homeland.

When this event reached the ears of the common people, an innumerable multitude came together from all the cities and neighboring regions to behold and venerate the blessed bodies. After sacred hymns had been sung for their sake and abundant lamps had been lit, someone might aptly and most appropriately have said there: “Lights around the sons and heirs of Light.” Their bodies were then buried clearly and magnificently in that church which Josaphat himself had built from its foundations. The Lord performed many miracles and expulsions of diseases through his pious servants, both during the transportation of their bodies, at their burial, and also in subsequent times. The king and the populace witnessed all the miracles performed through them. Many among the neighboring nations, suffering from the disease of unbelief and ignorance of God, came to the faith through the signs that took place at the tomb. All who saw and heard Josaphat’s life, fashioned in imitation of the angels, and his love for God burning from his earliest years, were seized with admiration and glorified God in all things, for he never ceases to bring aid and help to those who love him, and he rewards them with the most abundant blessings.

Here ends the present book, which I have written to the best of my ability, as I received it from distinguished men who transmitted these matters to me truthfully. May you, who read and hear this history profitable to the soul, be admitted through the prayers and intercessions of the blessed men Barlaam and Josaphat—concerning whom this history has been composed—to the company of those who have proved the conduct of their lives acceptable to God. This is through Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom belong honor, dominion, majesty, and magnificence, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and forever, unto ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0605]

## DECEMBER 25. THE LIFE OF SAINT EUGENIA [Note: [Col. 0619D] Eugenia.]

The Roman Martyrology, December 25: “At Rome, in the cemetery of Apronianus, Saint Eugenia, virgin. In the time of the Emperor Gallienus, after many distinguished deeds of virtue and after bringing sacred choirs of virgins into union with Christ, she underwent a long contest under Nicetius, prefect of the city, and was finally beheaded with the sword.”

The Greek Menologion, December 24, briefly recounting her Acts: “The contest of Saint Eugenia, martyr, and her companions. She lived under the Emperor Commodus and was the daughter of a tribune in the city of Rome. When her father was sent by the emperor to the city of Alexandria to exercise the office of tribune, he took his wife and children with him; among them was the blessed Eugenia. While she was learning literature and occupied herself with the reading of many books, she came upon the letters of the holy apostle Paul, from which she learned the faith of Christ. Accordingly, abandoning the disturbances of her father’s household and the deceit of the world, she withdrew with two eunuchs to the monastery situated before the city of Alexandria, dressed in male attire. Having been received as a guest by Bishop Helenus, and stating the reason why she had come, she was deemed worthy of divine baptism together with those whom she had brought with her. She was enrolled among the monks, and after some time was entrusted with the care of the monastery. There, because of the miracles God performed through her, she became acquainted with a certain woman of senatorial rank named Melanthia. Later she was accused by that woman as though she had invited her to intercourse—a charge contrary to Eugenia’s character. For Melanthia, believing her to be a man because of the appearance of her clothing, and wounded by her beauty after being repeatedly rejected when she made advances, reported her to the tribune Philip. When her father ordered her to be summoned, the truth was revealed: not only was the person in male clothing a woman, but she was also the tribune’s daughter. Consequently, she drew her father, her mother, and many members of the household to the Christian faith. Her father, having been stripped of his tribune’s rank, was baptized and afterward attained the perfection of martyrdom when unbelievers attacked him in an idol temple and killed him with swords. Saint Eugenia, however, was brought to Rome with her mother and brothers. The eunuchs Protus and Hyacinthus were beheaded; Eugenia herself was tied to a heavy stone and thrown into the river Tiber, but was saved from it and received her consummation by the sword.”

The Menaea, likewise on December 24, touch upon her life in a few iambic verses. Her Acts, written by Metaphrastes, are extant in Lippomanus, volume V, and Surius, volume VI, translated by Gentian Hervetus. These Acts agree completely with the Acts transmitted by Metaphrastes and are arranged in the same order. Thus either this ancient translation was rendered more closely from Metaphrastes, or, more probably, this translator and Metaphrastes drew from the same source, since the new translation by Metaphrastes contains some matters treated at greater length, while this ancient translation contains certain matters absent from the new one. Unless one prefers to suppose that Metaphrastes translated this Latin text into Greek, since he proceeds in the same order and sometimes appears not to have understood the Latin text correctly. Certainly, what is said here in chapter 1 about the seventh consulship of Commodus, he understood as the seventh year of Commodus’s reign—plainly in error, as I shall soon explain. The authors who followed, and who were earlier than Metaphrastes, also remembered Eugenia; it is plausible that they derived their accounts from this Latin source. Alcimus Avitus, bishop of Vienne, mentions Eugenia as a most celebrated martyr in book VI, chapter 20, of his poem to his sister Fuscina on the praise of chastity; Fortunatus does so in book VIII, poem 4, On Virginity; and Aldhelm likewise in On the Praise of Virginity.

## OF THE VIRGIN AND MARTYR, BY AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR [Note: [Col. 0621C] Unknown.]

I have given it this title because I found the name of no author either in the manuscript or in the printed editions. I see, however, that Goldast, in volume I, part II, of *Rerum Alemannicarum*, in his notes on Hepidanus’s *Life of Saint Wiborada*, book I, chapter 27, cites the Acts of Eugenia in the translation of Rufinus. If he drew this from manuscripts, I readily agree. Certainly the style does not differ from Rufinus’s style.

[Col. 0605D] **CHAPTER I.**—In his seventh consulship, Commodus [Note: [Col. 0621D] *In the seventh consulship of Commodus.*]

According to Baronius, volume II, this is the year of Christ 194, which was the thirteenth year of Commodus’s reign. Yet the same Baronius, under the year of Christ 188, the seventh year of Commodus’s reign, places the appointment of Philip as prefect of Augustal Egypt. For, he says, although Philip is said to have obtained it after the completion of Commodus’s seventh year, this happened because he did not receive the title and office at the very moment when he had been chosen by the emperor, but only when he entered Alexandria; and Ulpianus affirms that this was done according to the law of Augustus (*Digest*, single law, *On the Office of the Prefect of Augustal Egypt*).

Here Baronius follows the Acts of Eugenia transmitted in Greek by Metaphrastes, which express “the seventh year of the reign” in place of “the seventh consulship.” But Metaphrastes’ and Baronius’s position does not agree in any way with the Acts themselves, whether Latin or Greek. For here, in chapter 17, the pagans are said to have stated that when the persecution was raised by Severus, Philip had governed Egypt blamelessly for nine years and lost everything in the tenth, because he favored the Catholics. The same account is found in Metaphrastes.

Now more than ten years intervene between the seventh year of Commodus’s reign—which they take to be the year in which Philip was appointed prefect of Egypt—and the tenth year of Severus’s reign, in which they take the same prefecture to have been removed from him. Since, according to Baronius, the seventh year of Commodus’s reign corresponds to the year of Christ 188, and the tenth year of Severus to the year of Christ 204, it is clear that between the two years of Christ, even when reckoned exclusively, there are fifteen years; or seventeen years if both terminal years are counted. Yet Philip is said to have been removed from his administration in the tenth year of his prefecture.

Therefore the Latin text is entirely correct in stating that the prefecture of Egypt was conferred upon Philip in the seventh consulship of Commodus—that is, in the thirteenth year of Commodus’s reign, corresponding to the year of Christ 194. It is thus equally correct in saying that he was deprived of it in the tenth year of his prefecture, namely, in the tenth year of Severus’s reign, the year of Christ 204. From the year of Christ 194 to the year of Christ 204 there are exactly ten years. From this it is evident that the Latin Acts are more authentic than the Greek. I wish that the great Baronius, as he generally does elsewhere, had set aside the corrupted Greek texts and adhered to them.

The emperor sent the most illustrious man Philip [Note: [Col. 0622B] *Philip.*] to Egypt to serve as prefect of Alexandria, so that all the offices administered throughout Egypt should be subject to his authority. [Col. 0606D] When he therefore came from the city of Rome to the city of Alexandria with his wife Claudia, his two sons Avitus and Sergius, and his daughter Eugenia, and administered the prefecture with Roman dignity, ordering the whole province of Egypt according to Roman laws, he put an end to all who practiced magical curiosity. He did not even permit the Jews to retain the designation of their name, while he decreed that Christians should remain only at a distance from Alexandria. Although he was more a friend of philosophers than a supporter of idols, he nevertheless pressed the Roman superstitions as though he were a devout worshiper, agreeing not with reason but with tradition.

[Note: [Col. 0622B] *Philip.* Baronius, volume II, under the year of Christ 204, the second year of Pope Zephyrinus and the tenth of the Emperor Severus, says that those who thought this man was the same as the Emperor Philip were mistaken. Cedrenus is among them, in his account of Maximinus; Zonaras rightly refutes them in his account of the Emperor Philip, as Baronius himself notes under September 13.]

## CHAPTER II

After he had most thoroughly educated his daughter Eugenia in the liberal arts and instructed her both in Latin and in Greek eloquence, he also permitted her to be taught philosophy. For she was of keen intelligence and so capable of retaining what she learned that whatever she grasped once by hearing or reading, she kept forever. Eugenia was beautiful in face and graceful in body, [Col. 0607B] but more beautiful in mind and more lovely in chastity.

When, therefore, at the age of fifteen, she was sought in marriage by Aquilius, son of the consul Aquilius [Note: [Col. 0622B] *Aquilius, of Aquilius.*] The old edition has “Aquilius, of Aquilinus.” Baronius, volume II, under the year of Christ 188, reads “Acilio,” who held the consulship that year together with Commodus—unless, he says, we suppose this to have been one of the suffect consuls. [Col. 0622C] Dio records that Commodus designated twenty-five consuls for a single year, something that had never happened before. But since the name agrees with that of the ordinary consul, no other suffect consul need be sought. What Baronius supposes in the same place—that Eugenia was betrothed to the consul Aquilius—I believe he took from Metaphrastes, where Aquilius is said to have betrothed Eugenia. But this must be understood not as betrothing her to himself, but to his son, as this Latin text has it. For parents used to arrange and contract betrothals for their sons.]

Her father asked her whether she consented to the young man, born of the most illustrious lineage, who sought her. She replied: “A husband should be chosen for his character, not his birth; for it is with the man himself, not with his parents, that one must live.”

When she resisted one suitor after another with a steadfast spirit of chastity, the teaching of the blessed apostle Paul came into her hands. Although she lived under thoroughly pagan parents, she nevertheless began in spirit to be a Christian.

## CHAPTER III

Since the Christians had been ordered to leave the city of Alexandria, she asked her parents to allow her, for the sake of viewing the countryside, to travel around her estates situated in the suburbs of Alexandria. As soon as she had obtained what she requested and was hurrying from the city toward the estate, she heard Christians singing psalms and saying: “All the gods of the nations are demons, but our God made the heavens” (Ps. XCV).

When she heard this, she sighed and wept, and said to the eunuch youths named Protus and Hyacinthus:

“I know that you were educated in literature together with me. We have read the deeds of men, both worthy and unworthy, and with painstaking zeal have worked through the syllogisms of philosophers, constructed with empty labor: the arguments of Aristotle, the Ideas of Plato, the sects of Epicurus, and the counsels of Socrates and the Stoics. In short, whatever the poet sings, whatever the orator devises, whatever the philosopher thinks, is excluded by this one sentence, which we hear the Christians sing with rejoicing: ‘All the gods of the nations are demons, but our God made the heavens.’ ‘Confession and beauty are before him; holiness and magnificence are in his majesty.’

“Let us therefore confer together. Let the Apostle be read and the Prophet praised. Let there be harmony in faith, and let us determine through earnest counsel by what means we may reach the innermost chambers of divine wisdom without being separated from one another.

“Usurped authority has made me your mistress,” she said, “but wisdom has made me your sister. Let us therefore be brothers, as divine wisdom has ordained, not as human rashness boasts. Let us go together to the Christians and proceed as I shall arrange.

“I hear that a certain Helenus is called a bishop. His dwelling is that place in which men are heard singing to their God day and night; we too hear them singing whenever we pass by. [Col. 0608A] But this bishop is said to be occupied with various responsibilities of his Church. For those who devote themselves to divine praises, he has appointed a certain presbyter named Theodore, whose miracles are said to be so great that he even gives sight to the blind by his prayers, drives out demons, and restores health to the sick. Indeed, he allows no woman to come to the lodging of this community, where God is sung.

“Considering this, I think I should cut my hair, so that our journey by night tomorrow may be arranged and they may provide us passage. You two will walk beside the *basterna* [Note: [Col. 0622C] *Basterna.*] Shortly afterward he calls it a *vehiculum*. Ammianus, book XIV: “With such an entourage many matrons, their heads covered and traveling in *basternae*, traverse every side of the city.” See the *Onomasticon*.] while the others go ahead, and you will set me down at the place. When the empty *basterna* has passed, the three of us [Note: [Col. 0622C] *The basterna—the three of us.* Thus correctly in the manuscript. The printed editions incorrectly read *the three basternae*.], dressed alike in the clothing of our master, shall hasten together to the men of God.”

Both approved the plan, and on the following night it was carried out as she had arranged.

## CHAPTER IV

Christ deemed it worthy to show such grace to those who believed in him that, at the very hour when they arrived at the monastery, Saint Helenus the bishop arrived there. Since it is customary in Egypt that when bishops visit monasteries a company of singers accompanies them, Helenus, bishop of Heliopolis, arrived with more than ten thousand men singing and saying: “The way of the righteous has been made straight, and the path of the saints prepared.”

Hearing this, Eugenia said to her companions:

“Consider the power of the songs, and see that whatever they sing with melodious voices is directed toward us. When our discussion about the true God was taking place in the arrangement of our mutual conversation, we heard them sing this: ‘For all the gods of the nations are demons, but our God made the heavens.’ And now, as we undertake the journey by which we wish to withdraw from the worship of idols and merit grace so that we may reach Christian worship, behold, thousands of men meet us, crying out with one voice and saying: ‘The way of the righteous has been made straight, and the path of the saints prepared.’

“Let us therefore understand where this people is going. If they are going to the dwelling to which we have decided to go, let us join the singing crowds and, counted among those who arrive, enter as their companions, until we gather the necessary information.”

## CHAPTER V

When they had joined those singing psalms, they asked who the elder was who alone rode on a donkey in the midst of the people following and preceding him. They learned that this was Helenus the bishop, a Christian from infancy. While he had grown up as a small child in the monastery, he increased in the virtues of such great holiness that whenever he was sent to fetch fire from nearby, he would carry burning coals in his garment without damaging it. [Note: [Col. 0622C–D] *Fire.* A similar account of Abbot Helenus occurs in book II of the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 9, in the same words as here: “he carried burning coals in his garment without its being damaged.” I would not readily say which borrowed from the other. Rather, one may infer even from this that Rufinus was also the author of this Life, as of book II of the *Lives of the Fathers*. Palladius, chapter 59, has the same little story about Helenus.] [Col. 0608D]

“Indeed,” he said, “a few days ago a certain magician came who tried by arguments of words to overthrow the people of God. He said that this bishop was false and that he himself had been sent by Christ to teach. He was exceedingly cunning and led the people astray through the divine Scriptures.

“At last the entire Christian crowd approached this man whom you see, our Father, and said to him: ‘We have heard of Zareas, that he himself has been sent by Christ. Set a day on which you will either receive him as your companion or, if you can, prove that he speaks falsely.’

“Accordingly, a day and place were appointed in the middle of the city of Heliopolis. The magician Zareas came with his arts, and Bishop Helenus came with his prayers. After greeting the people, he said: ‘Now you will test the spirits that are from God’ (1 John IV).

“Then he turned to Zareas and began a great contest of words. But because Zareas was exceedingly cunning, and Helenus could not refute him by argument, he saw that the people were being gravely harmed because Zareas was prevailing in speech. He therefore asked for a brief silence and said to the people:

“‘The counsel of the apostle Paul must be followed in this matter. For he says to his disciple Timothy: “Do not contend with words; it is useful for nothing except the subversion of those who hear” (2 Tim. II). But lest we produce this testimony not as prudent men but as timid ones, let a fire be kindled in the middle of the city, and let us enter the flames together. Whoever is not burned, let us believe that Christ sent him.’”

Then everyone approved the decision. A great fire was immediately kindled. The blessed Helenus ordered Zareas to enter the flames. Zareas replied: “You enter first, since you proposed this.”

The most blessed Father Helenus therefore made the sign of the cross over himself, entered the great flames with outstretched hands, [Note: [Col. 0622D] *Enters the flames.*] This challenge to enter the fire occurs frequently in sacred histories when other arguments for proving and propagating the faith are lacking. I have collected various examples in my dissertation *On Faith to Be Kept with Heretics*, chapter 12.] and stood there for nearly half an hour. Neither his hair nor his clothing was harmed in any part. He then ordered Zareas likewise to enter.

But Zareas began to resist and flee. When the people delivered him unwillingly into the fire, the flame immediately surrounded him and began to burn him. Saint Helenus threw himself in and rescued him alive, though half-burned; the people then expelled him in disgrace from the borders of that region. This is the man whom, as you see, the people accompany daily in the praises of God wherever he goes.

## CHAPTER VI

When the blessed Eugenia heard this, she groaned and fell at the feet of the man who had told her these things. She said:

“I beg you to introduce me to him together with these two brothers of mine. We wish to turn from idols to Christ. Since we have determined this together and are brothers and sister, we also wish to obtain from him that he never permit us to be separated from one another.”

He replied: “Now be silent until he has entered the monastery to which he is going and has rested a little. When the time is suitable, I shall make everything known to him according to your request.”

Meanwhile, as he approached the monastery to which he was traveling, behold, the members of the community came out to meet the Father, singing a hymn to God: “We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple” (Ps. XLVII).

When the bishop and the people entered, Eugenia also entered with Hyacinthus and Protus, her companions; only the man with whom she had spoken knew who she was.

## CHAPTER VII

After the morning praises had been completed, the bishop rested briefly and ordered the preparation of the sixth hour, so that he could celebrate the divine mysteries and, once the sixth hour had begun, the ninth hour might arrive at the proper time for the meal of those who were fasting.

While the bishop was resting, he had a dream in which he was being led to a statue of a woman so that he might sacrifice to it. “Then,” he said, “I said in the dream to those who held me: ‘Permit me to speak with your goddess.’ When they allowed me to speak, I said to her:

“‘Recognize that you are a creature of God. Come down, and do not allow yourself to be worshiped.’

“When she heard this, she came down and followed me, saying: ‘I shall not leave you until you restore me to my Creator and Maker.’”

While these things were turning over in the bishop’s mind, Eutropius, the man who had spoken with Eugenia, approached him and said:

“Three brother youths, having unanimously abandoned the worship of idols and desiring to join the number of those serving Christ in this monastery, entered here today following your footsteps. They asked me with tears to request that they be granted an introduction to your blessed presence.”

Then the blessed Helenus said: “I give thanks to you, good Jesus, who have caused me to know this matter beforehand.”

He ordered the youths to be brought before him. Taking Eugenia by the hand, he poured forth a prayer. When he had finished it, he took them aside and questioned them with a very serious expression about what they said, and thought it necessary to inquire from what nation they came.

Eugenia replied: “Citizens—we are Romans. One of these two brothers of mine is called Protus, the other Hyacinthus; I am called Eugenius.”

The blessed Helenus said to her:

“You rightly call yourself Eugenius, for you act manfully, and may your heart be strengthened for the faith of Christ. Therefore you are rightly called Eugenius. For know also that through the Holy Spirit we foresaw beforehand that you are Eugenia in the body, how you came here, and that these men are yours; he did not permit me to overlook any of this. But the Lord deigned to reveal to me that you have prepared for him a most pleasing dwelling in your body by preserving the reward of virginity and rejecting the deceptive allurements of the present age.

“Know, however, that you will suffer much for chastity. But he to whom you have wholly given yourself will not abandon you.”

Turning to Protus and Hyacinthus, he said:

“Though placed in a body of servitude, you have courageously maintained and continue to maintain the freeborn dignity of the spirit. Therefore, while I remain silent, Christ the Lord speaks to you, saying: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you, I shall no longer call you servants, but friends’ (John XV). Accordingly, I proclaim you blessed, because you have agreed with the Holy Spirit and unanimously consented to the commands of the Savior, so that together you may reach glory and receive it.”

The blessed Helenus spoke these words publicly, with no other witness than God, and ordered her to remain in this male attire. They did not leave him until, instructed in the sanctification of baptism, they had been admitted to the monastery to which they had hastened.

## CHAPTER VIII

Let us return to the time when Protus and Hyacinthus departed, taking Eugenia with them. The *basterna*, with the animals walking and the youths going ahead, arrived empty at her mother. When they saw the youths hurrying from a distance and the *basterna* approaching, everyone ran out joyfully. But when they found the vehicle empty, all together uttered a cry, and suddenly the whole city resounded with uproar.

Who could hear that the prefect had lost his dearest daughter? There was immeasurable mourning and immense weeping. Everyone lamented in confusion: the parents, their daughter; the brothers, their sister; the servants, their mistress. Grief and infinite anguish of spirit held them all.

An investigation was conducted throughout the province. Diviners were questioned, and soothsayers sought. Demons were also questioned through sacrifices and criminal superstitions, so that they might reveal where Eugenia had gone. All said only that the gods had snatched her up to heaven.

Her father believed this had happened. Turning from tears to consolation, he instituted festivals in response to the oracles and, consecrating her among the number of the gods, had an image of her made from pure gold. It began to be worshiped in such a way that they paid it no less honor than to their other gods. Her mother Claudia, however, and her brothers Avitus and Sergius could find no consolation by any means; they mourned her unbearably.

## CHAPTER IX

The blessed Eugenia, male in attire and spirit, remained in the aforementioned monastery of men. She made such progress in divine learning that within two years she retained all the Lord’s Scriptures in memory. Such tranquility of spirit was in her that everyone said she was one of the number of the angels.

For who could detect that she was a woman, when the virtue of Christ and spotless virginity protected her, so that she was admirable even to men? Her speech was humble in charity, clear in moderation, free from vices, and avoided eloquence. She surpassed everyone in humility. No one was found more ready than she for prayer.

She became all things to all: she consoled the sorrowful, rejoiced with the joyful, and pacified the angry by a single word. Through her example she so edified the proud that he would rejoice to believe himself suddenly transformed from a wolf into a sheep. She obtained such grace from God that whenever she visited anyone in pain, all pain immediately departed and complete health arrived.

Her companions Hyacinthus and Protus accompanied her and obeyed her in all things.

## CHAPTER X

In the third year after her conversion, the abbot who presided over the brothers in the monastery departed to the Lord. After his departure, it seemed to everyone that they should choose the blessed Eugenia as their abbot.

The blessed Eugenia feared that, contrary to the rule, a woman might be placed over men. At the same time, she feared that she might disdain the unanimous request of them all. She said to them:

“I beg you to bring the Gospel here at once.”

When it had been brought, she said:

“Whenever Christians must choose something, Christ must be heard before all else. Let us therefore see in this election of yours what he himself commands, so that we may attend both to your order and to his instructions.”

Turning the book’s pages, she came to the passage and began to read:

“Jesus said to his disciples: ‘You know that the rulers of the nations are greater than those over whom they rule, and exercise authority over them’ (Matt. XX). ‘But it shall not be so among you; whoever among you wishes to be first shall be your last, and whoever among you wishes to be lord shall be your servant’ (Luke XXIII).”

After saying this, she added:

“Behold, obeying your order, I have decided to accept the primacy and obey the Lord’s commands. I make myself last for the sake of your love.”

Everyone rejoiced at her agreement. She herself, however, undertook before all the work of the monastery usually performed by the lowest-ranking person: carrying water in every circumstance, chopping wood, and attending to cleanliness. Finally, she chose her dwelling in the place where the monastery’s doorkeeper lived, so that she would not appear superior even to him.

She carefully attended to the brothers’ meals and rigorously maintained the order of singing praise to God. She devoted herself so attentively to the hours of terce, sext, none, evening, night, and morning that she seemed already to have perished to God if even the smallest part of any hour passed without divine praises.

Through this work she began to become so dear to God that she drove demons from possessed bodies and opened the eyes of the blind. But since I intend to relate many matters individually in order, let us proceed as far as brevity permits.

[Col. 0612B] ## CHAPTER XI

A certain Alexandrian matron, superior to the other matrons, named Melanthia, heard of Eugenia’s reputation and came to her, for she had been severely afflicted with quartan fever for a year and more. When the blessed Eugenia anointed her with oil, she immediately vomited out all the violence of bile. Restored to perfect health, she hurried on foot to her own lodging, which she possessed nearby the monastery.

Meanwhile she prepared gifts, filled three silver cups with solid coins, and sent them to the blessed Eugenia as a reward for her healing. Eugenia gratefully returned what had been sent and said:

“We abound and overflow with every good thing. Therefore, dearest relative Melanthia, I urge and admonish you to distribute these things more generously to the needy and those suffering want.”

[Col. 0612C] ## CHAPTER XII

When Melanthia heard this, she became distressed. Coming to Eugenia, she began to plead and promise still greater gifts. She became a constant visitor to the blessed Eugenia, and, finding nothing that revealed her to be a woman, was deceived by the elegance of her youth.

When she saw her, she supposed that she was truly a young man. Believing that she had been saved not by Eugenia’s holiness but by some art, she fell into desire for her. Thinking Eugenia greedy for greater wealth, she began to offer limitless sums and promise still more.

When she repeatedly made the same entreaties and saw that the gifts offered to Eugenia were returned with gratitude, she turned toward even greater destruction and pretended to be ill. When the blessed Eugenia visited her at her request, Melanthia began to address Saint Eugenia, who was sitting before her bed, as follows:

“An intolerable love for you torments my heart, and I have found no remedy for my distress except to appoint you master of all my possessions. Why do you torture yourself with empty and pointless fasts? Behold, there is an infinite abundance of estates, an immense weight of gold, a plentiful store of silver, and an unlimited number of servants. I possess the dignity of noble birth. This year I have been widowed without children. Take their place in my possessions; be now not only master of my property but of me as well.”

While she was saying these and similar things, Eugenia said to her:

“Your name rightly testifies to the blackness of your treachery; you have prepared a great dwelling place for the devil. Depart from the servants of God, deceitful and seductive Melanthia, for we serve in another manner. Let your riches have masters like yourself; we are content to beg with Christ. He is abundantly rich who is poor with Christ.

“Let the images of desire flee from you, for this madness that has invaded you is not conducive to your salvation. You have become a dwelling place of the dragon and pour forth poison; but, invoking the name of Christ, we escape the venom of your poisons and find the Lord’s mercy.”

## CHAPTER XIII

Then, unable to endure the shame of her deception and fearing that she would be exposed unless she herself exposed it first, she returned to Alexandria and decided to approach the prefect, saying as follows:

“I encountered a wicked young man pretending to practice the Christian religion. When I allowed him to come to me under the pretext of healing—for he was said to be able to help the sick—and he considered me one of those whose chastity he was accustomed to violate, he dared shamelessly to address me and, with impudent words, urge me to commit the crime. If I had not immediately raised an outcry and been rescued by the assistance of my maidservants, he would have taken me captive to his lust in barbarous fashion.”

When the prefect heard this, he was inflamed with immense fury and ordered men to be sent to the monastery district to imprison him in chains, together with all who were staying there. Accordingly, all were placed in chains; and since one prison could not contain them, they were divided among various places of detention. After this, a day was appointed for their execution, on which some would be condemned to the beasts, others to the fires, and others to various punishments.

An immense rumor arose, and shameless report spread throughout the whole province of Egypt. Everyone believed; everyone condemned them; and it seemed plausible to everyone that Melanthia, an illustrious woman, could not be lying. What more need be said? The appointed day of execution arrived, and the inhabitants of all the neighboring cities assembled to see the corrupters handed over to the bites of beasts. They were brought in chains, with the blessed Eugenia, held by iron collars; and, since no one recognized that she was a woman, the crowd cried out with various judgments.

Then the prefect ordered her to be brought nearer, so that he might hear her not through intermediaries but learn the truth from her own mouth. The racks, whips, flames, torturers, and all the other instruments that ordinarily bring hidden thoughts of the heart to light were prepared.

## CHAPTER XIV

Then the prefect Philip said:

“Speak, most wicked of Christians! Is this what your Christ handed down to you as a commandment: that you should devote yourselves to corrupting others and, by deceitful cunning, entrap the modesty and chastity of married women? Speak now, gallows-bird! What recklessness compelled you to desire the illustrious woman Melanthia and, entering under the guise of a physician, to provoke her most noble chastity toward the disgrace of a brothel?”

When the blessed Eugenia heard this, she lowered her head so that she could not be recognized, and gave the prefect this answer:

“My Lord Jesus Christ, whom I serve, taught chastity and promises eternal life to those who preserve the integrity of their bodies. We can now declare this Melanthia to be a false witness; but it is better that we suffer evils than that she, once convicted, should suffer anything, lest the fruit of our patience perish as well. Nevertheless, if Your Excellency will swear by the safety of the emperors that you will not turn the same sentence against her, and that this deceitful witness will suffer no harm, we shall now prove that the crime she charges against us rebounds upon her.”

When the prefect had sworn by the safety of the emperors, promising to fulfill everything she requested, Eugenia said:

“O Melanthia, whose name means ‘blackness,’ dark Melanthia, you have caused the goads to be applied and ordered Christians to be hanged. Condemn us, strike us, burn us—you treat us well enough; yet Christ does not have servants such as you testify that we are. Nevertheless, order the maidservant whom you said was a witness to our crime to be brought in, so that the lie may be stripped bare from her own mouth.”

When she had been brought before the judge, she began to say:

“This most shameless young man, often exposed in adulteries with low-born women, was driven by the very impunity he enjoyed to this point: he entered shamelessly, even into my mistress’s bedchamber, at the first hour of the day. At first, by his words, he indicated that he had come as though for her health; secondly, he revealed his own desire; and thirdly, he even resorted to violence, had I not quickly entered and summoned the household, which today is witness to this crime.”

Then the prefect ordered certain members of the household to appear and confirm by their testimony that this had happened. When they were brought forward, they each testified that it was as she had said. Then the judge, greatly agitated, said:

“What will you say to this, wretch, whom so many witnesses refute and so many proofs expose?”

## CHAPTER XV

To this the blessed Eugenia said:

“It is time to speak, because the time to be silent has passed” (Ecclesiasticus 3).

“I had indeed wished that the crime charged against me should be exposed at the future judgment, and that I should display my chastity to him alone for whose love it must be preserved. Nevertheless, lest deceitful audacity boast over the servants of Christ, I shall disclose the truth in a few words—not for the vanity of human eloquence, but for the glory of Christ’s name.

“For such is the power of his name that even women who live in his fear obtain the dignity of men; and the difference of sex cannot be found superior to faith in him, since the blessed apostle Paul, the teacher of all Christians, says that with the Lord there is no distinction between male and female, for we are all one in Christ (Galatians 3).

“Therefore, with a fervent spirit I adopted this rule. And because of the confidence I had in Christ, I did not wish to be a woman; rather, preserving immaculate virginity with the whole purpose of my mind, I steadfastly bore myself as a man in Christ. I did not assume a false appearance of modesty in order to pretend, as a man, to be a woman; rather, by acting manfully as a woman, I bore myself as a man, embracing firmly the virginity that is in Christ.”

And having said this, she tore from her head the tunic in which she was clothed, and she appeared as a woman. Immediately she said to the prefect:

“You are indeed my father according to the flesh; Claudia is my mother; and these two who sit with you, Avitus and Sergius, are my brothers. I am Eugenia, your daughter, who for the love of Christ rejected the whole world with its delights as dung.

“Here are Protus and Hyacinthus, my eunuchs, with whom I entered the school of Christ. Christ proved so powerful there that, by his mercy, he made me victorious over lust and every defilement. In him I believe that I shall remain continually to the end.”

## CHAPTER XVI

When the father recognized his daughter, the brothers their sister, and the servants their mistress, they immediately ran to her and, shedding tears before the people, embraced her. The event was announced to her mother Claudia, who at once hastened to the spectacle.

Garments woven with gold were brought, and, although unwilling, she was clothed in them. Placed upon a lofty tribunal, she was raised up on high, and the entire people cried out:

“One Christ, one true God of the Christians!”

The priests and bishops, who were before the amphitheater with a large Christian crowd and would have buried those accused if they had been killed, entered singing a hymn to God, and all cried with one voice:

“The right hand of the Lord has been glorified in power; your right hand, Lord, has crushed the enemies.”

Eugenia was therefore carried in triumph. And, lest the proof of her chastity be absent from the people’s great joy, a fire seemed to descend from heaven and surround Melanthia’s house so completely that no trace remained of anything belonging to her.

The people’s joy was mingled with the fear of God. The church, which had been closed for eight years as though widowed, was reopened. The Christian people were recalled; the prefect, still wearing the insignia of office, was baptized; his sons were baptized; and his mother Claudia was baptized.

He restored the privileges of the Christians and sent a report to the emperor Severus concerning them, stating that Christians greatly benefited the commonwealth and therefore ought to live in the cities without any persecution. The emperor agreed to the reports, and the whole city of Alexandria became, as it were, one church. There was joy in all the cities, and the dignity of the Christian name flourished.

## CHAPTER XVII

But because the enemy’s rivalry always follows holiness, and malice fights against goodness, certain distinguished men of Alexandria, worshipers of idols, were greatly displeased that he had granted privileges to the Christians. Coming to the emperor, they said that the state had been thrown into disorder by Philip, who, after having administered his office irreproachably for nine years, had now, in the tenth year, [Note: **In the tenth year.** Baronius, volume II, year of Christ 204, under Pope Zephyrinus II and Emperor Severus X. “It should not seem so very surprising,” he says, “that Philip continued so long in the exercise of that office. For since the prefecture called Augustal—the prefecture of Egypt—was of the greatest importance of all, and since Augustus had reserved it for himself as a hostage of the Roman Empire and had decreed that no senator should be sent to it, but rather some excellent man from the equestrian order who could never stir up disturbances out of desire for supreme power, once the emperor had found a most faithful man worthy of that prefecture, he did not easily remove him, knowing above all that this was advantageous to the peace and security of the Roman Empire, since the Egyptians were the most eager of all peoples for innovations and the most fickle in spirit for stirring up disturbances and rebellion. But Dio discusses these matters at greater length (Dio, *Roman History*, book 15).”]

“ruined everything. Finally, he has abandoned all the rites of the immortal gods and converted the whole city to the worship of a certain man whom the Jews killed. There is no reverence for your laws. Anyone at all enters the venerable temples whenever he wishes—not to profess goodwill toward the worship, nor to believe that the gods whom we worship exist, but to utter endless blasphemies and to call the signs of the divine name mere stones or metals.”

Many statements of this kind were made to the Augusti Severus and Antoninus. They, being provoked, [Note: **Being provoked.** Baronius, volume II, year of Christ 204, under Pope Zephyrinus I and Emperor Severus X, places the persecution raised by Severus. “It also seems,” he says, “that what stirred Severus’s anger and incited him to persecute the faithful was his realization that Philip, administering the most distinguished prefecture of all Egypt, the Augustal prefecture, had now become a Christian.” Thus far Baronius. Since this chapter says that it was the tenth year of Philip’s prefecture, this calculation does not agree with the seventh year of Commodus, in which he is said to have assumed the prefecture.]

sent him decrees of this sort:

“Divine Augustus, our father, the former Emperor Commodus, appointed and established you in Alexandria not as prefect but as king, [Note: **As king.** Baronius, above, under the year of Christ 204. As to the fact that Severus says in that letter, according to Metaphrastes in Hervetus’s translation, “He chose you as the ruler of Egypt rather as a king than as a prefect,” this clearly confirms what Tacitus writes in these words: “Ever since the divine Augustus, Roman equestrians have held Egypt in place of kings. It seemed expedient to retain at home a province difficult of access, fertile in grain, divided by superstition and licentiousness, noble, and ignorant of laws and magistrates” (Tacitus, book 17).]

so that, as long as you lived, you would accept no successor. Therefore, wishing to add to his benefits, we decree that you offer the customary worship to the almighty gods or, having relinquished your dignity, surrender even your personal possessions.”

## CHAPTER XVIII

After receiving this authority from the Augustus, he pretended to be ill until he had distributed and donated everything throughout the province to churches and the poor. The prefect himself, however, in the fear of God and in the worship of Christ, also strengthened others in Christ.

Meanwhile, all Alexandria conspired to make him a bishop. [Note: **To make him a bishop.** Baronius, volume II, year of Christ 204, under Pope Zephyrinus II and Emperor Severus X, says that the *Acts of Philip* should be corrected where they say that he was made bishop of Alexandria. For, he says in the note for 13 September, his prefecture was secular, not sacerdotal. Indeed, Eusebius, both in his *Chronicle* and in his *History*, when he records the succession of the bishops of Alexandria, as do Bishop Nicephorus, Nicephorus Callistus, and others who performed the same task, none of them numbers Philip among the Alexandrian bishops.]

The state continued to regard him as prefect because his successor had not yet arrived, while the Church regarded him as bishop because, on account of his faith, it had rightly chosen him as its priest. He remained in the episcopate for one year and three months.

## CHAPTER XIX

After this period of time, the prefect Perennius arrived. [Note: **Prefect Perennius.** So the manuscript reads. In the printed editions, *Herennius*. **At Metaphrastes**, *Terentius*. Baronius, under the year cited immediately above, says: “The man whom Eusebius calls Laetus (Eusebius, book 6, chapter 2) was perhaps also called Terentius Laetus. The *Menaea*, the manuscripts, Ado, and Usuard in the *Martyrology* have Perennius. Herennius Celsus also appears in these times in Trebellius Pollio’s *Thirty Tyrants*, in the life of Aemilianus. Hence it seems possible to infer that Herennius was then Augustal prefect of Egypt.”]

While he was seeking to strike him in Alexandria and could not do so because the entire city remained devoted to him, he sent men who pretended to be Christians. They entered and struck him. [Note: **They struck him.** Baronius, volume II, under the year cited immediately above: “As for the fact that Eusebius, when discussing the martyrs who suffered in Egypt, makes no mention of the martyrdom of this Philip, it perhaps happened because he passed over him as the cause of his death. Since he was secretly killed by assassins and no public confession of the Christian name known to anyone had preceded it, he may seem to have been omitted by Eusebius; although there is no doubt that many other matters of even greater importance were also passed over by him in silence, as can be seen in almost every year.”]

He was engaged in prayer to the Lord. The prefect Perennius then had the assailants brought before him. Conscious of his own command, he committed them to custody, as though they were to be tried, but after a few days released and dismissed them through the emperors’ clemency.

The most blessed Philip was permitted to remain alive for three days after the blow—not for any other reason than to strengthen wavering hearts. For, as he was about to depart to the Lord, he did not wish to be deprived of the crown of martyrdom, and he himself prayed to receive it. For the one who, while still in the body, drove out demons and enlightened the blind through prayer—how much less would he have wished to be deprived of the palm?

Without doubt, he could obtain whatever he wished. And so he received it, that as he shared the name of Philip, he might also share the crown; and the martyrs received as their companion one whom the Church had rightly received as its priest.

Near the courtyard there, his daughter, the holy Eugenia, had established a monastery for the virgins of Christ. In that place he ordered his little body to be laid, where the most blessed Claudia was building a hospice and had established estates to provide for the reception of travelers. She herself returned to Rome with her sons Avitus and Sergius and with the blessed Eugenia.

## CHAPTER XX

Accordingly, the Roman senate received Philip’s sons with every expression of joy, and they sent one proconsul to Carthage and another as deputy to Africa.

Many married women and nearly all the virgins whom the blessed Eugenia could make her acquaintances or friends were coming to her, so that she might lead them to believe in Christ and remain in the Lord’s virginity. A certain virgin of royal lineage, named Basilla, desired to approach her. But since she could not go to her because of the charge against the Christian name, she asked through a trustworthy intermediary that Eugenia instruct her in the Christian religion.

Then the blessed Eugenia summoned her most blessed companions, Protus and Hyacinthus, and said to them:

“Gird yourselves for the warfare to which Christ calls you. I shall offer you to Basilla under the guise of a gift, so that you may make her a servant in Christ.”

Thus they were given as a gift. Basilla received them as servants but honored them as apostles. She spent every hour with them; and, keeping them as eunuchs in her service, she ceased neither by day nor by night from conversations about God and from prayers.

Then Cornelius, who was the chief priest of the sacred law in the city of Rome, came secretly to her and baptized her. When the blessed Basilla had been strengthened in the fear of God through the working of Christ’s mercy, she and the blessed Eugenia enjoyed one another’s company by mutual visits on almost every night.

## CHAPTER XXI

All the Christian widows assembled with the blessed Claudia, and all the virgins assembled with the blessed Eugenia. The holy Cornelius, pope of the city of Rome, gave them each Saturday evening, as it passed into the Lord’s Day, a night of vigil with hymns. At the crowing of the cocks he celebrated the holy mysteries in the quiet of the night, and thus strengthened them on the Sabbath.

Eugenia and Basilla, as I have mentioned, enjoyed one another’s company in Christ on almost every night and renewed one another through their mutual conversation.

O how many virgins the Savior found through Eugenia! How many brides Christ gained through Basilla! How many women preserved widowhood with willing resolve through Claudia! How many young men believed in Christ the Lord through Protus and Hyacinthus!

## CHAPTER XXII

When Valerian and Gallienus were emperors, a sedition arose concerning the Christians, because Cyprian was overturning Carthage and Cornelius Rome. Authority was therefore given to the proconsul Paternus to kill Cyprian.

Cornelius, however, because he was supported by many distinguished Romans, was in hiding. Then the blessed Eugenia, seeing Basilla, said:

“It has been revealed to me by the Lord that you will suffer for your virginity.”

Basilla replied to Eugenia:

“The Lord has also deigned to reveal to me that you will receive a double crown of martyrdom: one, which you acquired at Alexandria through your righteous labors; and another, which you will obtain through the shedding of your blood.”

Then the blessed Eugenia stretched out her hands and said:

“Lord Jesus, Son of the Most High, who came for our salvation through the virginity of your mother, lead to the kingdom of your glory, through the reward of virginity, all those whom you have entrusted to me.”

## CHAPTER XXIII

While the holy virgins of Christ who were with Eugenia and Basilla were gathered together, the blessed Eugenia said to them all:

“Behold, it is the season of the vintage, when clusters of grapes are cut down and trampled underfoot, but afterward are set before royal banquets. No imperial power and no illustrious dignity is adorned without their blood. You, my branches and clusters born from my own inward being, be ready in the Lord.

“For virginity is the mark of the first virtue, close to God; like the angels; the parent of life; the friend of holiness; the way of security; the mistress of joy; the guide of virtue; the nourishment and crown of faith; the aid and support of charity.

“Nothing should be more laboriously pursued by us; nothing should be striven for more earnestly than to live with virginity—or, what is more glorious, to die even for virginity.

“The allurements of this world are utterly deceptive. They come with temporal joy and depart with everlasting grief. They produce momentary laughter in order to inflict eternal weeping; they bestow fleeting flowers in order to bring more enduring, withered blossoms; they falsely promise the security of passing time in order to hand people over to the torments of the everlasting age.

“Therefore, dearest virgins, who until now have run with me in the contest of virginity, remain in the love of the Lord which you have begun. Endure the time of temporal weeping without weariness or horror, so that you may be able to receive the times of eternal joy with complete love.

“For I have commended you to the Holy Spirit, and I believe that he will present you all to me whole and undefiled. Therefore, do not henceforth seek my face in bodily form, but contemplate my deeds and actions through the spirit.”

Having said this, she kissed them all and consoled them as they wept with the greatest courage. After Basilla and Eugenia had said farewell to each other, they departed following prayer.

## CHAPTER XXIV

Behold, on that same day one of the maidservants went to Pompeius, Basilla’s betrothed, and said:

“Since we know that you have obtained our mistress Basilla from the emperor, know that six years and more have passed since you postponed receiving her, when you were still a tender child, so that you might take her later. But know that her cousin Helenus is a Christian, and that he has made her a Christian in such a way that she will not marry you at all. For Eugenia has pretended to offer her as a gift two eunuchs, Protus and Hyacinthus, whom she honors as masters and whose feet she kisses every day as though they were immortal gods, because they are the teachers of the magic arts practiced by the Christians.”

After hearing this, Pompeius immediately ran to Helenus, her cousin, who was also her foster father and guardian, and said to him:

“I have decided to celebrate my wedding within these three days. For this reason, arrange for me to see my bride, whom the invincible rulers, lords of the world, have commanded to become my wife.”

When Helenus heard this, he realized that the affair had been betrayed. He said to him:

“I exercised guardianship over her, because of her father’s relationship to me and because I myself raised her, until the years of her childhood had passed. But now that she has begun to govern herself, she wishes to be under her own authority. Therefore, if you desire to see her, that will depend upon her will, not upon my command.”

## CHAPTER XXV

When Pompeius heard this, he began to burn with even greater passion. He went to Basilla’s house and ordered the doorkeepers to announce him. Basilla gave them this message for him:

“Know that I have absolutely no reason to see you, hear you, or greet you.”

When he heard this, he was greatly disturbed. Using nearly all the support of the senators, he prostrated himself before the emperor and said:

“Come to the aid of your Romans, most sacred rulers, and remove from this city the new gods whom Eugenia brought with her when she came from Egypt.

“It has long been the case that those called Christians harm the commonwealth. They mock the sacred rites of our laws and despise our almighty gods as though they were empty images. They also pervert the laws of nature, separate marriage, and associate themselves with the favor of brides. They say that it is unjust for a bride to receive her bridegroom.

“What shall we do, most merciful emperors? Gods have been found who forbid human beings, and to whom these things will be visible, if those who can be commanded are not born. Where is the restoration of Roman strength? Where are the renewed battles of the Roman armies? For whose sake will your victorious right hands make the necks of enemies bow, if wives are no longer to be taken, if we lose our brides and remain silent?”

## CHAPTER XXVI

While he was pursuing these and similar arguments, and the entire senate was uttering them in mournful complaint, the Augustus Gallienus decreed [Note: **The Augustus Gallienus decreed.** Baronius, volume II, year of Christ 262, under Pope Dionysius II and Emperors Valerian and Gallienus VIII. “As regards the martyrs who suffered at Rome, and the fact that some are said to have undergone martyrdom under the Emperor Gallienus, this did not happen because, after Valerian’s persecution ceased, they were crowned in martyrdom. For, as we shall say, after Valerian, his father, had been captured by the enemy, Gallienus soon ordered the persecution to cease, issuing edicts on behalf of the Christians. Rather, because Gallienus alone ruled at Rome while Valerian was with the army in the East, many martyrs, whether at Rome or elsewhere, are said to have suffered under Gallienus; among them was the most illustrious woman, the virgin Eugenia.”]

that Basilla should either accept her bridegroom or perish by the sword, and that Eugenia should either sacrifice to the gods or die cruelly. He also granted permission for anyone who concealed a Christian in his house to be punished.

Basilla was summoned so that she might receive her bridegroom. She said that she had the King of kings as her bridegroom, who is Christ, the Son of God. When she had said this, she was pierced with a sword.

Protus and Hyacinthus were immediately seized and dragged to the temple. But as they prayed, the statue of Jupiter to which they were being led in order to sacrifice fell at their feet. It was shattered so completely that no trace of it could be seen where it had stood. The prefect of the city, Nicetius, attributing this not to divine power but to magical art, ordered them to be beheaded.

## CHAPTER XXVII

He also summoned Eugenia before him and began to demand from her an account of her magical arts. But she boldly opened her mouth and said:

“I promise you that our art is more powerful still. For our teacher has a Father without any mother, and a mother without a father. The Father begot him in such a way that he never knew a woman at all; the mother begot him in such a way that she knew no male at all.

“He himself has a virgin wife, who daily creates children for him and gives birth to innumerable sons for him. Every day she joins her flesh to his flesh. His kisses are continually united with her; in their love they remain together completely; and they subsist with such integrity that every virginity, every charity, and every purity proceeds from their marriage.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII

When Nicetius heard this, he was astonished. And, lest the emperor learn that he had listened to her willingly, he ordered her to be led to the temple of Diana. The executioner stood over her and said:

“Redeem your life and your patrimony, Eugenia, and sacrifice to the goddess Diana.”

Then the blessed Eugenia stretched out her hands and began to pray, saying:

“God, who knows the secrets of my heart; who has preserved my virginity pure in your love; who has deigned to unite me to your Son, my Lord Jesus Christ; who has caused your Holy Spirit to reign in me: stand by me now in my confession of your name, so that all who worship this idol and glory in their images may be put to shame.”

While she was praying, an earthquake occurred in that place. The foundations of the temple sank together with the idol itself, so that nothing remained except the altar that had stood before the temple door, where the blessed Eugenia was standing.

These events took place on the island of Lycaonia before all who were following Eugenia’s contest. A crowd of Roman people gathered, with various acclamations. Some called her innocent, others a sorceress. The events were reported to the prefect, and the prefect made them known to the emperor.

The emperor ordered her to be bound to a stone and thrown into the Tiber. But immediately the stone burst apart. The blessed Eugenia, sitting upon the surface of the river, was borne along in such a way that it became clear to all the Christians that the one who had been with Peter in the sea so that he would not sink was with Eugenia in the river so that she would not be drowned.

## CHAPTER XXIX

From there she was taken away and sent into the furnaces of the Severan baths. These were immediately extinguished, so that the heat of the baths cooled and all the fires of the wood became nothing. They were thrown into such confusion that they could no longer be used.

After this she was sent into a dark prison and ordered to receive no food for ten days or see any light at all. Yet such an abundance of splendor shone there every day that, when the blessed Eugenia emerged, she seemed to radiate a kind of light.

The Savior appeared to her, carrying in his hand bread of snowy whiteness and immense sweetness and grace, and said to her:

“Eugenia, receive food from my hand. I am your Savior, whom you have loved and love with the whole intention of your mind and spirit. On the same day I shall receive you into heaven on which I descended to earth.”

Having said this, he departed.

On the very day of the Lord’s Nativity, a gladiator was sent who struck her while she was in custody. Her body was taken up by Christian relatives and placed not far from the city, on the Latin Way, in her own estate, where she herself had buried the remains of many saints.

## CHAPTER XXX

Her mother Claudia, while weeping at her tomb, saw her while awake in the silence of midnight. Eugenia appeared dressed in a gold-woven *cyclas*, together with a great multitude of virgins, and said to her:

“Rejoice and be glad, because Christ has also brought me into the exultation of the saints, and my father into the number of the patriarchs. Behold, on the Lord’s Day he will also receive you into everlasting joy. Commend to your sons, my brothers, that they guard the sign of the cross, and let them become participants with us.”

As she spoke, a brightness appeared that the eye could not bear, and angels passing by sang a hymn to God in inexpressible voices. Only this could be understood: the name of Jesus Christ and of the Holy Spirit resounded in those praises.

Glory and honor to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, now and always, and forever and ever. Amen.

---

## MARCH 13. THE LIFE OF SAINT EUPHRASIA, VIRGIN, BY AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR

[Note: **362. Of Euphrasia.** The Roman *Martyrology*, 13 March: “In the Thebaid, the burial of Saint Euphrasia, virgin.” Usuard also mentions her on this day.

The Greek *Menologion*, 25 July: “On the same day, Saint Eupraxia, daughter of a certain senator named Antigonus, and Eupraxia under the Emperor Theodosius, to whom she was related by blood. After Antigonus died, Eupraxia’s mother commended her to Theodosius, who betrothed her to a man of senatorial rank. But she departed with her mother and went to the Thebaid of Egypt. She entered a monastery in which there were one hundred and four virgins, leading a life equal to that of angels. Emulating their virtue, she did not permit herself to leave the monastery; she was then sixteen years old.

“Her mother, however, departing from there and visiting the monasteries of the East, distributed many possessions and benefactions to those in need. Afterward, when she fell ill, she returned to the dwelling where she had left her daughter. Having entrusted all her possessions to her daughter, she rested in the Lord.

“Eupraxia, after distributing all her goods to the poor and to the churches of God, embraced the discipline of the monastic life with distinction. She progressed so far in virtue and subjected the needs of the body so completely that she stood motionless for forty-five days, with her hands raised toward heaven.

“Thus, because of her outstanding virtue, the blessed Eupraxia received the grace of miracles, by which she freed many people from various illnesses. Having herself attained a blessed end, she was translated to the Lord.”

All editions contain the deeds of Euphrasia, except the first edition of the *Lives of the Fathers*. From these editions and from a manuscript codex, Surius transcribed them in volume II, altering the style. I have retained the old style, in accordance with the wish of many learned men who are still living.

John of Damascus, considering her Acts legitimately written, draws authority from them in his third discourse on images, where he cites the following passage in Greek:

> Λὲγει ἡ διάκονος τῷ κορασίῳ, Ὕπαγε κυρία μου εἰς τὸν οἶκόν σου, ὅτι οὐ δύνασαι ὧδε παραμεῖναι· οὐδὲ γὰρ δύναταί τις ὧδε παραμεῖναι, ἐὰν μὴ συντάξηται τῷ Χριστῷ. Λέγει αὐτῇ τὸ κοράσιον, Ποῦ ἐστιν ὁ Χριστός; Ἡ διάκονος ἐπέδειξεν αὐτῇ τὸν δεσποτικὸν χαρακτῆρα, καὶ στραφεῖσα λέγει τῇ διακώνῳ, Ἀληθῶς κᾀγὼ τῷ Χριστῷ συντάσσομαι, καὶ οὐκέτι ἀπέρχομαι μετὰ τῆς κυρίας μου· καὶ πάλιν ἀναστᾶσα ἡ Εὐπραξία, καὶ λαβοῦσα τὴν θνγατέρα ἑαυτῆς, παρέστησεν εἰς τὸν δεσποτικὸν χαρακτῆρα· καὶ ἐκτείνασα τὰς χεῖρας αὐτῆς εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν ἐβόησε μετὰ κλαυθμοῦ, Κύριε Ἰησοῦ Χριστὲ, σοὶ μελήσει περὶ τοῦ παιδίου, ὅτι σὲ ἐπόθησεν, καὶ σοὶ παρέθετο ἑαυτήν.

> “The deaconess said to the girl: ‘Go, my lady, to your home, because you cannot remain here; indeed, no one can remain here unless she joins herself to Christ.’ The girl said to her: ‘Where is Christ?’ The deaconess showed her the image of the Lord. Turning to the deaconess, the girl said: ‘Truly I too am joining myself to Christ, and I shall no longer depart with my mistress.’ Then Eupraxia rose again, took her daughter, and brought her before the Lord’s image. Raising her hands to heaven, she cried out with tears: ‘Lord Jesus Christ, take care of the girl, since she has desired you and has dedicated herself to you.’”

Damascus extracted this passage in abbreviated form from the Greek Acts of Eupraxia, which are narrated more fully in chapters 8 and 9 of this Latin Life.

She flourished in the time of the Emperor Theodosius, as is clear from the Life itself and from the *Menologion*. She is distinct from Euphrasia of Nicomedia, who cleverly eluded the shamelessness of a lustful young man; Nicephorus discusses her in book 7, chapter 13. The *Menaea* place Euphrasia of Nicomedia, a martyr under the Emperor Maximian, on 19 January.]

## CHAPTER ONE

In the days of Theodosius, the most pious emperor, there was a certain man who was a senator in the imperial city, named Antigonus. He was related to the emperor by birth and association, wise both in speech and in action, always especially inclined to recommend what was good, and piously administering the affairs of Lycia according to Roman law.

He was also a compassionate man, providing everyone with what they needed. The ruler loved him not only as a relative and senator, but also as a Christian, a pious man, and one who always offered useful counsel.

He was exceedingly wealthy, so much so that the imperial city had no other man comparable to him in wealth, speech, or action. He took a wife from his own family, descended from the same imperial bloodline. Her name was Euphraxia. She was a religious woman, greatly fearing the Lord, devoted to the Church, and offering prayers to God with tears.

She made many people capable of service in the work of God and offered many gifts in churches and sanctuaries. [Note: **Sanctuaries.** In my opinion, he uses this word to translate *semneia* (σεμνεῖα), meaning monasteries. Thus in chapter 5: “She too, while devoted there in the sanctuaries.”]

The emperor and the empress loved her greatly, especially because she was of their family, as well as well-mannered, honorable, and very religious. A daughter was born to them, and they named her Euphraxia after her mother.

## Chapter II

When they had this daughter, one day Antigonus said to Euphraxia: “You know, my sister Euphraxia, that this life is nothing, riches are nothing, and the vanity of this temporal age is nothing. For within eighty years a person’s allotted time is completed in ruin, whereas riches stored up in heaven remain for endless ages for those who fear God. Yet we deprive ourselves of those riches, bound by worldly thoughts; placed in the deceitfulness of temporal wealth, we consume our days in vain, acquiring nothing profitable for our souls.”

Hearing this, Euphraxia said to her husband Antigonus: “And what do you order me, my lord, that we should do?” Antigonus replied: “We have acquired one daughter through God, and she is enough for us. Let us by no means continue to submit ourselves to the unhappiness and misery of the world.”

Hearing this, Euphraxia rose, stretched out her hands toward heaven, and, groaning, said to her husband Antigonus: “Blessed be God, who has made you worthy of his fear and has brought you to knowledge of the truth. Truly, my lord, I have often entreated God to illumine your heart and make your mind perceive this matter clearly, but I did not dare to disclose it to you. Since you yourself have made the beginning, command me to speak.”

Antigonus said to her: “Say what you wish, my sister.”

She replied: “You know, my lord, that many generations ago the Apostle testified and said: ‘The time is short. It remains that those who have wives should live as though they had none’ (1 Cor. 7). For the desire for this age is passing away. Of what use will this money and such abundance of possessions be? None of these things can descend with us into hell. Therefore, with your good resolve, hasten to give much to the poor, lest the plan you have considered be found fruitless.”

Hearing this, Antigonus glorified God.

## Chapter III

When Antigonus had consequently embraced an excellent way of life and distributed much to the poor, he lived only one year after renouncing conjugal relations with his wife and ordering his life piously. When the year was completed, he died and was buried in peace.

Then the emperor and the Augusta alike mourned him, as a man descended from their family, just and religious. They also felt compassion for Euphraxia, not only as their own kinswoman but also because she was still young. For she had lived with her husband for two years and three months; during one of those years, by mutual agreement, they abstained from one another and lived as brother and sister.

After Antigonus had been buried, Euphraxia received much consolation from the emperor and the Augusta. Taking her own daughter, she placed her in the hands of the emperor and the Augusta; then she fell at their feet and said with cries and great lamentation: “Into the hands of God and into yours I now commend this orphan. Therefore, remembering Antigonus, who was yours, receive her and protect her; be a father and mother to her in his place.” Many of those who heard her uttered streams of tears and cries, so that even the rulers mourned.

## Chapter IV

After a short time, when the mourning for Antigonus had somewhat subsided, the emperor persuaded her to give her daughter Euphraxia in marriage to a very wealthy senator. Accordingly, Euphraxia received the betrothal pledge. After the pledge had been received, they awaited the girl’s coming of age. For she was exceedingly young—about five years old—when she received the pledge.

After some time, the senator himself considered having Antigonus’s wife joined to him in marriage. Through petitions or through married noblewomen, he persuaded the Augusta to send them without the emperor’s knowledge and to announce the proposal of marriage to Euphraxia.

When she heard this, she wept bitterly and said to the women who had been sent: “Woe to you in the age to come, who persuade me to such things and join together against a woman who is hastening to live according to God. Depart from me, for you have now undertaken an alien gathering against me.”

They departed in disgrace and reported to the Augusta what had happened. When the emperor learned what had been done, he severely rebuked the Augusta. Indignant with her, he said:

“Truly, Augusta, you have done something alien to this way of life. Are these the deeds of a Christian Augusta? Is this how you promised God that you would rule piously? Is this how you remember Antigonus, who always remained useful to us? You have done something foreign to our imperial authority: you are compelling a woman who is still of tender age, who lived with her husband scarcely one year, and who soon afterward, by mutual agreement, separated from him for the sake of the heavenly kingdom—you are compelling her to return again to the world. Did you not fear God when you wished to commit this injustice? Who will satisfy the people, since this was not done through me? You have done something indecent and incongruous, something that ought not to have been done without hearing my imperial command, especially because of my most sincere friend, Antigonus.”

## Chapter V

Hearing this, the Augusta changed her face in extreme shame and remained almost like a stone, without speaking, for about two hours. Great sadness then arose between the emperor and the Augusta because of Euphraxia, the wife of Antigonus.

When Euphraxia realized that great sadness had arisen between the emperor and the Augusta on her account, she became utterly downcast and mournful even unto death, and wished to leave the city. Weeping bitterly, she then said to her daughter Euphraxia:

“My daughter, we have abundant and great property in Egypt. Come, let us go there and visit your father’s possessions; everything I have is yours, my daughter.”

So Euphraxia departed with her daughter Euphraxia from the imperial city without the emperor’s knowledge and came to Egypt. There she also stayed, frequently visiting her estates. She proceeded into the interior of the Thebaid with her stewards and servants, who managed her affairs. There too she devoted herself to the sanctuaries and offered many gifts there, distributing much money among monasteries of men and women.

## Chapter VI

There was a women’s monastery in one city, containing one hundred and thirty *architria*.

[Note: *Architria.* Does he mean cells? In the *Life of Saint Antony*, chapter 53, one finds *archisterium*, referring to the inner and primary cell of Antony.]

People proclaimed great and wondrous virtues concerning them. In that monastery no one tasted wine; none of them ate fruit, grapes, figs, or any such good things that grow from the abundance of the earth. Some of them, having renounced the world, would not even eat oil. Some prolonged their fast from one evening until the next evening; others ate after two days, and others after three.

None of them washed her feet. Some, when they heard anyone speak of a bath, laughed and judged that they were hearing something shameful and greatly abominable; they would not even allow their ears to hear such a thing.

Each of them had a bed on the ground: a small haircloth, one cubit wide and three cubits long, on which she rested a little. Their garments too were of haircloth down to the bottom, binding the extremities of their feet. Each labored as much as she could.

Whenever one of them happened to fall ill, no fomentation or medical assistance was given to her. If any became sick, she received it as a very great blessing from God and endured the illness until divine medicine came to her aid.

None of them went out through the doors. There was a mature doorkeeper through whom all responses were given. Many healings also took place there.

## Chapter VII

Euphraxia, who admired these holy women because of their wondrous way of life, often went to the monastery and offered incense and candles there.
