One day she asked the abbess and the senior women of the monastery, saying to them: “I wish to offer a small gift, without causing you fear: twenty or thirty pounds of gold in revenue, so that you may pray for this servant of yours and for her father, Antigonus.”

The abbess replied: “My lady, your handmaidens have no need of revenues, nor do they desire money. For this reason they left everything and despise all things in this age, so that they may deserve to enjoy eternal goods. They wish to possess nothing, lest they be deprived of the heavenly kingdom. But so that I do not sadden you or send you away without fruit, bring a little oil for the lamps and incense into the oratory; this will serve us as a reward of righteousness.”

After offering these things, Euphraxia asked the abbess that all the sisters pray for Antigonus and for his daughter Euphraxia.

## Chapter VIII

One day the abbess, testing the child Euphraxia, said to her: “My lady Euphraxia, do you love our monastery and all the sisters?”

She replied: “Yes, lady, I love you.”

The abbess again said jokingly: “If you love us, remain with us in our habit.”

The little girl said to her: “Truly, if my mother would not be saddened, I would never again leave this place.”

The abbess said to her: “Between us and the bridegroom, whom do you love more?”

The girl said: “I do not know him, nor does he know me; but I know you, and I love you. Tell me: whom do you love, me or him?”

They replied: “We love you, and our Christ.”

The girl answered: “I too love you and your Christ.”

Her mother Euphraxia was sitting there, and there was no end to the streams of her tears. The abbess gladly listened to the girl’s words, because although she was still a child in age, she spoke in this way. She had not yet completed seven years when she spoke such words with the abbess.

Then her mother groaned and wept bitterly, saying to her daughter: “My daughter, come, let us go home, because it is already evening.”

The girl said to her: “I am staying here with the lady abbess.”

The abbess said to the girl: “Go, my lady, to your home; you cannot remain here. No one can remain here unless she has devoted herself to Christ.”

The girl replied: “Where is Christ?”

The abbess gladly showed her the image of the Lord. Euphraxia went and kissed the image of the Lord. Then, turning back, she said to the abbess: “Truly, I too devote myself to my Christ, and I will not go any farther with my lady mother.”

The abbess said to her: “Daughter, you have nowhere to stay here, and you cannot remain here.”

The girl said: “Where you remain, I too will remain.”

When it was already evening and her mother and the abbess had urged her repeatedly to leave, they could not remove her from the monastery. For many days her mother and the abbess repeatedly coaxed her, but they could not persuade her to leave the monastery.

Finally, the abbess said to the girl: “Daughter, if you wish to remain here, you must learn letters and the Psalter, and you must continue fasting until evening, like all the sisters.”

The girl said to her: “I will learn both fasting and everything else; only let me remain here.”

The abbess then said to her mother: “My lady, let this girl remain here. I see that the grace of God has shone upon her. The righteousness of her father, your honorable character, and the prayers of both of you are evidently preparing eternal life for her.”

## Chapter IX

Euphraxia rose, took her daughter, and brought her before the image of the Lord. Stretching out her hands toward heaven, she cried out with great shouting and weeping:

“Lord Jesus Christ, care for this little girl, because she has desired you and commended herself to you.”

Then she turned and said to her daughter: “Euphraxia, my daughter, may the God who established the immovable mountains also strengthen you in his fear.”

After saying this, she placed her in the hands of the abbess. Weeping and beating her breast, she left the monastery, while the entire community wept with her.

## Chapter X

The next day the abbess took Euphraxia into the sacristy. After praying over her, she clothed her in the monastic garment. Stretching out her hands toward heaven, she entreated God for her, saying:

“King of the ages, who have begun a good work in her, perfect it in peace. Grant that this little girl may walk according to your name and always find confidence in your presence.”

Then Euphraxia, her mother, also prayed and said: “My daughter, do you love being clothed in this habit?”

Euphraxia replied: “Indeed I do, my mother, because, as I have learned from the abbess and the sisters have said, the Lord Jesus Christ offers this habit as a pledge to those who love him.”

Her mother said to her: “May the one to whom you are betrothed make you worthy of his bridal chamber.”

Saying this, and praying for her daughter, she bade farewell to the abbess and the sisters and kissed her daughter. Then she went out and, according to her custom, went around distributing to the poor whatever they needed.

## Chapter XI

Everywhere Euphraxia’s excellent way of life was proclaimed, as was the extent of what she contributed to monasteries and venerable places, so that the emperor heard of it, and the entire senate loved her greatly and glorified God.

They heard that she neither tasted fish nor drank wine. Despite the great gifts she bestowed on everyone and the fame she received, she fasted from evening until evening, sometimes taking legumes and sometimes vegetables.

## Chapter XII

After a few days, the abbess summoned the girl’s mother and said to her privately: “Lady, I wish to tell you something; do not be troubled.”

She replied: “My lady, tell me what you command.”

The abbess said: “I saw your husband Antigonus in a dream, established in great glory. He asked the Lord Jesus Christ that you might depart from your body, thereafter be with him, and enjoy that glory which Antigonus, your husband, merited.”

Hearing this, the matron returned to her house as a religious woman. She was not troubled; rather, she rejoiced with great joy. She prayed that she might depart from human life and thereafter be with Christ.

Then she summoned her daughter and said to her: “My daughter, as my lady the abbess has told me, Christ has called me, and the days of my death have drawn near. Behold, I have given all my property and your father’s property into your hands. Distribute it piously, so that you may possess a heavenly inheritance.”

Hearing this from her mother, Euphraxia began to groan and weep, saying: “Woe is me, for I am a stranger and an orphan.”

Her mother said to her: “Daughter, you have Christ as father and bridegroom; therefore you are neither a stranger nor an orphan. You also have the lady abbess in the place of a mother. See, my daughter: hasten to fulfill what you promised. Fear God, and honor all the sisters, serving them with complete humility.

“Never think in your heart, ‘I am of royal blood,’ nor say, ‘They ought to serve me.’ Be poor on earth, so that you may become rich in heaven. Behold, you have everything under your authority. Bring the possessions and money into the monastery for your father and for me, so that we may find mercy with God and be freed from eternal punishment.”

Having given these commands to her daughter, she died on the third day, and they buried her in the monastery in a tomb.

## Chapter XIII

When the emperor heard that Euphraxia, the wife of Antigonus, had died, he summoned the senator to whom her daughter had been betrothed and informed him, saying: “The girl has entered the monastery.”

The man asked the emperor to write to the girl through couriers and command her to come to the city and celebrate the marriage.

When Euphraxia received the emperor’s letter, she wrote another letter in her own hand, as follows:

“Lord emperor, are you advising your servant to reject Christ and be joined to a corruptible man destined to be consumed by worms, who exists today and is gone tomorrow? Far be it from your servant to commit such an injustice.

“Therefore, lord emperor, do not allow that man to trouble you any further. I have consented to Christ, and it is impossible for me to deny him. But I beseech your authority to remember my parents. Therefore take all the property, distribute it among the poor and orphans alike, and give everything to the churches.

“For I know that you will remember my parents, especially my father. I have heard that he was never separated from you in the palace. Therefore, remembering them, dispose of this property well.

“Free all those placed under the yoke of slavery and grant them what is lawful. Command my father’s agents to remit every debt that the farmers have rendered from the day of my father until this day, so that, freed from concern for my earthly affairs, I may be able to serve Christ without any hindrance, since I have committed my soul to him.

“Pray for your servant, you and the Augusta, that she may be worthy to serve Christ as he deigns to allow his servant.”

Then she sealed the letter and gave it to the courier. When he returned, he presented the letter to the emperor to read again. He opened it and read it privately with the Augusta, and both shed many tears, praying fervently for Euphraxia.

When morning came, the emperor summoned the entire senate, together with the father of Euphraxia’s betrothed, and ordered the letter to be read aloud. When they heard the letter, all were filled with tears and said, as though with one voice:

“Truly, lord emperor, this girl is the daughter of Antigonus and Euphraxia, your kinspeople, and she is of their blood. Truly, the daughter of religious parents is religious; the holy branch comes from a holy root.”

All then glorified God in common agreement and prayed together for the girl. The senator was never again seen to be importunate.

## Chapter XIV

The emperor therefore arranged everything piously and distributed the girl’s property properly. He himself also died and was buried in peace with his fathers.

Euphraxia was honored and lived according to God, abstaining beyond measure. She was twelve years old and trained herself vigorously for the contests.

At first she ate from evening until evening, then after two days, and afterward after three days. No one other than she cleaned the refectory and made the sisters’ beds. She herself carried water to the kitchen.

This was the custom in the monastery: if it happened that a sister was tempted by the devil in sleep, she immediately disclosed it to the abbess. The abbess would ask God with tears that the devil depart from her, and would command her to carry stones, place ashes beneath the covering and scatter them over the haircloth, and sleep in this manner until the tenth day.

One day Euphraxia herself was tempted by the devil and placed ashes on her bed. When the abbess saw the ashes beneath Euphraxia’s bed, she laughed and said to one of the senior sisters: “Truly, this girl has begun to be tempted.”

Then the abbess prayed, saying: “God, who created her according to your will, strengthen her in your fear.”

Calling her, the abbess said to her: “Why did you not tell me of the demonic temptation?”

She fell at the abbess’s feet and said: “Forgive me, my lady, because I was ashamed to tell you about this matter.”

The abbess said to her: “My daughter, behold, you have begun to fight. Act courageously, so that you may conquer and be crowned.”

## Chapter XV

After a few days she was tempted again and told a certain sister named Julia, who loved Euphraxia greatly and also trained her in the contests.

Julia said to her: “My lady Euphraxia, do not conceal this from the abbess; report it so that she may pray for you. We are all tempted by the devil, but let us hope in the name of Christ, because we overcome him. Therefore, my sister, do not delay; tell the abbess about the matter, and do not be ashamed.”

Hearing this, Euphraxia thanked Julia and said to her: “May God help you, sister, because you have strengthened me and comforted my soul. Truly, I will go in and tell my lady abbess about the matter.”

Julia said: “Do so, that she may pray for you and increase your abstinence.”

She went in and reported the matter to the abbess. The abbess said to her: “Do not fear, daughter, the entire war of the devil by which he strives against us. Fight courageously, therefore, with steadfast mind, and he will not prevail against you. You will be greatly tempted by him; but fight so that you may conquer, receive victory and triumph from your bridegroom Christ, and increase your abstinence as much as you can. For whoever fights with exceptional zeal will receive exceptional gifts.”

After some time, the abbess asked her: “After how many days did you eat, daughter?”

The girl said: “After three days, my lady.”

The abbess said to her: “Add one more day.”

She received her command with great joy and departed.

## Chapter XVI

When she had reached the age of twenty, she grew stronger in body and prevailed. She was exceedingly beautiful, like a true noblewoman, and born of royal blood.

When she was again tempted, she told the abbess about it. The abbess said to her: “Do not fear, daughter; God is with you.”

There was a pile of stones in the monastery courtyard. Wishing to test Euphraxia and provoke her obedience to the Mother, the abbess said to her: “Come, my daughter, move these stones from here and place them beside the kiln.”

Euphraxia immediately approached to move the stones. Among them were large stones that two sisters could scarcely shift. She picked them up onto her shoulders, needing no assistance. She was young and very strong, and she did not say to the abbess, “Let another sister help me.” Nor did she say, “The stones are large; I cannot manage them.” Nor did she say, “I am fasting and growing weak, and this task is too great.” Rather, she fulfilled the command confidently through obedience.

## Chapter XVII

The next day the abbess said to her: “It is not right for these stones to be placed beside the furnace; carry them back to their proper place.”

Again she confidently fulfilled the command of her abbess. The abbess ordered her to do this work for twenty days, in order to test her patience.

All the sisters saw what was happening and admired the girl’s obedience. Some other sisters mocked her; others called out: “Act courageously, Euphraxia!”

Thirty days were completed. Then, after the celebration of the divine service, one day as Euphraxia was going to carry the stones, the abbess said to her: “Leave this task, daughter. Take flour, knead it, and bake bread in the furnace, so that you may be found serving the sisters by evening.”

She fulfilled the command with great joy and gladness.

## Chapter XVIII

Again, when the devil found her at leisure, he sent such a temptation upon her: it seemed that the senator to whom she had been betrothed was arriving with a large force, taking her away from the monastery and departing with her.

While she lay on her pallet, she cried out violently. The abbess and the other sisters awoke and heard her cries of distress. Awakening her, they said: “What is this anxiety, daughter?”

She immediately recounted the dream. The abbess roused the sisters and stood in prayer.

After completing the service until the third hour, Euphraxia held the Codex and stood reading while the others sat. Afterward she stood serving until the third hour.

When the third hour was completed, Euphraxia immediately prepared what the sisters needed: she cleaned the refectory, made the beds, filled vessels with water, and carried it to the kitchen; she broke wood and cooked legumes, kneaded flour with leaven, and baked bread in the furnace.

While doing all these things, she was absent neither from the nocturnal psalmody nor from the third, sixth, or ninth hours, nor from evening prayer. After completing the evening prayers, she performed the service herself, carrying things in. Julia also labored with her, for she loved Euphraxia very much.

## Chapter XIX

Again the devil vehemently tempted her in sleep and subjected her to a great struggle. She immediately confessed the struggle of her distress to the abbess.

The abbess prayed for her and said: “My daughter Euphraxia, this is the time of combat. Take care that the devil does not soften your mind and that you do not lose your labor. Fight with him for a little while longer; when he has been overcome by you, he will flee again.”

Julia likewise said to her: “My lady and sister, if we do not resist and overcome him now, what kind of battle will we wage with him in old age?”

Euphraxia replied: “As the Lord lives, sister Julia, if the abbess commands me, I will not taste bread for an entire week until, with the Lord’s help, I conquer him.”

Julia said to her: “If you can accomplish this on earth, you will be blessed in heaven. In this monastery no one has been able to remain without food for an entire week except our lady abbess.”

Euphraxia then went in and reported the devil’s temptation in sleep to the abbess, asking her to command that she remain without food for the entire week.

The abbess said to her: “Do whatever seems easy to you, my daughter. May God, who created you, strengthen you and grant you victory against the devil.”

Euphraxia therefore began to fast for the entire week. She abandoned neither the office of psalmody nor the service of the sisters, so that all admired her endurance, as well as her beauty and the youth of her age.

Some of their community said: “For a year now we have been watching Euphraxia, and we have not seen her sit, either by day or by night, except when she rested in her place at night. She never sat, not even when she ate bread.”

All the sisters therefore loved Euphraxia, because she exercised herself in such humility and served the sisters diligently, although she was especially descended from imperial blood. For this reason they prayed for her with great devotion, asking the Lord that she might be saved.

## Chapter XX

There was one among them named Germana, who was said to have been born of a slave woman. Out of envy toward Euphraxia, she secretly rose against her in the kitchen and said to her:

“Tell me, Euphraxia: behold, you eat once a week according to the abbess’s rule, while we cannot fulfill this. If we are compelled by the abbess, what shall we do?”

Euphraxia replied: “My lady, our lady abbess said that each one should strive as she is able. She did not impose this yoke on me without necessity.”

Germana said to her: “Deceiver, full of every kind of cunning! Who does not know that you are doing this by a trick, so that after the abbess rests you may yourself succeed her? I believe in Christ that she will never deem you worthy to come to the place of abbess.”

Hearing this, Euphraxia fell at her feet and said to her: “Forgive me, my lady, and pray for me.”

When the abbess learned what had happened, she summoned Germana before everyone and said to her:

“Wicked slave woman, alien to God, what harm did Euphraxia do to you, that you hastened to obstruct her zeal? You are excluded from the council of the sisters; you are unworthy of service and a stranger to the fellowship of the sisters.”

Euphraxia pleaded earnestly that she grant Germana forgiveness, but she did not move the abbess until thirty days had been completed.

On the thirtieth day, seeing that she gained nothing by pleading, Euphraxia took Julia and the senior women of the monastery with her and asked them to entreat the abbess to be reconciled with Germana.

When this had been done, the abbess summoned Germana before everyone and said to her:

“Did you not determine in your heart to cut short this girl’s zeal? Did you not consider that although she was a noblewoman and of imperial birth, she humbled herself and served you for God’s sake?”

When everyone pleaded for Germana, the abbess was appeased.

## Chapter XXI

Then the devil did not cease bringing struggles against Euphraxia. He was exceedingly enraged against her and wished to bring her quickly to an end.

One day, when she had gone down to the well to draw water, the devil seized her together with the pitcher and threw her down into the well, so that Euphraxia became nauseated and her head reached the bottom.

When she had risen from the water and was holding the bucket’s rope, she cried from the well: “Christ, help me!”

When she uttered this cry, it became known that Euphraxia had fallen into the well. The sisters and the abbess ran together and pulled her out.

She rose, made the sign of the cross over herself, smiled slightly, and said: “As my Christ lives, you do not conquer me, devil, nor do I yield to you. Until now I carried one pitcher of water to the kitchen; from today onward I will carry two pitchers of water.”

And she did so.

## Chapter XXII

When the devil saw that he had been unable to kill her in the well, he attacked her again on another occasion, when she had gone down to cut wood.

After she had cut a little, the devil stood watching her. As she raised the axe to cut a piece of wood, the devil bound her hands and dragged the axe down to her heel, and it reached as far as her shin.

When she saw the exceedingly cruel wound and the blood flowing profusely, she threw down the axe, became distressed, and fell to the ground.

Julia ran and announced to the sisters with a cry that Euphraxia had taken up the axe and had died from the axe-blow. When a commotion and shouting arose among all of them, a few sisters surrounded her together and wept.

Then the abbess approached, poured water on her face, and, making the sign of the cross over her and embracing her, said: “My daughter Euphraxia, why are you distressed? Recover yourself and speak to the sisters.”

[Note: [Col. 0643A] “She poured water upon her face.” When cold water was poured over them, those who had fainted came to themselves. Hence the proverb, “to sprinkle water,” that is, to give courage. Shortly afterward in the *Life of Euphrosyne*, ch. 15: “Water was thrown into that person's face.”]

She looked up, and the abbess said: “Lord Jesus Christ, heal your servant, for she suffers much on your account.”

After binding her foot with a piece of haircloth, the abbess raised her and, giving her her hand, led her toward the monastery.

Euphraxia looked back at the wood that had been thrown down and said to the sisters: “As my Lord lives, unless I gather the wood and complete my week, I will not go up.”

[Note: “And complete my week.” Hence *hebdomadarii* or *septimanarii* occur among various writers. See the *Onomasticon*.]

Julia said to her: “Do not, my lady sister; you are not able. Leave it; I will gather it. You go up and rest because of the pain.”

But she did not agree. Filling her hands with wood, she went up.

The devil nevertheless did not spare her. For when she had climbed the higher steps of the ladder, she stepped on the hem of her tunic, fell upon the wood she was carrying, and the wood was driven toward her face, so that the sisters thought that it had pierced her eye.

Then Julia cried out to her: “My lady, I told you that you could not rest, but you did not listen to me.”

Euphraxia said to her: “Carefully remove the wood from me; my eye is unharmed.”

Julia pulled the wood away from her, and a profuse flow of blood followed.

The abbess brought oil, prayed, and laid her hand upon her. Then she said to her again: “Go to your bed and rest; I will assign your service to the sisters.”

Euphraxia said: “As my Lord lives, I will not rest until I have completed my duty.”

The sisters repeatedly urged her to rest because of the wounds she had suffered, but she refused. Though wounded, with blood flowing from both injuries, she stood performing the service for the sisters. She was absent neither from the work of God nor from any other service.

## Chapter XXIII

Again, on another occasion, when she was climbing with Julia to the third upper terrace,

[Note: “The third upper terrace.” Thus there were several upper terraces or storeys in one house. Elsewhere *solarium*, that is, the highest storey exposed to the sun, was only one.]

the devil seized her and hurled her downward.

When Julia cried out, the sisters ran together, believing that they would find Euphraxia dead. But she rose and came toward them. They received her and brought her to the abbess, who asked whether she had been injured in any way.

Euphraxia replied: “As the Lord lives, my lady, I do not know either how I fell or how I rose.”

When the abbess heard that she had fallen from such a height and suffered no injury, she glorified God, saying: “Go, daughter, to your work, and the Lord will be with you.”

## Chapter XXIV

Again the enemy wished to kill her and attacked her in this way.

Euphraxia was holding a boiling pot in which vegetables were being cooked, intending to pour the vegetable broth into a vessel. The devil knocked her feet away; she fell backward and poured the contents of the pot over her face.

When all the sisters were terrified at what had happened, Euphraxia sprang up, smiled slightly, and said to them: “Why are you troubled?”

When the abbess saw that she had not been injured, she looked into the pot and saw that what remained was still boiling.

Euphraxia turned and said: “Truly, my lady, it came upon my face like cold water.”

The abbess marveled, looked at her, and said: “Daughter, may God protect you and grant you to endure without ceasing in his fear.”

The abbess entered the oratory, summoned the senior women, and said to them:

[Note: “Senior women.” Soon afterward, in chapters 27 and 30, *seniores sorores*, “senior sisters.” The term *seniores* often occurs among both men and women in these Lives.]

“You know that Euphraxia has obtained the grace of God. You have seen that neither when thrown down was she saddened, nor was she burned by the excessive heat.”

They replied: “Truly Euphraxia is a servant of God, and the Lord cares for her; for in such temptations she has been delivered by the Lord.”

## Chapter XXV

And so the whole city and province had the custom of bringing infants who were ill to that monastery, to the handmaids of God who performed miracles. The abbess received them, and they entered the oratory and entreated the Lord for them; immediately the infants were healed of every ailment, and their mothers received them back healthy, departing and glorifying God.

There was also in the monastery a woman possessed by a demon, bound there from infancy so that she might be saved. She had an unclean demonic spirit; her hands were tied, she foamed at the mouth, gnashed her teeth, and cried out so loudly that all who heard her fell into fear. Although the abbess and the senior sisters had frequently prayed for her recovery, they achieved nothing. Consequently, they were unable even to approach her to offer her food.

A small vessel was fastened to a rope. They placed vegetables or bread in the vessel, hoisted it, and thus extended it to her from a distance, so that she could eat. Often she would throw the vessel away and, with a stick, strike at the face of the person offering her food.

## Chapter XXVI

One day the doorkeeper came in and said to the abbess: “My lady, a woman has brought a little child and is weeping outside, standing at the door. The child is about eight years old, paralyzed, deaf, and mute.”

The abbess, perceiving through revelation of the Spirit that Euphraxia had received grace from the Lord against demons, said to the doorkeeper: “Call Euphraxia to me.”

When she came before the abbess, the abbess said to her: “Go, take the child from his mother and bring him here.”

She went out and, seeing the little child paralyzed and trembling, took pity on him. Groaning sorrowfully, she made the sign of the cross over the child and said to him: “May the one who created you heal you, my son.”

Taking him, she proceeded toward the abbess. As Euphraxia carried him, the child was healed and cried out to his mother. When Euphraxia saw that the child had begun to speak, she was terrified and threw him to the ground. But the child immediately got up and ran to the door, looking for his mother.

The doorkeeper ran and reported to the abbess what had happened. When she had summoned the child’s mother, she said to her: “Tell me, sister—have you come to test us?”

The child’s mother replied: “By our Lord Jesus Christ, my lady, this child has neither walked nor spoken until this present hour. But as soon as this sister received him, he immediately spoke. When she threw him to the ground, she stood there astonished; but the child rose and came to me, your handmaid.”

The abbess said to her: “Behold, then, you have him sound. Take him and go in peace.”

Taking her son, she departed, glorifying God.

## Chapter XXVII

Again the abbess said to the senior sisters: “What do you think of Euphraxia?”

They answered her: “She is truly a handmaid of God.”

She called her and said to her: “My daughter Euphraxia, I want you to offer food with your own hands to this possessed woman [Note: [Col. 0644A] ‘Patienti’: that is, the possessed woman; this is clear from Chapter 25.] who is in the monastery, if you do not fear her.”

Euphraxia replied: “I do not fear anything you command me, my lady.”

So Euphraxia took a small vessel, put vegetables and a piece of bread into it, and offered it to her. But the woman suddenly gnashed her teeth and roared loudly, then rushed at her. Seizing the vessel, she wanted to smash it.

Euphraxia, however, seized her hand and said: “As the Lord God lives, if I put you on the ground, I shall take the abbess’s stick and beat you with it so that you will never dare do this again.”

When the woman saw that Euphraxia had prevailed over her, she became quiet. After she had ceased, Euphraxia began to soothe her, saying: “Sit down, sister; eat and drink, and do not be upset.”

The woman sat down, ate, drank, and rested. From that hour onward, food was given to her together with the stick. All the sisters, seeing what Euphraxia had done, prayed to the Lord for her.

Whenever the woman began to stir and grow angry, the sisters would say to her: “Be quiet, sister, and do not behave wickedly; for if Lady Euphraxia comes, she will beat you.” At once she would become quiet.

## Chapter XXVIII

Again Germana was gnawed by envy, and her heart burned. She said to the sisters: “If Euphraxia had not been here, would no one else have been found to offer her food? I will take the food and serve her myself.”

So she took the woman’s food, approached her, and said: “Take your food, sister, and eat.”

The woman immediately sprang upon her, tore her clothing, beat her, and threw her to the ground. Then she fell upon her and began to eat her flesh.

When there was an outcry and no one dared approach her, Julia ran to the kitchen and said to Euphraxia: “Hurry, lady, for Germana has been torn apart by the possessed woman.”

Euphraxia ran up, seized the woman’s hands and throat, and rescued the bloody and mangled Germana from her.

Euphraxia said to the woman: “Have you done well to crush your sister in this way?”

The woman stood there foaming and gnashing her teeth.

Euphraxia said to her: “From this hour, if you behave wickedly toward the sisters, I will not yield to you or pity you. I shall take the stick of my lady the abbess and beat you with it without mercy.”

The woman sat down and immediately ceased.

## Chapter XXIX

When morning came, after the sacred office had been completed and they had gone out from the oratory, Euphraxia visited the possessed woman. She found that the woman had thrown her torn garment onto the ground, was sitting on it, gathering excrement and eating it.

When Euphraxia saw this, she wept and reported to the abbess what had happened. The sisters gathered and found the woman naked, gathering phlegm and eating it.

The abbess ordered that another tunic be given to her so that she might be clothed. Euphraxia took the tunic, a dish with vegetables, and a piece of bread, offered them to her, and said: “Take these, sister, clothe yourself, and taste some food. Why do you disgrace yourself in this way?”

The woman took them, ate, and drank. Euphraxia clothed her and ministered to her.

Euphraxia did not cease weeping for her until evening, mourning over her. When evening came, she immediately entreated the Lord with tears that the possessed woman might be healed.

At dawn the abbess called Euphraxia and said to her: “Why did you hide from me that you were offering prayers to God for this possessed woman? If you had told me, I too would certainly have come.”

Euphraxia said to her: “Forgive me, my lady. I saw her lying there shamefully and sick, and I grieved over her.”

The abbess said: “I have something to confess to you. Take care that Satan does not tempt you and that pride does not arise in you. Behold, Christ has given you power over them, so that you may cast them out.”

When Euphraxia heard this, she put ashes on her head, threw herself upon the ground, and cried out: “Who am I, wretched and unclean, that I should cast out a demon whom you have been unable to cast out despite praying for so long?”

The abbess said to her: “My daughter, this time has been awaiting you; your reward in heaven is abundant.”

Euphraxia entered the monastery, threw herself before the altar, and entreated God that the woman might be healed through her prayers and that help might be granted from on high.

Then she rose from the floor after praying and, at the abbess’s command, went again to the possessed woman. All the sisters followed her so that they might witness what was to be done.

When she approached her, she said: “May my Lord Jesus Christ, who created you, heal you.” Immediately she made the sign of the cross on the woman’s forehead.

The demon then cried out before everyone: “Oh! How am I to leave her at the hands of this impostor and deceiver, after dwelling in her for many years? No one was able to cast me out, and this unclean and lustful woman is attempting to drive me away!”

Euphraxia said to him: “It is not I who drive you away, but Christ, the God of all.”

The demon said to her: “I will not leave, unclean woman, for you have not received the power to cast me out.”

Euphraxia said: “I am unclean and full of every wickedness, as you yourself testify; nevertheless, at the Lord’s command, come out of her. For if I take the abbess’s staff, I shall beat you.”

But when the demon resisted and refused to come out, Euphraxia took the abbess’s staff and said to him: “Come out, or I shall certainly torment you.”

He answered her: “How can I depart from her, when I cannot withdraw from her?”

Then Euphraxia began to strike him. When she had struck him three times, she said: “Come out of God’s creature, unclean spirit. May the Lord Jesus Christ rebuke you.”

The demon said: “I cannot come out of her. Why do you persecute me? Where am I to go?”

Euphraxia said: “Into the outer darkness, into eternal fire, into endless torments prepared for you and for your father Satan and for those who do his will.”

All the sisters stood watching her and did not dare come nearer. Euphraxia, however, struggled fiercely with the resisting demon.

Looking toward heaven, she said: “Lord Jesus Christ, do not let me be put to shame at this hour, lest this unclean demon overcome me.”

Immediately the demon, foaming and gnashing his teeth, cried out in a loud voice and departed from the woman. From that hour she was healed.

The sisters ran up, glorifying God for this event, for great fear had seized them all. Euphraxia took the woman, washed her with water, clothed her, and led her to the abbess. The abbess, together with the sisters, brought her into the monastery, and they gave glory to God for the miracle that had occurred.

## Chapter XXX

From that hour Euphraxia humbled herself even more. She remained awake throughout the whole night and fasted every week, as was her custom. Without failing, she served all the sisters, and lived with complete diligence and joy in gentleness and humility.

One day the abbess saw a vision and was greatly troubled. All the sisters began to entreat her, pleading and saying: “Tell us, my lady abbess, why do you groan in this way and afflict our souls along with your own.”

She said: “Do not force me to speak until tomorrow.”

The senior sisters said to her: “Believe us, my lady: if you do not tell us, you will bring great distress upon our souls.”

The abbess said: “I did not wish to say until tomorrow what is going to happen; but because you compel me, listen now: Euphraxia is leaving us, for tomorrow she will be taken from this life. Let no one tell her, lest she be saddened.”

After these words, there was great lamentation for many hours.

One of the sisters, learning of this, ran to the oven and found Euphraxia baking bread; Julia was with her as usual.

The sister who had come said: “Know this, Lady Euphraxia: there is great mourning within, both with the abbess and among the sisters, because of you.”

When Julia and Euphraxia heard this, they were astonished and stood there for a long time.

Afterward Julia said: “Perhaps the abbess heard that, at the command of the one who was once your betrothed, the emperor ordered you to be brought from the monastery, and that is why they are lamenting?”

Euphraxia replied: “As my Lord Jesus Christ lives, even if all the foundations of the earth were shaken, they would not be able to persuade me to abandon Christ my Lord. Nevertheless, my lady Julia, while the bread is baking, go and see these mourners; see what has happened, lest my soul be troubled.”

Julia went and, standing outside the doors, heard the abbess recounting her dream in this way:

“I saw,” she said, “as though two men of a certain habit were coming here. They sought to take Euphraxia and said to me: ‘Send her; he has need of her.’

“Again others came and said to me: ‘Take Euphraxia with you and lead her before the Lord.’

“Immediately I took her and hurried along with them. When we came to a certain gate whose glory I cannot describe, it opened of its own accord for us. We entered and saw there an indescribable heavenly palace, containing a bridal throne not made by human hands.

“I could not approach farther inside. But they took Euphraxia and presented her to the Lord. She fell down and kissed his immaculate feet.

“I saw there ten thousand angels and an innumerable multitude of saints; all were standing and looking on. Then I saw—and behold, the Mother of the Lord took Euphraxia and led her to the bridal chamber, where she was preparing a crown of beauty.

“And I heard a voice saying to Euphraxia: ‘Behold your reward. Now go; after ten days, come and enjoy these things throughout the infinite ages.’

“Therefore, since today is the ninth day since I saw the vision, Euphraxia will die tomorrow.”

## Chapter XXXI

When Julia secretly heard the abbess recounting this, she beat her breast and face and came weeping bitterly to the oven.

When Euphraxia saw her weeping, she said to her: “I adjure you by the Son of God, Sister Julia, tell me what you heard and why you are weeping.”

Julia said to her: “I am weeping, my lady, because today we shall be separated from you. For, as I heard from my lady abbess, tomorrow you will breathe out your life from this body.”

When Euphraxia heard this, she was distressed and became fainthearted; she fell down. Julia sat beside her, weeping.

Euphraxia said to her: “Sister, give me your hand, raise me, and lead me to where the wood is stored; place me there. Then take the bread from the oven and carry it into the monastery.”

Julia did this but did not tell the abbess.

As Euphraxia lay on the floor, she cried out:

“Why, Lord, have you rejected me, a stranger and an orphan? Why have you despised me? Behold, the time has come when I was to fight against the devil, and my soul is being demanded from me.

“Have mercy on me, your handmaid, Lord Jesus Christ. Grant me even one year, so that I may mourn my sins, for I am without repentance and stripped of all repentance. There is no work of salvation in me, for no one in hell will confess you.

“There is no repentance in the grave; after death I cannot prevail through tears. For those who are in hell will not praise you, Lord, but the living will praise your holy name.

“Grant me even one more year, so that I may repent, for I am desolate like a fig tree without help.”

As she wept, one of the sisters heard her and informed the abbess and the sisters that Euphraxia was lying prostrate in the wood-storage room and crying out in this way.

Julia said: “It is true, my lady; she heard that she is dying, and that is why she is lamenting.”

The abbess then said to the sisters: “Who told her and afflicted her soul? Who informed her and crushed her heart? Did I not ask you not to tell her until her hour came? Why did you do this and afflict her soul? Go and bring her to me.”

They went and said to her: “Come, Lady Euphraxia; the abbess is calling you.”

She came out weeping and troubled. She entered, stood before the abbess, and wept and mourned, greatly afflicted by her groans.

The abbess looked at her and said: “What is wrong, my daughter, that you groan in this way?”

Euphraxia said: “I am weeping for myself, my lady, because you knew that I was going to die and did not tell me, so that I might mourn my sins, since I am defiled by every sin.”

After saying this, she threw herself onto the floor and clasped the abbess’s feet. Through the abbess, all her counsel was carried out with eagerness.

Euphraxia cried out and said: “Have mercy on me, my lady, and beseech the Lord to grant me even one year, for I am without repentance and do not know what darkness may cover me.”

The abbess said to her: “As the Lord lives, your King Christ has made you worthy of the heavenly senate.”

Then she began to recount to everyone the blessings that Euphraxia was to enjoy. She asked Euphraxia to pray to the Lord for her, so that she might be found worthy to share in them. She prayed that she might dwell with Euphraxia in Christ and enjoy the very gifts that Euphraxia herself was going to receive.

## Chapter XXXII

As Euphraxia lay at the abbess’s feet, she began to suffer cold and stiffness. A little later, a violent fever seized her.

The abbess said to the sisters: “Take her, and let us enter the oratory, for her hour is now approaching.”

They placed her in the oratory and watched over her until evening. When evening came and the hour for taking food had arrived, the abbess ordered the sisters to leave, retaining only Julia with her, so that Euphraxia would not be left alone at any hour. Having closed the doors, they remained with her until morning.

Julia pleaded with Euphraxia, saying: “My lady sister, do not forget me. Remember that I have always been inseparably joined to you on earth. Pray to God for me, that he may not separate me from you.

“Remember that I provided you with good contests. Entreat the Lord to release me from this burden of flesh, so that I may be found worthy to depart with you in confidence.”

When morning came, the abbess saw that Euphraxia was in her final breath and about to die. She sent word through Julia to the sisters, saying: “Come, my daughters, bid her farewell, for she is already failing.”

When they came, they bade her farewell, weeping and saying: “Remember us, Lady Sister Euphraxia, a name blessed by God, who loved you.”

After all the others, the woman who had long suffered from the demon—and had been saved through Euphraxia—also came. Mourning like everyone else, she kissed Euphraxia’s hands and said: “How much these hands have ministered to me, unworthy and sinful as I am! By God and by these hands, the demon was driven out from me.”

When Euphraxia was unable to answer, the abbess said to her: “My daughter, do you not have pity even on this sister? Why do you not speak to her, since she is so distressed on your account?”

Euphraxia replied: “Why do you mourn for me, sister lady? Let me rest, for I am failing. Nevertheless, bless God, and he himself will preserve you.”

And she said: “Pray for me, for there is a great struggle in my soul at this hour.”

When the abbess had prayed and all had answered “Amen,” Euphraxia gave up her spirit.

She was thirty years old. They buried her in the tomb where her mother Euphraxia also rested, and they glorified God because they had been found worthy to have a sister with God.

## Chapter XXXIII

Her teacher Julia remained at Euphraxia’s tomb for three days, weeping and not departing from it. She had taught Euphraxia letters and the Psalter and loved her greatly, since Euphraxia had been her disciple and was of imperial lineage.

On the fourth day Julia became joyful, approached the abbess, and said to her: “My lady, pray for me, for Christ has called me, with blessed Euphraxia interceding for me.”

Having said this, she kissed all the sisters.

On the fifth day after Euphraxia’s death, her teacher Julia also died and was buried in the tomb where blessed Euphraxia had been laid.

## Chapter XXXIV

After thirty days the abbess summoned the senior sisters of the monastery and said to them: “My daughters, choose a mother for yourselves and appoint in my place one who can preside over you.”

They replied: “My lady, tell us why you say this, for you have never said such a thing to your servants.”

The abbess said to them: “The Lord has called me. Lady Euphraxia prayed for me and labored greatly in her prayers so that I might be found worthy of the heavenly bridal chamber. Julia also, through holy Euphraxia, became her companion and entered that palace not made by human hands. I too am hastening to become worthy and to have a place with them.”

When the sisters heard that Euphraxia and Julia were in the greatest glory, they rejoiced and prayed together that they too might be found worthy to enter that bridal chamber.

They therefore chose one of the sisters, named Theogenia, to preside over them.

The abbess summoned her and said to her: “Behold the good testimony that all the sisters have given concerning you, and they have appointed you to the leadership and oversight of the handing down of the divine law and of our way of life.

“I adjure you by the undefiled and consubstantial Trinity: do not seek the riches or possessions of this world, nor occupy the sisters with earthly concerns. Rather, let them despise temporal goods and be found worthy to receive eternal ones.”

Again she said to the sisters: “Since you know perfectly the life and conduct of Euphraxia, imitate her, so that you may become her companions.”

When they had all said “Amen,” she bade them farewell, entered the oratory, and closed the doors. She ordered that none of them enter until dawn.

When morning came and they entered, they found that she had fallen asleep in the Lord. Singing a hymn to the Lord, they laid her in the tomb where blessed Euphraxia had been buried.

From that day onward, no other bodies were buried in that tomb.

## Chapter XXXV

Many signs and healings took place at the aforementioned tomb, and demons who had been expelled cried out: “Why does Euphraxia prevail against us after her death and persecute us?”

This is truly the Life of Euphraxia the matron, who was found worthy to take her place in the heavenly senate.

Let us therefore hasten, brothers and sisters alike, to adopt such a way of life and pursue humility, obedience, labor, gentleness, and patience, so that we too may be found worthy of an angelic manner of life and may rejoice with great joy in our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ.

To him belong honor and glory throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

---

## January 1. Life of Saint Euphrosyna, Virgin

**[Note: Euphrosyna.]** The Roman Martyrology, January 1: “At Alexandria, the burial of Saint Euphrosyna the virgin, who shone in the monastery through the virtue of abstinence and miracles.”

The Greek Menologion, September 25: “The natal day of our holy mother Euphrosyna, daughter of the blessed Paphnutius the Egyptian.”

The Menaea briefly express her Life in iambic verses.

Galesinius, in his note to the Martyrology, says that she was also called Euphrasia by others, and that she is mentioned by Damascene at the end of the third book *On Images*. There is indeed a correct mention of Euphrasia or Euphraxia in Damascene, but not of Euphrosyna, who is a different person. The feast day of Euphrasia occurs on March 13. See above, shortly before, under Euphrasia.

You have the Life of Euphrosyna by Metaphrastes in Lipomanus, volume VI, and in Surius, volume I. The version we give here has until now circulated among the Lives of the Fathers. We compared it with old editions and a manuscript.

**[Col. 0643A] VIRGIN. BY AN UNCERTAIN AUTHOR.**

## Chapter I

There was a man in Alexandria named Paphnutius, honorable in the eyes of all and observant of God’s commandments.

**[Note: Paphnutius.]** The Greek Menologion, September 25: “On the same day, the commemoration of the blessed Paphnutius, father of Euphrosyna.” The Menaea likewise speak of the same man on that day.

He took a wife worthy of his lineage and herself full of honorable character, but she was barren and did not bear children. Her husband was greatly troubled because he had no one to whom he could leave all his possessions, so that after his death that person might manage his property well and properly. He did not cease ministering to the needy night and day; he remained attached to the churches, praying and petitioning God through fasts and prayers that a son might be given to him.

His wife was likewise afflicted with great sorrow, seeing her husband so deeply troubled. She too gave much money to the poor and to oratories, asking that her desire might be fulfilled.

Her husband also went about seeking some person worthy of God who might, through his prayers, bring his longing to fulfillment. In this way he came to a monastery whose abbot was said to be a great man before God. He entered there and offered a large sum of money, and he gained great confidence with the abbot and all the brothers.

## Chapter II

After a considerable time he disclosed to the abbot the reason for his desire. The abbot sympathized with him and asked the Lord to grant him the fruit of the womb. God heard the prayers of both and granted them an only daughter.

When Paphnutius saw the abbot’s manner of life, he never withdrew from the monastery. He therefore brought his wife there, so that she might receive a blessing from the abbot and the brothers.

When the little girl was weaned, and she had reached the age of seven, she was baptized, and they gave her the name Euphrosyna.

Her parents rejoiced over her because she was pleasing to God and beautiful in appearance.

## Chapter III

When she was twelve years old, her mother departed from this world. Her father remained, educating her in letters and reading and in the other wisdom of this world.

The girl absorbed such instruction that her father marveled at her intelligence. Her reputation spread throughout the entire city: people spoke of her wisdom and learning, and of the fact that she was exceedingly beautiful and well composed in face and character.

Many men were stirred to seek her for their sons, and although many contended with her father, they could not bring the matter to completion. He nevertheless kept saying: “May the Lord’s will be done.”

But one man, surpassing all others in honor and wealth, summoned her father and asked him to give his daughter in marriage to his son, and Paphnutius consented.

## Chapter IV

After a considerable time, Paphnutius took her, when she was eighteen years old, and went with her to the monastery where he was accustomed to go. Again he gave a large sum of money for the needs of the brothers.

He said to the abbot: “I have brought you the fruit of your prayers, so that you may pray for her, because I now wish to give her in marriage.”

The abbot ordered that she be brought into the guest quarters of the monastery. He spoke with her, blessed her, and exhorted her concerning chastity, humility, patience, and the fear of the Lord.

For three days she remained there, daily listening to the psalms. Seeing the conduct and spiritual purpose of each of them, she marveled at their life, saying: “Blessed are these men, who are like angels even in this world and afterward attain eternal life.”

And her heart began to be troubled by zeal for the fear of God.

## Chapter V

After three days Paphnutius said to the abbot: “Come, Father, so that your handmaid may greet you, and pray for her, because we wish to go into the city.”

When the abbot came, the girl threw herself at his feet, saying: “I beseech you, Father, pray for me, so that God may gain my soul.”

He extended his hand and blessed her, saying: “O God, who know human beings before they are born, may you deign to care for this handmaid of yours, so that she may be found worthy to have a portion and fellowship in the kingdom of heaven.”

Entrusting her to the elder, they went into the city. Whenever her father happened to encounter a monk, he would bring him to his house and ask him to pray for her.

One year, on the anniversary of the day when the abbot of the monastery mentioned above had been ordained, the abbot sent one of the brothers to Paphnutius to invite him to the abbot’s solemn celebration. The brother went to his house and asked for him.

The servants said to him: “He has gone out.”

## Chapter VI

When Euphrosyna heard this, she summoned the brother and began to question him: “Tell me, for charity’s sake, my brother, how many brothers are you in the monastery?”

He said: “Three hundred and fifty-two.”

The girl said to him: “If someone wishes to go there to adopt the monastic life, does your abbot receive him?”

He replied: “Yes, he receives him with great joy, especially because of the Lord’s saying: ‘Whoever comes to me I will never cast out’” (John 6).

Euphrosyna said to him: “Do you all sing psalms in your church, and do you fast equally?”

That monk said to her: “We sing psalms together, but as for fasting, each one does as he wishes or as much as he can, so that the manner of life may not become willfully obstinate, but proceed from personal judgment and voluntary choice.”

After investigating the monks’ entire manner of life, she said to the monk: “I wanted to leave and attain such an indescribable life, but I am afraid of disobeying my father, because he wishes to give me to a husband for the sake of the vain and passing substance of this world.”

The monk said to her: “Sister, do not allow a man to defile your body and subject such beauty to disgrace. Rather, be betrothed to Christ, who can give you, in place of all these passing things, the kingdom of heaven and fellowship with the angels.

“Leave secretly and go to a monastery. Changing your worldly clothing, put on a monastic garment, so that you may escape.”

When she heard this, she was pleased and said to him: “And who will tonsure me?” She did not want to be tonsured by a layman who did not preserve the faith.

The monk said to her: “Behold, your father will come with me to the monastery and remain there for three or four days. You, however, bring one of the monks, and, in whatever way you wish, he will come to meet you with great joy.”

## Chapter VII

While he was saying these and similar things to Euphrosyna, Paphnutius arrived. Seeing the monk, he questioned him, saying: “Why have you taken upon yourself this trouble for us, my lord?”

He replied: “It is the anniversary of the monastery. The abbot sent me so that you would come and receive his blessing.”

Paphnutius rejoiced, entered a small boat with him, and they went to the monastery.

When he was there, Euphrosyna sent one of her most trustworthy servants and said: “Go to the monastery of Theodosius. Enter the church and bring with you whichever monk you find there.”

By God’s mercy, a monk was coming from the monastery, selling what he had with him. When the servant saw him, he asked him to come to Euphrosyna.

When the monk came, the girl saw him, rose, greeted him, and said: “Pray for me, Father.”

He prayed, blessed her, and sat down.

Euphrosyna said: “My lord, I have a Christian father and servant of God, a possessor of very great wealth. He had a wife who bore me, but she has now departed from this life.

“My father wishes to give me over to this wicked world in exchange for all his possessions. I do not wish to be defiled in it, but I am afraid of disobeying my father, and I do not know what to do.

“I have spent the whole night without sleep, asking God to show his mercy to my soul. When morning came, I decided to send someone to the church and bring one of the brothers, so that I might hear from him a word of salvation and learn what I ought to do.

“I ask you, Father, for the sake of your soul’s reward—I know that you have been sent by God—to teach me the things of God.”

The elder said to her: “The Lord says: ‘If anyone does not renounce father and mother and brothers and children, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple’” (Luke 14). “I know nothing more to tell you. Yet if you can endure the temptations of the flesh, leave everything and flee from your father’s possessions, which find many heirs.

“Behold: *ptochia* [Greek: πτωχεῖα], houses for the poor; *hierocomia*, homes for those with the ‘sacred disease’; guesthouses, monasteries, widows, orphans, strangers, the sick, and captives—wherever your father wills and decides, he will leave his possessions. Only do not lose your soul.”

**[Note: Ptochia.]** Here there is a remarkable variant reading among the various books. Most editions have *tapetia*, absurdly. In the Audomarian manuscript there was *topchia*. The *p* must undoubtedly be transposed, and the word read as *ptochia*, πτωχεῖα, that is, “a house for the poor.” Latin authors sometimes use Greek words when a suitable Latin translation does not readily occur.

**[Note: Hierocomia.]** Thus the Bertinian manuscript. The first edition has *ierocomia*, which arose from the spelling *ierocomia*. I understand *hierocomia* to mean a place where those suffering from the sacred disease, ἱερῇ νόσῳ—“the sacred disease”—are cared for.

The girl said to him: “I trust in God and in your prayers, because, with God’s help, I must labor for my soul.”

The elder said to her: “May such desires not fall away from steadfastness; for now is the time of repentance.”

Euphrosyna said to him: “That is why I have wearied you: fulfill my desire, pray over me and bless me, and cut the hair from my head.”

The elder rose, prayed, cut the hair from her head, and clothed her in a monastic garment.

**[Note: Tunicam schematis.]** Greek σχῆμα, the monastic habit. See the *Onomasticon*.

Praying for her, he said: “May the God who delivered all his saints himself guard you from every evil.”

After saying this, the elder departed from her and went on his way rejoicing.

[Col. 0646C] 665 **CHAPTER VIII.**—Euphrosyna, reflecting within herself, said: “If I go to a monastery of women, my father will find me when he searches for me, and will forcibly take me away because of my betrothed. Therefore I shall go to a monastery of men, where no one will suspect who I am.” Saying this, she threw off her woman’s clothing, put on a man’s, and, when evening came, left her house, taking with her five hundred solidi. She hid herself somewhere for the whole night. When morning came, her father arrived in the city and, God so willing, immediately went to the church.

Euphrosyna therefore reached that monastery, where her father was also very well known, and through the porter announced to the abbot: “A eunuch from the palace is standing before the door, wishing to speak with you.” When the abbot came out, Euphrosyna threw herself on the ground; after praying, they sat down. The old man said to her: “Why have you come here, my son?” Euphrosyna replied: “I was a eunuch from the palace, and I have always desired the monastic way of life. Our city is now greatly devoted to this way of life. I have learned of your good manner of life, and I wish to dwell with you. I possess many estates, and if the Lord grants me respite, I shall bring them here.”

The old man said to her: “You have come well, my son. Here is the monastery; if you wish, live with us.” Then the old man asked her: “What is your name?” She replied: “Smaragdus.” The abbot said to her: “You are young; you cannot live alone. You need a teacher, so that you may learn the rule and the way of life of the monks.” She said to the abbot: “As you command, my lord, so I shall do.” She placed five hundred solidi in the abbot’s hand, saying: “Take these for the present; and if I find that I can endure life here, the rest will also come.”

The abbot summoned a brother named Agapitus, a holy and passionless man, and placed Smaragdus in his hands, saying: “From now on he will be your son and disciple. Form him in such a way that he surpasses his teacher.” After kneeling and praying, he entrusted him to him. When all had responded “Amen,” Agapitus received him into his cell.

Because Smaragdus had a handsome appearance, whenever he came to church to pray to God, the devil stirred many men against the beauty of his face through evil thoughts, so that everyone troubled the abbot for having introduced such beauty into the monastery. When the abbot heard this, he summoned Smaragdus and said to him: “Your face is beautiful, my son, but it is a cause of weakness to the brothers. I want you to live alone in your cell, sing psalms there, and eat there, without going out anywhere.” He ordered Agapitus to prepare a solitary cell in which Smaragdus might live.

Agapitus did everything that the Father of the monastery had commanded him, introduced Smaragdus into the solitary cell, and there Smaragdus devoted himself to prayer and applied himself night and day to fasting and vigils, serving the Lord in simplicity of heart. The brother mentioned above, who had received him, marveled at him and reported his steadfastness to all the brothers. They all praised God, who performs such things even through human weakness.

[Col. 0647C] **CHAPTER IX.**—When Paphnutius, her father, had returned home, he hurried into the room in which his daughter had been accustomed to stay. Finding her absent, he became sad and sorrowful and began anxiously questioning the servants and maidservants about what had happened to Euphrosyna.

The servants said: “We saw her during the night, but in the morning she did not appear. We thought that the father of the young man to whom she had been betrothed had come and taken her away.” He sent his servants to that man’s house, but they did not find her there. When her betrothed and his father heard this, they were deeply saddened. Coming to Paphnutius, they found him greatly distressed, lying on the ground, and said to him: “Perhaps someone has seduced her and fled with her.”

Immediately his servants were sent with horses throughout Alexandria. There were also ships there, and they entered them and searched them by force. They searched the monasteries of women, the deserts and caves, and the houses of friends and neighbors. Since they did not find her, they mourned her as though she were dead: the father-in-law mourned his daughter-in-law, the betrothed his bride, and the father, mourning his daughter, said:

“Alas, alas, my sweetest daughter! Alas for me, consolation of my eyes! Who has invaded my estate? Who has scattered my possession? Who has dried up my vineyard? Who has extinguished my lamp? Who has cheated me of my hope? Who has violated my daughter’s beauty? What wolf, do you suppose, has torn apart my lamb? What place has touched such a face? What sea is carrying away that imperial countenance as a captive? She was the establishment of nobility, the comforter of the afflicted, the repose of those who labored, the harbor of those who groaned.

“Earth, earth, do not conceal my blood until I see what has happened to my daughter Euphrosyna.”

As Paphnutius continued with these and similar words, all who were present raised their voices and wept, so that the whole city lamented her.

**CHAPTER X.**—Unable to endure and finding no consolation, Paphnutius went to the aforementioned old man, of whom we spoke above. Falling at his feet, he said: “I beg you, do not cease praying, so that the result of your prayers may be found; for I do not know what has happened to my daughter.”

When the venerable old man heard this, he was deeply saddened. He ordered all the brothers to come to him and said to them: “Show charity, brothers. Let us ask the Lord to deem it worthy to show us what has happened to the daughter of our friend Paphnutius.”

They all fasted and prayed, but throughout the entire week nothing was revealed to them concerning Euphrosyna, as usually happened when they asked God about other matters. For Euphrosyna’s prayer to God was day and night that God would not reveal her during her lifetime.

When nothing had been revealed either to the old man or to any of the brothers, the abbot began to console him: “Do not abandon the discipline of the Lord, my son, for ‘the Lord disciplines the one whom he loves’ (Prov. 3). Know this also: without God’s will, not even one sparrow falls to the ground (Luke 12); how much less your daughter? Nothing happens without his command. I know that she has chosen the better part for herself, and for that reason nothing concerning her has been revealed to us. For I know that, God forbid, if she had fallen into evil deeds, God would never have disregarded the great labor of the brothers. I trust in the Lord that in this life God will show her to you.”

When Paphnutius heard this, he received consolation, giving thanks to God. He prayed daily and devoted himself to good works and almsgiving.

**CHAPTER XI.**—After some days he visited the monastery, commending himself to the prayers of the brothers. One day he came to the abbot, threw himself at his feet, and said: “Pray for me, Father, because I cannot endure the grief over my daughter. Rather, day by day my wound is renewed and grows, and my soul is afflicted.”

Seeing him so greatly distressed, the old man said to him: “Would you like to have a conversation with a spiritual brother who has come from the palace of Theodosius?” He did not know that she was his daughter.

Paphnutius replied: “I would.” The abbot summoned Agapitus and said to him: “Take Paphnutius and bring him into Smaragdus’s cell.” He brought him into Smaragdus’s cell without revealing anything to him beforehand.

When she suddenly saw her father and recognized him, she was completely filled with tears. Paphnutius thought that this was an expression of contrition; he did not recognize her, because the appearance of her face had withered from excessive abstinence, vigils, and tears. She covered her face with her hood so that he might in no way recognize her.

After praying, they sat down. She began speaking to him about the blessedness and eternal glory of the future kingdom, and about how one might attain it through humility and chastity, holy conduct, almsgiving, and charity. She spoke also about contempt for the world, and that children should not be loved more than God, who is the maker of all things. Interpreting the apostolic Scripture, she explained how “tribulation produces perseverance, and perseverance character” (Rom. 5).

Seeing her father in profound sorrow, she sympathized with him.

**CHAPTER XII.**—But fearing that she might be recognized and thereby become an obstacle to him, while wishing to console him, she said: “Believe me: God will not despise you. If your daughter’s soul had been lost, God would have revealed her to you, so that, held by the devil, she might not bring everlasting sorrow upon you and herself. But I believe in God, because she has chosen a good counsel for herself, as I have already said, according to the Gospel saying: ‘Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me’ (Matt. 10); and, ‘If anyone does not renounce all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple’ (Luke 14).

“God is also able to reveal her to you in this world. Stop, stop! Why are you destroying yourself by grieving? Rather, give thanks, despairing of nothing with respect to God. For my teacher Agapitus, often deeply saddened, used to say to me: ‘A certain man named Paphnutius, devoted to good works, has come here. He mourns his daughter as though she were dead, not knowing what has happened to her, and is afflicted by excessive lamentation, especially because she was his only child. With tears he threw himself at the abbot’s feet, asking that through the abbot’s prayers and those of all the brothers God might reveal the matter.’

“So you too should pray to God on her behalf. And I, although unworthy and conscious of my own sins, have often besought the Lord to grant you endurance and patience, and to fulfill what is expedient both for you and for your daughter. For this reason I have also often wished to see you and converse with you, so that perhaps through me, humble though I am, you might find some consolation.”

To prevent herself from being recognized through prolonged conversation, she said to Paphnutius: “Farewell, my lord.”

As Paphnutius was about to leave, her soul sympathized with him; her face grew pale and filled with tears. Because of excessive fasting and prolonged hunger, she was vomiting blood.

Paphnutius, greatly strengthened by her admonition, departed from her. Coming to the abbot, he said: “My soul has been built up by that brother, and through God’s grace I have become so joyful from his consolation that it is as though I had found my daughter.” Commending himself to the prayers of the abbot and all the brothers, he returned home, glorifying God.

**CHAPTER XIII.**—After Smaragdus had completed thirty-eight years in the solitary cell, he fell ill, and from that illness he died. One day, as usual, Paphnutius came to visit the monastery. After praying and greeting the brothers, he said to the old man: “If you command it, Father, let me go and see Smaragdus, because my soul greatly longs for him.”

The old man summoned Agapitus and ordered him to lead Paphnutius to visit Smaragdus. Entering the cell where the sick man lay, Paphnutius began to kiss him while weeping, saying:

“Alas for me! Where are your promises? Where are your sweet words, by which you promised that I would see my daughter with my own eyes? Look: I shall not only fail to see her, but you too, in whom I had a little consolation, are leaving us. Alas for me! Who will now console my old age? To whom shall I go? Who will be my helper?

“I mourn a double evil: it has been thirty-eight years since I lost my daughter, and nothing concerning her has been revealed to me, although I prayed day and night. I have found no one like her, and an incomparable grief holds me fast. What can I hope for now? Where shall I find consolation? I shall now descend mourning into hell.”

When Smaragdus saw him weeping bitterly and receiving no consolation, he said to him: “Why are you troubled and destroying yourself? Is the Lord’s hand powerless, or is anything difficult for God? Put an end to your grief. Remember how God revealed the patriarch Jacob’s Joseph, whom he had mourned as though dead (Gen. 46). But I beg you not to leave or abandon me for three days.”

Paphnutius hesitated within himself for three days, saying: “Perhaps God has revealed something about me to him.” On the third day he said to Smaragdus: “I have waited as you asked, my lord brother, and for three continuous days I have not gone anywhere.”

**CHAPTER XIV.**—Smaragdus, who was also Euphrosyna, recognizing that the day of her repose was approaching, summoned Paphnutius and said to him:

“The omnipotent God has arranged my misery well and fulfilled my desire, which I brought to completion by fighting courageously to the end—not through my own strength, but through the help of the one who guarded me from the enemy’s snares. Having completed the course, the crown of righteousness remains for me.

“I do not want you to be anxious any longer about your daughter Euphrosyna. I am that wretched woman, and you are my father. Look: you have now seen her, and you are satisfied. But let no one know this. Do not permit anyone else to strip and wash my body; do this yourself.

“Since I promised the abbot that I possessed many estates and that, if I could endure and remain in this place, I would bring them here, fulfill what I promised. This place is venerable. Pray for me.”

Saying this, she gave up her spirit on the Kalends of January.

**CHAPTER XV.**—When Paphnutius heard these words and saw that she had fallen asleep, his entrails were shaken, and he fell to the ground, becoming like a dead man.

Agapitus ran up. Seeing that Smaragdus was dead and Paphnutius lying half alive on the ground, he threw water onto his face [Note: [Col. 0652B] “He threw water onto his face.” Thus, in former times, cold water was accustomed to be poured over those who had lost consciousness. Above, *Life of Euphrasia*, chapter 22: “He sent water onto his face.”] and raised him, saying: “What is wrong, my lord Paphnutius?”

Paphnutius replied: “Let me die here, for today I have seen wonders.”

He rose, fell upon her face, poured out a flood of tears, and cried:

“Alas for me, my sweetest daughter! Why did you not reveal yourself to me earlier, so that I too might die with you of my own free will? Woe is me! How did you remain hidden? How did you pass through the snares of the adversaries and the spiritual wickedness of the darkness of this life, and enter eternal life?”

**CHAPTER XVI.**—When Agapitus heard this and learned of so extraordinary a matter, he was astonished and ran to report everything to the abbot.

The abbot came, fell upon her, and lamented, saying:

“Euphrosyna, bride of Christ and daughter of saints, do not forget your fellow servants and this monastery, but pray for us to the Lord Jesus Christ, that he may cause us, fighting courageously, to reach the harbor of salvation and to have a share with him and with his saints.”

He ordered all the brothers to assemble, so that her holy body might be committed to burial with due honor.

When they had assembled and had seen so astonishing a miracle, they glorified God, who performs such great miracles even through the frail female sex. One brother had only one eye. He kissed her face with tears, and as soon as he touched her, his eye was restored.

When all the brothers who were present saw what had happened, they blessed God [Col. 0652A], giving thanks to him to whom belong all good things. Greatly strengthened and edified, they buried her in the tomb of the fathers.

Her father, offering everything he possessed to the church, the hospice, and the monastery, entered that same monastery. He offered a very large portion of his wealth there and remained in that same cell, sleeping on the same *psiathium* [Note: [Col. 0652B] “On the same *psiathium*.” The Bertinian manuscript reads: “on the same *phisiata*.” The printed editions have “on the same bed.” The correct reading is *psiathium*, that is, a mat, as has often been stated already. See the *Onomasticon*.] on which Euphrosyna had slept.

Paphnutius lived in the holy vocation for ten years and departed to the Lord. They buried him beside his daughter, while the abbot and the whole congregation glorified God.

The day of their departure to the Lord is celebrated in that same monastery even to the present day, glorifying God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0651] **OCTOBER 29. THE LIFE OF SAINT MARY THE HARLOT** [Note: [Col. 0659C] “Of Mary the harlot.” Her feast is not found assigned to a definite day in any ecclesiastical calendars, except that in the *Menaea*, on October 29, Mary is joined to Abraham. Until now the *Life of Abraham and Mary his niece* had also been printed together, with Ephraem as author. I have separated them so that you may have the male ascetics distinguished from the female ascetics.]**, NIECE OF ABRAHAM THE HERMIT. BY SAINT EPHRAEM THE ARCHDEACON, TRANSLATED BY AN ANONYMOUS INTERPRETER.**

This is the section of the *Life of Saint Abraham* found above, column 281.

[Col. 0651D] **CHAPTER I.**—I wish, dearly beloved, to relate to your united company another remarkable deed that the blessed man performed in his old age. It is full of edification for wise and spiritual men, and likewise an example of humility and compunction. The event occurred as follows:

**CHAPTER II.**—The blessed man Abraham had a blood brother. When that brother died, he left behind a daughter, his only child, seven years old. When her father’s relatives and friends saw that she had been deprived of her parents, they brought her without delay to her uncle.

When the old man saw her, he ordered her to be enclosed in the outer cell of his own cell. There was a very small window between the two cells, through which he taught her the psalter and other Scriptures. With him she kept vigil in the praises of the Lord, sang the psalms with him, and strove in every form of abstinence to imitate her uncle.

She also advanced eagerly in the discipline she had undertaken and hastened to fulfill every virtue of the soul. For the most holy man continually entreated the Lord for her with tears, so that her mind would not become entangled in the care of earthly affairs, since her father, when he died, had left her immense sums of money. After his brother’s death, when his brother’s daughter had come to him, the servant of Christ immediately ordered this money to be distributed to the poor and orphans.

She also begged her uncle daily to pray to the Lord for her, so that she might be rescued from evil thoughts and from the snares of the devil’s various traps. Thus she steadfastly maintained the rule of her discipline.

Her uncle rejoiced to see her advancing so readily and without hesitation in every virtue: in tears, humility, modesty, and quiet; and, higher than all these, in exceptional love toward God. For twenty years she lived with him in abstinence, like a most chaste lamb and an undefiled dove.

When that period of years had been completed, the devil raged against her and displayed his customary snares, considering how he might entangle her in his nets, so that at least in this way he might bring sorrow and anxiety upon the blessed man and separate his mind, however slightly, from the Lord.

**CHAPTER III.**—There was a certain man who was a monk in name only, and who often used to visit him under the pretext of edification. By looking at the blessed woman through the window, he was also stirred by the goads of lust and wished to converse with her, for the love of desire had kindled his heart like a fire.

He lay in wait for her for a long time, until a full year had passed, weakening her resolve by the persuasive softness of his words. Finally, opening the window of her cell, she went out to him, and he immediately defiled and polluted her with the crime of wickedness and lust.

After the deed of so great a sin had been committed, her heart was terrified. Tearing apart the hair shirt in which she was clothed, she struck her face with her hands, wishing in her excessive grief to surrender herself to death. Overwhelmed by the weight of her anxiety, and seeing no harbor of deliberation, she was tossed amid various waves of thought. She mourned that she was no longer what she had been, and repeatedly cried out with lamentation:
