“Now I feel that I am dead. I have lost my days and the labor of my abstinence. The tears of my prayers and the work of my vigils have been brought to nothing. I have angered my God and destroyed myself. Alas for me, wretched woman, deserving to be mourned with every fountain of tears! I have plunged my holy uncle into the bitterest grief. Reproach against my soul has covered me; I have become the devil’s mockery.

“What further life is there for me, unhappy woman? Alas for me! What have I done? Alas for me! What has happened to me? Alas for me! What evil have I suffered? Alas for me! From where and how have I fallen? How has my mind been darkened? I did not understand how I fell; I did not know how I was polluted. I do not know how a dark cloud covered my heart, or how I could have been ignorant of what I was doing.

“Where shall I hide? Where shall I go? Into what pit shall I throw myself? Where is the teaching of my most holy uncle? Where are the admonitions of his companion Ephraem, who taught me to persevere in my virginity and urged me to preserve my undefiled soul for the immortal Bridegroom? ‘Your Bridegroom,’ they used to say, ‘is holy and jealous.’

“Alas for me! What shall I do? I no longer dare to look toward heaven, knowing that I am dead before God and men. I shall not dare approach that window again. How shall I, a sinner filled with filthy pollution, attempt once more to speak with my holy uncle? And even if I dared, would not fire leap from the window and immediately consume me?

“It is better for me, then, to go to another country, where no one can recognize me, since I am already dead once and no hope of salvation remains for me.”

She rose and immediately went to another city, where she took lodging in a certain inn, changing her former dress [Note: [Col. 0659D] “In an inn.” That is, in a lodging-house or brothel. Below, chapter 6, *stabularius* means the innkeeper.].

**CHAPTER IV.**—When this downfall had overtaken the woman mentioned above, the following vision was shown to the blessed man during sleep.

He saw a terrible and enormous dragon, exceedingly foul even in appearance and hissing with great strength, as though coming out of some place and advancing all the way to his cell. He saw it find a dove there, swallow it, and return again to its pit.

When he awoke, he was deeply saddened and wept bitterly. He thought that Satan’s persecution was being stirred up against the Church of God and that many were being turned away from the faith of truth, or that perhaps some schism had arisen in the holy Church.

He therefore fell upon his knees and prayed to the Lord, saying: “You, God who foreknows all things and loves humanity, know what this vision means.”

Two days later he saw the same dragon come to his cell in a similar way and place its head beneath his feet, whereupon it was torn apart. The dove that it had swallowed was found alive in its belly. He stretched out his hand and received her alive.

When he awoke, he called the blessed woman again and again, thinking that she was in her little cell, and said: “Why have you grown weary, daughter Mary”—for that was her name—“of opening your mouth in the praises of God for two days now?”

When she gave him no answer and he did not hear her singing psalms for two days in the customary manner, he realized that his vision certainly concerned her. Then he groaned and wept bitterly. Pouring out tears, he said:

“Alas for me, for the most savage wolf has snatched away my lamb, and my daughter has been taken captive!”

Raising his voice, he said with tears: “Christ, Savior of the world, turn my lamb Mary back to me and restore her to the sheepfold of life, so that my old age may not depart from this world in grief. Do not despise my prayer, Lord, but send your grace swiftly, so that it may cast her unharmed from the dragon’s mouth.”

Thus the two days revealed to him in the vision were fulfilled in the course of two years, during which his niece spent her slippery life as though in the belly of the most savage dragon. But throughout that entire period the holy man never relaxed his spirit from praying to the Lord for her, day and night.

**CHAPTER V.**—After two years, when he had discovered where she was and how she was living, he asked a man well known to him to go to her and learn everything carefully.

The man whom he had sent went, and, reporting everything truthfully—including that he had seen her herself—was asked by the holy man to bring him a military garment and a horse to ride. When the door had been opened, he went out and immediately put on the military clothing. He also placed a long *camelauchium* over his head so that his face would be covered [Note: [Col. 0659D] “*Camelanchium*.” This is the correct reading. The printed editions have *calamanchum*, that is, a cap. It also occurs below, in chapter 9, where the Cologne edition has *calamanen*. See the *Onomasticon*.]. Carrying with him one solidus in coins, he mounted the horse and hastened rapidly.

Just as someone wishing to explore another’s country or city assumes the clothing of the inhabitants of that place so that he will not easily be recognized, so this blessed Abraham used the enemy’s clothing in order to put the enemy to flight.

“Come, then, dearly beloved brothers, marvel at this second Abraham. The first Abraham went forth to battle against kings, struck them down, and brought back his nephew Lot. This second Abraham went forth to battle against the devil, so that, after defeating him, he might bring back his niece with a greater triumph.”

When he reached the place, he turned aside into an inn. Looking around anxiously in every direction to see her, he searched for her. After many hours had passed without an opportunity being given him to see her, he smiled and said to the innkeeper:

“I have heard, my friend, that you have an excellent girl. If you would order her to come, I would gladly look at her.”

The innkeeper, seeing the old man’s gray hair and his age already wearied by the number of his years, did not suspect that he wished to see her because of lust, and replied:

“She is, as you have learned, exceedingly beautiful.”

Indeed, this Mary was almost beyond what nature required, beautiful in the loveliness of her appearance. When the old man asked her name, the innkeeper replied that she was called Mary.

Then, with a cheerful expression, he said: “Please bring her into my presence, so that I may feast with her today. I have heard much praise of the girl.”

When she was summoned and appeared, and the holy man—her uncle—saw her in the dress of prostitutes, almost his entire body dissolved with grief. He concealed the bitterness of his soul beneath a cheerful expression and restrained the tears that burst forth as a man, lest, if the woman recognized him, she might seek the protection of flight.

**CHAPTER VII.**—When they had sat down and begun drinking, the remarkable man began to jest with her. She rose, embraced his neck, and caressed him with kisses.

As she kissed him, she smelled his little body exuding the sweetest fragrance of abstinence. She remembered the days during which she had lived in the greatest abstinence and, as though struck in the heart by a weapon, groaned deeply and shed tears. Unable to endure the force of her emotion, she burst out with these words:

“Woe, woe is me, miserable and alone!”

The innkeeper, astonished, said: “What is the matter, Lady Mary, that you have suddenly burst into such profound sighs? You have lived here for two years, and never has a groan or a sadder word been heard from you. But now I do not know what has happened to you.”

She replied: “I would be blessed if I had died three years ago.”

At this the blessed old man, so that he would not be recognized, spoke to her with an appearance of calmness: “Now, when we are occupied with joy, have you come to recall your sins?”

O God most high, how admirable is the dispensation of your mercy! Surely the girl did not say in her heart: “How closely this man’s appearance resembles that of my uncle”? But you alone, God who loves humanity, from whom all good wisdom comes, so arranged matters that she could not recognize him and perhaps, troubled by confusion, flee.

This must be believed for no other reason than that the tears of your servant, her uncle, obtained such standing before you that you deigned to make possible what seemed impossible.

The holy man produced the solidus he had brought and gave it to the innkeeper, saying: “Please, my friend, prepare an excellent dinner for us, so that I may feast with the girl. I have come because of my love for her, after a long journey.”

O true wisdom according to God! O truly spiritual understanding! O truly praiseworthy discernment for salvation! For fifty years he had never tasted bread during his abstinence; now, without hesitation, he ate meat in order to save a lost soul.

The choir of the holy angels, rejoicing over this blessed man’s discernment, marveled greatly. He ate and drank eagerly, without any hesitation, so that he might draw out the soul fixed in the mire.

O wisdom of the wise, and understanding of those who understand! O discernment of those who discern! Come, marvel at this apparent ignorance; come, be astonished at this transformation: how this perfect, wise, discerning, and prudent man became ignorant and undiscerning, so that he might rescue a soul swallowed from the lion’s mouth and release from bonds and a dark prison a soul hidden and chained.

**CHAPTER VIII.**—After they had feasted, the girl invited him to lie down with her, so that they might enter the bedroom. He replied: “Let us go.”

When he had entered, he saw a bed raised high, and immediately sat down upon it eagerly.

“How shall I address you, or by what name shall I call you, most perfect athlete of Christ? I am utterly at a loss. Shall I call you continent or incontinent? Wise or foolish? Discerning or undiscerning?

“For fifty years you had lain on a *psiathium* [Note: [Col. 0659D] “On a *psiathium*.” The old edition has “on a space of ground.” But *psiathium* has already occurred several times in other Lives, so there can be no doubt about the correctness of the reading.]. How is it that you now confidently climb upon a bed of this kind?

“But you did all these things for the praise and glory of Christ: you undertook the longest journey, ate meat, drank wine, and turned aside into an inn, so that you might save a lost soul.

“We, however, if we merely wish to speak a useful word with our neighbor, make distinctions about everything at the wrong time.”

## CHAPTER IX

While he was sitting on the bed, the girl said to him: “Come, sir, so that I may remove your shoes from your feet.” But he said to her: “Close the door carefully, and then you shall remove them.” The girl first wished to take off his shoes; but when he would not allow it, she came to him after the doors had been closed.

Then the old man said to her: “Lady Maria, come near me.” When she had approached, he firmly took her hand, as though he intended to kiss her. Removing his *camelaucium* from his head and breaking into tears, he said to her:

“My daughter Maria, do you not recognize me? My very entrails, am I not the one who nourished you? What has happened to you, my daughter? Who has destroyed you? Where is that angelic way of life which you once had, my daughter? Where is self-restraint? Where are the tears? Where are the vigils? Where are the lying-on-the-ground practices (*chameuniae*)?

[Note: [Col. 0660C] *Chameuniae.* The old edition has *continentiae* (“self-restraint”); the Cologne edition has *caumeniae*. The reading given here is the correct one. They are *χαμευνίαι* (*chameuniai*), “sleeping on the ground.” Above, in the *Life of Abraham*, chapter 18: “He was never at all wearied by lying on the ground and by bodily mortification.” See the *Onomasticon*.]

“How have you fallen from the height of heaven into this pit, my daughter? Why, when you sinned, did you not tell me? Why did you not immediately report it to me? I certainly would have done penance for you with my beloved Ephraem. Why did you do this? Or why did you abandon me in this way and bring me into this intolerable grief? Yet who is without sin except God alone?”

When he had said these and many other things, she remained in his hands like an immovable stone, overcome alike by fear and shame. Again the blessed man added with tears:

“Will you not speak to me, my daughter Maria? Will you not speak to me, part of my very being? Was it not for your sake, my daughter, that I came here? Let this sin rest upon me, my daughter; on the day of judgment I shall give an account to the Lord for you; for this sin I shall make satisfaction to God.”

Until the middle of the night he consoled her with words of this kind and admonished her with abundant tears. When she had gained a little confidence, she addressed him, weeping in this manner:

“I cannot,” she said, “look at you because of the shame on my face.” And how can I pour out a prayer to God when I have been polluted in this way by the filth of this mire?’

“The holy man said to her: ‘Let your iniquity rest upon me, my daughter; let God demand this sin from my hands. Only listen to me, and come; let us go to our place. For your beloved Ephraem also grieves deeply for you and diligently entreats the Lord on your behalf. Do not despair, daughter, of the Lord’s compassion. Even if your sins are like mountains, his mercy surpasses the whole of creation.

“‘As we read, an impure woman approached the Pure One, and did not pollute him; rather, she herself was cleansed by him. She washed the Lord’s feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair (Luke VII). If a spark can set the sea ablaze, can your sins pollute his purity? It is not unusual to fall in the struggle; but it is evil to lie there after being cast down. Vigorously turn back from where you had advanced your foot. When you fell, the enemy laughed; but let him find you stronger when you rise.

“‘Have pity, I beg you, on my old age; grieve, I beseech you, over the labor of my gray hairs; rise and come with me to the cell. Do not fear. The human race is prone to slip; but just as it falls quickly, so by God’s help it rises again more swiftly. He does not wish sinners to die, but to be healed and live (Ezekiel XVIII).’

“She replied to him:

“‘If you know that I can do penance and that God will accept my satisfaction, behold, I shall come as you command. Go ahead, and I shall follow your holiness and kiss your footprints, because you have grieved over me so deeply that you might draw me out of this abyss of impurity.’

“And placing her head at his feet, she wept throughout the night, saying: ‘What shall I repay you, Lord my God, for all these things?’”

## CHAPTER X

When daybreak came, blessed Abraham said to her: “Rise, daughter, and let us go from here to our cell.” She replied to him: “I have here a little gold and some clothing. What do you command should be done with them?”

Blessed Abraham answered: “Leave all these things here; they were acquired through the Evil One.” Then they rose and departed.

Immediately he placed her on a horse and led it ahead of him, just as a shepherd, when he finds a lost sheep, joyfully carries it upon his shoulders (Luke XIII). Thus blessed Abraham, rejoicing in his heart, made the journey with his granddaughter.

When he had reached his own place, he shut her in the inner cell—the one in which he himself had previously lived—while he remained in the outer cell. Clothed in sackcloth, she persevered in humility of spirit and heart, and in tears of the eyes. She also exhausted herself with vigils and the strictest labors of abstinence, continually crying out to the Lord with modesty and quietness. With the firmest hope of forgiveness, she mourned her crime, devoting herself so wisely and constantly to supplication that no one, however devoid of compassion, could fail to be moved when he heard the sound of her weeping.

For who could be found so merciless that, recognizing her lamentation, he would not himself weep? Or who could fail to give thanks to our God for the true compunction of her heart? Indeed, compared with our own petitions, her repentance exceeds every measure of grief. She prayed so fervently that the Lord might forgive her for what she had done that she even asked for a sign from God if her repentance had been accepted.

Thus the most merciful God, who does not wish anyone to perish but all to return to repentance (I Timothy II), accepted her worthy satisfaction in such a way that, after the completion of three years, health was restored to many through her prayers. For crowds of people flocked to her with ever greater eagerness, and she fervently prayed to the Lord for their salvation.

## CHAPTER XI

Blessed Abraham continued in this life for another ten years. Seeing her excellent repentance and glorifying God, he rested in peace in the seventieth year of his life. For fifty years he had fulfilled his way of life with great devotion, humility of heart, and sincere charity.

## CHAPTER XII

He never showed partiality toward anyone, as is customary among many, so that they prefer one person out of love while despising another. Nor did he alter his rule of abstinence; he did not grow numb through laziness or act sluggishly, but always lived as though he were to die each day.

Such was the manner of blessed Abraham, and such were his life and his contests of endurance. He stood in the battle line against the adversary in such a way that he never turned his back. Neither in the tribulations that he suffered in the village nor in the battle in which he fought against the demons’ fantasies did he relax his spirit or tremble in any respect.

But his greatest and most remarkable struggle was the one he undertook on behalf of the most blessed Maria: how, through spiritual wisdom—by prudence, I mean, and inexperience—and through indifference and lack of self-restraint, he drew her out of the abyss of iniquity.

O miracle! He entered the very den of the dragon, trampled him there beneath his feet, and snatched the prey from between his teeth. Such were the struggles and labors of the blessed man.

## CHAPTER XIII

We have written these things in this manner for the consolation and devotion of all who wish to order their lives piously and courageously, and for the praise and glory of God, by whose grace all that is necessary is abundantly granted to us. In another volume we have described the rest of his virtues.

At the hour when he rested, departing to the Lord, nearly the whole city gathered. Each person approached his most pure body with complete devotion and tore a blessing for himself from his garments. Whenever anyone suffering from any illness received something that had been torn away, health followed without delay.

## CHAPTER XIV

Maria also lived for another five years. Ordering her life beyond measure, she persevered day and night in great lamentation and tears, praying to the Lord. Many passersby, when they crossed that place at night and heard the sound of her weeping, were nevertheless turned to mourning and joined their own tears to hers.

At the hour of her falling asleep, when she was taken from this life, all who saw her gave glory to the Lord because of the radiance of her face.

## CHAPTER XV

[Note: [Col. 0660D] “Woe to me.” The three following chapters are absent both from Ephraem, volume III, in the *Life of Abraham*—and Ephraem’s translator Vossius states that he did not find them in the Greek manuscripts—, and from Metaphrastes, volume VI of Lipomanus, and volume II of Surius. They were also absent from our manuscripts. But because the Cologne edition contains them, I have printed them as well. Vossius thinks that these clauses were composed from other passages of Ephraem in which he has certain similar expressions.]

“Woe is me, most beloved, because these indeed have fallen asleep and have gone to the Lord with complete confidence. Their minds were in no way entangled in worldly affairs, but solely in the love of the Lord. But I remained by my own will unready and unprepared; and behold, winter has overtaken me, and an endless storm will find me naked and stripped, without the perfection of good works.”

## CHAPTER XVI

“I marvel at myself, most beloved, at how I sin every day and repent every day; for hours I build, and for hours I overturn what I have built. In the evening I say: ‘Tomorrow I shall repent.’ But when morning comes, carried away, I let the day pass.

“Again in the evening I say: ‘I shall keep vigil at night and entreat the Lord with tears to be merciful to my sins.’ But when night arrives, sleep seizes me instead.

“Behold, those who received money with me strive to trade day and night, so that they may obtain the praise of public acclaim and rule over ten cities. But because of my laziness I hid mine in the earth, and my Lord has drawn near to come. Behold, my heart trembles, and I mourn the days of my negligence, having no excuse that I can offer.”

## CHAPTER XVII

“Have mercy on me, O God, who alone are without sin, and save me, who alone are kind and merciful. For besides you, the blessed Father, your only-begotten Son who was incarnate for us, and the Holy Spirit who gives life to all things, I know no other, nor do I believe in another.

“And now remember me, lover of humankind, and lead me out of the prison of my iniquities, because both things belong to you, Lord: when you wished me to enter this world and when you command me to depart from it.

“Remember me, defenseless as I am, and save me, a sinner. May your grace, which in this age has become my help, refuge, and glory, itself shelter me beneath its wings on that dreadful and terrible day.

“For you know—as the searcher of heart and kidneys—that I have rejected many forms of wickedness and paths of scandal, the vanity of the shameless, and the defense of heretics. And this was not from myself, but from your grace, through which my mind has been enlightened.

“Therefore I beseech you, holy Lord: save me in your kingdom, and deem me worthy to be blessed with all who have pleased you, for glory, worship, and majesty are fitting for you, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen.”

[Col. 0661]

# OCTOBER 8. LIFE OF SAINT THAIS

[Note: [Col. 0661D] *Thais.* Her commemoration occurs in the Greek *Menologion* on October 8: “The feast of Saint Thaisia, who had been a prostitute. From adolescence she had been corrupted by her own mother and thus made herself a workshop of the devil. But she was won over by the holy man Paphnutius. Having been converted and pierced with repentance for her crimes, she distributed all her possessions, valued at a price of four hundred, to the poor and shut herself in a cell, where, with tears and groans issuing from the depths of her heart, she cried: ‘You who fashioned me, have mercy on me.’ She spent three years in this discipline; then, leaving at the abbot’s command, she departed after fifteen days.”

“These words are taken verbatim from the *Menaea*, in which, however, her place of origin is specified, though it is missing here. It says there *Σιδώνιος* (*Sidonius*, ‘Sidonian’). The manuscript *Florarium Sanctorum*, August 28: ‘The conversion of Thais the sinner.’ And October 8: ‘The deposition of Saint Thais the sinner, converted from prostitution by Saint Paphnutius. Having found a monastery of virgins, he shut her in a small cell and sealed the door with lead, leaving her a small window through which a little food could be brought to her. After three years of repentance, Abbot Paphnutius returned and, following a revelation given to him by God, broke open the door which he had sealed with lead and said to her: “Come out, for God has forgiven you your sins.” But she said: “I call God to witness that from the moment I entered here I made a burden of all my sins, set it before my eyes, and just as breath has never ceased from my nostrils, so my sins have not departed from me for even one moment up to this hour.” She flourished in the year of salvation 344.’

“This life is placed separately in some manuscripts, while in others it is inserted among other books, such as Book II, chapter 16, because of Paphnutius, who converted her. I have given it separately so that a woman might be joined to women.”]

## OF THE PROSTITUTE, BY AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR

### CHAPTER I

[Col. 0661A] 374

There was a prostitute named Thais, of such great beauty that many, selling their property because of her, reached extreme poverty. Moreover, when her lovers quarreled among themselves, the threshold of the girl’s house was frequently filled with the blood of young men.

When Abbot Paphnutius heard this, he put on secular clothing, took one solidus, and set out to her in a certain city of Egypt. He gave her the solidus as the price of sin. After receiving the payment, she said: “Let us enter the house.”

Then he entered. As though he intended to climb onto a bed spread with costly fabrics, he invited her and said: “If there is an inner chamber, let us go there.”

She replied: “There is one; but if you fear human beings, no one enters even this outer chamber. If, however, you fear God, there is no place hidden from the eyes of his divinity.”

When the old man heard this, he said to her: “And do you know that there is a God?”

She replied: “I know God, the kingdom of the age to come, and also the future torments of sinners.”

He said to her: “If you know these things, why have you destroyed so many souls, so that you may be condemned when an account is demanded not only for your own crimes but also for theirs?”

When Thais heard this, she fell at the feet of the monk Paphnutius and entreated him with tears, saying: “Impose repentance upon me, Father. For I trust that through your prayer I shall obtain forgiveness. I ask only for a delay of three hours; after that I shall come wherever you command, and whatever you order, I shall do.”

When Abbot Paphnutius had appointed the place to which she should come, she departed, gathered everything she had received through sin, brought it out into the middle of the city before the watching people, and set it on fire, crying:

“Come, all of you who have sinned with me, and see how I shall burn the things you have given me.”

The value, however, was forty pounds.

### CHAPTER II

When she had consumed everything, she went to the place which the abbot had appointed for her. He found a monastery of virgins, led her into a small cell, sealed the door of the cell with lead, and left only a small window through which a little food could be brought to her. He ordered the sisters of the monastery to provide her each day with a little bread and a small amount of water.

As he was leaving her behind the lead-sealed door, Thais said to him: “Where do you command me, Father, to pour out my water?”

He answered: “In the cell, as is fitting for you.”

When she again asked how she should pray to God, he said to her: “You are not worthy to name God or to bring the name of his divinity to your lips; nor are you worthy to raise your hands toward heaven, since your lips are full of iniquity and your hands are polluted with filth. Instead, sitting and facing east, look toward that direction and frequently repeat only this saying: ‘You who fashioned me, have mercy on me.’”

[Note: [Col. 0664A] “You who fashioned me, have mercy on me.” The same prayer of Thais is found in the *Menaea* and the *Menologion*.]

### CHAPTER III

After she had been shut up in this manner for three years, Abbot Paphnutius felt compassion and immediately went to Abbot Antonius to ask him whether the Lord had forgiven her sins or not.

When he arrived and had carefully related the whole matter to him, Abbot Antonius summoned his disciples and ordered them all to keep vigil that night and persist individually in prayer, so that God might reveal to one of them the reason for which Abbot Paphnutius had come.

When each had withdrawn and they were praying without ceasing, Abbot Paul, the chief disciple of Saint Antonius, suddenly saw in heaven a bed adorned with costly fabrics, guarded by three virgins shining with radiant faces.

When Paul said to himself, “This gift belongs to none other than my father Antonius,” a voice came to him: “It does not belong to your father Antonius, but to the prostitute Thais.”

When Abbot Paul had plainly reported this, Abbot Paphnutius, having learned God’s will, departed. He returned to the monastery where she had been shut up and broke open the door which he had closed.

But she requested that she remain shut up as before. When he had opened the door, he said to her: “Come out, for God has forgiven your sins.”

She replied: “I call God to witness that from the moment I entered here I set all my sins before my eyes like a burden. My sins did not depart from my eyes; rather, I always wept as I looked upon them.”

Abbot Paphnutius said to her: “God did not forgive you because of your repentance, but because you always kept the remembrance of these things in your mind.”

After he had brought her out from there, Thais lived only fifteen days, and then rested in peace.

[Col. 0663]

# OCTOBER 8. LIFE OF SAINT PELAGIA

[Note: [Col. 0671A] *Pelagia.* The Roman Martyrology, October 8: “At Jerusalem, Saint Pelagia, surnamed the Penitent.”]

## OF THE PROSTITUTE, BY JAMES THE DEACON

[Note: [Col. 0671A] *James the Deacon.* The author calls himself this here in the preface.]

## TRANSLATED BY EUSTOCHIUS

[Note: [Col. 0671A] *Eustochius.* The translator gives his own name in the prologue, which is absent from the Cologne edition but is found in the manuscript of Saint-Omer and in the old editions.]

### TRANSLATOR’S PROLOGUE

[Col. 0663A]

“I, Eustochius, with Christ’s help, have translated the words of so great a priest, hidden from the Latins.

“But you, readers, weigh the labor with me, and, remembering us, pour forth words to God.”

## AUTHOR’S PREFACE

[Col. 0663]

[Col. 0663] 376

We must always give great thanks to our Lord, who does not wish sinners to perish in death but desires all to be converted through repentance to life (I Timothy II).

Hear, therefore, the miracle that took place in our own days. I, the sinner James, thought that I should write to you, holy brothers, so that by hearing or reading you might know it and gain for your souls the greatest help of consolation.

For the merciful God, who wishes no human being to perish, established in this age that sins should be forgiven through satisfaction, because in the future there will be a just judgment in which each person will receive according to his works.

Now, therefore, grant me silence and observe with me with every diligence of heart, because our account is filled with abundant compunction.

# LIFE

[Col. 0663]

### CHAPTER I

[Col. 0663B]

The most sacred bishop of the city of Antioch summoned to himself all the bishops living nearby for a certain matter. Eight bishops therefore assembled, among whom was the most holy man of God, Nonnus, my bishop, a remarkable man and a most effective monk, from the monastery called that of the Tabenesiots.

Because of his incomparable life and most honorable manner of living, he was taken from the monastery and ordained bishop. After we had assembled in the aforesaid city, its bishop ordered us to remain in the basilica of the blessed martyr Julian.

[Note: [Col. 0671A] *Julian.* Various Julians occur in the Martyrology. I think that the one meant here is one of those who suffered in Syria, where Antioch is located.]

We entered and took our places, while the other bishops who had assembled sat before the door of the basilica.

### CHAPTER II

While they were sitting there, some bishops asked my lord Nonnus to teach them something. Immediately the holy bishop began to speak from his mouth for the edification and salvation of all who were listening.

While we were all admiring his holy teaching, behold, the foremost of the female mimes of Antioch passed by us. She was the foremost of the pantomime dancing women, sitting upon a little donkey.

[Note: [Col. 0671A] *The foremost of the pantomime dancing women.* I have emended this conjecturally. In place of *choreutriarum*, the old edition has *thorentriarum* and the Cologne edition *thorentiarum*. The manuscript of Saint-Omer has: “The first chaos into the pantomime theater.” Perhaps some will conjecture that *theatricarum* should be read in place of *thorentiarum*. The *χορευταί* (*choreutai*, “dancers”) are known from Plato and Aristotle; they both sang and danced. Such was Pelagia, a pantomime dancer.]

She proceeded with the greatest display, adorned in such a way that nothing seemed to be upon her except gold, pearls, and precious stones. The nakedness of her feet was covered with gold and pearls. She was accompanied by a great procession of boys and girls dressed in costly garments, and she wore a golden necklace around her neck.

Some went before her, while others followed. The beauty and splendor of her appearance could not satisfy the eyes of all worldly men. As she passed us, she filled the entire air with the scent of musk and the fragrance of other extremely sweet perfumes.

[Note: [Col. 0672A] *Musk.* Below, in the *Life of Saint Marcella*, chapter 3: “to smell fragrant with *musco mure* [perhaps ‘mouse-musk’].” See the *Onomasticon*.]

When the bishops saw her pass by in this manner, bareheaded and indecently displaying the whole arrangement of her limbs, with such a retinue that she had neither a veil placed over her head nor anything over her shoulders, they groaned in silence and turned their faces away as though from a grave sin.

### CHAPTER III

But the most blessed Nonnus looked at her intently and for a long time, so that after she had passed he continued to gaze at and observe her. Then he turned his face away and said to the bishops sitting around him:

“Were you not delighted by her great beauty?”

When they gave no answer, he placed his face upon his knees and, with the holy handkerchief which he held in his holy hands, filled his entire lap with tears. Sighing heavily, he said again to the bishops:

“Were you not delighted by her great beauty?”

When they still gave no answer, he said:

“Indeed, I was greatly delighted, and her beauty pleased me, because God has destined and appointed that she should stand before the sight of his awesome and wondrous throne, where he will judge both us and our episcopate.

“And again I say to you, bishops: What do you think? How many hours did this woman spend in her chamber, washing and arranging herself, adorning herself for the spectacle with every care and concentration of mind, so that nothing might be lacking from her bodily beauty and adornment, in order that she might please everyone and not appear ugly to her lovers, who exist today and do not exist tomorrow?

“Therefore, since we have a Father in heaven, the Almighty, and an immortal bride who grants promises to those who guard them—promises containing heavenly riches and eternal rewards that cannot be measured, things which the eye has not seen, nor the ear heard, nor entered into the human heart, which God has prepared for those who love him—why do I say more?

“Since we have the promise of seeing that great and splendid face, the inestimable countenance of the Bridegroom, at which the cherubim do not dare to look, we neither adorn nor cleanse the filth from our wretched souls, but negligently leave them lying there.”

### CHAPTER IV

After saying all these things, he took me, the sinful deacon, with him, and we came to the lodging where a cell had been given to us.

When he entered his room, he threw himself upon the floor, with his face toward the ground. Beating his breast, he wept and said:

“Lord Jesus Christ, forgive me, a sinner and an unworthy man, because the adornment of a prostitute for a single day has surpassed the adornment of my soul. With what face shall I look upon you? With what words shall I be justified in your sight?

“For I shall not hide my heart from you, since you see my secrets. Woe is me, a sinner and an unworthy man, because I stand before your altar and do not offer the beautiful soul that you require from me.

“She promised to please human beings, and she did so; I promised to please you, and through my laziness I lied. I am naked both in heaven and on earth, failing to fulfill the commands of your commandments.

“Therefore I have no hope from good works, but my hope is in your mercy, through which I trust that I shall be saved.”

While he was saying these things and wailing exceedingly because of them, we celebrated a solemn feast with great fervor that same day.

### CHAPTER V

When the following day, which is Sunday, arrived, after we had completed the nocturnal prayers, Saint Nonnus the bishop said to me:

“I tell you, brother deacon, that I had a dream and am greatly troubled because I cannot understand it.”

He immediately told me that he had dreamed that a black dove stood at the horn of the altar, covered with much filth. It flew around him, and he could not endure the stench and foulness of its filth.

It remained around him until the prayer of the catechumens was dismissed.

[Note: [Col. 0672A] “The prayer of the catechumens was dismissed.” The Mass of the faithful, or of the faithful, follows immediately. In former times the divine office was divided in such a way that one part was called the Mass of the catechumens and the other the Mass of the faithful.]

When the deacon proclaimed to the catechumens, “Depart,” it immediately disappeared from sight.

But after the Mass of the faithful and the completion of the offering, when the church had been dismissed and I was leaving the threshold of the house of God, that same dove came again, covered with much filth, and once more flew around me.

I stretched out my hand, seized it, and threw it into a basin that was in the courtyard of the holy church. It released into the water all the filth with which it had been covered, and it rose from the water white as snow. Then, taking flight, it was carried upward and was completely removed from my sight.

When the holy bishop Nonnus of God had related the dream, he took me with him. We came to the larger church with the other bishops and greeted the bishop of the city.

### CHAPTER VI

When he entered, he exhorted all the people of the church, who entered and sat upon their thrones. After the entire canonical celebration and the reading of the holy Gospel, the same bishop of the city handed the holy Gospel to the most blessed Nonnus and urged him to address the people.

He opened his mouth and spoke the wisdom of God that dwelt in him. He used neither rhetorical composition nor philosophy, nor did he speak anything confused or inappropriate, having nothing superfluous of human nature in him. Rather, filled with the Holy Spirit, he rebuked and admonished the people, speaking with complete sincerity about the future judgment and the eternal blessings that have been stored up.

The whole people was pierced with compunction by the words through which the Holy Spirit spoke by him, so that the pavement of the holy Church was flooded with the people’s tears.

### CHAPTER VII

By the working of divine mercy it happened that this prostitute also came to the same church, the woman about whom we have been speaking. And what is astonishing, she was a catechumen who had never shown concern for her sins and had never before come to the church of God.

Suddenly she was pierced by fear of the Lord when Saint Nonnus was rebuking the people. She despaired of herself, and the woman, weeping, poured forth streams of tears and could in no way restrain herself from crying.

Immediately she ordered two of her servants, saying:

“Wait here, and when Saint Nonnus the bishop has gone out, follow him and find out where he is staying. Then come and report it to me.”

The boys did as their mistress had commanded them. Following us, they came to the basilica of the blessed martyr Julian, where our lodging or cell was.

They returned and came to their mistress, saying: “He is staying in the basilica of the blessed martyr Julian.”

When she heard this, she immediately sent through the same boys a diptych of tablets containing the following:

[Note: [Col. 0672A] *Diptych of tablets.* Diptychs were two-leaved tablets used for various purposes. See the *Onomasticon*.]

“To the holy disciple of Christ, from the sinner and disciple of the devil.

“I have heard about your God, that he bowed the heavens and descended upon earth, not for the sake of the righteous but to save sinners (Matthew IX). He humbled himself so greatly that he approached tax collectors, and he lived among sinners, although the cherubim do not dare to look upon him.

“And you, my lord, who possess great holiness—even if you have not seen with bodily eyes the Lord Jesus Christ himself, who revealed himself to that sinful Samaritan woman at the well (John IV)—you are nevertheless his true worshiper, as I have heard Christians report.

“If you are truly a disciple of that Christ, do not reject me, who through you desire to see the Savior, so that through you I may be deemed worthy to see his holy face.”

Then Saint Nonnus the bishop wrote back to her:

“Whatever you are, you are manifest to God—both you and your purpose and your will. Nevertheless I tell you not to attempt my humility, for I am a sinful man and a servant of God.

“If you truly possess a desire for divinity, the power to obtain virtue, and faith, and if you wish to see me, other bishops are with me. Come, and you will see me before them; you will not be able to see me alone.”

When the prostitute had read it, filled with joy she ran to the basilica of the blessed martyr Julian and announced to us her arrival.

When the holy bishop Nonnus heard this, he summoned all the bishops who were there and ordered her to come to him.

When she approached the place where the bishops were gathered, she threw herself upon the floor and seized the feet of the blessed bishop Nonnus, saying:

“I beg you, my lord, imitate your teacher, the Lord Jesus Christ. Pour out your goodness upon me and make me a Christian. For I, my lord, am a sea of sins and an abyss of iniquity. I ask to be baptized.”

## Chapter VIII

When the holy Bishop Nonnus had scarcely persuaded her to rise from his feet, and she had risen, he said to her:

“The priestly canons contain a prohibition against baptizing a prostitute unless she has provided sponsors, so that she may not return again to those same evils.”

[Note: The canons formerly forbade anyone to be admitted to baptism without a sponsor or guarantor. This was observed with much greater care in the case of prostitutes and actors, whose conversion was more doubtful.]

When she heard this sentence from the bishop, she threw herself once more upon the pavement, seized the feet of Saint Nonnus, washed them with her tears, and wiped them with her hair, saying:

“You will have to give an account to God for my soul, and I shall charge you with the guilt of my deeds if you delay baptizing me, wicked and utterly disgraceful as I am. May you find no portion with God among the saints unless you now make me a stranger to my evil deeds. May you deny God and worship idols unless you cause me today to be reborn as Christ’s bride and offer me to God.” [Col. 0667D]

Then all the bishops and clerics who had assembled, seeing such a sinner uttering such words out of desire for God, said in amazement that they had never seen such faith and desire for salvation as this prostitute’s.

Immediately they sent me, the sinful deacon, to the bishop of the city, so that I might report all these things to him and ask his Blessedness to send with me one of the deaconesses. When he heard this, he rejoiced with great joy, saying:

“Well, venerable father; these are the works awaiting you. I know that you will be my mouth.” [Col. 0668A]

At once he sent with me the lady Romana, chief of the deaconesses. When she arrived, she found her still at the feet of the holy Bishop Nonnus. She could scarcely persuade her to rise from his feet, saying:

“Rise, daughter, so that you may be exorcized.”

And she said to her:

“Confess all your sins.”

She replied:

“If I were to search through the knowledge of my heart, I would find no deeds of goodness in myself. I know that my sins are heavier than the sand of the sea; indeed, water is very small compared with the mass of my sins. Yet I trust in your God, that he will forgive the weight of my iniquities and look upon me.”

Then the holy Bishop Nonnus said to her:

“What is your name?”

She replied:

“My natural name, given to me by my parents, is Pelagia; but the citizens of Antioch call me Margarita, ‘Pearl,’ because of the weight of the ornaments with which my sins have adorned me. For I was the adornment and decorated workshop of the devil.”

Again the holy Bishop Nonnus said to her:

“Are you called Pelagia by your natural name?”

She replied:

“Yes, my lord.”

When he heard this, the holy Bishop Nonnus exorcized her and baptized her. He placed upon her the sign of the Lord and gave her the body of Christ.

Her spiritual mother was the holy Lady Romana, chief of the deaconesses. She took her up into the catechumenium, since we also were staying there.

[Note: “Catechumenium” means the place of the catechumens in the church, which was separated from the place of the faithful.]

Then the holy Bishop Nonnus said to me:

“I tell you, brother deacon, let us rejoice today with the angels of God, and let us take oil in our food beyond the customary measure, and receive wine with spiritual joy, because of this girl’s salvation.” [Col. 0668C]

## Chapter IX

While we were eating, voices were suddenly heard, like the voice of a man undergoing violence. For the devil cried out, saying:

“Woe, woe! What am I suffering at the hands of this decrepit old man? Were the thirty thousand Saracens whom you snatched away from me, baptized, and offered to your God not enough for you? Was Heliopolis not enough for you? Although it was mine, and all who dwelt in it worshiped me, you snatched it away from me and offered it to your God. And now you have taken away my greatest hope; now I can no longer endure your schemes. Oh, what I am suffering at the hands of this accursed man! Cursed be the day on which you were born! Rivers of tears flood my wretched dwelling; now my hope has been taken away.” [Col. 0668D]

The devil cried out all these things and lamented before the doors, and he was heard by everyone.

Then, repeating himself, he said to the newly baptized girl:

“You do this to me, my lady Pelagia, and do you imitate my Judas? He was crowned with glory and honor and appointed an apostle, yet he betrayed his Lord; so you have done to me.”

Then the holy Bishop Nonnus said to her:

“Sign yourself with the cross of Christ and renounce him.”

She made the sign of the cross in Christ’s name and blew upon the demon, and immediately he disappeared completely.

## Chapter X

Two days later, while she was sleeping in her room with her spiritual mother, Saint Romana, the devil appeared at night and awakened God’s servant Pelagia. He said:

“I beg you, my lady Margarita, were you not enriched with gold and silver? Did I not adorn you with gold and precious gems? I beg you, what have I done to grieve you? Answer me, so that I may satisfy you; only do not make me a reproach among Christians.”

Then God’s servant Pelagia made the sign of the cross and blew upon the demon, saying:

“My God, who rescued me from the midst of your teeth and led me into his heavenly bridal chamber—he himself will resist you on my behalf.”

Immediately the devil disappeared completely. [Col. 0669A]

## Chapter XI

On the third day after Saint Pelagia had been baptized, she summoned the young man who managed all her affairs and said to him:

“Go to my wardrobe and write down everything that is there, whether gold, silver, ornaments, or costly garments, and bring it to me.”

The young man did as his mistress commanded and brought all her wealth. [Col. 0669B]

She immediately summoned the holy Bishop Nonnus through her spiritual mother, Saint Romana, and placed all her wealth in his hands, saying:

“These are the riches with which Satan enriched me. I hand them over to your holiness’s discretion; do with them what you know to be expedient. For the riches I desire are those of my Lord Jesus Christ.”

He immediately summoned the senior church steward and, with her present, placed all her wealth in his hands, saying:

“I adjure you by the indivisible Trinity: do not allow anything from this to enter the bishop’s residence or the church. Rather, distribute it to widows, orphans, and the poor, so that what was wrongly acquired may be rightly distributed, and the wealth of the sinner may become treasures of righteousness.

“But if, disregarding this oath, whether by yourself or through anyone else, you remove anything from it, may anathema enter his house, and may he share the lot of those who said, ‘Let him be crucified, let him be crucified.’”

She then summoned all her young men and young women and set them all free. She also gave them gold neck-rings (*tortos*) from her own hand, saying:

“Hasten and free yourselves from this wicked world, full of sins, so that just as we were together in this world, so we may remain together without sorrow in that life which is supremely blessed.” [Col. 0669C]

[Note: “Tortos.” So the old edition reads. The Cologne edition has *torques*, necklaces.]

## Chapter XII

On the eighth day, when she was to remove her white baptismal garments, she rose at night without our knowledge, took off her baptismal clothing, and put on a *tricina* tunic and the *birra* of the holy Bishop Nonnus. From that day she was nowhere seen in the city of Antioch. [Col. 0669D]

[Note: “Tricinam.” The edited copies add, “that is, made of haircloth.”]

[Note: “Birram.” *Birra* now signifies either a costly or an inexpensive garment. See the *Onomasticon*.]

Saint Romana wept for her most bitterly, but Saint Nonnus consoled her, saying:

“Do not weep, daughter, but rejoice with great joy, because Pelagia has chosen the better portion, like Mary, whom the Lord in the Gospel preferred to Martha.”

She went away to Jerusalem and built herself a cell on the Mount of Olives, where the Lord prayed.

## Chapter XIII

After some time the bishop of the city summoned all the bishops, so that each might return to his own place.

After three or four years had passed, I, the deacon Jacob, desired to go to Jerusalem, so that I might worship there the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ. I asked my bishop to permit me to go.

When he had permitted me to leave, he said to me:

“I tell you, brother deacon: when you reach Jerusalem, seek out there a certain brother Pelagius, a monk and eunuch, who has lived enclosed in solitude for many years, as though you were going to visit him. For you will truly be able to receive help from him.” [Col. 0670A]

He said all this to me about God’s servant Pelagia without revealing the truth openly.

## Chapter XIV

I therefore reached Jerusalem and worshiped the holy resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ. The next day I sought out the servant of God.

I approached and found him on the Mount of Olives, where the Lord prayed, in a small cell enclosed on every side, with a little window in the wall.

I struck the door of the little window, and he immediately opened it and recognized me. I, however, did not recognize her. For how could I have recognized the woman whom I had formerly seen possessed of indescribable beauty, now withered in face from excessive abstinence? Her eyes appeared like hollows.

She said to me:

“Where do you come from, brother?”

I answered:

“I have been sent to you at the command of Bishop Nonnus.”

She said to me:

“Pray for me, for he is truly a holy man of God.”

Immediately she closed the little window and began to sing the office of the third hour.

I prayed beside the wall of her cell and departed, greatly helped by the angelic vision of her. [Col. 0670B]

When I returned to Jerusalem, I began to visit the brethren by walking among the monasteries.

## Chapter XV

A great reputation for the lord Pelagius was spreading through the monasteries. Therefore I decided to return to him once more and refresh myself with his salutary teachings. [Col. 0670C]

When I reached his cell and dared to knock—or rather, to call to him by name—he gave no answer.

I waited, persevering through the second and third days, calling Pelagius by his proper name, but I heard no one.

So I said within myself:

“Either no one is here, or the monk who was here has departed.”

Then, warned by God’s prompting, I said again:

“Let me consider whether he may perhaps be dead.”

I opened the little window, looked inside, and saw him dead. I closed the window, carefully filled it with mud, and hurried to Jerusalem. I reported to those living there that the holy monk Pelagius, who had performed wonders, had fallen asleep.

Then the holy fathers came with monks from various monasteries. The opening of the cell was unsealed, and his little holy body was carried outside. They placed it honorably in gold and precious stones. [Col. 0670D]

While the holy fathers were anointing the body with myrrh, they discovered that it had been a woman. They wanted to conceal the miracle, but it could not be hidden from the people themselves. So they cried out in a loud voice, saying:

“Glory to you, Lord Jesus Christ, who have many hidden riches upon the earth—not only those of men, but also those of women.”

The news was spread among all the people. All the monasteries of virgins came, both from Jericho and from the Jordan, where the Lord was baptized, carrying candles, lamps, and hymns. Thus the holy relics of Pelagia were laid to rest and carried by the holy fathers.

This is the life of a prostitute; this is the conduct of one who had despaired. May the Lord cause us, together with her, to find his mercy on the day of judgment; for his are honor and glory, power and dominion forever and ever. Amen. [Col. 0671]

# April 2. The Life of Saint Mary the Egyptian, the Prostitute, by Sophronius, Bishop of Jerusalem; Translated by Paul, Deacon of the Holy Church of Naples

[Note: “Mariae.” The Roman Martyrology, April 2: “In Palestine, the burial of Saint Mary of Egypt, who is called the Sinner.” The Greek Menologion, April 1: “Of our holy mother Mary of Egypt, who, after having led a wanton and shameful life for seventeen years, turned to a better way of life and became such that she also demonstrated her virtue by many miracles; for she lived forty-seven years in such a way that she had no spectator except God himself.”

“Mary of Egypt flourished during the reign of the elder Emperor Justin, around the year of our Lord 520. At nearly the same time there lived another repentant woman, also named Mary, formerly a prostitute and a native of Tarsus, who practiced the monastic life in a monastery situated at Aegae. She is mentioned in the *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 21.”]

[Note: “Sophronio.” Nicephorus testifies that Sophronius was the author of this Life, book VII, chapter 5. The same work is cited under Sophronius’s name at the Second Council of Nicaea, act 4, and by Saint John of Damascus in his third Oration on Images.

The *Triodion* also mentions it when, on Thursday of the fifth week of Lent, it speaks of Andrew of Crete, archbishop and author of the Great Canon:

Greek: “He composed this when the great Sophronius, patriarch of Jerusalem, had also written the Life of Mary of Egypt; for this Life too is presented as full of infinite compunction and gives much consolation to those who have fallen and sinned, if only they are willing to withdraw from wicked deeds.”

Sophronius’s annual commemoration is celebrated by the Latins on March 11. The Roman Martyrology: “At Jerusalem, Saint Sophronius, bishop.” The Greek Menologion on the same day: “Of our holy father Sophronius, patriarch of Jerusalem, from the city of Damascus, distinguished by manifold learning, knowledge of divine letters, and piety.”

For the beginning of his episcopate, see Baronius under the year 633; and for his death, under the year 636. Sophronius is also discussed in the *Miscellaneous History*, book XVIII, year 20 of the Emperor Heraclius, and book XIX, year 26 of the same emperor; by Cedrenus, year 20 of the same emperor; and by Zonaras, in the third part of the *Annals*, under Heraclius.]

[Note: “Paulo.” Sigebert, in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 69: “Paul, a deacon of the Neapolitan church, translated the Life of Saint Mary of Egypt from Greek into Latin.”

Bishop Hildebert of Le Mans also expressed the same account in verse, as Henry of Ghent reports in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Writers*, chapter 8: “Hildebert, first bishop of Le Mans and afterward archbishop of Tours, who flourished in both prose and verse, wrote the Life of Mary of Egypt in elegant meter.” I possess a manuscript copy of it.]

## Preface of the Translator

To the most glorious and eminent lord, King Charles. [Col. 0671]

Knowing that your most glorious Majesty takes great pleasure both in divine sayings and in the examples of the saints who came before us, I had previously offered my lord a little book concerning the conversion of Mary of Egypt, together with a short account of the repentance of a certain vicedominus.

[Note: “Vicedomini.” This refers to Theophilus, whose feast occurs on February 4. His story may be found in Surius, volume I, though by another translator. See the *Onomasticon*.]

Since that work was lost through some accident, I have now obediently devoted myself to restoring it at your command. [Col. 0690B]

It was also an act of my service and devotion that I should present not merely the simple text of the work mentioned, but should add other matters worthy of investigation, concerning, namely, the venerable constitutions and deeds of the prelates of the Roman Church, whose sanctions the Church uses with such reverence, as your Majesty knows very well.

[Note: “Constitutis.” I do not know what constitutions are meant here.]

Your servant adopted this concise form for the sake of brevity so that your Serenity, whom I understand to be greatly burdened with the affairs of the state and unable to traverse at leisure the scattered volumes of different writers, might possess certain ecclesiastical customs collected briefly, as in a kind of *Enchiridion*. [Col. 0671]

I have learned that, in accordance with your royal diligence, my lord’s zeal burns in this matter: that the direction of your actions and words according to irrefragable authority, and the careful investigation and examination of what ought to be maintained and what rejected in the worship of God, are the subject of continual study—so that, strengthened by the help of his divinity, you may be enabled to proceed toward all things with prosperous success.

## Prologue of the Author

To conceal a king’s secret is good; but to reveal and confess the works of God is honorable (Tobit XII). [Col. 0671]

Thus, it is read, the angel spoke to Tobit after the loss of his sight and his glorious illumination, and after those dangers had passed through which he was delivered and obtained God’s mercy.

For to disclose a king’s secret is harmful and exceedingly dangerous, while to keep silent about God’s glorious works is a great loss to the soul.

Therefore, although I hesitate to conceal divine matters in silence and fear the impending judgment and condemnation of the lazy servant who, having received a talent from his lord, dug in the earth, hid it, and concealed the gift given for use instead of putting it to work (Matthew XXV), I shall by no means keep silent about the sacred account brought to me.

Let no one disbelieve me as I write about what I have heard, nor let anyone, doubting the greatness of the matter, think that I am lying. Far be it from me to lie about sacred matters or corrupt the word where God is mentioned.

The danger will not belong to me if someone understands little, or judges unworthily concerning the greatness of God, who assumed flesh, and is unbelieving toward the one who tells these things.

But if there are some who read the text of this writing and indeed refuse to believe the glorious wonder of the event, may the Lord have mercy on them and make them capable of understanding the sacred word, lest they become guilty concerning God’s miracles, of which he predestined many to occur among his chosen ones. [Col. 0673]

For they too, considering the weakness of human nature, declare impossible those things that are gloriously said to have occurred among holy people.

I shall now take up the narrative itself, reporting the event that is known to have taken place in our own generation, as it was related by a holy man trained both to perform and to teach divine things.

But, as stated above, let no one be led to disbelief by considering it impossible that so great a miracle could occur in our generation. For the grace of God, passing through holy souls in every generation, makes them friends of God and prophets, as Solomon taught according to God’s wisdom (Wisdom VII).

It is now time to disclose the beginning of the sacred account: the great and manly contest of the venerable Mary of Egypt, namely, how she completed the course of her life.

# Life

## Chapter I

In a monastery of Palestine there was a man adorned in conduct and speech, who from his earliest infancy had been carefully instructed in monastic practices and truthfully formed in the monastic way of life. His name was Zosimas. [Col. 0673A]

[Note: “Zozimas.” Elsewhere, Sosimus. The Roman Martyrology, April 4: “In Palestine, Saint Zosimas the anchorite, who cared for the burial of Saint Mary of Egypt.”]

Let no one suppose that we mean that Zosimas who was accused of belonging to another sect’s erroneous doctrines. This is one man, and that is another; there is much difference between them, although both happened to bear the same name.

This Zosimas had lived from the beginning in one of the monasteries of Palestine. Passing through the whole monastic discipline, he became outstanding among all in the practice of abstinence.

He observed irreproachably every commandment of the rule handed down to him by those who had been trained from childhood, maintaining the struggle of perfect monastic discipline. [Col. 0673B] He also added many things of his own, wishing to subject the flesh to the spirit. He is not known to have offended in any matter.

Indeed, he was so perfect in all monastic practices that many monks, coming to him repeatedly from the monasteries of that region and from distant places, bound themselves by his examples and teachings and subjected themselves even more strictly to abstinence in imitation of him.

## Chapter II

Possessing all these qualities, he never departed from meditation on sacred discourse. Whether resting on his bed, rising, working with his hands, or taking food when it was appropriate for him to do so, he used spiritually the good in which he was accustomed to partake.

He had one task that was never interrupted and never failed: to sing psalms frequently and meditate on sacred discourse. [Col. 0673C]

Many times, they say, he was also deemed worthy of divine illumination, and visions were shown to him by God. This is neither astonishing nor unbelievable. For if, as the Lord says, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew V), how much more do those who have purified their flesh, always sober and watchful in spirit, behold with the eyes of divine illumination, receiving in this way an indication of the goodness of the vision prepared for them?

Zosimas himself said that he had been handed over to this monastery, so to speak, from his mother’s arms, and that he had completed the monastic course there up to his fifty-third year. [Col. 0674A]

After this he was troubled by certain thoughts, as though he were already perfect in every respect and needed no instruction from anyone in anything.

As he said, he thought within himself:

“Is there a monk on earth who could teach me something new, someone able to help me in something I do not know or in something I have not fulfilled in monastic practice? Is there among those who have lived in solitude a man who surpasses me in his works?”

While he was thinking these and similar thoughts, someone stood before him and said:

“O Zosimas, you have indeed decided well, and as far as was possible for a human being; you have brought your monastic course to a good completion. Yet no human being demonstrates that he is perfect. The present struggle is greater than the one that has passed, although you do not know it. [Col. 0674B]

“But so that you may learn how many other paths of salvation there are, go out from your land, your kindred, and your father’s house, like that outstanding patriarch Abraham (Genesis XII), and come to the monastery situated beside the Jordan River.”

## Chapter III

Immediately, therefore, he followed the speaker. He left the monastery in which he had lived from infancy and, reaching the Jordan, the holiest of all rivers, was directed by the one who had called him to the monastery to which God had commanded him to go.

When he knocked at the monastery door, he first spoke with the monk who guarded it, and that monk announced him to the abbot.

The abbot received him and, seeing from his habit and appearance that he was a religious man, knelt—as is customary among monks—and, after receiving the prayer, asked him:

“Where have you come from, brother, and for what reason have you joined these humble monks?” [Col. 0674C]

Zosimas replied:

“Where I have come from, I do not think it necessary to say. But I have come, Father, for the sake of edification. I have heard great and praiseworthy things about you, and that you are able to join a soul to God.”

The abbot said to him:

“May God, brother, who alone heals the sickness of the soul, teach both you and us his divine commandments and direct everyone to do what is appropriate. For one human being cannot edify another unless each person frequently pays attention to himself and, with sober understanding, does what is beneficial, having God as his co-worker. [Col. 0675A]

“Nevertheless, since, as you have said, the love of Christ has brought you to see us humble monks, remain with us if this is why you have come. May the good shepherd nourish us all with the grace of his Holy Spirit, he who gave his soul for our deliverance and calls his own sheep by name (Matthew XX; John X).”

When the abbot had said this, Zosimas knelt again, received the prayer, answered “Amen,” and remained in that monastery.

## Chapter IV

There he saw elders shining in conduct and appearance, fervent in spirit and serving the Lord. [Col. 0675B]

There was continual psalmody, with unceasing vigils throughout the whole night; work was always in their hands, and divine psalms were continually in their mouths, without diminution.

[Note: “Psallentia.” This was the expression they used at that time. The term *psallentium* frequently occurs in Gregory of Tours. See the *Onomasticon*.]

Idle speech had no place there. There was no thought among them of gold, silver, or any other possession. The expenditure of the entire year, its measure, or reflections on temporal life—matters appropriate to sorrow—were not even known by name among them.

There was only one first concern, which all hastened to accomplish: that each person should be dead in body, as though dead once for all to the world, mortified to the things of the world, and no longer living.

Their unfailing food was the utterances of divinity. They nourished the body with bread and water, so that they might appear all the more effective before the divine mercy.

## Chapter V

Seeing these things, Zosimas, as he said, was greatly edified. He stretched himself toward perfection and caused his own course to grow, finding co-workers who were renewing God’s paradise in an excellent manner. [Col. 0675C]

After some days had passed, the time approached when the sacred fasts handed down to Christians were celebrated, when they purified themselves in preparation for the day of the divine Passion and the celebration of the Resurrection.

The monastery’s main gate was never opened; it was always closed. The monks completed their course without any disturbance. It was not permitted to open it except, perhaps, when a monk came for some necessary task.

That place was solitary and was not only unfamiliar but unknown to most of the neighboring people.

Such was the rule observed from ancient times. For this reason, as I understand it, God led Zosimas to that monastery. [Col. 0675D]

[Note: “Regia.” Thus the manuscript reads. Other editions have “door.” It refers to the monastery’s first gate, which was called the *Regia*. See the *Onomasticon*.]

## Chapter VI

I shall now relate how the tradition of that monastery was observed.

On the Sunday customarily called the first week of the fast, the divine mysteries were celebrated as usual, and everyone partook of the life-giving and undefiled body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.

After taking a small amount of food, as was customary, they all gathered in the oratory. With knees bent and prayer offered humbly, the monks greeted one another. Each, kneeling publicly, embraced the abbot and asked for his prayer, so that they might have him as a co-worker and companion in the contest they were beginning.

When these things had been done, the monastery doors were opened. Singing with one voice, “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the defender of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?” and so forth (Psalm XXVI), they went out, leaving one or two monastery guardians behind—not to guard what had been stored inside, for there was nothing among them suitable for thieves, but so that the oratory would not be left without the divine offices. [Col. 0676A]

Each person carried provisions according to what he could or wished to carry.

[Note: “Annonabat.” Thus the manuscript reads. Surius has, “He carried provisions.” Another version has, “He carried what was necessary for life.”]

One carried something sufficient for the body in measured quantity.

[Note: “Something sufficient for the body in measured quantity.” Surius has, “Water sufficient for the body in measured quantity.” Another version has, “A small loaf to support the frailty of the body.” I suspect that the word *paximatium*, which another version interprets as “a small loaf,” has been omitted in our text.]

Another carried dried dates; another, palm fruits; another, legumes soaked in water; and another nothing except his own body and the clothing he wore. [Page 384]

When nature’s necessity demanded it, they were nourished by the herbs that grew throughout the wilderness.

Each person was his own canon and law, without transgression, so that no one knew how his companion practiced abstinence or how he conducted himself. [Col. 0676B]

For as soon as they crossed the Jordan, they separated far from one another, and no one joined himself to another, considering the solitude a city.

If one of them saw someone approaching from a distance, he immediately turned aside from the path and went in another direction.

He lived for himself and God, frequently singing psalms and taking food at the appointed time.

They observed all the fasts in this way and returned to the monastery before the life-giving day of the resurrection of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, the solemn Sunday that the holy Church has received as the feast celebrated with palm branches.

Each returned bearing as the witness of his own labor his own conscience, which knew how he had worked and what seeds of labor he had sown. No one in any way asked another how or in what manner he had completed the contests of labor. [Col. 0676C]

## Chapter VII

This, then, was the rule of that monastery, and it was guarded perfectly and excellently.

As has been said, each person was joined to God through the wilderness and fought within himself, so that he might please not human beings but God alone.

For the things done for human beings, and those performed in order to please human beings, will not only fail to benefit those who do them but will also bring many harms upon the people who perform them.

At that time Zosimas crossed the Jordan according to the monastery’s customary rule, carrying a small amount suitable for the body’s needs and the clothing he wore. [Col. 0676D]

He observed the rule as he traversed the wilderness and satisfied nature’s need at the time of eating.

At night he sat upon the ground, resting a little and taking a little sleep wherever the evening hour found him.

At dawn he began to hasten onward, always holding the same unceasing purpose. As he said, he desired to enter deeper into the wilderness, hoping to find some father living there who might edify him in the way he desired.

He continued on his journey without stopping, as though hurrying toward someone plainly visible.

After completing a journey of twenty days, when the sixth hour had arrived, he stopped briefly on the road. Turning toward the east, he performed his customary prayer.

For he was accustomed, at the appointed time of day, to halt his journey, stand, sing psalms, and pray on his knees. [Col. 0677A]

While he was singing psalms and gazing intently into heaven, he saw on the right-hand side, where he was praying, what appeared to be a shadow in the form of a human body.

At first he was disturbed and trembled, thinking that he had seen the apparition of some spirit. But he fortified himself with the sign of the cross and cast fear away from himself—for the end of his prayer was already approaching.

Then, turning his eyes, he saw someone truly hastening toward the west.

It appeared to be a woman, her body exceedingly blackened by the heat of the sun, with hair on her head white like wool, though scanty and reaching no farther than her neck.

## Chapter VIII

When Zosimas saw this, he was filled with joy at the sweetness he had long desired, and began to run swiftly toward the place to which the other apparition was hastening. For during those days he had seen neither human form nor the shape of any animal, bird, or wild beast. He wished to know what, or what sort of creature, it was that he saw, hoping that it might bring him some profit from the elders.

But when the fugitive saw Zosimas coming toward it, it began to run away toward the lower part of the wilderness. Zosimas, forgetting the infirmity of old age and reckoning nothing of the toil of the journey, ran at the utmost speed, desiring to see the one who fled. He pursued, and it went on ahead. Zosimas ran more swiftly and gradually came nearer.

When he was close enough that his voice could be heard, Zosimas began to cry out with tears:

“Why do you flee from me, an old and sinful man, servant of God? By God, whoever you are, for whose name you inhabit this wilderness, wait for me. Wait for me, infirm and unworthy as I am. Wait for me for the hope you have of the recompense of so great a labor. Stop, and grant prayer and blessing to an old man, for the sake of God, who has never cast anyone away.” [Col. 0677C]

As Zosimas made this plea with tears, they came running to a place marked out like a dry torrent-bed. He judged that a torrent had once been there; the place had the appearance appropriate to such a feature in that land.

When they came to the said place, the fugitive descended into it and climbed up again on the other side. Zosimas, unable to go forward anywhere, stood on the other side of the torrent-bed, which seemed to have the appearance of a torrent. He added tears to tears and increased sighs upon sighs, so that he might hear more closely the harsh sound of lamentation. [Col. 0677D]

### Chapter XI

Then that fleeing body uttered such a voice:

“Abba Zosimas, forgive me for God’s sake, because I cannot turn and reveal myself to you. For I am a woman, and, as you see, naked of every bodily covering, with the shame of my body uncovered. But if you truly wish to offer a prayer to a sinful woman, throw me the garment with which you are clothed, so that, turning toward you, I may cover my feminine weakness, and receive your prayers.”

Then excessive trembling, great fear, and mental bewilderment seized Zosimas. For that man was exceedingly vigorous, and, by the gift of divinity, most discerning; and he understood that she would not have called him by name—someone whom she had never seen and of whom she had never heard—unless the grace of providence had most manifestly enlightened her.

He promptly did what he had been told. Removing the cloak with which he was clothed, he threw it backward to her. Taking it, she covered as much as she could of that part of her body which ought to be covered more than the rest, girded herself, and, turning toward Zosimas, said to him:

“What did you think, abba, on seeing a sinful woman? What do you seek to see or learn from me, since you have not been too reluctant to endure such labor?”

But he, prostrate on the ground, asked to receive a blessing according to custom. She too prostrated herself, and both lay upon the ground, each asking a blessing from the other.

### Chapter X

After many hours had passed, the woman said to Zosimas:

“Abba Zosimas, it is fitting for you to bless and pray; for you are supported by the dignity of the priesthood, have served at the holy altar for many years, and by the gifts of Christ’s divinity search out the mysteries.”

These words drove Zosimas into even greater fear and struggle, and the trembling old man was drenched in drops of sweat. Exhausted and almost breathless, he said to her:

“By the very vision, O spiritual mother, you are already manifest: you have departed to the Lord, and have died in the stronger part. But above all, grace has been granted to you, that you should call by name one whom you had never seen. Yet since grace is not recognized by dignity, but is customarily revealed through the actions of souls, bless me for God’s sake, and grant the prayer of your perfect indulgence.”

Moved with compassion for the holy old man’s steadfastness, she said:

“Blessed is the Lord, who provides salvation for souls.”

When Zosimas answered, “Amen,” both rose from the ground.

The woman said to the old man:

“Why, then, have you come to me, a sinful woman? Nevertheless, since the grace of the Holy Spirit has directed you to offer some service suited to the smallness of my body, tell me how the most Christian people is governed today, how the emperors fare, and how the flock of the holy Church is fed.”

Zosimas answered:

“Mother, through your holy prayers God has granted lasting peace. But receive the consolation of an unworthy monk, and pray to the Lord for the whole world and for me, a sinner, so that the labor of this journey and course may not prove fruitless for me on the road through so great a solitude.”

She replied:

“You, abba Zosimas, being possessed of the honor of the priesthood, as I said, ought to pray for everyone and for me; for this purpose also you were called. But since we have the commandment of obedience, I shall willingly do what you have ordered me.”

Saying this, she turned toward the east, raised her eyes on high, stretched out her hands, and began to pray, moving only her lips in silence. Her voice could not be heard at all distinctly. Thus Zosimas could recognize none of the words of her prayer.
