As she stood—so he said—trembling, looking at the ground and saying nothing at all, he swore, calling God to witness his statement, that when he saw her persevering steadfastly in prayer, he raised his eyes a little from the ground and saw her lifted about one cubit above the earth, praying suspended in the air.

When he saw this, he was seized with overwhelming fear, threw himself upon the ground, drenched in sweat and terrified beyond measure, and dared say nothing. Within himself he said:

“Lord, have mercy on me.”

### Chapter XI

As he lay prostrate upon the ground, he was troubled in mind, wondering whether she might be a spirit pretending to pray. But the woman turned, raised the monk, and said:

“What is troubling you, abba? Why are your thoughts making you suspicious of me, because I am a spirit and am offering a feigned prayer? Be assured, man, that I am a little sinful woman, though I have been enclosed within holy baptism. I am not a spirit, but dust and ashes, wholly flesh, and I have never entertained in my mind any spiritual apparition.”

Saying this, she made the sign of the cross upon her forehead, her eyes, and her lips; and at the same time, impressing the banner of the cross upon her breast, she said:

“May God, abba Zosimas, free us from the adversary and from his assaults, for his envy against us is great.”

Hearing this, the old man prostrated himself and grasped her feet, saying with tears:

“I beseech you by the Lord Jesus Christ, our true Lord, who deigned to be born of a virgin, for whose sake you have put on this nakedness, for whose sake you have spent these bodily members: hide nothing from your servant. Tell me who you are, from where you came, when you came, and for what reason you inhabit this solitude; and tell me everything concerning you, so that you may make God’s mighty works manifest.

“For what benefit are hidden wisdom and a concealed treasure, as it is written (Ecclus. XX)? Tell me everything for God’s sake. You do not speak for boasting or display, but to satisfy me, a sinner and an unworthy man. I believe in the God for whom you live and with whom you converse, that for this very purpose I have been directed into this solitude: so that God may make manifest what concerns you.

“For it is not within our power to resist God’s judgments. If it had not been pleasing to Christ the Lord to reveal you and how you struggled, he would not have permitted you to be seen by anyone, nor would he have strengthened me to hasten along so great a road, unable to advance or even to leave my cell.”

### Chapter XII

While he was saying this and much more, the woman raised him and said:

“I am truly ashamed, my abba, to tell you of the shamefulness of my deeds. Nevertheless, since you have seen my naked body, I shall also lay bare before you the works of my actions, so that you may know how full my soul is of the shame of lust and the disgrace of confusion.

“For I do not wish to relate what concerns me for the sake of any glory, as you yourself have understood. What could I glory in, when I became a vessel chosen for the devil? Yet I know that if I begin to tell what concerns me, you will flee from me, as one flees from the face of a serpent, unable to hear with his ears the things I have done, which cannot be endured.

“I shall speak, denying nothing, but reporting everything truthfully. First I beg you not to cease praying for me, so that I may merit and find mercy on the day of judgment.”

The old man, drenched in tears, wept. Then the woman began to relate what concerned her, saying:

### Chapter XIII

“I had Egypt as my homeland, Father. While my parents were still living, when I was twelve years old, scorning their affection, I came to Alexandria. I am ashamed to consider how I first violated my virginity and how I lay continually and insatiably enslaved to the vice of lust.

“For it would take too long to tell. I shall say this more briefly, so that you may recognize the insatiable ardor of my vice, which I possessed for the love of fornication. For seventeen years and more I spent my time publicly lying in the fire of lust. I did not lose my virginity in exchange for anyone’s gift; nor did I accept anything from those who wished to give me something. For, inflamed by the madness of lust, I considered this: that I should make more people run to me, freely satisfying the desire of my fornication and crime.

“Nor should you suppose that I accepted nothing because of wealth. I lived by begging, or very often by spinning flax. For, as I said, I had an insatiable desire, so that I continually wallowed in the dungheap of lust. This pleased me, and I regarded this as life: to commit violence against nature without ceasing.

“While I was living in this manner, during a season of intense heat I saw a multitude of Libyans and Egyptians running as if toward the sea. I found someone and asked him:

‘Where are these men hurrying, running as they are?’

“He said to me:

‘They are all going up to Jerusalem because of the Exaltation of the holy Cross, which is customarily celebrated after a few days.’

“I said to him:

‘Do you think they will receive me if I wish to go with them?’

“He said:

‘If you have the fare, no one will prevent you.’

“I said to him:

‘Indeed, brother, I have neither fare nor provisions. I shall go and board one of the ships they have hired. Even if they refuse, I shall surrender myself; for, having my body in their power, they will accept it as my fare.’

“I wished to travel with them for this reason—my abba, forgive me—so that I might have many accomplices in the passion of my lust.”

### Chapter XIV

“I told you, my lord and old man, forgive me; do not force me to speak of my shame. I tremble, for the Lord knows that these words of mine defile even the air.”

Zosimas, watering the ground with his tears, answered her:

“Speak for God’s sake, my mother; speak, and do not omit what follows in so salutary a narrative.”

Adding this to her earlier account, she continued:

“But when that young man heard the obscurity of my words [Note: [Col. 0690D] *Obscuritatem.* So read by three manuscripts. Surius and other editions have *scurrilitatem*, ‘vulgarity.’ But Paulus may have formed *obscuritatem*, or *obscurritatem*, from *scurra*, ‘buffoon.’], he laughed and went away.

“I threw down the distaff that I held in my hand—for after some time it would have been fitting for me to hold it—and ran to the sea. There I saw them running, and I saw several young men standing on the shore, about ten in number, very vigorous in body and sharp-featured, and excellent for what pleased me. Others had already boarded the ships.

“Impudently, as was my custom, I rushed into their midst, saying:

‘Take me with you wherever you are going; I shall not be disagreeable to you.’

“Adding still filthier words, I made them all laugh. When they saw my shameless behavior, they took me up and carried me into the small boat. From there we began our voyage.

“But how can I tell you, man of God, what happened afterward? What tongue can speak, or ear hear, the things that took place in the little boat and on the journey? How I, willingly, compelled those wretched men to sin when they did not wish it! It is not something that can be narrated, but an unspeakable and utterly wicked spectacle, of which I then became the wretched instructress in crimes.

“So now be satisfied. I am astonished that that sea endured the lusts of my iniquities; that the earth did not open its mouth and plunge me alive into hell, when I led so many souls into the snare of death.

“But, as I believe, God—who does not wish anyone to perish but all to be saved (1 Tim. II)—was seeking my repentance. For he does not desire the death of a sinner, but patiently awaits his conversion (Ezek. XVIII).

“Thus we went up to Jerusalem with great haste. For however many days I remained in the city before the festival, I devoted myself to similar and even worse wicked deeds. I was not satisfied with the young men who had lusted with me at sea and on the journey; I also gathered many other foreigners and citizens into my criminal acts, defiling and seducing them.”

### Chapter XV

“When the festival of the Exaltation of the precious Cross arrived, I went ahead as before, ensnaring and capturing the souls of young men.

“At first light I saw everyone running together in agreement toward the church. I too went, running with those who ran, and entered with them into the temple courtyard. When the hour of the Exaltation of the divine Cross arrived, I pushed and was pushed, and was in some way repelled as I hurried to enter with the people. I was pressed up to the temple door with those who were entering, approaching in great hardship, wretched as I was.

“But when I wished to enter, they all went in without hindrance, while some divine power prevented me and did not permit me to enter. Immediately repelled, I was cast outside; and once expelled, I found myself standing alone in the courtyard.

“Considering that this was happening to me because of feminine weakness, I again mingled with others and forced myself somehow to enter; but I labored in vain.”

### Chapter XVI

“For whenever I touched the threshold with my foot, everyone inside was received without hindrance, but it did not receive me alone. It was as though a military force had been assigned to close the entrance against me; so some sudden power prevented me, and again I found myself in the courtyard.

“After suffering this three or four times and attempting to enter without accomplishing anything, I finally despaired. I could advance no farther at all—for my body had been badly battered by the force pressing against me—and I withdrew.

“I stood in a corner of the temple courtyard. At last, with difficulty, I brought to mind the reason why I was forbidden to see the life-giving wood. Understanding the matter touched the eyes of my heart with the awareness of salvation: I reflected that the filthy crimes of my actions were barring my entrance.

“I began, therefore, to be exceedingly troubled and to weep, beating my breast, bringing sighs from the depth of my heart, groaning and lamenting. I looked upward at the place where I stood and saw an image of the holy Mother of God.

“Fixing my attention upon her and gazing at her without turning away, I said:

‘Lady Virgin, who according to the flesh gave birth to God, I know that it is neither fitting nor appropriate for me, so filthy, to adore or contemplate your image with eyes polluted by such defilements. You are recognized as a virgin and chaste, possessing an immaculate body and soul. It is just that you should abhor and reject me, a lustful woman, from the purity of your most pure chastity.

‘Nevertheless, since I have heard that God became man for this reason: that he might call sinners to repentance—and he whom you, worthy one, gave birth to—help me, solitary and without any assistance. Receive my confession, and grant me permission to enter through the opened doorway of the church. Do not make me deprived of the sight of the most precious wood, upon which God the Word was fastened—he whom you, the virgin, conceived and bore, and who gave his own blood for my liberation.

‘Command, O Lady, that the door also be opened to me, unworthy as I am, for the veneration of the divine Cross. I take you, most worthy through Christ born from you, as my surety: never again will I defile my flesh through the dreadful mockeries of sexual intercourse. But as soon as I see the wood of your Son, holy Virgin, I renounce the world, its deeds, and everything in it; and immediately I shall depart wherever you, as my surety, lead me.’”

### Chapter XVII

“Saying this, and as though receiving some assurance, inflamed with the warmth of faith and presuming upon the compassionate heart of the Mother of God, I moved from the same place where I had stood to pray.

“When I came, I again mingled with those entering, and there was no one any longer to repel me or prevent me from approaching the doors through which they entered the temple. A powerful trembling and ecstasy seized me, and I was utterly shaken in every way.

“Thus I joined myself to the door whose entrance had first been closed to me—as though the power that had previously prevented my entry had afterward prepared the way for me—and I entered without the labor of any hindrance. So I found myself within the Holy of Holies, and was deemed worthy to adore the mystery of the precious, life-giving wood of the Cross.

“Then I saw the mysteries of God, and how ready he is to receive penitents. I threw myself face down upon the ground, kissed that holy pavement, and went out.

“Running to her who had become my surety, I came and stood before her. I went to the place where the written document of my pledge was inscribed, and, bending my knee before the face of the holy Virgin Mother of God, I invoked her in these words:

‘You, most gracious Lady, have always displayed the mercy of your compassion; you have not rejected an unworthy supplication. I have seen the glory which we sinners do not rightly see: the glory of almighty God, who through you receives the repentance of sinners.

‘What more can I, a sinful and wretched woman, remember or relate? It is now time to fulfill what I pledged, pleasing through the faith of my love for you. Now, wherever it pleases you, direct me. Be my guide to salvation and teacher of truth, going before me on the road that leads to repentance.’

“Saying this, I heard the voice of someone crying out from far away:

‘If you cross the Jordan, you will find a good rest.’

“Hearing this voice and believing that it had been spoken for me, I cried out in tears. Looking toward the image of the Mother of God, I shouted:

‘Lady, Lady, Queen of the whole world, through whom salvation has come to the human race, do not abandon me!’

“Saying this, I went out from the temple courtyard and walked hastily.

“As I was leaving, someone saw me and gave me three coins, saying:

‘Take these, *nonna*.’ [Note: [Col. 0690D] *Nonna.* So the manuscripts read. The old edition has *numos*, ‘coins’; Surius has *mater*, ‘mother.’ See the *Onomasticon*.]

“I took them and bought three loaves with them, accepting them as suitable provisions for my journey. I asked the man who sold the bread:

‘Where is the road, and what kind of road is it, man, that leads to the Jordan?’

“When he pointed out the city gate that led in that direction, I hurried along the road, weeping.”

### Chapter XVIII

“Joining one question to another, I spent the remainder of the day hastening on my journey. It was the third hour of the day when I was deemed worthy to see the precious and holy Cross.

“When the sun was already declining toward sunset, I caught sight of the church of blessed John the Baptist, situated beside the Jordan. I entered that temple, immediately worshiped, and then descended into the Jordan, where I washed my hands and face in the holy water.

“I received the life-giving and undefiled mysteries of Christ the Lord in that same holy basilica of the Forerunner and Baptist John. Then I ate half of one loaf, drank from the water of the Jordan, and rested for the night on the ground.

“When dawn came the next day, I crossed to the other side and again asked my guide to direct me wherever it pleased her. I came into this solitude, and from then until today I have withdrawn, fleeing and awaiting my God, who saves the small and the great who turn to him (Ps. LIV).”

Zosimas said to her:

“How many years has it been, Lady, since you began to inhabit this solitude?”

The woman answered:

“As I reckon it, forty-seven years have passed since I left the holy city.”

Zosimas said:

“And what were you able to find for food, my lady, or what do you find now?”

The woman answered:

“I crossed the Jordan carrying two and a half loaves. After a short time they became dry and hard like stones, and by eating a little of them I survived for some years.”

Zosimas said:

“And so, without pain, did you pass through the length of so much time? Did you feel no sudden change or disturbance from the heat?”

She said:

“You now ask me about a matter that makes me tremble greatly when I recall it: the many dangers I endured and the thoughts that wickedly troubled me. For I fear that I may suffer some affliction from them again.”

Zosimas said:

“Do not leave anything out, Lady, but tell everything. Since we have come to know you revealed in this manner, you must teach us everything without omission.”

### Chapter XIX

She said to him:

“Believe me, abba, for seventeen years I wrestled with savage and untamed desires. Whenever I began to eat, I desired meat; I craved the fish that Egypt had; I also desired wine that was pleasant to me. I took great delight in wine and drank excessively, even to drunkenness; and now I had a very strong desire for it, because I had used it so much while I was in the world.

“But here I had no water at all, and I was burned with the most violent thirst, enduring the peril of necessity. I also experienced an intense desire for lustful songs, which disturbed me and brought back to my memory the songs of demons that I had learned in the world.

“Then, weeping and beating my breast, I brought back to mind the fitting pledge I had made when I set out toward this solitude. I would come in my thoughts before the image of the holy Mother of God, who had received me under her protection of faith, and I would weep before her, asking her to drive away from me the thoughts that afflicted my wretched soul.

“When I wept excessively and painfully and beat my breast manfully, I then saw a light shining all around me, and immediately a certain enduring serenity came upon me.

“But how can I tell you about the thoughts that again compelled me toward fornication? Abba, forgive me. An inner fire inflamed my wretched body exceedingly, burned me throughout, and dragged me toward the desire for intercourse.

“Whenever such a thought arose in me, I threw myself upon the ground, watered the earth with tears, and hoped that she who had become my surety would truly stand beside me. I imagined her threatening me, intensifying her rebuke against my frenzy as against one who had broken faith, and directing against me the punishments due for my betrayal, as though in anger she wielded a sword against me.

“I would not rise from the ground until that sweetest light had first illuminated me as usual and driven away the thoughts that troubled me. Thus I continually raised the eyes of my heart without ceasing toward that surety of mine, begging her to help me in this solitude and repentance.

“I therefore had her as my helper and fellow-worker, her who gave birth to the author of chastity. Thus, throughout seventeen years, I struggled against many dangers, as I have said, continuing until today.

“From that time onward, the Mother of God stood by me as my help, directing me in every way and in all things.”

Zosimas said:

“Did you have no food or clothing?”

She said:

“As I have already said, I used up those loaves over seventeen years; afterward I was nourished by herbs found throughout the desert. The garment I had, after I crossed the Jordan, was torn and worn out through extreme age.

“I endured great hardship from icy cold and burning heat, scorched by the heat’s burning and stiffened and trembling in the frost of excessive cold. Many times I fell to the ground and lay motionless, without breath, struggling against many different necessities and immeasurable temptations.

“Through everything, until this day, God’s power has preserved my wretched soul and body in many ways. Remembering from what evils the Lord has delivered me, I am nourished by food that does not perish and possess the feasts of the hope of my salvation.

“I am nourished and covered by the covering of the word of God, who contains all things (Deut. VIII). For man does not live by bread alone (Matt. III), and those who have stripped themselves of the tunic of sin, having no covering, are surrounded by the covering of the rock (Job XXIV, according to the Septuagint).”

### Chapter XX

When Zosimas heard that she was bringing forth testimonies from the Scriptures, namely from the books of Moses, blessed Job, and the Psalms, he said to her:

“Mother, did you learn the Psalms, or have you read other books of sacred Scripture?”

Hearing this, she smiled and said to him:

“Believe me, I have not seen a human being since I crossed the Jordan—until you today. Nor have I seen any wild animal or any other creature at all since I came into this solitude.

“I never learned letters anywhere, nor did I ever listen to anyone singing the Psalms or reading. But the word of God, living and effective, teaches the human mind inwardly (Heb. IV).

“This is the end of what concerns me. Now I beg you, by the incarnation of the Word of God, to pray for me, a lustful woman.”

When she had said this, the old man ran forward and, bending his knee, threw himself upon the ground, crying out and saying:

“Blessed is the Lord God, who alone does great wonders, glorious and exceedingly astonishing, without number (Job IX). Blessed are you, Lord God, who have shown me how much you grant to those who fear you. For truly you do not forsake those who seek you, Lord (Ps. IX).”

The woman took hold of the old man and did not allow him to prostrate himself completely upon the ground. She said to him:

“I adjure you by the Lord our Savior Jesus Christ: tell no one what you have heard, until God releases me from the bond of the flesh. Having received all these things in peace, when this same season returns next year I shall appear to you again, and you shall see me, with God’s grace governing us.

“Do for the Lord’s sake what I now command you: when the sacred fasts of the coming year return, do not cross the Jordan, as you customarily do in the monastery.”

Zosimas was astonished to hear her speak as though she knew the monastery’s rule, despite being unfamiliar with it. He cried out nothing else except praise of God, who grants greater things than are asked to those who love him.

She said:

“Wait, as I have said, abba, in the monastery. Even if you wish to leave, you will not be able to go anywhere.

“On the most sacred evening of the Lord’s Supper, bring in a sacred and worthy vessel a portion of the divine Body and life-giving Blood, and wait for me on the side of the Jordan that borders the inhabited world. When I come, I shall receive the life-giving gifts.

“Since I received Communion in the church of the most blessed Forerunner before I crossed the Jordan, I have never received Communion again until now; until now I have never partaken of this portion of sanctification. Therefore, I beg you, do not despise my request. Bring these life-giving and divine mysteries in every respect at the hour when the Lord made his disciples participants in the divine Supper.

“Also tell John, the abbot of the monastery where you live:

‘Pay attention to yourself and to your flock; for certain things are happening there that require correction.’

“But I do not wish you to tell him this now, only when God commands you.”

Saying this and asking the old man for his prayers, she hastened more quickly into the inner desert.

### Chapter XXI

Zosimas prostrated himself and kissed the place on the ground where her footprints had stood, giving glory to God. Offering immense thanks, he returned, praising and blessing the Lord our God Jesus Christ.

He joined again to the monastery the road through that same solitude by which he had come, returning at the time when those who lived there were accustomed to return. He remained silent throughout that entire year, daring not to say anything at all about what he had seen. Within himself he entreated God to show him the desirable face once again.

He sighed, considering the slowness of the annual cycle. When the first Sunday of the sacred fasts arrived, immediately after the customary prayer the others went out singing the Psalms. He, however, detained by a slight fever, remained inside the monastery.

Zosimas remembered what that holy woman had said to him:

“Even if you wish to leave, you will not be able to go out.”

After several days had passed, he recovered from his illness and continued living in the monastery.

When the monks returned on the evening of the sacred Supper, he did what he had been commanded. He placed in a small cup a portion of the undefiled Body and the precious Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. In a basket he put a few figs and dates—the fruit of palm trees—and a little lentil soaked in water.

He arrived late and sat on the bank of the Jordan, awaiting the holy woman. Since that most blessed woman was delayed, Zosimas did not sleep but watched the solitude attentively, waiting to see what he desired.

He said within himself:

“Perhaps she came and, finding me absent, turned back?”

Saying this, he wept. Raising his eyes to heaven, he prayed earnestly to God:

“Do not deprive me, Lord, of seeing again the one whom you granted me to see. I shall not go away empty, carrying my sins for condemnation.”

### Chapter XXII

As he prayed these things with tears, another thought came upon him:

“What if she comes? What will she do? How will she cross the Jordan, since there is no boat? How will she reach me, unworthy as I am? Woe to me, wretched man! Woe to the one who has made me a stranger to such a righteous beauty!”

While the old man was thinking these things, behold, the holy woman arrived and stood on the opposite side of the river, from which she had come.

When Zosimas saw her, he rose, rejoicing, and glorified God with great exultation. But the struggle of the contest fluctuated in his thoughts, since she could not cross the waters of the Jordan.

The old man looked and saw her making the sign of the cross over the waters of the Jordan. The splendor of the moon illuminated all the darkness of that night, for it was the time of her return.

As soon as she had impressed the sign of the cross, she stepped upon the waters. Walking over the liquid surface of the sea, she came as if along a solid road.

Zosimas, astonished and trying to bend his knees, cried out from above the waters and stopped her:

“What are you doing, abba? You are a priest of God and are carrying the divine mysteries.”

He immediately obeyed her. Coming down from the waters, she said to the old man:

“Bless me, Father; bless me.”

He immediately answered with great haste—for overwhelming astonishment had seized him at so glorious a miracle—and said:

“Truly God does not lie, who promised that those who purify themselves would become like him.

“Glory to you, Christ our God, who have shown me through this handmaid of yours how far below the measure of true perfection I am in my own estimation.”

As he was saying this, the woman asked him to recite the holy Creed and then begin the Lord’s Prayer. When the “Our Father” had been completed, the holy woman, as is customary, offered the elder the kiss of peace.

Then, receiving the life-giving gifts of the mysteries, she raised her hands toward heaven and, groaning with tears, cried out:

“Now dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace; for my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke II).

She said to the old man:

“Forgive me, abba, and fulfill another command of my request. Go now to the monastery, guided by God’s peace. When the coming year returns, come again to that torrent where I previously spoke with you. Do not omit this in any way; come for God’s sake, and you will see me again, as God wills.”

He answered her:

“If only it were possible now to follow your footsteps and enjoy the sight of your most precious face! I beg you, mother, grant one small request of an old man and deign to eat a little of the food I brought here.”

Saying this, he showed her what he had carried with him in the basket.

She touched the lentils with the tips of her fingers, took three grains, and put them into her mouth, saying that the grace of the Spirit was sufficient to preserve the substance of the soul undefiled.

Then she said to the old man:

“Pray for me for God’s sake, and always remember my wretchedness.”

Touching her holy feet, he begged her with tears to pray for the Church, for the empire, and for him. Then he let her depart, weeping and lamenting. For he did not dare detain her long, since, even if he had wished to, she could not be detained.

### Chapter XXIII

Again marking the Jordan with the sign of the cross, she stepped upon the liquid element, walked across it, and crossed just as she had done when she came before.

The old man returned filled with joy and trembling. He reproached himself and repented that he had not asked the holy woman’s name, so that he might know it. Nevertheless, he hoped to learn it when she came the following year.

### Chapter XXIV

When that year had passed, he again came into the vast solitude of the desert. Having completed everything according to custom, he hastened to behold that glorious vision.

As he traversed the solitude and found no signs indicating the desired place, he looked to right and left, directing his eyes about and searching everywhere like the swiftest hunter, seeking wherever he might capture the sweetest quarry.

But when he saw nothing moving anywhere at all, he began to pour himself out in lamentation and tears. Then he raised his eyes and prayed:

“I beseech you, Lord, show me in the body the angel to whom the whole world is unworthy to be compared.”

## Chapter XXV

While praying thus, she reached the place that had been indicated as resembling a streambed. At its uppermost end she saw the sun shining; and, looking, she saw the holy woman’s dead body lying there, with her hands arranged as was proper, and her body lying facing east.

He ran to it and washed the most blessed woman’s feet with his tears, for he did not dare touch any other part of the body. After weeping for some time and reciting psalms suitable to the occasion and the circumstances, she offered the prayer for burial and said to herself: “Perhaps the holy woman does not approve of this being done.”

While she was thinking this, writing had been traced on the ground, where the following could be read:

“Bury, Abba Zosimas, the little body of wretched Mary. Return to the earth [Note: “Return to the earth.” A similar expression occurs in the Life of Saint Paul the First Hermit.], what belongs to it, and add dust to dust. Pray only for me, for the Lord’s sake, when the month of Parmothi [Note: “Parmothi.” Thus in the manuscript. Surius has *Parmathi*, and in the margin *Parmenuthi*. The old edition has *Parmenothi*. Pharmuthi is the eighth month of the Egyptians. See the table of the months in the *Onomasticon*.] has passed according to the Egyptians; according to the Romans this is April, on the ninth day, that is, the fifth day before the Ides of April, the day of the saving Passion, after participation in the divine and sacred banquet.”

## Chapter XXVI

When the old man had read these words, he first wondered who had written them, since she had said that she did not know writing. Yet he rejoiced exceedingly because he had learned her holy name.

He reflected that, immediately after she had partaken of the divine mysteries in the Jordan, she had come at that very hour to the place where she soon afterward departed from this world; and that Mary had completed in the course of a single hour the same journey which Zosimas, walking for twenty days, had scarcely completed with great labor. She had then immediately departed to the Lord.

Zosimas glorified the Lord and poured his tears over her body. “It is time,” he said, “wretched Zosimas, to complete what is yours. But what shall I do, unhappy man? I have nothing with which to dig. I lack a hoe; there is no spade; I have nothing of all these things at hand.”

As he said this in his heart, he saw a small piece of wood lying nearby. Taking it up, he began to dig. The earth, however, was exceedingly hard and very compact, and he could not dig at all, since he was exhausted by fasting and utterly weakened by the fatigue of the long journey. He labored, was oppressed by heavy sighs, and, drenched in sweat, groaned bitterly from the depths of his heart.

Looking up, he saw a lion of enormous size standing beside the holy woman’s body and licking her feet. At the sight of it he trembled greatly in fear of the huge beast, especially because he had heard the holy woman say that she had never seen any wild animal. But he strengthened himself on every side with the sign of the cross, believing that the power of the one lying there was able to keep him unharmed.

The lion began to signal to the old man, greeting him with gentle gestures. Zosimas said to the lion:

“Since you have come sent by God, greatest of beasts, so that the body of this servant of God may be committed to the earth, complete the work required by your office, so that her little body may be buried. I, weakened by old age, cannot dig, nor do I have anything suitable with which to carry out this task; and, because of the length of this journey, I cannot hurry elsewhere to fetch something. By divine command, perform this work with your claws, so that we may commit this holy body to the earth.”

## Chapter XXVII

Immediately, in accordance with the old man’s words, the lion itself dug with its forelegs a pit large enough to suffice for burying the holy woman’s little body.

The old man washed the holy woman’s feet with his tears and, with many prayers poured forth, begged her to pray for everyone then and thereafter, and especially for him. With the lion standing by, he covered the naked little body with earth, as he had found her earlier, having nothing else except that torn garment which Zosimas had previously thrown to her, and from which Mary had covered certain parts of her body.

Then they departed together. The lion withdrew into the depths of the desert like a gentle sheep; but Zosimas returned, blessing and praising God and singing a hymn of praise to Christ our Lord. When he came to the monastery, he reported everything to them from the beginning and concealed nothing of what he had seen and heard. All who heard these mighty works of God marveled with immense astonishment, and with fear, love, and great faith celebrated the day of the most blessed holy woman’s departure.

Abbot John found certain men who needed correction, in accordance with that holy woman’s words, and, through the mercy of the Lord God, corrected them. Zosimas, while continuing to live in that same monastery, completed one hundred years and then departed to the Lord in peace, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom, with the Father, glory, honor, and dominion belong, together with the holy life-giving and adorable Spirit, now and forever and unto ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0691]

# February 12. Life of Saint Marina, Virgin, by an Unknown Author

[Note: “Marina.” I find three Marinas in ecclesiastical calendars: the Alexandrian, the Antiochene, and the Spanish; but they are so confused with one another that it is difficult to determine whether there were only two or three. Let us examine each of them, comparing them with one another and collating the authorities.

The memory of our Marina, who is the Alexandrian, is found assigned to a definite day in the *Menaea*, on February 12, where she is first called Maria and then, after changing her clothing, Marinus. There is no mention of her in the *Menologion*, but there is mention there of another Marina, virgin and martyr, on July 17, who is called Margaret by the Latins.

Among the Latins, I fear that nothing certain can be established. The ancient and more recent Martyrologies vary greatly concerning the day, the place, and the crown of martyrdom, so that this Marina of ours, who was only a virgin, appears to have been confused through similarity of name with another who was both virgin and martyr. I think the cause of this variation and confusion arose from the fact that Saint Margaret, virgin and martyr of Antioch, was called Marina by the Greeks.

Thus Bede, Rabanus, and Notker, who place Marina the martyr on June 18 at Antioch under the prefect Olybrius, place the same woman at the same location under the name Margaret on July 13. Rabanus and Notker indeed also name the same prefect, Olybrius, there; the Roman Martyrology, however, has Margaret on July 20.

Usuard, in Molanus’s first recension, has on June 18: “At Alexandria, the passion of Saint Marina, virgin,” but this is omitted in Usuard’s second recension by Molanus; nor is there any mention in that edition of a Marina who suffered at Alexandria. Yet Molanus, in both the first and second recension of Usuard, places Margaret’s feast on July 20—not in Usuard’s text, but in the additions. In his note, based on the second recension, he says that Usuard, under the name Marina, has her on June 18; this must be understood of Usuard according to his first recension, since in the second, as I have said, it is omitted.

Moreover, in the notes to the second recension, under July 20, he adds that perhaps “at Alexandria” wrongly entered the text on June 18 through the copyist’s carelessness. “For Bede,” he says, “has her on that day according to the historical account at Antioch.” From this it is clear that Molanus in both places took Marina and Margaret to be the same person.

Again, in the additions to Usuard, both in his first and second recension, under July 13, he says that Margaret is honored by many on that day. My manuscript Usuard also expressly has Margaret on that day, and thus agrees with Bede, Rabanus, and Notker concerning Margaret’s day.

After examining four ancient writers of Martyrologies, then, we still do not have a certain feast day for our Marina among the Latins—or indeed even a record of her. She is certainly found in the commonly published Ado on June 18: “At Alexandria, Saints Marina, virgin and martyr, and Balbina.” But Mosander, the editor of Ado, has prefixed an asterisk here, because this entry was absent from the other three manuscripts he used, except for one augmented by a certain Benedictine. Certainly, in my two oldest manuscripts there is no mention here in Ado of our Marina. Therefore the statement that she was a martyr cannot be attributed to Ado, as Baronius thought.

Rather, because she is called a martyr, the entry must be understood of Marina or Margaret, as Molanus understood it in his notes on Usuard; and “at Alexandria” must be replaced by “at Antioch,” since the place is incorrectly given by Galesinius as Achaia. Thus, in the manuscript Ado, there is no memory either of Marina or of Margaret. For the fact that Margaret is found in Mosander’s edition on July 13 is likewise marked with an asterisk, since it is absent from the other manuscripts.

What day, then, will be assigned to our Marina among the Latins? Baronius’s Roman Martyrology does indeed have on June 18: “At Alexandria, the passion of Saint Marina, virgin,” and Baronius thinks that this is our Marina. But how does the passion suit her? Why should it not rather be understood of Marina or Margaret, virgin and martyr, as Bede, Rabanus, and Notker indicate? Unless we wish to say that these three writers confused Marina or Margaret, virgin and martyr, with our Marina, who was only a virgin, since they again discuss Margaret on July 13.

Accordingly, on June 18 the Roman Martyrology should read: “At Alexandria, Saint Marina, virgin,” with the word “passion” omitted, as Bellinus long ago expressed it in the Roman Martyrology. My manuscript Usuard has the same reading.

Unless someone prefers to interpret “passion” and the designation “martyr” as referring to the many sufferings she endured from her brethren in religious life, just as Basilissa is called a martyr on January 9 because she suffered much, although she did not undergo martyrdom. Certainly the manuscript *Florarium of the Saints*, on June 18, recognizes our Marina with the word “passion.” It says: “At Alexandria, the passion of Saint Marina, virgin, whose acts are found near the end of the fifth book of the *Lives of the Holy Fathers.” It refers to the first edition of the *Lives of the Holy Fathers*, since she is found there at the end of the fifth book.

Concerning the translation of our Marina’s remains to Venice, the Roman Martyrology has on July 17: “At Venice, the translation of Saint Marina, virgin.” I think this was added to Baronius’s Roman Martyrology from Peter Aquilinus’s *Catalogue of the Saints*, book VI, chapter 108, since it is not found in Bellinus’s Roman Martyrology.

The Roman Martyrology of Baronius presents another Marina, virgin and martyr, on July 18: “In Galicia in Spain, Saint Marina, virgin and martyr.” I find this in no ancient Martyrology, not even in Bellinus’s Roman Martyrology, and therefore I suppose that Baronius inserted it into the Roman Martyrology from Spanish writers.

Hence some perhaps not without reason doubt whether this Spanish Marina is the same as either of the other Marinas already mentioned—that is, either the Alexandrian or the Antiochene. Villegas reports in the first part of the *Flower of the Saints of Spain*, under July 18, that some consider her to be the same as the Marina virgin who appears here in the *Lives of the Fathers*. But since that Marina was only a virgin and not also a martyr, as the Spanish Marina is believed to have been, their opinion seems less probable.

He reports that others identify her with Marina or Margaret, virgin and martyr, who suffered at Antioch. Molanus, in his notes on Usuard under July 20 according to the second recension, asserts that in their readings on June 18—he means, I think, July 18—the Spaniards say that Marina came from Antioch in Galicia. Since there is no Antioch in Galicia, it does not seem improbable that the Spaniards honor Margaret under the name Marina.

This opinion is supported by the fact that the feast days of the two fall almost on the same date. Marina or Margaret of Antioch is placed in the *Menologion* on July 17 and in the Roman Martyrology on July 20; the Spanish woman is placed in the Roman Martyrology on July 18 and in the *Treasury of Sermons* on July 19.

Nevertheless, Villegas above, and the *Treasury of Preachers* of Thomas de Trujillo, volume III, under July 19, assign certain features specifically to the Spanish Marina, such as the furnace into which she is said to have been thrown and the spring in which certain miracles are reported to have been performed through her intervention. Learned men who are familiar with these matters may determine to whom such details ought to be referred.]

[Col. 0691A]

# Chapter I

There was a certain layman who had one small daughter. Wishing to convert, he entrusted her to one of his relatives and departed for a monastery thirty-two miles distant from the city. Upon entering it, he performed every task belonging to the monastery, so that its abbot loved him more than the others who were in the monastery, because he was faithful and obedient.

After some time, however, he remembered his daughter’s affection and began to grieve and suffer inwardly. When he had done this for many days, his abbot saw that he was troubled and said to him:

“What is wrong, brother, that you walk about so sadly? Tell me, and God, who comforts everyone, will give you help.”

Then the man fell weeping at his feet and said:

“I have a son in the city whom I left when he was little, and when I remember him I am distressed on his account.”

He did not tell him that the child was a girl. The abbot, not knowing this and unwilling to lose him because he was useful to the monastery, said to him:

“If you love him, go and bring him here, so that he may be with you.”

He went and brought her, and she was called Marina. He changed her name and called her Marinus. He gave her instruction in reading and writing within the monastery, and she remained there with him. None of the brothers knew that she was a girl, but they all called her Marinus.

When she was fourteen years old, her father began to teach her the way of the Lord. He said to her:

“See, daughter, that no one learns your secret until the end of your life. Be watchful against the devil’s snares, lest he deceive you and this holy monastery appear to be dissolved through us, so that in the presence of Christ and his holy angels we may receive a crown rather than eternal condemnation with the impious.”

Every day he taught her many other things concerning the kingdom of God.

# Chapter II

When she was seventeen years old, her father died. She remained alone in her father’s cell and observed all her father’s teachings. She was obedient to everyone in the monastery, so that she was loved by her abbot and by all the others.

The monastery had a pair of oxen and a cart, since it was near the sea, where there was a market three miles away. The monks went there and brought back whatever the monastery needed.

One day her abbot said:

“Brother Marine, why do you not also go with the brothers and help them?”

She replied:

“You have commanded it, Father?”

There was an inn in that market town. [Note: “Pandochium.” Thus in the manuscripts. The Cologne edition has *pandocium*, that is, “tavern.” The old edition has *homo manens nomine pandox*. The correct form is *pandochium*, πανδοχεῖον, “tavern.” Thus *pandox*, “tavernkeeper.”]

Brother Marinus therefore began to travel frequently with the cart. If she was slow in returning, she stayed at the inn with the other monks.

# Chapter III

It happened through the snares of the enemy that the innkeeper had a virgin daughter. A certain soldier entered her room, slept with her, and the girl conceived by him.

When her parents learned of it, they began to torment the girl, saying:

“Tell us by whom you conceived.”

She replied:

“By that monk called Brother Marinus, who frequently stayed here with the cart. He forced me, and I conceived.”

Immediately her parents went to the monastery and said to the abbot:

“Look, lord abbot, what your monk Marinus has done. How he deceived our daughter!”

The abbot said to them:

“Wait; let us see whether what you say is established.”

When he came, the abbot said to him:

“Brother Marine, did you commit this crime against their daughter?”

He stood for a long while, then reflected and, groaning inwardly, said:

“I have sinned, Father. I repent of this sin. Pray for me.”

The abbot became angry and ordered him to be beaten and tormented. He said:

“I tell you truly: you who have committed this evil will not remain in this monastery.”

And he cast her out.

She never confessed her secret to anyone. Instead, she went away and threw herself down before the monastery gate, lying on the ground in penance and afflicting herself as though she herself had sinned. She asked the brothers entering whether one of them would give her even a single morsel of bread.

Doing this for three years, she did not leave the monastery.

The innkeeper’s daughter gave birth to a male child. After she had weaned him, the girl’s mother brought him with her, threw him down there before the monastery, and said to her:

“Look, Brother Marinus, how well you know how to nourish your son.”

She left him there and departed.

The holy virgin took him in as though he were her own son and, from the same morsel of bread that she received from those entering the monastery, fed the child of another. This continued for another two years.

# Chapter IV

Afterward, when the brothers saw this, they were moved by compassion. They went to the abbot and began to ask him to receive her into the monastery, saying:

“Abba, forgive and receive Brother Marinus. Behold, it has been five years that he has lain in penance before the monastery gate and has never left this place. Receive him into penance, as our Lord Jesus Christ commanded.”

Only with difficulty did they persuade him. He ordered her to enter, summoned her, and said:

“Your father was a holy man, as you know, and brought you here as a little child into this holy monastery. He did not commit any of the evil that you imagined and did, nor did anyone else in this holy monastery.

“Now you have entered with your son, whom you have by adultery, and therefore you must repent. You have committed a grave sin.

“I command you to perform all the monastery’s cleaning alone every day, to carry water for the necessary washing, and to complete the *calcearium* [Note: “Calcearium.” Thus in the Cologne edition. The old edition has *calcarium*. I think it refers to the service of cleaning the others’ shoes. In the manuscript it is *caldarium* or *caliclarium*. Does it therefore mean the service of preparing hot water, or of washing the brothers’ little cups?] for everyone each day, and to serve everyone. In this you will have my favor.”

The holy woman willingly accepted this and performed every task that had been assigned to her.

# Chapter V

After a few days, it happened that she fell asleep in the Lord.

The brothers went and announced to the abbot:

“Brother Marinus has died.”

The abbot said to them:

“See what sort of sin he committed, that he was not even deemed worthy of penance. Nevertheless, go, wash him and bury him far from the monastery.”

They went, and while washing him they discovered that he was a woman. They all began to cry aloud, beating themselves and shouting:

“Such holy conduct and patience were found in her, yet no one knew her secret; and she had been afflicted by them in this way!”

They came weeping to the abbot and said:

“Abba, come and see Brother Marinus.”

He said:

“What is this?”

The brothers replied again:

“Come and see the wonders of God, and see what you have done.”

Terrified, he went and came to the body. Raising the cloak with which it was covered, he saw that she was a woman. At once he fell down, struck his head against the ground, and cried out:

“I adjure you by Jesus Christ the Lord: do not condemn me before God’s presence because I afflicted you, for I did it in ignorance. You, lady, did not reveal your secret, and I truly did not know your holy way of life.”

He ordered her holy body to be placed inside the monastery, in the oratory.

# Chapter VI

On that same day the girl who had been possessed by the demon came to the monastery and confessed the crime she had committed and by whom she had conceived.

On the seventh day after the virgin’s repose in the Lord, she was delivered from the demon there, inside the oratory.

When those who were in the market town and the neighboring monasteries heard of the wonders that had occurred, they took up crosses and candles and came to the same monastery with hymns, songs, and psalms, blessing God. They entered the oratory where her body rested and blessed God.

To this day Christ performs many wonders there through the prayers of the holy virgin, to the praise of his name. God lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0695]

# Life of Blessed Fabiola, by Saint Jerome the Priest

(The text of this letter may be read in *Patrologia*, volume XXII, column 690.)

[Note: “Fabiola.” The day of her death is unknown, and her memory does not appear in the ecclesiastical calendars.

“Among us.” Cato, in his speech *On the Dowry*, quoted by Gellius, book X, chapter 23: “If you had caught your wife in adultery, you could kill her with impunity and without a trial; if she caught you in adultery, she would not dare touch you with a finger, nor is it lawful.” See the Code, book IX, under the Julian law on adultery and illicit sexual relations. It is a different law among Christians.

“Lateran.” This was Plautius Lateranus, concerning whom see Tacitus, book XV, and Arrian, book II, chapter 1. Juvenal mentions the Lateran residence in satire 10, and Julius Capitolinus in *Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher*: “He was educated in the place where he was born, and in the house of his grandfather Verus beside the house of Lateranus.” The same author, in the life of Verus the emperor, mentions Sextilius Lateranus, the consul.

“She stood in the order of penitents.” Baronius, volume IV, under the year of Christ 390, the fourth year of Pope Siricius, the fifteenth of Valentinian, and the twelfth of Theodosius, after narrating the penance of the emperor Theodosius, adds: “How vigorously the severity of public penance prevailed in the Church at this time, from which neither nobility, dignity, nor sex could free or excuse anyone, is clearly shown by another example of the most illustrious Roman woman named Fabiola, who was still a noble branch of the ancient Fabian family. It happened that, because she had contracted a second marriage unlawfully after divorcing her first husband, she performed public penance at Rome around these very days.”

“Clinic.” Below, in the Life of Paula, number 5: “Which sickbed patient was not supported by her resources?” A *clinicus* is one confined to a bed—κλίνη, “bed”—and unable to move from it because of illness. See the *Onomasticon*.

“Thus she traveled through the islands and the whole Etruscan Sea.” Baronius, volume V, under the year of Christ 390, the fourth year of Pope Anastasius and the fourth year of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius. “From this,” he says, “you clearly understand how, in so short a time, the shoots planted from the vine of Egypt in Roman soil extended as far as the sea, and sent their branches into the islands and throughout the sea. The monks propagated among later generations who lived along the coasts and islands of the Tyrrhenian Sea; and we can clearly understand from the letters of Saint Gregory the Pope that even the island of Gorgonia, where Rutilius says there had previously been only one person [Rutilius, *Itinerary*, book I], was enriched by numerous monastic shoots. Gregory mentions the monks of Palmaria and other islands, as well as the many monasteries gathered on the island of Gorgonia and later restored by Gregory himself to better order.”

“The swarms of the Huns burst forth.” Jerome, in the *Chronicle*, under the eighteenth year of Valens: “The nation of the Huns ravages the Goths, who, having been received by the Romans without laying down their arms, were compelled through the greed of the general Maximus, and by hunger, to revolt.” See Orosius, book VII, chapter 33.

Baronius, volume V, under the year of Christ 395, the eleventh year of Pope Siricius and the first year of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius: “In this year Fabiola, the most illustrious woman, who had gone to Jerusalem so that she might spend the rest of her life there, terrified by these incursions, was compelled, together with others, to board a ship and return to Italy.” See the fuller discussion there concerning the incursion and ravaging of the Huns.

“The Roman army was absent at that time and was occupied with civil wars in Italy.” Baronius, in the passage just cited: “For the army which Theodosius had taken with him from the East into the West against the tyrant Eugenius was being held in Italy by Stilicho, in accordance with the will of the deceased Theodosius.” Concerning that Roman army and the war against Eugenius, see Baronius himself, volume IV, under the year of Christ 394 and the following years.

“Herodotus.” Book I and the beginning of book IV, where he calls them Scythians and says that they held Asia for twenty-eight years.

“Because of their excessive greed for gold.” Baronius, in the previously cited volume: “That this race of men was indeed the greediest of all mortals is affirmed by Ammianus when he describes their customs at length” (Ammianus, book XXXI).

“There was at that time a certain disagreement among us.” Baronius, volume V, under the year of Christ 395, the eleventh year of Pope Siricius and the first year of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius: “What those disagreements were, through which the faithful in Palestine disputed with one another with tireless zeal, has been explained above in the previous volume” (Baronius, volume IV, under the years of Christ 392, 393, and 394). They had evidently been stirred up by the wickedness of the Origenists, whose principal supporters were John, bishop of Jerusalem; Evagrius Ponticus; Palladius of Galatia; Isidore of Alexandria; and Rufinus of Aquileia.

“She fell asleep.” Baronius, volume V, under the year of Christ 400, the third year of Pope Anastasius and the sixth of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, places Fabiola’s death and concludes as follows: “In this year, when the holy Fabiola, a widow renowned for her distinguished holiness and the nobility of her family, had died, Saint Jerome, at the request of Oceanus, wrote her epitaph. In its opening he counts the various intervals of time in such a way as to establish approximately the year in which the event occurred, saying: ‘Several years have passed since, upon the death of Blesilla, I consoled Paula, that venerable woman, while the wound was still fresh; the cycle of the fourth summer is turning since, when writing the epitaph of Nepotian to Bishop Heliodorus, I exhausted whatever strength I possessed in the grief of that moment; and almost two years ago I sent my dear Pammachius a brief letter concerning Paulina’s sudden departure, blushing to say more to a most eloquent man,’ and so forth. Shortly afterward he says: ‘At the present time you are entrusting Fabiola to me, the praise of Christians, the wonder of pagans, the grief of the poor, and the comfort of monks,’ and so forth (Jerome, letter 30). Since Saint Jerome himself counts four years from Nepotian’s death and two from Paulina’s repose, it is sufficiently clear from what was said above that he assigns the present year to Fabiola’s funeral, leaving no real opportunity for doubt concerning these matters.

“Unless, however, one finds that in letters written by Saint Jerome ten years later—namely, after the destruction of the city—to Marcellinus and Anapsychia, Fabiola is mentioned as though she were still alive. The same saint testifies that he sent Fabiola two books on Ezekiel composed by him (Jerome, letter 8; preface to book I on Ezekiel), and it is clear that he did not compose them until after the city’s destruction. It is therefore necessary to affirm that this was another Fabiola, to be considered younger; and this is not surprising, since at the same time we may count two Paulas and likewise two Melanias, elder and younger.

“Furius.” See Livy, book V, chapter 49; Florus, book I, chapter 13.

“Papirius.” Livy, book X, chapter 39; Florus, book I, chapter 16.

“Scipio.” Florus, book II, chapter 18; Orosius, book VI, chapter 5.

“Pompey.” Florus, book III, chapter 5; Appian, *Mithridatic History*; and Plutarch, *Life of Sulla.”]

[Col. 0697]

# January 26. Life of Saint Paula, Roman Widow, by Saint Jerome the Priest

[Note: “Paula.” The Roman Martyrology, January 26: “At Bethlehem, the repose of Saint Paula, widow and mother of Eustochium, virgin of Christ. She was of a most noble senatorial family; renouncing the world and distributing her possessions to the poor, she withdrew to the Lord’s manger. There, endowed with many virtues and crowned by a long martyrdom, she passed to the heavenly kingdom. Saint Jerome wrote her life, admirable for its virtues.”

Paula was born at Rome to her father Rogatus and her mother Blesilla, as stated below in chapter 2; her birth is assigned to the eleventh year of Constantius, A.D. 351.

There was another Paula the Younger, the granddaughter of this woman, born from her son Toxotius and Laeta, as stated below, chapter 23.

“By fleeing glory.” Sallust, in the *Catiline*: “Therefore, the less he sought glory, the more he attained it.” Nazarius, in the *Panegyric of Constantine*: “You never lifted your step anywhere without glory accompanying you everywhere like a shadow.”

“Blesilla.” Baronius, volume IV, under the year of Christ 382, the sixteenth year of Pope Damasus, the sixteenth of Gratian, the seventh of Valentinian, and the fourth of the emperors Theodosius. He says that Blesilla possessed such virtue that, having been widowed at the age of twenty after being left by a husband with whom she had lived only seven months, she—according to Jerome—“grieved more deeply over the loss of her virginity than over her husband’s death” (Jerome, letter 25).

How Saint Jerome trained her in contempt for the world, he himself explains in a letter to her sister Eustochium, in these words: “I remember that nearly five years ago, when I was still at Rome and reading Ecclesiastes with the holy Blesilla, so that I might urge her to despise this world and consider everything she saw in the world as worthless, she asked me to explain obscure passages in the manner of a little commentary, so that she could understand what she read even without me. Since she was suddenly taken away by death while our work was still in progress, and so forth” (the same author, letter 116).

Moreover, the same Saint Jerome describes at greater length the virtues of this young widow in the consolation on her death that he wrote to her mother Paula (the same author, letter 25).

He also states that she was educated in Greek and Latin literature, saying: “If you had heard her speaking Greek, you would have thought that she did not know Latin. If her tongue turned toward the Roman sound, her speech showed no trace at all of foreignness.” Of the same woman he adds: “In not many months—but in days—she had overcome the difficulties of the Hebrew language so completely that, in learning and singing the Psalms, she competed with her mother.”

Among Paula’s four daughters—Paulina, Eustochium, Blesilla, and Ruffina—Blesilla was the first to depart from this life, as Saint Jerome states in a letter to Pammachius (the same author, letter 26). His letter to Saint Marcella concerning Blesilla’s conversion to Christ is also extant; there he discusses Blesilla’s illness (the same author, letter 23). Thus far Baronius.

Concerning her death, Jerome says in letter 10, to Furia: “I pass over Blesilla, who, in the short span of life that followed her husband—your brother in the world—completed many seasons of virtue.”

“Paulina.” Baronius, in the same place. Concerning Paulina, daughter of the same holy Paula and sister of Blesilla, there is a letter written by Saint Jerome to Pammachius, the cousin of Saint Marcella, upon her repose; Saint Jerome gives the date elsewhere (the same author, letters 56, 25, and 50). Pammachius had been Jerome’s fellow student at Rome.

“Eustochium.” Baronius, in the same place: “All the praises given to Eustochium are surpassed by the holy purpose she adopted and the manner of life she undertook; she increased them daily through greater growth in virtue and finally brought them to a blessed completion.” Jerome writes concerning her to Pammachius: “What was stronger than Eustochium, who broke the gates of nobility and the arrogance of consular ancestry through her virginal purpose, and subjected the foremost lineage in the foremost city to chastity?” (the same author, letter 26).

Saint Jerome assisted her as she climbed to a higher rank than the others by writing for her the treatise *On the Preservation of Virginity* (the same author, letter 22). Saint Jerome relates in a letter to Laeta—who knew the matter well—what terrible event befell Praetextata, the aunt who attempted to drag the virgin away from the purpose she had undertaken (the same author, letter 7). Laeta had dedicated to God, while she was still very young, her daughter Paula, born in fulfillment of a martyr’s vow, so that she would remain a virgin.

“Ruffina.” Baronius, in the same place: “Ruffina was born fourth and married the distinguished man Aletius. Her premature death,” Jerome says, “struck her pious mother’s heart with dismay” (the same author, letter 27). Saint Paulinus of Nola, bishop, wrote of her outstanding virtues in his consolation on her death addressed to her husband Aletius (Paulinus, letter 31).

She was the younger daughter and had not yet married when her mother Paula left Rome to travel to Jerusalem. But she had already reached marriageable age, as Saint Jerome testifies (Jerome, letter 27), and, through her mother’s holy upbringing, had likewise been joined to a holy man. Paulinus writes of her: “For she is a spouse of faith, a sister of virginity, a daughter of perfection; to her Paula is mother, Eustochium sister, and you her husband” (Paulinus, letter 31).]

**Toxotius.** Baronius, in the same place: Toxotius married Laeta, daughter of Albinus, a pagan and priest of ancestral superstition; from them was born [Col. 0699D] Paula the Younger. It was truly a remarkable event that, through the devout conduct of Toxotius and Laeta, Albinus the priest—an implacable enemy of the Christian religion—became a Christian, to the astonishment of the city at so great a miracle. Saint Jerome relates this in these words, writing to Laeta concerning her daughter Paula:

> “Who would have believed,” he says, “that the granddaughter of Albinus the priest would be born in fulfillment of a martyr’s promise? That, while her grandfather was present and rejoicing, a tiny tongue, still stammering, would sound Christ’s Alleluia? That an old man would nourish Christ’s virgin in his own embrace? And rightly and happily did we await this. A holy and faithful household sanctifies the unbeliever. He is now a candidate for the faith, surrounded by a believing throng of children and grandchildren. I think that even Jupiter himself, if he had possessed such relatives, might have believed in Christ” (Jerome, Letter 7).

Thus far Jerome himself. It was indeed a great miracle that an old man could be born again, and that a priest of idols could enroll among the faithful at the very end of life [Col. 0700A] and begin learning the rudiments of religion—one who among his own people had served as chief priest of sacred rites—and that the decrepit old man, drawn forth by his infant granddaughter’s stammering tongue, should give back an Alleluia. Her mother Laeta, a most holy woman, eager to dedicate her as a virgin to Christ, requested and received from Saint Jerome a paraenetic letter on the education of that daughter. How greatly she advanced may be sufficiently indicated by this alone: having grown older, she sailed to Jerusalem to join her grandmother Paula, and there, together with Saint Eustochium, she grew old in holy virginity dedicated to God (Jerome, Letter 7).

**Clinicorum.** In some manuscripts, incorrectly, *clericorum* (“of clerics”). Above, in the *Life of Fabiola*, no. 6: “Whom, naked and bedridden, did Fabiola’s garments not clothe?” See the *Onomasticon*.

**And when the bishops of the East, etc.** Baronius, volume IV, under the year of Christ 382—the sixteenth year of Pope Damasus, the sixteenth of Gratian, the seventh of Valentinian, and the fourth of the emperors Theodosius—asserts that 416 bishops of East and West assembled at the Roman council [Col. 0700B].

**When winter had ended.** Baronius, in the same place: Not only is the arrival of the bishops in Rome for the council indicated, but the length of their stay in Rome is likewise made known: namely, that they remained in Rome until the spring of the following year.

**She descended to the harbor.** Baronius, volume IV, under the year of Christ 385—the first year of Pope Siricius, the tenth of Valentinian, and the seventh of the emperors Theodosius—places Paula’s departure for Jerusalem in this year. “To establish,” he says, “the chronology with certainty, first grasp the following point. Since Saint Jerome states that Paula died when Honorius was consul for the sixth time and Aristaenetus was consul, and again says that she lived in Jerusalem for twenty years, it is necessary to affirm that she departed for Jerusalem in this year, and so forth.”

As for Paula’s departure from the city, Rome then witnessed a spectacle wholly worthy of a Christian: a woman of consular rank, abandoning forever the splendor of her homeland and parents, her wealth, and her beloved children [Col. 0700C], and sailing together with her daughter, dedicated to Christ, across so many expanses of sea and dangers of life to the cradle of Christ, and so forth.

**To the island of Pontia.** Concerning the Pontian islands, see Pliny, Book III, chapter 6; Mela, Book II, chapter 7; Suetonius, *Caligula*, chapter 15.

**Flavia Domitilla.** Eusebius, in his *Chronicle*, under the sixteenth year of Domitian: “Bruttius writes that very many Christians suffered martyrdom under Domitian. Among them was Flavia Domitilla, the niece, through his sister, of Flavius Clemens the consul, who was banished to the island of Pontia when she testified that she was a Christian.” He says the same of her in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter 19. See also the Roman Martyrology and Baronius’s *Annals*.

**Segor, a three-year-old heifer.** In this passage he understands *conternantem* as τριετῆ (*trietē*), “three years old.” See Saint Jerome, *Hebrew Places*, under Zoar and Baba. See also the *Onomasticon*.

**Through the error of Dositheus.** Dositheus was among the first heretics, [Col. 0700D] from whom came the heresy of the Dositheans. See Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*.

**For he was seeing.** Baronius, volume IV, under the year of Christ 385—the first year of Pope Siricius, the tenth of Valentinian, and the seventh of the emperors Theodosius—relates similar things. Saint Hilary also tells such stories in his *Book on the Synods*, as does Saint Paulinus in *The Seventh Birthday Poem of Saint Felix*, and Severus in *Dialogue*, Book III. They add concerning women possessed by spirits that, although they were hung by the feet with their heads downward, nevertheless, by a divine miracle, their garments clung to their feet, so that feminine modesty might be protected. Jerome perhaps refers to these women in his *Apology Against Rufinus*: “I saw many miracles, and what rumor had previously brought to my ears I confirmed by the judgment of my eyes.”

**The fields of Taphneos.** Thus read Surius and the Reatinus edition. The old edition has “Thaneos,” without “fields,” joining it with “the land of Goshen.”

**Bishop Isidore the Confessor.** His memory occurs in the Roman Martyrology on January 2: “At Nitria in Egypt, blessed Isidore, bishop and confessor.” Here the Reatinus edition incorrectly understands Isidore of Pelusium.

**Arsatas.** The old edition and the Reatinus read *Arsenios*. I think Arsacius is meant, of whom Palladius speaks in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 7, where he joins Serapion with him, as Jerome does here. Unless Arsisius is intended, of whom Palladius also speaks in chapters 7 and 117, and Sozomen in Book III, chapter 13, and Book VI, chapter 30, where they likewise mention Serapion together with him. H. Gravius conjectured *Arsenitas*. Does he mean *Arseniotas*? But that is an entire people named after a place. I have no doubt that Jerome here gave the particular name of someone, as the accompanying circumstances suggest.

**A certain cunning deceiver.** Baronius, volume IV, under the year of Christ 388—the fourth year of Pope Siricius, the thirteenth of Valentinian, and the tenth of the emperors Theodosius. Palladius also, adhering to Evagrius, withered under the contagion of the same disease—that is, the disease of the Origenists. Concerning him Jerome, writing against the Pelagians, says:

> “Palladius attempted to revive that same heresy through servants of wickedness, and to construct against me a new charge concerning the Hebrew translation; surely, did we envy his talent and nobility? Even now he is working the mystery of iniquity,” etc. (Jerome, preface to *Against the Pelagians*).

For this reason Saint Epiphanius, lamenting that the same man was teaching these things in Palestine, says:

> “But beware of Palladius the Galatian, who was once dear to us and now needs God’s mercy, because he preaches and teaches the heresy of Origen, lest he perhaps lead some of the people entrusted to you into the perversity of his error” (in Jerome, Letter 60).

Jerome wrote this to John, bishop of Jerusalem, when Palladius had already abandoned the desert of Nitria and, as he himself testifies (Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 22), had gone to Palestine because of his illness. After remaining there for some time, he taught the heresies of Origen; Epiphanius therefore warned John, the bishop of that place, to beware of him as soon as possible. Since Epiphanius names no other Origenist except Palladius, it is clear that, even if others were infected with the same stain, no one but Palladius undertook the task of teaching the ravings of Origen. Therefore, when Jerome writes that an Origenist attempted Saint Paula, I can see no one other than Palladius who was then residing in Palestine.

**The globes of the Stoics.** The Stoics believed that the souls of the good dwell after this life in celestial spheres. See Lipsius, *Physiology*, Book III, dissertation 14.

**He answered in the Greek language.** Gravius here records the Greek words: Οὐδὲν ἐμοὶ γέγονε χεῖρον—“Nothing worse has happened to me.” In Plutarch’s *Consolation to Apollonius*, Diogenes, lying near death, was roused by a physician and asked, μή τι περὶ αὐτὸν εἴη χαλεπόν;—“Had anything difficult happened to him?” He replied: Οὐδέν—“Nothing,” meaning that no evil had occurred.

**Meat broths.** All printed editions read *virulentias* (“poisonous substances”). See the Reatinus edition, which attempts to interpret this. But Jerome often uses *jurulentia* (“broth” or “juicy gravy”). Thus, in Book I *Against Jovinian*: “meat broths taken in.” And in chapter XL of Ezekiel: “the ashes of burnt offerings and meat broths.” Likewise in chapter IV of Zechariah: “And instead of meat broth they began to bear various flowers of virtues.” Celsus, Book II, chapter 27: “All flesh is full of juice.” [Col. 0702B] Thus it can scarcely be doubted that *virulentia* arose from its resemblance to *jurulentia*.

**He slept.** Baronius, volume V, under the year of Christ 404, places Paula’s death in this year, drawing the conclusion, as he says, from the chronological calculation. Understand it as follows. Jerome writes that Paula died “when Honorius Augustus was consul for the sixth time and Aristaenetus was consul, on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, on the third day of the week.” From this indication of the weekday, Baronius correctly concludes that the consulship of Honorius VI and Aristaenetus fell in the year of Christ 404. It did not fall on “the third day of the week, the seventh day before the Kalends of February” (that is, January 26) in the year 405, or 403, or any other nearby year, but only in 404. Hence it is clear that in Eusebius of Scaliger this consulship of Honorius and Aristaenetus is incorrectly assigned to 405, and in Eusebius of Pontacus even more incorrectly to 407. Our Dionysius Petavius also correctly joined this consulship to the year 404 in his splendid work *On the Doctrine of Times*, placing the dominical letter C before the leap day. [Col. 0702C] Sethus Calvisius had also thought of this.

*(For the text of this letter, see Migne,* Patrologia*, volume XXII, column 878.)*

[Col. 0701]

# JANUARY 31. LIFE OF SAINT MARCELLA, WIDOW, BY SAINT JEROME THE PRIEST

[Note: [Col. 0701D]]

**421 Marcella.** The Roman Martyrology, January 31: “At Rome, Saint Marcella, widow, whose illustrious praises the blessed Jerome wrote.” Her memory is celebrated in various writings of Saint Jerome.

**In the seventh month.** Jerome, Letter 10, to Furia, here—and again shortly afterward in this very chapter—draws a comparison between Marcella and the Anna of the Gospel:

> “Holy Marcella is sufficient for you, who, answering to her lineage, has brought us something from the Gospel (Luke II). Anna had lived seven years with her husband after her virginity; this woman, seven months. The former awaited the coming of Christ; the latter holds the one whom the former had received. The former sang of him as he wailed; the latter proclaims him in triumph. The former spoke of him to all who awaited Israel’s redemption; the latter, together with the redeemed nations, cries out: ‘A brother does not redeem; a man will redeem’ (Psalm XLVIII). And from another psalm: ‘A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her’ (Psalm LXXXVI).”

[Col. 0702D] **And when Cerealis [her].** Baronius, volume IV, under the year of Christ 368—the ninth year of Pope Damasus and the twelfth of the emperors Valentinian and Valens. “On the sixth day,” he says, “after the death of his father, Valentinian the Younger, then four years old, son of Justina, was formally proclaimed Augustus through the agency of his uncle Cerealis” (Socrates, Book IV, chapter 26).

As for Cerealis, the uncle in whom such authority to create a new emperor seemed to reside, he should not be thought to be anyone other than the man who held the urban prefecture under Constantius and later the consulship under him. For no other Cerealis of distinction is found in the records of that time. We may therefore rightly say that this is the same man whom Saint Jerome recalls as having sought the marriage of Saint Marcella (Jerome, Letter 16; this is the present *Life*).

**Whose name is illustrious among the consuls.** Baronius, in the same place: His consulship occurred in the year of the Lord 358, together with his colleague Dacianus. [Col. 0703A] An inscription of this kind dedicated to him is also found on the base of a statue in Rome, in the Cevoli residence on the Via Julia:

> NERATIUS CEREALIS, VIR CLARISSIMUS, ORDINARY CONSUL, RESTORER OF THE BATHS, DECREED THIS.

Another inscription of the same sense, concerning the restoration of the baths by the consul Cerealis, exists on the Via Lata. There is also another mentioning his urban prefecture, restored above in volume III, second edition, in its proper place; it had been incorrectly assigned to the time of Constantine (Baronius, under the year 353).

From the very distinguished name and authority of Cerealis, measure the eminent greatness among all Roman women of Saint Marcella, a woman of the highest rank. Her greatness increased all the more because, for Christ’s sake, she despised those things more profoundly; so that she truly shone forth not merely in the city but throughout the Roman world as an outstanding example of Christian devotion.

**To give off the fragrance of musk.** Above, in the *Life of Pelagia*, chapter 2 [Col. 0703B]: “She filled the whole air with the scent of musk.”

**And Pope Athanasius.** Baronius, volume III, under the year of Christ 340—the fourth year of Pope Julius and of the emperors Constantine, Constantius, and Constans. “How beneficial,” he says, “Athanasius’s arrival in Rome was may be understood from this alone: he was the first to bring to the city the institution of the Egyptian monks, and he brought with him the admirable life of the great Antony, which he had written, although Antony was still alive. This way of life, adapted to every aspect of evangelical perfection, was also taken up by the noblest Roman women.” Thus far Baronius.

There is no doubt that Marcella learned much about the *Life of Antony* from the reports of Athanasius and other Alexandrian priests; nevertheless, Athanasius had not yet written the *Life of Saint Antony* at that time. See what is said above in the prefaces to the *Life of Saint Antony*, no. 3.

**As though they had fled to Rome as to the safest harbor of religion.** This was always the ancient practice: in matters of faith, people hastened to Rome as to the metropolis of the other churches.
