See the letters of Athanasius to Popes Julius and Mark, and Baronius throughout the *Annals* [Col. 0703C].

**Tower-like.** This explains the surname of Magdalene. For *Magdal*, or *Migdal*, is called “tower” by the Hebrews; hence the name Magdalene, meaning “Tower-like,” derives its significance. Saint Jerome indicates this in Letter 140, to Principia, in his explanation of Psalm XLIV:

> “Magdalene,” he says, “truly *pyrgitis* (πυργίτης), truly a tower of whiteness and of Lebanon, which looks toward the face of Damascus—that is, toward the blood of the Savior, calling her to repentance in sackcloth.”

**Finally, when she also summoned me to Rome.** Baronius, volume IV, under the year of Christ 382—the sixteenth year of Pope Damasus, the sixteenth of Gratian, the seventh of Valentinian, and the fourth of the emperors Theodosius. In this year a council was held at Rome, consisting of bishops from various provinces, namely from the East and from other regions of the Catholic world, and so forth. Jerome clearly indicates in these words that he was summoned by Damasus.

[Col. 0703D] Concerning this entire journey of Jerome and his arrival in Rome, see what is said above from Baronius in the prefaces to Book I, where Jerome’s various journeys are discussed.

**She conferred with him.** How eager Marcella was to learn is testified by Jerome himself in the preface to his letter on Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians:

> “I know her ardor; I know her faith—which she always keeps as a flame in her breast—surpassing her sex, forgetting human concerns, and, while the drum of the divine books resounds, crossing the red sea of this world. Certainly, when I was in Rome, she was never so hurried that she did not ask me something about the Scriptures. Nor, in Pythagorean fashion, did she regard whatever I answered as necessarily correct; nor did a presupposed authority prevail with her without reason. She examined everything and weighed it all with a discerning mind, so that I felt I had not so much a disciple as a judge.”

Through either a lapse of memory or an error of the pen, Baronius, in the passage cited shortly afterward, thought that Jerome had said this about Albina, Marcella’s mother. But it is clear that he is speaking there about Marcella, since Albina was already dead, as the same passage makes clear.

Baronius, volume IV, under the year of Christ 382—the sixteenth year of Pope Damasus, the sixteenth of Gratian, the seventh of Valentinian, and the fourth of the emperors Theodosius—says: Saint Marcella, whenever she wished to learn something, did not always visit him [Jerome] in person, but was also accustomed to do so by letter, as the same Saint Jerome relates (Jerome, Letter 147). Among many other things, he taught her the ten words by which God’s name is called among the Hebrews (Letter 136). He explained to her the Hebrew expressions *Alleluia*, *Maranatha*, and also *Diapsalma*, a Greek word (Letter 137 and Letter 138), as well as a treatise on blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (Letter 147). He also discussed various other questions (Letter 148).

**A ship full of blasphemies.** He means Rufinus’s arrival in Rome. Jerome, *Apology*, Book II:

> “O most richly laden trireme, which came to enrich the poverty of the city of Rome with Eastern and Egyptian merchandise:
>
> > … You are that greatest one,
> >
> > the one who restores the commonwealth to us by writing.
>
> Therefore, unless you had come from the East, that most learned man would still be lingering among the mathematicians.”

I think he alludes to Macarius the Roman, whom Gennadius, in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Church Writers*, chapter 28, says composed a book against the mathematicians, and who was very close to Rufinus. A little later Jerome says:

> “For a long time Pharos taught you what Rome did not know; Egypt instructed you in what Italy until now did not possess.”

See below, in the prefaces to Book II, concerning Rufinus’s journey.

**Let the false fortune-teller beat the buttocks of fools.** This is the correct reading, not “noses,” as Erasmus, the Reatinus, and the other editions have it. Jerome himself, Book II *Against Jovinian*: “Every day in the circles of the streets the false fortune-teller beats his buttocks.” Concerning the beating of buttocks, see Lucian, *Life of Peregrinus*. See the *Onomasticon* [Col. 0704C].

**Then the blessed disciple, and truly worthy of his name, etc.** Baronius, volume V, under the year of Christ 397—the thirteenth year of Pope Siricius and the third of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius. “What,” he asks, “is this speech of Saint Jerome, as though shaded by riddles? What does he mean by ‘the blessed disciple, and truly worthy of his name,’ if he had not stumbled upon such a teacher?” The author clearly alludes to that writing of Rufinus addressed to Macarius concerning the adulteration of Origen’s books, published in Rome to prepare the way for the errors of Origen. He also dedicated to Macarius the preface *Concerning First Principles* (*περὶ ἀρχῶν*). Since Macarius was his name, Jerome says that he should truly be called *olbios* (ὄλβιος), that is, “blessed”—Macarius by name—if he had not fallen in with such a teacher. But who this Macarius was, consult what we have noted in the Roman Martyrology (January 2), so that you may distinguish him from the other holy men of the same name. Thus far Baronius.

But Baronius incorrectly distinguished this Macarius of Rufinus from the Macarius of Palladius and confused him with Macarius the Roman, mentioned above in Book I. See what is said there, no. 1 [Col. 0704D].

**Then Saint Marcella.** Baronius, in the same place: At that time the Roman Church was tossed about amid immense danger, when that treasure-house of heresies—the book of Origen, *Concerning First Principles* (*περὶ ἀρχῶν*)—was carried about in the hands of clerics, imprudently praised, copied, and multiplied everywhere like a brood of vipers. Thus, unless the Roman Church, founded upon the firmest rock in Peter by Christ’s most steadfast promises, had been strengthened, its fall could rightly have been feared, and Peter’s little ship itself would then have dreaded shipwreck, unless Christ had been sailing in it (Luke XI). It happened plainly that, just as when Christ was being assailed by the insults of the Pharisees a certain woman raised her voice and began fearlessly to magnify him, so the Catholic faith was preserved unharmed from the blasphemies of the Origenists through the confession of a Roman woman. While he confounded the wisdom of the wise, and those whose duty it was to rise and stand as a wall for the house of Israel remained silent, the Lord stirred the spirit of a woman. For then the woman arose, a new Deborah, and overthrew the battalions of the Canaanites [Col. 0705A].

**And would mock the bishop’s simplicity.** Baronius, in the same place: Saint Jerome criticizes the simplicity of Pope Siricius, not his deceit. Since Siricius could not be persuaded to believe that a heresy could conceal such poison in men so renowned for their Christian reputation, he was, as he says, through the honesty of his own character unable to suspect evil of others. He did not immediately destroy with the spiritual sword of authority—as was proper—that deformed monster, nor did he promptly condemn to the flames that translation of Origen’s *Concerning First Principles* (*περὶ ἀρχῶν*), filled with poison. Although he could at least partly have invoked as an excuse the example of the evangelical householder who allowed the weeds to grow until the harvest, lest the wheat be uprooted with them, waiting for those who were truly heretics to become manifest through more certain signs when the crop had matured. For he was dealing with men who had come in sheep’s clothing, though inwardly they were ravenous wolves, and who, under an assumed sanctity—not merely an ordinary one, but one renowned throughout the world—were hatching the eggs of vipers.

Moreover, although Siricius did not act swiftly when the Church was endangered by the errors of Origen, he was removed from this life very soon, at the beginning of the following year. Anastasius, a most vigorous opponent of the Origenist heretics, was then raised to Peter’s chair. It has often been demonstrated beforehand by frightening examples that those pontiffs who handled the cause of faith somewhat sluggishly and cared for it too negligently were very quickly taken from this life by Christ, the chief shepherd of all. It was thus plainly shown that divine providence has always watched over the Roman Church with the highest and continual zeal and particular diligence, so that it might not be stained even by the slightest suspicion of heretical contagion.

**When the heretics saw.** Baronius, above: From these few facts we can understand that Marcella acted forcefully and restored the contest [Col. 0705C], and furthermore put the enemies to flight. For, when openly exposed by her, they denied that the *Periarchon*—the storehouse of heresies—had been translated into Latin through their own work, and likewise denied that they agreed with Origen. Presenting themselves as adherents of Catholic discipline and as communicants of the Catholic Church, they requested letters of communion from the Roman pontiff, so that by their testimony they might prove themselves Catholic everywhere and, protected by these letters, appear to have departed from the city as approved Catholics.

**They obtained ecclesiastical letters.** Baronius, in the same place: As for Rufinus, although he was about to depart for Aquileia and requested and received from Siricius, the Roman pontiff, only the customary letters of communion—letters, as we have often said, ordinarily granted only to Catholics—Siricius was not at all blameworthy. Since the heretical translation of Origen’s *Periarchon* itself lacked the author’s name, and it was unclear who had written the preface, there was nothing that should have excluded Rufinus from Catholic communion while he had not yet been exposed, indeed while he proclaimed himself Catholic and outwardly professed himself alien to every heresy. Nor is it the custom of the Roman see to condemn anyone who has not been convicted.

Furthermore, that Rufinus was accustomed to display the letter he had received from Siricius in order to demonstrate to everyone that he was a Catholic is testified by Saint Jerome in the apology composed against him, where he says: “You produce the letter of Siricius, who now sleeps in the Lord, and disregard the words of Anastasius, who is alive.” Thus far Jerome. For afterward, when Anastasius had learned the facts, Rufinus himself received the sentence he deserved.

**This distinguished man Anastasius succeeds him in the pontificate.** Baronius, volume V, under the year of Christ 398—the first year of Pope Anastasius and the fourth of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius [Col. 0706A]. He found, Baronius says, the apostolic see, Peter’s little ship, whose helm he had undertaken to govern, tossed by the storms of heretics. For, as was explained more fully in the preceding year, when Rufinus came into the city with Melania, he brought the heresies of Origen into it, having published his Latin translation of the same author’s *Periarchon*, a new Trojan horse filled with enemies within but veiled in religious language—a treasury of heresies from which deceptive wares were displayed in the Roman Church. Their merchants had fallen into such madness that they attempted to bring them even to the Apostolic throne, while Marcella alone protested and raised her voice like the woman in the Gospel (Luke XI).

Saint Jerome indicates that Anastasius found the Roman Church wavering in such a condition in his letter to Principia, which is this very *Life of Marcella* (Jerome, Letter 16). Concerning Anastasius’s role, the same Saint Jerome writes to Demetrias:

> “While she was still a little girl, and Anastasius, of holy and blessed memory, governed the Roman Church, a savage storm of heretics from the regions of the East attempted to pollute and undermine the simplicity of the faith praised by the Apostle’s voice (Romans XII). But this man, rich in the wealth of poverty and in apostolic vigilance, immediately struck down the harmful head and silenced the hissing mouths of the hydra” (Jerome, Letter 8).

**This was the beginning of the condemnation of the heretics.** Baronius adds: What happened when Pope Anastasius began to sit on the throne, Saint Jerome briefly summarized in writing to Principia, showing that Saint Marcella was responsible for the condemnation of Origen’s heresy at Rome.

**So that they might be condemned in their absence.** Baronius, volume V, under the year of Christ 397—the thirteenth year of Pope Siricius and the third of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius—says: Jerome adds that the matter had been advanced by Saint Marcella to such an extent that, when the heretics understood that they had now been openly exposed at Rome, they deserved to be condemned in their absence. Although summoned by Anastasius, the successor of Siricius, they utterly refused to come. Thus it became perfectly clear to everyone that the one who guards Israel neither sleeps nor slumbers, even if those charged with keeping watch sometimes slept.

[Col. 0706C] **Marcella is the source of this most glorious victory.** Baronius, in the same place: How splendidly was the contest weighed and balanced according to the judgment of God, when he chose to destroy through a woman what the devil had contrived through his followers under the leadership of a woman! Melania, as was also shown above, raised the standard of impiety, though marked with the appearance of piety, at great cost to Catholic truth. Under that banner, Pelagius the arch-heresiarch also soon afterward drew up his ranks. Hence Saint Jerome’s just complaint as he reviews the standard-bearers of this entire campaign:

> “What do the wretched little women want—burdened with sins, carried about by every wind of doctrine, always learning and never arriving at knowledge (2 Timothy III)—and the other companions of little women, itching to hear, not knowing what they hear or what they say?” (Jerome, Letter to Ctesiphon, *Against the Pelagians*).

He then gives a highly learned catalogue of the principal heresies that unhappily emerged, always preceded by some woman associated with the heresiarch. [Col. 0706D] But Christ set a woman against a woman, and Marcella against Melania; Marcella raised triumphant trophies from the condemned impiety.

**Rome was besieged.** Concerning this most disastrous period for the city, see Baronius, volume V, under the year of Christ 410—the ninth year of Pope Innocent, the sixteenth of Honorius, and the third of the emperors Theodosius—when the city was captured by Alaric, king of the Goths.

**Marcella’s house as well.** It was on the Aventine. Jerome, Letter 154: “If you should wish to borrow copies, you can obtain them either from Saint Marcella, who lives on the Aventine, or from the Lot of our age, the most holy man Domnio.”

**And when they brought both her and you to the basilica of the blessed Apostle Paul.** Baronius, in the volume and year cited immediately above: The barbarians who found the sacred vessels brought them to the basilica of Saint Peter so that they might remain unharmed. These same Goths, having found and recognized the most holy women—living vessels of Christ more precious than gold—brought them to the basilica of the Apostle Paul [Col. 0707A], situated on the Ostian Way, so that, as the outcome proved, they might be kept untouched.

**After a few days.** Baronius, in the same place: Saint Jerome likewise teaches that, a few days later, Saint Marcella departed this life. At this time, while he was laboring over his commentaries on Ezekiel, he heard in one and the same message of the siege and capture of the city, as well as the departure to God of Saint Marcella and his dear Pammachius. For he writes in the preface:

> “I was eager to pass on”—that is, after completing my interpretation of Isaiah—“and to place, as they say, the final hand upon the prophetic work. And behold, suddenly the death of Pammachius and Marcella, the siege of the city of Rome, and the falling asleep of many brothers and sisters were announced to me. I was so struck down and stupefied that day and night I thought of nothing except the salvation of all, and I considered myself captive in the captivity of the saints. Nor could I open my mouth before I learned something more certain, anxiously suspended between hope and despair and tormented by the sufferings of others. But after the brightest light of all the lands had been extinguished—or rather, after the head of the Roman Empire had been severed, and, to speak more truly, after the whole world had perished in one city—I fell silent, was humbled, and kept silence concerning good things (Psalm XXXVIII),” etc.

Thus Jerome indicates that, shortly after the city was stormed, Saint Marcella ended her life. The ecclesiastical records preserve her memory on an annual day, though not the day on which she herself died, but the day on which she was transferred and given a more fitting burial: the day before the Kalends of February. Pammachius, who died at the same time, is commemorated on the third day before the Kalends of September. Thus those who were joined by blood and companions in the practice of a holy life—for both cultivated the monastic discipline—also died in this same year.

After all that has been said above about both of them, this is sufficient for their praise: Saint Jerome writes in the preface to his work on Daniel, addressed to them:

> “I beseech you, most eager for learning (*philomathestatos*, φιλομαθέστατε), Pammachius, and Marcella, the unique model of Roman holiness, joined by faith and blood, to support my efforts with your prayers.”

*(For the text of this life, see Migne,* Patrologia*, volume XXII, column 1087.)*

# BOOK TWO OF THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS, OR THE HISTORY OF THE MONKS, BY RUFINUS OF AQUILEIA, PRIEST

## PREFACES TO BOOK TWO

[Col. 0707]

### To the Reader

**424** Since two books follow here, either by Rufinus as author or as translator—a matter discussed in Prolegomenon 4, § 10—it seemed appropriate here, as we did with Jerome in the first book, to select Rufinus’s journey from the *Annals* of the great historian and to represent it in Baronius’s words [the manuscript reads *repraestare*; read *repraesentare*]. If anything is obscure, or if we do not entirely agree on some point, the Note will provide both illumination for the obscurity and the grounds for the differing opinion.

Since Baronius believed that Rufinus remained at Melania’s side and accompanied her on her journey, he intertwined their journeys like one wheel within another. I have not thought it appropriate to separate them now, but present them connected as Baronius understood them, even though Melania is not mentioned anywhere in this book; she is treated explicitly only in the eighth book, in Palladius’s *Lausiac History*.

Throughout this book Rufinus—if indeed he is its author and not rather its translator—describes his journey through Egypt. **425** Baronius does not treat this journey from the present book because he believed Evagrius to be the book’s author; we have taught that another view should be held in Prolegomenon 4, § 5. If Rufinus is the author of this book, you will read his journey through Egypt throughout the entire work; if he is the translator, these prefaces present Rufinus’s various journeys, collected from different sources.

[Col. 0707]

# THE JOURNEY OF RUFINUS AND MELANIA
[Note: [Col. 0727C] *Of Ruffinus and Melania.*] Baronius repeatedly treats the pilgrimage of Ruffinus and Melania as one and the same. I do not know whether this can altogether be accepted. For since their pilgrimage together is posited as threefold—first, from Rome to Egypt; then from Egypt to Jerusalem; third, from Jerusalem to Rome, followed later by Melania’s return alone [Col. 0727D] to Jerusalem—the first joint pilgrimage, as Baronius presents it, cannot stand. For when he himself gathers from Palladius that in the year of Christ 372, the sixth of Pope Damasus and the ninth of the emperor Valens, Melania spent no more than eight months in Egypt and wishes her to have migrated from there to Jerusalem with Ruffinus, while Ruffinus writes in *Invective* 2 (as we present it here, under letter l) that he spent six years in Alexandria, it follows either that Ruffinus came to Egypt earlier, if he went to Jerusalem with Melania after her eight-month survey of Egypt, or certainly that he accompanied Melania on the Jerusalem pilgrimage for several years—namely, five years and four months. Now it is certain from Jerome that Ruffinus and Melania migrated together from Egypt to Jerusalem. Therefore, if Melania remained in Egypt for only eight months according to Baronius’s view, while Ruffinus spent six years in Alexandria, it follows that they did not undertake the Egyptian pilgrimage together. But if Baronius believed that Ruffinus too remained in Egypt for only eight months, he believed this without a witness, as will be explained more fully below in these notes, under letter l. If, however, one holds that Melania stayed in Egypt for several years (whether this should be done will be considered under letter t), then perhaps it could be thought that Ruffinus and Melania [Col. 0728D] sailed together from Rome to Egypt. Yet I do not presently see how solidly this can be maintained. Nor is the third joint pilgrimage of Ruffinus and Melania, in which they are said to have gone together from Jerusalem to Rome, altogether certain, as we shall later see under letter bb. Thus, concerning only the second pilgrimage undertaken together—that by which they proceeded from Egypt to Jerusalem to the settled abodes of the hermits—we have certain testimony in the holy Jerome’s Letter 5 to Florentius.]

[Note: [Col. 0727] Let the reader remember that when Baronius repeatedly cites Palladius’s *Lausiac History*, he used the edition of Aloysius Lipomanus, which appears in volume III of his *Lives of the Saints*, printed in Venice in 1554 in quarto. That text differs very little from the *Paradise* of Heraclides, printed in folio at Paris in 1504. Much more complete than both is the edition of Palladius prepared by Gentianus Hervetus at Paris in 1555, in quarto, and carefully edited. See General Prolegomenon 14, before the first book.]

## Egyptian Departure

In this year of Christ 372, the fifth of Pope Damasus and the ninth of the emperor Valens, when, as we shall say, the great Athanasius had died and a dreadful persecution was harassing the Alexandrian church and all Egypt, Jerome wrote from the Syrian desert to Ruffinus, who was making for Egypt and visiting the monks confessors there [Col. 0709A], as the letters [Note: [Col. 0728D] *The letters.*] of Jerome indicate (Jerome, Letter 41 to Ruffinus):

> “I hear that you are penetrating the hidden places of Egypt, visiting the choirs of the monks, and moving throughout the heavenly family on earth. The first report of this unexpected joy was brought to me by my brother Heliodorus. I did not believe what I desired to be certain, especially since he said that he had heard it from another, and the novelty of the matter deprived the report of credibility. Again, my mind, suspended in wavering hope, was impelled toward belief by an Alexandrian monk who had previously been sent, through the devout service of the people, to the Egyptian confessors—already martyrs in intention—and who was an unmistakable author of the report [Col. 0729A]. I confess that even then my judgment faltered; for although he did not know your homeland or your name, he nevertheless seemed to bring greater confirmation because he asserted the same things that another had already reported. At last the full weight of the truth burst forth. A great crowd of travelers reported that Ruffinus was in Nitria and had gone to the blessed Macarius. Then I completely loosened the reins of my credulity.”

What Jerome says here about Nitria and Macarius having been visited by Ruffinus is attested by Ruffinus himself both in *Invective* 2 and in Book II of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapters 3 and 4.] This indicates that the letter was sent by him at that time, etc.

That Ruffinus undertook such a pilgrimage with Melania, a most distinguished Roman woman, to Jerusalem, but first sailed to Egypt to visit the holy monks living there, the same holy Jerome declared in two letters—one to Florentius, who was living at Jerusalem, and the other to Ruffinus [Note: [Col. 0729A] *Jerome.*] [Note: [Col. 0729A] *Ruffinus.*] We have already given Jerome’s passage here above, under letter b.] (Jerome, Letters 5 and 41), which he sent from the Syrian desert. In his Letter 5 to Florentius at Jerusalem he writes:

> “And because brother Ruffinus, who is said to have come from Egypt to Jerusalem with the holy Melania, is joined to me by an inseparable affection of brotherhood, I ask that you not hesitate to return to him my letter, enclosed with this letter of yours.”

Other witnesses are added to these. For the holy Paulinus confirms this very pilgrimage of Ruffinus with Melania in his letter to Severus (Paulinus, Letter 9) [Note: [Col. 0729A] *Paulinus.*] “I have sent a note to the presbyter Ruffinus, the spiritual companion of the holy Melania on her journey.”] and Palladius likewise, when he discusses the same Melania [Note: [Col. 0729B] *Palladius.*] He himself, *Lausiac History*, chapter 33, in the edition of Lipomanus used by Baronius.]

At what particular time this pilgrimage of Ruffinus with Melania occurred, however, different opinions are found on the matter [Col. 0709B]. For Palladius seems to assert at the very beginning of the reign of Valens [Note: [Col. 0729B] *At the beginning of the reign of Valens.*] Palladius’s Lipomanian text has this concerning the date; Baronius cites it, or rather Heraclides:

> “She [Melania], reduced to widowhood in the twenty-second year of her age, deserved, through love of the Divinity, to be joined to the eternal bridegroom, loving him until the end of her life. Revealing the secrets of her heart to no one—for she was being prevented from doing so at the beginning of the reign of Valens—she appointed her son as administrator and sent aboard ship, with certain boys and girls, what she appeared to possess in movable goods.”

Hervetus’s Palladius expresses the time as follows:

> “For she was being prevented at that time, while Valens held the empire,”

without indicating any precise date. The Greek reads:

> Ἐκωλύετο γὰρ ἐν τοῖς καιροῖς Οὐάλεντος, ἀρχὴν ἔχοντος τῆς βασιλείας.

This may be translated in two ways: either, “For she was being prevented during the times of Valens, at the beginning of his reign,” or, “while he held imperial authority.” Since the Greek text is ambiguous, and different translators have understood it differently, it is difficult to determine from it the date of Melania’s departure, when she sailed from Rome to Jerusalem. If one places Melania’s departure at the beginning of the reign of Valens—namely, in the fourth year of Valens, or in some nearby year—then Melania’s entire chronology must be arranged accordingly: her birth, the year of her widowhood, and the year of her departure. But if that departure is placed in the tenth year of Valens, everything must be arranged differently.]

Palladius seems to affirm that this occurred at the beginning of the reign of Valens (Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 33). But in the *Chronicle* of Saint Jerome, under the tenth year of the same emperor, we read:

> “Melania, the most noble of Roman women, and daughter of Marcellinus, formerly consul [Note: [Col. 0729C] *Daughter.*] Others call her his granddaughter. See below under number 21.], leaving behind her only son, then urban praetor [Note: [Col. 0729C] *Then urban praetor.*] See below under letter u concerning how this should be read and understood.], sailed to Jerusalem, where she was such a marvel of virtues, especially humility, that she received the name of Thecla.”

This is what Jerome says there. We think it should be understood not as referring to the time when she first departed from Rome, but to the time when she reached Jerusalem from Egypt. As for the departure to Egypt, neither in Ruffinus himself nor in Palladius [Note: [Col. 0729C] *Ruffinus and Palladius.*] In Ruffinus, Book II, chapter 4 of the *Ecclesiastical History*—the passage cited shortly below in the text—there is no mention of Athanasius or Melania; hence it cannot be inferred from it that Melania reached Alexandria while Athanasius was alive. In Palladius 441 as well, since Baronius did not assign the passage, I searched for this history for a long time, and found no other account in the commonly circulated Hervetian edition than that Melania received that hide from Macarius himself, with no mention of Athanasius. Palladius, however, in the Lipomanian edition, chapter 6—which you have in volume III of his *Lives of the Saints*, and which I see Baronius also used—relates that Melania received a sheepskin from Athanasius, who had received it not from Macarius but from Mark. Yet he does not say that she received it on this pilgrimage. Although, if she really received that hide from Athanasius himself, it could scarcely have happened otherwise than on this pilgrimage. For although Athanasius had at some time been in Rome, Melania was then either not yet born or merely a little girl. Athanasius’s final departure from Rome occurred in the year of Christ 349, the thirteenth year of Pope Julius and the thirteenth of the emperor Constantius; Melania, however, was either born [Col. 0730A] around the year of Christ 347, if her departure for Jerusalem is placed at the beginning of the reign of Valens—namely, in its fourth year—or born still later, if one places it in the tenth year of Valens. I thought it useful to point out this differing account in the editions of Palladius concerning the sheepskin—one saying that it was given to Melania by Macarius, the other by Athanasius—so that if anyone should wish to defend Jerome’s *Chronicle*, which places Melania’s departure for Egypt in the tenth year of Valens, by which time Baronius places Athanasius’s death, he will not be disturbed by that edition of Palladius which says that Melania received the hide from Athanasius himself.]

Since it is established by the testimony of Ruffinus and Palladius that Melania and her companions were in Alexandria while Athanasius was still alive, and it is clear that he departed this life in that very year, it is necessary to affirm that she and her companions set out for Egypt before the tenth year of Valens. For Palladius seems clearly to demonstrate that Melania reached Alexandria while the holy Athanasius was still alive, when he says that Athanasius himself gave Melania a sheepskin which he had received as a gift from Macarius the abbot—Macarius having been given it by a lion in thanksgiving for the cubs whose sight he had restored. Ruffinus relates the history of this astonishing event, and says that he himself was present when persecution was inflicted on the monks by the Arians after Athanasius’s death:

> “For I speak of what I myself saw while present, and report the deeds of those whose sufferings I was privileged to share” (Ruffinus, Book II, chapter 4).

This is what he himself says.

While Palladius discusses the same pilgrimage of Melania (Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 2, Lipomanus, volume III), he says that she traversed the Egyptian desert under the guidance of Isidore and visited, among other monks of great renown, Pambus [426], to whom she gave three hundred pounds of silver for the use of the monks.

Since, as we have said, Jerome wrote that letter to Ruffinus when Ruffinus was visiting monks harassed by the persecution—which happened in that same year after Athanasius’s death, about which we shall speak shortly—it seems necessary to affirm that those letters were also sent by Saint Jerome to Ruffinus in that same year. Among other things, he writes:

> “I hear,” he says, “that you are penetrating the hidden places of Egypt, visiting the choirs of the monks [Col. 0710A], and moving throughout the heavenly family on earth” (Jerome, Letter 41).

And below:

> “Again, my mind, suspended in wavering hope, was impelled by a certain Alexandrian monk [Note: [Col. 0730A] *A certain Alexandrian monk.*] Was it Piammon, or one of his companions? In Cassian, *Conferences* VIII, chapter 7, Piammon says, while speaking of the holy monks who were then banished under Lucius to Pontus and Armenia: “In the time of Lucius, who was a bishop of the Arian perfidy under the reign of Valens, while we were bringing assistance to our brothers—namely, to those who had been exiled from Egypt and the Thebaid to the mines of Pontus and Armenia because of their perseverance in the Catholic faith—although in certain cities we saw the discipline of coenobitic communities to be extremely rare, we nevertheless discovered that among them not even the name of anchorites had been heard.” Jerome must certainly be understood as referring to these same confessors. For in order that assistance might be carried to those staying in Pontus and Armenia, it was necessary to cross Syria and the desert of Chalcis, where Jerome was living.], who had previously been sent to the Egyptian confessors—already martyrs in intention—through the devout service of the people, and who was an unmistakable author of the report, impelling me toward belief.”

And shortly afterward:

> “A great crowd of travelers reported that Ruffinus was in Nitria and had gone to the blessed Macarius.”

This is what Jerome himself says.

All these considerations make it clear that Melania reached Alexandria with Ruffinus in this year, while Athanasius was still alive, and that Saint Jerome, after Athanasius’s death, when persecution had been stirred up by the Arians in that year against the Alexandrian church [Col. 0710B] and the inhabitants of the desert, wrote that letter to Ruffinus from the Syrian desert, where he was living in poor health, etc.

But at what particular time should we think that Melania came from the city to Alexandria with Ruffinus and his companions before Athanasius’s death, which we have said is certain? If we agree with Palladius, who asserts that this happened around the beginning of the reign of Valens, we might add Ruffinus himself as a supporting witness, where he says that he spent six years [Note: [Col. 0730B] *Six years.*] Ruffinus, in his second *Invective*, describes his residence in Alexandria and Egypt as follows:

> “Moreover, this man [Jerome], who in all his life did not spend a full thirty days in Alexandria, where Didymus was, boasts far and wide throughout almost all his little books that he was Didymus the Seer’s disciple and had Didymus as his *kathēgētēs*—that is, his teacher—in the Holy Scriptures. And all this boasting was acquired in a single month. I, who spent six years there for the sake of God, and again, after an interval, some additional days—where Didymus was, about whom alone you boast; and where there were others no less than he, whom you do not know even by sight: Serapion and Menites, men alike in nature, character, and learning; where there was Paul, an old man and disciple of Peter the martyr; and, to come to the teachers of the desert, to whom we devoted ourselves more attentively and more frequently: where there was Macarius, the disciple of Antony, and the other Macarius, and Isidore, and Pambus, all friends of God [Note: [Col. 0729D] Concerning these and others, see Ruffinus, Book II, chapters 4 and 8 of the *History*.]—who taught us these things which they themselves had learned from God, what material for boasting I could have had about all of them, if it were appropriate or expedient to do so! But I am ashamed even to unfold these matters, while I wish to show you that, contrary to what you say, our teachers were not deficient in intellect, but—what grieves me more—our own intellect was more deficient than our teachers.”

Why should we not believe Ruffinus when he asserts these things about himself? The testimony even of his antagonist Jerome supports it, for in his *Apology*, Book II, against Ruffinus, Jerome says:

> “Pharus taught you over a long period what Rome did not know; Egypt instructed you in what Italy has until now not possessed.”

By these words Jerome implies that Ruffinus devoted himself to study both in Alexandria—which he designates by Pharus—and among the monks of Egypt. When he says that Ruffinus was at Pharus for a long time, he indicates those six years which Ruffinus says he spent in Alexandria. Nor does Jerome’s Letter 46 contradict this. Even if we grant, according to Palladius’s view, that Melania set out for Egypt around the beginning of the reign of Valens—that is, in the third or fourth year of his reign, when he began his persecution, as Palladius seems to imply above under letter g—nothing follows from this against that letter of the holy Jerome. For it is not established that Ruffinus set out for Egypt together with Melania. And even if we grant that this is established, no difficulty follows, since Ruffinus could have been in Egypt for several years before reliable news reached Jerome concerning him, as Jerome himself sufficiently implies in the same letter when he says that he learned it from different messengers at different times.]

It happened that he had stayed in Alexandria and afterward returned there again and remained for several days (Ruffinus, *Invective* against Jerome 2). But this again dissuades us from believing it, because from the recently cited letter of Jerome to Ruffinus his arrival in Egypt seems previously unheard-of, unexpected, and very recent, as was said above, etc.

**Baronius, later in the same year.**—As for the monks of Egypt, who were most cruelly harassed by Lucius, Ruffinus, who was living in Egypt with Melania, handed down these things from the records of the writers for posterity to read (Ruffinus, Book II, chapters 3–4):

> “Then, after the flight and exile of citizens, after the slaughter, torture, and flames by which he had destroyed countless people, he turned the weapons of his rage against the monasteries [Note: [Col. 0731A] *Against the monasteries.*] This may perhaps refer to what Jerome has in the *Chronicle* under the twelfth year of Valens: “Many of the monks of Nitria were killed by tribunes and soldiers.” In the same place: “When Valens issued a law that monks should serve in the army, he ordered those unwilling to do so to be killed with clubs.”], ravages the desert, and declares war against those who were at peace. He undertakes to attack at once three thousand men, or more, scattered throughout the whole desert in hidden and solitary dwellings. He sends an armed force of cavalry and infantry; he chooses tribunes, commanders, and generals of war, as though he were going to fight against barbarians. When they arrived, they saw a new kind of warfare: their enemies presenting their necks to the sword and saying nothing except, ‘Friend, why have you come?’ At that time the fathers of the monks [Note: [Col. 0731A] *The fathers of the monks.*] Thus they were called because of the distinction afforded them by their life and antiquity. Ruffinus gives a longer catalogue of these men in Book II, chapter 8 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, whom he says he himself saw: “At that time Egypt flourished not only with men learned in Christian philosophy, but also with those who, living throughout the vast desert, performed apostolic signs and wonders through simplicity of life and sincerity of heart. Among them, for the present, are those whom we ourselves saw and whose hands we were privileged to receive in blessing: Macarius of the upper desert, another Macarius of the lower desert, Isidore in Scetis, Pambus in the Cells, Moses and Benjamin in Nitria, Sybrion [variant: Scyrion], Elias, and Paul in Apeliote, another Paul in Focis, Poemen and Joseph in Pispiri, which was called the mountain of Antony. We also learned through reliable report that many other such men lived in the regions of Egypt. Thus the Apostle’s saying was truly fulfilled: ‘Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more’ (Romans 5).” *Invective* 2 likewise mentions the two Macarii, Isidore, and Pambus; Ruffinus says that he devoted himself more attentively and more frequently to these teachers in the desert. In the same place he says that in Alexandria he studied under Didymus, Serapion, Menites, and Paul, the disciple of Peter the martyr. He also mentions Didymus, his teacher, in Book XI, chapter 7 of his *History*: “For we who were in some measure hearers of his living voice, and who have read what some wrote down while he was speaking, recognized in those discourses that came from his own mouth a far greater grace and something divine, sounding beyond the human voice.” Ruffinus later adds the following, from which we infer that he also traveled in Mesopotamia: “At that same time Mesopotamia also had distinguished men, powerful in the same studies. Some of them we ourselves saw at Edessa and in the regions of Carrhae; of more we learned by report.”] Macarius, Isidore, another Macarius, together with Heraclides and Pambus, disciples of Antony, were regarded throughout Egypt, especially in the regions of the desert of Nitria, as men who were believed to share not the life and conduct of other mortals but those of the angels above. I speak of what I saw while present, and report the deeds of those whose sufferings I was privileged to share.”

And in his letter to Anastasius, the Roman pontiff, he likewise boasts that he had suffered these things, saying:

> “Although, therefore, our faith was tested during the persecution of the heretics, when we were living in the holy Alexandrian Church, in prisons and exiles inflicted on us for the faith, nevertheless, even now, if there is anyone who wishes to test our faith, let him know, etc.”

But the holy Jerome exclaims that this entire account of himself was composed by Ruffinus in an excess of self-boasting. After quoting Ruffinus’s words, he adds:

> “I am surprised that he did not add: ‘A prisoner of Jesus Christ’; and: ‘I have been delivered from the mouth of the lion’; and: ‘At Alexandria I fought with beasts’; and: ‘I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; there remains for me the crown of righteousness.’ What evil, what exiles, what prisons is this man naming? I am ashamed of such an obvious lie, as though prisons and exiles were inflicted without the sentences of judges. Yet I want to know the very prisons and the provinces whose exiles he says he endured. Certainly he has the opportunity to name one prison out of many and one exile out of countless exiles. Let him produce for us the records of his confession, which until now we have not known, so that among the other martyrs of Alexandria we may also recount his acts, and so that against his detractors he may say: ‘From now on let no one trouble me, for I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus Christ’ (Galatians 6).”

This is what Jerome says (*Apology*, Book II).

Certainly Melania, a most distinguished woman and granddaughter of the consul Marcellinus [Note: [Col. 0731C] *Granddaughter of the consul Marcellinus.*] See below under letter u.], made famous throughout the entire Roman world by her ancient nobility and by her son’s urban prefecture [Note: [Col. 0731C] *Her son’s urban prefecture.*] See below under letter v.], was attended by the services of all prefects wherever she went, while Ruffinus held the first place with her. So far was it from being the case that either she herself or anyone of her household had been sent into exile, as Ruffinus boasts, that even those who suffered persecution for the sake of the faith fled to her as to an asylum, and were by her likewise placed in safety and even supported. What we shall shortly say about her, when she appeared before the judge, provides reliable confirmation of this. But why did Ruffinus, as Paul the Apostle did, not also recount his own confession along with those of others? Especially since he knew that so great a claim would not readily be accepted by his opponents without some more certain proof, whereas he describes the confessions of others with such exactness [Note: [Col. 0731C] *With such exactness.*] Indeed, Ruffinus does not describe very accurately the persecution of the Arians, instituted by order of Valens against the Orthodox, as is clear from Socrates, Book IV, chapters 16, 17, and 19; Sozomen, Book VI, chapters 19 and 20; Theodoret, Book IV, chapters 18, 19, and 20; and Gregory Nazianzen, in his oration in praise of Athanasius, who enumerate far more outrageous deeds committed by the Arians. Indeed, Ruffinus himself does not even mention the constancy and generosity which Melania—whose side he nevertheless often kept—showed to the monks in Egypt and Palestine, as Paulinus, Letter 10, and Palladius, chapter 125, report. Peter, bishop of Alexandria, also recounts in his letter preserved by Theodoret, Book IV, chapter 20, the horrifying deeds of the Arians against the Catholics. Among other things he says:

> “Nineteen presbyters and deacons were transported to the city of Heliopolis in Phoenicia to live there, and from there to the mines at Pheno and Proconnesus; among them were twenty-three monks, etc. Eleven Egyptian bishops were sent to Diocaesarea, etc. They banished the clergy of Antioch to Neocaesarea, a city of Pontus.”

Epiphanius (*Against Heresies* 68), besides other matters, reports that “some were condemned to the beasts.” Cassian (*Conferences* VIII, chapter 7) mentions certain men “banished to the mines of Pontus and Armenia.”]

If Ruffinus made any confession at Alexandria at that time, it is thought to have been only this [Note: [Col. 0731D] *It is thought to have been only this.*] If he was Melania’s companion throughout the pilgrimage, as most believe, it may be thought that he was thrown into the same storm of persecution, or even a greater one—for it is easier to persecute men than women, especially women of high rank. Yet since he himself asserts in Book II, chapter 4, that he shared the sufferings of the fathers, why should we disbelieve him? Certainly Socrates, Book IV, chapter 19, does not disbelieve Ruffinus when he tells these things about himself.] when Melania, having been summoned to judgment because she favored the Orthodox, is thought to have been accompanied by him. But once she was dismissed as quickly as possible, those who were with her also presumably returned home. Enough of this.

**Baronius, shortly afterward in the same year.**—But what Ruffinus passed over in silence, namely, the memorable service then performed by Melania, the most noble Roman woman, let us join to these words from Paulinus. For in writing to Severus, among other worthy praises of this Christian consular woman, he says:

> “At the time of Valens, when the fury of the Arians, with the emperor himself as an accomplice of its impiety, was persecuting the Church of the living God, she was the leader and partner of all who were struggling for the faith. She received the fugitives or accompanied those who had been arrested. But when she had received in hiding those who, because of their outstanding faith, were exposed to the greater hatred of the heretics, and when those concealing them too incurred hostile envy, a grave disturbance was then inflamed by diabolical torches. She was ordered, as though she were defying the public law, to be dragged out and to suffer what awaited those men unless she preferred to betray them. She came forward fearlessly, eager for suffering and exulting in the insult of public exposure. Indeed, she did not wait to be dragged out, but hurried ahead of those who were to drag her before the judge. He, overcome by reverence for her presence, did not carry out the rage of his unbelief, while he marveled at the audacity of her faith.

> “In that same period, for three days she fed five thousand hidden monks on her own bread (Matthew 14; Mark 6; Luke 9), so that through her hand the Lord Jesus might again feed the former number in the desert [Col. 0712B], with a mercy now all the more abundant because those hidden men were protected under less freedom, unlike those who had once come voluntarily to the Lord in liberty and peace. Yet although she was not timid when discovered, she confidently provided the forbidden service; and although she did not wish the glory of her deed to be acknowledged, she was nevertheless revealed by the magnitude of her work, glorious among human beings through as many witnesses as there were people fed, while God alone knew the deed” (Paulinus, Letter 10).

This is what Paulinus says, celebrating with wondrous praise such eminent deeds, which certainly occurred in Egypt [Note: [Col. 0732A] *Occurred in Egypt.*] I agree with Baronius that these deeds occurred in Egypt—not, however, for the reason that throughout Palestine there was no equally large number of monks, capable of reaching five thousand, but because it is likely that these events took place in Nitria, a region of Egypt, which Melania is known to have visited, according to Palladius, Lipomanian chapter 33 and Hervetian chapter 117. Jerome also testifies, in Letter 22 to Eustochium on the guardianship of virginity, that “in that same place about five thousand lived in separate cells.” You also have this passage here in Ruffinus, Book III, number 219, drawn from the same Jerome.], and not in Palestine. This is suggested by the fact that nowhere except Egypt does one find so vast a number of monks gathered together at one time.

That Melania herself remained in Egypt for eight months [Note: [Col. 0732A] *Eight months.*] There is nothing of this sort in Palladius. He merely says that she remained for six months on the mountain of Nitria. In any case, if I draw the right conclusion, Melania stayed in Egypt for several months; indeed, it is possible to infer that she remained there for several years, as follows:

1. Ruffinus is said by Baronius to have been her companion; yet Ruffinus says that he remained for six years even in Alexandria alone.

2. Jerome, in Letter 41 to Ruffinus, says that he learned from three different messengers that Ruffinus was in Egypt: from Heliodorus; from an Alexandrian monk who had previously been sent, through the devout service of the people, to the Egyptian confessors—already martyrs in intention; and from the report of a great crowd of travelers. But there is a very great distance between Alexandria, from which that monk was coming, and the desert of Chalcis, where Jerome was living, since the monk was hurrying through Syria and the desert of Chalcis to Armenia and Pontus, where the confessors were. Months would have to be spent before one could reach Chalcis from Alexandria. If that monk had been sent long before, and Jerome still did not then have more certain knowledge of Ruffinus’s residence in Egypt unless a great crowd of travelers arrived to confirm it, it is certain that Ruffinus and Melania had remained in Egypt for a considerably longer time.]

Palladius teaches this (Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 33). Moreover, the things that Palladius relates concerning the services by which the same Melania assisted confessors exiled in Palestine are known to be different from these. We shall recount them shortly [Col. 0712C].

That the prefect, as though provoked by insults, willingly yielded to her replies in so great an undertaking—concealing and feeding five thousand monks in the desert—was due to the woman’s immense distinction, which won her reverence even among her enemies. Melania’s name, as has been said, was known and honored not only in Rome but everywhere throughout the Roman empire, both because of the nobility of her family and because of the excellence of her piety. Concerning her, the same Paulinus mentioned above says:

> “A woman of higher rank was cast down into the service of humility through love of Christ, sublimely humbled, so that by her strength in a weak sex she might rebuke sluggish men, and by her humility in both sexes confound arrogant persons; rich though impoverished, noble though humbled. Thus, when Marcellinus the consul was her grandfather [Note: [Col. 0732B] *Marcellinus the consul as grandfather.*] Baronius, under the year of Christ 372, the sixth of Pope Damasus, and the ninth of Valentinian and Valens. Jerome calls her his daughter (Jerome, *Chronicle*), whereas Ruffinus agrees with Paulinus, who also calls her the granddaughter of the consul Marcellinus (Ruffinus, *Invective* 1 against Jerome). Palladius, however, when describing her deeds, calls her the daughter of Marcellinus, together with Jerome (Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 33). Marcellinus is found to have held the ordinary consulship with his colleague Probinus in the year of the Lord 341, as the official consular Fasti indicate. Arnoldus Pontacus, in his notes on Jerome’s *Chronicle*, says that the consular Fasti can support both accounts, so that Melania may have been both the daughter and the granddaughter of Marcellinus, formerly consul. For, he says, two ordinary consuls of this name are found: one a hundred years earlier—Pontacus’s words should be transposed—colleague of Aurelian, around the year 278 of Christ; the other colleague of Probinus, around the year 343 (Baronius says 341). Pontacus adds: Perhaps the word “daughter” is being used for “granddaughter,” just as the Gauls call grandsons *petits-fils* and granddaughters *petites-filles*.], she suffered marriage while still in tender years because of the splendor of her family and wealth, and soon became a mother, but by the misfortune of mortals did not enjoy this state for long, lest she love earthly things for too long. For besides the other bereavements that, together with her husband, she mourned after the fruitless labor of miscarried pregnancies, her sorrows increased until she lost two sons and her husband within a single year, with only one little child left to her more as a memorial than as compensation for her affections” (Paulinus, Letter 10).

These and other things Paulinus says about her, etc.

[Col. 0713A] Moreover, at this time, when Melania’s son was serving as urban praetor [Note: [Col. 0732D] “When he was serving as urban praetor.”], the illustrious Cardinal Baronius wishes Melania either to have sailed from Rome to Egypt or, rather, as he himself interprets Jerome, to have departed from Egypt for Jerusalem while her son was serving as urban praetor. And indeed Jerome seems to assert this in his *Chronicle*, under the tenth year of the emperor Valens:

“Melania, the most noble of Roman women and daughter of Marcellinus, formerly consul, leaving behind her only son, then urban praetor, sailed to Jerusalem. There she became such a marvel of virtues, especially of humility, that she acquired the name of Thecla.”

It might seem doubtful how Melania’s son could at that time have been serving as urban praetor, since he was a boy, indeed almost an infant. For it is certain that when Melania departed from Rome for Jerusalem, her son was only a few years old—a boy rather than a man. Rufinus, in Book II of his *Invectives*,

[Col. 0733A] says:

“Nor must that other remarkable deed of his be passed over in silence, lest we cause shame to those who hear it: namely, that he had written in his very own *Chronicles* that the granddaughter of the consul Marcellinus, whom he had described as the foremost woman of the Roman nobility, after leaving her little son behind at Rome, went to Jerusalem and was there named Thecla on account of the distinction of her virtue; but afterward he erased this from his copies when he saw that her actions displeased a woman of stricter discipline.”

Paulinus, in Letter 10 to Severus:

“She was so overwhelmed by misfortunes that within the space of a year she lost two sons and her husband, with only one little child left to her, more as a reminder than as compensation for her affections.”

And below:

“Thus, accompanied in mourning by three funerals, at once widowed and bereaved, she came to Rome with her only child, more an inciter than a consoler of her tears: whether, sensing misfortune before he could understand himself, the infant already knew how to mourn another’s death, although he did not yet know his own life; or whether, in the ignorance of an infancy heedless of evil, he laughed in pitiable play amid his mother’s laments.”

Instructed by these examples that life in this frail world does not endure, and that one must place one’s hope solely in God, whom alone we cannot unwillingly lose, she adopted a salutary understanding for herself and her son, so that by neglecting her little one she might love him, and by leaving him she might retain him; she would possess him more securely in his absence, once she had entrusted him to the Lord, than she could embrace him in the present if she had entrusted him to herself.”

Since, therefore, he was still a little boy, it was also necessary that a procurator and guardian be appointed for him. Heraclides, or Palladius in Lipomanus and Baronius, chapter 33, speaking of her departure when she sailed from Rome, says: “After a procurator had been appointed for her son.” And in chapter 42, when she was already living in Jerusalem and distributing generous alms: “Her parents also, and the guardians of her son, supplied her with much from their own resources.” Palladius, in Hervetus’s chapter 117:

“When she had arranged that someone should be named guardian of her son.”

In Greek: Ποιήσασα ἐπίτροπον τῶν υἱοῦ αὐτῆς ὀνομασθῆναι — “Having arranged that someone should be appointed guardian of her son.”

Likewise, in chapter 118:

“His relatives, his own son, and his guardians supplying her each year with money.”

In Greek: Χορηγούντων αὐτῇ καὶ τῶν πρὸς γένος, καὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ υἱοῦ, καὶ τῶν ἰδίων ἐπιτρόπων τὰ χρήματα — “Her kinsmen, her own son, and her appointed guardians supplying her with money.”

For this reason, in the first edition of my *Lives*, I thought that an error had crept into Jerome’s *Chronicle*. Against the testimony of all the manuscripts—for their general authority with me is nevertheless usually very great—I altered a single letter in Jerome and read *praetori*, “to the praetor,” rather than *praetore*, “the praetor.” Thus Melania would have departed from Rome leaving her only son in Rome to the urban praetor, namely as his guardian, rather than her son himself then being urban praetor.

Now, however, after examining the matter more carefully, let the ancient books retain their authority, and let us keep *praetore*, “the praetor”; and let us say that the praetorship was conferred upon Melania’s son even though he was a boy. Clearly, the highest offices, although more rarely, were sometimes conferred in later times upon boys in consideration of the family or of parents who had deserved well of the state. Thus Honorius, the infant son of the emperor Theodosius,

[Col. 0733D] was created consul. Claudian, in his panegyric on the fourth consulship of Honorius, says:

“Amid your cradle, consul,

You are advanced, entering the fasti with your name newly inscribed,

And the year that brought you forth is bestowed upon you.”

Hence, in the edict of Theodosius (*Book 1, On Those Who Contend over Religion*, *Theodosian Code*), by which he restrained the heretics, writing to Eusignius, the praetorian prefect, we read: “With Honorius, the noble boy, and Evodius as consuls,” assigning to them the year of Christ 386. Likewise Theodosius the Younger, son of Arcadius, was consul with Rumoridus before he was three years old; they are assigned to the year of Christ 303.

Of Olybrius, a boy who was consul, Jerome says in his letter to Demetrias:

“A pious son, an amiable man, a kindly master, an approachable citizen, consul indeed in boyhood, but more distinguished as a senator by the goodness of his character” (Jerome, Letter 8).

Boethius also saw two of his children, still boys, serving as consuls. Philosophy, consoling him, brings this joint consulship before him:

“You saw your two sons alike advanced from your house as consuls amid the attendance of the senators and the enthusiasm of the people” (Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy*, Book II, Prose 3).

That they were boys at the time is clear from what follows:

“What shall I say of your consular sons, in whom, as is appropriate in boys of that age, the evidence of either their father’s or their grandfather’s intellect already shines” (the same, Prose 4).

Baronius had forgotten that boys had sometimes been consuls (Baronius, volume VIII, under the year of Christ 526); hence he interpreted *consulares* here as “sons of a consul.” But Sirmond, our own scholar, has rightly restored these two consuls—Symmachus and Boethius, sons of the elder Boethius—to the *Fasti* (Sirmond, on Letter 1 of Book VIII of Ennodius), although their grandfather and father have until now been so regarded. Their consulship fell in the year of Christ 522.

Therefore, just as it is established that boys, and even infants, were created consuls in those times, so it is not surprising that praetors were sometimes appointed at the same age. For they were not selected on account of jurisdiction or any major administration, but for spectacles—that is, for the expenditures which either they themselves or their fathers, the senators, bore on their behalf. They were indeed chosen as praetors from the senatorial order, as the first law of the *Theodosian Code*, *On Praetors and Quaestors*, declares. Boethius, *Consolation*, Book III, Prose 4:

“Indeed, he says, the praetorship was once a great power; now it is an empty name and a burdensome charge upon senatorial wealth.”

Here Bernartius has incorrectly read *praefectura*, “prefecture.”

Symmachus testifies in many letters that he devoted himself entirely to arranging his son’s praetorship and preparing the games. Thus, in Book IV, Letter 59, to Eufrasius:

“Since the occasion has arisen, it seems appropriate to solicit your diligence with my prayers, so that noble horses, distinguished in appearance and in speed, may be prepared for the performance of my son’s praetorship.”

He recommends the same matter to the same man in the following two letters. He also mentions his son’s praetorian dignity in Book VIII, Letters 21, 70, and 71.

How much Symmachus spent on his son’s praetorian games is reported by Olympiodorus of Thebes, the historian of that age, in Photius, codex 80, where he discusses the wealth and property of Roman citizens and the expenses of the praetorian games. He says that Symmachus spent twenty gold centenaria on his son’s praetorship—that is, approximately two hundred thousand gold pieces; and that Maximus spent forty gold centenaria on his son’s praetorship—that is, forty thousand gold pieces.

In view of these facts, it ought no longer to seem surprising if the son of the most noble and wealthiest Roman woman, Melania, was elected praetor while still a boy.

Gregory of Tours slipped in the same way at this passage of Jerome’s *Chronicle*, in Book I of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 40. He thought that Melania’s son had been named Urbanus, whereas Jerome is to be understood as speaking of the urban praetor. He expressed and paraphrased Jerome’s passage from the *Chronicle* as follows:

“Melania, a noble matron and resident of the city of Rome, went to Jerusalem out of devotion, leaving her son Urbanus at Rome. He conducted himself in every respect with such goodness and holiness that the inhabitants called him Thecla.”

As you can see, he omitted *praetore*, “the praetor.”

It is established that Albina was joined in marriage, while Melania the Younger, her granddaughter, was given in marriage to Pinianus (Palladius, chapter 33); but more will be said about them below.

Saint Jerome praises the woman’s extraordinary steadfastness [Note: [Col. 0734D] “Extraordinary steadfastness.”] Jerome, Letter 25:

“Saint Melania, the true nobility among the Christians of our time, with whom may the Lord grant you and me a share on his day, while her husband’s body was still warm and not yet buried, lost her two sons at once, etc.”

He praises her because she had buried her husband and two sons at once with dry eyes. Leaving behind one survivor, she traveled first to Egypt and then to Jerusalem; and there, Paulinus reports, she remained for five lustrums, that is, twenty-five years (Paulinus, *To Severus*, Letter 10). Palladius, however, asserts that she remained two years longer, namely twenty-seven years [Note: [Col. 0734D] “Twenty-seven years.”] So Palladius says. But Paulinus, in Letter 9 to Severus, says that she remained in Jerusalem for five lustrums, that is, twenty-five years.

Palladius, in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 33, confirms this.

Melania’s stay in Egypt brought great harm both to her and to Rufinus [Col. 0713B]. For, having formed an intimate association with Didymus of Alexandria, a man of great renown and, because of his extraordinary learning joined to blindness, altogether admirable to everyone, and having drunk from the cup he offered them as they thirsted—he whom he extolled with astonishing praise—they drank together with the sweet beverage the poison of his Origen, and so forth.

He poured Origen’s *Peri Archon* into their minds in such a way that, enriched by it as by a great treasure, they desired to enrich the entire Catholic world. But in fact they brooded over the eggs of an asp; when these burst open, serpents emerged, and by their deadly poison very many miserably perished.

But these matters will have to be treated more fully in their proper places below. For the present, what has been said is sufficient concerning Melania’s and Rufinus’s association with Didymus in Egypt during the period when they traveled there.

## Departure for Palestine

In the year of Christ 372—In this same year, when from the letters of Peter of Alexandria we learned that the bishops and monks of Egypt had been exiled to Diocaesarea, a town situated in Palestine, Melania, inflamed by great zeal for the faith, departed for Jerusalem in order to minister to them. What she did there Palladius teaches in these words (Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 33):

“After the Augustal prefect of Alexandria had condemned Isidore, Pithymus [Euthymius] [Note: [Col. 0734D] “Pithymus.” Baronius printed *Euthymius*. But *Pithymus*, or *Pissimius*, is correct, as is clear from the Greek text of Palladius.], Adelphius, Paphnutius, Pambo, among whom was also the elderly Ammonius, who had only one ear, together with twelve bishops, priests, and certain others, numbering altogether one hundred and twelve, to exile in the region of Diocaesarea in Palestine, this most blessed woman followed all of them and provided them with her service from her own resources.

“When those who were guarding the exiles mentioned above tried to prevent her from doing this—for they often reported it to me themselves, and I too saw the holy Pithymus, Isidore, and Paphnutius—the blessed woman then took servant’s clothing and, toward evening, brought them everything necessary for life.

429

“When the consular governor of the province of Palestine learned of this, believing that he could fill his pockets from her money by some trickery and intimidation, he ordered her—he did not know who she was—to be seized and thrown into prison. From there that holy woman sent him the following message through certain intermediaries:

“‘I was the daughter of that man and the wife of that man; now, however, I am Christ’s servant. Therefore do not suppose that I should be despised because of my present humble clothing, for, if I wished, I could easily exalt myself. You cannot frighten me in any way, nor can you take anything from my possessions. And so, lest you incur some danger or offense through ignorance, I have sent you this message.’

“It was as though she were saying: ‘Sometimes such measures must be taken against the imprudent, and arrogance must be employed against them like a hawk or a dog, which at the appropriate time imitates what will seize the proud.’

“Terrified immediately by such words, the judge excused his action to her, honored her as she deserved, and ordered that she might approach those men whenever she wished.”

Thus far concerning the service she rendered to the confessors.

## Her Journey to Jerusalem and Residence There

[Col. 0714B]

In the year of Christ 372—Concerning her residence in Jerusalem he immediately adds:

“After the aforementioned men had been recalled from exile, she established a monastery for herself near Jerusalem, where she completed a period of twenty-seven years, having with her fifty virgin sisters. A certain Rufinus, an Italian from the town of Aquileia, was also with her. He was a man of noble birth and sufficiently firm character in his singular vocation, and he later deserved to attain the priesthood. No one of the male sex could be found more gentle, more steadfast, or more serene, as though he knew everything.”

This is what Palladius says about Rufinus, an adherent of Origen and an Origenist, toward whom Jerome was intensely hostile for that reason. Thus it should not surprise us if someone who adorns Rufinus with immense praises tears Jerome apart with insults in the same commentary.

But more about Palladius will be said in its proper place below. Concerning Melania’s and Rufinus’s manner of life throughout the whole period during which they lived in Jerusalem, he adds:

“These people, then, during those twenty-seven years, were accustomed to receive and support at their own expense all the saints in Jerusalem, as well as visiting bishops, monks, and virgins—for this they had vowed to God—and they made all who came to them better through contemplation of such great and remarkable things.

“They restored to the holy Church those four hundred monks who had separated themselves from the Church because of Paulinus, namely, the bishop of Antioch. Besides these, they also recalled to our Church all people of the perverse sect and those who were contending with sacrilegious mouths against the Holy Spirit, by persuading them of the truth and continually instructing everyone. They honored and often fed the clergy of that place; and, doing these things together, they completed their lives in pious devotion, giving no one even the slightest suspicion of scandal arising from them, and leaving the whole world filled with spiritual edification.”

Thus far Palladius.

Baronius, under the year of Christ 385—As for Melania, whom Paula followed to Jerusalem, Jerome suffered slander on her account. He lists this among the accusations made against him by his detractors after the death of Damasus, accusations carried out under the prompting of hatred and envy. In the very letter that he wrote to Asella as he was about to board ship in the Roman harbor, he reviews them in detail. Among other things he says (Jerome, Letter 99):

“Nothing else is brought against me except my sex; and this is never brought against me except when Paula and Melania depart for Jerusalem.”

And afterward:

“No other women have provided the city of Rome with a story except Paula and Melania. They have despised their possessions and abandoned their children, raising the Lord’s cross like a certain banner of devotion. If they sought baths, chose perfumes, and possessed wealth and widowhood as material for luxury and freedom, they would be called ladies and saints. But now they wish to appear beautiful in sackcloth and ashes and to descend into the fire of Gehenna with fasts and filth; clearly, with the people applauding, they are not allowed to perish with the crowds.”

As far as Melania is concerned, when Jerome calls her a widow, there can be no doubt that he means the elder Melania, for the husband of the younger Melania, Pinianus, was still alive. Nor does he mention her here as though she were then in Rome, since we saw above that several years earlier she had first departed for Egypt and then for Jerusalem, where she was still living at that time. Rather, Saint Jerome mentions her because the detractors had seized upon the occasion both of her migration to Jerusalem and of Paula’s undertaking the same journey—the journey which Jerome himself had also taken—as an opportunity to slander her. He continues:

“If pagans criticized this life, if Jews had the consolation of not pleasing those to whom Christ is displeasing. But now, shame upon it, Christian men neglect the beam in their own eye and search for a speck in another’s eye (Luke 6). They tear apart a holy vocation and regard it as a remedy for their own punishment if no one is holy, if everyone is slandered, if there is a crowd of those who are perishing, if there is a multitude of sinners.

“You enjoy washing every day; another considers such cleanliness filth. You belch up a pheasant and boast of having eaten sturgeon; I fill my stomach with beans. You take pleasure in crowds of laughing people; I take pleasure in Paula and Melania weeping. You desire what belongs to others; they despise what belongs to themselves. You delight in wines steeped in honey; they drink cold water, which is sweeter. You consider yourself lost if you do not possess, eat, and devour everything in the present; they desire the future and believe the things that have been written to be true.

“Grant that those persuaded of the resurrection of bodies are foolish and vain; what is that to you? We, on the contrary, dislike your life. May you be fat for your own good; I take pleasure in thinness and pallor. You consider such people wretched; we consider you more wretched. Like is repaid with like, and each of us seems mad to the other.

“I wrote this hurriedly, weeping and grieving, Lady Asella, when I had already boarded the ship. I give thanks to my God that I am worthy to be hated by the world. Pray, however, that I may return from Babylon to Jerusalem; let Nebuchadnezzar not rule over me, but Jesus, the son of Josedech (Haggai 2). Let Ezra come—his name means ‘Helper’—and restore me to my homeland.

“Fool that I was, wanting to sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land and, after abandoning Mount Sinai, seeking help from Egypt (Jeremiah 42). I did not remember the Gospel: whoever goes out from Jerusalem immediately falls among robbers, is stripped, wounded, and killed (Luke 10). But although the priest may look away, and the Levite likewise, that merciful Samaritan is present. When they said to him, ‘You are a Samaritan and have a demon’ (John 8), while rejecting the demon he did not deny being a Samaritan, because the one whom we call guardian the Hebrews call a Samaritan.

“Some chatter that I am a sorcerer; as a servant I acknowledge the title of faith. The Jews also call my Lord a magician (Mark 3). The Apostle too has been called a deceiver. May no temptation seize me except one that is human (1 Corinthians 10). What part of my afflictions have I suffered, since I serve the cross? They charged me with the disgrace of a false accusation; but I know that through good report and bad report (2 Corinthians 6) one reaches the kingdom of heaven.

“Greet Paula and Eustochium, whether the world wishes it or not, my sisters in Christ. Greet Albina, the mother, and Marcella, the sister; also Marcellina and holy Felicitas. And say to them: ‘We shall stand together before the tribunal of Christ; there it will become clear with what intention each person has lived.’ Remember me, distinguished example of chastity and virginity, and calm the waves of the sea by your prayers.”

Thus far Jerome’s letter to Asella.

The fact that you see him offer no greeting to Melania sufficiently indicates that in this letter he understands Melania the Elder, who had departed for Jerusalem long before and was living there.

## The Miserable Fall of Rufinus and Melania

[Col. 0716C]

Baronius, under the year of Christ 393—How afterward Rufinus and Melania themselves became Jerome’s principal opponents and patrons of the Origenists is shown by Jerome in his letter to Pammachius, *On the Best Kind of Translation*, where he exposes the frauds of the false monks:

“This is not the fault of the man who, under another’s persona, is playing the tragedy, but of Rufinus and Melania, his teachers, who for a great reward taught him to know nothing” (Jerome, Letter 101).

Alas! To the scandal of the entire Catholic Church, that very dear Rufinus, who had been Jerome’s close friend, was so changed into Jerome’s enemy. Jerome himself indicates, even by that single eulogy, how closely he had been bound to him by the ties of friendship and the unbreakable bonds of affection. When Rufinus, together with Melania, was visiting the monasteries of Egypt, Jerome, writing from his solitude in Syria to visit and greet him, says among many other signs of affection:

“Believe me, brother: a sailor tossed by storm does not look toward harbor so eagerly; thirsty fields do not desire rain so greatly; a mother anxiously seated on the curving shore does not await her son so intensely, as I have longed for you ever since a sudden storm tore me from your side, ever since an impious rupture tore away one who clung to me by the bond of charity” (Jerome, Letter 41), and so forth.

With how much anxious concern he wished Rufinus to remain safe and feared that their friendship might suffer even the slightest loss because of their absence, he added at the end words that he wished to impress more firmly upon his memory:

“I beg you not to let the mind lose, together with the eyes, a friend who is long sought, scarcely found, and difficult to preserve. Let gold glitter for whomever wishes, and let shining metals sparkle from ceremonial dishes and gleam from baggage. Charity cannot be bought; affection has no price. A friendship that can cease was never true.”

With such words he surrounds his friend with walls, so that Rufinus, even if he wished, could not leap over them without the mark of disgrace. But unhappy Rufinus, following others, turned his back on his friend; grieving as a deserter in the camp of the enemies, he raged from there against his friend and brother and came forth armed as the leader of the impious. He was compelled by no other cause than the desire to preserve and defend the errors of Origen against those who opposed the Catholic truth.

That he himself fought for Origen with no little zeal, and not in the last place but among the foremost, Epiphanius seems to indicate in the letter just mentioned to John. Among so many defenders of Origen, he names only Rufinus and prays for him in these words:

“But may God deliver you, brother, and the holy people of Christ entrusted to you, and all the brothers who are with you, and especially the presbyter Rufinus, from the heresy of Origen and from the other heresies and their destruction” (Jerome, Letter 60).

Thus far Epiphanius.

But Melania’s most bitter fall wounds me with greater pain, torments me with anguish, and overwhelms me with sorrow. Is this that illustrious widow, the ornament of Roman women, the supreme glory of Christians, and the living model of Christian philosophy, who had set forth that remarkable example at Rome when, at the same time, she buried her husband and two beloved children with eyes entirely dry?
