Jerome himself had once admired and praised her incredible holiness and proposed her for imitation to others. He expressed it in these words of such great confidence:

“Saint Melania, the true nobility among the Christians of our time, with whom may the Lord grant you”—he is addressing Paula—“and me a share on his day, while her husband’s body was still warm and not yet buried, lost her two sons at once” (Jerome, Letter 25), and so forth.

But what follows is plainly more glorious in a woman: triumphing over the city that had conquered all others, now herself conquered, and overcoming the love of an only child implanted by nature, she despised Rome, left her only son there, became an exile from the world and a citizen of heaven, and, victorious even over winds and waves, sailed to Jerusalem as winter was already approaching, as she says.

For this reason Saint Jerome, rightly and deservedly astonished by the greatness of her deeds,

[Col. 0717D] considered her worthy to be called by the name of Thecla (Jerome, in the *Chronicle*). He could find no nobler title with which to honor Melania than the name of the most holy virgin, Paul’s firstborn and the first martyr among women. For she, the first of all the most distinguished Roman women, gave the example of despising Rome for Christ, disdaining wealth, abandoning children, and seeking Jerusalem; and she opened the way for the others to undertake the same deed, perhaps [p. 432] having undertaken a bold enterprise herself. She herself first surpassed the other noble Roman women, leaving Egypt and crossing the sea. On the shore of Palestine, the land of promise and possession of the saints, more fortunate than Mary in the wilderness, beating the tambourine of repentance, she led the way in singing a new song to the Lord.

Other illustrious Roman women, truly restored as Israelites, virgins and widows, followed her, forming choruses and singing with her the same praises to Christ the victor.

But, tested at the waters of contradiction—O incredible deception of the enemy of the human race!—she was deceived, overcome, and failed. Such a ship, laden with goods of such precious worth—for divine Scripture compares the virtuous woman to a merchant’s ship—suffered shipwreck in the very harbor of tranquility, if one can believe it, when she struck the shoals of Origen unwarily. Thus stained with the soot of Origen, she was changed from Naomi into Mara, and from Thecla returned to being Melania—a name of ill omen, derived from darkness.

Such is the human condition: while one lives, no one may claim anything as secure.

## Return to Rome

[Col. 0718B]

In the year of Christ 397—The following year of Christ, during the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus, is entered in the *Fasti*. In that year the heresies of Origen were brought into the city under a cloak of piety by the presbyter Rufinus of Aquileia, returning from Palestine to Rome with Melania. They were offered in Babylon’s golden cup, but before the faithful could be intoxicated by them, they were exposed and rejected.

How these events unfolded must be explained one by one; but first the chronology must be clarified.

That Rufinus was Melania’s inseparable companion, having departed with her for Egypt [Note: [Col. 0734D] “Having departed with her for Egypt.”] This is uncertain: whether Rufinus departed from Rome for Egypt together with Melania. Jerome does not imply this. See the remarks in note a. and for Palestine, and that he spent his life with her there, in Jerusalem, for as long as she remained there, is sufficiently indicated by what was said above.

But when she finally returned

[Col. 0718C] to Rome, it is established by the testimony of Palladius and Paulinus that Rufinus followed in her footsteps [Note: [Col. 0734D] “Palladius and Paulinus.”] Neither of them says that Rufinus went from Jerusalem to Rome together with Melania. In this journey they mention only Melania.

Palladius does indeed say that Rufinus was with Melania, but at that time they were in Jerusalem. Nor should Paulinus be understood otherwise when he calls Rufinus “Melania’s companion on the spiritual journey” (Paulinus, Letter 9). He surely would not have omitted Rufinus’s arrival in Letter 10, in which he follows Melania’s arrival at Naples, if Rufinus had arrived with her.

Unless someone should say that Melania and Rufinus first landed at Rome together; that Melania then went on to Naples; and that Rufinus remained in Rome or departed for Aquileia. But Paulinus, who received Melania, says that she landed at Naples. Palladius and Heraclides, however, simply say that she landed at Rome from Caesarea. They are to be interpreted as referring to Naples on the basis of Paulinus, who was present.

Palladius says:

“There was also with her a certain Rufinus by name, an Italian citizen from the town of Aquileia, a man of noble birth and sufficiently firm character in his singular vocation, who later deserved to attain the priesthood. No one of the male sex could be found more gentle, more steadfast, or more serene, as though he knew everything. These people, then, during twenty-seven years, received at their own expense all the saints and visiting bishops, monks, and virgins in Jerusalem—for this they had vowed to God” (Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 33, in Lipomanus, volume III), and so forth.

Shortly afterward he speaks of their return to Rome, as do we.

This is what Palladius says about Rufinus, who was also in agreement with him concerning the errors of Origen, as has been demonstrated more fully above. Paulinus, too, calls Rufinus Melania’s companion (Paulinus, *To Severus*, Letter 9), and praises him, although he had not yet known him sufficiently well.

After these events Saint Jerome also sent a letter to Rufinus, who was living in Rome (Jerome, Letter 66), so that there would seem to be no doubt [Note: [Col. 0736A] “So that there would seem to be no doubt.”]—indeed, a very great doubt remains. We do not deny that Rufinus was in Rome when Jerome wrote that letter to him; what we deny is that he went to Rome together with Melania. It appears that domestic necessity had already summoned Rufinus to Rome, when he had to depart for Aquileia. Melania went to Rome on account of her granddaughter, as is clear above from Palladius.

Thus it is not certain that Rufinus arrived in Rome at the same time as Melania. But in what particular year of the Lord Melania returned to the city must now be investigated more carefully.

It has already been demonstrated clearly enough above that she departed with Rufinus first for Egypt and then for Jerusalem in the year of our Lord 372, the ninth year of the emperors Valentinian and Valens. But how many years they spent on this journey and in their residence there is disputed, since Palladius, as we recently saw, counts twenty-seven years, while Paulinus counts twenty-five.

But Paulinus’s testimony is more carefully established and more solid. He received this information from Melania herself, whom, on her return to Rome—as we shall say immediately—he received as a guest when she turned aside to Nola.

The testimony of Paulinus is rendered still more certain, and Palladius’s assertion of twenty-seven years is disproved, by the fact that it is established that they returned to Rome while Pope Siricius was still alive. If we assign their arrival to the number of years prescribed by Palladius, we would necessarily have to affirm that their return occurred not under Siricius but under his successor Anastasius.

According to Paulinus, therefore, who counts five lustrums from Melania’s absence from the city, we must say that she returned to Rome in this very year, as though by right of return.

That Rufinus departed from Palestine with the peace of Saint Jerome is asserted by the testimony of both men. Saint Jerome himself quotes Rufinus’s words in his later *Apology*, which are as follows:

“You gave us peace as we departed.”

He replied:

“We gave peace; we did not receive heresy. We joined right hands and accompanied you as you departed, so that you might be Catholics,” and so forth.

Palladius gives the following publicly alleged reason for Melania’s return to the city:

“After a long time, when she heard that her granddaughter Melania had married a man, and learned that after the marriage she wished to renounce this world, she feared that men of evil life and of a bad, perverse doctrine might be joined to her. For this reason, when she was already very old—that is, sixty years of age—she sailed from the city of Caesarea to the city of Rome within a period of twenty days” (Palladius, at the place cited above, chapter 33).

This is Palladius’s account of the alleged and publicly circulated external reason for her return.

The fact that Melania and Rufinus were in agreement concerning the errors of Origen, however, as has been explained more fully above, was the true reason for their coming to the city; the preceding discussion makes this clear. They desired that the opinions of Origen which they had favored and nurtured throughout that entire period—opinions of which there were many defenders among the monks living in Egypt, including the better-known Evagrius and Isidore, and among the bishops John, the distinguished bishop of Jerusalem—should be approved by the bishop of the Roman see, so that they might thereby be accepted by the universal Church.

But with what diligence this was pursued, and under what coverings this elegantly disguised heresy was brought into the city along with them, let us examine.

First, let us reproduce what Saint Paulinus, who received Melania at Nola, describes concerning her return in his letter to Severus:

“The Lord added this grace to the gifts and letters you sent, so that our brother Victor should meet us precisely on those days when we received that holy woman herself—Melania, that is—returning from Jerusalem after five lustrums.

“But what sort of woman was she? If one may call a person a woman who was so manly a Christian. What am I to do here? The fear of unbearable tedium forbids me to add anything further to my volumes; but the dignity of the person, or rather the grace of God, seems to require that I not hastily pass over the memory of so great a soul, but pause a little to recount her to you” (Paulinus, *To Severus*, Letter 10), and so forth.

He continues by recounting her noble ancestry, since she had as her grandfather the ordinary consul Marcellinus, who held the consulship together with Probino in the year of the Lord 341, as well as her ardent zeal in following the Christian life and many other things about her, which we have arranged above in their proper chronological order.

Finally, concerning her arrival at Naples on her return, he adds:

“She was brought to Naples, a city separated by a short distance from Nola, where we live. There she was welcomed by the meeting of her sons and grandsons, and immediately hastened to Nola, to the lodging of our humility. She came to us surrounded by the splendid retinue of her immensely wealthy descendants.

[The supplied source ends here, mid-sentence.]

“We saw the glory of the Lord in that journey of mother and children: their route was indeed one, but their manner of travel was far different. She was thin and cheaply dressed, seated on a little donkey; while senators, honored and wealthy, surrounded her with all the pomp of this world that their rank and means allowed—following in swaying carriages, on caparisoned horses, in gilded carriages and numerous wagons, while the Appian Way groaned and glittered. Yet the grace of Christian humility shone more brightly than the splendors of vanity. The rich admired the poor woman, the profane admired the holy one, and our poverty laughed at them. [Col. 0720C] We saw a confusion worthy of God: purple, silk, and gilded furnishings serving old and black rags. We blessed the Lord, who makes the humble and the exalted wise, fills the hungry with good things, and sends the rich away empty (Luke I). Yet in these rich people we were astonished to see, on that same day, a poverty of spirit derived from their mother’s possessions: they gloried more in their holy mother’s want than in their own visible abundance. It seemed, moreover, that the glory of the Lord was working the very thing that we saw the poor woman’s riches in her children, so that she might already receive the fruit of her faith, since she herself could look upon her victory over this world’s vanity, seeing close at hand everything that she had abandoned for Christ and continued to despise. Those sons, clad in silk and accustomed, each according to his sex, to shine in the toga or the stola, rejoiced to touch with their hands that coarse tunic, like the warp of broom-fiber, and the cheap little cloak; and they eagerly spread their garments—of wool, gold, and costly workmanship—beneath her feet and covered them with cloth. They judged themselves cleansed from the contagion of their wealth if they were privileged to gather any dirt from her cheapest garment or footprint.

“Our hut, extending farther than its single upper room raised above the ground, with a portico separating the guest-cells, seemed enlarged by the grace of the Lord. It provided not only sufficient cramped space for the holy people who accompanied her in great numbers, but also for the crowds of those wealthy men. In it, the neighboring roofs of our little domain of Felix echoed with the voices of boys and virgins; nor did the guests of that same dwelling, although discordant in their station, make a disturbance. Rather, even among them religious modesty imitated the silence of our discipline. Though, if they were drowsily asleep with sluggish bellies, they pretended not to join those keeping vigil, they nevertheless did not dare to clash with pious voices, restrained by faithful fear; and, while the tumult of worldly crowds was suppressed by the pleasing voices of the psalm-singers, they too joined in silently.

“But, to return to the Lord’s perfect dove, know now that in this great woman, despite the weakness of her sex, the power of God has made refreshment into fasting, rest into prayer, bread into the word, clothing into a rag, a bed into a rough blanket and sackcloth, and the hard ground into softness through the written word, by which the pleasure of reading eases the hardship of a rigid couch. For the holy soul, to keep vigil and to rest in the Lord are one and the same.

“This daughter of Zion has hitherto possessed and desired her; now the daughter of Babylon possesses and admires her, because that city itself is already more a daughter of Zion than a daughter of Babylon in many respects. Therefore it marvels at her, living amid the obscurity of humility and the light of truth, supplying encouragement in faith to the rich and consolation amid hardship to the poor. Yet, amid the Roman crowds, she cries out from her quiet and hidden place in Jerusalem: ‘Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged’ (Psalm CXX); ‘Is this why I have been extended, that I should now dwell with those who dwell in Cedar?’ For, as I have learned, among the Hebrews this name signifies ‘obscurity.’ Therefore, I think she should be congratulated on the virtues just mentioned in such a way that fear should nevertheless be felt concerning her present dwelling: that so distinguished a soul may contribute more to Rome than she draws from Rome, and may sit beside the rivers of Babylon in such a way that she remembers Zion (Psalm CXXXVI). Let her not cease to flourish, established in the constancy of her purpose as upon willows ever living by their native moisture, with the instrument of her body suspended beyond all the snares and allurements of hostile Babylon; and, with the constancy of faith and the grace of virtue enduring, let her leaf not fall, so that, just as her life is admired on the journey, her praise may also be sung at its end.”

Thus far Paulinus on Melania’s arrival in Rome. Since he calls that city the daughter of Babylon, yet says that in many respects it displays the daughter of Zion, I think you readily understand that, through this variation in the name of one city, pagans and Christians are distinguished: Rome is called Babylon insofar as pagan impiety still flourished in it; but it is Zion in many respects, since it abounded in Christians among whom the worship of the true religion shone forth. Thus, from the judgment of so great a man, you can plainly understand in what sense Rome is called Babylon by John in the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0721] See this explained in Rosweyde’s notes on Paulinus’s Letter 10 and in his *Anticapellus*, chapter 5.]. But enough has already been said about this in the first volume of the *Annals*.

But let us return to Melania. When you see her praised in this manner by Paulinus, do not be surprised. To those who did not know what had been accomplished in Palestine, in the presence of only a few witnesses, not so much by her as through her by her associates, concerning the introduction of Origen’s errors into the Church—against the opposition of Saint Jerome and the resolute resistance of Saint Epiphanius—she and her ancestors seemed worthy of such praises, and even greater ones. How, I ask, could Paulinus know what not even those who were in Jerusalem could have known? As was demonstrated above, in that controversy between Saint Epiphanius and John, bishop of Jerusalem and patron of the Origenists—although he denied that he defended Origen’s errors—the matter became known only through Saint Jerome’s letters to Pammachius. You see, therefore, that Paulinus, entirely ignorant of all these matters, had sound reason to praise Melania so extraordinarily. And who could doubt that he also celebrated Ruffinus, her companion on the journey, with immense praises in other letters addressed to the same Severus, so that the enthusiasm of all Christians was turned toward their celebration (Paulinus, Letter 9)? Behold, then, by what sort of attendants the heresy of Origen was brought into the city. It would plainly have had to be called a miracle if, after hearing the sound of the trumpet, pipe, lyre, harp, psaltery, symphony, and every kind of music, everyone had not worshiped the golden statue (Daniel III); if, I say, they had not received with equal applause those whom they heard almost divinely exalted by the praises of the holiest men, and if everyone had not accepted with outstretched hands what was offered by them, bearing outside it the title of holiness, etc.

At that time Paulinus received from Melania a very small fragment of the wood of the most holy cross, sent to her by John, bishop of Jerusalem. Paulinus himself bears witness to this when, after taking a small portion from it, he sent it in the name of his wife Therasia to Severus’s mother-in-law, Bassula. He writes:

“Of the wood of the divine cross—a part of a fragment—which blessed Melania brought to us from Jerusalem as a gift from the holy bishop there, John, this small remnant has been sent especially to our venerable sister Bassula by your common servant. But what is given to one of you belongs to both, because the same principle remains in both of you, and faith abolishes sexual distinction, by which you both advance toward the perfect man. Receive, therefore, from brothers united in mind, who desire to share with you in every good. Receive a great gift in a small thing; and in this almost atom-sized fragment of a short little stick, accept a reminder of the present and a pledge of eternal salvation. Let your faith not be constricted by bodily eyes, which see only what is small; rather, with intent vision, let it perceive in this tiny object the whole power of the cross. While you think of looking upon that wood on which our salvation—and the Lord of majesty—hung, while the world trembled, rejoice with trembling. Let us also remember the rocks split apart at the impact of this cross, and at least in imitation of the stones let us split our inmost hearts through divine fear (Paulinus, to Severus, Letter 11),” etc.

With regard again to this same wood of the most holy cross, which Melania gave to Paulinus, a plainly remarkable miracle occurred. A cottage packed with hay was burning, and the flames, spreading with violent force, consumed everything and were advancing upon Paulinus’s lodging. When he presented that same wood of the cross to the balls of fire, the fire immediately recoiled and was completely extinguished. Paulinus himself celebrated this miracle, which deserved to be consecrated to perpetual memory, in verse (Paulinus, *On the Birthday of Saint Felix* 10).

The same Paulinus was also given by the same Melania a tunic woven from the fleece of harmless lambs. Having received it, he sent Severus in return a shaggy cloak made of camel hair; concerning the tunic he later wrote to him:

“We,” he says, “without weighing what would be worthy either in words or in gifts, have nevertheless sent you the one resource in which charity makes us your equals—for in that alone are we equal to you—a tunic which, since it was part of my own clothing, I ask you to accept as though it were a cloth gathered from the vileness of dung. For even this suits your innocence, since, woven from the tender fleece of lambs, it caresses the touch. I add still more to its value and grace: so that it might be proved more worthy of your use, it is for me a pledge from the blessing of the holy and illustrious woman Melania, holy among God’s saints. Thus she seemed more worthy to you, whose faith is closer to hers than our blood is” (Paulinus, to Severus, Letter 10).

By these final words Paulinus indicates that he was related to Melania by blood.

Not long before Melania’s arrival, Severus had sent Paulinus at Nola a little book written about the deeds of Saint Martin. Paulinus testifies that Melania, who eagerly desired it, had read it, and that he had also shown it to Saint Nicetas, bishop of the Dacians, who at that same time had made a pilgrimage to Italy out of devotion. For in the letter returned to Severus he says:

“I myself recited our Martin to her—Melania, who was exceedingly devoted to such histories. In this manner I revealed you, too, to the venerable and most learned bishop Nicetas, who had come from Dacia to the Romans, deservedly admired, and to many saints of God, boasting in truth not so much as your herald as my own” (Paulinus, Letter 10), etc.

We can derive a correct and well-established chronology for the arrival of that great man Nicetas from the number of Saint Felix’s birthday poems published by Paulinus. Since Paulinus himself, writing to Severus (Paulinus, Letter 9), testifies that he had decided to compose a birthday poem for Felix in verse every year, it will plainly be possible to count the years in sequence from their number. But since Paulinus’s ninth published *Birthday Poem* mentions a later arrival of the same Nicetas at Nola and says that it occurred in the fourth year after his earlier arrival, we must affirm that his first arrival took place at the time when Paulinus composed the fifth birthday poem. Concerning his later arrival, in which he mentions the earlier one, these are the verses (Paulinus, *Birthday Poem* 9):

“You came at last, restored to me in the fourth year;

But thanks be to Christ, because even late he brought you back.”

Since, then, on this reckoning his first arrival must have occurred at the time of the fifth published birthday poem, we must determine in which year of the Lord that fell. It can be understood clearly enough from Paulinus himself that those birthday poems must be counted from the last year in which, while still detained in Spain, he was preparing to travel to Rome. That was the year of the Lord, as we have seen, 393. In the following year, when he had already gone to Nola for the birthday of Saint Felix, he published the second birthday poem in sequence. When, as his testimony makes clear, he had already spent a year with the same Saint Felix in the territory of Nola, and had received the embassy from the African bishops—which was in the year of the Lord 395—he wrote the third birthday poem; in the following year, namely the preceding year, the fourth. Therefore, it must necessarily be said that in this very year of the Lord 397 he composed the fifth birthday poem. It is equally necessary to affirm that Nicetas’s arrival occurred at that time, since from the fifth birthday poem through the ninth there is a total of four years, the period by which Nicetas postponed his return to Italy, etc.

Now that we have stayed long enough with Paulinus at Nola, let us accompany Melania and Ruffinus as they return to the city. They had been absent from the city for a long time, residing at Jerusalem, as it were in a kind of spiritual academy, in order to cultivate true wisdom; they had remained there, as we have seen, for five lustra—that is, twenty-five years. When they first came to Rome, they plainly turned everyone’s eyes toward themselves in astonishment. People were delighted to see present what rumor had often conveyed about them in their absence with the highest praise. But they were concerned not merely to see them, but also to hear them; and thus they hung upon their mouths as upon some heavenly oracle brought into Rome. Since they displayed, in the Stoic apathy they had learned from the books of Origen, a model of a most perfect Christian life, complete in every respect, they enjoyed the highest esteem among all the Christians in Rome, with the exception of a very few learned men whom Saint Jerome had previously warned by letter. When Ruffinus understood that the citizens’ feelings toward himself and his associates were so favorably and warmly disposed, he immediately opened the chests containing the impiety he had first brought with him from Egypt and then from Jerusalem. From them he brought forth pestilential wares, but wrapped in such deceptions and embellished with such gold that they could have deceived even the truly prudent and wise.

When Saint Jerome discusses their arrival in the Roman harbor, he writes the following by antiphrasis (Jerome, *Apology*, Book II):

“O richest trireme, which had come to enrich the poverty of the city of Rome with Eastern and Egyptian merchandise.

. . . . . . . . . You are that greatest one

who restores our property to us by writing. Therefore, unless you had come from the East, the most learned man would still be stuck among the mathematicians.”

And shortly afterward:

“For a long time Pharos taught you what Rome did not know; Egypt furnished what Italy until now did not possess,” etc.

Melania Leaves Rome for Sicily and Returns to Jerusalem

In the Year of Christ 408.—In this year, which preceded the siege of the city, the Roman widow Melania, whom we have often mentioned above, remembering the ancient prophecy issued four hundred years earlier, as Palladius says, sold her estates and, together with her granddaughter Melania, her husband Pinianus, and her daughter-in-law Albina, withdrew from Rome to escape the disaster threatening the city. She went once more to Jerusalem, where, after forty days, she departed this life. This account comes from Palladius (Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 33). He also relates that, through this prophetic oracle, which she had proclaimed at Rome and repeatedly impressed upon people, many Christian citizens of Rome were led to despise temporal possessions. They judged it wiser, for the love of Christ and in hope of heavenly reward, to squander their wealth on the poor than to leave it as booty for the barbarians. When the outcome of events proved the oracle true, they gave immense thanks to God. Melania’s exhortation had still greater force because she kept saying—as she believed—that the world would fall together with the city.

When the same Palladius says that the younger Melania, her granddaughter, withdrew from Rome together with the elder Melania, as well as her husband Pinianus and Melania’s daughter-in-law Albina, understand the relationship of these people to Melania as follows. Her only surviving son married Albina, by whom, Palladius says, the younger Melania was born, the granddaughter of the elder Melania. She was married to Pinianus, whose mother-in-law was Albina (Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 33). That Albina occupied the place of a mother to Pinianus is shown by Saint Augustine, who, writing to her, calls Pinianus her son and frequently uses these names (Augustine, Letter 227). Here again note that this Albina, Melania’s daughter-in-law, was entirely different from Albina, the mother of Saint Marcella, whom Saint Jerome often mentions. From the testimony of that same Saint Jerome, we learned that the latter had departed this life many years earlier. What happened when those whom we have said withdrew from the city this year crossed over into Africa, we shall relate in its proper chronological place in the following year.

But here Palladius must be corrected when he says that Melania’s son, being very young, accompanied Melania on her journey as far as Sicily. For how could he have been very young when it is established that the elder Melania had been left a widow approximately forty years earlier? Or how could he have accompanied her only as far as Sicily, when he sailed with them to Africa, where he also died? This is established by the letters of Augustine and Paulinus, which we shall discuss in the following year. From them a much more reliable account of the deeds of Melania, Pinianus, and their companions is obtained than from Palladius, who made no mention whatsoever of Africa. It is clear from this omission that they all departed there in the following year and remained there for a considerable time.

In this same year of Christ 409—the eighth year of Pope Innocent, the fifteenth of Honorius, and the second of Theodosius, emperors—Pinianus, a man of illustrious rank, together with the elder Melania, his wife the younger Melania, and Albina, the mother of the younger Melania and mother-in-law of the elder Melania’s son, sailed to Carthage after selling the possessions he had in Rome and Italy the preceding year. There, enriching the poor of the Church from the funds he had collected, he proceeded from there to Saint Alypius at Tagaste (Jerome, *Commentary on Isaiah*, Book X, preface; Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 9). When Saint Augustine first heard of their arrival, he wrote to them, excusing himself for being unable to hasten to visit them because of the harsh winter that had descended and the unsettled condition of the church at Hippo. The letter itself survives, and its title is “To Albinus, Pinianus, and Melania” (Augustine, Letter 227). But I think “Albina” should be restored in place of “Albinus,” since a woman of that name, Pinianus’s mother-in-law, traveled with them to Africa, as is sufficiently apparent both from Palladius and from Augustine’s own testimony, etc.

While these same people were staying in Africa, the elder Melania’s son died. The mother mourned the loss of her only child with such restraint that it became a great example of Christian steadfastness. Saint Augustine, who witnessed this, wrote about it with the highest praise to Paulinus, bishop of Nola. The letter itself does not survive; but from Paulinus’s letters written in reply to him, all these matters, which others have buried in silence, become sufficiently clear. Paulinus says:

“Because you taught me, in the spirit of truth, to preserve moderation in governing the temperament of the soul amid Western mortals, you saw that blessed mother and grandmother Melania mourned the bodily death of her only son, with a silent grief, yet not with a sorrow dry of maternal tears” (quoted in Augustine, Letter 249).

He calls Melania both mother and grandmother: mother in relation to her deceased son, grandmother in relation to her granddaughter. But Paulinus continues:

“You, as a spirit nearer and more equal to her soul, understood more deeply her restrained and dignified tears; and, preserving the strength of a manly soul, you contemplated the mother’s heart more accurately and fairly through the likeness of your own heart, so that you perceived that she first wept because of natural affection, and then was moved by a higher cause—not so much because, through mortal necessity, she had lost in the present world her only son, who had died, as because he had been, so to speak, overtaken by worldly vanity. For he had not yet abandoned the ambition of senatorial rank, and, contrary to the holy poverty of his vows, he had not considered himself taken up so as to pass from the glory of conversion to the glory of resurrection and obtain with his mother a common rest and crown, if in this world’s life he had preferred sackcloth to the toga and the monastery to the Senate, following his mother’s example. Nevertheless, that same man, as I have already reported, departed enriched by these works through the vow of your holiness, so that, if he did not wear the nobility of his mother’s humility in his clothing, he nevertheless carried it before him in his mind.

“For, in accordance with the word of the Lord, he was gentle in character and humble of heart, so that he may rightly be believed to have entered into the Lord’s rest, since ‘there are remains for the peaceful man, and the meek shall possess the earth’ (Matthew XI), pleasing God in the land of the living. Certainly he fulfilled that saying of the Apostle not only through the silent affection of his mind, but also through conspicuous religious deeds. Though he was a colleague of the great ones of this world in rank and honor, he did not, as one glorious, set his mind on the high things of the earth; rather, as a perfect imitator of Christ, he agreed with the humble and continued throughout the whole day to show mercy and lend assistance (Romans XII). Thus his offspring became mighty upon the earth (Psalm XXXVI) among those who are mighty of the earth and excessively exalted (Psalm XLVI), so that the holy merit of the man might also be revealed through the visitation of his most blessed family and household. ‘The generation of the upright,’ he says, ‘shall be blessed’ (Psalm CXI): glory that does not perish and riches that do not fade are in his house—a house built in heaven, not by the labor of hands, but by the holiness of works. But I shall cease to say more about the memory of a man so dear to me and so devoted to Christ, since I recall that I have already narrated no small part about him in letters previously delivered to you, and since I could proclaim nothing better or holier about the blessed mother of this son and the father of saints, Melania, the root of branches, than what your holiness has deigned to speak and discuss about her. For, since I, a sinner with unclean lips, could say nothing worthy, being far removed from the merits of her faith and the virtues of her soul, you, that man of Christ, a teacher in the Church of truth, with the grace of God directing you toward what is better, might be prepared as a worthier herald of so manly a soul in Christ. You saw, as I said, her mind strengthened by divine power through a more favorable spirit, and you praised her piety joined with virtue in more fitting language.”

Thus far Paulinus concerning Melania deprived of her son.

As for the elder Melania’s remaining children, we have already said that two of them were buried at nearly the same time as their father, and that only one male child was left to her. Saint Jerome states that she left him at Rome when she set out for Jerusalem (Jerome, Letter 25). This is the very man whom we have said died in Africa. Saint Paulinus, moreover, testifies that daughters also survived her when she returned from Jerusalem to Rome, describing them as meeting their mother with great pomp (Paulinus, to Severus, Letter 10). Palladius reports that the son under discussion had a wife named Albina (Palladius, *Lausiac History*), as we stated above. But in this matter we rightly corrected Palladius entirely on the basis of Paulinus and Augustine, when he says that this son of the elder Melania, being very young, followed his mother as far as Sicily when she returned to Jerusalem. For from what has been said it is sufficiently clear that he followed his mother into Africa and there ended his life.

But there is another point—and it is the more important one—for the sake of which we wished to recount from Paulinus this well-known account of Melania’s son’s death. Although at this time she is exalted by the praise of Saint Augustine and Paulinus, this serves as evidence that she had completely washed away the stains that had clung to her through her patronage of Origen’s errors, after she learned that those errors had been condemned at Rome by Pope Anastasius and by the council of the bishops of Italy. Since, as has been said, the elder Melania sailed to Jerusalem as soon as possible after being deprived of her son, the *Acts of the Younger Melania* report that Pinianus and her companions remained in Africa. It is clear that they departed from there for Alexandria and afterward went on to Jerusalem. But, says Palladius, when the elder Melania reached Jerusalem, she departed this life within forty days. It is right to believe that she had already been reconciled with Saint Jerome, who seems to have associated most familiarly there both with her traveling companions and with her relatives; this can also be understood from his letter to Augustine (Jerome, Letter 79).

[Col. 0735]

ON RUFFINUS THE PRIEST AND HIS BOOK, WITH PRAISES AND TESTIMONIES FROM ILLUSTRIOUS MEN

PRAISES OF RUFFINUS

[Col. 0735A]

Jerome, Letter 5, to Florentius

445 “And since Brother Ruffinus [Note: [Col. 0737C] Ruffinus.] You see, reader, what Jerome writes about Ruffinus before that closest and sweetest bond was turned into hateful slander. Who would not exclaim with Augustine: ‘O miserable and pitiable condition! O uncertain knowledge of present circumstances in the wills of friends, where there is no foreknowledge of the future! And finally, what friend would not be feared as a future enemy, if what we lament could arise between Ruffinus and Jerome? When, toward whom, and where should ruin not be feared by a human being, since it could happen to men mature in age and rich in the Lord’s eloquence—at the very time when, having already cast aside worldly burdens and become free, you were following the Lord, and were living together in that land where the Lord, walking on human feet, said, ‘My peace I give you, my peace I leave you’ (John XIV)? Truly, the life of man upon earth is a trial (Job VII). Alas for me, who cannot find you together somewhere! Perhaps, as I am moved, grieve, and fear, I would fall at your feet, weep as much as I could, and beg as much as I loved: now each of you for himself, now both for one another, and for others, especially the weak for whom Christ died. They watch you, as though in the theater of this life, at great risk to themselves, lest by writing about you they spread things that, if you should ever become reconciled, you could not erase’ (Augustine, Letter 15 to Jerome, and in Jerome, Letter 93.)”], who is said to have come from Egypt to Jerusalem with holy Melania, is joined to me by an inseparable bond of brotherly affection. I ask you not to hesitate to deliver to him the letter of mine attached to this letter of yours. Do not judge us by his virtues. In him you will see the unmistakable traces of holiness, while I am ash and the vilest part of clay—and now, as I am turned into dust, I am content if the weakness of my eyes can endure the radiance of his character. He has just washed and is clean, whitened like snow. I, stained with every filth of sin, wait day and night in trembling to pay the last quarter.”

The same author, in the appendix to Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, under the fourteenth year of Valentinian

Florentinus, Bonosus, and Ruffinus are regarded as distinguished monks. Florentinus was so compassionate toward the needy that he was commonly called “the father of the poor.”

[Col. 0735C]

Paulinus, Letter 9, to Severus

I have sent to the presbyter Ruffinus the very annotation that you had sent as a memorandum and that I had inserted in my letter. He is the spiritual companion of holy Melania on her journey, truly holy and devoutly learned, and for that reason bound to me by intimate affection. If he does not explain to you the causes of the discrepancy in the reckoning of years or reigns that rightly troubles you, and the reasons for the gap in the historical narrative—for he is rich in both scholarly and secular literature, in Greek no less than in Latin—I fear that we shall seek in vain for another person in these regions.

Cassian, *On the Incarnation*, Book VII, chapter 27

Ruffinus also, a man of Christian philosophy, was no insignificant member of the body of ecclesiastical teachers.

Pope Gelasius, at the Roman Council of seventy bishops

[Col. 0735D] Likewise, Ruffinus, a devout man, published many books of ecclesiastical works and also interpreted several Scriptures. But since blessed Jerome censured him in certain matters concerning free choice, we hold the views that we know blessed Jerome held.

Sidonius, Book II, Letter 9, to Donidius

Among them, Adamantius Origen, translated by Tyrannius Ruffinus, was carefully studied by readers of our faith. Likewise, as they expressed differing opinions according to each person’s preference, they discussed why he was rejected by some of the foremost initiates as a sinister and dangerous author, although he had been translated so closely word for word that neither Apuleius rendered Plato’s *Phaedo*, nor Cicero Demosthenes’ *Ctesiphon*, so fully into the usage and standard of Roman speech.

Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men of the Church*, chapter 17

Ruffinus, a presbyter of the Church of Aquileia, was no small part of the Church’s teachers, and in translating from Greek into Latin he possessed an elegant talent. In the end he made available to Latin readers a very large part of the Greek library: namely, the works of Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia; of Gregory of Nazianzus, a most eloquent man; the books of Clement of Rome’s *Recognitions*; Eusebius of Caesarea in Palestine’s *Ecclesiastical History*; the *Sentences* of Sixtus; and the *Sentences* of Evagrius.

He also translated the *Sentences* of the martyr Pamphilus against the mathematicians.

All those works that are read by Latins with the prologues mentioned above were translated by Ruffinus; those without a prologue were translated by another person, who did not wish to compose a prologue.

Not all of Origen’s works were translated by him, since Jerome also translated some, which are distinguished by his own prologue.

Through his own labor—or rather, by the grace and gift of God—the same Ruffinus expounded the Creed, so that, by comparison with his exposition, others may be thought not to have expounded it at all.

He also discussed Jacob’s Blessing over the patriarchs in three senses: historical, moral, and mystical.

He also wrote many letters exhorting people to the fear of God, among which those he sent to Proba are preeminent.

He added a tenth and an eleventh book to the *Ecclesiastical History* that, as we have said, had been written by Eusebius and translated by Ruffinus himself.

He also replied to a detractor of his little works in two volumes, arguing and proving that he had exercised his talent out of regard for God and with the Lord’s help for the benefit of the Church, whereas the other, driven by the spur of rivalry, had turned his pen to slander.

Honorius, *On Illustrious Men of the Church*, chapter 17

Ruffinus, a presbyter of the Church of Aquileia and no small part of the Church’s teachers, possessed an elegant talent in translating from Greek into Latin and made available to Latin readers a very large part of the Greek library: namely, the works of Basil, bishop of Caesarea; of Gregory of Nazianzus, a most eloquent man; the books of Clement of Rome’s *Recognitions*; the nine books of Eusebius of Caesarea in Palestine’s *Ecclesiastical History*, to which he added two; and the *Sentences of Sixtus the Philosopher* [Note: [Col. 0737D] Sixtus the philosopher.] It is plainly evident whom Honorius habitually copied from Gennadius. But what I noted above, in prolegomenon 4, section 5—that either Honorius is corrupt or Gennadius was read by him superficially—applies here as well. For he conflates the *Sentences of Sixtus* with those of the martyr Pamphilus. Sixtus did not write against the mathematicians; the martyr Pamphilus did, as Gennadius clearly states.], against the mathematicians.

Not all of Origen’s works were translated by him, since Jerome also translated some.

He expounded the Creed in such a way that, in comparison with his exposition, others may be thought not to have expounded it at all.

He also discussed Jacob’s Blessing over the patriarchs in three ways: historically, morally, and mystically.

He also wrote many letters exhorting people to the fear of God.

He replied to his detractor in two volumes.

TESTIMONIES CONCERNING THIS VERY BOOK

Ruffinus, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 4

After mentioning the two Macarii, Heraclides and Pambo, and recounting certain miracles of Macarius, he adds:

“But if we wished to relate the deeds of each individual miracle, we would be excluded from the brevity we have proposed, [Col. 0738A] especially since these matters deserve a narrative in a work of their own [Note: [Col. 0737D] “A work of their own.” Ruffinus seems here to indicate that, when writing the *Ecclesiastical History*—in which he incidentally mentions the holy Fathers who flourished in the desert—he intended to treat their deeds more fully in a work of his own. We learn from the following testimony of Saint Jerome that he did so, although it seems to me more likely that this book was not composed by Ruffinus so much as extracted by him from the Greek text of Palladius, Heraclides, or an anonymous author. See what was said in prolegomenon 4.]”

Jerome, Letter to Ctesiphon against the Pelagians, chapter 2
Ruf[inus] also wrote a book, ostensibly about monks, in which he enumerates many who never existed [Note: “Who never existed.”] I cannot detect in this book any such persons who never existed, since scarcely one appears for whom other authors do not also provide testimony. I except only the city of Oxyrhynchus, whose name and bishopric, although they are found among historians and the Fathers, I do not remember ever having read anything concerning the history narrated here. Yet I know of no one who has ever doubted its existence. Indeed, Baronius incorporated it into his Annals, volume III, under the year of Christ 316, the third year of Pope Sylvester and the eleventh of the emperor Constantine.]; and those whom he says were Origenists [Note: “Origenists.” Consult what we said in the general prolegomenon 15.]—there is no doubt that they were condemned by the bishops: namely Ammonius, Eusebius, and Euthymius [Note: “Namely Ammonius, Eusebius, and Euthymius.” These are discussed here in chapter 23.], and Evagrius himself [Note: “Evagrius.” Concerning him, see chapter 27.], as well as Or [Note: “Or.” Concerning him, see chapter 2.] and Isidore [Note: “Isidore.” He and his monastery are discussed in chapter 17.], together with many others whom it would be tedious to enumerate. And in accordance with that passage of Lucretius:

> And just as when physicians try to give  
> bitter wormwood to children,  
> first they touch the rim of the cup  
> with the sweet, golden-yellow liquid of honey,

so he placed one John [Note: “John.” He appears here in chapter 1, and Saint Jerome states that he was placed at the beginning of the book.] at the very beginning of the book, a man who was undoubtedly Catholic and holy, in order by means of him to introduce into the Church the other men whom he had presented as heretics.

From the words of Saint Apollonius, in Part III of the Decree, chapter 3, concerning Consecration, chapter 16 [Note: “From the words.” It is noted in the Decree concerning this chapter: “This chapter is found in Palladius, in the Life of Abbot Apollo.” This was noted in the time of Gregory XIII, after Palladius had appeared in Hervetus’s translation; in that translation the same account is found in chapter 52, although in different words. In Palladius’s older translation there is no mention of this matter. But this narrative, both in substance and in wording, has been taken from this book, chapter 7, which Ruffinus translated, as I think, from an anonymous Greek book. For what is now found under Palladius’s name, chapter 52, in Hervetus’s translation, is also found under the name of Heraclides, in an uncertain translator, chapter 2. See the prolegomena on Ruffinus, Palladius, and Heraclides.]:

The appointed fasts—namely, on Wednesday and Friday—are not to be broken unless some great necessity arises, because on Wednesday Judas conceived the betrayal of the Lord, and on Friday the Savior was crucified. Therefore, anyone who breaks the prescribed fast on these days without some necessity may seem either to betray the Savior together with the betrayer, or to crucify him together with those who crucified him.

# THE THIRD BOOK OF THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS, OR THE SAYINGS OF THE ELDERS, PROBABLY BY RUFFINUS [Note: “Ruffinus.” See general prolegomenon 5, at the beginning of these books.] THE PRESBYTER OF AQUILEIA

[Col. 0739]

## Prologue

[Col. 0739] 492 Who would doubt that the world truly stands by the merits of the saints? [Note: “Who would doubt that the world truly stands by the merits of the saints?” From this, too, it may in some way be inferred that Ruffinus is the author of this book, as I touched upon in prolegomenon 5. Here Ruffinus repeats what he had said in the prologue to the preceding book—or rather, he responds epiphonematically to that book’s prologue. For whereas there he had said, “so that it should not be doubted that the world still stands by their merits,” he now concludes epiphonematically, alluding to what was said earlier: “Who, truly, would doubt that the world stands by the merits of the saints?” Moreover, just as the prologue of the preceding book alludes in certain respects to Palladius’s preface to the *Lausiac History*, so this one has more openly certain common elements with Palladius’s letter to Laus, which is placed there after the preface. I now set these out individually. [Col. 0810D] “Therefore do not despise simplicity and unpolished speech.” Palladius, at the beginning of the *Lausiac History*, in his letter to Laus: “Nor reject rough and unadorned diction.” “For it is not the task of my work to mark out the words of divine teaching and Scripture with sophistry and eloquence.” Palladius, in the same place: “It does not belong to divine teaching to use speech adorned and composed for displaying wisdom.” “But to persuade the minds of human beings to faith and works of truth.” Palladius, in the same place: “But to persuade by words of truth.” “Finally, the faith of the holy fathers, patriarchs, and prophets—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, Moses, Elijah, and John—has therefore been set down,” etc. Palladius, in the same place: “For those who wrote the Lives of the Fathers—of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Elijah, John, and those who followed thereafter—did not narrate them so that their glory might be displayed, but so that they might benefit those who read them.”], namely, of those whose life shines forth in this volume; they have wholly avoided every stain of luxury, and, having abandoned the world, they search out the vast solitudes of the desert. There, keeping watch amid terrifying cliffs and dreadful caves, they neither hunger nor thirst, because the right hand of God sustains and feeds them. By their merits may you be lifted up; by their supplications may you obtain forgiveness of sins, my lord Fidosus [Note: “My lord Fidosus.” At first I thought that *Phidose* should be read, a Greek name, since I knew that a similar name existed elsewhere: Phidus, bishop of Joppa at the Council of Ephesus, and Phidus the deacon in the *Life of Saint Euthymius* under 20 January. Athanasius, in his letter concerning the Synods of Ariminum and Seleucia, also has a certain Φιδήλιον, *Phidelius*, a bishop; in Socrates, book II, chapter 32, the form is Φιλήδιος, *Philedius*. But after examining various possibilities, I found nothing that suited this passage. Finally, when I was reading Palladius attentively—for I saw that this prologue had been modeled on him—and noticed that in both the Preface and the letter to Laus the word *fidelissimus* occurred several times—“the splendor of your most faithful and religious authority, Laus,” in the Preface; and “Since you know these things, most faithful Laus,” in the letter; and in chapters 19, 20, and 34, “most faithful Laus,” where the Greek has πιστότατε—it seemed to me that Ruffinus had written *fidosum* for “most faithful,” and had thus covertly indicated Laus. For I do not think Ruffinus prefixed his own name to this book, since he either translated it from another work or published someone else’s book with a preface. Just as I found this prologue in all manuscripts and editions except the first, so I have printed it here. The first edition, however, presents what follows after *Fidose* in this form and with additions; I append it here so that you would not miss anything omitted: “I therefore bless and admire your praiseworthy purpose, as it deserves, because, while very many who profess the religious life devote their attention to the empty and vain pursuits of the present age, and, according to the prophet’s oracle, ‘the stones of the sanctuary have been scattered at the head of every street,’ I rejoice greatly that you desire to be instructed by the word of edification and the teaching of Holy Scripture, and that you seek out the reflections and institutions of the holy Fathers. “Accordingly, as I enter my twentieth year in the episcopate, I shall attempt to explain, in a concise account of the present little book, the life and moral teaching of those spiritual men whom I have seen and heard distinguished in the things of God, so that in your purpose of piety you may become a guide to yourself in good works, and a teacher of the unlearned—of those who are with you and of those who will come after you. “But I ask you not to despise the simplicity of my speech, nor to demand from me the elegance of a polished style. For it is not the task of divine Scripture to set forth its words with sophistry and eloquence, but to persuade human minds to faith and works of truth, according to what is written: ‘Open your mouth with the word of God’ (Prov. 31); and again: ‘Do not despise the words of the elders, for they too learned from their fathers’ (Eccles. 8). “Finally, the faith and conduct of the holy patriarchs and prophets—Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Elijah, and John—were set down by those who came before us not merely so that they might glorify them, whom the Lord had certainly glorified and held glorious in his kingdom, but so that they might provide later readers with the teaching of truth and examples of salvation. “Therefore, receiving from us not eloquence but strength, truths rather than embellishment, imitate the saints whom you read and proclaim those whom you love. For through this your hearers, having become lovers of Christ, will advance toward eternal salvation.” From these passages it becomes even clearer how Ruffinus reproduced this prologue from Palladius’s Preface. Compare them with one another, and you will recognize for yourself that my conjecture is not groundless.] Therefore do not despise simplicity and unpolished speech. For it is not my task to mark out the words of divine teaching and Scripture with sophistry and eloquence, but to persuade human minds to faith and works of truth. Finally, the faith and conduct of the Fathers, the holy patriarchs and prophets—namely Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Elijah, and John—were set down not merely so that we might glorify those whom God had certainly glorified and held glorious in his kingdom, but so that they might provide later readers with the teaching of truth and examples of salvation.

[Col. 0740]

# SAYINGS OF THE ELDERS

[Col. 0739A] 1. One of the holy elder Fathers, when monks asked him about the reason for abstinence, said:

“My little sons, we must hate every comfort of the present life. We must neither seek bodily pleasures and the sweetness of the belly, nor honor from human beings; and the Lord Jesus will give us heavenly honors, rest in eternal life, and glorious joy with his angels.”

2. The same elder said:

“Because hunger is naturally present in human beings, we ought to take food to sustain the needs of the body, but not in a state of passion or satiety of the belly. Sleep, too, is naturally present in human beings, but not to the point of surfeit or bodily relaxation, so that we may humble the passions and vices of the flesh. For an excess of sleep makes the mind and senses of a human being dull and sluggish, whereas wakefulness makes both the senses and the mind more subtle and pure. Thus the holy Fathers also said that holy vigils purify and enlighten the mind.

“Anger, too, is naturally present in human beings—not as an upheaval of passion, but so that one may be angry against oneself and one’s vices, in order readily to correct and cut them away from oneself. Likewise, if we see others doing something wrong and contrary to God’s commandments, we ought indeed to be vehemently angry against their vices, but carefully correct, rebuke, and admonish the persons themselves, so that, once corrected, they may be saved and attain eternal life.”

3. There was an elder in the inner desert who for many years labored exceedingly in abstinence and in every spiritual discipline (Pelagius, booklet VII, no. 25). Some brothers came to him and, admiring his perseverance, said:

“How do you endure this place, so dry and desolate, Father?”

He answered them:

“All the labor of the whole period during which I have lived here does not yet amount to the span of a single hour of the eternal torments of Gehenna. We must,” he said, “endure labor in the short time of this life and mortify the passions of our body, so that in that future and eternal age, which never fails, we may find perpetual rest.”

4. The holy elders told us about a certain brother, saying that at one time he was so assaulted by demons that, from the first hour of the day, they caused such hunger and physical weakness in him that he could not endure it at all (Pelagius, booklet I, no. 58). Nevertheless, he said in his heart:

“However hungry I may be, I must wait at least until the third hour, and then take food.”

When the third hour had come, he again said to his thoughts:

“Now too I must forcibly endure until the sixth hour.”

When the sixth hour arrived, he soaked bread in water, saying:

“While this bread is soaking, I must also wait until the ninth hour.”

When the ninth hour arrived, according to custom he completed all his prayers and psalmody in accordance with the rule, and set out the bread to eat. He endured this for many days.

One day, then, he did the same from the first hour [Col. 0741B] until the ninth. When the ninth hour arrived and he had sat down to take food, he saw a great smoke rise from the little basket in which the bread—namely, the *paximatia* [Note: “Paximatia.” These are loaves commonly used by the Egyptian monks. See the *Onomasticon*.]—had been placed, and pass out through the window of his cell.

From that day onward, neither hunger nor bodily weakness afflicted him. Rather, his heart was so strengthened in faith and abstinence that even after two days he no longer desired to take food. Thus, with the grace of God assisting his struggle, the brother through his patience extinguished the passion of *gastrimargia*, that is, gluttony and desire.

5. Once some brothers left the monastery to visit the Fathers who lived in the desert (Pelagius, booklet X, no. 92). When they came to an elderly hermit, he received them with great joy and, as is customary, set a little table before them. Seeing that they were tired from the journey, he had them refresh themselves before the ninth hour and set before them whatever he had in his cell to eat, giving them rest.

When evening came, they completed prayers and psalms according to custom, and did the same during the night. The elder mentioned above rested separately in another place, and heard them speaking among themselves and saying:

“These hermits are fed more and better for refreshment than those who live in monasteries.”

The elder heard this but remained silent. When day dawned, they set out to go to another hermit who lived nearby. As they were leaving, the elder said to them:

“Greet him for me, and say to him: ‘Be watchful, and do not water the vegetables.’”

When they reached the other elder, they delivered the message. He understood the reason and detained the brothers, giving them work weaving baskets. He himself sat with them and did not cease from manual labor.

In the evening, when the lamps were lit, he added some psalms beyond the usual number. After completing the prayers, he said to them:

“We do not customarily take food every day, but because of your arrival we must dine today.”

He set dry bread and salt before them, saying:

“Because of you we must dine on something more.”

He then added a little vinegar, salt, and a little oil. When they had risen from the table, he began again to sing psalms until nearly dawn, and said to them:

“Because of you we cannot sing the entire canon. Therefore rest a little, since you are tired from the journey.”

When morning came and the first hour arrived, they wished to leave him, but the elder did not permit them, saying:

“Rather, stay with us for several days. I shall not let you leave today; out of charity I shall keep you for at least three more days.”

When they heard this, they rose during the night and, before daybreak, secretly fled from the place.

6. One of the holy elders went to visit another elderly hermit. The latter received him with complete joy and, for his guest’s arrival, prepared cooked lentils for refreshment. They agreed first, according to custom, to complete their prayers and psalmody, and afterward to take food.

When they had entered, they sang psalms and completed the entire Psalter. They also recited passages from the Holy Scriptures as though they were reading, having two prophets absent from them. The day had already passed, and the night likewise was drawing to a close. While they were praying and singing psalms attentively, another day dawned, and then they realized that the night had passed.

Again they spoke to one another about the word of God and explained spiritual meanings to each other. It came to about the ninth hour, and the visiting elder took his leave and returned to his cell. They had forgotten to eat the food that had been prepared while they received spiritual nourishment. In the evening, the elder found the pot full, just as it had been prepared, and, saddened, said:

“Alas! How we have forgotten this stew.”

7. Abba Zeno told us that once, while traveling to Palestine, he became tired from the labor of the journey and sat down beneath a tree (Pelagius, booklet IV, no. 17). Nearby there was a field full of cucumbers. He thought in his heart that he should rise and take some of those cucumbers for refreshment.

“It is nothing great,” he said, “that I am going to take.”

Then, answering himself in his thoughts, he said:

“Since thieves are sent to punishments at the command of judges, I too must test myself to see whether I can endure the torments that thieves suffer.”

He rose at once, stood in the heat for five days, and scorched his body. Then he said to his thoughts:

“Since I cannot endure torments, I must not commit theft. Rather, I must continue, according to custom, the work of my hands and refresh myself from my labors, as Holy Scripture says in the Psalms: ‘You shall eat the labors of your hands; you are blessed, and it shall be well with you’ (Ps. 127), which indeed we sing every day in the presence of the Lord.”

8. A disciple of a certain holy elder was assaulted by the spirit of fornication. But, with the Lord’s grace assisting him, he bravely resisted the wicked and impure thoughts of his heart, afflicting himself severely with fasts and prayers and with manual labor.

The blessed elder, seeing him laboring in this way, said to him:

“If you wish, my son, I shall beseech the Lord to take this assault away from you.”

He answered:

“I see, Father, that although I endure labor, I nevertheless feel that good fruit is being brought to completion in me, because through the occasion of this assault I fast more, and endure more in vigils and prayers. Nevertheless, I ask you to intercede for me and entreat the Lord’s mercy, that he may give me strength so that I can endure and fight lawfully.”

Then the holy elder said to him:

“Now I know, my son, that you understand faithfully that this spiritual struggle, through patience, advances toward the eternal salvation of your soul. Thus the holy Apostle said: ‘I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; from now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me’—and not for me alone, but for all who love his appearing (2 Tim. 4).”

[Col. 0743B] 9. Another brother, too, was violently assaulted by an unclean spirit of fornication. He rose during the night and went to a certain holy elder proven in virtues, confessing to him that he was suffering an assault from the spirit of fornication.

When the elder heard this, he comforted him, teaching him through spiritual words about the virtue of patience. He said, as it is written:

“Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord” (Ps. 26).

The brother returned to his cell, and behold, the assault again pressed upon him. He hastened once more to the elder mentioned above. When the elder saw him, he again taught him to endure patiently and without weariness, saying:

“Believe, my son, that the Lord Jesus Christ will send you help from his holy heaven, so that you may overcome this passion.”

Strengthened by the holy elder’s counsel, the brother returned to his cell. Again the assault greatly troubled his heart. Immediately, at that same hour of the night, he returned to the elder and begged him to pray to the Lord for him with greater earnestness.

The elder said to him:

“Do not be afraid, my son; do not give way, and do not conceal your thoughts. For the unclean spirit departs from you in confusion when the secrets of unclean thoughts are revealed to holy and most blessed Fathers. Act manfully, my son; let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord (Ps. 26). For where the battle is harder, there the crown will also be more glorious.

“Finally, the holy prophet Isaiah says: ‘Has the hand of the Lord become powerless to save, or has his ear grown heavy so that he does not hear?’ (Isa. 59). Consider, therefore, little son, that the Lord awaits your struggle and prepares for you, as you fight against the devil, the crown of eternity. For this reason Holy Scripture warns us, saying: ‘Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of heaven’ (Acts 14).”

When the brother heard this, his heart was strengthened in the Lord. He remained with the elder and no longer wished to return to his cell.

10. At one time the demon of fornication inflicted so harsh an assault upon blessed Abba Moses, who lived in a place called Petra, that he could no longer remain seated in his cell. He went to Saint Abba Isidore and reported the violence of his assault (Pelagius, booklet XVIII, no. 12).

Abba Isidore brought testimonies from the Holy Scriptures to comfort him and urged him to return to his cell, but Abba Moses did not wish to go back. Then Abba Isidore and Abba Moses together went up to the upper part of his cell.

Isidore said to him:

“Look toward the west and see.”

When he looked, he saw a multitude of demons violently disturbed in fury, as though prepared for battle and hastening to fight.

Then Abba Isidore said to him:

“Look again toward the east and see.”

When he looked, he saw an innumerable multitude of holy angels, a glorious and shining army of heavenly powers, brighter than the light of the sun.

Abba Isidore said to him:

“Those whom you saw in the west are the ones who assault the saints of God. Those whom you saw toward the east are the ones whom God sends to the assistance of his saints. Know, therefore, that there are more with us, as the prophet Elisha says (2 Kings 6). Saint John likewise says: ‘Greater is he who is in us than he who is in the world’ (1 John 2).”

When he heard this, Saint Abba Moses was strengthened in the Lord and returned to his cell, giving thanks and glorifying the patient goodness of our Lord Jesus Christ.

11. There was a certain brother in the desert of Scetis, ready and eager for the work of God and for spiritual conduct (Pelagius, booklet V, no. 22). The devil, the enemy of the human race, introduced thoughts into him so that he would remember the beauty of a certain woman known to him and be violently troubled in his thoughts.

It happened, by the providence of the Lord Jesus, that another brother came from Egypt to visit him in the charity of Christ. While they were speaking with one another, the conversation came around to the point that the brother from Egypt said:

“That woman has died.”

She was the very woman whose love had been the occasion of the other brother’s assault.

When he heard this, after a few days he went to the place where the body of the dead woman had been laid. He opened her tomb during the night, wiped the pus of her corruption with his cloak, and returned to his cell. He kept the stench before his eyes and said to his thoughts:

“Behold the object of your desire. You sought this; satisfy yourselves with it.”

Thus, in that stench, he tormented himself until the most filthy assault ceased.

12. Two monk brothers went to a nearby city to sell the things they had worked at with their hands throughout the year (Pelagius, booklet V, no. 27). One of them went out to buy certain necessities, while the other remained alone at the lodging; and, instigated by the devil, he fell into fornication.

When his brother returned, he said to him:

“Behold, we have sold the things that were necessary. Let us now return to our cell.”

The other brother answered:

“I cannot return.”

His brother begged him, saying:

“Why will you not return to the cell?”

He confessed to him:

“Because, when you left me, I fell into fornication; therefore I do not wish to return.”

Wanting to gain and save his soul, his brother said to him under oath:

“When I was separated from you, I too fell similarly into fornication. Nevertheless, let us return to the cell and place ourselves in repentance” [Note: Note that a well-intentioned lie is not lawful; perhaps he understood that he had fornicated spiritually.].

“For all things are possible with God” (Luke 1), so that he may deign to grant forgiveness to us who repent, lest we be tormented in eternal fire and in the punishments of hell in Tartarus, where there is no repentance, but fire always without end and dreadful torments.

Thus they returned to their cell. They went to the holy Fathers and threw themselves at their feet, groaning with great wailing and tears. They confessed to them the temptation and ruin that had befallen them. Whatever the holy elders commanded and taught them concerning repentance, they did in every respect.

The other brother, who had not sinned, did penance for the brother who had sinned as though he himself had sinned, because he had great charity toward him. When the Lord saw the labor of his charity, he soon revealed to the holy Fathers what the true circumstances were; and because the sinless brother had afflicted himself for the salvation of his brother, the Lord therefore granted forgiveness to the one who had sinned.

Behold, this is so, as it is written:

“He laid down his life for the salvation of his brother” (1 John 3).

13. Another brother was suffering trouble from the spirit of fornication. He went to a very experienced elder and begged him:

“Take this concern upon yourself, most blessed Father, and pray for me, because the passion of fornication is grievously assaulting me” (Pelagius, booklet V, no. 19).

When the elder heard this, he prayed earnestly, entreating the Lord’s mercy for him by day and by night.

The same brother came again and asked the elder to pray for him with still greater earnestness. The blessed elder prayed for him with equal and complete concern. But when the elder frequently saw the monk coming to him and begging him to pray, he became very sad and wondered why the Lord did not hear his prayer.

That same night the Lord revealed to him what negligence, sluggish relaxation, and bodily pleasures were present in that monk’s heart. This was shown to the holy elder: he saw the monk sitting, while the spirit of fornication played before him in various female forms, and he himself took pleasure with them. He also saw an angel of the Lord standing nearby and gravely indignant against that brother, because he did not rise or prostrate himself in prayer to God, but rather took pleasure in his thoughts.

These things were shown to the holy elder by revelation. He understood that the fault and negligence of the monk were the reason that his prayers were not heard. Then the elder said to him:

“It is your fault, brother, because you take pleasure in evil thoughts. It is impossible for the unclean spirit of fornication to depart from you merely because others are praying and entreating God for you, unless you yourself also undertake labor in fasts, prayers, and many vigils, beseeching the Lord Jesus Christ with groaning to grant you his mercy and the help of his grace, so that you may resist evil thoughts.

“Physicians, who prepare and apply medicines for human bodies, may indeed do everything with the greatest care; nevertheless, if the sick person refuses to abstain from harmful foods or from other things that customarily aggravate illnesses, the physicians’ treatment, care, and concern do him no good. The same thing happens in illnesses of the soul.

“Although the holy Fathers, who are spiritual physicians, may with complete concentration and from their whole heart pray for the mercy of our Lord and Savior on behalf of those who ask to be helped by their prayers, unless those persons themselves, with complete attention of mind, do what is pleasing to God both in prayer and in every spiritual work, the prayers of the saints will not benefit them in their negligence and relaxation, while they give no thought at all to the salvation of their souls.”

When the brother heard this, his heart was pierced. According to the elder’s teaching, he afflicted himself with complete concern in fasts, prayers, and vigils, and he obtained the Lord’s mercy. The spirit of the unclean passion departed from him.

14. There was a certain monk who lived in the desert. After many years, a certain girl from his family and kindred discovered where the monk mentioned above lived, and, instigated by the devil, went into the desert looking for him (Pelagius, booklet V, no. 24). When she found him, she entered his cell and told him that she was of his family and kinship. She remained there with him and fell with him into the ruin of sin.

There was another monk, also living in the desert. Whenever the hour for refreshment came, the *gello* [Note: “Gello.” Later, *gellanculus*. In Pelagius, booklet V, no. 24, the word is *suriscula*. A water vessel is meant. See the *Onomasticon*.] containing the water that he had prepared for himself to drink would tip over, and all the water would spill onto the ground. This happened for several days whenever he came to take refreshment, and the water was poured onto the ground so that he could not drink.

He thought to himself that he should go to the other monk and tell him about the *gello* that kept tipping over and spilling all the water. While he was on the way, at evening he slept in an ancient, ruined temple of idols and heard demons speaking among themselves:

“This night we have thrown that monk into fornication.”

When he heard this, he was astonished.

When day dawned, he reached the monk and found him overcome by the deepest sadness. He said to him:

“What am I to do, brother? Whenever I wish to take refreshment, the *gello* that I use for water immediately tips over, the water spills out, and I have nothing to drink.”

Then the monk mentioned above answered:

“You came to ask me why the little *gello* tips over and the water spills out? What am I to do? I fell into fornication last night.”

The other brother answered:

“I already know that.”

The monk said:

“How were you able to know this?”

He replied:

“When I was resting on the road during the night, I heard the demons speaking among themselves and rejoicing over your fall, and I was deeply saddened.”

Then the monk said:

“Behold, I am leaving and returning to the world.”

When the other heard this, he begged him:

“Do not do this, brother. Rather, endure patiently and remain in this place. Let us drive the woman away, and let her return to her own place. This pursuit is plainly a device of the evil devil. You ought rather to remain in this place, in affliction of heart and body, and with inward groaning of heart and tears, to entreat the mercy of our Lord and Savior until the end of your life, so that you may find mercy on that terrible day of the great judgment of God.”

15. There was a brother in the desert who lived in a place called Cellia, and the demons assaulted him with the passion of fornication. He thought to himself:

“Perhaps I ought to labor more at manual work, so that my carnal sense may be extinguished.”

That brother was a potter by trade. He rose, took clay, and molded something resembling the figure of a woman. He said to his thoughts:

“Behold, your wife. Therefore it is necessary for you to add to your manual labor beyond what is customary.”

After some days he did the same again with clay and molded something resembling a daughter for himself. He said to his thoughts:

“Behold, your wife has given birth to a daughter. Therefore it is necessary for you to exercise your manual labor more and more, so that you may feed and clothe yourself, your wife, and your daughter.”

Thus, through excessive labor, he so mortified his body that he could no longer endure such toil. Then he said to his thoughts:

“If you cannot endure this excessive labor, neither should you seek a woman.”

When God saw the fervent purpose of his mind in the struggle for chastity, he took away from him the trouble of the demons’ assault. And he glorified God for the greatness of his grace.

16. A brother asked blessed Abba Poemen:

“What shall I do, Father? The passion of fornication assaults me, and I am carried away into the passion of anger.”

The holy elder answered him:

“For this reason the prophet David said: ‘I used to strike the lion, and I frequently strangled the bear’ (1 Sam. 17). This is understood as follows: I cut anger away from my soul, but I afflicted fornication through labors.”

### 17

The holy elder Fathers used to speak of a certain monk, already advanced in age, who lived in the desert of Scetis.
