He was a slave belonging to certain men, and each year he would descend from the desert to Alexandria, where his masters lived, bringing them their annual payment, as slaves customarily give such payments to their masters (Pelagius, *Little Book* 15, no. 31, under the name Olympius). But his masters, moved by greater reverence because of the fear of God, honored him when they met and greeted him, and asked him to pray to the Lord on their behalf. He, however, would put water into a basin and hasten to wash the feet of his masters, wishing to offer them service with all humility. They, for their part, refused to allow him to wash their feet, saying: “Do not, most blessed Father, burden our souls.” But he answered them: “I am your servant, for almighty God has appointed you as my masters. And I give thanks to your lordships, because you have deigned to permit me to serve the living and true God, the creator and ruler of heaven and earth. Indeed, I have brought you the payment of my servitude.”

His masters, however, insisted and refused to accept the payment he had brought. The monk replied: “If you are unwilling to accept my payment, I have resolved not to return to the desert, but to remain here and serve you.” When his masters heard this, they agreed to accept the payment, lest he be saddened, and especially so that he might return to the desert places and his cell. Whatever he gave his masters as his payment, even against their will, they immediately distributed to the poor as soon as they received it.

The brothers questioned this same elder and said to him: “We beg you, Father, tell us why, with such determination, you insisted on giving your masters the payment for your service, even though they were unwilling and resisted you so strongly.” The elder replied: “Brothers, I hasten to fulfill the payment which, as to my masters, I owe them for my service each year, so that whatever, with the Lord’s help, I have labored at in fasting and prayer, in holy vigils, or in every spiritual work, with Christ the Lord assisting me, may benefit me in eternal life and contribute to the salvation of my soul. Otherwise, if I should fail to bring the payment for my service, perhaps all my spiritual labor would benefit as their reward those who permitted me to serve Christ the Lord and to live a spiritual life.”

### 18

There were two brothers, brothers by birth and related by blood, yet both were monks living according to the spiritual vocation. The wicked devil plotted against them, seeking by some means to separate them from one another (Pelagius, *Little Book* 15, no. 89).

One evening, therefore, as was customary, the younger brother lit a lamp and placed it upon a lampstand. Through the malice of the demons the lampstand fell, and the lamp was extinguished. By this opportunity the wicked devil plotted against them, in order to provoke them to quarrel. The elder brother rose and began to strike his brother furiously. But the younger, throwing himself upon the ground, pleaded with his brother, saying: “Be magnanimous, my lord, and I will light the lamp again.”

Because he did not answer him with an angry word, the evil spirit immediately departed from them in confusion. That same night he went and reported to the prince of the demons: “Because of the humility of that monk who, prostrate on the ground, asked his brother’s forgiveness, I had no power over them.” And he continued: “Seeing his humility, God poured out his grace upon him; and I feel myself greatly tortured and tormented because I was unable to separate them from one another.”

A pagan priest who lived there heard all these words and, pierced with compunction by the fear of the Lord and love of Jesus Christ, reflected that the worship of idols was rather the deception and destruction of souls. He abandoned everything and hastened to the holy Fathers at the monastery, reporting to them all that the demons had said among themselves through their wickedness.

When the holy Fathers had instructed him with salutary exhortations in the teaching of the Lord and Savior, he was baptized, undertook the monastic life and its holy vocation, and, with the grace of God assisting and cooperating with him, became a highly approved monk. He so revered and practiced the virtue of humility that everyone admired his extraordinary humility. For he used to say that the practice of humility dissolves all the power of our adversaries, the demons.

Indeed, our Lord Jesus Christ also triumphed over the devil through humility and crushed all his power. He added that he had often heard the demons speaking among themselves: “When we set human hearts ablaze with anger, if anyone patiently endures insulting abuse and instead turns and asks for what makes for peace, saying, ‘I have sinned,’ we immediately feel all our power wither, because the grace of divine power draws near to them.”

### 19

The blessed elder Poemen reported to the brothers, saying that recently there had been a certain monk in Constantinople during the reign of the emperor Theodosius (Pelagius, *Little Book* 15, no. 66). He lived in a small cell outside the city, near a suburb called the Septimum.

[Note: “Suburb.” Here the manuscript reading is remarkably varied. Audomarensis has *prastro*, “which is called insentimo”; Aquicinctinus has *proastion*, “which is called setimo”; the printed editions have *prope prascium* or *prastium*. Cedrenus, in the twentieth year of the reign of Theodosius the Younger, relates the same little story, where the Greek is *προάστειον* (*proasteion*). Below, in Pelagius, *Little Book* 15, no. 66, in this same matter, the word is *suburbanum*, “suburb.” Above, in the *Life of Saint Basil*, chapter 2, one likewise finds *proastium*. See the *Onomasticon*.]

[Note: “Septimum.” The seventh district or region of Constantinople is understood, situated in a suburb, or *proastion*. Sometimes Latins retain a Greek word and call it *hebdomon*. See the *Onomasticon*.]

The place was one where emperors, after leaving the city, were accustomed to spend their leisure willingly. When the emperor heard that there was a solitary monk there who never left his cell, he began walking toward the place where the aforementioned monk was staying. He ordered the eunuchs who followed him not to approach the monk’s cell. He himself went alone and knocked at the door.

The monk rose and opened it for him, without recognizing that he was the emperor. For the emperor had removed his crown from his head so that he would not be recognized. After prayer they sat down together, and the emperor asked him: “How are the holy Fathers living in Egypt?” The monk replied: “They all pray to God for your salvation.”

The emperor gazed attentively around the cell and saw nothing in it except a few dry loaves hanging in a basket. He said to him: “Give me your blessing, abba, so that we may have some refreshment.” The monk immediately hurried, brought water and salt, set out pieces of bread, and they ate together. He then offered him a cup of water, and the emperor drank.

Then the emperor Theodosius said: “Do you know who I am?” The monk replied: “I do not know who you are, lord.” He said to him: “I am the emperor Theodosius, and I have come here out of devotion.” When the monk heard this, he prostrated himself before him.

But the emperor said to him: “Blessed are you monks, who, secure and free from worldly affairs, enjoy a tranquil and peaceful life, having concern only for the salvation of your souls: how you may attain eternal life and heavenly rewards. For I tell you truly that I was born into a kingdom, and now I live in a kingdom, yet I never take food without anxiety.”

After this the emperor greeted him with great honor and departed from him. That same night the man of God began to consider within himself: “I ought no longer to remain in this place. For many, not only from the populace but also from the palace and from the senators, will follow the emperor’s example and come to see me; they will not cease to honor me as a servant of God. They will do this for the Lord’s name, but I fear that perhaps the wicked devil may steal away from me”—that is, “may secretly snatch away”—“and that I may gladly begin receiving them, and that my heart may take pleasure in their praise and honor. Through this I would begin to lose the virtue of humility and to delight in human praises and honors.”

[Note: “May steal away.” That is, “may secretly snatch away.” The printed editions add “my merit.” Likewise above, in Rufinus, Book II, chapter 15: “One day Satan, wishing to steal this from him …”]

While the man of God was considering all these things within himself, he fled from there that same night and went to Egypt, to the holy Fathers in the desert. Let us therefore consider, dearly beloved brothers, with what concern the servant of God strove to preserve the virtue of humility, so that he might deserve to receive from Christ the Lord, in the heavenly kingdom, eternal glory in return for the labor of the holy life which he had practiced for the Lord’s name.

### 20

Other holy elders also spoke about this same holy Poemen, saying that once, when the provincial governor arrived and heard of the blessed Poemen’s holy reputation, he desired to see him and sent a messenger to ask that he receive him (Pelagius, *Little Book* 8, no. 13).

The blessed Poemen was greatly saddened, thinking to himself: “If distinguished persons begin coming to greet and honor me, it is clear that many other ordinary people will also visit me. As a result, the secluded conduct of my life will necessarily be disturbed, and I may lose, through the theft of the wicked devil, the grace of humility which, with such labor and with the Lord’s help, I have striven to preserve from my youth; I may fall into the snares of vainglory.”

After considering these matters within himself, he decided that he should make an excuse and not receive the governor. The governor was saddened that Poemen had not received him and said to his officials: “Because I was not worthy to see the man of God, I attribute it to my sins.” Nevertheless, he very greatly desired to see the holy man by some means.

He therefore devised a plan that would give him an opportunity to see him. He seized the son of the blessed Poemen’s sister and put him in prison, so that by this means Poemen would either receive the governor or himself come to ask the governor for the young man’s release. He said to his officials: “So that the holy elder may not be saddened, send him word that, if he wishes to come to me, we must immediately bring the young man out of prison. For his case is such that it cannot pass without punishment.”

When the young man’s mother—that is, the sister of the holy Poemen—heard this, she went to the desert where her brother was. She stood at the door of his cell with much weeping and wailing, begging him to descend to the governor and plead on behalf of her son.

The blessed Poemen not only said nothing to her, but did not even open the door to come out to her. Then she began to curse him and say: “You are utterly hard and impious, with an iron heart! How can so great the grief of my weeping fail to move you to mercy, when I have only this one son, whom I see placed in danger of death?”

Then the elder sent her a message through the brother who served him: “Go and tell her: Poemen has not fathered children, and therefore he does not grieve.”

When the governor heard this, he said to his friends: “Write to him that he at least compose a letter of intercession to me, so that I may be able to release him.” Then, after many people had urged him, the holy elder wrote to the governor:

“Let your nobility carefully investigate the case of that man. If he has committed anything worthy of death, let him die, so that in this present age he may pay the penalty for his crime and escape the eternal and everlasting punishments of Gehenna. But if he has committed nothing worthy of death, order that he be judged according to what appears just under the laws.”

### 21

There was also among the great Fathers an elder named Agathon, highly renowned for the virtue of humility and patience (Pelagius, *Little Book* 10, no. 10).

Once some brothers went to visit him. They had heard that he possessed great humility and, wishing to test whether he truly possessed the patience of humility, said to him: “Many are scandalized by you, Father, because you are excessively afflicted by the vice of pride, and therefore despise others and consider them worthless. You also never cease speaking slanderously against the brothers. Many further assert that you do these things because you are afflicted by the vice of fornication, and, so that you may not appear to be the only one in error, you therefore never cease slandering others.”

The elder replied: “I recognize that all the vices you have mentioned are in me, and I cannot deny my many iniquities.” He fell prostrate upon the ground and worshiped those same brothers, saying: “I beg you, brothers, do not cease praying earnestly to Christ the Lord for me, a wretched man subject to many sins, that he may grant forgiveness for my many and evil iniquities.”

The brothers mentioned above added: “Let this also not be hidden from you: many are prepared to assert that you are a heretic.”

When the elder heard this, he said to them: “Although I am subject to many other sins, I am certainly not a heretic. May this be far from my soul!”

Then all the brothers who had come to him prostrated themselves on the ground at his feet, begging him and saying: “We ask you, abba, tell us why, when we spoke to you of so many vices and sins, you were not disturbed at all, but were greatly disturbed by the word ‘heretic,’ abhorred it, and could not endure hearing it.”

The elder said to them: “I endured those earlier faults and sins out of humility, so that you would believe me to be a sinner. For we know that, if the virtue of humility is preserved, it is great salvation for the soul.

“Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, when the Jews inflicted many insults and abuses upon him, endured everything patiently in order to provide us with examples of humility. False witnesses were brought forward and spoke many false things against him, and he patiently endured everything even to the death of the cross. Thus the apostle Peter also proclaimed, saying: ‘Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his footsteps’ (1 Peter 2). Therefore we ought patiently and humbly to endure every adversity.

“But I could not endure the statement you made concerning heresy, and I greatly abhorred it, because heresy is separation from God. A heretic is separated from the living and true God and joined to the devil and his angels. Having been alienated from Christ, he no longer has God to whom he may appeal for his sins, because he has perished utterly.

“But if he turns to the true and catholic faith of the holy Church, he is received by our good and merciful Savior Christ and reunited to the true God, our creator and Savior Christ, who is the Son in the Father, eternally with the Holy Spirit. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.”

### 22

The elder Fathers and all the monks living in the desert of Scetis held counsel among themselves and agreed that Father Isaac should be ordained priest for them in the church situated in that same desert. On the appointed day and hour a multitude of monks living in that desert gathered there (Paschasius, chapter 33, no. 2).

When the aforementioned abbot Isaac heard of this plan, he fled to Egypt and hid himself in a field among the bushes, considering himself unworthy of the honor of the priesthood. Very many monk-brothers followed him in order to seize him.

When they had arrived at the same field toward evening, farther away, so that they might refresh themselves after the fatigue of the journey—for it was night—they released the little donkey that carried their provisions, so that it could graze. While it was grazing, the donkey reached the place where the aforementioned abbot Isaac was hiding.

When day had dawned, the monks searched for the donkey and came to the same place where the elder had concealed himself. They were greatly astonished at the divine dispensation. They seized him and wanted to bind and restrain him and lead him away in that condition.

But the venerable elder did not permit this, saying: “I can no longer resist you, because perhaps it is God’s will that, although unworthy, I should receive the order of the priesthood.”

### 23

There were two monk-brothers living together in a cell, whose humility and patience were praised by many even among the holy Fathers.

A certain holy man heard of them and wished to test whether they possessed true and perfect humility. He therefore came to visit them. When they had received him joyfully and had completed their prayers and psalmody according to custom, he went outside the cell and saw a small garden where they grew vegetables for themselves.

Taking up a stick, he began with all his strength to strike and destroy all the vegetables, so that nothing at all remained. When the aforementioned brothers saw this, they said absolutely nothing and did not show sad or troubled faces.

They went back into the cell, completed the evening prayers, and, worshiping him, said: “If you command, lord, we will go and cook and taste the stalk that remains, since it is already time for us to eat.”

Then the elder worshiped them and said: “I give thanks to my God, because I see the Holy Spirit resting in you. Therefore I exhort and admonish you, dearly beloved brothers, to preserve the virtue of holy humility and patience to the end, so that this same virtue may cause you to appear great and exalted in the sight of the Lord in the heavenly kingdom.”

### 24

There was a certain elderly and highly approved monk in a coenobium, and he fell into a very serious illness. Exhausted by an excessive and unbearable infirmity, he suffered for a long time through many pains. The brothers could not find how to help his illness, because the monastery did not possess the things which the needs of his sickness required.

A certain woman devoted to God heard of his suffering and illness. She begged the Father of the monastery to take him to her cell so that she might care for him, especially since she could more easily find in the city what seemed necessary for his illness.

The Father of the monastery therefore ordered the brothers to carry him to the cell of the woman devoted to God. She received the elder with every reverence and served him for the Lord’s name, in return for the eternal reward which she believed she would receive from Christ our Savior.

After she had diligently served the man of God for more than three years, people of corrupted minds began, according to the uncleanness of their own minds, to suspect that the elder did not have a pure conscience toward the virgin who served him.

When the elder heard this, he prayed to the divinity of Christ, saying:

“You, Lord our God, who alone know all things and see that my illnesses and misery are many, and who consider the affliction of this great infirmity, which has consumed me for so long that I need the service of this woman of yours, who ministers to me for your name’s sake: grant her, my Lord and God, a worthy reward in eternal life, as in your goodness you have deigned to promise to those who, for your name’s sake, offer their service to the needy and infirm.”

When the day of his departure drew near, very many holy elder brothers from the monastery gathered around him. The elder said to them:

“I beg you, lords, fathers, and brothers, that when I have died you take my staff, plant it upon my grave, and, if it takes root and produces fruit, then you will know that my conscience toward the woman of God who served me is clean. But if it does not put forth leaves, know that I am not clean toward her.”

When the man of God had departed from the body, the holy Fathers, according to his command, planted his staff upon his grave. It put forth leaves, and when the season came it produced fruit. Everyone marveled and glorified God.

Because of this miracle, many also came from the neighboring regions and magnified the Savior’s grace. Indeed, we ourselves saw that little tree and blessed the Lord, who protects in all things those who serve him in sincerity and truth.

### 25

Once they brought to the blessed abbot Apollonius a possessed man who was being severely tormented by a demon (Pelagius, *Little Book* 15, no. 65).

For three days those who had brought him kept watch, begging the elder to heal him in Christ’s name through prayers poured out to God. The elder replied that he did not possess such merit as to command demons.

But when those who had come persisted, asking him and pleading with abundant tears, he finally consented. He commanded the demon in the name of our Lord and Savior, saying: “Come out, unclean spirit, from God’s creature.”

Then the demon replied: “I am indeed going out at the command of Christ’s power, but I will ask you a question, and you must answer me: What does it mean that it is written in the Gospel, ‘Who are the goats, and who are the sheep?’” (Matthew 25).

The elder replied: “The goats are the unjust, among whom I too am a sinner, subject to many sins. But God knows who the sheep are.”

Then the demon cried out with a loud voice: “Because of your humility I cannot stand at all!” And immediately he came out of the man whom he had possessed.

When all who were standing there saw this, they gave glory to God.

### 26

The holy elders reported to us, saying that there was a certain monk in the desert of Scetis. He came to visit the holy Fathers at a place called the Cells, where a multitude of monks lived in separate cells.

Since he could not at that time find a cell in which he could stay, one of the elders, who had another vacant cell, gave it to him, saying: “Rest for the time being in this cell, until you find a place where you can remain.”

Many brothers gathered to visit him, desiring to hear from him a word of eternal salvation, for he possessed a spiritual gift for teaching the word of God.

The elder who had lent him the cell was wounded in his heart by the poison of envy. He began to be indignant and say: “I have lived in this place for so many years, and the brothers come to me only very rarely, and then on feast days; but behold, very many brothers go to this impostor almost every day!”

He said to his disciple: “Go and tell him to leave that cell, because I need it.”

When his disciple went to the brother, he said to him: “My abba has sent me to ask how your holiness is, for he has heard that you are ill.”

The brother sent him this reply: “Pray for me, lord Father, because I have a severe stomachache.”

The disciple returned and said to his abba: “He begs your holiness to grant him even two days’ delay, so that he may arrange another cell for himself.”

After three days had passed, he again sent his disciple, saying: “Go and tell him to leave my cell. If he delays again, tell him that I am coming immediately and will drive him from my cell by beating him with a stick.”

The disciple went to the aforementioned brother and said to him: “Because my abba is very concerned about your illness, he has sent me to ask whether you are better.”

He replied: “I give thanks, holy lord, for your love, because you are concerned for me. Nevertheless, through your prayers I am better.”

The disciple returned and said to his abba: “Even now he begs your holiness to wait until Sunday, and then he will leave immediately.”

When Sunday arrived and he did not leave, the elder took a bar and, inflamed by the spirit of envy and anger, went to drive him from his cell by force.

His disciple approached him and said: “If you command, Father, I will go ahead of you and see whether perhaps some brothers have come to greet him; if they see you, they may be scandalized.”

The disciple went ahead and entered the brother’s cell, saying: “Behold, my abba has come to greet you. Come out quickly, therefore, and meet him with thanksgiving, because he has come to you out of his great love and affection.”

The brother immediately rose and went to meet him with great eagerness. When he saw him before he had drawn near, he prostrated himself on the ground and worshiped the elder with thanksgiving, saying:

“May the Lord repay you, dearest Father, with eternal blessings for your cell, which you granted me for his name’s sake; and may Christ the Lord prepare for you a glorious and splendid dwelling in the heavenly Jerusalem among his saints.”

When the elder heard this, he was pierced in his heart. He threw down the stick, ran to embrace him, kissed him, and invited him to his cell so that they might eat together with thanksgiving.

The elder then summoned his aforementioned disciple and asked him: “Tell me, son, did you say to this brother the words which I ordered you to say concerning the cell?”

His disciple confessed, saying: “Truly, lord, I say that, because of the humility which I owe you as my Father and lord, I did not dare to answer you anything when you sent me to him. Nevertheless, I did not say to him any of the things you ordered me to say.”

When the elder heard this, he immediately prostrated himself at his feet, saying: “From this day forward, you shall be my father and I shall be your disciple, because, through your haste, discretion, fear, and conduct in the love of God, Christ the Lord has freed both my soul and that brother’s from the snare of sin.”

This happened because of the faith, holy concern, and intention of the disciple, who perfectly loved his abba in the love of Christ and anxiously feared that, through the vice of envy and anger, his spiritual father might do something of the kind and lose all the holy labors which, from the beginning of his life, he had undertaken in Christ’s service for the rewards of eternal life.

Therefore the Lord granted his grace, so that they might rejoice together in the peace of Christ.

### 27

The holy elders used to speak of a disciple of Abba Paul named John, saying that he possessed great humility and the virtue of obedience, so that, even when his abba commanded difficult things, he never resisted in the slightest and did not even murmur lightly about anything (Pelagius, *Little Book* 14, no. 4).

Once manure from oxen was needed for the monastery’s uses. The abba sent him to the neighboring village to look for ox manure there and bring it quickly to the monastery.

There was a savage beast, a lioness, in that place. John, his disciple, immediately went out and proceeded according to the abba’s command. As he was leaving, he said to his abba: “Lord Father, I have heard many people say that there is a savage lioness in that place.”

Then the elder, as though joking, said to him: “If she comes upon you, seize her, tie her up, and bring her back with you.”

When he reached the place toward evening, the lioness immediately came out and sprang upon him. He tried to seize and hold her, but she shook herself free and escaped from his hands. He followed her, saying: “My abba commanded me to bring you to him bound.”

At once the beast stopped. Holding her, he returned to the monastery.

When he was delayed on the journey, the abba became very anxious and was deeply saddened on his account. Suddenly his disciple appeared, holding the lioness bound.

When the elder saw this, he marveled greatly and gave thanks to our Savior and Lord. His disciple said: “Behold, lord, as you commanded, I have brought the lioness bound.”

The elder wished to humble his disciple’s mind, lest the disciple become elated in his thoughts. He therefore said to him: “Just as you are senseless, so you have brought this senseless beast. Untie her, then, and release her, so that she may return to her place.”

### 28

One of the holy elders sent his disciple to draw water (John, *Little Book* 2, no. 17). The well was a considerable distance from the elder’s cell.

His disciple forgot to take with him the rope with which he was to draw the water. When he reached the well, he was very saddened, because their cell was far away. He did not know what to do or where to turn, for he hesitated to return to the cell without water.

Then, in great anxiety, he prostrated himself in prayer with tears, saying: “Lord, have mercy on me according to your great mercy” (Psalm 50); “you who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them; you who alone have done great wonders, have mercy on me for the sake of your servant who sent me.”

When he had risen from prayer, he cried out: “O well, well, my abba, the servant of Christ, sent me to draw water!”

Immediately the water rose up to the mouth of the well. After the brother had filled his flask, he departed, glorifying the power of the Lord our Savior. The water of the well returned to its place.

### 29

There was a certain brother in the monastery named Eulalius, richly adorned with the grace of humility (Pelagius, *Little Book* 15, no. 86).

Whenever, as commonly happens, the more negligent brothers committed some fault, they excused their own faults by claiming that the aforementioned brother was responsible. When he was rebuked by the elder brothers, he did not deny it, but prostrated himself upon the ground, worshiped them, and said that he had sinned and acted negligently.

When they accused him again and again, and, according to the monastic rule, imposed two- and three-day fasts upon him, he patiently endured everything.

The brothers did not know that he patiently endured all these things because of the virtue of humility. They gathered together, especially the elder brothers, and went to the Father of the monastery, saying:

“Consider, Father, what should be done. How long can we endure the negligence and damage which that brother Eulalius causes in the monastery? Almost all the monastery’s vessels and implements have already been broken and ruined through his negligence. How, then, can such a man be tolerated?”

The Father of the monastery replied: “For the time being let us endure the brother for a few days; afterward we will decide what ought to be done with him.”

Having said this, he dismissed the brothers. He entered his cell and prostrated himself in prayer, imploring the Lord’s mercy to reveal to him what he could arrange or decide concerning the brother so often mentioned.

Then it was revealed to him what he should do. The abbot therefore summoned all the brothers and said to them:

“Believe me, brothers: I would rather have the mat of brother Eulalius, together with his humility and patience, than all the works of those who, while murmuring in their hearts, labor in the monastery.”

To show you what merit this same brother has before God, I command you to bring me the mats of all the brothers.

When they had brought them, he ordered them to light a fire and placed all the brothers’ mats in it. They were immediately burned, except for the mat of brother Eulalius, which was found whole and had not been burned.

When all the brothers saw this, they were greatly afraid. They prostrated themselves on the ground, asking Christ the Lord for pardon and forgiveness, and greatly admiring brother Eulalius’s patience and humility.

From that time onward they honored and magnified him as one of the great Fathers. Brother Eulalius, however, could not endure these honors and praises. He said:

“Woe to me, unhappy man, because I have lost my humility, which for so long I hastened to acquire with the help and assistance of Christ the Lord.”

He rose during the night, left the monastery, and fled into the desert, where no one would recognize him. There he lived in a cave. For he did not desire the temporary praises of human beings, but wished to receive from Christ our Savior, in the age to come, heavenly and eternal glory.

### 30

We ought to know the praiseworthy humility and virtue of patience of the blessed abbot Anastasius, so that, considering his admirable magnanimity and tranquility of soul, we may imitate his example (Pelagius, little book XVI, no. 1, under the name of Gelasius).

This Anastasius had a codex written on very fine parchment, worth eighteen solidi; for it contained the whole Old and New Testament. When a certain brother had come to him for a visit, he saw the codex in his cell, coveted it, stole it, and departed. The aforementioned abbot Anastasius, when that same day he had looked for his codex in order to read and had not found it, understood that the brother had stolen it. He did not send after him or seek him out, lest, in addition to the theft, perjury should also be added.

The brother, however, went down to the nearby city and wished to sell the codex. He asked sixteen solidi for it. The man who wished to buy it said to him, “Give me the codex, so that I may determine whether it is worth so great a price.” He therefore gave him the codex for examination. Immediately that brother went with the codex to the holy Anastasius and asked him, saying, “Father, please examine this codex and assess whether it is worth sixteen solidi, since the man who is selling it asks that much for it.”

Abbot Anastasius said, “Because the codex is good, it is worth that much.” When the prospective buyer returned, he said to the seller, “Here, take the price, because I showed the codex to Abbot Anastasius, and he said to me, ‘The codex is good, and it is worth that much.’”

The brother asked whether the blessed Anastasius had said anything else. The buyer replied, “Believe me, he said absolutely nothing else to me.”

When the brother heard this, he said to him, “I have reconsidered, brother, and I do not wish to sell my codex,” for he had been pierced with remorse of heart. He hastened to Abbot Anastasius, threw himself on the ground at his feet, and begged him with weeping and tears, in repentance, to take back his codex. But the abbot would not agree, saying, “Go in peace, brother. See, with my consent, keep that very codex.”

The other, however, persisted in asking for it with tears, saying, “If you do not receive the codex, lord Father, my soul will in no way find rest.” After this he received his codex; and that brother remained with the blessed Anastasius in his cell until the end of his life.

### 31

There was a certain hermit named Pior, one of the ancient Fathers, whom the blessed Antony instructed as a young man in the holy vocation of the monks. He remained with the blessed Antony for a few years. When he was twenty-five years old, he went to another secluded place in the desert in order to live alone, with the consent and approval of the blessed Antony.

Saint Antony said to him, “Go, Pior, and live wherever you wish; and when the Lord reveals to you, through some reasonable circumstance, that you should come to me, then you shall come.”

When this Pior had reached the place situated between Nitria and the desert of Scetis, he dug a well, thinking to himself: “Whatever sort of water I find, I must be content with it.” This happened, as an opportunity for the increase of his merits: the water was found to be so salty and bitter that, if anyone came to visit him, he carried water for himself in his own vessel.

He remained in that place for thirty years. The brothers therefore told him to leave the place because of the bitterness of the water. But he said to them:

“If we flee the bitterness and labor of abstinence and wish to have rest in this world, after the end of this life we shall not receive those eternal and truly sweet goods, nor shall we enjoy the perpetual delights of blessed paradise.”

The brothers said that he took only one biscuit and five olives as food, and even that while walking outside.

Many of the holy Fathers also affirmed this about him: that for thirty years and more after he had left his parents’ house, he was never persuaded—even when he heard that his parents had died—to go to seek out or visit his relatives (Pelagius, little book IV, no. 34).

Nevertheless, his sister, who was a widow and had two sons already grown to youth, sent them into the desert to seek their brother Pior. After they had gone around various monasteries looking for him, they finally found him with difficulty and said to him:

“We are the sons of your sister, who ardently desires to see you before her death.”

But he did not consent to their request. The young men then went to the holy man Antony and told him why they had come. The blessed Antony sent for him and summoned him to his presence, saying:

“Why, brother, have you not come to me for so long?”

He answered him, “Most blessed Father, you commanded me that, when the Lord had revealed to me through some circumstance that I should come to you, I was to come; and behold, until now it has not been revealed to me.”

The blessed Antony said to him, “Go, so that your sister may see you.”

Then he took another monk with him and went to the place and house of his sister. Standing outside near the courtyard door, he stood with his eyes closed so that he would not see his sister. When she came, she threw herself at his feet, for she was overcome with exceedingly great joy.

Pior said to her, “Behold, I am Pior, your brother. Look at me as much as you wish.” After this he immediately returned to the desert, to his cell.

He did this in order to instruct the monks, so that they would not be given permission, whenever they pleased, to visit their parents or relatives.

### 23

The abbot John, who lived on the mountain called Calamus, also had a sister. From childhood she had lived according to the holy vocation, and she herself instructed and taught her brother, that same abbot John, to abandon the vanities of this world and enter a monastery.

When he had entered the monastery, he did not leave it for twenty-four years, nor did he visit his sister. She greatly desired to see him, however, and frequently wrote and sent letters to him, asking him to come to her before she departed from this body, so that she might rejoice in the charity of Christ at his presence. But he excused himself and did not wish to leave the monastery.

The venerable servant of God and his sister wrote to him again, saying:

“If you do not wish to come to me, I must come to you, so that after so long a time I may deserve to adore your holy charity.”

When the aforementioned John heard this, he was greatly distressed and thought to himself:

“If I permit my sister to come to me, permission will henceforth also be given for our other parents and relatives to come to visit me.”

Therefore he decided that he himself should go and visit his sister. He also took two other brothers from the monastery with him.

When he came to the door of his sister’s monastery, he cried out, saying, “Bless us, and listen to travelers.”

His sister came out with another servant of God and opened the door. She did not recognize her brother at all; he recognized his sister, but did not speak a word, lest she recognize him by his voice.

The monks who were with him said to her, “We ask you, lady mother, to order that water be given us to drink, because we are weary from the journey.”

When they had received and drunk it, they offered prayer and gave thanks to God, then departed and returned to their monastery.

After some days his sister again wrote to him, asking him to come and see her before her death and to pray in her monastery. Then he wrote back to her and sent the letter through a monk from his monastery, saying:

“By the gracious favor of Christ I came to you, and no one recognized me. You came out to us, gave us water, and I received it from your hands and drank it; giving thanks to the Lord, I returned to the monastery. Let it therefore be enough for you that you have seen me. Do not trouble me any further, but pray for me without ceasing to our Lord Jesus Christ.”

### 33

Another monk also went to his sister to visit her, for he had heard that she was ill in the monastery (Pelagius, little book IV, no. 61). She was a servant of God, renowned for her holy way of life. Therefore she did not consent to receive or see her brother, lest through that occasion he should enter the women’s monastery. Instead, she sent word to him, saying:

“Go, lord brother, and pray for me. By the gracious favor of God and our Savior, I shall see you in the future age, in the kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

### 34

We must also bring forward examples of virtue from the abbot Theodorus. This blessed Theodorus was a disciple of Saint Pachomius, a man numbered among the holy Fathers, who was the father of an immense multitude of monks and the father of many monasteries in the region of the Thebaid [Note: [Col. 0759] Above, book I, in the Life of Saint Pachomius, chapter 28, it is said that Pachomius had a sister.].

Since he shone with the virtues of holiness in every respect, he also earned from the Lord the grace of prophecy, for the Lord revealed many future things to him.

At a certain time the sister of the aforementioned Theodorus came to the monastery in which the same blessed Theodorus lived, in order to see her brother after many years. When they had announced to him the arrival of his sister, he immediately sent two monks to keep watch at the monastery door and instructed them to say to his sister:

“Behold, sister, you have heard and learned that I am alive. Do not be distressed because you have not seen me. Rather, consider the vanity and instability of the present world; turn your heart and embrace the way of holy life, so that you may attain eternal life and the heavenly goods that the Lord has prepared for those who love him and keep his commandments.

“Consider within yourself that this is the only true and firm hope: that a person should keep God’s commandments, so that he may deserve to attain the glorious and eternal promises of the Lord, our Savior Christ.”

When she heard this, she was immediately pierced in her heart and poured out tears in the presence of the Lord. Shortly afterward she entered the monastery of the virgins, servants of God, which had been built in the same village; as time passed, the handmaid of Christ increased in her holy vocation.

When their mother heard of these events, she petitioned the bishops, and they gave her letters to the aforementioned holy Pachomius, the Father of monasteries, concerning her son (above, book I, in the Life of Saint Pachomius, chapter 31).

When she arrived, she went to the monastery of the servants of God and sent a letter to the Father of the monastery, begging to see her son. The blessed Pachomius summoned her son Theodorus and said to him:

“I have heard, son, that your mother has arrived on your account. Therefore, because of the letters of the bishops who wrote to me, go and let your mother see you.”

Theodorus said to him:

“You have commanded me, lord, to see my mother. If, then, I go to see her after having attained such spiritual knowledge, I fear that I may be found guilty before God. For I ought to demonstrate the strength of my spirit as an example to the other brothers.”

When the mother heard that he had not consented to see her, burning with intense affection for her son, she did not wish to return to her home but remained in the monastery of the virgins, saying:

“If I remain here, I shall often see my son when he goes out with the other brothers on the necessary business of the monastery. I shall be able to profit from his admonitions and exhortations, and his spiritual teaching will strengthen my heart, so that I may deserve to attain the eternal rest that our Lord Jesus Christ promised to those who love him.”

The Lord also performed many great miracles through the holy Pachomius. Frequently, after the name of Christ the Lord had been invoked, he healed those possessed by demons. The Lord also had mercy, through his prayers, on many who suffered from various illnesses and on the paralyzed.

### 35

For a long time the blessed abbot Pachomius fought the good fight against the exceedingly filthy attacks of demons, like an athlete of truth, just as did the blessed Antony (above, book IV, in the Life of Saint Pachomius, chapter 20).

With very fervent prayers he entreated the Lord that he might not sleep for a certain period, so that he could remain continually awake by day and night, fighting against the opposing demons until he cast them down and overcame them, as it is said in the psalm: “And I shall not turn back until they fail” (Psalm XVII).

The Lord therefore granted and conceded his request. For demons are powerless and weak when one of us, with complete faith and the whole intention of his heart burning with holy desire, and with the help of the power of our Savior Jesus Christ, contends against them.

The brothers told us about that most blessed Father Pachomius, who, as we have said, was superior of many monasteries in the region of the Tabennesiots (in the Life of Pachomius by Metaphrastes, chapter 55, in Surius, volume III, May 14). They said that he frequently told the brothers:

“For, as the Lord God is my witness, I have often heard unclean demonic spirits speaking among themselves about the various and manifold arts they practice against those who serve God, and especially against monks.

“One of them would say: ‘I am engaged in combat against an exceedingly tough man. Whenever I send evil thoughts into him, he immediately rises and throws himself into prayer, praying with groans that divine help be given him. When he rises in this way, I depart in great confusion.’

“Another demon would say: ‘When I send thoughts into the heart of the man I watch, he consents, receives them, and carries them out. Often I make him blaze with anger, fall into disputes and quarrels, become sluggish in prayer, and sleep during psalmody, and he does not oppose me.’

“Therefore, my most beloved brothers, you must always guard your understanding and your mind, invoking the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and live according to the commandments of God both in prayer and in psalmody, as the Apostle says: ‘Persist in prayer, and be watchful in it.’

“Therefore, if we remain watchful with compunction and fear of heart, our adversaries, the exceedingly filthy demons, will not prevail against us or harm us.”

The blessed Father Pachomius himself taught the brothers always to remember the word of God, for the salvation of their souls. Afterwards each of the brothers would go away to his cell, working with his hands and meditating on what he had learned from the holy Scriptures.

For it is impossible for anyone among them to speak an idle word. They discussed among themselves only what they had learned from the holy Scriptures, explaining passages from Scripture that would strengthen and enlighten their souls in the fear of the Lord.

### 36

There was a certain great man among the holy elders, to whom Christ had given such grace, through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, that he saw what others did not see (John, little book I, no. 3).

The holy elders related that on one occasion a very large number of brothers were sitting together, speaking among themselves and discussing the holy Scriptures that concern the salvation of souls. Holy angels stood around them, rejoicing with cheerful countenances as they watched; for they delighted in the Lord’s utterances.

But whenever they spoke to one another about anything else whatsoever, the holy angels immediately withdrew farther away, indignant at them. Then exceedingly filthy and diseased pigs came and wallowed among them; for demons, in the form of pigs, delighted in their superfluous and idle talk.

When the blessed elder saw this, he went to his cell and throughout the entire night mourned our miseries with great weeping and wailing. He therefore exhorted the holy Fathers throughout the monasteries and warned the brothers, saying:

“Beware, brothers, of excessive speech, and restrain your tongue from idle words. Through such speech a deadly destruction of the soul is generated, and we do not understand that by these things we become hateful both to God and to the holy angels.

“For Scripture says: ‘Through much speaking you will not escape sin’ (Proverbs X). These things make our mind and soul weak and empty.”

### 37

There was a certain man of high rank in the imperial palace under the emperor Theodosius, named Arsenius, whose sons—Arcadius and Honorius—Augustus had taken from the baptismal font (Pelagius, little book XV, no. 6).

This Arsenius, inflamed by desire for divine love, abandoned all the temporal glory of the world and went to the desert of Scetis, so that among the holy Fathers he might lead a secluded and peaceful life, free from all the tumult of this world. Separated from bodily enticements and pleasures, he might cling with the full intention of his mind to the Lord Savior, as it is written: “My soul has clung to you; your right hand has received me” (Psalm LXII).

The holy elders said of him that, just as while he was engaged in worldly life he wore clothing more expensive than anyone else, so afterward, living in the desert of Scetis, he took pains to have clothing poorer and more contemptible than that of all the monks.

### 38

Abbot Daniel also said that the holy Arsenius related to the brothers—as though he had heard it from someone else, although, as far as can be understood, he himself had seen the vision—that he once saw the following (Pelagius, little book XVIII, no. 2):

“A certain elderly monk,” he said, “was sitting in his cell, and suddenly a voice came to him saying, ‘Come outside, and I shall show you the works of human beings.’

“He rose and went outside. The voice led him on and showed him a black Ethiopian cutting wood with an axe and making a great bundle. He tried to lift the bundle, but because of its size he could not carry it. He returned, cut more wood, and added it to the bundle.

“Again it showed him another man standing beside a lake, drawing water from the lake and pouring it into a reservoir; but from the other side the water flowed out through holes and ran down beneath, into the same place.

“Again it said to him, ‘Come, follow me, and I shall show you something else.’

“He saw what appeared to be a temple building and two men sitting on horses. Each carried upon his shoulders one piece of wood—that is, a long beam. They wished to enter together through the gate of that temple, but the wood they carried crosswise prevented them from entering through the gate. Neither humbled himself before the other; instead, both contended, each wishing to enter at the same time. They could not succeed, for neither of them humbled himself so as to give the other room.”

He explained these visions to him, saying:

“Those who carry the wood are those who bear the holy yoke of the monks. But, justifying themselves in their hearts with the exaltation of pride, they do not humble themselves before one another. They were unwilling to walk in humility along the way of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, who said: ‘Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls’ (Matthew XI). Therefore, because of the pride of their hearts, they remained outside, excluded from the kingdom of Christ, the heavenly King.

“The man who was cutting wood and adding more to the bundle is a man burdened with many sins who continually adds other sins to the burden of his sins. He ought rather to repent of his earlier sins; but, neglecting to correct his former vices, he adds still more to his previous sins.

“The man who was drawing water from the lake is a man who performs some good works, but because he also commits even more evil through sins, the good works he performs perish and are erased. Therefore, as the Apostle says, a person must work out his salvation with fear and trembling (Philippians II).”

### 39

Abbot Daniel also said concerning Abbot Arsenius (Pelagius, little book IV, no. 5) that, when he was making baskets from palm leaves, he put water into a basin so that the palms could be soaked. When the thick, foul-smelling water stank [Note: [Col. 0812A] *Brumosa*. Thus the manuscript reads; the printed editions read almost uniformly *bramosa* and *bromosa*. It is understood here as thick and foul-smelling water. Isidore’s Glosses: “*Bromosa*, dirty. *Brumosus*, old, resinous. *Brumalia*, resinous rain. See the Onomasticon.”], he did not permit them to replace it with other water but added more water to the foul water, so that it would always stink.

The brothers asked him, saying, “Why, Father, do you not allow the water to be changed, but let your entire cell be filled with this most dreadful stench?”

The blessed elder replied:

“Because of the incense, perfumes, and musk [Note: [Col. 0812A] *Muscata*. There is a variant reading here in the manuscripts: *musica* in Aquicinctus; *musaco* in Audomarensis. Above, in the Life of Pelagia, chapter 2: ‘Yet as she passed by us, she filled the whole air with the scent of musk.’ In the Life of Marcella, chapter 3: *fragraremusco muro* [in Vallarsius’s edition, [Col. 0812B] no. 3, *fragrare mure*]. See the Onomasticon.], and the various other things which, while living in the world, I enjoyed without interruption, I must now, while I am in this body, endure a stench of this kind in place of that exceedingly sweet fragrance, so that on the day of judgment the Lord may free me from the unspeakable stench of Gehenna and may not condemn my soul with that rich man who feasted luxuriously and splendidly in this world (Luke XVI).”

### 40

One of the brothers said to the blessed Arsenius (Pelagius, little book V, no. 32):

“Behold, most blessed Father, I hasten to meditate on the holy Scriptures that I have learned, but I do not feel compunction in my heart, because I do not understand the power of divine Scripture; and therefore my soul is greatly distressed.”

The blessed Arsenius replied:

“You ought, son, to meditate continually on the Lord’s utterances. For I have heard that the blessed abbot Poemen and many other holy Fathers said that those enchanters who are accustomed to charm snakes do not themselves understand the words they utter, but the snakes, hearing them, understand the power of those words, become quiet, and submit to them.

“Let us do the same. Although we are unable to understand the power of the divine Scriptures, nevertheless, when the demons hear them, they are terrified by the power of the divine word and, driven away, depart from us, unable to endure the utterances of the Holy Spirit, which he spoke through his servants the prophets and apostles.”

### 41

At a certain time, when a murder had been committed in the vicinity of the blessed Macarius and the crime was being charged to an innocent man (Rufinus, book II, chapter 28, on Macarius the Egyptian, almost word for word), the man who was suffering the accusation rose and fled to the cell of the blessed Macarius.

Those who were pressing him also arrived and bound him, saying that they themselves would be in danger unless they seized and handed the murderer over to the authorities. But the man to whom the crime was being attributed affirmed under oath that he had no knowledge of that bloodshed.

After there had been a long dispute on both sides, Saint Macarius asked where the man who was said to have been killed had been buried. When they had shown him the place, he went with them to the tomb. There, kneeling and invoking the name of Christ, he said to those standing nearby:

“Now the Lord will show whether this man whom you are pressing is truly guilty.”

Then, raising his voice, he called the dead man by name. When the man, summoned from the tomb, answered him, Saint Macarius said to him:

“By faith in Christ I adjure you to say now whether you were killed by this man who is accused in your case.”

Then the man answered from the tomb in a clear voice, saying that he had not been killed by him.

When everyone, overcome with astonishment, had fallen to the ground and was groveling at Macarius’s feet, they began to beg him to ask by whom the man had been killed. Then the holy man said:

“I shall not ask him that. It is enough for me that the innocent man is set free. It is not my task to expose the guilty man; perhaps he will yet be pierced with remorse for the crime he committed and will do penance, so that his soul may be saved.”

### 42

At another time, when a certain brother had brought grapes to Saint Macarius, Macarius—who, in accordance with charity, considered not his own interests but those of another (Philippians II)—carried them to another brother who appeared weaker because of illness (Rufinus, book II, chapter 29, on Macarius of Alexandria, almost word for word).

Then the sick man gave thanks to God for his brother’s service and received the grapes. Yet he too, thinking more of his neighbor than of himself, carried them to another sick brother. That brother in turn carried them to another; and so, after the grapes had been carried through all the cells scattered far apart throughout the desert, none of them knowing who had first sent them, they were finally brought back to the one who had sent them.

The holy Macarius rejoiced that he saw such abstinence and such charity among the brothers, and he devoted himself to even more demanding exercises of the spiritual life.

### 43

This account about him was also confirmed to us by those who heard it from his own mouth: at a certain time, during the night, a demon in the form of a monk knocked at the door of his cell, saying:

“Rise, Abba Macarius, and let us go to the assembly where the brothers gather for the vigils” (Rufinus, book II, chapter 29, word for word).

But he, filled with the grace of God, could not be deceived. He understood that it was the devil’s deception and said:

“O liar and enemy of truth, what fellowship, what association do you have with the assembly and gathering of the saints?”

But the demon said:

“Are you unaware, Macarius, that no assembly and no gathering of monks takes place without us? Come, then, and you will see our work there.”

Saint Macarius said:

“May the Lord command you, unclean demon” (Epistle of Jude).

Then he turned to prayer and asked the Lord to show him whether what the demon had boasted was true. He went to the assembly, where the brothers were already celebrating the vigil, and again besought the Lord in prayer to show him the truth of this matter.

And behold, he saw what seemed to be certain little black Ethiopian children running throughout the church, here and there, and as if flying about. As those Ethiopian children ran about, they mocked each of the brothers who was praying and singing psalms. If they pressed a brother’s eyes with two little fingers, he immediately fell asleep; but if they thrust a finger into someone’s mouth, they made him yawn.

Again, after the psalm, when the brothers had thrown themselves down to pray, they ran among them one by one. Before one who was lying in prayer they appeared as if in the form of a woman; before another they appeared as if building, carrying something, or doing various other things. Whatever the demons, as if playing, had fashioned, the praying brothers turned over in the thoughts of their hearts.

But when they began to do any of these things before some of the brothers, they were violently repelled and hurled away, so that they did not dare to stand or pass before them. Before others they even played upon their necks and backs.

When Saint Macarius saw this, he groaned bitterly and, pouring out tears before God, said:

“Look, Lord, and do not be silent; do not be appeased, O God. Rise up, and let your enemies be scattered, and let them flee from your presence, for our soul is filled with illusions” (Psalms LXXXII, LXXXVII).

After the prayer, in order to examine the truth, he summoned separately each of the brothers before whose faces he had seen the demons playing in various forms and images. He asked whether, during prayer, they had entertained thoughts of building, traveling, or other things that he had seen the demons represent to each one.

Each of them confessed that such thoughts had indeed been in his heart, just as Macarius had alleged.

Then it was truly understood that all the evil, superfluous, and vain thoughts that each person conceives in his heart while singing psalms, dreaming, or praying arise through the illusion and instigation of demons.

But from those who guard their hearts with all vigilance in the fear and love of the Lord, those dark Ethiopians and the thoughts they send forth are repelled. For a mind joined to Christ, especially when intent upon prayer, receives nothing evil and nothing superfluous.

### 44

A certain brother asked Abbot Sisoes how he ought to live in his own cell (Paschasius, chapter I, no. 1). He replied:

“Eat your bread with salt and water, and you will have no need to cook anything or wander farther afield.”

### 45

When Abbot Poemen was asked how one ought to fast (Pelagius, little book X, no. 44), he replied:

“I want a monk to eat so little each day that he is not satisfied. For two- and three-day fasts are for vainglory. The holy Fathers examined all these matters and found that it is good to fast every day and eat little, so that one may also be hungry every day. They have shown us that this is an easy royal road.”

### 46

When Abbot Silvanus had arrived at a certain monastery with his disciple Zacharia, before they departed the monks made them eat a little (Pelagius, little book IV, no. 40).

After they had gone out, his disciple found water and wished to drink. Abbot Silvanus said to him, “Zacharia, today is a fast day.”

He replied, “Father, did we not eat today?”

The elder said to him, “That food was an act of charity, son; but let us keep our fast.”

### 47

Some of the brothers in Panephos went to Abbot Joseph to ask him about receiving brothers—whether at that time it was permissible to show them confidence or joy (Pelagius, little book XIII, no. 1).

Before they questioned him, he said to his disciple:

“Do not be surprised, son, at what I am going to do today.”

He placed two seats for those who had come and said to them, “Sit down.” He placed one seat on his right and another on his left. Then he entered his cell, put on tattered clothing, and came out and passed between them. He entered again, put on other, better clothing of the kind he used on feast days, and afterward came out to them. Then he entered again, put on his everyday clothing, and came and sat among them.

They were amazed and astonished at what he had done.

The elder said to them, “Did you see what I did?”

When they had nodded, he said to them, “And what did I do?”

They replied, “At first you used tattered clothing, and afterward other, better clothing.”

He said to them, “Did I change from that disgraceful clothing, or from that better clothing?”

They said, “No.”

The elder said to them:

“If, then, I am the same person in both garments and have not changed, and just as the first garment did not harm me, so the second did not change me, then we ought to act in the same way when brothers arrive: when they are present, we should receive them with confidence and joy; but when we are alone, mourning and abstinence should remain within us.”

When they heard what they already had in their hearts before they had questioned him, they glorified God and departed joyfully.

### 48

One of the Fathers said:

“A person may be found who eats a great deal and, while still hungry, restrains himself so that he is not satisfied; another eats little and is satisfied” (Pelagius, little book X, no. 99).

Therefore, the one who eats much and, while still hungry, restrains himself has a greater reward than the one who eats little and is satisfied (Paschasius, chapter 1, no. 3).

### 49

A certain elder said:

“Never eat what you have desired. When you eat what has been sent to you by the Lord, give thanks without ceasing” (Paschasius, chapter 1, no. 4).

### 50

The brothers related of a certain elder that he had desired a cucumber. When one had been brought to him, he hung it before his eyes. To avoid being overcome by desire, he did not touch it; instead, he did penance, punishing himself because he had desired it (Pelagius, little book IV, no. 60).

### 51

One of the elders became ill and for many days could not take any food. His disciple urged him, saying:

“If you command it, Father, I shall make you a little cake.”

When he nodded to him, the disciple made it (Pelagius, little book IV, no. 59).

The elder had a small vessel containing honey and another similar vessel containing oil pressed from flaxseed. The latter smelled foul and was useful for nothing else except perhaps in a lamp. The deceived brother put some of it into the elder’s food, thinking that he had put in honey.

When the elder tasted it, he said nothing but ate in silence. The third time the disciple gave it to him, the elder said, “I cannot eat, son.”

The disciple, as though wishing to encourage him, said, “Here, Abba, it is good, and I eat from it myself.”

After he tasted it and realized what he had done, he fell on his face, saying:

“Woe to me, Abba, for I have killed you! You have placed this sin upon me because you did not speak.”

The elder said to him:

“Do not be distressed, son, on account of this. If God had wished me to eat something good, you would have put in honey, and not what you put in.”

### 52

Abbot Poemen said:

“Unless Nebuzaradan, the chief of the cooks, had come to Jerusalem, the temple of the Lord would not have been burned with fire” (2 Kings XXV).

This means that unless the desire of gluttony entered the soul, the human mind would not be inflamed by the assault of the devil (Pelagius, little book IV, no. 29).

53. Whenever Abba Macarius refreshed himself with the brothers after an act of charity, he resolved in his heart that for as many cups of wine as he had drunk when they were offered to him, for that many days afterward he would not taste even water at all (Pelagius, little book IV, no. 26). Thus, when the brothers offered him wine, he accepted it joyfully, so that afterward he might afflict himself with thirst. When his disciple learned of this, he disclosed the old man’s plan and begged the brothers not to offer him wine, declaring that the winecups were torture for him rather than refreshments.

54. When a feast was being celebrated in the church and the other monks were eating, one of them said to those serving: “Since I eat nothing cooked, order salt to be brought to me” (Pelagius, little book VIII, no. 21). Hearing these words, the servant, loudly and so that the others could hear, ordered another, saying: “Since that brother does not eat cooked food, bring him a little salt.” Then blessed Theodore said: “You ought rather, brother, to have eaten meat in your cell than to have heard him say this in the presence of the brothers.”

55. A brother from abroad came to Abba Silvanus on Mount Sinai (Pelagius, little book X, no. 69), and he saw the brothers working. He said to them: “Why are you working for food that perishes? Mary chose the good portion” (Luke 10). Then the old man said to his disciple Zacharias: “Give him a codex to read, and put him in a cell that has nothing in it.” At the ninth hour that brother kept looking along the road, wondering whether the old man might perhaps call him to eat. But after the ninth hour had passed, he came to the old man and said to him: “Have the brothers not eaten today, abba?” When the old man admitted that they had, he said: “Why did you not call me?” Then Abba Silvanus said to him: “You are a spiritual man and have no need of this food; but we, being carnal, need to eat. Therefore we work, whereas you have chosen the good portion. For you read every day and do not wish to receive carnal food.” When he heard this, he began to repent and say: “Forgive me, abba.” Then Silvanus answered him: “Therefore Martha is necessary to Mary; for Martha’s sake, Mary too is praised.”

56. Abba John [Note: [Col. 0812B] Abba John.] Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, at the end of his letters, after a hymn on the Nativity of Christ and the Epiphany, rendered this story of John the Little in the verse and rhythms of his own age, from this passage or from Pelagius below, little book X, no. 27:

> In the Lives of the ancient fathers I read something delightful,  
> Yet useful as an example, which I tell you in rhythmic verse.  
>   
> Abba John was little in stature, not in virtues;  
> With an older companion, with whom he was in the desert,  
> He said: “I wish to live securely, as the angels do,  
> Enjoying neither clothing nor food produced by human hands.”  
>   
> His brother replied: “I advise you not to be rash in what you have begun;  
> It would be better for you afterward not to have begun it at all.”  
>   
> But he answered: “He who does not fight neither falls nor conquers.”  
> And naked he entered the inner desert;  
> For seven days he endured on grass as his food beneath the snow;  
> On the eighth, hunger commanded him to return to his companion.  
>   
> When the door was closed late, he sat entirely in the cell;  
> When the younger one called in a weak voice: “Brother, open!”  
>   
> 535 John, lacking help, stands at the familiar doors:  
> “Let your kindness not reject one whom necessity has brought back.”  
>   
> The other answered from within: “John has become an angel;  
> He gazes upon the hinges of heaven and no longer cares for human beings.”  
>   
> Outside, John keeps watch and endures the evil night,  
> And besides this voluntary ordeal undergoes penance.  
>   
> When morning came, he was received and sufficiently scorched by words;  
> So intent upon the little crusts, he patiently endured everything.  
>   
> Refreshed, he gave thanks to the Lord and to his companion,  
> Then tried with weakened arms to move a little rake.  
>   
> Chastened by hardship for his excessive levity,  
> When he could not be an angel, he learned to be a good man.

[Col. 0812C] Abba John used to say to his elder brother: “For I would like to be secure, as the angels are secure, doing nothing but always praising God” [Col. 0769A] [Note: [Col. 0769] Pelagius, little book X, no. 27. In the printed editions this is the text of Pelagius. I have presented it as it appears in the manuscripts.]. And throwing off his cloak, he went out into the desert. After spending a week there, he returned to his brother. When he knocked at the door and his brother did not open it, he said: “Who are you?” But he replied: “I am John.” When the other still did not open to him, he begged, saying: “I am he.” Yet he would not open the door to him until dawn. When morning came, he said to him: “You are a man, and you must work in order to eat.” Then the other threw himself at his feet and said: “Forgive me, abba.”

57. A certain brother was assailed by a spirit of blasphemy and was ashamed to speak of it. Whenever he heard of any great old men, he would go to them to disclose it, but as soon as he arrived he was again too ashamed to tell them. When he therefore came frequently to Abba Poemen [Col. 0769B], the old man saw that he was troubled by thoughts and said to him: “Behold, you frequently come to me troubled by thoughts, and then return sadly, carrying them away with you again. Tell me, then, my son, what is troubling you.” He replied (Paschasius, chapter 1, no. 5): “The devil attacks me with blasphemy, and I was ashamed to speak of it. But as soon as he disclosed the matter, his attack appeared lighter. The old man said to him: “Do not be distressed, my son. Whenever this thought comes to you, say: ‘I am not responsible for it; let your blasphemy be upon you, Satan, for my soul does not want this matter.’ Whatever the soul does not want will not remain long.” And thus that brother departed healed.

58. Abba Moses said: “Passion is generated through these four things: excessive food and drink, excessive sleep, idleness and joking, and walking about in ornate clothing” (Paschasius, chapter 1, no. 6).

59. Abba Poemen said: “Just as the emperor’s sword-bearer always stands beside him armed, so the soul ought always to be prepared against the demon in this manner” (Pelagius, little book V, no. 8).

60. A certain old man said: “Just as stronger herbs or medicines drive away poisonous creatures, so prayer with fasting drives away filthy thoughts.”

61. While Abba Macarius was living in that desert—where he was alone—and the lower desert was full of many brothers (Pelagius, little book XVIII, no. 9; Paschasius, chapter 1, no. 8), one evening he was looking along the road and saw a demon coming in the form of a man. He was clothed in a linen tunic pierced with openings, and from each opening small vessels were hanging. The old man said to him: “Where are you going, evil one?” He replied: “I am going to stir up the brothers who are below.” The old man said to him: “And why do you carry so many vessels with you?” He replied: “I am carrying tastes for the brothers, and therefore I carry so many, so that if one displeases them I may show them another; and if that one does not please them, I may offer another. It cannot happen that at least one of them will not please them.” Saying this, he departed.

The old man remained, again watching the road until the demon returned. When he came back, the old man said to him: “May you be safe.” He replied: “How can you say that to me, since they have all become opposed to me, and no one complies with my counsels?” The old man said to him: “Then do you have no friend?” He replied [Col. 0770A]: “I have one friend; he himself agrees with me, and whenever he sees me, he quickly turns this way and that.” When the old man asked him his name, he said: “He is called Theopemptus” [Note: [Col. 0812C] Theopemptus.] In the Greek Menaia, on 19 January in the Life of Macarius of Egypt, he is called Θεόπεμπτος (*Theopemptus*). In the manuscripts and printed editions this name is variously corrupted as *Theopentus* and *Theopentius.].

As soon as he had departed, Abba Macarius rose and went down to the lower desert. When the brothers heard of it, they went out to meet him, each hoping that he would stay with him and making preparations accordingly. But he sought out Theopemptus’s cell and went to him. When Theopemptus had received him joyfully and the two were alone together, the old man said to him: “How are things with you, my son?” He replied: “By your prayers, I am well.” The old man said: “Do thoughts not attack you?” He replied: “For the moment I am well.” For he was ashamed to speak. The old man then said to him: “See, I have been in the desert for so many years and am honored by everyone; yet, although I am an old man, my thoughts trouble me.” Theopemptus replied: “Believe me, abba, they do the same to me.”

Then the old man pretended that each of the thoughts was attacking him, until Theopemptus confessed everything to him. Afterward he said to him: “How do you fast?” He replied: “Until the ninth hour.” The old man said to him: “Fast until evening, and continually meditate without ceasing on something from the Gospel or from the other Scriptures. And whenever an unclean thought comes upon you, never look downward, but upward, and immediately the Lord will be your helper.” Then Abba Macarius departed again for his own solitude.

Again watching along the road, he saw the demon returning and asked him: “Where are you going?” He replied [Col. 0770C]: “To stir up the brothers in the same way.” When he returned, the old man asked him how the brothers were doing. He replied: “Badly, because they have all become boorish; and what is worse than everything else, the one whom I had as a friend and obedient to me has somehow changed, and he seems harsher toward me than all the others.” He swore that he would not go there again until a long time had passed. Saying this, he departed.

62. A certain brother asked an old man: “What shall I do, Father? I cannot endure my thoughts.” The old man replied: “In this matter I have never been attacked” (Pelagius, little book V, no. 31). The brother was scandalized and went to another old man, saying to him: “See what that old man said to me! I was scandalized by him, because he spoke beyond human nature.” The second old man said to him: “That man of God did not say those words to you without reason. Go, then, and do penance before him, so that he may tell you the power of his words.”

The brother returned to the old man and began to say: “Forgive me, abba, because I acted foolishly by not saying farewell to you and departing in that manner. But I beg you, explain to me how you are not attacked.” The old man said to him: “Since I became a monk, I have not been satisfied with bread, water, or sleep. The thought of all these things has not allowed me to engage in the struggle you described.” And that brother departed from him helped by his counsel.

[Col. 0771A] 63. When a certain man again asked about thoughts, Abba Poemen said: “If a monk restrains his belly and his tongue, and does not follow wandering, let him trust that he will not die but will live forever” (Paschasius, chapter 1, no. 9).

64. Two brothers came to Abba Elias, troubled by their thoughts (Paschasius, chapter 1, no. 10). When the old man saw that they were corpulent, he smiled as though at his disciple and said: “Truly, brother, I am ashamed for you, because you have nourished your body so greatly, although you profess to be a monk. Pallor and emaciation, together with humility, are the adornment of a monk.”

He also said: “A monk who eats much and works much should not be confident; but he who eats little, even if he works little, should be confident and act manfully.”

[Col. 0771B] 65. While Abba Arsenius was sitting in the field (Palladius, *Canopus*), a certain virgin woman, wealthy and God-fearing, having learned of Abba Arsenius’s reputation, came from the city of Rome to Alexandria so that she might be worthy to see him (Pelagius, little book II, no. 7). When she had been honorably received by Theophilus, the archbishop of that city, she asked him to persuade blessed Arsenius to receive her. He therefore went to him and said: “A Roman woman, distinguished above the others in rank, wealth, and reputation, has come from such a distant region wishing to see you and receive your blessing. I beg you to go out to meet her.”

But when Arsenius refused to go out to meet her, she, learning this, ordered her animals to be saddled, saying: “I trust in my God that I shall see him and shall not be deprived of this intention. I have not come to see human beings, for there are plenty of them in our own city; I wished to see a prophet.”

When she had come to the cell of blessed Arsenius, she happened to see him walking outside. At once she fell prostrate before his feet. He quickly raised her and addressed her sternly, saying: “If you desire only to see my face, look—here it is.” But out of shame she did not dare raise her eyes. The old man said to her: “If you have heard anything about my conduct, that is what you ought to have looked upon. How, then, did you dare to cross so vast a sea? Or do you not know that you are a woman, for whom it is not permitted to go out everywhere? Did you come here so that, on returning to Rome, you might boast to other women that you had seen Arsenius, thereby making the sea accessible to women coming to me?”

She replied [Col. 0771D]: “If God wills it, may he permit no woman to come here.
