But I beg you to pray for me and to deign to remember me.” Arsenius said to her: “I pray to my God that he may erase the memory of you from my heart.” When she heard these words, she returned to the city and was overcome with illness because of her distress.

When the bishop came to visit her and asked what was wrong, she recounted the old man’s final words concerning the erasure of her memory and confessed that in her grief she wished to die. But the bishop consoled her with these words: “Do you not know that you are a woman? And because the enemy commonly attacks a man through a woman, he said that he wished to erase your face from his heart. For he is praying to the Lord for your soul.” At these words the woman was restored.

66. Abba Moses said: “If an emperor wishes to conquer a city belonging to his enemies, first he cuts off their food and water, and thus his enemies, compelled by hunger and want, submit themselves to his rule” (Pelagius, little book IV, no. 19). In the same way, if you wish to live in fasting and hunger, carnal passions grow weak and are not strong against the soul. For who is as strong as a lion? Yet because of its belly it enters a cage, and all its strength is humbled.

67. A certain young man wished to renounce the world, but thoughts frequently recalled him as he was leaving, entangling him in various affairs; for he was rich (Pelagius, little book XIV, no. 4; Paschasius, chapter 2, no. 1). One day, therefore, as he was leaving, demons surrounded him and raised a great cloud of dust before him. He immediately stripped himself, threw away his clothes, and ran naked to the monastery. God revealed this to an old man, saying: “Rise and receive my athlete.”

The old man rose, went to meet him naked, recognized the cause, marveled, and gave him a monastic habit. Whenever brothers came to that old man to ask him about various conditions, he answered them; but when they asked about renunciation, he said: “Ask this brother, for I have not yet attained to his renunciation.”

68. A certain brother renounced the world. After distributing his possessions to the poor, he kept some things for himself and came to Abba Antony (Pelagius, little book VI, no. 1). When the old man learned of this, he said to him: “If you wish, go into the village, buy some meat, place it upon your naked body, and come back to me.”

When the brother had done this, both dogs and birds tore at his entire body, trying to seize the meat, with their teeth and claws. When he came to Antony, the old man asked whether he had done what he had commanded. When the brother showed him his lacerated body, Saint Antony said to him: “Those who renounce the world but still wish to possess money are torn apart by demons in this way.”

69. A certain brother asked an old man: “Do you wish me to keep two solidi for myself because of bodily illness?” (Pelagius, little book VI, no. 22). Seeing his thoughts and that he wished to keep them, the old man said: “Keep them.” The brother returned to his cell and began to wrestle with his own thoughts, saying: “I wonder whether the old man blessed me or not.”

He rose, returned to the old man, and begged, saying: “For God’s sake, tell me the truth, because my thoughts trouble me on account of those two solidi.” The old man said to him: “Because I saw that your thought wished to keep them, I told you to keep them; for it is not good to retain more than the body needs. Thus the two solidi are your hope. And if it should happen that they perish, does God not care for us? Cast your thought, therefore, upon God, for he cares for us.”

70. A certain monk named Serapion possessed only a Gospel. He sold it and gave the proceeds to the hungry, imitating this memorable saying: “I sold,” he said, “the very word that was always saying to me: ‘Sell what you possess and give to the poor’” (Pelagius, little book VI, no. 5).

71. When a certain man asked Abba Agathon to accept his money for safekeeping, Agathon refused, saying: “I have no need of it, because the work of my hands feeds me” (Pelagius, little book VI, no. 17). When the man persisted, saying: “At least accept it for the sake of those in need,” he replied: “It is a double shame: I accept what I do not need, and, by dispensing what belongs to another, I shall become subject to vainglory.”

72. Abba Paul said: “If a monk wishes to keep in his cell anything beyond what he cannot live without, he is frequently compelled to leave his cell, and thus he is deceived by the demon” (Paschasius, chapter 2, no. 2). Paul himself observed this during one Lent: he endured with a sextarius of lentils and a small vessel of water, and, making one mat, he wove and unwove it so that he would not go outside even once.

73. When Abba Macarius was in Egypt and had gone out of his cell, he returned and found someone stealing what he had in his cell (Pelagius, little book XVI, no. 6; Pachomius, chapter 3, no. 1). He therefore stood there himself like a traveler, loaded the animal together with the thief, and escorted him in complete tranquility, saying: “We brought nothing into this world. The Lord gave, the Lord took away; as he himself willed, so it happened” (Job 1). “Blessed be the Lord in all things” (1 Timothy 6).

74. A certain brother came to the cell of a great old man, entered, and stole his food (Pelagius, little book XVI, no. 19; Paschasius, chapter 3, no. 2). When the old man saw this, he did not rebuke him but worked still more, saying: “I think that brother is in need.” The old man was suffering greatly because of the scarcity of bread.

When the elder was dying and the brothers surrounded him, he saw the brother who had been accustomed to steal his bread and said to him: “Come here to me, brother.” He took his hand and kissed it, saying: “I give thanks to these hands, brothers, because I believe that through them I shall enter the kingdom of heaven.” The other, pierced by this word, repented and became an energetic monk, following the old man’s example, which he had witnessed.

75. Abba Agathon governed himself and excelled in discretion in everything, both in the work of his hands and in clothing. He wore garments that appeared to no one either particularly good or particularly bad.

76. A certain old man said: “Anger arises through these four things: through the desire of avarice, in giving and receiving; when someone loves his own opinion and defends it, so that it appears neither particularly good nor particularly bad to anyone; when someone wishes to be raised to honors; and when someone wishes to be a teacher and hopes to be wiser than everyone else” (Paschasius, chapter 6, no. 1).

“Anger also darkens the human senses through these four things: if a man hates his neighbor, envies him, considers him worthless, or disparages him. The retribution of this passion therefore has four forms: first, from the heart; second, from the face; third, from the tongue; fourth, in deed.

“If someone can bear the evil in such a way that it does not enter the heart, it does not reach the face. But if it comes to the face, let him guard his tongue so that he does not speak it. If he has spoken it, let him at least guard against carrying it out in deed, but immediately let it go.

“For there are three classes of people in the passion of anger. He who is voluntarily harmed and insulted, yet spares his neighbor, is according to the nature of Christ. He who neither harms nor wishes to be harmed is according to the nature of Adam. But he who harms or insults, brings accusations, or exacts interest is according to the devil.”

77. One of the brothers, having suffered an injury from another, came to Abba Sisoes (Pelagius, little book XVI, no. 10; Paschasius, chapter 7, no. 1). After explaining the nature of the insult, he added: “I wish to avenge myself, Father.” The old man began to ask him to leave vengeance to God. But he said: “I will not desist until I have taken a strong revenge.”

The old man said to him: “Since you have once fixed this in your mind, let us at least pray now.” The old man rose and began to pray in these words: “God, you are no longer necessary to us to care for us, because we ourselves, as this brother says, both wish and are able to avenge ourselves.” When that brother heard this, he threw himself at the old man’s feet and asked forgiveness, promising that he would never again contend with the man against whom he was angry.

78. A certain brother, while being insulted by another, came and reported it to an old man (Paschasius, chapter 7, no. 2). The old man answered him: “Satisfy your thought, because the brother does not wish to insult you, but your sins do. In every temptation that comes to you through a human being, do not accuse him, but simply say: ‘These things happen to me because of my sins.’”

79. Abba Poemen frequently said: “Never let malice overcome you. If someone does evil to you, return good to him, so that by good you may conquer evil” (Pelagius, little book X, no. 53; Paschasius, chapter 7, no. 3).

80. A certain brother rejoiced all the more the more someone insulted or mocked him (Pelagius, little book XVI, no. 12; Paschasius, chapter 7, no. 4), saying: “These are the people who give us an opportunity for our progress; but those who bless us disturb our souls. For it is written: ‘Those who bless you deceive you’” (Isaiah 3).

[Col. 0774D] 81. Another old man, if someone spoke ill of him, hastened—if the man was near him—to repay him with good himself; but if he lived farther away, he sent him gifts (Paschasius, chapter 7, no. 5).

82. A certain brother asked Abba Sisoes: “If thieves or barbarians attack me, wishing to kill me, and if I am able to prevail, do you command me to kill them?” He replied: “Do not do so at all; but commit yourself wholly to God. Whatever adversity befalls you, acknowledge that it comes to you because of your sins; for you must ascribe everything to divine providence.”

83. There was a great hermit on a mountain called Athlibeus, and thieves came upon him [Col. 0775A] (Paschasius, chapter 8, no. 2). When he raised his voice, other brothers from the neighboring places gathered and seized them. The judge had them taken to the city and sent them to prison.

The brothers were saddened because the thieves had been handed over to the judge on their account. They came to Abba Poemen and reported what had happened. He wrote to the hermit, saying: “Remember where the first betrayal came from, and then you will see the second. For if you had not been betrayed by what was within you, you would never have committed the second betrayal.”

When he was pierced by these words—for he was renowned throughout that whole region and had not gone out for a long time—he rose at once and came to the city. Publicly bringing the thieves out of prison, he freed them from their punishments.

84. A disciple of a certain philosopher sinned [Col. 0775B] (John, little book 4, no. 12). When he wished to be forgiven, the philosopher said to him: “I will not forgive you unless for three years you carry the burdens of others.” When he returned after three years, having made satisfaction for his sin, the philosopher said to him: “Even now I do not yet forgive you unless for another three years you give payment to those who afflict you with insults and abuse.”

When he had completed this as well, and his sin had been forgiven, his teacher said to him: “Now go and enter the city of Athens, so that there you may learn wisdom.” There was an old man there devoted to wisdom who sat at the gate and, in order to test everyone entering, afflicted them with insults [Note: [Col. 0812C] *Conviciis affligebat.* Concerning this Athenian custom, see Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration in Praise of Saint Basil*. See *Onomasticon*, under “Depositio.”].

When the old man did the same to the young man as he entered, the young man burst into laughter. The old man said to him: “What are you doing? I insult you, and you laugh?” The young man replied: “Would you not have me laugh, when I have paid for three years in order to endure what I am suffering from you today for free?”

Then the old man said to him: “Enter the city, for you are worthy.” Abba John used to relate this, and he himself added these words: “This is the gate of God, through which our fathers entered the city of God rejoicing, after many tribulations and insults.”

85. A certain brother asked an old man: “Give me, Father, one thing that I may guard and by which I may be saved.” The old man replied: “If you can be insulted and subjected to abuse, and endure it and remain silent, this is a great thing and is above all other commandments” (Pelagius, little book XV, no. 83).

86. When certain brothers asked Abba Moses for a word, he encouraged his disciple Zacharias to say something to them. Then Zacharias removed his cloak, placed it beneath his feet, trampled upon it, and said: “Unless a person is trampled upon in this way, he cannot be a monk” (Pelagius, little book XV, no. 17).

87. Abba Macarius said: “He is truly a monk who conquers himself in everything. For if someone, while rebuking another, is moved to anger, he fulfills his own passion. He ought not to lose himself in order to save another.”

88. In the presence of Abba Antony, other brothers were praising a certain brother. But when the old man tested him, he discovered that he could not endure insult. The old man said to him: “You, brother, are like a building which, although it has an ornamented entrance, is attacked by thieves through its back doors” (Pelagius, little book VIII, no. 2).

89. A certain brother asked Abba Isaac: “Abba, why are the demons so afraid of you?” (Pelagius, little book, no. 22, under the name of Isidore.) The old man replied: “Since I became a monk, I have resolved that my anger would not pass outside my throat; and therefore the demons fear me.”

90. When one of the fathers came to Abba Achilles (Pelagius, little book IV, no. 9), he saw him spitting blood and asked what this was. He replied: “It was a word spoken by a brother that had saddened me. I resisted so that I would not say it, but I asked the Lord to take it away from me. That word became blood in my mouth, and after I spat it out, I found relief. I also forgot both the sadness and that word.”

91. Certain brothers came to a holy old man who was sitting in the desert (Pelagius, little book XV, no. 14). They found children pasturing livestock and sometimes speaking filthy words among themselves. After asking the old man about each of their thoughts and receiving his answer, they said to him: “How can you endure, abba, the voices of these children, and why do you not command them not to shout in this way?”

The old man said to them: “Truly, brothers, for many days my thought wanted me to say something to them, but I rebuked myself, reasoning: ‘If I cannot bear this little thing, how shall I bear it if a greater temptation comes upon me?’ Therefore I say nothing to them, so that endurance may become habitual for me” [Col. 0776C].

He also said: “If someone does not restrain his tongue in a time of anger, he will never be able to control the passion of his flesh.”

92. While Abba John was sitting among the brothers (Pelagius, little book XVI, no. 3), and each of them was asking him about his own thoughts and he was answering them all, a certain old man, out of envy, said to him: “This John is like a prostitute adorning herself in order to gather lovers for herself.”

Abba John said to him: “You speak truly, abba, and it is no different; for God himself has revealed this to you.” The old man replied again: “Indeed, John, your vessel is full of poison.” John said to him: “It is as you have said, abba; and you say this because you see only what is outside. If you saw what is within, how much more would you have to say!”

After this, one of his disciples said to him: “Are you not inwardly disturbed, abba, by the words of this old man?” He replied: “No; but as I am outwardly, so I am inwardly.”

93. There was a certain old man in Egypt who, before Abba Poemen came there, was held in great reverence by everyone (Pelagius, little book XVII, no. 8). When Abba Poemen came there from Scetis, many, leaving that old man, came to Poemen; and for this reason the old man began to envy and disparage him.

When Abba Poemen heard of this, he was saddened and said to his brothers: “What shall we do? People have placed us in a difficult position by leaving that holy old man and looking to us, who are nothing. How shall we heal this great man? Come, then, let us prepare some small foods, take them to him, and bring a little wine, so that we may taste it together with him. Perhaps in this way we can appease his spirit.”

They set out, knocked at his door, and his disciple, hearing them, said: “Who are you?” They replied: “Tell your abba that Poemen has come to receive his blessing.” When he heard this through his disciple, he answered him: “Go and tell them: ‘Leave me; I am not free.’”

They nevertheless remained there sadly [Alternative: in distress], saying: “We will not leave this place unless we are found worthy to venerate him.” When he perceived their humility and patience, he was pierced with remorse, opened the door, and they kissed one another and tasted food together.

Then the old man himself said to them: “Truly, what I have heard about you is not all there is; I have seen a hundred times as much in your conduct.” From that day he became Poemen’s dearest friend.

94. Abba Muthues once built himself a cell in a place called Heracleona (Paschasius, chapter 10, no. 1). While he was being troubled there by many people, he went to another place and likewise built a dwelling there. But through the devil’s snares a certain brother was found there who, out of envy, was constantly quarreling with him. For this reason he rose, left that place, returned to his own village, built a cell there as well, and shut himself inside it.

After some time, the old men of the place from which he had departed gathered together, bringing with them also the brother with whom he had quarreled, so that they might ask him to return to his cell. When they came near the place, they left both their *melotes* and that brother there; they themselves went on to the old man and knocked. He opened a window, looked out, recognized them, and said: “Where are your *melotes*?” They replied: “Here nearby, together with that brother who was angry with you.”

When the old man heard this and recognized them, he joyfully broke open with an axe the door through which he had entered, went out, ran to the place where the brother was, and himself took the initiative in doing penance before him. He embraced him, brought them into his cell, and feasted with them for three days, although he had never been accustomed to break his fast. Afterward he rose and departed with them.

93. Abba Agathon used to say: “I have never gone to sleep while quarreling with anyone; nor, insofar as it depended on me, have I allowed anyone who was quarreling with me to go to sleep until I had returned with him in peace” (Pelagius, little book XVII, no. 6).

515 96. Two old men were sitting together in one cell, and they had never had even the slightest disagreement between them (Pelagius, little book XVII, no. 22). One said to the other: “Let us too have at least one quarrel, as other people do.” The other replied: “I do not know how a quarrel is made.” The first said to him: “Look, I will place a brick between us and say: ‘It is mine’; and you say: ‘It is not yours, but mine.’ From this contention and strife arise.”

When they had placed the brick between them, one said: “It is mine.” The other replied first: “I hope it is mine.” When the first again said: “It is not yours, but mine,” the other replied: “And if it is yours, take it.” At this they could find no way to quarrel.

97. At a certain time, while the blessed Abba Macarius was praying (John, booklet III, no. 17), a voice sounded to him, saying: “Macarius, you have not yet attained the measure of the two women who live together in the neighboring city.” On hearing this, the old man rose, took his staff, and reached the designated city. When he knocked at the door of the house he had sought and found, one of the women came out and received him with great rejoicing. The old man summoned both women and addressed them as follows:

“I have come from a distant solitude and endured such labor solely on your account, so that I might learn of your deeds. Tell me and relate them to me.”

They said to him: “Believe us, most holy Father, for we have not been separated from our husbands’ beds even this present night. What deeds, then, do you seek from us?”

But the old man persisted in prayer that they explain to him the order of their life. Then, compelled, they said to him:

“We are not related to one another by any family connection. It happened, however, that we were married to two brothers. We remained together with them in one household for fifteen years, and neither of us ever spoke an indecent word to the other, nor did we ever quarrel; rather, we have lived in peace until now. By mutual agreement we resolved that, leaving our husbands together, we would go to a community of religious virgins, but despite many prayers we were unable to obtain this from our husbands. Since we could not accomplish it, we made a covenant between ourselves and God that until our death we would not speak any worldly word at all.”

When the blessed Macarius heard this, he said: “In truth, there is neither virgin nor married woman, neither monk nor layperson; God seeks only the purpose, and he supplies the spirit of life to all.”

98. A certain brother, while living in a coenobium and frequently being provoked to anger (Pelagius, booklet VII, no. 33), said to himself: “I will go into the desert; and since I shall have no one with whom to quarrel, perhaps this passion will cease troubling me.” [Col. 0778D] When he had gone out and was living alone in a cave, one day he filled a vessel with water and set it on the ground, and suddenly it overturned. When he had filled it a third time and the same thing happened, he seized the vessel and angrily smashed it. When he had come to his senses, he reflected that he had been deceived by the spirit of anger, and said:

“Behold, I am alone, and yet I have been conquered by anger. I will return to the coenobium, because everywhere there is need of struggle and patience, and above all of God’s help.”

And so he rose and returned to his place.

[Note: [Col. 0777] In the printed editions this is the text of Pelagius; I have set it as it is in the manuscripts.]

99. The blessed Macarius used to relate the following about himself:

“When I was young, although I was living in a cell, they seized me against my will and ordained me cleric in a village (Pelagius, booklet XV, no. 25). Since I did not wish to remain there, I fled to another village. A devout layman sold the products of my work and supplied me with what I needed. It happened that a certain virgin conceived a child through fornication. When her parents asked who had violated her, she said: ‘That anchorite of yours committed this deed against me.’

“Her parents went out, seized me, hung earthen vessels around my neck, and led me through every lane, beating me mercilessly and mocking me with these words: ‘This monk has violated our daughter.’ When they had nearly beaten me to death with clubs, one of the elders said to them: ‘How long will you beat this foreign monk so mercilessly?’ But they also insulted the man who ministered to me, who followed me with his face flushed in shame, saying: ‘See what this man has done for whom you gave testimony!’

“The girl’s parents said: ‘We will release him on no account unless someone comes forward as surety for him and undertakes to provide support for the girl.’ When I signaled to the man who ministered to me to do this, he accepted responsibility for me on the strength of his pledge.

“I therefore returned to my cell and gave him whatever baskets I found. After selling them, he provided food for me and my supposed wife. I used to say: ‘Well, Macarius, you have found yourself a wife; therefore you must work harder, so that you may be able to feed her.’ I worked both day and night, so that I could provide her daily food.

“But when the wretched woman’s time for giving birth arrived, she was unable to deliver for many days, suffering terribly. When she was asked what she had done, she replied: ‘Because I had no cause against that anchorite, I falsely accused him. The young man who lives near us violated me.’

“When the man who ministered to me heard this, he came filled with joy, crying out that the wretched girl who had falsely fabricated an accusation against me had been unable to give birth until she confessed this. He summoned all the neighbors to come and ask my pardon. When I learned this, I quickly departed, lest those people trouble me further, and I came to this place. This is the reason for my arrival in these regions.”

100. A certain brother asked Abba Poemen, saying: “What shall I do, Father, for I am troubled by sadness?”

The old man said to him: “Regard no one as worthless, condemn no one, slander no one, and the Lord will give you rest” (Paschasius, ch. 39, no. 2; Pelagius, booklet IX, no. 8; Appendix to Martin, no. 39).

101. Abba Poemen used to say of Abba Isidore that he alone had known himself (Paschasius, ch. 11, no. 3). For whenever his thought said to him, “You are great,” he himself replied: “Am I perhaps such as Antony, or indeed Abba Pambo, or the other fathers who pleased God?” Whenever he reflected on these things, he became calm. But when the demon who troubled him suggested despair and punishments, saying, “After all these things you are going to torments,” he again said: “Even if I am sent into torments, I shall nevertheless find you beneath me.”

[Col. 0780A] 102. Demons also frequently appeared to Abba Moses, cursing him and saying: “You have prevailed over us, Moses, and we can do nothing to you. Whenever we wish to humble you through despair, you are exalted; but whenever you are exalted, you humble yourself so greatly that none of us comes near you” (Paschasius, ch. 11, no. 4).

103. When a certain brother repeatedly asked Abba Sisoes the same question, saying, “What shall I do, Father, for I have fallen?” he answered, “Rise” (Paschasius, ch. 11, no. 5).

The brother replied, “I have risen,” and confessed that he had fallen again. The old man said: “Rise again.”

When the brother repeatedly reported that he had risen and repeatedly fallen, the old man continued to use the same expression, crying out: “Do not cease rising, my son.”

The brother said to him: “How long can I keep rising, Father? Explain this to me.”

Then the old man said: “Until you die, having been found either in a good work or in an evil one. For in whatever work a person is found, in that work he will be judged.”

104. A certain old man was gravely tempted by thoughts for ten years, so that he finally despaired, saying: “I have already lost my soul; but since I have perished once, I will return to the world” (Pelagius, booklet VII, no. 42).

As he was departing, a voice came to him, saying: “The ten years in which you struggled [Note: [Col. 0812D] ‘You struggled.’ Elsewhere: ‘You fought.’ But this form of speech, common in that period, occurs frequently in these books.] will be your crown. Return, therefore, to your place, and I will free you from every evil thought.”

He immediately returned and persevered in the work he had begun. It is therefore not good for anyone to despair on account of thoughts. For if we deal with them profitably and pass through them, they provide us with crowns all the more.

105. At a certain time, while Abba Antony was sitting in the desert, tempted by the spirit of acedia and entangled in various thoughts, he said to God:

“Lord, I desire to be saved, but various thoughts do not permit me. Show me graciously what I should do in my distress, and how I may be saved” (Pelagius, booklet VII, no. 1).

After a little while he rose and saw someone resembling himself sitting, twisting a cord, then rising from his work and praying. It was an angel assigned for Antony’s correction, from whom he also heard these words: “Do this, Antony, and you will be saved.”

Filled with the greatest joy, he received confidence and was saved.

[Col. 0780D] 106. A certain brother asked an old man, saying: “What shall I do, Father, for I perform none of the works of a monk? Living in negligence, I eat, drink, and sleep, and from hour to hour I pass from one thought to another. For this reason I am saddened and despair.”

The old man said to him: “Remain sitting in your cell and do what you can without disturbance of mind. Put your trust in God, for whoever remains in his cell for God’s sake will be found in the place where Abba Antony is” (Pelagius, booklet VII, no. 34).

107. Another brother asked Abba Achilles: “Why, while sitting in my cell, do I suffer acedia?”

The old man said to him: “Because you have not yet seen the rest that we hope for, my son, nor the torments that we fear. If you examined these carefully, even if your cell were filled with worms up to your neck, you would nevertheless remain lying among them without acedia” (Pelagius, booklet VII, no. 28).

108. A certain brother asked Abba Antony, saying: “By observing what shall I please God?”

The old man replied: “Keep what I tell you. Wherever you go, always have God before your eyes. Whatever work you undertake, take examples from the divine Scriptures. Wherever you settle, do not move away from there too quickly, but remain patiently in the same place. If you observe these three things, you will be saved” (Pelagius, booklet I, no. 1).

109. A certain brother, having sought a word from Abba Moses, heard the old man say to him: “Go and sit in your cell. Your cell can instruct you in everything, if you remain there. For just as a fish taken out of water immediately dies, so a monk perishes if he wishes to delay outside his cell” (Pelagius, booklet II, no. 1, under Antony’s name; Life of Antony, ch. 52).

110. A certain brother asked Abba Poemen: “Is it better to live farther apart, or to remain with others?” (Paschasius, ch. 12, no. 2).

The old man replied: “If a person reproves himself, he can persevere anywhere; but if he glorifies himself, he never stands firm. Whatever good a person may have done, let him not rejoice in it, for he will soon lose it.”

111. Once a certain Egyptian brother came to Abba Zeno in Syria (Paschasius, ch. 12, no. 4), [Col. 0781C] and began accusing his own thoughts in the old man’s presence.

The old man, astonished, said: “The Egyptians conceal the virtues they possess and reveal the faults they do not possess. But the Syrians and Greeks proclaim the virtues they do not possess and conceal the faults they do possess.”

112. A certain old man said: “Whoever is honored or praised more by human beings suffers no small loss of soul; but whoever is not honored at all by human beings will receive glory from God above” (Pelagius, booklet XV, no. 56; Paschasius, ch. 13, no. 1).

113. The same man said: “It is impossible for grass and seed to grow at the same time; so it is impossible for those who possess the praise and glory of worldly people also to produce heavenly fruit” (Pelagius, booklet VIII, no. 20, under Syncletica’s name; Paschasius, ch. 12, no. 2).

[Col. 0781D] 114. The same man said: “Just as an exposed treasure is diminished, so virtue perishes when it is made public. For just as wax melts before the face of fire, so the soul, dissolved by praise, perishes with respect to its purpose” (Pelagius, booklet VIII, no. 19, under Syncletica’s name).

115. The same man said: “When a thought of vainglory or pride attacks you” (Pelagius, booklet XV, no. 54; Paschasius, ch. 13, no. 3), “examine yourself: have you kept all God’s commandments? Do you love your enemies? Do you rejoice in the glory of your enemy and grieve at his downfall? Do you hold this conviction: ‘I am an unprofitable servant and a greater sinner than all human beings’? Yet even then do not think highly of yourself, as though you had done some good, knowing that an exalted thought dissolves all those good things.”

116. When a certain old man came to another old man, he said to him: “I am already dead to this world” (Pelagius, booklet XI, no. 38; Paschasius, ch. 12, no. 5).

The other replied: “Do not trust yourself until you have departed from this body. Even if you say, ‘I am dead,’ the devil is not yet dead, and his crafty evils are innumerable.”

117. A certain old man had been in the desert for fifty years, neither tasting bread nor taking water to satiety. He said: “I have killed vainglory and greed” [Note: [Col. 0781] Pelagius, booklet X, no. 15. In the printed editions this wording belongs to Pelagius. I have set it as it is in the manuscripts.]

When Abba Abraham heard this, he came to him and asked whether he himself had said this. When the old man admitted it, Abraham said to him:

“Suppose, while walking along the road, you see stones and fragments of bricks, and among them a mass of gold. Can your thought judge that gold to be like those other things?”

The old man said: “No, but I am still fighting against my thoughts. Behold, greed is alive, but it is bound.”

Abba Abraham also said: “One person loves and praises you, while another fears and slanders you. If both come to you, do you not regard them equally?”

The old man said: “No, but I am again fighting with my thought, so that I may love the one whom I abhor.”

Abba Abraham said to him: “Behold, then, the passions still live in you, but they are bound by the saints; perhaps they remain in you on account of your life.”

118. A certain old man lived in the lower regions of the desert and sat in repose in a cave; a devout layman ministered to him (John, booklet IV, no. 35; Paschasius, ch. 12, no. 7).

It happened that the layman’s son fell ill. He therefore begged the old man with many prayers to come to his house and pray for the child. The old man rose and walked with him. The man went ahead, entered his house, and said: “Come out to meet the anchorite.”

When the old man saw them coming from a distance with lamps [Note: [Col. 0812D] “With lamps.” Men of rank, or those distinguished by holiness, were met with fire, candles, lamps, and incense. See the remarks on the Life of Saint Basil, ch. 9, no. 44. Consult also the Onomasticon.], he realized that they were coming toward him. He therefore stripped off his clothes, threw them into the river, and began washing them while standing naked.

The man who ministered to him saw this, was ashamed, and said to the people: “Go back, for our old man has lost his senses.” Then he hurried to him and said: “Abba, why have you done this? Everyone who saw you said: ‘The old man is possessed by a demon.’”

He replied: “That is precisely what I wanted to hear.”

119. When a certain provincial judge wished to venerate Abba Moses, the latter, on hearing of it, fled from his place (Pelagius, booklet VIII, no. 13). When by chance he met him, the judge asked him:

“Tell us where Abba Moses’s cell is.”

He replied: “Why do you wish to see that foolish and heretical man?”

When the judge heard this, he went to the church and reported to the clergy:

“I had heard various things about Abba Moses and wished to receive a blessing from him. But a monk who met me told me that he was a heretic.”

When the clergy heard this, they were saddened and began asking what kind of monk had said this. He replied: “He was an old man, dressed in very old garments, tall and dark.”

Then, recognizing from their description that it was Moses himself, the judge departed in great amazement.

120. While Abba Sisoes was living on the mountain where the blessed Antony had been enclosed (John, booklet II, no. 13), a layman was hastening to him with his little son to receive a blessing. It happened that the child died on the way.

Without any disturbance of mind, the father lifted him and carried him in faith to the old man. Entering the cell, he threw himself and the child to the ground, as is customary for those asking a blessing. When the prayer had ended, the father rose and went outside, leaving the child’s body before the abbot’s feet. The old man, still supposing that he was lying there for the sake of prayer, said: “Rise, son, and go outside.” He did not know that the child was dead.

Immediately the boy rose and went out. When his father saw him, he was astonished. He returned to the cell, venerated the old man, and related in faith both what had happened to his son and his grief.

The old man became very sad, for he did not wish to hear that anything of this kind had been accomplished through him. Through his disciple, he commanded the man not to tell anyone about this until the old man’s death.

121. When a certain layman came into the church possessed by an unclean spirit (John, booklet II, no. 4; Paschasius, ch. 14, no. 2), everyone prayed, but the unclean spirit would not leave him. The brothers therefore said among themselves:

“What can we do to this spirit? No one can drive it out except Abba Besarion. But if we tell him this, he will not agree to come to the church. Let us proceed in this way: since he usually comes to the church before everyone else, let us make the sufferer sit down, and afterward let us say to the abbot: ‘Abba, awaken this man who is sleeping.’”

They did so. When Abba Besarion came, they all stood in prayer and said to him: “Abba, awaken this man who is also sleeping.”

He awakened him, saying: “Rise and go outside.” Immediately the unclean spirit departed from him, and from that hour he was made well.

122. There was a certain man in Egypt who had a paralytic son. He brought him to the cell of the blessed Abba Besarion and left him crying at the door, then went far away (John, booklet II, no. 7, under Macarius’s name).

The child began to weep. When the old man saw him through the window, he said: “Who brought you here, son?”

The child replied: “My father brought me, and he himself went away.”

The old man said to him: “Rise and join him.”

Immediately the child rose, healed, and reached his father.

123. Abba Muthues said: “The nearer a person comes to God, the more he will see himself as a sinner” (Pelagius, booklet XV, no. 28).

For the prophet Isaiah, when he saw the Lord, called himself wretched and unclean. Let us therefore not remain here without care. Scripture says: “Let anyone who stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10).

We therefore sail uncertainly in this world. Yet we appear to sail as though on a calm sea, while worldly people sail as though in dangerous places (Pelagius, booklet XI, no. 34, under Syncletica’s name). We are as though in daylight, illumined by the sun of righteousness; but they are in ignorance, as though in the night.

It frequently happens, however, that a worldly person sailing through a dark night, remaining vigilant and crying out, saves his own ship, while we, sailing in calm waters, often grow negligent through that very security and perish, abandoning the rudder of humility. For just as it is impossible for a ship to be made firm without nails, so it is impossible for a person to be saved without humility.

124. As Abba Macarius was returning to his cell at dawn, carrying palm leaves, the devil met him with a very sharp sickle and wished to strike him, but was unable to do so (Pelagius, booklet XV, no. 26; Paschasius, ch. 13, no. 6).

He cried out and said: “I suffer great violence from you, Macarius. When I wish to harm you, I cannot; yet whatever you do, I do even more in my own way. You fast at times, whereas I am never refreshed by food. You often keep vigil, whereas sleep has never overcome me. But in one matter you defeat me—I admit it.”

When the blessed Macarius asked him what that matter was, he said: “Your humility alone defeats me.”

As the enemy said this and the blessed Macarius stretched out his hands in prayer, the unclean spirit vanished into the air.

125. One of the old hermit monks was struck by a man possessed by an evil spirit, who, foaming at the mouth, struck him violently on the cheek. The old man offered him the other cheek to strike; but the devil, unable to endure the fire of his humility, immediately departed (Pelagius, booklet XV, no. 53).

126. One of the Fathers used to say: “All a monk’s labor is vain without humility. For humility is the forerunner of charity, just as John was the forerunner of Jesus, drawing everyone to him; so humility draws one to charity, that is, to God himself, because God is charity” (Paschasius, ch. 13, no. 7).

127. At a certain time, as Abba Macarius was ascending Mount Nitria, he ordered his disciple to go a little ahead. As the disciple went before him, he encountered a pagan priest coming rapidly and carrying a large piece of wood. The disciple cried out to him:

“Where are you running, demon?”

The priest became angry and beat him with such blows that he nearly left him lifeless. Then he left him and continued running.

After going a little farther, he met the blessed Macarius, who said to him: “Be saved, laborer; be saved.”

Amazed, the priest replied: “What good have you seen in me, that you greeted me?”

The old man said: “Because I saw you laboring, and running without understanding.”

The priest said to him: “And I, moved by your greeting, have recognized you as a great servant of God. For another wretched monk met me and insulted me, and I repaid his words with blows.””

Then, seizing the blessed Macarius by the feet, he cried out: “Unless you make me a monk, I will not stop.”

They went on together and reached the place where the beaten brother was lying. Since he could not walk, they both lifted him and carried him in their arms to the church.

When the brothers saw that priest accompanying the blessed Macarius, they were astonished. With wonder they made him a monk, and because of him many pagans became Christians.

Abba Macarius therefore used to say: “Since an arrogant and evil word turns even good people toward evil, a humble and good word changes even evil people for the better.”

128. The blessed Antony often used to say: “Unless the baker covered the eyes of the millstone [Note: [Col. 0812D] ‘The baker covered the eyes of the millstone.’ The first part of this number is missing from the manuscripts up to ‘Never.’ The printed editions contain it, and therefore I have retained it. But whose eyes are meant by ‘the millstone’? I believe it should be read: ‘unless the baker covered the eyes of the animal at the mill.’ Thus Pelagius, booklet XV, no. 80.] he would consume his own wages while receiving them” (Pelagius, booklet XV, no. 80; Paschasius, ch. 15, no. 1).

So too, by God’s dispensation, we receive a covering, so that we cannot notice the good things we do, lest, blessing ourselves, we become exalted and lose our proper reward.

For this reason also, when we are left amid filthy thoughts, it is necessary that we attend only to this: that we condemn ourselves and our own judgment, lest the filth within us obscure in us that small good work of ours.

A person is never good, even if he desires to be good, unless God dwells in him, because no one is good except God alone. We must therefore always accuse ourselves truthfully. For when each person reproves himself, he does not lose his proper reward.

129. The blessed Antony also related that he had seen all the snares of the enemy spread over the whole earth. When he sighed and said, “Who can pass through these?” he heard a voice saying to him: “Humility alone passes through them, Antony; the proud can in no way touch it.”

130. The blessed Antony also, while praying in his own cell, heard a voice say to him: “Antony, you have not yet attained the measure of the leatherworker who is in Alexandria” (Paschasius, ch. 15, no. 2).

On hearing this, the old man rose in the morning, took his staff, and hastened to the city of Alexandria. When he entered the house of the designated man, the latter was astonished at the sight of so great a man.

The old man said to him: “Tell me about your deeds, for on your account I have left the desert and come here.”

He replied: “I do not know that I have ever done anything good. Nevertheless, when I rise in the morning from my bed, before I begin my work, I say that the whole city, from the least to the greatest, will enter the kingdom of God because of their righteousness, while I alone will enter everlasting punishment because of my sins. Each evening, before I rest, I recall these words truthfully in my heart.”

When the blessed Antony heard this, he replied: “In truth, my son, like a good goldsmith sitting peacefully in your house, you have attained the kingdom of God; but I, living all my time in the desert without discernment, have not yet attained the measure of your word.”

131. A certain brother asked Abba Poemen, saying: “What does the Apostle mean when he says, ‘All things are pure for the pure’ (Titus 3)?”

He said to him: “If someone can attain to understanding this saying, he will see himself as less than the whole of creation.”

The brother said to him: “How can I regard myself as less than one who is a murderer?”

The old man replied: “If a person can attain to this saying of the Apostle, and sees someone who perhaps has killed another, he says within himself: ‘That man has committed only this one sin, whereas I commit murder every hour, killing myself through sin.’”

When the brother asked how this could happen, he replied: “This alone is a person’s righteousness: to reproach himself. For then he is righteous, when he condemns his own sins.”

132. When some brothers were sitting near Abba Poemen, one praised another brother, saying: “That brother is good, because he hates evil.”

The old man said to him: “What does it mean to hate evil?”

Not knowing what to answer him, the brother begged: “Tell me, Abba, what does it mean to hate evil?”

The old man said to him: “He hates evil who hates his own sins, and who blesses and loves every one of his brothers.”

133. A certain brother asked Abba Poemen, saying: “How can a person avoid speaking evil about his neighbor?” (Paschasius, ch. 16, no. 1).

The old man replied: “I and my neighbor are two images. When I look at my own image and reproach myself, the image of my brother is found honorable in my sight. But when I praise my own image, then I see my brother’s image as deformed. Therefore I do not slander another if I always reproach myself.”

134. Abba Hyperichius said [Note: [Col. 0812D] “Hyperichius.” In the printed editions this number contained various brief sayings, which are found in the same words in Pelagius, booklet LV, numbers 45 through 54 inclusive, under Hyperichius’s name, except for the final two, which appear under the title “Anonymous.” I have substituted here what was in the manuscripts.]:

“It is better to eat meat and drink wine than to eat the flesh of one’s brothers in slander. For just as the whispering serpent drove Eve from paradise, so whoever slanders his brother destroys not only his own soul but also the soul of the listener” (Pelagius, booklet IV, nos. 51–52).

135. Abba John used to say: “We have laid down a small burden—that is, reproving ourselves—and chosen to carry a heavy one: justifying ourselves and condemning others.”

136. Once, after the assembly had concluded at Scetis, while the Fathers were speaking about the lives of many people and about numerous matters, Abba Pior remained silent [Note: [Col. 0785D] Pelagius, booklet IX, no. 9. In the printed editions this wording belonged to Pelagius. I have set it as it is in the manuscripts.].

Afterward he went out, took a sack, filled it with sand, and carried it on his back. Then he put some more sand into another small cloth and carried it before him.

When the other brothers saw this, they asked him what this example meant. He replied:

“This sack, which contains much sand, represents my sins, for my iniquities are many. Behold, I have placed them behind my back, unwilling to see them, so that I might grieve or weep over them. But behold, I have placed these few sins of my brother before my eyes, and I am tormented by them as I condemn my brother.

“It is not right to judge in this way. Rather, I should bring them before me, reflect upon them, and ask God to forgive me.”

When the Fathers heard this, they said: “In truth, this is the way of salvation.”

137. Abba Isaac once came to a coenobium [Note: [Col. 0786D] Pelagius, booklet IX, no. 3. In the printed editions this wording belonged to Pelagius. I have set it as it is in the manuscript.], [Col. 0787A] and saw there a negligent brother. In anger he ordered him to be expelled from the coenobium.

As the brother was going out toward his dwelling, an angel of the Lord came and stood before the door of his cell, saying: “I will not permit you to enter.”

The old man begged that his fault be made known. The angel answered him:

“God sent me, saying: ‘Go and say to Isaac: Where do you order us to send the brother who sinned?’”

At once he repented, saying: “I have sinned, Lord; forgive me.”

The angel said to him: “Rise; God forgives you. But do not do this again, condemning anyone before God judges him.”

“Human beings have taken judgment upon themselves and do not entrust it to me,” says the Lord. This was said because, if one of those perfected people should happen to sin even in a small matter, he is immediately exposed.

138. A certain brother committed a fault in the coenobium. When the others rebuked him, he went to Abba Antony. The brothers followed, wishing to bring him back, and began reproaching him for his faults. But he denied having committed the fault.

Abba Paphnutius, surnamed Cephalas, happened to be there. He related this previously unheard parable in the assembly of the brothers:

“I saw,” he said, “a man on the bank of a river, sunk in mud up to his knees. Some people came to pull him out by extending a hand, but they sank him as far as his neck.”

Then the blessed Antony said of the blessed Paphnutius: “Behold a man who truly can save souls.”

Moved by these words, the brother’s companions repented and brought back to the coenobium the one who had departed.

139. One of the elders said: “If you see someone sinning, do not place the blame on him, but on the one who is attacking him, saying: ‘Woe to me, for this man has been overcome against his will, just as I have.’ Weep and seek God’s consolation, for we are all deceived.”

140. A certain anchorite named Timothy, hearing that a brother was negligent, was asked by that brother’s abbot what should be done with him. He advised that the brother be expelled from the coenobium.

When the brother had been expelled, temptation came upon Timothy. As he wept before God and said, “Have mercy on me,” a voice came to him, saying:

“Timothy, this has come upon you because you despised your brother at the time of his temptation.”

141. One of the Fathers, being in an ecstasy, saw four orders before God [Note: [Col. 0787D] Pelagius, booklet XIV, no. 19. In the printed editions this wording belonged to Pelagius. I have set it as it is in the manuscripts.].

The first consisted of people who were sick and gave thanks to God. The second consisted of those who practiced hospitality, persevered in it, and ministered to others. The third consisted of those who pursued solitude and did not see human beings. The fourth consisted of those who, for God’s sake and out of obedience, were solicitous and subject to their fathers.

The order that exhibited obedience was superior to those three orders. It wore a golden collar and possessed greater glory than the others.

The old man said to the one who had shown him this in the ecstasy: “Why does this fourth order possess greater glory than the others?”

He replied: “Because all the others obtain some rest by fulfilling their own wills, even when they are engaged in good works. But the obedient person, abandoning his own will, hangs upon the will of the father who commands; therefore he has received greater glory than the others.”

142. A certain old man said: “If someone imposes a task on his brother with the fear of God and with humility, that word, because it proceeds for God’s sake, compels the brother to obey and to do what has been imposed on him” (Pelagius, booklet XV, no. 73).

“But if someone wishing to command his brother seeks to do so not according to the fear of God, but from authority and his own will, he who sees the hidden things of the heart does not permit him to be obeyed, lest the brother do what has been commanded him. For the work of God, which is done for God’s sake, is manifest, while human authority, arranged through boasting, is manifest.

“Whatever is from God possesses humility from the beginning; whatever comes from authority, anger, or agitation is from the enemy.”

143. Abba Silvanus had a disciple named Mark, whose obedience was great; for this reason the old man loved him (Pelagius, booklet XIV, no. 5). He also had eleven other disciples, who were saddened because he loved Mark more than them.

When the other elders heard this, they came to him in sorrow to report that the brothers living with him were troubled. But before they told him anything, he went with them to the cells of each one. He called each by his own name, saying:

“Come outside, brother, because I need you.”

None of them wished to come out.

At last they came to Mark’s cell. When they knocked at the door, Abba Silvanus called his name. As soon as Mark heard the old man’s voice, he came outside.

The abbot entered Mark’s cell. Since Mark was a scribe, he found there a gathering of sheets on which he was writing, and observed that, at the very hour when he had been called, Mark had abandoned the letter he was forming halfway through, solely in order to fulfill his obedience.

After hearing the old man’s voice, he did not wish to complete the letter he had begun [Note: [Col. 0788D] The printed editions insert *O*, and so does Pelagius.].

Therefore the other elders said to him: “In truth, the one whom you love we now also love, because God too loves him on account of his obedience.”

### 144

A certain solitary elder had a servant who ministered to him and lived in a village (Pelagius, *Book* XIV, no. 16). When the man had been delayed for several days, and the elder’s necessities had run out, and he had neither anything to work at nor anything with which to refresh himself, and was consequently distressed, he said to his disciple [Note: In the printed editions this is word for word from Pelagius; I have given it as it appears in the manuscripts]: “Go to the village.” He replied: “Whatever you wish, Father, I will do.”

The brother feared approaching the village because of the danger of scandal, yet, in order to obey the Father, he promised that he would go. The elder said to him: “Because I trust in the God of our fathers, that he will protect you from every temptation.” After praying, he sent him on his way.

When the brother had arrived in the village and had asked where the man who served the elder lived, he found the house. When he knocked at the door, it happened that no one was found in the house except the daughter of that servant. When she had opened the door and the brother asked her where her father was and why he had been delayed for so many days, she urged him to enter the house with her and pulled him along. When he would not consent, she overpowered him and dragged him toward her.

When he saw that he was being drawn into sin and his thoughts were pressing him, he groaned and cried out to God, saying: “Lord, because of the prayer of the one who sent me, save me at this hour.” When he had said this, he suddenly found himself beside the river near his monastery, and he returned to his Father without stain.

### 145

Two brothers who were related by blood came to live in a certain monastery. One of them was exceedingly devout [Col. 0789B], while the other possessed great obedience (Pelagius, *Book* XIV, no. 17). Whenever the abbot ordered him, “Do this,” he did it; and again, “Do that,” and he did it. He was glorified in the monastery for possessing such obedience.

His devout brother, however, becoming envious [Pelagius has “abstinent”], said within himself [Note: In the printed editions this is word for word from Pelagius; I have given it from the manuscripts]: “Now I will test my brother, to see whether he has steadfast obedience.” He went to the abbot and said to him: “Send my brother with me, because I am needed in a certain place.” The abbot allowed him to go.

As they were traveling together, wishing to test him, when they reached a river filled with a multitude of crocodiles, he said to him: “Go down into the river and cross it.” The brother went down, and the crocodiles came and began to lick his body, but they did him no harm.

When the devout brother saw this, he said to him: “Come up out of the river, and let us go.” As they continued on their way, they found a dead body lying on the road. The devout brother said: “If we had something of old clothing, we could place it over him.” His brother replied: “Let us pray, in case God might raise him.”

While they stood in prayer, the dead man was raised. The devout brother then boasted, saying: “This dead man rose because of my devotion.” But God revealed to their Father in the monastery everything that had happened: how he had tested his brother with the crocodiles, and how the dead man had risen.

When they returned to the monastery, the abbot said to the devout brother: “Why did you do this to your brother? Know that it was because of his obedience that the dead man rose.”

### 146

One of the elders of Scetis sent his disciple to Egypt to lead a camel there, so that it might carry to Egypt the baskets he had made. As he was leading the camel, another elder met him and said: “If I had known, brother, when you were going to Egypt, I would have asked you to bring another camel for me as well.”

When the brother had reported this to his own abbot, the latter, out of great charity, said to him: “Go, my son, and lead the camel to that man, saying to him: ‘Because we are not yet ready, meet your need; and you yourself go with this camel all the way to Egypt, and bring the camel back to us, so that we too may transport our vessels.’”

The brother did so. When he had gone to the elder, he said: “Abba Pambo says: ‘Because we are not yet ready, take it and meet your need.’” The elder loaded the camel and went to Egypt.

When he had unloaded it, the brother again led the camel back and said: “Pray for me, Father.” When the elder asked where he was going, he replied: “I am going to Scetis, so that I may bring our baskets here as well.”

When the elder heard this, he was pierced with remorse and began to repent, saying with tears: “Forgive me, most beloved, because your charity has taken away my profit.”

### 147

Another elder had finished his baskets (Pelagius, *Book* XVII, no. 16) and had already attached their straps when he heard his neighbor saying: “What shall I do? The market is near, and I have nothing with which to attach straps to my baskets.”

The elder immediately went in, dismantled his own straps, and brought them to his brother, saying: “Here, I have these extra ones. Take them and attach them to your baskets.” Thus, through his excessive charity, he brought his brother’s work to completion while leaving his own unfinished.

### 148

Abba John, through the grace of charity, had forgotten every form of malice. Once he had borrowed one solidus from a brother and had purchased flax with which to work. Another brother came and asked him for a little flax in order to make himself a sack, and he gave it to him gladly. Then another came asking him for flax, and he gave it to him. Likewise, when many others came and asked, he gave to them all gladly.

After this, the man who had lent him the solidus came and asked him to repay it. He said: “I will go and bring it to you.” Since he had nothing with which to repay it, he rose and went to Abba Jacob to ask him to repay the man from whom he had borrowed.

As he was going along the road, he found a solidus lying there, but he did not touch it. After praying, he returned to his cell. When the brother again demanded what he owed, he said to him: “I will bring it from somewhere now.”

Again he went out and found the solidus lying where it had been before. After praying, he returned, and behold, the brother came again, troubling him about the solidus.

Then the elder said decisively: “Now I will go and bring it.” As he went out, he found the solidus lying in the same place. After praying, he picked it up and went to Abba Jacob, saying: “Abba, as I was coming to you, I found this solidus on the road. Therefore do me the kindness of proclaiming it here in the city, in case someone has lost it; and if its owner is found, return it to him.”

The elder went out and proclaimed it for three days, but no one was found who had lost that solidus. Then John said to Abba Jacob: “If no one has lost it, I will return it to that brother, because I owe it to him. When I came to you to borrow—or rather, to receive in charity—and repay my debt to him, I found it.”

The elder marveled that, although John both owed the money and had found it, he had not immediately taken it and returned it, but had gone back twice and proclaimed it a third time.

This was also remarkable about him: if anyone wished to borrow something from him, he did not hand it over himself, but said to the brother: “Go and take whatever you need.” When the item was returned, he said: “Go and put it back where you took it.” But if nothing was returned, he said absolutely nothing.

### 149

Abba Poemen said: “Never fulfill your own will, but rather humble yourself, so that you may do the will of your neighbor” [Note: Pelagius, *Book* IV, no. 30. In the printed editions this passage follows Pelagius’s wording; I have given it from the manuscripts.]

Again, whenever Abba Poemen was summoned to eat against his own will, he went weeping, lest by disobeying his brother he should distress him.

Likewise, having slain his own will and humbled himself, he followed another’s will.

### 150

A certain anchorite sat in a cave near a coenobium, practicing many virtues (Pelagius, *Book* XIII, no. 8; Paschasius, ch. 18, no. 1). Some monks came from the coenobium and compelled him to eat at an unusual hour.

Afterward the brothers said to him: “Are you distressed about anything, abba, because today you did something outside your custom?” He replied: “I am in tribulation whenever I do my own will.”

### 151

Abba Paphnutius never tasted wine (Pelagius, *Book* XVII, no. 12). Once, while traveling, he came upon robbers. When he found them drinking on the road, the chief of the robbers recognized him, for he knew that he did not drink wine. Seeing, however, that he was exhausted from the labor of the journey, he filled a large cup with wine, held a sword in his hand, and said to the elder: “Unless you drink this cup, I will kill you.”

The elder recognized that the man wished to do this by God’s command; wishing to win him, he took the cup and drank. The chief of the robbers then began to say to him: “Forgive me, abba, because I have troubled you.”

The elder replied: “I trust in my God that, because of this one cup of wine, he will show you mercy both in the present age and in the age to come.”

The chief of the robbers said to him: “And I trust in God that, from today onward, I will harm no one.” Thus the elder won over the entire company of robbers.

### 152

There were two brothers. One of them was an elder who asked the younger, saying: “I beg you, brother, let us live together” (Pelagius, *Book* XVII, no. 14).

The other replied: “I am a sinner, and you cannot live with me.” But the elder continued to ask him, saying: “We can.”

The elder was pure and did not wish to hear that a monk might ever have an evil thought. The younger said to him: “Allow me to rest for this one week, and afterward we shall speak again.”

When the elder came to him after the week, the younger, wishing to test him, said: “I have fallen into a great temptation this week, abba. I went to the village because of a necessity, and I sinned.”

The elder said to him: “And do you wish to repent?” When the younger had promised that he did, the elder said: “I will carry half of that sin with you.”

Then the brother said: “Now we can both remain together.” And they lived together until the time of their departure.

### 153

One of the elders used to say: “Whatever a person detests, let him absolutely not do to another” (Pelagius, *Book* I, no. 21; Paschasius, ch. 16, no. 2).

You detest it when someone slanders you? Then do not slander another. You detest it when someone brings a false accusation against you, or when someone takes something away from you? Then do not do this, or anything similar, to anyone.

For whoever keeps this saying may find it sufficient for salvation.

### 154

After Abba Poemen and Abba Nuph had come into the desert, their mother longed to see them and often came to their cell, yet she was unable to see them there (Pelagius, *Book* IV, no. 33).

Accordingly, watching for an opportunity, she met them as they were hurrying to the church. When they saw her, they quickly turned back and closed the door of the cell. She stood outside, weeping and searching for them.

Then Abba Nuph went out to blessed Poemen and said: “What shall we do about this mother of ours, who is weeping at the door?”

Abba Poemen then rose and went to the door. Without opening it, he heard her lamenting continuously and said to her: “Why are you making such great cries and pouring out lamentation, now that you are already wearied by age?”

When she recognized the voice of her son, she cried out even more loudly, saying: “Because I desire to see you, my sons. What is it, after all, if I see you? Am I not your mother? Did I not nurse you at these breasts of mine? I am already filled with every delay, and, hearing your voice, all my inward parts have been stirred by longing.”

Poemen said to her: “Do you desire to see us here more, or in the age to come?”

She replied: “What then? If I do not see you here, am I somehow certain that I shall see you there?”

The elder answered: “If you can restrain yourself here from seeing us, you will undoubtedly see us there forever.”

Then she departed joyfully, saying: “If I am certainly going to see you there, I no longer wish to see you here.”

### 155

John the Younger of Thebes, a disciple of Abba Ammonas, ministered for twelve years to a certain sick elder (Pelagius, *Book* XVI, no. 4; Paschasius, ch. 19, no. 2).

Yet when the elder saw him laboring, he never spoke a gentle or kindly word to him. When he was departing from the body, while other elders were sitting there, he took John’s hand and said to him three times: “Farewell. Farewell. Farewell.”

Then he handed him over to the elders, saying: “This man is not a human being but an angel, who for so many years ministered to me in my sickness, although he never heard a good word from me.”

### 156

When Abba Agathon came into the city to sell his handiwork, he found a sick stranger lying in a narrow alley, with no one to care for him. The elder remained there, rented a cell for himself, and from the work of his hands provided service for the sick man.

He remained there for four months, until the sick man was healed; then he returned to his own cell.

### 157

A certain great elder said to his sick disciple: “Do not be distressed, my son, by the illness or wound of your body, for it is the highest form of devotion for someone to give thanks to God in sickness” (Pelagius, *Book* VII, no. 16, under the name of Syncletica; Paschasius, ch. 20, no. 1).

“If you are iron, you lose your rust through fire; but if you are gold, then, tested by fire, you advance from great things to greater. Do not be anxious, therefore, brother. For if God wishes you to be tormented in the body, who are you to take it badly? Endure, then, and ask God to grant what he himself wills.”

### 158

A certain elder was frequently sick in body and languished. It happened, however, that during one year no illness touched him. For this reason he wept and bore it grievously, saying: “You have abandoned me, Lord, and have not wished to visit me in this present year” (Pelagius, *Book* VII, no. 41; Paschasius, ch. 20, no. 2).

### 159

When a certain elder was dying in Scetis, and the brothers had surrounded his bed, arranged him properly, and were weeping, he opened his eyes and laughed. Again he opened them and laughed, and the third time he did the same (Pelagius, *Book* XI, no. 52).

When the brothers asked him, saying: “Tell us, abba, why do you laugh while we are weeping?” he replied: “The first time I laughed because you are all afraid of death; the second time I laughed because you are not prepared; but the third time I laughed because I am going from labor to rest.”

### 160

At the very hour when Abba Pammon was passing from the body, he said to the other holy men standing beside him: “From the time I came, brothers, to this desert place and built this little cell for myself, apart from the work of my hands I do not remember having tasted bread, nor do I repent of any word that I have spoken, up to this hour. Yet even so I am going to God as though I had not even begun to worship him” (Pelagius, *Book* I, no. 16).

### 161

When Abba Agathon was dying, he kept his eyes open for three days without moving them (Pelagius, *Book* XI, no. 2). The brothers touched him and said: “Where are you now, abba?”

He replied: “I stand in the presence of God’s judgment.”

The brothers said to him: “Do you also fear?”

He answered them: “As far as it lay within my virtue, I always took care to do the commandments of my God. But I am a human being; and how do I know whether my works are pleasing to God?”

The brothers said to him: “Do you not trust that your works are according to God?”

He replied: “I do not trust this in the presence of God, because God’s judgment is one thing, and human judgment another.”

### 162

When the time of Abba Sisoes’s repose had arrived and many other elders had gathered there, they saw his face shining with a certain radiance. He said to them: “Behold, Abba Antony has come to us” (John, *Book* III, no. 6).

After a little while he said: “Behold, also the choir of the prophets.” Again his face was covered with brighter light, and he said to them: “The blessed apostles are here as well.” He appeared to be speaking with certain people.

When the Fathers asked him to tell them with whom he was speaking, he said: “The angels have come to take my soul, and I am begging them to hold me for a little while so that I may perform repentance.”

The Fathers said to him: “You no longer need to perform repentance, abba.”

He replied: “Truly I tell you, I do not remember having even begun repentance.”

From this saying they understood that he was perfect in the fear of the Lord. Then, while his likeness shone with the brightness of the sun, he said to them: “See, see, for the Lord is coming.”

With these words spoken, he gave up his spirit, and that entire place was filled with a pleasant fragrance.

### 163

As the time approached for blessed Arsenius to depart from this world, he said to his disciples: “Let no one show me charity except in the matter of an offering; if I have shown charity, I will find it” (Pelagius, *Book* X, no. 9).

When his disciples were troubled, as though his time were already near, he said to them: “My hour has not yet come; but when it comes, I will not be silent” (Pelagius, *Book* XV, no. 9).

“Nevertheless, you will stand with me in the divine judgment before the tribunal of Christ if you give anyone anything from my little body as though it were a relic.”

When they replied: “What shall we do, Father? We do not know how to bury a man,” he answered: “Do you not know how to put a rope around my feet and drag me in that way to the mountain?”

The hairs of his eyelashes fell out from continual weeping. Throughout his entire life, while sitting and working, he kept a cloth in his lap because of the tears flowing from his eyes (Pelagius, *Book* III, no. 1).

When he was dying (Pelagius, *Book* XV, no. 9), he began to weep. When his brothers asked him, saying: “Why are you weeping, Father? Are you also afraid?” he replied: “Truly I am afraid; and this fear that is with me now has always been in me from the time I became a monk.”

When Abba Poemen saw that he had departed, he said: “Blessed are you, Abba Arsenius, because you mourned yourself so much in this world. For whoever does not mourn himself here will mourn forever there. Therefore, either here by his own will or there because of torments, it is impossible for a person not to weep.”

### 164

Blessed Athanasius the bishop once asked Abba Pammon to go to Alexandria (Pelagius, *Book* XVII, no. 11). When he went down with the brothers and saw some secular people, he said to them: “Rise and greet the monks, so that you may be blessed by them” [Note: Pelagius, *Book* III, no. 14. A similar account occurs in the *Life of Pelagia*, chapter 3.]

“For these men frequently speak with God, and their mouths are holy.”

When he saw an actress there, he began to weep. The bystanders asked why he was weeping. The elder replied: “Two things compelled me to these tears. The first is the destruction of that woman; the second is that I do not take as much care to please God as this woman takes to please depraved men.”

### 165

It was said of a certain elder that whenever his thought said to him: “Put it off today, and tomorrow you will repent,” he would answer it in turn: “Not so; today we must repent, and tomorrow let God’s will be done in us” (Pelagius, *Book* XI, no. 44).

### 166

One of the Fathers related the following about a certain bishop, saying that he had heard that two men from his congregation were adulterers of extreme impurity (John, *Book* I, no. 16; Paschasius, ch. 23, no. 1).

He therefore asked God that, if this were true, he might know it. After the consecrated offering, when each person approached for communion, he understood their souls from their faces. For he saw the faces of sinners as black as coal and their eyes filled with blood; but others he saw with bright faces and clothed in white garments.

When they had received the Lord’s body, light appeared on the faces of some, and flame on the faces of others. In order to identify those whose crimes he had heard about, he offered them communion. He saw one of them with a bright and honorable face, surrounded by white garments; but the other was black and had a horrible face.

After they had received the grace of the divine mystery, a certain force of light illumined the first, while the other was set ablaze as though by flame.

The bishop prayed to be instructed concerning what had been shown to him about each of them. An angel of the Lord stood beside him and said: “Everything you heard about them is true. But that one remains in his filth and in the will to sin; therefore you saw him with a black face and being consumed by flame.

“The other was indeed like him, as you had heard. But you saw him illumined with a bright face because, remembering what he had done before, he renounced those evil works and, with tears and groans, sought God’s mercy, promising that, if his former sins were forgiven him, he would not return to them again.

“Therefore, after his former crimes had been blotted out, he attained the grace you saw.”

When the bishop marveled at God’s grace, because God had not only rescued a man from the torments deserved by such a shameful life but had also honored him with such dignity, the angel replied:

“You marvel rightly, for you are a human being. But our Lord and your Lord is naturally good and humane toward those who cease from sins. When people seek him through confession, he not only forgives their sins but also makes them worthy of honor.

“For God so loved the human race that he sent his only-begotten Son for sinners and gave him over to death for them (John 3). If, while they were his enemies, he chose to die for them (Romans 5), how much more when they become his own.

“Know this, then: no human sin overcomes the goodness of God, provided that each person, through repentance, blots out the evils he previously committed. For God is merciful and knows the weakness of the human race, the strength of its passions, and the power or malice of the devil.

“When people fall into sin, he indulgently awaits their correction, as with sons. But when they repent, he has compassion on them as on the sick; and, immediately forgiving their sins, he also grants them the rewards of the righteous.”

When the bishop heard these things, he marveled greatly and glorified God.

### 167

Abba Paul the Simple had received this grace: when people entered the church, he could look at them and perceive from their faces each person’s thoughts, whether they were evil or good (Pelagius, *Book* XVIII, no. 20; Paschasius, ch. 23, no. 2).

When they came to the church and entered, the elder saw them entering with bright faces and joyful spirits, and their angels with them, likewise rejoicing. But one man he saw as black, with a body enveloped in darkness; demons were dragging him here and there toward themselves, having sent a bridle into his nostrils, while his holy angel followed him from afar in sadness.

Blessed Paul began to weep most bitterly and beat his breast, sitting before the church because of the man he had seen in this condition. All the other elders, seeing him weeping in this way, began to ask him to reveal whatever he had seen in them or to enter the assembly with them. He, however, did not wish to enter, but continued to weep for the man he had seen in such a state.

After a little while, when the assembly had ended and they were leaving, he again examined all their faces to see whether they were coming out as they had entered. He saw that the man whom he had previously seen as black and darkened was leaving the church with a bright face and a shining body, while the demons followed him from afar. His holy angel, however, was near him, exceedingly joyful and rejoicing over him.

Then Paul rose with joy and cried out, blessing God and saying: “How great is the mercy and kindness of God! How great is his compassion!”

Going up to a higher place, he said in a loud voice: “Come and see the works of God” (Psalm 45); “come and see how he wishes all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2). “Come, let us worship him, saying: ‘For you alone can take away sins.’”

When everyone had gathered, Paul explained to them what he had seen before the man entered the church and what he had seen afterward. He asked the brother whom he had seen in this condition to disclose to him his thoughts and actions, and how God had granted him such a great transformation.

Before them all, the man began to relate what had happened, saying:

“I am a sinful man, and for many years I have continually practiced fornication. But when I entered the church of God just now, I heard the words of the prophet Isaiah—or rather, of God speaking through him:
