“‘Wash yourselves; be clean. Take away your evil deeds from your souls before my eyes. Learn to do good; seek justice. And if your sins are like scarlet, they shall be made white as snow; and if you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land’ (Isaiah 1).

“But I, wretched fornicator that I am, was pierced by this saying of the prophet. I entered into my own heart and said to God: ‘Lord, you are the one who came to save sinners. Fulfill in me, an unworthy sinner, these things that you have now promised through the prophet.

“‘Behold, from this moment I confess to you with all my heart that I will no longer commit this evil. I renounce every form of injustice, and from now on I will serve you with a clean conscience. From today, Lord, and from this hour, receive me as one who repents, worships you, and renounces all sins. I have sworn and resolved within myself to keep all your ordinances’ (Psalm 118).

“Under this pledge I came out of the church, resolving within myself no longer to commit any of my former sins.”

Then all the elders cried out to the Lord with a loud voice, saying: “How greatly your works have been magnified, O Lord! You have made all things in wisdom” (Psalm 103).

### 168

When Abba Joseph [Note: Joseph. The Aquicinct manuscript has *Jusefet*; the Audomar manuscript, *Tusefel*; others, *Josephel*.] had come with other elders to Abba Poemen (John, *Book* II, no. 10), one of the aforesaid elder’s relatives brought an infant whose face had been disfigured by disease. The child’s father sat outside the monastery with him and wept.

When one of the elders had gone out at the sound of the weeping and asked him why he was crying, he replied: “I am a relative of this Abba Poemen, and for this reason I came, so that he might see this infant whom affliction is crushing. Until now we were afraid to bring him here, because he does not wish to see us; and now, if he learns that I am here, he may drive me away again.

“But when I saw you, Fathers, who have just come to him, I dared to come here. What do you think, abba? Have mercy on me, take this infant, and carry him inside with you so that he may pray for him.”

After the elder had brought him into the cell, he acted with wise discretion: he did not present him first to Abba Poemen. Beginning with the younger brothers, he said: “Sign this infant, brothers, while praying for him,” and he made the same request of each of the elders.

After all the others, he brought him to Abba Poemen. The latter did not wish to touch him. But when the elder asked him to pray, as all the others had done, he rose, groaned, and prayed, saying: “God, heal your creation, so that the enemy may not dominate it.”

He made the sign over the infant, and immediately the child was returned healthy to his father.

### 169

One of the Fathers was asked whether poverty was a perfect good. He replied: “Need is a great thing. For whoever willingly endures it has tribulation in the flesh, but finds rest for his soul.”

### 170

A brother asked an elder: “If a brother owes me a few coins, do you order me to ask him for them?” The elder replied: “Tell him only once, with humility” (Paschasius, ch. 5, no. 2).

The brother said: “But if I tell him once and he gives me nothing, what shall I do?”

The elder replied: “Say nothing more to him.”

The brother said: “And what shall I do, since I cannot overcome my thought unless I persist with him?”

The elder said to him: “Let your thought burst; only do not distress your brother, because you are a monk.”

### 171

A brother asked an elder: “How can the soul acquire humility?” He replied: “If it considers only its own evils and not those of another” (Paschasius, ch. 13, no. 10).

He also used to say: “The perfection of a human being is humility. For to whatever extent a person lowers himself in humility, to that extent he advances in honor. Just as pride, if it ascends to heaven, is brought down to hell, so humility, if it descends to hell, is then exalted to the heavens” (Pelagius, *Book* XV, no. 77; Paschasius, ch. 13, no. 5).

### 172

Abba Macarius [Note: Macarius. The number and the little story of Macarius were worded as follows in the Aquicinct manuscript:

“While Abba Macarius was walking through the desert, he found a certain dead man lying face down on the ground. He placed his staff over him and said: ‘In the name of Jesus Christ, arise.’ Immediately the man who had been lying dead rose and threw himself at the feet of Saint Macarius.

“He began to proclaim how he had been led by the angels of Satan to the place of torments, but, because of Macarius’s request, had been released by the Ethiopians.” When Macarius asked him to what place he had been destined, he groaned deeply and said: ‘As far as heaven is distant from earth, so high is the fire in whose midst I had been cast.’

“When the elder heard this, he shed tears and said: ‘Woe to that man who has transgressed God’s commandments!’”

The account in the printed text concerning the refreshment of the damned does not fit very well with the opinions of scholastic theologians. The same little story, narrated somewhat differently, is also found below in John, *Book* III, no. 16; see the note there.]

While he was walking in the desert, he found the dry skull of a man lying on the ground [Note: John, *Book* III, no. 16, tells the story somewhat differently.]. When he turned it over with his staff, it seemed to emit a voice. The elder asked who it was, and it replied:

“I was once the chief priest of the idols who lived in this place. But you are Abba Macarius, filled with the divine Spirit. For whenever you take pity on those who are in punishment and pray for them, they feel some consolation” [Note: This must of course be understood in the proper sense. See the note.].

The elder said to him: “And what is your consolation, or your punishment? Tell me.”

Groaning more deeply, he replied: “As far as heaven is distant from earth, so high is the fire in whose midst we are, drenched in it from our feet to our heads on every side. No one is permitted to look upon another’s face; rather, our faces are joined to one another’s backs.

“But whenever you pray for us, we see one another in part, and this is a consolation for us.”

When he heard this, Macarius shed tears, saying: “Woe to that day on which a human being transgressed God’s commandments!”

He again asked him whether there was another punishment greater than this. The skull replied: “There are others far below us.”

When Macarius asked who they were, he said: “We, who did not know God, experience at least some mercy; but those who denied the God whom they had known are tortured beneath us with more grievous and unspeakable punishments.”

When blessed Macarius heard this, he departed after burying the skull more deeply in the earth.

### 173

A brother asked an elder: “Abba, why are we attacked so violently by demons?” The elder replied: “Because we throw away our weapons from us—that is, patience, humility, gentleness, and obedience” (Pelagius, *Book* XV, no. 58; Paschasius, ch. 25, no. 1).

### 174

A brother asked Abba Sisoes: “Do you think, abba, that the devil now persecutes us as he persecuted the ancient Fathers?”

He replied: “He persecutes us more now, because, as the time of punishments approaches, he is more distressed. Yet he does not even deign to attack the weak, whom he quickly overthrows whenever he wishes; rather, he attacks strong and great men” (Pelagius, *Book* XV, no. 45; Paschasius, ch. 25, no. 2).

### 175

Some brothers asked Abba Silvanus by what path he had acquired such prudence. He replied to them: “I have never allowed evil thoughts that would provoke God to anger to remain in my heart” (Pelagius, *Book* XI, no. 29).

### 176

Blessed Antony used to say: “If it can be done, a monk ought to inform the elders how many steps he walks and how many cups of water he drinks in his cell, so that he may not go astray in these matters.”

### 177

Abba Poemen said: “The enemy rejoices in nothing so much as in the person who does not wish to reveal his thoughts.”

### 178

A brother said to an elder: “Behold, abba, I frequently ask the elder Fathers to give me an admonition for the salvation of my soul, and whatever they say to me, I retain nothing” (Pelagius, *Book* X, no. 92).

The elder had two empty vessels. He said to him: “Go, bring one of those vessels, put water into it, wash it, pour the water out, and put the clean vessel back in its place.”

The brother did this once and twice. Then the elder said to him: “Bring both vessels together.”

When he had brought them, the elder said: “Which of the two is cleaner?”

The brother replied: “The one into which I put water and washed.”

Then the elder said to him: “So it is also with the soul, my son. Although it retains nothing of the words of God that it hears and asks about so frequently, it is nevertheless cleansed more than the soul that does not inquire.”

### 179

A certain elder said: “When a monk practices good works, the devil comes but finds no place in him, and immediately departs. But if he practices an evil work, the Spirit of God frequently comes, sees the evil work, does not approach him, but withdraws.

“Yet if he is sought again with the whole heart, he will quickly return” (Paschasius, ch. 26, no. 3).

180. A certain elder said: “A monk must labor until he possesses Christ” (Pasch., ch. 28, no. 3). But once he has attained him, he no longer labors. Nevertheless, the Lord permits his chosen ones to labor so that they may remember the labors of their trials and thereby guard themselves, fearing that they might lose such great labors. For this reason also God led the children of Israel around through the desert for forty years, so that, remembering their trials, they would not turn back.

181. A certain brother asked an elder, saying: “Tell me, Father, why do monks who now labor in the monastic life not receive grace as the ancient Fathers did?” The elder said to him: “At that time there was such great charity that each person lifted his neighbor upward; but now, after charity has grown cold and the whole world lies in the power of the evil one, individuals drag their neighbors downward, and therefore we do not obtain grace in this way” (Pelag., little book XVII, no. 19; Pasch., ch. 28, no. 4).

182. A certain brother asked an elder, saying: “Do you think, abba, that holy men know when grace comes upon them?” The elder replied: “They do not always know. For when the disciple of a certain great elder had sinned in some matter, the elder, becoming angry, said to him loudly: ‘Go and die.’ Immediately the disciple fell down and died. When the elder saw him dead, great fear seized him, and with profound humility he prayed, entreating God and saying: ‘Lord Jesus Christ, raise him up, and henceforth I will never again utter such a word without due consideration.’ When he had said this, his disciple immediately rose.”

183. Abba Poemen said: “A man who teaches others but does not do what he teaches is like a deep spring, which washes everyone’s things and satisfies everyone with drink, but cannot wash itself; rather, it contains both filth and mud” (Pelag., little book X, no. 50).

He also said: “Teach your soul to keep what your tongue teaches others.”

[Col. 0799D]

184. When a certain anchorite came to Abba Poemen, the elder received him gladly (Pelag., little book X, no. 39). After they had embraced one another, the anchorite began to speak about the Holy Scriptures and heavenly matters. Then the elder turned his face toward another brother and gave the anchorite no answer. Seeing that he would not speak with him, the anchorite went out sadly and said to the elder’s disciple: “I have undertaken all this journey and labor for nothing, to come to one who does not deign to speak with me.”

The disciple entered to Abba Poemen and said: “Because of you this abba has come here—a man so great, possessing such renown in his own region—and you do not wish to speak with him?”

The elder replied [Col. 0800A]: “This man is from above and speaks of heavenly things; I am from below and can scarcely speak of earthly things. If he had spoken to me about the passions of a monk, perhaps I would have answered him. But if he speaks of heavenly things, I confess that I do not know them.”

The disciple went out and said to the anchorite: “Our elder does not wish to speak about higher questions; but if someone speaks to him about the passions, he answers him.”

Cut to the heart by these words, the anchorite entered to the elder and said: “What shall I do, abba, since the passions of my heart rule over me?”

Then the elder looked at him joyfully and said: “Now you have come well, Father. I open my mouth; fill it with your good things.”

By these words the anchorite was helped, and he said: “In truth, this way that you follow is good and true.” After thanking the elder, he returned to his own region.

[Col. 0800B]

185. A certain elder said: “If someone speaks either about the Scriptures or about any other matter, do not argue with him. If he speaks well, agree with him; but if he speaks badly, say to him: ‘You know how you are speaking’” (Pasch., ch. 31, no. 1). By observing this, you will possess humility and avoid hatred. For if you persist in arguing and wish to defend your own statement, scandal will arise. Therefore, if you do not avoid arguments in any matter, you will in no way possess rest.

186. A certain brother asked an elder, saying: “How long, Father, must silence be observed?” The elder replied: “Until you are questioned. For in every place, if you remain silent, you will possess rest” (Pasch., [Col. 0800C] ch. 32, no. 3).

187. A certain elder used to say: “Just as a bee produces honey wherever it goes, so also a monk, wherever he travels, if he has gone for the work of God, can always bring forth the sweetness of good deeds” (Pasch., ch. 32, no. 7, under the name of Ammon).

188. Abba Muthues once came from a place called Ragitham, in the region of Gebalon; his disciple was also with him (Pelag., little book XV, no. 17; Pasch., ch. 33, no. 3). When the bishop of that place saw him, he took hold of him and made him a presbyter against his will. While they were staying together, the bishop said to him: “Forgive me, abba. I know that you did not want this, but I presumed to do it because I desired to receive a blessing from you.”

Because of his humility, the elder replied [Col. 0800D]: “My own inclination was somewhat unwilling as well; but my difficulty is that I shall have to be separated from the brother who is with me, and by myself I am not sufficient to complete my prayers.”

The bishop said to him: “If you know him to be worthy, I will ordain him also.”

Abba Muthues replied: “Whether he is worthy, I do not know; but I do know one thing: he is better than I am.”

The bishop ordained him also. Nevertheless, both of them remained in such a way until the end of their lives that they never approached the altar for the consecration of the offering. Therefore the elder used to say: “I trust in my God that I do not bear a grave judgment because of this ordination, since I did not presume to offer the oblation myself. For this ordination belongs to those who are righteous and undefiled, without fault; but I know myself well.”

[Col. 0801A]

189. A certain brother asked blessed Macarius to give him a word by which he might be saved. The elder said to him: “It is necessary to flee from people, sit in a cell, and continually lament over one’s sins; and, above all virtues, to restrain both the tongue and the belly.”

190. While Abba Arsenius was still living as a layman in the palace, he prayed to the Lord, saying: “Lord, show me the way by which I may be saved” (Pelag., little book II, no. 3). And he heard a voice saying to him: “Arsenius, flee from people, and you will be saved.”

After he had withdrawn into solitude, he prayed the same prayer again and once more heard a voice saying to him: “Arsenius, flee, be silent, and remain at rest. These are the beginnings of salvation.”

191. When Archbishop Theophilus came to the same Arsenius to hear from him some word of edification (Pelag., little book II, no. 4), Saint Arsenius said to all who were present [Col. 0801B]: “If I tell you something, will you keep it?”

When they had gladly promised him this, he added: “Wherever you hear that Arsenius is, do not go there again.”

Again, when the archbishop wished to see him, he first sent someone to find out whether Arsenius would open the door to him. But Arsenius sent him this reply: “If you come alone, I will open to you; but if you come with several others, Arsenius will no longer remain here.”

When the archbishop heard this, he postponed the journey he had begun, lest the hermit leave that place because of him.

[Note: [Col. 0801D] In the printed editions another saying concerning Arsenius occurs here, namely the one about the reed-bed. The style in the printed editions is different. I have placed here the reading from the manuscripts: Pasch., ch. 34, no. 2.]

192. While certain brothers were traveling from the Thebaid to buy flax, they said to one another: “On this occasion we shall see blessed Arsenius.”

When they reached his cave, his disciple Daniel announced them to him [Col. 0801C]. He said to him: “Go, my son, receive them and show them hospitality; but leave me to look toward heaven, and send them away again, for they shall not see my face.”

193. When one of the brothers came to the same blessed Arsenius wishing to see him, he knocked at the door.

[Note: [Col. 0802D] The style in the printed editions is different. I have placed here the reading from the manuscripts.]

Abba Arsenius, thinking that it was his disciple, opened the door to him. But after he saw that it was someone else, he immediately threw himself face down upon the ground. When the man asked him to rise, Arsenius replied: “I will not rise from here unless you leave.”

Although the brother begged him for many hours, he would not consent to rise until the man had departed.

Whenever the same blessed Arsenius gathered in church with the other Fathers, he sat behind a column, so that neither he himself could look upon another’s face nor another upon his [Col. 0801D] (Pelag., little book XV, no. 10).

[Note: [Col. 0802D] Another saying about Arsenius is added here in the printed editions.]

194. As Abba Besarion was walking through the desert with his disciple (Joan., little book III, no. 1; Pasch., ch. 34, no. 3), they came to a certain cave. When they entered, they found a brother sitting and making a cord. He neither looked at them nor greeted them nor spoke any word to them.

Abba Besarion therefore said to his disciple: “Let us go away from here, because this elder does not wish to speak with us.” They went on to Abba John [Col. 0802A].

When they were returning, they came to the same cave, and Besarion said to his disciple: “Let us enter again to this brother, in case God may perhaps have persuaded him by now to speak with us.”

When they had entered, they found only a dead body. Groaning, he said to his disciple: “Come, brother, let us arrange it, because on account of him the Lord sent us here.”

When they were burying the body, they discovered that it was a woman. They were amazed and said: “See how women also wrestle with demons and conquer them.”

Praising and glorifying God, who is the protector of all, they departed from that place.

195. Once two young men came to blessed Macarius (Joan., little book III, no. 2), one fully instructed, while the other was still inexperienced [Col. 0802B].

[Note: [Col. 0802D] The style here is different in the printed editions.]

They fell at his feet and asked him to permit them to live with him. When he saw that they were delicate in body, he thought that they could not endure the desert. He said to them: “My brothers, you cannot remain here.”

They said: “Father, if we cannot live with you, what then shall we do?”

Hearing this, he began to reason within himself: “If I drive them away from here, they will be scandalized. I will say to them: ‘Come, build yourselves a cell, if you can.’”

When they asked him merely to show them the place, he led them and showed them a rock which they could cut and use to prepare a dwelling for themselves, and cover with wood brought from the marsh. Macarius thought that they would immediately depart because of the labor imposed on them.

But they asked him [Col. 0802C]: “What work do you command us to do, Father?”

Then he gathered palm leaves and showed them how to weave a cord, instructing them to sell it for their sustenance, and so he left them.

They, however, completed with the greatest patience whatever had been commanded them. When the elder saw them growing daily in good works and frequently remaining in the church in silence and prayer, he wished to know their true practices.

He therefore fasted for a full week and asked the Lord to deem it worthy to show him their works. After this he went to them and knocked at the door of their cave. When they opened it and saw the man of God, both prostrated themselves on the ground.

After the customary prayer had been made, they sat down. The elder brother signaled to the younger and went outside. The younger himself sat twisting a cord, saying absolutely nothing.

At the ninth hour the younger brother knocked at the door and entered with food for them to eat. Commanded by the same signal from the elder brother, he set out a little table with three pieces of dry bread, and stood there silently.

When they had eaten, they said to blessed Macarius: “Are you leaving, Father, or not?”

He replied that he wished to rest there. Then they placed a small mat in one corner for him, while they themselves rested in another corner, as though they had thrown themselves down to sleep.

Macarius again asked the Lord to reveal their works to him. And behold, as though the roof had been removed [Col. 0803A], a bright light filled that cell like midday, though they did not perceive it.

After they supposed that the elder was asleep, they rose and devoted themselves to prayer, stretching their hands toward heaven. The elder watched what they were doing, but they could not see him.

Looking more intently, the elder saw demons, like flies, coming and attempting to settle upon the younger brother’s mouth and eyes. But an angel of the Lord, armed with a fiery sword, surrounded and defended him, while driving back and expelling the demons. They were in no way able to approach the elder brother.

When it was already near dawn, they threw themselves down again upon their same bed. Then Macarius, as though awakening, rose; and they likewise rose, as though awakened from a long sleep.

The elder brother approached the elder [Col. 0803B] and said: “Father, shall we sing perhaps twelve psalms?”

While they were singing the psalms, a torch of fire came forth from the younger brother’s mouth with each verse and rose toward heaven. Likewise, whenever the elder brother drew his lips together to sing, something like a cord of fire likewise extended from his mouth toward heaven.

After they had completed Matins, Macarius went out and begged them to pray for him. They, however, remained silent, fell at his feet, and commended themselves to his prayers.

The elder understood that the elder brother was perfect in the fear of God, while the younger was still being attacked by demons. After a few days the elder brother was received into peace; on the third day the younger followed him.

196. Abba Moses used to admonish the brothers, saying [Col. 0803C]: “There are four principal things for a monk to observe: to be silent, to keep the commandments of God, to humble himself, and to endure the hardship of poverty” (Pasch., ch. 35, no. 1). A monk must therefore always mourn, always remember his sins, and at every hour place death before his eyes.

197. The holy Fathers gathered together and prophesied about the last generation. One of them, a distinguished man named Squirion [Vulgate: Isquirio], said: “We still fulfill the commandments of God” (Joan., little book I, no. 14).

The other Fathers asked him [Col. 0803D]: “What of those who will come after us?”

He replied: “Perhaps they will fulfill half the commandments of God and seek the eternal God.”

The holy Fathers said: “And after those who come, what will they do?”

He replied: “The people of that generation will not possess the works of God’s commandments, and they will forget the precepts of God. Iniquity will then abound, and the charity of many will grow cold (Matt. XXIV). But temptation will come upon them, and those who are found proved in that temptation will be better than both us and our Fathers, happier, and more approved.”

198. A certain brother asked Abba Agathon, saying: “Father, I wish to remain in the community with the brothers. Tell me how I should live with them.”

The elder replied: “Observe this above all: that just as you enter among them on the first day, so also spend all your remaining days, with humility” (Pelag., little book X, no. 1; Pasch., ch. 42, no. 1).

[Col. 0804A]

199. When the Mazices came upon Scetis and killed many of the Fathers (Pelag., little book XV, no. 11; Pasch., ch. 42, no. 4), Abba Poemen fled from there with another elder abba named Nub and five other Fathers. They came to a place called Therenuthi.

[Note: [Col. 0813B] Therenuthi.] This is clearly the correct reading, as is established from Pelagius, little book XV, no. 2. The manuscript and printed editions have a corrupt form, perhaps *teneritudinis*, *terenitudinis*, or something similar. See the *Onomasticon*.

There they found a deserted temple and remained in it together for seven days, until they could determine where each one would stay in Egypt. Abba Nub therefore said to them: “During this week let each one remain by himself and not speak with another.”

As they were doing this, there was a statue of an idol in that temple. Abba Nub rose in the morning, stoned it, and in the evening, when he returned, said to it: “I have sinned; forgive me.” He did the same throughout the entire week.

On Saturday, when they had gathered together, Abba Poemen said to him: “What did you intend by doing this all week, saying to an idol, ‘Forgive me,’ as though it were a faithful person?”

The elder replied: “I did this for your sake. Tell me: when I was stoning this idol, did it speak or become angry? And again, when I asked it for forgiveness, did it exalt itself or boast?”

Abba Poemen answered him: “Certainly not.”

Then the elder said: “Brothers, behold, there are seven of us. If you wish us to remain together, let this idol be an example to us, so that no one may become angry when he is insulted, nor boast or exalt himself when forgiveness is requested from him. But if you do not wish this, let each one go wherever he wishes.”

They threw themselves upon the ground and replied that they would do so. Thus they remained for many years with great humility and patience [Col. 0804C]. They slept four hours at night, sang psalms for four, and worked for four. During the day they worked until the sixth hour; then they read until the ninth hour. After this they prepared their food, gathering various plants of the earth.

[Note: [Col. 0813B] Mazices.] The printed text has *Mazines*. The Aquileian manuscript has *Amazones*. But *Mazices* should be read. In Pelagius it is “the people of the Mazici.” See the *Onomasticon*.

200. There were also seven other men, likewise exceptionally tried, who lived in that desert adjoining the Saracens. Their cells were separated from one another by some distance, but they themselves were joined by the bond of charity. One was called Peter, another Stephen, the third John, the fourth George, the fifth Theodore, the sixth Felix, and the seventh Laurus.

They lived in a barren and immensely desolate solitude, scarcely habitable by human beings, and showed themselves to one another only once a week. On the Sabbath, at the ninth hour of the day, each came from his own place to an agreed meeting place, bringing whatever he had been able to find [Col. 0804D].

One brought nuts, another *lactorones*.

[Note: [Col. 0813B] *Lactorones*.] This is the reading of the printed editions. The Aquileian manuscript has *lactopones*, and reads the entire passage as follows: “Another, *lactopones*; another, dates; another, figs; another, edible herbs, namely lapsanum, parsnips, wild chard, and parsley.” The Audomar manuscript lacks the earlier items and reads the remainder as follows: “lapsanum, parsnips, and figs from the rocks.” The Cologne edition has: “lapsanum and parsnips, gourds, and parsley.” Some editions omit the figs. It is altogether difficult to decide the matter here. Could *lacterones* mean lettuces, from *lac*, “milk”? Or could it be a corruption from the Greek *γαλακτέρονες* (*galakterones*, perhaps “milky ones”)? I do not recall having read this word, however. Perhaps *scarvitae* is a genuine word, whence the French *chervis*, among edible herbs. See the *Onomasticon*.

Another brought dates, another figs, another edible herbs, namely lapsanum, parsnips, figs, and parsley. For this was their principal food; bread, oil, and drink were outside their use. They were sustained solely by the herbs and fruits mentioned above. The palm supplied them with clothing; water was scarcely found in those regions.

They did not drink in any other way than by going out in the morning and roaming among the various herbs, gathering the dew, which falls there in great abundance, and drinking only from it [Col. 0805A].

When, as we have said, they gathered together in one place, they gave thanks to God and ate their food. After the meal they sat until evening meditating on the Holy Scriptures. No worldly conversation passed among them, no concern for the world, no activity of earthly affairs, but only spiritual discussion: remembrance of the desirable heavenly kingdom, future blessedness, the glory of the righteous, the punishment of sinners, and the rest of the saints.

As they recalled these things, they sighed from the depths of their hearts and wept profusely. Remaining awake throughout the entire night and celebrating praises to the Lord, they brought their time for speaking with and seeing one another to an end on Sunday at the ninth hour.

Each returned to his own cell, where he devoted himself alone to God, day and night [Col. 0805B].

While they were occupied in these practices, the Saracens, roaming widely through the desert, discovered them. They attacked them, drove them out of the desert, bound them, and hung them by their feet. After afflicting them with many insults, they finally piled bitter herbs beneath them and set them on fire. There they were tortured terribly, and through the bitterness of the smoke they lost the sight of their eyes.

After tormenting them for a long time, the Saracens left them half alive. We know that one of them survived for a considerable time afterward in a certain place; but where the others were taken, we have no knowledge at all.

201. A certain brother asked Abba Poemen [Note: [Col. 0805D] Pelag., little book XVII, no. 10; Pasch., ch. 37, no. 3; Appendix to Martin, no. 14.], saying: “What does the Lord mean when he says in the Gospel, ‘No one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friend’ (John XV) [Col. 0805C]? How is this done?”

The elder replied: “If someone hears an evil word from his neighbor and, although he could answer him with similar words, nevertheless bears it in his heart and imposes force and labor upon himself so that he may not answer him with evil and sadden him, that person lays down his life for his friend.”

202. A certain elder said: “If a person does not remember his own deeds in prayer, he labors in vain when he prays” [Note: [Col. 0805D] John, little book IV, no. 4, under the name of Moses; Appendix to Martin, no. 35. The printed editions have a different style.]. “When someone abandons the desire to sin and walks on, remaining in the fear of God, God immediately receives him with joy.”

203. A brother asked a holy elder [Appendix to Martin, no. 36], saying: “What should a person do whenever temptation comes upon him and whenever a thought is injected by the enemy?”

He replied: “He ought to mourn in the presence of God’s goodness, so that God may come to his aid and help him. For it is written [Col. 0805D]: ‘The Lord is my helper, and I shall look down upon my enemies’ (Psalm CXVII).”

204. A certain elder said: “Just as flies do not approach a pot that has been heated red-hot, but if it has become lukewarm they settle upon it and produce worms, so demons flee from a monk who has been kindled by the fire of divine love, but mock and pursue one who is lukewarm” (Pasch., ch. 39, no. 3, under the name of Pimen).

205. As Abba Silvanus was sitting in a cave, he fell into ecstasy and remained hanging with his face toward the ground [Col. 0806A] [Note: [Col. 0806D] Pelagius, little book III, no. 15; this is also the style of the printed editions. I have placed here the reading from the manuscripts, Appendix to Martin, no. 48.]. After several hours he rose and wept bitterly.

His disciple, standing nearby, said to him: “What is wrong, Father?” But he remained silent and wept. When the disciple pressed him to tell him why he was weeping, he said: “I was carried away to the judgment, my son, and I saw many of those wearing our monastic habit going to punishment, while many laypeople were going into the kingdom of God.”

Saying this, the elder mourned grievously.

206. A certain elder said to a brother: “Think every day that death is near you; as though you were already shut in a tomb, care nothing for this world” [Note: [Col. 0806D] Pasch., ch. 43, no. 2, under the name of Silvanus. Appendix to Martin, no. 108.]. Let the fear of God remain continually within you, at every hour. Believe yourself inferior to all people. Do not speak evil of anyone, because God knows everything; but be at peace with everyone [Col. 0806B], and the Lord will always give you rest.

207. When certain brothers asked blessed Macarius how they should pray (Pelag., little book XII, no. 10), he replied to them: “We do not need superfluous words; we should merely stretch out our hands and say: ‘God, as you will, and as it pleases you, so let it be.’ But if temptation or assault suddenly comes upon us, we should say: ‘God, help us’—for he himself knows what is beneficial for us.”

208. Abba John used to say: “A monk should be like a man sitting beneath a tree who, seeing various wild beasts and serpents coming toward him, climbs into the tree to escape when he cannot resist them. So also a monk should sit in his cell and, seeing evil thoughts coming against him [Col. 0806C], flee through prayer to the Lord when he cannot resist them, and he will be saved.”

209. He also said: “A monk should be like a man who has fire on his left and water on his right. Whenever the fire is kindled, he takes water and extinguishes it. So too the monk must act at every hour: whenever an impure thought has been kindled by the enemy, he should pour out the water of prayer and extinguish it.”

210. While Abba Zeno was in Scetis (Pelag., little book XVIII, no. 7), he went out from his cell at night to walk through the desert. As he went farther, he lost his way and walked for three days and nights. Exhausted almost to death, he fell down [Col. 0806D].

And behold, a child stood before him, holding bread in his hand, and said to him: “Rise and eat.”

He rose and prayed, for he thought it was an apparition. The child said to him: “You did well to pray; now rise and eat.”

Abba Zeno would not comply until he had prayed a second and a third time. When the child praised him for praying, he then rose and ate.

After this the child said to him: “The farther you have walked, the farther you are from your cell. But rise, follow me.” And immediately he found himself before his cell.

The elder therefore said to him: “Enter my cell [Col. 0807A] and pray.” When the elder had entered his cell, the child disappeared.

211. Abba Daniel related this about blessed Arsenius: On Saturday evening he let the setting sun shine behind his back while he remained persevering in prayer. Stretching his hands toward heaven, he did not cease praying until the sun rose again the following day and filled his eyes (Pelag., little book XII, no. 1).

He spent the other nights awake as well. Near dawn, when he wished to rest a little because of the frailty of nature, he would say to sleep: “Come, wicked servant.” Then, immediately closing his eyes, he would steal a little sleep while sitting, and at once rise again (Pelag., little book IV, no. 2).

This same Arsenius, throughout his entire life, sat at his manual work [Col. 0807B] and kept a cloth in his lap for the tears that frequently flowed from his eyes out of longing for eternal life (Pelag., little book III, no. 1; Rufinus, above, no. 163).

212. When certain brothers came to Abba Lucius [Note: [Col. 0807D] Pelag., little book XII, no. 9. This is also the style of the printed editions.], the elder asked them: “What work do you usually do with your hands?”

They said: “We do no manual work, but, according to what the Apostle says, we pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. V).

The elder said to them: “Do you not eat?”

They admitted: “Yes.”

He said to them: “Then when you eat, who is praying for you?”

They fell silent.

Again he asked them: “Do you sleep?”

When they said that they did sleep, he said to them: “Then when you sleep, who is praying for you?”

They could find nothing to answer him [Col. 0807C].

Then he said to them: “Forgive me, therefore, because you do not do as you say. But I will show you how, while working with my hands, I pray without ceasing.

“I sit from morning until the appointed hour, soak a few palm leaves, and make cords from them. Meanwhile I pray, saying: ‘Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy, and according to the abundance of your mercies blot out my iniquity’ (Psalm L).

“When I have completed my manual work and made some vessels or a few cords, and have obtained ten coins from them, of these coins I give two to the poor and eat the rest. Therefore, when I eat or sleep, they complete my prayer without ceasing for my sins.”

213. Once, as Abba Macarius was carrying the baskets he had woven from Scetis, burdened by the great labor of the journey, he sat down and said: “God, you know that I am no longer able to walk.”

Immediately he found himself at the river, although he had still been many intervals away from it (Joan., little book II, no. 6).

214. When Abba Ammon came into the desert to a certain place to draw water, he saw a basilisk. Throwing himself face down, he said: “Lord, either I must die or this beast.”

Immediately, by the power of God, the basilisk was dispersed.

215. One day, when Dulas, the disciple of Abba Besarion [Col. 0808A], was walking with him along the seashore, he became very thirsty and said to the elder: “Thirst is tormenting me, Father” (Joan., little book II, no. 1).

Blessed Besarion prayed and ordered him to draw water from the sea and drink it. When he had done so and found the water exceedingly sweet, he filled the small vessel that he was carrying with him.

When Abba Besarion saw this, he said to him: “Why have you filled the vessel with water, my son?”

He replied: “Forgive me, Father, for I was afraid that I might become thirsty later.”

The elder said to him: “May the Lord forgive you, my son; for God is everywhere and can provide you with sweet water.”

216. A certain brother wished to depart into solitude, but was prevented by his own mother [Note: [Col. 0808D] Pelagius, little book III, no. 20. This is also the style of the printed editions. I have placed here the reading from the manuscript.]. He said to his mother: “Permit me, mother, for I wish to save my soul” [Col. 0808B].

When his mother could no longer hold him back, she released him. He went into the desert, but through negligence spent his entire life there.

His mother died, and after some time he himself became ill. He was carried away in ecstasy to the judgment and found his mother among those being judged.

When she saw him, she was astonished and said: “What is this, my son? You too have been brought to this place to be condemned? And where are those words you used to say: ‘I wish to save my soul’?”

Ashamed by the words he heard, he stood there with nothing to answer. And behold, a voice sounded ordering that he be recalled, as though another person had been commanded to leave the brothers’ monastery. Coming back to himself, he reported to those standing there everything he had learned and heard.

To confirm his words, he asked that someone present go to the monastery to see whether a brother of the same name, about whom he had heard, had died. The man went and found that it was so.

After he had recovered his health, he shut himself away and sat, pondering his salvation, repenting and weeping over what he had previously done in negligence. His compunction was so great that, although many begged him to rest a little lest he suffer harm from his incessant weeping, he refused, saying: “If I have not endured my mother’s reproach, how shall I endure reproaches or torments in the presence of Christ and his angels on the day of judgment?”

217. A certain brother lived in Egypt and was outstanding in great humility (Pasch., ch. 24, no. 2). He had a sister in the city who was a prostitute and had been the ruin of many souls.

The elders frequently admonished this brother, and they could scarcely persuade him to go to her, so that through his admonition he might overcome the sin being committed through her. When he came to the place, one of her acquaintances saw him, went ahead, and announced to her: “Behold, your brother has come to you from the desert.”

When she heard this, she left the lovers whom she was serving and went out to meet her brother with her head uncovered. When she saw him and attempted to embrace him, he said to her: “My dearest sister, spare your soul, for many are perishing because of you. Consider how many torments have been prepared for you unless you hasten to repent.”

Trembling, she said to him: “And do you know, brother, whether there is salvation for me even now?”

He said to her: “If you are willing, there is still salvation for you.”

She threw herself at her brother’s feet and begged him to take her with him into the desert. The brother said to her: “Go, cover your head, and follow me.”

She replied: “Let us go quickly. It is better for me to disfigure myself and walk among people with my head uncovered than to enter again into the workshop of my sin.”

As they walked together, the brother admonished her to repent. Seeing that some brothers were meeting them, he said to her: “Since not everyone yet knows that you are my sister, withdraw a little from the road until they have passed” [Col. 0809B].

She did so. After they had passed, her brother called to her, saying: “Come, sister; let us go on our way.”

But she did not answer him.

Searching carefully for his sister, he found her dead, and her footprints full of blood, for she had been barefoot.

Weeping and wailing, he then reported everything that had happened to the elders. They debated among themselves concerning her salvation.

But God revealed her case to one of the elders: she had shown no concern for bodily matters, but only for healing her own wound; she had neglected everything that belonged to her, sighed deeply, and wept over her sins. Therefore God had accepted her repentance.

### 218. At a Certain Time

[Note: “At a certain time.” This is taken from Saint Jerome, Letter 33, to Castrutianus; yet the passage here includes material lacking in Jerome at the end: “Those who by sight alone, through lust, are able to send a man into the destruction of Gehenna.” Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 7; Socrates, Book IV, chapter 20; Jerome, in the preface to Didymus’ *On the Holy Spirit*: “But my Didymus, having the bride’s eye in the *Song of Songs*, and those eyes which Jesus commanded to be raised toward the shining crops, looks from afar into deeper things.” And Letter 32, to Abigaus: “But rejoice that you possess that eye of which it is said in the *Song of Songs*: ‘You have wounded me, my sister, my bride, with one of your eyes’ (Song of Songs 4).”]

When blessed Antony had been brought to the city of Alexandria by Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, for the refutation of the heretics [Column 0809C] (from Jerome, Letter 33, to Castrutianus), Didymus, a most learned man who had lost his sight, went to him. As they spoke at length about the Holy Scriptures, among their other conversations concerning the sacred Books, Antony, marveling at his intellect and praising the sharpness of his mind, asked him:

“Are you not saddened that you lack bodily eyes?”

Since he remained silent out of shame, Antony questioned him a second and a third time, and at last drew from him a frank admission of the sorrow in his heart. Antony then said to him:

“I am astonished that a prudent man should grieve over the loss of what ants, flies, and gnats possess.”

[Note: “What ants, flies, and gnats possess.” Jerome, Letter 32, to Abigaus, a consolatory letter on blindness: “Nor should you grieve if you do not possess what ants, flies, and serpents possess.” There he also reports that certain philosophers of the world, “so that they might force their whole thought toward purity of mind, tore out their own eyes.” And in Book II, *Against Jovinianus*: “We read that certain men gouged out their own eyes.” Cicero, *On Ends*, Book V: “Democritus, who is said—truly or falsely—to have deprived himself of his eyes.” Concerning him also: Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book V; Gellius, Book X, chapter 7; Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 46.]

He should rather rejoice in possessing those eyes which the saints and the apostles deserved. For it is far better to see with the spirit than with the flesh, and to possess those eyes into which the splinter of sin cannot fall, than those which by sight alone, through lust, can send a man into the destruction of Gehenna.

### 219. A Certain Brother

[Note: “A certain brother.” The following passage may perhaps be related to what Saint Jerome has in Letter 4, to Rusticus:

“We recently saw and lamented the wealth of Croesus exposed by the death of one man, and the contributions of a city, gathered as though for the uses of the poor, left to his family and descendants. Then the iron that lay hidden in the depths floated upon the water (2 Kings 6), and among the palm trees the bitterness of the water was revealed (Exodus 15). Nor is this surprising: he had such a companion and teacher, one who made the hunger of the needy his wealth and reserved what had been left to the wretched for his own wretchedness. Their cry at last reached heaven and overcame God’s most patient ears, so that an evil angel sent to Nabal of Carmel (1 Samuel 25) might say: ‘Fool, this night they will take your soul from you; and whose will those things be which you have prepared?’ (Luke 12). Here understand the iron allegorically as the monk’s hidden and grave iniquity; and let us find in the bitterness of the water by Moses, near the seventy palms, the crime that is covered by palms, as though by the shadow of holiness.

“I do not know whether by ‘companion and teacher’ he is insinuating Rufinus, whom he designates by the name Grunnius. Concerning him he says in the same letter: ‘This well-moneyed man was especially welcome at banquets. Nor is it surprising, since one who was accustomed to bait many people, having formed a wedge of chattering men shouting around him, would go out in public—Nero within, Cato without.’”]

A certain brother from Nitria, more frugal than avaricious, and unaware that the Lord Jesus had been sold for thirty pieces of silver, died and left behind one hundred solidi, which he had collected by weaving linen (from Jerome, Letter 22, to Eustochium, *On the Preservation of Virginity*).

A council was therefore held among the monks—for about five thousand lived in that same place in separate cells [Note: “For about five thousand lived in that same place in separate cells.” Above, Book II, which is Rufinus’ first book, in the prologue: “They remain scattered and separated throughout the desert in cells.” He did not say “in separate cells” without reason, since he was indicating the *Cellia*, or laura.]—to determine what ought to be done. Some thought that the money should be distributed to the poor; others that it should be given to the church; several that it should be returned to his parents. But Macarius, Pambo, Isidore, and the other elder Fathers, with the Holy Spirit speaking through them, decreed that it should be buried with its owner, saying: “May your money be with you for destruction” (Acts 8).

But lest anyone think that this was done cruelly, such terror and dread seized all the monks throughout Egypt that among them it was considered a grave crime to have left behind even one solidus.

### 220. A Certain Greek Youth

[Note: “A certain Greek youth.” This is almost word for word from Saint Jerome, Letter 4, to Rusticus.]

There was a certain Greek youth living in Egypt in a coenobium who could extinguish the flames of the flesh by neither abstinence nor any degree of labor. When this temptation of his had been reported to the monastery’s Father, he saved him by the following method.

He ordered a serious and harsh man to harass the youth with quarrels and insults and, after inflicting the injury, to be the first to come forward with a complaint. When the man carried out what had been commanded, witnesses were even summoned who spoke in his defense—the man who had insulted the youth. But the youth began to weep at the false accusation. Every day there were groans; every day tears flowed. He sat alone, because he was filled with bitterness, and deprived of every form of assistance, he lay at the feet of Jesus.

What more need be said? A whole year passed in this way. When it was over, the youth was questioned about his former thoughts—whether, if he still had to endure some distress, he would do so. He replied:

“Father, I have no leisure even to live; how could I have any desire to fornicate?”

Thus, through the providence of his spiritual Father, the youth overcame lust and was saved.

# BOOK FOUR OF THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS, BY SEVERUS SULPICIUS AND JOHN CASSIAN

[Note: “By the authors.” I have entitled this fourth book as being by Severus Sulpicius and John Cassian because this book has been excerpted from their works in their own words. Who made the excerpts is not entirely certain. See what was said in the general prolegomenon, section 6.]

[Note: “By Severus Sulpicius.” You will find various eulogies of him at the beginning of his works, composed by various learned men. Here I shall give only those that mention the *Dialogues*, from which these excerpts are taken. Gelasius, *Decree*, Part I, distinction 15, chapter 3: “The little works of Posthumianus and Gallus are apocryphal.” Jerome, Book XI on Ezekiel, chapter 36, after listing the followers of the error of the Millenarians, adds: “And recently our Severus, in the dialogue which he entitled *Gallus*.”]

Do not be surprised that Severus’ *Dialogues*, in which Posthumianus and Gallus converse, are numbered by Pope Gelasius among the apocrypha. For they contain certain blemishes, which are noted in the index of prohibited books by Father Giovanni Maria Brasichelli, master of the Sacred Palace, and in Bellarmine’s book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, in various places in Baronius’ *Annals*, and in our Possevinus’ *Sacred Apparatus*. Nevertheless, no such blemishes occur in these excerpts.

Regarding the year in which Severus Sulpicius wrote his *Dialogues*, Baronius says the following in volume V, under the year of Christ 402, in the eighth year of Pope Innocent I and of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius:

“In what year of the Lord Severus wrote that dialogue can likewise be understood from the following. Since Saint Jerome says that they had recently been written by Severus, and since it is established that the commentaries on Ezekiel, in which he discusses them, were written in the year when the city was captured by the Goths, as appears from the prefaces attached to those books—namely, eight years after this time—it must certainly be admitted that Severus composed this work long after the death of Saint Martin, although Posthumianus’ journey to the East, from which he begins the dialogue, took place while Saint Martin was alive, namely in the year when the Alexandrian church was thrown into turmoil because of the Origenists.”

The same Baronius, in volume V, under the year of Christ 431, the eighth year of Pope Celestine, the twenty-fourth of Theodosius, and the seventh of the emperors Valentinian, demonstrates that the author of the *Dialogues*, Severus Sulpicius, was different from Severus Sulpicius, bishop of Bourges. In this matter Severus’ commentators—Carlo Sigonio, Pietro Galesini, and Victor Giselinus—had gone astray. Joseph Scaliger also noted this in the prolegomena to his books *On the Correction of Chronology*, as did Nicolas Faber in his posthumous *Opuscula*, in the essay on Dionysius the Areopagite, where he says that our Severus was a monk of Primuliacum.

The journey of Posthumianus, who converses in Severus’ *Dialogues*, to Egypt is described in Severus’ first dialogue, from which the excerpts you are reading here are taken. For the year of Christ in which it is thought to have occurred, see the note here on chapter 2, section 4. Victorius of Reate errs in the *Life of Saint Jerome*, where he thought that Severus had traveled to Egypt, whereas Severus himself is relating Posthumianus’ journey.]

# AND JOHN CASSIAN

[Note: “And John Cassian.” You will find various eulogies of him before his works, revised by Henry Cuyckius and Pietro Ciacconius, who at the same time indicate what must be guarded against in Cassian’s works. Nothing worthy of a censor’s mark occurs in these excerpts.]

Regarding Cassian’s journey to Egypt, Baronius says the following under the year of Christ 404, the third year of Pope Innocent, and the tenth of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, after discussing Cassian’s being sent as an envoy to Pope Innocent in the matter of John Chrysostom:

“After this, Cassian journeyed to Egypt and there began to cultivate the monastic life; from there he drew the material for writing the *Conferences of the Fathers*. A letter of Isidore of Pelusium to Cassian is extant (Isidore of Pelusium, Book I, Letter 309), written when he had begun to undertake the monastic life, in which Isidore chiefly admonished him that he must restrain his tongue.”

Thus far Baronius. I do not see how Baronius’ opinion concerning Cassian’s journey to Egypt can agree with Cassian’s writings. For Cassian says that he lived among the hermits from childhood. He writes this in the preface to Bishop Castor, which he placed before his books *On the Institutes of the Coenobia*, when he explains why he is now less capable of recalling and collecting the institutions of the Egyptian monks:

“Secondly, because, although from our childhood we lived among those same men and, encouraged by their daily exhortations and examples, either attempted to do, or learned, or perceived by sight, the things in question, we can no longer retain them completely, having been separated for so many years from their companionship and from the imitation of their way of life.”

From this it may also be inferred that he is not the same Cassian to whom Isidore of Pelusium writes.

These excerpts are from Severus Sulpicius’ first dialogue and from the *Institutes* and *Conferences* of John Cassian.

## [EXCERPTS]

### Prologue

**536** You have frequently and repeatedly demanded of me, brothers, that, for your edification, I should explain, after my return from overseas regions, the story of my journey: how the faith of Christ flourishes in the East; what peace there is among the rulers; what rest there is among the saints; what the institutions of the monks are; what the life and manner of the hermits are; whether Christians are permitted to live in the desert; with how many signs and miracles Christ works in his servants; how my voyage prospered; and where and by what route my overland journey brought me.

Therefore, aided by your prayers, I shall do what I see you desire. I ask you most willingly to lend your ears to what I relate.

[Note: Severus Sulpicius, *Dialogue* 1, chapter 1, has some words of this prologue. Everything is to be understood as spoken in the name of Posthumianus, who is the speaker.]

### CHAPTER I  
### On a Solitary Monk Who Lived in a Small Hut in the Territory of Cyrene

[Column 0815A]

Three years ago, at the time when I left here (Severus Sulpicius, *Dialogue* 1, chapter 2), after we had set sail from Narbonne, we entered the port of Africa on the fifth day; so favorable was our voyage by God’s will. I wished to visit Carthage, to see the places of the saints, and especially to pray at the tomb of Cyprian the martyr.

On the fifteenth day, therefore, we returned to the port and set out into the open sea, making for Alexandria. Because the South Wind opposed us, we were almost carried into the Syrtis. The prudent sailors, guarding against this danger, cast anchors and brought the ship to a halt.

The mainland lay before our eyes. We went ashore in boats, and when we saw that everything was empty of human cultivation, I went farther inland, being especially eager to explore the region. About three miles from the shore I saw a small hut among the sands. Its roof, like the keel of a ship, was joined closely to the ground and constructed of fairly strong boards.

This was not because any force of rain was feared there—for no one had ever heard that rain had fallen there—but because the force of the winds is so great that, whenever a breeze begins to blow under even a gentler sky, there is a greater shipwreck in those lands than on any sea. No shoots grow there, and no crops are produced, since the unstable soil consists of dry sands that yield to every movement of the winds.

Yet wherever certain headlands projecting from the sea resist the winds, the soil is somewhat firmer and produces sparse, bristly grass, which is sufficiently useful as food for sheep. The inhabitants of that region live on milk. Those who are more industrious—or, so to speak, wealthier—use barley bread.

That is the only crop there, and because of the rapidity of its growth, owing to the nature of the sun or air, it usually escapes the violence of the winds. For it is said to ripen on the thirtieth day from the sowing of the seed.

The only reason people remain there is that they are all exempt from tribute. For it is the extreme coast of Cyrene, adjoining that desert which lies between Egypt and Africa, through which Cato once led his army while fleeing Caesar.

When, therefore, I reached the hut that I had seen from a distance, I found an old man there in a garment of animal skin, turning a millstone by hand. When greeted, he received us most kindly.

We explained that we had been cast out and put ashore on that coast and were detained by the calmness of the sea, so that we could not immediately resume our voyage. Having come ashore, we wished—as is the habit of the human mind—to learn about the nature of the region and the customs of its inhabitants. We especially asked whether there were any Christians among those solitudes.

Then, weeping for joy, he fell at our knees. He kissed us repeatedly and invited us to prayer. Next, spreading animal skins on the ground, he made us recline and set before us a truly sumptuous meal: half a barley loaf.

There were four of us, and he was the fifth. He also brought in a bundle of a herb whose name has escaped me. It resembles mint and, being abundant in leaves, offered the taste of honey. We were delighted and satisfied by its exceedingly sweet flavor.

We stayed with him for seven days. On the following day, when some of the inhabitants began to gather around us, we learned that our host was a priest, something he had concealed from us with the utmost discretion.

We then went with him to the church, which lay nearly two miles away and was hidden from our sight by an intervening mountain. It was woven from worthless brushwood and was scarcely more elaborate than our host’s hut, in which hardly anyone could stand except while bent over.

When we inquired into the customs of the people, we noticed this remarkable thing: they neither sold nor bought anything. They knew nothing of fraud or theft. They had neither gold nor silver, nor did they desire to possess them.

For when I offered that priest ten gold pieces, he refused them. When he would not accept them, we gave him some clothing instead. He received this kindly. Then, when the sailors called us back to the sea, we departed from him.

### CHAPTER II  
### On the Sayings of Origen, and That They Are Heretical

With a favorable voyage, therefore (Severus Sulpicius, *Dialogue* 1, chapter 3), we reached Alexandria on the seventh day. There ugly disputes were being waged between the bishops and the monks, on this occasion or for this reason: priests had often gathered together and seemed, through frequent synods, to have decreed that no one should read or possess the books of Origen [Note: “Of Origen.” Baronius, volume V, under the year of Christ 399, the second year of Pope Anastasius, and the fifth of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius. It happened that, when such great and numerous disturbances had been stirred up in Alexandria and throughout Egypt over Origen’s books, by Theophilus, bishop of that city, and other bishops against the monks who supported Origen’s writings, that Posthumianus—the man who converses with Gallus in Severus’ dialogue—arrived in Alexandria and witnessed in person many of the events that took place between the two opposing parties. For, setting out from Narbonne for Africa to visit the tomb of Saint Cyprian the martyr, he proceeded from there along the coast of Cyrene and reached Egypt, intending to go on to Jerusalem to visit the holy places, and so forth. His pilgrimage to Egypt and Jerusalem, even if it did not occur in this year, could nevertheless have taken place not long afterward.]—although Origen was regarded as a highly skilled interpreter of the Holy Scriptures.

The bishops, however, recalled that certain passages in his books had been written with great recklessness. Origen’s supporters, not daring to defend them, said instead that they had been deceitfully inserted by heretics. Therefore, they argued, the rest should not be condemned on account of passages that deserved criticism, since the faith of readers could readily distinguish between them, so that they would not follow what was false while retaining what had been discussed in a Catholic manner.

They said that it was not surprising if heretical fraud had operated in new and recently written books, since in certain places it had not feared to attack the truth of the Gospel.

The bishops, resisting this more obstinately, used their authority to compel people to condemn everything sound together with what was corrupt, and to condemn the author himself as well, since the books that the Church had already accepted were sufficient for these matters. They declared that reading which would harm the ignorant more than it benefited the wise ought to be rejected entirely.

As for me, when I investigated certain passages from those books with particular curiosity, I found many things highly pleasing. But I also found some passages that deserved criticism, in which it is beyond doubt that he held erroneous opinions, although his defenders maintain that they were falsified.

I marvel that one and the same man could have been so unlike himself: in the part for which he is approved, no one after the apostles has an equal; in the part for which he is rightly criticized, no one is taught to have erred more disgracefully.

For when the bishops read many excerpts from his books that were clearly written against the Catholic faith, the passage that aroused the greatest hostility was one in which it was read that:

“Our Lord Jesus Christ, just as he had come in the flesh for the redemption of humanity, had suffered the cross for humanity’s salvation and tasted death for humanity’s immortality, so, following the same order of suffering, he would also redeem the devil, because it was fitting to his goodness and compassion that he who had restored fallen humanity should also free the fallen angel.”

When the bishops brought forward this and other statements of the same kind, a great revolt arose from the rival factions. Since it could not be suppressed by the authority of the priests, a prefect was appointed, as a harsh precedent, to enforce the discipline of the Church. Through fear of it, the brothers were dispersed and the monks driven into various regions, so that, when edicts had been issued, they were not allowed to remain in any place.

What greatly troubled me was that Jerome, a most Catholic man and highly skilled in sacred learning, was thought at first to have followed Origen. Yet that same Jerome now condemned Origen above all others, together with all his writings.

Nor did I dare to pass rash judgment on anyone. Nevertheless, the most outstanding and learned men were said to disagree in this controversy.

Whether this is an error, as I think, or a heresy, as it is believed, it could not be suppressed by the many punishments imposed by the priests. Nor could it have spread so widely if it had not grown through contention.

When I arrived amid this disturbance, Alexandria was in turmoil. The bishop of that city received me with great kindness—better than I had expected—and tried to keep me with him. But I had no desire to remain where the resentment arising from the recent slaughter of the brothers was still burning.

### CHAPTER III  
### On the Way of Life of Jerome of Jerusalem

After leaving there (Severus Sulpicius, *Dialogue* 1, chapter 4), I made for the town of Bethlehem, which was six miles from Jerusalem. The church of that place, governed by the presbyter Jerome, is sixteen stages from Alexandria. For the bishop who holds Jerusalem has jurisdiction over it.

Jerome, whom I had come to know on my previous pilgrimage, had long before easily persuaded me that I ought to seek no one more suitable than him. For, apart from the merit of his faith and the endowment of his virtues, he was learned not only in Latin and Greek but also in Hebrew letters, so that no one would dare compare himself with him in any branch of knowledge.

I lived with him for six months. His continual struggle and perpetual battle against the wicked had stirred up the hatred of the depraved. Truly, I confess, he seemed to me to have painted the vices of many people in certain of his little works (Jerome, Letter 22, to Eustochium, *On the Preservation of Virginity*); indeed, since he omitted absolutely nothing that he did not criticize, tear apart, and expose, he attacked avarice in particular, and vanity no less.

He discussed pride at length and superstition in not a few passages. Moreover, how truthfully and forcefully he argued concerning the familiar relations of virgins and monks, and even of clerics! For this reason some are said not to love him.

Heretics hate him because he never ceases to attack them. Clerics hate him because he assails their vices and crimes. But good people plainly admire and love him.

Those who think him a heretic are insane. I may truly say that the man’s Catholic learning is sound doctrine: he is wholly devoted to reading and wholly devoted to books. He rests neither by day nor by night; he is always either reading something or writing.

If I had not firmly resolved in my mind—and, with God as my witness, promised beforehand—to visit the desert, I would not have wished to leave such a great man even for the briefest moment.

Having therefore entrusted and committed all my possessions and my entire household to him—the household that had followed me against my will and kept me entangled—I was in a manner relieved of a heavy burden and completely free. I departed for Alexandria.

After visiting the brothers there, I proceeded from that place to the upper Thebaid, that is, to the farthest regions of Egypt. It was said that a great many monks lived there in the vast, open solitude of the desert.

It would take too long to relate everything I saw. I shall touch on only a few things.

### CHAPTER IV  
### On Abbots’ Supplying Food to Brothers Established in the Desert with Their Permission

[Column 0818C]

Not far from the desert, adjoining the Nile, there are many monasteries (Severus Sulpicius, *Dialogue* 1, chapter 5). Usually one hundred men live in a single place. Their supreme rule is to live under the authority of an abbot, to do nothing according to their own judgment, and in all things to depend upon his will and power.

If any of them conceive in their minds the desire for greater virtue, so that they may go to the desert and lead a solitary life, they do not depart unless the abbot permits it. Their first virtue is obedience to another’s authority.

After they have gone to the desert by the arrangement of that abbot, bread and every other kind of food are supplied to them.

### CHAPTER V  
### On a Brother Being Fed in the Desert with Heavenly Bread

[Column 0818D]

It happened during the days when I had arrived there (Severus Sulpicius, *Dialogue* 1, chapter 5) that the abbot sent bread through two boys to a certain solitary who had recently withdrawn to the desert and had built his hut no more than six miles from that monastery.

The older of the boys was fifteen years old; the younger was twelve. As they were returning from there, an asp of extraordinary size came toward them. They were not at all frightened by its appearance. When it came before their feet, it lowered its blue neck as though enchanted by spells.

The younger boy seized it by hand, wrapped it in his cloak, and began to carry it. Then, entering the monastery like a victor, he set down the captive beast before the brothers, after untying his cloak, not without some swelling of pride.

But when the others praised the boys’ faith and courage, the abbot, following a more profound judgment lest their weaker age grow insolent, restrained both of them with rods. He severely rebuked them because they themselves had revealed what the Lord had done through them. The deed belonged not to their faith but to divine power.

They should learn instead to serve God in humility, not to glory in signs and miracles, because consciousness of weakness was better than the vanity of virtues.

When the solitary brother heard this—that the boys had been endangered by the serpent and, in addition, had deserved many blows after conquering it—he begged the abbot not to send him any bread or food from then on.

Eight days had now passed since the man of Christ had shut himself up within the danger of starvation. His limbs were parched by fasting, but his mind, intent upon heaven, could not fail. His body was wasting away from hunger; his faith remained firm.

Meanwhile, the abbot was warned by the Spirit to visit his disciple. Wishing, in pious concern, to learn by what means of life the faithful man was being sustained, since he had refused to have bread supplied by a human being, the abbot himself set out to seek him.

When the solitary saw the old man approaching from a distance, he went to meet him, gave thanks, and led him to his cell. When the two entered together, they saw a palm-fiber basket filled with hot bread, hanging from a post beside the door.

At first the hot bread was perceived by its smell; by its touch it was shown to have been taken from the hearth only a short while earlier. Yet it could not be recognized as Egyptian bread.

Both men were astonished and recognized the heavenly gift. The solitary declared that it had been provided through the abbot’s arrival, while the abbot attributed it to the solitary’s faith and virtue. Thus, with great rejoicing, they both broke the heavenly bread.

When the abbot later returned to the monastery and reported this to the brothers, such ardor had inflamed every soul that they hastened eagerly, vying with one another, to go to the desert and the sacred solitudes.

[Note: “I saw two old men.” What is related here about the two old men without names is related by Cassian, Book V of the *Institutes*, chapter 27, about Paesius and John as follows:

“When the old man John, who was in charge of a great coenobium and a multitude of brothers, had come to the old man Paesius, who lived in the vastest desert, and, as though from a very old companion, asked him what he had done throughout the forty years during which he had been separated from him in solitude and had been disturbed by none of the brothers, he replied: ‘The sun has never seen me eating.’ And he said to him: ‘Nor has it seen me angry.’”

The same account is found in Pelagius, Book IV, section 24.]

In this monastery I saw two old men who were said to have lived there for forty years, without ever having departed from the place (ibid., chapter 6). For I heard the following celebrated with unanimous testimony concerning their virtues, both from the abbot himself and from all the brothers: the sun had never seen one of them eating, and had never seen the other angry.

But since you have learned the virtue of one hermit, I shall tell you a few more things about several others.

### CHAPTER VI  
### On a Lioness Taking Food from an Old Man as from a Tame Animal

When I entered the first part of the desert (Severus Sulpicius, *Dialogue* 1, chapter 7), we traveled about twelve miles from the Nile—I had one of the brothers as a guide who knew the region—and came to a certain old monk living beneath the foot of a mountain.

There was a well there, which is exceedingly rare in those regions. He had one ox, whose entire labor consisted in drawing up water by means of a wheel-operated machine, for the well was said to be a thousand feet deep or more.

There was also a garden, rich in many vegetables. This was contrary to the nature of the desert, where everything is dry and scorched by the sun’s heat, and no seed ever produces even a small root.

But the holy man’s labor, shared with the animal, and his own industry accomplished this. For frequent irrigation with water gave such richness to the sand that we saw the vegetables in his little garden grow green and bear fruit in a marvelous way.

The ox lived on these vegetables together with its master, and the holy man gave us dinner from the same abundance.

After dinner, when evening was already approaching, he invited us to a palm tree whose fruit he sometimes used. It was nearly two miles away. These are the only trees found in the desert, though they are rare. Whether diligent people in ancient times cultivated them, or whether nature itself produces them, I do not know—unless God, knowing the future, prepared them for his servants because the desert would one day be inhabited by the saints.

For in most of the secluded places among them, since no other shoots grow, the inhabitants are nourished by the fruit of these trees.

When we reached the tree to which our host was leading us, we encountered a lion there. At the sight of it, my guide and I trembled. The holy man approached without hesitation, and we, although frightened, followed him.

At his command the wild beast withdrew calmly and stood still while he picked fruit from the branches that were within reach. When he offered a hand full of dates, the beast came forward and took them as freely as any domestic animal.

After it had eaten, it went away. As we watched this, still trembling, we could readily recognize how great was the power of faith in him and how great was the weakness in us.

### CHAPTER VII  
### On a She-Wolf Being Fed by an Old Man and Asking Forgiveness as Guilty of Theft

**540** We saw another remarkable and singular man living in a small hut that could accommodate no more than one person (Severus Sulpicius, *Dialogue* 1, chapter 8).

A she-wolf was accustomed to stand beside him while he ate. The beast was scarcely ever late, but came to him at the proper hour of his meal and waited for a long time outside the door until he offered her the bread left over from dinner. She would lick his hand and then depart, as though she had completed her duty and received consolation.

It happened by chance that the holy man, while escorting a brother who had come to visit him, was away for a longer time and did not return until nightfall. Meanwhile, the beast arrived at the customary time for dinner.

Finding the cell empty and sensing that her familiar patron was absent, she entered and carefully investigated where its inhabitant might be. By chance, a palm-fiber basket containing five loaves was hanging nearby. She took one of them and devoured it; then, having committed the crime, she departed.

When the hermit returned, he saw that the little basket had been opened and that the number of loaves was no longer complete. He understood that his household had suffered a loss and, near the threshold, recognized fragments of the loaf that had been taken.

There was no uncertainty, however, about the person who had committed the theft.

When, therefore, the beast did not come on the following days as usual—plainly, because she was conscious of her bold deed and pretended not to approach the man whom she had injured—the hermit found it painful to be deprived of the consolation of his fosterling.

At last, recalled by his prayer, she appeared on the seventh day, as usual, before the door of the man who was eating dinner. But so that you might easily see the shame of the penitent, she did not dare to come nearer. With her eyes cast down toward the ground in profound embarrassment, she plainly seemed to be asking for pardon.

The hermit took pity on her confusion, ordered her to come closer, and gently stroked her sorrowful head with his hand. Then he restored his guilty fosterling with a double portion of bread. Having thus obtained forgiveness, she set aside her grief and resumed her accustomed service.

Consider, I ask you, the power of Christ even in this matter: everything brute is intelligent to him, and everything savage is gentle. The she-wolf performs her duty; the beast recognizes the crime of theft; the she-wolf is confounded by conscious shame; when called, she comes; she offers her head; and she possesses a sense of the pardon granted to her, just as she bore the shame of her fault.

This virtue is yours, Christ; these miracles are yours, Christ. For the things your servants perform in your name are your wonders. And in this we groan: wild beasts perceive your majesty, while human beings do not fear it.

But lest this seem incredible to anyone, I shall relate still greater things. The faith of Christ is present, assuring me that I will invent nothing, but explain what I have learned with certainty.

### CHAPTER VIII  
### On Five Blind Lion Cubs Being Given Sight by an Anachoretic Monk
Most of them lived in the desert without any kind of shelter; they are called anchorites (Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* 1, chapter 9).
