They live on the roots of plants and never remain in any fixed place, so that they will not be visited by human beings. [Col. 0821C] Accordingly, two monks from Nitria, although from a very distant region, traveled toward a certain man who lived according to this custom and rule, because he had once been dear and familiar to them in the monastic life, and they had heard of his virtues. After searching for him long and diligently, they finally found him in the seventh month, dwelling at the far end of that desert adjoining Memphis. He was said to have inhabited those solitudes for twelve years.

Although he avoided the company of all human beings, when he recognized the brothers he did not shun them, but did not refuse to remain with his beloved friends for three days. On the fourth day, after advancing a short distance as he accompanied them on their departure, they saw a lioness of extraordinary size coming toward him. Although the beast had found the three men, she was not uncertain whom she was seeking: she threw herself at the anchorite’s feet [Col. 0821D] and then went on ahead of them. For she would proceed before them and then pause, looking back at them, so that it could easily be understood that she wanted the anchorite to follow wherever she led.

What more need be said? They reached the beast’s cave, where she was nurturing five already-grown cubs. Because they had emerged from their mother’s womb with their eyes closed, they were afflicted with perpetual blindness. The mother carried them out one by one from the rocky cavern and placed them before the anchorite’s feet. Then at last the holy man understood what the beast was asking. Having invoked the name of Christ, he touched the cubs’ closed eyes with his hand; immediately their blindness was driven away, and the beasts’ eyes opened to a light long denied them.

Thus, after visiting the anchorite whom they had desired to see, the brothers returned to the monastery with the fruitful reward of their labor [Col. 0822A], and recounted the faith of the holy man and the glory of Christ that they themselves had witnessed.

## CHAPTER IX. How a certain brother learned from the example of an ibex what herbs he ought to eat and what he ought to reject

There was also another anchorite in those regions who lived in the part called Syene (Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* 1, chapter 10). When he first withdrew to the desert, intending to live on herbs and the roots of plants—for the sand there sometimes produces plants of exceedingly sweet and remarkable flavor—he was ignorant of how to distinguish the edible growths and often gathered harmful ones. Nor was it easy to distinguish the potency of the roots by their taste, since all were equally sweet, although most concealed deadly poison within their more insidious nature.

When, therefore, an internal force tortured him as he ate, and all his vital organs were shaken by immense pains, while frequent vomiting, amid intolerable suffering, dissolved the very seat of life as his stomach was already failing, the hermit became utterly afraid of everything that might be eaten and no longer dared to touch or taste anything. He was passing the seventh day without food, his spirit already failing, when a wild animal called an *ibex* approached him. Standing near him, it threw down a bundle of herbs which had been gathered the day before and which the hermit had not dared to touch. The animal, however, rejected with its mouth those that were poisonous and selected those it knew to be harmless.

Thus the holy man, taught by its example what he ought to eat and what he ought to reject, both escaped the danger of starvation and avoided the poisons of the herbs.

## CHAPTER X. How a certain brother, established for fifty years on Mount Sinai, did not permit the approach of other brothers

[Col. 0822C]

But it would take too long to recount everything we have learned about those who inhabit the desert (Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* 1, chapter 11). I spent a full year and nearly seven months in the desert, although I often lived with that old man who had a well and an ox. I visited the two monasteries of the blessed Antony, which are still inhabited by his disciples. I also went to the place where the most blessed Paul, the first hermit, had sojourned. I saw the ridge of Mount Sinai, whose summit, almost touching heaven, cannot be approached.

Among the retreats of this mountain, an anchorite was said to live, but although I searched long and diligently, I could not see him. He had withdrawn from human society for nearly fifty years and used no clothing [Col. 0822D], but was covered with the hair of his body. Whenever religious men wished to visit him, he would flee human contact, rapidly seeking trackless places. He was said to have allowed only one man to see him, about five years earlier; I believe that man obtained this privilege through the power of his faith.

When that man asked him, during a long conversation, why he fled human beings so completely, he is said to have replied: “He who is frequented by human beings cannot be visited by angels.” Hence, with good reason, popular belief had spread the report that this holy man was visited by angels.

I, however, departed from Mount Sinai (ibid.) and returned to the river Nile, traveling along both its banks, which are thickly lined with monasteries. [Col. 0823A] I often saw—as I had said earlier—a hundred monks living in one place; indeed, it was reported that two or three thousand lived in the same villages. You should not suppose that the virtue of the monks who dwell there is less because of their numbers than that of those whom you have known to withdraw from human gatherings.

As I have already said, their chief and foremost virtue is obedience. For no newcomer is received by the abbot of a monastery unless he has first been tested and proved, prepared to refuse no command of the abbot, however arduous, difficult, or seemingly unreasonable.

## CHAPTER XI. Great miracles of incredible obedience

I shall relate to you two great miracles of incredible obedience (Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* 1, chapter 12). A certain brother, having renounced the affairs of the world, entered a monastery governed by a strict rule and asked to be received into the community. The abbot began to set many things before him: the labors of that discipline were severe, and his own commands were harsh—commands that scarcely anyone’s patience could fulfill. He advised him instead to seek another monastery where he could live under easier laws, and not to attempt what he could not accomplish.

The man, however, was not moved by these repeated warnings. Rather, he began to promise complete obedience, saying that if the abbot ordered him to enter fire, he would not refuse to do so. When the abbot had heard this declaration, he did not hesitate to test it, but ordered him to enter the furnace prepared for baking bread.

The man did not delay in obeying the command. At once, without hesitation, he entered the midst of the flames. But the flames were immediately overcome by such bold faith and yielded, as they once had to the Hebrew youths; the fire at once fled. The man who had entered and was expected to burn was astonished to find himself as though drenched with cool dew.

But what wonder is it if that fire did not touch your recruit, Christ, so that the abbot was not ashamed to issue a difficult command, nor the disciple regret having fulfilled his obedience? From this we should understand how much obedience deserves to obtain from God: the man who had arrived weak on the very day he was tested was found perfected through the agility of obedience. Rightly judged blessed, rightly judged glorious, he was tested through obedience and glorified through suffering.

## CHAPTER XII. Another miracle of obedience

Likewise, another brother came to the same monastery to be received by the same abbot 542 (Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* 1, chapter 13). When the first law of obedience was set before him and he promised perpetual endurance even in the most extreme circumstances, the abbot happened by chance to be carrying a dry storax branch in his hand. He planted it in the ground and assigned the newcomer this task: he was to water the little branch continually until—against nature—a dry branch should become green in the dry soil [Note: [Col. 0823D] A similar account appears in Pelagius, *Booklet* IV, no. 3].

Subjected to the command of this harsh rule, the brother carried water every day on his own shoulders. He had to fetch it from the river Nile, nearly two miles away. Even after a year had passed, the labor of the worker did not cease. There could be no hope that his work would produce any result, yet the virtue of obedience endured in the labor.

The following year likewise mocked the brother’s labor with its futility. Finally, in the third year, as the succession of seasons ran its course, while the water-carrier did not cease either by night or by day, the branch blossomed. I myself saw from that little branch a young tree which still remains within the monastery courtyard, green with spreading branches as a testimony. It demonstrates both what obedience deserved and what faith was capable of accomplishing.

## CHAPTER XIII. He who expelled demons was himself possessed by a demon, but was restored with a salutary outcome

One of the holy Fathers, endowed with extraordinary power to drive demons from possessed bodies, performed many signs (Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* 1, [Col. 0824B] chapter 14). He cured possessed bodies not only when present and not merely by his word, but sometimes even when absent, by sending pieces of the fringe of his hair shirt or letters.

Accordingly, people flocked to him in a remarkable manner, coming from many regions. I say nothing of lesser persons: prefects, counts, and judges of various authorities often lay before his doors. He completely abstained from every drink and sustained himself as food on only seven dried figs.

Meanwhile, just as honor arose for the holy man from his virtue, vanity began to creep in through his honor. When he first became aware that this evil was spreading within him, he tried for a long time and with great effort to examine it, but he could not entirely drive it away. Everywhere the demons acknowledged his name. He was unable to exclude the crowds that streamed to him. Meanwhile, the hidden poison crept through his heart, and he whose command drove demons from the bodies of others could not cleanse himself of the secret thoughts of vanity.

He therefore turned to the Lord with all his prayers and asked that, by permitting the devil to exercise power over him, God would make him like those whom he himself had healed. What more need be said? That powerful man, known throughout the East for signs and miracles, that man to whose threshold crowds had once flocked, was seized by a demon. Held in chains, he endured everything that is usually inflicted upon one possessed. Finally, in the fifth month, he was cleansed not only of the demon but also—and this was more useful and desirable for him—of vanity.

## CHAPTER XIV. How an anchorite was punished when he returned to the world

[Col. 0824D]

A certain young man, exceedingly rich in possessions and illustrious by birth, who had a wife and a small son, was serving as a military tribune in Egypt. When, during several expeditions against the Blemmyes [Perhaps *Blemyes*], he had come near some part of the desert and had seen several shelters of the saints, he received from the blessed hermit John a word of salvation (Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* 1, chapter 15).

He did not delay to despise his useless military service and its empty honor. Instead, he entered the desert resolutely and within a short time shone forth as perfect in every kind of virtue [Note: [Col. 0824D] Ruffinus, Book II, chapter 1, speaks of him]. Powerful in fasting, conspicuous for humility, and firm in faith, he had easily equaled the ancient monks in zeal for virtue.

Meanwhile, a thought sent by the devil entered his mind: it would be better for him to return to his homeland and save his only son, his entire household, and his wife. Surely this would also be more pleasing to God than to save himself alone from the world while neglecting the salvation of his family.

Overcome, therefore, by this appearance of false righteousness, after four years the hermit abandoned his cell and his way of life. When he reached the nearest monastery, inhabited by many brothers, he confessed the reason for his departure and sought their advice. Although everyone opposed him, especially the abbot of the place, the decision fixed in his ill-considered mind could not be dislodged.

Thus, breaking away in unhappy obstinacy, he departed from the brothers amid universal grief. He had scarcely withdrawn from their sight when he was immediately filled with a demon. Vomiting bloody foam from his mouth, he tore himself with his own teeth. Then he was carried back to the same monastery on the shoulders of the brothers. Since the unclean spirit could not be restrained there, necessity compelled them to bind him with iron chains; his feet and hands were shackled. It was a punishment well deserved by a deserter.

After two years, he was freed from the unclean spirit through the prayers of the saints. He immediately returned to the desert from which he had departed. He himself was corrected, and he became an example to others, lest anyone be compelled by either the shadow of false righteousness or uncertain instability to abandon with useless fickleness what he had once begun.

## CHAPTER XV. The dress or clothing of the Egyptian monks

534 There are also certain features of the Egyptians’ very clothing that correspond not merely to the care of the body but also to the formation of character (Cassian, *Institutes* I, chapter 4). [Col. 0825C] They constantly wear very small hoods, by day and by night, so that they may continually be reminded, even by imitating this covering, to preserve the innocence and simplicity of little children.

They also wear linen *colobia* (ibid., chapter 5), which scarcely reach as far as the elbows; their arms otherwise remain bare, so that the cutting off of the sleeves may suggest that they have cut off their actions and works belonging to this world.

After this, they cover their necks and shoulders alike with a narrow cloak, humble in its covering and cheap in its material, which is called a *maforte* both in our language and in theirs (ibid., chapter 7).

Their final item of clothing is a goatskin, called a *melotes* (ibid., chapter 8). This goatskin garment signifies that, with their members mortified to every wantonness of carnal passions, they ought to stand firm in the utmost gravity of virtue.

They also refuse sandals as though they were forbidden by the Gospel command (Matthew and Luke, chapter 10). But when bodily weakness, the morning cold of winter, or the heat of midday requires it, they protect their feet. Although they lawfully use these shoes, since they are permitted by the Lord’s command (Acts, chapter 12; Mark, chapter 6), they nevertheless do not allow them to remain attached to their feet when they approach to celebrate or receive the sacred mysteries. They believe that the command given to Moses and to Joshua son of Nave must also be observed literally: “Loosen the strap of your sandal, for the place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exodus, chapter 3; Joshua son of Nun, chapter 5).

## CHAPTER XVI. The prescribed manner of prayer and complete renunciation of the world

Throughout Egypt and the Thebaid, wherever monasteries are found, they maintain a prescribed manner of prayer at evening assemblies and during nightly vigils (Cassian, *Institutes* II, chapter 3). No one there is permitted to take part in the congregation of the brothers unless he has first been made estranged from all his possessions. Whoever has entered the community is compelled to obey everyone, so that he recognizes that, in accordance with the Lord’s teaching, he must return to his former childhood. He presumes nothing for himself on account of his age or the number of his years, considering that the time he foolishly wasted in the world has been lost; but because of the inexperience proper to a beginner and the novelty of his service—which he recognizes that he bears in the army of Christ—he is compelled to submit even to those younger than himself.

Throughout Egypt, therefore, as we have said, a number of twelve psalms is observed at both evening and nighttime celebrations (ibid., chapter 4), with this proviso: after the psalms, two readings follow, one from the Old Testament and the other from the New. This practice, established in ancient times, has remained inviolate through so many centuries because the elders affirm that it was not instituted by human invention but was delivered from heaven to the ancient Fathers through angelic ministry.

## CHAPTER XVII. How an angel was seen to sing twelve psalms in an assembly of elders

In the beginnings of the faith, when there were few but exceptionally approved men who were counted by the name of monks, and who had already received their rule of life from the successors of the apostles, they withdrew to more secluded places outside the cities and lived under such strict abstinence that everyone marveled at the severity of their way of life (Cassian, *Institutes* II, chapter 5).

These venerable Fathers, carefully providing for posterity, gathered together in one place to deliberate what manner of daily worship should be prescribed throughout the whole body of the brotherhood. They wished to transmit to their successors an inheritance of piety and peace free from every dispute about arrangements. They feared that some disagreement or variation in the daily celebrations among men devoted to the same worship might arise and eventually produce a harmful seed of error.

Each, according to his own fervor, proposed a different number of psalms. Some proposed fifty, others sixty; some, not even content with that number, thought it ought to be exceeded. A pious rivalry arose among them for the glory of religion, and the time of the evening celebration was being consumed by this most sacred dispute.

Suddenly, one of them rose in their midst to sing psalms to the Lord. While all looked on in amazement, he sang eleven psalms, divided by interjected prayers and rendered in successive verses with equal recitation. He completed the twelfth with the response of “Alleluia,” and then suddenly disappeared from the eyes of all, bringing an end both to the dispute and to the ceremonies.

From this the holy elders who were present understood that, through angelic instruction and not without the Lord’s providence, a general rule had been established for the gatherings of the brothers. They decreed that this number should be observed both at evening celebrations and during nighttime vigils (ibid., chapter 6).

544 They begin and conclude the prayers mentioned above in this manner (Cassian, *Institutes* II, chapter 7). When a psalm has been completed and is followed by the *Gloria*, they do not immediately fall to their knees. Before bending their knees, they pray for a short while; and while standing [Col. 0827B] in supplication, they spend the greater part of the hours. After this, they briefly prostrate themselves on the ground, as though praying only for the divine mercy, and then rise again with the utmost speed. Once more, with hands extended, they pray standing in the same manner as before, lingering more intently over their prayers.

They themselves say that a monk who remains prostrate on the ground for too long, as though laboring more earnestly in prayer, is attacked not only by various thoughts but also more heavily by sleep. Experience has taught us that many lie prostrate on the ground not so much for the sake of prayer as for the sake of refreshment, and therefore appear to prolong their prayer for a longer time.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How much discernment and care must be observed in prayer

When they assemble to celebrate the aforesaid solemnities, which they call *synaxes* (Cassian, *Institutes* II, chapter 10), everyone maintains such silence that, although so large a multitude of brothers gathers together, no voice is heard except that of the one singing. During this prayer there is no spitting, no throat-clearing, no drowsy yawn, and no voice is heard apart from that of the priest who concludes the prayer.

When the man who is to gather up the prayer rises from the ground, no one dares to bend his knee before he bows down, nor to linger after he has risen from the ground. They conclude their prayers quickly for this reason: if they lingered longer, an excess of spittle or phlegm might interrupt the outpouring of prayer. Therefore, while it is still fervent, prayer must be snatched quickly from the enemy’s throat, as it were. Since that enemy is always hostile to us, he is especially hostile when he sees us offering prayers to the Lord against him.

For this reason, they consider it more useful for prayers to be brief but very frequent (ibid., chapter 11). They say that it is better to sing ten verses of a psalm with contrition of heart and reasonable attention than to pour out ten whole psalms with a distracted mind.

## CHAPTER XIX. That at the response “Alleluia” no psalm is sung except one bearing that title

They carefully observe this rule among themselves (Cassian, *Institutes* II, chapter 11): at the response “Alleluia,” no psalm is sung except one whose title is marked with the inscription “Alleluia.”

They also permit no period of time to pass free from the exercise of work (ibid., chapter 12). They strive to carry out with complete diligence by their hands everything that the light of day makes possible; but they also search with attentive minds for kinds of work that even the densest darkness of night cannot prevent. They believe that they will seek a more exalted purity of spiritual contemplation through the mind’s gaze the longer they remain devoted to work and labor.

We must also know this (ibid., chapter 18): from the evening of the Sabbath, which gives light to the Lord’s Day, until the following evening, they do not bend their knees [Col. 0828B], nor do they do so throughout all fifty days.

## CHAPTER XX. Manual labor, and why psalms are sung at the third, sixth, and ninth hours

They practice manual labor continually and privately in their cells (Cassian, *Institutes* III, chapter 2), so that, while constantly meditating throughout the whole day on the psalms and on the other Scriptures, they spend the entire day in the tasks that we celebrate at fixed times.

They conclude the third, sixth, and ninth hours each day with three psalms (ibid., chapter 3). For we know that the prophet Daniel also poured out prayers to the Lord every day at these three times, with the windows of his upper room open (Daniel, chapter 6). These times have not without reason been assigned more particularly to religious observances, since in them the fulfillment of the promises and the culmination of our salvation were accomplished.

At the third hour, the Holy Spirit, once promised through the prophets, descended upon the apostles and gave them knowledge of all languages (Acts, chapter 2). At the sixth hour, our Lord Jesus Christ, the spotless sacrifice, was offered to the Father. Ascending the cross for the salvation of the whole world, he destroyed the sins of the human race (Colossians, chapter 2).

At that same hour, while Peter was in an ecstasy of mind, the calling of the Gentiles and the purification of every kind of living creature contained in the vessel brought down from heaven were revealed to him by a heavenly voice, which said: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat” (Acts, chapter 10). It is clearly understood that the vessel, lowered from heaven by its four beginnings, signifies nothing other than the Gospel.

At the ninth hour, Christ, penetrating the regions below, extinguished the impenetrable darkness of Tartarus with the radiance of his splendor (Matthew, chapter 27). Breaking its bronze gates and crushing its iron bars, he carried with him into the heavens the captivity of the saints that had been held shut away. Removing the fiery sword, he restored the ancient inhabitant to paradise.

At that same hour, the centurion Cornelius, persisting in prayer, learned from an angel who spoke to him that his prayers and almsgiving had been remembered before God (Acts, chapter 10). These testimonies clearly prove that, with good reason, these hours were consecrated to religious observances by the holy and apostolic men, and that we too ought similarly to observe them. Unless we are compelled, as by a law, to discharge these duties of piety at least at the appointed times, we shall spend the entire day entangled in forgetfulness, idleness, or empty occupations, without interruption for prayer.

## CHAPTER XXI. With how much discernment and caution those who renounce the world are received into the monastery

When someone wishing to renounce the affairs of the world asks to be received into a monastery, he is not admitted before he has demonstrated the evidence of his perseverance, as well as his humility and patience, by keeping watch at the monastery doors for ten days or more (Cassian, *Institutes* IV, chapter 3).

He must fall on his knees before all the brothers who pass by, be rejected and despised by everyone as though he desired to enter the monastery not for the sake of religion but out of necessity, and, after suffering many insults, provide proof of his constancy. His endurance of disgrace must show what he will be like in temptations.

Afterward, when he has been received, he is examined with the utmost care to ensure that not even the contagion of a single coin remains attached to him from his former possessions. They know that he cannot remain long under the discipline of the monastery, nor obtain humility or obedience, if even a small amount of money is hidden in his possession.

For this reason, once received, each man is stripped of all his former property so completely that he is not even permitted to keep the garment he is wearing (ibid., chapter 5). He is brought into the middle of the assembly of the brothers, stripped of his own clothing, and dressed by the hands of the abbot in the monastery’s clothing. Thus he knows not only that he has been stripped of all his former possessions, but also that, having laid aside all worldly pride, he has descended to the poverty and want of Christ.

The garments he had put off (ibid., chapter 6) are kept in the monastery until they clearly recognize the progress he has made and the virtue of his conduct and endurance. If they see that he can persevere there, they distribute those garments to the needy. But if they detect him in any complaint or disobedience, they strip him of the monastery clothing with which he had been dressed, put back on him the old clothing that had been preserved, and expel him from the community.

When someone has been received, has been approved through this perseverance of which we have spoken, and has exchanged his own clothing for the monastic habit (ibid., chapter 7), he is not immediately permitted to mingle with the congregation of the brothers. Instead, he is assigned to an elder who lives separately, not far from the entrance of the monastery, and is charged with the care of travelers and newcomers, providing them with every attention of welcome and hospitality.

After serving there with him for a full year and demonstrating his service to travelers without any complaint, having been instructed through this first training in humility, he is afterward admitted to the congregation of the brothers.

[Col. 0830A] Finally, he is first taught to conquer his own desires, and they take care to command him frequently to do what they perceive to be contrary to his inclination (ibid., chapter 8). For they declare that a monk can never prevail over anger, sadness, or the spirit of fornication unless he has first learned through obedience to mortify his own desires. Nor can he retain true humility of heart, firm harmony with the brothers, or remain long in the monastery if he has not learned to overcome his own desires.

## CHAPTER XXII. That no one in the monastery should presume to do anything without the order of the elders

After this, the rule of obedience is maintained among them with such care (Cassian, *Institutes* IV, chapter 10) that the younger brothers do not presume to go even to attend to their natural needs without the knowledge or permission of their superior. They hasten to fulfill every command given to them by the abbot as though it had been issued from heaven by God. Thus, when things impossible for them are sometimes commanded, they receive them with such faith and devotion that they strive with all their strength to carry them out and complete them.

Accordingly, while they sit within their cells and devote themselves equally to work and meditation (ibid., chapter 12), whenever they hear some signal inviting them to prayer or to another task, each one bursts eagerly from his cell. Thus the man who is practicing the Scriptures, if he is found to have begun a letter, does not dare to finish it. At the very point when the sound of the ringing signal reaches his ears, he springs up with the utmost speed, not allowing himself even as much delay as would be needed to complete the form of the letter he had begun.

Among their other practices, we have recognized this as a great virtue (Cassian, Book IV, chapter 13): no one is permitted to possess a basket, a private satchel, or anything else as his own, nor does anyone dare even to say that something is his.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The three lentils carelessly left behind

During the week of a certain brother who served in the kitchen (Cassian, *Institutes* IV, chapter 20), the monastery superior happened to see three lentils lying on the ground. They had slipped from the brother’s hands as he hurried to prepare them for cooking, while the lentils were being washed in water. He immediately consulted the abbot about the matter.

The brother was then judged to be a pilferer and negligent custodian of sacred property and was suspended from prayer. The guilt of his negligence was not remitted to him until he had expiated it through public penance.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. The two monks during whose week the wood ran out

I know of other brothers (Cassian, *Institutes* IV, chapter 21) whose week coincided with such a shortage of wood that there was absolutely no means of preparing the customary food for the brothers. Until purchased wood could be brought, the abbot had ordered them to be content with *xerophagia*—dry food. This had been approved by everyone, and no one could hope for any cooked dish.

Yet those two brothers, as though they would be deprived of the fruit and reward of their labor and service if they did not prepare food for the brothers according to custom during their assigned week, imposed upon themselves so much voluntary labor and care that, in those dry and barren regions—where wood can be found only if it is cut from fruit-bearing trees, since no wild thickets grow in those places—they nevertheless managed to obtain it.

They ran across the extended wastes and went toward the desert that stretches in the direction of the Dead Sea. Gathering thin stalks and little thorns that the wind had scattered here and there, they prepared the entire customary meal through their voluntary service. They offered these gifts to the brothers with such faith that, although they could honorably have excused themselves either on account of the shortage of wood or by appealing to the abbot’s command, they did not wish to misuse the permission for their own advantage and reward.

## CHAPTER XXV. The blessed John who lived near the town of Lycus

I think it necessary for this work to commemorate the blessed John (Cassian, *Institutes* IV, chapter 23; Rufinus, Book II, chapter 1), who lived near Lycus, a town of the Thebaid, and who was exalted to the grace of prophecy because of the virtue of his obedience.

He became so renowned throughout the whole world that, through his own merit, he was made illustrious even among the kings of this world. For although he lived, as I have said, in the remotest parts of the Thebaid, the emperor Theodosius did not presume to advance against powerful tyrants in war before he had been encouraged by John’s prophetic utterances and responses. Trusting in these as though they had been delivered to him from heaven, he always carried away trophies from wars and enemies that had seemed hopeless.

## CHAPTER XXVI. The obedience of that same John

This blessed John served a certain elder from his adolescence until he reached full and mature manhood (Cassian, *Institutes* IV, chapter 24). As long as the elder remained in the conduct of this life, John clung to him with such humility that his obedience caused even the old man the greatest astonishment.

The elder wished to investigate more clearly whether this virtue arose from genuine faith and profound simplicity of heart. He therefore frequently assigned him many tasks, including superfluous and impossible ones. I shall relate a few of them.

The elder took from his woodpile a branch that had once been cut and prepared for use as firewood. After planting it in the ground before the young man, he ordered him to bring water and water it twice every day.

The young man received the command with his customary reverence, without considering its impossibility, and fulfilled it day after day. Carrying water continually for two miles, he never ceased to water the wood. Throughout the entire year, neither bodily weakness nor any necessary occupation was able to prevent him from observing this command.

The old man secretly examined his diligence day after day. When he saw that the young man was observing his command with a simple affection of heart, as though it had been given by God, he at last took pity on the perseverance of his long labor. Approaching the dry branch, he said: “Son John, has this tree put down roots or not?”

When John said that he did not know, the elder, as though testing whether it was now held by its own roots, pulled up the branch before him. Throwing it some distance away, he ordered his disciple to stop watering it from then on.

## CHAPTER XXVII. The enormous stone that the same John brought by obedience

547 When the fame of his obedience had already spread throughout all the monasteries (Cassian, *Institutes* IV, [Col. 0832B] chapter 25), certain brothers came to the elder for the sake of testing—or rather, edifying—the young man.

Then the elder called his disciple and said to him: “Run, John, and roll that stone here as quickly as possible.”

Immediately, John attempted to roll the enormous stone, applying first his neck and then his whole chest to it. He exerted such effort and force that the sweat from his limbs not only soaked his entire garment but also moistened the stone itself beneath his neck.

He showed little understanding of the impossibility of the command or the task. Out of reverence for the elder and the sincere simplicity of his service, he believed with complete faith that the elder could command nothing useless or unreasonable.

It is enough to have said this much of the few among the many deeds of the abbot John. I shall now relate the memorable deed of the abbot Mutius.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The remarkable patience of Abbot Mutius

[Col. 0832C]

This Abbot Mutius, wishing to renounce this world, sought a monastery (Cassian, Book 4 of the *Institutes*, chapter 27). He kept watch for so long before the monastery gate with his little son, about eight years old, until he was deemed worthy of being received. When at last they had both been admitted, they were immediately separated from one another, lest, through the constant sight of the child, the father be reminded of the wealth he had abandoned; and just as he knew that he was no longer rich, so also he would cease to know himself as a father. To test more fully whether he would act more strongly under the influence of natural affection or obedience, the boy was neglected and clothed in rags rather than garments. He was also exposed to the blows and slaps of various people, which the father, often [Col. 0832D] before his own eyes, saw inflicted even gratuitously upon the innocent child, so that he never saw the boy’s cheeks without their being stained by the dirty traces of tears. Though the child was treated in this way before his eyes day after day, Mutius, for the love of Christ and by the power of obedience, remained always rigid and unmoved. For he no longer regarded as his own the son whom he had offered together with himself to Christ, nor did he care about the injuries presently inflicted upon him. Rather, he rejoiced that the boy could in no way soften the firmness of his mind or his unshakable rigor.

When the father of the monastery saw this, and wished to test his constancy still further, one day, when he had seen the child crying, he pretended to be angry and ordered the boy’s father to take him and throw him [Col. 0833A] into the water. Then Mutius, as though this command had been given to him by the Lord, immediately seized his son and, running swiftly, brought him to the bank of the river in order to throw him in. Indeed, this would have been carried out in action through the fury of his faith and obedience, had not the abbot arranged for brothers to keep careful watch over the riverbank in order to rescue the child. As soon as the child had, so to speak, been thrown into the riverbed, they snatched him up and, with the deepest devotion having fulfilled the father’s command, prevented the deed from being completed.

His faith, obedience, and devotion were so pleasing to God (ibid., chapter 28) that they were immediately confirmed by divine testimony. For it was at once revealed to the elder that, through this obedience, Mutius had fulfilled the deed of the patriarch Abraham. When, after a short time had passed, that same [Col. 0833B] abbot departed from this world, he commended this Father Mutius to all the brothers for his obedience and left him to the monastery as his successor and abbot.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Of a monk, the son of a certain count, who had been ordered to carry baskets through the streets

We knew a certain brother who, according to the order of this world, was of the highest rank, for he was born of a count and a very wealthy father (Cassian, Book 4 of the *Institutes*, chapter 29). When he had left his parents and hastened to the monastery, an elder immediately ordered him, in order to test his humility, to place ten large baskets upon his shoulders and carry them through the streets for sale. A condition was added so that he might be detained longer in this service [Col. 0833C]: if someone happened to wish to buy them all together, he was not to yield them, but was to sell them individually to those who asked for them. He fulfilled this with complete devotion; trampling down all shame for his desire for Christ, he placed the baskets upon his shoulders, carried them through the streets, sold them at the fixed price, and brought the money back to the monastery.

## CHAPTER XXX. Of Abbot Pinuphius, who, fleeing for the sake of humility, withdrew far from the monastery

We also saw Abbot Pinuphius (Cassian, Book 4 of the *Institutes*, chapter 30). He was a priest of a great monastery in Egypt, not far from the city of Panephysis, and, on account of his life, age, and priesthood, was honored by everyone. Seeing that, because of this very honor [Col. 0833D], he could not maintain humility, he secretly fled from the monastery and withdrew alone to the remotest parts of the Thebaid. There, laying aside the clothing of the monks [p. 548], he put on secular dress and sought the monastery of the Tabennesiots, which he knew to be stricter than all other monasteries and in which, because of the distance of the region, he believed he would remain unknown.

There he persisted for a very long time before the gate, falling at the knees of all the brothers and pleading with the greatest urgency to be received. After being tested with much contempt, he was finally admitted. At once, as an old man fit for no other task, he was assigned the care and cultivation of the garden. He performed this work under a younger brother who had been entrusted with him and to whom he was subject. He fulfilled not only the duties [Col. 0834A] connected with tending the garden but also, every day with complete diligence, all the tasks that were harsh or degrading for the other brothers. Often rising even at night, he worked so secretly and without a witness that no one could discover who had done the work.

While he was hiding there for three years and was being sought throughout Egypt by the brothers scattered everywhere, he was at last seen by a certain brother who had come from the regions of Egypt. Because of his humble appearance and the lowly work he was performing, he could scarcely be recognized. Bent over with a hoe, he was preparing the earth for vegetables; then, carrying manure on his shoulders, he was placing it around their roots. The brother who saw this was held for a long time in profound hesitation as he tried to recognize him. At last he came nearer and carefully examined not only his face [Col. 0834B] but also the sound of his voice; then he threw himself at his feet at close range.

The brothers began to be astonished and asked why he had done this to a man who, in their view, was regarded as the lowest, as though he had only recently come out of the world. When that brother had explained to them the whole story and identified the abbot, they were struck with even greater amazement, since he had also been held in high esteem among them. They then asked his forgiveness for their ignorance, because they had assigned him for so long to the company of the younger and least important brothers. But he wept and mourned greatly because, through the envy of the devil, he had been exposed and had not been permitted to remain longer in such humility and abasement. The brothers then brought him back unwilling and weeping to his own monastery, guarding him with the greatest care so that he would not similarly [Col. 0834C] slip away and flee again.

After he had remained there for a short time (Cassian, Book 4 of the *Institutes*, chapter 31), inflamed once more by the same desire for humility, he waited for the silence of night and fled in such a way that he now sought not a neighboring province but unknown regions. For he boarded a ship and arranged to travel to the parts of Palestine, believing that he would hide more safely if he carried himself to places where even his name had never been heard.

When he arrived there, he immediately sought our monastery, which was not far from the cave in which our Lord deigned to be born of the Virgin. Abbot Pinuphius hid in that monastery for a short time, but, in accordance with the Lord’s saying, like a city set upon a mountain, he could not remain hidden [Col. 0834D] for long (Matthew 5). For some brothers who had come from Egypt to the holy places for the sake of prayer recognized him and, with much pleading and especially against his will, brought him back once more to his own monastery.

## CHAPTER XXXI. An excellent exhortation to a novice monk

Because of the familiar friendship that we had enjoyed with this elder in our monastery, we later sought him out in Egypt. While we were staying there, it happened that he received a certain brother into his monastery (Cassian, Book 4 of the *Institutes*, chapter 32). In our presence he gave him an extraordinary exhortation, which I have wished to insert into this little work. He [Col. 0835A] therefore said to him:

“You know, my son, how many days you kept watch before the gate before you were received today. You must first understand the reason for this difficulty. Once you have understood it, it can greatly benefit you in the life that you desire to enter, if you approach the service of Christ as you ought.

“For just as immense glory is promised in the future to those who serve God faithfully and adhere to him according to the institutions of this rule (ibid., chapter 33), so the gravest punishments are prepared for those who have carried it out lukewarmly and negligently, and who have failed to offer God the fitting fruits of holiness in accordance with what they professed or what people believe them to be. For it is better not to vow than to vow and not fulfill one’s vow (Ecclesiastes 5); and cursed is the one who [Col. 0835B] performs the work of the Lord negligently (Jeremiah 48). Therefore we rejected you for so long, not because we do not desire with all our heart to embrace your salvation and that of everyone else, but lest, if you were rashly received, we should make both ourselves guilty before God of levity and you liable to a harsher punishment—if, having been readily accepted for the present and not understanding the burden of this profession, you should afterward either abandon it or become lukewarm.

“Know, therefore, that today you have died to this world and its practices (Cassian, Book 4 of the *Institutes*, chapter 34), and that, according to the Apostle, you have been crucified to this world and this world to you (Galatians 6). But perhaps you will say: ‘How can someone who is alive be crucified?’ Listen briefly to the explanation.

“Our cross is the fear of the Lord (Cassian, Book 4 of the *Institutes*, chapter 35) [Col. 0835C] [p. 549]. For just as someone who has been crucified no longer has the power to move or turn his limbs anywhere according to the impulse of his mind, so we too must apply our wills and desires not according to what presently pleases us, but according to the command of the Lord by which he has bound us. And just as the one who is fastened to the cross no longer looks upon present things, nor thinks about his affections, nor is moved by any desire of possessing anything, and, while still breathing in the body, believes himself dead to all the elements, so we too must be crucified by the fear of the Lord to all carnal vices and must always keep the eyes of our mind fixed upon the place where we ought to hope that we shall depart at every moment.

[Col. 0835D] “We must therefore take care never to presume to take up any of the things that we cast away when we renounced the world (Cassian, Book 4 of the *Institutes*, chapter 36). For it is not the one who begins these things but the one who perseveres in them to the end who will be saved (Matthew 10; 24).

“For the crafty serpent always watches our heel (Cassian, Book 4 of the *Institutes*, chapter 37); that is, he lies in wait for our departure and continually tries to trip us until the end of life. Therefore it will profit nothing to have begun well if the work is not brought to a good completion (Genesis 3).

“Therefore, according to the saying of Scripture, having entered to serve the Lord (Cassian, Book 4 of the *Institutes*, chapter 38), stand in the fear of the Lord and prepare your [Col. 0836A] soul not for rest or pleasures but for temptations and hardships (Ecclesiasticus 2); for through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14). The gate is narrow and the way is constricted that leads to life, and few are those who find it (Matthew 7).

“The beginning of our salvation is therefore the fear of the Lord (Cassian, Book 4 of the *Institutes*, chapter 39). Through it the beginning of conversion and the protection of virtue are acquired. When it has penetrated the human mind, it produces contempt for all things and engenders horror of the world. Through contempt and deprivation of all possessions, true humility is acquired.

“Humility is demonstrated by these signs: first, if the monk keeps all his own desires mortified within himself; second, if he does not conceal his actions and thoughts [Col. 0836B] from his elder; third, if he entrusts everything not to his own judgment but to the elder’s decision; fourth, if in all commands he preserves the gentleness of obedience and the steadfastness of patience; fifth, if he inflicts injury upon no one and patiently endures injuries inflicted upon himself; sixth, if he does nothing beyond the examples of the rule; seventh, if, in everything commanded of him, he judges himself to be a bad and unworthy laborer; eighth, if he declares himself inferior to everyone; ninth, if he restrains his tongue and is not loud in speech; tenth, if he is not quick and ready to laugh. By such signs true humility is recognized.

“You must also necessarily observe these things within the community (Cassian, Book 4 of the *Institutes*, chapter 41): according to the Psalmist’s saying, be like one who is [Col. 0836C] deaf and does not hear, and like one who is mute and does not open his mouth (Psalm 37), discerning and judging nothing among the things that have been commanded to you.

“Therefore you must not expect your patience to depend upon the virtue of others (ibid., chapter 42)—that is, suppose that you possess it only when no one has provoked you.

“The beginning of our salvation, as has already been said, is the fear of the Lord (ibid., chapter 43). From the fear of the Lord arises salutary compunction; from compunction of heart proceeds contempt for all possessions and nakedness; from nakedness proceeds humility; from humility is generated the mortification of the will; through the mortification of the will all vices are uprooted; when the vices have been expelled, the virtues bear fruit and grow; through the flourishing of the virtues purity of heart is acquired; and through purity [Col. 0836D] of heart the perfection of apostolic charity is possessed.”

## CHAPTER XXXII. Of the monk who compelled travelers to eat before the appointed hour

When we had traveled from the regions of Syria to the province of Egypt (Cassian, Book 5 of the *Institutes*, chapter 24), a highly esteemed elder monk received us graciously and prepared a meal for us before the appointed hour of fasting had ended. When we asked why he was compelling us to eat before the canonical hour of the meal, he replied:

“Fasting, brothers, is always with me; but since I am about to send you away, I shall not be able to keep you continually with me. Therefore, receiving Christ in you, I ought to refresh [Col. 0837A] him; and after I have sent you on your way, I shall be able to make up the strictness of the fast in myself. The children of the bridegroom cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them; but when he has departed, then they may fast lawfully” (Luke 5; Matthew 9).

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Of the monk who was never accustomed to eat alone

We also saw another monk living in the desert (Cassian, Book 5 of the *Institutes*, chapter 26), who had never been accustomed to take food alone. Even if no brother came to his cell for five whole days, he continually postponed his meal and remained fasting until, on Saturday or Sunday, going out [p. 550] for the sake of assembling with the community at church, he found [Col. 0837B] some traveler. He then brought the traveler back to his cell and took food together with him.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Of the old monk Machete

We also saw another old monk named Machete (Cassian, Book 5 of the *Institutes*, chapter 29), a solitary, to whom the Lord had granted this favor: whenever a spiritual discussion was held in the gathering of the brothers throughout the entire night and day, he was never overcome by sleep; but if someone attempted to introduce a word of detraction or idle talk, he immediately fell asleep.

When letters from his father, mother, friends, and many others in the province of Pontus were once sent to this elder (ibid., chapter 32), he received a large bundle of letters, turned the matter over in his mind [Col. 0837C] for a long time, and said:

“How many thoughts will reading these letters cause me—thoughts that will drive me either to empty joy or to fruitless sadness? For how many days will the memory of those who wrote them recall me from the contemplation to which I have devoted my heart?”

As he turned these things over in his heart, he decided not only not to open any letter but not even to unseal the bundle itself, lest, by reviewing the names of those who had written or recalling their faces, he should cease from the concentration of his spirit. Thus, just as he had received it bound, he handed it over to the fire to be burned, saying: “Go, thoughts of my homeland; burn together, and do not try to recall me any longer to the things from which I fled.”

## CHAPTER XXXV. Of Abbot Theodore

[Col. 0837D] We also saw another Abbot Theodore (Cassian, Book 5 of the *Institutes*, chapter 33), endowed with the highest holiness and knowledge, not only in the active life but also in knowledge of the Scriptures—a knowledge given to him not so much by the study of reading as by purity of heart alone. When he was seeking the explanation of an exceedingly obscure question, he persisted tirelessly in prayer for seven days and nights, until the Lord revealed to him the solution of the question he had posed.

This same blessed Theodore came unexpectedly to my cell in the dead of night. Secretly and with fatherly concern he investigated what I, still a new hermit, was doing alone [Col. 0838A]. When I, after completing the evening service, had begun to refresh my weary body and he had found me lying on a mat, he drew deep sighs from his heart and, calling me by name, said:

“How many, O John [Note: [Col. 0837] The author calls himself John. He is John Cassian.], speak about God and embrace him within themselves, while you are deprived of this light, released into idle sleep?”

Then, waking me, he thereafter compelled me to keep watch for my salvation.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Of the anchorites living in the vastest desert

When we had come from the monasteries of Palestine to the Egyptian town called Diolcos, and had seen there a very large multitude bound by the discipline of the cenobium (Cassian, Book 5 of the *Institutes*, chapter 36) [Col. 0838B], we hastened, urged on by the praises of everyone, to see with our keenest understanding another order, which is considered higher: that of the anchorites.

These men, first carefully instructed in monasteries under the strictness of the rule, then penetrate the profound recesses of the desert in order to engage in the fiercest battles with demons. We discovered that men of this way of life lived on this side of [variant: *circa*, “around,” for *citra*, “on this side of”] the channel of the Nile, in a place surrounded on one side by the Nile and on the other by the vastness of the sea, making it an island desirable only to monks seeking solitude. The salinity of the soil and the barrenness of the sands do not permit the land to be suitable for cultivation by anyone.

As we hurried to these men with the greatest desire, we marveled beyond measure at their immense labors [Col. 0838C], which they endure in solitude. They are constrained by such a great scarcity of water that they ration it with the care that no one would use for the most precious wine. They bring it from the Nile for their necessary uses from a distance of three miles or more; yet this interval, divided by sandy mountains, is doubled by the extreme difficulty of the labor.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Of the monk Archebius

After seeing these things, when the ardor of imitating them had inflamed us (Cassian, Book 5 of the *Institutes*, chapter 37), one of their most esteemed hermits, named Archebius, led us to his cell out of kindness. When he discovered that we intended to remain there, he pretended [Col. 0838D] that he wished to leave the same place and began to offer us his cell as though he were about to depart. He said that he would do this even if we had not come.

We therefore took possession of his cell together with all its equipment. He remained there only a few days while he prepared the expenses required to build another cell, and then he departed from that place. Afterward he returned and built another cell for himself with great labor. Not long afterward, when brothers arrived, he likewise handed it over to them, together with all its equipment [p. 551], for the sake of charity. He himself, tireless in the work of charity, continued and built a third cell for himself in which to live.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Of two young men who died on the road while carrying figs to a sick man

[Col. 0839A] A certain brother, having brought figs from Mareotis to Abbot John in the Scetis desert, immediately sent them through two young men to an old man who was suffering from illness in the inner desert (Cassian, Book 5 of the *Institutes*, chapter 40). This solitary lived eighteen miles from the church.

When the young men had received the fruit and were making their way to the old man’s cell, a very dense cloud suddenly arose and they lost the path of the straight road. Although they wandered throughout the day and night through the pathless vastness of the desert and could not find the cell of the sick hermit, they were exhausted both by the weariness of the journey [Col. 0839B] and by hunger and thirst. With their knees fixed upon the ground, they gave up their spirit to the Lord while praying.

Afterward they were sought for a very long time by the signs of their footprints, which are marked in those sandy places as though in snow, until the fine sand, driven by a light breath of wind, should cover them. At last they were found lying just as they had prayed, still preserving the figs untouched, as they had received them. They chose to lose their lives rather than violate the trust committed to them, lest they presume to take any food without the abbot’s command. They preferred to lose their temporal life rather than violate the elder’s order.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. How constant the labors of the Egyptian monks are

Throughout Egypt the monks in no way [Col. 0839C] permit themselves to be idle (Cassian, Book 10 of the *Institutes*, chapter 22), but obtain their food by the labor of their hands. They not only refresh travelers and visiting brothers with the products of their labors, but also provide a great quantity of food throughout the regions of Libya, which suffer from famine, and in the cities they supply those who are held in prisons and various bonds. Through such an offering, they believe that they offer themselves to the Lord as a reasonable sacrifice from the fruit of their hands.

For they say that a working monk is always assaulted by one demon, while an idle monk is devastated by innumerable spirits (ibid., chapter 23).

## CHAPTER XL. Of Abbot Paul

Finally, Abbot Paul, one of the most approved of the Fathers (ibid., [Col. 0839D] chapter 24), while dwelling in the vast desert called Porphyrius, was sustained only by the fruit of palm trees and a small garden. He could practice no other occupation by which he might support himself, because he was more than seven stages away in the desert from human beings or habitable land.

Therefore, so that he would not stand entirely idle even for a moment, he gathered palm leaves and continually imposed upon himself a daily quota, as though he were to be supported by it. When his cave had been filled with the work of an entire year and he had no one to whom he could sell it, while he himself could not remain idle, he burned everything for which he had labored with anxious care, year after year, by setting fire to it. In this way he demonstrated that without the work of his hands a monk can neither remain in that place [Col. 0840A] nor ever ascend to the summit of perfection.

## CHAPTER XLI. Of the blasphemous brother who was burning with intolerable heat of lust

I knew another brother who confessed to a highly esteemed elder that he was being gravely assaulted by the vice of the flesh; for he was burning with an intolerable heat of lust (Cassian, Book 12 of the *Institutes*, chapter 20). Then the elder, immediately perceiving, like a spiritual physician, the inner cause and origin of this illness, sighed deeply and said:

“By no means, my son, would the Lord have handed you over to so wicked a spirit unless you had blasphemed against him.”

When the brother heard this, he immediately fell face down at the elder’s feet and, struck with the greatest astonishment [Col. 0840B], confessed that he had blasphemed against the Son of God through an impious thought. From this it is clear that the one who is a blasphemer against God, as one who inflicts an injury upon him, is deprived of the integrity of perfection and does not deserve the sanctification of chastity.

## CHAPTER XLII. Where many elders assembled with Saint Antony for the sake of consolation

At a certain time many elders came together to the blessed Antony, who was living in the regions of the Thebaid, for the pursuit of perfection and for discussion (Cassian, *Conferences* 2, chapter 2). Their discussion continued from the evening hours until daylight, and the question of discernment consumed most of the night [Col. 0840C].

For a very long time they asked which virtue or practice could preserve a monk unharmed from the snares of the devil or, at least, lead him to God by a straight path and a firm step. Each person brought forward an opinion according to the capacity of his understanding. Some placed it in devotion to fasts and vigils; others in nakedness and contempt [p. 552] for possessions; others judged that it lay in a more remote life and the solitude of the desert; and some defined charity, that is, acts of kindness, as the first thing to be pursued, since such acts are performed through devoted hospitality toward brothers and travelers.

As they contended in this pious dispute, and most of the night had already been spent, the blessed Antony finally replied to them all:

“All the things you have mentioned are necessary and useful [Col. 0840D] to those who thirst for God. But the countless falls and experiences of many brothers do not permit us to assign the primary place to these things. We have often seen brothers who practiced these observances deceived by a sudden fall because they did not maintain discernment at all in the good they had begun.

“No other cause of their fall is found except that, having been insufficiently instructed by the elders, they could not attain the principle of this discernment. It teaches the monk always to walk along the royal road, neither permitting him to pass beyond the proper measure through excessive self-restraint nor allowing him to turn aside into vices.

“Therefore, in everything we do, discernment must be placed first. It is most clearly shown that no virtue can either be perfectly [Col. 0841A] accomplished or remain firm without the grace of discernment.”

When Antony had said this, the judgment of everyone concluded that discernment is what leads the monk, with firm step, unafraid, to God and continually preserves the virtues mentioned above unharmed. For discernment is the mother, guardian, and guide of all the virtues.

## CHAPTER XLIII. Of the elder Heron

To confirm these things with more certain examples (Cassian, *Conferences* 2, chapter 5), I shall tell you about a certain elder named Heron, who, failing to retain discernment, lost all his former labors and, in addition, ended his life miserably. Only a few days ago he was cast down from the heights to the depths through a deception of the devil.

He had lived in the desert for fifty years [Col. 0841B], maintained an extraordinary strictness of life, and pursued the solitude of the wilderness with marvelous fervor beyond all others. After so many labors, he was deceived by the ambusher and fell into a most grievous error, striking all who lived in the desert with sorrowful grief. He would not have fallen if he had been willing to preserve the virtue of discernment.

With such rigor of mind did he constantly practice unchanging abstinence from food and continually pursue the solitude of the desert and of his cell that he did not relax the severity of his abstinence even on the holy day of Easter. When all the hermits gathered together at the church for so great a solemnity, he alone was absent, lest by taking even a small portion of vegetables he should appear to have relaxed his purpose.

Deceived by this presumption, he received an angel of Satan as though he were an angel of light and obeyed his commands with the greatest reverence [Col. 0841C]. He threw himself headlong into an exceedingly deep well, intending to prove the great merit of his virtue if he emerged from it unharmed. The brothers extracted him from the well with great labor, half alive, and he died on the third day. What is worse, he persisted so obstinately in his deception that he could in no way be persuaded that he had been deceived by the cunning of demons.

## CHAPTER XLIV. Of two monks who, traveling through the desert, decided not to eat unless God sent them food

What shall I say about those two brothers who lived beyond the desert [Col. 0841D] where the blessed Antony had once dwelt (Cassian, *Conferences* 2, chapter 6)? Moved by insufficiently cautious discernment, they traveled through the vast expanse of the wilderness and resolved not to eat any food at all except what the Lord himself might provide for them.

While they were wandering through the deserts and were already failing from hunger, the Mazices saw them from a distance. This people is more savage and cruel than all other nations; they are impelled not by a desire for plunder leading to bloodshed but solely by the ferocity of their minds. Yet when they saw the monks, contrary to the nature of their savagery, they ran to meet them with bread.

Then one of the brothers, aided by discernment, received the bread with thanksgiving as though it had been handed to him by God, reasoning that food had been divinely supplied to him and saying [Col. 0842A] that it had not happened without God’s command that those who always delighted in human blood should now provide the substance of life to men who were failing from hunger.

The other, however, refused the food as though it had been offered to him by a human being and, consumed by the hardship of starvation, died. Although the beginnings of both had arisen from a blameworthy conviction, one is recognized as having corrected, through the assistance of discernment, what he had conceived imprudently; the other, persisting in foolish presumption, brought upon himself the death that the Lord had wished to avert from him.

## CHAPTER XLV. Of the monk who, deceived by the devil, wished to sacrifice his son

What shall I say about that monk whose name I omit because he is still alive (Cassian, [Col. 0842B] *Conferences* 2, chapter 7)? For a long time [p. 553] he received the devil in the splendor of an angel and, often deceived by his revelations, believed him to be a messenger of justice. Every night in his cell the devil provided light without the aid of any lamp. Finally, he ordered the monk devoutly to offer his son, who lived with him in the same monastery, as a victim to God, so that by this sacrifice he might be made equal to the merits of the patriarch Abraham.

The monk was so deceived by the devil’s words that he would immediately have carried out the deed if the boy had not slipped from his hands and fled swiftly from the cell.

## CHAPTER XLVI. Of the monk to whom the devil showed an army of Christians and Jews

[Col. 0842C] There was also another monk (Cassian, *Conferences* 2, chapter 8) who always practiced excessive abstinence and who, shut away alone in his cell for many years, displayed an abstinence that very few could imitate. In the end he was so deceived by diabolical revelations that, after years of labors and virtues by which he had surpassed other monks, he fell miserably into Judaism and the circumcision of the flesh.

After a long time the devil, as though a messenger of truth, showed him through empty dreams and certain vain revelations a dark and dreadful army of Christians and monks, wasted away by extreme emaciation and completely deformed. In contrast, he showed him the people of the Jews dancing with the greatest joy and flashing with immense light. He therefore urged him that [Col. 0842D], if he wished to become a participant in their blessedness, he should hasten to receive circumcision as well.

From this it is entirely clear that none of the men mentioned above would have been deceived so grievously if they had worked to attain the principle of discernment. Their falls demonstrate by experience how dangerous it is not to possess the grace of discernment.

## CHAPTER XLVII. Of Abbot Serapion
Abbot Serapion was accustomed frequently to tell the younger brothers, for their instruction, about himself (Cassian, *Conference* II, chapter 11), saying:

“When I was still a little boy and was living with Abbot Theon, I had this habit when the enemy was pressing me: after I had eaten my fill with the old man at the ninth hour, I would secretly hide one *paximatium* each day in my bosom; in the evening, without the old man’s knowledge, I would eat it in secret. Although I carried out this theft every day, once my fraudulent desire had been satisfied and I returned to myself, I was tormented much more severely over the theft I had committed than I had rejoiced over eating it.

“Since I was compelled to complete this most burdensome task every day, not without sorrow of heart, and was ashamed to disclose the secret theft to the old man, it happened by God’s providence that certain brothers, seeking the old man’s cell most eagerly for the sake of edification, came to visit him. When the meal was over and spiritual conversation had begun, the old man answered their questions and was explaining the vice of gluttony and hidden thoughts. At last he added:

“‘Nothing is so harmful to monks, and so pleasing to demons, as concealing their thoughts from spiritual fathers.’

“Then, struck with compunction of heart, I thought that the secrets of my breast had been revealed to the old man. First I was moved to hidden groans; then, as compunction of heart increased, I burst into open sobs and tears and began to weep most bitterly. Immediately I threw from my bosom the *paximatium* that, following my vicious habit, I had secretly prepared to eat.

“Bringing it into their midst, I explained how I had wrapped it up and secretly eaten it each day. Then, prostrate on the floor, I confessed with a plea for pardon; and, with abundant tears pouring forth, I asked them to obtain forgiveness for me from God by their prayers.

“Then the old man said: ‘Take courage, son, because this confession of yours has freed you from that captivity. Today you have triumphed over your adversary as victor, striking him down more powerfully by your confession than you had been cast down by him through your silence. Therefore, after this disclosure of yours, that evil spirit will no longer rule over you, nor will that most terrible serpent henceforth claim a hiding-place in you, because by this confession he has been driven out of the darkness of your heart.’

“The old man had not yet finished speaking when suddenly, like a lamp being brightly rekindled, something came forth from my bosom and filled the cell with such a stench that we could scarcely remain there.

“The old man resumed: ‘Behold, the Lord has proved to you the truth of my words, so that by the eyes of faith you might perceive that the instigator of that passion had been driven from your heart by a saving confession, and that, with the enemy exposed and expelled, you might recognize that he would never again have a place of habitation in you.’

“Thus, in accordance with the old man’s judgment, the devil’s dominion was extinguished in me by the power of confession, so that afterward the enemy never again attempted to bring upon me even the memory of this desire.”

## Chapter XLVIII. On the Monks Killed by the Saracens

In the regions of Palestine, near the village of Thecue (Cassian, *Conference* VI, chapter 1)—[Note: “Near the village of Thecue.” The Roman Martyrology, 28 May: “At Thecue in Palestine, the holy monk-martyrs who were killed by the Saracens in the time of Theodosius the Younger. The inhabitants gathered their sacred remains and held them in the highest veneration.”]—Baronius notes:

“These appear to be the men about whom John Cassian speaks in *Conference* VI, chapters 1 and following. The same Baronius, volume V, in the year of Christ 410, the ninth year of Pope Innocent, the sixteenth of Honorius, and the third of the emperors Theodosius, says that Cassian, throughout the whole of *Conference* VI, is concerned with explaining why God permits holy men to be killed by the wicked. This question was plainly on everyone’s lips at that time because of the disasters breaking in everywhere and the barbarians ravaging far and wide. For Cassian was not the only one to discuss it: on the same occasion Augustine also treated it in his letter to Victorianus (*Letter* 122), when the latter had asked among other things: ‘Why were servants of God also killed by the sword of the barbarians, and maidservants of God led away captive?’ Augustine likewise discusses the matter at greater length in his writings to Marcellinus in the books *On the City of God.’”

Thus far Baronius.

Baronius there also believes that, at the same time, Egypt suffered a disaster inflicted by barbarians, and he proves this from Augustine’s letter to Victorianus:

“Indeed, the whole world is afflicted by such great disasters that scarcely any part of the earth exists where events such as those you have described are not committed and mourned. For even shortly before this, in those deserts of Egypt where monasteries, separated from every disturbance, lived as though in security, brothers were killed by barbarians” (Augustine, *Letter* 122).

Cassian, however, who was living in Egypt at this time, makes no mention of the devastation inflicted by barbarians upon the monasteries of Egypt. For after narrating the killing of monks in the regions of Palestine, he adds:

“Sorrowful, we went to the holy Theodore, a man outstanding in active conduct. He was living in the Cells, a place situated between Nitria and Scetis. It lies five miles from the monasteries of Nitria and is separated from the desert of Scetis, where we were staying, by an intervening wilderness of eighty miles” (Cassian, *Conference* VI, chapter 1).

But the principal monasteries of Egypt were in Scetis, Nitria, and the Cells. Therefore, what Saint Augustine says about the monasteries of Egypt being devastated should be understood of those situated at the outermost edge and boundary of Egypt.

I gather this from Saint Jerome, *Letter* 82, to Marcellinus:

“This year, after I had completed three books—namely, of Ezekiel—the sudden onslaught of the barbarians, of whom your Virgil says (*Aeneid* IV):

> Wandering far and wide,  
> the Barcaeans . . .

“and of whom Holy Scripture says concerning Ishmael, ‘He shall dwell over against all his brothers’ (Genesis 16), swept along the boundary of Egypt, Palestine, Phoenicia, and Syria, and, carrying everything with it like a torrent, so that scarcely by the mercy of Christ could we escape their hands.”

Thecue, which deserved to produce the prophet Amos, is a vast and utterly desolate wilderness extending in the broadest expanse as far as Arabia and the Dead Sea, where the waters of the Jordan enter and disappear and where the ashes of Sodom lie.

In this wilderness, monks of the highest sanctity had lived for a very long time. Suddenly they were killed by Saracens roaming about. Their bodies were received with such veneration both by the people of that region and by the entire Arab population that countless crowds came running from both sides and engaged in a most serious contest over their relics, piously striving with one another in devotion over the sacred spoils, each side claiming to have the better right to bury them and possess their relics: some boasting of their residence near the monks, others of their closeness by origin.

## Chapter XLIX. On Abbot Daniel

Among the other hermits, we also saw Abbot Daniel, equal to the others in every virtue but especially endowed with the grace of humility (Cassian, *Conference* IV, chapter 1). Because of his purity and gentleness, he was chosen for the diaconate by Saint Paphnutius, presbyter of that same desert. The blessed Paphnutius rejoiced so greatly in his virtues that, knowing him to be his equal in merit of life and grace, he hastened to make him his equal also in priestly rank. Finally, wishing while still alive to provide himself with a most worthy successor, he advanced him to the honor of the priesthood.

Yet Daniel did not abandon his former habit of humility. In Paphnutius’s presence he never claimed anything for himself from the addition of the higher order; rather, whenever Abbot Paphnutius offered spiritual sacrifices, Daniel remained, as a deacon, in the service of his former ministry.

Nevertheless, although blessed Paphnutius was such a great man and possessed, among many other gifts, the foreknowledge granted by grace, his hope concerning the choice of a successor was frustrated. For not long afterward, he sent to God before himself the very successor whom he had prepared.

## Chapter L. On Abbot Serenus

We saw Abbot Serenus, a man of the highest sanctity and continence, a mirror of his own name, whom we admired with singular veneration above the others (Cassian, *Conference* VII, chapter 1). Among all the virtues that shone forth by God’s grace not only in his actions and conduct but even in his very face, he had received the gift of chastity through a special favor to such a degree that he did not feel himself disturbed even by the natural impulses themselves, not even in sleep.

Since this purity of the flesh seems to exceed the condition of human nature, I think it necessary to explain how he attained it.

The blessed Serenus, therefore, striving tirelessly by prayers both day and night, as well as by fasts and vigils, for inward purity of heart and bodily purity, saw that he had obtained the requests of his prayers and that all the heats of desire had been extinguished in his heart. As though inflamed by the sweetest taste of purity, he burned with an even greater thirst and zeal for chastity and began to devote himself to more intense fasts and supplications, so that the mortification of this passion—attributed to the inner person solely by God’s gift—might also reach outward purity, to the point that he would no longer be troubled even by any simple and natural movement of the kind aroused even in little children and nursing infants.

As he persisted tirelessly in his prayer, petition, and tears, an angel came to him in a nocturnal vision. The angel seemed to open his abdomen, drew out from his entrails a fiery mass of flesh, and cast it away. Then, restoring all his intestines to their proper places, the angel said to him:

“Behold, the incitements of your flesh have been cut away. Know that today you have obtained the perpetual purity of body which you faithfully requested.”

Let it suffice to have spoken briefly about this grace of God, which was peculiarly granted to the man mentioned.
