When we came to him on the fortieth day and asked him about various questions (ibid., chapter 2), we finally questioned him about the assaults of demons. Then, answering with the most peaceful expression, as was always his custom (ibid., chapter 22), he said:

“Demons cannot have the power to harm any human being. The example of blessed Job plainly demonstrates this (Job 2), where the enemy dares to test him no further than divine providence permits.”

## Chapter LI. That Demons Now Have No Equal Power Against Monks as in Earlier Times

Our own experience and the report of our elders have made it sufficiently clear that demons do not now have the same power against monks that they had in earlier times, at the beginnings of the anchorites, when monks were still few in number in the desert (Cassian, *Conference* VII, chapter 23).

At that time the ferocity of demons was so great that scarcely a very few could endure dwelling in solitude. Indeed, even in the coenobia where ten or twelve lived together, their violence raged so fiercely, and visible attacks were so frequently experienced, that no one dared sleep at night with all the others at once. Instead, while some tasted sleep in turn, others kept vigil, occupied with psalms, prayers, or readings. When natural necessity invited the others to sleep, those who had awakened took their turn guarding those who were about to sleep, and likewise gave themselves to vigil.

There can therefore be no doubt that one of two things is now the case: either, because the power of the cross has penetrated even the deserts and its grace shines everywhere, the wickedness of demons has been blunted; or our negligence has made them slower to attack us than before, since they disdain to fight against us with the same determination with which they once raged against those most proven soldiers of Christ.

We also know that holy men have sometimes been handed over bodily to Satan or to serious illnesses (Cassian, *Conference* VII, chapter 25), for the lightest offenses, although divine mercy does not permit even the slightest sin or stain to be found in them on the day of judgment. In this way it sends them, like tested gold, into that glorious eternity, needing no penal purification, in accordance with the saying:

> The righteous person is tested in the furnace of humiliation.  
> (Ecclesiasticus 27)

And:

> For whom the Lord loves, he chastises; and he scourges every son whom he receives.  
> (Hebrews 12; Proverbs 3)

Our own times have also shown this clearly, and the case of Abbot Paul or Moses provides an open proof. They lived in the place in this desert called Calamus (Cassian, *Conference* VII, chapter 26).

Paul lived in the desert adjoining the city of Panephysis. We know that this wilderness was long ago turned into a body of exceedingly salty water. Whenever the north wind blows, the water, driven from its pools and poured over the neighboring lands, covers the entire surface of that region so completely that it makes the ancient villages there—which, for this very reason, were once abandoned by every inhabitant—appear like islands.

## Chapter LII. On Abbot Paul

This Abbot Paul had advanced so far in purity of heart through the tranquility and silence of solitude that he could not endure the sight not only of a woman’s face but even of a woman’s clothing (Cassian, *Conference* VII, chapter 26).

One day, as he was going to the cell of a certain elder, a woman happened by chance to meet him. When he saw her, he ran back to his own monastery, abandoning the road he had begun, with as much haste as no one would flee from the face of a lion or a most savage dragon.

Although this was done from zeal for chastity and fervor for purity, it was nevertheless an act of presumption not according to knowledge. Since it exceeded the limits of disciplined observance, he was immediately struck with such a correction that his entire body was paralyzed, and no limb in him was able to perform its proper function.

Not only his feet and hands but also the movement of his tongue, and even his ears, lost the sense of their proper hearing, so that nothing human remained in him except the appearance of an immobile statue. He was reduced to such a state that the care of men could in no way suffice to serve his infirmity; only the attentiveness of a woman could assist him.

He was carried to a monastery of sacred virgins, where food and drink were administered to him by female service. The same attentiveness served him in fulfilling every natural need for nearly four years—that is, until the end of his life.

Although all his limbs were so bound by weakness that none of his joints retained living movement, such grace of virtues proceeded from him that, when the sick were anointed with oil that had touched his body, they were immediately healed of every illness. Thus, in connection with his illness, it clearly became evident both that the weakness of his limbs had been assigned to him out of love for the Lord and that the grace of healing had been prepared by the power of the Holy Spirit as a testimony and manifestation of his merits.

## Chapter LIII. On Abbot Moses

The second man whom we mentioned, Moses, who lived in this desert (Cassian, *Conference* VII, chapter 27), was himself an exceptional and incomparable man. Because of a single saying that he had spoken too harshly against Abbot Macarius, he was immediately handed over to a demon of such a terrible kind that it forced human excrement into his mouth.

That this scourge of purification had been inflicted upon him by divine providence, so that not even the stain of a momentary sin might remain in him, was demonstrated by the speed of his healing. For as soon as Abbot Macarius prostrated himself in prayer, the evil spirit was driven from Moses and departed more quickly than words can tell.

From this it is plainly understood that we ought not to abominate or despise those whom we see handed over to various temptations or evil spirits (ibid., chapter 28), because we must hold two things firmly:

First, no one is ever tempted without God’s permission.

Second, everything inflicted upon us by God is imposed for our benefit, as by a most loving father and most merciful physician.

## Chapter LIV. On the Monk Who Saw a Multitude of Demons at Night in the Desert

A certain brother, while traveling through the desert, found a cave as evening approached and stopped there (Cassian, *Conference* VIII, chapter 16). While he was singing psalms there as usual, the hour of midnight passed. When the vigil was over, he sat down for a little while to refresh his weary body.

Suddenly he began to see innumerable troops of demons converging from every direction. Advancing in endless compact formation, some went before their prince and others followed him. Their prince appeared both taller than all the rest in stature and more terrifying in appearance.

When he had seated himself upon a most lofty throne, he began carefully to examine the actions of each one. Those who said that they had not yet been able to outwit their rivals he ordered to be driven from his presence as useless, angrily reproaching them for the great amount of time and the labor they had wasted.

But those who reported that they had deceived the human beings entrusted to them, he sent forth before everyone else with the highest praise and exultation, amid the applause of all, like the bravest warriors and the most glorious examples for the rest.

Among them a certain very wicked spirit arrived more joyfully than the others, as though about to announce a great triumph. He identified a monk whom he knew very well and asserted that, after besieging him continually for five [Cassian: fifteen] years, he had at last, that very night, plunged him into the ruin of fornication.

When this report had been made, the joy of everyone arose, and the spirit, exalted by the highest praises of their prince and crowned with great acclamations, departed.

When dawn came and the entire multitude of demons had vanished from his sight, the brother doubted the unclean spirit’s assertion. He also remembered the Gospel saying that the devil “did not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him; when he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own nature” (John 8).

He went to Pelusium, where he knew that the brother in question lived. Another brother, well known to him, was also there. When he asked him about that brother, he discovered that on the very night when the most terrible demon had announced his downfall to its prince, the monk had abandoned his former monastery, gone to a village, and fallen miserably into fornication.

When the brother heard this, he returned to his own place, sighing and weeping.

## Chapter LV. On Two Philosophers Who Went to Saint Antony

At a certain time, two philosophers, having heard the reputation of blessed Antony, went to him (Cassian, *Conference* VIII, chapter 18). After they had discussed certain questions among themselves, they despised Saint Antony as an uneducated and illiterate man and departed from him.

Then, wishing—if they could do him no further harm—to disturb him in his cell by magical tricks and the intervention of demons, they sent the most wicked demons against him, struck by envy and resentment because many people came to him daily as to a servant of God.

But Antony impressed the sign of the cross now upon his breast and forehead, and now devoted himself earnestly to prayer. The most violent demons did not even dare approach him; they returned to those who had sent them without accomplishing anything.

Then the philosophers sent others again, as though more powerful. When these too returned exhausted, they sent still others, no less powerful and more violent, against the soldier of Christ. They accomplished absolutely nothing, because Antony resisted them manfully.

Thus their plots—so great and so many, contrived through every magical art and necromancy—achieved nothing. By this it was most clearly demonstrated that great power resides in the Christian profession, since those savage shadows were unable not only to harm Antony but even to disturb him for a moment in his dwelling.

Struck with amazement at this, the philosophers immediately came to Saint Antony (ibid., chapter 19). They disclosed to him the magnitude of their attacks, their causes, and the schemes arising from their envy, and at once asked to become Christians. When he asked them to identify the day on which the attack they had revealed took place, they told him. Blessed Antony declared that at that very time he had been struck by the most bitter goads of thoughts.

We also know that blessed Antony sometimes persisted in prayer in such a way (Cassian, *Conference* IX, chapter 31) that, while he was frequently praying in the same ecstasy of mind, and sunrise had begun to spread, we heard him crying out in the fervor of his spirit:

“Why do you hinder me, sun, which rise for this purpose—to draw me away from the brightness of this true light?”

# BOOK FIVE OF THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS, OR THE SAYINGS OF THE ELDERS, BY AN UNKNOWN GREEK AUTHOR

Translated by Pelagius, Deacon of the Holy Roman Church.

[Note: “By an unknown Greek author.” It is sufficiently clear from Photius that this book had a Greek author, since Photius used a Greek copy and refers to a translator who translated from Greek. Yet, whatever some may have conjectured, the author remains uncertain, as Photius indicates by naming no one. See the remarks in the general prolegomena, sections 7 and 8.]

[Note: “Pelagius.” Consult what I noted about him in the fourteenth section of the general prolegomena.]

## Preliminary Remarks on Book Five

### On the Book’s Title among the Greeks, Its Subject, Division, and Usefulness

Photius.

It is certain that the book which Photius mentions as existing in Greek in his own time is this same book, which you have here in Latin, translated partly by Pelagius, deacon of the Holy Roman Church, in this Book V, and partly by John, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, in Book IV.

Since among both Greeks and Latins there is one book, we have divided it into two because of the different translators, following Sigebert of Gembloux in his *On Illustrious Men*, chapters 116 and 117.

Photius nevertheless cites two sections that seem to be lacking from the Latin copy.

First, this book is lacking here, which Photius lists as number 21 and which contains conferences among the elders concerning their own reflections. It does not appear to be present here in this place, but it is found at the end of Book VII, translated from Greek by Paschasius, deacon of the Holy Roman Church, under this title: “On the Meditations of Twelve Anchorites.” In Greek it exists in the Augsburg Library, manuscript 78, no. 2, and is described in that library’s catalogue as: “An account of the Twelve Fathers who met concerning their own righteous deeds.”

Second, this book is lacking here, which Photius lists as number 22. For here you do not have the maxims or sayings of Hesychius; but they were published separately, both in Greek and Latin, in two centuries addressed to Theodulus, by John Pico at Paris in the year of Christ 1563, printed by Frederick and William Morel, after the minor works of Mark the Ascetic—if, indeed, these are the same sayings that Photius cites together with the published book of Hesychius.

Photius, Patriarch of Constantinople, *Bibliotheca*, codex 198.

[Note: “Photius.” The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

We read the *Book of Holy Men*, which narrates their manner of life and their righteous deeds for spiritual progress and benefit.

It was apparently an epitome and abridgment of the great work called the *Spiritual Meadow* (*Limonarion*), which recounts the lives and deeds both of the men associated with Antony the Great and of those who flourished after them. Likewise, the work called the *New Garden* describes the lives and religious practices of more recent men, extending down to the age of the emperor Heraclius and to those somewhat nearer to his time.

This present book, however, is condensed into twenty-two sections and sets forth, through various narratives, the usefulness of each subject and the means of attaining it.

1. The first section is an exhortation toward progress in perfection, drawn from various persons.

2. The second shows the fruit of a tranquil and solitary life.

3. The third treats of continence and teaches that it must be practiced not only in food but likewise in the other movements of the soul.

4. The fourth explains how one must fortify oneself against the battles arising from fornication.

5. The fifth concerns poverty and the need to avoid greed.

6. The sixth concerns patience and courage.

7. The seventh teaches that nothing should be done for display.

8. The eighth teaches that no one should judge.

9. The ninth concerns discernment.

10. The tenth teaches that one must always be sober, or watchful.

11. The eleventh teaches that one must pray constantly and attentively.

12. The twelfth teaches that hospitality and mercy must be practiced cheerfully.

13. The thirteenth teaches obedience.

14. The fourteenth concerns humility.

15. The fifteenth concerns endurance of evils.

16. The sixteenth concerns love.

17. The seventeenth concerns those who have seen visions. [Note: “Those who have seen visions.” Our Schott translates the Greek *dioretikón* in this way and therefore thought that the title in the printed books should be corrected. It must be considered whether the translation should instead be amended on the basis of the printed editions: “On foresight, or insight, and contemplation.” For *dioráō* means “to look through,” a verb used in this sense by Lucretius and Lactantius, or “to perceive clearly.” Hence *dioratikós* means “discerning,” able to distinguish, as Chrysostom, Damascenus, and Aphrodisaeus use it. See Budaeus.

“Thus in Athanasius, *Life of Saint Antony*: ‘For I believe that a soul purified from every side and standing according to nature, having become discerning, can see more and farther than the demons.’ David Haeschelius translates this: ‘For I am fully persuaded that a mind free from the filth of disturbances and stable according to nature, endowed with the gift of discernment, can perceive much more and much farther than demons.’

“Sozomen, Book I, chapter 13, concerning Saint Antony: ‘If anyone is concerned about this,’ he says, ‘let him purify his soul; for this alone can make it discerning and knowledgeable of future things, since God reveals beforehand what is going to happen.’”]

18. The eighteenth concerns elders who performed miracles.

19. The nineteenth concerns the lives of various holy Fathers that were pleasing to God.

20. The twentieth contains the apt sayings of some who had grown old in monastic practice.

21. The twenty-first contains conferences among elders concerning their own reflections.

22. The twenty-second and final section contains the sayings of Hesychius, presbyter of Jerusalem.

With these sections the whole book is completed.

It is supremely useful—more useful than almost any other book—for those who order their lives in preparation for the heavenly inheritance.

It also possesses the clarity that it promised; otherwise it is of such a character as suits men who do not labor over words but devote all their effort and endeavor to the practice of deeds.

[Greek parallel text:] “A Book of Holy Men was read, recounting their ways of life and righteous deeds for spiritual progress and benefit.

“It was apparently an epitome and synopsis of the great work called the *Limonarion* (*Spiritual Meadow*), which recounts the lives and deeds of those associated with Antony the Great and of those who flourished after them. Likewise, the work called the *New Paradise* [alternative reading: *paradeisin*, ‘paradise’] records the ways of life and ascetic struggles of those still more recent, down to the reign of the emperor Heraclius and even somewhat later.

“Yet the present book, divided into twenty-two subjects, displays by various narratives both the usefulness of each and the means of acquiring it.

“1. The first chapter contains exhortation toward progress in perfection, from various persons. 2. The second shows the gain arising from stillness. 3. The third treats continence, and teaches that continence must be exercised not only with respect to foods [alternative reading: *brōmatōn*, ‘of foods’], but likewise with respect to the other movements of the soul. 4. The fourth teaches how we must protect ourselves against the wars that rise against us from fornication. 5. The fifth concerns renunciation of possessions and the need also to guard against covetousness. 6. The sixth concerns patience and courage. 7. The seventh teaches that nothing should be done for display. 8. The eighth teaches that no one ought to judge. 9. The ninth concerns discernment. 10. The tenth concerns the need always to be watchful. 11. The eleventh teaches that one must pray without ceasing and watchfully. 12. The twelfth teaches that hospitality and mercy must be exercised cheerfully. 13. The thirteenth instructs concerning obedience [alternative reading: ‘and instruction’]. 14. The fourteenth concerns humility. 15. The fifteenth concerns endurance of wrongs. 16. The sixteenth concerns love. 17. The seventeenth concerns those endowed with discernment. 18. The eighteenth concerns wonder-working elders. 19. The nineteenth concerns the God-beloved ways of life of various Fathers. 20. The twentieth contains sayings of those grown old in ascetic practice. 21. The twenty-first presents discourses of elders with one another concerning their thoughts. 22. Finally, the twenty-second contains the maxims of Hesychius, presbyter of Jerusalem.

“In these the entire account of the book is completed.

“It is exceedingly useful, if anything is, to those who practise their life with a view to the inheritance of heaven.

“It also has, as promised, clarity; and in other respects it is such as would suit men not devoted to contests of words, but who have undertaken all their labor and zeal in the practice of deeds.”

## SAYINGS OF THE ELDERS

# FIRST BOOK: On the Progress of the Fathers

### 1

A certain man asked Abbot Antony (Rufinus, Book III, no. 108):

“What must I keep in order to please God?”

The old man answered:

“Keep what I command you. Wherever you go, always have God before your eyes. In everything you do, use the testimony of the Holy Scriptures. Wherever you sit, do not move quickly. Keep these three things, and you will be saved.”

### 2

Abbot Pambo asked Abbot Antony (Appendix of Martin, no. 54):

“What shall I do?”

The old man answered:

“Do not trust in your own righteousness; do not regret what has already happened; and exercise restraint over your tongue and your belly.”

### 3

Saint Gregory said:

“God requires these three things from every person who has received baptism: a right faith with the whole soul and strength, restraint of the tongue, and purity of body.”

### 4

Abbot Evagrius said: [Note: “Evagrius.” This was Evagrius of Pontus, an Origenist; see the remarks on Book II of Rufinus, chapter 27. Father John Maria Brasichellensis, master of the Sacred Palace, notes in the index of prohibited books: “This Evagrius of Pontus, an Origenist, inculcates his Stoic apatheia, which Saint Jerome so often condemned as an obvious error.”]

“Some of the Fathers used to say that a drier and even diet, joined with love, brings the monk more quickly into the harbor of apatheia.” [Note: “Into the harbor of apatheia.” Here Evagrius insinuates his Stoic doctrine of *apatheia*, against which Saint Jerome argues in his letter to Ctesiphon against the errors of the Pelagians.] [Note: “Not uneven.” This is how it should be read; the printed editions omit *not*. In Greek, this apophthegm from Evagrius’s *Praktikos*, or *The Monk*, is given by Socrates, Book IV, chapter 23 in the Greek text and chapter 18 in the Latin, as follows: “Ὅτι τὴν ξηροτέραν, καὶ μὴ ἀνώμαλον δίαιταν, ἀγάπῃ συζευχθεῖσαν θᾶττον διάγειν τὸν μοναχὸν εἰς τὸν τῆς ἀπαθείας λιμένα”: ‘A drier, and not uneven, diet, joined to love, brings the monk more swiftly into the harbor of apatheia.’ Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 43, reads it in the same way.

“Suida, in the section on the Macarii, where he also lists certain works of Evagrius, wrongly reads *anōmalon* instead of *mē anōmalon*. The omission of the negation has caused interpreters great difficulty. Hieronymus Wlofius conjectured *anaimakton* in place of *anōmalon*, as though a bloodless diet were intended if one abstained from fish and meat in the Pythagorean manner. Zacharias Palthenius, who translated the homilies of Saint Macarius from Greek and prefixed the words of Suida, rendered *anōmalon diaitan* as ‘a harsh way of life.’ I understand ‘an even diet’ to mean an even manner of living, so that one does not eat sparingly at one time and lavishly at another, or use one kind of food at one time and another kind at another.”]

### 5

Again he said:

“The death of a man’s father was announced to a certain monk.” [Note: “Was announced.” In Socrates, Book IV, chapter 23 in Greek and chapter 18 in Latin, this saying from Evagrius’s *Praktikos*, or *The Monk*, is expressed as follows: “It was reported to one of the monks that his father had died. But he said to the one who announced it: ‘Stop blaspheming; for my father is immortal.’” Nicephorus cites the same saying from the same Evagrius in Book XI, chapter 43.]

But he said to the one who announced it:

“Stop blaspheming, for my father is immortal.”

### 6

Abbot Macarius said to Abbot Zacharias:

“Tell me: what is the work of a monk?”

He said to him:

“Are you asking me, Father?”

Abbot Macarius said to him:

“I am certain about you, son Zacharias, for there is someone urging me to ask you.”

Zacharias said to him:

“As for me, Father, I think that whoever subjects and compels himself to necessities is a monk.”

### 7

They used to speak about Abbot Theodore, whose designation is “of Pherme.” [Note: “Of Pherme.” Both the printed editions and the manuscripts vary here, some reading *Ferine*, others *Firme*. I have no doubt that the correct reading is “of Pherme.” In Palladius, in the account of Abbot Paul, chapter 23, Pherme is a mountain in Egypt leading into the vast desert of Scetis, where five hundred monks practiced asceticism. It is also mentioned by Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 29, and by Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 36.

“Abraham Ortelius, in his *Geographical Treasury*, believes that this region is described by Philo in *On the Contemplative Life*, although Philo does not name it. This Theodore, therefore, is called ‘of Pherme’ to distinguish him from another Theodore, called ‘of the Ninth’ of Alexandria in Pelagius’s Booklet VII, no. 7, or ‘of Ennaton’ in Booklet XI, no. 10. Elsewhere Theodore is sometimes mentioned without qualification. Who can say whether this refers to one of these men or to a third?”]

He was said to have possessed these three principles above many others: possessing nothing, practicing abstinence, and avoiding people.

8. Abba John the Dwarf said: “I want a person to partake of every virtue. Therefore, rising each morning day by day, begin with every virtue, and keep God’s commandment with great patience, with fear and perseverance, in the love of God, with resolve of soul and body, and with great humility: in patience, in anguish of heart and watchfulness, in abundant prayer and supplications, with groanings; in purity and cleanliness of speech, and in guarding the eyes; suffering insult and not becoming angry; peaceful and not returning evil for evil; not paying attention to the faults of others, nor exalting yourself; but be subject and humbler than every creature, renouncing every bodily possession and the things that belong to the flesh, in affliction, in struggle, in humility of spirit, in good will and spiritual abstinence; in fasting, in patience, in weeping, in the struggle of combat, in discernment of judgment, in purity of soul, in perceiving what is good in quiet, and [Col. 0856A] in the work of your hands; in nightly vigils, in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness, in labors, shutting yourself in the tomb as though already dead, so that death may seem to you near every day.” [Col. 0855D]

9. Abba Joseph [Note: [Col. 0987C] Joseph. On this saying the same Friar John Maria, Master of the Sacred Palace, notes [Col. 0987D]: “Read cautiously; for it seems to suggest Evagrius’s impassibility. And whose works in this life have been so pure that they had nothing human mingled with them, except those of Christ and his Mother?”] the Theban said: “There are three honorable states in the sight of the Lord. The first is when a person falls ill, temptations are added to him, and he receives them with thanksgiving. The second is when someone performs all his works purely before God, having nothing human in him. The third is when someone sits in submission and obedience to his spiritual father and renounces all his own wishes.”

10. Abba Cassian related concerning a certain abba John, who was first of the community, that he had indeed been great in his way of life (Cassian, *Institutes*, book V, chapter 28). When he was about to die and depart joyfully and with a firm purpose of mind to the Lord, the brothers surrounded him, asking him to leave them, in place of an inheritance, some brief and saving word by which they might ascend to the perfection that is in Christ. But he groaned and said: “I have never done my own will, nor have I taught anyone anything that I had not first done myself.” [Col. 0856B]

11. A brother asked an old man, saying: “What good thing can I do and live in it?” The old man said to him: “God alone knows what is good. Nevertheless, I heard that one of the Fathers asked the great abba Nisteron, who was a friend of abba Antony, and said to him: ‘What good work should I do?’ He answered him: ‘All works are not equal. Scripture says (Genesis 18) that Abraham was hospitable, and God was with [563] him. Elijah loved quiet, and God was with him. David was humble, and God was with him. Therefore, whatever you see according to God’s will for your soul, do that, and guard your heart.’” [Col. 0856C]

12. Abba Pastor said: “To guard oneself, to examine oneself, and to possess discernment—these three are works of the soul.”

13. A certain brother asked him, saying: “How ought a person to conduct himself?” The old man answered him: “We saw Daniel, for no accusation was found against him except concerning the service that he rendered to his God.” [Col. 0856D]

14. He said again: “Poverty, affliction, and discernment—these are the works of the solitary life” (*Appendix to the Martyrdoms*, no. 8, under the heading “Moses”). For it is written (Ezekiel 14): “If these three men were present, Noah, Job, and Daniel”: Noah represents those who possess nothing; Job represents those who suffer affliction; Daniel represents those who discern. If, then, these three practices are found in a person, God dwells in him.

15. Abba Pastor said: “If a monk hates two things, he can be free from this world.” The brother said: “What are they?” The old man said: “Carnal ease and vain glory.” [Col. 0857A]

16. They said concerning abba Pambo (Rufinus, book III, no. 160) that at the very hour when he was departing this life, he said to the holy men standing around him: “From the time I came to this place of solitude, built myself a cell, and dwelt here, I do not remember having eaten bread except through the labor of my hands, nor do I repent of any word that I have spoken up to this hour. And thus I go to the Lord, as one who has not even begun to serve God.”

17. Abba Sisoes said: “Be despised, and cast your pleasures behind you; be free and secure from worldly cares, and you will have rest.”

18. When abba Chame was about to die, he said to his sons: “Do not dwell with heretics; do not associate with judges; and do not let your hands be open for gathering anything, but let them rather be extended for giving.” [Col. 0857B]

19. A brother asked an old man: “How does the fear of God come to a person?” The old man said: “If a person has humility and poverty, and does not judge another, the fear of the Lord comes into him” (Paschasius, chapter 21, no. 2).

20. The old man said: “Let fear, humility, lack of provisions, and mourning remain in you” (Paschasius, chapter 21, no. 3).

21. Some of the old men therefore said: “Whatever you hate, do not do to another” (Rufinus, book III, no. 153; Paschasius, chapter 16, no. 2). “If you hate one who speaks evil of you, do not speak evil of anyone yourself; if you hate one who slanders you, do not slander anyone yourself; if you hate one who brings you into disgrace, attacks you with insults, takes away what belongs to you, or does anything of this kind, do none of these things to anyone. Whoever, then, can keep this saying has enough for salvation.” [Col. 0857C]

22. The old man said: “The monk’s life consists in these things: works, obedience, meditation, and not judging, speaking against others, or grumbling. For it is written: ‘You who love the Lord, hate evil’ (Psalm 96). The monk’s life is this: not entering in with an unjust person; not seeing evil with his eyes; not acting inquisitively; not investigating; not listening to what belongs to others; not seizing with his hands, but rather giving; not being proud in heart; not entertaining wicked thoughts; not filling his belly; but doing everything with discernment. Behold, in these things is the monk.” [Col. 0857D]

23. The old man said: “Ask God to give mourning and humility to your heart; always look upon your sins, and do not judge others; but be subject to everyone. Do not have friendships with a woman, with a child, or with heretics. Cut off confidence in yourself, restrain your tongue and your belly, and abstain from wine. If someone speaks with you about any matter, do not argue with him. If he speaks well, say: ‘Yes.’ But if he speaks badly, say to him: ‘You know what you are saying.’ Do not argue with him about what he has said, and then your mind will be peaceful.”

## BOOK TWO. On Quiet

[Col. 0858A]

1. Abba Antony said: “Just as fish die if they remain too long on dry land, so monks who linger outside their cells or remain among worldly people are drawn away from their purpose of quiet” (Rufinus, book III, no. 109, under the name of Moses; and in the *Life of Antony*, chapter 52). Therefore, just as a fish returns to the sea, so we too ought to return to our cell, lest, by lingering outside, we forget the inner watchfulness.

2. He said again: “The one who sits in solitude and keeps quiet is delivered from three battles—that is, of hearing, speech, and sight—and will have only one battle, namely, that of the heart.”

3. While abba Arsenius (Rufinus, book III, no. 190) was still in the palace, he prayed to the Lord, saying: “Lord, guide me to salvation.” A voice came to him, saying: “Arsenius, flee from human beings, and you will be saved.” When he himself later withdrew to the monastic life, he prayed again, saying the same words. And he heard a voice saying to him: “Arsenius, flee, be silent, keep quiet; for these are the roots of not sinning.” [Col. 0858B]

4. Once Theophilus, archbishop of blessed memory, came to abba Arsenius with a certain judge (Rufinus, book III, no. 191). The archbishop questioned [564] the old man, wishing to hear a word from him. After remaining silent for a little while, the old man answered him, saying: “And if I speak to you, will you keep it?” They promised that they would. The old man said to them: “Wherever you hear that Arsenius is, do not approach.” [Col. 0858C]

On another occasion, when the archbishop wished to see him, he first sent someone to find out whether he would open the door to him. The old man sent him word, saying: “If you come, I will open to you. But if I open to you, I open to everyone, and then I will no longer sit here.” When the archbishop heard this, he said: “If I go in pursuit of him, I shall never again go to a holy man.”

5. Once abba Arsenius came to a certain place where there was a reed-bed, and it was being stirred by the wind. The old man said to the brothers: “What is this movement?” They said to him: “They are reeds.” The old man said to them: “Truly, if someone sits in quiet and hears the voice of a bird, his heart will not retain the same quiet; how much less when he hears the sound of these reeds?” [Col. 0858D]

6. They said concerning him that his cell was thirty-two miles away, and he did not go out quickly, but others performed services for him. When the place called Scetis was depopulated, he went out weeping and saying: “The world has lost Rome, and the monks have lost Scetis.”

7. Once, while the same abba Arsenius was sitting in Canopus (Rufinus, book III, no. 65), a Roman matron, a virgin, very rich and fearing God, came to see him, and the archbishop Theophilus received her. She asked him to arrange for her to see the old man. He went to him and asked, saying: “A certain matron has come from Rome and wishes to see you.” But the old man did not consent to her coming to him. When this was reported to the matron, she ordered the animals to be saddled, saying: “I believe in God that I shall see him. There are many people in our city also, but I have come to see prophets.” [Col. 0859A]

When she reached the old man’s cell, by God’s providence the old man happened to be outside the cell at that moment. When the matron saw him, she fell at his feet. But he raised her up indignantly and, looking at her, said: “If you wish to see my face, behold, look.” But out of shame she did not look at his face. The old man said to her: “Have you not heard of my way of life? This is what you ought to see. How did you dare undertake such a long voyage? Do you not know that you are a woman and ought not to go anywhere? Or is it so that you may go back to Rome and say to other women: ‘I saw Arsenius,’ and make the sea a road for women coming to me?” [Col. 0859B]

She said: “If God wills me to return to Rome, I will not allow anyone to come here. But pray for me and remember me always.” In reply he said to her: “Pray to God that he may erase the memory of you from my heart.” When she heard this, she departed troubled. When she reached the city, she began to suffer from a fever because of her grief. It was reported to the archbishop that she was ill, and he came to comfort her, asking what was wrong with her. She said to him: “Would that I had never come here! For I said to the old man, ‘Remember me,’ and he said to me, ‘Pray to God that the memory of you may be erased from my heart.’ And behold, I myself am dying of grief.” [Col. 0859C]

The archbishop said to her: “Do you not know that you are a woman, and that the enemy attacks holy men through women? Therefore the old man said this, for he is always praying for your soul.” Thus her mind was restored, and she departed joyfully to her own home.

8. Abba Evagrius said: “Cut off from yourself the attachments of many people, lest your mind be thrown into confusion and destroy the measure of quiet.”

9. A certain brother came to Scetis to abba Moses, asking him for a word. The old man said to him: “Go and sit in your cell, and your cell will teach you everything.”

10. Abba Moses said: “The person who flees from human beings is like a ripe grape; but the one who associates with human beings is like an unripe grape.”

11. Abba Nilus said: “The one who loves quiet remains impenetrable to the arrows of the enemy; but the one who mingles with the crowd will receive frequent wounds.”

[Col. 0859D]

12. Abba Pastor said: “The beginning of evils is to distract the mind.” He said again: “It is good to flee from bodily things. When a person is near bodily warfare, he is like a man standing above a very deep lake, so that whenever his enemy sees him, he can easily push him down. But if he is far from bodily things, he will be like a man positioned far from a well, so that even if his enemy drags him in order to throw him down, while he is dragging him violently, God directs help to him.”

On one occasion Abraham, the disciple of abba Sisoes, said to him: “Father, you have grown old; let us go out for a little while near the world.” Abba Sisoes said to him: “Let us go wherever there is no woman.” His disciple said to him: “And where is there a place without a woman, except perhaps in the desert?” The old man said to him: “Then take me into the desert.” [Col. 0860A]

14. Abbess Matrona said: “Many who were situated on the mountain and engaged in popular activities perished. It is better to be with many people while living a solitary life in one’s will than, while being alone, to be with a crowd in one’s purpose of mind.”

565 15. The old man said: “A monk ought always to purchase quiet for himself, even if a bodily loss should occur.”

16. Someone related: “Three diligent men who loved one another became monks. One of them chose to reconcile disputing people, in accordance with what is written: ‘Blessed are the peacemakers’ (Matthew 5). The second chose to visit the sick. The third went away to keep quiet in the desert.” [Col. 0860B]

“The first, laboring because of people’s disputes, could not heal everyone. Overcome by weariness, he came to the one who served the sick, and found him also failing in spirit and unable to fulfill the commandment. The two agreed together and went to see the one who had withdrawn into the desert, and they told him of their tribulations. They asked him to explain to them what progress he himself had made.

“He remained silent for a little while, then poured water into a cup and said to them: ‘Look at the water.’ It was turbid. After a short time he said again: ‘Look now at how clear the water has become.’ When they looked into the water, they saw their faces as though in a mirror. Then he said to them: ‘So it is with the one who lives among people: because of the disturbance, he does not see his sins. But when he has become quiet, and especially in solitude, then he sees his offenses.’” [Col. 0860C]

## BOOK THREE. On Compunction

1. They said concerning abba Arsenius that throughout his whole life, while sitting at his manual work, he kept a cloth in his lap because of the tears that frequently flowed from his eyes (Rufinus, book III, nos. 163, 211).

2. A certain brother asked abba Ammon, saying: “Tell me a word.” The old man said to him: “Go, and make your thoughts like those of the wicked who are in prison. For they ask people: ‘Where is the judge, and when will he come?’ And while awaiting their punishments they weep. Thus the monk also ought always to be apprehensive and rebuke his soul, saying: ‘Woe is me! How shall I stand before the tribunal of Christ, and how shall I give him an account of my deeds?’ If you always meditate in this way, you will be able to be saved.” [Col. 0860D]

3. Abba Evagrius said: “When you sit in your cell, gather your understanding to yourself, and remember the day of death. Then you will see the mortification of your body. Consider the destruction; accept the pain. Let the vanity of this world fill you with dread. Be modest and attentive, so that you may always remain in the same purpose of quiet, and you will not grow weak.

“Remember also those who are in hell. Consider within yourself what the souls there are like now: in what bitter silence, or with what terrible groaning, or in what fear and struggle, or in what expectation and pain; souls possessing innumerable tears without relief. [Col. 0861A]

“Remember also the day of resurrection, and imagine that divine, fearful, and terrible judgment. Bring before your mind the shame reserved for sinners, which they will suffer in the presence of Christ and God, before angels and archangels, powers, and all human beings; and also all the punishments—the eternal fire, the immortal worm, the darkness of Tartarus, and, above all these, the gnashing of teeth, fears, and torments.

“Bring before your mind also the good things reserved for the righteous: confidence before God the Father and his Son Christ, before angels and archangels and powers and the whole people; the kingdom of heaven and its gifts, joy and rest.

“Keep the remembrance of both before you. Over the judgments reserved for sinners, groan and weep; put on the appearance of mourning, fearing lest you too should fall into these things. But over the good things reserved for the righteous, rejoice, exult, and be glad. Hasten to enjoy the latter, and become a stranger to the former. See that you do not ever forget them, whether you are inside your cell or somewhere outside; and do not let your mind cast away their remembrance, so that through these things at least you may escape filthy and harmful thoughts.” [Col. 0861B]

4. Abba Elias said: “I fear three things: one, when my soul is about to depart from the body; another, when I am about to meet God; and the third, when sentence is about to be pronounced against me” (*Appendix to the Martyrdoms*, no. 97, under the heading “The Old Man”).

5. When Theophilus, archbishop of blessed memory, was about to die, he said: “Blessed are you, abba Arsenius, because you always kept this hour before your eyes.” [Col. 0861C]

6. The brothers said that once, while the brothers were eating together in charity, one brother laughed at the table. When abba John saw him, he wept, saying: “What do you think this brother has in his heart, that he laughed when he ought rather to have wept because he is eating charity?”

7. Abba James said: “Just as a lamp illuminates a dark room, so the fear of God, when it comes into a person’s heart, illuminates him and teaches him all the virtues and commandments of God.”

8. Some of the Fathers asked abba Macarius the Egyptian: “How is it that your body is so dry, both when you eat and when you fast?” The old man said to them: “Just as wood in a person’s hand, with which brushwood is turned and turned back in the fire, is continually consumed by the fire, so, if a person purifies his mind in the fear of God, that fear of God also consumes his bones.” [Col. 0861D]

9. Once the old men from Mount Nitria sent to abba Macarius in Scetis, asking him to come to them. Otherwise, he should know that the whole multitude would come to him if he did not come to them, because they desired to see him before he departed to the Lord.

When he came to the mountain, the entire multitude of the brothers gathered around him. The old men asked him to give a word to the brothers. Weeping, he said: “Let us weep, brothers, and let our eyes bring forth tears before we go from this place, where our tears burn our bodies.” They all wept and fell prostrate on their faces, saying: “Father, pray for us.” [Col. 0862A]

10. Once, while passing through Egypt, abba Pastor saw a woman sitting in a tomb and weeping bitterly, and he said: “If all the delights of this world were to come, they would not move her soul away from mourning. So also the monk ought always to have mourning within himself.”

11. On another occasion he was traveling with abba Anub in the region of Diolcos. When they came near the tombs, they saw a woman beating herself severely and weeping bitterly. They stood and watched her. After proceeding a little farther, they met someone, and abba Pastor asked him: “What is wrong with this woman, that she weeps so bitterly?” He said to him: “Her husband, son, and brother have died.” [Col. 0862B]

Abba Pastor replied to abba Anub: “I tell you that unless a person mortifies all the desires of his flesh and possesses this mourning, he cannot become a monk. For this woman’s whole life and mind are in mourning.”

12. Abba Pastor said again: “Mourning is twofold: it works, and it guards.”

13. A brother asked him (*Appendix to the Martyrdoms*, no. 34), saying: “What shall I do?” He said to him: “When Abraham came into the promised land, he acquired a tomb for himself, and through the grave he received the land as an inheritance.” The brother said to him: “What is the grave?” The old man said: “A place of weeping and mourning.”

14. Athanasius of blessed memory asked abba Pambo to come down from the desert to Alexandria [Note: [Col. 0861] Rufinus, book III, no. 164. A similar account occurs in the *Life of Pelagia*, chapter 3.]. When he had come down, he saw there a theatrical woman, and he wept. Those who were present asked him why he had wept, and he said: “Two things moved me. One was her destruction; the other, that I do not possess such zeal to please God as she possesses to please disgraceful men.” [Col. 0862C]

15. Once abba Silvanus was sitting with the brothers, and he fell into an ecstasy of mind and fell on his face (Rufinus, book III, no. 205; *Appendix to the Martyrdoms*, no. 48). After a long time he rose, weeping. The brothers asked him, saying: “What is wrong, Father?” But he remained silent and wept. When they pressed him, he said to them: “I was carried away to the judgment, and I saw many of those wearing our habit going to torments, and many worldly people going to the kingdom.” [Col. 0862D]

The old man mourned and did not wish thereafter to leave his cell. But if he was forced to go out, he covered his face with his hood, saying: “Why is it necessary to see this temporal light, in which there is nothing useful?”

16. Syncletica of blessed memory said: “There is labor and great struggle for the impious who turn to God, and afterward unspeakable joy. Just as those who wish to kindle a fire are first filled with smoke and weep because of the irritation of the smoke, and thus obtain what they desire, so it is with us. For it is written: ‘Our God is a consuming fire.’ Therefore we too ought to kindle the divine fire within ourselves with tears and labors.”

17. Abba Hyperichius said: “Night and day the monk labors, keeping vigil and remaining in prayers; and by pricking his heart he brings forth tears and more quickly calls forth the mercy of God.” [Col. 0863A]

18. The brothers came to abba Felix, bringing with them some worldly people, and asked him to give them a word. The old man remained silent. When they continued asking him for a long time, he said to them: “Do you wish to hear a word?” They answered: “Yes, Father.” The old man therefore said: “Now there is no word. In former times, when the elders were asked questions and the brothers did what they told them, God granted them what to say. But now, since some ask questions without doing what they hear, God has taken grace away from the elders, so that they do not find what to say, because there is no one who practices what is taught.” [Col. 0863B]

When the brothers heard this, they groaned, saying: “Pray for us, Father.”

19. They related concerning abba Hor [Note: [Col. 0987C] Hor. Here Friar John Maria, Master of the Sacred Palace, notes concerning the passage above: “This is that heretical Hor, the Origenist, whom Saint Jerome mentions in his letter to Ctesiphon, and whom wretched Evagrius attempted to pass off as a saint” (rather, Rufinus, as I have shown in the general prolegomenon 4). “For this reason, the shadows of his virtues have vanished into the wind.”] and abba Theodorus that they had placed a goatskin in their cell and said to one another: “If God visits us now, what shall we do?” And weeping, they left the place made of bricks and withdrew to their cells (*Appendix to the Martyrdoms*, no. 47).

20. An old man related that when a certain brother wished to convert, his mother opposed him (Rufinus, book III, no. 216). He did not cease from his purpose, saying: “I wish to save [567] my soul.” She resisted him strongly, but when she could not prevent his desire, she eventually gave permission.

He went away, became a monk, and spent his life negligently. It happened that his mother died, and after some time he himself fell ill with a serious illness. When he fell into an ecstasy of mind, he was carried away to judgment, and found his mother among those being judged. [Col. 0863C]

When she saw him, she was astonished and said: “What is this, my son? Have you too been condemned and ordered to come to this place? Where are the words you used to say: ‘I wish to save my soul’?”

Confounded by what he had heard, he became numb with grief and stood there, unable to answer his mother. But, through God’s merciful providence, after he had seen these things, it happened that he recovered and escaped the illness that threatened him. [Col. 0863D]

Considering within himself that this vision had been divinely given, he shut himself in thereafter and sat, thinking about his salvation, repenting and weeping over what he had previously done in negligence. His fervor was so great that, although many asked him to relax a little lest he suffer some injury from the excessive weeping he poured forth, he refused to be comforted, saying: “If I could not endure the reproach of my mother, how shall I be able to endure the shame brought against me by Christ and his holy angels on the day of judgment?”

21. The old man said: “If, at God’s coming after the resurrection, it were possible for human souls to perish from fear, the whole world would die from terror and dread. For what will it be like to see the heavens torn open, and God revealed with wrath and indignation, and innumerable hosts of angels, and the whole human race gathered together and looking on? Therefore we ought to live in such a way that we are those from whom God will demand an account of every one of our movements.” [Col. 0864A]

22. A brother asked the old man (Paschasius, chapter 21, no. 4; *Appendix to the Martyrdoms*, no. 22), saying: “Why, abba, is my heart hard, and why do I not fear the Lord?” The old man said to him: “I think that if a person holds rebuke in his heart, he will possess fear.”

The brother said to him: “What is rebuke?” The old man said: “It is for a person to rebuke his soul in every matter, saying to it: ‘Remember that you must meet God.’ Say this also: ‘What have I to do with human beings?’ I think that if someone remains in these things, the fear of God will come to him.”

23. The old man saw someone laughing and said to him: “We shall give an account of our whole life before the Lord of heaven and earth, and you are laughing?” [Col. 0864B]

24. The old man said: “Just as we carry the shadow of our bodies everywhere with us, so we ought to carry weeping and compunction with us wherever we are.”

25. A brother asked the old man, saying: “Abba, tell me a word.” The old man said to him: “When God struck Egypt, there was no house without mourning.”

26. A brother asked another old man, saying: “What shall I do?” The old man said: “We ought always to weep.”

For it happened that once an old man died and, after a long time, returned again to himself. We questioned him, saying: “What did you see there, abba?” Weeping, he related to us: “I heard a mournful voice there, without ceasing, saying: ‘Woe is me, woe is me.’ So we too ought always to say this.” [Col. 0864C]

27. A certain brother asked the old man, saying: “How is it that my soul desires tears, as I hear the old men weeping, but they do not come, and they afflict my soul?” The old man said: “The children of Israel entered the promised land after forty years. Tears, then, are like the promised land: if you reach them, you will no longer fear warfare. For God wishes the soul to be afflicted in such a way that it always desires to enter that land.”

## BOOK FOUR. On Continence

1. Some brothers wishing to come to abba Antony from Scetis entered a ship to go to him. They found in the same ship an old man who also wished to go to Antony, but the brothers did not know him. [Col. 0864D]

As they sat in the ship, they spoke of the sayings of the Fathers, of the Scriptures, and again of their manual work. But the old man remained completely silent. When they reached the harbor, they recognized that the old man too was going to abba Antony.

When they came to him, abba Antony said to them: “You have found a good traveling companion in this old man.” He also said to the old man: “You have found good brothers with you, abba.” The old man said to him: “They are good indeed, but their dwelling has no door. Whoever wishes enters the stable and unties the donkey.” He said this because whatever came into their hearts, they spoke with their mouths.

[Col. 0865A]

2. Abba Daniel said concerning abba Arsenius that he would pass the night keeping vigil (Rufinus, book III, no. 211). For he kept vigil all night, and when, toward morning, he wished to sleep because of bodily nature, he said to sleep: “Come, wicked servant,” and he stole a little sleep while sitting; then he immediately rose. 568

3. Abba Arsenius said: “It is enough for a monk to sleep one hour, provided that he is a warrior.”

4. Abba Daniel said concerning him: “He remained with us for so many years, and each year we gave him a small measure of food; and whenever we came, we ate from it as well.”

5. He said again that he changed the water of the palms only once a year, merely adding more to it (Rufinus, book III, no. 39). He also made a braided mat from those palms [Note: [Col. 0987D] A braided mat made from palms. The word *plecta* occurs frequently in these books, sometimes *plecta*, apparently from the Greek πλεκτόν (*plektón*, “braided”), and sometimes *flecta*. These are straps woven from palm, reed, broom, or a similar material, from which baskets, hampers, and other such objects are made. The Egyptians call them σειρές (*seirés*). See Cassian, *Conference* XVIII, chapter 15. [Col. 0988A]] and sewed [Note: [Col. 0988A] “And sewed.” Some manuscripts read *cusibat*. This is absent from the Paris edition. After twisting and preparing the palm braid, they wove baskets from those braids and sewed them together. The translator renders this *cusare* or *cusire*, “to sew,” like the French *coudre*. Elsewhere in these books this word will also occur.] until the sixth hour. [Col. 0865B]

The elders therefore asked him why he did not change the water of the palms, which stank. He said to them: “In place of the incense and the fragrant perfumes that I used in the world, I must now use this stench.”

6. He said again: “When he heard that every kind of fruit had ripened, he said: ‘Bring them to me.’ He tasted a little of everything only once, giving thanks to God.”

7. They said concerning abba Agathon that for three years he put a stone in his mouth, until he learned silence.

8. Once abba Agathon was traveling with his disciples (*Appendix to the Martyrdoms*, no. 6). One of them found a small bundle of green chickpeas on the road and said to the old man: “Father, if you order me, I will pick it up.” But the old man looked at him in astonishment and said: “Did you put it there?” The brother answered him: “No.” The old man said: “How do you wish to take what you did not put there?” [Col. 0865C]

9. Once one of the old men came to abba Achilles (Rufinus, book III, no. 90) and saw him spitting blood from his mouth. He asked him, saying: “What is this, Father?” The old man said: “It is the word of a certain brother who saddened me, and I tried very hard to retain it within myself. I begged God that it might be taken away from me, and that word became blood in my mouth. Behold, I have spat it out, and I have found rest, and I have forgotten that pain.”

10. Once abba Achilles came to the cell of abba Isaiah in Scetis and found him eating. He had put salt and water in a small bowl. When he saw that Isaiah had hidden it behind the palm braids, he said to him: “Tell me what you were eating.” He replied: “Forgive me, abba, for I was cutting palms and became overheated [Note: [Col. 0988A] “I became overheated.” That is, “I grew hot.” He uses in Latin the Greek καῦμα (*kaûma*, “heat”), which you will also find elsewhere here. Thus shortly afterward, no. 17: “He stood in the heat and cooled himself in the sun.”]. Therefore I dipped a morsel in salt and put it in my mouth, because my throat had dried out. Since the morsel that I had put in my mouth would not go down, I was compelled to pour a little water over the salt, so that I might swallow it even in this way. But forgive me.” [Col. 0865D]

Abba Achilles said: “Come and see Isaiah eating broth in Scetis. If you want to eat broth, go to Egypt.”

11. They said concerning abba Ammoy that he fell ill and, lying in bed for many years, never relaxed his mind enough to look into the inner parts of his cell and see what he possessed. For many things were brought to him as to a sick man; but whenever his disciple John entered and left, he kept his eyes closed so that he would not see what John was doing. For he knew that John was a faithful monk. [Col. 0866A]

12. Abba Benjamin, who was a presbyter in the Cells, said that when he had come to Scetis to a certain old man and wished to give him a little oil, the old man said to him: “Behold that little vessel which you brought me three years ago; and just as you placed it, so it has remained.” When we heard this, we marveled at the old man’s way of life.

13. They related concerning abba Dioscorus of Namisias that his bread was barley bread and his flour was lentil flour. Each year he imposed upon himself a rule of one particular observance: either not to meet anyone for a year, or not to speak, or not to taste anything cooked, or not to eat any fruit or vegetables. In all his work he acted in this way. When he completed each practice, he took up another, doing this year by year. [Col. 0866B]

14. Abba Evagrius said that an old man had said: “For this reason I cut off carnal pleasures from myself, so that I may also cut off the occasions of anger. For I know that anger always fights against me for the sake of pleasures, disturbs my mind, and drives away my understanding.”

15. Bishop Epiphanius of Cyprus once sent word to Abba Hilarion, asking him and saying: “Come, so that we may see one another before we depart from the body.” When they had come together, while they were eating, some poultry was brought. The bishop took a piece and gave it to Abba Hilarion. The old man said to him: “Forgive me, Father, for ever since I received this habit I have eaten nothing that has been killed.” Epiphanius said to him: “But ever since I received this habit, I have neither allowed anyone who had anything against me to go to sleep, nor have I myself gone to sleep while holding anything against anyone.” The old man said to him: “Forgive me, for your way of life is greater than mine.”

16. They said of Abba Elladius [Note: [Col. 0988A] Elladius. Older editions: Palladius.] that he spent twenty years in a cell and never raised his eyes upward to see its roof.

[Col. 0866D] 569

17. Abba Zeno was once walking in Palestine (Ruffinus, Book II, no. 7). When he became weary, he sat down to eat beside a cucumber plot. His mind began to persuade him, saying: “Take one cucumber for yourself and eat it.” But he answered his thought: “Thieves go to torments. Test yourself in this matter, then, to see whether you can endure torments.” He rose and stood in the burning heat for five days, scorching himself in the sun, saying—as though his mind were speaking to itself—“I cannot endure torments.” So he said to his mind: “If you cannot endure torments, then do not steal in order to eat.”

18. Abba Theodorus [Al.: Theodotus] said: “Lack of bread wastes away a monk’s body.” Another elder said: “The body wastes away even more through vigils.”

19. Abba John, who was short in stature, said: “If a king wishes to take possession of an enemy city, he first controls its water and the provisions of those in the city; then, when they are endangered by hunger, they submit to him. So it is also with the passion of the belly. If a person lives in fasting and hunger, his enemies, who trouble his soul, become weak” (Ruffinus, Book III, no. 66, under the name of Moses).

20. He said again: “Once, as I was going up along the road leading to Scetis, carrying palm-leaf plaits, I saw a camel-driver speaking and provoking me to anger. I dropped what I was carrying and fled” (Appendix to the Martyrdom, no. 12).

21. Abba Isaac, priest of the Cells, said: “I know of a brother who was reaping in a field and wanted to eat an ear of wheat. He said to the owner of the field: ‘Do you want me to eat one ear?’ When the man heard this, he was astonished and said to him: ‘Father, the field is yours, and you ask me?’ Such was the scrupulousness of that brother.”

22. One of the brothers asked Abba Isidore, the elder of Scetis (Ruffinus, Book III, no. 89, under the name of Isaac): “Why are the demons so greatly afraid of you?” The old man said to him: “Ever since I became a monk, I have taken care not to allow anger to rise as far as my throat.”

23. He said again that for more than forty years he had felt the movement of sin in his mind, but had never consented either to lust or to anger.

[Col. 0867C]

24. Abba Cassian told of a certain Abba John who had lived with Abba Esius [Note: [Col. 0988A] Esius. In Cassian, Institutes, Book V, chapter 27, the name is Paesius or Phesius.] at the summit of the desert for forty years [Note: [Col. 0867D] In Cassian, Institutes, Book V, chapter 27. Something similar appears above, Book IV, chapter 5.]. Because he had great affection for him, and because of the confidence arising from that affection, he asked him: “After living so long in such seclusion, easily suffering harassment from no one, tell me: what progress have you made?” He replied: “Ever since I began to live alone, the sun has never seen me eating.” Abba John said to him: “Nor has it seen me angry.”

25. He said again: “Abba Moses told us that Abba Serapion said to him: ‘When I was young and sat with my abba, Theona, and we were eating, I rose from the meal and, following the devil’s works, stole a piece of paximate bread [Note: [Col. 0988A] Paximate bread. Elsewhere, paxamatem. It was bread of a definite weight provided for the monks’ meals in Egypt. See the Onomasticon.] and ate it secretly, without my abba knowing [Note: [Col. 0868D] Cassian, Conferences, II, chapter 11. Above, Book IV, chapter 47.]. After I continued doing this for some time, the vice began to dominate me, and I could not overcome myself. I was merely condemned by my own conscience, and I was ashamed to tell the old man.

“‘It happened, by the providence of the merciful God, that some people came to the old man for the benefit of their souls and asked him about their thoughts. The old man answered them: “Nothing is so harmful to monks, and so pleasing to demons, as concealing their thoughts from spiritual Fathers.” He also spoke to them about continence. While these things were being said, I thought that God had revealed my situation to the old man. I was pierced with remorse and began to weep. I took from my bosom the paximate which I had wrongly made a habit of stealing, and, prostrating myself on the floor, asked forgiveness for the past and prayer for caution in the future.

“‘Then the old man said: “My son, even though I remained silent, your confession has freed you from this captivity; and by confessing now against yourself, you have killed the demon that darkened your heart through silence—the demon you had until now allowed to dominate you, neither contradicting nor rebuking it in any way. From now on it will have no place in you, since it has been driven out of your heart into the open.”

“‘Before the old man had finished speaking, the truth of his words appeared in action: something like a fiery lamp came out of my bosom and filled the whole house with a foul odor, so that those present thought that a great quantity of sulfur had been burned. The old man said: “My son, by the sign that has occurred, the Lord has provided proof of my words and of your deliverance.”’”

26. They said of Abba Macarius that, when he was free among the brothers, he set himself a limit: whenever wine was found and he drank it for the brothers’ sake, he would not drink water for an entire day for each cup of wine (Ruffinus, Book III, no. 53). The brothers, wishing to refresh him, would give him wine. The old man accepted it joyfully, so that he might afterward afflict himself. But his disciple, knowing the reason, said to the brothers: “For God’s sake, do not give him any, because afterward in his cell he subjects himself to torture.” When the brothers learned this, they no longer gave him wine.

27. The elder Abba Macarius of Scetis said to the brothers after the dismissal from church: “Flee, brothers.” One of the brothers said to him: “Father, where can we flee farther than from this solitude?” He put his finger to his lips and said: “This is what I mean we must flee.” Then he entered his cell, closed the door, and sat alone.

28. Abba Macarius also said: “If, wishing to rebuke someone, you provoke him to anger, you are satisfying your own passion. Do not lose yourself in trying to save another.”

29. Abba Pastor said: “If Nabuzardan, the chief cook, had not come, the temple of the Lord would not have been burned with fire (2 Kings 25). So also, unless indulgence of throat and belly enters the soul, the mind will by no means fall while fighting against the enemy” (Ruffinus, Book III, no. 52).

30. They said of Abba Pastor that when he was summoned to eat, he went against his will, weeping, lest he disobey his brothers and grieve them (Ruffinus, Book III, no. 149).

31. Some people told Abba Pastor about a monk who did not drink wine. He said to them: “Wine is absolutely not for monks.”

32. Abba Pastor said again: “Just as bees are driven away by smoke so that the sweetness of their labor may be taken, so bodily ease drives the fear of the Lord from the soul and removes from it every good work.”

33. An elder told of Abba Pastor and his brothers, who lived in Egypt (Ruffinus, Book III, no. 154). Their mother desired to see them but could not. One day she kept watch, and when they were going to church she presented herself to them. When they saw her, they turned back to their cell, entered, and shut the door in her face.

She stood at the door crying and weeping with great compassion. Abba Anub heard her and went in to Abba Pastor, saying: “What shall we do with this old woman, who is weeping so before the door?” Abba Pastor rose, came to the door, and, standing inside, heard her weeping most bitterly. He said: “Why are you crying so, old woman?”

When she heard his voice, she cried out all the more, weeping and saying: “I want to see you, my sons. What does it matter if I see you? Am I not your mother? Did I not nurse you, and am I not now completely gray with age? Yet even hearing your voice has distressed me.”

The old man said to her: “Do you want to see us here, or in the age to come?” She replied: “And if I do not see you here, shall I see you there, my sons?” He said to her: “If you can bear calmly not to see us here, you will see us there.” So the woman departed rejoicing and saying: “If I shall certainly see you there, I do not want to see you here.”

34. They said of Abba Pior that he ate while walking (Ruffinus, Book III, no. 31). When someone asked him why he ate in this way, he replied that he did not do it as some kind of task, but used it as something superfluous. To another who asked him about it he replied: “So that the soul may not have bodily pleasure even while eating.”

35. They said of Abba Peter, surnamed Pionius, who was in the Cells, that he did not drink wine. When he grew old, they asked him to take a little wine. Since he did not agree, they warmed water and offered it to him. He said: “Believe me, children, I receive it as though it were a condiment.” He resolved to be content with warm water.

36. Once a celebration of the liturgy took place on the mountain of Abba Antony, and a little wine was found there. One of the elders took a small cup, carried it to Abba Sisoes, and gave it to him. He drank once; then he received it a second time and drank. The man brought it to him a third time, but he did not accept it, saying: “Stop, brother. Do you not know that it is Satan?”

37. A brother asked Abba Sisoes: “What shall I do? Whenever I come to church, the brothers often detain me out of charity for a meal.” The old man said to him: “It is a burdensome matter.” His disciple Abraham said: “If a brother is met on the Sabbath and Sunday on the way to church, and he drinks three cups, is that not much?” The old man said: “If Satan did not exist, it would not be much.”

38. The disciple often said to Abba Sisoes: “Rise, abba; let us eat.” He replied: “Have we not eaten yet, my son?” The disciple answered: “No, Father.” The old man said: “If we have not yet eaten, bring something; let us eat.”

39. Abba Sisoes once said confidently: “Believe me: for thirty years now I have not asked God concerning sin, but while praying I say: ‘Lord Jesus Christ, protect me from my tongue.’ And to this day I fall through it [Note: [Col. 0988B] “I fall through it.” The Paris edition reads: “I care for those works themselves,” which is not correct.] and sin.”

40. Abba Silvanus and his disciple Zacharias once came to a monastery, and the monks made them taste a little food before they departed (Ruffinus, Book III, no. 46). As they were leaving, his disciple found water along the road and wanted to drink. Abba Silvanus said: “Zacharias, today is a fast day.” He replied: “Have we not eaten today, Father?” The old man said to him: “That eating was charity; but let us keep our fast, my son.”

571

41. Saint Syncletica said: “We who have undertaken such a way of life must preserve chastity, which is supreme. Chastity even appears to be observed among worldly people; but folly accompanies it, on account of which they sin with all their other senses. They look indecently and laugh without restraint.”

42. She said again: “Just as venomous animals drive away stronger medicines from themselves, so fasting with prayer drives an impure thought from the soul.”

43. She said again: “Let not the delicacies of the rich of this world deceive you, as though they contained something useful. They honor the art of preparing food in various ways for the sake of pleasure. But by fasting and rejection of foods, surpass the abundance of their delights. Do not be satisfied with bread, and do not desire wine.”

44. Abba Sisoes said: “Our exile is that a person should keep his mouth” (Paschasius, chapter 32, no. 4; Appendix to the Martyrdom, no. 72).

45. Abba Hyperichius said: “Just as a lion is terrifying to wild asses, so an approved monk is terrifying to thoughts of lust.”

46. He said again: “Fasting is a bridle for the monk against sin. Whoever rejects fasting is carried away like a horse burning with desire for a woman.”

47. He said again: “The body of a monk dried out by fasting raises the soul from the depths, and the monk’s fasting dries up the channels of pleasure.”

48. He said again: “The chaste monk will be honored on earth and crowned in heaven by the Most High.”

49. The same man said: “A monk who does not restrain his tongue in a time of anger [Note: [Col. 0988B] “His tongue in a time of anger.” The Paris edition reads: “the excess of dew,” which has no meaning.] will at some time also fail to restrain bodily passions.”

50. He said again: “Let your mouth not utter an evil word, for a vine does not bear thorns.”

51. He said again: “It is better to eat meat and drink wine than to eat the flesh of the brothers through slander” (Ruffinus, Book III, no. 134).

52. He said again: “The whispering serpent drove Eve out of paradise. Like him is the person who speaks against his neighbor, for he destroys the soul of the one who listens to him and does not save his own.”

53. Once there was a festival in Scetis, and they gave an old man wine in a cup. Rejecting it, he said: “Take this death away from me.” When the others who were eating with him saw this, they too did not drink.

54. On another occasion a small vessel of wine from the first-fruits was brought there to be distributed to the brothers, a cup for each. A certain brother entered, and when he saw that they were receiving wine, he fled into a crypt; the crypt collapsed. When they heard the sound, they ran and found the brother lying half-dead, and they began to rebuke him, saying: “It serves you right, because you had vainglory.”

But the abba restored him and said: “Leave my son alone; he has done a good work.” And, as the Lord lives, this crypt will not be rebuilt in my lifetime, so that the world may know that in Scetis a crypt collapsed because of a cup of wine.

55. A priest once went up from Scetis to the bishop of Alexandria. When he returned to Scetis, the brothers asked him: “How is the city?” He said to them: “Believe me, brothers, I saw no human face there except the bishop’s.”

When they heard this, they were astonished and said: “What do you think happened to all that multitude?” The priest reassured them in their perplexity, saying: “I forced my mind not to look upon a human face.” The brothers profited from this account and guarded themselves against lifting up their eyes.

56. An old man once came to another old man. The latter said to his disciple: “Make us a little lentil stew.” He did so. “And soak some bread for us.” He soaked it. They remained like this until the following day at the sixth hour, speaking about spiritual matters.

Again the old man said to his disciple: “Make us a little lentil stew, my son.” He replied: “I made it yesterday.” So they rose and ate.

57. Another old man came to one of the Fathers. The latter cooked a little lentil stew and said: “Let us do the work of God and taste it.” One of them completed the entire Psalter; the other recited two of the major prophets from memory [Note: [Col. 0988B] “From memory.” A Gallicism, *par coeur*, that is, by heart. Likewise in Book X, no. 91, in the same Pelagius: “We completed David from memory.” Hildegard, 642, in her explanation of the Rule of Saint Benedict: “They shall recite the readings mentioned above from memory and by heart, that is, without a book, since they are short.” Similarly, in Greek, ἀπὸ στήθους λέγειν (“to speak from the breast,” i.e. from memory) and ἀποστηθίζειν (“to learn by heart”).] in the order used by a reader. When morning came, the old man who had arrived departed, and they forgot to eat.

58. A brother was hungry from morning onward and struggled with his mind so as not to eat until the third hour (Ruffinus, Book III, no. 4). When the third hour came, he compelled himself to wait until the sixth. He soaked some bread and sat down to eat. Then he rose and said: “I shall remain like this until the ninth hour.”

At the ninth hour he prayed and saw the devil’s work departing from him like smoke. Thus his hunger ceased.

59. One of the elders fell ill (Ruffinus, Book III, no. 51). Since he could not take food for many days, his disciple begged him to allow something to be prepared for him so that he might be refreshed. The disciple went and made a little lentil stew from flour, together with zippulae [Note: [Col. 0988B] “Zippulae.” This is the reading of most manuscripts and printed editions. In the Vedastine manuscript it is *pulmentum*. Above, in Ruffinus, Book III, no. 51, in this same story, the word is *placentas*. Perhaps *zippulae*, *sippulae*, or *sipulae*, from the old verb *sipare*? See the Onomasticon.].

There was hanging there a small vessel containing a little honey, and another containing *raphanelaeum* [Note: [Col. 0988B–C] “Raphanelaeum.” The Paris edition: “oil pressed from flaxseed.” The old edition: *rafenealion*, that is, flax oil. Why not oil from the radish, as in Pliny, Book XIX, chapter 5? See the Onomasticon.], which smelled so foul that it was useful only for a lamp. The brother made a mistake and put *raphanelaeum* into the stew instead of honey.

572

When the old man tasted it, he said nothing but silently ate. The disciple continued to urge him to eat. He forced himself and ate, and the disciple gave him a third serving. The old man did not want to eat, saying: “Truly, I cannot, my son.”

The disciple encouraged him, saying: “It is good, abba. Look, I am eating with you.” When he tasted it and realized what he had done, he fell on his face, saying: “Woe is me, Father, for I have killed you, and you have placed this sin upon me by not speaking.”

The old man said to him: “Do not be distressed, my son. If God had wished me to eat honey, you should have put honey into these zippulae.”

60. They told of an old man who once desired to eat a cucumber (Ruffinus, Book III, no. 50). When he had obtained one, he first hung it before his eyes. Since he had not been overcome by the desire, he disciplined himself and did penance merely because he had desired it.

61. A brother once went to visit his sister, who was ill in a monastery (Ruffinus, Book III, no. 33). She was exceptionally faithful. At one point she refused to see a man and would not give her brother an occasion to come among women on her account. She sent word to her brother: “Go, brother, and pray for me, for by Christ’s grace I shall see you in the kingdom of heaven.”

62. A monk encountered some servants of God on a journey. When he saw them, he turned aside from the road. The abbess said to him: “If you were a perfect monk, you would not look at us in such a way as to recognize that we were women.”
