63. Some brothers once entered Alexandria, invited by Archbishop Theophilus, so that, in their presence and after prayer, he might destroy the temples of the pagans. While they were eating with the archbishop, veal was served, and they ate without distinguishing what it was.

The archbishop took a piece of meat [Note: [Col. 0988C] “Piece of meat.” The Paris edition reads *compadium*. The older German editions have, in the following word, *capadium*, that is, “a little piece.” The German translation conveys the matter. Nevertheless, I think *copadium* should be written, from Greek κοπάδιον (“a small cut piece”), from ἀκόπτω (“to cut”), whence the French *couper*, “to cut.” Yet it seems that *compadium* was also read long ago. A manuscript of the Camberon Glossary: “*Compadium*, a stew, so called as though *compan ium*, because it is eaten with bread,” with N changed into D. Thus each person invented an etymology for himself.] and gave it to an old man reclining beside him, saying: “Here is a good piece of meat; eat, abba.”

They replied: “Until now we thought that we were eating vegetables. If this is meat, we do not eat it.” And none of them would agree to taste any more.

64. A brother brought fresh bread into his cell and invited the elders to the table. After they had each eaten one paximate, they stopped. Knowing the labor of their abstinence, the brother began humbly to plead, saying: “For God’s sake, eat today until you are satisfied.”

So they ate ten more paximates each. Behold, then, how much more than was necessary the true monks, who practiced simple abstinence, ate for God’s sake.

65. One of the elders once fell seriously ill, so that he discharged a great deal of blood from his bowels. A brother brought dried nixas [Note: [Col. 0988C] “Dried nixas.” The Camberon Glossary says: “*Nixa* is a kind of tree, so called from the likeness of its fruit to *enixa*.” This was derived in outline from Isidore’s *Etymologies*, Book XVII, chapter 7. See the Onomasticon.], made them into a porridge, put them into it, and offered it to the old man, begging him and saying: “Eat, for perhaps it will benefit you.”

The old man gazed at him for a long time and said: “Truly I tell you, I wished God would allow me to remain in this illness for another thirty years.” The old man would in no way agree to take even a little food in such an illness, so that the brother took away what he had brought and returned to his cell.

66. Another old man lived far out in the desert. It happened that a brother came to him and found him ill. The brother washed his face and prepared a meal for him from what he had brought. When the old man saw this, he said: “Truly, brother, I had forgotten that human beings find comfort in food.”

The brother also offered him a cup of wine. When the old man saw it, he wept and said: “I did not expect that I would drink wine until death.”

67. An old man decided not to drink for forty days. Whenever the burning heat came, he washed a small water vessel [Note: [Col. 0988C] “Small water vessel.” This reading is consistently found in all the books. A manuscript of the Camberon Glossary: “*Suriscula*, a water vessel.” It is not correct to read, in the Glosses of Isidore, as printed by Bonaventure Vulcanius, *sirascula*, “a water vessel.” Read *suriscula*.], filled it with water, and hung it before his eyes.

When the brothers asked him why he did this, he replied: “So that, while seeing what I desired, I may not taste it; thus I may endure greater ardor and, because of this, may deserve to obtain a greater reward from the Lord.”

68. A brother was traveling with his elderly mother. When they came to a river, the old woman could not cross it. Her son took his cloak, wrapped it around his hands so that he would not in any way touch his mother’s body, and carried her across the river.

His mother said to him: “Why did you cover your hands in this way, my son?” He replied: “Because a woman’s body is fire. From the very moment I touched you, the remembrance of other women came into my mind.”

[Col. 0873C]

69. One of the Fathers said that he knew of a brother who fasted throughout the whole week of Easter. When he came late on Saturday to the liturgy, he received communion and immediately fled, lest the brothers compel him to eat in the church. At home he ate only a little boiled beetroot with salt, without bread.

70. The brothers were assembled at Scetis to eat dates. One of them was ill from excessive abstinence and, coughing, spat out phlegm, which, against his will, landed on another brother.

When his thought compelled him to say: “Stop now, and do not spit on me,” in order to overcome his thoughts he took what he had spat out, put it into his mouth, and immediately ate it.

573

Then he began to say to himself: “Either do not say to your brother anything that would grieve him, or eat what you abhor.”

# BOOK FIVE  
## On Fornication

Abba Antony said: “I think that the body has within it a natural movement, which does not act when the mind does not will it, but is merely signified in the body, as a movement without passion.

“There is another movement, arising from the fact that the body is nourished and strengthened by food and drink, through which the heat of the blood arouses the body to action. Therefore the Apostle says: ‘Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery’ (Ephesians 5). And again, in the Gospel, the Lord commanded his disciples, saying: ‘Take care lest your hearts at any time become weighed down with carousing and drunkenness’ (Luke 21).

“There is yet another movement that comes upon those who struggle in the monastic life through the ambushes and envy of demons. Therefore it is necessary to know that there are three bodily movements: one natural; another arising from an abundance of food; and the third from demons.”

2. Abba Gerontius of Petra said: “Many who have been tempted by bodily pleasures, although they did not approach bodies, have fornicated in their minds; while preserving bodily virginity, they fornicate according to the soul. Therefore, beloved, it is good to do what is written: ‘With all vigilance guard each person’s heart’ (Proverbs 5).”

3. Abba Cassian said (Cassian, *Conferences*, II, chapter 10) that Abba Moses had told us: “It is good not to conceal thoughts, but to reveal them to spiritual elders who possess discernment—not to those who are merely old in years. For many who looked only at age and disclosed their thoughts to people without experience reached utter despair instead of consolation.”

4. There was a certain brother who was extremely diligent in the monastic life (Cassian, *Conferences*, II, chapter 13). When he was severely troubled by the demon of fornication, he came to an old man and reported his thoughts to him.

When the old man, being without experience, heard this, he was indignant and called the brother wretched and unworthy of the monastic habit, since he admitted such thoughts. When the brother heard this, he despaired of himself, left his cell, and was returning to the world.

By God’s providence, Abba Apollo met him. Seeing him disturbed and exceedingly sad, he asked him: “My son, what is the cause of your great sadness?” At first, because of his profound confusion, the brother gave him no answer. But after the old man had questioned him at length about what was happening to him, he confessed, saying:

“Thoughts of fornication trouble me. I confessed this to that old man, and, according to his words, I now have no hope of salvation. Therefore, despairing of myself, I am returning to the world.”

When Father Apollo heard this, like a wise physician he earnestly entreated and admonished him, saying: “Do not be astonished, my son, and do not despair of yourself. For at my age and in this way of life I too am greatly troubled by such thoughts. Do not therefore faint in this circumstance, which is cured not so much by human effort as by God’s mercy. Grant me only what I ask today, and return to your cell.”

The brother did so. Abba Apollo then left him and went to the cell of the old man who had driven him to despair. Standing outside, he entreated the Lord with tears, saying:

“Lord, who beneficially bringest temptations upon us, turn the battle that this brother suffers against this old man, so that by experience in his old age he may learn what over a long time he has not learned, namely, to sympathize with those troubled by such temptations.”

When he had finished praying, he saw an Ethiopian standing beside the cell and shooting arrows at the old man. As though pierced by them, the old man was immediately carried here and there like a man drunk with wine. Unable to endure it, he came out of his cell and took the same road by which the young man had been returning to the world.

Abba Apollo understood what had happened and went to meet him. Approaching him, he said: “Where are you going, and what is the cause of the disturbance that has overcome you?”

The old man realized that the holy man understood what had happened to him, but out of shame he said nothing. Abba Apollo said to him:

“Return to your cell. From now on, acknowledge your weakness and keep it before you. Until now you were either unknown to the devil or despised by him, and for this reason you did not deserve, like men of virtue, to have struggles against the devil.

“What do I mean by struggles? You could not endure even one day of his assault. This has happened to you because, when you received that young man who was being attacked by the common adversary, instead of anointing him with words of consolation for the diabolical battle—as you ought to have done—you drove him into despair. You did not consider that most wise command by which we are ordered to rescue those being led to death and not to neglect to redeem those being killed (Proverbs 14). Nor did you consider the parable of our Savior, who said (Matthew 12) that a bruised reed must not be broken and a smoldering wick must not be extinguished.

“No one could withstand the ambushes of the adversary or extinguish or restrain the fire of a nature boiling within, unless the grace of God preserved human weakness. Let us all implore the Lord in our prayers, in his saving providence, to turn away from you the scourge that has been sent against you, for he both causes grief and restores to salvation; he strikes, and his hand heals; he humbles and exalts; he puts to death and gives life; he leads down to the underworld and brings back” (1 Samuel 2).

Having said this, he completed the prayer, and at once the old man was freed from the battle that had been inflicted upon him. Abba Apollo urged him to ask God to give him an educated tongue, so that he might know the time when it is fitting to speak a word.

5. When Abba Syrus [Al.: Cyrus] of Alexandria was questioned about the thought of fornication, he replied:

“If you have no thoughts, you have no hope; for if you have no thoughts, you have actions. The reason is this: whoever does not fight against sin in thought and contradict it sins bodily. But whoever sins bodily has no trouble from thoughts.”

6. An old man asked a brother: “Do you have the habit of conversing with a woman?” The brother said: “No.” The old man said: “My thoughts are old and new painters, and certain memories that trouble me through the likenesses of women.”

The old man then said to him: “Do not fear the dead, but flee the living: that is, consent to sin and its actions. Instead, extend your prayer.”

7. Abba Mathois said that a certain brother once came and said that the person who speaks against another is worse than the person who fornicates. The old man replied: “That is a hard saying.”

The brother said to him: “How, then, do you want the matter to stand?” The old man said: “Speaking against another is indeed evil, but it finds a quick remedy, and the person who has spoken against another often repents, saying: ‘I spoke wrongly,’ and the matter passes. Fornication, however, is death by nature.”

8. Abba Pastor said: “Just as the prince’s swordsman always stands beside him, ready, so the soul must always be ready against the demon of fornication” (Ruffinus, Book III, no. 59).

9. A brother once came to Abba Pastor and said: “What shall I do, Father? I am afflicted by fornication” (Ruffinus, Book III, no. 63; Paschasius, chapter 1, no. 9). “I went to Abba Hybistion, and he said to me: ‘You must not allow it to dwell in you for a long time.’”

Abba Pastor said to him: “Abba Hybistion’s works are above in heaven with the angels, and this is hidden from him. But you and I are in fornication. Therefore, if a monk restrains his belly and his tongue and remains in solitude, let him be confident that he will not perish.”

10. They told of the abbess Sarah that for thirteen years she was fiercely attacked by the demons of fornication. She never prayed that this battle should depart from her, but said only: “Lord, give me strength.”

11. They said again of her that at one time the same demon of fornication pressed upon her more violently than before, placing the vanities of the world in her thoughts. But she did not relax her mind’s hold on the fear of God or on her resolve of abstinence. Once she went up onto her bed to pray, and the spirit of fornication appeared to her bodily and said: “You have defeated me, Sarah.”

She replied: “I have not defeated you, but my Lord Christ.”

12. A certain brother was being tormented by fornication, and the torment was like a burning fire in his heart day and night. The brother struggled, neither yielding nor consenting to his thought. After a long time the torment departed from him, unable to prevail because of the brother’s perseverance. Immediately light appeared in his heart.

### 13

Another brother was troubled by fornication. He rose at night, went to an old man, and told him his thought; the old man consoled him. Strengthened by this consolation, he returned to his cell. And behold, again the spirit of fornication tempted him. Again he went to the old man. This happened frequently. The old man did not distress him, but spoke to him about what was beneficial for him, saying:

“Do not yield to the devil, nor relax your courage; rather, whenever the demon troubles you, come to me, and, being rebuked, he will depart. For nothing so wearies the demon of fornication as the exposure of his assaults; and nothing pleases him so much as the concealment of his thoughts.”

The brother therefore came to the old man eleven times, confessing his thoughts. Afterwards the brother said to the old man: “Show me charity, abba, and tell me a word.”

The old man said to him: “Believe me, son: if God were to permit my thoughts, by which my soul is troubled, to be transferred to you, you would not be able to bear them, but would utterly fall down.”

When the old man had said this, the brother’s temptation of fornication ceased, because of the old man’s profound humility.

### 14

Another man, likewise troubled by fornication, began to struggle and to extend his abstinence. For fourteen years he guarded his thoughts so as not to consent to his desire. Afterwards, when he came to the church, he revealed to the entire assembly what he was suffering. An order was then given, and everyone afflicted himself on his behalf for a week, praying continually to the Lord; and his temptation ceased.

### 15

Concerning the thought of fornication, an old man said:

“Eremite, are you sleeping? Do you wish to be saved? Go, work; go, afflict yourself; go, seek, and you will find. Watch, knock, and it will be opened to you.

“For there are pancratiarii in the world [Note: [Col. 0988D] Pancratiarii: thus called from *pancratium*, a type of gymnastic contest, because they are said to fight with all their strength, from ἀπὸ τῶν πάντων κρατῶν, ‘because they fight with all their powers.’ Gellius, Book III, chapter 15, calls one a *pancratiastes*: ‘Diagoras had three sons: one a boxer, another a pancratiast, and the third a wrestler.’ Benedict’s Glosses: *Pancratiarii*, παγκρατιάριοι.] who, after they have been beaten severely and have stood firm and appeared strong, receive crowns. Sometimes one man is beaten by two, yet, strengthened by the blows, he conquers those who beat him. Do you see what strength he has acquired through the exercise of the flesh? You too stand firm and take courage, and the Lord will fight the enemy on your behalf.”

### 16

Concerning this same thought of fornication, another old man said:

“Be like one who passes through a street or by a cookshop and catches the smell of some cooked food or roast meat. Whoever wishes enters and eats; whoever does not wish merely smells it and passes on. So you too shake the stench from yourself, rise, and pray, saying: ‘Lord, Son of God, help me.’

“Do this also against other thoughts. For we are not uprooters of thoughts, but wrestlers against those same thoughts.”

### 17

Another old man said:

“We suffer these things because of negligence. For if we consider that God dwells within us, we will not bring a foreign vessel inside ourselves. The Lord Christ, dwelling in us and sharing our dwelling, observes our life. Therefore, since we bear him and contemplate him, we must not be negligent, but sanctify ourselves, just as he is holy.

“Let us stand upon the rock, and the evil one will be shattered. Do not fear, and he will not prevail against you. Sing psalms with strength, saying: ‘Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion; he who dwells in Jerusalem will not be shaken forever’ (Psalm 124).”

### 18

A brother asked an old man, saying:

“If a monk falls into sin, he is distressed like one who has gone from progress into a worse condition, and he struggles until he rises again. But the one who comes from the world, like someone making a beginning, makes progress.”

The old man replied:

“A monk who falls into temptation is like a house that collapses. If he is sober in his thinking, he rebuilds the house that has fallen, finding materials useful for the construction, since he already has foundations, stones, sand, and the other things necessary for the building; thus the structure quickly advances.

“But the one who has neither dug nor laid a foundation, and possesses none of the necessary materials, builds only in hope that it may somehow be completed one day.

“So it is with a monk who falls into temptation and turns back to the Lord: he has abundant equipment—meditation on the divine law, psalmody, manual labor, prayer, and the other things that serve as foundations. But the one who is newly converted, until he learns these things, will occupy the first place.”

### 19

A certain brother, held by the spirit of fornication, went to a great old man and begged him, saying:

“Show me charity and pray for me, for I am troubled by fornication” (Ruffinus, Book III, no. 13).

The old man prayed to the Lord. When he came to the old man a second time, he repeated the same words. The old man likewise did not neglect to pray for him, saying:

“Lord, reveal to me from where this demonic activity in this brother arises. I have prayed to you, yet he has still found no rest.”

The Lord revealed what was happening concerning that brother. The old man saw him sitting, with the spirit of fornication beside him and, as it were, playing with him; an angel sent to help him was standing there and was indignant against the brother because he did not prostrate himself before God, but seemed rather to delight in his thoughts, inclining his entire mind toward them.

The old man understood that the cause lay chiefly with the brother himself, and he announced this to him, saying: “You consent to your thought.” He taught him how he ought to resist such thoughts. The brother, recovering his breath through the old man’s instruction and prayer, found rest from his temptation.

### 20

The disciple of a great old man was once tempted by fornication. When the old man saw him suffering, he said to him:

“Do you wish me to ask the Lord to lift this distress from you?”

He replied: “I see, abba, that although I suffer, I perceive from the burden of this suffering that I am bearing fruit. But ask God in your prayers to give me endurance, by which I may persevere.”

His abba said to him: “Now I know that you are making great progress, my son, and that you surpass me.”

### 21

They told of an old man who went down to Scetis and had a son who was still nursing. Since the boy had been raised in the monastery, he did not know what women were. When he became a man, the demons showed him women’s forms at night. He told his father, who was astonished.

Once, therefore, he went up with his father to Egypt. On seeing women, he said to his father: “Abba, these are the women who came to me at night in Scetis.”

His father said to him: “These are the monks of the world, my son. These wear one kind of clothing, while the hermits wear another.” The old man was astonished that the demons had shown him images of women in Scetis, and they immediately returned to their cell.

### 22

A certain brother, tested by temptations in Scetis, was assailed by the adversary, who cast into his mind the memory of a beautiful woman and greatly distressed him (Ruffinus, Book III, no. 11).

It happened, by God’s providence, that another brother coming down from Egypt arrived in Scetis. As they spoke, he told him: “The wife of that man has died.” It was the very woman over whom the brother had been troubled.

When he heard this, he took his garment at night and went up to the place where he had heard that she was buried. He dug up the place, wiped the putrefying blood from her remains onto his garment, and returned with it to his cell.

Whenever it became exceedingly foul, he placed the stench before him and, reproaching his thought, said: “Behold the desire you were seeking. You have it; satisfy yourself with it.” In this way, by means of that stench, he chastised himself until his desires died.

### 23

A man once came to Scetis to become a monk. He also brought his son, recently weaned. When the boy became a young man, the demons began to attack and trouble him. He said to his father:

“I am going back to the world, because I cannot endure carnal desires.”

His father consoled him. The young man then said: “I can no longer endure it, father. Let me return to the world.”

His father said to him:

“Listen to me once more, my son. Take forty loaves and palm leaves for forty days, go into the inner desert, and remain there for forty days; then God’s will shall be done.”

Obeying his father, he rose and went into the desert. He remained there, laboring and making mats from dry palms and eating dry bread. When he had rested there for twenty days, behold, he saw a demonic apparition coming upon him. It stood before him in the form of an Ethiopian woman, foul and ugly to look at, so that he could not endure her stench; and he drove her away from him.

She said to him:

“I am the one who appears sweet in human hearts. But because of your obedience and the labor you are enduring, God did not permit me to deceive you; instead, he made my stench known to you.”

He rose, gave thanks to God, returned to his father, and said to him: “I no longer wish to go back to the world, father. I have seen the devil’s activity and his stench.”

His father already knew about this, and said to him: “If you had remained for forty days and kept my command to the end, you would have seen greater things.”

### 24

An old man lived in a remote desert. He had a female relative who wished to see him after many years. She asked where he lived, rose, and came to the road leading to his desert (Ruffinus, Book II, no. 14).

Finding some camel-drivers, she joined them and entered the desert with them. She had been driven to this by the devil. When she came to the old man’s door, she began to identify herself by signs, saying: “I am your relative.” She remained with him.

There was another monk sitting in the lower part of the place. At the hour when he wished to eat, he filled a small water-vessel for himself; suddenly the vessel overturned and the water spilled out. Inspired by God, he said to himself:

“I shall enter the desert and tell the elders what has happened to me concerning the water.”

He rose and went away. When evening came, he slept in a temple of idols beside the road. At night he heard demons saying:

“Tonight we have thrown that monk into fornication.”

When he heard this, he was saddened. Upon reaching the old man, he found him sorrowful, and said to him: “What shall I do, abba? I fill my little vessel with water, and at the hour of eating it is spilled.”

The old man said to him: “You came to ask me why your vessel overturns; but what shall I do, since I fell into fornication tonight?”

He replied: “I know that too.”

The old man said: “How do you know?”

He answered: “I was sleeping in the temple and heard the demons speaking about you.”

The old man said: “Behold, I am going back to the world.”

The other begged him, saying: “Do not, father; remain in your place. As for the woman, send her away from here. This happened because of the enemy’s assault.”

When he heard this, the old man persevered, intensifying and increasing the rigor of his way of life with tears, until he returned to his former standing.

### 25

An old man said:

“Security, silence, and hidden meditation produce chastity.”

### 26

A brother asked an old man:

“If a person happens to fall into temptation, what becomes of those who are scandalized by him?”

The old man related the following:

“There was a deacon appointed in a monastery in Egypt. When a certain curialis [Note: [Col. 0988D] *Curialis*: there were *curiales*, men enrolled in the municipal councils. Cassiodorus, *Variarum* Book VI, letter 3: ‘He also scourges the curiales, who are called by the laws the lesser senate.’ But the word was also used in other ways.] was suffering persecution from a judge, he came with his entire household to the monastery.

“Through the working of the evil one, that deacon fell into fornication with the man’s wife, and confusion arose among all the brothers. The deacon went to a certain old man and told him what had happened. The old man had a hidden inner cell. When the deacon saw it, he said: ‘Bury me alive here, and tell no one.’

“He entered the darkness of that cell and truly performed his repentance there.

“After a long time, it happened that the water no longer rose in the river Nile. While everyone was performing litanies, it was revealed to one of the saints that unless the deacon who was hidden with that particular monk came, the waters of the river would not rise.

“When they heard this, they were astonished. They came and brought him out from the place where he was. He prayed, and the water rose. Those who had once been scandalized by him were later edified by his repentance, and glorified God.”

### 27

Two brothers went to the city to sell what they had made. When they became separated from one another in the city, one of them fell into fornication (Ruffinus, Book III, no. 12).

Afterwards, when his brother arrived, he said to him: “Let us return to our cell, brother.”

The other replied: “I am not coming.”

He asked him: “Why, brother?”

He answered: “Because when you left me, I fell into temptation and committed fornication.”

Wishing to save him, the other began to say: “The same thing happened to me. When I was separated from you, I too fell into fornication. But let us go and together perform our repentance with every effort, and God will forgive us sinners.”

When they came to the cell, they told the elders what had happened to them, and the elders gave them instructions concerning how they should perform their repentance. One of them, however, performed repentance not for himself but for the other brother, as though he too had sinned.

When God saw his labor and charity, after a few days he revealed to one of the elders that, because of the great charity of the brother who had not sinned, he had forgiven the one who had committed fornication. Truly, this is laying down one’s life for one’s brother.

### 28

A brother once came to an old man and said to him:

“My brother leaves me and goes here and there, and because of this I am distressed.”

The old man urged him, saying: “Bear it calmly, brother. When God sees the labor of your endurance, he will bring him back to you. For it is not possible to recall someone easily from his purpose through harshness and severity. The demon does not drive out the demon; rather, you will recall him to yourself through kindness. For our God also draws people to himself by advising them.”

He also related the following:

“There were two brothers in the Thebaid. When one of them fell into fornication, he said to the other: ‘I am returning to the world.’

“The other wept, saying: ‘I will not let you leave, brother, and lose your labor and your virginity.’

“But the first would not listen, saying: ‘I will not remain here; I am going. Either come with me and return with me again, or at least let me go and remain in the world.’

“As the brother was leaving, he reported this to a great old man. The old man said to him: ‘Go with him, and God, because of your labor, will not permit him to fall.’

“He rose and went with him to the world. When they reached a certain village, God saw the labor of the one who followed his brother out of charity and necessity, and he removed the desire from his brother.

“Then the brother said: ‘Let us return to the desert, brother. Behold, I think I have now sinned with a woman; what have I gained from this?’

“They returned unharmed to their cell.”

### 29

A brother tempted by a demon went to an old man, saying:

“Those two brothers are together and live badly.”

The old man recognized that he was being deceived by a demon and sent for the two brothers. When evening came, he spread a mat for them and covered them with a single blanket, saying:

“They are great and holy sons of God.”

He said to his disciple: “Shut this brother up separately in a cell, for he has in himself the passion that he attributed to them.”

### 30

A brother said to an old man:

“What shall I do? An impure thought is killing me.”

The old man said to him:

“When a woman wishes to wean her child, she smears something bitter on her breasts. When the infant, accustomed to sucking milk, comes to nurse and tastes the bitterness, he withdraws.

“You too must put bitterness into your thought.”

The brother said: “What is the bitterness that I should put there?”

The old man said to him: “The thought of death and of the torments prepared for sinners in the world to come.”

### 31

A brother asked an old man about such a thought (Ruffinus, Book III, no. 62). The old man said to him:

“I have never been troubled by this matter.”

The brother was scandalized by him and went to another old man, saying: “Behold what that old man said to me, and I was scandalized by him, because what he said is beyond nature.”

The old man said to him:

“That man of God did not say this to you without reason. Rise, go, and perform repentance before him, so that he may reveal to you the power of his words.”

The brother rose and came to the old man, performing repentance in his presence. He said:

“Forgive me, father, because I acted foolishly. I did not say farewell to you as I departed; rather, I beg you to explain to me how you have never been troubled by fornication.”

The old man said to him:

“From the time I became a monk, I have not been satisfied with bread, water, or sleep. While the appetite for these things by which we are nourished was tormenting me, I was not permitted to feel the assaults of fornication.”

The brother departed, making progress through the old man’s account.

### 32

A brother asked an old man:

“What shall I do? My thought is always intent upon fornication and does not let me rest for even an hour, and my soul is distressed by this” (Ruffinus, Book III, no. 40).

He said to him:

“When the demons sow thoughts in your heart and you perceive this, do not converse with your mind, because suggesting is the demons’ work. Although they do not neglect to cast such things into you, the demons do not compel you. It is therefore in your power to accept or not to accept.”

The brother replied: “What shall I do? I am weak, and this passion overcomes me.”

He said to him:

“Pay attention to this. Do you know what the Midianite women did? They adorned their daughters and placed them before the Israelites. They did not compel anyone to join with them; rather, those who wished fell into their snare (Numbers 25). Others, however, became indignant, threatened them, and avenged the fornication by destroying those who had presumed to act so. The same must be done concerning fornication.

“When such thoughts begin to speak in your heart, do not answer them. Instead, rise, pray, and perform repentance, saying: ‘Son of God, have mercy on me.’”

The brother said to him:

“Behold, abba, I meditate, but there is no compunction in my heart, because I do not know the power of the word.”

He said to him: “Nevertheless, meditate. For I have heard that Abba Pastor, and also the other Fathers, said this: ‘The magician does not know the power of the words he speaks, but the serpent hears and knows the power of what is being enchanted; it submits to the magician and is humbled. So it is with us: although we do not know the power of what we say, the demons nevertheless are terrified when they hear it and depart.’”

### 33

An old man said:

“The thought of fornication is fragile, like papyrus. Therefore, if it is cast against us and we reject it without consenting to it, it is easily torn apart.

“It is necessary, then, that there be discernment in our thinking, by which we recognize that those who consent to it have no hope of salvation, while for those who do not consent, a crown has been reserved.”

### 34

Two brothers, assailed by fornication, went away and took wives. Afterwards they said to one another:

“What have we gained by abandoning the angelic order and coming into this impurity, and after this going to fire and torment? Let us return to the desert and perform repentance for what we have presumed to do.”

They came to the desert and begged the Fathers to receive them as penitents confessing what they had done. The old men shut them up for an entire year. Equal amounts of bread were assigned to both, according to the measure, and water according to the measure. They were alike in appearance.

When the time of repentance had been completed, they came out. The Fathers saw that one was extremely pale and sad, while the other was robust and radiant. They were astonished, since both had received equal food and drink.

They questioned the one who was sad and afflicted, saying: “What did you occupy yourself with in your cell, in your thoughts?”

He replied: “I kept revolving in my mind the punishments for the evils I had committed and the torments into which I was going. Because of fear, my bones clung to my flesh.”

They also questioned the other, saying: “What did you think about in your cell?”

He said: “I gave thanks to God because he had rescued me from the defilement of this world and from the punishments of the world to come, and had recalled me to this angelic way of life. As I continually remembered my God, I rejoiced.”

The old men said: “The repentance of both is equal before God.”

### 35

There was an old man in Scetis who, when he fell into a serious illness, was attended by the brothers. Seeing that they were laboring, the old man said:

“I am going to Egypt, so that I will not burden these brothers.”

Abba Moses said to him: “Do not go, for you will fall into fornication.”

The old man, distressed, said: “My body is dead, and you say this to me?”

He rose and went to Egypt. When the people living throughout the surrounding area heard of it, they brought him many things. A faithful virgin also came to him, wishing to offer her service to the sick old man.

After some time, when he had improved somewhat from the illness that afflicted him, he fell into fornication with her, and she conceived. When the neighbors asked her where she had conceived, she replied: “From this old man.”

They did not believe her. But the old man said: “I did this; only preserve for me the child she has borne.”

When she had given birth to a boy and he had been weaned, the old man carried the infant on his shoulders. On the day of the festival at Scetis, he came there and entered the church before the multitude of brothers.

When they saw him, they wept. He said to the brothers:

“Do you see this infant? He is the son of my disobedience. Therefore beware, brothers, for I did this in my old age, and pray for me.”

He returned to his cell and went back to the beginning of his former way of life.

### 36

A certain brother was very grievously tempted by demons. They had taken the form of beautiful women and persisted for forty continuous days, fighting against him in order to draw him into shameful intercourse. But he resisted manfully and was not overcome in the least. When God saw his good struggle, he granted him that thereafter he should suffer no heat of carnal desire.

### 37

There was a solitary in Lower Egypt, very famous because he alone sat in a church in a deserted place. Behold, in accordance with Satan’s activity, a shameless woman who had heard about him said to some young men:

“What will you give me if I bring down this solitary of yours?”

They agreed upon a definite payment for her. She went out in the evening and came to his cell as though she were lost. When she knocked at the cell, he came out. Seeing her, he was troubled and said:

“How did you come here?”

She, as though weeping, said: “I came here while wandering.”

Moved by compassion, he brought her into the little courtyard of his cell. He himself went farther inside and closed the door.

Behold, the wretched woman cried out: “Abba, wild beasts will eat me here!”

He was troubled again, fearing also God’s judgment, and said: “From where has this anger come upon me?”

He opened the door and brought her inside. The devil began to prick his heart toward her as with arrows. When he understood that these were the devil’s assaults, he said to himself:

“The ways of the enemy are darkness, but the Son of God is light” (Psalm 34).

He rose and lit a lamp. As desire inflamed him, he said:

“Those who do such things go into torments” (Galatians 5). “Test yourself by this: can you endure the eternal fire?”

He put his finger into the lamp. When it had caught fire and was burning, he did not feel it because of the excessive flame of carnal desire. Continuing in this way until morning, he burned all his fingers.

The wretched woman, seeing what he was doing, became as if turned to stone with fear. In the morning the young men came to the monk and said: “Did a woman come here last night?”

He replied: “Yes; behold where she is sleeping.”

They entered and found her dead. They said: “Abba, she is dead.”

Then he pulled back the little cloak he wore and showed them his hands, saying:

“Behold what this daughter of the devil has done to me: she has destroyed all my fingers.”

As he related what had happened, he said:

“It is written: ‘Do not repay evil for evil’” (Proverbs 17; 1 Thessalonians 5; 1 Peter 3).

He prayed and raised her up. After her conversion, she lived chastely for the remainder of her life.

### 38

A brother was assailed by fornication. It happened that he came to a village in Egypt. Seeing the daughter of a pagan priest, he fell in love with her and said to her father:

“Give her to me as a wife.”

The man replied: “I cannot give her to you unless I ask my god.”

He went to the demon he worshiped and said to it: “Behold, a monk has come to me wishing to take my daughter. Shall I give her to him?”

The demon replied: “Ask him whether he denies his God, his baptism, and his monastic profession.”

The priest came and said to him: “Deny your God, your baptism, and your monastic profession, and I will give you my daughter.”

The brother consented. Immediately he saw what appeared to be a dove come out of his mouth and fly up into heaven.

The priest went to the demon and said: “Behold, he has promised to do these three things.”

The devil replied: “Do not give him your daughter in marriage, because his God has not departed from him, but will still help him.”

The priest came and said to the brother: “I cannot give her to you, because your God is still helping you and has not departed from you.”

When he heard this, the brother said to himself:

“If God has shown such goodness toward me, even though I, wretched man, denied him, my baptism, and my monastic profession; if the good God nevertheless continues to help me in this way, why should I depart from him?”

Coming to his senses, he regained sobriety of mind, went into the desert to a certain great old man, and told him what had happened.

The old man replied:

“Remain with me in the cave, fast for three consecutive weeks, and I will pray to God for you.”

The old man labored on behalf of the brother and prayed to God, saying:

“I beg you, Lord, grant me this soul and receive his repentance.”

God heard his prayer.

When the first week had been completed, the old man came to the brother and asked him: “Have you seen anything?”

The brother replied: “Yes. I saw a dove standing high in the sky above my head.”

The old man said to him: “Pay attention to yourself and pray earnestly to God.”

During the second week, the old man again came to the brother and asked him: “Have you seen anything?”

He replied: “I saw a dove coming near my head.”

The old man instructed him: “Be sober in mind and pray.”

When the third week had been completed, the old man came again and asked him: “Have you seen anything more?”

He replied: “I saw the dove come and stand upon my head. I stretched out my hand to seize it, but it rose and entered my mouth.”

Giving thanks to God, the old man said to the brother:

“Behold, God has received your repentance. From now on, pay attention to yourself and be vigilant.”

The brother replied: “Behold, from now on I will remain with you until I die.”

### 39

One of the Theban elders said that he had been the son of a priest of idols. When he was a small child sitting in the temple, he often saw his father enter and offer sacrifices to the idol. Once, when he secretly entered after him, he saw Satan sitting there, with all his army standing before him. Behold, one of his princes came and worshiped him.

The devil said to him: “Where do you come from?”

He replied: “I was in that province. I stirred up wars and many disturbances there, causing bloodshed, and I have come to report to you.”

The devil asked him: “In how much time did you do this?”

He replied: “In thirty days.”

The devil ordered him to be scourged, saying: “You did this in so much time?”

Another came and worshiped him. He said to him: “Where do you come from?”

The demon replied: “I was at sea. I stirred up storms, sank ships, and killed many people, and I have come to report to you.”

The devil said: “In how much time did you do this?”

He replied: “It has been twenty days.”

He ordered this one likewise to be scourged, saying: “Why did you accomplish so little in so many days?”

A third came and worshiped him. He said to him: “And you, where do you come from?”

He replied: “I was in that city. While a wedding was taking place there, I stirred up quarrels and caused much bloodshed; moreover, I killed the bridegroom himself, and I have come to report to you.”

He said to him: “In how many days did you do this?”

He replied: “Ten.”

As though he had delayed, he ordered this one also to be scourged.

Another came to worship him. He said to him: “Where do you come from?”

He replied: “I was in the desert. Behold, it has been forty years that I have been fighting against a certain monk, and only last night did I prevail sufficiently to make him commit fornication.”

When the devil heard this, he rose and kissed him. Taking the crown that he himself wore, he placed it on the other’s head and made him sit with him on the same throne, saying:

“You have accomplished a great deed with courage.”

“When I heard and saw this, I said within myself: ‘The order of monks is exceedingly great.’”

### 40

They said of a certain Father that he had been a secular man and afterwards was converted. He was frequently troubled by desire for his wife, and he told the Fathers about it. When they saw that he was a laborer and that he was doing more than they prescribed, they imposed certain things upon him to weaken his body, until he could not even rise.

By God’s providence, a certain Father came to visit Scetis. When he arrived at the man’s cell, he saw it open and passed by, wondering that no one had come out to meet him. He turned back and knocked, saying:

“Perhaps the brother who lives here has fallen ill.”

When he knocked, he entered and found him extremely weak. He said to him: “What is wrong, Father?”

The man told him:

“I come from secular life, and now the enemy troubles me concerning my wife. I told the Fathers, and they imposed various burdens of monastic discipline upon me. When I wished to fulfill them obediently, behold, I collapsed; yet the temptation continues to grow.”

When the old man heard this, he was saddened and said to him:

“The Fathers, as strong men, have indeed imposed good burdens upon you, but you are weighed down by them. If you will listen to me, a little one, cast these things from you, take a small amount of food at the proper time, and regain your strength. Do some work for God, and cast your thought upon the Lord (Psalm 54), for by your own labor you will not be able to overcome this matter.

“Our body is like a garment. If you care for it diligently, it will endure; but if you neglect it, it will rot.”

When he heard this, he did so. Within a few days, that temptation departed from him.

Source/review notes: The second listed edit is a no-op and should be disregarded; it was included accidentally. The substantive corrections are the translation of the corrupted editorial term in note 2 and the reversed comparison in Booklet VII, §17.

41. An ancient solitary monk, advancing in his way of life, was sitting on a mountain in the region of Antinoe, as we heard from monks who knew him; by his words and conduct many were making progress. Since he was such a man, the devil was stirred up against him by envy, as also against all men of virtue, and cast into his mind this thought: a man living such a life ought not to be served or assisted by another, but rather ought himself to serve others. If he did not provide service for others, he should at least serve himself, saying:

“Go, then, sell in the city the little baskets you make, buy what you need, and return to your place; be a burden to no one.”

The devil suggested this because he envied his quiet and his timely leisure for the Lord, as well as his usefulness to many. For the enemy was hastening to hunt him down and seize him from every side.

He, however, as though consenting to a good thought, descended from his monastery. He was admired by everyone, yet no one knew that he was subject to such ambushes of cunning; he was known and famous to all by whom he was seen. After a long time he saw a woman, and through his lack of caution was overthrown and fell into sin with her. Then, coming into a deserted place while the devil followed in his footsteps, he fell beside a river.

Thinking that the enemy had rejoiced at his ruin, he wished to despair of himself, because he had greatly grieved the Spirit of God and the holy angels, as well as the venerable Fathers, many of whom, even while living in cities, had overcome the devil. Since he could not make himself like any of them, he was deeply distressed and did not remember that God is the one who grants strength to those who turn to him with the greatest devotion.

Blinded, and not seeing the remedy for his sin, he wished to throw himself into that river, so as to give the enemy perfect joy. From his great anguish of spirit he fell ill in body; and unless merciful God had afterward granted him help, he would have died without repentance, bringing the enemy perfect joy.

At last, coming to himself, he resolved to show greater labor in the affliction of repentance and to entreat God with weeping and mourning. Thus he returned to his monastery. He sealed the door of his cell, as is done over a dead man, and wept, entreating God. Fasting and keeping vigil with complete anxiety, he weakened his body; yet even then he did not think that his soul had been satisfied, since he had not repented adequately.

When the brothers often came to him for their own benefit and knocked at the door, he said that he could not open it, explaining:

“I have bound myself by a sacred vow to practice repentance devoutly for one year; but pray for me.”

He could find no other way to excuse himself to them, for they were scandalized when they heard this about him, since he was honorable among them and a very great monk.

He spent the entire year fasting intensely and practicing repentance devoutly. On Easter Day, during the very night of the Lord’s Resurrection, he took a new lamp and placed it in a new pot. Having covered it with a lid, he rose from evening prayer and said:

“Merciful and compassionate is the Lord, who wishes even barbarians to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. To you, Savior of the faithful, I flee for refuge. Have mercy on me, who have greatly embittered you, caused the enemy to rejoice, and—behold—I am dead because I obeyed him.

“You, Lord, who have mercy on both the impious and those without mercy, and who also command us to extend mercy to our neighbors, have mercy on my lowliness. For nothing is impossible with you, since my soul has been scattered like dust beside the underworld.

“Show mercy, because you are kind and compassionate, to your creature, who will also raise up on the day of resurrection the bodies that do not now exist. Hear me, Lord, for my spirit has failed, and my wretched soul. My body too has wasted away—the body I defiled. And now I cannot live, because I did not believe.

“Forgive my sin through repentance, since in despair I have a double sin. Give life to me, who am crushed, and command this lamp to be kindled by your fire. Then, receiving confidence in your mercy and pardon, may I keep your commandments for the remaining time of my life that you grant me, and never depart from your fear, but serve you thereafter with greater devotion than before.”

Saying these things during that very night of the Resurrection with many tears, he rose to see whether the lamp had been lit. When he uncovered the pot, he saw that it had not been lit. He fell again on his face, entreating the Lord and saying:

“I know, Lord, that a contest was set before me so that I might be crowned, but I did not stand firm, choosing instead, for the sake of the pleasure of the flesh, to be handed over to the torments of the impious. Spare me, therefore, Lord.

“For behold, again I confess my disgrace before your goodness, before your angels and before all the righteous; and, if they could do so without being scandalized, I would confess it even before all human beings. God, have mercy on me, so that I may instruct others also. Lord, give me life.”

Praying in this way three times, he was heard. Rising, he found the lamp burning brightly. Filled with hope, he was strengthened by joy of heart, marveling at the grace of God, who had both pardoned his sins and granted his request according to his desire and intention. He said:

“I give you thanks, Lord, because you have had mercy even on one unworthy of this worldly life, granting confidence through this great and new sign. For you, in your mercy, spare the souls whom you create.”

While he continued in confession, day broke. He rejoiced in the Lord, forgetting bodily food. He preserved the fire of that lamp throughout his life, periodically pouring in oil and placing something above it to prevent it from being extinguished.

Thus the divine Spirit once more dwelt in him, and he became distinguished among all, displaying humility in confession and thanksgiving to the Lord with joy. A few days before his death, his departure was also revealed to him.

## SIXTH BOOKLET

### On the fact that a monk ought to possess nothing

1. A certain brother renounced the world and gave to the poor what he possessed, but retained a little for his own account. He came to Abba Antony (Ruffinus, book III, no. 68). When the old man learned this, he said to him:

“If you wish to become a monk, go to that village, buy some meat, put it on your naked body, and then come here.”

When that brother had done so, dogs and birds tore his body. When he came to the old man, Antony asked whether he had done what he had commanded him. When the brother showed him his lacerated body, Saint Antony said:

“Those who renounce the world but wish to possess money are attacked and torn apart by demons in just this way.”

2. Abba Daniel related concerning Abba Arsenius that on one occasion Magistrianus came to him, bringing the testament of a senator who was his relative and who had left him a very large inheritance.

[Note: [Col. 0888D] *Magistrianus.* Ado of Vienne, in the *Martyrology*, 2 July, in the booklet *On the Feasts of the Apostles*: “The feast of Saints Processus and Martinianus, who, being *magistriani*, were leaders in the military service.” I showed there in the notes that this passage should be read in this way, and I also explained what office they held in the palace guard.]

Taking the testament, he wished to tear it up. But Magistrianus fell at his feet, saying:

“I beg you, do not tear it up, for my head will be cut off.”

Abba Arsenius said to him:

“I died before he did. He himself has only now died; how, then, did he make me his heir?”

And he returned the testament, accepting nothing.

3. The aforementioned Abba Arsenius once fell ill in Scetis and needed, in his distress, no more than a single *silique* coin. When he could not find one, he accepted what seemed to be alms from someone and said:

“I thank you, Lord, that you have deemed me worthy, for your name, to reach the point of needing to ask for alms.”

4. They related concerning Abba Agathon that for a long time he had been building a cell for himself and his disciples. When they had completed it and he had begun to live there, he saw during that very week that it was not useful to him, and he said to his disciples what the Lord had said to the apostles:

“Rise; let us go from here” (John 14).

The disciples were greatly distressed and said:

“If you had any intention of moving from here, why did we endure so much labor, building the cell over such a long time? People will begin to be scandalized by us and say: ‘Look, they are moving again; they never settle anywhere.’”

When he saw that they had become discouraged, he said to them:

“Even if some are scandalized, there are others who will be edified and say: ‘Blessed are these men, because they moved for God’s sake and despised all that was theirs.’ Nevertheless, I tell you: whoever wishes to come, let him come, for I am going away meanwhile.”

But they prostrated themselves on the ground, asking that he allow them to depart with him.

5. Abba Evagrius said:

[Note: [Col. 0989A] *Evagrius.* You have this in Greek in Socrates, book IV, chapter 18, from Evagrius’s *Praktikos*: “One of the brothers possessed only a Gospel, and, selling it, gave the proceeds as food to the hungry, uttering a saying worthy of remembrance: ‘I have sold the very word,’ he said, ‘which says: Sell what you possess and give to the poor.’”]

There was a certain brother who possessed nothing at all except a single Gospel, and he sold even that to provide food for the poor (Ruffinus, book III, no. 70, under the name Serapion). He uttered a saying worthy of being remembered:

“I have sold even the very word that commands: ‘Sell everything and give to the poor’” (Matthew 19).

6. Abba Theodore, surnamed of Pherme, possessed three good books. When he came to Abba Macarius, he said to him:

“I have three books, and I make progress through reading them. The brothers also ask for them to read, and they too make progress. Tell me, then, what should I do?”

The old man answered:

“They are indeed good actions, but better than all of them is to possess nothing.”

When he heard this, he went away, sold the books mentioned, and gave their price to those in need.

7. One of the Fathers related concerning Abba John the Persian that, through his many virtues, he had attained profound simplicity and innocence (Ruffinus, book III, no. 148). He lived in Arabia near Egypt.

On one occasion he borrowed a solidus from his brother and bought flax in order to work. A brother came and asked him:

“Give me, Abba, some flax, so that I may make myself a garment to use.”

He gave it to him gladly. Likewise, another came and asked him to give him some flax so that he might make a covering for himself, and he gave it to him. He gave simply and gladly to many others who asked him.

Afterward the owner of the solidus that he had borrowed came wishing to recover what he had lent. The old man said to him:

“I will bring it to you.”

But since he had nothing with which to repay him, he went to Abba Jacob the steward to ask him to give him a solidus. As he was going, he found a solidus lying on the ground. He did not touch it, but prayed and returned to his cell.

The brother came again and began to trouble him about the solidus. The old man said to him:

“I will repay you.”

He went away again and found the solidus lying in the same place as before. After praying again, he returned.

Then the brother again began to trouble him, and the old man said:

“Wait for me once more, and I will bring you your solidus.”

He rose, came to that place, and found the solidus there. After praying, he took it and went to Abba Jacob, saying:

“Abba, when I was coming to you, I found this solidus on the road. Show your charity and announce it, in case someone has lost it.”

Abba Jacob announced it, but no one was found who had lost it. Then the old man said to Abba Jacob:

“If no one has lost it, I will give it to that brother, since I owe him a solidus. When I was coming to you so that you might lend me a solidus and I could repay my debt, I found it on the road.”

Abba Jacob marveled that, compelled by his debt, he had found it but had not immediately taken it; nevertheless, he gave the solidus to that brother.

This was also remarkable about him: if anyone came to ask him to lend him something, he did not give it himself, but said to the brother asking for the loan:

“Go and take for yourself what you need.”

When the borrower reported that he had taken the loan, he said to him:

“Put it back again where you took it from.”

But if the one who had borrowed it reported nothing, the old man said nothing to him.

8. Some of the Fathers related that a certain brother once came to the assembly of the Cells before Abba Isaac, wearing a small hooded garment. The old man looked at him and said:

“This is the dwelling of monks; you are a man of the world and will not be able to remain here.”

9. Abba Isaac said to the brothers:

“Our Fathers and Abba Pambo used to wear old garments patched from many pieces, but now you wear costly clothing. Leave this place; you have abandoned this place.”

When they were about to go out to the harvest, he said to them:

“I will give you no further commands, because you do not observe them.”

10. Abba Cassianus said (Cassianus, *Institutes*, book VII, chapter 19) that a certain Syncleticianus had renounced the world and, dividing his possessions among the poor, had kept some for his own use, unwilling to receive completely the humility of those who renounced everything or the rule of the common monastic life. To him Saint Basil of blessed memory said:

“You have ceased to be a senator, but you have not become a monk.”

11. A certain brother said to Abba Pisterammon:

“What should I do? It is difficult for me to sell what I produce by the labor of my hands.”

He answered:

“Since Abba Sisoes and the others sold the work of their hands, this will not harm you. But when you sell, state the price of the item you are selling only once. If you wish to lower the price a little, that is up to you; in this way you will also find peace.”

The brother asked him again:

“If I have enough elsewhere to meet my needs, do you think I should not concern myself with manual labor?”

The old man answered:

“However much you have, do not neglect to work; do as much as you can, provided it is not with disturbance of spirit.”

12. A brother asked Abba Serapion:

“Tell me one word.”

The old man said:

“What can I tell you, since you have taken what belonged to widows and orphans and placed it in the window?”

For he had seen the window full of books.

13. Syncletica, of blessed memory, was asked:

“Is it a perfect good to possess nothing?”

She answered:

“It is a very great good for those who can endure it. For those who can bear it have tribulation of the flesh, but possess rest of soul. Just as strong garments, when trampled and repeatedly trodden underfoot, are washed and whitened, so a strong soul is strengthened still more through voluntary poverty.”

14. Abba Hyperichius said:

“The monk’s treasure is voluntary poverty. Therefore, brother, store up treasure for yourself in heaven, because there the ages are for resting without end.”

15. There was one of the saints named Philagrius. He lived in Jerusalem and worked so that he could provide himself with enough bread. As he stood in the marketplace wishing to sell what he had made with his hands, it happened that a small bag containing a thousand solidi fell from someone. When the old man found it, he remained in the same place, saying:

“Now the person who lost it must come here.”

And behold, the one who had lost it came, weeping. The old man took him aside and returned his bag. The man asked him to accept some portion of it, but the old man would not agree in any way. Then the man began to shout:

“Come and see what a man of God has done!”

But the old man secretly fled and left the city, lest he be recognized for what he had done and honored.

16. A certain old man was asked by a brother what he should do to be saved. The old man stripped off his garment, girded his loins, stretched out his hands, and said:

“Thus must the monk be naked of every worldly possession and crucify himself against the temptations and struggles of the world.”

17. Someone asked an old man to accept money that would be useful for his needs. But he did not wish to do so, since he was self-sufficient through the work of his hands (Ruffinus, book III, no. 71). When the other persisted in begging him at least to accept it for the needs of the poor, the old man replied:

“It would be a double reproach to me: I would accept what I do not need, and, by distributing what belongs to another, I would gather vain glory.”

18. Some Greeks once came to give alms in the city of Ostracine.

[Note: [Col. 0989A] *Ostracine.* The Paris edition has *ostiatim*, “from door to door.” Other editions have *ostracen*. Note that Ostracine is a city in Egypt.]

They appointed for themselves the church’s stewards, so that these men might show them those who had the greatest need. The stewards led them to a certain leper and gave the alms to him. But he did not wish to accept them, saying:

“Behold, I have a few palm leaves. I work them and make mats, and from these I eat bread.”

Again they led them to the cell of a widow who lived with her daughters. When they knocked at the door, her daughter ran to the door naked. Her mother had gone to some work, for she was a bleacher, and they gave her daughters clothing and money.

But the girl did not wish to accept them, saying that her mother had come and told her:

“Take courage, because God has willed it, and I have found work to do today from which we shall have our sustenance.”

When her mother came, they asked her to accept the gifts, but she refused, saying:

“I have God as my provider, and today you wish to take him away from me?”

Recognizing her faith, they glorified God.

19. A great and unknown man came to Scetis carrying gold with him and asked the priest of the desert that it be distributed among the brothers. The priest said to him:

“The brothers have no need of it.”

When the man was exceedingly insistent and would not agree, he placed a basket of solidi at the entrance of the church and said:

“Let whoever needs it take it.”

No one touched it; some did not even look at it. Then the old man said to him:

“God has accepted your offering. Go and give it to the poor.”

He departed greatly edified.

20. Someone brought money to an old man and said:

“Keep this for your expenses, because you have grown old and are ill.”

For he was a leper. The old man answered:

“You have come after sixty years to take away my provider? Behold, having been ill for so long, I have lacked nothing, since God has provided for me and fed me.”

He did not agree to accept it.

21. The old men related concerning a certain gardener that he worked and spent all his labor on almsgiving. He kept for himself only enough to provide his food.

Afterward Satan put this thought into his heart:

“Save some money for yourself, lest, when you grow old or fall ill, you need money for expenses.”

He collected money and filled a jar with coins. It happened that he fell ill and that his foot began to putrefy. He spent on physicians what he had collected, but it did him no good.

Later a certain experienced physician came and said to him:

“Unless you have your foot amputated, it will putrefy.”

They appointed a day for amputating his foot. But during that night he came to himself, repented of what he had done, groaned, and wept, saying:

“Remember, Lord, my former works, which I used to do when I worked in my garden, from which I served the poor.”

When he had said this, an angel of the Lord stood before him and said:

“Where are the coins you collected, and where is the hope about which you deliberated?”

Then, understanding, he said:

“I have sinned, Lord. Forgive me, and from now on I will do this no more.”

Then the angel touched his foot, and he was healed immediately. Rising in the morning, he went into the field to work.

The physician came at the appointed time with his instruments to cut off his foot, but they told him:

“He went out at dawn to work in the field.”

The physician marveled and went to the field where the man was working. When he saw him digging the earth, he glorified God, who had restored his health.

22. A brother asked a certain old man:

“Do you wish me to keep two solidi for myself because of the weakness of my body?” (Ruffinus, book III, no. 69.)

Seeing his thought—that he wished to keep them—the old man said:

“Yes.”

The brother went to his cell and was tormented by his thoughts, saying:

“Did the old man really tell me this, or not?”

He rose, returned to the old man, repented, and begged him, saying:

“For the Lord’s sake, tell me the truth, because my thoughts afflict me concerning the two solidi.”

The old man said to him:

“Because I saw that you wished to keep them, I told you to keep them. Nevertheless, it is not good to keep more than the body needs. If, therefore, you keep two solidi, your hope will be found in those coins. And if it should happen that they perish, God will no longer care for us. Let us therefore cast our thought upon the Lord, for he himself cares for us.”

## SEVENTH BOOKLET

### On patience or fortitude

1. Saint Abba Antony was once sitting in the desert (Ruffinus, book III, no. 105), when his spirit was overcome by weariness and confusion of thoughts. He said to God:

“Lord, I wish to be saved, but my thoughts do not allow me. What shall I do in this tribulation? How shall I be saved?”

Rising a little, he began to go outside. He saw someone like himself sitting and working, then rising from his work and praying, then sitting again and making a mat from palm leaves, and then rising once more to prayer.

It was an angel of the Lord, sent to correct Antony and give him a warning. Antony heard the angel’s voice saying:

“Do this, and you will be saved.”

When he heard this, he experienced great joy and confidence. By acting in this way, he found the salvation he had sought.

2. A certain brother asked Abba Agathon:

“A command has come to me, and I face a severe struggle in the place where the command is to be carried out. I wish, therefore, to go there because of the command, but I fear the battle.”

The old man said to him:

“Agathon was like that: he fulfilled the command and conquered the battle.”

3. Abba Ammonas said that he had spent fourteen years in Scetis, entreating God day and night to give him power to overcome anger.

4. Abba Besarion said that he had remained standing among thorns for forty nights and had not slept.

5. A certain solitary brother was troubled. He went to Abba Theodore of Pherme and told him that he was disturbed. The old man said to him:

“Go, humble your mind, submit yourself, and live with others.”

He went into the mountain and remained with others. Later he returned to the old man and said:

“Even while living with other people, I find no rest.”

The old man said to him:

“If you do not find rest alone or with others, why did you wish to become a monk? Was it not so that you might endure tribulations? Tell me, how many years have you worn this habit?”

He said:

“Eight.”

The old man said:

“Believe me, I have worn this habit for seventy years, and I have not been able to find rest for a single day; and you wish to have rest in eight years?”

6. A brother asked him again:

“If the sound of some collapse suddenly occurred, would you be afraid, Abba?”

The old man said to him:

“If heaven were joined to the earth, Theodore would not be afraid.”

For he had asked God in prayer that fear be taken away from him, and for this reason the brother had questioned him.

7. They related concerning Abba Theodore and Abba Lucius of the Ninth [district] of Alexandria:

[Note: [Col. 0989A] *Of the Ninth of Alexandria.* The Paris edition has *of the New*. Others have *of Nonnus*; others, *of the place*. Likewise below, in Booklet XI, no. 2, Theodore is called “of Ennaton,” which in Latin is “of the Ninth.” The ninth district or region of Alexandria is meant. Elsewhere it is similarly called the Seventh or Hebdomon.]

They spent fifty years deceiving their own minds by saying:

“After this winter has passed, we shall move away from here.”

Then, when summer came, they would say:

“After the summer has passed, we shall leave here.”

They did this throughout the whole period of their monastic life, always remembering the Fathers.

8. Abba Poemen said concerning Abba John, who was short in stature, that he had asked the Lord to remove all passions from him. He became secure and came to a certain old man, saying:

“Look at a tranquil man who has no struggle.”

The old man said to him:

“Go and ask the Lord to command that a struggle be stirred up in you, because the soul makes progress by fighting.”

When the struggle returned to him, he no longer prayed that it be taken away, but said:

“Lord, give me endurance to bear these struggles.”

9. Abba Macarius the Great came to Abba Antony on the mountain. When he knocked at the door, Antony came out and said to him:

“Who are you?”

He answered:

“I am Macarius.”

Antony closed the door, went inside, and left him outside. When he later saw Macarius’s patience, he opened the door to him. Rejoicing at his arrival, Antony said:

“It is a long time since I have wished to see you, having heard about you.”

He offered him hospitality and refreshed him, for he was exhausted from much labor.

When evening came, Abba Antony soaked a few palm leaves. Abba Macarius said to him:

“Give them to me, so that I may soak what I will work.”

Antony said:

“I have no more.”

Macarius made a larger bundle, soaked it, and sat down. From evening onward they spoke about the benefit of souls and made mats, and the mats descended through the window into the cave.

When Saint Antony went out in the morning, he saw the collection of mats made by Abba Macarius. He marveled, kissed his hands, and said:

“Much virtue proceeds from these.”

10. Macarius himself once descended from Scetis to a place called Terenuthis and entered a tomb in which the bodies of pagans had formerly been buried. He pulled one body beneath his head as a pillow made of rushes.

[Note: [Col. 0989A] *A pillow made of rushes.* This is the correct reading in the manuscripts and older editions. The Paris edition incorrectly has “of feathers from a branch.” See the *Onomasticon*.]

When the demons saw his confidence, they were enraged. Wishing to frighten him, they called out as though to a certain woman:

“Nonna, come with us to the bath.”

[Note: [Col. 0989B] *Nonna.* This is the reading of the manuscripts and older editions. The Paris editions incorrectly have *Nonne*. The demons pretend to address a certain woman whom they call *Nonna*, or “lady”—as though they were saying in French, “That lady there, come here.” See the *Onomasticon*.]

Another demon, from beneath him, as though from among those dead bodies, answered:

“I have a stranger lying on me; I cannot come.”

The old man was not frightened. Trusting in God, he beat that body and said:

“Get up and go, if you can.”

When the demons heard this, they cried out in a loud voice:

“You have defeated us!”

And they fled in confusion.

11. Abba Mathois said:

“I prefer a light and continuous task to a heavy one that is quickly finished.”

12. They related concerning Abba Milido:

[Note: [Col. 0989B] *Milido.* In the *Menologion*, 10 November, he is called Milus: “Commemoration of Saint Milus the martyr and bishop, and of his two disciples, who, having been converted and baptized from the region of the Persians to the faith of Christ and instructed in the divine Scriptures, together with his two disciples attained an immortal and heavenly life in place of mortal and earthly life.”]

When he was once living with two disciples in the territory of the Persians, two sons of the emperor went out hunting according to custom. They cast nets for forty thousand [paces], so that whatever was found within the nets might be killed.

The old man and his two disciples were found within the nets. When the princes saw that he was hairy and terrifying in appearance, they marveled and said to him:

“Are you a human being or some kind of spirit? Tell us.”

He said to them:

“I am a sinful human being. I came out to mourn my sins, and I worship the Son of the living God.”

They said to him:

“There is no other god except the Sun, Fire, and Water. Worship and sacrifice to them.”

[Note: [Col. 0989B] *Except the Sun, Fire, and Water.* These three were worshiped as gods by the Persians, as is known from Persian histories.]

He answered:

“These are creatures, and you are in error. But I beg you: turn and acknowledge the true God, who created these things and everything else.”

They mocked him and said:

“You say that one who was condemned and crucified is the true God?”

“Yes,” he replied. “I say that the very one who was crucified and killed death is the true God.”

They then inflicted tortures on him and on the brothers who were with him, compelling them to sacrifice. After many tortures they beheaded the two brothers, but tortured the old man for many days.

Afterward they placed him in a certain location and shot arrows at him as though at a target—one from behind and the other from the front. The old man said to them:

“Since you have agreed together as one to shed innocent blood, tomorrow at this very hour, which is now, your mother will remain without her sons, be deprived of your affection, and you will pour out one another’s blood with your own arrows.”

They mocked his words and went out the next day to hunt. It happened that a deer escaped from their net. They mounted their horses and raced to catch it. When they shot their arrows after it, they struck each other in the heart and died beside one another, according to the old man’s prophecy.

13. Abba Poemen said:

“The monk’s virtue appears in temptations.”

14. The same man said again that Isidore the priest of Scetis once addressed the assembly of the brothers, saying:

“Brothers, did we not come to this place to labor? And now I see that there is no labor here. Therefore, having gathered up my skin, I am going where there is labor; and there I shall find rest.”

15. Saint Syncletica said:

“If you live with others in a monastery, do not move from place to place; you will be harmed if you do this. For just as a hen, if it abandons its eggs after brooding them, causes them to hatch without chicks, so a monk or virgin grows cold and dies in faith by moving from place to place.”

16. She said something else:

“When the devil cannot move a person through the goads of poverty, he employs riches to seduce him” (Ruffinus, book III, no. 157; Paschasius, chapter 20, no. 1). “When he cannot prevail through insults and reproaches, he employs praise and glory. If he cannot bring about bodily satiety and cannot seduce through pleasures, he attempts to overthrow the soul through troubles that occur contrary to one’s purpose.

“He also brings severe illnesses against the one being tempted, seeking them out so that, by making monks fainthearted through them, he may disturb the love they have for God.

“But even if the body is broken, inflamed by severe fevers, and afflicted with intolerable thirst, if you are a sinner who suffers these things, remember the punishments of the age to come, the eternal fire, and the judicial torments; then you will not fail because of what is happening in the present. Rather, rejoice, because God has visited you.

“Keep on your lips that celebrated saying: ‘The Lord has chastened and chastened me, but he has not handed me over to death’ (Psalm 117).

“If you are iron, through the fire applied to you, you will lose your rust. But if you are righteous and suffer these things, you are being advanced from great things to greater. You are gold, but through fire you will be proved more excellent.

“For ‘an angel of Satan has been given to you, a thorn in your flesh’ (1 Corinthians 12). Rejoice when you see whose likeness you have received, for you have merited receiving a gift like Paul’s.

“If you are chastened by fevers or by the severity of cold, remember what Scripture says: ‘We passed through fire and water; what remains is that we may be brought into refreshment’ (Psalm 65). You have obtained the first; await the second, doing what belongs to virtue.

“Cry out the words of the Prophet, who says: ‘I am poor and needy and suffering’ (Psalm 68). Through such tribulation you will become perfect. For he says: ‘In tribulation you enlarged me’ (Psalm 4).

“Let us therefore test our souls especially in these exercises, since we have our adversary before our eyes.”

17. He said again:

[Note: [Col. 0895D] This is absent from the Paris edition.]

“If illness troubles us, let us not be distressed, as though because of bodily sickness and wounds we could not stand for prayer or sing psalms aloud. All these things are necessary for us to destroy the desires of the body, since fasts and labors have been established for us because of shameful pleasures.
