“If, therefore, this illness blunts them, it is unnecessary to be excessively concerned with observing those practices. For just as illness is removed by a great and powerful medicine, so vices are cut away by bodily illness.

“It is a great virtue when there is endurance in illnesses and thanksgiving is offered to God.

“If we lose our eyes, let us not bear it heavily. We have lost an instrument of pride, but let us contemplate the glory of the Lord with our inward eyes.

“Have we become deaf? Let us not be distressed, because we have lost vain hearing.

“Have your hands been weakened by some illness? Let us keep our inner hands ready against the temptations of the enemy.

“Does illness possess our whole body? Yet health is growing in our inner man.”

18. He said again what was stated above [Note: [Col. 0896D] This is absent from the Paris edition.]: Those who have committed some crimes in this present age are sent to prison even against their will; so let us reduce ourselves, because of our sin, to custody, in order that the voluntary punishment of our mind may remove from us the punishments that are to come. If you fast, do not find yourself an excuse for saying that, because you were afflicted, you fell into illness, since those who do not fast also suffer similar illnesses. Have you begun some good work? Do not be turned back by the obstacles of the enemy, for the enemy himself will be destroyed by your endurance. Indeed, those who begin to sail first spread their sails and find a favorable wind; afterward, however, a contrary wind meets them. But sailors do not immediately, because of the assault of the contrary wind, either unload or abandon the ship; rather, enduring for a little while or struggling against the storm, they again find a straight course. So also, when we encounter an opposing spirit, let us raise up the cross as a sail, 587 and we shall complete the voyage through this present age without danger.

19. They said of the abbess Sarah, a virgin of blessed memory, that she lived for sixty years above the channel of a river [Col. 0897A], and never bent down to look at the river itself.

20. Abbot Hyperichius said: Let spiritual hymns be in your mouth, and let constant meditation lighten the burden of the temptations that come upon you. A clear example of this is the traveler weighed down by a load of some burden: by blowing and breathing, he gradually diminishes the labor of the burden and of the road.

21. The one mentioned above said again: We must arm ourselves against temptations, for they come in every possible way; thus, when they come upon us, we shall appear tested.

22. A certain old man said: When temptation comes upon a person, tribulations multiply around him on every side, so that he becomes fainthearted and murmurs. The old man related it in this way:

There was a certain brother in a cell, and temptation came upon him. If anyone saw him, no one wanted to greet him or receive him into his cell; if he needed bread, no one would lend him any; and if he came from the harvest, no one invited him, as was customary, to refresh himself. Once he came back from harvesting through the heat, and had no bread in his cell; yet in all these circumstances he gave thanks to God.

When God saw his patience, he took away from him the battle of temptation. And behold, immediately someone knocked at the door, leading a camel loaded with bread from Egypt. When that brother saw this, he began to weep, saying: “Lord, I am not worthy even to be afflicted a little.” When his tribulation had passed, the brothers kept him in their cells and in the church, and gave him rest.

[Col. 0897C] 23. The old man said: For this reason we do not advance: we do not know our measure, nor do we have patience in the work that we have begun; yet without any labor we wish to possess virtue.

24. A certain brother asked an old man, saying: What shall I do? My thought does not allow me to sit in my cell for even one hour. The old man said to him: “My son, return, sit in your cell, work with your hands, pray to God without ceasing, cast your thought upon the Lord, and let no one deceive you into leaving it.” And he said:

There was a certain worldly young man who had a father and desired to become a monk. Although he repeatedly begged his father to allow him to enter the monastic life, his father would not agree. At last, after being urged by faithful friends, he reluctantly consented.

That young brother departed and entered a monastery. Once he had become a monk, he began to complete every task of the monastery perfectly and to fast every day. He also began to abstain for two days at a time, and likewise to eat only once a week. His abbot saw him, marveled, and blessed God for his abstinence and labor.

After some time, the brother began to beg his abbot, saying: “I ask you, abba, to let me go into the desert.” The abbot said to him: “My son, do not think of this. You cannot endure such labor, and, besides, the temptations and cunning of the devil. When temptation comes upon you, you will find no one there to comfort you amid the disturbances of the enemy that will be inflicted upon you.”

But the brother began to urge him even more [Col. 0897D] to permit him to leave. When his abbot saw that he could not keep him, he prayed and let him go.

Afterward he said to his abbot: “I ask you, abba, to provide people to show me the road I must take.” The abbot assigned two monks of the monastery to him, and they departed with him.

As they traveled through the desert for one day and then another, they became exhausted from the heat. They threw themselves on the ground and lay there, falling into a brief sleep. Behold, an eagle came, struck them with its wings, went some distance ahead, and settled on the ground.

When they awoke, they saw the eagle, and said to him: “There is your angel; rise and follow it.” He rose, bade farewell to the brothers, and followed it. He came to the place where the eagle was standing; immediately it rose and flew about one stadium, then settled again. The brother likewise followed it. Again it flew and settled not far away, and this continued for three hours.

Afterward, as he followed it, the eagle turned to the right, away from the one following it, and disappeared. The brother nevertheless continued on. Looking around, he saw three palm trees, a spring of water, and a small cave, and said: “Behold the place that the Lord has prepared for me.”

He entered it and began to live there, eating dates and drinking water from the spring. He remained there alone for six years, seeing no one.

And behold, one day the devil came to him in the likeness of a certain elderly abbot, with a terrifying face. When the brother saw him, he was afraid; he fell into prayer and then rose. The devil said to him: “Let us pray again, brother.”

When they had risen, [Col. 0898C] the devil said: “How long have you been here?” He replied: “Six years.” The demon said to him: “Behold, I have been your neighbor, and I did not know until four days ago that you lived here. I too have a monastery not far from you; and behold, it is eleven years since I left the monastery—except today, when I learned that you lived near me.

“I thought to myself: ‘I will go to this man of God and discuss with him what might contribute to the salvation of our souls.’ And I tell you this, brother: We gain nothing by sitting in our cells, because we do not receive the body and blood of Christ; and I fear that we may become outsiders to him if we distance ourselves from this mystery.

“But I tell you, brother, behold, three miles from here there is a monastery with a priest. Let us go every Sunday, or every two weeks, receive the body and blood of Christ, and return to our cells.”

This devilish counsel pleased the brother. When Sunday came, behold, the devil came and said to him: “Come, let us go, for it is time.” They went out and traveled to the monastery mentioned above, where the priest was. After entering the church, they devoted themselves to prayer.

When the brother rose from prayer, he looked around and did not find the one who had brought him there. He said: “Where do you suppose he has gone? Perhaps he has gone to attend to a common necessity.” He waited a long time, but the other did not come.

Then he went outside and searched for him. When he did not find him, he asked the brothers of that place: “Where is the abbot who entered the church with me?” They said to him: “We saw no one else except you.”

Then the brother understood that it had been a demon, and said: “See with what cunning the devil drove me out of my cell. Nevertheless, this does not concern me, since I came for a good work: I shall receive the body and blood of Christ and then return to my cell.”

After the offices had been celebrated in the church, the brother wished to return to his cell. The abbot of that monastery detained him, saying: “Unless you eat with us, we will not let you return.” After he had eaten, he returned to his cell.

And behold, again the devil came in the likeness of a certain worldly young man. He began to look him over from the crown of his head to his feet and to say: “Is this the man? No, he is not.” And he continued examining him.

The brother said to him: “Why are you looking at me like that?” The other replied: “I suppose you do not recognize me; yet after so long a time, how could you recognize me? I am your father’s neighbor, the son of that man. What? Was your father not called so-and-so? Did your mother not have such-and-such a name? Was your sister not called so-and-so? Are you not called by this name? Were those slaves not called by those names?

“Your mother and sister died three years ago; your father has just died, and he made you his heir, saying: ‘To whom shall I leave my property except to my son, the holy man who abandoned the world and went after God? To him I leave all my goods.’

“Now, whoever has the Lord and knows where he is, let him say so, so that he may come, dispose of all the property, and distribute it to the poor for my soul and his. Many went searching for you, but they did not find you. I came here by chance on some business and recognized you. Therefore, do not delay: come, sell everything, and act according to your father’s will.”

The brother replied: “I have no need to return to the world.” The devil said: “If you do not come and that property is lost, you will afterward have to give an account of it before God. What evil am I telling you to do? Come and distribute it to the poor and needy, like a good steward, so that what was left to the poor may not be squandered on prostitutes and evil livers. Or what burden is it to come, give alms according to your father’s will for the sake of your soul, and return to your cell?”

Why say more? By persuading the brother, he brought him back into the world; and when he had come with him as far as the city, he left him.

The brother wished to enter his father’s house, thinking that his father had already died. Behold, his father himself came out alive. When he saw him, he did not recognize him and said to him: “Who are you?” The brother, confused, could not answer. His father began to ask him again where he was from.

Then, ashamed, he said to him: “I am your son.” His father said to him: “Why have you returned?” He was ashamed to say what had brought him back, but said: “Your affection made me return, because I longed for you.”

And he remained there. After some time he fell into fornication, and although his father afflicted him with many punishments, the wretched man did not repent but remained in the world. Therefore I say, brothers, that a monk must never, persuaded by anyone for any reason, leave his cell.

25. Some people came in the desert to a certain great old man and said to him: “How are you content here, abba, and how do you endure this labor?” (Ruff., book III, no. 3.) The old man said to them: “All the labor of my lifetime that I endure here is not worthy to be compared with one day of the torments prepared for sinners in the age to come.”

26. The old man said: The ancients did not quickly move from place to place except for perhaps three reasons: if someone was angry with them and, although they had made every effort to satisfy him, they could not appease him; or if it happened that they were praised by many; or if they had fallen into the temptation of fornication.

[Col. 0900B] 27. A certain brother said to Abbot Arsenius: “What shall I do, abba? I am afflicted by my thought, which says: ‘You cannot fast, work, or visit the sick, although this too is a reward.’”

When the old man saw that these were diabolical seeds, he said to him: “Go, eat, drink, and sleep; only do not leave your cell, knowing that perseverance in the cell brings the monk to his proper order.”

After he had done this for three days, he became weary. Finding a few palm fronds, he split them; on the following day he again began to braid them. When he became hungry, he said to himself: “Here are a few more palm fronds; I will unweave them and eat.” After he had unbraided them, he said again: “I will weave a little, and then eat.” After he had woven, he said: “I will recite a few psalms, and then eat securely.”

Thus, little by little, with God’s cooperation, he advanced until he reached his proper order. Once he had gained confidence against his evil thoughts, he conquered them.

28. An old man was asked why a brother sitting in his cell suffered from weariness. The old man said to him: “Because you have not yet seen either the hoped-for resurrection or the kindled torments. If you had seen these, even if your cell were so full of worms that you were submerged in them up to your neck, you would certainly endure it and would not become weary.”

29. The brothers urged a certain old man to rest from his severe labor. He replied to them: “Believe me, my children, Abraham repented when he saw the great and splendid gifts of God, wondering why he had not contended in labors even more.”

[Col. 0900D] 30. A brother asked an old man, saying: “My thoughts waver, and I am troubled.” He said: “Remain in your cell, and the thoughts will come again. For just as, when a she-ass is tied up, her foal wanders and runs here and there but always returns to its mother wherever it goes, so will the thoughts of one who, for God’s sake, has tolerably remained seated in his cell be: even if they waver for a little while, they return again to him.”

31. A certain old man sat in the desert, and water was far from his cell, twelve miles away. Once, while he was going to draw water, he became exhausted and said: “Why must I endure this labor? I will come and live near this water.”

After saying this, he turned and saw someone following him and counting his footsteps. He asked him: “Who are you?” The other said: “I am an angel of the Lord, and I was sent to count your footsteps and give you your reward.”

When the old man heard this, he became courageous and more eager, and placed his cell even farther from that water.

32. The Fathers said: If temptation befalls you in the place where you live, do not leave the place during the time of temptation. For if you leave, wherever you go you will find before you what you were fleeing. Be patient until the temptation passes, lest your departure become a stumbling block to others, and lest perhaps your departure bring tribulation upon those who live around that place.

33. There was a certain brother in a community who was restless and frequently moved to anger (Ruffin., book III, no. 98). He said to himself: “I will go and live alone somewhere. Since I will have no one with whom to speak or listen, I shall be quiet, and the passion of anger will leave me.”

He went out and lived alone in a cave. One day, after filling his small water vessel, he placed it on the ground; suddenly it tipped over. He filled it a second time, and again it tipped over. Then, after filling it a third time, he set it down, and once more it tipped over.

Moved by fury, he seized the vessel and smashed it. Turning inward upon himself, he realized that he had been mocked by the same demon of anger and said: “Behold, I am alone, and it has conquered me. I will therefore return to the community, because everywhere labor and patience are necessary, and above all the help of God.”

He rose and returned to his place.

[Col. 0901C] 34. A brother asked an old man (Ruff., book III, no. 106), saying: “What shall I do, Father? I do no monastic work, but live in a certain negligence, eating, drinking, and sleeping; moreover, I am occupied with shameful thoughts and much agitation, passing from one task to another and from one thought to another.”

The old man said to him: “Remain in your cell and do what you can without agitation. For what you are doing now, little though it is, is like what Abba Antony did when he was accomplishing great and numerous works in the desert. I believe in God that whoever, for his name’s sake, sits in his cell and guards his conscience will himself be found in the place of Antony.”

35. An old man was asked how a vigilant monk ought not to be scandalized when he sees some returning to the world. He replied:

A monk should look at dogs hunting hares. When one of them sees the hare, it pursues it; the others, seeing only a dog running, run with it for a while, but afterward, becoming tired, turn back. The one who saw the hare alone continues until it catches it. It is not hindered in its purpose or its running by those who turn back behind it. It does not think about precipices, forests, or thorns; sometimes it runs into the briars, is scratched and pricked, and does not rest until it catches the hare.

So also the monk, or anyone who seeks the Lord Christ, continually fixes his attention on the cross, passing through all the scandals that arise [Col. 0902A] until he reaches the one who was crucified.

590 36. The old man said: Just as a tree cannot bear fruit if it is transplanted too often, so a monk who frequently moves cannot bear fruit.

37. A certain brother was troubled by his own thoughts, which urged him to leave the monastery, and he reported this to the abbot. The abbot said: “Go, sit down, pledge your body to the wall of your cell, and do not leave it. As for your thought, let it think as much as it wishes; only do not throw your body out of your cell.”

38. The old man said: The monk’s cell is that Babylonian furnace where the three youths found the Son of God; but it is also the pillar of cloud from which God spoke to Moses.

39. A certain brother remained for nine years besieged by his thoughts, which urged him to leave the community of the brothers. Every day he would take up the little hide on which he usually slept, intending to leave. When evening came, he would say to himself: “Tomorrow I will depart from here.” In the morning he would say in his thought: “Let us force ourselves to remain here today also for the Lord’s sake.”

After he had done this day after day for nine years, the Lord took away his temptation.

40. A certain brother fell into temptation and, through his distress, lost the monastic rule. When he again wished to lay the foundations of a disciplined life for himself, distress hindered him, and he said to himself: “When will I find myself as I once was?” [Col. 0902C] Losing heart, he could not even begin the work of a monk.

He came to a certain old man and related what was happening to him. When the old man heard what afflicted him, he gave him this example:

A certain man owned an estate, but through his negligence it became overgrown with thorns and filled with briars and brambles. Later he decided to cultivate it and said to his son: “Go and clear that field of the estate.”

His son came to clear it. When he looked at it, he saw that a multitude of briars and thorns had grown up in it. Losing heart, he said to himself: “When shall I ever uproot and clear all this?” He threw himself on the ground and began to sleep; he did this for many days.

Afterward his father came to see what he had done and found that he had accomplished nothing. He said to him: “Why have you done nothing until now?” The young man said to his father: “As soon as I came to work, father, when I saw this multitude of briars and thorns, I was turned back from undertaking the labor; and because of my distress I threw myself on the ground and slept.”

Then his father said to him: “My son, work each day an area as wide as the space you occupy while lying on the ground. In this way your work will gradually advance, and you will not become fainthearted.”

When the young man heard this, he did so, and in a short time the estate was cleared and cultivated.

“You too, brother, work little by little and do not lose heart, and God by his grace will restore you again to your former order.”

After hearing this, the brother departed and, sitting with complete patience, did as the old man had taught him. Thus, finding rest, he advanced through the Lord Christ.

41. There was a certain old man who frequently fell ill (Ruffin., book III, no. 158; Pasch., chapter 20, no. 2). It happened one year that he did not become ill; he was deeply distressed and wept, saying: “God has abandoned me and has not visited me.”

42. The old man said that a brother was once tormented by his thoughts for nine years, to the point that through fear itself he despaired of his salvation (Ruffin., book III, no. 194). He condemned himself, saying: “I have lost my soul.” And since he was already ruined, he said: “I will go to the world.”

As he was leaving, a voice came to him on the road, saying: “The temptations that you endured for nine years will be your crowns. Return, therefore, to your place, and I shall lift you up from your evil thoughts.”

From this it is understood that it is not good for anyone to despair of himself because of what comes into his thoughts. For if we deal with these thoughts well, they provide us with a crown all the more.

43. There was a certain old man in the Thebaid who sat in a cave and had a tested disciple. It was the old man’s custom to teach his disciple in the evening and remind him of what would benefit his soul. After the admonition, he would pray and dismiss him to sleep.

It happened that certain devout laypeople, who knew of the old man’s great abstinence, came to him. After he had comforted them, they departed.

After they had left, the old man again sat down in the evening, after the offices, according to his custom, admonishing and instructing that brother. While he was speaking, he became weighed down with sleep. The brother waited until the old man awoke and prayed for him as usual.

Since the old man did not awaken and the disciple had sat for a long time, the distress of his thoughts compelled him to leave and sleep. But he forced himself to resist the thought and remained seated.

Again he was compelled by sleep, but he did not leave. The same thing happened up to seven times, and he resisted his own will.

Afterward, once midnight had passed, the old man awoke and found him sitting beside him. He said: “You have not left until now?” He replied: “No, Father, because you had not dismissed me.” The old man said: “Why did you not awaken me?” He replied: “I did not presume to disturb you, lest I trouble you.”

They rose and began to say the morning prayers. After the morning prayers, the old man dismissed the disciple.

When the disciple was sitting alone, he fell into an ecstasy of mind. And behold, someone was showing him a glorious place, and a seat in it, and seven crowns above the seat. He asked the one who was showing him these things: “Whose are these?” The other said: “They belong to your disciple. God has given him the place and the seat for his manner of life; but he earned these seven crowns this night.”

When the old man heard this, he marveled and trembled. He called the disciple and said to him: “Tell me what you did this night.” He replied: “Forgive me, Father, for I did nothing.”

The old man, supposing that he was concealing the matter out of humility, said to him: “Believe me, I shall not rest unless you tell me what you did or what you thought this night.”

The brother, conscious of nothing that he had done, could find nothing to say. He said to the old man: “Forgive me, Father; I did nothing except this: compelled by the movement of my thoughts, I was about to leave and sleep seven times, but because you had not dismissed me as usual, I did not leave.”

When the old man heard this, he immediately understood that each time the brother resisted his thought, he was crowned by God. For the brother’s benefit he told him none of this, but he related it to other spiritual Fathers, so that we may learn that God grants us a crown even for small thoughts.

It is therefore good for a person to force himself in everything for God’s sake; for, as it is written, “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matthew 11).

44. Once a certain old man who lived as a solitary became ill. Since he had no one to serve him, he would rise and eat whatever he found in his cell. This continued for several days, and no one came to visit him.

After thirty days had passed without anyone coming to him, the Lord sent his angel to minister to him. When this had continued for seven days, the Fathers remembered him and said to one another: “Let us go and see whether perhaps that old man has become ill.”

When they arrived and knocked, the angel departed from him. The old man called out from inside: “Go away from here, brothers.” But they lifted the door from its hinge, entered, and asked him why he had shouted.

He said: “For thirty [Col. 0904C] days I have been laboring under illness, and no one visited me. And behold, it has now been seven days since the Lord sent an angel to minister to me; when you came, he departed from me.”

After saying this, he fell asleep in peace. The brothers marveled and glorified God, saying: “The Lord does not abandon those who hope in him.”

45. A certain old man said: If bodily illness overtakes you, do not become fainthearted. For if the Lord God wishes you to become bodily weak, who are you to regard it with displeasure? Does he himself not care for everything concerning you? Do you live without him? Endure patiently, therefore, and ask him to grant you what is necessary—that is, to do what is his will—and sit patiently, eating what you have in charity.

[Col. 0904D] 46. One of the Fathers related, saying: When I was in Oxyrhynchus, poor people came there on the evening of the Sabbath to receive the agape. While they were sleeping, there was a certain man who had nothing but a mat: he placed half of it beneath himself and covered himself with the other half, for there was severe cold.

When he went out to urinate, I heard him murmuring and groaning because of the cold, and comforting himself by saying: “I give you thanks, Lord. How many rich people are now in prison, sitting even in irons or having their feet bound in stocks, unable to urinate freely; but I am like an emperor, stretching out my feet and walking wherever I wish.”

While he was saying this, I stood listening to his words. When I went inside, I related them to the brothers, and when they heard them they were greatly edified.

47. A brother asked a certain old man, saying: If I am in some place and tribulation arises for me, and I have no one to whom I can entrust myself and disclose the suffering of my soul, what shall I do?

The old man said to him: Trust in God, for he will send his angel and his grace, and he himself will be your consolation if you ask him in charity.

He added: For I heard that something of this kind happened in Scetis. There was a certain man who was enduring temptations, and, having no confidence in anyone to whom he could confess, he prepared his cloak in the evening to leave.

And behold, during the night the grace of God appeared to him in the form of a virgin and begged him, saying: “Go nowhere, but remain here with me; none of the things you have heard will come to harm.”

Believing her words, he sat down, and his heart was immediately healed.

# THE EIGHTH BOOK  
## On the fact that nothing should be done for display

1. Abba Antony once heard about a certain young monk that he had performed a particular conspicuous deed on the road: when he saw some old men traveling and laboring as they walked, he ordered onagers to come and carry them until they reached their destination.

Those old men reported this to Abba Antony, and Abba Antony said: “It seems to me that this monk is like a ship loaded with every good thing, though it is uncertain whether it will be able to reach the harbor.”

After some time, Abba Antony suddenly began to weep, pull his hair, and mourn. When his disciples saw this, they said to him: “Why are you weeping, abba?” The old man replied: “A great pillar of the Church has just fallen.”

He was speaking of that young monk, and he added: “Go to him and see what has happened.”

His disciples therefore went and found that monk sitting on a mat and weeping over the sin he had committed. When he saw the old man’s disciples, he said to them: “Tell the old man to beseech God to grant me only ten days’ reprieve, and I hope that I shall make satisfaction to him.”

He died within five days.

2. A certain brother was praised by the monks before Abba Antony. When he came to him, Antony tested whether he could endure an insult. When he discovered that he could not bear it, he said to him: “You are like a house that is adorned on its front but stripped by thieves from behind.”

3. They said of Abba Arsenius and Abba Theodore of Pherme that they hated human glory above all things. Abba Arsenius did not readily approach anyone; Abba Theodore did approach people, but to him it was like a sword.

4. A certain man named Eulogius was a disciple of John the archbishop. This Eulogius was a presbyter and an ascetic, breaking fasts of two days’ duration; sometimes he even prolonged his fast for a week, eating only bread and salt, and for this he was praised by people.

[Note: [Col. 0989B–C] “Breaking fasts of two days’ duration” (*biduanas levando*). Thus above, Book VII, no. 24, “abstaining for two days”; below, Book X, no. 44, “breaking fasts of two days’ duration.” They would sometimes abstain for two days, sometimes for three, sometimes longer; when they broke the fast, they were said to “break two-day or three-day [fasts],” that is, periods of abstinence.]

He came to Abba Joseph at the place called Panepho, believing that he would find a stricter asceticism with him. The old man received him joyfully and, as an act of charity, had prepared for him what he himself had.

Eulogius’s disciples said: “The presbyter eats nothing but bread and salt,” while Abba Joseph silently ate.

After they had spent three days there, they heard neither singing psalms nor praying, for their work was hidden, and they departed without being edified.

By God’s providential arrangement, a mist arose, and, having lost their way, they returned to the old man. Before they knocked at the door, they heard psalms being sung. After waiting a long time to listen, they knocked, and the old man received them again with joy.

Those who were with Eulogius, because of the heat, took up the small water vessel and gave it to him to drink. The water had been mixed with sea water and river water, and he could not drink it.

As he considered this in his mind, he began to ask the old man to explain his practice, saying: “What is this, abba? At first you were not singing psalms, but now you began after we had gone out; and when I wanted to drink water, I found it salty.”

The old man said to him: “A brother was distracted and mistakenly mixed in sea water.”

Eulogius continued to ask the old man, wishing to know the truth. The old man said to him: “That small cup is for the wine that charity provides; this one is for the water that the brothers continually drink.”

By these words he taught him discernment of thoughts and cut away from him all the human impulses that moved his mind. Eulogius became like everyone else, thereafter eating everything that was set before him. He also learned to work in secret and said to the old man: “Truly, your work is performed in charity.”

5. Abba Zeno, the disciple of Abba Silvanus, said: Never remain in a renowned place, never sit with a man of great reputation, and never lay a foundation in order to build yourself a cell somewhere.

6. A certain brother once came to Abba Theodore of Pherme and spent three days asking him to hear a word from him. The old man did not answer him, and the brother departed sadly.

His disciple said to him: “Abba, why did you not speak to him? Behold, he has gone away sad.”

The old man said: “Believe me, I did not speak to him because he is a merchant: he wishes to boast in other people’s words.”

7. Another brother asked the same Abba Theodore, saying: “Would you approve of my not eating bread for several days?” The old man said: “You are doing well; I too have done this.”

The brother said to him: “I want to take a small quantity of chickpeas to the bakery and make flour from them.” Abba Theodore said to him: “If you are going to the bakery, make yourself bread. What need is there for this additional step?”

8. Another brother asked the same old man, Abba Theodore, and began to speak and inquire about matters that he had not yet put into practice. The old man said to him: “You have not yet found a ship for yourself, nor put your vessels into it, nor begun to sail, and already you have arrived at the city where you intended to reach? When you have first put into practice the matter about which you are speaking, then speak from the matter itself.”

[Col. 0907A] 9. Then Abba Cassian said that a certain brother came to Abba Serapion, and the old man encouraged him to pray according to the custom. But the brother, saying that he was a sinner and unworthy even of the habit of a monk, would not consent.

The old man also wished to wash his feet, but the brother again used the same words and absolutely refused. The old man had him taste some food and began, in charity, to admonish him, saying:

“My son, if you wish to advance, remain in your cell, attend to yourself and to the work of your hands; for it is not as beneficial for you to make progress as it is to remain seated.”

When the brother heard this, he became so embittered and changed his expression so visibly that the old man could not fail to notice it.

Abba Serapion therefore said to him: “Until now you were saying, ‘I am a sinner,’ and accusing yourself as unworthy even to live; but when I admonished you with charity, were you right to become so embittered? If you truly wish to be humble, learn to bear courageously what is imposed upon you by another, and do not pour hateful words upon yourself.”

When the brother heard this, he repented before the old man and departed greatly advanced.

10. Once a provincial judge heard about Abba Moses (Rufinus, book III, no. 119), he went to Scetis to see him. Some people announced his arrival to an old man, who rose and fled toward the marsh. The judge and his companions came upon him and asked him:

“Tell us, old man, where is the cell of Abba Moses?”

He replied: “Why do you want to look for him? He is a foolish man and a heretic.”

When the judge came to the church, he said to the clergy:

“I heard about Abba Moses and came to see him. But behold, an old man traveling toward Egypt came upon us, and we asked him where the cell of Abba Moses was. He said to us: ‘Why are you looking for him? He is foolish and a heretic.’”

When the clergy heard this, they were distressed and said:

“What sort of old man was it who spoke these things about the holy man to you?”

They replied: “An old man wearing extremely worn clothing, tall and dark.”

They said: “That is Abba Moses. Since he did not wish to be seen by you, he said these things about himself to you.”

The judge departed greatly edified.

[Col. 0907C]

11. A brother asked Abba Mathoēs:

“If I go to live somewhere, how do you want me to conduct myself there?”

The old man said to him:

“If you settle in a place, do not seek to make a name for yourself there in any matter by saying, ‘I do not attend the brothers’ gathering,’ or, ‘I do not eat this or that.’ Such things make a vain reputation for you, and afterward you will suffer harassment, because once people hear this, they will run there.”

[Col. 0907D]

12. Abba Nisteron the Elder was walking in the desert with a brother, and when they saw a dragon, they fled. The brother said to him:

“Do you also fear, Father?”

The old man replied:

“I do not fear, my son; but it was better that, on seeing the dragon, I fled, because I had no way to escape the spirit of vainglory.”

13. A provincial judge once wished to see Abba Pastor, but the old man would not consent (Rufinus, book III, no. 20). The judge seized his sister’s son as though he were a criminal and put him in prison, saying:

“If the old man comes and asks for him, I will release him.”

The boy’s mother came to her brother, Abba Pastor, and began to weep at his door. He gave her no answer at all. Overcome by grief, she reproached him, saying:

“Even if you have entrails of iron and no compassion moves you, let pity for your own flesh and blood move you at least.”

He sent her this message:

“Pastor has not fathered children.”

And so she departed.

When the judge heard this, he sent word:

“Let him command it with a word, and I will release him.”

But the old man sent him this reply:

“Examine the case according to the law. If he is worthy of death, let him die; but if he is not, do as you wish.”

[Col. 0908A]

14. Abba Pastor said again:

“Teach your heart to keep what your tongue teaches others.”

He said again:

“Because people want to appear perfect in speaking, but in doing what they say they are inferior.”

[Col. 0908B]

15. Abba Adelphius, who had been bishop of Nilopolis, once came to Abba Sisoes on the mountain. Since he was about to leave, the old man had food tasted in the morning, although it was a fast day. When they were setting the table, behold, some brothers knocked.

The old man said to his disciple:

“Give them a few fritters, since they are worn out from their labor.”

Abba Adelphius said to him:

“Let it be for now, lest they say, ‘Abba Sisoes has eaten since morning.’”

The old man looked at him and said to the brother:

“You go and give them some.”

When they saw the porridge, they said:

“Do you have some visitors? Surely the old man is eating with you?”

The brother replied:

“Yes.”

They began to grieve and say:

“May God forgive you, because you allowed the old man to eat at this hour. Do you not know that he will have to labor for many days?”

[Col. 0908C]

When the bishop heard this, he began to do penance before the old man, saying:

“Forgive me, Abba. I was thinking in a merely human way, but you did what belongs to God.”

Abba Sisoes said to him:

“Unless God glorifies a person, human glory never stands.”

16. Abba Ammonas of the place called Raythum asked Abba Sisoes:

“When I read the Scriptures, my mind wants to adorn my speech so that I will be ready to answer questions.”

The old man said to him:

“There is no need for that. Rather, from purity of mind provide yourself with confidence in speaking.”

[Col. 0908D]

17. A provincial judge once came to see Abba Simon. The latter took the strap with which he was girded and climbed a palm tree to clean it.

The judge’s party came and asked him:

“Where is the old man who lives in this solitude?”

He replied:

“There is no solitary here.”

After saying this, the judge departed.

18. On another occasion, a different judge came to see him. The clergy who went ahead of him said:

“Abba, prepare yourself, because a judge who has heard about you is coming to receive your blessing.”

He said:

“I, too, will prepare myself.”

He covered himself with his sackcloth, took bread and cheese in his hand, sat at the entrance of his little cell, and began to eat.

The judge then arrived with his official retinue. When they saw him, they despised him, saying:

“Is this the solitary monk about whom we have heard such things?”

Immediately they departed and returned to their own affairs.

[Col. 0909A]

19. Saint Syncletica said:

“Just as an exposed treasure is quickly spent, so every virtue, once it becomes known or is publicized, will be destroyed” (Rufinus, book III, no. 114).

“For just as wax melts before the face of fire, so the soul is emptied by praise and loses the firmness of its virtues.”

20. She said again:

“Just as it is impossible for grass and seed to exist at one and the same time, so it is impossible for those who possess worldly glory to produce heavenly fruit” (Rufinus, book III, no. 113; Paschasius, chapter 13, no. 2).

21. Once, when a feast was being celebrated at Cellia, the brothers were eating in the church (Rufinus, book III, no. 54, under the name of Theodore). A certain brother said to the server:

“I do not eat anything cooked, but only salt.”

The server called another brother in the presence of the assembly and said:

“That brother does not eat cooked food; bring him salt.”

One of the elders rose and said to him:

“It would have been better for you to eat meat in your cell today than to have this statement heard before so many brothers.”

[Col. 0909B]

22. There was a man who abstained from foods and did not eat bread. He came to a certain old man. Other visitors happened to arrive there as well, and the old man prepared a little stew for them.

When they sat down to eat, the abstaining brother put soaked chickpeas before himself alone and ate them.

When they had risen from the table, the old man took him aside and said:

“Brother, if you come to someone, do not display your way of life to him. But if you wish to maintain your way of life, sit in your cell and never go out.”

The brother accepted the old man’s words and became one who lived the common life, in that he came to eat with the brothers.

[Col. 0909C]

23. The old man said:

“Human prudence cuts away all a person’s fat and leaves him dry.”

24. The old man said:

“Either flee from people by fleeing, or, while mocking the world and the people who are in it, make yourself a fool among many.”

## NINTH BOOK  
### On the fact that no one should be judged

1. A temptation once befell a brother in the congregation of Abba Elias. He was expelled from there and went to the mountain to Abba Antony. After remaining with him for some time, Antony sent him back to the congregation from which he had departed.

When they saw him, they expelled him again. He went in the same way to Abba Antony and said:

“They would not receive me, Father.”

The old man sent them this message:

“A ship suffered shipwreck at sea and lost the cargo it was carrying. With difficulty, the empty ship was brought to land. Do you therefore wish to sink the ship that has been brought safely to land?”

When they recognized that Abba Antony had sent him back, they immediately received him.

[Col. 0909D]

2. A certain brother had sinned, and the presbyter ordered him to leave the church. But Bessarion rose and went out with him, saying:

“I too am a sinner.”

3. Abba Isaac of the Thebaid came to the brothers’ congregation and saw one of the brothers at fault, and he condemned him (Rufinus, book III, no. 137).

When he had gone out into the desert, an angel of the Lord came and stood before the door of his cell, saying:

“I will not allow you to enter.”

He asked:

“What is the reason?”

The angel of the Lord answered him:

“God sent me to say to you: ‘Where do you command me to send that guilty brother whom you condemned?’”

Abba Isaac immediately did penance, saying:

“I have sinned; forgive me.”

The angel said:

“Rise; God forgives you. But from now on take care not to condemn anyone before God condemns him.”

[Col. 0910A]

4. A brother was once found at fault in Scetis. The elders held a council and sent to Abba Moses, asking him to come. He did not wish to come.

The presbyter sent to him, saying:

“Come, because the whole assembly of the brothers is waiting for you.”

He rose and came. Taking with him a very old basket, he filled it with sand and carried it behind him.

They went out to meet him and said:

“What is this, Father?”

The old man said to them:

“My sins are running behind me, and I do not see them; yet I have come today to judge another’s sins?”

When they heard this, they said nothing to the brother, but forgave him.

[Col. 0910B]

595 5. Abba Joseph asked Abba Pastor:

“Tell me how I may become a monk.”

The old man said to him:

“If you wish to find rest both in this age and in the age to come, say in every matter, ‘Who am I?’ and do not judge anyone.”

6. A certain brother asked him again:

“If I see my brother’s fault, is it good to conceal it?”

The old man said to him:

“Whenever we cover our brother’s sin, God will also cover ours; and whenever we disclose the faults of our brothers, God will likewise disclose ours.”

[Col. 0910C]

7. A brother once offended in the congregation. There was a certain solitary in that region who had not gone outside for a long time.

The abba of that congregation came to him and told him about the brother who had offended. He said:

“Expel him.”

After the brother had been expelled from the congregation, he threw himself into a ditch.

[Note: [Col. 0989C] “Ditch.” Here *fossatum* or *fossatus* seems to be used for a pit, perhaps for a marsh, from which they carried material for making their cells and baskets. In military matters, *fossatum* means something else.]

He remained there. It happened that other brothers, going to Abba Pastor, heard him weeping in the ditch. They went down to him, found him in great distress, and asked him to go to that solitary old man.

He refused, saying:

“I will die in this place.”

The brothers came to Abba Pastor and told him about him. He asked them to go to him and say:

“Abba Pastor is calling you to himself.”

When they had said this to him, he went to him.

When the old man saw him afflicted, he rose, kissed him, and rejoiced with him, asking him to take food.

Then Abba Pastor sent one of his brothers to that solitary, saying:

“I have wanted to see you for many years since I heard about you, but through the laziness of us both we have not been able to see one another. Now, God willing, since an opportunity has arisen, tire yourself by coming here so that we may see one another.”

For he did not leave his cell.

When the solitary heard this, he said:

“Unless God had inspired that old man concerning me, he would not have sent for me.”

He rose and came to him. They greeted one another joyfully and sat down.

Abba Pastor said to him:

“There were two men in one place, and both had their own dead. One of them left his own dead and went away to mourn for the other man’s dead.”

When the old man heard this, he was pierced by his words and remembered what he had done. He said:

“Pastor is above in heaven, but I am below on earth.”

[Col. 0911A]

8. A certain brother asked Abba Pastor:

“What shall I do? I become fainthearted while sitting.”

The old man said to him:

“Despise no one, condemn no one, and speak evil of no one. Then God will grant you rest, and your sitting will be without disturbance” (Rufinus, book III, no. 100; Paschasius, chapter 39, no. 2; Appendix of Martin, no. 39).

9. A council was once held in Scetis, and the Fathers were speaking about a certain brother who was at fault (Rufinus, book III, no. 136).

Abba Pior remained silent. Later he rose, went out, took a sack, filled it with sand, and carried it on his shoulders. He put a little of the same sand into a small basket and carried that in front of him as well.

When the Fathers asked him what this meant, he replied:

“This sack, which contains a great deal of sand, represents my sins. Because they are many, I have placed them behind me so that I will not grieve over them or weep for them. This little sand represents the sins of that brother; they are before my face, and I occupy myself with them by judging my brother. That ought not to happen. Rather, my own sins should be before me, and I should think about them and ask God to forgive me.”

When the Fathers heard this, they said:

“Truly, this is the way of salvation.”

[Col. 0911C]

10. The old man said:

“Do not judge a fornicator if you are chaste, because you likewise transgress the law. For the one who said, ‘You shall not fornicate,’ also said, ‘Do not judge.’”

11. A presbyter of a certain basilica came to a solitary to consecrate an offering for him to receive communion. But someone came to that solitary and accused the same presbyter before him.

When the presbyter later came again, as was customary, to consecrate the offering, the solitary was scandalized and did not open the door to him. Seeing this, the presbyter departed.

And behold, a voice came to the solitary, saying:

“Human beings have taken my judgment upon themselves.”

He fell into a state of ecstasy and saw what appeared to be a golden well, a golden bucket, a golden rope, and very good water.

He also saw a leper drawing water and pouring it back into the vessel. He wanted to drink but could not, because the one drawing the water was a leper.

And behold, a voice came to him again, saying:

“Why do you not drink from this water? What difference does it make who fills the vessel? He merely fills it and pours it into the vessel.”

When the solitary came to himself and considered the power of the vision, he called the presbyter and had him consecrate the offering for him as before.

[Col. 0911D]

12. There were two brothers of great spiritual stature in the congregation, and each had been worthy to see God’s grace in the other.

It happened once that one of them went out of the congregation on a Friday and saw someone eating in the morning. He said to him:

“Are you eating at this hour on Friday?”

The next day, the celebration of the Eucharist took place as usual. But his brother saw that the grace which had been given to him had departed from him, and he was grieved.

When he came to his cell, he said to him:

“What have you done, brother? I do not see God’s grace in you as I did before.”

He replied:

“I am conscious of no evil in either my actions or my thoughts.”

His brother said:

“Have you not spoken some offensive word?”

He remembered and said:

“Yes. Yesterday I saw someone eating in the morning and said to him, ‘Are you eating at this hour on Friday?’ This is my sin. But labor with me for two weeks, and let us ask God to forgive me.”

They did so. After two weeks, the brother saw God’s grace once again coming upon his brother, and they were comforted, giving thanks to God, who alone is good.

## TENTH BOOK  
### On discernment

1. Abba Antony said:

“There are some who wear out their bodies through abstinence, but because they have not possessed discernment, they have become far from God.”

2. Some brothers came to Abba Antony to report to him the phantasms they saw and to learn from him whether they were real or whether they were being deceived by demons.

They had a donkey with them, and it died on the road.

When they came to the old man, he forestalled them, saying:

“How did that donkey die on the road?”

They said to him:

“How do you know, Father?”

He said:

“Demons showed me.”

They said to him:

“That is why we have come to ask you: we have seen phantasms, and often they come true, so that we might not be mistaken.”

The old man satisfied them by using the example of the donkey to show that such things come from demons.

A hunter then came by, hunting wild animals in the forest. He saw Abba Antony rejoicing with the brothers, and this displeased him.

The old man wished to show him that one must sometimes accommodate oneself to the brothers. He said to him:

“Put an arrow in your bow and draw it.”

He did so.

He said to him:

“Draw again.”

He drew it.

Again he said:

“Draw still further.”

[Col. 0912D]

He drew it.

The hunter said to him:

“If I draw it beyond measure, the bow will break.”

Abba Antony said to him:

“So it is also in the work of God: if we stretch the brothers beyond measure, they quickly fail. It is therefore fitting to relax their strictness from time to time.”

When the hunter heard this, he was pierced with remorse. He departed, greatly profiting from the old man’s words, and the brothers, strengthened, returned to their place.

3. A brother said to Abba Antony:

“Pray for me.”

The old man answered him:

“Neither do I have pity on you, nor does God, unless you are concerned for yourself and ask God.”

4. Abba Antony said again:

“God does not permit wars to arise in this generation, because he knows that they are weak and cannot bear them.”

5. Abba Evagrius once said to Abba Arsenius:

“How is it that we, who have been raised amid learning and knowledge, possess no virtues, while these peasants living in Egypt possess so many virtues?”

Abba Arsenius replied:

“We, because we are occupied with the disciplines of worldly learning, possess nothing. But these Egyptian peasants have acquired virtues through their own labors.”

[Col. 0913A]

6. Abba Arsenius of blessed memory used to say:

“A monk living as a foreigner in another province should not involve himself in any affairs, and he will be at peace.”

7. Abba Mark asked Abba Arsenius:

“Is it good not to have any consolation in one’s cell? For I saw a brother who had a small vegetable garden in his cell, and he uprooted it.”

Abba Arsenius said:

“It is good, but one must act according to each person’s discipline. Even if he does not possess the strength to endure such a thing, he will plant it again.”

[Col. 0913B]

8. Abba Peter, who was a disciple of Abba Lot, related this (Rufinus, book III, no. 128; Paschasius, chapter 42, no. 1):

“I was once in the cell of Abba Agathon, and a brother came to him, saying:

“‘I want to live with the brothers, but tell me how I should live with them.’

“The old man said to him:

“‘Just as on the first day when you enter among them you preserve your status as a stranger, so preserve it all the days of your life, and do not assume familiarity.’

“Abba Macarius said:

“‘What does familiarity do?’

“The old man said:

“‘It is like a great heat. When it blazes up, everyone flees from its face, because heat also spoils the fruit of trees.’

“Abba Macarius said:

“‘Is familiarity therefore a bad thing?’

“Abba Agathon replied:

“‘There is no passion worse than familiarity, for it is the mother of all the passions. It is therefore fitting for a monk to practice not assuming familiarity, even if he is alone in his cell.’”

9. Abba Daniel said:

“When Abba Arsenius was about to die, he entrusted this to us:

“‘Take care not to wish to hold an agape for me, because if I held one for myself, I find it.’” (Rufinus, book III, no. 163.)

10. They said of Abba Agathon (Rufinus, book III, no. 21) that some people went to him, having heard that he was a man of great discernment. Wishing to test whether he would become angry, they said to him:

“Are you Agathon? We have heard about you that you are a fornicator and proud.”

He replied:

“Yes, that is so.”

They said to him:

“Are you Agathon the talkative and slanderer?”

He replied:

“I am.”

They said to him again:

“Are you Agathon the heretic?”

He replied:

“I am not a heretic.”

They asked him:

“Tell us why you patiently endured all the other insults we directed against you, but did not tolerate this statement when we said, ‘You are a heretic.’”

He replied:

“I attribute the first things to myself, because they are useful for my soul. But when you said that I was a heretic, I did not agree, because that means separation from God, and I do not wish to be separated from God.”

When they heard this, they admired his discernment and departed edified.

[Col. 0913D]

11. The same Abba Agathon was asked:

“What is greater: bodily labor or guarding the inner person?”

The abba said:

“A human being is like a tree. Bodily labor is therefore like the leaves of the tree, while guarding the inner person is its fruit. Since, as it is written, ‘Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire’ (Matthew 3), all our concern ought to be directed toward our fruit—that is, toward guarding the mind.

“Nevertheless, we also need the covering and adornment of leaves, which are bodily labor.”

Abba Agathon was wise in understanding, diligent in labor, sufficient in all things, and constantly devoted to manual work. He was sparing in food and clothing.

[Col. 0914A]

12. When a council had been held in Scetis concerning a certain matter and the matter had been settled, Abba Agathon later came and said to them:

“You have not settled the matter well.”

They said to him:

“Who are you even to speak?”

He replied:

“A son of man. For it is written: ‘If indeed you speak justice, judge rightly, sons of men’ (Psalm 57).”

[Col. 0914B]

13. Abba Agathon said:

“If an angry man were to raise the dead, he would not please God because of his anger.”

14. Three old men once came to Abba Achilles, and one of them had a bad reputation.

One of the old men said to him:

“Abba, make me a fishing net.”

He said:

“I will not.”

Another said to him:

“Make one for us, so that we may have a remembrance of you in our monastery.”

He replied:

“I have no time.”

The third, the one who had the bad reputation, said:

“Make a fishing net for me, so that I may receive a blessing from your hands, Abba.”

He immediately replied:

“I will make one for you.”

The first two, to whom he had not consented, said to him privately:

“How is this? When we asked you, you did not wish to make one, but to this man you said, ‘I will make one for you.’”

The old man replied:

“I said to you, ‘I will not,’ because I had no time, and you would not be distressed. But if I did not make one for him, he would say, ‘The old man heard about my bad reputation and therefore did not want to make a fishing net for me.’ Thus we would immediately cut the cord to soothe his mind, lest he be swallowed up by such sorrow.”

[Col. 0914C]

15. They said of a certain old man that he had spent fifty years neither eating bread nor readily drinking water (Rufinus, book III, no. 117). He used to say:

“I have extinguished fornication, avarice, and vainglory.”

When Abba Abraham heard that he had said these things, he came to him and said:

“Did you say this?”

He replied:

“Yes.”

Abba Abraham said to him:

“Suppose you enter your cell and find a woman lying on your mat. Can you avoid thinking that she is a woman?”

He said:

“No, but I fight my thought so that I will not touch that woman.”

Abba Abraham said:

“Then you have not killed fornication, since the passion itself is alive, though bound.”

“Again, suppose you are walking along the road and see stones and potsherds, with gold lying among them. Can you regard what you see as though it were stones?”

He replied:

“No, but I resist my thought so that I will not collect it.”

Abba Abraham said to him:

“Then the passion is alive, but bound.”

Abba Abraham said again:

“Suppose you hear of two brothers: one loves you and speaks well of you, while the other hates you and slanders you. If both come to you, do you receive them equally?”

He said:

“No, but I constrain my mind (sic) to treat the one who hates me as well as the one who loves me.”

Abba Abraham said to him:

“Then the passions are alive, but they are in some way bound by holy men.”

[Col. 0915A]

16. One of the Fathers related that a certain old man was laboring diligently in his cell and wore a mat.

When he went to Abba Ammonas, Abba Ammonas saw him using a mat and said to him:

“This is of no benefit to you.”

The old man said to him:

“Three thoughts trouble me. One compels me to withdraw somewhere into the desert; another urges me to go as a stranger to a place where no one knows me; the third urges me to shut myself in my cell, see no one, and eat every other day.”

Abba Ammonas said to him:

“It is beneficial for you to do none of these three things. Rather, sit in your cell and eat a little every day, always keeping in your heart the saying of that publican who is mentioned in the Gospel (Luke 18). In this way you will be able to be saved.”

[Col. 0915B]

17. Abba Daniel said:

“To the extent that the body flourishes, the soul withers; and to the extent that the body is dried up, the soul flourishes.”

Abba Daniel said again:

“To the extent that the body is pampered, the soul becomes subtle; and to the extent that the body has been made austere, the soul is pampered.”

18. Abba Daniel related again that when Abba Arsenius was in Scetis, there was a certain monk who stole whatever belonged to the old men.

Abba Arsenius wished to win him over and provide the old men with peace. He took him into his cell and said to him:

“Whatever you want, I will give you; only do not steal.”

He gave him gold, coins, small objects,

[Note: [Col. 0989C] “Small objects.” *Rescellas* also occurs in this same book, no. 76. It is a diminutive of *res* (“thing”); hence *reculas*, *rescellas* were formed.]

and everything he had in his *responso*,

[Note: [Col. 0989C] “*Responso*.” Thus the Audomaren manuscript and the Paris edition read. Other editors replaced it with *expensu* (“expense” or “expenditure”), which I think they did in order to depart as little as possible from the traces of the manuscript in which they found *responsum*. At first I conjectured *reposito*, which is used below, in Book XIII, no. 15, in a similar matter: “and he saw the storage place in which bread was usually kept.” But I scarcely doubt that the translator found the Greek προσφωνάριον (*prosphōnárion*), which indeed means “answer” in the sense in which it is commonly understood, as a response. Here, however, it seems to be used for a small basket or carrying basket. The Edessene monk uses this Greek word in this sense in the *Elenchus of the Agarene*:

“Καὶ μετὰ μικροῦ ἀπέστειλεν αὐτὴν βόσκειν τοὺς καμήλους κατὰ τὴν τῶν Ἀράβων συνήθειαν ἐπιφερομένην τὸ ὀψώνιον αὐτοῖς ἐν προσφωναρίῳ ἐπὶ τοῦ ὤμου αὐτῆς.”

“And shortly afterward he sent her to pasture the camels according to the custom of the Arabs, carrying their provisions in a *prosphonarion* on her shoulder.”

Again later:

“Καὶ λαβοῦσα ἐν τῷ προσφωναρίῳ κατὰ τὸ σύνηθες ἑσπέρας τὴν τῶν καμήλων κόπρον, καὶ ἄνωθεν τοῦ μουχαμὲτ, ἦλθεν ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ τοῦ κυρίου αὐτῆς.”

“And, according to the customary practice, taking in the *prosphonarion* in the evening the camels’ dung, with the *muchamet* on top, she came into her master’s house.”]

and gave it to him.

But he stole again.

When the elders saw that he had not stopped, they expelled him, saying:

“If a brother is found to have some bodily infirmity, one ought to endure him. But if he has stolen and, after being admonished, does not stop, expel him, because he harms his own soul and disturbs all who live in that place.”

[Col. 0915C]

19. At the beginning of his monastic life, Abba Evagrius came to a certain old man and said:

“Tell me, Abba, a word by which I may be saved.”

He said to him:

“If you wish to be saved, when you go to someone, do not speak before he asks you something.”

Evagrius was pierced by this saying, did penance in the old man’s presence, and made amends to him, saying:

“Believe me, I have read many books, but I have never found such learning.”

He departed, greatly profiting.

[Col. 0915D]

20. Abba Evagrius said:

“Reading, vigils, and prayer stabilize the wavering or wandering mind. Hunger, labor, and anxiety moisten the burning desire. Psalmody, patience, and mercy restrain disturbed anger—but these must be applied at appropriate times and in due measure. If they are practiced at an inappropriate time or without measure, they help only for a short while; and what lasts only briefly will be more harmful than useful.”

[Col. 0916A]

21. As Abba Ephraem was once passing by, a prostitute, prompted by someone, began to flatter him (Idem, book I, *Life of Ephraem*, chapter 7). She wanted either to entice him, if possible, into shameful intercourse or, if she could not do that, at least to provoke him to anger, since no one had ever seen him angry or quarreling.

He said to her:

“Follow me.”

When they had come to a crowded place, he said to her:

“Come here, and as you wished, I will have intercourse with you.”

Seeing the crowd, she said to him:

“How can we do this here, with such a crowd standing around? We would be ashamed.”

He said:

“If you are ashamed before human beings, how much more ought we to be ashamed before God, who reveals the hidden things of darkness (1 Corinthians 4)?”

Ashamed and confounded, she withdrew without carrying out her lustful purpose.

[Col. 0916B]

22. Some brothers once came to Abba Zeno and asked him:

“What does it mean that it is written in the Book of Job, ‘Not even heaven is clean in God’s sight’ (Job 15)?”

The old man replied:

“People have abandoned their own sins and are investigating heavenly things.”

This is the interpretation of the saying you asked about: since God alone is clean, it is said that even heaven is not clean in his sight.

23. Abba Theodore of Pherme said:

“If you are friends with someone and it happens that he falls into the temptation of fornication, then, if you can, give him your hand and pull him back up. But if he falls into some error of faith and does not listen to you, quickly turn back and cut off your friendship with him, lest, by lingering, you be dragged with him into the abyss.”

24. The aforementioned Abba Theodore once came to Abba John, who had been a eunuch from birth.

As they were speaking, Abba Theodore said:

“When I was in Scetis, our work was the work of the soul, while we regarded manual labor as something incidental. But now the work of the soul has become incidental, as though manual labor were the work.”

[Col. 0916C]

25. One of the Fathers once came to the same Abba Theodore and said to him:

“Behold, a certain brother has returned to the world.”

Abba Theodore said to him:

“Do not marvel at this. If you ever hear that someone has escaped from the mouth of the enemy, marvel at that.”

[Col. 0916D]

26. The aforementioned Abba Theodore said:

“Many choose temporal rest in this age before the Lord grants them rest.”

27. They said of Abba John, who was short in stature, that he once said to his older brother:

“I wanted to be secure as the angels are secure: doing nothing, but serving God without interruption.”

He stripped off the clothing he was wearing and went into the desert (Rufinus, book III, no. 56).

After spending one week there, he returned to his brother. When he knocked at the door, his brother answered before opening it, saying:

“Who are you?”

He said:

“I am John.”

His brother replied:

“John has become an angel and is no longer among human beings.”

He kept knocking and saying:

“It is I.”

But his brother did not open to him and allowed him to suffer distress.

Later he opened the door and said to him:

“If you are a human being, you must work again in order to live. But if you are an angel, what are you seeking by entering a cell?”

He did penance and said:

“Forgive me, brother, for I have sinned.”

[Col. 0917A]

599 28. Some elders once came to Scetis, and Abba John the Dwarf was with them.

While they were eating, a certain tall presbyter rose to give each person a small vessel of water to drink. No one consented to accept it from him except John the Short.

The others marveled and said to him:

“How, being the least of all, did you presume to make use of the service of such a tall old man?”

He said to them:

“When I rise to give water, I rejoice if everyone drinks, so that I may gain a reward. Now I accepted it for this reason: so that I might enable the one who had risen to receive a reward, lest he perhaps also become distressed because no one took anything from him.”

When he had said this, they all marveled at his discernment.

[Col. 0917B]

29. Abba Pastor once asked Abba Joseph:

“What should I do when some temptations draw near me? Should I resist them, or should I allow them to enter?”

The old man said to him:

“Let them enter, and fight with them.”

When he returned to Scetis, he sat there. It happened that someone coming from the Thebaid to Scetis told the brothers that he had asked Abba Joseph:

“When temptation draws near me, should I resist it, or should I let it enter?”

And that Joseph had said to him:

“Do not allow temptation into yourself at all, but cut it off immediately.”

When Abba Pastor heard that he had said this to the man who had come from the Thebaid, he rose and went again to Panephos, to Abba Joseph, and said to him:

“Abba, I entrusted my thoughts to you, but you said one thing to me and another to the brother from the Thebaid.”

The old man said to him:

“You know that I love you?”

He replied:

“Yes.”

“Did you not tell me that I should speak to you what I thought, just as I would to myself? For if temptations enter and you give and receive with them, they make you more tested. But I spoke to you as I would to myself. There are others, however, for whom it is not beneficial even to let the passions approach; they must cut them off immediately.”

[Col. 0917C]

[Col. 0917D] **30.** Abba Pastor also said: Once I came to Lower Heraclea to Abba Joseph, and he had in his monastery a very beautiful sycamore tree. From morning onward he kept saying to me, “Go, gather some for yourself and eat.” It was Friday. I did not eat because of the fast, but I asked him, saying, “Tell me, for the Lord’s sake, the reason for this, since you said to me, ‘Go, eat.’ I did not go because of the fast, but I was ashamed because I had not carried out your command, thinking that you had not ordered this of me without reason.” He replied, “The elder Fathers do not at first speak straightforwardly to the brothers, but rather in a distorted way; and if they see that they do what is [Col. 0918A] twisted, they no longer speak to them except what is useful, recognizing that they are obedient in everything.”

**31.** A brother asked Abba Joseph, saying, “What shall I do? I can neither endure hardship, nor work, nor give alms.” The old man said to him, “If you can do none of these things, at least keep your conscience from every evil against your neighbor, and so you will be saved; for God seeks a soul without sin.”

**32.** Abba Isaac the Theban said to his brothers, “Do not bring boys here, for because of the boys four churches in Scetis have become a desert.”

**33.** Abba Longinus asked Abba Lucius, saying, “I have three thoughts. One is that I should go into exile.” The old man replied, “If you do not restrain your tongue wherever you go, you will not be an exile. But restrain your tongue here, and you will also be an exile here.” Abba Longinus said to him, “My other thought is to fast by extending the fast to two days.” Abba Lucius replied, “The prophet Isaiah said, ‘Even if you bend your neck like a circle, not even then will your fast be acceptable’ (Isaiah 58); rather, restrain your mind from evil thoughts.” Abba Longinus said, “The third is my intention: to avoid the sight of people.” Abba Lucius replied, “Unless you first correct your life while associating with others, you will not be able to correct yourself even while living alone.”

**34.** Abba Macarius said, “If we remember the evils inflicted upon us by human beings, we cut off from our mind the power of remembering God. But if we remember the evils stirred up by demons, we shall be unpierceable” (Paschasius, ch. 37, no. 4; Appendix of Martyrius, no. 15).

**35.** Abba Mathois said, “Satan does not know by which passion the soul may be seduced. Therefore he does indeed sow his own tares in it, but he does not know how to reap them. Sometimes he scatters seeds of fornication, sometimes of detraction, and likewise of the other passions; and whichever passion he sees the soul inclining toward, that one he supplies to it. For if he knew toward what the soul was inclined, he would not sow diverse or varied things in it.”

**36.** They related concerning Abba Nathyra, who was a disciple of Abba Silvanus, that while he was sitting in his cell on Mount Sinai, he governed his life moderately with regard to the things necessary for the body (Appendix of Palladius, ch. 20, no. 18). But when he became bishop in [Col. 0918D] Pharan, he afflicted his soul greatly by the severity of his self-restraint. His disciple said to him, “Abba, when we were in the desert, you did not torment yourself in this way.” The old man said, “My son, there was solitude, quiet, and poverty there. Therefore I wished to care for my body, lest I become ill and seek what I did not have. But here there is the world, and there are many opportunities for excess; and if I fall into illness, there are people here to come to my aid, so that I do not lose the monk’s purpose.”

**37.** A brother asked Abba Pastor, saying, “I am troubled, and I want to leave this place.” The old man said to him, “For what reason?” He replied, “Because I hear things about a certain brother that do not edify me.” The old man said to him, “Are the things you heard untrue?” He said, “No, Father, they are true; for the brother who told me is trustworthy.” He answered, “The one who told you is not trustworthy. For if he were trustworthy, he would certainly not tell you such things. When God heard the outcry of Sodom, he did not believe it until he came down and saw with his own eyes (Genesis 18).” The brother said, “But I saw with my own eyes.” When the old man heard this, he looked down at the ground, picked up a small straw, and said to him, “What is this?” He replied, “A straw.” Again the old man looked up toward the roof of the cell and said to him, “What is this?” He replied, “A beam that supports the roof.” The old man said to him, “Put this in your heart: your sins are like this beam, while those of the brother about whom you are speaking are like this small straw.” When Abba Sisoes heard [Col. 0919B] this discourse, he marveled and said, “With what shall I call you blessed, Abba Pastor? Yet, like a precious stone, your words are full of grace and glory.”

**38.** Once the presbyters of that region came to the neighboring monasteries, where Abba Pastor was also present. Abba Anub entered and said to him, “Let us ask these presbyters today to receive here, in charity, the gifts of God.” He stood for a long time without giving him an answer, and Abba Anub went out sorrowfully. Those sitting beside Abba Pastor said to him, “Why did you not answer him?” Abba Pastor said to them, “I have no cause to answer; for I am already dead. A dead man does not speak. Therefore do not count me as being here with you.”

[Col. 0919C] **39.** Once a certain brother went from Abba Pastor’s monastery into a foreign land (Rufinus, book III, no. 114), and came to a certain solitary. That man had charity toward everyone, and many people came to him. The brother told him certain things about Abba Pastor, and when he heard of his virtue of soul, he desired to see him.

When that brother had returned to Egypt, after some time the aforementioned solitary rose and came as a stranger into Egypt to the same brother who had previously stayed with him, for the brother had told him where he lived. When the brother saw him, he was astonished and very glad. The solitary said to him, “Show me the charity you have toward me, and take me to Abba Pastor.” He took him and led him to the old man, and announced him, saying, [Col. 0919D] “A great man, possessed of much charity and of very great honor in his own province, has come wishing to see you.”

The old man received him gladly, and after greeting one another they sat down again. The visiting brother began to speak about the holy Scriptures and spiritual and heavenly matters. Abba Pastor, however, turned his face away and gave him no answer. Seeing that he would not speak to him, the man went out sorrowfully and said to the brother who had brought him, “I have undertaken this journey in vain. I came to the old man, and look—he does not even consider me worthy of speaking with him.”

The brother entered Abba Pastor’s presence and said to him, “Abba, this great man, who possesses such glory in his own place, came because of you. Why did you not speak with him?” [Col. 0920A] The old man replied, “He is from above and speaks of heavenly things, whereas I am from below and speak of earthly things. If he had spoken to me about the passions of the soul, I would certainly have answered him; but as for spiritual matters, I do not know them.”

The brother went out and said to him, “The old man does not quickly speak about the Scriptures; but if someone speaks to him about the passions of the soul, he answers him.” The visitor, moved to compunction, entered again to the old man and said to him, “What shall I do, Abba, since the passions of the soul dominate me?” The old man looked at him joyfully and said, “Now you have come well; now I shall open my mouth concerning these matters and fill it with good things.”

The man, greatly edified, said, “Truly, this is the way of charity.” Giving thanks to God that he had been found worthy to see such a holy man, he returned to his own country.

[Col. 0920B] **40.** A brother asked Abba Pastor, saying, “I have committed a great sin, and I want to repent for three years.” Abba Pastor said to him, “That is a long time.” The brother said to him, “Do you command one year?” Again the old man said, “That is a long time.” Those who were present said, “Up to forty days?” Again the old man said, “That is a long time.” And he added, “I think that if a person repents with his whole heart and does not again undertake the thing for which he is repenting, God will accept even three days of repentance.”

**41.** Abba Ammon asked him about impure thoughts, which the human heart generates, and about vain desires. Abba Pastor said to him, “Will the axe boast without the one who cuts with it (Isaiah 10)?” Therefore you too must not stretch out your hands toward them, and they will remain idle.

**42.** Abba Isaiah asked him the same question. Abba Pastor said, “Just as clothes in a chest full of garments rot if it is left for a long time, so it is with the thoughts in our heart. If we do not carry them out bodily, in the course of time they will be destroyed and rot.”

**43.** Abba Joseph asked about the same matter, and Abba Pastor said, “Just as someone who shuts up a serpent or scorpion in a vessel and seals it causes it to die completely as time passes, so evil thoughts, which spring up through the activity of demons, gradually weaken through the patience of the person into whom they are cast.”

**44.** Abba Joseph asked Abba Pastor, saying, “How ought one to fast?” (Rufinus, book III, [Col. 0920D] no. 45). Abba Pastor said, “I want a person who eats every day to take a little away from himself from time to time, so that he may not become satiated.” Abba Joseph said to him, “So when you were young, did you not fast by extending the fast to two days?” The old man said, “Believe me, I also fasted for three days and for a week. But the great elders tested all these practices and found that it is good to eat every day, a little less on each day. They showed us this royal road, because it is lighter and easier.”

**45.** Abba Pastor said, “Do not live in a place where you see people who are jealous of you, for there you will make no progress.”
