**46.** A brother came to Abba Pastor and said to him, “I sow my field, and from it I provide an agape-meal.” The old man said to him, [Col. 0921A] “You are doing a good work.” The brother went away with this purpose in mind and continued to add to the meal he was making.

When Abba Anub heard this, he said to Abba Pastor, “Do you not fear God, since you spoke to that brother in this way?” The old man was silent. After two days Abba Pastor sent for that brother, called him to himself, and said to him in the hearing of Abba Anub, “What did you ask me that day? My mind was elsewhere.” The brother said, “I said this: ‘I sow my field, and from what I gather I provide an agape-meal.’” Abba Pastor said to him, “I thought you were speaking about that other brother of yours, who is a layman. But if you do these things, it is not the work of a monk.”

Hearing this, the brother was saddened and said, “I neither do nor know any other work besides this. May I not sow my field?” When he had gone away, Abba Anub began to repent before Abba [Col. 0921B] Pastor, saying, “Forgive me.” Abba Pastor said to him, “Behold, from the beginning I knew that it was not the work of a monk, but I spoke to him according to his state of mind and stirred his mind toward progress in charity. Now he has gone away sorrowful, and yet he continues to do this work.”

**47.** A certain brother asked Abba Pastor, saying, “What does this mean that is written: ‘Whoever is angry with his brother without cause’ (Matthew 5 in the Greek)?” He replied, “For every matter by which your brother may wish to trouble you, if you become angry against him until you tear out your right eye and cast it away from you, you are angry with him without cause. But if someone wishes to separate you from God, be angry for this reason—”

[Col. 0921C] **48.** Abba Pastor said, “If a person sins and does not deny it, saying, ‘I have sinned,’ do not rebuke him, for you destroy his resolve. But if you say, ‘Do not be distressed, brother, but be watchful from now on,’ you stir his mind toward repentance.”

**49.** The same man said again, “Experience is good. For through experience people become more proven.”

**50.** The same man also said, “If someone teaches something and does not do what he teaches, he is like a well that refreshes all who come to it and washes away their filth, but cannot cleanse itself; rather, all foulness and impurity are in it” (Rufinus, book III, no. 183).

**51.** He said again, “There is a person who knows himself.” He said again, “There is a person who appears to be silent with his mouth, but his heart condemns others; such a person is speaking without ceasing. There is another who speaks from morning until evening and keeps silence. He said this because he never spoke without benefit to those listening.”

**52.** He said again, “If there are three together, one of whom rests well, another is ill and gives thanks, and the third ministers to them with sincere willingness, these three are alike, as though they were engaged in one and the same work.”

**53.** He said again, “Malice never drives out malice. But if someone does evil to you, do good to him, so that by your good work you may destroy his malice” (Rufinus, book III, no. 79; Paschasius, ch. 7, no. 3).

[Col. 0922A] **54.** He said again, “The one who is given to complaint is not a monk; the one who repays evil for evil is not a monk; the one who is irascible is not a monk.”

**55.** A brother came to Abba Pastor and said to him, “Many thoughts come into my soul, and I am endangered by them.” The old man led him outside under the open sky and said to him, “Spread out your cloak and catch the wind.” He replied, “I cannot do that.” The old man said to him, “If you cannot do this, neither can you prevent the thoughts from entering; but it is yours to resist them.”

**56.** A certain brother asked him, saying, “An entire inheritance has been left to me. What shall I do with it?” Abba Pastor said to him, “Go, and come back after three days, and I will tell you.” He came at the appointed time, and [Col. 0922B] the old man said to him, “What can I tell you, brother? If I say, ‘Give it to the church,’ the clergy will make banquets for themselves from it; if I say, ‘Give it to your relatives,’ you will have no reward; but if I say, ‘Give it to the poor,’ you will be secure. Whatever you wish, go and do it; I have no reason to decide for you” (Paschasius, ch. 36, no. 4, under the name of Sisoes; Appendix of Martyrius, no. 7).

**57.** Abba Pastor said again, “If a thought concerning things necessary for the body comes to you and you dismiss it once, and it comes again and you dismiss it, what happens? If it comes a third time, do not pay attention to it; it is idle.”

**58.** A certain brother said to Abba Pastor, “If I see something, do you want me to tell it?” The old man said to him, “It is written: ‘Whoever answers before he hears, it is folly and disgrace for him’ (Ecclesiasticus 11). Therefore, if you are asked, speak; otherwise, be silent.”

**59.** Abba Pastor said again that Abba Ammon had said, “There is a person who carries an axe throughout his whole life and cannot cut down a tree; but there is another who has skill in cutting and fells a tree with a few blows.” He said that the axe signified discernment.

**60.** He said again, “The human will is a bronze wall and a stone barrier between a person and God. If he abandons these things, he too may say what is written in the psalm: ‘In my God I shall leap over a wall,’ and, ‘My God, his way is undefiled’ (Psalm 17). For if righteousness comes to the aid of the will, a person labors.”

**61.** A brother asked Abba Pastor, saying, [Col. 0922D] “I suffer harm to my soul because I am with my abba. What, then, do you command? Shall I remain with him?” Abba Pastor knew that his soul was being harmed by his abba, and he was astonished that the man should even ask whether he ought to remain with him. He said to him, “If you wish, stay.” The brother went away and remained with him.

He came again and said to Abba Pastor, “I am burdening my soul.” Abba Pastor did not say to him, “Leave him.” He came a third time and said, “Believe me, I will no longer be with him.” The old man said to him, “Behold, now you are saved; go, and do not remain with him any longer.”

For Abba Pastor had said to the same man, “A person who sees that his soul is suffering harm has no need to ask. One asks about hidden thoughts, so that the elders may test them; but concerning manifest sins there is no need to ask—one must cut them off immediately.”

**62.** Abba Abraham, who was a disciple of Abba Agathon, asked Abba Pastor, saying, “Why do the demons attack me in this way?” Abba Pastor said to him, “Do the demons attack you? Demons do not fight against us when we do our own wills; for our own wills have become demons, and they are what trouble us so that we may do them. But if you want to know the sort of people against whom demons fight, look at Moses and those like him.”

**63.** Abba Pastor said that a certain brother had asked Abba Moses, saying, “What does it mean for a person to mortify himself in relation to his neighbor?” He replied, “Unless a person places in his heart that he has been three years in the grave, he does not attain to this saying” (Rufinus, book III, no. 102; Paschasius, ch. 43, no. 2, under the name of Silvanus; Appendix of Martyrius, no. 108).

**64.** A brother asked Abba Pastor, saying, “How ought a monk to sit in his cell?” The old man said to him, “To sit in the cell, as regards what is visible, means that he should do manual work, eat once, be silent, and meditate. Secretly to make progress in the cell means that each person should bear his own reproach in every place wherever he goes, observe the hours of the service, and not neglect what is hidden.

“If a time comes when he is free from manual work, let him enter upon the service of the work of God and complete it without any disturbance. The end of these things is that you should keep the company of those who live together in goodness and be recalled from the company of the wicked.”

**65.** Once two brothers came to Abba Pambo, and one of them asked, saying, “Abba, I fast for two days and eat two paximates. Do you think I shall save my soul, or am I deceived?” The other said, “I earn two siliquae a day from my manual work, and I retain a little of them for food, while I spend the rest on almsgiving. Do you think I shall be saved, or am I deceived?”

Although they pleaded with him at length, he did not answer them. After four days, when they were about to leave, the clergy said to them, “Do not be sad, brothers; God will grant you your reward. This is the old man’s custom: he does not speak quickly unless God gives him what he is to say.”

They therefore entered to the old man and said to him, “Abba, pray for us.” He said to them, “Do you want to depart?” They said, “Yes.” Looking at them and taking their works into himself, he wrote on the ground and said, “Pambo fasts for two days and eats two paximates. Is he a monk on this account?” No. Again he said, “And Pambo works for two siliquae a day and gives them in alms. Is he a monk on this account?” Not yet.

After remaining silent for a little while, he said to them, “You are indeed doing good work, but if you keep your conscience with your neighbor, you will be saved in this way.” Thus edified, the brothers departed joyfully.

**66.** A certain brother asked Abba Pambo, saying, “Why do certain spirits prevent me from doing good to my neighbors?” The old man said to him, “Do not speak in this way, lest you make God a liar. Rather say, ‘I absolutely do not want to show mercy.’ For God, going before you, said, ‘I have given you authority to trample on scorpions and serpents, and over all the power of the enemy’ (Luke 10). Why, then, do you not trample on the unclean spirits?”

**67.** Abba Palladius said, “The soul that lives according to Christ’s will ought either faithfully to learn what it does not know or openly to teach what it knows. If, when it can do both, it is unwilling to do either, it suffers from the disease of insanity. For the beginning of turning away from God is disgust with instruction, when the soul does not desire that for which the soul that loves God always hungers” (Palladius, Letter to Lausos, under the title of Heraclides, in Hervetus’s edition).

**68.** A brother said to Abba Sisoes, “Why do the passions not depart from me?” The old man said to him, “Because the vessels of those passions are within you. But give them their pledge, and they will depart.”

**69.** A certain brother came to Abba Silvanus on Mount Sinai and saw the brothers working. He said to the old man, “Do not work for the food that perishes (John 6); but Mary chose the better part (Luke 10).” The old man said to his disciple, “Call Zacharias and put this brother in the cell where there is nothing” (Rufinus, book III, no. 55).

When the ninth hour came, he watched the door to see whether they would send for him and call him to eat. When no one spoke to him, he rose, came to the old man, and said to him, “Abba, did the brothers not eat today?” [Col. 0924C] The old man said, “Yes, they have already eaten.” The brother said, “Why did you not call me?” The old man replied, “You are a spiritual man and have no need of this food; but we are carnal and wish to eat, and therefore we work with our hands. You, however, have chosen the better part, reading all day and refusing to take carnal food.”

When he heard this, he prostrated himself in repentance, saying, “Forgive me, my abba.” The old man said, “I think that Mary certainly needs Martha, for Mary is praised through Martha.”

**70.** Saint Syncletica said, “Those who gather earthly riches through labor and the dangers of the sea, when they gain much, then desire more, and regard what they have as nothing; toward what they do not yet have they direct all the attention of their mind. But we possess nothing even of the things that must be sought, and through fear of God we do not wish to possess what is necessary.”

**71.** She said again, “There is a useful sadness, and there is a sadness that corrupts. Useful sadness is that we should groan over our sins and over the ignorance of our neighbors, and that we should not fall away from our purpose but attain the perfection of goodness. These are forms of true sadness.

“There is also a certain association of our adversary with these things. For he sends sadness without any reason, which they have called weariness or listlessness. Such a spirit must therefore be driven away more often by prayer and the singing of psalms.”

**72.** She said again, “There is an extended and severe abstinence that comes from the devil’s instigation, for his followers also do this. When, then, do we distinguish divine and royal abstinence from tyrannical and diabolical abstinence?

“It is clear: throughout the moderate course of your life, let one rule of fasting be yours. Do not suddenly fast for four or five consecutive days and then dissolve your discipline by an abundance of food; for this makes the devil glad. Everything without measure is corruptible.

“Do not suddenly expend your weapons, lest you be found naked in battle and easily captured. Our weapons are our body, and our soul is the soldier. Therefore give careful attention to both, so that you may be ready for what is necessary.”

**73.** Once two old men came from the region of Pelusium to the abbess Sarah. As they walked, they said to one another, “Let us humble this old woman.” They said to her, “Take care that your mind is not exalted and you do not say, ‘Look, solitary men are coming to me, who am a woman.’” The abbess Sarah said to them, “In sex I am a woman, but not in spirit.”

**74.** The abbess Sarah said again, “If I asked God that all human beings might be edified through me, I would be found repenting before the door of each one. Rather, I pray that my heart may be pure with everyone.”

**75.** Abba Hyperichius said, “He is truly wise who teaches others by his deed, not by his words.”

**76.** Once a certain monk came from the city of Rome. He had held a high position at the palace and lived in Scetis near the church. He had with him a single servant who ministered to him.

When the presbyter of the church saw his infirmity and realized that the man had come from a life of luxury, whatever the Lord granted him, or whatever entered the church, he sent to him. After he had spent twenty-five years in Scetis, he became a contemplative man, gifted with foresight and renowned.

When one of the great Egyptian monks heard of his reputation, he came to see him, hoping to find his bodily discipline more severe. When he entered, he greeted him, and after praying they sat down. Seeing the Roman clothed in soft garments, with a papyrus *buda* and a skin spread beneath him, and with a small pillow of *cartica* under his head [Note: [Col. 0989D] “*Buda* of papyrus, etc., pillow of *cartica*.” Thus consistently in the manuscripts. Some editions have *matta* instead of *buda* and omit *de cartica*. It is difficult to decide between the two, since they are scarcely found elsewhere. It is certain that *buda* means a bed-covering or bedding, as it is called immediately below in this very passage. The Cambridge Glossary manuscript: “*Buda*, bedding for a bed made of *biblos*, that is, papyrus.” Isidore’s Glosses: “*Buda*, history.” I read *storea* [mat]. For *historia* in place of *storea* is said in the manner in which *Hispania* is used for *Spania*. I cannot say precisely what *cartica* is. Joannes Meursius, in his Greek-Barbarian Glossary, under Καρτζὰ [*Kartzā*], cites *Cartica* from excerpts of the Arabic-Latin Glossaries without interpretation. In the Excerpts from an Old Greek-Latin Lexicon, he gives *Carticula*, δεῖπνον [a meal]; that meaning does not suit this passage.

“In Cassian, Conference 1, chapter 23, one finds *embrimium* or *embrymium*, used for the monks’ pillow in Egypt, and he describes it thus: ‘He warns them to lie upon reed mats, with *embrimia* likewise placed beneath our heads in place of pillows. These, made from thicker papyrus reeds fitted into long, slender bundles and softly bound at intervals of a cubit and a half, now provide the brothers sitting in the assembly with a very low seat in place of a stool; now, placed beneath their necks, they offer the heads of those sleeping a support that is not excessively hard but pliable and suitable. These materials are considered especially convenient and appropriate for the monks’ use because they are somewhat soft and can be prepared with little labor and at little cost, since papyrus grows abundantly along the banks of the Nile and no one prevents anyone who wishes to use it from cutting it down; and because they are easy to remove or, when necessary, to put in place, being light and easily handled.’”]

and also had clean feet with little shoes, he was inwardly scandalized by him, because in that place it was not customary to live in such a manner; rather, they were accustomed to practicing severe abstinence.

The Roman old man, possessing contemplation or the grace of foresight, understood that the Egyptian monk had been scandalized inwardly by him, and said to his servant, “Prepare a good day for us today, for the sake of the abba who has come.” He cooked the few vegetables he had, and at the proper hour they rose and ate. He also had a little wine because of his infirmity, and they drank it.

When evening came, they recited twelve psalms and slept; likewise during the night. In the morning the Egyptian said to him, “Pray for me,” and went out, not having been edified by him.

After he had gone a little way, the Roman old man, wishing to heal him, sent after him and called him back. When he came, he received him again with joy and asked him, saying, “From what province are you?” He said, “I am an Egyptian.” He said to him, “From what city?” He replied, “I have never been from a city at all, nor have I ever lived in a city.” He said to him, “Before you became a monk, what work did you do on the estate where you lived?” He replied, “I was a field watchman.” He said to him, “Where did you sleep?” He replied, “In the field.” He said, “Did you have anything on which to lie?” He replied, “When I was in the field, did I have bedding on which to sleep?” He said, “And how did you sleep?” He replied, “On the bare ground.” He said, “What did you eat in the field, or what sort of wine did you drink?” Again he replied, “What food or what drink is there in the field?” He said, “How, then, did you live?” He replied, “I ate dry bread, and if I found anything salted, and I drank water.”

The old man said, “That was a great hardship.” He said, “Was there at least a bath on the estate where you could wash?” He said, “No, but I washed in the river whenever I wished.”

After the old man had drawn all these answers from him and learned the manner of his former life and labor, wishing to help him make progress, he told him about his own former life, which he had lived as a secular person, saying, “I, wretched man whom you see, am from that great city of Rome, and I held the highest position at the palace with the emperor.”

When the Egyptian heard the beginning of his words, he was moved to compunction and listened attentively to what was being said. The old man continued, “So I left Rome and came into this desert.” Again he said, “I, whom you see, had great houses and much money, and despising them I came to this little cell.” Again he said, “I, whom you see, had beds covered with gold and furnished with the most precious bedding; in place of these God has given me this papyrus bedding and this skin.”

“My garments too were worth an incalculable price, and in place of them I use these cheap little rags. At my lunch much gold was spent; in place of it he has given me these few vegetables and this little cup of wine. I had many servants who served me, and look: in place of them the Lord moved this one man to serve me.

“In place of a bath, I pour a little water over my feet, and because of my infirmity I wear little shoes. Again, in place of the reeds, lyres, and other music by which I delighted in my banquets, I recite twelve psalms to myself by day and twelve by night. And in place of the sins I formerly committed, I now, with rest, offer God a small and worthless service.

“Therefore, Abba, take care not to be scandalized because of my infirmity.”

When the Egyptian heard this and came to himself, he said, “Woe is me! I came from much tribulation and very great labor in the world into the monastic life in order to rest, and now I possess what I did not have then. But you came from much worldly delight and by your own will into tribulation; from great glory and riches you came into humility and poverty.”

After this, he departed having made much progress, became his friend, and often came to him for his own benefit. For he was a discerning man, filled with the good fragrance of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0927A] **77.** The old man used to say, “Words alone are not necessary, for there are many words among people at this time; but deeds are necessary. This is what God seeks, not words that have no fruit.”

**78.** A certain brother asked some of the Fathers, “Is a person defiled when he thinks about filthy things?” When the matter was investigated among them, some said, “Yes, he is defiled”; others said, “No. For if we are defiled, we cannot be saved—we who are simple people. Rather, salvation depends on our not carrying out bodily the things we think about.”

The brother who had asked, however, judging the Fathers’ varied answer insufficient for him, went to a more proven old man and asked him about this. The old man replied, “What is required of each person is according to his measure.”

The brother therefore asked the old man, saying, “For the Lord’s sake, explain this saying to me.” The old man said to him, “Suppose a desirable vessel is lying here. Two brothers entered, one possessing the great measures of an experienced life, the other possessing small ones.

“If the thought of that perfected brother is stirred at the sight of the vessel and he says within himself, ‘I wish I had this vessel,’ but does not remain in this thought and quickly cuts off such desire, he is not defiled.

“But if the one who has not yet reached the greater measures desires that vessel and struggles with his thought, driven by desire, yet does not take it, he too is not defiled.”

**79.** The old man said, “If someone remains in a particular place and bears no fruit of that place, the place itself expels him, since he has not borne the fruit of that place.”

**80.** The old man said, “If someone does something by following his own will, seeking what is not according to God, but does it through ignorance, afterward he ought to return to the Lord’s way. But whoever clings to his own will, which is not according to God, and does not wish to listen to others but thinks himself knowledgeable—such a person will scarcely reach the Lord’s way.”

**81.** The old man was asked, “What is meant by what is read, ‘The way is narrow and constricted’ (Matthew 7)?” The old man replied, saying, “This narrow and constricted way is for a person to do violence to his own thoughts and, for God’s sake, cut off his own wills. This is also what is written concerning the apostles: ‘Behold, we have left everything and followed you’ (Matthew 19).”

**82.** The old man said, “Just as the order of monks is more honored than secular people, so a monk who is a stranger ought in every way to be a mirror for the local monks.”

**83.** One of the Fathers said, “If a worker remains in a place where there are no workers, he cannot make progress; for this is the virtue of a worker: to strive not to diminish in his work. Even a lazy person, if he remains with a worker, makes progress; and if he does not make progress, at least he does not sink lower.”

[Col. 0928A] **84.** A certain old man said, “If a person has words but no deeds, he is like a tree that has leaves but no fruit. For just as a tree full of fruit is also green with leaves, so speech accompanies the person who has good works.”

85. An old man said that once someone had fallen into a serious sin and, struck with remorse, went to tell an old man about it. He did not tell him what he had done, but asked as though inquiring: “If such a thought should arise in someone, is there salvation for him?” But the other, because he lacked discernment, answered him: “You have lost your soul.” Hearing this, the brother said: “Then if I am lost, I shall go back to the world.”

As he went away, however, he resolved to go and disclose his thoughts to Abba Silvanus, for this Silvanus was a great discerner. So the brother came to him and did not tell him what he had done, but again asked him in the same way as he had asked the first old man: “If such thoughts should arise in someone, is there salvation for him?”

Abba Silvanus opened his mouth and began to speak to him from the Scriptures: “The judgment concerning thoughts is not at all the same as that concerning sin.” When the brother heard this and received the power of these words into his heart, he took courage and also disclosed to him what he had done.

When Abba Silvanus heard what he had done, like a good physician he applied to his soul a poultice taken from the divine Scriptures, saying that there is repentance for those who truly turn to God out of love. After some years it happened that the aforesaid abbot came upon the old man who had caused the brother’s despair. He told him these things and said: “Behold, that brother who had despaired because of your answer and had returned to the world is like a brilliant star in the midst of the brothers.”

I have recounted this so that we may know what danger there is when someone discloses something sinful, whether of thought or of deed, to those who lack discernment.

86. A certain old man said: “It is not because evil thoughts enter us that we are condemned, but because we use the thoughts wrongly. For it happens that through thoughts we suffer shipwreck, and again through thoughts we are crowned.”

87. A certain old man said: “Do not give or receive in dealings with secular people; do not associate with a woman; and do not place prolonged confidence in a boy.”

[Col. 0928D] 88. A certain brother asked an old man: “What shall I do? Many thoughts trouble me, and I do not know how to resist them.” The old man said: “Do not resist them all, but one. For all the thoughts of monks have one head. It is therefore necessary to consider which one it is and what sort it is, and to resist that one; for in this way the remaining thoughts also are humbled.”

89. Against evil thoughts a certain old man said: “I beg you, brothers: just as we have restrained evil deeds, let us also restrain our thoughts.”

90. A certain old man said: “Whoever wishes to dwell in the desert ought to be a teacher, not one who needs to be taught, lest he suffer loss.”

606

[Col. 0929A] 91. An old man was asked by a certain brother: “How do I find God—in fasts, or in labors, or in vigils, or in mercy?” He replied: “In the things you have listed, and in discernment. For I tell you that many have afflicted their flesh and, because they did this without discernment, went away empty-handed, possessing nothing. Our mouth reeks of fasting; we have learned all the Scriptures; we have mastered David by heart—and we do not possess what God requires, namely humility.”

92. A brother asked an old man: “Abba, I ask the elders, and they speak to me about the salvation of my soul, but I retain nothing of their words. Why, then, do I ask them and make no progress? For I am wholly in uncleanness” (Ruf., book III, no. 178).

[Col. 0929B] There were two empty vessels. The old man said to him: “Go, take one of these vessels, put oil in it, light tinder inside it, pour out the oil, and put the vessel back in its place.” He did so. The old man said to him: “Do the same again.” When he had done this repeatedly, the old man said to him: “Now bring both vessels and see which of them is cleaner.” He replied: “The one in which I put the oil.” The old man said to him: “So it is also with the soul concerning the things about which it asks. Although it retains nothing of what it hears, it will nevertheless be cleansed more than the soul that does not ask anything at all.”

93. A brother was sitting at rest in his cell, and the demons wanted to deceive him under the appearance of angels. They woke him so that he would go to the gathering, and they showed him a light. He went to a certain old man and said to him: “Abba, angels come with a light and wake me for the gathering.” The old man said to him: [Col. 0929C] “Do not listen to them, my son, for they are demons. When they come to wake you, say: ‘I rise when I wish; I do not listen to you.’”

Having received the old man’s instruction, he returned to his cell. The following night the demons again came as usual and woke him. [Col. 0929D] But he answered them as he had been instructed: “I rise when I wish; I do not listen to you.”

They said to him: “That wicked old man, that deceiver, has misled you. A brother came to him wishing to borrow money; although he had some, he lied to him, saying that he had none, and did not give him any. From this, then, know that he is a deceiver.”

The brother rose at dawn, went to the old man, and reported these things to him. The old man said to him: “It is true that I had money, and that a brother came wishing to borrow it, and I did not give it to him. But I knew that, if I gave it to him, I would cause harm to his soul. I therefore considered it better to transgress one commandment than to transgress ten, by which we might have come into trouble on his account if he had received money from me. As for the demons who wish to deceive you, do not listen to them.” Greatly strengthened by the old man’s words, he went away to his cell.

94. Three brothers once came to a certain old man in Scetis. One of them asked him: “Abba, I have committed the Old and New Testaments to memory.” The old man replied: “You have filled the air with words.”

[Col. 0930A] The second asked him: “I myself have written out the Old and New Testaments.” He said to this one also: “And you have filled the windows with papers.”

The third said: “For me, the weeds have grown up in the hearth.” The old man replied: “And you have driven hospitality away from yourself.”

95. Some of the Fathers told of a great old man that, whenever someone came to ask him for a word, he would say with great confidence: “Behold, I take the place of God and sit upon the judgment seat. What, then, do you want me to do for you?”

If you said to him, “Have mercy on me,” God says to you: “If you want me to have mercy on you, you too must have mercy on your brothers, and I will have mercy on you.”

If you want me to forgive you, you too must forgive your neighbor.

“Is the matter, then, from God?” By no means; it lies with us, if we wish to be saved.

[Col. 0930B] 96. They said of a certain old man in the Cells that he was a great worker. While he was doing his work, another holy man happened to come to his cell and heard him outside arguing with his thoughts and saying: “How long, on account of one word, shall I lose all those things?”

Standing outside, the other thought that he was arguing with someone else. He knocked so that he might enter and reconcile them. When he entered and saw that there was no one else inside, and since he had confidence with the old man, he said to him: “With whom were you arguing, abba?”

He replied: “With my thoughts. I had committed fourteen books to memory, and I heard one small word outside. When I came to perform the work of God, I lost all those things, and that one thing I had heard outside came to my memory during the hour of my service. That is why I was arguing with my thought.”

[Col. 0930C] 97. Brothers from a community came into the desert and visited a certain hermit, who received them gladly. As is customary among hermits, when he saw that they were tired from their labor, he set a table outside the usual hour, placed before them what he had in his cell, and gave them rest.

When evening came, they recited twelve psalms, and likewise during the night. While the old man was keeping vigil, he heard them 607 saying to one another: “Solitary men receive more rest in the desert than we do in the community.”

In the morning, when they were about to go to another man living nearby, he said to them: “Greet him for me and say to him: ‘Do not water the vegetables.’”

When he heard this, the other understood the saying and kept them laboring and fasting until evening. When evening came, he made them perform an extended work of God, then set out what he had and said: “Let us stop for a little on your account, because you are tired from your labor.”

[Col. 0930D] He said again: “We do not usually eat every day, but for your sake let us taste a little.” He set before them dry bread and salt and said: “Behold, today we are keeping a feast for your sake.” He put a little vinegar into the salt.

They rose and began to chant psalms until morning. He said: “For your sake we cannot fulfill our rule, so that you may rest a little, because you are visitors.”

When morning came, they wanted to flee. But he entreated them, saying: “Remain with us for a little while; or, for the sake of the commandment, spend three days with us according to the custom of the desert.” When they saw that he would not release them, they secretly fled.

[Col. 0931A] 98. A brother asked a certain Father: “If I should become weighed down by sleep and the hour of my service pass, my soul, out of shame, does not wish to perform its duty.” The old man said: “If it happens that you sleep until morning, when you awaken, rise, close your door and your windows, and perform your task. For it is written: ‘The day is yours, and the night is yours’ (Ps. 73). God is glorified at every time.”

99. A certain old man said: “There is a person who eats much and is still hungry; there is also another who eats little and is satisfied. The one who eats more and remains hungry receives the greater reward than the one who eats little and is satisfied” (Ruf., book III, no. 48; Pasch., ch. 1, no. 3).

[Col. 0931B] 100. A certain old man said: “If some unpleasant conversation has occurred between you and another person, and he denies it, saying, ‘I did not say that,’ do not quarrel with him and say, ‘You did say it,’ because he will become irritated and say to you, ‘Yes, I did say it.’”

101. A certain brother asked an old man: “My sister is poor. If I give her alms, is she not like one of the poor?” The old man said: “No.” The brother said: “Why, abba?” The old man replied: “Because the blood relationship itself draws you a little.”

102. An old man said: “A monk ought neither to be a hearer of slanderers, nor to be slandered, nor to be scandalized.”

103. A certain old man said: “Let not everything that is said please you, and do not agree with every word. Believe slowly, and speak what is true quickly.”

[Col. 0931C] 104. A certain old man said: “If a word arises in the heart of a brother sitting in his cell, and, turning the word over in his mind, the brother cannot reach the measure of the word, nor is he drawn onward by God, the demons stand by him and show him from that word whatever they themselves wish.”

105. Some of the old men said: “When at the beginning we gathered together with one another and spoke about something that would be useful to our souls, we would each withdraw separately and ascend to heaven. But now we gather together, occupy ourselves with slander, and each drags the other into the depths.”

106. Another of the Fathers said: “If our inner person acts soberly, he can also guard the outer person. But if this is not so, by what virtue can we guard the tongue?”

[Col. 0931D] 107. The same man who was mentioned above also said: “Spiritual work is necessary, because this is why we have come. It is a great labor to say with the mouth what is not accomplished through bodily work.”

108. Another of the Fathers said: “A person absolutely ought to have work within his cell at which he can labor. If he is occupied with the work of God, the devil comes to him day after day, but does not find a place in which to remain.

“If, however, the enemy again gains mastery over him and brings him into captivity, the Spirit of God comes frequently again. But if, because of our wickedness, we do not make room for him, he departs.”

[Col. 0932A] 109. Monks once came down from Egypt to Scetis to see the elders of that place. When they saw them emaciated by hunger and eating impatiently because of excessive abstinence, they were scandalized by them.

Recognizing this, the presbyter wished to heal them and send them away restored. He therefore preached in the church to the people, saying: “Fast and extend your abstinence, brothers.”

The Egyptians who had come there wanted to leave, but he detained them. When they had fasted at first, they became distressed, for he had made them fast for two consecutive days. The inhabitants of Scetis fasted for a whole week.

When Saturday came, the Egyptians sat down to eat with the old men. As the Egyptians hurried themselves in eating, one of the old men held their hands and said: “Eat with discipline, as monks do.”

One of the Egyptians pushed his hands away and said: “Leave me, for I am dying. I have eaten nothing cooked for an entire week.”

The old man said to him: “If you have become so weak after eating at two-day intervals, why were you scandalized by the brothers who always preserve their abstinence in this manner for entire 608 weeks?”

[Col. 0932B] They did penance before them and, edified by their abstinence, departed with joy.

110. A certain brother renounced the world and received the monastic habit. Immediately he shut himself in, saying: “I want to be a solitary.”

When the neighboring elders heard this, they came and expelled him. They made him go around the brothers’ cells, do penance before each one, and say: “Forgive me, for I am not a solitary; I have only just begun and recently taken up the monastic life.”

[Col. 0932C] 111. Some old men said: “If you see a young man ascending to heaven by his own will, seize his foot and throw him to the ground, because this is not beneficial for him.”

112. A brother said to a certain great old man: “Abba, I wanted to find an old man according to my own will and remain with him.”

The old man said to him: “You are seeking well, my lord.”

But he maintained that this was his desire, not understanding what the old man had said. When the old man saw that he thought he had spoken well, he said to him: “So, if you find an old man according to your own will, do you want to remain with him?”

He said: “Yes, I certainly want this, if I find one according to your will.”

The old man then said to him: “Not so that you may follow that old man’s will, but so that he may follow your will, and so that you may rest in him.”

[Col. 0932D] The brother understood what he was saying, rose, and prostrated himself in repentance, saying: “Forgive me, for I was greatly conceited, thinking that I was speaking well, when I possessed nothing good.”

113. Two brothers who were blood relatives renounced the world. One of them, the younger in age, had begun the monastic life first. When one of the Fathers came to them and stayed with them, they set out a basin.

The younger brother came to wash the old man’s feet, but the old man took hold of his hand and moved him away. He made the one who was older in age perform the task that those who had first entered the monastery were accustomed to perform.

The brothers standing by said to him: “Abba, the younger one was first in the monastic life.”

The old man answered them: “I am taking precedence away from the younger and giving it to the one who is older in age.”

[Col. 0933A] 114. A certain old man said: “The prophets wrote books. Our fathers came after them and put many things into practice from them, and their successors again committed them to memory. But this generation that now exists has written them on sheets and parchments and put them away idle in the windows.”

115. An old man said: “The hood that we use is a sign of innocence; the shoulder-cloth with which we bind our shoulders and neck is a sign of the cross; and the belt with which we gird ourselves is a sign of strength. Let us therefore conduct ourselves according to what our habit signifies, for if we do everything with desire, we shall never fail.”

# BOOK ELEVEN: On the Need to Live Soberly

[Col. 0933B] 1. A brother asked Abba Arsenius to hear a word from him. The old man said to him: “Whatever virtue you possess, strive that your inner work may be according to God and overcome the passions of the outer person.”

He said again: “If we seek God, he will appear to us; and if we hold fast to him, he will remain with us.”

2. Abba Agatho said: “A monk ought not to permit his conscience to accuse him in any matter” (Ruf., book III, no. 161).

[Col. 0933C] When the aforesaid Abba Agatho was about to die, he remained motionless for three days, keeping his eyes open. The brothers questioned him, saying: “Abba, where are you?”

He replied: “I stand before the sight of the divine judgment.”

They said to him: “Are you afraid?”

He said: “So far I have labored as best I could in keeping God’s commandments; but I am a human being, and I do not know whether my works have pleased God.”

The brothers said to him: “Do you not have confidence that your works are according to God?”

The old man said: “I do not presume to, until I have come before God. For God’s judgments are one thing, and human judgments another.”

When they wanted to ask him something else, he said to them: “Show love, and do not speak with me, because I am occupied.”

Having said this, he immediately gave up his spirit with joy. They saw him gathering in his spirit as someone might greet his beloved friends.

He had exercised great vigilance in everything and used to say: “Without vigilance, a person rises to no virtue.”

[Col. 0933D] 3. They said of Abba Ammoys that when he went to church, he did not permit his disciple to walk beside him, but made him follow from a distance. If the disciple came near him to ask him about anything, he immediately spoke to him and sent him back, saying: “Lest, while we are speaking about something useful to the soul, some conversation irrelevant to the matter should also intrude, I do not permit you to remain beside me.”

4. At the beginning, Abba Ammoys said to Abba Arsenius: “How do you see me now?”

He said: “Like an angel, Father.”

609

Later he said to him again: “How do you see me now?”

He said: “Like Satan; for even if you speak a good word, it is like a sword to me.”

[Col. 0934A] 5. Abba Allois said: “Unless a person says in his heart, ‘I alone and God are in this world,’ he will have no rest” (Appendix to Matthew, no. 71).

6. He said again: “If a person wishes, in a single day he can reach the measure of divinity by evening.”

7. As Abba Besarion was dying, he said: “A monk ought to be wholly an eye, like the Cherubim and Seraphim.”

8. Abba Daniel and Abba Ammoys were once traveling together. Abba Ammoys said: “Do you suppose, Father, that we shall ever sit in a cell?”

Abba Daniel said to him: “Who, then, takes God away from us? For God is outside as well as in the cell.”

[Col. 0934B] 9. Abba Evagrius said: “It is a great thing to pray without distraction; it is greater to sing psalms without distraction.”

10. The same man said: “Always remember your departure, and do not forget the eternal judgment, and there will be no sin in your soul.”

11. Abba Theodorus of Ennato [Note: [Col. 0990B] Theodorus of Ennato. The same is found above, in Book Seven, no. 7, concerning Nono of Alexandria. By Ennatus or Nonus of Alexandria is understood the ninth district or region of Alexandria.] said: “If God counts against us the negligences of the time when we pray, and the captivities that we suffer while we sing psalms, we cannot be saved.”

12. Abba Theonas said: “Because our mind is hindered and drawn back from contemplation of God, we are therefore led captive by carnal passions.”

13. Some of the brothers once came to test John the Short, because he did not allow his mind to spread itself among worldly thoughts and did not speak about worldly affairs. They said to him: “We give thanks to God, because it has rained abundantly this year, and the palm trees, having been adequately watered, are beginning to put forth branches well. The brothers who are accustomed to occupy themselves with the work of their hands will find the means by which to labor.”

[Col. 0934C] Then Abba John said to them: “So it is when the Holy Spirit descends into the hearts of the saints: they become green, in a manner of speaking, and are renewed, and they put forth leaves in the fear of God.”

14. They said again of Abba John that he once made mats for two baskets, but spent them on one basket and did not realize it until he brought it against the wall. His mind was occupied in contemplation of God.

[Col. 0934D] 15. There was a certain old man in Scetis who possessed bodily endurance but was not very careful about retaining what he had heard. He went to Abba John the Short to ask him about forgetfulness.

After hearing a word from him, he returned to his cell and forgot what Abba John had said. He went again and asked him. After hearing him, he likewise returned; but as soon as he reached his cell, he forgot what he had heard. Thus, going and returning many times, forgetfulness held him in its power.

Afterward, meeting the old man again, he said: “Do you know, abba, that I have again forgotten what you said to me? But, so as not to trouble you, I did not come.”

Abba John said to him: [Col. 0935A] “Go, light a lamp.” He lit it. He said to him: “Bring other lamps and light them from it.” He did so.

Abba John said to the old man: “Was the lamp harmed in any way because you lit other lamps from it?”

He said: “No.”

“So John too is not harmed if all Scetis comes to me, nor does this hinder me from the love of God. Whenever you wish, therefore, come without hesitation.”

And so, through the patience of both, God took forgetfulness away from the old man. For this was the work of those who lived in Scetis: to encourage those who were attacked by any passion, and to impose labor upon themselves, so that they might gain one another through goodness.

16. A brother asked Abba John: “What shall I do? A certain brother frequently comes to take me with him to the work at which he labors, but I am a poor, sick man and fail at such a task. What, then, shall I do concerning the commandment of God?”

[Col. 0935B] The old man replied: “Caleb son of Jephunneh said to Jesus son of Nun (Joshua IV): ‘I was forty years old when Moses, the servant of the Lord, sent me with you to this land; and now I am eighty years old. As I was strong then, so I am now able to enter and go out for war.’ So you too, if you can go in such a way that you can also come out, go. But if you cannot do this, sit in your cell and weep over your sins. And if they find you grieving, they will not compel you to leave.”

17. Abba Isidore, who was a presbyter in Scetis, said: “When I was young and sat in my cell, I had no fixed number of psalms that I recited in the service of God; for night and day were spent by me in this.”

[Col. 0935C] 18. Abba Cassian told of a certain old man sitting in the desert who asked God to grant him that he might never fall asleep while engaged in spiritual matters. But if the words were words of slander or hatred, he would immediately fall asleep, so that his ears would not receive such poison.

He said that the devil is zealous to move people to idle words and is also the enemy of all spiritual teaching. For this he used the following example:

“Once, while I was speaking with certain brothers about the benefit of souls, they were so overcome by deep sleep that they could not even move the eyelids of their eyes. But, wishing to show that this was a demonic work, I introduced words about idle matters. At this they rejoiced and immediately struggled against sleep.

“I groaned and said: [Col. 0935D] ‘Until now 610 we were speaking about heavenly matters, and the eyes of all of you were weighed down by the heaviest sleep. But when idle conversation appeared, you all became eager to listen.’

“For this reason I ask you, most beloved brothers: recognizing that this is the work of the evil demon, pay attention to yourselves and guard yourselves against sleep whenever you are either doing or hearing something spiritual.”

[Col. 0936A] 19. When Abba Pastor was still young, he once went to a certain old man to ask him about three matters. When he reached the old man, he forgot one of the three matters and returned to his cell.

When he stretched out his hand to take the key, he remembered the matter he had previously forgotten. He withdrew his hand from the key and returned to the old man. The old man said to him: “You have hurried to come, brother.”

He told him that when he had stretched out his hand to take the key, he remembered the matter he had been asking about, and had not opened his cell but immediately returned to him. The journey was very long.

The old man said to him: “Truly, a shepherd of flocks; for your name will be called throughout the whole land of Egypt.”

20. Abba Ammon came to Abba Pastor and said to him: “If I go to my neighbor’s cell, or if he comes to me for some matter, we are afraid that some unsuitable conversation, foreign to the monk’s purpose, may intrude.”

The old man said to him: “You do well; youth requires vigilance.”

Abba Ammon said to him: “What, then, did the old men do?”

He said to him: “The old men who were already progressing and established had nothing foreign in themselves or in their mouths to say.”

He said: “If, then, it becomes necessary to speak with a neighbor, does it seem good to you that I speak with him about the Scriptures, or about the words and sayings of the elders?”

[Col. 0936B] The old man said to him: “If you cannot remain silent, it is better for you to speak about the words of the elders than about the Scriptures. For the danger is not small.”

21. Abba Pastor was asked about defilements, and he replied: “If we establish our active life upon the fear of God and sobriety, we do not find defilements in ourselves.”

[Col. 0936C] 22. They said of Abba Pastor that, when he was about to go out to perform the work of God, he would first sit for an hour, continually discerning his thoughts, and only then would he go out.

23. Abba Pastor said that someone asked Abba Paysius: “What shall I do for my soul, since it has become insensible and does not fear God?”

He said to him: “Go and attach yourself to a person who fears God. When you have clung to him, you too will be taught to fear God.”

24. He said again: “The beginning and the end are the fear of the Lord. For it is written: ‘The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom’ (Ps. 110). And again, when Abraham had completed the altar, the Lord said to him: ‘Now I know that you fear God’ (Gen. II).”

25. He said again: “Withdraw from every person who is incessantly contentious in conversation.”

[Col. 0936D] 26. He said again (Appendix to Mark, no. 25): “I once asked Abba Peter, the disciple of Abba Lot: ‘When I am in my cell, my soul is at peace; but when a brother comes to me and reports to me the words of those outside, my soul is troubled.’

“Abba Peter told me that Abba Lot used to say: ‘Your key has opened my door.’

“I said to him: ‘What does this saying mean?’

“He said: ‘If someone comes to you and you ask him, “How are you? Where have you come from? How are things with this or that brother? Did they receive you or not?” then you open the door of your mouth to your brother and hear things you do not wish to hear.’

“I said to him: ‘That is true. But what should a person do when a brother comes to him?’

“The old man said to him: ‘In mourning there is instruction; but where there is no mourning, it is impossible to guard the mind.’

“He said to him: ‘When I am in my cell, mourning is with me. But when someone comes to me, or when I leave my cell, I do not find mourning.’

“The old man said to him: ‘It is not yet subject to you, but is employed for a time, as occasion requires.’

“He said to him: ‘What is this saying?’

“He said to me: ‘If a person labors for something according to virtue, whenever he seeks it for his benefit, he finds it.’”

[Col. 0937A] 27. A brother asked Abba Sisoe: “I desire to guard my heart.”

The old man said to him: “How can we guard our heart if our tongue has an open door?”

[Col. 0937B] 28. Abba Silvanus was once sitting on Mount Sinai. His disciple, wishing to leave to attend to one of his duties, said to the old man: “Release the water and water the garden.”

When he went out to release the water, he covered his face with his hood, looking only at his feet. It happened that someone came upon him at that very hour and, seeing him from a distance, observed what he was doing.

When he reached him, he said to him: “Tell me, abba, why did you cover your face with your hood and water the garden in this way?”

The old man said to him: “So that my eyes might not see the trees and my mind be occupied with contemplating them instead of with its work.”

611

29. Abba Moses asked Abba Silvanus: “Can a person make a beginning of the monastic life throughout the whole day?”

Abba Silvanus replied: “If a person is a worker, he can make a beginning of his monastic life at any moment and at any hour” (Ruf., book III, no. 175).

[Col. 0937C] 30. Some people once asked Abba Silvanus: “In what kind of monastic life did you labor in order to receive this understanding?”

He replied: “I never permitted a thought to remain in my heart that irritated me.”

31. Abba Serapion said: “Just as the emperor’s soldiers, when they stand before him, ought not to look to the right or to the left, so also a monk, when he stands in the presence of God and is intent every hour upon his fear, has nothing that can terrify him from the evils of the adversary.”

[Col. 0937D] 32. Saint Syncletica said: “Let us live soberly, because through the senses of our body thieves enter, even if we do not wish it. For how can a house not be darkened if smoke rising from outside finds its windows open?”

33. The same woman mentioned above said: “We must be armed on every side against the demons, because they enter from outside and are stirred up from within, since our soul also suffers this.

“For just as a ship is sometimes overwhelmed from outside by the mass of the waves, but at other times sinks from within when its bilge rises, so we are sometimes condemned by the iniquity of works committed outwardly, while at other times we are given over inwardly to the wickedness of thoughts.

“Therefore we must not only watch for the outward assaults of unclean spirits, but also drain away the uncleanness of our inner thoughts.”

[Col. 0938A] 34. She said again: “We have no security in this world. For, as the Apostle says, ‘Let the one who stands take heed lest he fall’ (1 Cor. 10). We sail in uncertainty, since, as the Psalmist says, ‘Our life is like the sea’ (Ps. 103).

“Nevertheless, there are places in the sea: some are full of dangers, while others are calm. We appear to sail in the calm part of the sea, whereas secular people sail in dangerous places” (Ruf., book III, no. 123).

“And again, we sail by day, with the sun of righteousness providing us guidance, while they are carried along at night in ignorance. Yet it often happens that those secular people, sailing in storm and darkness, save their ship through fear of danger by crying out to God and keeping vigil, while we, in calm waters, are ourselves sunk through neglect, abandoning the rudders of righteousness.”

[Col. 0938B] 35. Abba Hyperichius said: “Let your thought always be in the kingdom of heaven, and soon you will receive it as your inheritance.”

36. He said again: “Let the life of the monk be made according to the imitation of the angels, burning up and consuming sins.”

[Col. 0938C] 37. Abba Orsisius said: “I think that unless a person guards his heart, he will forget and neglect everything he hears and sees. Finally, when the enemy finds a place in him, he trips him up.

“For just as a lamp prepared with oil and a wick [Note: [Col. 0990B] *Lychino.* Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read *lychno*. I think *ellychnium* is meant, unless one reads *licinio*. For in Isidore *licinium*, as if *lucinium*, is the same as *ellychnium*.] shines, but if through negligence it does not receive oil, it is gradually extinguished and darkness grows strong against it, so also, if a mouse comes to it and wants to eat its wick [Note: [Col. 0990B–C] *Myxum.* This is the reading I have restored. Yet all the manuscripts and printed editions read *nixum*. I think *ellychnium* is meant, which the Greeks also call μύξα (‘mucus’).] before it is completely extinguished, it cannot do so because of the heat of the fire. But if it sees that the lamp has neither light nor any heat of fire remaining, then, wishing to pull out its wick, it also throws the lamp itself to the ground. If it is earthenware, it is shattered; if it is bronze, its owner repairs it.

“So also, if the soul is negligent, the Holy Spirit gradually withdraws from it until its warmth is completely extinguished. Then the enemy consumes and devours the purpose of that soul and also destroys the body of wickedness.

“But if someone is good through the affection he has for God, yet is simply carried away into negligence, God, who is merciful, awakens in him his understanding and the memory of the punishments prepared for sinners in the age to come. He ensures that the person becomes sober and henceforth guards himself with great caution, until the time of his visitation.”

[Col. 0938D] 38. A certain old man came to another old man. As they were speaking, one of them said: “I am dead to this world” (Ruf., book II, no. 116; Pasch., ch. 12, no. 5).

The other said to him: “Do not put confidence in yourself until you leave this body. For if you say of yourself that you are dead, Satan is not dead.”

39. A certain old man said: “Every morning and evening a monk ought to consider within himself what he has done of the things God wills and what he has not done. Thus a monk ought to spend his whole life doing penance; for Abba Arsenius lived in this manner.”

[Col. 0939A] 40. An old man said: “If someone loses gold or silver, he can find something in place of what he lost.”

41. An old man said: “Just as a soldier and a hunter, setting out toward the labor they have undertaken, do not consider whether one will be wounded or another remain unharmed, but each fights for himself alone, so also the monk ought to be.”

612

42. An old man said: “Just as no one can harm one who is at the emperor’s side, so Satan cannot harm us in any way if our soul clings to God. For it is written: ‘Draw near to me, and I will draw near to you’ (Zech. I). But because we are frequently lifted up with pride, the enemy easily snatches our wretched soul into the disgrace of passion.”

43. A brother said to an old man: “I see no struggle in my heart.” The old man said to him: “You are like a fourfold gate, so that whoever wishes may enter you by whichever way he wishes and leave by whichever way he wishes, while you do not understand what is happening. If you had a door and closed it, not permitting evil thoughts to enter through it, then you would see them standing outside and fighting against you.” [Col. 0939B]

44. They said of a certain old man that whenever his thoughts said to him, “Put it off today; tomorrow you will repent,” he contradicted them, saying: “No, but today I will repent; tomorrow let the Lord’s will be done” (Ruff., bk. III, no. 165).

45. An old man said: “Unless our outward person behaves soberly, it is impossible to guard the inward person.”

46. An old man used to say: “There are three powers of Satan that precede every sin: first, forgetfulness; second, negligence; third, desire. For when forgetfulness comes, it produces negligence; from negligence desire is born; and through desire a person falls. If the mind is so sober that it rejects forgetfulness, it does not come to negligence; and if it does not neglect, it does not admit desire; and if it does not admit desire, it will never fall, with the grace of Christ helping it.” [Col. 0939C]

47. An old man said: “Devote yourself to silence, think of nothing vain, and attend to your meditation, whether resting or rising, with the fear of God. If you do these things, you will not fear the assaults of the wicked.”

48. An old man said to a brother: “The devil is the enemy, and you are the house. The enemy therefore never ceases to throw upon you whatever filthy thing he finds, pouring every impurity into you. But your task is not to neglect throwing outside what he has thrown in. For if you are negligent, your house will be filled with filth, and you will in no way be able to enter it. From the beginning, however, cast out little by little whatever he throws in, and your house will remain clean through the grace of Christ.” [Col. 0939D]

49. One of the old men said: “When an animal’s eyes are covered, it goes around the mill; but if it has its eyes uncovered, it does not walk around the millstone. So too, if the devil succeeds in covering a person’s eyes, he brings him low into every sin; but if his eyes are not closed, he can more easily escape from him.”

[Col. 0940A] 50. The old men said: “On Abba Antony’s mountain seven monks were sitting during the date season, and one of them drove the birds away from them. There was also an old man who, on the day when it fell to him to guard the dates, cried out: ‘Go away from within, evil thoughts, and from without, birds!’”

51. A certain brother in the cells was soaking his palm leaves. When he had sat down to make braids, his thought told him to go visit a certain old man. Then, thinking within himself again, he said: “After a few days I will go.” His thought said to him once more: “What will you do if he dies in the meantime?” “I will go now to speak with him, because it is the summer season,” he said. Again he said within himself: “But now is not the right time.” He thought again, saying: “When you have cut the rushes for the mats, then it will be the right time.” Again he said: “I will spread out these palm leaves, and then I will go.” Once more he said within himself: “But today the weather is fine.”

He rose, left the soaked palm leaves, took his melote, and went. There was an old man living near him, a perceptive man. When he saw him walking hurriedly, he cried out: “Prisoner, prisoner, where are you running? Come here to me.” When he came, the old man said to him: “Return to your cell.”

The brother then told him of the waves he had endured in his thoughts, and so he returned to his cell. When he entered it, he prostrated himself and repented. After he had done this, the demons suddenly cried out in a loud voice: “You have conquered us, monk; you have conquered us!” His mat, on which he had been lying, became as though scorched by fire, while the demons were driven away like smoke. Thus that brother learned their wiles. [Col. 0940B–C]

52. They said of a certain old man that he was dying in Scetis. The brothers surrounded his bed, clothed him, and began to weep. He opened his eyes, laughed, and then laughed again (Ruff., bk. III, no. 159). This happened three times. When the brothers saw it, they asked him: “Tell us, abba, why do you laugh while we are weeping?” He said to them: “The first time I laughed because you fear death; the second time I laughed because you are not prepared; but the third time I laughed because I am going from toil to rest, and you are weeping.” After saying this, he immediately closed his eyes, as one dying. [Col. 0940D]

53. A brother who lived in a cell once came to one of the Fathers and said that he was afflicted by his thoughts. The old man said to him: “You have thrown upon the ground a great tool, which is the fear of God, and have taken into your hand a reed, which is evil thoughts. Take instead for yourself the fire, which is the fear of God. When an evil thought approaches you, it will be burned up like a reed by the fire of the fear of God. For wickedness cannot prevail against those who possess the fear of God.”

54. One of the Fathers said: “Unless you first hate, you cannot love. Unless, therefore, you hate sin, you will not practice righteousness, as it is written: ‘Turn away from evil and do good’ (Ps. XXXVI). Nevertheless, in all these matters the purpose of the mind is required everywhere. Adam, while standing in paradise, transgressed God’s commandment; but Job, while sitting on the dung heap, kept it. Hence it is clear that God seeks from a person a good purpose, so that he may always hold fast to it.” [Col. 0941A]

## BOOK TWELVE

### On the necessity of praying without ceasing and soberly

1. They said of Abba Arsenius that, on the evening of the Sabbath, as Sunday was dawning, he left the sun behind him and stretched out his hands toward heaven in prayer until the morning of Sunday, when the rising sun illumined his face; and thus he sat down (Ruff., bk. III, no. 21).

2. The brothers asked Abba Agathon: “Father, which virtue in the ascetic life requires the greater labor?” He said to them: “Forgive me, for I think that there is no labor like praying to God. Whenever a person wishes to pray to his God, the enemy demons always hasten to interrupt his prayer, knowing that they are hindered by nothing except prayer poured out to God. Every other labor undertaken by a person engaged in the religious life, however earnestly and patiently he performs it, nevertheless has and possesses some respite. Prayer, however, requires labor in a great struggle until the final breath.”

3. Abba Dulas, who was a disciple of Abba Bessarion, recounted: “Once I came to my abba’s cell and found him standing in prayer, with his hands extended toward heaven. He continued doing this constantly for fourteen days. Afterward he called me and said: ‘Follow me.’

“We went out into the desert. When I became thirsty, I said to him: ‘Abba, I am thirsty.’ He took his melote, went away from me about a stone’s throw, prayed, and brought it back full of water.

“We went on to the city of Lyco and came to Abba John. After greeting him, we prayed. Then, when we had sat down, they began to speak about the vision they had seen. Abba Bessarion said: ‘A command has gone forth from the Lord that the temples be destroyed.’ And so it happened, and they were destroyed.” [Col. 0941B–C]

4. Abba Evagrius said: “If you lose heart, pray. Pray with fear, trembling, and labor, soberly and vigilantly. Thus one ought to pray, especially because of our invisible enemies, the wicked ones devoted to evil, who strive above all to hinder us in this.”

5. He said again: “When an opposing thought comes into your heart, do not seek one thing instead of another through prayer, but sharpen the sword of tears against the one who attacks you.”

6. It was reported to Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus, of blessed memory, by the abbot of his monastery, which he had in Palestine: “Through your prayers we have not neglected the rule, but with diligence we celebrate the third, sixth, and ninth hours, and Vespers.” He rebuked him and instructed him: “It is evident that you are free from prayer at the other hours. But the true monk ought to pray without ceasing, or at least to sing psalms in his heart.”

7. Abba Isaiah said: “When the presbyter of Pelusium was giving an agape, and the brothers were eating and speaking to one another in the church, he rebuked them, saying: ‘Be silent, brothers. For I know that one brother is eating with you whose prayer rises before God like fire.’” [Col. 0941D–0942A]

8. Abba Lot came to Abba Joseph and said to him: “Abba, according to my ability I keep a modest rule, a small fast, prayer, meditation, and quiet; and according to my ability I strive to purify my thoughts. What ought I to do from now on?”

The old man rose, stretched out his hands toward heaven, and his fingers became like ten lamps of fire. He said to him: “If you wish, become wholly like fire.”

9. Some monks called Euchites came at one time to Abba Lucius in Enaton—that is, “praying ones.” [Note: [Col. 0990C] Euchites. Some editions have *Euschiti*; others, above, in Rufinus, book III, no. 212, have *Cochiti*. The well-known Euchites were heretics; their name derives from Greek *εὔχομαι*, “I pray.”] The old man asked them: “What is the work of your hands?” (Ruff., bk. II, no. 212). They said: “We do not engage in any manual labor, but, as the Apostle says (1 Thess. V), we pray without ceasing.”

The old man said to them: “Do you not eat?” They said: “Yes, we eat.” He said to them: “When you eat, then who prays for you?”

Again he asked them: “Do you not sleep?” They said: “We sleep.” The old man said: “And when you sleep, who prays for you?” They could find nothing to answer him.

He said to them: “Forgive me, brothers, for behold, you do not do as you said. But I will show you that, while working with my hands, I pray without ceasing. I sit, with God’s help, soaking a few palm leaves, and I make a mat from them, saying: ‘Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy, and according to the multitude of your mercies blot out my iniquity’ (Ps. L).”

He said to them: “Is this prayer or not?” They said: “Yes.”

He said: “When I spend the whole day laboring and praying in heart or mouth, I make roughly sixteen coins. I set aside two of them at the door, and eat the rest. Whoever receives those two coins prays for me while I eat or sleep. Thus, by God’s grace, what is written is fulfilled in me: ‘Pray without ceasing’ (1 Thess. V).” [Col. 0942B–D]

10. Some people asked Abba Macarius: “How ought we to pray?” (Ruff., bk. III, no. 207). The old man said to them: “There is no need to speak much in prayer, but frequently to stretch out one’s hands and say: ‘Lord, as you will and as you know, have mercy on me.’ If a battle presses upon the soul, say: ‘Help me.’ Since he himself knows what is useful, he shows us mercy.”

11. They said of Abba Sisoes that, unless he quickly lowered his hands when he stood in prayer, his mind was carried away into the higher realms. Therefore, if a brother happened to be praying with him, he hastened to lower them, lest his mind be carried away and he remain there.

12. An old man said: “Constant prayer quickly corrects the mind.”

13. One of the Fathers said: “Just as it is impossible for anyone to see his face in troubled water, so the soul, unless it has been cleansed of alien thoughts, cannot pray to God contemplatively.” [Col. 0943A]

14. An old man once came to Mount Sinai. As he was leaving, a brother met him on the road and groaned, saying to the old man: “We are afflicted, abba, because of the drought; it has not rained for us.”

The old man said to him: “Why do you not pray and entreat God?” He replied: “We do pray and continually beseech God, but it does not rain.”

The old man said: “I believe that you are not praying attentively enough. Do you wish to know that this is so? Come, let us stand together in prayer.”

He stretched out his hands toward heaven and prayed. Immediately rain descended. When the brother saw this, he was afraid and fell down to worship him. But the old man immediately fled from there.

15. The brothers recounted: “Once we came to certain old men. After the customary prayer had been made, we greeted one another and sat down. After we had spoken, when we were leaving, we asked that prayer be made again.

“One of those elders said to us: ‘What? Have you not prayed?’

“We said: ‘Yes. When we entered, Father, prayer was made; and from that hour until now we have been speaking.’

“He said: ‘Forgive me, brothers, for while I was sitting with you, a certain brother made one hundred and three prayers while speaking.’

“After saying this, he made a prayer and dismissed us.”

## BOOK THIRTEEN

### On the necessity of being hospitable and merciful with cheerfulness

1. Some of the Fathers once went to Abba Joseph in Panephysis to ask him about receiving brothers who came to them—whether they ought to relax their abstinence with them and rejoice with them (Ruff., bk. III, no. 47).

Before they could question him, the old man said to his disciple: “Observe what I do today, and wait.”

He placed two reed seats, tied together in bundles, one on the right and one on the left, and said: “Sit down.” He entered his cell and put on his old clothes. Coming out, he passed through their midst. Then he entered again and put on his better clothes, which he had been wearing before. Coming out again, he sat among them.

Amazed at what the old man had done, they asked him what it meant. He said to them: “Did you see what I did?” They said: “Yes.”

He said: “Was I changed by the disgraceful clothing?” They said: “No.”

He asked again: “Was I harmed by the better clothing?” They said: “No.”

He said: “I myself am the same in both. Just as I was not changed by the earlier clothing, nor harmed by the later, so we ought to act in receiving the brothers, as is read in the holy Gospel: ‘Give to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s’ (Matt. XXII; Mark XII; Luke XX).

“When the brothers are present, we ought to receive them with joy; but when we are alone, we need to mourn.”

When they heard this, they marveled, because he had already understood what they had in their hearts to ask him, and they glorified God. [Col. 0943B–D]

2. Abba Cassian said: “We came from Palestine to Egypt to one of the Fathers (Cassian, *Institutes*, bk. V, ch. 24). After he had shown us hospitality, we asked him: ‘Why, when receiving brothers, do you not keep the rule of fasting, as is done in Palestine?’

“He replied: ‘Fasting is always with me; you I cannot always keep here. Fasting, although it is a useful and necessary practice, lies within our own will. But the fullness of charity is required of us by God’s law. Therefore, in receiving Christ in you, I must show you the things that belong to charity with every care. When I have dismissed you, I can recover the rule of fasting, since the children of the bridegroom cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them; but when he has been taken away from them, then they fast of their own accord’ (Matt. IX).” [Col. 0944A]

3. The same man said again: “We came to another old man, and he made us taste food. After we were full, he urged us to eat more. When I said that I could no longer eat, he replied: ‘I have already set the table six times for different brothers who came, and while urging each one, I also ate; yet I am still hungry. But you, after eating only once, are so full that you can no longer eat?’”

4. Once in Scetis an order was issued that they should fast during that week and celebrate Easter. It happened that, during that same week, certain brothers came from Egypt to Abba Moses. He made them a little broth. When the neighbors saw the smoke, they said to the clergy of the church there: “Behold, Moses has broken the order and cooked broth in his place.”

They said: “When he comes, we will speak with him.”

When the Sabbath came, the clergy, seeing the great ascetic conduct of Abba Moses, said to him before all the people: “O Abba Moses, you have broken the commandment of men, but you have firmly bound the commandments of God.” [Col. 0944B–C]

5. A brother came to Abba Pastor in the second week of Lent and told him his thoughts. Finding rest in the old man’s answer, the brother said to him: “I was almost prevented from coming to you today” (Append. Mart., no. 43).

The old man said: “Why?”

He replied: “I was afraid that, because of Lent, the door would not be opened to me.”

Abba Pastor answered him: “We have not learned to close a wooden door; rather, we desire to keep the door of the tongue closed.” [Col. 0944D]

6. A brother said to Abba Pastor: “If I give my brother a little bread or something else, the demons defile it, so that it appears to be done to please people.”

The old man said to him: “Even if such a deed is done to please people, we nevertheless ought to provide our brothers with what they need.”

He told him this parable: “There were two farmers living in one city. One of them sowed and gathered a small and poor harvest; the other, neglecting to sow, gathered absolutely nothing. If famine comes, which of the two can escape?”

The brother replied: “The one who produced something, even though it was little and impure.”

The old man said to him: “So let us also sow a little, even if it is impure, lest we die in a time of famine.” [Col. 0945A]

7. A brother came to a certain solitary. As he was leaving him, he said: “Forgive me, abba, because I have interrupted your rule.”

The solitary replied: “My rule is to receive you hospitably and dismiss you in peace.”

8. A certain solitary lived not far from the community of the brothers and performed many works. It happened that some men came to the monastery where the community was, turned aside to the solitary, and caused him to eat outside the appointed hour.

Afterward the brothers said to him: “Are you not grieved, abba?”

He replied: “My grief is to do my own will” (Ruff., bk. III, no. 150; Pasch., ch. 18, no. 1). [Col. 0945B]

9. They spoke of a certain old man in Syria who lived beside the road to the desert. His work was that, whenever a monk came from the desert, at whatever hour, he confidently made him eat.

A solitary once came, and the old man asked him to taste something. When he refused, saying, “I am fasting,” the old man was grieved and said to him: “Do not pass over your child, I beg you; do not despise me, but come, let us pray. Behold, there is a tree here. If it bows when the one who bends his knee and prays bows, let us follow it.”

The solitary bent his knee in prayer, but nothing happened. The old man who had received him also bent his knee, and immediately the tree bent with him. When they saw this, they rejoiced and gave thanks to God, who always performs wonders. [Col. 0945C]

10. Two brothers once came to a certain old man. It was the old man’s custom not to eat every day. When he saw the brothers, he received them joyfully and said: “Fasting has its own reward.”

And again: “Whoever eats for the sake of charity fulfills two commandments, because he has abandoned his own will and fulfilled the commandment by refreshing the brothers.”

11. There was an old man in Egypt living in a deserted place. Another man lived far away, a Manichaean who was a presbyter among those whom they themselves called presbyters. When he wished to go to a man of the same error, night overtook him in the place where the holy and orthodox man lived.

He was anxious and wanted to knock so that he might stay with him. He knew that the old man would recognize that he was a Manichaean, and his thought held him back, lest the old man perhaps refuse to receive him. Compelled by necessity, however, he knocked.
