The old man opened the door, recognized him, received him cheerfully, compelled him to pray, refreshed him, and showed him where to sleep. During the night the Manichaean reflected and marveled, saying: “How did he have no suspicion of me? Truly, this man is a servant of God.”

In the morning he rose, fell at the old man’s feet, and said: “From today I am orthodox, and I will not leave you.” From then on he remained with him. [Col. 0945D–0946A]

12. A Theban monk received from God the grace of ministry, so that he might provide each person in need with whatever was necessary.

Once, in a certain village, he was giving an agape. A woman came to him to receive something. She was clothed in extremely old garments. When he saw her dressed in such old clothing, he filled his hand in order to give her much; but his hand closed, and he drew out only a little.

Another woman came, well dressed. Seeing her clothing, he extended his hand to give her little; his hand opened, and he drew out much.

He inquired about both women and learned that the woman who wore fine clothing had fallen from respectable circumstances into poverty and, because of her former social standing, had been dressed in good garments; whereas the other had put on old clothing in order to receive alms.

13. A monk had a poor lay brother, and whatever the monk earned he gave to him; but the more the monk gave, the poorer the layman became.

The monk went and reported this to an old man. The old man said to him: “If you wish to listen to me, give him nothing more. Say to him: ‘Brother, when I had anything, I gave it to you. Now you work, and from what you earn give something to me.’ Whatever he brings you, accept from him, and wherever you know there is a poor stranger or old man, give it to him and ask them to pray for him.”

The brother followed these instructions. When his lay brother came, he spoke to him as the old man had said, and the man went away sadly.

One day he gathered small vegetables from the garden and brought them to him. The monk accepted them, gave them to the old men, and asked them to pray for him. After receiving their blessing, the layman returned home.

Later he brought vegetables again and three loaves. His brother accepted them and did as before. After receiving the blessing, he went away again.

The third time he came, he brought many provisions, wine, and fish. When his brother saw this, he marveled, summoned the poor, and refreshed them. He then said to his lay brother: “Do you need a few loaves?”

He said: “No, lord. For whenever I received anything from you, it was as though fire entered my house and consumed it. But now, when I receive nothing from you, I abound, and God blesses me.”

The monk went and reported everything that had happened to the old man. The old man said to him: “Do you not know that the work of monks is fire, and wherever it enters, it consumes? It is beneficial for your brother that he should give alms from his own labor and receive prayer from holy men. Thus, receiving a blessing, his labor will multiply.” [Col. 0946B–D]

14. One of the old men said: “There is a certain man who frequently does many good things, and the devil sends scrupulosity into his mind over small matters, so that he loses the reward for everything else he does.

“Once, while I was sitting in Oxyrhynchus with a presbyter who gave many alms, a widow came asking him for a little wheat. He said to her: ‘Go, bring a measure, and I will measure it for you.’

“She brought it. As he measured the measure by hand, he said to her: ‘It is too large,’ and he put that widow to shame.

“When she had gone away, I said: ‘Abba, did you lend this wheat to the widow, or what?’

“He said: ‘No, I gave it to her.’

“I said: ‘Then, if you gave it all freely, why did you wish to be so scrupulous over a small matter and put the woman to shame?’” [Col. 0946D–0947A]

15. A certain old man shared a common life with one other brother; for that old man was merciful. A famine occurred, and some people began coming to his lodging to receive an agape. The old man gave bread to everyone who came.

The brother, seeing what was happening, said to the old man: “Give me my share of the loaves, and do whatever you wish with your share.”

The old man divided the loaves and continued to give alms from his share as usual. Many people flocked to the old man when they heard that he gave to everyone. God, seeing the purpose of his will, blessed the loaves.

The brother who had taken his share and gave nothing away consumed his loaves. Then he said to the old man: “Since I have only a little of my loaves left, abba, receive me again into the common life.”

The old man said: “As you wish, so I will do.” They again began to live together in common.

When provisions again became scarce, needy people came once more to receive an agape. One day the brother entered and saw that the loaves had run out. A poor man came asking for an agape.

The old man said to the brother: “Give him bread.”

He replied: “I have none left, Father.”

The old man said: “Go inside and look.”

The brother entered, examined the place, and saw that the storage room where the bread was usually kept was full of loaves. When he saw this, he was afraid; he took bread and gave it to the poor man. Thus, recognizing the faith and virtue of the old man, he glorified God. [Col. 0947B–C]

## BOOK FOURTEEN

### On obedience

1. Abba Arsenius, of blessed memory, once said to Abba Alexander: “When you have finished your palm leaves, then come and let us taste food. But if some strangers arrive, eat with them.”

Abba Alexander worked slowly and carefully. When the hour for eating arrived, he still had some palm leaves remaining. Wishing to keep the old man’s command, he waited until he had finished spreading out the palm leaves.

Abba Arsenius, seeing that he was delayed, ate, supposing that perhaps guests had arrived for him and that he had eaten with them. After Abba Alexander had finished spreading out the palm leaves in the evening, he went to Abba Arsenius.

Abba Arsenius said to him: “Did you have any guests?”

He said: “No.”

The other said: “Why, then, did you not come?”

He replied: “Because you said to me, ‘When the palm leaves are finished, then come.’ Since I kept your word in mind, I did not come, because I have only now completed the work.”

The old man marveled at the exactness of his obedience and said to him: “Break away from your work more quickly, so that you may also perform the ministry of psalmody and hasten to fill water for yourself; otherwise your body will quickly become weak.” [Col. 0947C–D]

2. Abba Abraham came to Abba Ares. While they were sitting together, a brother arrived and said to Abba Ares: “Tell me what I should do in order to be saved.”

The old man said to him: “Go, and throughout this entire year eat bread and salt in the evening; then come again, and I will speak to you.”

The brother went and did so. When the year was completed, he came again to Abba Ares. It happened that Abba Abraham was again with him.

The old man said again to the brother: “Go, fast this year, and eat after two days.”

When he had left, Abba Abraham said to Abba Ares: “Why do you place a light yoke upon all the brothers, but load this brother with a heavy burden?”

The old man said to him: “The other brothers come seeking advice and depart in the same way. But this man has come for God’s sake to hear a word, and he is a great worker; whatever I say to him, he does with every care. Therefore I speak the word of God to him.” [Col. 0948A]

3. They told of Abba John, who was short in stature, that he went to a certain old man, a Theban by birth, who lived in Scetis and sat in the desert. [A similar account appears here in Book IV, ch. 12, from Sulpicius.]

The old man once took a dry stick, planted it, and said to him: “Give it a jar of water every day until it bears fruit.” The water was far from them, so that he had to leave in the evening and return in the morning.

After three years the stick came to life and bore fruit. The old man took some of its fruit, brought it to the church, and said to the brothers: “Take and eat the fruit of obedience.” [Col. 0948B]

4. They said of John, who was a disciple of Abba Paul, that he possessed great obedience (Ruff., bk. III, no. 67; Pasch., ch. 2, no. 1).

There was a memorial monument in a certain place, and a very savage lioness lived there. The old man saw the lioness’s dung around the place and said to John: “Go and bring that dung.”

He said to him: “What shall I do, abba, because of that lioness?”

The old man smiled and said to him: “If she comes against you, tie her up and bring her here.”

The brother went there in the evening, and behold, the lioness came upon him. In accordance with the old man’s word, he rushed at her in order to seize her. The lioness fled, and he followed her, saying: “Wait, because my abba told me to tie you up.”

When he caught her, he tied her up. The old man, who had been waiting for him and had sat there for a long time in distress, saw him finally arrive, with the lioness tied up.

When the old man saw this, he marveled. Wishing to humble him, he struck him and said: “Bavose”—[Note: *Bavose*. Thus the manuscripts and the Paris edition. Other editions have *stulte*, “foolishly.” Rufinus, book III, no. 27, in this same account has *insensibilis*, “senseless.”]—“What a senseless dog you have brought me!” The old man immediately untied her and let her return to her place. [Col. 0948C–D]

5. They said of Abba Silvanus that he had in Scetis a disciple named Mark, who possessed great obedience and was also a professional copyist. The old man loved him because of his obedience (Ruff., bk. III, no. 143).

He had eleven other disciples, who were grieved that he loved Mark more than them. When the neighboring old men heard that he loved him more than the others, they took it badly.

One day they came to him. Abba Silvanus took them with him, went out of his cell, and began knocking at the cells of each of his disciples, saying: “Brother, come, because I need you.”

One of them did not immediately follow him. He came to Mark’s cell and knocked, saying: “Mark.”

When Mark heard the old man’s voice, he immediately came out, and the old man sent him on a certain task.

Abba Silvanus then said to the old men: “Where are the other brothers?”

He entered Mark’s cell and found a quire that Mark had begun at that very hour. He was forming the letter O. When he heard the old man’s voice, he did not complete or turn the pen further to finish and close the letter he had in hand.

The old men said: “Truly, abba, the one you love, we too love, because God also loves him.” [Col. 0948D–0949A]

6. The mother of the aforementioned Mark once came to see him, bringing a large retinue. The old man went out to her, and she said to him: “Abba, tell my son to come out to me, so that I may see him.”

The old man entered and said to him: “Come out, so that your mother may see you.”

He was wearing a torn sack patched with pieces of cloth, and his head and face were stained with the smoke and soot of the kitchen. Out of obedience to the abba he did come out, but he closed his eyes and thus greeted his mother and those who had come with her, saying: “Be well.”

None of them, not even his mother, recognized that it was he. She sent again to the old man, saying: “Abba, send my son out, so that I may see him.”

He said to Mark: “Did I not tell you, ‘Come out, so that your mother may see you’?”

Mark said to him: “I came out according to your word, Father. Nevertheless, I beg you not to say this to me again, that I should come out, lest I appear disobedient to you.”

The old man went out and said to his mother: “He is the one who came out to you and greeted you, saying: ‘Be well.’” He comforted her and sent her away. [Col. 0949B–C]

7. Four brothers from Scetis once came to Abba Pambo dressed in leather tunics. Each praised the virtue of the others, without the one being praised being present.

One of them fasted greatly; another possessed nothing; the third had very great charity; and of the fourth they said that he had remained in obedience to his elders for twenty-two years.

Abba Pambo answered them: “I tell you that this man’s virtue is greater than that of the others. Each of you has retained the virtue he possesses by his own will; but this man, cutting off his own will, has made himself the servant of another’s will. Such men are confessors, if they remain so to the end.” [Col. 0949D]

8. A certain man came to Abba Sisoi the Theban, wishing to become a monk. The old man asked him whether he possessed anything in the world. He replied, “I have one son.” The old man said to him, “Go, throw him into the river, and then you will become a monk.” When he had gone away to throw him in, the old man sent one of the brothers to stop him. As he was about to cast the boy in, the brother said to him, “Stop! What are you doing?” He replied, “The abba told me to throw him in.” The brother said to him, “But the abba now says: Do not throw him in.” He then left his son and came to the old man, and through his obedience became a most exemplary monk.

9. Saint Syncletica said: “While living in community, we place obedience above every form of self-control, because self-control contains arrogance, whereas obedience promises the humility that is fitting.”

10. The same woman said again: “We ought to govern the soul with discernment; and while living in community, we should not seek what belongs to us, nor serve our own will. For, as though banishing ourselves into exile, we have entrusted ourselves in faith to one Father, having been separated from worldly affairs. Therefore, from the place where we departed, let us seek nothing further. There we had glory; there we had abundance of food; here, even bread itself is scarce.”

11. Abba Hyperichius said: “The monk’s ministry is obedience. Whoever possesses it will be heard in whatever he asks, and will stand before the Crucified One with confidence. For the Lord likewise came to the cross, becoming obedient even unto death.”

12. The old men said: “If someone has faith in another person and submits himself to him, he ought not to concern himself with God’s commandments, but should entrust his entire will to his spiritual father; for by obeying him in everything, he will not incur sin before God.”

13. An old man said: “God asks this of Christians: that one obey the divine Scriptures, since from them he will receive the pattern for what he should say and do, and that he agree with orthodox superiors and Fathers.”

14. A certain brother from Scetis, going out to the harvest, came to a great old man and said to him: “Tell me, abba, what should I do as I go to reap?” The old man said to him: “If I tell you, will you obey me?” The brother replied, “Yes, I obey you.” The old man said to him: “If you obey me, rise, go, and renounce this harvest; then come back, and I will tell you what to do.” The brother renounced the harvest and came to the old man.

The old man said to him: “Enter your cell and spend fifty continuous days there, eating bread with salt once a day. Then I will tell you something else.” He did so and returned again to the old man. Knowing that he was a diligent man, the old man instructed him how he ought to live in his cell.

The brother went down into his cell, prostrated himself face down on the ground for three days and three nights, and wept before God. Afterwards, when his thoughts said to him, “You have been exalted; you have become great,” he restrained the vices of his thoughts and humbly recalled his sins before himself, saying: “And where are all those sins of mine that I committed?” But if the thought arose in him that he had greatly neglected God’s commandment, he also said within himself: “Yet I will offer a small service to my God, and I believe that he will show me mercy.”

In this way, having conquered the spirits of evil thoughts, they later appeared to him visibly and said: “We are disturbed by you.” He said to them, “Why?” They replied: “Because if we exalt you, you return to humility; but if we humble you, you raise yourself up on high.”

15. The old men said: “God asks nothing so much from those who are beginning the monastic way of life as the labor of obedience.”

16. A certain solitary old man had a servant who lived on an estate. Once, because the servant was delayed, the old man’s necessities ran out (Ruffinus, book III, no. 144). When some time had passed and the servant had not come, the old man ran out both of the food he needed to live and of work for his hands.

As he was distressed because he had nothing to work at and no means of living, he said to his disciple: “Would you like to go to that estate and call the servant who customarily brings us what we need?” He replied, “I will do whatever you command.” The old man continued to delay, not daring to send the brother.

When they had waited a long time and were suffering because the servant did not come, the old man said again to his disciple: “Would you like to go to the estate and bring him?” He replied, “I will do whatever you wish.”

The disciple also feared going down to the estate, lest he be scandalized in some other way; but, so as not to disobey his father, he agreed to go. The old man said to him: “Go and trust in the God of your fathers, for he will protect you from every temptation.” After praying, he sent him on his way.

When the brother arrived at the estate, he asked where the servant lived and found his lodging. It happened that the servant was away from the estate with all his household, except for one daughter. When she heard the brother knocking, she came to the door and opened it. When he asked her about her father, she urged him to enter the lodging and at the same time pulled him inside.

He did not agree to enter. But when she pressed him for a long time, she prevailed and brought him inside to her. Embracing him, she began to entice him to sexual intercourse. When he saw that he was being drawn into lust and was confused by his thoughts, he groaned and cried out to God, saying: “Lord, for the sake of my father’s prayers, deliver me at this hour.”

After he had said this, he suddenly found himself on the road beside the river, going toward the monastery, and was restored unharmed to his abba.

17. Two brothers who were blood relatives came to live in a certain monastery. One of them was distinguished for great self-restraint, the other for great obedience (Ruffinus, book III, no. 145). The Father would say to the obedient one, “Do this,” and he did it; “Do that,” and he did it; “Eat in the morning,” and he ate.

Because he was so obedient, he had a great reputation in the monastery. But his brother, the self-restrained one, pierced by the sword of envy against him, said to himself: “I will test whether this man truly has obedience.”

He approached the father of the monastery and said to him: “Send my brother with me, so that we may go somewhere.” The abba allowed them to leave. The abstinent brother took him with him, intending to test him.

When they came to a river where there were many crocodiles, he said to him: “Go down into the river and cross.” The other immediately went down. The crocodiles came and licked his body, but did him no harm. When his brother saw this, he said to him: “Come up out of the river.”

As they continued on their way, they found a human body lying in the road. The abstinent brother said to his brother: “If we had something old, we would throw it over that body.” The obedient brother replied: “Rather, let us pray, and perhaps he will rise.”

They stood for prayer and prayed fervently, and the dead man rose. After this, the abstinent brother became proud and said: “This dead man was raised because of my self-restraint.”

God revealed all these things to their abba, including how he had tested his brother with the crocodiles and how the dead man had been raised. When they returned to the monastery, the abba said to the abstinent brother: “Why did you do this to your brother? Yet see: the dead man rose because of his obedience.”

18. Another man, who had lived a worldly life and had three sons, renounced the world and came to a monastery, leaving his sons in the city. After he had spent three years in the monastery, his thoughts began frequently to bring his sons to his remembrance, and he became very sorrowful over them. He had not told the abba that he had sons.

Seeing him sad, the abba said to him: “What is wrong, that you are sad?” He told him that he had three sons in the city and that he wished to bring them to the monastery. The abba ordered him to bring them.

When he went to the city, he found that two of them had already died and that only one remained. Taking him, he came to the monastery. When he sought the abba, he did not find him there. He asked the brothers where the abba was. They said: “He has gone to the bakery.”

He took the son he had brought and went to the bakery. When the abba saw him coming, he greeted him. He took the child he had brought and embraced him. Then he said to the father: “Do you love him?” He replied, “Yes.” Again he said to him: “Do you love him completely?” He replied, “Yes.”

When the abba heard this, he said to him: “Then take him, if you love him, and throw him into the furnace while the furnace is burning.” The father took his son and threw him into the burning furnace. Immediately the furnace became like dew. Because of this, he won glory at that time, like the patriarch Abraham.

19. A certain old man said: “The brother who has given his mind to obedience to a spiritual father has a greater reward than the one who has withdrawn alone into the desert” (Ruffinus, book III, no. 141).

He also said: “Someone among the Fathers related that he had seen four orders in heaven. The first order consisted of sick people giving thanks to God; the second, of those who pursued hospitality and diligently ministered to the sick; the third, of those living in solitude and not seeing human beings; the fourth, of those who, for God’s sake, submit themselves to spiritual Fathers in order to obey them.

“The order of the obedient wore a golden necklace and crown and possessed greater glory than the others. I said to the one who showed me all these things: ‘How does this order, which is small, possess greater glory than the others?’ He answered me: ‘Those who pursue hospitality do so according to their own will. Likewise, those who withdraw into the desert have departed from the world by their own decision. But this order, which has given itself to obedience, casting away all its own desires, depends upon God and upon the command of its spiritual father. Therefore it has greater glory than the others.’

“Therefore, my son, obedience is good when it is performed for God’s sake. Pay attention, then, children, to some trace of this virtue. Obedience is the salvation of all the faithful. Obedience is the mother of all virtues. Obedience is the discoverer of the kingdom of heaven. Obedience opens the heavens and raises human beings from the earth. Obedience is the companion of angels. Obedience is the food of all the saints. Through it they were weaned, and through it they came to perfection.”

# FIFTEENTH BOOKLET: ON HUMILITY

[Col. 0953B]

1. Abba Anthony, unable to fathom the depth of God’s judgments, asked, saying: “Lord, why do some die after a short time of life, while others reach extreme old age? Why are some destitute, while others are enriched with possessions? Why are the unjust wealthy, while the just are oppressed by poverty?”

A voice came to him, saying: “Anthony, attend to yourself. These are God’s judgments, and it is not fitting for you to know them.”

2. Abba Anthony said to Abba Pastor: “This is the great work of a human being: that each person place his own fault upon himself before the Lord and await temptation until the final moment of his life.”

3. Abba Anthony said again: “I saw all the snares [Col. 0953C] of the enemy spread out upon the earth, and, groaning, I said: ‘Who, do you think, can pass through these?’ And I heard a voice saying: ‘Humility.’”

[Note: “[Col. 0990C] Snares.” Thus Ecclesiasticus 9:20 warns us: Ἐπίγνωθι ὅτι ἐν μέσῳ παγίδων διαβαίνεις—“Know that you are passing through the midst of snares.” Saint Augustine, on Psalm 141: “‘What does “in the midst of snares” mean? On the way of Christ: snares on this side and snares on that side. Snares on the right, snares on the left. Snares on the right: the prosperity of the world; snares on the left: the adversity of the world. Snares on the right: promises; snares on the left: terrors. Walk in the midst of snares; do not depart from the way. Let neither promise capture you nor terror shatter you.’”]

4. Once some old men came to Abba Anthony, and Abba Joseph was with them. Wishing to test them, Abba Anthony brought up a matter from the holy Scriptures. He began by asking the younger men what this or that word meant. Each answered as best he could. But he said to them: “You have not yet found it.”

After them he said to Abba Joseph: “How do you say that this word should be understood?” He replied: “I do not know.” Abba Anthony said: “Truly, Abba Joseph alone has found the way, since he answered that he did not know.”

5. Once demons stood by Abba Arsenius while he was sitting in his cell and troubled him. The brothers who used to minister to him arrived, and, standing outside the cell, they heard him crying out to the Lord and saying: “Lord, do not abandon me, because I have done no good before you. But grant me, Lord, according to your kindness, at least now to make a beginning of living well.”

6. They said of the man mentioned above that, just as no one in the palace wore better clothing than he did, so, when he lived the monastic life, no one was clothed more poorly than he was (Ruffinus, book III, no. 37).

7. Once, when Abba Arsenius was asking an Egyptian old man about his thoughts, another man who saw him said: “Abba Arsenius, how can you, who have been educated in such great learning in the Latin and Greek languages, question this rustic about your thoughts?”

He replied: “As far as worldly matters are concerned, I acquired Latin and Greek learning; but I have not yet been able to learn the alphabet of this rustic.”

8. The old men said that once, in Scetis, some people gave the brothers a few figs. Because there were so few, they did not send any of them to Abba Arsenius, lest he suffer what might seem an insult.

When he heard this, he did not go out, as was customary, to celebrate the work of God with the brothers, saying: “You have excommunicated me by not giving me the blessing [eulogia] that the Lord sent to the brothers, from which I was not worthy to receive.”

When everyone heard this, they were edified by the old man’s humility. The presbyter went and brought him some of those figs and led him into the assembly rejoicing.

9. They said of him that no one could comprehend the manner of his life. Once, while Abba Arsenius was living in the lower regions of Egypt and was suffering harassment there, it seemed good to him to leave his cell. Taking nothing with him, he said to his disciples Alexander and Zoilus: “You, Alexander, go up into a boat; and you, Zoilus, come with me as far as the river and seek a little boat sailing to Alexandria. You too shall sail to your brother.”

Zoilus was troubled by these words and remained silent, and so they separated from one another. The old man went down toward the region of Alexandria and fell seriously ill.

His disciples said to one another: “Do you think that one of us has grieved him, and that this is why he separated himself from us?” They found no cause of ingratitude in themselves, nor any occasion when they had disobeyed him.

When the old man had recovered, he said to himself: “I will go to my fathers.” Thus he came to a place called Petra, where the servants mentioned above were.

While he was beside the river, an Ethiopian girl came and touched his melote. The old man rebuked her. She said: “If you are a monk, go to the mountain.”

The old man was pierced by these words and said to himself: “Arsenius, if you are a monk, go to the mountain.” While this was happening, his disciples Alexander and Zoilus came upon him.

When they fell at his feet, the old man threw himself upon the ground, and they wept together. The old man said: “Did you not hear that I became ill?” They replied: “Yes, we heard.” He said to them: “Why did you not come to see me?”

Alexander said: “Because your separation from us was intolerable to us; many people were also saddened by it, saying: ‘If they had not disobeyed the old man, he would never have separated himself from them.’”

The old man said to them: “I knew that this would be said. Yet people will also say again: ‘Because the dove found no rest for the sole of its foot, it returned to Noah in the ark’” (Genesis 8).

By these words the spirits of his disciples were healed, and they remained with him until the end of his life.

When he was dying, they were greatly troubled (Ruffinus, book III, no. 163). He said to them: “The hour has not yet come. When it comes, I will tell you. I shall have to be judged with you before the tribunal of Christ if you allow anyone to do anything to my body.”

They said to him: “What shall we do, then? We do not know how to clothe or bury the dead.” The old man said: “Do you not know how to put a rope around my foot and drag me to the mountain?”

When he was about to give up his spirit, they saw him weeping and said to him: “Truly, Father, are you also afraid of death?” He said to them: “Truly. The fear that is upon me at this hour has always been in me, from the time I became a monk, and I am very afraid.” Thus he fell asleep in peace.

This saying was always in Arsenius’s mouth: “Why did you go out?” I have always regretted speaking; I have never regretted being silent.

When Abba Pastor heard that Arsenius had departed this life, he wept and said: “Blessed are you, Abba Arsenius, because you wept for yourself in this world. For whoever has not wept for himself in this world will weep forever there. Whether here willingly or there under the compulsion of torments, it is impossible not to weep.”

10. Abba Daniel related of Abba Arsenius that he never wished to speak about any question concerning the Scriptures, although he could have done so splendidly if he had wished, nor did he quickly write a letter to anyone (Ruffinus, book III, no. 198).

When he came to the assembly after some time, he sat behind a column so that no one could see his face and so that he himself would not look upon another. His appearance was angelic, like Jacob’s: adorned with gray hair, elegant in body, though thin. He had a long beard reaching all the way to his belly. The hairs of his eyelids had fallen out from excessive weeping. He was tall, but bent by prolonged old age; he died at the age of ninety-five.

He served for forty years in the palace of the emperor of blessed memory, the elder Theodosius, who was the father of Arcadius and Honorius. He spent forty years in Scetis, ten years in the place called Trohen, above Babylon and opposite the city of Memphis, and three years in Cinopo of Alexandria. Returning again to Trohen, he spent another two years there, completing his course in peace and in the fear of God, for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith (Acts 11).

11. Abba John related that Abba Anub, Abba Pastor, and the rest of their brothers were monks in Scetis, born from one womb (Ruffinus, book III, no. 199; Paschasius, chapter 42, no. 4).

When the people called the Mazices came there and laid waste to the place, they first departed from it and came to a place called Therenuthi, until they had decided where they ought to live. They remained there for a few days in an ancient temple.

Abba Anub said to Abba Pastor: “Show charity, both you and your brothers, and let us each live separately and not come to one another during this week.” Abba Pastor replied: “Let us do as you wish.” And they did so.

There was a stone statue in the temple. Every morning Abba Anub would rise and stone the face of that statue; in the evening he would say: “Forgive me.” He did this throughout the week.

On Saturday they met one another. Abba Pastor said to Abba Anub: “I saw you, abba, stoning the face of this statue throughout the week and then doing penance before it. Yet a faithful person does not do this.”

The old man replied: “I did this for your sake. When you saw me stoning the face of that statue, did it speak? Did it become enraged?” Abba Pastor said: “No.”

“Again, when I did penance before it, was it troubled? Did it say, ‘I do not forgive’?” Abba Pastor replied: “No.”

The old man said: “Then we too, who are seven brothers, if you want us to remain together, must become like this statue, which is not troubled when insulted. If you do not want this, behold, there are four entrances to this temple; let each one leave by whichever entrance he wishes and go wherever he wishes.”

When they heard this, they all prostrated themselves on the ground before Abba Anub and said to him: “As you command, Father, so let it be. We will do what you tell us.”

Afterward Abba Pastor related: “We remained together for the whole time of our lives, laboring and doing everything according to the old man’s word, which he had spoken to us.

“He appointed one of us as steward, and whatever he set before us, we ate. It was impossible for anyone among us to say, ‘Bring something else,’ or, ‘I do not want to eat this.’ Thus we passed the whole time of our lives in quietness and peace.”

12. They said of Abba Ammon that certain people came to him asking him to judge between them, but the old man pretended not to hear. Then a woman said to another woman standing beside her: “This old man is a fool.”

The old man heard her, called her to himself, and said to her: “How many labors do you think I endured in different solitudes in order to acquire this foolishness? And because of you I am about to lose it today.”

13. They related concerning the bishop of the city called Oxyrhynchus, named Affy, that when he was a monk he treated his life with excessive severity. When he became bishop, he wished to use in the city the same severity he had practiced in the desert, but he could not.

Therefore he prostrated himself before the Lord, saying: “Do you suppose, Lord, that your grace has departed from me because of the episcopate?” And it was revealed to him: “No; rather, because then you were in solitude, and since there was no human being, your God was your protector. Now, however, you are here in the world, where human beings assist you.”

14. Abba Daniel said that in Babylon there was the daughter of a certain leading man who had a demon. Her father loved a certain monk. The monk said to him: “No one can heal your daughter except certain solitaries whom I know. If you go to them, they will not agree to do this because of their humility.

“But let us do this: when they come bringing things for sale that they have made, say that you wish to buy what they are selling. When they come into the house to receive the price, we will ask them to pray, and I believe that your daughter will be saved.”

They went out into the street and found one of the old men’s disciples sitting and selling his baskets. They took him with them into the house, as though he were to receive the price of the baskets.

When that monk entered the house, the girl who was tormented by the demon came and slapped him. He turned his other cheek to her, in accordance with the divine commandment.

The demon was forced to cry out: “O violence! The commandments of Jesus Christ are driving me out of here!” And immediately the girl was cleansed.

When they came to the old men, they told them what had happened. They glorified God and said: “The custom and pride of the devil have been overthrown by the humility commanded by Christ Jesus.”

15. Abba Evagrius said: “The beginning of salvation is to rebuke yourself.”

16. Abba Serapion said: “I have performed more bodily labors than my son Zacharias, yet I have not attained the measure of his humility and silence.”

[Col. 0957B] 17. Abba Moses said to Brother Zacharias: “Tell me what I should do.” When he heard this, Zacharias threw himself face down upon the ground at his feet, saying: “You are asking me, Father?” (Ruffinus, book III, no. 86; Append. Mart., no. 49).

The old man said to him: “Believe me, son Zacharias, I have seen the Holy Spirit descend upon you, and for this reason I am compelled to ask you.”

Then Zacharias took his cowl from his head, placed it beneath his feet, and, trampling upon it, said: “Unless a human being has been trampled in this way, he cannot become a monk.”

18. Abba Pastor said: “When Abba Moses questioned Brother Zacharias at the time of his death, he said: ‘What do you see?’ He replied: ‘There is nothing better than silence, Father.’ He said to him: ‘It is true, my son. Be silent.’”

At the hour of his death, Abba Isidore was sitting nearby. He looked up toward heaven and said: “Rejoice, my son Zacharias, for the gates of the kingdom of heaven have been opened to you.”

19. The bishop of Alexandria, Theophilus, of holy memory, once came to the mountain of Nitria. The abba of that mountain came to him, and the bishop said to him: “What more have you found on this way, Father?”

The old man replied: “To accuse and reproach myself without ceasing.” The bishop said to him: “There is no other way that should be followed except this one.”

20. When Abba Theodorus ate with the brothers, they took the cups with reverence and silence, and did not say, as was customary, “Forgive me.”

21. They said of that same Abba Theodorus that, when he had become a deacon in Scetis, he was unwilling to minister and fled here and there. Again the old men brought him back, saying: “Do not abandon your ministry.”

Abba Theodorus said to them: “Let me go, and I will beseech God. If he shows me that I ought to remain in this ministry, I will do so.”

As he prayed to God, he said: “If it is your will, Lord, that I remain in this ministry, show me.” A pillar of fire appeared, rising from earth to heaven, and a voice sounded, saying: “If you can become like this pillar, go and minister.”

When he heard this, he resolved never to minister. When he came to the church, they did penance before him, saying: “If you wish to minister to us, at least hold the cup.” He did not agree, saying: “If you do not let me go, I will leave this place.” And so they let him depart.

22. Abba John the Short said: “Humility is the door of God. Our fathers, driven by many insults, entered rejoicing into the city of God.”

The same man said again: “Humility and the fear of God surpass all virtues.”

23. Abba John the Theban said: “The monk ought to possess humility above all things, for this is the Savior’s first commandment: ‘Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven’” (Matthew 5).

24. Once the brothers who lived in Scetis gathered together and began to inquire among themselves about Melchizedek the priest. But they forgot to call Abba Copres.

Afterward they called him and asked him about the same question. He struck his mouth three times and said: “Woe to you, Copres, because you have abandoned what God commanded you to do, and you presume to investigate what he has not required of you.”

When the brothers heard this, they each fled to his own cell.

25. Abba Macarius once related about himself, saying: “When I was young and sitting in my cell in Egypt, they seized me and made me a cleric in a village (Ruffinus, book III, no. 99).

“Since I did not wish to agree to minister, I fled to another place. A certain secular man, though religious in his way of life, came to me. He took from me the work I was doing with my hands and supplied me with what was necessary.

“But it happened, when the devil tempted me, that a certain virgin in that village was violated and fell into sin. When she began to conceive, they asked who had fathered the child in her womb. She said: ‘This solitary, who slept with me.’

“They came out from that village, seized me, brought me back to the village, hung cooking pots and the handles of vessels around my neck, and made me parade through the village, beating me along the road and saying: ‘This monk has corrupted our daughter! Take him away, take him away!’ They beat me almost to death.

“A certain old man arrived and said: ‘How long will you beat this foreign monk?’ The man who used to provide me with necessities followed behind in shame, for they had also treated him with many insults, saying: ‘Behold the solitary monk for whom you testified—see what he has done!’

“The girl’s parents said: ‘We will not release him until he provides a surety that he will support her.’ I asked the man who used to provide for me to become my surety, and he stood surety for me.

“I returned to my cell and gave him all the baskets I had, saying: ‘Sell them and give the proceeds to that woman of mine for food.’ I said in my heart: ‘Macarius, behold, you have found yourself a wife; now you must work still harder to feed her.’

“I worked not only by day but also by night, and sent the proceeds to her. When the time came for that wretched girl to give birth, she remained in labor for many days and did not give birth.

“They said to her: ‘What is the matter?’ She replied: ‘I know why I am suffering for so long.’ Her parents asked her: ‘Why?’ She answered: ‘Because I falsely accused that monk and entangled him through deceit, although he was not responsible. It was such-and-such a young man who did this.’

“When my servant heard these words, he came to me rejoicing and said: ‘That girl could not give birth until she confessed that you had no responsibility before her, but that she had lied against you. And behold, all the inhabitants of that village wish to come here to your cell to glorify God and do penance before you.’

“When I heard this from my servant, I rose and fled here to Scetis, so that the people would not distress me. This was the beginning of the reason why I began to live here.”

26. Once, as Abba Macarius was returning from the marsh to his cell, he was carrying palm branches. Behold, the devil met him on the road with a sickle (Ruffinus, book III, no. 124; Paschasius, chapter 13, no. 6).

He wanted to strike him with that sickle but could not, and said to him: “I suffer great violence from you, Macarius, because I cannot prevail against you. For whatever you do, I also do: you fast, and I do not eat at all; you keep vigil, and I do not sleep at all. There is only one thing in which you surpass me.”

Abba Macarius said to him: “What is it?” The devil replied: “Your humility, through which I cannot prevail against you.”

27. Once Abba Mathois went from Raythu into the region of Gebalon; his brother was with him (Ruffinus, book III, no. 188; Paschasius, chapter 33, no. 3).

The bishop of that place came to the old man mentioned above and ordained him a presbyter. While they were eating together, the bishop said: “Forgive me, abba, because I know that you did not want this; but, in order to receive your blessing, I presumed to do it.”

The old man said to him humbly: “My mind did desire this a little; nevertheless, I bear it heavily because I am compelled to be separated from my brother who is with me. For I am not able to complete all the prayers that we used to perform together.”

The bishop said: “If you know that he is worthy, I will ordain him too.” Abba Mathois said to him: “Whether he is worthy, I do not know; but I know one thing: he is better than I.”

The bishop ordained him also. Thus both departed from this life without ever approaching the altar to offer the sacrifice.

The old man used to say: “I believe in God that perhaps I will not endure a severe judgment because of the ordination I received, since I do not dare to consecrate the offering. This office belongs to those who live without reproach.”

28. Abba Mathois said: “The closer a person comes to God, the more he sees himself as a sinner” (Ruffinus, book III, no. 123). For the prophet Isaiah, when he saw the Lord, called himself wretched and unclean (Isaiah 6).

29. They said of Abba Moses that he had become a cleric and that they had placed an omophorion upon him. The archbishop said to him: “Behold, Abba Moses, you have become a candidate.”

He replied: “Do you mean outwardly, lord pope, or inwardly?”

Wishing to test him, the bishop said to the clerics: “When Abba Moses enters the altar area, drive him out and follow him, so that you may hear what he says.”

When they began to drive him out, they said to him: “Go out, Ethiopian!” As he went out, he said: “They have treated you well, you ash-covered and pot-covered one” [cinerente et caccabate]. [Note: “[Col. 0990C] Cinerente et caccabate.” Thus the Vedastine and Audomare manuscripts. The printed editions vary: some have cinerose et caccabate; others, cinerate et caccabate. I think cinerentum is formed in the manner of pulverulentus and similar words. See the Onomasticon.]

“Since you are not a human being, why did you presume to place yourself among human beings?”

### 30.

While Abba Pastor was in the assembly, he heard about Abba Nesteron and desired to see him. He therefore instructed Nesteron’s abbot to send him to him. But since that abbot did not wish to let him go alone, he did not send him. A few days later, the monastery’s steward asked his abbot to permit him to go to Abba Pastor, so that he might tell him his thoughts. When his abbot released him, he said to him:

“Take this brother with you, because the old man instructed me concerning him; and since I did not dare let him go alone, I have delayed until now.”

When the steward had come to the old man, he spoke to him about his thoughts, and the old man healed him by his answer. Afterward the old man questioned that brother, saying:

“Abba Nesteron, how did you acquire this virtue, that whenever some tribulation arises in the monastery, you neither speak nor become annoyed?”

When the brother was pressed greatly by the old man, he said to him:

“Forgive me, Abba. When I first entered the assembly, I said to myself: ‘You and the donkey must be one.’ For just as a donkey is beaten and does not speak, suffers injury and does not answer, so must you. As it is also written in the Psalm: ‘I became like a beast before you, and I am always [Col. 0960C] with you’—[the supplied text reads *per tecum*] (Ps. 72).”

### 31.

They said of Abba Olympius in Scetis (Ruff., book III, no. 17) that he was a slave, and that every year he went down to Alexandria, carrying his wages to his masters. They would come out to meet and greet him. The old man would pour water into a basin and bring it, so that he could wash his masters’ feet.

But they would say to him: “No, Father; do not trouble us.”

He would answer them: “I confess that I am your slave, and I give thanks because you have allowed me to serve God as a free man. Nevertheless, I wash your feet. Here, then, accept my wages.”

But they would refuse. When they would not accept them, he said: “Believe me: if you do not wish to accept my wages, I shall remain here and serve you.”

Out of reverence for him, they then placed him in charge, allowing him to do whatever he wished. When he returned, they escorted him with honor, providing him with whatever was necessary for him to make an *agapē* for them. Through this he became renowned in Scetis.

### 32.

Abba Pastor said:

“A person must always and unceasingly breathe humility and the fear of God, just as he breathes the breath that he draws in and expels through his nostrils” (Append. Mart., no. 101).

### 33.

A brother asked Abba Pastor:

“How ought I to conduct myself in the place where I live?”

The old man answered him:

“Exercise prudence as a stranger. Wherever you are, do not seek to have your word prevail before you, and you will have rest.”

### 34.

He said again:

“To cast oneself down before God, not to exalt oneself, and to put one’s own will behind one’s back—these are the tools with which the soul works.”

### 35.

He also said:

“Do not measure yourself; rather, cling to one who conducts himself well.”

### 36.

He said again:

“A brother asked Abba Alonius: ‘What is contempt?’ The old man said: ‘To be beneath irrational animals; then you will know that they are not condemned.’”

### 37.

The same man also said:

“Humility is the earth on which the Lord commanded that sacrifice be offered.”

### 38.

Again he said:

“If a person keeps his proper order, he will not be disturbed.”

### 39.

Again he said:

“Once, when the old men were sitting and eating, Abba Alonius stood and served them. When they saw this, they praised him, but he made no reply at all.

“Someone therefore said to him privately: ‘Why did you not answer the old men when they praised you?’

“Abba Alonius said: ‘If I had answered them, I would have been found taking delight in their praise of me.’”

### 40.

Abba Joseph related:

“Once, when we were sitting with Abba Pastor, he mentioned Abba Agatho. We said to him: ‘He is a young man; why do you call him “Abba”?’

“Abba Pastor said: ‘His mouth caused him to be called “Abba.”’”

### 41.

They said of Abba Pastor that he never wished to set his statement above the word of another old man; rather, he always praised whatever the other had said.

### 42.

Once Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, of holy memory, came to Scetis. The brothers assembled and said to Abba Pambo:

“Speak one word to the pope, so that his spirit may be edified in this place.”

The old man answered:

“If he is not edified by my silence, neither will he be edified by my speech.”

### 43.

Brother Pystus related, saying:

“We seven solitary brothers went to Abba Sisoi, who lived on the island of Clysma. When we begged him to tell us something, he answered:

“‘Forgive me, for I am an ignorant man. But once I came to Abba Hor and Abba Athre. Abba Hor had been ill for eighteen years, and I began to beg them to tell me some word. Abba Hor said: “What can I tell you? Do whatever you see. For God belongs to the one who exacts from himself beyond his capacity and does violence to himself in everything.”

“‘These two men—Abba Hor and Abba Athre—were not from the same province. There was great grace between them until they both departed from the body. Abba Athre was outstanding in obedience, while Abba Hor possessed great humility.

“‘I stayed with them for a few days, investigating their virtues, and I saw something wondrous that Abba Athre did. Someone had brought them a small fish, and Abba Athre, who was the elder, wanted to prepare it for the old Abba Hor. He therefore set down a knife and began cutting the fish. Abba Hor called him, saying: “Athre, Athre!”

“‘He immediately let go of the knife in the middle of the cut fish, without cutting it through, and ran to him. I was amazed at such obedience, because he did not say: “Wait until I have cut the fish.”

“‘I said to Abba Athre: “Where did you find this obedience?”

“‘He answered me: “It is not mine; it belongs to this old man.” He took me and said: “Come, see his obedience.”

“‘He then cooked the small fish badly, deliberately ruining it, and set it before the old man. The old man ate it without saying anything.

“‘He said to him: “Is it good, old man?”

“‘He answered: “Very good.”

“‘Afterward he brought him a small fish, cooked exceedingly well, and said: “Here, old man, I ruined this; I cooked it badly.”

“‘The old man answered: “Yes, it turned out a little badly for you.”

“‘Then Abba Athre turned to me and said: “Do you see that this old man’s obedience is like this?”

“‘I departed from them, and whatever I saw, I did according to my ability.’

“These things Abba Sisoi said to the brothers. One of us then asked him:

“‘Show us charity, and tell us one word.’

“He said:

“‘Whoever possesses what is immeasurable in knowledge fulfills all of Scripture.’

“Another of us said to him:

“‘What is pilgrimage, Father?’

“He answered:

“‘Be silent, and wherever you come, say: “I have no cause.” That is pilgrimage.’”

### 44.

A brother came to Abba Sisoi on the mountain of Abba Antony. While they were speaking, he said to Abba Sisoi:

“Have you still not reached the measure of Abba Antony, Father?”

The old man answered:

“If I possessed even one thought of Abba Antony, I would become entirely like fire. Nevertheless, I know a man who can bear his thoughts only with labor.”

### 45.

That brother asked him again:

“Do you think Satan persecuted the ancients in this way?”

Abba Sisoi said to him:

“Now more than ever, because his time has drawn near, and he is troubled” (Ruff., book III, no. 174; Pasch., chap. 25, no. 2).

### 46.

Some others came to him to hear a word from him, but he said nothing to them. He always said:

“Forgive me.”

When they saw his baskets, they said to his disciple Abraham:

“What do you do with these baskets?”

He answered them:

“We sell them here and there.”

When the old man heard this, he said:

“And Sisoi eats from here and there.”

When they heard this, they were greatly edified by his humility and departed with joy.

### 47.

A brother asked Abba Sisoi:

“I see that my mind is intent upon God.”

The old man said to him:

“It is not a great thing for your mind to be with God. It is great, however, if you see yourself beneath every creature. Bodily labor corrects this and leads to the path of humility.”

### 48.

Blessed Syncletica said:

“Just as it is impossible to build a ship without nails, so it is impossible for a person to be saved without humility.”

### 49.

Abba Hyperichius said:

“The tree of life is high above, and the monk’s humility climbs up to it.”

### 50.

The same man also said:

“Imitate that publican, lest you be condemned with the Pharisee; and follow the gentleness of Moses, so that, cutting off the heights of your heart, you may turn them into springs of water.”

### 51.

Abba Crsisius said:

“If a fragment of an unbaked tile is placed in a foundation beside a river, it will not last a single day; but if it is baked, it remains like a stone.

“So it is with a person who possesses carnal wisdom and has not been hardened in the fire of temptations, as Joseph was. Such a person is dissolved by the word of God: when he has made a beginning, he is beset by many temptations among human beings.

“It is good for a person to know his own measure and, at the beginning, to avoid a burden. But those who are strong in faith stand firm and unmoved. For if someone wishes to speak of the holy Joseph himself, he will say that he was not earthly: how greatly he was tempted, and in what sort of province, where there was not even a trace of divine worship! Yet the God of his fathers was with him. He rescued him from every tribulation, and now he is with his fathers in the kingdom of heaven.

“Let us, therefore, recognize our own measure and strive; for scarcely are we able to escape the judgment of God.”

[Col. 0963B]

### 52.

There was a solitary old man living in the desert, and he said to himself that he was perfect in the virtues. He prayed to God, saying:

“Show me what the perfection of the soul is, and I shall do it.”

But God, wishing to humble his thoughts, said to him:

“Go to that archimandrite, and whatever he tells you, do.”

Before the old man came to him, God revealed to that archimandrite:

“Behold, that solitary is coming to you. Tell him to take a whip and go to pasture your pigs.”

The old man came, knocked at the door, and entered the archimandrite’s dwelling. After they had greeted one another, they sat down. The solitary who had come said to him:

“Tell me what I must do in order to be saved.”

He said to him:

“Will you do whatever I tell you?”

He answered:

“Yes.”

He said to him:

“Take this whip and go pasture the pigs.”

Those who knew him and had heard about him, when they saw him pasturing pigs, said:

“Did you see that great solitary about whom we had heard? Behold, his mind has been deranged, he is tormented by a demon, and he is pasturing pigs.”

When God saw his humility and how patiently he endured the insults of people, he commanded him to return to his own place.

### 53.

A man who was tormented by a demon and foamed violently struck a certain solitary old monk on the cheek. The old man immediately turned the other cheek to him. The demon, unable to endure the fire of his humility, immediately departed from him (Ruff., book III, no. 125).

### 54.

The old man said to someone:

“When a thought of pride or exaltation enters you, examine your conscience: whether you keep all the divine commandments; whether you love your enemies; whether you rejoice when your adversary is glorified; whether you are grieved at his being brought low; whether you recognize yourself to be an unprofitable servant; and whether you consider yourself worse than all sinners.

“But if you now think of yourself as though you had corrected everything, know that such a thought of yours will dissolve all things” (Ruff., book III, no. 115; Pasch., chap. 13, no. 3).

### 55.

The old man said to someone:

“Do not set your heart against your brother, saying that you are more sober, more self-controlled, and more intelligent than he. Rather, submit yourself to the grace of God in a spirit of poverty and in genuine love, lest, lifted up by a spirit of exaltation, you lose your labor. But be seasoned with spiritual salt in Christ.”

### 56.

The old man said:

“Whoever is honored or praised beyond what is deserved suffers the greater loss. But whoever is not honored at all by people will be glorified from above” (Ruff., book III, no. 112; Pasch., chap. 13, no. 1).

### 57.

A brother asked the old man:

“Is it good to repent continually?”

He answered him:

“We saw Jesus the son of Nun: when he was lying face down, God appeared to him.”

### 58.

When the old man was asked why we are so troubled by demons, he answered:

“Because we throw away our weapons, namely insult, humility, poverty, and patience” (Ruff., book III, no. 173; Pasch., chap. 25, no. 11).

### 59.

A certain brother asked the old man:

“If one of the brothers brings me thoughts from outside, do you wish me to tell him not to bring them to me?”

The old man answered:

“No.”

The brother said:

“Why?”

The old man answered:

“Because we cannot keep this ourselves either. And perhaps, when we say to our neighbor, ‘Do not do that,’ we may afterward find ourselves doing the very same thing.”

The brother said:

“What, then, ought to be done?”

The old man answered:

“If we wish to preserve silence, that very manner is sufficient for our neighbor.”

### 60.

The old man was asked what humility was. He answered:

“If you forgive a brother who has sinned against you before he repents before you.”

### 61.

The old man said:

“In every temptation, do not blame another person, but blame yourself alone, saying: ‘These things have happened to me because of my sins.’”

### 62.

The old man said:

“I have never passed beyond my proper order in order to walk higher; nor have I ever been disturbed when placed in humility. For all my thought was directed toward this: to entreat the Lord to strip me of the old person.”

### 63.

A brother asked the old man:

“What is humility?”

The old man answered:

“To do good to those who do evil to you.”

The brother said:

“If a person does not reach that measure, what should he do?”

The old man answered:

“Let him flee, choosing silence.”

### 64.

A brother asked the old man:

“What is the work of pilgrimage?”

He said to him:

“I know a brother who was on pilgrimage. When he was detained in a church and an *agapē* happened to be held there, he sat at the table to eat with the brothers.

“Some said: ‘Who has kept this man here?’

“They said to him: ‘Rise and go outside from here.’

“He rose and went away. But others, grieved at his expulsion, went out and called him back.

“Afterward someone asked him: ‘What, do you think, was in your heart when you were expelled and then called back?’

“He said: ‘I put it in my heart that I should be like a dog, which, when chased away, goes outside, and when called, comes in.’”

### 65.

Some people once came to the Thebaid to a certain old man, bringing with them a man who was tormented by a demon, so that the old man might cure him (Ruff., book III, no. 25). After the old man had been entreated for a long time, he said to the demon:

“Come out of God’s creature.”

The demon answered:

“I am coming out, but I ask you one question, so that you may tell me: which are the goats, and which are the lambs?”

The old man said:

“The goats are such as I am; who the lambs are, God knows.”

When the demon heard this, he cried out in a loud voice:

“Behold, because of this humility of yours I am coming out.”

And he came out at that very hour.

### 66.

A certain Egyptian monk lived in a suburb of the city of Constantinople (Ruff., book III, no. 19, according to Poemen). When the emperor Theodosius the Younger was passing along that road, he left behind all those who were in his service and came alone to the monk’s cell. He knocked at the monk’s door, and the monk opened it.

When he saw him, he recognized that he was the emperor, but nevertheless received him as though he were one of the military officials. When he had entered, they prayed and sat down.

The emperor began to ask:

“How are the fathers in Egypt?”

He answered:

“They are all praying for your well-being.”

The emperor looked around his cell to see what he had. He saw nothing there except a small basket containing a little bread and a flask of water.

The monk said to him:

“Taste a little.”

He served him bread and set before him oil and salt. The emperor ate, and the monk gave him water to drink.

The emperor said to him:

“Do you know who I am?”

He said:

“God knows who you are.”

Then he said to him:

“I am the emperor Theodosius.”

The monk immediately bowed down and greeted him humbly.

The emperor said:

“Blessed are you, because you have a secure life and do not think about this world. But I will tell you the truth: I was born into imperial power, and I have never enjoyed bread and water as I have today. I ate with great pleasure.”

From that time onward the emperor began to honor him. But the old man, when he went out, fled and returned again to Egypt.

### 67.

The old men used to say:

“When we are tempted, then we are humbled all the more, because God, knowing our weakness, protects us. But if we glorify ourselves, he takes his protection away from us, and we perish.”

### 68.

The devil appeared to a certain brother transformed into an angel of light and said to him:

“I am the angel Gabriel, and I have been sent to you.”

But he said to him:

“See to it that you have not been sent to someone else. I am not worthy that an angel should be sent to me.”

The devil immediately disappeared.

### 69.

The old men used to say:

“Even if an angel truly appears to you, do not readily receive him. Rather, humble yourself, saying: ‘I am not worthy to see an angel while living in sins.’”

### 70.

They related of another old man that, as he sat in his cell and endured temptations, he saw demons openly and despised them. When the devil saw that he was being defeated by the old man, he came and showed himself to him, saying:

“I am Christ.”

When the old man saw him, he closed his eyes.

The devil said to him:

“I am Christ. Why have you closed your eyes?”

The old man answered:

“I do not wish to see Christ here, but in that life.”

When the devil heard this, he disappeared.

[Col. 0966A]

### 71.

When the demons wished to deceive another old man, they said to him:

“Do you wish to see Christ?”

He said:

“Anathema to you and to the one of whom you speak! I believe my Christ, who says: ‘If anyone says to you, “Behold, here is Christ,” or, “There he is,” do not believe it.’”

After he had said this, they immediately disappeared (Matt. 24).

### 72.

They related of another old man that he persevered in fasting for seventy weeks, eating once a week. He asked God about a certain saying from the Holy Scriptures, but God did not reveal it to him.

He therefore said to himself:

“Behold, I have undertaken such labor and have achieved nothing. I will go to my brother and ask him.”

When he had gone out and closed his door to depart, an angel of the Lord was sent to him, saying:

“The seventy weeks during which you fasted did not bring you near to God. But now, when you have humbled yourself so as to go to your brother, I have been sent to disclose the saying to you.”

After revealing to him what he had asked about, the angel departed from him.

### 73.

A certain old man said (Ruffin., book III, no. 73):

“If someone, with humility and the fear of God, enjoins his brother to do something, the very word that goes forth for God’s sake causes that brother to become subject to him and to fulfill what has been commanded.

“But if someone wishes to command his brother and does not do so according to the fear of God, but as though by authority, wishing to establish his power over him, God, who sees the hidden things of the heart, does not permit the other to hear or do what is commanded.

“For it is clear which work is done according to God, and it is likewise clear which is enjoined according to one’s own will or authority. What is from God is commanded with humility and entreaty; what is from authority is commanded with fury and disturbance, as something that comes from the evil one.”

### 74.

The old man said:

“I would rather be defeated with humility than conquer with pride.”

### 75.

The old man said:

“Do not condemn the one who stands before you, because you do not know whether the Spirit of God is in you or in him. By ‘the one who stands before you’ I mean the person who is your servant.”

### 76.

A brother asked the old man:

“If I live with other brothers and see something improper, do you wish me to speak?”

The old man said to him:

“If there are some older than you or your equals, you will have greater rest by remaining silent. For by making yourself lesser in this matter, you will also make yourself secure.”

The brother said to him:

“What then shall I do, Father? The spirit troubles me.”

The old man said:

“If you are troubled, admonish them once, humbly. But if they do not obey you, leave your trouble before God, and he himself will comfort you. For this is what it means for the worshiper of God to cast himself before God and to abandon his own wishes.

“Take care that your concern be according to God. Nevertheless, as I see it, it is good to remain silent; for silence is humility for you.”

### 77.

A brother asked the old man:

“What is a person’s progress?”

The old man answered:

“A person’s progress is humility. For in whatever measure someone inclines toward humility, in that measure he will be raised toward progress” (Ruff., book III, no. 171; Pasch., chap. 15, no. 5).

### 78.

A certain old man said:

“If someone says, ‘Forgive me,’ humbling himself, he burns the demons who tempt him.”

### 79.

The old man said:

“If you acquire silence, do not regard it within yourself as some virtue, even if you have attained it. Rather, say: ‘I am unworthy to speak.’”

### 80.

A certain old man said:

“Unless the baker blindfolded the eyes of the animal going around the mill, the animal would turn around and eat its own labor” (Ruff., book III, no. 128; Pasch., chap. 15, no. 1). “So we too receive a veil according to God’s dispensation, lest we see the good things we accomplish and, perhaps, bless ourselves, thereby losing our reward.

“For this reason we are sometimes allowed, at intervals, to take up filthy thoughts, so that when we look upon those same thoughts, we may condemn ourselves by our own judgment. Those very thoughts are a veil over the small good work itself. When a person accuses himself, he does not lose his reward.”

### 81.

A certain old man said:

“I would rather be taught than teach.”

He also said:

“Do not teach before the proper time; otherwise you will be diminished in understanding throughout the whole time of your life.”

### 82.

A certain old man was asked:

“What is humility?”

He answered:

“Humility is a great and divine work. The way of humility is this: bodily labors must be undertaken; a person must reckon himself among sinners; and he must place himself subject to everyone.”

The brother said:

“What does it mean to be subject to everyone?”

The old man answered:

“It means not to pay attention to the sins of others, but always to look at one’s own and to pray to God without ceasing.”

### 83.

A certain brother asked the old man:

“Tell me one thing which I may keep and by which I may live.”

The old man said to him:

“If you can endure and bear insult, that is a great thing, above all the virtues” (Ruff., book III, no. 85).

### 84.

The old man said:

“Whoever patiently bears contempt, injury, and loss can be saved.”

### 85.

The old man said to someone:

“Do not cultivate familiarity with the abbot, nor attach yourself to him frequently. For from this you will acquire confidence, and you will begin to desire to hold the primacy yourself.”

### 86.

A certain brother was in the assembly, and he took upon himself every burden that fell upon the brothers, even to the point of accusing himself of fornication (Ruff., book III, no. 29, under the name Eulalius).

Some of the brothers, however, unaware of his actions, began to murmur against him, saying:

“How many evils this man commits, and he does not even work!”

The abbot, knowing what he was doing, said to the brothers:

“I would rather have one mat of his with humility than all your mats with pride.”

To demonstrate, by God’s judgment, what kind of brother he was, he brought all the things that those brothers had made, as well as the mat of the man about whom they complained. He lit a fire and threw everything into it.

All their works were consumed, but that brother’s mat remained unharmed.

When the brothers saw this, they were afraid and did penance before him, thereafter regarding him as a father.

### 87.

The old man was asked how certain people said that they saw the appearance of angels. He answered:

“Blessed is the one who always sees his own sin.”

### 88.

A certain brother was grieved against another brother. When the latter heard this, he came to make amends to him. But the other did not open the door of his cell to him.

The man therefore went to a certain old man and told him the matter. The old man said to him:

“See to it that you do not regard your cause as just in your own heart, as though you were going to accuse your brother, reproach him, and justify yourself—and that, because of this, God has not touched his heart so that he would open the door to you.

“Nevertheless, this is what I tell you: even if he has sinned against you, put it in your heart that you have sinned against him. Justify your brother, and then God will grant his heart to be reconciled with you.”

He told him an example of this kind:

“There were two devout laymen who were conversing with each other. They went out and became monks. In their zeal for the Gospel saying—but without understanding—they castrated themselves, supposedly for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.

“When the archbishop heard of it, he excommunicated them. But since they thought they had acted well, they became angry with him, saying:

“‘We castrated ourselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, and he has excommunicated us? Let us go and appeal against him to the archbishop of Jerusalem.’

“They went and reported everything to him. The archbishop of Jerusalem said to them:

“‘I also excommunicate you.’

“Again grieved, they went to Antioch to the archbishop and told him everything that had happened to them. He likewise excommunicated them.

“They said to one another:

“‘Let us go to Rome, to the patriarch, and he will avenge us against all these men.’

“They went to the supreme archbishop of the city of Rome and reported to him what the aforementioned archbishops had done to them, saying:

“‘We have come to you because you are the head of all.’

“He too said to them:

“‘I excommunicate you, and you are separated.’

“Then, being excommunicated, they lost all reason and said to themselves:

“‘These bishops defer to and agree with one another, which is why they assemble in synods. But let us go to that holy man of God, Bishop Epiphanius of Cyprus, because he is a prophet and does not show partiality to anyone.’

“When they were approaching his city, it was revealed to him concerning them. He sent someone to meet them and said:

“‘Do not enter this city.’

“Then, coming to their senses, they said:

“‘In truth, we are guilty. Why then do we justify ourselves? Granted that they excommunicated us unjustly—but is this prophet also unjust? For behold, God has revealed to him what concerns us.’

“They severely reproached themselves for the fault they had committed.

“When the one who knows hearts saw that they had truly made themselves guilty, he revealed this to Bishop Epiphanius. The bishop voluntarily sent for them and brought them in, consoled them, and received them into communion.

“He wrote about them to the archbishop of Alexandria, saying:

“‘Receive your sons, because they have truly repented.’

“The old man who had related this example added:

“‘This is the healing of a person, and this is what God desires: that a person cast his own fault before God.’”

When the brother heard this, he acted according to the old man’s word. He went and knocked at his brother’s door. As soon as the other perceived him, he first repented inwardly before him; then he immediately opened the door, and they kissed one another sincerely. Great peace was established between them.

### 89.

Two monks, who were also brothers by birth, lived together, but the devil wished to separate them from one another (Ruff., book III, no. 18).

One day the younger brother lit a lamp and placed it on a lampstand. The demon performed its work and overturned the lampstand. Because of this, the older brother struck him angrily.

The younger brother repented and said to him:

“Have patience with me, brother, and I will light it again.”

And behold, the power of the Lord came and tormented that demon until morning.

The demon reported to its chief what had happened. A pagan priest heard what the demon had reported, went out, and became a monk. From the beginning of his conversion he maintained humility, saying:

“Humility dissolves all the power of the enemy, as I heard them saying among themselves: ‘When we trouble the monks, one of them turns, repents, and destroys all our power.’”

## THE SIXTEENTH BOOKLET

### On Patience

### 1.

The brothers said of Abba Gelasius that he possessed a parchment Codex worth eighteen solidi (Ruff., book III, no. 30, under the name Anastasius). It contained the entire Old and New Testament, and the Codex itself was kept in the church so that any of the brothers who wished could read it.

A visiting brother arrived and came to the old man. When he saw the Codex, he coveted it, stole it, and went away. The old man did not pursue him in order to seize him, since he understood what he had done.

The brother went into the city and looked for someone to whom he could sell it. When he found a buyer, he began asking sixteen solidi for it. The man who wished to purchase it said:

“First give it to me so that I may show it to someone; then I will give you its price.”

The seller gave him the Codex to show. The man who wished to buy it took it to Abba Gelasius, to determine whether it was a good Codex and whether it was worth that much. He also told him the price that the seller was asking.

The old man said:

“Buy it, because it is a good Codex and is worth the price he told you.”

The man returned to the seller and spoke differently, not as he had heard from the old man. He said:

“Behold, I showed it to Abba Gelasius, and he told me that it was expensive and not worth as much as you said.”

When the seller heard this, he said to him:

“Did the old man tell you nothing else?”

He answered:

“Nothing.”

Then the seller said:

“I no longer wish to sell this Codex.”

Stricken with remorse, he came to the old man, repenting and asking him to take back the Codex. But the old man did not wish to receive it.

Then the brother said to him:

“If you do not receive it, I cannot be at peace.”

The old man said to him:

“If you cannot be at peace unless I receive it, behold, I receive it.”

That brother remained with him until his death, advancing through the patience of the old man.

### 2.

Once an assembly was held at Kellia on a certain matter. A certain Abba Evagrius spoke, and the priest of the monasteries said to him:

“We know, Abba Evagrius, that if you were in your homeland, you might perhaps be a bishop or the head of many people. But now here you are like a stranger.”

Stricken with remorse, he did not answer with agitation. He merely shook his head, looked at the ground, wrote with his finger, and said to them:

“Truly, Fathers, it is so. Nevertheless, I have spoken once; in the Scriptures I will add nothing a second time.”

### 3.

Once Abba John the Short was sitting before the church. The brothers surrounded him, each asking him about his thoughts (Ruff., book III, no. 92).

A certain old man, seeing this, was inflamed with envy and said to him:

“Your *suriscula* [perhaps ‘little vessel’], Abba John, is full of poison.”

Abba John answered him:

“So it is, Abba. You said this because you see only what is outside. But if you saw what is within, what would you say?”

### 4.

They said of John the Younger of the Thebaid, who was a disciple of Abba Ammonas, that he served the old man during his illness for twelve years (Ruff., book III, no. 155; Pasc., chap. 19, no. 2). Afterward he sat upon a mat, while the old man was distressed on his behalf.

Although he had labored greatly with him, the old man never said to him, “Be well.” When he was now near death, and the old men of the place were sitting around, he took John’s hand and said:

“Be well, be well, be well.”

Then he handed him over to the old men, saying:

“This is an angel, not a human being.”

### 5.

They said of Abba Isidore, who was a presbyter in Scetis, that if someone had a sick, fainthearted, or abusive brother and wished to drive him away, he would say:

“Bring him to me.”

He would take hold of him and, by his patience, heal that brother’s spirit.

[Col. 0970D]

### 6.

Abba Macarius, who was in Egypt (Ruff., book III, no. 73; Pasch., chap. 3, no. 1), found a man who had brought an animal and was stealing what the old man possessed. Macarius himself stood beside the thief as though a stranger and helped him load the goods onto the animal. With complete calm he saw him off, saying to himself:

“We brought nothing into this world, but the Lord gave it. As he himself willed, so it came to pass. Blessed is the Lord in all things” (1 Tim. 6).

### 7.

Once, when an assembly of the brothers had been held in Scetis, the old men wished to test Abba Moses. They despised him, saying:

“Why has this Ethiopian come among us?”

When he heard this, he remained silent. After the assembly had been dismissed, those who had treated him insultingly said to him:

“Are you not even disturbed now?”

He answered:

“I was disturbed, and I did not speak” (Ps. 67).

### 8.
