Paysius, the brother of Abba Pastor, had an attachment to a certain monk from his cell. Abba Pastor did not approve of this. He therefore arose, fled to Abba Ammonas, and said to him:

“My brother Paysius has an attachment to certain people, and I do not willingly endure this.”

Abba Ammonas said to him:

“Abba Pastor, are you still alive? Go to your cell and put it in your heart that you have already spent a year in the tomb.”

### 9.

Abba Pastor said:

“Every labor that befalls you will be overcome by silence.”

10. A certain brother, having been injured by another brother, came to Abba Sisoi the Theban and said to him: “I have been injured by a certain brother, and I wish to avenge myself” (Ruf., book III, no. 77; Pasch., chapter 7, no. 1). But the old man entreated him, saying: “Do not, my son; rather leave vengeance to God.” He replied: “I will not rest until I have avenged myself.” The old man said: “Let us pray, brother.” Then the old man rose and said: “God, we no longer need You to concern Yourself with us, since we ourselves carry out our own vengeance.” When the brother heard this, he fell at the old man’s feet, saying: “I will no longer contend with that brother; but I beg you, forgive me.”

11. A certain man, seeing a religious carrying a dead man on a bed, said to him: “Are you carrying the dead? Go, carry the living.”

12. They told of a certain monk that the more anyone attacked or provoked him with insults (Ruf., [Col. 0971C] book III, no. 80; Pasch., chapter 7, no. 4), the more he ran to meet that person, saying: “Such men become a means of correction for those who are earnest in their way of life. For those who praise them lead their souls still further astray.” For it is written: “Those who call you blessed lead you astray” (Isaiah 3).

13. Once robbers came to the monastery of an old man (Prat. spirit. chapter 212), and said to him: “We have come to take away everything that is in your cell.” He replied: “As much as seems good to you, my sons, take it.” So they took whatever they found in the cell and departed. But they forgot there a small sack that had been hidden in the cell. The old man picked it up and followed after them, shouting and saying: “My sons, take what you forgot in the cell.” They, astonished at the old man’s patience, brought everything back into his cell and all repented, saying to one another: “This truly is a man of God.”

14. Some brothers came to a certain holy old man who was sitting in a desert place, and outside, beyond the monastery, they found a boy pasturing animals and saying things that were improper (Ruf., book III, no. 91). After they had seen the old man, disclosed their thoughts to him, and felt that they had profited from his answer, they said to him: “Abba, how can you tolerate having these boys with you, and not command them not to [Col. 0990D] quarrel [Note: “Ne strinientur.” Thus in the Audomarensis manuscript. The first edition has “ne hystrientur”; the Cologne edition, “ne histrientur”; the Paris edition, “ne struentur.” Some editions have “ut constringantur” [“that they be restrained”]. In Rufinus, book III, no. 91, where the same account is related, the reading is “vociferentur” [“shout at one another”]. In Flemish, strijen means “to contend,” as in French estriver, “to quarrel.” I do not know whether there is an allusion to this Latin word. See the Onomasticon.]?” The old man said: “Believe me, brothers, I have had days when I wanted to command them, and I rebuked myself, saying: ‘If I cannot bear this small thing, how shall I be able to bear a greater temptation, should God allow one to come upon me?’ For this reason I say nothing to them, so that I may acquire the habit of bearing whatever comes upon me.”

15. They told of a certain old man who had a little boy living with him. Once, seeing him do something that was not good for him, he said to him: “Do not do this.” But the boy did not obey him. When the old man saw this, he dismissed concern for him from his thoughts, casting his own judgment upon him. The boy, however, shut the door of the cell in which the bread was kept for three days, leaving the old man fasting; and the old man did not say to him: “Where are you?” or “What are you doing outside?” The old man had a neighbor. When the neighbor realized that the boy was taking so long, he made a little stew, gave it to him through the wall, and urged him to taste it. He said to the old man: “Why is that brother delaying outside?” The old man replied: “When he has time, he will return.”

16. Some people related that certain philosophers once wanted to test the monks. One monk came by, dressed in a robe and well clothed (Ruf., book II, no. 74; Pasch., chapter 3, no. 2). The philosophers said to him: “You—come here.” But he became indignant and attacked them with insults. Another monk then passed by, a great monk, of peasant birth. They said to him as well: “You, bad old monk, come here.” He came running. They began slapping him, but he turned the other cheek toward them. At once the philosophers rose and venerated him, saying: “Truly, behold a monk.” They made him sit in their midst and questioned him, saying: “What is it that you do more than we do in this solitude? You fast, and we fast; you discipline your bodies, and we discipline ours; and whatever else you do, we also do. What more, then, do you do as you sit in the desert?” The old man answered them: “We place our hope in the grace of God, and we guard our minds.” They said to him: “We cannot guard this.” And, being edified, they dismissed him.

17. A certain old man had a tested disciple, whom one day, being distressed, he drove outside. The disciple sat waiting outside. When the old man opened the door, he found him there and repented before him, saying: “You are my father, because your humility and patience have conquered the faintheartedness of my spirit. Come inside; from now on you are the old man and the father, while I am the young man and the disciple, because by your conduct you have surpassed my old age.”

18. One of the old men said that he had heard certain holy men say that the young are those who provide guidance to the old in this life. They related the following: There was a drunken old man who made one mat each day, sold it in the neighboring village, and drank whatever he received for its price. Then a certain brother came to him and stayed with him. He too made one mat. The old man would take it and sell it, spending the price of both mats on wine, while bringing that brother only a little bread toward evening. He did this continually for three years, and the brother said nothing.

Afterward the brother said to himself: “Look, I am naked, and I eat bread in poverty. I will rise and leave this place.” Again he thought to himself, saying: “Where shall I go? I will remain here, for I remain in this common life for God’s sake.” Immediately an angel of the Lord appeared to him, saying: “Do not leave anywhere; for tomorrow we will come to you.”

That same day the brother urged the old man, saying: “Do not leave this place for anywhere, because my people will come today to take me away.” When the hour came at which the old man usually went down to the village, he said to the brother: “They will not come today, my son; it is already late.” But the brother insisted in every way that they would come. While he was speaking with him, he fell asleep in peace. The old man wept, saying: “Alas for me, my son, for I have lived many years in negligence, while you have saved your soul through patience in a short time.” From that day the old man became sober and approved.

19. They told of a certain brother who lived near a great old man that he would enter and seize whatever the old man had in his cell (Ruf., book III, no. 74; Pasch., chapter 3, no. 2). The old man saw him, but did not rebuke him; instead, he forced himself to work more with his hands than usual, saying: “I believe this brother is in need of work.” He imposed on himself more labor than usual and tightened his stomach so that he would eat his bread with deprivation.

When that old man began to die, the brothers surrounded him. Looking toward the man who had stolen from him, he said: “Come close to me.” He took and kissed his hands, saying: “I thank these hands, brother, because because of them I am going into the kingdom of heaven.” The other, pierced with remorse and repenting, himself became an approved monk, taking an example from the deeds of that great old man [Note: In the printed editions this was followed by no. 20, concerning Thais the prostitute; but you will find it in Book I among the Lives.].

## BOOK SEVENTEEN. On Charity

1. Abba Antony said: “I no longer fear God, but love Him, because love has driven out fear” (1 John 4).

2. He said again: “Life and death are near at hand. For if we gain our brother, we shall gain God; but if we scandalize our brother, we sin against Christ.”

3. Abba Ammon of Nitria came to Abba Antony and said to him: “I see that I endure greater labor than you, and how is it that your great name among people is greater than mine?” Abba Antony said to him: “Because I love God more than you do.”

4. Once Abba Hilarion came from Palestine to Abba Antony on the mountain, and Abba Antony said to him: “You have come well, Lucifer, who rises in the morning.” Abba Hilarion said: “Peace be with you, pillar of light, who sustain the inhabited world.”

5. Abba Mark said to Abba Arsenius: “Why do you flee from us?” The old man said to him: “God knows that I love you; but I cannot be with God and with human beings. For the thousands and thousands of the higher virtues have one will, while human beings have many wills. Therefore I cannot leave God and come to be with human beings.”

6. Abba Agathon said: “I have never, according to my own will, gone to sleep while retaining resentment in my heart against anyone, nor have I allowed another who had anything against me to go to sleep” (Ruf., book III, no. 95).

7. Once, as Abba John of Scetis was going up with some other brothers, the brother who was guiding them lost the way; for it was night. The brothers said to Abba John: “What shall we do, abba? This brother has lost the road; perhaps we shall die while wandering.” The old man said to them: “If we say anything to him, he will be saddened. But look: I will pretend to be weak, and say that I cannot walk, and I will lie here until morning.” And they did so. The others also said: “We will not go either, but will sit with you.” And they sat until morning, so as not to rebuke that brother.

8. There was a certain old man in Egypt, before Abba Pastor came there. That old man had a reputation among people and much honor (Ruf., book III, no. 95). When Abba Pastor came up from Scetis with his companions, they left that old man and went to Abba Pastor. The old man, becoming envious, spoke badly about them.

When Pastor heard this, he was saddened and said to his brothers: “What shall we do about this great old man? People have left him in distress and have turned their attention to us, who are nothing. How, then, can we heal him?” He said to them: “Prepare something to eat, take a small vessel of wine, and let us go to him and eat together. Perhaps by this means we can heal his spirit.”

So they took the food they had prepared and went to him. When they knocked at the door, his disciple answered, saying: “Who are you?” They said: “Tell the abba that Pastor is here and desires to receive a blessing from you.” His disciple announced this to him. He sent word, saying: “Go away, for I have no time.”

But they persisted in the heat, saying: “We will not leave until we have deserved the old man’s blessing.” When the old man saw their persistence and humility, he was pierced with remorse and opened to them. They entered and ate with him. As they were eating, the old man said: “In truth I tell you, I heard less of you than what is actually the case; for what I see in your conduct is a hundred times greater.” From that day he became their friend.

9. Abba Pastor said: “Strive, according to your strength, never to do harm to anyone at all, and keep your heart pure toward every person.”

10. He said again: “There is nothing greater than love, even to the point that someone lays down his life for his neighbor. For if someone hears a distressing word, and although he himself could do the same, struggles and endures it without causing distress in return; or if, having been injured in some matter, he bears it patiently without repaying the one who distressed and injured him—such a person lays down his life for his neighbor” (Ruf., book II, no. 201; Pasch., chapter 37, no. 3; Appendix to Martin, no. 14).

11. Once Abba Pambo was traveling with some brothers in the regions of Egypt. Seeing certain laypeople sitting there, he said to them: “Rise, greet, and kiss the monks, so that you may be blessed; for they frequently speak with God, and their mouths are holy” (Ruf., book III, no. 164).

12. They told of Abba Paphnutius that he did not readily drink wine (Ruf., book III, no. 151). Once, while traveling, he came upon a band of robbers and found them drinking. The leader of the robbers recognized him and knew that he did not drink wine. Seeing him exhausted from great labor, he filled a cup with wine, held a drawn sword in his other hand, and said to the old man: “If you do not drink, I will kill you.”

The old man, knowing that he wished to carry out God’s commandment, and wishing to gain him, accepted the cup and drank. The robber chief repented before him, saying: “Forgive me, abba, because I have distressed you.” The old man said to him: “I believe in my God that through this cup He will show you mercy both in this age and in the age to come.” The robber chief replied: “And I believe in God that from now on I will do no one any harm.” Thus the old man won over their entire company of robbers by surrendering himself to their will for God’s sake.

13. Abba Hyperichius said: “Rescue your neighbor from sins, insofar as you have the strength, without reproach, because God does not reject those who turn back to Him. Let no word of malice or wickedness dwell in your heart against your brother, so that you may be able to say: ‘Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors’” (Matthew 6).

14. There were two brothers in the Cells. One of them was an old man, and he urged the younger one, saying: “Let us remain together, brother.” The other said to him: “I am a sinner, and I cannot remain with you, abba” (Ruf., book III, no. 152). But the old man urged him, saying: “We can indeed.”

The old man was pure and did not want to hear that a monk harbored fornication in his thoughts. The brother said to him: “Give me one week, and we will speak again.” The old man came. The younger man, wishing to test him, said: “I have fallen into a great temptation this week, abba. While going into the village on some service, I encountered a woman.”

The old man said to him: “Is there repentance?” The brother said: “Yes.” The old man replied: “I will bear half of this sin with you.” Then the brother said: “Now I know that we can remain together.” And they remained together until their death.

15. One of the Fathers said: “If someone asks you for something and you are compelled to give it to him, let the disposition of your heart accord with what is given, as it is written: ‘If anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two’” (Matthew 5). This means that if someone asks you for something, you should give it willingly and wholeheartedly.

16. They told of a certain brother that, after making baskets and putting handles on them (Ruf., book III, no. 147), he also heard his neighboring monk say: “What shall I do? The market is near, and I have no handles to put on my baskets.” The other removed the handles he had put on his own baskets and brought them to that neighboring brother, saying: “Look, I have these extra; take them and put them on your baskets.” He completed the work his brother needed to finish, but left his own work incomplete.

17. They told of a certain old man in Scetis that he fell ill and wanted to eat a little fresh bread. When one of the brothers who practiced the ascetic life heard this, he took his melote, put dry bread into it, and, going to Egypt, exchanged it for fresh bread and brought it to the old man.

When the brothers saw those fresh loaves, they were amazed. But the old man refused to taste them, saying: “It is the blood of a brother.” The old men urged him, saying: “For God’s sake, eat, so that this brother’s sacrifice may not be in vain.” Thus, being urged, he ate.

18. A brother asked a certain old man: “There are two brothers. One remains in his cell, prolonging a six-day fast and imposing much labor on himself; the other serves the sick. Whose work is more acceptable to God?” The old man answered him: “Even if that brother who fasts for six days were to hang himself by his nostrils, he could not be equal to the one who serves the sick.”

19. Someone asked a certain old man: “How is it that some people now labor in the monastic life and do not receive grace as the ancients did?” (Ruf., book III, no. 181; Pasch., chapter 28, no. 4). The old man said to him: “Because then there was love, and each person lifted his neighbor upward. Now, however, as love has grown cold, each person drags his neighbor downward; and for this reason we do not deserve to receive grace.”

20. Once three brothers went to harvest and undertook a certain area of sixty measures to reap (Appendix to Martin, no. 9). On the very first day one of them began to fall ill and returned to his cell. The two who remained said one to the other: “Look, brother, you see that our brother has fallen ill. Let us each force ourselves a little, you in your spirit and I in mine, and let us trust in God, because through his prayer we two will complete the work and reap his portion.”

When they had finished harvesting the entire area they had undertaken, they came to receive their wages. They called that brother, saying: “Come, brother, receive your labor.” He said to them: “What labor should I receive, since I did not reap?” They replied: “The harvest was completed through prayers. Come, therefore, and receive your wages.”

After much dispute had arisen among them about this—the brother saying, “I will not accept them, since I did not labor,” while the others refused to yield unless he also received his share—they went to the judgment of a great old man.

That brother said to him: “The three of us went to reap in a field for wages. When we came to the place we were to harvest, I fell ill on the very first day and returned to my cell, unable to reap with them even for one day. Now these men compel me, saying: ‘Brother, come and receive wages where you did not labor.’”

The other brothers also said: “In truth, we went to reap and undertook an area of sixty measures. If all three of us had been present, we could scarcely have completed it with great labor. Through this brother’s prayers, however, we two reaped the field more quickly than three could have done, and we say to him: ‘Come, receive your wages.’ But he does not wish to.”

When the old man heard this, he marveled and said to one of his monks: “Strike the signal [Note: “Strike the signal.” So also in John below, Book III, no. 2, “striking it.” In former times they struck pieces of wood to produce a sound and summon the brothers. See the Onomasticon.] in the brothers’ cell, so that they may all gather here.”

When they had come, he said to them: “Come, brothers, and hear a just judgment today.” The old man told them everything and adjudged that brother to receive his wages and to do with those wages whatever he wished. The brother departed saddened and weeping, as though he had suffered an injustice.

21. A certain old man said: “Our Fathers had the custom of coming to the cells of new brothers who wished to live as solitaries. They visited them so that none of them, if tempted by demons, would be harmed by his own thoughts. If one of them was found to be injured, they brought him to the church. A basin of water was set out, and prayer was made for the one who was troubled by temptations. All the brothers washed their hands in the basin, and that water was poured over the brother who was being tempted; and thus the brother was immediately cleansed.”

[Col. 0977C] 22. Two old men had lived together for many years and had never quarreled with each other (Ruf., book III, no. 96). One said to the other: “Let us also have one quarrel, as human beings do.” The other replied: “I do not know how a quarrel is made.” He said: “Look, I will place a brick in the middle, and I will say: ‘This is mine.’ You say: ‘No, it is mine.’ Let that be the beginning of the quarrel.”

So they placed a potsherd between them, and one of them said: “This is mine.” The other said: “No, it is mine.” The first replied: “Yes, it is yours; take it and go.” And they departed, unable to quarrel with one another.

23. A certain brother asked an old man: “If I see a brother of whom I have heard some fault, I cannot persuade myself to bring him into my cell. But if I see a good brother, I gladly receive him.” The old man said to him: “If you do good to a good brother, it is little; bestow twice as much on the other, for he is the one who is sick.”

24. A certain old man said: “I have never desired a work that would benefit me and harm my brother, holding this hope: that my brother’s gain is a work of fruitfulness for me.”

25. A certain brother was the servant of a Father. It happened that a wound developed on the old man’s body, and much pus flowed from it with a foul odor. His thought said to the brother who served him: “Leave this place, because you cannot endure the stench of this rottenness.”

But the brother, in order to restrain such a thought, took a vessel and washed the old man’s wound, collecting that very water in the vessel. Whenever he became thirsty, he drank from it. His thought again began to trouble him, saying: “If you do not wish to flee, at least do not drink this stench.”

But the brother struggled and bore it patiently, drinking the water with which that wound had been washed. As he continued serving the old man in this way, God saw the love expressed in his labor, turned that water from the wound into the purest water, and healed the old man with an invisible medicine.

## BOOK EIGHTEEN. On Foreknowledge, or Contemplation

1. A brother went to the cell of Abba Arsenius in Scetis and looked through the window. He saw the old man entirely like fire; that brother was worthy to behold such things. When he knocked, the old man came out, saw that brother amazed, and said to him: “Have you been knocking here for a long time? Did you perhaps see something?” He answered: “No.” The old man spoke with him and then dismissed him.

2. Abba Daniel, who was a disciple of Abba Arsenius, said (Ruf., book III, no. 38) that Abba Arsenius had related the following to him, speaking as though of someone else—although I think it was said of him.

As a certain old man sat in his cell, a voice came to him saying: “Come, I will show you the works of human beings.” He rose, went out, and was led to a certain place. He showed him an Ethiopian cutting wood, making a large bundle, and trying to carry it, but being unable to do so. Instead of removing some of the bundle, he went back again, cut wood, and added it to the bundle. He did this for a long time.

Going a little farther, he showed him another man standing beside a lake. That man filled a vessel with water and poured it from the vessel into a leaky cistern, which again emptied that very water back into the lake.

He said to him again: “Come, I will show you something else.” And behold, he saw a temple and two men sitting on horses, carrying a single crossbeam, one opposite the other. They wanted to enter the temple through the door, but could not because of the beam they carried crosswise. Since they did not bend down, one behind the other, so that the beam could be made straight, they remained outside the temple door.

When he asked what this meant, the other answered him: “These are those who carry what resembles the yoke of righteousness with pride, and have not humbled themselves so as to correct themselves and walk humbly on the way of Christ. Therefore they remain outside the kingdom of God.

“The one who cuts wood is a man with many sins who does not repent of them, does not remove any of his sins, but adds iniquities upon his iniquities.

“The one who fills the cistern with water is a man who indeed performs good works, but because he also has evil things mixed in with them, he loses even his good works. Therefore every person must be sober in considering his works, lest he seem to endure labors in vain.”

3. Abba Daniel related again, saying: “Our Father Abba Arsenius spoke of a certain old man who was great in this life but simple in faith. Because he was unlearned, he went astray and said that, by nature, the body of Christ was not the bread that we receive, but that it was its figure.

“When two old men heard him saying this, and knew that his life and conduct were exemplary, they thought that he was saying it innocently and simply. They came to him and said: ‘Abba, we have heard the statement of a certain unbeliever who says that the bread we receive is not by nature the body of Christ, but its figure.’

“The old man said to them: ‘I am the one who said this.’

“They entreated him, saying: ‘Do not hold this view, abba, but hold what the catholic Church has handed down. We believe that the bread itself is the body of Christ, and that the cup itself is the blood of Christ according to truth and not according to figure. Just as in the beginning, taking dust from the earth, He fashioned a human being in His own image—and no one can say that it was not the image of God, although it is incomprehensible—so also with the bread of which He said, “This is my body”: we believe that it is truly the body of Christ.’

“The old man said to them: ‘Unless I know this in reality, your answer does not satisfy me.’

“They said to him: ‘Let us entreat God during this week concerning this mystery, and we believe that God will reveal it to us.’

“The old man gladly accepted this proposal and entreated God, saying: ‘Lord, if You know that I am unbelieving concerning this matter not through malice but through ignorance and error, reveal to me, Lord Jesus Christ, what is true.’

“The old men also departed to their cell and entreated Him, saying: ‘Lord Jesus Christ, reveal this mystery to the old man, so that he may believe and not lose the fruit of his labor.’

“God heard both parties. When the week was complete, they came to church on the Lord’s Day. The three of them alone sat on a seat of rushes bound together like a bundle, and the old man sat in the middle.

“The eyes of their understanding were opened. When the breads were placed on the altar, only those three saw what appeared to them to be a little child lying upon the altar. When the priest stretched out his hands to break the bread, an angel of the Lord descended from heaven with a knife in his hand and cut the little child, while catching his blood in the cup. As the priest broke the bread into small portions, the angel likewise cut the child’s limbs into small portions.

“When the old man came forward to receive Holy Communion, flesh covered with blood was given to him alone. When he saw this, he was terrified and cried out, saying: ‘I believe, Lord, that the bread placed upon the altar is Your body, and that the cup is Your blood.’

“Immediately that portion in his hand became bread, according to the mystery, and he took it into his mouth, giving thanks to God.

“The old men said to him: ‘God knows human nature: it cannot eat raw flesh. Therefore He transforms His body into bread and His blood into wine for those who receive them in faith.’

“They gave thanks to God for that old man, because God had not allowed his labors to perish, and they returned joyfully to their cells.

4. The same Abba Daniel again related the story of another great old man who lived in the lower regions of Egypt. Because of his simplicity, he said that Melchizedek himself was the Son of God. This was reported to Cyril, of holy memory, archbishop of Alexandria, and he sent for him.

Knowing that the old man was a visionary, and that whatever he asked of God was revealed to him, and knowing also that he said this simply, Cyril used the following approach. He said: “Abba, I beg you, for I have this thought: that Melchizedek himself is the Son of God. But another thought tells me that he is not, but was a human being and a high priest of God. Since I am uncertain about this, I have sent for you so that you may entreat God to deem it worthy to reveal to you what the truth is in this matter.”

The old man, relying on his manner of life, confidently said: “Give me three days’ time. I will entreat God about this matter and report to you what is revealed to me.”

He entered his cell and entreated God concerning this statement. After three days he came and said to Cyril, of holy memory: “Melchizedek was a human being.”

The archbishop replied: “How has this become certain to you, abba?”

He said: “God showed me all the patriarchs, so that each of them passed before me, from Adam up to Melchizedek. The angel sitting beside me said: ‘Behold, this is Melchizedek.’ Therefore, archbishop, be certain that this is so.”

The old man departed and began proclaiming everywhere that Melchizedek was a human being. Cyril, of holy memory, greatly rejoiced.

5. Ephraem, of holy memory, was still a boy when he saw a dream or revelation: a vine had been born upon his tongue, grown, and filled the whole earth with exceedingly abundant fruit. All the birds of heaven came and ate from the fruit of that vine; and the more they ate, the more abundantly it was filled with fruit (above, in The Life of Ephraem, chapter 1).

6. Again, one of the saints saw in a dream an angelic order descending from heaven (above, in The Life of Ephraem, chapter 3), according to God’s command, carrying in its hand a book—that is, a volume written inside and out. They said to one another: “To whom should this be entrusted?” Some named one person, others another. They answered and said: “Truly, both of those whom you name are holy and righteous; nevertheless, this cannot be entrusted to them.”

After naming many other saints, they said: “This can be entrusted to no one other than Ephraem.” The old man to whom this appeared in a dream saw that they gave that volume to Ephraem.

In the morning, when he arose, he heard Ephraem teaching, as though a fountain were bubbling forth from his mouth. The old man who had seen the dream recognized that what came from Ephraem’s lips was the work of the Holy Spirit.

7. They told of Abba Zeno that, while he was living in Scetis, he went out at night from his cell, as though going to the marsh (Col. 0981A; Ruf., book III, no. 210). After losing his way, he spent three days and three nights walking and laboring. When his strength failed, he fell half-dead.

And behold, a little boy stood before him, holding bread and a small flask of water, and said to him: “Rise and eat.” He rose and prayed, thinking that it was a phantom. The boy answered him: “You have done well.” He prayed a second time, and a third time. The boy said to him: “You have done well.”

He rose, took the food, and ate. Afterward the boy said to him: “You have walked as far as you are from your cell; but rise and follow me.” Immediately he found himself in his cell.

The old man said to him: “Come inside and give us a prayer.” When the old man had entered, the boy suddenly disappeared.

8. Abba John said: “One of the old men saw, in a state of ecstasy, three monks standing beyond the sea. A voice came to them from the opposite shore, saying: ‘Take fiery wings and come to me.’

“Two of them took wings and flew to the other shore, from which the voice had come. The third remained behind, weeping and crying out loudly. Later, wings were given to him, but they were not fiery; they were weak and feeble, so that he came there only with great labor, sinking down and rising again, and suffering greatly.

“So it is with this generation: even if it receives wings, they are not fiery; it can scarcely receive wings that are weak and feeble.”

9. Abba Macarius lived in a very remote place; he was the sole solitary there (Ruf., book III, no. 61; Pasch., chapter 1, no. 8). Below it was another desert, in which very many brothers lived. The old man was watching the road, and he saw Satan coming in the guise of a man, so as to pass by his cell. He appeared to be wearing a linen tunic, completely worn out and full of holes, and from all its openings little flasks hung down. The old man said to him: “Ho there, chief! Where are you going?” He replied: “I am going to remind the brothers.” The old man said to him: “What are these flasks for?” He replied: “I am carrying tastes for the brothers.” The old man said to him: “And do you carry all of them together with the taste?” He replied: “Yes. If one does not please someone, I will offer another; if that one does not please him either, I will give him a third, and so on in sequence, until at least one of them pleases him in every possible way.” Having said this, he passed on. The old man continued watching and guarding the road until he returned again. When the old man saw him, he said to him: “Good health to you.” He replied: “Where is there health for me?” The old man said to him: “Why?” He replied: “Because now everyone has been sanctified, and no one yields to me.” The old man said to him: “Then do you have no friend there?” He replied: “I have only one brother there; he alone yields to me, and whenever he sees me, he turns like a weather-vane.” The old man said to him: “And what is that brother called?” He replied: “Theoctistus [Rufinus: Theopemptus].” Having said this, he passed on.

Then Abba Macarius arose and went to the lower desert. When the brothers saw him, they took palm branches and went out to meet him, and each of them prepared his cell, uncertain at whose place he would stay. The old man asked which of them was called Theoctistus in that place. When he found him, he entered his cell. Theoctistus received him joyfully. When they had begun to speak privately, the old man said to him: “How is your brotherly life going for you?” He replied: “Well, through your prayers.” The old man said: “Do thoughts attack you?” He replied: “For the moment I am well.” For he was ashamed to tell him. The old man said to him: “See how many years I have spent in the discipline of this place, and everyone honors me; yet even in my old age the spirit of fornication troubles me.” Theoctistus replied: “Believe me, abba, it troubles me also.”

The old man pretended that other thoughts were troubling him, until he made him confess. Then he said to him: “How do you fast?” He replied: “Until the ninth hour.” The old man said to him: “Fast until evening, and abstain; commit the Gospels to memory so that you may retain them by heart, and meditate inwardly also on the other remaining Scriptures. If an evil thought rises within you, never look downward, but always upward; and immediately the Lord will help you.”

Having corrected that brother, the old man returned to his solitude. While he was watching, he saw that demon again and said to him: “Where are you going again?” He replied: “To remind the brothers.” And he went away. When he returned, 638 the old man said to him: “How are the brothers there?” He replied: “Badly.” The old man said: “Why?” He replied: “Because they are all holy; and what is worse, even the one whom I had as my friend and obedient to me has somehow been overthrown, I do not know how, and he too no longer yields to me, but has become holier than everyone else. Therefore I have sworn not to set foot there again until a long time has passed.” Saying this, he went away, leaving the old man. But the holy old man entered his cell, worshiping and giving thanks to God the Savior.

10. Abba Macarius, wishing to console the brothers, used to say: “A boy once came here with his mother; he was being tormented by a demon, and he said to his mother: ‘Get up; let us leave here.’ She replied: ‘I cannot walk on my feet.’ Her son said to her: ‘I will carry you.’” And I marveled at the demons’ cunning: how he wanted to drive them away from there.

11. He also spoke to the brothers about the desolation of Scetis: “When you see a cell built beside a marsh, know that the desolation of Scetis is near. When you see trees, it is already before the door. But when you see children, take up your melotes and depart.”

12. Abba Moses, who lived at Petra, was once attacked very severely by fornication. Since he could not remain in his cell, he went and told Abba Isidore about it; and the old man urged him to return to his cell (Ruf., book III, no. 10). But he did not consent, saying: “I cannot, abba.” He took him with him and brought him up onto the roof. He said to him: “Look toward the West.” When he looked, he saw a multitude of demons; they were confused and jostling one another to attack. Again Abba Isidore said to him: “Look toward the East.” He looked and saw an innumerable multitude of angels in glory.

Then Abba Isidore said: “These are the ones sent to help us; those who rise toward the West are the ones who attack us. Therefore, those who are with us are more numerous than those who are against us” (2 Kings 6). Thus, giving thanks to God, Abba Moses took courage and returned to his cell.

13. Abba Moses used to say in Scetis: “If we keep the commandments of our fathers, I confidently promise you before God that the barbarians will not come here. But if we do not keep them, this place will be desolated.”

14. Once, while the brothers were sitting with that same Abba Moses, he said to them: “Look, the barbarians will come to Scetis today; but rise and flee.” They said to him: “And will you not flee, abba?” He said to them: “For so many years I have been waiting for this day, so that the saying of my Lord Jesus Christ might be fulfilled: ‘All who take the sword will perish by the sword’” (Matthew 26). They said to him: “Neither will we flee, but we will die with you.” He said to them: “I have no reason to do so; let each of you see how he should remain.”

There were seven brothers with him. They said to him: “Look, the barbarians have approached the door.” Immediately the barbarians entered and killed them. One of them, terrified by carnal fear, fled and hid behind palm mats. He saw seven crowns descending and crowning Abba Moses and the six brothers who had been killed with him.

15. They said about Abba Silvanus that he once wanted to go to Syria. His disciple Marcus said to him: “Father, I do not want to leave here, nor do I allow you to depart, abba. Therefore wait here another three days.” While the abba was waiting, Marcus, his disciple, fell asleep in peace on the third day.

16. Abba John, who had been exiled by Marcian, used to say: “We once came from Syria to Abba Poemen, wishing to ask him about hardness of heart. The old man did not know Greek, and no interpreter could be found. Seeing us distressed, the old man began to speak in the Greek language, saying:

‘The nature of water is soft, but that of stone is hard. If a vessel full of water hangs above a stone, and a drop continually falls from it upon the stone, it perforates it. So also the divine word is gentle, but our heart is hard. Therefore, when a person frequently hears the divine word, his heart is opened to fear God.’”

17. Abba Poemen said: “It is written: ‘As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God’” (Psalm 40). Since deer in the desert swallow many serpents, and when they have been inflamed by their venom they long to reach the waters, yet when they drink they are tormented by the burning of the serpents’ poison, so also monks living in the deserts are inflamed by the venom of wicked demons. Therefore they long to come on the Lord’s Sabbath to the springs of water—that is, to the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ—so that they may be cleansed from all the bitterness of the wicked demons.

18. Someone asked Abba Poemen: “What does it mean that it is written, ‘Do not repay evil for evil’” (1 Thessalonians 5; 1 Peter 3)? Abba Poemen said to him: “This passion has four stages: the first is in the heart, the second in the gaze, the third in the tongue, and the fourth is to do evil for evil. If you are able to cleanse the heart, it does not proceed to the gaze. Guard yourself also against speaking; but if you have spoken, correct yourself quickly, lest you do evil for evil.”

19. Saint Basil the bishop narrated the following: There was in a certain women’s monastery a virgin who pretended to be foolish and possessed by a demon (Palladius, chapters 41–42). She was regarded by all the others as deranged, to such an extent that they would not even eat with her. She had chosen such a way of life that, never leaving the kitchen, she performed every duty of service there. In accordance with the popular proverb, she was the sponge of the whole household, proving in herself what we read written in the holy books: “If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this world, let him become foolish, so that he may become wise” (1 Corinthians 3).

With her head wrapped in rags, she served in every way. The other virgins wore their hair shorn and covered by cucullae. Of the four hundred virgins, no one ever saw her eating; throughout her entire life she never sat at table. She never received even a small piece of bread from anyone, but merely wiped away crumbs from their tables and washed the pots, living content with these foods alone. She never injured anyone; no one ever heard her murmur; she never spoke to anyone, whether little or much.

Although everyone beat her, although she lived hated by all and endured everyone’s insults, the angel of the Lord once appeared to the holy Pyoterius—this was his name—a most distinguished man who always lived in the desert. He was sitting one day in a place of porphyry, and the angel addressed him in these words:

“Why do you think that you are something great, as a holy man living in such a place? Do you want to see a woman holier than you? Go to the monastery of the women of Tabennesi, and there you will find one of them wearing a crown on her head; know that she is better than you. While she alone fights against such a multitude day and night, her heart has never departed from God. But you, sitting in one place and never going anywhere, wander through all the cities in spirit and thought.”

He immediately went to the monastery mentioned above and asked the superiors of the brothers to introduce him into the women’s quarters. Since he was a man renowned not only for his life but also for his advanced age, they brought him in with great confidence.

When he entered, he wished to see all the sisters. Among them, however, he did not see the one for whom he had come. Finally he said: “Bring them all to me. It seems to me that one is missing.” They replied: “We have one foolish woman [Palladius: *salem*] inside in the kitchen.” For that is what they call women afflicted by a demon.

He said: “Bring her to me also, so that I may see her.” On hearing this, they began to call the woman mentioned above. Since she did not wish to respond, sensing, I believe, something—or perhaps recognizing this very thing by divine revelation—they said to her: “Saint Pyoterius wishes to see you.” He was a man of great reputation and renown.

When she had been brought to him, and he saw that her forehead was wrapped in a cloth, he threw himself at her feet and said: “Bless me.” She likewise fell at his feet and said: “You bless me, lord.”

All the sisters were astonished and said: “Do not endure such an insult, abba; she is foolish, as you can see.”

But Saint Pyoterius said to all of them: “You are the foolish ones. For she is both your Amma and mine.”

[Note: [Col. 0990D] There is great variation here, partly among the printed books and partly among the manuscripts. The Paris edition and Palladius, chapter 42, have *anima* (“soul”); others have *nonna* (“nun”), others *domna* (“lady”). The Audomarensis manuscript has *Amma*. This is the truest reading. Firmian’s Greek version of Palladius: “For she, being better than both you and me, is an Amma” (*Αὕτη γὰρ καὶ ὑμῶν, καὶ ἐμοῦ ἀμείνων οὖσα Ἀμμᾶς ἐστὶν*), “for that is what they call spiritual mothers.” Thus in the same Palladius, chapter 37, Amma Piamun; chapter 137, Amma Taor; chapter 138, Amma Talida. See the *Onomasticon*.]

That is what they call spiritual women. “And I pray God,” he said, “that I may be found worthy of her on the day of judgment.”

When they heard this, all of them fell together at her feet, each confessing to her various sins of her own. One said that, while washing dirty dishes, she had poured the filth over her; another repeatedly recalled that she had beaten her with blows; another lamented that she had stuffed her nostrils with mustard. The others likewise reported that they had inflicted various injuries upon her.

After praying to God for all these matters, that holy man departed. A few days later, unable to bear such honor for herself, unwilling to be heaped with so much respect by the sisters, and believing herself burdened by the apologies of each one, she secretly left that monastery. Where she went, where she placed herself, or what end she met, no one was ever able to learn.

20. The blessed Paul the Simple, disciple of Abba Antony, told the fathers the following story: He once came to a monastery to visit and to instruct the brothers. After the customary mutual consolation, they entered the church of God to celebrate the liturgy in the usual manner.

[Note: [Col. 0985] Rufinus, book III, no. 167; Paschasius, chapter 23, no. 2. A similar account occurs in Rufinus, book II, chapter 14, concerning Eulogius.]

As the blessed Paul watched each person entering the church, he observed with what disposition each entered. For God had given him this grace: he could see what disposition each person possessed, just as we see one another’s faces; and he could also see the angel of each person rejoicing over him.

When everyone entered with a bright face and radiant appearance, he saw one man whose whole body was black and dark. Demons held and dragged him on both sides toward themselves, putting a halter into his nostrils; while his holy angel followed him from a distance, mourning and grieving.

Paul, weeping and frequently beating his breast with his hand, sat before the church, grieving intensely over the man who had appeared to him in such a condition. Those who saw what he was doing, and his sudden change, his tears, and his mourning, questioned him and begged him to say what he had seen, fearing that he had observed something reproachable in everyone, on account of which he acted thus. They also asked him to enter the liturgy with them.

But Paul drove them away and refused to enter. He sat outside, lying there and weeping bitterly over the man who had appeared to him in such a state.

A little later, when the assembly had left the church, Paul again watched each person coming out, so that, having recognized the condition in which they had entered, he might know what sort of people they were when they came out. He saw that the man who had previously been black and dark throughout his body was leaving the church with a bright face and a radiant body. The demons who had previously held him were now following him from a distance, while his holy angel walked beside him, joyful, eager, and greatly rejoicing over him.

Paul leaped for joy and cried out, blessing God and saying: “O ineffable mercy and goodness of God! O his divine compassion and immeasurable goodness!”

Running and climbing onto a high step, he said in a loud voice: “Come, see the works of the Lord, how dreadful they are and worthy of all astonishment. Come, see him who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2). “Come, let us worship and fall down before him, and say: ‘For you alone are powerful to forgive sins.’”

At these words all ran together, eager to hear what he was saying. When everyone had assembled, Paul told them what he had seen before they entered the church and what he had seen afterward.

He questioned the man, asking him to tell why God had granted him such a sudden transformation. The man, convicted by Paul, openly recounted the matter before everyone around him, saying:

“I am a sinful man, and until now I lived for a long time in fornication. But when I entered the holy church of God just now, I heard the voice of the prophet Isaiah as it was being read—rather, I heard God’s voice speaking through him—where he says:

‘Wash yourselves; be clean. Remove the evil of your thoughts from my sight. Learn to do good. And if your sins are like scarlet, they will be made white like snow. And if you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land’” (Isaiah 1).

“I,” he said, “a fornicator, was pierced exceedingly by this saying. Groaning within my conscience, I said to God: ‘You are God, who came into the world to save sinners, and who promised through the prophet these things that have just been read. Bring them to completion in effect and deed even in me, unworthy and sinful as I am. For from this moment I promise and pledge to you in words, and confess with my heart, that I will no longer do that evil. I renounce every iniquity and from now on serve you with a clean conscience. Today, Lord, and at this hour, receive me as one who repents, appeals to you, and renounces every sin.’

“Having made these promises,” he said, “I came out of the church, determining in my soul to do nothing evil any longer before the eyes of the Lord.”

When they heard this, everyone cried out to the Lord with a loud voice, saying: “How greatly your works have been magnified, O Lord! You have made all things in wisdom” (Psalm 103).

Therefore, recognizing through the holy Scriptures and divine revelations how great is God’s goodness toward those who devoutly flee to him and cleanse their former offenses through repentance, Christians should understand that such people are not only spared punishment for sins previously committed, but also obtain the promised blessings.

Let us not despair of our salvation. For just as God promised through the prophet Isaiah to wash again those who are entangled in sins, make them white like wool and snow, and fill them with the heavenly blessings that are in the city of the heavenly Jerusalem, so also now, through the prophet Ezekiel, he has promised with an oath: “‘As I live,’ says the Lord, ‘I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live’” (Ezekiel 18).

[Note: [Col. 0991A] Observe that in the first and third editions of this book, at no. 13, the following story is inserted:

“There was a certain very devout priest named Plegus [variant: Plecgils], who frequently celebrated the solemnities of the Mass at the body of Saint Ninian [variant: Ninianus], bishop and confessor. Since he led a holy life with worthy moderation, by Christ’s favor, he began to beseech almighty God in prayer to show him the nature of Christ’s body and blood. He asked this not out of unbelief, as often happens, but out of devotion of heart. From childhood he had been instructed in divine laws; and out of love for the heavenly King he had once left the boundaries of his homeland and its pleasant fields, so that in exile he might diligently learn the mysteries of Christ. Therefore, burning more greatly with love for him, he daily offered precious gifts and asked that the form hidden beneath the appearance of bread and wine be shown to him—not because he doubted Christ’s body, but because he wished to see Christ, whom no mortal, once he has been raised above the stars, can freely behold on earth.

“The day came. While he was devoutly celebrating the solemnities of the Mass according to custom, he fell upon his knees and said: ‘I beseech you, almighty God, reveal to me, insignificant in this ministry, the nature of Christ’s body, so that I may see him present with bodily sight, and now touch with my hands the form of the child whom his mother’s womb once carried crying.’

“As he prayed these things, an angel came from heaven and addressed him: ‘Rise quickly, if you desire to see Christ. He is present, clothed in the bodily garment worn by the holy woman who bore the child.’

“Then the venerable priest, afraid, lifted his face from the ground and saw upon the altar the Son of the Father as a child, whom Simeon was deemed worthy to carry as an infant in his arms. The angel said to him: ‘Since you have desired to see Christ, whom previously you used to consecrate under the appearance of bread with mystical words, now look upon him with your eyes and touch him with your hands.’

“Then the priest, relying upon the heavenly gift—and what is astonishing to say—took the child in his trembling arms and joined his own breast to Christ’s breast. Then, pouring himself into an embrace, he kissed God and pressed Christ’s holy lips with his own lips.

“When these things had been accomplished, he restored the glorious limbs of the Son of God to the top of the altar and filled Christ’s table with heavenly nourishment. Then the man again prostrated himself and asked God to deign to change himself again into his former form. When this prayer had been completed, he rose from the ground and found that Christ’s body had returned to its former form, as he had requested.”

But this story is absent from the other editions and manuscripts. It is certain that it was inserted from English histories. Saint Ninian certainly lived in England. It is found in Paschasius, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, chapter 14, and Saint Thomas cites it in *Opusculum* 58, chapter 11; likewise William of Malmesbury, book III of *The Deeds of the English*. A similar vision occurs in the *Life of Saint Basil*, above, chapter 7. See there what is said at no. 36.]

BOOK SIX OF THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS, OR THE SAYINGS OF THE ELDERS, BY AN UNKNOWN GREEK AUTHOR

[Note: [Col. 0991C] “By an unknown Greek author.” See the general preface, sections 7 and 8, where we proved that neither Evagrius nor Palladius was the author of this book or of the preceding one, which are usually joined together and treated as one. For this reason I have attributed the book to an unknown Greek author, since even in Photius’s time it circulated without an author’s name and was entitled in Greek *ΑΝΔΡΩΝ ΑΓΙΩΝ ΒΙΒΛΟΣ*, “Book of Holy Men.” See it in the *Bibliotheca*, codex 198.]

TRANSLATED BY JOHN, SUBDEACON OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

[Note: [Col. 0992C] “By John.” See the general preface, section 14, where, from Sigebert’s *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 117, and from manuscripts, we demonstrated that the translator of this book was John, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church.]

[Col. 0991]

## PREFACE

644 Nothing in particular needs to be prefixed to this book, since it is part of the preceding book, which Sigebert, in chapter 117 of *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, cites as distinct from the earlier one because it has a different translator. We too have published it separately under that name, so that its citation—since it must often be cited elsewhere—might be easier and clearer.

[Col. 0993]

## SAYINGS OF THE ELDERS (C, S)*

### FIRST BOOK: On Foreknowledge or Contemplation

[Col. 0993A]

Zacharias once went to his abba Silvanus and found him in an ecstasy of mind, with his hands extended toward heaven. When he saw this, he closed the door and went out. Returning around the sixth and ninth hours, he found him in the same condition. Around the tenth hour he knocked, entered, and found him resting. He said to him: “What happened to you today, Father?” He replied: “I was weakened today, my son.” But Zacharias held his feet and said: “I will not let you go unless you tell me what you saw.” The old man answered: “I was carried up into heaven, and I saw the glory of God. I remained there until now, and now I have been released.”

2. Saint Syncletica said: “Let us become prudent like serpents and innocent like doves, so that we may cleverly understand the snares of the devil. For the command to become prudent like serpents was given so that we might not be ignorant of the devil’s attacks and devices. Indeed, one likeness is overcome by another likeness; and the innocence of the dove is also demonstrated.”

3. One of the Fathers used to say: “Once, while the elders were sitting and speaking about edifying matters, there was among them one who possessed foreknowledge. He saw angels moving their hands and washing the elders” (Ruf., book III, no. 35). But when worldly conversation began, the angels departed, and pigs rolled about in their midst, full of filth and stench, defiling them. When they again spoke about edification, the angels returned and washed them once more.

[Col. 0993C] 4. An old man said: “This is what is written: ‘For two and three sins of Tyre I shall turn myself away; but for four I shall not turn away’ (Amos 1): to think evil, to consent to the thought, and to speak it. The fourth is to carry out the deed. In this, therefore, the Lord’s anger is not turned away.”

5. They said about a certain great old man in Scetis: Whenever the brothers were building a little cell, he would go out joyfully, and after laying the foundation he would not leave until he had stayed with them. But once, when he went out to build a cell, he was greatly saddened. The brothers said: “Why are you sad and mournful, abba?” He replied: “This place is going to be desolated, my children. For I saw that a fire had been kindled in Scetis. The brothers took palm branches, beat at it, and extinguished it. Then it was kindled again, and the brothers again took palm branches, beat at it, and extinguished it. A third time it was kindled and filled all Scetis, and now it could not be extinguished. Therefore I am sorrowful and mournful.”

[Col. 0993D] 6. An old man said: “It is written: ‘The righteous will flourish like a palm tree.’ This saying signifies the high, upright, and sweet fruit of good works. There is, however, in the palm tree an *incarduum* [inner core].”

[Note: [Col. 1021B] 662 *Incarduum.* Thus the Paris edition and the Aquicinctine manuscript; but the German edition has *incardium*, and the Lyon edition *incordium*. Is it not the same as the Greek *ἐγκάρδιον*, the middle of anything, or the inner part and marrow of every tree, also called *ἐντεριώνη*? Let *ἐγκάρδιον* be understood here in the palm tree. See the *Onomasticon*.]

“and it itself is white, possessing within it every operation. Something similar is also found in the righteous: his heart is one and simple, looking toward God alone. It is also white, possessing the illumination of faith, and every operation of the righteous is in his heart; for the sharpness of his thorns is a bulwark against the devil.”

7. Another old man once said: “The Shunammite received Elisha because she had no attachment to any man” (Pasch., chapter 37, no. 4, under the name of Macarius; Appendix to the Martyrologies, no. 16). The Shunammite is said to represent the soul, and Elisha the Holy Spirit. Therefore, whenever the soul withdraws from worldly confusion and turmoil, God’s Spirit will come to it, and then it will be able to give birth, although it is barren.”

8. Another of the Fathers said: “The eyes of a pig have a natural formation such that, by necessity, they always look toward the earth and can never look up toward heaven. So also the soul of one who delights in the sweetness of pleasures, once it has fallen into the mire of lust, can scarcely look toward God or conceive anything worthy of God.”

9. There was a great man among those possessing foreknowledge. He affirmed: “The virtue that I saw standing over baptism I also saw over the monk’s garment when he receives the spiritual habit.”

[Note: [Col. 1021B] “The virtue.” See the discussion above, book I, *Life of Saint Antony*, chapter 37, no. 78, concerning the similarity between baptism and entry into religious life.]

10. An old man was given the grace of seeing what was happening, and he said: “I once saw a brother meditating in his cell in a coenobium. And behold, a demon came and stood outside the cell. While that brother was meditating, the demon could not enter; but when he stopped meditating, then the demon entered.”

11. They said about a certain old man that he prayed to God to see the demons. It was revealed to him: “You have no need to see them.” But the old man pleaded, saying: “Lord, you are able to protect me by your grace.” Then God opened his eyes, and he saw them: they surrounded the man like bees, gnashing their teeth over him. But God’s angels rebuked them.

12. An old man said: “Two brothers lived near one another, one a stranger and one a local.”

[Note: [Col. 1021B] “One a stranger, and one a local.” Thus the manuscripts and older editions. In place of *inchoris*, the Paris edition has *incola* (“inhabitant”). That is a good interpretation, but the author used a Greek-derived word, *ἐγχωρής*. Thus in Holy Scripture: “A graceless man,” from Ecclesiasticus 20, as though “a vain tale.” The Cologne edition and the latest revised *Speculum Exemplorum* incorrectly have *in choris*. See the *Onomasticon*.]

“The stranger was somewhat more negligent, while the local was exceedingly diligent. It happened that the stranger fell asleep in peace. Since the old man who lived near them possessed foreknowledge, he saw a multitude of angels escorting the stranger’s soul. When it reached heaven to enter, a judgment was held concerning him. A voice came from above, saying: ‘It is clear that he was somewhat negligent, but because of his foreign sojourn, open the way for him.’

“After this the local also fell asleep, and all his relatives came to him. The old man saw that no angels came to escort his soul, and he marveled. Falling on his face before God, he said: ‘How did that stranger, though more negligent, receive such glory, while this man, though diligent, received nothing of the kind?’

“A voice came to him, saying: ‘When this diligent man came to die, he opened his eyes and saw his relatives weeping, and his soul was comforted. But that stranger, although more negligent, saw none of his own; he wept, and God comforted him.’”

646

13. Another of the Fathers narrated that there was a solitary in the desert of Nilopolis, and a certain layman, though faithful, ministered to him. In the same city there was a rich and impious man. It happened that the rich man died, and the whole city, together with the bishop, escorted him with lamps.

The man who ministered to the solitary also went out, as usual, carrying bread to him. He found that a wild beast had devoured him, and he fell on his face before the Lord, saying: “I will not rise from here until God shows me what this means. That impious man had such a procession at his burial, while this man, who served you day and night, suffered this.”

And behold, an angel of the Lord came and said to him: “That impious man had a small good work in this world, and he received its reward here, so that he may find no rest there.”

[Note: [Col. 1021C] “That impious man.” See the discussion concerning the *Life of Saint Pachomius*, chapter 39, no. 39, on how burial contributes to reward or punishment.]

“But this solitary, because he was adorned with every virtue, also had, as a human being, a small amount of guilt; he received its punishment here, so that there he might be found pure before God.”

Thus comforted by these words, he departed, glorifying God for his judgments, because they are true.

14. The holy Fathers of Scetis prophesied concerning the last generation, saying: “What have we accomplished?” (Ruf., book III, no. 197). One of them, a man of great life, named Cyrion,

[Note: [Col. 1021C] Cyrion. The reading varied here, making it difficult to recover the true name. The Paris edition has Histirion; the Audomarensis manuscript, Cyrion, which I have retained. That name occurs for a soldier in the Roman, Bedean, Usuardian, and Adoian Martyrologies, on March 9, who suffered martyrdom at Sebaste under the emperor Licinius. Another, a presbyter and martyr crowned with laurels, is commemorated on February 14, at Alexandria. Perhaps this is our man, who lived in Scetis near Alexandria. Rufinus, book II of the *History*, chapter 8, has a monk named Scyrion, a monk in Apeliotes in his own time. The following prophecy of the elders is, I think, recalled by Theodore of Alexandria in Sophronius’s *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 54:

“‘We later came to Theremithes to Abba Theodore of Alexandria. The old man said to us: “My little children, the monks of Scetis have indeed lost much, in accordance with the prophecy of the elders. Believe me, children, for among the monks of Scetis there was great charity, great abstinence, and great discernment.”’”]

Cyrion [variants: Squirion, Isquirion, or Histirion] said: “We do not keep God’s commandments.”

They replied: “What, then, will those who come after us do?”

He said to them: “They will perform half of our work.”

They said to him: “And what will those who come after them do?”

He replied: “That coming generation will have absolutely no work at all. Yet I see that they will have temptations; and those who are found approved in that time will be better than us and our fathers.”

15. A certain old man related the following:

There was a very elderly virgin who had advanced greatly in the fear of God. When I asked her what had led her to this way of life, she sighed and began to say:

“While I was still a little girl [Col. 0995D], my father was modest and gentle in character, but weak and infirm in body. He lived in such a way, taking care of himself, that he was scarcely ever seen by those who lived in the same village. He continually worked his own land and always occupied his life there. If perhaps he was healthy, he brought the produce of his cultivation home; but most of the time he was confined to bed by illness. His silence was so great that those who did not know him would have thought him voiceless.

“My mother, however, was quite the opposite: immoderately curious and more shameful than all the women in that region. Her conversation was directed toward everyone in such a way that one might have thought her whole body was a tongue. She frequently stirred up quarrels against everyone [Col. 0996A]. When drunk with wine, she consorted with dissolute men. She distributed the things kept inside our house as though she were the worst sort of prostitute, so that even our considerable property could not suffice for us. My father had entrusted her with the management of the household. She abused her body in such shameful ways that scarcely anyone in the village was able to escape her lust. Yet her body never suffered any illness, nor did she feel even the slightest pain; from her birth until her final day she possessed a sound and healthy body.

“Meanwhile, my father, exhausted by a long illness, died. Immediately the weather became disturbed: rain, lightning, and thunder troubled the air. The rain did not cease either by night or by day, and for three days it kept him lying on his bed without burial [Col. 0996B]. The villagers, shaking their heads, marveled that such wickedness had been hidden from everyone, saying: ‘He must have been God’s enemy, since even the earth refuses to receive him for burial.’ Nevertheless, lest his dismembered body prevent the inhabitants from entering the house, while the stormy weather still threatened and the rain continued to fall, we scarcely managed somehow to commit him to burial.

“After this, my mother, having received the greatest freedom, indulged her lust with extreme shamelessness. She turned our house into a brothel and lived thereafter in much wantonness and luxury. While I was still a little girl and our resources were failing, she scarcely ever [reading uncertain: *cum timore*], as it seems to me, when her death came, received such a splendid funeral [Col. 0996C] that it was even thought that the weather itself was accompanying her bier.

“After her death, I passed beyond childhood. When the desires and stirrings of the body began to move me, one evening, as usually happens, I began to think and consider whose life I should choose to imitate: whether my father’s, who had lived modestly, gently, and soberly. But then I reflected that he had achieved nothing good in his life; he had spent all his time in illness and tribulation, and had ended his life in such a way that even the earth refused to receive him for burial. If such a way of life was good in God’s sight, why, then, had my father, who had chosen to live in this manner, suffered so many evils?

“‘But,’ my thought said, ‘look at my mother: it is good to live by surrendering oneself to pleasure, wantonness, and lust [Col. 0996D]. She left no shameful deed undone; while drunk, she spent all her time healthy and prosperous, and so completed her life. What, then, should I do? I must live as my mother lived. It is better to trust my own eyes concerning what is plainly known, and to omit nothing.’

“When I, miserable woman, had resolved to devote myself to such a life, night came, and sleep immediately overtook me. After these thoughts, someone appeared before me, very large in body and terrifying in appearance. Looking at me, he frightened me with an angry aspect and a harsh voice, and asked me: ‘Tell me,’ he said, ‘what are the thoughts of your heart?’

“Terrified by his appearance and bearing, I trembled and did not dare look at him. In a louder voice he again ordered me to declare what I had resolved upon. Dissolved with fear and having forgotten all my thoughts, I said that there was nothing. But when I denied it, [Col. 0997A] he recalled everything to me that I had meditated in my heart.

“Convicted, I turned to prayer and begged to obtain forgiveness, and I explained to him the cause of those thoughts. He said to me: ‘Come and see both your father and your mother, and afterward choose for yourself whichever life you wish.’ Taking me by the hand, he drew me along.

“He led me into a great field containing many gardens, different kinds of fruit, various trees, and indescribable beauty, and brought me inside. My father came to meet me, embraced me, and kissed me, calling me his daughter [Col. 0997B]. I embraced him and asked to remain with him. But he said: ‘You cannot remain here now. If you wish to follow in my footsteps, you will come here before long.’

“While I continued to beg him to let me stay with him, the one who had led me there again took me by the hand and said: ‘Come, I will show you your mother, who is being consumed by fire, so that you may know toward which of these two lives you ought to incline.’

“He set me in a dark and gloomy house filled with every kind of shrieking and disturbance. He showed me a blazing furnace and boiling pitch, with certain terrifying figures standing over the furnace. Looking downward, I saw my mother plunged into the furnace up to her neck, gnashing her teeth and burning in the fire; and a great stench arose from many worms [Col. 0997C].

“When she saw me, she cried out with a howl, calling me her daughter: ‘Alas, my daughter! I suffer these things because of my own deeds. Everything that concerned sobriety seemed to me mere madness. I did not believe that fornication and adultery would bring me torment; I did not regard drunkenness and wantonness as punishments. And behold, because of a little lust, what hell I receive and what punishments I endure! Behold, because of brief pleasures, what torments I am paying! Behold, because I despised God, what rewards I receive! All these immovable evils have seized me.

“‘Now is the time for help, my daughter; now remember the nourishment you received from me; now repay me if you ever received any benefit. Have pity on me,’ she said, ‘for I burn in fire and am consumed by it. Have pity on me [Col. 0997D], for I am dying amid such tortures. Have pity on me, my daughter, and stretch out your hand and draw me from this place.’

“When I refused to do this because of those who were standing there, she cried out again with tears: ‘My daughter, help me, and do not despise the tears of your own mother. Remember my pain on the day when I gave birth to you, and do not despise me, who am perishing in the fire of hell.’

“Moved to tears by her voice, I suffered a human compassion and began, crying aloud, to lament with her. Those who were in the house arose, lit a fire, and asked me the reason for my groaning. I told them what I had seen.

“And so I resolved that I would follow my father’s life, convinced, through the ineffable mercy of God, of the punishments laid up [Col. 0998A] for those who wish to live wickedly. For that blessed virgin, having learned from the vision that there is a great reward for good works and that the evil deeds of a shameful life receive the greatest punishments, declared this. Let us therefore become people of better counsel, so that we may be made blessed.”

16. An old man again related the following concerning a certain bishop, so that, receiving the greatest confidence from it, we might maintain our diligence in God for salvation (Ruf., book III, no. 166; Pasch., ch. 23, no. 1).

Some people reported concerning a bishop who was staying among us—as the bishop himself related—that two faithful women of the secular class, married ladies, were living as though immodestly. The bishop was disturbed by what those who reported this had told him [Col. 0998B]. Suspecting that there might perhaps be others like them, he turned to entreat God, asking to become certain of the matter; and he obtained what he requested.

After that divine and terrible consecration, when each person approached to partake of the holy mysteries, he could discern from their faces the souls subject to the sins of each. He saw the faces of sinful men black; some of them had faces as though scorched by heat, with eyes red and bloodshot; others had bright faces but white garments. When some received the Lord’s body, it burned and consumed them; in others it became like a light within them, entered through their mouths, and illuminated their entire bodies [Col. 0998C].

Among them were also some who had chosen the solitary life, as well as those who lived in marriage; and they too appeared in the same manner.

Then he turned and began distributing the sacrament to the women as well, so that he might learn what their souls were like. In the same way he saw their faces become black and red, some bloody and others white.

Among them came those two women who had been accused before the bishop and on whose account he had especially undertaken this prayer and inquiry. He saw them too, as they approached the holy mystery, with bright and honorable faces and clothed in white robes. After they had partaken of Christ’s mystery, they became as though illuminated by light.

Again the bishop turned to his customary prayer, beseeching God and desiring to learn [Col. 0998D] the meaning of the revelations shown to him. An angel of the Lord appeared and commanded him to inquire about each person.

The holy bishop immediately asked about the two women, whether the original accusation against them was true or false. The angel affirmed that everything said about them was true.

The bishop said to the angel: “How, then, when they received Christ’s body, were their faces radiant, their robes white, and their brightness so great?”

The angel replied: “Because they repented of their deeds and, turning away from them with tears, groans, and almsgiving to the poor, they deserved, through confession, a divine ‘number’ [reading uncertain: *numerum*]; and henceforth they promised [Col. 0999A] never again to walk in those evils, if indeed they might obtain forgiveness for their former sins. For this reason they deserved a divine transformation, were released from their crimes, and thereafter lived soberly, devoutly, and justly.”

The bishop said that he marveled not so much at the transformation of those women—for this has happened to many—as at God’s gift: that he not only refused to subject them to punishments but also deigned to grant them such great grace.

The angel said to him: “You marvel at this justly, as a human being. But our Lord and your Lord and God, being naturally good and merciful toward those who turn away from their sins and approach him through confession, not only does not allow them to go to punishment, but also withdraws his anger from them and makes them worthy of honor. For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for it [Col. 0999B] (John 3).

“Therefore, if he chose to die for people when they were enemies, will he not much more release them from punishments once they have become his household and repent of what they have done? He will grant them the good things prepared by him to be enjoyed.

“Know this, then: no human sins overcome God’s clemency, provided that through repentance one washes away by good deeds the evils one formerly committed. Since God is merciful, he knows the weakness of your race, the strength of its passions, and the power and cunning of the devil. When people fall into sins, he forgives them as children and patiently waits for their correction. When they turn back and implore his goodness, he has compassion on them as on the weak [Col. 0999C], immediately releases them from their punishments, and grants them the good things prepared for the righteous.”

The bishop said to the angel: “I beg you, tell me also the differences among the faces, and to what sins each of these people is subject, so that, recognizing these things as well, I may be freed from all ignorance.”

The angel said to him: “Those who have bright and cheerful faces live in sobriety, chastity, and righteousness. They are also modest, compassionate, and merciful.

“Those who have black faces are workers of fornication and lust, and are devoted to other crimes and sins.

“Those who appeared bloody and red live in wickedness and injustice; they love slander, are blasphemers, deceitful, and murderers.”

Again the angel said to him: “Help them, if you desire their salvation [Col. 0999D]. For this reason you obtained the fulfillment of your prayers: so that by seeing the sins of your disciples, and by admonishing and entreating them, you might make them better through repentance for him who died for them and rose from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord.

“Whatever virtue, zeal, and love you possess toward the Lord your Christ, exercise complete care for all of them, so that they may turn from their sins to God. Clearly persuade them of the sins to which they are subject, lest they despair of their own salvation.

“When those souls repent and turn to God, their salvation will be assured, together with the abundance of future blessings. You, however, will receive a great reward by imitating your Lord, who left the heavens [Col. 1000A] and dwelt on earth for the salvation of humanity.”
