17. One of the Fathers related: “There are three honorable things among monks, to which we ought to approach with fear, trembling, and spiritual joy: participation in the holy sacraments, the table of the brothers, and the basin in which the brothers’ feet are washed.”

He offered the following example, saying:

“There was a great old man gifted with foresight, and it happened that he ate with several brothers. While they were eating, the old man saw in the spirit that some sitting at the table were eating honey, others bread, and others dung.

“He marveled within himself and entreated God, saying: ‘Lord, this mystery is truly astonishing to me: the same food has been set before everyone on the table, but in eating it appears to have been changed. Some eat honey, some bread, and others dung.’

“A voice came to him from above, saying: ‘Those who eat honey are those who eat at the table with fear, trembling, and thanksgiving, and who pray without ceasing. Their prayer rises before God like incense; therefore they also eat honey [Col. 1000B].

“‘Those who eat bread are those who receive what has been given by God while giving thanks.

“‘Those who eat dung are those who murmur and say, “This is good and that is bad” (1 Corinthians 10).’

“We ought not to think such thoughts, but rather glorify God and offer him praise, so that what has been said may also be fulfilled in us: ‘Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory [Col. 1000C] of God’ (1 Corinthians 10).”

## SECOND BOOK

### On the holy elders who performed signs

Abba Dulas, the disciple of Abba Besarion, said:

“While we were walking beside the seashore, I became thirsty and said to Abba Besarion: ‘Abba, I am very thirsty’” (Ruf., book III, no. 215).

When the old man had prayed, he said to me: “Drink from the sea.” The water became sweet, and I drank. I drew only a little into a vessel, lest I become thirsty again.

When the old man saw this, he said to me: “Why have you filled the vessel with water?”

I said to him: “Forgive me, lest I become thirsty again.”

The old man said: “God is here, and he is everywhere.”

2. At another time, when it was necessary for him, he prayed and crossed the Chrysoroas River on foot [Col. 1000D]. I marveled and asked him: “How did you feel your feet while you were walking in the water?”

The old man said: “I felt the water up to my ankles; everything beyond that was solid beneath my feet.”

3. Again, as we were going to another old man, the sun was setting. The old man prayed, saying: “I beg you, Lord, let the sun stand still until I reach your servant.” And it happened so.

4. Once a man possessed by a demon came to Scetis, and prayer was made for him in the church, but the demon did not leave him, because it was obstinate (Ruf., book III, no. 121; Pasch., ch. 14, no. 2).

The clergy of that place said to one another: “What shall we do with this demon? No one can cast it out except Abba Besarion [Col. 1001A]; and if we ask him on the man’s behalf, he will not even come into the church.

“Let us do this: he will come into the church in the morning before everyone else. Let us make the afflicted man sit in his place, and when he enters, let us stand for prayer and say to him: ‘Raise up this brother, Abba.’”

They did so. When the old man came in the morning, they stood for prayer and said to him: “Raise up this brother, Abba.”

The old man said to the afflicted man: “Rise and go outside.”

Immediately the demon left him, and from that hour he was healed.

5. The elders once spoke to Abba Elias in Egypt about Abba Agathon, saying: “He is a good brother.”

The old man said to them: “He is good according to his generation.”

They said to him: “But what is he according to the ancients?”

He replied: “I have already told you that he is good according to his generation. But according to the ancients, I saw a man in Scetis [Col. 1001B] who could make the sun stand still in the heavens, as Jesus son of Nun did.”

When they heard this, they were astonished and glorified God.

6. They said of that great Abba Macarius that, as he was going up from Scetis, he was carrying baskets. Exhausted, he sat down and prayed, saying: “God, you know that I can no longer continue.”

Immediately he was lifted up and found himself over the river (Ruf., book III, no. 213).

7. A certain man in Egypt had a paralytic son. He brought him to the cell of blessed Macarius and, leaving him weeping at the door, went a long way off (Ruf., book III, no. 122).

The old man looked out, saw the child crying, and said to him [Col. 1001C]: “Who brought you here?”

He said: “My father threw me here and went away.”

The old man said to him: “Rise and take hold of him.”

Immediately the child was healed. He rose, took hold of his father, and they went away together to their home.

8. Abba Sisoes said:

“When I was in Scetis with Abba Macarius, we went up with him to reap seven *nomina* [Note: [Col. 1021D] *Reap with him seven nomina.* I do not adequately understand what these *nomina* are. If a Greek text were available, it might perhaps shed some light. In Pelagius, book XVII, no. 20: ‘They undertook a defined area of sixty *modii* to reap.’ In Rufinus, above, book II, chapter 18, in the story of Serapion: ‘And from that payment each one would gather more or less eighty *modii* of grain.’ Yet these passages still do not make clear what the *nomina* are. Our Peter Larisselius suggested *nomia*, from Greek νέμω (*nemō*, ‘to distribute’), whence *nomoi* and *nomai* among the Egyptians, so that it may be understood as a definite portion of land. [Col. 1022B]]

“And behold, a widow was gathering ears of grain behind us and did not cease weeping. The old man therefore called the owner of that field and said to him: ‘What is the matter with this old woman, that she is always weeping?’

“He said to him: ‘Her husband held someone’s deposit and died without speaking; he did not say where he had put it, and the owner of the deposit wants to take her and her children into slavery.’

“The old man said: ‘Tell her to come to us where we are resting in the heat.’

“When she came [Col. 1001D], the old man said to her: ‘Why are you always weeping?’

“She said: ‘My husband died after receiving something entrusted to him by another, and when he died he did not say where he had put it.’

“The old man said to her: ‘Come and show us your husband’s grave.’

“Taking the brothers with him, he went with her. When they came to the place where the man had been laid, the old man said to her: ‘Withdraw from here to your house.’

“While they were praying, the old man called out to the one who had died, saying to him: ‘Where did you put the other man’s deposit?’

“He answered him: ‘It is hidden in my house beneath the foot of the bed.’

“The old man said to him: ‘Sleep again until the day of resurrection.’

“When the brothers saw this, they fell at his feet. The old man said to them: ‘This was not done on my account, for I am nothing. God did this for the sake of that widow and her orphans [Col. 1002A]. For this is the great thing: God desires the soul to be without sin, and if it asks for something, it receives it.’

“The widow came and was told where the entrusted property was. She took it, returned it to its owner, and freed her children. Those who heard this glorified God.”

9. Once, as Abba Emilis was passing through a certain place, he saw a monk being held by some people as a murderer. The old man approached, questioned the brother, and discovered that he had been falsely accused. He said to those holding him: “Where is the man who was killed?”

They showed him. Then, approaching the dead man, he said to everyone: “Pray.”

As he himself stretched out his hands toward God, the dead man rose [Col. 1002B].

The old man said to him in the presence of everyone: “Tell us: who killed you?”

He said: “When I entered the church, I entrusted money to the presbyter. He himself rose up, killed me, carried me away, and threw me into this abbot’s monastery. But I beg you to take the money from him and give it to my children.”

Then the old man said to him: “Go, sleep until the Lord comes and raises you.”

Immediately he fell asleep.

10. Many brothers once came to Abba Pastor (Ruf., book III, no. 168). One of his relatives had a son whose face, through the devil’s activity, had been turned backward. When his father saw the multitude of Fathers, he took the child and sat outside, weeping.

It happened that one of the elders went outside. When he saw the father [Col. 1002C], he said: “Why are you weeping, man?”

He said: “I am a relative of Abba Pastor. Behold, this affliction has happened to this child. I wanted to present him to this elder so that he might cure him, but I was afraid, for he does not want to see us. Now, if he discovers that I am here, he will send someone to drive me away and threaten me out of this place [Note: [Col. 1022B] ‘And threaten me out of this place.’ The verb *minare* is used not only by ecclesiastical writers but also by secular authors. See the *Onomasticon*.].

“Seeing your presence, I dared to come here. Therefore, however you wish, Abba, have mercy on me, bring this child inside, and pray for him.”

The old man took him, entered, and acted wisely. He did not immediately present him to Abba Pastor, but began with the younger brothers, saying: “Make the sign of the cross over this child.”

After he had had all of them make the sign over him in order, he finally presented him to Abba Pastor, who did not want to touch him. But they begged him, saying: “As everyone else has done, so do you too, Father.”

He groaned [Col. 1002D], rose, and prayed, saying: “God, save your creation, so that the enemy may not rule over it.”

After making the sign of the cross over him, he healed him and restored him sound to his father.

11. One of the Fathers related concerning a certain Abba Paul, who was in the lower regions of Egypt, living near the Thebaid. This Paul held in his hands those creatures called horned serpents, as well as asps, snakes, and scorpions, and tore them in two.

When the brothers saw this, they were amazed and asked him: “Tell us what you have done to receive this grace.”

He said to them: “Forgive me, brothers. If someone possesses purity, everything is subjected to him, as it was to Adam when he was in paradise before the transgression of the divine command.”

[Col. 1003A] 12. In the time of Julian the Apostate [Note: [Col. 1022B] *In the time of Julian.* Authors give various accounts of the agent responsible for Julian’s death. See Baronius, volume IV of the *Annales*, where he discusses this matter at length.], when Julian was descending into Persia, a demon was sent by that same Julian to go swiftly to the West and bring him some answer from there.

When the demon reached a certain place where a monk lived, he stood there motionless for ten days, because he could not go farther: the monk did not cease praying, either by night or by day.

The demon returned without accomplishing his task to the one who had sent him. Julian said to him: “Why were you delayed?”

The demon answered him: “I was delayed and returned without accomplishing anything. For I had to wait ten days for the monk Publius, in case he might cease praying and allow me to pass. But he did not cease, and I was prevented from passing. I returned having accomplished nothing.”

Then the most impious Julian, enraged, said: “When I return, I will take revenge on him.”

Within a few days, however, he was killed by the providence of God. Immediately one of the prefects who had been with him went away, sold everything he possessed, gave it to the poor, came to that old man, became a great monk, and so fell asleep in the Lord.

13. Once a certain layman came to Abba Sisoes on the mountain of Abba Antony, bringing his son with him [Col. 1003B] (Ruf., book III, no. 120). On the journey his son died, but the father was not disturbed. With faith he carried him to the old man, fell down with his son as though doing penance, and asked to receive the old man’s blessing.

The child’s father rose, left his son before the old man’s feet, and went outside the cell [Col. 1003C]. The old man, thinking that the boy was doing penance at his feet, said to him: “Rise and go outside.” For he did not know that he was dead.

The boy immediately rose and went outside. When his father saw him, he was terrified. He entered, worshiped the old man, and told him what had happened.

When the old man heard this, he was saddened, for he did not want this to happen. The old man’s disciple therefore ordered him to tell no one about it until the old man’s death.

14. Abraham, the disciple of that same Abba Sisoes, was once tempted by a demon. When the old man saw that he had fallen, he rose and stretched out his hands toward God, saying: “God, whether you wish it or not, I will not let go until you have healed him.”

And that brother was healed.

15. A certain solitary old man lived near the Jordan River [Col. 1003D]. Once, entering a cave because of the heat, he found a lion there. The lion began gnashing its teeth and roaring.

The old man said to it: “Why are you distressed? There is room enough for both you and me. If you do not wish to stay, rise and go outside.”

The lion could not endure this and went out.

16. Once an old man went up from Scetis to Teremuthis and stayed there. Seeing the severity of his abstinence, they offered him a little wine.

Others, hearing about him, brought him a man possessed by a demon. The demon began cursing the old man, saying: “You have brought me to this wine-drinker?”

Because of his humility, the old man did not want to cast the demon out. But because of the demon’s insult [Col. 1004A] he said: “I believe in Christ that, before I finish drinking this cup, you will leave him.”

When the old man began to drink, the demon cried out: “You are burning me!”

Before the old man had finished drinking, the demon left the man through the grace of Christ.

17. One of the Fathers sent his disciple to draw water. The well was very far from their cell, and the brother forgot to take a rope with him (Ruf., book III, no. 28).

When the brother reached the well and realized that he had not brought the rope, he prayed and cried out: “O well, well, my abba told me to fill this flask with water.”

Immediately the water rose to the top of the well. The brother filled his flask, and the water returned again to its place [Col. 1004B].

## THIRD BOOK

### On the excellent conduct of various holy men

Abba Dulas related:

“Once, as Abba Besarion, my abba, and I were walking in the desert (Ruf., book III, no. 194; Pasch., ch. 34, no. 3), we came beside a certain cave. When we entered it, we found a brother sitting there and weaving a mat from palm leaves. He did not wish to look at us, greet us, or speak with us at all.

“The old man said to me: ‘Let us go away from here; perhaps this brother does not want to speak with us.’

“We left and immediately went to see Abba John. When we returned, we again came by that cave [Col. 1004C] where we had seen the brother.

“The old man said to me: ‘Let us enter to see this brother, in case God has revealed to him that he should speak with us.’

“When we entered, we found that he had fallen asleep in peace.

“The old man said to me: ‘Come, brother, let us gather his body, for God sent us here for this very purpose: to bury him.’

“As we gathered him, we discovered that by nature he was a woman.

“The old man marveled and said: ‘Behold how women too struggle against the devil in the desert, while we are dishonored in the cities.’

“Therefore, glorifying God, who protects those who love him, we departed from there.”

2. Abba Vindemius said that Abba Macarius related the following:

Once, while I was sitting in Scetis, two young foreign visitors came down (Ruffinus, Book III, no. 195). One of them was beginning to grow a beard, while the other had not yet begun. They came to me and said, “Where is the cell of Abba Macarius?” I said to them, “Why do you want him?” They replied, “Having heard about him, we have come to Scetis to see him.” I said to them, “I am he.” They, repenting, said, “We wish to remain here.”

But when I saw that they were delicate, as though accustomed to wealth, I said to them, “You cannot stay here.” The older one said, “And if we cannot stay here, we shall go elsewhere.” So I said within myself, “Why am I driving them away and causing them to stumble? The labor itself will make them flee from themselves.” Then I said to them, “Come, make yourselves a little cell, if you can.” They said, “Only show us how, and we will do it.”

I gave them an axe, a basket [Col. 1005A] full of bread, and some salt. I also showed them a hard rock and said, “Cut here, and bring yourselves wood from the marsh; and when you have put on a roof, stay in the same place.” I thought they would flee because of the labor. But they asked me, “What shall we do here?” I said to them, “Plaiting palm leaves.” Taking palm leaves from the marsh, I showed them how to begin the plaiting and how they ought to sew it together. I also said to them, “Make baskets and give them to the church’s custodians; they will bring you bread.”

After this I withdrew from them. They patiently did everything I had told them, and they did not come to me for three years. I too endured, struggling with my thoughts, saying, “I wonder what their practice is, since they have not come to ask me about their thoughts? Those who come from far away come to me, but these, who are near me, have not come to me. Indeed, they have gone to no one else, except to the church, silently to receive the offering.”

Accordingly, I prayed to God while fasting for one week, asking him to show me their way of life. After that week I rose and went to see how they were living. When I knocked, they opened the door and silently greeted me. After making a prayer, I sat down. The older one signaled to the younger one to go out, and he himself sat down to plait, saying nothing.

At about the ninth hour he gave a signal by striking, and the younger one came and cooked a little stew. At the older one’s indication, he also set the table, placed three biscuits upon it, and stood there [Col. 1005C] silently. I said, “Rise; let us eat.” We rose and ate. He brought a small flask, and we drank.

When evening came, they said to me, “Are you going away from here?” I replied, “No, I will sleep here.” They placed a mat for me in one part of the cell and one for themselves in another corner. They also removed their belts and their half-belts, and lay down together on the mat before me.

When they had reclined, I prayed to God to reveal to me their practice. The roof of the cell opened, and there was a great light as bright as day, but they did not perceive that light. When they thought that I was asleep, the older one touched the younger one on the side. They rose, girded themselves, and, stretching out their hands toward heaven, stood silently.

I saw them, but they did not see me. I saw demons like flies coming upon the younger brother: some came to sit upon his mouth, others upon his eyes. And I saw an angel of God, bearing a fiery sword, surrounding him and driving the demons away from him. They could not approach the older one.

Toward morning they reclined again. I pretended to be waking up, and they did likewise. The older one said only this: “Shall we say twelve psalms?” I replied, “Yes.”

The younger one sang five psalms, six verses each, and one alleluia. With each word, a flame of fire came out of his mouth and ascended into heaven. Likewise, when the older one opened his mouth to sing, something like fiery smoke came out of his mouth and reached heaven. And I too said a little from my heart, as they did: “The work of God.”

As I went out, I said, “Pray for me.” They responded by silently bowing to me. I understood that the older one was perfect, while the enemy was still attacking the younger one.

After a few days the older brother fell asleep in the Lord, and on the third day the younger one did likewise. Whenever some of the Fathers came to Abba Macarius, he would lead them to their cell, saying, “Come and see the martyrdom of these young foreign visitors.”

2. Two of the Fathers asked God to show them to what measure they had attained. A voice came to them, saying, “In that village in Egypt there is a certain layman named Eucharistius, and his wife is called Maria; you have not yet attained their measure.”

The two elders rose and came to that village. After making inquiries, they found his cell and his wife. They said to her, “Where is your husband?” She replied, “He is a shepherd and is tending the sheep.” She brought them into her house.

When evening came, Eucharistius himself arrived with the sheep. Seeing the elders, he prepared a table for them and put water into a basin so that he might wash their feet. They said to him, “We will taste nothing unless you tell us about your way of life.”

Then Eucharistius said to them humbly, “I am a shepherd of sheep, and this is my wife.” But when the two elders persisted, asking him to tell them everything, he did not want to speak. Then they said to him, “The Lord has sent us to you.”

Hearing this, he was afraid and said to them, “Behold, we have these sheep from our parents. Whatever God gives me from them, we divide into three parts: one part for the poor, one part for receiving strangers, and the third part for our own use.

“Since I took a wife, neither I nor she has been defiled; she is a virgin. We sleep apart from one another; at night we put on sackcloth, and during the day our ordinary clothing. Until now no one has known these things.”

When the Fathers heard this, they were astonished and withdrew, glorifying God.

4. Once Abba Macarius the Egyptian [Col. 1006D] came from Scetis to the mountain of Nitria on the day of the offering, to the monastery of Abba Pambo. The elders of that place said to him, “Father, speak an edifying word to the brothers.”

He said to them, “I have not yet become a monk, but I have seen monks.” And he said:

“Once, while I was sitting in my cell in Scetis, my thoughts pressed me hard, saying, ‘Rise, go into the desert, and consider what you see there.’ For five years my mind resisted this, saying, ‘Perhaps this suggestion comes from demons.’

“When this thought persisted in me, I went into the desert and found a pool of water, with an island in its midst. Various animals of the desert came and drank from it. Among them I saw two naked men, and my body trembled, for I thought that they were spirits.

“When they saw me trembling, they spoke to me, saying, ‘Do not be afraid; we too are human beings.’ I said to them, ‘Where are you from, and how did you come to this desert?’ They said, ‘We were from a coenobium, but we reached an agreement and came out here. Behold, it has been forty years.’

“One of them was Egyptian, the other Libyan. They too asked me, saying, ‘How is the world? Has the water risen at its appointed season? Does the world still have its abundance?’ I answered them, ‘Yes.’

“I also asked them, ‘How can I become a monk?’ They said to me, ‘Unless someone renounces everything that is in the world, he cannot become a monk.’ I said to them, ‘I am weak and cannot be like you.’ They replied, ‘If you cannot be like us, remain in your cell and weep over your sins.’

“I asked them, saying, ‘Do you not feel cold in winter, or does your body not burn in the heat of summer?’ They said, ‘God has made this provision for us, so that in winter we feel neither cold, nor in summer the heat.’

“And so I said to you, ‘I have not yet become a monk. Forgive me, brothers.’”

5. Once Abba Sisoes was sitting alone on the mountain of Abba Antony. Because his attendant was delayed in coming to him, he had not seen a human being for ten months. As he was walking through the mountain, he found a Pharanite catching wild animals.

The elder said to him [Col. 1007C], “Where are you from, and how long have you been here?” He replied, “Truly, Abba, I have been on this mountain for eleven months, and I have seen no human being except you.”

When the elder heard this, he entered his cell and beat himself, saying, “Behold, Sisoes, you thought that you had accomplished something, yet you have not done what this layman has done.”

6. The same Abba Sisoes, while sitting in his cell, always kept his door closed (Ruffinus, Book III, no. 162). It was said of him that on the day of his falling asleep, while the Fathers were sitting around him, his face shone like the sun. He said to them, “Behold, Abba Antony has come.”

After a little while he said to them again, “Behold, the choir of prophets has come.” Again his face shone even more, and he said, “Behold, the choir of apostles has come.” [Col. 1007D] His face shone twice as brightly again, and behold, he seemed to be speaking with certain persons.

The elders asked him, saying, “With whom are you speaking, Father?” He said to them, “Behold, angels have come to take me, and I am asking that I be allowed to remain a little while to repent.”

The elders said to him, “You have no need of repentance, Father.” But he said to them, “Truly, I do not know that I have even made a beginning of repentance.”

And they all understood that he was perfect. Suddenly his face again became like the sun, and they were all afraid. He said to them, “Look, the Lord has come, saying, ‘Bring me the chosen vessel of the desert.’” Immediately he gave up his spirit. He became like lightning, and the whole place was filled with a fragrance of sweetness.

[Col. 1008A] 7. They said of Abba Hor [Note: [Col. 1022B] Hor.]:

Brother John Maria, master of the Sacred Palace, notes here in his index of expurgated books: “This is that heretical Origenist Hor or Or, whom Jerome mentions in his letter to Ctesiphon, whom the wretched Evagrius tried to pass off as a saint; therefore the shadow of his virtues has vanished into thin air.” Thus far his note.

But I have shown at length in the fourth general prologue that it was not Evagrius but Ruffinus who was the author of Book II of the Lives of the Fathers, in whose second chapter Hor or Or is mentioned.

They said of him that he never lied, never swore, never cursed anyone, and never spoke to anyone unless necessity required it.

8. The same Abba Hor said to his disciple, “Take care never to bring someone else’s word into this cell.”

9. Two great elders were walking in the desert near Scetis. Hearing the murmur of a voice from the ground, they searched for the entrance to a cave. Entering it, they found an old woman there, a holy virgin, lying sick.

They said to her, “When did you come here, old woman, and who serves you?” For they found nothing in the cave except her alone, lying there sick.

She said [Col. 1008B], “I have spent thirty-eight years in this cave of the desert, serving Christ with complete sufficiency, and I have seen no human being until today. God sent you, so that you might bury my body.”

When she had said this, she rested in peace. The Fathers glorified God, buried her little body, and returned to their own place.

10. They related concerning a certain solitary that he went out into the desert wearing only a linen sackcloth. After he had walked for three days, he climbed upon a rock and saw beneath it green grass and a man grazing like an animal.

He descended secretly and seized him. But since that elder was naked and could not endure the smell of human beings, he was distressed and could scarcely escape from his hands; then he fled. The brother also went out after him, running and shouting, “Wait for me, for I am following you because of God.”

But the elder turned and said to him, “I too am fleeing from you because of God.” After this the brother threw off the *levitio* (a garment) [Note: [Col. 1022C] *Levitionem*.] with which he was clothed and followed him.

The elder, seeing that he had cast off his clothing, waited for him. When he had come near, the elder said to him, “When you threw the material of the world away from you, I too waited for you.”

The brother asked him, saying, “Father, tell me a word by which I may be saved.” He said to him, “Flee human beings, be silent, and you will be saved.”

*Levitionem*: Thus the manuscripts and the Paris edition read it. Some printed editions have *lebetonem*, others *lebitonem*. This name is written and pronounced in various ways in Greek, hence the variation in Latin. See the *Onomasticon*.

11. A certain solitary was telling the brothers who were at Raithu, where there are seventy palm trees [Col. 1008D] [Note: [Col. 1022C] “At Raithu, where there are seventy palm trees.” The *Menologium*, January 14, concerning the forty-three martyrs at Raithu, says: “Where there are twelve springs and seventy palm trees,” which is likewise found in Greek in the *Menaea*. In Holy Scripture these palms are mentioned in Exodus 15, to which Saint Jerome alludes in Letter 4, to Rusticus: “And among the palm trees the bitterness of myrrh was displayed.”], about the place where Moses arrived with the people when he had come out of the land of Egypt (Exodus 15). He said:

“Once I thought that I ought to enter the inner desert, to see whether I might perhaps find someone living farther within the desert and serving our Lord Jesus Christ.

“Walking for four days and nights, I found a cave. When I came near, I looked inside and saw a man sitting there. I knocked according to the custom of monks, so that I might greet him when he came out. But he did not move, for he had rested in peace.

“Without hesitation I entered. When I took hold of his shoulder, he immediately dissolved and became dust. Then I looked and saw a *colobium* hanging there. When I took hold of that too, it dissolved and was reduced to nothing [Note: [Col. 1009D] Something similar, or perhaps the same account, is narrated by Paphnutius in the Life of Saint Onuphrius, chapter 2, by Metaphrastes, in Surius, volume III.].

“While I was troubled by this, I went out from there and walked through the desert. There I again found another cave and traces of a human being [Note: [Col. 1009D] In the already cited Life of Saint Onuphrius, chapter 3.]. I became more cheerful.

“When I approached the cave and knocked again, no one answered me. I entered, but found no one. Standing outside the cave, I said within myself, ‘This servant of God must come here, wherever he may be.’

“When the day had already passed, I saw buffaloes coming, and with them the servant of God, naked, covering the shameful parts of his body with the hair of his head. As he approached me, he thought that I was a spirit and stood in prayer, for, as he later said, he had often been troubled by spirits.

“Understanding this, I said to him, ‘Servant of God, I too am a human being. Look at my footprints and touch me, because I am flesh and blood.’ When, after the prayer, he had said ‘Amen,’ he looked at me, and, having been reassured, brought me into the cave. He asked me, saying, ‘How did you come here?’ I said to him, ‘I came into this solitude seeking servants of God, and God did not disappoint my desire.’

“I in turn asked him, saying, ‘How did you come here, how long have you been here, what is your food, and how, being naked, do you not need clothing?’ He said to me [Note: [Col. 1010D] In the already cited Life of Onuphrius, chapter 5, this hermit is called Timothy.]:

“‘I was in a coenobium in the Thebaid [Alternative: Thebaïs], and my work was weaving linen. A thought entered my mind that I should leave there and live alone: “You will be able,” it said, “to be at peace, receive strangers, and have a greater reward from what you earn by your work.”

“‘When I consented to this thought and carried it out, I left and built a monastery for myself. People came there and assigned work to me. When I had already accumulated a great deal, I was eager to distribute it to the poor and to strangers.

“‘But our adversary, the devil, envious of me—as he always is, and was then—was devising a way to deprive me of the reward that was to come to me, because I was eager to offer my labors to God.

“‘He saw a holy virgin assigning me patterns, which I completed and returned to her, and he prompted her to commission other patterns from me again. When familiarity had been established and confidence had increased, there was finally also touching of hands, laughter, and eating together. At last we conceived sorrow and gave birth to iniquity.

“‘After I had remained in that ruin for six months, I later thought, saying: “Whether today, tomorrow, or many years from now, I am destined for death, I shall have eternal punishment. If someone violates another man’s wife, he is rightly subjected to eternal penalties; of how many torments, then, is he worthy who has violated Christ’s bride?”

“‘Thus I secretly fled into this desert, leaving everything to that woman. Coming here, I found this cave, this spring, and this palm tree, which brings me twelve clusters of dates. Each month it brings me one cluster, which suffices for me for thirty days, and after that another ripens.

“‘After a long time my hair grew greatly, and when my garments began to tear apart, I covered with my hair the part of my body that ought to be covered.’

“While I was asking him again whether he had experienced difficulty at the beginning there, he said to me:

“‘At the beginning I was greatly afflicted with pain in the liver, so that, lying on the ground, I could not say a psalm standing; prostrate upon the earth, I cried out to the Most High.

“‘When I was in the cave in severe pain and weakness, so that I could no longer even go outside, I saw a man enter, stand beside me, and say, “What are you suffering?”

“‘Strengthened a little by him, I said, “My liver hurts.” He said to me, “Where do you feel pain?” When I had shown him, he joined the fingers of his hand together and divided that place as though with a sword. Tearing out the liver, he showed me its wounds; scraping the liver with his hand, he put the scabs into a cloth. Then, replacing the liver with his hands, he closed the place again.

“‘He said to me, “Behold, you have been healed. Serve our Lord Jesus Christ as you ought.” From that time I became well, and I have been here without difficulty.

“‘I earnestly asked him to let me remain in the inner desert. He said to me, “You cannot endure the attacks of the demons.” Considering this myself, I asked him to pray for me and then let me go. After he had prayed, he dismissed me.

“‘I have told you these things for your edification.’”

12. Another elder said the following [Note: [Col. 1010D] See also above, Book I, in the Life of Saint Onuphrius, chapters 1 and 2.]—he who also became bishop of the city of Oxyrhynchus, as though he had heard this from another, although he himself had done it:

“Once it seemed to me that I should enter the inner desert around Oase, where the Mazices live, to see whether I might perhaps find someone serving Christ.

“Taking a few biscuits and about four days’ supply of water in a vessel, I set out. After four days had passed and my food had been consumed, I wondered what I should do. Trusting, I set myself to continue.

“I walked another four days without food. When my body could no longer endure the fasting and the labor of the journey, I became faint-hearted and lay upon the ground.

“Someone came and touched my lips with his finger, as a physician might pass saliva over an eye. Immediately I was strengthened, so that I thought I had neither walked nor endured hunger.

“When I saw this power coming upon me, I rose and continued through the desert. After another four days had passed, I again became exhausted and collapsed. When I stretched out my hands toward heaven, behold, the man who had earlier strengthened me came again and, as though applying something to my lips with his finger, strengthened me.

“Seventeen days had passed, and after this I found a hut, a palm tree, and a man standing there, whose head-hair served as his clothing. His hair was entirely white with age, and he was terrifying in appearance.

“When he saw me, he stood in prayer. When he had finished with ‘Amen,’ he realized that I was human. Taking my hand, he asked me, saying, ‘How did you come here? Is everything in the world still as it was? Are there still persecutions?’

“I said to him, ‘For the sake of you who truly serve the Lord Jesus Christ, I traverse this desert. The persecution has ceased through the power of Christ. But please tell me: how did you come here?’

“He began to weep and lament, and said to me: ‘I was a bishop. When persecution arose and many punishments were inflicted upon me, and I could no longer endure the tortures, I later sacrificed.

“‘Then, coming to myself, I recognized my iniquity and gave myself over to death in this desert. I have lived here for forty-nine years in confession and supplication to God, asking whether my sin might perhaps be forgiven.

“‘The Lord has provided me with food from this palm tree, but I did not receive the comfort of pardon until forty-eight years had passed. In this present year I have been comforted.’

“As he said this, he suddenly rose, ran outside, and stood in prayer for a long time. When he had finished praying, he came to me. Looking at his face, I was terrified and trembled, for he had become like fire.

“He said to me, ‘Do not be afraid. God sent you so that you might carry my body to burial and commit it to the grave.’

“When he had finished saying this, he immediately stretched out his hands and feet and ended his life. I tore my tunic, kept half for myself, and wrapped the holy little body in the other half, hiding it in the earth.

“When I had buried him, the palm tree immediately withered and the hut collapsed. I wept bitterly, asking God whether he might somehow grant me that palm tree, so that I could remain in that place for the rest of my life.

“When this did not happen, I said within myself, ‘It is not God’s will.’ Praying, I again turned toward the inhabited world. And behold, the man who had anointed my lips appeared to me, strengthened me, and thus I recovered sufficiently to reach the brothers.

“I related these things to them, asking them not to despair of themselves, but through repentance to find God.”

13. A certain brother asked an elder, saying, “Is it a name that saves, or a work?” The elder replied, “A work.”

The elder continued: “I know of a brother who was once praying, and his prayer was immediately heard. A thought entered his mind: he wanted to see how the soul of a sinner and that of a righteous person are taken from the body.

“Since God did not wish to grieve him by denying his desires, while he was sitting in his cell a wolf entered, took the brother’s clothing in its mouth, and dragged him outside. The brother rose and followed it. The wolf led him to a certain city and then, leaving the brother there, withdrew.

“When the brother was sitting outside the city, at a monastery where someone lived who had a reputation like that of a great solitary, the solitary himself was ill and awaiting the hour of his death.

“The brother who had come there saw many candles and lamps being prepared because of that solitary, as though through him God supplied bread and water to the inhabitants of that city and preserved them. They were saying, ‘If he dies, we shall all die together.’

“When the hour of his departure came, the brother saw a Tartarean demon of hell descending upon that solitary, holding a fiery trident. He heard a voice saying, ‘Just as this soul did not let me rest, not even for one hour, so do not have mercy on it; tear it out.’

“The Tartarean demon then placed the fiery trident he was holding into the solitary’s heart, tortured him for many hours, and dragged out his soul.

“After this the brother entered the city and found a foreigner lying sick in the street, with no one to care for him. He stayed with him for one day.

“When the hour of his falling asleep came, the brother saw Michael and Gabriel descending for his soul. One sat at his right and the other at his left, and they asked his soul to come out. But it did not come out, as though unwilling to leave its body.

“Gabriel said to Michael, ‘Take this soul now, so that we may go.’ Michael replied, ‘We have been commanded by the Lord that it be brought out without pain; therefore we cannot tear it out by force.’

“Michael then cried out in a loud voice, saying, ‘Lord, what do you desire concerning this soul? It will not consent to us and come out.’

“A voice came to him: ‘Behold, I am sending David with the harp, and all those singing psalms to God in Jerusalem, so that when it hears the psalm at their voice, it may come out.’

“When they had all descended around that soul, singing hymns, the soul came out in this way and sat in Michael’s hands, and it was taken up with joy.”

14. The same person related again concerning a certain elder that he once came into a city to sell vessels that he had made. When he had spread them out, it happened that he sat before the door of a certain rich man who was already dying.

As the elder sat there, he saw black horses and their riders, black and terrifying, each holding a fiery staff in his hand. When they had reached the door, they left their horses outside, and each entered hurriedly.

When the sick man saw them, he cried out in a loud voice, saying, “Lord, help me!” But they said to him, “Now you remember God, when the sun has been darkened for you? Why did you not seek him until today, while the light of day still shone for you? Now, at this hour, you have no share in hope or consolation.”

15. The Fathers said that there was a certain Macarius who first established a monastery in Scetis (Ruffinus, Book I, chapter 29). That desert place is far from Nitria, requiring a day and a night of travel. There is also great danger for those going there: if someone strays even a little, he wanders in peril through the desert.

All the men there are perfect; no imperfect person can remain in that place so harshly, for it is utterly arid, without any consolation from the necessities of life.

Now this aforementioned Macarius, being a man from the city, once joined himself to the elder Macarius. When they came to cross the river Nile, it happened that they boarded a larger ship. Two military tribunes had also boarded it with great pomp. They had inside a carriage entirely of bronze, horses whose bridles were golden, attendant soldiers, boys wearing necklaces, and others with golden belts.

When those tribunes saw the two monks dressed in old rags and sitting in a corner, they praised their poverty. One of the tribunes said to them, “Blessed are you, who have mocked this world.”

The city-dwelling Macarius replied to them, “We have indeed mocked this world, but this world has mocked you. Yet know that you said this without intending it; both of us are called blessed, that is, both Macarii.”

The tribune was moved by his words. Returning home, he stripped off his clothing, became a monk, and began giving many alms.

16. They said concerning the same Abba Macarius [Note: [Col. 1022C] “Macarius.” Brother John Maria of Brisighella, mentioned above, notes here: “Read carefully this account of the skull found by Macarius, for since it does not fit well with the accepted theological positions, many reject it as apocryphal. See Bellarmine, Book II on Purgatory, chapter 18. Saint Thomas explains the same matter in Book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 45, question 2, article 2, response to objection 4. Consult Sixtus of Siena, annotation 45, Book V of the *Bibliotheca*. Thus far his note.

“Dionysius Carthusianus cites this story of the skull from Book IV of the *Lives of the Fathers*, in his booklet on the four last things, article 52. He abbreviates it, however, omitting what is said here about the relaxation of the punishments of the damned. I believe he did so because he saw that the matter was especially controversial among the scholastics, each of whom tried to interpret it.

“Bellarmine, volume II, controversy 3, Book II on Purgatory, chapter 18, thought that this story was found only in John Damascene, in his discourse on the dead. Since Damascene cites it from the *Historia Lausiaca* of Palladius, where it is not now found, Bellarmine considered the story false and apocryphal.

“But the story is mentioned in the Greek *Menaea*, January 19, and in this place in Pelagius, and above in Ruffinus, Book III, no. 172. John Damascene also relates it in his book on those who have fallen asleep in the faith, where he tells the story of Macarius in Greek as follows:

> Having questioned the dry skull about the dead, he learned many things. Moreover, no consolation at all is found for anyone. For the saint was accustomed to offer prayers for the dead, and he desired to know whether they were of any benefit. Therefore the Lord, who loves souls, wishing to show this and to assure his servant, breathed a word of truth into the dried skull: “Whenever you offer prayers for the dead, we perceive a little consolation.”

“Therefore some interpretation must be sought. See Saint Thomas on this matter in Book IV, distinction 45, article 2, question 2. He says that the damned do not receive any genuine mitigation of their punishments, but only some empty and deceptive joy—namely, when they see that they have companions in their punishments, just as demons rejoice when they deceive someone. In the same place Saint Thomas refutes the interpretations of various scholastics concerning this passage.

“Certainly, since the ancient scholastics labored to explain this matter, they did not regard it as apocryphal.”] the elder Macarius—because once, while walking through the desert, he found the head of a dead man lying on the ground (Ruffinus, Book III, no. 172, relates it somewhat differently). When he moved it with the palm branch that he held in his hand, the head spoke to him.

The elder said to it, “Who are you?” The head replied to the elder, “I was a priest of the pagans who lived together in this place. You, however, are Abba Macarius, who have the Holy Spirit of God.

“Whenever you have compassion upon those who are in torments and pray for them, they are then comforted a little.”

The elder said to it, “What is this consolation?” The head replied, “As far as heaven is from earth, so far is the fire beneath our feet and above our head. While we stand in the midst of the fire, no one can see his neighbor face to face.”

The elder said with tears, “Woe to the day on which a human being was born, if this is the consolation of punishment.”

Again the elder said, “Is there a torment worse than these?” The head replied, “A greater punishment lies beneath us.”

The elder said to it, “Who are those there?” The head said to him, “We who did not know God have at least a little mercy; but those who knew God and denied him, and did not do his will, are beneath us.”

After this the elder took the head and buried it.

17. Once, while the same Abba Macarius was praying in his cell (Ruffinus, Book III, no. 97), a voice came to him, saying, “Macarius, you have not yet attained the measure of those two women of that city.”

The elder rose in the morning, took his palm staff, and set out for the city. When he arrived, he found the place and knocked at the door. One woman came out and received him into her house. After he had sat down, he summoned the two women. When they came, they sat with him.

The elder said to them, “For your sake I have endured so much labor. Tell me now about your practice: what is it, and how do you live?”

They said, “Believe us: last night we were not without our husbands. What practice could we have?”

But the elder earnestly begged them to reveal their way of life. Then they said to him:

“We are strangers to one another according to the world, but it pleased us to marry two brothers according to the flesh. For fifteen years now, the two of us have lived in one house, and we do not know whether we have ever quarreled with one another, or whether one of us has ever spoken an indecent word to the other. We have passed all this time in peace and concord.

“A thought entered our minds to enter a monastery of virgins. We asked our husbands, but they did not consent to this. Since we were entirely unable to obtain such permission, we made a covenant between ourselves and God that until death no worldly speech would come out of our mouths.”

When Abba Macarius heard this, he said, “Truly I tell you: neither virgin, nor one living under a husband, nor monk, nor layperson; but according to each person’s purpose, God grants the Holy Spirit to all.”

18. The Fathers used to tell of a certain great elder that, as he was walking in the desert, he saw two angels accompanying him, one on his right and the other on his left [Col. 1014C]. As they walked, they came upon a corpse lying on the road. The elder covered his nostrils because of the stench, and the angels did likewise. After they had gone a little farther, the elder said: “Did you also smell that?” They replied: “Not at all; we covered our noses on your account as well. For we do not smell the uncleanness of this world, nor does it come near us; rather, we smell the souls that possess the stench of sins.”

## BOOK FOUR

Seven chapters of sayings sent by Abba Moses to Abba Poemen. Whoever observes them will be delivered from punishment.

1. The elder Moses said: “A person ought to be as one dead to his companion—that is, to die to his friend—so that he does not judge him in any matter” (Appendix to Martin, no. 109).

2. He said again: “A person ought to mortify himself with respect to every evil thing before he departs from the body, so that he may harm no one.”

3. He said again: “Unless a person has in his heart that he is a sinner, God does not hear him.”

A brother said to him: “What does it mean to have in one’s heart that one is a sinner?”

The elder said: “If someone carries his own sins, he does not see the sins of his neighbor.”

4. The elder said again: “Unless one’s conduct agrees with one’s prayer, a person labors in vain” (Ruffinus, book III, no. 202; Appendix to Martin, no. 35, under the name of Moses).

The brother said: “What does it mean for conduct to agree with prayer?”

The elder replied: “That we no longer do the things for which we pray. For when a person abandons his own will, God is reconciled to him and receives his prayers.”

The brother asked: “In all a person’s labor, what is it that helps him?”

The elder said to him: “It is God who helps. For it is written: ‘Our God is our refuge and strength, our helper in the tribulations that have come upon us exceedingly’ (Psalm XLV).”

5. The brother said: “What do the fasts and vigils that a person practices accomplish?”

The elder said to him: “They are what humble the soul. For it is written: ‘See my humility and my labor, and forgive all my sins’ (Psalm XXIV). If, therefore, the soul undertakes these labors, God will have mercy on it because of them.”

[Col. 1015B] 6. A brother asked the elder: “What should a person do in every temptation that comes upon him, or in every thought of the enemy?”

The elder said to him: “He ought to weep in the presence of God’s goodness, asking him to help him; and he will quickly find rest if he asks with understanding. For it is written: ‘The Lord is my helper, and I will not fear what man can do to me’ (Psalm CXVII).”

7. The brother asked him again: “Suppose a man beats his servant because of the sin he has committed. What should that servant say?” (Appendix to Martin, no. 37.)

The elder said to him: “If he is a good servant, he will say: ‘I have sinned; have mercy on me.’”

The brother said to him: “Nothing else?”

The elder said to him: “No. For as soon as he takes the blame upon himself and says, ‘I have sinned,’ his master immediately has mercy on him. The conclusion of all this is not to judge one’s neighbor.

“When the hand of the Lord killed the firstborn in the land of Egypt, there was no house in which someone had not died (Exodus XII).”

The brother said to him: “What does this saying mean?”

The elder replied: “If we look upon our own sins, we will not see the sins of our neighbor. For it is folly for someone who has his own dead person to leave him and go weep over the death of his neighbor.

“To die to your neighbor means to carry your own sins and to be without speculation about anyone—saying that this person is good and that one is evil. Do not do evil to anyone, do not think evil of anyone, do not despise anyone who does evil, do not consent to someone doing evil to your neighbor, and do not rejoice with one who does evil to his neighbor. This is to die to your neighbor.

“Do not speak evil of anyone, but say: ‘God knows each person.’ Therefore do not obey one who slanders, nor rejoice with him in his slander. Do not obey one who speaks evil of his neighbor. This is what is meant by: ‘Do not judge, and you will not be judged’ (Matthew VII).

“Do not be hostile toward anyone, do not retain hostility in your heart, do not hate the person who is hostile toward his neighbor, and do not consent to his hostility. Do not despise the person who is hostile toward his neighbor. This is peace.

“Console yourself with these thoughts: the labor is short, and the rest is everlasting, by the grace of God the Word. Amen.”

8. Another elder said: “For your sake, O man, the Savior was born; for this reason the Son of God came, so that you might be saved. He became man while remaining God; he became a child; he became a reader, taking the book and reading in the synagogue, saying: ‘The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach good news to the poor’ (Luke IV).

“He became a subdeacon; for, making a whip out of cords, he drove everyone—sheep, oxen, and the rest—out of the temple (John II).

“He became a deacon; for, girding himself with a linen cloth, he washed the feet of his disciples, commanding them to wash one another’s feet (John XIII).

“He became a presbyter and sat in the midst of the teachers, teaching (Luke XIII).

“He became a bishop; and, taking bread, he blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples (Matthew XXVI), and so forth.

“He was scourged for your sake, crucified, and died; on the third day he rose again and was taken up. He took everything upon himself for your sake; everything according to the divine dispensation, everything in order, everything consecutively he accomplished, so that he might save us. And you, for his sake, cannot endure?

“Let us be sober, let us keep watch, let us devote ourselves to prayers, so that by doing what pleases him we may be able to be saved.

“Was Joseph not sold in Egypt, in a foreign land? Were the three youths, captives in Babylon, known to anyone? Yet God protected them, received them, and glorified them, because they feared him.

“Whoever gives his soul to God has no will of his own; rather, while awaiting God’s decision, he does not labor anxiously. For if you wish to do your own will without God’s cooperation, you will be exceedingly wearied.”

9. A brother asked Abba Pastor: “What does it mean when it is written: ‘Do not worry about tomorrow’ (Matthew VI)?”

The elder said to him: “This is addressed to the person who is placed in temptation and is failing: he should not consider how much time he will spend in it, but should willingly accept what is for today and what is daily, as it comes.”

10. A brother asked Abba John: “How does a soul that has its own wounds not blush to slander its neighbor?”

The elder answered him by means of a parable: “There was a poor man who had a wife. When he saw another woman who was more beautiful, he also took her in marriage. Both women were naked.

“When there was a market in a certain place, they both asked him, saying: ‘We wish to go with you.’ He put them naked into a barrel, crossed over in a small boat, and came to the place.

“At midday, when one of them saw that the people had departed and that there was silence, she quickly leapt into a place near the barrel. Finding some old and torn rags, she girded herself with them and then confidently appeared to walk about.

“But the other, sitting naked inside, said to her husband: ‘Look, that prostitute is naked, and she is not ashamed.’

“The husband answered her sorrowfully: ‘What a marvel! She has at least covered her shame, whereas you, naked on every side, are not ashamed to condemn one who is partly clothed.’

“So it is with every slanderer who, not seeing his own evils, always accuses the faults of others.”

11. Certain brothers said to Abba Antony: “We wish to hear from you a word by which we may be saved.”

The elder said: “You have heard the Scriptures; let that be sufficient for you.”

They said: “But we also wish to hear it from you, Father.”

The elder answered them: “You have heard the Lord say: ‘If someone strikes you on the left cheek, offer him the other also’ (Matthew V).”

They said to him: “We cannot fulfill this.”

He said to them: “If, then, you cannot offer him the other also, at least endure patiently what comes upon one cheek.”

They replied: “We cannot do that either.”

He said to them: “If you cannot do even this, do not wish to strike rather than to be struck.”

They said to him: “We cannot do that either.”

Then the elder said to his disciple: “Prepare some broth for these brothers, because they have become exceedingly weak.”

Then he said to them: “If you can do neither this nor that, what shall I do for you? Therefore only prayer is necessary for you.”

12. Abba John used to tell certain brothers: “There were three philosopher friends, one of whom, when he was dying, entrusted his son to another” (Ruffinus, book III, no. 84).

“When the boy had advanced into young manhood, he committed adultery with the wife of the man who had raised him. When the crime became known, he was sent away.

“Afterward, when he repented exceedingly, the man did not permit him to return, but said to him: ‘Go and spend three years among the condemned men who deposit metals in the river; then I will forgive your offense.’

“When he returned after three years, he again said to him: ‘Go for another three years; pay to endure insults.’ He did this for another three years.

“Then the man said to him: ‘Now go to the city of the Athenians [Note: [Col. 1023B] “To the city of the Athenians.” The same passage occurs above, at Book CXI, no. 84. Gregory of Nazianzus, in his Oration in Praise of Basil, describes the ceremony by which young newcomers arriving at Athens were received: [Greek passage below].] so that you may learn philosophy.’

“There was an elderly philosopher sitting at the city gate, insulting those who entered. He therefore insulted that young man also. But the young man laughed at the insult.

“The elder said to him: ‘What is this? I insult you, and you laugh?’

“The young man said: ‘Do you not want me to laugh? For I have paid for three years in order to endure insults, and today I endure them for nothing. That is precisely why I laughed.’

“The elder said to him: ‘Go up and enter the city.’”

When Abba John had related this, he said: “This is the gate of the Lord, and our Fathers entered through it, rejoicing amid many insults.”

[Greek passage:]

“Whenever some young man arrived and came into the hands and power of those who had taken charge of him—for he came either by compulsion or willingly—this was their Attic custom, a game mingled with seriousness.

“First he was received as a guest by one of those who had taken him in hand earlier, whether a friend, a relative, or someone from the same homeland, or one of those who were distinguished in sophistry and skilled in attracting fees; and for this reason they were held in especially high honor by them, since it was a reward for them to obtain students.

“Then he was mocked by everyone who wished to do so. They did this, I think, in order to humble the spirit of the newcomers and bring them under their control from the beginning.

“He was mocked by the bolder men more boldly, and by the more reasonable men more reasonably, according as he possessed rusticity or urbanity.

“To those who did not know the custom, the affair seemed exceedingly frightening and savage; but to those who knew it beforehand, it was very pleasant and humane. For the display of threats was greater than the actual deed.

“Then he was led in procession through the marketplace to the bath. The procession was as follows: those who were conducting the young man arranged themselves in pairs, standing in a line at intervals, and escorted him to the bath.

“When they drew near, they raised a great shout and leapt about as though possessed by divine frenzy. The shout commanded them not to proceed farther but to stand still, as though the bath refused to admit them. At the same time they struck the doors, frightening the young man with the noise. Then, having allowed him to enter, they finally granted him his freedom, receiving him as their equal and as one of themselves when he came out of the bath.

“This was for them the most delightful part of the whole ceremony: the speedy release and liberation from those who had been troubling him.”

“From this custom there seems to have arisen the practice in certain academies by which newcomers proceeding from elementary schools to the public gymnasia of the academies were examined, trained, and ‘polished,’ as happens at Cologne, Basel, and several other academies of Germany. They call this the deposition of the Beanus. Elsewhere they are said to be stripped of their pupillage. See our Antonius Possevinus, Book I of the *Select Bibliotheca*, chapter 19; our Jacobus Pontanus, volume I of the *Dialogues on Latinity*, preliminary exercise 84; Jacobus Middendorpius, Book I *On Academies*, chapter 16.”]

13. Abba John said concerning a soul that desires to repent: “There was a very beautiful prostitute in a certain city who had many lovers. A certain man from among the rulers came to her and said: ‘Promise me your chastity, and I will take you as my wife.’

“When she had made the promise, he took her and brought her into his house.

“When her former lovers sought her, and learned that such a great man had taken her as his wife, they said: ‘If we approach the door of so powerful a man, and he discovers the desires of those who seek her, we shall undoubtedly be punished. But come behind the house and use our customary whistle. When she hears the sound of us whistling, she will come down to us, and we shall be found blameless.’

“When she heard this, she covered her ears, leapt into the inner part of the house, and shut herself in.

“Having spoken this way, the elder said that the prostitute is the soul, her lovers are the vices, the ruler or prince is Christ, and his house is the everlasting dwelling of the heavens; the whistlers are the evil demons. If, therefore, the soul remains chaste and faithful, it always runs to God.”

14. Abba Pastor said: “It is written in the Gospel: ‘Whoever has a tunic, let him sell it and buy himself a sword’ (Luke XXII). This means: Whoever has rest, let him abandon it and take up warfare.” By “warfare” he meant warfare against the devil.

15. The same elder said: “A certain elder lived in a cell in the regions of Egypt, and a brother and a certain virgin ministered to him. It happened one day that both of them arrived at the elder’s place at the same time. Since it was already late and they could not return to their own places, the elder placed a mat between them so that they could sleep.

“But the brother, unable to withstand the struggle with his flesh, violated the unfortunate virgin and ruined her. After the sin was completed, he departed in the morning.

“When the elder learned what had happened, he foresaw what was to come and remained silent at the time. As the elder accompanied them on their return, without showing any sign of distress, after he had left them they said to one another: ‘Do you suppose this elder understood our crime or not?’

“Then they returned, moved by repentance, and said: ‘Holy Father, did you understand how the enemy deceived us and cast us down, or not?’

“He answered: ‘I understood, my children.’

“They said to him: ‘And where was your thought at that hour of our death?’

“He said to them: ‘My thought was there at that hour where Christ was crucified. I was standing and weeping both for myself and for you. But because the Lord has promised your repentance, I urge you to apply yourselves diligently to treating the wound that you have suffered through pride.’

“After receiving from him a rule of repentance, they departed, each one courageously striving, until they could become chosen vessels.”

16. A certain philosopher asked Saint Antony: “How, Father, are you content when you are deprived of the consolation of books?”

He replied: “My book [Note: [Col. 1024C] ‘My book.’ Socrates, Book IV, chapter 18, citing this saying of Antony from Evagrius’ *Praktikos* or *The Monk* according to the Latin text, gives it in this form: [Greek passage]. ‘A certain one of those who at that time were considered wise approached Antony and asked: “How can you endure, Father, deprived of the consolation that comes from books?” Antony said: “My book, O philosopher, is the nature of created things, and whenever I wish, it is present to me so that I may read the words of God.”’ Thus it is customary for holy men to read God in created things.] is the nature of created things, which is accustomed to be present to me whenever I wish to read the words of God.”

[Greek passage:]

“A certain one of those who were then regarded as wise approached Antony and said: ‘How can you endure, Father, deprived of the consolation that comes from books?’

“Antony said: ‘My book, O philosopher, is the nature of created things, and whenever I wish to read the words of God, it is present to me.’”

17. Once, when someone came to Abba Macarius at midday, burning with excessive thirst in the heat and asking for water to drink, he said: “This shade is sufficient for you, though many travelers and sailors now need it and do not enjoy it.”

18. While I was speaking with the same elder about the practice of self-control, he said: “Take courage, my son; for I too, for twenty continuous years, was satisfied neither with bread, nor water, nor sleep. I received bread by weight and water by measure; as for sleep, I hurried to snatch only a little of it, merely leaning against the walls.”

19. A brother asked an elder whether he ought to eat when he went to visit certain brothers. The elder replied: “You will not eat with a woman.”

20. A certain brother asked Abba Isidore of Scetis about the thought of fornication. The elder answered him: “The thought of fornication does indeed come, disturbing and occupying the mind, but it is unable to bring the act to completion and makes no progress; it merely hinders virtue. But a sober man, driving it away from himself, immediately turns to prayer.”

21. The elder answered concerning the same thought: “If we had no thoughts, we would be like beasts. But just as the enemy demands what belongs to him, so we must fulfill what belongs to us. Let us persist in prayer, and the enemy is put to flight. Devote yourself to meditation on God, and you will conquer. Perseverance in what is good is victory. Strive, and you will be crowned.”

22. The elder said: “A person who keeps death before his eyes conquers cowardice at every hour.”

23. Abbess Syncletica said: “Our adversary is more easily overcome by those who possess nothing. For he has nothing with which to harm them, since most people, mindful of the distress and temptations that separate them from God, are accustomed to be struck through the loss of money and other possessions.”

24. Again the same woman said: “Those who gather visible riches through many labors and dangers at sea, while they acquire more, desire still more, and regard what they possess as nothing. But we refuse to possess even necessities for fear of God.”

25. The elder said: “Whoever binds a remembrance of malice in his soul is like someone hiding fire among straw.”

26. A certain elder said: “If you speak to someone about eternal life, speak the word to a listener with compunction and tears. Otherwise do not speak, lest you be found useless, hastening to save others by words that are not your own.

“For God said to the sinner: ‘Why do you recount my righteous acts and take up my covenant in your mouth?’ (Psalm XLIX).

“Say instead: ‘I am a dog; indeed, a dog is better than I, because it loves its master and will not come to judgment.’”

27. A brother asked an elder: “How does the soul love uncleanness?”

The elder said to him: “The soul often desires bodily passions, but it is the Spirit of God that restrains it. Therefore we must weep and attend carefully to our uncleanness.

“You have seen Mary: when she bent over the Lord’s tomb and wept, the Lord called her. So it will also be with the soul.”

28. A brother asked the elder: “What are sins?”

The elder said to him: “Sins are when a person despises his own offenses as though they were nothing and tries to teach others. Therefore the Lord says: ‘Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your eye, and then you will see to remove the splinter from your brother’s eye’ (Matthew VII).”

29. A brother asked the elder: “What shall I do, since my spirit wounds me over a small labor?”

The elder said to him: “We do not marvel at Joseph, when he was a boy in Egypt, in the land of those who worship idols: see how courageously he endured temptations, and God glorified him to the end.

“Let us also look at Job, who did not slacken in fearing God until the end; therefore no one was able to move him from hope in God.”

30. A certain soldier asked the elder whether God receives a repentant person. After strengthening him with many words, the elder finally said to him: “Tell me, my beloved: if your cloak is torn, do you throw it away?”

He answered: “No, but I mend it and use it.”

The elder said to him: “If, then, you spare your own garment, will God not show mercy to his own image?”

[Col. 1020A] 31. There was a brother in a cell who, after the sacred services had been completed and the priest had dismissed the church, would wait until everyone had gone out, so that someone might invite him to eat.

“One day, after the assembly had ended, he went out before everyone else and ran to his cell. The priest saw him running and was astonished.

“When that brother came to the church gathering a week later, the priest said to him: ‘Tell me, brother, what is the truth? What was the reason that at every assembly of the church you remained later than everyone else, whereas at the previous gathering you went out before everyone?’

“The brother answered him: ‘I was abstaining so that I would not have to cook for myself, and therefore I waited for someone to take me home to eat. But before coming to that gathering, I cooked a little lentil stew for myself; therefore, when the sacred mystery was completed, I went out before everyone else.’

“When the priest heard this, he issued an instruction in the church, saying: ‘Brothers, before you come to the church gathering, cook a little food for yourselves, so that because of it you may hasten eagerly back to your cells.’”

32. Once a judge of a certain region came into the province of Abba Pastor. The inhabitants of that place came and asked the abbot to go and plead with him.

He said to them: “Allow me three days, and then I will go.”

The elder prayed to the Lord, saying: “Lord, do not grant me this favor; otherwise people will not allow me to remain seated in this place.”

Then the elder went and pleaded with the judge.

The judge said: “Are you pleading for a robber, abba?”

The elder rejoiced because he had not obtained from the judge the favor he had requested, and so he returned to his cell.

33. The elders used to say: “When Moses entered the cloud, he spoke with God; when he came out of the cloud, he spoke with the people. So also, when a monk is in his cell, he speaks with God; when he leaves his cell, he is with the demons.”

34. A young man came to Abba Macarius to be healed of a demon. While he was standing outside, a certain brother from another monastery arrived and committed the sin of intercourse with that young man.

The elder came out, saw the brother sinning with the boy, and did not rebuke him, saying: “If God, who formed them, saw them and exercised patience toward them—though, if he wished, he could burn them—who am I to rebuke them?” [Note: [Col. 1019D] Macarius’ judgment is astonishing, but not to be imitated.]

35. They told of a certain elder who lived quietly in the lower regions of Egypt, and a faithful layman ministered to him. It happened that the layman’s son fell ill. The man earnestly begged the elder to come and pray for the boy.

The elder rose and went with him. The layman hurried ahead and confidently entered his house, saying: “Come out to meet the solitary.”

When the elder saw them coming out from a distance with lamps, he understood that they were coming to meet him. He removed his garments, threw them into the river, and began washing them while standing naked.

His lay attendant was ashamed when he saw him naked and said to those men: “Turn back, for this elder has lost his mind.”

Then he came to the elder and said: “Why have you done this? Everyone is saying: ‘This elder has a demon.’”

The elder said: “That is precisely what I wanted to hear.”

36. Certain elders asked Abba Pastor: “If we see a brother sinning, shall we rebuke him?”

Abba Pastor answered them: “For my part, if it is necessary to pass by that place and I see him sinning, I pass by and do not rebuke him. But because it is written: ‘Give testimony concerning what your eyes have seen’ (Proverbs XXV), I say to you: if you have not touched the matter with your own hands, do not testify.

“Sometimes a certain brother was deceived in a matter of this kind. It appeared to him that a brother was sinning with a woman. When he was greatly troubled by his thoughts, supposing that they were having intercourse, he went and kicked them with his foot, saying: ‘Stop now!’ And behold, they were bundles of wheat from the harvest.

“Therefore I say to you: unless you have touched the matter with your own hands, do not testify.”

37. They told of a certain brother who lived in the desert and was deceived by demons for many years, while he himself thought that they were angels.

His father according to the flesh would come from time to time and visit him. One day he took a double-bladed axe with him, saying: “When I return, I will bring back a little firewood.”

One of the demons went ahead and said to his son: “Look, the devil is coming to you in the likeness of your father, carrying a double-bladed axe in his basket, in order to attack you. Therefore, get ahead of him, take the axe from him, and resist him.”

His father then came as usual. The son took the axe from him, struck him, and killed him. Immediately the evil spirit clung to him and strangled him.

# THE SEVENTH BOOK OF THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS, OR SAYINGS OF THE ELDERS, BY AN UNKNOWN GREEK AUTHOR, TRANSLATED BY PASCHASIUS, DEACON OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH

[Col. 1025]

## PRELUDE

664 I have nothing to place before this book except what has already been said in General Prolegomenon 9, where we stated that its author is an unknown Greek whom I have not yet seen published by anyone, and in Prolegomenon 14, where we investigated Paschasius the translator.

[Col. 1025]

## Prologue

Paschasius to the venerable father Martin, presbyter and abbot.

At your command, most holy Father, you have ordered me to translate into Latin the *Lives of the Greek Fathers*, which, like the other books, were carefully composed with eloquence. If it had been permitted, I would have declined a work so unfamiliar. For nothing can ever be written, read, or published when talent or the conscience of the heart forbids it.

I do not dare to say that I know that I know nothing, lest I steal this saying from the most wise Socrates. But since it is equally necessary for me to make use of your command, I will not boast of talent; rather, I will fulfill even in this assigned work the fidelity that I owe you.

Since, however, there are very many books of eloquent men written in Latin, and although you yourself affirm and testify that you are experienced in reading them, if you happen to find anything from them inserted here that has been expressed less elegantly, I beg that it not be attributed to my fault. For just as I found those things written in the Codex given to me, so I translated them, although I do not claim that I am able to present even those passages with studied elegance.

It therefore remains for me to complete, with your prayers, what I began at your command. If, however, you decide that these things should be written down, I ask that you deign to polish them in your own style. For I will not know that some things pleased you unless I also learn that some displeased you.

[Col. 1025]

## SAYINGS OF THE ELDERS

[Note: [Col. 1061C] 686 A few things in this book require notice, since light is shed upon them by what was said above.] (G)*

## CHAPTER ONE

For overcoming gluttony and the desires of the belly

[Col. 1025A]

1. A certain brother asked Abba Sisoi how he ought to live in his own cell (Ruffinus, book III, no. 44).

Abba Sisoi answered him: “Eat your bread, your salt, and do not make it necessary for you to cook anything or wander farther away.”

To another who asked the same question, the prophet Daniel replied with the words: “I did not eat the bread of desires” (Daniel X).

2. One elder said to another elder who possessed love and received both many monks and laypeople: “A lamp indeed gives light to many, but it burns its own beak” (Appendix to Palladius, chapter 20, no. 9).

3. One of the Fathers said: “There is a person who eats a great deal and is still hungry, yet exercises self-control; another eats little and is satisfied. But the one who eats much and, while still hungry, exercises self-control has a greater reward than the one who eats little and is satisfied” (Ruffinus, book III, no. 48; Pelagius, booklet X, no. 99).

[Col. 1027A] 4. A certain elder said: “Never eat what you have desired; eat instead what the Lord has sent you, and give thanks” (Ruffinus, book III, no. 49).

5. A certain brother was troubled by a spirit of blasphemy and was ashamed to speak of it. Whenever he heard of any renowned elders, he went to them in order to disclose it to them; but as soon as he arrived, he was ashamed to speak (Ruffinus, book III, no. 57).

When he nevertheless came frequently to Abba Pimen, the elder saw that he had thoughts and said to him: “Look, you frequently come to me with thoughts, and then you return again in sorrow, carrying them with you. Tell me, my son, what is it that you have?”

He said: “The devil troubles me with blasphemy, and I am ashamed to speak of it.”

As soon as he disclosed the matter, his affliction appeared lighter.

The elder said to him: “Do not be troubled, my son. Whenever this thought comes, say: ‘I have no need of this matter. Let your blasphemy be upon yourself, Satan.’ For the soul does not desire this matter, and whatever the soul does not desire will not remain long.”

And so that brother departed.

6. Abba Moses said: “The passion of impurity is generated by these four things: abundance of food and drink, satiety of sleep, idleness and joking, and walking about in ornate clothing” (Ruffinus, book III, no. 58).
