7. The same man said: “There are many bodily passions.”

The brother said to him: “And what are they, abba?”

He replied: “The apostle Paul says: ‘Fornication and uncleanness, or every kind of greed, must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints’ (Ephesians V). Sight also and self-confidence frequently come to battle.”

8. Abba Macarius related that, while he was living in that solitude where he dwelt alone—below it there was another desert, full of many brothers—he was looking along the road one evening and saw a demon coming in the form of a man dressed in a linen tunic pierced with holes. Small vessels hung from each of the holes.

The elder said to him: “Where are you going, evil one?”

He answered: “I am going to remind the brothers who are below.”

The elder said: “Why are you carrying so many little vessels with you?”

He said: “I am bringing tastes for the brothers. I carry so many so that, if one does not please them, I may offer another; and if that one also displeases them, I may show them another. Thus it cannot fail that one of them will please them.”

Having said this, he departed.

The elder remained in the same place, again watching the road, until the demon returned and he learned what he had accomplished.

When he returned, the elder said to him: “May you be safe.”

He answered: “What use is that word to me? Everyone has become opposed to me, and no one accepts my counsels.”

The elder said to him: “Then do you have no friend there?”

He replied: “I have one friend; he agrees with me. Whenever he sees me going here and there, he quickly turns toward me like the wind.”

When the elder asked him his name, he said: “He is called Theopistus” [Ruffinus: Theopemptus; Pelagius: Theoctistus]. And immediately he vanished.

Abba Macarius rose at once and went down to the lower desert.

When the brothers saw him from a distance, they came out to meet him, and each one, hoping that he would remain with him, prepared himself.

But he asked for the cell of Theopistus and went to him. When Theopistus had received him joyfully and the two were alone, Abba Macarius said to him: “How are things with you, brother?”

He answered: “For the present, through your prayers, things are well.”

The elder said: “Do thoughts not trouble you?”

He replied: “For the present I am well.” For he was ashamed to speak.

The elder said to him: “Look, I have been in the desert for so many years, and I am honored by everyone; yet at this age, although I am an old man, troublesome thoughts still afflict me.”

Theopistus answered: “Believe me, abba, they afflict me as well.”

Then the elder pretended that each thought was attacking him, until Theopistus confessed everything to him.

Afterward the elder said: “How do you fast?”

He answered: “Until the ninth hour.”

The elder said to him: “Fast until evening, and from the Gospel or the other Scriptures meditate continually on something without ceasing. Whenever a thought comes upon you, never look downward, but direct the eyes of your heart upward, and immediately the Lord will be your helper.”

And so he departed for his own solitude.

While he persisted in prayer and watched the road, he again saw the same demon and asked him: “Where are you going?”

He gave the same answer, that he was going to remind the brothers.

When he was returning, the elder asked him: “How are the brothers now?”

He said: “Badly, because they have all become wild; and what is worse than everything else, the one friend I had who obeyed me has somehow changed and is more difficult than all the rest. I have sworn not to set foot in that place again until a long time has passed.”

Having said this, he departed.

9. A certain brother asked Abba Pimen about his thoughts. The elder answered: “If a monk rejects the belly, luxury, and the tongue, and does not pursue wandering, I trust that he will not die but will live forever” (Ruffinus, book III, no. 63; Pelagius, booklet V, no. 9).

10. Two brothers came to Abba Elijah, troubled by thoughts (Ruff., bk. III, no. 64). Seeing that they were corpulent, the old man, smiling as though at his disciple, said: “Truly, brother, I am ashamed on your account, because you have so fattened your body in this way [Col. 1028D]; for we are food for worms, while you profess to be a monk. Pallor together with humility, and emaciation, are a monk’s adornment.” He also said: “A monk who eats much and works much should not be confident; but he who eats little—even if he works little—should be confident and act manfully.”

## CHAPTER II. Against love of money, and concerning complete renunciation

1. A certain young man wanted to renounce the world (Ruff., bk. III, no. 67; Pelag., booklet XIV, no. 4), but whenever he went out of his house, thoughts entangling him in many affairs called him back; for he was extremely wealthy. One day, as he went out, unclean enemies surrounded him and raised a great cloud of dust [Col. 1029A] before him. He immediately stripped himself, threw away his clothes, and ran naked to the monastery. God revealed this to a certain old man, saying: “Rise and receive my athlete.” So the old man arose and went out to meet him naked. After learning the reason, he marveled and gave him the monastic habit. Whenever people came to the old man to ask about various thoughts, he instructed them concerning renunciation of the world and said: “Ask that brother who did not even keep the clothing on his body, for I have not yet attained the measure of this man’s renunciation.”

2. Abba Paul of Galatia used to say: “If a monk wants to keep in his cell any possessions beyond those without which he cannot live, he is often compelled [Col. 1029B] to leave his cell, and in this way he is led astray and deceived by demons” (Ruff., bk. III, no. 72). This same Paul once endured an entire Lent with a sextarius of lentils and a small vessel of water, making one mat and repeatedly weaving and unweaving it, so that he would not go outside even once.

3. A certain brother asked an old man, saying: “Do me a kindness, abba, and tell me what I should accumulate in my youth so that I may have it in old age.” The old man replied: “Either acquire Christ and think about yourself, or else acquire money, so that you will not have to beg. Therefore it is yours to choose either the Lord God or Mammon.”

4. Abba Agathon frequently admonished his disciple, saying: “Never acquire anything for yourself that you would be reluctant to give to a brother who asks you for it, and thereby be found transgressing God’s commandments. Give to the one who asks you, and do not turn away from the one who wants to borrow from you” (Luke VI).

## CHAPTER III. A monk should grieve over nothing if he has lost or been deprived of something

1. While Abba Macarius was in Egypt, he went out of his cell. When he returned, he found a thief stealing whatever he had in his cell (Ruff., bk. III, no. 73; Pelag., booklet XVI, no. 6). He therefore stood there himself like a traveler, loaded the animal together with the thief, and with great patience led him away, saying: “We brought nothing into this world” (1 Tim. VI). “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased him, so it has happened. Blessed be the Lord in all things.”

[Col. 1029D] 2. A certain brother who lived near a great old man would secretly enter his cell and steal whatever the old man had (Ruff., bk. III, no. 74; Pelag., booklet XVI, no. 19). When the old man noticed this, he did not rebuke him, but worked even more, saying: “I suppose that brother is in need.” The old man consequently suffered great hardship from lack of bread. When he was about to die and the other brothers had gathered around him, he saw the brother who used to steal from him and said: “Come here to me, brother.” Taking his hands, he kissed them and said: “I give thanks to this brother’s hands, because on his account I believe I am going into the kingdom of heaven.” The other man [Col. 1030A], pierced with remorse and repenting, himself became an earnest monk, having observed these deeds.

## CHAPTER IV. Endurance of poverty leads to rest

1. One of the old men used to say: “We find nothing written about that poor Lazarus indicating that he had performed any virtue, except this alone: he never murmured against the rich man, although the latter showed him no mercy. Rather, he bore the burden of his poverty with thanksgiving; and therefore he was received into Abraham’s bosom.”

2. He also said: “No one ought to think about anything except the fear of God. For even if he is compelled to be concerned about bodily necessity, he should never think about it before the proper time.”

## CHAPTER V. On restraining greed

[Col. 1030B]

1. When Abba Silvanus had gone a short distance from his cell, his disciple Zacharias, together with other brothers, removed the garden fence and enlarged the garden. When the old man returned and learned what had happened, he took up his cloak to leave. They threw themselves at his feet and begged him to explain why he was doing this. Then the old man said: “I will not enter this cell unless the fence has been restored to its place.” As soon as this had been done, he returned.

2. A certain brother asked an old man: “If a brother owes me a few coins, do you command me to ask him for them again?” (Ruff., bk. III, no. 170.) The old man replied: “Tell him just once, with humility.” He said: “But if I tell him once and he gives me nothing, what should I do?” The old man said: “Say nothing more to him.” He replied again: “And what should I do? I cannot overcome my thought unless I persist with him.” The old man said to him: “Dismiss your thoughts; only do not distress your brother, because you are a monk.”

3. When people wanted to buy the work of his hands, Abba Agathon sold it peacefully. The price was one hundred coins for a sieve, and two hundred fifty for a basket. He stated the price to those who wished to buy, and whatever they gave him, he accepted silently, never counting it. He used to say: “What benefit is it to me to argue with them, perhaps causing them to sin by swearing, and then, when the coins exceed the price, distributing them [Col. 1030D] to the brothers? For God does not want such almsgiving from me, nor does he approve of my allowing anyone to sin while making an offering.” When a brother said to him: “Where, then, will bread for the cell come from?” he replied: “What business does human bread have in the cell?”

## CHAPTER VI. Against anger, and concerning the origin of anger

1. One of the holy Fathers said (Ruff., bk. III, no. 76): “Anger arises through these four actions: through the greed of giving and receiving, and of seizing what belongs to others; when someone loves and defends his own opinion; when someone wants to be considered worthy of honors; and when someone wants to be a teacher, hoping to be wiser than everyone else. Anger also darkens the human senses through these four things: when a person hates his neighbor, regards him as worthless, envies him, or disparages him. In support of this I will present the holy evangelist John as an authority: ‘The one who hates his brother,’ he says, ‘is in darkness, and does not know where he is going, and remains in death’ (1 John II).

“The retribution for this passion has four forms: first, in the heart; second, in the face; third, in the tongue; fourth, in deed. If someone can bear an evil in such a way that it does not enter his heart, it does not reach his face. If it reaches his face, let him guard his tongue so that he does not speak it. But if he has spoken it, let him at least guard himself from carrying it out in deed, and immediately cut it off from his heart.

“There are three classes of people in the passion of anger. The one who willingly harms no one, does not insult those who resist him, and spares his neighbor is according to the nature of Christ. The one who neither harms another nor wants to be harmed is according to Adam. But the one who harms others, insults them, brings accusations against them, or exacts interest is according to the devil.”

2. Some brothers came to Abba Antony and asked to hear from him a word by which they might be saved (Joan., booklet IV, no. 11). He said to them: “You have heard the Scriptures, and you know what is sufficient for you from Christ.” But they persisted, asking him to be willing to say something to them himself. Then he said to them: “The Gospel says: ‘If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also’” (Matt. V). They said that they could not do this. The old man replied: “You cannot offer the other? Then at least endure it if he wishes to strike that one again.” When they testified that they could not do even this, the old man said to them: “Then if you cannot do this, do not repay evil for what you have received.” When they repeated the same statement they had made earlier, Abba Antony said to his disciple: “Go and prepare food for them, so that they may eat; you see that they are very weak.” And he said to them: “If you cannot do this, and do not want to do the other, what are you asking of me? As I see it, you need prayer, by which your weakness may be healed.”

## CHAPTER VII. Returning good for evil

1. One of the brothers, having suffered an insult from another, came to Abba Sisoes. After explaining the kind of abuse, he added: “I want to avenge myself” (Ruff., bk. III, no. 77; Pelag., booklet XVI, no. 10). The old man asked him to leave vengeance to God. But he said again: “I will not stop until I have taken strong revenge.” Abba Sisoes replied: “Since you have once set this in your heart, at least let us pray.” The old man rose and began to pray in these words: “God, you are no longer necessary to us, to care for us, since we ourselves, as this brother says, both want and can take revenge.” When that brother heard this, he fell at the old man’s feet and begged forgiveness, promising that he would never again quarrel with the man against whom he was angry.

2. When a certain brother was being insulted by another, he came and reported it to an old man (Ruff., bk. III, no. 78). The old man [Col. 1032A] replied: “Satisfy your thought, for the brother does not want to insult you; rather, your sins are bringing this upon you. In every temptation that comes upon you, do not accuse him in any way; say only: ‘These things are happening to me because of my sins.’”

3. Abba Pimenius often used to say: “Evil never overcomes evil; but if someone does evil to you, return good to him, so that through goodness you may conquer evil” (Ruff., bk. III, no. 79; Pelag., booklet X, no. 53).

4. There was a certain brother (Ruff., bk. III, no. 80; Pelag., booklet XVI, no. 12) who, the more someone insulted or provoked him, the more he went back to that person, saying: “These are the people who give us the opportunity for our perfection; those who bless us deceive us and overturn the path of our feet [Col. 1032B]” (Isa. III).

5. There was another old man who, if anyone slandered him, hurried—if the person lived nearby—to repay him with good in person; but if he lived farther away, he sent him gifts (Ruff., bk. III, no. 11).

## CHAPTER VIII. Not retaliating against enemies

1. A certain brother asked Abba Sisoes (Ruff., bk. III, no. 82): “If thieves or barbarians attack me, intending to kill me, and I overcome them, do you command me to kill them?” He replied: “Do not do this, lest you be called a murderer; but commit everything to God. Whatever adversity befalls you, acknowledge that it comes upon you because of your sins; but if you obtain anything good, you must attribute it all to divine providence.”

2. There was a great hermit on a mountain called Athabeos [Ruffin.: Athlibeus], and thieves came upon him (Ruff., bk. III, no. 83). When he raised his voice, other brothers from the surrounding places gathered and seized them. The judge had them taken to the city and sent to prison. The brothers were greatly distressed because the thieves had been handed over to punishment on their account. They came to Abba Pimenion and told him what had happened. He wrote to the hermit, saying: “Remember the first betrayal—where it came from—and then you will see the second betrayal. For if you had not been betrayed by what was within you, you would never have committed this second denunciation.”

When he heard such words, he was pierced with remorse [Col. 1032D]. Since he was well known in that region and had not left his cell for a long time, he nevertheless rose, went into the city, drove the thieves from the prison, and publicly set them free.

## CHAPTER IX. Perfect patience

1. Someone saw a man laboriously carrying a dead person on a bed (Pelag., booklet XVI, no. 11) and said to him: “Are you carrying the dead? If you want to do something better, carry the living, for the peacemakers will be called sons of God” (Matt. V).

2. When some brothers asked Abba Moses for a word, he encouraged his disciple Zacharias to say something to them. Then Zacharias took off his cloak, put it under his feet, trampled on it, and [Col. 1033A] said: “Unless someone has been trampled in this way, he cannot be a monk” (Ruff., bk. II, no. 86; Pelag., booklet XV, no. 17).

3. Blessed Antony prophesied to Abba Ammon, saying: “You have much progress to make in the fear of God.” He led him out of his cell, showed him a stone, and said to him: “Go and insult this stone and beat it without ceasing.” When he had done this, Saint Antony asked him whether the stone had answered him anything. He said: “No.” Abba Antony said to him: “You too will reach this measure, so that you will consider no insult to have been done to you.”

## CHAPTER X. That, for the sake of peace, one ought to abandon works even though they are good

1. Abba Motois built a monastery for himself in a place called Heracleona (Ruff., bk. III, no. 94). When he was troubled there by many people, he moved to another place and likewise built a monastery there. But through the envy of the devil, a certain brother was found there who was always angry with him. So he rose, left that place, and returned to his own village. There he built a monastery and shut himself in.

After some time, the old men of the place from which he had returned gathered together, bringing with them the brother with whom he had quarreled, so that they could ask him to take them back into his monastery. When they had reached the neighboring area, they left both their cloaks and that brother there, and went on to the old man themselves. When they knocked, he opened the window, looked out, and recognized them. After prayer, Abba Motois said to them: “Where are your cloaks?” They replied: “Look, they are nearby, together with the brother who had been angry with you.”

When the old man heard this, and learned that brother’s name and that he had come, he broke down with an axe the door through which he had entered, went out, ran to the place where the brother was, and himself began first to repent before him. Embracing him, he brought him into his cell and feasted with them for three days, although he had never been accustomed to break his fast. Then he rose and departed with them.

2. A certain brother asked Abba Elijah: “If I have saddened someone, how should I ask forgiveness?” The old man replied: “From the depths of your heart, repent before him with sorrow [Col. 1033D]; and when God sees your purpose, he will reconcile him to you.”

## CHAPTER XI. Against the spirit of sadness, which produces despair

1. Abba Arsenius said: “An unbaked brick, if it is placed in a foundation near a river, cannot endure even for one day; but if it has been well baked, it remains like a stone” (Pelag., booklet XV, no. 51, under the name of Orsisius). So too the person who has not been baked and kindled, as it is said of Joseph, “The word of the Lord kindled him” (Ps. CIV), is immediately dissolved at the beginning of a carnal thought.

2. The same old man was questioned by another brother, who said: “If I sin—even in some very small sin—and my thought consumes me and reproves me, saying, ‘Why did you sin? What shall I do?’” The old man replied: “At whatever hour a person falls into guilt and says from the heart, ‘Lord God, I have sinned; forgive me,’ that consuming of thought or sadness will immediately cease.”

3. Abba Pimenius used to say of Abba Isidore that he alone had known himself (Ruff., bk. III, no. 101). Whenever his thought said to him, “You are great,” he would answer himself: “Surely I am not such as Antony, or perhaps Abba Piamon, or the other Fathers who pleased God?” Whenever he considered these things, he found rest. But when the enemy, troubling him, suggested despair and punishment, saying, “After all this you are going to torments,” he said: “Even if I am sent to torments, I shall still find you beneath me.”

4. Evil spirits often appeared to Abba Moses (Ruff., bk. III, no. 102), saying: “You have defeated us, and we can do nothing to you. Whenever we want to humble you through despair, you are exalted; whenever we want to exalt you, you humble yourself so much that none of us approaches you.”

5. When someone frequently asked Abba Sisoes this question (Ruff., bk. III, no. 103), “What shall I do, Father, because I have fallen?” he replied: “Rise.” And he rose. Again he confessed that he had fallen. The old man said: “Rise again.” When the brother repeatedly reported that he had fallen, the old man used the same word, crying out: “Do not stop rising, my son.” The brother said to him: “How long can I keep rising, Father? Explain this to me.” The old man said: “Until you are found lying down either in a good work or in an evil one. For in whatever work a person is found, he will be judged.”

6. He also said: “The one who labors and supposes that he has done something receives his reward here.”

## CHAPTER XII. Against the spirit of vain glory

1. A certain brother asked Abba Pimenius whether it was better to live farther away or to remain with others (Ruff., bk. III, no. 110). The old man replied: “If a person reproves himself, he can persevere anywhere; but if he magnifies himself, he stands nowhere, as it is written: ‘The one who considers himself to be something, when he is nothing, deceives himself’” (Gal. VI). Whatever one person does for another, let him not exult in it, because he will soon lose it.

[Col. 1034D] 2. If anyone wished to hear Abba Macarius with fear, as though he were a holy man, he, being viewed with suspicion, received absolutely no answer from the old man. But if someone addressed him as though despising him, with words such as: “Abba Macarius, when you were a camel-driver and stole nitre, were you not beaten by your masters when you were caught stealing?” he gladly answered him with joy, whatever he asked.

3. As Abba Nesteron was walking with other brothers in the desert, they saw a dragon and fled (Pelag., booklet VIII, no. 12). One of them said to him: “Do you also fear, abba?” The old man replied: “I do not fear, my son, but I ought to flee; for if I had not fled, I would not have escaped the thought of vain glory.”

[Col. 1035A] 4. Once an Egyptian brother came to Abba Zeno in Syria and began accusing his own thoughts in the old man’s presence (Ruff., bk. III, no. 111). When he heard this, the old man marveled and said: “The Egyptians conceal the virtues they possess and reveal the vices they do not possess; but the Syrians and Greeks proclaim the virtues they do not possess and conceal the vices they do possess.”

5. When one old man came to another old man, he said: “I am dead to this world” (Ruff., bk. II, no. 116; Pelag., booklet XI, no. 38). The other replied: “Do not trust yourself until you have left this body. Even if you say, ‘I am dead,’ the devil is not yet dead, and his evil arts are innumerable.”

6. When Abba Sisoes had fallen into ecstasy while sitting in the presence of another brother, and had sighed without knowing that the other was listening [Col. 1035B], he began to repent and say: “Forgive me, brother, I beg you; for I do not yet know myself to be a monk, since I sighed while another was listening.” Whenever the same old man stood in prayer and raised his hands to heaven, he quickly lowered them, lest, if another were present, the act itself should count as praise for him.

7. A certain old man lived in the lower parts of Egypt and sat in quiet (Ruff., bk. III, no. 118; John, booklet IV, no. 35). A devout layman ministered to him. It happened that the layman’s son fell ill. After many prayers, he begged the old man to come to his house and pray for the child. The old man rose and walked with him. The layman went ahead, entered his house, and said: “Come out to meet the hermit.” When the old man saw them coming from a distance with lamps, he realized that they were coming to meet him. He immediately stripped off his clothes, threw them into the river, and began washing while standing naked. His attendant, seeing this, was ashamed. He begged the people, saying: “Go back; our old man has lost his senses.” Coming to him, he said: “Abba, what is this that you have done? Everyone who saw you said: ‘The old man is possessed by a demon.’” He replied: “That is precisely what I wanted to hear.”

8. On another occasion, one of the judges wanted to see him. Clerics went ahead and said to him: “Abba, prepare yourself, because the judge, having heard of your deeds, will come to you, wishing to receive your blessing” (Pelag., booklet VIII, no. 18, under the name of Simon). He replied: “I will do so; I will prepare myself.” He put on his lebeton [Note: [Col. 1061C] Pelagius, booklet VIII, no. 18, has ‘sackcloth.’ See the Onomasticon.] and, taking bread and cheese in his hands, climbed up to the gate. Sitting there with his legs spread apart, he began to eat. When the judge arrived with his retinue and saw him, he said: “Is this the hermit of whom we heard such things?” And despising him, he departed.

## CHAPTER XIII. Against the spirit of pride

1. A certain old man said: “The one who is more greatly honored or praised by people suffers no small loss; but the one who is not honored by people receives glory from above” (Ruff., bk. XIII, no. 112; Pelag., booklet XV, no. 56).

2. He also said: “It is impossible for grass and seed to grow at the same time; so it is impossible for us, while possessing the praise and glory of worldly people, also to produce heavenly fruit” (Ruff., bk. III, no. 113; Pelag., booklet VIII, no. 20, under the name of Syncletica).

3. He also said (Ruff., bk. III, no. 115; Pelag., booklet XV, no. 54): “When the thought of pride—or of vain glory—attacks you, examine yourself: Have you kept all God’s commandments? Do you love your enemies? Do you rejoice in the glory of your enemy and grieve at his downfall? Do you regard yourself as an unprofitable servant and as a greater sinner than all other people? Even then, do not think yourself anything great, as though you had done some good, knowing that this exalted thought dissolves all good things.”

4. The old man said to someone (Pelag., booklet XV, no. 55): “Do not set your heart against your brother, saying: ‘How are you more sober than he, and more self-controlled?’ Rather, submit yourself to God’s grace in a spirit of poverty and through genuine love, lest you lose your labor through a spirit of exaltation.”

5. The old man also said: “To the extent that a person lowers himself in humility, to that extent he also advances upward” (Ruff., bk. III, no. 171; Pelag., booklet XV, no. 77). For just as pride, if it rises to heaven, is brought down to hell, so humility, if it descends to hell, will then be exalted to heaven.

[Col. 1036C] 6. When Abba Macarius was returning to his cell at dawn, carrying palm leaves, the devil met him with a very sharp sickle, wanting to strike him, but he was unable to do so (Ruff., bk. II, no. 124; Pelag., booklet XV, no. 26). The devil cried out: “I suffer great force from you, Macarius. When I want to harm you, I cannot; yet in everything you do, I surpass you even more. You sometimes fast, but I am never refreshed by any food. You often keep vigil, but sleep has never overcome me. In one thing, however, you defeat me—I confess it.” When Macarius asked him what that was, he replied: “Your humility alone defeats me.” As the enemy said this and blessed Macarius stretched out his hands in prayer, the unclean spirit vanished into the air.

7. One of the Fathers used to say: “Every labor without humility is vain” (Ruff., bk. III, no. 126). Humility is the forerunner of love. Just as John was the forerunner of Jesus, drawing everyone to him [671], so humility draws one to love—that is, to God himself—because God is love.

8. A certain brother asked an old man: “What is humility?” The old man replied: “It is a tree of life, growing upward” (Pelag., booklet XV, under the name of Hyperichius).

9. He also said: “The earth on which God said that he wished sacrifice to be offered is humility” (Pelag., booklet XV, no. 37, under the name of Pastor).

10. When an old man was again asked, “How can the soul attain humility?” he replied: “If a person considers only his own evils.” He also said [Col. 1037A]: “Humility is the perfection of a person” (Ruff., bk. III, no. 171; Appendix to Martin, no. 58).

11. Abba Motois said: “Humility neither becomes angry itself nor permits others to become angry.”

12. He also said: “Humility is this: if your brother has sinned against you, forgive him before he repents” (Pelag., booklet XV, no. 60).

## CHAPTER XIV. How perfect men, although able, do not wish to perform miracles, lest they become exalted

1. As Abba Joseph was coming with other brothers to Abba Pimenius (Ruff., bk. III, no. 168; John, booklet II, no. 10), one of the relatives of the aforementioned old man Pimenius brought a child whose face had been disfigured by a seizure of the devil. The child’s father sat outside the monastery with him and wept. When one of the old men came out at the sound of the weeping and asked him why he was crying, he replied: “I am a relative of Pimenius, and for this reason I have come, so that he might see this child. You see, lord, what affliction Satan has brought upon this child. Until now we were afraid to bring him here, because he does not want to see us. Now, when I saw you Fathers who have just come to him, I ventured to come here. Therefore, please go and take pity on me, abba; take this child and bring him inside with you, so that he may pray for me.”

The old man took him and entered the cell. Using wise judgment, he did not present him first to Abba Pimenius, but to the lesser Fathers. He said: “Sign the child, brothers, and pray,” asking each of the old men in turn. After all the others, he brought him to Pimenius. But Pimenius did not want even to look at him. When they asked him to pray as all the others had done, he groaned, rose, and prayed, saying: “God, heal your creation, and do not let the enemy rule over it.” He signed the child, and immediately the child was restored healthy to his father.

2. When a layman came into the church possessed by an unclean spirit, and everyone had prayed, the unclean spirit would not leave him at all (Ruff., bk. II, no. 121; John, booklet II, no. 4). The brothers therefore said among themselves: “What can we do to this spirit? No one can drive it out except Abba Besarion; but if we tell him this, he will not agree to come to the church. Let us do this: since he usually comes to the church before everyone else, let us make the afflicted man sit down, and afterward say: ‘Abba, abba, awaken this sleeping man.’”

They did so. When Abba Besarion came, they all stood in prayer and said to him: “Abba, awaken this man who is sleeping.” He said: “Rise and go outside.” Immediately the unclean spirit left him, and from that hour he was healed.

## CHAPTER XV. How it is sometimes beneficial for us to be left in sordid thoughts, lest we become exalted

1. Blessed Antony often used to say: “Unless a baker covered the eyes of the animal, while receiving his wages, the animal itself would consume them” (Ruffin., bk. III, no. 128; Pelag., booklet XV, [Col. 1038A] no. 80). So too, by God’s providence, we receive a covering, so that we are unable to perceive the good things we do, lest we bless ourselves and become exalted, thereby losing our own reward.

For this reason also, when we are left in sordid thoughts, we must take care only to condemn ourselves and our own judgment, so that the sordid things within us may obscure our small good work in our own eyes. For no person is good—even if he desires to be good—unless God dwells in him, because no one is good except God alone (Luke XVIII). We must always accuse ourselves truthfully. For whenever someone does not reproach himself, he loses his own reward.

2. The same blessed Antony was praying in his cell when a voice came to him saying: “Antony, you have not yet attained the measure of the tanner who is in Alexandria” (Ruff., bk. III, no. 130). Hearing this, the old man rose in the morning, took his staff, and hurried into the city. When he reached the man identified by the voice and entered, the man was astonished at seeing so great a person. The old man said to him: “Tell me about your deeds, for I have left the desert and come here because of you.”

He replied: “I do not know that I have ever done anything good. Therefore, rising from my bed in the morning, before I sit down to my work, I say that this whole city, from the least to the greatest, will enter the kingdom of God because of its righteousness, while I alone, because of my sins, will enter everlasting punishment. I feel the truth of this in my heart each morning and each evening before I rest.”

When blessed Antony heard this, he replied: “Truly, my son, sitting in your house like a good craftsman, you have attained the kingdom of God in peace; but I, having spent all my time in the desert without discernment, have not yet attained the measure of your words.”

3. A certain brother asked Abba Pimenius: “What does the Apostle mean when he says, ‘All things are clean to the clean’?” (Ruff., bk. III, no. 131.) He replied: “If someone can attain to understanding this saying, he will see himself as less than the whole of creation.” The brother said: “How can I see myself as less than one who is a murderer?” The old man replied: “If a person can attain to this saying of the Apostle and sees someone who has perhaps killed another, he says within himself: ‘That man committed only this one sin, but I commit murder every hour, killing myself.’”

When the brother asked how this could be, the old man replied: “This alone is a person’s righteousness: always to reproach himself. He will then be justified when he condemns his own sins.”

4. A certain brother said to an old man: “My thought tells me, ‘I am good.’” The old man replied: “The one who does not see his sins always believes that he is among the good; but the one who sees them cannot be persuaded by his thoughts that he is among the good, for he knows what he sees. Therefore, each person must labor greatly to examine himself, because negligence, laziness, and laxity blind the eyes of our heart.”

[Col. 1039A] 5. A certain brother said to Abba Pimenius: “My thoughts do not allow me to look at my sins, but my Fathers compel me to think about my sins.” Abba Pimenius replied by relating something about Abba Isidore. He said: “While Abba Isidore was weeping in his cell and his disciple was sitting in another cell, it happened that the disciple came to him at the very hour when he was weeping and asked him: ‘Why are you weeping, Father?’ He replied: ‘I am weeping over my sins, my son.’ Again he said to him: ‘You have no sins, abba.’ The old man replied: ‘O my son, if God were to reveal my sins to people, neither three nor four would be enough—nor even more.’”

## CHAPTER XVI. How detraction may be avoided

1. A certain brother asked Abba Pimenius [Col. 1039B]: “How can a person avoid speaking evil of his neighbor?” (Ruff., bk. III, no. 133.) The old man replied: “My neighbor and I are two images. When I condemn my own image, my brother’s image is found venerable in my eyes; but when I praise my own, I look upon my brother’s image as deformed. Therefore I do not disparage another if I always reproach myself, because the one who does not examine himself despises a great man.”

2. One of the Fathers used to say: “Whatever you hate, do not do to another” (Ruff., bk. III, no. 153; Pelag., booklet I, no. 21). “If you hate the one who speaks evil to you, do not speak evil of another. If you hate the one who slanders you, do not slander anyone. If you hate the one who treats you with contempt, attacks you with insults, takes away what belongs to you, or does anything of that sort, do none of these things to anyone. Whoever can keep this word has enough for salvation.”

3. One of the holy Fathers, seeing another person negligent, wept bitterly, saying: “Woe to me, because just as this man sins today, so will I tomorrow.” He admonished his disciple, saying: “Even if someone has committed a grave sin in your presence, do not condemn him. Rather, regard it as though you sin more than he does, even if he is a layman—unless perhaps he has blasphemed God, which is characteristic of heretics.”

4. A certain hermit named Timothy, hearing of a negligent brother, asked an abba what should be done with that brother and advised that he be expelled (Ruff., bk. II, no. 140). When the brother had been expelled, temptation came upon Timothy. As he implored God’s presence and said, “I have sinned; have mercy on me,” a voice came to him saying: “Timothy, this has happened to you because you despised your brother at the time of his temptation.”

## CHAPTER XVII. Doing the will of one’s neighbor
1. A certain brother asked Abba Pimenion, saying: “What is faith?” The old man replied: “To live always in charity and humility, and to do good for one’s neighbor.”

2. When Abba Theodore was speaking about the work of the soul and of the hands, a brother said to him: “Explain to us, abba, the work of the soul and the works of the hands.” The old man replied: “Everything that we do because of God’s commandment is to be reckoned among the works of the soul; but whatever we do for our own advantage or profit is understood to be a work of the hands.”

3. Whenever one of the brothers asked Abba Apollo about his work and labor, he immediately went with complete joy, saying: “Today I am going to work for my soul with my king, Christ.” For this is the reward reckoned to the soul.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Rejecting One’s Own Will

1. A certain anchorite sat near a coenobium, performing many virtues (Ruff., bk. III, no. 150; Pelag., booklet XIII, no. 8). When some monks from the coenobium came to him, they compelled him to eat at an unusual hour. Afterward the brothers said to him: “Are you troubled about something, abba, because today you did something contrary to your custom?” He replied to them: “I am troubled when I have done my own will.”

2. A certain brother came to Scetis and asked to see Abba Arsenius. When the other brothers urged him to rest for a little while, he replied: “I will not eat bread unless I have been deemed worthy to see him.” Then one of the brothers led him to Abba Arsenius. After knocking at the door of his cell, he brought him in. They were received, and after prayer they sat down. When the blessed Arsenius remained silent, the one who had brought the brother said: “I am leaving.” But the man who had come out of great desire, seeing that Abba Arsenius had said nothing to him, sat silently out of embarrassment and said: “I too, brother, will leave with you.” And so both departed.

He had also asked to be taken to Abba Moses, who had been converted from among the robbers. Moses received him, showed him hospitality, and dismissed him. The brother who had taken him to both men said to him: “Behold, you have seen both of those whom you requested. Which of the two pleases you more?” He replied: “For the moment, this one seems better to me, because he received us both kindly and fed us well.”

When one of the Fathers learned of this exchange, he prayed to the Lord, saying: “Lord, I beg you to show me the meaning of this matter: one man, for your name’s sake, refuses to see or address anyone; the other, for your name’s sake, is accessible to everyone.”

And behold, in an ecstasy, two boats were shown to him traveling along a river. In one he saw the Holy Spirit sailing with Abba Arsenius in silence and repose. In the other boat he saw Abba Moses, while the angels of God were placing honey and a honeycomb in his mouth and between his teeth.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Attending the Sick, or on Illness Itself

1. A certain brother asked the old men, saying (Pelag., booklet XVII, no. 18): “If two brothers are in one cell, and one of them fasts for six complete days while the other attends to his illness, whose work is greater before God?” The old man replied: “If the one who fasts for six days were to hang himself by the nostrils, he would not be like the other in God’s sight.”

2. John the Younger of the Thebaid, a disciple of Abba Ammonas, attended the old man during his illness for twelve years. Yet when the old man saw him laboring, he never addressed him with a kind or pleasing word (Ruff., bk. III, no. 155; Pelag., booklet XVI, no. 4).

When the old man was departing from this world, and the other elders were sitting there, he took John’s hands and said to him three times: “May you be saved; may you be saved; may you be saved.” Then he entrusted him to the elders, saying: “He is not a man but an angel: for all these years he served me in my illness, and although he heard no kind word, he nevertheless performed his service with great patience.”

3. Accordingly, brothers suffering from various kinds of need gathered around Saint Antony (Pallad., ch. 26). Among them were Eulogius [Note: [Col. 1061C] Eulogius.] The same story, with the same meaning, appears in Palladius, chapter 26, translated into Latin by Hervetus. [Col. 1061D] Paschasius differs from him in the translation of certain words, as does the old translator of Palladius. Here is one passage, but a noteworthy one, no. 4.] a certain Alexandrian monk, and another man tormented by elephantiasis; they were said to have come there for this reason.

This Eulogius the scholar [Note: [Col. 1061D] Scholar.] The meaning of this word varies. It is generally taken to mean an advocate or a declaimer. See the *Onomasticon*.] was educated in secular letters. Captivated by the desire for immortality, he had renounced this world. After dividing and scattering all his possessions, he had retained a small amount of money for himself, so that he could use it because he was unable to work for himself.

When a certain weariness of spirit afflicted him, and he could neither live patiently with many others in a monastery nor endure a solitary life, he found someone lying publicly in the street, so afflicted by the illness mentioned above that he appeared to be without feet or hands. Only his tongue was free from those great torments, so that by it he might more effectively obtain relief for his misery from those who looked upon him.

When Eulogius saw him lying there, he prayed to God and made a certain agreement with the Lord. Then he addressed him in these words: “Lord God,” he said, “in your name I take responsibility for this man afflicted by such a terrible disease, so that through him I too may be saved. Therefore stand by me, Jesus Christ, and grant me patience in this service.”

Then he said to the man lying there: “Brother, do you wish me to take you into my house and support you by whatever means I can?” When the sick man said that he would gladly accept this, if Eulogius was willing, Eulogius replied: “Then I will go and bring a donkey for you to ride.” The sick man consented with great joy.

Eulogius immediately did this and carried the man without delay to his lodging. For fifteen years he served him with constant care and unceasing concern. During all that time, the man to whom such service was rendered endured everything with thanksgiving, and was cared for by the hands, medicines, food, and baths of Eulogius, as his condition required.

After fifteen years, however, the sick man, moved by the devil and forgetful of all the labors and great merits of Eulogius, began wanting to leave him and to assail him with many insults and reproaches, saying: “Runaway!” [Note: [Col. 1061D] “Runaway, you who have devoured your own house and stolen another person’s property.” The old translator of Palladius: “You have committed many evils, perhaps as a runaway from your master; you have stolen other people’s money.” Hervetus, the more recent translator of Palladius: “Go away from here, wicked runaway; you have stolen other people’s money and robbed your master.” Meursius represents the Greek manuscript as follows: Σχάτα, γλούττον, φαγοκύρι, ἀλλότρια χρήματα ἔκλεψας, “Excrement, buttock, master-devourer, you have stolen another’s money.” Yet he reads it as one word, σκατογλούττων, and wants Palladius’s σκατογλούττων to be the same as Aristophanes’ σκατοφάγος, that is, “dung-eater.” For the same Meursius, φαγοκύρις means “master glutton.” Should it not rather be “master’s glutton,” if that is the meaning—“you have robbed your master,” as Hervetus has it? Paschasius also seems to have read φαγοκύρις, but in another sense, for he translates it: “you have devoured your own house.” Thus for him φαγοκύρις is as though it meant κυρίων φάγος, “devourer of his own possessions.” It is an easy step from squandering one’s own property to theft; hence the two expressions are properly joined: devouring one’s own and stealing another’s. The old translator of Palladius seems to have read φυγοκύρι, for he translates it “runaway from your master.” What Meursius derives from σχάτα, γλούττον as σκαταγλούττων I cannot yet approve; I would rather say that these are two insulting words, even if they are not now well understood.]

“You who have devoured your own house and stolen another’s property—do you think that in me you have found an opportunity for your salvation?”

Eulogius, however, pleaded with him and tried to satisfy his mind, saying: “My lord, do not speak in this way. Rather tell me what I have done to grieve you, and I will correct it.”

The man with elephantiasis, raging, said: “Go away. I do not want your flattery; cast me into the street. I have no need of your cooling relief.”

Eulogius replied: “I beg you, be calm. Or tell me, venerable old man, what I have done to grieve you.”

The man with elephantiasis, still more violent in his anger, said to him: “I can no longer endure your deceitful mockery; I cannot tolerate your flattery and derision. Nor is this dry and meager life pleasing to me. I want to be satisfied with meat.”

When Eulogius, that most patient man, had provided him with meat, the sick man began shouting again: “You cannot satisfy my will, nor am I able to live alone with you. I want to see people and go out in public.”

Eulogius said to him: “I will bring you a crowd of brothers.”

The sick man, now even more savage and almost blasphemous, replied: “I do not even want to see your face, and you bring me people like yourself, devourers of bread alone.” Shaking himself, he cried out in an agitated voice: “I do not want to remain here; I want to go out in public. O violence! Throw me back into the place from which you took me.”

His madness was so great, and the devil had so perverted his impaired senses and, in a manner of speaking, his character [perhaps: his humors], that he might even have hanged himself, if he had possessed hands with which to do so.

Eulogius therefore went to the neighboring monks and said to them: “What am I to do? This man with elephantiasis has driven me to utter despair.”

They asked him: “Why?”

He replied: “Because the things he is trying to impose upon me are harsh, and I do not know what to do. Should I cast him out? Yet I have otherwise given my right hand to God regarding him, and I am very afraid of doing so. I will not cast him out, but I cannot endure so many and such great evils through days and nights again. What, then, should I do with him? I do not know.”

They said to him: “While that great man Antony is still alive—for that is what he was called—go up to him. Place the sick man on a boat and take him to Antony’s monastery, remaining there until Antony comes out of his cave. When you see him, tell him what you are suffering and ask his advice. Whatever he tells you to do regarding this matter, do it and obey his instructions, knowing that what he commands you has been ordered by God.”

Thus, willingly instructed by the brothers’ words, Eulogius overcame the sick man with gentle entreaties, placed him in a small coastal boat, and carried him out of the city by night to the dwelling of Saint Antony’s disciples.

It happened that blessed Antony arrived there the following day toward evening. Cronius told me that he came wearing a cloak made of skins.

Whenever he came to the brothers’ monastery, he used to call for Macarius and ask him: “Have any more brothers arrived?” Macarius would reply that some had arrived. Antony would then ask: “Are they from Egypt or from Jerusalem?”

He had instructed them to give this sign: whenever people not sufficiently worthy of his conversation arrived, they were to say that Egyptians had come; whenever certain holy and spiritual men appeared, they were to announce that men from Jerusalem had come.

On this occasion, then, when he arrived and, according to his custom, asked whether the brothers there were from Jerusalem or from Egypt, Macarius replied that he had seen some of both kinds.

When Saint Antony told him: “Make them welcome, let them eat, and then, after prayer has been completed with them, let them depart,” this was what was done with the others. But when he learned that men from Jerusalem had arrived, he sat with them throughout the night and spoke to them about matters that would benefit their salvation.

They reported that on that night he sat with them and summoned each of those who had gathered to him. When he heard that no one had called for Eulogius, he himself called him three times by name in the darkness.

When the scholar mentioned above did not answer, thinking that some other Eulogius was being called, Antony said to him again: “I am calling you, Eulogius, who came from the city of Alexandria.”

Eulogius said to him: “What do you command, I pray?”

Antony replied: “Why have you come here?”

Eulogius answered: “The one who was willing to reveal my name to you has surely also revealed the reason for my coming.”

Then Antony said: “I know why you have come, but tell it before all these brothers, so that everyone may hear.”

Thus commanded by the great Antony, the servant of Christ Eulogius recounted before them all: “I found this man with elephantiasis thrown out in the public street, and no human being cared for him. I promised God that I would serve his illness as best I could, so that I might be saved through him and he through me. It is now fifteen years since we have been together, as I believe everything has also been revealed to your holiness.

“Although he had never suffered any harm from me during all these years, after so long a time he now afflicts me with various storms and tempests. Because of this I considered casting him away from me, and for that reason I have come to your holiness, asking you to teach me by your counsel what I should do and to assist me by your prayers. For I am completely wearied and tormented by the worst impulses.”

To this Antony replied in a stern and angry voice: “You are casting him away from you, Eulogius? But he does not cast him away who recognizes that he was made by God. You are casting him away? He will find someone better than you, and God will choose someone to gather up the abandoned man.”

Eulogius was terrified by these words and fell silent. Saint Antony then left Eulogius and began to chastise the sick man with his own words, addressing him with a very loud cry:

“You man with elephantiasis, dreadful with filth and mud, worthy neither of earth nor of heaven—will you never cease shouting insults against God? Do you not know that the one serving you is Christ? How have you dared to speak such things against Christ? For Christ’s sake this man has subjected himself to such servitude and service, and you have left him wounded by your biting words.”

Then Antony turned to the other brothers and addressed each one according to what was appropriate. Afterward he returned to Eulogius and the sick man and said to them:

“Let neither of you, my sons, turn elsewhere; let neither separate from the other. Return peacefully to your cell, in which you have lived for so long, laying aside all sadness. For now the Lord God will send help to you. This trial has come upon you because both of you have reached the end of your lives, and each of you will deserve to be crowned.

“Therefore do nothing differently. Otherwise, if an angel should come and be unable to find you in the place I have mentioned, both of you might be deprived of your crowns.”

They quickly returned to their cell and arrived there in restored peace. Within forty days Eulogius died first, and a few days later the aforementioned sick man died, sound in mind.

Cronius had spent a considerable time in the regions of the Thebaid and then went down to the monasteries near Alexandria. It happened that he arrived there on the day which the brothers were celebrating as the fortieth day for one man and the third day for the other.

When Cronius heard this, he was astonished. He took the holy Gospel, placed it in the midst of the brothers, and solemnly explained everything to them in order, saying:

“I myself interpreted all the conversations I have recounted, because Saint Antony did not know how to speak Greek. I knew both languages and served as interpreter between them, answering Antony in Egyptian and the others in Greek.”

4. Cronius himself also told us the following [Note: [Col. 1043D] The same account appears in the *Life of Antony*, chapter 38.]: on that very night when Saint Antony dismissed blessed Eulogius, Antony had said that for an entire year he had been praying that the dwelling places of sinners and of the righteous might be shown to him by revelation.

He said that he saw a certain giant, tall enough to reach the clouds, of a gloomy color, holding his outstretched hands toward heaven. Beneath his feet a lake was spread out like the sea. There Antony saw souls flying about like restless birds.

All those that flew above the giant’s hands and head were preserved; but all those found beneath his hands were plunged into the lake.

He reported that a voice then came to him, saying: “Know that all the souls you see flying are the souls of the righteous, who rest in the dwelling of paradise. The other souls are sent to the underworld. This is what all those suffer who have obeyed the fleshly will, and all those who, retaining anger, have attempted to repay evil with evil.”

5. Both Cronius and Saint Hierax, together with many other neighbors of the brothers, related to us the following.

A certain old man said: “If a monk knows of someone from whom he could make progress, but has difficulty obtaining the necessities of the body and therefore does not go to him, such a monk does not believe that God exists.”

6. A certain old man said: “Whoever wishes to dwell in the desert must be a teacher, not one who needs instruction, lest he appear to suffer harm” (Pelag., booklet X, no. 90).

## CHAPTER XX. That Bodily Illness Benefits the Soul

1. A certain great old man said to his sick disciple: “Do not be saddened, my son, by the illness or wound of your body” (Ruff., bk. III, no. 157; Pelag., booklet VII, no. 16, under the name of Syncletica). “For it is the highest form of devotion for someone to give thanks to God in illness.

“If you are iron, you lose your rust through fire; but if you are gold, once tested through fire, you advance from great things to greater. Therefore do not be anxious, brother. If God wishes you to be tormented in the body, who are you to resist his will or to take it badly? Endure, then, and ask God to grant what he himself wills.”

2. A certain old man was frequently sick in body and weak. It happened that in one year no illness touched him. For this reason he wept and took it very hard, saying: “You have abandoned me, Lord, and have not wished to visit me in this present year” (Ruff., bk. III, no. 158; Pelag., booklet VII, no. 41).

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Fear of God

1. A brother asked Abba Piemon how the soul might resist when it does not wish to fear God. The old man replied: “The soul does wish to fear God, but the time has not yet come. For the fear of the Lord is great perfection.”

2. A certain brother asked an old man, saying: “How does the fear of God enter the soul?” The old man replied: “If someone first possesses humility, so that he judges or condemns no one, gives alms generously, and possesses nothing, then the fear of God enters the soul” (Pelag., booklet I, no. 19).

3. The old man said: “Let fear, humility, and poverty of provisions remain in you” (Pelag., booklet I, no. 20).

4. A certain brother asked the old man, saying: “Why, abba, is my heart hard and does not fear God?” (Pelag., booklet III, no. 22; Appendix of Mart., no. 22). The old man said to him: “I think that if a person holds reproof in his heart, he possesses the fear of the Lord.”

The brother said to him: “What is reproof?”

The old man replied: “For a person to reprove his soul in everything, saying to it: ‘Remember that you must meet God.’ He also says here: ‘What did I want with a human being?’ I think that if someone remains in these things, the fear of God will come to him.”

## CHAPTER XXII. On Repentance

1. A certain brother asked Abba Pimenion, saying: “What is repentance?” The old man answered: “Repentance for sins is not to sin again. For this word continually cries out to a person until his final breath: ‘Turn back today, lest sudden death come upon you like a thief.’”

2. Abba Pimenius said with a groan: “All the virtues have entered my cell except one virtue, and a person stands through its labor” (Appendix of Mart., no. 59).

The brothers asked him: “What virtue is this, abba?”

The old man replied: “That a person should always blame himself.”

## CHAPTER XXIII. That Through Repentance a Person Can Be Reconciled to God in One Day

1. One of the Fathers recounted the following about a certain bishop. He had heard that two men from his congregation were exceedingly impure and adulterous (Ruff., bk. III, no. 166; John, booklet I, no. 16). He therefore asked God to let him know whether this was true.

After the consecrated offering had been made, when each person approached for communion, he recognized their minds through their faces. He saw the faces of sinners black like coals, with eyes filled with blood; but he saw others with bright faces and dressed in white garments.

When they had received the body of the Lord, a light appeared on the faces of some, while on others there appeared a flame. To determine which of the men were those whose crime he had heard about, he offered them communion. He saw one of them with a bright and honorable face, surrounded by white garments; the other was black, with a terrible face.

After they had received the grace of the divine mystery, a certain light illuminated one, while the other was set ablaze as though by a flame.

The bishop therefore prayed to God to teach him the meaning of what had been shown concerning each man. An angel of the Lord stood beside him and said: “Everything you heard about these men is true. But one of them remains in his filth and in his desire to sin; that is why you saw him with a black face and burning with flame.

“The other was indeed like him, as you had heard. But you saw him illuminated with a bright face because, remembering what he had previously done and renouncing those evil works, he was asking God’s mercy with tears and groans. He promised that if his past sins were forgiven him, he would not return to them again. Therefore, with his former crimes blotted out, he attained the grace you saw.

“When the bishop marveled at God’s grace—because God had not only set a man free from the torments of such a shameful life but had also adorned him with such honor—the angel replied: ‘You marvel rightly, for you are a human being. But our Lord and your Lord is naturally good and humane toward those who cease from sin and repent in confession. He not only forgives their torments but also makes them worthy of honor.

“‘For God loved human beings so greatly that he gave his Only-begotten for sinners and destined him to death on their behalf (John 3). If, when they were his enemies, he chose to die for them, how much more will he show mercy to them when they belong to him?

“‘Know this, then: no sins of human beings overcome God’s goodness, provided that each person, through repentance, wipes away the evils he previously committed. For God is merciful. He knows the weakness of the human race, the power of the passions, and the strength or malice of the devil. When people fall into sin, he waits for their amendment, showing indulgence as to children; but when they repent, he sympathizes with and pities them as with the sick. Immediately he releases them from their sins and grants them even the rewards of the righteous.’”

When the bishop heard this, he was greatly astonished and glorified God, making known to everyone what had happened.

2. Abba Paul the Simple possessed this grace: while sitting and looking at those entering the church, he perceived from their faces the thoughts of each one, whether they were evil or good (Ruff., bk. III, no. 167; Pelag., booklet XVIII, no. 20).

Once, when some people came to the church, he saw them entering with bright faces and joyful hearts, accompanied by their angels, who were rejoicing with them. But he saw one man with a black and clouded body, while demons on either side pulled him toward themselves, having placed a bridle in his nostrils. His holy angel followed him from a distance, sorrowful.

Blessed Paul began to weep bitterly and beat his breast as he sat before the church, because of the man whom he had seen in this condition.

All the other elders, seeing him weeping in this way, began to ask him either to reveal what he had seen in them or to enter the assembly with them. He refused to enter, but continued always to weep because of the man whom he had seen in that state.

After a little while, when the assembly had ended and they were leaving, he again looked carefully at the faces of everyone, to see whether they were leaving in the condition in which they had entered.

He saw the man whom he had previously seen black and clouded leaving with a bright face and a white body. The demons followed him from a distance, while his holy angel was near him, exceedingly joyful and glad on his account.

Then Saint Paul rose up and cried out with joy, blessing the Lord and saying: “O how great is the mercy and kindness of God! How great is his compassion!”

Going up to a higher place, he said in a loud voice: “Come and see the works of God; come and see how he wishes all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. 2). “Come, let us worship him, saying: ‘For you alone can forgive sins.’”

When everyone had gathered, Paul explained to them what he had seen before entering the church and what he had seen afterward. He asked the brother whom he had seen in this state to disclose to him his thoughts and actions, and how God had granted him such a great change.

The man began to recount everything before them all, saying:

“I am a sinful man, and for many years I was always devoted to fornication. But when I entered the church of God just now, I heard the words spoken by the Lord through the prophet Isaiah, saying (Isa. 1):

“‘Make yourselves clean, and remove the evil from your souls before my eyes. Learn to do good; seek justice. And if your sins are like scarlet, they shall be made white as snow. If you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the land.’

“I, a fornicator, was pierced by this saying of the prophet. Groaning within my heart, I said to the Lord: ‘Lord, you are the one who came to save sinners. Therefore fulfill in me, unworthy and sinful as I am, the things you have now promised through the prophet.

“‘Behold, from this moment I confess to you and promise with all my heart that I will no longer do this evil. I renounce all injustice, and from now on I will serve you with a clean conscience. From today and from this hour, Lord, receive me as one who repents, worships you, and renounces all sins.

“‘I have sworn and resolved to keep all your ordinances’ (Ps. 118). With this promise I left the church, resolving within myself never again to commit any of my former sins.”

When everyone heard this, they cried out to the Lord with one voice, saying: “How great are your works, Lord! You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103).

## CHAPTER XXIV. That Even if a Person Dies in the Intention of Repentance, He Is Nevertheless Received

1. A certain brother came to Abba Pimenion and said that he had suffered a great tribulation. The old man said to him: “Flee from that place as far as you can walk in three days and three nights, and spend an entire year fasting until evening.”

The brother said to him: “If I die before the year is completed, what will become of me?”

Abba Pimenius replied: “I trust in God that if you leave me with such an intention—to do this—even if you die immediately, your repentance will be received by God with good desire.”

2. A certain brother lived in his cell in Egypt, outstanding in great humility. He had a sister in the city who was a prostitute and had brought ruin upon many souls (Ruff., bk. III, no. 217).

The elders often reproached that brother and scarcely managed to persuade him to go to her, so that through his admonition he might overcome the sin committed through her.

When he arrived at the place, one of her acquaintances saw him, went ahead, and announced to her: “Behold, your brother has come to you.”

She, rejoicing greatly, left the lovers whom she was serving and went out to meet her brother with her head uncovered.

When she tried to embrace him, he said to her: “My dearest sister, spare your soul, because many are perishing on your account. How will you be able to endure those bitter and eternal torments?”

Trembling, she said to him: “Do you know, brother, whether there is salvation for me from now on?”

He replied: “If you are willing, there is salvation.”

She threw herself at her brother’s feet and asked him to take her with him into the desert.

The brother said to her: “Go, cover your head, and follow me.”

She replied: “Let us go. For I would rather be disfigured among people by walking with my head uncovered than enter again the workshop of my sin.”

As they walked together, he urged her to repent. When he saw that some people were coming toward them, he said to her: “Since not everyone knows that you are my sister, step a little way off the road until they have passed.”

After they had gone by, he called her and said: “Come, sister, let us continue on our way.”

When she did not answer, he searched for her and found her dead. Her footprints were full of blood, for she had been barefoot.

When he reported the event to the elders, they disputed among themselves about her salvation. But God revealed the matter to one of the elders: during the journey she had felt no concern for bodily use or comfort; she had disregarded her own wound and groaned over such great ruin. Therefore, because of the devotion of her heart, God received her repentance.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Assaults of Demons

1. A certain brother asked an old man, saying: “Why, abba, are we assaulted by demons?”

The old man replied: “Because we have cast away our weapons—that is, repentance, humility, obedience, and poverty” (Ruff., bk. III, no. 173; Pelag., bk. XV, no. 58).

2. A certain brother asked Abba Sisoes, saying: “Do you think, abba, that the devil persecutes us now as he persecuted the ancients?” (Ruff., bk. III, no. 174; Pelag., booklet XV, no. 45).

He replied: “Now he persecutes the people of our age more intensely, because the kinds of punishments are drawing near. There he will be tormented with his legions, since he knows the lake in which he will burn in fire and sulfur; therefore he is hostile toward human beings.

“Yet he does not even deign to attack the weak, whom he quickly overthrows whenever he wishes. Rather, he attempts to trip up the strong and the great through various precipices.”

3. Abba Pimenius asked Abba Abraham: “How do demons assault us?” (Pelag., booklet X, no. 62).

The old man replied: “Demons do not fight against us, because we do their will. Rather, our own wills have become demons for us, and they trouble us. Hence the Apostle says: ‘The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you may not do whatever you wish’ (Gal. 5).

“Do you want to know against whom demons fought? Against Abba Moses and those like him. But the desires of our hearts assault us.”

4. A certain brother asked Abba Achilles [also: Achilleus]: “How can demons act against us?”

The old man replied: “Through our desires.”

He added: “The cedars of Lebanon said: ‘How great and tall we are, yet we are cut down by a very small tool.’ Therefore let us give it nothing of ourselves, and it will not be able to cut us down.

“Then men came and made a handle for an axe out of the cedars themselves, and so they cut them down. The trees, therefore, are souls; the axe is the devil; the handle is our will. Through our evil desires, therefore, we are cut down.”

## CHAPTER XXVI. How a Person Can Mortify Vices Within Himself

1. A certain brother asked Abba Moses, saying: “How can a person mortify himself?”

The old man said to him: “Unless someone considers himself to have already spent three years in the tomb, he cannot attain this understanding” (Pelag., booklet X, no. 63).

2. Abba Pimenius said: “That monk can be as one dead to this world who has come to hate two things: the repose of his flesh and vain glory.”

3. A certain old man said: “A monk will be free from everything when he is intent only upon doing good” (Ruff., bk. III, no. 179). For when he practices good works, the devil comes and finds no place, and departs. But if he practices an evil work, the devil comes repeatedly, attacks him, and overturns him into worse things.

4. Blessed Antony admonished his disciple, saying: “Hate your belly, the necessities of this world, evil desire, and honor, as one who is absent from this world; and you will possess rest.”

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Perseverance

1. Abba Antony said: “If a monk labors for a few days and then relaxes again; if he labors again and afterward neglects his labor, he accomplishes nothing and will not possess perseverance in patience.”

2. The old man said: “What is the point of beginning a craft if one does not learn to complete it? Therefore nothing is gained by beginning what is not completed” (Appendix of Mart., no. 102).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the Labor of the Saints

1. A certain old man said: “Let a person labor until he possesses Christ” (Ruff., bk. III, no. 180). Whoever has once attained him is no longer in danger. Nevertheless, he is permitted to labor so that, remembering the tribulation of his labor, he may guard himself on every side, fearing that he might lose such great labors.

For this reason also God led the children of Israel around through the desert for forty years: so that, remembering the tribulation of the journey, they would not wish to turn back.

2. A certain brother asked an old man: “How do those who seek remission of sins labor?” The old man replied: “Before the grace that works on behalf of their labor reaches them, they are pale and toil-worn; but those upon whom, because of their former endurance, the grace of Christ has already come, flourish, and their souls rejoice, and their faces are bright like the sun when it has no cloud and shines. But when the sun is covered by a cloud, it grows pale; so too the soul, when passions and temptations darken it. But the soul that has been cleansed by the grace of God shines in this way, as it is written: ‘Great is his glory in your salvation’ (Psalm 20).”

3. He also said: “Although holy men labor here, they nevertheless possess some rest, because they are free from the thoughts of this world.” [Col. 1050C]

4. A certain brother asked an old man, saying: “Why do men who now labor in the ascetic life not receive grace as the ancients did?” (Rufinus, Book III, no. 181; Pelagius, Book XVII, no. 19). The old man said: “At that time there was charity, and each person lifted his neighbor upward; but now, after charity has grown cold, individuals drag their neighbors downward. Therefore they do not deserve the grace of God.”

## CHAPTER XXIX. On Exhortation in Teaching

1. When someone asked Abba Pimenion about hardness of heart, the old man replied: “The nature of water is soft, and that of stone hard; yet if water frequently drips upon a stone, by dripping it pierces the stone. So too the word of God is sweet and soft, but our heart is hard. Therefore a person who frequently hears or meditates upon the word of God gives room for the fear of God to enter him.” [Col. 1050D]

## CHAPTER XXX. On Avoiding Curiosity

1. A certain old man said: “A monk ought not to inquire what someone is like, or how this or that person behaves, because through such questioning he is drawn away from prayer and slips into detraction and excessive talk. Therefore nothing is better than silence.”

2. A certain brother asked an old man, saying: “If some brother comes bringing me outside reports about other people, do you command me to tell him not to bring them to me?” The old man said: “Say nothing, because we ourselves have not been able to keep this rule. We must therefore beware lest, while telling our neighbor, ‘Do not do this,’ we later do the same things—or worse—ourselves.” The brother said to him: “What, then, should one do?” The old man replied: “If we wish to be silent, example alone is sufficient for our neighbor.” [Col. 1051A]

## CHAPTER XXXI. On Avoiding Disputes

1. A certain old man said (Rufinus, Book III, no. 185): “If someone speaks with you about the Scriptures or about any other matter, do not argue with him. If he speaks correctly, agree with him; but if he speaks incorrectly, say to him: ‘You know how you speak.’ The Apostle says: ‘Do not quarrel about words’ (2 Timothy 2). By observing this, you will possess humility and avoid hatred. For if you persist in arguing and wish to defend your own statement, scandal arises from it. Often, therefore, while praising another person, an argument arises even from one’s defense of oneself. If you argue heatedly about any matter, you will suffer no small harm and will in no way possess rest. Rather, strive to guard silence and be anxious about nothing. Attend to your meditation, rising with the fear of God both morning and evening, and you will not fear the assaults of the enemies.” [Col. 1051B]

## CHAPTER XXXII. On Silence

1. Blessed Antony used to say to his disciple: “If you desire silence, do not suppose that you are practicing a virtue; rather, confess that you are unworthy to speak.”

2. When a certain brother had said to Abba Sisoes, “I want to save my soul,” he replied: “By what means can we save our soul, when our tongue often leaps forth through an open door?” (Pelagius, Book XI, no. 27). [Col. 1051C]

3. A certain brother asked an old man, saying: “How long, Father, must silence be kept?” The old man replied: “Until you are questioned. For in every place, if you are silent, you will possess rest” (Rufinus, Book III, no. 186).

4. The old man said: “Silence is pilgrimage” (Pelagius, Book IV, no. 44, under the name of Sisoes).

5. A certain old man said: “Pilgrimage undertaken for God is good if it also includes silence; for self-confidence is not pilgrimage” (Appendix of Martin, no. 72). [Col. 1051D]

6. Abba Arsenius used to say: “A monk who is a stranger in a foreign land should not become an intermediary in any matter, and he will be able to attain quiet.”

7. Abba Ampo said: “Just as a bee produces honey wherever it goes, so too a monk, wherever he travels, if he has gone for the work of God, can bring the sweetness of good deeds” (Rufinus, Book III, no. 189).

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On Fleeing Clerical Honor

1. When Abba Theodore had been ordained deacon in Scetis, he was in no way willing to remain there, but fled to many places. The old men repeatedly brought him back, saying: “Do not abandon your place.” He said to them: “Permit me to ask God whether he commands me to minister in my office.” And he prayed as follows: “Lord, if it is your will that I remain in my ordination, show me.” A fiery column appeared to him, reaching from earth to heaven, and a voice came to him: “Theodore, if you can become like this column, go and minister.” It is enough that what was said through Moses to the Levites and priests should be fulfilled: that with pure heart and body, blameless hands, and the purest garment, they should offer sacrifices for the children of Israel. When he heard this, he was no longer willing in any way. But when he came to the church, they begged him, if he would not minister, at least to hold the chalice. He would not consent, saying: “If you say anything more to me about this, I will leave here.” And so they let him go. [Col. 1052A]

2. When Abba Isaac heard that the Fathers wanted to make him a presbyter in Scetis, he fled to Egypt and, entering a field, hid among the plants (Rufinus, Book III, no. 22). It happened that the Fathers who were pursuing him rested in that same field, since it was already night, and they released the donkey to graze. While grazing, it reached the place where Abba Isaac was hiding. When morning came, they searched for the donkey and found the old man as well, and they were astonished. When they wanted to bind him, he said to them: “I am no longer fleeing, because I know that this is by God’s command; and wherever I flee, I shall eventually arrive at this.”

3. Abba Motois once came from a place called Ragita, in the region of Gehilon (Rufinus, Book III, no. 188; Pelagius, Book XV, no. 27). His disciple was also with him. When the bishop of that place saw him, he seized him and made him a presbyter against his will. While they were eating together, the bishop said to him: “Forgive me, Abba. I know that you did not want this honor, but because I desired to receive your blessing, I presumed to do this.” The old man replied humbly: “My own thought was also reluctant, but I am troubled by this: I shall have to be separated from the brother who is with me, and alone I am not sufficient to fulfill my prayers.” The bishop said to him: “If you know him to be worthy, I will ordain him also.” Abba Motois replied: “Whether he is worthy, I do not know; but I know one thing: he is better than I am.” So the bishop ordained him also. Yet both of them remained until the end of their lives without ever approaching the altar for the offering to be consecrated. Therefore the old man used to say: “I trust in my God that I shall not incur a great judgment because of this ordination, since I did not presume to offer the oblation.
