For ordination belongs to those who are without fault, righteous and immaculate; but I know myself well.” [Col. 1052D]

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the Desert, and Why They Fled into Solitude

1. Abba Arsenius was once asked by Abba Mark why he fled from people (Pelagius, Book XVII, no. 5). He replied: “God knows that I love people, but I cannot be with God and with people at the same time. The heavenly multitudes and powers are of one will, whereas human beings have many and diverse wills. For this reason I cannot leave God and be with people.” [Col. 1053A]

2. While certain brothers were traveling from Thebaid to buy flax, they said: “Let us take the opportunity to see blessed Arsenius” (Rufinus, Book III, no. 192). When his disciple Daniel announced this to him, Arsenius ordered him to ask them for what reason they had come there from Alexandria. When Daniel reported that they were going to purchase flax, Arsenius replied: “Then they shall not see my face, because they have come not on my account but for their own business. Go, therefore, receive them courteously and dismiss them, saying: ‘The old man cannot come out to meet you.’”

3. While Abba Besarion was walking through the desert with his disciple, they came to a certain cave (Rufinus, Book III, no. 194; John, Book III, no. 1). Entering it, they found a brother sitting and making a cord. He neither looked at them nor greeted them nor spoke anything else to them. Abba Besarion therefore said to his disciple: “Let us leave here, because this old man does not wish to speak with us.” They went on to Abba John. When they were returning, they came to the same cave, and Abba Besarion said: “Let us enter again to see this brother, in case God may perhaps persuade him even now to speak with us.” When they had entered, they found him dead. He said to his disciple: “Come, brother, let us prepare him for burial, because on his account God sent us here.” When they were burying him, they discovered that the person was a woman. They were astonished and said: “Great indeed is the mercy of the Lord, since women also wrestle with demons and conquer them.” And glorifying God, who is the protector of all, they returned to their own place, relating what they had seen. [Col. 1053C]

## CHAPTER XXXV. What the Hermit’s Observance Is

1. Abba Moses used to address a discourse to the solitaries, saying: “There are four principal elements of regular observance: keeping silence, observing the commandments of God, humbling oneself, and the hardship of poverty” (Rufinus, Book III, no. 196). A person possesses these three virtues with difficulty: always mourning, always remembering his sins, and placing death before his eyes every hour.

2. Blessed Antony used to say: “The ancient Fathers went out into the desert, and once they themselves had been healed, they became physicians; then they returned and healed others. But if one of us happens to go out into the desert, before we ourselves have been healed we undertake the care of others. Then our illness returns to us, and our last state becomes worse than the first. Therefore it is said to us: ‘Physician, first heal yourself’ (Luke 4).” [Col. 1053D]

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Who Are Brothers of Equal Merit

1. A certain brother asked Abba Pimenion, saying: “Who are brothers of equal merit?” (Pelagius, Book X, no. 52). The old man replied: “If three are together, one resting in every word and deed, another suffering weakness and giving thanks, and the third serving them with a pure conscience, these three are of equal merit.” [Col. 1054A]

2. The old man said: “To insult, to lie, or to swear falsely is foreign to Christ. Through these four things the soul is stained: if someone has friendship with the powerful while devoting himself to carnal desires; if he has slandered his neighbor; if, while walking through the city, he has not guarded his eyes; and if he has had any acquaintance with a woman.”

3. Blessed Arsenius related that, while he was sitting in his own cell, he heard a voice telling him to go outside to contemplate the works of men’s hands (Rufinus, Book II, no. 38; Pelagius, Book XVIII, no. 2). Going out, he saw a man drawing water from a well and pouring it into a vessel full of holes; the water ran out and flowed back into the well. Going a little farther, he saw an Ethiopian making a bundle from wood he had cut. When he tried to lift it and found it too heavy, he piled more wood upon it. Trying again, and still unable to move it, he nevertheless did not stop adding wood.

Going farther again, Arsenius saw two young men sitting on horses before the city gate. They were carrying a crosswise beam of wood and could not enter the city. The beam they carried prevented them from entering, and neither one wished to follow or humble himself before the other; thus both remained outside the city.

The one who was showing these things to holy Arsenius in the spirit said to him: “The man whom you first saw drawing water from the well and pouring it back into the well through a perforated vessel is like a person who performs almsgiving and appears to practice a good work; but because he frequently commits iniquity in other works, he stains and loses that small amount of good through these evils.

“The man whom you saw cutting wood, adding a heavy load and making it heavier, is a person established in many sins who, after repentance, increases another burden upon his sins.

“And those whom you saw unable to enter the city because of the crosswise beam resisting them are people who appear to bear the pitiable yoke of pride, and who were unwilling to humble themselves before one another so that, being corrected by this, they might follow the humble way of Christ. Therefore both these and those remained outside the kingdom of God.” [Col. 1054C]

4. A brother asked Abba Sisoes, saying: “An inheritance has been left to me by my parents; what should I do with it?” The old man replied: “If I say, ‘Give it to the church and its clergy,’ they will feast upon it. If I say, ‘Give it to your relatives,’ you will receive no reward. Therefore, if you wish to fulfill the divine commandment, give it to the poor and needy, and you will be perfect” (Pelagius, Book X, no. 56, under the name of Pastor; Appendix of Martin, no. 7).

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Temporal Advancement Must Be Abandoned for the Sake of Charity

1. Abba Sisoes said: “Once, when I was in the marketplace selling my baskets to a brother, I saw that anger was approaching me, so I abandoned my wares and fled” (Appendix of Martin, no. 11).

2. Abba John said: “Once I was going up along the desert road in Scetis, weaving a basket, and I heard a camel-driver speaking idle words. So that I would not perhaps become angry, I abandoned my basket and fled” (Appendix of Martin, no. 12). [Col. 1055A]

3. A brother asked Abba Pimenion, saying: “What does the Lord’s saying mean: ‘Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends’ (John 15)? How does one do this?” The old man replied: “If someone hears an evil word from his neighbor and, although he could answer with similar words, nevertheless struggles in his heart to bear the distress and constrains himself not to return evil, so as not to grieve him, such a person lays down his life for his friend” (Rufinus, Book III, no. 201; Pelagius, Book XVII, no. 10; Appendix of Martin, no. 14).

4. Abba Macarius said: “If we remember the evils we suffer from human beings, we lose the virtue of memory. But if we recall the evils sent against us by demons, we shall be without disturbance, knowing that from the beginning God created good, whereas the devil sowed evil over it. Behold, there are countless destructions” (Pelagius, Book X, no. 34; Appendix of Martin, no. 15).

He added: “It is the monk’s fault if, after being injured by the brothers, he does not come forward first in charity with a purified heart” (John, Booklet I, no. 7; Appendix of Martin, no. 16). For the Shunammite would not have deserved to receive the prophet Elisha into her house unless she had had no dispute with anyone else. The Shunammite represents the soul, while Elisha represents the Holy Spirit; for unless the soul is pure, it does not deserve to receive the Spirit of God. Thus long-standing anger blinds the eyes of the heart and excludes the soul from prayer. [Col. 1055B]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. What Mourning or Poverty Undertaken for God Accomplishes

[Col. 1055C]

1. A brother asked holy Antony: “What should I do for my sins?” He replied: “Whoever wishes to be freed from sins will be freed from them through weeping and lamentation; and whoever wishes to be built up in virtues is built up through the weeping of tears. The very praise of the psalms is lamentation.

“Remember the example of King Hezekiah of Judah, as it is written through the prophet Isaiah (Isaiah 38): by weeping he not only received health, but also obtained an increase of life for fifteen years. And when the army of the enemy came upon him—namely, one hundred and eighty-five thousand men—the power of the Lord struck them down to death through the watering of his tears.

“Holy Peter the Apostle, by weeping, received forgiveness for what he had done in denying Christ. Mary, because she watered the Lord’s feet with tears, deserved to hear that she had chosen the better portion. ‘The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever and ever.’” [Col. 1055D]

2. Blessed Macarius said: “Truly, if contempt has become for a monk like praise, poverty like riches, and want like a feast, he never dies” (Appendix of Martin, no. 23). “It is impossible for one who believes rightly and worships God devoutly to fall into an unclean passion and into the error of demons.”

## CHAPTER XXXIX. In This Life a Person Cannot Find Rest

1. A brother asked Abba Sisoes: “After how much time should a person cut passions away from himself?” (Appendix of Martin, no. 26). He replied: “It is written in the Gospel: ‘God does not hear sinners, but if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, he hears him’ (John 9). Therefore, when an assault comes, cut it off, because the soul is fragile; let it be armed before it is defiled by sins.” [Col. 1056A]

2. A brother asked Abba Pimenion: “What shall I do? Thoughts trouble me while I sit in my cell.” He replied: “Despise no one, judge no one, speak evil of no one; and God will give you rest and establish your sitting without disturbance” (Rufinus, Book III, no. 100; Pelagius, Book IX, no. 8; Appendix of Martin, no. 39).

“Consider the discipline and quiet of the elders. Meditate on the divine offices, and know the canonical hours by day and by night. Let the fear of the Lord not depart from your heart. Do not boast, nor consider yourself among the righteous. Guard yourself with all your strength so that you do not do your own will.” [Col. 1056B]

3. He also said: “Just as flies do not approach a heated pot, but if it has become lukewarm they settle upon it and produce worms, so demons flee from a monk heated by the fire of the divine Spirit, but they mock and pursue one who is lukewarm” (Rufinus, Book III, no. 204; Appendix of Martin, no. 42).

## CHAPTER XL. From Where Vices Arise

1. A brother asked holy Antony: “How does God promise good things to the soul through constant attention to the Scriptures, while the soul does not wish to remain in good things but turns toward transient, perishable, and unclean things?” He replied: “To this must be joined what the Psalmist says: ‘If I had seen iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have heard me’ (Psalm 65).

“Do you not know that when the belly has been filled with food, great vices immediately boil up—those which our Savior foretold through the Gospel: ‘What enters the mouth does not defile a person, but what comes out of the heart is what plunges a person into destruction’ (Matthew 15)?

“See what he named first: evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, and blasphemies. Because the person who has not yet tasted the sweetness of heavenly things so as to seek God with all his heart therefore returns to uncleanness. Who could rightly say: ‘I have become like a beast before you, and I am always with you’ (Psalm 72)?”

## CHAPTER XLI. How Virtues Must Be Obtained

[Col. 1056D]

1. A brother asked a certain old man, saying: “Teach me, Father” (Appendix of Martin, no. 46). He said to him: “Go, love to do violence to yourself. Draw your sword and go out to battle.” The brother said to him: “My thoughts do not permit me.” The old man replied: “It is written: ‘Call upon me in the day of your tribulation; I will deliver you, and you will glorify me.’ Call upon God, therefore, and he will deliver you” (Psalm 80).

2. Two brothers went to a holy old man sitting alone in Scetis. One of them said: “Abba, I have learned the whole Old and New Testament by heart” (Pelagius, Book X, no. 94). The old man said to him: “You have filled the air with words.” The other said: “I have written out the whole Old and New Testament, and I possess it.” To him he replied: “And you have filled your windows with papers.

“Do you not know who said: ‘The kingdom of God is not in speech but in power’ (1 Corinthians 4)? And again: ‘It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified’ (Romans 2)?”

They were therefore asking him about the way of salvation. He said to them: “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord (Psalm 110), and humility with patience. When all these things are inserted into one’s life and practiced, little is sufficient.” [Col. 1057A]

## CHAPTER XLII. How One Should Live in Cenobitic Communities

1. When a young brother asked Abba Agathon, saying: “I wish to remain with the brothers; tell me how I should live with them,” the old man replied: “Above all, observe this: whatever you are when you first enter among them, remain that way for the rest of your time, and you will complete your pilgrimage in peace” (Rufinus, Book III, no. 198; Pelagius, Book X, no. 8).

“Guard yourself against ever assuming confidence in speaking, as the Apostle says: ‘No one serving as a soldier for Christ entangles himself in worldly affairs’ (2 Timothy 2).”

2. Agathon also said: “If you live with your neighbor, be like a stone column: if it is insulted, it does not become angry; if it is praised, it is not exalted” (Appendix of Martin, no. 10).

3. Abba Pimenion asked Abba Nesteron, who was sitting in a cenobium: “From where did you acquire this virtue, brother—that whenever trouble occurs in the community, you neither speak nor intervene as mediator?” (Pelagius, Book XV, no. 30). When he did not wish to answer, the old man pressed him, and he said: “Forgive me, Abba. At the beginning, when I entered, I said to my thought: ‘Behold, you and this donkey are equals. For just as this donkey is beaten and does not speak, is insulted and answers nothing, so you too must be. For thus the psalm says: “I have become like a beast before you, and I am always with you”’ (Psalm 72).”

4. When the people of the Mazices invaded Scetis [Note: [Col. 1057] Rufinus, Book III, almost word for word; Pelagius, Book XV, no. 11.] and killed many of the Fathers, Abba Pimenion, together with another elder Father named Anub and five other Fathers, fled from there and came to a place called Terenuthi. There they found an ancient deserted temple, and all seven remained together in it until each should learn where he would stay in Egypt.

They agreed among themselves, saying: “During this week, let each person remain by himself, and let one not speak to another.” While they were doing this, there was a statue of an idol in that temple. Abba Anub therefore rose in the morning and stoned it in the face; then, returning in the evening, he said to it: “I have sinned; forgive me.” He did this throughout the entire week.

On Saturday, when they had assembled together, Abba Pimenion said to him: “What did you intend to accomplish during this whole week, saying to an idol, as a faithful man would, ‘Forgive me’?” The old man Anub replied: “I did this for your sake. Tell me: when I was stoning this idol, did it speak or become angry? Or when I asked it for forgiveness, did it exalt or glorify itself?”

Abba Pimenion answered him: “Certainly not.” Then the old man said: “Brothers, there are seven of us. If you wish, therefore, to remain together so that we may gain profit for our souls, let this idol be an example to us: when someone is insulted, let him not become angry; when forgiveness is sought from him, let him not glorify or exalt himself. But if you do not wish this, let each one go wherever he wishes.”

They threw themselves upon the ground and promised to do this. And so they remained for many years with great humility and abstinence, appointing one of their number as steward. They attained perfection and had one desire. Whatever was placed on the table, they were refreshed by it, and no one said, “Bring us that,” or, “I do not want to eat this.”

They slept four hours at night, sang psalms for four hours, and worked for four hours. During the day, at intervals, they devoted themselves to the divine offices, working and reading, and weaving palm leaves until the ninth hour. After this they prepared food for themselves, gathering certain herbs of the earth. [Col. 1058B]

## CHAPTER XLIII. What the Observance of Spiritual Discipline Is

1. A certain brother (Appendix of Martin, no. 106) asked holy Abba Serapion, who had ten thousand monks under his governance, saying: “Other brothers from the community have chosen me to command them. Show me how I should give orders.” Serapion replied:

“My command may perhaps be a difficult one. For our Lord Jesus Christ instructs us through his Gospel, saying: ‘If you love me, keep my commandments’ (John 14). And when the disciples were disputing among themselves about precedence, asking which of them was the greatest, he said to them: ‘If anyone wishes to become great among you, he shall be your servant; and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be the servant of all’ (Mark 10).

“The Apostle Peter, in his letter, instructs shepherds: ‘Feed the flock of God that is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion but willingly according to God; not for shameful gain but eagerly; not as lording it over the allotments, but becoming examples to the flock. And when the chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the unfading crown of glory’ (1 Peter 5).

“Therefore first do what you command, so that you may offer them not only commands but also a model for imitation of your example. Do not be a hireling but a shepherd of sheep, because our Savior called blessed the one whom he appointed over his household to give them food at the proper time (Matthew 24).” [Col. 1058D]

2. Abba Moses asked Abba Silvanus, saying: “Can a person each day take hold of the beginning of the ascetic life?” He replied: “One must take hold of something from everything” (Appendix of Martin, no. 108).

“Rising in the morning, let him take the beginning of wisdom: in every virtue and every commandment of God; in great patience, endurance, and love of God; with humility of soul and body; in much perseverance and remaining in the cell; in prayer [Col. 1059A] and supplication, with groaning; with purity of heart and eyes; with guarding of the tongue and of speech; in renunciation of material things and desires of the flesh; possessing anguish in the contest; in spiritual self-control and the struggle of battle; in repentance and mourning; in simplicity of soul and silence; in fasts and night vigils; in the work of one’s hands, according to what the Apostle Paul says, ‘working with your hands’; in hunger and thirst; in cold and nakedness; in labors, hardships, and persecutions; in pits, caves, and caverns (2 Corinthians 11).

“Be a doer of the word and not merely a hearer (James 1), working the talent to double its value, wearing the wedding garment, and established upon the firm rock.

“Let almsgiving and faith not abandon you” [Note: [Col. 1059] Rufinus, Book III, no. 206; Pelagius, Book X, no. 63, under the name of Moses; Appendix of Martin, no. 108.].

“Consider every day that death is near; and as though already shut in a tomb, care nothing for this world, because worldly anxiety and the desire for riches are the thorns that the Lord said in the Gospel must be avoided, for they choke the good seed (Luke 8).

“Fasting from food, humility, and mourning must not depart from you, because the Lord scatters the bones of those who please themselves. Let fear remain in you every hour, as it is written: ‘Because of your fear, O Lord, we conceived, and we travailed, and we gave birth to the spirit of salvation’ (Isaiah 26).

“Look to these things, and to whatever other virtue there may be among them. Do not measure yourself against the great, nor consider yourself righteous; rather, believe yourself lower than every creature, that is, more contemptible than any sinful person. ‘Whoever thinks himself to be something, when he is nothing, deceives himself’ (Galatians 6).

“Do not judge your neighbor, nor despise the faults of others; but mourn your own sins, and do not be concerned about the conduct of any person. Be gentle in spirit and not angry. Have nothing in your heart—neither hatred nor anything against an enemy without cause. Do not despise him in his tribulation, and do not return evil for evil, but be peaceful with everyone: this is the bond of perfection.

“Do not trust one who does evil, nor rejoice with one who has done evil to his neighbor. Do not slander others, because God is judge and witness in all things. Do not hate anyone because of his sin, for it is written: ‘Do not judge, so that you may not be judged’ (Matthew 7).

“When you rebuke another, take care that you do not commit worse things. Do not despise the sinner, but pray for him, that God may grant him conversion to repentance. And if you hear that someone is doing evil, answer by saying: ‘Am I the judge of these things? I am a sinful person, dead beneath my sins.’ A dead man has no reason to concern himself with anyone.

“Whoever attends to and considers all these things is a worker of every righteousness, while the prophet proclaims concerning Christ our Redeemer: ‘But I am a worm and not a man’ (Psalm 21). And another prophet, Habakkuk, says: ‘The stone will cry out from the wall, and the beetle will speak from the wood’ (Habakkuk 2). But while we exalt ourselves in many things, in many things we are tripped up.

“Whoever guards these things lives under the grace and power of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

## CHAPTER XLIV. On the Meditations of Twelve Anchorites

[Note: [Col. 1062D] On the Meditations.] “Since some time ago I received from the Augustan Library, most promptly supplied by David Roeschelius, this same chapter expressed in Greek, it is worthwhile to append it here:

### Narrative of Twelve Fathers Who Met Together Concerning Their Own Achievements

Once twelve wise and spiritual anchorites had gathered together, they asked themselves, each to state what he had accomplished in his cell, and what ascetic practice and spiritual virtue he had practiced.

[Col. 1063A] The first, who was also the eldest among them, said:

“Brothers, from the time when I began to live in quiet, I completely crucified myself to external affairs, remembering what is written (Psalm 2): ‘Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke from us.’ And, making something like a wall between my soul and bodily affairs, I said in my mind: ‘Just as the one inside the wall does not see the person standing outside, so you too must not wish to look upon external affairs, but attend to yourself, awaiting the hope of your God.’

“Treat evil desires like serpents and the offspring of vipers. Whenever I feel them growing in my heart, I attend to them with threat and anger and dry them up. I have never ceased becoming angry with my body and my soul, lest they do anything evil.” [Col. 1060A]

The anchorites, once wise, holy, and spiritual, twelve in number, having gathered together, asked themselves, each to say what he had corrected in his cell and what spiritual meditation he had practiced.

1. The first, who was also the eldest among them, said: “Brothers, from the time I began to live in quiet, I crucified myself completely to external activities, remembering what is written: ‘Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke from us’ (Psalm 2). And, making something like a wall between my mind and bodily affairs, I said in my mind: ‘Just as the one who is inside the wall does not see the person standing outside, so you too must not wish to look upon external affairs, but look to yourself, awaiting the hope of God every day.’ Thus I regard evil thoughts or evil desires as the offspring of serpents and scorpions. Whenever I sense them arising in my heart, I attend to them with threat and anger and dry them up; nor do I ever cease being angry with my body and my mind, lest they do anything wicked.” [Col. 1060B]

2. The second said: “I said to myself, from the time I renounced the earth: ‘Today you have been reborn; today you began to dwell here. Be a stranger each day, and tomorrow you will be released.’ And this I advise myself every day.”

3. The third said: “From early morning I ascend to my Lord, and after worshiping him I throw myself upon my face, confessing my transgressions. Then I descend, worshiping the angels of God and asking them to pray for me and for all creation. When I have completed this, I descend into the abyss. And just as the Jews once went toward Sodom and Gomorrah, tearing themselves and weeping and mourning over the misfortune of their fathers, so I go about among the punishments, contemplating my own limbs being tormented, and I weep with those who weep.” [Col. 1060C]

4. The fourth said: “I am as though I were sitting on the Mount of Olives with the Lord and his Apostles, and I said to myself: ‘From now on know no one according to the flesh; rather, remain always with them, imitating their zeal and manner of life, like the good Mary sitting at the Lord’s feet and listening to his words:

“‘Become holy, for I am holy’ (1 Peter 1:16).

“‘Become compassionate, as your Father who is in heaven is compassionate’ (Luke 6:36).

“‘Become perfect, as your Father who is in heaven is perfect’ (Matthew 5:48).

“‘Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart’ (Matthew 11:29).” [Col. 1063C]

5. The fifth said: “I contemplate the angels ascending and descending at every hour to the summons of souls. And, always awaiting the end, I say: ‘My heart is ready, O God.’”

6. The sixth said: “Every day I imagine hearing these words from the Lord: ‘Act for my sake, and I will give you rest. Struggle a little longer, and you will see my salvation and my glory. If you love me, keep my commandments (John 16:15). If you are my children, be ashamed before me, who am your father, as one who has endured so much for you. If you are my sheep, listen to the voice of the shepherd (John 10:27). If you are my slaves, follow the sufferings proper to your master.’”

7. The seventh said: “I continually meditate on these three things and unceasingly repeat them to myself: hope, faith, and love, so that I may rejoice in hope, be strengthened by faith, and never grieve anyone through love.” [Col. 1063D]

8. The eighth said: “I see the devil fallen [the printed text is uncertain: πέ . . . Ἴσ., πέσοντα], and wherever I go I see him with my inner eyes. I appeal to the Lord God against him, so that he may remain ineffectual and have power over no one, especially not over those who fear the Lord.”

9. The ninth said: “Every day I contemplate the assembly of the holy, and the Lord of glory shining in their midst above all. Whenever I become fainthearted, I ascend into the heavens and contemplate the most beautiful ranks of angels, the hymns they continually send up to God, and their melodies. I am lifted above the sounds and voices, so as to understand what is written: ‘The heavens declare the glory of God’ (Psalm 18:2). And I regard all things upon earth as ashes and refuse.” [Col. 1064A]

10. The tenth said: “I always see the angel who remains beside me standing near, and I guard myself while considering what is written: ‘I foresaw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken’ (Psalm 15:8). I therefore fear him as one who watches my ways, ascending every day to God and displaying my deeds and words.”

11. The eleventh said: “I set before myself the virtues as though they had faces—self-control, prudence, patience, and love—and surrounded myself with them. Wherever I go, I say: ‘Where are your instructors? Do not be careless; do not become fainthearted. Keep them always near you. Speak as you wish about virtue, so that after your death they may testify on your behalf before God, that he may find rest in you.’”

12. The twelfth said: “You, Fathers, possessing a heavenly way of life, have acquired heavenly thoughts; and this is not surprising. For I see you perfected in deeds and pursuing the things above. And what shall I say? You are lifted up even in your thoughts, for by your power you are transferred from the earth, having completely alienated yourselves from it.

“What shall I call you? Earthly angels and heavenly human beings—and I would not be wrong. But I still judge myself unworthy of such a state. Wherever I go or turn, I see my sins going before me, and I continually see them on my right and on my left. Having condemned myself among those beneath the earth, I say: ‘Be with those of whom you are worthy; for among them you will shortly be reckoned.’

“There I contemplate, Fathers, unceasing groans and tears, which no one can describe. I see some gnashing their teeth, shaking throughout their whole bodies, and trembling from head to foot. I throw myself upon the ground, cover myself with ashes, and beseech God not to let me experience those calamities.

“I also see a sea of fire, boiling without measure, breathing out flames and roaring, so that one might think that the roar of the fire reaches to heaven. In that fearful sea I see innumerable people thrown in by terrifying and savage angels, and all crying and howling together with one voice—such howls and voices as no one has heard upon earth—and all burning like brushwood, while the mercies of God turn away from them because of their lawlessness.

“Then I mourn the human race: how does it dare to speak a word or give heed to anything, when so many evils are reserved for the world? Holding my mind upon these things, I practice the mourning of which the Lord spoke, judging myself unworthy of both heaven and earth and considering what is written: ‘My tears have been my bread day and night’ (Psalm 41:4).”

These are the sayings of wise and spiritual Fathers who truly sought the Lord. May we also receive a way of life worthy of remembrance and narration, so that, having become blameless, perfect, and irreproachable, we may please God, to whom be glory forever. Amen.

[Note continued:] I do not present these things in Latin, because you have them here expressed in Latin by Paschasius, and anyone can readily compare them with the Latin text. Would that more learned men, if they possess in Greek anything relating to the Lives of the hermit Fathers, either publish it or supply it, so that the fidelity of translators may become evident and the history may retain its proper authority. [Col. 1064D]

2. The second said: “I said, ever since I renounced the earth: ‘Today you were reborn; today you began to serve God; today you began to dwell here. Thus be every day a stranger, and one who will be set free tomorrow.’ This was my daily counsel to myself.

3. The third said: “At dawn I ascend to my God; and, worshiping him, I throw myself on my face, [Col. 1060C] confessing my faults. Then, descending, I worship the angels of God, asking them to intercede with God for me and for every creature. When I have fulfilled these things, I go down into the abyss; and what the Jews do when they go to Jerusalem—cutting themselves, weeping, and mourning the downfall of their ancestors—I imitate by going around and waiting, subjecting my own limbs to torments; and I weep with those who weep.

4. The fourth said: “I am as though sitting on the Mount of Olives with the Lord and his disciples. And I said to myself: ‘Recognize no one according to the flesh, but always be an imitator of heavenly conduct with these men, like the good Mary Magdalene, sitting at Jesus’ feet and listening to his words.’ ‘Become holy and perfect, just as your Father who is in heaven is’ (Matt. [Col. 1060D] V). And: ‘Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart’ (Matt. XI).

5. The fifth said: “I behold angels ascending and descending at the summons of souls, and I always await my end, saying: ‘My heart is ready, O God; my heart is ready’ (Ps. CVII).

6. The sixth said: “Every day I resolved that my words should be heard by the Lord, thinking that I was being told: ‘Labor for my sake, and I will give you rest. Struggle a little longer, and you will see my salvation and my glory. If you love me, if you are my children, return to the Father, entreating him. If you are my brothers, be ashamed for my sake, just as I have suffered many things for you [Col. 1061A]. If you are my sheep, follow the Lord’s Passion.’

7. The seventh said: “I constantly meditate on these things, and without interruption I converse with myself about faith, hope, and charity: so that in hope I may rejoice, in love never distress anyone, and in faith grow strong.

8. The eighth said: “I await the devil, who is willing and seeking someone to devour. Wherever he strikes, I await him with my inward eyes, and I appeal to the Lord God against him, so that he may remain without effect and prevail in nothing, especially against those who fear God.

9. The ninth said: “Every day I await the church of intellectual virtues, and I see the Lord of glory shining in their midst above them all. When [Col. 1061B] I depart from him, I ascend into heaven, awaiting the angels’ wondrous beauties and the hymns they ceaselessly send forth to God, together with their sweet songs. I am carried away by their sounds, voices, and sweetness, so that I delight in recalling what is written: ‘The heavens declare the glory of God, and the works of his hands proclaim the firmament’ (Ps. XVIII). And I regard everything that is upon the earth as ashes and dung.

10. The tenth said: “I await my angel, standing beside me; and I guard myself, remembering what is written: ‘I kept the Lord always before my eyes, because he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken’ (Ps. XV). Therefore I fear him as one who guards my ways, ascends daily to God, and makes known my deeds and [Col. 1061C] words.

11. The eleventh said: “I put a face upon the virtues—as though upon temperance, chastity, kindness, and love—and have stood within myself. Surrounding myself with them, and wherever I go, I say to myself: ‘Where are your followers? Do not lose heart; do not fail, since you always have them beside you.’ Whatever you please, speak about virtue, so that after death they may testify concerning you before God, because they found rest in you.

[Col. 1062A] 12. The twelfth said: “You, Fathers, possessing a heavenly way of life, also possess heavenly wisdom. There is nothing surprising in that. I see you raised up by your works and pursuing higher things. What shall I say? By virtue you have even been transported beyond the earth, wholly estranging yourselves from it. What shall I say? In calling you earthly angels and heavenly men, I shall not have spoken falsely. But I, judging myself unworthy of these things, see that my sins always go before me, wherever I go, on my right and on my left. As for hell, I have sentenced myself to it, saying: ‘Be with those of whom you are worthy; after a little while you will be numbered among them.’

“I see there equal groans and unceasing tears, which no one can recount. I behold some gnashing their teeth, leaping with their whole bodies, and trembling [Col. 1062B] from head to foot. Throwing myself upon the ground and embracing the ashes, I beseech God never to let me experience the reality of their fate. I also see an immeasurable sea of boiling fire, surging and roaring, so that some might think the waves of fire reach as far as heaven; and in that terrifying sea innumerable people cast down by wild beasts. All together, with one voice, they cry out and howl—such howls and voices as no one on earth has ever heard—and burn like every dry shrub, while God’s mercy turns away from them because of their injustices.

“Then I lament the human race, which dares to speak or pay attention to anyone, while such evils have been stored up for the world. And in these thoughts I hold my mind, meditating on the Lord’s saying, judging myself unworthy of [Col. 1062C] heaven and earth, and considering what is written: ‘My tears have become my bread day and night’ (Ps. XLI).”

These are the responses of the wise and spiritual Fathers. May a worthy remembrance of them also come to us, so that we may be able to demonstrate by our deeds the narrative of their way of life, and, having become blameless, perfect, and irreproachable, please our Savior. To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1064D]

Observe that I obtained only two manuscript copies of this book; yet they did not entirely agree in their chapters and numbers, either with one another or with the printed editions. In one of them, a very old copy, the following chapter was additionally inserted before chapter 5:

**On the Worthlessness of Clothing**

“Abba Agathon disciplined himself and excelled in all things with discretion, both in the work of his hands and in clothing. For he used garments that appeared neither sufficiently good nor sufficiently bad to anyone. He used to say to his disciples: ‘Let a monk’s clothing also be such as repels nakedness and cold, not of an ostentatious color, by which the soul may be tossed about in the arrogance of self-display or in vanity.’”

Here a certain little know-it-all had corrected *inditi* to *indici*. [Col. 1066A] But the correct reading is *inditi*, that is, “acquired” or “assumed.”

Observe also that many passages which Paschasius shares with Rufinus are found in nearly the same words in Rufinus and Paschasius.]

**BOOK EIGHT OF THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS, OR THE LAUSIAC HISTORY, BY PALLADIUS, BISHOP OF HELENOPOLIS, TRANSLATED BY GENTIANUS HERVETUS**

**PRELIMINARY REMARKS ON THE BOOK OF PALLADIUS, AND PRAISES OF THE SAME BOOK**

[Col. 1065]

**To the Reader**

What we did in the first and second books—namely, present at a single glance, from the *Annals* of the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius, the journeys of those authors whose activities occupied the greater part of those books—we shall likewise attempt here. Receive, then, Palladius’ journey, arranged in some general fashion by years and places. You will read the remaining minor details and particular encounters in his own text. I have also added the various journeys of Melania the Younger, to illuminate Palladius, who mentions only certain matters concerning her journey in passing. Concerning Melania the Elder, whom Palladius also mentions, you have an extensive account above in the preliminary remarks to Book Two, where we discussed the journey of Rufinus, who is either the author or translator of that book, and whom Baronius holds to have remained at Melania’s side and to have been her companion on her journey.

[Col. 1065]

**[JOURNEYS]**

**THE JOURNEY OF PALLADIUS, BISHOP OF HELENOPOLIS**

[Col. 1065B]

**Journey to Egypt**

In the year of Christ 388. Baronius, vol. IV, under that year.—In this same year [of Christ 388, the fourth of Pope Siricius, the thirteenth of Valentinian, and the tenth of the emperors Theodosius], specifically during the second consulship of Theodosius, Palladius of Galatia, as he himself testifies (Palladius, in the *Lausiac History*, chap. 1), went to Alexandria. Thereafter, both from what he saw while traveling through the Egyptian desert and from what he heard from others, he wrote an account for the prefect Lausos. For this reason they sometimes called the same book the *Lausiac* [Note: [Col. 1083A] *Lausiaca*. Thus this history is called in the *Triodion*: εἶτα ἀνάγνωσις εἰς τὸ Λαυσαϊκόν, “then a reading for the Lausiac.” Hence one reads, “in the Lausiac,” which expression also occurs later in the same place. It was so called from Lausos, a high official of the empire; concerning him, see below at no. 7.] and that title is also found prefixed to it in some places, so that it is called the *Paradise of Heraclides* [Note: [Col. 1083B] *Paradise of Heraclides*. Here you have this *Paradise* as it was formerly published, after all the books of the *Lives of the Fathers*, in an appendix. See what was said in General Prolegomena 14.].

He remained in [Col. 1065C] the desert with Evagrius Ponticus for several years; he himself mentions the three years spent there (Palladius, chap. 12). Moreover, through his association with Evagrius Ponticus, he became imbued with Origen’s errors.

[Col. 1066B] We were surprised [Note: [Col. 1083B] *We were surprised*.] I think that Aloysius Lipomanus is meant here. In volume III of his *Lives of the Saints*, he reprinted at Venice in 1554, with a preface commending the book, Palladius’ work, which had earlier appeared at Paris in 1504 under the title *Heraclides*. But if Lipomanus’ meaning is correctly understood, he does not so much doubt whether Palladius of Galatia is the author of this book as say that Jerome, in his letter to Ctesiphon, is not speaking about this book of Palladius but about that of Evagrius—or rather of Rufinus—which is true. Nevertheless, the same six monks who appear in Rufinus’ book and are branded Origenists by Saint Jerome also appear in this book. But, says Lipomanus, “after setting aside these six, do not hesitate to read about the others.” See the General Prolegomenon, where we discussed the authority of these books.]

Some have wondered whether this Palladius is the same man whom Saint Jerome records as having been a Galatian by nation and an Origenist by profession. Yet Palladius himself professes this in that account, in these words (Palladius, chap. 22): “I answered that I was a stranger and came from the regions of Galatia, and I confessed that I was one of Evagrius’ brothers.” This is his own statement. Moreover, both Jerome and Epiphanius explicitly affirmed that Palladius and Evagrius had been corrupted by Origen’s errors.

Thus Palladius, clinging to Evagrius, also wasted away through infection with the same disease. Jerome, writing against the Pelagians, says the following about him: “Palladius, in servile wickedness, attempted to revive the same heresy [Col. 1066C] and to fabricate a new accusation against my Hebrew translation. Did we also envy his talent and nobility? Even now he is working the mystery of iniquity” (Jerome, preface to *Against the Pelagians), and so forth. For this reason Saint Epiphanius, lamenting the same man as he taught these doctrines in Palestine, says [Col. 1067A]: “Beware of Palladius the Galatian, who was once dear to us and now needs God’s mercy, because he preaches and teaches the heresy of Origen, lest perhaps he lead some of the people entrusted to you into the perversity of his error” (in Jerome, Letter 60).

He wrote this to John, bishop of Jerusalem, when Palladius had already left the desert of Nitria and, as he himself testifies (Palladius, in the *Lausiac*, chap. 22), had gone to Palestine because of his illness. There he remained for some time and taught Origen’s heresies; Epiphanius promptly warned John, bishop of that place, to beware of him. Since he names no other Origenist besides Palladius, it is certainly evident that, even if others were infected with the same stain, no one but [Col. 1067B] Palladius had taken on the task of teaching Origen’s ravings.

Therefore, the Origenist whom Jerome says tried to test the holy Paula was, as I see it, no one other than Palladius, who was then staying in Palestine. Jerome writes the following about this in Paula’s epitaph (Jerome, Letter 27):

“Let me briefly relate how she avoided the filthy pools of the heretics and regarded them as pagans. A certain clever and crafty man, learned and, as he thought, knowledgeable, began, without my knowledge, to put questions to her and say: ‘What sin did an infant commit to be seized by a demon? At what age shall we rise again? If at the same age at which we die, then after the resurrection we shall need nurses; if at another, there will be no resurrection of the dead but a transformation into others. Will there also be a difference of sex between male and female, or will there not? If there is, marriage and intercourse will follow, as will generation; if there is not, once the difference of sex has been removed, the same bodies will not rise again. For an earthly dwelling weighs down the sense that thinks of many things (Wis. IX); but they will be subtle and spiritual [Col. 1067C], as the Apostle says: “It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body” (1 Cor. XV).’

“From all this he wished to prove that rational creatures had fallen into bodies because of certain vices and ancient sins, and that, according to the diversity and merits of their sins, they were generated in one condition or another: either they would enjoy bodily health and the wealth and nobility of their parents, or, entering diseased flesh and the homes of the poor, they would pay the penalties of their former sins and be confined in the present age and in bodies as in a prison [Col. 1067D].

“When she had heard this and reported the man to me, the necessity fell upon me of resisting the most wicked viper and deadly beast of which the Psalmist speaks, saying: ‘Do not hand over the souls of those who confess you to the beasts’ (Ps. LXXV); and: ‘Rebuke, O Lord, the beasts of the reed, which, writing iniquity, speak lies against the Lord and lift their mouth on high’ (Ps. LXVII). I met the man and, with a brief question, brought to a close the arguments of the woman whom he was trying to deceive, saying,” and so forth.

He reports the disputation then held with him and finally adds: “From that day Paula began to detest the man and all who held the same doctrine, so that she publicly proclaimed them enemies of the Lord.”

This is Jerome’s account. Thus Palladius, having been refuted by Saint Jerome [Col. 1068A], turned his pen against him and first spewed forth the following about Paula in his account for Lausos:

“I saw many women and knew very many widows and virgins, among them Paula the Roman, mother of Toxotius, a woman of the most skillful intelligence for the way of life according to the spirit. Her progress in this way of life was hindered by a certain Jerome, a Dalmatian by birth, who, moved by envy, drew into his own peculiar rule of life a woman of the finest natural gifts, although, had she devoted herself to the perfect way of life, she seemed capable of leaving many—indeed, perhaps all—far behind her. Her daughter, Eustochium by name, is still practicing the monastic life at Bethlehem. I have never spoken with her; nevertheless, she is said to possess outstanding chastity and to govern a community of fifty virgins” (Palladius, in the *Lausiac*, chap. 29).

This is Palladius’ statement. That he himself remained in [Col. 1068B] Palestine at least until the year 392 will be stated below from Epiphanius’ letter to John.

**Journey to Bithynia**

In the year of Christ 392. Baronius, vol. IV, under the year of Christ 388.—But what happened afterward to Palladius? It happened that, leaving Palestine for Bithynia, he assumed the persona of a Catholic and, associating with Catholics, afterward insinuated himself into the friendship of John Chrysostom, bishop of Constantinople [Col. 1068C].

“And from where,” you will ask, “did you learn this about his association with John?” Chiefly from the fact that he supported that same John Chrysostom. He was connected with him not only by Catholic communion but also by sharing in the sufferings that befell him. For what he endured in defense of John he himself declares in these words:

“From Palestine I came to the province of Bithynia, where, I do not know how—whether through human zeal or by divine will (God knows)—I was made bishop beyond my merits. There I shared in the sufferings of that upheaval which arose under Saint John; and, hidden for ten months in a most obscure cell, I began to recall the sayings of that holy man” (Palladius, in the *Lausiac*, chap. 22), and so forth.

**Journey to Asia**

[Col. 1068D]

In the year of Christ 400. Baronius, vol. V, under that year.—In the year of Christ 400, the third of Pope Anastasius and the sixth of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, a synod of twenty-two bishops was held at Constantinople concerning the Asian bishops, when the case of Antoninus, bishop of Ephesus, was examined; and Palladius was sent to Asia with two others (Palladius, in the *Dialogue*).

Palladius—or whoever the author was—relates the matter in this way in the *Dialogue on the Affairs of John Chrysostom*:

“After the present synod had taken counsel, it sent certain bishops from among those present to Asia to question the witnesses. Three were chosen from the whole number: Syncletius the Metropolitan, Hesychius the Oparian, and Palladius of Helenopolis. The synod [Col. 1069A] instructed them that anyone who did not appear within two months at Hypaepa, a city of Asia, to defend his rights—since the accusers and the remaining bishops who were to be judged by Syncletius and his associates were neighbors—was to be excommunicated.

“Accordingly, the aforesaid bishops Syncletius and Palladius went down to Smyrna. Hesychius, however, because he favored Antoninus, pretended to be ill. They immediately announced their arrival by letter to both parties, so that, assembling in the city mentioned, they might fulfill what they had promised.

“Before the judges arrived, those men had entered into friendships, some persuaded by gold, others bound by an oath. When they had assembled in the city itself, the judges thought they could trifle with them by delaying the witnesses, as though the witnesses had gone abroad for various reasons. The judges then [Col. 1069B] asked the accuser within how many days he would produce the witnesses, promising that they would wait for him.

“Thinking that the judges found the harshness of the climate difficult to endure and therefore wished to depart—for the heat of the summer sun was intense—he promised to produce the witnesses within forty days, voluntarily subjecting himself otherwise to the penalty of the canons. The judges waited forty days. Meanwhile, the accuser, who had been sent to seek out the witnesses, neglected this business and came to Constantinople, where he went into hiding. When he did not appear anywhere, the judges wrote to all the bishops of Asia, declaring him excommunicated, whether as a deserter or as one who had withdrawn. After remaining there another forty days, since he did not appear at all, they returned to Constantinople. There they found Eusebius and reproached him for what he had done. Again he pleaded bodily illness [Col. 1069C] and promised to produce the witnesses.”

**Journey to Rome**

In the year of Christ 404. Baronius, vol. IV, under the year 308, and vol. V, under the year 404.—At that same time, while a more violent persecution against Chrysostom was raging, Palladius departed from the East and went to Rome to Innocent, by whom he was received together with others.

“And from where,” you will ask, “do you derive this?” He himself bears witness to it. Speaking of Pinianus and his wife Melania the Younger, by whom he was received in the city, he says:

“Even to us, certainly, although we were very many gathered together, who had traveled to Rome [Col. 1070D] on account of the blessed Bishop John, they did not render insignificant services. While we were staying in those regions, they received us with the greatest hospitality and, when we departed from there, honored us with the most lavish expenditure [Col. 1069D]” (Palladius, in the *Lausiac*, chap. 49).

This is his own statement.

[Note: [Col. 1083C] *When this occurred*.] I do not think that the passage taken from Palladius’ *Dialogue on the Affairs of Saint Chrysostom* clearly concerns our Palladius of Galatia. For although that Palladius is called bishop of Helenopolis there, on page 5, how can he later in the same dialogue be called bishop of the Blemmyes or Ethiopians? For on page 30 of Chrysostom’s edition, which Baronius cites, Theodore asks:

“Tell me, please, what happened to those bishops who were sent with our men—namely, Eulysius, Palladius, Cyriacus, and Democritus [read: Demetrius]?”

Palladius replies: “Cyriacus of Emesa was led eighty thousand paces to Palmyra, a Persian town; Eulysius was banished to a fortress of the Arabs at Bostra called Nusphas, adjacent to the Saracens; Palladius, bishop of the Blemmyes or Ethiopians, is being held near a place called Syene; and Demetrius is being held within the Oasis nearest to the Mazices, for there are other Oases as well.”

Yet these four are said on page 5 of the same work to have come to Rome, where Eulysius is called bishop of Apamea in Bithynia and Demetrius bishop of Pisinuntus; and it is said that he came to Rome a second time. On page 6, Cyriacus is said to have been sent with Demetrius, Eulysius, Palladius, and several Roman companions from the Roman Church to the East. There it is also said of the Romans who had returned after four months:

“Nor could they tell us anything more certain about the blessed John, nor where Demetrius, Cyriacus, Eulysius, and Palladius now are.”

Therefore one of the two passages is corrupt. If in the first passage, on page 5, that Palladius is correctly called bishop of Helenopolis, it should be considered whether in the later passage, on page 30, the words have been transposed, so that one should read: “Palladius, bishop, is being held near the place of the Blemmyes or Ethiopians, which is called Syene.” Certainly Syene is near the Blemmyes and Ethiopians. This conjecture of mine [Col. 1084A] will stand only if it is supported by some Greek manuscript.]

When this occurred, you have it set out in the *Dialogue on the Affairs of the same holy John* [Note: [Col. 1069D] It is found in volume I of John Chrysostom, Paris edition, col. 10.] in these words:

“Hardly a month had passed when Palladius also, bishop of Helenopolis—for Helenopolis is a city in Bithynia, as stated above—arrived without letters. He too said that he had fled from the madness of the rulers; but he related everything more explicitly and pointedly, and produced the very copy of the edict,” and so forth.

Although the Palladius under discussion must be different from the one who speaks in that dialogue—for he says [Col. 1070A] that he came to Rome for the first time only when, under Pope Zosimus, he undertook that embassy on behalf of the peace of the churches—what then? That he temporarily changed his outward persona rather than his mind, which was filled with impiety, is strongly indicated by the fact that in the book he wrote after those disturbances, as is evident from the fact that he mentions Melania’s death, which occurred after the sack of Rome, he praised numerous Origenists and exalted Evagrius, who was branded with Origen’s errors, to the heavens.

**Palladius’ Second Arrival at Rome with Coelestius in the Case of Pelagius the Heresiarch**

In the year of Christ 417. Baronius, vol. V, under that year.—The four hundred seventeenth year of Christ [the sixteenth of Pope Innocent, the twenty-third of Honorius, and the tenth of the emperors Theodosius], beginning with the eleventh consulship of Honorius Augustus and the second of Constantius [Col. 1070B], was the year in which Pelagius the heresiarch, having learned that his acquittal, secured in the Palestinian council, had not been accepted by Innocent, the Roman pontiff, but that he remained bound by the earlier condemnation pronounced against him, employed every artifice of deception in order to mislead him. For he himself sent a letter to Pope Innocent in which he professed that he was truly a Catholic. Prailius of Jerusalem also sent another letter on the same matter, stating that Pelagius’ acquittal had been lawfully accomplished.

It was arranged that Coelestius, his disciple, who was likewise branded with heresy, should be sent to Rome with these letters, to conduct his own case and appeal to the judgment of the apostolic see against his accusers, as though harassed by calumnies, thereby declaring that he believed no differently from what the Catholic Church held.

[Col. 1070C] How much weight this view has [Note: [Col. 1084A] *How much weight this view has*.] I do not see how this opinion rests on a solid foundation, since that Palladius, the author of the *Dialogue on the Affairs of Saint Chrysostom*, appears wholly distinct from Palladius of Galatia. Baronius himself acknowledges this shortly before, under the year of Christ 404, where he discusses the journey to Rome of Palladius of Galatia. Accordingly, this embassy of Palladius to Pope Zosimus must be understood as belonging to Palladius, the author of the dialogue, not to the Galatian writer of the *Lausiac*.]

It is nevertheless permissible to suppose that, among all these men and in connection with all these matters, Palladius the Galatian, bishop of Helenopolis, was also an envoy; it was stated above, on the testimony of Saint Jerome, that he favored Pelagius. For Palladius himself, in the dialogue he wrote about the affairs of Saint John Chrysostom, testifies at its very beginning that he came to Rome under Pope Zosimus.

**Palladius the Galatian Accused of Impurity by Jerome**

Baronius, vol. V, under the year of Christ 413.—That this proud man, Pelagius, was carried to such madness that he asserted it was within human power, by free choice, not merely to avoid sin but also not to be tempted, is shown by Jerome, who, speaking in Pelagius’ person and using his words, says:

“Others, shut up in cells and not seeing women, are tortured by desires because they are wretched and do not hear my words. But even if I am surrounded by bands of women, I have no desire. For it has been said of me: ‘Holy stones roll upon the earth’ (Zech. IX); and therefore I do not feel desire, because by the power of free choice I carry Christ’s trophy” (Jerome, *Against the Pelagians*, book II).

It appears that Saint Jerome struck at such heretics elsewhere as well, when he says:

“If they had made my words known to my people without flattering them and ruining them by adulation, so as to say, ‘You have no sins; you possess perfect righteousness; holiness, chastity, and righteousness are found in you alone,’ I would not have handed them over to impurity and disgrace, to do what is improper and follow their worst thoughts. Let us observe the heretics: how, once they have despaired of salvation, they give themselves over to gluttony and luxury; let them eat meat, frequently visit the baths, smell of musk, be drenched in various perfumes, and seek bodily beauty” (Jerome, *On Jeremiah*, book IV, chap. 23), and so forth.

In this way Saint Jerome was attacking Pelagius and the Pelagians; and without doubt, among others, he was also taunting Palladius the Galatian, bishop of Helenopolis in Bithynia. He mentions him explicitly in the preface to the same books written against Pelagius: Palladius habitually associated with religious women, yet boasted with great ostentation that he was entirely free from desire [Col. 1071A]. This was so even though, particularly in Egypt, while visiting the monks, he traveled in the company of women.

For this reason he was also rebuked [Col. 1071B] in a letter from Isidore of Pelusium, one worthy to be reproduced here, since it may serve everyone as a beneficial memorial of so great a man. It reads as follows (Isidore, Letter 284, book II):

“**To Bishop Palladius**

“Flee, most excellent man, as far as possible from meetings with women. For those who exercise the priestly office ought to be holier and purer than those who have withdrawn to the mountains. The former have charge both of themselves and of the people, whereas the latter care only for themselves. The former have been placed upon the summit of such dignity, and everyone scrutinizes and examines [Col. 1071C] their life; the latter sit in a cave, either tending their own wounds, concealing their faults, or even weaving crowns for themselves.

“If necessity should bind you to meet with them, keep your eyes cast down toward the ground, and teach the women themselves how they ought to be regarded. For it is not enough to teach how one ought to look; one must also teach how to look as one ought. When you have said a few things capable of fastening themselves upon and enlightening their minds, fly away at once, lest prolonged familiarity soften and weaken your strength and, having found you like some dreadful and lofty lion, cut off the mane—the hair that truly makes the lion a lion and preserves his royal dignity—while tearing out his teeth and claws [Col. 1071D], by whose aid he overcomes even the strongest beasts; and then, having disfigured and made ridiculous that dreadful, intolerable animal, which by its roar alone shakes a mountain, it may offer itself to children for mockery.

“If you desire to be honored by women—which is especially unbecoming to a spiritual man—whatever the circumstances [Col. 1072A], have no dealings with women, and then you will receive honor from them. This will be especially advantageous to us when it is not sought from us. Everyone usually despises those by whom he is honored and caressed, but admires those by whom he is not at all soothed by flattery. The female nature is particularly subject to this impulse. It becomes intolerable when someone flatters it; conversely, it most esteems and admires those who possess greater freedom and exercise greater authority over it.

“If you say that you often associate with them without suffering any harm from it, I may perhaps allow myself to be persuaded of that. But I also wish everyone to believe this: they say that water wears away stones and that a rock is hollowed out by drops of water falling continuously. The meaning of these words is as follows: What can be imagined harder than a rock? What, again, is softer than water, and indeed than a drop of water [Col. 1072B]? Yet persistence overcomes nature. If nature, which is difficult to move, is moved, and endures what it least possessed, by what reasoning will the will, which is easily moved, not be overcome and overturned by habit?”

Thus far Isidore, with excellent reasoning and an example, demolishes what those men asserted: that our will by its own nature can, if it wishes, avoid sin without the help of grace, or even cannot be tempted if it does not wish to be. For Isidore taught that nature is overcome by persistence.

**THE JOURNEY OF MELANIA THE YOUNGER AND HER HUSBAND PINIANUS WITH ALBINA, HER MOTHER**

**Journey to Sicily**

In the year of Christ 408. Baronius, vol. V, under that year.—In this same year [of Christ 408, the seventh of Pope Innocent, the fourteenth of Honorius, and the first of the emperors Theodosius], which preceded the siege of the city [Col. 1072C], Melania the Roman widow, whom we have often mentioned above, recalling an ancient prophecy uttered four hundred years earlier, as Palladius says, sold her estates and, together with Melania her granddaughter, Pinianus, Melania’s husband, and Albina, her daughter-in-law, left Rome to escape with them from the impending disaster of the city. She traveled again through Sicily to Jerusalem, where she departed this life after forty days. This is taken from Palladius (Palladius, in the *Lausiac*, chap. 33).

**Journey to Africa, and First to Carthage and Tagaste**

In the year of Christ 409. Baronius, vol. V, under that year.—In this same year [of Christ 409, the eighth of Pope Innocent, the fifteenth of Honorius, and the second of the emperors Theodosius], Pinianus, a man of illustrious rank, together with Melania the Elder, Melania the Younger, his wife [Col. 1072D], and Albina, the mother of the younger Melania, his mother-in-law, having, in the previous year, sold the property he possessed at Rome and in Italy, sailed to Carthage. There, enriching the poor of the Church from the money he had amassed, he departed from there to Saint Alypius at Tagaste (Palladius, in the *Lausiac*, chap. 9).

When Saint Augustine first heard of their arrival, he sent them a letter in which he excused himself for being unable to hurry to visit them because of the severe winter that had descended and the unsettled condition of the Church at Hippo. The letter itself survives, entitled *To Albinus, Pinianus, and Melania* (Augustine, Letter 227).

[Note: [Col. 1084B] *But instead of Albinus, Albina*.] Baronius’ conjecture that Albina is meant here is probable, but it is not necessary to restore *Albina* in place of *Albinus*. For it is established that in that age women’s names were sometimes expressed with masculine endings. Thus, in ancient authors, the woman now called Melania appears as *Melania*, *Melanius*, and *Melanium*. So in Jerome, Letter 79—the letter cited here in connection with Melania’s journey to Jerusalem—we read: “Albinus, Pinianus, and Melania send you many greetings.”

Nor is there any need to correct the text or conjecture a son named Albinus. Thus in Palladius, chapter 117, where the Latin reads *Concerning Saint Melania*, the Greek has Περὶ τῆς μακαρίας Μελανίου, “Concerning the blessed Melanius.” Likewise, Saint Paulinus is to be understood in Letter 249 to Augustine, which is included among Augustine’s letters:

“And I can proclaim nothing better or holier concerning the blessed mother of this son and the father, the root of holy branches, Melanius, than what your Holiness has deigned to say and discuss about her.”

For by *Melanius* he means Melania herself, as is clear even from what follows, “about her.” For if the passage concerned Melania herself and her father Melanius, as the compiler of the marginal notes and index at Baronius, volume V, under the year of Christ 409, supposed, Paulinus would have said “about them,” not “about her.” And from where, I ask, is it established that Melania’s father was called Melanius? It is established that he was called Marcellus or Marcellinus.

Therefore, by *Melanius*, as I have said, he means Melania herself, whom he calls the mother of the son and the father, the root of holy branches, because several persons distinguished by holiness proceeded from her, such as Melania her granddaughter and other persons. Were these women, Melania and Albina, called *Melanius* and *Albinus* because of the manly courage by which they overcame every passion and the world, just as the Phrygians were called “Phrygian” from the effeminacy of Phrygia?]

I therefore think that the reading should be restored, because a woman of that name, Pinianus’ [Col. 1073A] mother-in-law, traveled with them to Africa. This is sufficiently clear both from Palladius and from the testimony of Augustine himself.

But when Pinianus was at Tagaste, he enriched that church with such lavish generosity that he aroused the envy of some toward its bishop Alypius, as Saint Augustine testifies in a letter written to him; and the Acts of Saint Melania themselves confirm this in the following words:

> “The city in which they were staying was called Tagaste. In it there was a sacred temple and a priest skilled in preaching, who by his discourse could lead many to salvation, named Alypius. While staying with him, they devoted themselves to the sacred Scriptures. They enriched the temple in which Alypius served with great generosity, with golden ornaments and shining jewels [Col. 1073B], and with the produce of many estates. They also built two monasteries, to which they gave abundant wealth and revenues. One of them had a community of eighty men; the other had one hundred and thirty virgins” (Epistle 224; Metaphrastes, 31 January).

This is what may be said concerning the gifts bestowed by Pinianus upon the church of Tagaste.

## The Journey to Hippo

Baronius, vol. V, under the year 499 of Christ.—Pinianus decided, together with Melania, to travel to Hippo to visit Saint Augustine, who was serving there as bishop. Alypius accompanied them [695]. Since Pinianus feared that Augustine might compel him to be ordained a presbyter, Alypius reassured him that this would never happen; for he had received Augustine’s pledge that he would not do so.

It was customary—and we have already recalled this above when treating Paulinus—that when someone distinguished by religious devotion stood out among other Christians, he might sometimes be seized by the faithful in the church and handed over to the bishop for ordination, even if he were married, while his wife likewise professed continence with the same resolve as her husband. The example previously recounted concerning Paulinus and Therasia demonstrates this.

Pinianus, therefore, perhaps sensing that this might happen, delayed his arrival. But reassured by Alypius’ promise, he went to Hippo to see Saint Augustine. While he was there, and while no such event was expected, it happened that, during the celebration of the synaxis in the church, before the catechumens were dismissed according to custom, the faithful people rushed upon Pinianus and surrounded him so that he could not escape [Col. 1073D], demanding that he be ordained a presbyter.

This greatly displeased Alypius, who had stood surety for him; and Pinianus himself and his mother-in-law Albina bore it with deep indignation, believing that the whole affair had been arranged at Augustine’s initiative. Consequently they were somewhat angered against him, and Alypius especially. But Saint Augustine explained how the matter had occurred in letters sent to them after they had immediately departed from Hippo and returned to Tagaste. He excused himself and declared at length that nothing had been done with his knowledge.

Writing to Albina, Pinianus’ mother-in-law—although he customarily called her Pinianus’ mother—Augustine sent a sufficiently lengthy letter in his own defense [Col. 1074A], satisfying all her complaints and ill-founded suspicions. He begins as follows (Augustine, Epistle 225):

> “It is right to console the distress of your heart, which you say you are unable to express, not to increase it; so that, if possible, we may heal your suspicions, rather than, by becoming angry with them on our own behalf, disturb still further your venerable heart, dedicated to God.
>
> “No fear of death was inflicted upon our holy brother, your son Pinianus, by the people of Hippo, even if he himself perhaps feared something of the kind. For we too were afraid that some desperate men, who often mingle secretly with the crowd through conspiracy, might burst into violent recklessness when they found an opportunity for sedition, which they would stir up as though in righteous indignation [Col. 1074B]. But, as we were later able to learn, no one said or attempted anything of the sort. Rather, they shouted many insulting and outrageous things against my brother Alypius. Would that through his prayers they might deserve to be absolved from so great a guilt.
>
> “After their first shouts, I told them that he could not be ordained against his will and explained by what promise I was bound. I added that, if they made him a presbyter in violation of my pledge, they would no longer have me as their bishop. I then left the crowd and returned to our seats. At that my unexpected response caused them for a while to hesitate and become confused; but soon, like a flame briefly pressed down by the wind, they began to flare up much more fiercely. They thought that either I might be forced not to keep my promise, or that, if I maintained my pledge, he might be ordained by another bishop.
>
> “I told those whom I could—the more distinguished and influential men who had come up to us in the apse—that I could neither be moved from keeping my promise nor permit him to be ordained by another bishop in the church entrusted to me unless I had been consulted and had given permission. If I permitted it, I would nevertheless be departing from my pledge. I also said that, if he were ordained against his will, they would accomplish nothing except that he would leave once ordained. They did not believe that this could happen.
>
> “But the crowd, stationed on the steps and persisting in the same resolve with a dreadful and unremitting roar of shouting, rendered both mind and counsel uncertain. Then those unworthy cries were directed against my brother Alypius; then more serious dangers were feared by us. Yet although I was shaken by so great an upheaval of the people and so great a disturbance of the [Col. 1074D] Church, and although I had said nothing else to that packed crowd except that I could not ordain him against my will, I was nevertheless not induced—though I had also promised this—not to urge him to accept the presbyterate [696]. If I had been able to persuade him, he would no longer have been ordained against his will.
>
> “I kept faith with both promises: not only the one I had already made public to the people, but also the one by which, so far as human beings were concerned, I was bound by a single witness. I kept, I say, the faith of a promise, not of an oath, in so great a danger. Although—as we later discovered—this danger was falsely feared, it nevertheless threatened everyone in common, and the fear itself was shared by all. I was especially afraid to leave the church in which we were [Col. 1075A]. Yet it had to be feared that, in my absence, they might do something of the kind even more readily, since reverence would be diminished and anger more inflamed.
>
> “Furthermore, if I were to leave with my brother Alypius through the crowd packed around us, it had to be feared that someone might dare to lay hands upon him. But if I left without him, what would become of my reputation if something perhaps happened to him and I seemed to have abandoned him for that very reason, so that he might be handed over to the raging crowd?
>
> “Amid these agitations of mine, this heavy sorrow, and this breathless absence of any counsel, behold, suddenly and unexpectedly our holy son Pinianus sent me a servant of God to say that he wished to swear before the people that, if he were ordained against his will, he would leave Africa. He evidently believed that, since he could not commit perjury, they would no longer persist in fruitless shouting to expel from this place a man whom at least we ought to have as a neighbor.
>
> “Because I thought that after this oath I would have to fear a still more violent expression of their grief, I kept the matter silently to myself. Since he had also asked me to come to him, I did not delay. When he had told me this, he immediately added to the same oath what he had sent me word of through another servant of God while I was coming to him: namely, that he would remain present [Col. 1075B] if no one imposed the burden of the clergy upon him against his will.” That is, he would not leave Hippo if he were allowed to remain free, without the obligation of the clergy.

> “Here, in such great distress, I was refreshed as though by a breathing of air. I said nothing to him, but hastened to my brother Alypius and told him what Pinianus had said. [Col. 1075C] But he, as I suppose, avoiding any action being taken on his authority that might cause you offense, said: ‘Let no one consult me in this matter.’
>
> “When I heard this, I went to the tumultuous crowd. After silence had been made, I disclosed what had been promised, together with the oath. But those who were thinking only of his presbyterate and desiring it did not receive the offer as I had expected. After muttering among themselves for a little while, they requested that the same promise and oath should include this addition: if he should ever decide to consent to receive clerical office, he should consent only to the church of Hippo.
>
> “I reported this to him, and without hesitation he agreed. I announced it to them; they rejoiced and immediately demanded the promised oath. I returned to our son Pinianus and found him wavering over the words by which that promise, together with the oath, could be framed, because of unforeseen necessities that might compel him to leave [Col. 1075D]. He also revealed what he feared: that some hostile invasion might occur, which would have to be avoided by departure.
>
> “He wanted holy Melania and the reason of the unhealthy climate to be added, but Melania rebuked him in her reply. I said that a serious and by no means negligible necessity had been brought forward by her, one that could compel even citizens to emigrate. But if these things were told to the people, we would have to fear appearing to wish them evil; whereas, if an excuse were made under the name of necessity, it would be thought nothing but a fraudulent necessity.
>
> “Nevertheless, it was decided that we should test the people’s mind on this matter, and we found nothing other than what we had expected. When his words were repeated by the deacon and everything had pleased them, as soon as the name of the intervening necessity was heard, an immediate outcry arose. The promise displeased them, the disturbance broke out again, and the people concluded that nothing but deception was being practiced against them.
>
> “When our holy son Pinianus saw this, he ordered the word ‘necessity’ to be removed; and the people returned once more to rejoicing. When I excused myself on the grounds of weariness, he refused to approach the people without me, and we went together. He told them that he had instructed the deacon to say what they had heard, that he had sworn it, and that he would carry it out; then he proceeded to state everything in the wording he had dictated.
>
> “They replied, ‘Thanks be to God,’ and requested that the entire document be signed. We dismissed the catechumens, and he immediately signed the document. Then we bishops [697] began to be asked—not by the voices of the people, but by the people through respectable faithful men—to sign also. But when I began to sign, the holy Melania objected. I was astonished that she did so only so late, as though we could make that promise and oath void by refusing to sign.
>
> “Nevertheless, I obeyed; and thus my signature remained incomplete. No one thereafter thought that we should be pressed further to sign.”

This is Saint Augustine’s account.

## Return to Tagaste

Baronius, vol. V, under the year 409 of Christ.—Since Pinianus knew very well that he was not truly bound by promises made under force and fear, he secretly returned to Tagaste with his companions the following day.

Augustine reports in the same letter to Albina what the people of Hippo did when they learned of this. He says that he had indicated it to her in another writing:

> “As for the disturbances and the words of the people on the following day, after they learned that he himself had departed, I have taken care to make them known to your holiness by a memorandum, insofar as I judged sufficient.
