Therefore, whoever may have told you anything contrary to what I have related either is lying or is mistaken” (Augustine, Epistle 215).

This is his own statement.

Albina had complained in a letter, first, against Augustine, because he had induced Pinianus to swear; and she had also reproached the people of Hippo, suggesting that, enticed by love of money, they had tried to claim for themselves a very rich man. Since Augustine’s reputation was indirectly attacked by these allegations, he added a defense in the same letter, both for himself and for the people [Col. 1076D]. Among other things, he insists that he himself, formerly a citizen of Tagaste, had suffered the same pressure from the people of Hippo. They had been moved to act not by any other motive than piety: believing him to be a respectable man, they wanted to set him over themselves as presbyter.

But let us hear his own words:

> “How, then,” he says, “do you say that they did this from the most shameful greed for money? First, because this has nothing at all to do with the people who were shouting. Just as the people of Tagaste, concerning what you have entrusted to the church of Tagaste, possess nothing except joy in your good work, so also the people of Hippo—and the people of any other place where you have obeyed, or may at any time obey, the Lord’s commands concerning the mammon of unrighteousness.
>
> “Therefore, when the people most earnestly demanded that such a great man should serve their church [Col. 1077A], they were not seeking their own financial advantage from you; rather, they loved in you your contempt for money. For if they loved in me what they had heard—that I had abandoned a few small paternal fields and turned to the free service of God—they did not envy the church of Tagaste, my earthly homeland. But since that church had not imposed the clerical office upon me, whenever they could, they seized me in order to have me. How much more passionately, then, could they love in our Pinianus the conquest and trampling underfoot of so great a desire for this world, so great wealth, and so great a hope?
>
> “In the judgment of many who compare themselves with one another, I seem not to have abandoned riches but to have come into riches. For scarcely a twentieth part [Col. 1077B] of my paternal property can be considered mine in comparison with the estates of the church, which I am now regarded as possessing like a master.”

Since, on the contrary, those who had been elevated to the presbyterate in the African churches had been extremely wealthy, he adds:

> “In any of the African churches—and especially in the greater ones—let our man be not merely a presbyter but a bishop. Compared with his former wealth, even if he acted with the spirit of a master, he would be exceedingly poor.
>
> “Thus Christian poverty is loved much more clearly and securely in one whose desire for greater possessions cannot be suspected. This inflamed the hearts of the people; this raised them to that violence of unremitting shouting. Let us not accuse them additionally of shameful greed, but rather allow them, without guilt, to love in others the good that they themselves do not possess” [Col. 1077C].

Augustine brings forward these and many other arguments in his defense.

Alypius, like Albina, also thought that the people of Hippo had attempted to use force against Pinianus out of love of money; and both held the same view that an oath extracted by force and fear had no validity [698]. Saint Augustine therefore wrote to Alypius as well as to Albina in opposition to these claims (Augustine, Epistle 124). From this it clearly appears that the matter was settled among them not without mutual offense; but charity quickly wiped away all the rust produced by such an altercation.

## The Journey to Jerusalem

Baronius, vol. V, under the year 419 of Christ.—I would also have you observe from the same letter of Saint Jerome that he sends greetings to the bishops Augustine and Alypius not only in the name of Paula’s granddaughter, but also in the names of Albina, Pinianus, and Melania, whom we said had been in Africa seven years earlier and afterward came together to Jerusalem. He says (Jerome, Epistle 79):

> “Our holy mutual children, Albinus [Albina], Apinianus [Pinianus], and Melania, greet you very warmly.”

That is what the letter says. But *Albinus* should be corrected to *Albina*, and *Apinianus* to *Pinianus*, unless a son named Albinus was present there in addition to his mother Albina.

“But when,” you ask, “did they arrive in Jerusalem?” Three years earlier. And lest you think that we are proceeding by conjecture or guessing, [Col. 1078A] the matter is expressly demonstrated in the Acts of Melania the Younger [Note: [Col. 1077D] They are extant in Metaphrastes, 31 January, and in Surius, vol. I.]. There it is said that she spent seven years in Africa. If you recall the time of her departure from Rome for Africa—which we said occurred in the year preceding the city’s disaster, namely 409—and count seven years from that time, you will certainly find that she and her companions arrived in Jerusalem three years earlier, as stated. Her mother Albina, the mother of Melania the Younger, came with her, as her Acts testify. That this Albina was the wife of the son of Melania the Elder is taught by Palladius (Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 33).

Palladius relates that Melania the Elder died forty days after her arrival in Jerusalem (same author, chapter 47), although he makes no mention of the others [Col. 1078B]. When he later says that they lived in Campania and Sicily (same author, chapter 49), he seems plainly to have been unaware that Augustine establishes with certainty that they lived in Africa, and likewise unaware that Saint Jerome makes it clear that they went to Jerusalem. All these matters are attested at greater length by the Acts of Saint Melania the Younger.

Indeed, it is also clear from Saint Augustine that when they reached Jerusalem and found Pelagius there, they admonished him to condemn outright whatever the orthodox were bringing against him. He, as though complying with them, wrote an anathema against those errors that Westerners had charged him with. But how deceitfully and craftily Saint [Col. 1078C] Augustine exposed this is another matter. For now, hear what he records in writing about them when they were dealing with Pelagius:

> “You wrote to me that you dealt with Pelagius so that he would condemn in writing whatever was said against him, and that he said in your hearing: ‘I anathematize’” (Augustine, *On the Grace of Christ*, book I, chapter 1), and so forth.

Albinus [Albina], Pinianus, and Melania sent Pelagius’ statements to Augustine himself. Later, under Pope Zosimus, Augustine demonstrated in opposing writings the deceptions of that impious heresiarch. But more on this elsewhere.

As for the deeds of Melania the Younger, her husband Pinianus, and their companions, the Acts of Melania’s life make clear that they traveled to Egypt to visit the holy monks dwelling in the desert, leaving her mother Albina in Jerusalem because of her advanced age [Col. 1078D]. On their return to Jerusalem, Pinianus pursued the monastic life separately from his wife, while Melania remained enclosed in a cell near the Mount of Olives for fourteen years and lived there, in a confined place, a life like that of the angels.

These things will indeed seem extraordinary. But if anyone reads what Palladius, the same author mentioned above, wrote about Melania’s way of life before she went to Jerusalem, while she was still living in Italy and especially at Rome (Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 49), as well as what the same Acts relate about her manner of life while she was in Africa, he will not be greatly surprised that both she and [Col. 1079A] her husband attained such a high degree of monastic life, since from the beginning they had both devoted themselves entirely to God.

## The Journey to Constantinople

In the year of Christ 434.—In this same year [Christ 434; Pope Sixtus III; Theodosius 27; Valentinian 10; emperors], in which Proclus assumed the governance of the see of Constantinople, Saint Melania the Younger—who, as we said, was leading a monastic life in Jerusalem—was summoned to Constantinople by a letter from her uncle Volusianus. When she arrived, she converted Volusianus, who until then had resisted, to the faith of Christ, and worked tirelessly, both by prayers to God and by words addressed to him, so that he might die a Christian and attain eternal life.

Let us recall a history worthy of illustrious remembrance. Photius recognized it as authentic in his *Bibliotheca* when he discussed the embassy of Volusianus, Melania his niece, and the bishop Proclus, who baptized Volusianus at Constantinople. We mentioned them above when discussing the edict of that same Volusianus against the Pelagian Caelestius.

In brief, it must be repeated that this is the same Volusianus whose conversion prompted his Christian mother to appeal to Saint Augustine through the tribune Marcellinus, so that Augustine might convert him to the faith of Christ. But although letters had been exchanged for this purpose, Saint Augustine was then unable to persuade him to do so. At last, however, God brought it about that he accomplished it, albeit late. The occasion is revealed in the Acts of Saint Melania [Note: [Col. 1079D] They are extant in Metaphrastes, 31 January, and in Surius, vol. I, on the same day], which, although written in a simple and plain style, relate the truth in these words [Col. 1079C]:

> “A letter was delivered to Melania from her uncle Volusianus, who at that time had been appointed prefect of the city of Rome and had been sent as ambassador to Byzantium to the empress Eudocia. The letter indicated that he had long desired to see her.
>
> “She too wished to see her uncle and persuade him to abandon the opinion of the pagans. But, uncertain in mind and fearful lest she do anything imprudent or contrary to God’s will, she consulted the matter with certain other monks. When they permitted her to depart, blessed Melania left Jerusalem and set out for Constantinople.
>
> “Through every city and region she passed, everyone honored her with the respect and services that were fitting. The priests and bishops of the cities treated her with no small honor; venerable virgins and all the distinguished monks worshiped and greeted her, and looked upon her as though she had come from heaven.
>
> “When she came to Chalcedon and reached the seashore, she was afraid to embark and appeared troubled. A woman who had lived in ascetic discipline, who had devoted herself above all to solitude and silence, and who had not experienced the disturbances found in a city, was rightly fearful and reluctant to enter the greatest city. She turned aside to a place where there was a church entirely dedicated to the blessed martyr Euphemia.
>
> “Around midnight the martyr emitted from herself an abundance of exceedingly sweet fragrance and filled the place with ineffable delight. Therefore, taking good courage, at dawn she boldly crossed the strait and entered Byzantium. She was received as a guest by a certain distinguished and otherwise good man named Lausus [Note: [Col. 1084D] Lausus. Life of Melania the Younger by Metaphrastes, 31 January, concerning her host at Byzantium: ‘She was received as a guest by a certain distinguished and otherwise good man named Lausus, who had risen to the honor of the praepositura.’ Baronius, vol. V, under the year 434 of Christ, Pope Sixtus III, Theodosius 27, Valentinian 10, emperors. This appears to be the Lausus to whom Palladius wrote his *Lausiac History*. Palladius likewise calls him *praepositus*, and also names him guardian of the empire. What this office of *praepositus* was, the same author explains at the end of his work, where he says that Lausus was in charge of the sacred bedchamber], who had risen to the honor of the *praepositura*.
>
> “She found her uncle Volusianus overcome by a serious illness. Astonished at her appearance and struck with wonder at the incredible and unexpected change in her face and clothing—for her countenance had become exceedingly emaciated through ascetic discipline—he exclaimed in a loud voice: ‘O Melania, dearest, what I see you to be now compared with what you were!’
>
> “Taking the opportunity offered by his words, she replied: ‘Learn from me also, blessed uncle, and receive a judgment concerning the good things to come. I would never have held so great a glory in contempt, nor money, nor have cast aside care for the body, unless I had been persuaded that shortly I would receive things far greater than these.’
>
> “Blessed Melania gradually entered his mind not only by herself but also through many others, and she sought to undermine his false religion. She did so also through the most wise Proclus, to whose faith the sacred office of the Constantinopolitan church had then been entrusted. When Proclus came to him and, at the urging of blessed Melania, directed him toward piety, Volusianus is said to have admired him so greatly that, after recognizing the truth, he even said that if Rome had three such men, the name of the pagans would never be heard there. But more on this later.
>
> “When Volusianus realized that Melania also wished to urge the emperor toward this matter, he immediately feared that the baptism would be considered violent and involuntary, and that he himself would lose the reward he expected to gain from it, and he prevented her from pursuing what she had begun. He, however, as we shall say shortly, completed the matter himself and, renouncing the opinion of the pagans, was led over to Christ.
>
> “But she did not abandon concern for others. When the blasphemy of Nestorius had then arisen, and the evil one was leading many into error, even among those who belonged to the word of truth, she was the one who undertook a great contest against him. She made his sophistry vain and empty, answering from morning until evening those who questioned her, and persuading and bringing back many who had been deceived.
>
> “Therefore, unable to endure being defeated by her, the evil one turned against her husband—namely Pinianus—and appeared to him in pitiable form. Wearing a mournful black garment, he approached her, terrifying her and making grave threats. First, he said that he would change the heart of the emperor himself and of his servants and turn them against her; then he threatened to bring about her death through a miserable end, after she had been worn down by the most grievous sufferings.
>
> “Understanding that this was the evil one’s stratagem, she invoked the name of Christ, which inflicts upon him the gravest wound, and caused him immediately to disappear. Then she summoned the priest who was with her and began to relate what she had seen and heard. Suddenly she felt pain in her hip, so acute that she lost her voice, and no one doubted that it was a manifest assault of the enemy.
>
> “When the pain had continued for six days, and the evil was especially intensified at the hour when she had seen the black figure and heard the threats—for the seventh day had arrived—someone came to announce that her uncle Volusianus was in danger of soon ending his life by a sudden death.
>
> “When she heard this, although because of the pain in her hip she could scarcely move, she immediately set out to him, carried by hand and in a litter. She was deeply distressed, not because he was dying, but because he was undergoing the death of the soul, since he had not yet obtained the incorruptibility of baptism.
>
> “Then another person came and informed her that Volusianus had been baptized. He had often sought her but had not found her; learning that she was detained by illness, he had found another guide, and through him had become a son of light and received baptism.
>
> “When this was told her, the bodily illness ceased together with the anguish of her soul. Her hip was free even from pain, her foot moved, and the common enemy was put to shame. She completed the rest of the journey by herself; and those who had carried her, instead of carrying her as before, immediately stretched out their hands to praise God.
>
> “When she came to her uncle, strengthened him with words, and discoursed on the life that is there, she sent him forth rejoicing and furnished with good hope upon the road that leads to God. She had equipped him with the most beautiful provision for the journey, namely the precious body and blood of Christ, and had made it possible for him to depart in safety. This is how these things occurred.”

## Return to Jerusalem

> “After she had spent many days here and had benefited many people greatly in a short time, especially the empress and the emperor himself—for they needed greater healing, since their minds were swollen with greater worldly glory—after she had done these and many other things, she left the city,” and so forth.

The author adds that she reached Jerusalem by Easter, so that it is entirely clear that she returned to Jerusalem in the year following her arrival. That Eudocia benefited somewhat from her admonition may be understood from the fact that Melania also inspired her to undertake a pilgrimage to Jerusalem later; when this occurred, we shall say in its proper place.

Furthermore, we may infer from what followed that not only the Augusta Eudocia but also Theodosius was made better through his encounter with Melania. Since Melania burned with zeal for the Catholic faith, it is reasonable to believe that she stirred and moved him against the Nestorians, and persuaded him to have the books of Nestorius prohibited by imperial edict. This edict was promulgated in the following year, when she departed from Constantinople, as we shall relate.

The statements made both about Melania herself [Col. 1082A] and about her grandmother Melania the Elder demonstrate that Melania was highly renowned both because of the ancient nobility of her parents and because of her admirable holiness, and that she had become known throughout the Christian world.

## Melania Meets Eudocia on Her Journey to Jerusalem

In this same year, which followed Eudoxia’s marriage, Eudocia, the mother, made a pilgrimage to Jerusalem to fulfill a vow, as Socrates relates in these words:

> “Thereafter the emperor Theodosius began to offer prayers to Christ, giving thanks for the benefits he had received—namely, after the translation of the body of John Chrysostom—and to honor the name of Christ with the highest honors by performing this service. Indeed, he also sent his wife Eudocia to Jerusalem. For he had promised that she would fulfill this vow if he should see his daughter married.
>
> “She herself also honored the churches of Jerusalem and all the other churches situated in the cities toward the East, both on her journey there and on her return home, adorning them with various ornaments” (Socrates, book VII, chapter 46).

This is Socrates’ account.

The Acts of Melania also testify that Eudocia undertook this pilgrimage to Jerusalem at the urging of Saint Melania the Younger, while Melania was, as we have seen, in Constantinople. Concerning Eudocia they say:

> “Meanwhile, while these things were taking place, the empress Eudocia [Eudoxia] had gone to Antioch. She had obeyed Melania’s advice when Melania came to Byzantium and urged her to undertake this pilgrimage and come to Jerusalem, so that she might see the holy places and become a participant in the sanctification received from them.
>
> “When Melania therefore went out to meet her, she was treated with great honor by the empress, who regarded her as a mother and gave thanks to divine providence for two reasons: first, that she had been deemed worthy to see Jerusalem, so renowned, and the holy places; and second, that she had become, in spirit, the daughter of such a mother.
>
> “The empress’ great love for Melania is demonstrated by the fact that she did not hesitate to undertake so long a journey, approach her, and greet and embrace the virgins who were there as sisters.
>
> “When the dedication of the new church was celebrated, she too was present and took part in the festival. Something then occurred that was worthy of the evil one’s wickedness and the good God’s power. The empress’ foot, which had been dislocated from its joint through the injury inflicted by a demon, she restored properly and correctly to its place without pain.
>
> “After receiving this and many other benefits from the great Melania, and after satisfying herself with the spectacles there, she decided to return to Constantinople. Melania sent her away, giving her prayers as good companions” (Metaphrastes, 31 December; Surius, 31 January).

That is what the account says. We shall discuss Eudocia’s return to Constantinople in the following year, when it occurred.

As for Melania, it is not known how long she survived thereafter. But this is certain: after practicing the monastic life with great discipline and being distinguished by many miracles, she departed to God on the final day of December, which she had foretold, and was enrolled among the saints, whose annual commemoration is celebrated in the Church.

## Concerning Palladius

[Note: [Col. 1084D] Palladius.] Brother John Maria Brasichellensis, master of the Sacred Apostolic Palace, writes the following about Palladius in the Index of Expurgated Books, so that you may know well, reader, who this Palladius was. Hear the judgments of the Fathers concerning him [Col. 1085A].

Saint Jerome, whose judgment in this matter is approved by Saint Gelasius I, says in the preface to his book against the Pelagians:

> “Palladius attempted to revive the Pelagian heresy of servile wickedness.”

Saint Epiphanius writes as follows in his letter to John of Jerusalem:

> “Beware of Palladius the Galatian, who was once dear to us and now needs the mercy of God, because he preaches and teaches the heresy of Origen, lest perhaps he lead some of the people entrusted to you into the perversity of his error.”

This is Saint Epiphanius’ statement.

The Ecclesiastical Annals, vol. V, explain at greater length Palladius’ deeds, his deceitfulness, and his hatred of Saint Jerome. From all this you will learn what credence should be given to a heretical Origenist and Pelagian, especially in what he reports in this work about certain monks like himself, stained with the same soot. It is especially to be feared that he may pass off as saints men who were Origenists or Pelagians. [Col. 1086A] By careful conjecture, we shall point out certain examples of this kind in their proper places in the work.

To enable you to see more deeply into Palladius’ character and innermost dispositions, know that he was a disciple of Evagrius Ponticus, the heretic Origenist repeatedly condemned by the Church. We have discussed him at greater length in volume V of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, at the beginning of the book of Evagrius.

Palladius himself testifies to this in the *Lausiac History*, when he says:

> “I answered that I was a foreigner, that I came from the regions of Galatia, and I confessed that I was one of Evagrius’ brothers.”

Socrates, book IV, chapter 18, and Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 44, likewise affirm this. It is therefore not surprising if Palladius, like his master, was stained with the same mire of errors.

Accordingly, although Socrates and Nicephorus praise this work—and we do not deny that it contains much that is useful and correct—it is nevertheless certain that they did not have a complete understanding of what kind of man Palladius was.

Thus far he.

## Eulogies of the Book

[702] See what was said above in the general prolegomena, section 10 [Col. 1083A], where, from Socrates, we cited an illustrious eulogy of Palladius’ book. The following may be added.

Cassiodorus, book VIII of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 23, from Socrates:

If anyone wishes to know what these men themselves did and accomplished, and what they said for the benefit of those who heard them, and how wild animals obeyed them, Palladius the monk wrote one book, who was indeed a disciple of Evagrius but treated all these matters carefully. In it he also mentions women who undertook the same manner of life as the men mentioned above.

[Col. 1084A] John of Damascus, *On Those Who Have Fallen Asleep in Faith*:

“I mean Palladius’ historical book addressed to Lausus, in which the miracles performed by the great Macarius, renowned for signs, are recorded with complete truthfulness.” The Greek reads: «Λέγω δὴ τὴν Παλλαδίου πρὸς Λαῦσον ἱστορικὴν βίβλον, ἐν ᾗ τὰ κατὰ τὸν μέγαν καὶ θαυματουργὸν Μακάριον, παναληθῶς ἀναγέγραπται θαύματα·»

Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 44:

“Palladius, the disciple of Evagrius, arranged the Lives of the Saints extremely well.”

[Col. 1085]

## Author’s Preface

[Col. 1085] 704 In this book is written the exercise in which the blessed and holy Fathers who lived in the desert practiced virtue, and the admirable manner of life they followed, so that those who wish to lead a heavenly life and enter the path that leads to the kingdom of heaven may emulate and imitate them. It also contains a memorial of women and of illustrious mothers inspired by God, who with great and steadfast courage completed the contests of the exercise of virtue, so that an example might be set before those who wish to be crowned with the crown of continence and chastity, and so that their love might be stirred.

This is written at the command and desire of a man endowed with varied and manifold learning, peaceful in character, pious in heart and religious in mind, generous in sharing with those in need what they require, and, because of his goodness of character, placed above many distinguished men in the highest offices; one who is altogether guarded by the virtue of the divine Spirit. He ordered us—or, if one should speak more accurately, awakened our dull and obtuse intellect to the contemplation of better things—to send him a description of the life of our holy, immortal, and spiritual Fathers, who, in order to please God, lived under harsh and rigorous bodily discipline. We were to present the contests of these renowned athletes, proclaiming the strenuous virtues of each of the great men.

Lausus is a lover of this divine and spiritual desire. To him, after divine assistance, has been entrusted the guardianship of the divinely inspired and religious government.

I, therefore, who am unlearned in speech, who have touched spiritual knowledge, so to speak, only with the tips of my lips, and who am unworthy to catalogue the holy Fathers who live a spiritual life—although I shrink from the greatness of the command, which surpasses my strength, and reluctantly undertake an order that requires both extensive secular learning and spiritual understanding—nevertheless, out of reverence first for the virtue of him who urged us to carry this out, and considering the benefit of those who will read these things, and fearing the task I was about to undertake, even though I would rightly have refused to obey, since I had ascribed the excellent command first of all to divine Providence, and had applied great diligence, strengthened by the intercession of the holy Fathers, I set about the task. I have described, as though in a kind of abridgment, only the chief contests and signs of the illustrious athletes and great men.

705 Nor have I described only renowned men who led the best and most excellent life of virtue, but also blessed women who honorably practiced themselves in the most outstanding manner of life. Some of them I was privileged to see face to face, their holy countenances, those who had already completed their contest of piety; from divine athletes I learned the heavenly discipline of life of others.

I visited on foot many cities and villages, caves, and all the dwellings of the monks in the desert, and examined their piety and religion with the greatest care. Having written down some things that I myself saw and others that I heard from the holy Fathers—namely, the contests of great men and of women who, because of their hope in Christ, were stronger than their nature ordinarily allowed—and having committed these things to writing, I sent to your friendly ears, which are devoted to divine utterances, O glory of excellent and religious men, most faithful and religious splendor of the government, genuine servant of God and friend of Christ, Lausus, as my small ability permitted, the distinguished name of each of Christ’s athletes, both male and female. From the many and great contests of each, I briefly set forth a few, also adding the lineage of most of them, their city, and the place of their dwelling.

We also remember men and women who perfectly ordered their lives according to virtue, but who, because of the empty mother of arrogance called glory, had been hurled into the lowest abyss and depths of hell. What they had obtained through long time and much labor—those benefits of spiritual discipline that should be embraced and sought with the keenest zeal—they lost in a single moment through arrogance and vain self-opinion. But by the grace of our Savior, through the providence of the holy Fathers and the compassion of their hearts, they were rescued from the spiritual snares of the devil, and through the prayers of the saints they recovered the former virtuous life they had led.

[Col. 1087]

## Copy of the Letter Written to Lausus the Governor by Heraclides, Bishop of Cappadocia

[Note: [Col. 1087] In Greek it reads, παρὰ Παλλαδίου ἐπισκόπου, “by Palladius the bishop.”]

[Col. 1087] I greatly praise your undertaking. It is fitting that a letter should begin with praise: while everyone else clings to empty things and builds stones from which they will obtain no benefit, you build books and wish to be taught. For the one God of all is alone incapable of being taught, since he exists of himself and has no one before him. Everything else can be taught, because everything else both exists and has been created.

The highest orders have the holy Trinity as their supreme teacher; the second orders learn from the first, the third from the second, and so on in succession and order down to the lowest. Those who are superior in honor and virtue teach those who are inferior in knowledge. Those, therefore, who think that they do not need teachers, or who do not obey those who teach in charity, suffer from the disease of ignorance, which is the mother of arrogance.

Among these, the foremost destined for destruction are the demons who, because of this same vice, fell from their heavenly dwelling and now fly in the air, having fled from the teachers who were in heaven. Doctrine does not consist in expressions or syllables, which sometimes even the worst people possess, but in rightly ordered character; freedom from trouble, terror, fear, and anger; confidence and freedom of speech in all things; and gentleness, which produces words just as fire produces flame.

For if this were not so, the great Teacher would not have said to his disciples: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew 11). He was not forming and directing the apostles through verbal ornament, but through goodness of character, harming no one except those who hate the word and hate teachers.

The soul that is trained in accordance with Christ must either faithfully learn what it does not know or openly teach what it knows. If it refuses either of these, it suffers from madness. For satiety with teaching and disgust with the word are the beginning of defection; the soul of one who loves God is always hungry.

Farewell, therefore, and be healthy and strong; and—what is most important—may God grant you knowledge of Christ.

[Col. 1087]

## Copy of the Letter Written to Lausus the Governor by Palladius, Bishop of Cappadocia

[Col. 1087] Although many people have left to this age, at different times, writings of many and varied kinds—some inspired by God’s heavenly grace and composed for the edification and security of those who faithfully follow the Savior’s doctrines; others, arising from a corrupt purpose that seeks to please human beings, luxuriating for the consolation of those who suffer from the disease of empty glory; and still others, arising from a certain untimely madness and from the prompting of the devil, who hates what is honorable, bursting in anger and arrogance into the minds of foolish people for the destruction of the frivolous and the defilement of the undefiled Catholic Church, in order to obscure an honorable and pure life—I too, humble because of my hope in Christ and reverent toward the command of your magnificence, most zealous man, thought it right above all to narrate everything concerning me: my age and the progress of my mind toward virtue in God, beginning from my youth.

When I was in my thirty-third year of living with the brethren and leading a solitary life, in the twentieth year of my episcopate, and in the fifty-third year of my entire life, I considered it necessary, for the sake of spiritual benefit, to write for you—who desire to have these things in writing—what the holy Fathers, both men and women, did rightly and virtuously. Some I myself saw; concerning others I heard from men of thoroughly faithful character, with whom I lived in the solitude of Egypt, Libya, and the Thebaid, and in Syene, under which are also those called the Tabennesiotes; then in Mesopotamia, Palestine, and Syria; in the regions of the West; at Rome; in Campania; and in the regions around them.

I thought that I should set everything before you from the beginning, with the greatest accuracy, in this book, in the form of a narrative. Thus, when you possess an honorable and soul-profitable memorial—a perpetual and uninterrupted medicine of piety and religion—you may through it drive away every drowsiness of forgetfulness, which is produced in the soul by irrational desire; every doubt in faith; every uncleanness and stinginess in the use of material things; every hesitation and vice of a timid and contemptible spirit; excessive inclination to anger and disturbance; irrational distress; and untimely fear. You may also escape dependence on the empty hope of the corrupt world, and advance perpetually in hope toward God and in the purpose of piety.

May you be a guide on the way both to yourself and to those who are with you, to those subject to you, and especially to pious emperors. Through such good deeds, all who love Christ hasten to be united with God, awaiting each day the release of the soul from the body, as it is written: “I am hard pressed, desiring to depart and to be with Christ, for that is much better” (Philippians 1). And again: “Prepare your works for departure, and make yourself ready for the field” (Proverbs 24).

For whoever always remembers death—which will certainly come and will not delay—will not stumble in important matters, as it is written: “In all your works remember your last end, and you will never sin” (Ecclesiasticus 7).

Nor should this brief admonition concerning the narratives deceive you in any respect; nor should you reject their rough and unadorned diction. Divine teaching does not consist in using ornate speech composed to display wisdom, but in persuading the mind through an understanding of truth, as it is written: “Open your mouth with the word of God, and judge all things rightly” (Proverbs 31). And again: “Do not decline from the narrative of the elders, for they learned from their fathers” (Ecclesiasticus 8).

[Col. 1089] I, therefore, most zealous man in the knowledge of God, following this saying in part, met with many holy men. This thought did not come to me while I was engaged in some other pursuit; rather, after I had completed a journey of thirty days, and then twice that number, and by God’s grace had traversed the whole region of the Romans on foot, I regarded the hardship of the road as nothing if I could meet a pious man and friend of God, so that I might gain what I did not possess.

For if blessed Paul the apostle—who was far superior to me, and perhaps even to the whole world, and who surpassed many in manner of life, knowledge, spiritual understanding, and faith in Christ—went from Tarsus to Judaea to meet Peter, John, and James, and therefore recounts this as though boasting, reporting his labors to spur on those who spend their lives in laziness and idleness, saying: “I went up to Jerusalem to see Cephas” (Galatians 2)—not content with merely hearing of his virtue, but desiring also to behold his face—how much more ought I, who am a debtor of innumerable talents, to have done this. I did not thereby confer a benefit on those holy men, but brought benefit to myself, a sinner.

For those who wrote the Lives of the Fathers—of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Elijah, John, and those who follow after them—did not narrate them in order to glorify those men, but to benefit those who would read them.

Knowing this, therefore, most faithful and especially venerable servant of Christ, Lausus, and often reminding yourself of it, bear patiently with our foolishness, so that you may guard your pious mind. By nature it is agitated like waves by various faults, both those that fall under observation and those that do not; but it can be calmed only by continual prayer and care for yourself.

For many even among the somewhat more religious brethren, who took pride in their labors of ascetic discipline and almsgiving, boasted of celibacy and perfect and complete virginity, devoted their minds intensely to meditation on the divine utterances, and relied on the discipline of good works, strayed from freedom from passion [read cautiously], serving their rash opinion. Under a pretext of piety, they were afflicted with a desire to conduct business; from this arise excessive anxieties about business and the attachment of the mind to evil enterprises, followed by concern for other people’s affairs. Such concerns uproot completely the care of honorable affairs, which is the mother of proper self-care.

Be strong, then, I beg you, in all understanding. Do not merely produce rich and splendid wealth—for you have certainly done this, reducing it sufficiently by distributing it to those in need—but let it serve you in the exercise of virtue. You have not bound your free power of choice by any impulse, by any irrational anticipation, or by any pretext for pleasing people, as has happened to many who, after subjecting their free will to empty vainglory by refusing to eat or drink, miserably succumbed again to the necessity of their oath, whether through love of life and indolence, bodily weakness, or desire for some pleasure, and suffered the ruin of perjury.

If, therefore, you partake with reason and abstain with reason, you will never sin. For reason is divine within us: through the admonitions present in us it drives away what is harmful and takes up what is useful. “The law is not made for the just,” he says (1 Timothy 1).

It is better, therefore, to drink wine with reason than water with disdain and arrogance. Observe: those who drink wine with pious and religious judgment are holy men; those who drink water inconsiderately and without reason, with arrogance, are profane and corrupt.

Do not condemn or praise the material of food or drink any further; rather, judge blessed or miserable the mind of those who use the material rightly or wrongly. Joseph once drank wine among the Egyptians, but his mind was not harmed, for his spirit was fortified.

Pythagoras, Diogenes, and Plato drank water; among them were also the Manichaeans and the rest of the company of theological philosophers. The intemperance of their vain opinion led them so far that they failed to recognize God, the creator of all, and worshiped lifeless images.

Those who were disciples with the blessed apostle Peter also partook of wine, to such an extent that this was reproached to the Lord himself, their teacher and the Savior of all (Matthew 11), when the Jews rebuked them for their participation, saying: “Why do your disciples not fast, as John’s disciples do?” (Mark 2). Again the unbelievers insulted the disciples and reproached them, saying: “Your teacher eats and drinks with tax collectors and sinners” (Luke 5).

They would not have criticized bread and water, but food and wine, those who condemn drinking wine while praising and admiring water. The Savior answers beautifully, saying: “John came in the way of righteousness, neither eating nor drinking”—that is, flesh and wine, for without other food he could not have lived—“and they say, ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Behold, a glutton and a wine-drinker, a friend of tax collectors and sinners’” (Matthew 11), because he eats and drinks.

What, then, shall we do? Let us follow neither those who condemn nor those who praise. Either let us fast wisely with John, even if the Jews say to us, “You have a demon,” or let us drink wine wisely with Jesus if the body needs it, even if they say to us, “Behold, gluttonous men and wine-drinkers.”

For food is nothing, nor drink, but faith working through love in deeds. When faith accompanies every action, the one who eats and drinks cannot be condemned because of faith. “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Romans 14).

But when someone from among the pleasure-seekers, or among those who commit any other sin, says, “I partake by faith,” or “I do something else by faith,” relying on faith while driven by an irrational desire or a corrupt conscience, he falls. For the Savior distinguished the matter, saying: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matthew 7).

That the fruit of those who order their lives according to divine reason and spiritual understanding is, according to the judgment of the divine Apostle, “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control, chastity” (Galatians 5), is beyond dispute. Blessed Paul himself said: “The fruit of the Spirit is this and this.”

But whoever strives to have such fruits will not, without reason, inconsiderately, or at an improper time, eat meat, drink wine, or live with any evil conscience. Again the same blessed Paul said: “Everyone who competes abstains from everything” (1 Corinthians 9).

When the flesh is healthy, he abstains from what makes it fatten; but if it is sick, worn down by grief, or afflicted by some misfortune, then he will use food or drink as medicine to heal what causes distress. He will abstain from what harms the soul: anger and envy, empty glory, sadness and slander, pride and exaltation, giving thanks to God.

Having said enough about these matters, I bring another exhortation to your docility. Flee as far as you can the company of men who have no benefit to offer and who strip away the skin improperly, even if they are orthodox and not heretics, and who injure by hypocrisy, even if they display the length of their years with white hair and a wrinkled brow.

For even if their honorable character prevents you from being harmed by them in any other way, that which seems least will wound you. Made insolent, you will become proud in spirit and mock them. This will bring you harm, since you will fall into arrogance.

Pursue instead, as though looking through a bright window, the holy company of men and women, so that through their book, written as it were in fine script, you may clearly see your own heart and test your laziness or diligence by comparison.

Many things bear witness to uprightness: the color of the face, which blossoms in the life one leads; the adornment of clothing; well-ordered conduct; modesty in speech; words that are neither elaborate nor affected; an elegant judgment; and considered and perceptive wisdom.

The Lord will give strength to your gentleness and to all who pursue the goal of piety, even if something happens through indolence or by chance. “Dress, the movement of the foot, and the laughter of the teeth will announce a person,” as the proverb says (Ecclesiastes 10).

I shall therefore begin to narrate the life of the holy Fathers. I will not pass over in silence those who are unknown to you, whether they live in cities, villages, caves, or solitudes, and I will also add those who live in monasteries. For it is not the place in which they rightly and virtuously conducted themselves that is sought, but the manner of their proper discipline, through which, with Christ’s help, they led an angelic life.

[Col. 1091]

# The Lausiac History

[Note: [Col. 1217A] In preparing this book for a new edition, in the first edition I had obtained a few excerpts from Palladius—some promptly supplied from the Augsburg Library by David Hoeschel, and some obtained in Greek at Venice from Gabriel, archbishop of Philadelphia—and from them at that time we drew some light in the darkness. Now, after Palladius’ Greek-Latin edition appeared at Paris from the Royal Manuscript, which he also collated with the Palatine Manuscript published by Meursius at Leiden, under the care of our Fronto Ducaeus, we have been illumined by greater light. It will also be useful in doubtful passages to consult the old translation of Palladius and the *Paradise of Heraclides*, which constitutes a large part of Palladius’ history. You have both in the appendix.]

## Chapter I. The Life of Isidore the Presbyter and Keeper of a Hostel

[Note: [Col. 1217B] Isidore. Concerning him see Socrates, book IV, chapter 18; Sozomen, book VI, chapter 29; Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 34. Baronius, volume III, under the year of Christ 340. As for his statement concerning Athanasius’ arrival at Rome, we find that among others he brought with him that Isidore about whom Palladius says more and whom he highly praises (*Palladius, Lausiac History*, chapter 1).]

[Col. 1091A] When I first came to the city of Alexandria, during the second consulship of the great emperor Theodosius, who because of his right faith in Christ is now with the angels, I encountered in that city a remarkable man, adorned in every respect with speech, character, and knowledge—namely Isidore, who was both presbyter and keeper of the hostel of the Alexandrian church.

It was said that in his first youth he had lived in the desert and completed the contests of ascetic discipline. I myself saw his cell on the mountain of Nitria. I encountered him as an old man of seventy years; after living another fifteen years, he died in peace.

This holy man [Col. 1091B] wore nothing made of linen until the hour of his death, except for a headband [Note: [Col. 1217B] “Except for a headband.” This is clearly the correct reading from Heraclides, who here speaks of a covering for the head. In the Venetian Manuscript the Greek is ἐκτὸς φακιολίου; in the Royal and Palatine Manuscripts, φακιαλίου. See the *Onomasticon*.]. He did not use a bath, did not touch meat, and never left the table filled to satiety.

His body was so well regulated by the grace of God that all who did not know his manner of eating were convinced that he lived luxuriously and sumptuously. If I wished to recount his virtues of soul individually, time would fail me as I narrated them.

He was so gentle, kind, and peaceable that even unbelievers who were his enemies because of his right faith in Christ revered at least his shadow because of the man’s outstanding goodness.

He possessed such spiritual grace, knowledge of the holy Scriptures, and understanding of divine doctrines [Col. 1092A] that even during the customary hour of the brethren’s meal, this holy man would fall into an ecstasy of mind, becoming mute and standing in amazement. When he was asked to relate what had happened during his ecstasy, he would say: “In my mind I have traveled abroad, seized by some contemplation.”

I often saw him at table in tears. When he was asked why he had wept, I heard him say: “I am ashamed to eat food contrary to reason, since I am endowed with reason; and I ought to be dwelling in the paradise of delights, being filled with ambrosial nourishment, because of the power given to us by the Lord.”

He was known at Rome to the entire senate and to the wives of the leading men, at the time when he had first withdrawn with the blessed Bishop Athanasius and afterward with Saint Bishop Demetrius.

Although he possessed abundant wealth and the necessities of life, when he died he neither made a will nor left money or any property to his sisters, who were virgins. Instead, he commended them to Christ, saying: “The God who created you will also provide you with food, just as he has provided for me.”

There was a community of seventy virgins with his sisters.

When I came to him as a young man and asked to be admitted to the monastic life, while my age was still inclined to frivolity and I needed not words but labors to subdue the flesh, and a hard and austere manner of life to restrain the body, he—like a good trainer of young colts—led me outside the city to the place called [Col. 1093A] the Hermit Cells, about five miles from the city.

## Chapter II. Dorotheus the Theban

[Note: [Col. 1217B] Dorotheus. Concerning him see Sozomen, book VI, chapter 29; and from him Cassiodorus, *Tripartite History*, book VIII, chapter 1; and Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 35.]

He handed me over to a certain Dorotheus, a Theban ascetic who had reached his sixtieth year, living in a cave, and ordered me to complete three years with him in order to subdue the disturbances of the soul—for he knew that the old man lived a very hard and austere life. After I had completed the number of years, he ordered me to return to him for the remainder of my spiritual instruction.

But because I could not complete the three years with him, having fallen into a severe illness, I left him before the appointed time. His manner of life was exceedingly harsh, squalid, [Col. 1093B] and utterly arid.

All day long, even in the very heat of midday, in the solitude beside the sea, he gathered stones, continually building with them and making cells, which he gave to those who could not build, making one cell each year.

Once I said to this holy man: “What are you doing, Father, killing your little body with such intolerable heat at your great age?” He answered me: “That kills me, and I will kill it too.”

Each day he ate six ounces of bread and a bundle of small vegetables [Note: [Col. 1217C] “And a bundle of small vegetables.” The Greek is Το λεπτολαχάνων δέμα, “a bundle of small vegetables.” Hervetus seems to have read λεπτολαχάνων δέκα, for he translates “ten small vegetables,” but the translator of Heraclides defends the accepted reading: “one bundle of the cheapest vegetables.” So does another old translator in the appendix to the *Lives of the Fathers*: “a bundle of small vegetable condiments.” Thus in Pollux we read φρυγάνων δεσμὸς and δέσμη, “a bundle” and “a sheaf” of kindling. Nicephorus, speaking of this same Dorotheus, book XI, chapter 35: Ἕξ δ` οὐγκίαι ἄρτου ἦν αὐτῶ τροφὴ, καὶ ἀπόδεσμος λαχάνων λεπτῶν: “His food was six ounces of bread and a bundle of tender vegetables.” Fronto.]; he drank only a little water.

I call God to witness that I never knew him to stretch out his feet, deliberately sleep on a mattress, or sleep upon a bed. Rather, throughout the entire night, sitting, he wove a cord from branches [Note: [Col. 1217C] “A cord from branches.” We preferred this to the translator’s “a chain from branches.” σειρά means not only “chain” but also “cord.” According to Eustathius, πλέγματά τινα ἀπὸ σχοινίων, ἢ σπάρτων, ἢ καννάβεως, “certain plaited things made from ropes, rushes, or hemp.” Heraclides has “a certain cord from a palm tree.” Synesius, *Dion*, on the Life of the Monks, p. 46: Ἢ τί αὐτοῖς οἱ [Col. 1217D] κάλαθοι βούλονται, καὶ τὰ πλεγμάτια ἅπτα μεταχειρίζονται: “What do they mean by the baskets, and what are the woven things that they handle?” Fronto.], from palm branches [Col. 1093C], so that he might obtain food from it.

Suspecting that he practiced such extreme discipline only while I was present, I asked several of his disciples whether he had always practiced such careful and exacting asceticism. They themselves remained afterward in separate places, conducting themselves rightly and virtuously. They told me that from his youth he had ordered his life in this way, never deliberately sleeping, except that sometimes, while working or eating, he would doze with his eyes lowered. So excessive was his drowsiness that often even bread [Note: [Col. 1217D] “Even bread.” Ψωμός here means bread, not a piece, as Hervetus translated it. See the *Onomasticon*.] would fall from his mouth while he was eating.

Once, when I compelled this holy man to lie down for a little while on a mat, he angrily said to me: “When you have persuaded the angels to sleep, then you will also persuade the lover of virtue.”

One day he sent me to his well, around the ninth hour, to fill a jar, which he would use for refreshment when the hour of eating approached. When I arrived, I saw a viper below in the well. I was so afraid that I did not draw the water at all, but ran back and reported to him, saying: “We are ruined, abba! I saw a viper down in the well.”

He smiled courteously, because he cared greatly for me, shook his head, and said: “If it should please the devil to put snakes and vipers, or tortoises or other poisonous animals, into every well and every spring of water, will you remain forever without drinking?”

He himself left the cell, drew water, and drank while fasting, first fortifying himself with the sign of the cross and saying: “Where the cross is present” [Note: [Col. 1217D] “Where the cross is present.” Hervetus translated this as though he had read σωτήρ, “savior,” rather than σταυρός, “cross”: “Where the Savior comes.” But Heraclides’ translator is correct: “Where the cross is present, there the devil’s wickedness has no power.” Another old translator has: “Where the cross of Christ is imposed, the devil’s malice will not prevail.” Jerome, in the *Life of Hilarion*: “He signed Christ’s cross on his forehead.” Prudentius, in the hymn before sleep:

> The cross drives away every crime,  
> The darkness flees the cross;  
> When the mind is dedicated  
> To such a sign, it knows no wavering.

So Fronto.], “there the devil’s wickedness is powerless.”

## Chapter III. The Deeds and Ascetic Discipline of Potamiaena

[Note: [Col. 1218A] Potamiaena. Baronius, volume III, under the year of Christ 310, the second year of Pope Eusebius and the fifth year of the emperor Constantine. If one considers her name and the kind of final punishment, she might seem to be the same woman as the one mentioned by Eusebius, book VI, chapter 4. But several differences establish that this woman is different: namely, the different status of the persons—for the former was freeborn, whereas this one was a slave—and the clearly different time of the punishment. This woman suffered under Maximian, while the other suffered under Severus. The former was called not Potamenia but Potamiaena; and she was not cast into a cauldron but merely covered with pitch.

Moreover, who could easily deny that, in so large a city, several virgins of the same name might have lived at different times and suffered the same punishments? Thus far Baronius.

As for Baronius’ statement that this woman is called Potamenia by Palladius and the other Potamiaena by Eusebius, this should rather be attributed to the corrupt text of Palladius used by Baronius. For this is how the *Paradise of Heraclides*, which Lipomanus published under Palladius’ name, reads; but the first edition of Hervetus has Potamiana. The Greek text has Ποταμιαίνα. In the old translator of Palladius the name is absent. Potamiaena could easily have become Potomenia.

The memory of Potamiaena, martyred under Severus, is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology on June 28; Eusebius speaks of her in book VI, chapter 4. Laurentius de la Barre, in his edition of Palladius, considered her the same as our woman.

Throughout Hervetus’ edition of Palladius, Maximianus is printed as Maximinus; the Paris Greek edition likewise has Maximinus. I fear this is erroneous, for the other Greek manuscripts have Μαξιμιανοῦ, “of Maximian.” The old translator of Heraclides and Palladius also read it this way.]

The blessed Isidore, keeper of the hostel, who had visited the blessed Antony, told me that he had heard from him an account worthy of being committed to writing.

A certain girl named Potamioena, exceedingly beautiful, was a slave during the persecution of the emperor Maximinus to a certain intemperate and lustful man. Although her master repeatedly pleaded with her and promised her various things, he could not deceive her. As a result, he was finally driven mad with rage and handed her over to the prefect of Alexandria [Note: [Col. 1218C] “The prefect of Alexandria.” The Greek is ἐπάρχῳ Ἀλεξανδρίνῳ. Hervetus did not translate this correctly as “the governor.” The old translator of Palladius and the translator of Heraclides correctly have “the prefect.” See the *Onomasticon*.], who was then in office, as a Christian woman who insulted the times and emperors with curses because of the persecutions.

He promised the prefect a large sum of money in return for the girl’s ruin, saying: “If you persuade her to submit to my desire, keep her in custody without subjecting her to any punishment. But if she remains in the severity she displayed at the beginning, I ask that she be put to death by punishment, lest, while alive, she mock my intemperance.”

The brave virgin was brought before the tribunal. Various instruments had been prepared for inflicting punishment, and her body was tortured; but in mind she resisted the many and varied methods of torture like a firm and steadfast tower.

Among the instruments of punishment, the judge then devised a torture more cruel than the others. He ordered a large cauldron filled with pitch to be heated over an extremely fierce fire. When the pitch was boiling and burning intensely, the savage governor turned to the blessed woman and said: “Go, obey your master’s will; otherwise, so that you may understand, I order you to be thrown into the cauldron.”

She replied: “God forbid that there should be a judge so unjust as to order me to obey lust and intemperance.”

The man, driven into a fury, ordered her to be stripped and thrown into the cauldron. She cried out, saying: “By the head of the emperor” [Note: [Col. 1218C] “By the head of the emperor.” It was once customary to swear by the emperor’s head. See the *Onomasticon*.], “whom you fear, if you have decided to punish me in this way, do not order me to be stripped; instead, order me to be lowered gradually into the boiling pitch, so that you may see how much patience Christ, whom you do not know, has granted me.”

Thus she was lowered gradually over the course of three hours, and she gave up her spirit when the pitch had reached her neck.

## CHAPTER IV. Life of Didymus the Blind

[Note: Here Didymus was initially distinguished for holiness and learning, but at the end he became an Origenist.]

[Note: Didymus.]

Concerning him, Jerome writes in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 109; Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 2, and Cassiodorus after him, *Tripartite History*, Book VIII, chapter 8; Nicephorus, Book IX, chapter 17, and Book X, chapter 35.

[Note: Brother John Maria Brasichellensis, Master of the Sacred Palace, writes as follows in the index of expurgated books: “Although Didymus was a great man in holiness and learning from the beginning, as the many encomia of the Fathers concerning him testify, he was eventually plunged into Origen’s error, regarded as a leading Origenist, and condemned as a heretic together with Origen and Evagrius Ponticus at the Fifth General Council, as Saint Tarasius, bishop of Constantinople, testifies in the confession of faith found in the Seventh Council, session 3; Nicephorus, *History*, Book XVII, chapter 27; and Cedrenus in his *Annals*. Saint Martin, pope and martyr, likewise condemned him with the same men at the Lateran Council, secretariat V, canon 18.”]



[Col. 1094D]

A very large company of holy men and women was then perfected in the Alexandrian church, who were found worthy of the land of the meek. Among them the blessed writer Didymus the blind was also perfected.

[Note: Blind. Lacking eyes. In Greek, ὁ ἀπὸ ὀμμάτων γενόμενος, “one who has become bereft of eyes.” This is a phrase commonly used by the Greeks. See the *Onomasticon*.]

I met him four times, traveling to him at intervals of ten years. He completed his life at the age of eighty-five. He was blind because, when he was four years old, he lost his eyes, as he himself told me; he neither learned letters nor attended teachers. For he had, by nature, a firm and reliable teacher: his own conscience.

He was adorned with such a great grace of spiritual knowledge that what is written was truly fulfilled in him: “The Lord enlightens

[Note: “The Lord gives light to the blind.” The Lyon edition mistakenly has σοφοιτίζει. The common edition of the Psalms, Psalm 145:8, has σοφοῖ τύφλους, “he makes the blind wise.” Augustine and the Old Psalter have *sapientificat*, “he makes wise”; and the interpreter of Heraclides has here, “The Lord makes the blind wise.” But Chrysostom notes that another Greek interpreter published Κύριος φωτίζει, “The Lord gives light,” from which come the Roman Psalter and the Vulgate Latin: *Dominus illuminat*. — Fronto.]

the blind” (Psalm 145). For he interpreted the Old and New Testaments word for word; but he explained doctrines so subtly and energetically that in knowledge he surpassed all the ancients.

Once, when he was compelling me to pray in his cell, while I was unwilling, he said to me, relating the following story:

“Three times blessed Antony entered this cell to visit me. When I asked him to pray, he immediately knelt in this cell and did not allow me to repeat what I had said, teaching by his action the meaning of obedience. Therefore, if you too follow the footsteps of his life, since you are a monk and a guest on account of your virtue, lay aside all contention.”

He himself also told me the following:

“Once, because I was anxious about the life of the wretched emperor Julian, who was a persecutor, and was troubled in spirit, it happened that, on account of this anxiety, I ate nothing until late in the evening. As I sat on a seat, sleep overcame me, and in an ecstasy I saw white horses with riders passing by and announcing: ‘Tell Didymus that Julian died today at the seventh hour. Rise, therefore, and eat; and send what you know to Bishop Athanasius, so that he too may know.’ I took note,” he said, “of the hour, the day, the week, and the month, and so I found it to be.”

## CHAPTER V. The Life of Alexandra

[Col. 1095C]

This blessed man also told me about a certain maidservant named Alexandra, who, after leaving the city, enclosed herself in a tomb. Through an opening she received what was necessary, and for ten years she appeared in the sight of neither men nor women.

In the tenth year, they say, the blessed woman, having fallen asleep, composed herself so completely that the woman who was accustomed to come to her, when she received no answer, reported the matter to us. When we came and removed the door of the tomb, we entered and found that she had fallen asleep.

The most blessed Roman Melania, whose life I shall relate at the appropriate time and place,

[Col. 1095D]

also spoke about her.

[Note: Below, here, chapter 117.]

“I was unable to look upon the face of this blessed woman,” she said. “But while I stood near the opening, I asked her to tell me the reason why she had withdrawn from the city and enclosed herself in a tomb. Through the opening she addressed me, saying:

“‘A certain man was consumed by a mad love for me. So that I might not appear to distress him or provoke him to resentment, I preferred to bury myself alive in this tomb rather than offend a soul that had been made in the image of God.’

“When I said to her, ‘How can you endure, servant of Christ God, having no conversation with anyone at all, but fighting alone against idleness and thoughts?’ she answered me:

“‘From morning until the ninth hour I pray; during the ninth hour I spin flax. During the remaining hours I turn over in my mind the lives of the holy Fathers and patriarchs, and the contests of the blessed apostles, prophets, and martyrs. When evening comes, after I have glorified my Lord, I take food—bread—and persevere for many hours of the night in prayer, awaiting the time when I shall be released from here with good hope and shall appear before the face of Christ God.’”

I shall not omit in this account those also who lived in such a way that they presented an appearance of piety and religion but despised it in reality, both for the praise of those who conduct themselves rightly and virtuously and so that those who read may be cautious and attentive.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning a Certain Virgin Who Was Afflicted with a Love of Wealth

[Col. 1096B]

There was a certain virgin in Alexandria in name only: humble in appearance, but sparing in her disposition, proud and insolent, and afflicted by avarice—loving gold rather than Christ. From her possessions she never gave anything to anyone: not to a guest, a poor or afflicted person, a monk, a virgin, or a church—not even a single obol.

Though urged by many admonitions from the holy Fathers, she did not cast off the heavy burden of her wealth. She also had a relative, whose daughter she had adopted as her own daughter. To her she promised her possessions night and day, although she herself had fallen away from heavenly riches.

For this too is one form of the devil’s fraud: under the pretext of love for relatives, he causes avarice to arise. That he has no concern for the family itself is clear from this: he taught people to kill brother, mother, and father. This is beyond dispute from the Scriptures. And although he may appear to some to insert concern for relatives (Deuteronomy 12), he does not do this because he wishes them well, but so that he may openly train the soul of those who obey him in injustice, since he knows the sentence that says: “The unjust shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6).

A person may, moved by spiritual understanding and divine desire, neither neglect his own soul nor fail to help relatives if they lack something. But when someone orders his whole soul in such a way that it is despised and overwhelmed by concern for relatives,

[Note: “That it be overwhelmed by concern for relatives.” See the excellent Conference of Saint Antony on this subject in Cassian, Conference 24, chapter 11.]

he falls under the law, treating his own soul as worthless.

The holy psalmist David also sings of those who care for their souls, saying in the fear of God:

“Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?”—that is, the rare one—“Or who shall stand in his holy place? He who is innocent in his hands and pure in heart, who has not received his soul in vain” (Psalm 23).

For those receive their soul in vain who think that it is dissolved together with this little flesh, and who neglect spiritual virtues.

When this virgin, who had acquired a title for herself in name alone but in conduct was alien to ascetic practice, wished, as the saying goes, to cut the vein in order to relieve her avarice, the most holy Macarius,

[Note: Macarius. Heraclides attributes this story to Isidore. And so that there may be no confusion concerning the ambiguous word Μακάριος, which is sometimes translated appellatively as “blessed” and sometimes as the proper name Macarius, he gives the name Isidore.]

presbyter and superintendent of the hospice for those physically mutilated, devised the following scheme.

He had been a lapidary from his youth.

[Note: Lapidary. Meursius notes in his *Greek Barbarous Lexicon* that the Greek here has καβιδάριος. Certainly Hervetus, the recent translator of Palladius, and the old interpreter of Heraclides both translate it as “lapidary.” In the Greek text recently published it is: Λιθουργὸς, ὃν λέγουσι καβιδάριον, “a worker in stone, whom they call a *kabidarios*.]

Approaching her, he said:

“Beautiful gems have fallen into my hands—emeralds and hyacinths—and I do not know whether they are stolen or belong to some merchant. No price can properly be set for them, since they exceed all valuation. Whoever possesses them is selling them for five hundred solidi. If you wish to acquire them, give five hundred solidi. From one gem alone you can obtain five hundred; with the rest you can adorn your niece, your daughter.”

Since the so-called virgin depended entirely upon the girl, she was ensnared by the desire to adorn her. She fell at his feet and said:

“I beg you not to let anyone else take them.”

The saint therefore urged her, saying:

“Come to my house and look at them.”

But she refused. Instead, she gave him five hundred solidi, saying:

“I beg you to take them yourself as you wish; for I do not want to see the man who is selling them.”

When Saint Macarius had received the five hundred solidi from her,

[Col. 1097B]

he devoted them to the use of the hospice.

After a considerable time had passed—for that man was highly esteemed among the Alexandrians, being exceedingly pious and merciful—she was afraid to question him. He lived to the age of one hundred years, during which time we too were alive.

At last, when she found him in the church, she said to him:

“I beg you, what do you command concerning the stones for which we gave five hundred solidi?”

He answered her:

“From the day you gave me the gold, I spent it on the purchase of gems. If you wish to see them, come to my hospice. The gems are placed there. Look at them; and if they do not please you, take back your gold.”

She came very eagerly.

The hospice had women in its upper section and men in its lower section. When she had arrived, he brought her into the vestibule and Saint Macarius said to her:

“What do you wish to see first, the hyacinths or the emeralds?”

She answered him:

“Whatever seems best to you.”

He led her to the upper section and showed her women whose limbs were torn apart and whose faces were wholly disfigured by various diseases. He said to her:

“Here are the hyacinths.”

Then he brought her down to the lower section and showed her the men, saying:

“Here are the emeralds. I do not think more precious ones can be found. If they do not please you, take back your gold.”

After this had happened, the virgin departed in shame. Returning home, she was deeply grieved that she had not undertaken this matter for God’s sake but had been driven by necessity. Later, however, she gave thanks to the presbyter, when the girl under her care died after marriage without children; thereafter she spent her own possessions for proper purposes.

## CHAPTER VII. The Life of Abbot Arsisius

[Note: Arsisius. I have entitled this chapter in this way because he is called Arsisius later in the text. In Hervetus’s editions of Palladius, this chapter was previously entitled “Arsacius.” There was indeed a certain Arsacius, Persian by birth, formerly a soldier and keeper of the royal lions, a confessor during the time of Licinius, and later a monk in the fortress of Nicomedia, where he also died. Concerning him, see Sozomen, Book IV, chapter 15, and Nicephorus, Book IX, chapter 38. But this Arsisius appears to be another man, with whom Palladius says that he lived. Concerning him, see Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 30, and Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 37. Here Meursius, in the preface to Pachomius’s rule, substitutes *Arsesii* for *Orsiesii*, less correctly. Orsiesius lived with Pachomius and succeeded him after Petronius, as stated in his Life, chapter 53. Arsisius says incidentally that he saw him.]

…and of those who were with him on Mount Nitria.

[Col. 1097D]

After I had met many holy men and had spent three years in the monasteries around Alexandria, where I remained with about two thousand great, most zealous, and excellent men adorned with every virtue, I departed from there and came to Mount Nitria.

Between this mountain and Alexandria lies a lake called Maria; it extends for about seventy miles. After crossing it, I reached the southern side of the mountain in a day and a half.

[Col. 1098A]

On this mountain there is a vast desert extending as far as Ethiopia, the Mazices, and Mauretania. About five thousand men live there,

[Note: Five thousand men. Thus today on Mount Athos there are twenty-two notable monasteries of Greek monks of the order of Saint Basil. Each year they pay the Turkish tyrant, as tribute, six thousand Turkish obols from their vineyards and olive groves. The mountain is called by Christians ἅγιον ὄρος, that is, “holy mountain”; by the Ruthenians, *Suvata hora*. Thus John Langus noted concerning Book XI of Nicephorus, chapter 38.]

and they follow various ways of life, each according to his ability and desire, so that one may live alone, with two or three others, or with any number one chooses.

On this mountain there are seven bakeries, which serve both them and the anchorites living in the immense desert—six hundred perfect men.

After I had lived for an entire year on the mountain among the blessed and holy Fathers—Arsisius the great, Putuphastus, Hagion,

[Note: Hagion. In Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 30, and Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 37, Arsion is joined to Arsisius or Arsesius. Heraclides has *Agion* here; perhaps *Arsion* is corrupted from *Agion*, or conversely.]

Cronius, and Serapion—and after I had been stimulated by their many spiritual accounts of the ancient Fathers, I went into the innermost desert.

On Mount Nitria there is one very large church, and in the church are three palm trees, from each of which a whip is suspended.

[Note: Whip. Here we have an ancient memorial of what are called disciplinary practices. See our Gretzer discussing them carefully in a special book on the subject.]

One is for chastising monks who commit offenses; another for punishing robbers, should any happen to appear; and the third for correcting those who happen to come and fall into some offense. Thus whoever commits an offense and is convicted of deserving punishment embraces the palm tree, receives the prescribed blows on his back, and is then dismissed.

Near the church stands a guesthouse, where they receive any guest who comes for as long as he wishes to remain—even two or three years—until he chooses of his own accord to depart. They permit him to remain at leisure for one week. On the following days, however, they occupy him with work, either in the garden, the bakery, or the kitchen.

If someone is deserving of special consideration, they give him a book to read and do not allow him to converse with anyone until the sixth hour. Physicians and pastry-cooks also live on this mountain. They use wine, and wine is sold there.

All of them make linen clothing with their own hands, so that they are entirely free from want. Around the ninth hour, one may stand and listen in each monastery to hymns and psalms sung to Christ and to prayers uttered with the hymns, so that one might think oneself lifted aloft and transported into a paradise of delights. They come to the church only on Saturday and Sunday.

There are eight presbyters who preside over this church. As long as the first presbyter of the church lives, no other presbyter offers, gives judgment, or delivers a sermon; they merely sit silently with him.

This great Arsisius and many other old men with him, whom we saw, were contemporaries of the great Antony. This great Arsisius told me that he had also seen Amon of Nitria, whose soul Antony saw taken up by angels and led into heaven (*Life of Antony*, chapter 32; Rufinus, Book II, chapter 30).

He also said that he had seen Pachomius of Tabennisi, a man renowned for prophetic grace and archimandrite of three thousand men. I shall later relate his virtues.

[Below, chapter 38.]

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning Saint Amon and His Wife

[Note: Amon. Concerning him, see Socrates, Book IV, chapter 18; Sozomen, Book I, chapter 14; and Cassiodorus after him, *Tripartite History*, Book I, chapter 11; Nicephorus, Book VIII, chapter 41. See also what was said above concerning Rufinus, Book II, chapter 30.]

[Col. 1099A]

Amon, he said, lived in the following manner:

“When he was an orphaned young man of about twenty-two years of age, his paternal uncle forcibly joined him in marriage to a woman. Since he was unable to resist the necessity imposed upon him by his uncle, it seemed best to him to be crowned,

[Note: Both bridegroom and bride were formerly accustomed to be crowned. See the *Onomasticon*.]

to sit in the bridal chamber, and to endure everything that takes place in marriage.

“When everyone who had arranged the bridal chamber and bed had gone out, blessed Amon rose and closed the doors. Sitting down, he called his blessed and lawful wife and said to her:

“‘Come here, mistress and sister,

[Note: Mistress and sister. Those who lived continently in marriage called their wives “sisters.” See the *Onomasticon*.]

for I shall explain the matter to you. This marriage by which we have been joined has nothing extraordinary about it. We shall therefore do well if from now on each of us sleeps separately, so that we may please Christ by returning our virginity to him intact.’

“Then he drew from his bosom a small book. As though speaking in the person of the Apostle and the Savior, he read to the girl, who was ignorant of letters, a great part of the text, adding from his own divinely inspired teaching and instructing her in how to live in life, virginity, and chastity.

“Thus, filled with the grace of Christ, she said:

“‘I too, my lord, am persuaded that I shall gladly live a chaste life. Whatever you command, I shall henceforth do.’

“He answered:

“‘I command and ask that each of us live separately.’

“But she could not accept this, saying:

“‘Let us remain in the same house, but in separate beds.’

“Thus he lived with her for eighteen years in the same dwelling, spending the entire day in the garden and balsam plantation. He cultivated balsam, which is planted like a vine and requires much labor in its cultivation and pruning.

“In the evening he entered the house, said prayers, and ate with her. Then, again offering night prayers and celebrating the synaxis, he went into the garden early in the morning.

“When these things had continued and both had reached impassibility,

[Note: Read this cautiously.]

the prayers of Amon proved powerful and effective.

“Finally the blessed woman said to him:

“‘There is something I wish to say to you, my lord. If you listen to me, I shall know for certain that you truly love me for God’s sake.’

“He answered:

“‘Say whatever you wish.’

“She said:

“‘It is fitting that you, who are a pious and religious man and practice justice, and I likewise, who have followed the same path of discipline, should live separately, so that many may benefit from it. It is not right that, on my account, so great and noble a virtue of philosophy should be concealed—your virtue, by which you live with me in chastity for Christ’s sake.’

“He thanked her and gave glory to God, saying:

“‘You have judged rightly, mistress and sister. If this pleases you, keep this house; I shall leave and build another house for myself.’

“When he had left her, he entered the interior of Mount Nitria. At that time there were not yet many monasteries there. He built for himself two vaulted cells.
