“After living another twenty-two years and practicing the full virtue of ascetic discipline, holy Amon died in the monastic life—or rather, he was translated—at the age of sixty-two. Twice each year he saw the blessed companion of his life.

“When he was living alone in Nitria, people brought him a boy tormented by rabies and bound in chains. A rabid dog had infected him by biting him. He tore himself to pieces because he could not endure the intolerable disease.

“When he saw the boy’s parents approach him in supplication, he said:

“‘Why do you present me with these labors, people, asking for things beyond my merits, when the remedy is in your own hands? Return to the widow the ox that you secretly killed, and your boy will be restored to health.’

“When they were convicted, they gladly did what they had been commanded. As he prayed, the boy recovered.

“Others came to visit him. To test their disposition, the holy man said to them:

“‘Bring me a jar, so that I may have enough water to receive those who come.’

“They promised that they would bring one. But when one of them changed his mind and had reached the village, he said to the other:

“‘I do not want to kill the camel or put the jar on it, lest it die.’

“On hearing this, the other, joining his donkeys together, carried the jar up with great difficulty.

“Amon, however, anticipated him and said:

“‘What? Did your companion’s camel die while you were coming here?’

“When he returned, he found that it had been devoured by wolves. This man also performed many other deeds.

“Blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, related this miracle when writing the *Life of Antony*:

“‘Once, when monks had been sent to Antony—for Antony was in the inner desert—and had come to him, the old man rose and walked with them. When he was about to cross the Lycus River with his disciple Theodore, he was afraid to undress, lest he should at some time see himself naked. While he was discussing this matter, he was found on the other side of the river, as though he had crossed in an ecstasy without a boat, having been transported by an angel. The brothers, however, crossed by swimming.

“‘When he approached Antony, Antony said to him first:

“‘“Since God had revealed many things to me about you and had made known to me your translation, I necessarily summoned you to me, so that, since we were permitted to enjoy one another’s company, we might intercede for one another.”

“‘He placed him in a certain secluded place and urged him not to leave before his translation. When he himself had been perfected apart from others, Antony saw his soul taken up into heaven by angels.’

“This, then, is Amon, who lived and died in this manner. I myself once crossed the Lycus River with fear in a ferryboat. It is a ditch and channel of the great Nile.”

## CHAPTER IX. The Life of Abbot Or

[Note: Here Or was an Origenist.]

[Note: Or. Concerning him, see Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 34. See also what was said above concerning Rufinus, Book II, chapter 2. This is that heretical Origenist Or whom Evagrius Ponticus—indeed Rufinus, as I demonstrated in the fourth prologue—wrongly inserted among the other saints in his book on the *Lives of the Fathers* (above, here, Book II, chapter 2), as Saint Jerome testifies in his letter to Ctesiphon. Behold the sort of saints Palladius imposes upon us. See our scholium, volume V of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, at the beginning of Evagrius’s work, where we also observed that, according to the decree of Saint Gelasius I, the Roman Church’s judgment concerning such men is the same as Saint Jerome’s. Thus the previously cited Master of the Sacred Palace.]

On this Mount Nitria there was an admirable abbot named Or, who had monasteries of a thousand brothers and was endowed with an angelic appearance (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 2). Though he was ninety years old, he had lost nothing in his body;

[Col. 1101A]

indeed, his face was bright and cheerful, so that even when he was seen alone he appeared to be a venerable man.

After he had practiced asceticism for a long time in the farther desert, he later gathered monasteries in the nearer desert. There he planted a grove with his own hands, although there was no timber in that place, until there was a dense forest in the desert.

The Fathers who were with him told us that not even a shoot had existed there when that man came from the desert. He planted the forest so that the brothers who came to him would not be forced to travel about in search of necessities. He cared for them in every respect, praying to God and striving for their salvation, so that they would lack nothing necessary and have no pretext for negligence.

When he first lived in the desert, he ate herbs and sweet roots. He also drank water whenever he found it, persevering continually in prayers and hymns.

After he reached full old age, an angel appeared to him in a dream while he was in the desert and said:

“‘You shall become a great nation, and a great people shall be entrusted to your faith. Those who will be saved through you shall number ten thousand. If you win that many here, the same number shall obey you in the age to come. Do not doubt anything,’ the angel said to him. ‘Nothing necessary for your use shall fail you until your death whenever you call upon God.’

“When he heard this, he came to the nearby desert, at first living apart in a small hut that he had built for himself and contenting himself with cooked vegetables, often eating only once a week.

“At first he was uneducated. But after he came from the desert into an inhabited land, divine grace was given to him, and he recited the Scriptures from memory. When the brothers gave him a book, he thereafter read as though he were skilled in letters.

“He had also received another grace, namely, the expulsion of demons, so that many of those who suffered, even against his will, cried out and revealed his life. He did not cease performing other healings as well.

“As a result, three thousand monks gathered around him. When the man saw them, he rejoiced, greeted them, and embraced them. After washing their feet with his own hands, he turned to teaching, for he was highly skilled in letters, having received this grace from God.

“When he had expounded many passages of Scripture and handed on the orthodox faith, he urged them to prayer. Great men have the custom of admitting no bodily food before they have given spiritual nourishment to the soul; this is the communion of Christ.

“When they had partaken of it and given thanks, he invited them to the table. While always sitting among them, he admonished them concerning what is good and honorable and told them what pertained to salvation.

“This man was renowned among many Fathers. When many monks came to him, he summoned all the brothers present and built cells for them in a single day: one supplied mud, another bricks, and another drew water. When the cells were finished, he provided those who came with whatever was necessary.

“Once he publicly exposed a false brother who had come to him and hidden his clothes. As a result, no one afterward dared to lie before him, since he possessed such great grace, which he had acquired through his upright life.

“It was possible to see the multitude of monks who were with him in the church, like choirs of angels praising God.”

The entire brotherhood bore witness to this saint’s great virtue, especially the servant of God Melania, who entered this mountain before me. I did not encounter him alive. She related these distinguished things about him: that he had never lied, never sworn an oath, never cursed anyone, and never spoken unless it was necessary.

## CHAPTER X. The Life of Abbot Pambo

[Note: Pambo. Concerning him, see Socrates, Book IV, chapter 18, and Nicephorus, Book IX, chapter 14.]

[Col. 1102B]

Abbot Pambo was also an inhabitant of this mountain. He was the teacher of Bishop Dioscorus; of the brothers Ammonius, Eusebius, and Euthymius; and of Origen, son [and] brother of Dracontius, an illustrious and admirable man.

[Note: “Ammonius, Eusebius, and Euthymius, the brothers, and Origen, the son.” This has been supplied from the Greek codex of the Paris edition; previously the text read, “the sons of Ammon and John.” Heraclides is correct; see him.]

This Pambo possessed many and varied privileges. Among the things he did rightly and virtuously, he had this excellence above the others: he despised gold and silver as far as the law of the Lord requires.

Blessed Melania told me that when she first came from Rome to Alexandria and heard of his virtue from the blessed Isidore, presbyter and keeper of the hospice, who told me about him and led me to him in the desert, she brought him silver vessels containing three hundred pounds of silver, asking him to share in her possessions.

“He was working,” she said, “and weaving branches, and he blessed me, saying in a loud voice: ‘May God give you your reward.’ Then he said to his steward Origen [or Theodore]: ‘Take them and distribute them among all the brotherhood in Libya and on the islands, for those monasteries are more needy.’ He ordered him to give nothing from them to those in Egypt, because that region is richer and more abundant.

“I stood waiting for him either to honor me with blessings or at least to praise me in words for so great a gift. When I heard nothing from him at all, I said to him:

“‘My lord, so that you may know its value, there are three hundred pounds of silver.’

“He did not even nod in response to this. Without paying attention even to the case containing the vessels, he answered:

“‘The one to whom you have brought these things, daughter, does not need to learn from you the weight of their amount. He who weighs the mountains and the hills in a balance (Isaiah 40:12) knows much more the quantity of your silver. If you were giving these things to me, you would rightly tell me their weight; but if you have offered them to God—who did not despise even two obols,

[Note: “Who did not despise even two obols.” These obols are the λεπτά mentioned in Mark 12:42. See the *Onomasticon*.]

but valued them above everything (Mark 12:42)—be silent.’

“Thus,” she said, “the grace of the Lord disposed of the matter when I entered this mountain.

“Not long afterward the man of God fell asleep, without illness and without feeling pain in any part of his body. He was weaving a basket, summoned me, and when the final moment was already at hand, said:

“‘Take this basket from my hands, so that you may remember me. I have nothing else to leave you.’

“After saying this, he departed without fever at the age of seventy, commending his spirit to the Lord.

“When I had cared for him

[Note: *Curassem.* In Latin, *curare* means what the Greek ἐνταφιάζειν means. Here Hervetus translated it as “to bury,” incorrectly. See the *Onomasticon*.]

and wrapped and laid down the holy body in linen cloths, I left the desert, keeping that basket with me until the day of my death.”

When Pambo was dying, at the very hour of his departure, with the presbyter and steward Origen

[Note: “With the presbyter and steward Origen.” This is how it appears in the Paris Greek edition. In others: Μακαρίῳ τῷ πρεσβυτέρῳ, “with the blessed presbyter,” which here seems to be a proper name, not an appellative, as Hervetus understood it when he translated “with the blessed presbyter.” In Heraclides, chapter 2, it is “with the presbyter Paul.” Unless perhaps “the blessed presbyter” means Isidore.]

and Ammonius, illustrious men, and the remaining brothers standing around him, he is said to have spoken as follows:

“From the time I came to this place of solitude, built my cell, and lived here, there was no day on which I did not do some work with my hands. I do not remember ever eating bread given to me freely by anyone; nor, up to this hour, do I regret any word that I have spoken. And so I depart to God, as one who has not even begun to be pious and religious.”

Origen and Ammonius, servants of Christ, also bore this testimony about him: whenever he was asked a question concerning Scripture or some action or practical matter, he never answered immediately. Instead, he would say:

“I have not yet found what to answer.”

Often three months passed without his giving an answer, and he would say:

“I have not yet understood it.”

He gave answers so carefully and with such divine guidance that everyone received them from God with great fear. For he was said to have exercised this virtue above even the great Antony and all the saints: precision and perfection in speech.

## CHAPTER XI. The Life of Abbot Pior

[Note: Pior. Concerning him, see below, chapter 87.]

Among the other deeds of Saint Pambo, the following is also reported. Pior, who practiced the monastic life, once approached his cell and brought his own bread. When Pambo reproved him, saying, “Why did you do this?” Pior replied, “So that I would not burden you.” Pambo therefore dismissed him silently.

After some time, the great Pambo approached Pior’s cell and brought his own bread, moistened. When Pior asked why he had brought moistened bread, Pambo answered:

“I moistened it so that I would not burden you either.”

## CHAPTER XII. The Life of Abba Ammonius and of His Brothers Together with Their Sisters

[Note: Here Ammonius was an Origenist.]

[Note: Ammonius. Concerning him, Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 30; and from him Cassiodorus, *Tripartite History*, Book X, chapter 7; Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 32. See what was said above, concerning Rufinus, Book II, chapter 23. Baronius, volume III, in the year of Christ 340, under Pope Julius IV and the fourth year of the emperors Constantine, Constantius, and Constans. With respect to Athanasius’s arrival in Rome, he says that we find Athanasius bringing with him, among others, Ammonius, a man of admirable holiness (a different man from the one whom we said had fallen asleep in the Lord during Constantine’s time; for this man died long after Antony’s death), as his companion. Concerning him Socrates says, Book IV, chapter 18: “There was another monk, a truly admirable man, whose name was Ammonius. He was so little given to curiosity that, when he happened to be staying at Rome together with Athanasius, he desired to see nothing at all among the city’s magnificent works except the church dedicated to Peter and Paul.” He lived down to the time of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria. When Theophilus was about to ordain him bishop together with Evagrius, Ammonius cut off his own earlobe lest he himself be chosen, since, as he thought, he was unworthy. The above-mentioned Master of the Sacred Palace notes here: “This Ammonius and his brothers, together with their sisters, were openly heretical Origenists [Col. 1220C]. Fleeing from Egypt to Constantinople, they caused great disturbances in the Church. Jerome, in his letter to Ctesiphon, and Theophilus of Alexandria, in his letter to Saint Epiphanius, which is Letter 67 among Saint Jerome’s works, cursed them exceedingly. In volume V of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, he most fully sets forth, from thoroughly reliable authorities and records, their wicked deeds and the upheavals they stirred up.” Thus he.]

Ammonius, who was a disciple of the great Pambo, came with three brothers and two sisters, and after they had attained the summit of piety and religious devotion, they went into the desert and established two separate monasteries, one for men and one for women, with a considerable distance between them.

Because the excellent Ammonius was exceptionally learned, a certain city desired to have him as its bishop. Its inhabitants approached blessed Timothy, the bishop, and asked him to ordain Ammonius as their bishop. He replied: “Bring him to me, and I will ordain him for you.”

So they went with a large force to seize him. He fled, but when he saw that he had already been surrounded, he stopped and begged them. Since they would not yield, the old man swore that he would neither accept the office nor leave the desert. When they still would not give way, he seized a pair of scissors before their eyes and cut off his left ear down to the base, saying to them: “Now understand that it is impossible for me to become what you are forcing me to become, since the law forbids anyone whose ears have been cut off to be promoted to the priesthood.”

They therefore released him and withdrew, and when they came to the bishop they reported what had happened. He said to them: “That law is in force among the Jews. But if you bring me a man of good character even with his nose cut off, I will ordain him.”

They went back and pleaded with him again. When he still would not comply, they attempted to bring him by force. He swore to them, saying: “If you compel me, I will cut out my tongue as well.” After they had left him, they withdrew.

The following miracle is reported of this Ammonius. “Never,” they say, “when an uprising of the flesh of shameful desire invaded his body, did he spare his own flesh; rather, he would apply red-hot iron to his limbs, so that he became entirely covered with sores.”

From his youth until his death, his table was of this kind: he ate only raw foods, for he never ate anything that had been exposed to fire, except bread.

He recited the Old and New Testaments from memory [Note: “From memory.” The Greek is ἀποστηθίζειν, *to recite by heart*. The Greeks use almost this very word in this sense; it occurs below, in chapter 21, in the account of Mark, and in chapter 39, in the account of Aphthonius.]. He was so thoroughly versed in the writings of the learned men Origen, Didymus, Pierius, and Stephen that he had gone through six million lines, as the great Fathers in the desert also testify concerning him.

Prophecies are also attributed to him. He was as powerful in consoling the brothers who lived in the desert as anyone else.

Evagrius, a man endowed with the power of discernment, attributed this to him as a special distinction: he said that he had never seen anyone more “impassible” [Note: “Apathetic.” Poor Palladius is trying here to impose upon his teacher Evagrius’s teaching concerning Stoic impassibility. See Saint Jerome’s letter to Ctesiphon. Thus the Master of the Sacred Palace notes here. Immediately before Benjamin, Heraclides inserts certain material concerning Evagrius and Ammonius and the Rufinian church. He seems to attribute to Evagrius the fact that he received Rufinus from the “spring,” and Baronius cites and understands it in this way in volume IV, in the year of Christ 394.] and free from every disturbance of soul. (Read this cautiously.)

In the Greek text, certain material follows here; it is translated in Heraclides, chapter 2.

## CHAPTER XIII. The Life of Abba Benjamin

[Note: Benjamin. Concerning him, Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 29; and from him Cassiodorus, *Tripartite History*, Book VIII, chapter 10; Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 35.]

In this mountain of Nitria there was an admirable man named Benjamin, who rightly and virtuously lived for eighty years. After he had practiced virtue to the highest degree, he was deemed worthy of the grace of healing, so that anyone upon whom he laid his hands, or to whom he gave oil that he had blessed, was freed from every illness.

This man, who had been deemed worthy of so great a grace, suffered from dropsy for eight months before his death. His body swelled to such a degree from the pain that he was regarded as another Job of our time.

When Bishop Dioscorus, who at that time was a presbyter of the mountain of Nitria, had taken us with him—namely, me and blessed Evagrius—he said to us: “Come and see the new Job, who, amid such a grave bodily illness and such swelling, possesses immense patience together with thanksgiving.”

When we approached, we saw such a mass of his body that we could not encircle even his little finger with the fingers of both hands. Since we could not look directly at the severity of his disease, we turned our eyes away.

Then blessed Benjamin said to us: “Pray, my children, that my inner man may not be dropsical. For this body, when it was well, profited me nothing; nor, when it was ill, did it harm me.”

During those eight months, a very broad seat was made for him [Note: “A very broad seat.” Δίφρος πλατύτατος, “a very broad seat.” Hervetus translated it as “a very broad carriage.” We preferred to render it “seat,” together with Heraclides; Nicephorus Callistus’s translator also supports this, Book XI, chapter 35: δίφρῳ πλατυτέρῳ ἐκάθητο, “he sat on a broader seat.” FRONTO.], on which he sat continually, since he could not lie in bed because of the bodily necessities involved.

Although he suffered from this incurable disease, he healed others who were afflicted by various illnesses. I therefore considered it necessary to describe the illness of this holy man, so that it would not seem strange to us if some misfortune should befall righteous men.

When that outstanding man died, the threshold and doorposts were removed so that his body could be carried out of the cell. So great was the mass of the body of the blessed and renowned father Benjamin.

## CHAPTER XIV. The Life of Apollonius

[Note: Apollonius. He is also mentioned by Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 29; and from him Cassiodorus, Book VIII, chapter 1; Nicephorus, Book IX, chapter 14, and Book XI, chapter 35.]

He was surnamed ἀπὸ πραγματευτῶν, that is, “from the merchants.”

A certain man named Apollonius, surnamed ἀπὸ πραγματευτῶν, that is, “from the merchants,” after renouncing the world and settling on the mountain of Nitria, was unable, because he was advanced in age, either to learn a trade or to study letters. During the twenty years he lived on the mountain, he adopted the following discipline.

With his own money and through his own labor, he bought every kind of medical and pantry supply in Alexandria [Note: “Every kind of medical vessel.” Παντοῖα ἰατρικὰ, καὶ κελλαρικά. Heraclides: “purchasing every kind of remedy and provisions.” In his *Glossary*, Meursius explains τὰ κελλαρικά as “things customarily stored in a cellar and pantry,” and cites Harmenopulus, Book II, title 10. [Col. 1221A] What is called frivolous at the end is γρυτάρια in Greek. See the *Onomasticon*.] and supplied them to the entire brotherhood for their illnesses.

He could be seen from first light until the ninth hour going about, visiting the monasteries, entering the cells, and checking whether anyone was bedridden. He carried raisins, pomegranates, eggs, rye bread, and whatever the sick required.

The servant of Christ continued this way of life until old age. When he was about to die, he left his supplies to another man like himself, asking him to carry out the same ministry. For since five thousand monks inhabited that mountain, such care was also necessary, because the place was deserted.

## CHAPTERS XV AND XVI. The Lives of Paeesius and Isaiah

[Note: Paeesius and Isaiah. Concerning them, Nicephorus, Book IX, chapter 14.]

There were two brothers named Paeesius and Isaiah, whose father was a Spanish merchant [Note: “Spanish merchant.” In Greek, ἐμπόρου Σπανοδρόμου. The old translator of Heraclides rendered it: “He always traveled as far as Spain, conducting trade.” I have seen excerpts in which the reading was Πανοδρόμου. Could it refer to the city of Panos in Egypt? Below, in chapter 39: Εἰς Πανὸς τὴν πόλιν, “to the city of Panos.” Above, in the *Life of Saint John the Almsgiver*, chapter 36, *Gallodromus* occurs.]

When their father died, they divided among themselves the property he had possessed: five thousand coins in money, and whatever was found in clothing and slaves. They deliberated together and, taking counsel for themselves, said: “What path of life shall we enter, brother? If we practice the commerce practiced by our father, we shall leave our labors to others, and perhaps fall into the dangers of either robbers or the sea. Come, then, brother, let us undertake the monastic life, so that we may both profit from our father’s possessions and not lose our souls.”

Both therefore approved the aim of the solitary life, but they were found to differ from one another. After they had divided the money and everything else, they both set before themselves the aim of pleasing God, but by different ways of life.

One of them scattered everything, giving it to monasteries, churches, and prisons. After learning a trade by which he could earn his bread, he devoted himself to discipline and prayer.

The other did not distribute any of his property. Instead, he built a monastery for himself, took in a few brothers, and received every guest, cared for every sick person, sheltered every old person, and gave to every poor person. On Saturdays and Sundays he set out three or four tables and welcomed those who were needy. In this manner he spent his life.

When both had died, the brothers assigned different forms of blessedness to each of them, since both had been found perfect in virtue. Some approved the life of the one who had renounced everything; others approved the life of the one who shared with all the needy.

When a dispute arose among the brothers because of these blessed men’s different ways of life, and especially because of the different praises given to them, they went to blessed Pambo and asked him to answer the question, wishing to know which way of life was better.

He said to them: “Both are perfect before God. One performed the work of Abraham, who welcomed everyone; the other embraced the firmest and most steadfast zeal of the prophet Elijah, in order to please God.”

When some said to him: “How can this be? We beg you—our touching your feet [Note: “Our touching your feet.” This has been restored from the Greek, since Hervetus’s reading, “from your feet,” made no sense. Touching the feet and falling at someone’s feet are forms of entreaty. See the *Onomasticon*.]—tell us how they can be equal,” while others preferred the ascetic and said: “He fulfilled the Gospel command, selling everything and giving it to the poor, persevering in prayer by night and by day, carrying the cross and following the Savior,” others, on the contrary, argued for the other, saying: “This man showed such and so great compassion to all the needy that he went out and sat along the royal roads, gathering those who were afflicted and bringing them aid. He refreshed not only his own soul but also the souls of others, caring for the sick and giving them assistance.”

Blessed Pambo said: “Again I tell you: both are equal before the Lord, and I will satisfy each of you concerning them.

“If this man had not practiced such great discipline, he would not have been worthy for me to compare him with the other’s goodness.

“The other, who refreshed and restored guests and served the needy, was shown to be equal before the Lord according to his strength. For he himself said: ‘I did not come to be served, but to serve’ (Matthew 20).

“Although this servant seemed to bear a burden because of his labor, he also found refreshment in that very labor.

“Wait a little, so that I may also receive a revelation from God concerning them. Afterwards, when you return, you will know.”

After several days had passed, they returned and asked the great man about them. The old man answered them: “I speak to you before God” [Note: “God.” The Greek reads, as Heraclides translated it, “I speak to you before God, and I have found both of them standing together in paradise.” Thus Paul says, 2 Corinthians 12:19: Κατενώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐν Χριστῷ λαλοῦμεν, “We speak before God in Christ”; and Galatians 1:20: Ἰδοὺ ἐνώπιον τοῦ Θεοῦ οὐ ψεύδομαι, “Behold, before God, I do not lie”; so that this may be understood as a form of oath, as in 2 Timothy 2:14: Διαμαρτυρόμενος ἐνώπιον τοῦ Κυρίου, “testifying before the Lord.” A similar expression occurs below, chapter 113: Ὡς ἐπὶ Θεοῦ ἡμᾶς ἔπεισεν, “He persuaded us as one speaking before God.” FRONTO.] “I saw both of them standing together in paradise.”

## CHAPTER XVII. The Life of the Younger Macarius

[Note: The younger Macarius. Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 29; and from him Cassiodorus, *Tripartite History*, Book VIII, chapter 1; Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 35.]

A certain younger man named Macarius, eighteen years old, was grazing livestock and playing with his companions beside the lake called Maria when he accidentally committed a killing. He told no one about it, but went into the desert. His fear of God and of human beings became so great that he did not realize that he had spent three years in the desert without shelter.

That land is dry, and everyone knows this, both those who have learned it by report and those who know it from experience. Later this Macarius built a cell for himself. After living in it for another twenty-five years, he was deemed worthy of such great grace that, taking delight in the desert, he despised the demons [Note: “Desert.” The translator had published the reading “so that he might spit at the demons who insulted the desert,” as though the Greek were ἐντρυφῶντας. Heraclides, however, defends the received reading in chapter 4: “So that, exulting in the solitary life, he might mock and despise the demons.” FRONTO.].

I spent a long time with him and learned from him what his attitude had been toward the sin of killing. He said that he was so far from grieving over it that he even gave thanks for the crime. “The accidental killing,” he said, “became for me the cause of salvation.”

He cited as testimony from the Scriptures the killing committed in Egypt by Moses, the great servant of God. He said that, if not for the killing and his fear of Pharaoh, Moses would not have been deemed worthy of the vision of the Lord, of so great a gift, or of writing down the holy utterances of the Spirit. After fleeing from Egypt, he came to Mount Sinai.

I say this not to prepare the way for any killing, but rather to show that virtues can also arise from an accident, when someone does not willingly approach the good of his own accord. For some virtues arise from the will and from the disposition of our own mind, while others arise from accident.

## CHAPTER XVIII. The Life of Abba Nathanael

Among the ancient saints there was another man, an excellent athlete of Christ, named Nathanael. I did not encounter him in the flesh, for he had fallen asleep fifteen years before my arrival on the mountain. When I met those who had practiced with this saint and had been his contemporaries, I gladly questioned them about the man’s virtue.

They also showed me his cell, in which no one yet lives, because it is nearer to inhabited territory. That blessed man had established it at a time when anchorites were still few.

They told me of his outstanding discipline: he had such endurance in his cell that he was never moved from his purpose. At the beginning he had been deceived by the demon who deceives everyone. The demon had caused him to lapse into indolence and grief of spirit and had driven him from his cell, for he had appeared sad and distressed in the first cell.

After leaving it, he built another closer to the village. When he had completed the cell and had lived in it for three or four months, the demon came at night holding a whip, like the lictors, and presenting the appearance of a soldier dressed in rags. He made a noise with the leather strap [Note: “And the whip.” Not “clothed in bull’s hide,” as Hervetus had written. See the *Onomasticon*.].

Enraged, blessed Nathanael said to him: “Who are you, that you do these things in my dwelling?”

The demon replied: “I am the one who drove you from your first cell, and now I have come to drive you from this one as well.”

When blessed Nathanael realized that he had been deceived, he returned to the first cell. For thirty-seven years he did not go outside the door, contending with the demon, who had done so much to him and inflicted such things upon him in order to force him to leave the cell that it is not even permissible to recount them.

Among other things, the enemy of the good devised this scheme: to bring him disgrace and dishonor and thereby break his resolve.

When seven holy bishops visited the saint, either through God’s providence or through the suggestion of that temptation, the demon almost drove him from his purpose. After the bishops had visited him and prayed, when they were leaving after the prayer, the outstanding man did not accompany them even a single footstep, lest he give the enemy an opportunity.

The bishops’ deacons therefore said to him: “You behave arrogantly, Abba, because you do not escort the bishops.”

He replied to them: “I honor my lords, the bishops, and I respect the entire clergy. I am the refuse of all human beings. But with respect to all these things, and with respect to the whole course of life, I am dead to the purpose that is in me. For I have a hidden aim, known to the Lord who knows the secrets of my heart, and that is why I did not accompany them.”

When this action too had failed for the demon, he assumed another form. Nine months before the athlete’s death, he transformed himself into a twelve-year-old boy, as though he were leading an ass carrying bread in a basket.

When the boy was near the cell late in the evening, he pretended that the ass had fallen and began to cry out: “Abba Nathanael, have mercy on me and give me your hand.”

Nathanael certainly heard the boy’s voice. He opened the door of the cell, stood inside, and said to him: “Who are you, and what do you want me to do for you?”

The demon replied: “I am this monk’s servant, and I am carrying bread, since there is a love-feast for your acquaintance, and at daybreak tomorrow, on the Sabbath, offerings will be needed. I beg you not to despise me, lest I be devoured by hyenas. There are hyenas in these regions.”

Blessed Nathanael stood silent. Because of his immense compassion, he was darkened and troubled in his entrails, and he considered what he should do, saying to himself: “Either I shall transgress the commandment, or I shall fall from my purpose.”

After reflecting within himself with pious understanding, he said: “It is better not to undermine the purpose of so many years, but to put the devil to shame and defeat him.”

Having therefore asked the Lord, he said to the boy who was speaking with him: “Listen, boy—or whoever you are. I believe in the God whom I worship, who rules every spirit, and I am sure that, if you truly need help, God will send you help. Neither hyenas nor anything else will harm you. But if you are a temptation, God will also reveal this to me from now on.”

He then entered and closed the door of the cell. The demon, ashamed that he had been defeated even in this way, dissolved into a whirlwind, resembling wild asses rejoicing, fleeing, and making a noise; thus he vanished.

This was the contest of blessed Nathanael; these were the virtues of his discipline and his unconquered battle against the adversary; and this was the celebrated conclusion of his life.

## CHAPTERS XIX AND XX. The Lives of Abba Macarius the Egyptian and Macarius the Alexandrian

[Note: Macarius the Egyptian and Macarius the Alexandrian. Concerning them, Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 29; Socrates, Book IV, chapter 18; and from him Cassiodorus, *Tripartite History*, Book VIII, chapter 7; Nicephorus, Book IX, chapter 14, and Book XI, chapters 42–43. Concerning the man raised from the dead by Macarius, Cassian, *Conferences*, conference 15, chapter 3. Concerning the punishment he inflicted upon gnats, Peter Damian, Book V, Letter 8: “Surely that blessed Macarius will not rightly be laughed at, who, when he repented of having committed some offense against the enemy, exposed his naked limbs for six months to the sharpest beaks of gnats—beaks that could pierce even boars?”]

The honorable contests of the saints and immortal Fathers, Macarius the Egyptian and Macarius the Alexandrian (Rufinus, Book II, chapters 28–29), those outstanding and unconquered athletes—contests numerous and great, and almost unbelievable to those who do not believe—both frighten me to recount and make me hesitate to commit them to writing, lest I be mentioned as a liar.

But since God destroys all who speak falsehood (Psalm 5), this can plainly be seen, as the Holy Spirit declares.

Since, then, by the grace of God I do not lie, most faithful Lausus, do not yourself disbelieve the contests of the Fathers. Rather, glory in imitating the discipline of those who are truly called Macarii, that is, “blessed.”

The first athlete of Christ, named Macarius, was Egyptian by birth. The second, younger in age but holding first place in the chief matters of monks, was also called Macarius and was an Alexandrian who sold delicacies.

First I shall narrate the virtues of Macarius the Egyptian, who lived a full ninety years. Of these, he spent sixty years in the desert.

When he was thirty years old and still young, he endured the labors of discipline with such perseverance for an entire decade that he was deemed worthy of great and remarkable discernment. He was called παιδαριογέρων, that is, “an old man in a boyish age,” because he advanced in virtue more quickly than his age would suggest.

When he was forty years old, he received power over spirits, the grace of healing, and the spirit of predicting future events. He was also deemed worthy of the honor of the priesthood.

Two disciples lived with him in the deepest part of the desert called Scete. One was his attendant and was always found near him because of those who came to be healed; the other sat apart in his cell.

As time passed, the saint foresaw something with his discerning eye and said to his attendant, whose name was John and who later became a presbyter in the place of Saint Macarius—for the great Macarius had been deemed worthy of the presbyterate:

“Listen to me, brother John, and bear my admonition patiently; it will benefit you. You are being tempted,” he said, “and the spirit of greed is tempting you. This is what I have seen, and I know that, if you bear my exhortation patiently, you will be perfected in the fear of God and in his work. In this place you will be praised, and the scourge will not approach your dwelling.

“But if you do not listen, the end of Gehazi will come upon you (2 Kings 5), whose vice afflicts you.”

It happened that, after the saint’s death, John did not obey him but obeyed the one who, because of greed, tied the noose around Judas’s neck. After another fifteen or twenty years, when he had appropriated the property of the poor, he suffered so severely from elephantiasis that no sound place could be found on his body where one might set a finger.

This was the prophecy of Saint Macarius.

It is superfluous to speak about food and drink, since even among the more negligent monks who live outside, gluttony cannot be found, nor any other way of life apart from the disciplined manner of those who live in those regions—both because of the scarcity of necessities and because of their zeal for God, with each person striving to surpass his neighbor through different forms of discipline.

Concerning the other discipline of this heavenly man, Macarius, it was said that this saint was continually in ecstasy and spent more time with God than occupied with the affairs of this world [Note: “Spent more time with God than occupied with the affairs of this world.” The translator Hervetus rendered it differently: “and spent more time either with God or engaged in heavenly matters.” Ἡ ὑπ᾽ οὐρανὸν means “the inhabited world.” See the *Onomasticon*.]. Various miracles are also attributed to him.

A lustful Egyptian (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 28), seized by love for a certain freeborn woman who was married, was unable to entice her because of her chastity and her virginity toward her husband [Note: “Toward her husband, her virginity.” We published this reading, whereas previously it had read *erga suum maritum Parthenicum*, as though *Parthenicus* were the husband’s proper name. In fact, παρθενικὸς ἀνὴρ is used in Scripture, and in Plutarch’s *Life of Pompey* one finds παρθένιος ἀνήρ: Πόπλια τὸν παρθένιον ἄνδρα κείμενον, “Publius, who married me while I was still a virgin.” Joel 1:8: Θρήνησον ὑπὲρ νύμφην περιεζωσμένην σάκκον ἐπὶ τὸν ἄνδρα τὸν παρθένιον, “Mourn more than a bride girded with sackcloth for her virginal husband.” The Latin Vulgate has: “Mourn for the husband of her youth.” Among poets there is κουρίδιος πόσις, ὁ ἐκ παρθενίας γεγαμηκὼς γυναῖκα, “a wedded husband, one who has married a woman from her virginity.” Thus in *Iliad* 5: Κουρίδιον ποθέουσα πόσιν τὸν ἄριστον Ἀχαιῶν, “longing for her wedded husband, the best of the Achaeans.” FRONTO.].

He went to a wicked sorcerer and said: “Either make her fall in love with me, or by your art cause her husband to divorce her.”

When the sorcerer had received a sufficient payment from him, he employed his magic and incantations. Since he could not move her mind to consent to him, he caused her to appear as a mare to those who looked at her.

When her husband returned from outside, he saw his wife in the form of a mare. When she lay down in her own bed, it seemed strange to him that a mare should be lying in his bed. Her husband therefore wept and lamented that he could not discover what had happened and that, although he thought he was speaking to the animal, he could obtain no reply, except that he saw her becoming angry.

He was all the more distressed when he understood that she was his wife, but that human arts had changed her into a mare. For these reasons he summoned the presbyters of the village and brought them into the house and showed her to them, but they too did not recognize the calamity that had befallen her.

For three days she ate neither hay as a mare nor bread as a human being, being deprived of both kinds of food. At last, so that God might be glorified and the power of Saint Macarius might be revealed, it entered her husband’s heart to take her into the desert to the holy man.

After tying her with a halter like a mare, he led her into the desert. When they had come near, the brothers stood near Saint Macarius’s cell, arguing with her husband and saying: “Why have you brought this mare here?”

He replied: “So that she may receive mercy through the saint’s prayer.”

They said to him: “What is wrong with her?”

He replied: “The mare you see was my unfortunate wife. I do not know how she was changed into a mare, and it is now three days since she has eaten anything.”

When they heard this, they reported it to God’s servant Macarius, who was already praying inside for her. God had revealed the matter to him while they were coming to him, and therefore he was praying that the cause of what had happened might be disclosed to him.

The holy man replied to the brothers who had reported that someone had brought a horse there: “You are the horses, since you have the eyes of horses. She is a woman as she was created—not transformed, but merely appearing so to the eyes of those who have been deceived.”

When she had been brought in, he blessed water, poured it over her bare head, and prayed over her. Immediately he caused her to appear as a woman to everyone who saw her.

When he ordered food to be brought to her, he enabled her to eat, and after healing her he sent her away with her husband, giving thanks to God.

The man of God admonished her, saying: “Never abandon the church, and never abstain from communion in the sacraments of Christ. For these things happened to you because you have not approached the undefiled sacraments of our Savior for five weeks.”

Here is another deed of his great discipline. For a large part of his life, he dug a tunnel from his cell for a distance of half a stadium and made a large cave at its end. Whenever several people troubled him, he would secretly leave his cell and go into the cave, and no one could find him.

One of his devoted disciples told us that, as he went through the tunnel to the cave, he recited twenty-four prayers, and as he returned, he recited the same number.

A report went forth about him that he had raised a dead man (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 28), in order to persuade a heretic who did not confess the resurrection of bodies. This report remained firmly established in the desert.

Once a young man tormented by a demon was brought to this saint by his grieving mother. Two young men held him tightly on either side.

The demon tormented him in the following way: after he had eaten three *modii* of bread and drunk a Cilician amphora of water [Note: “A Cilician amphora.” In Greek, Ἀμφορέα Κιλικίσιον ὕδατος, “a Cilician amphora of water.” See the *Onomasticon*.], he would belch up both, reducing the food to vapor. For what he ate and drank was consumed by the demon just as if by fire. There is also an order of demons called fiery. For there are distinctions among demons just as among human beings: their essence is not changed, but they are distinguished by their will.

When the young man’s mother did not supply him with food, he would often eat his own excrement and drink urine.

His mother wept, grieving over the alien calamity of her son, and earnestly implored and entreated the saint. The unconquered athlete of Christ, Macarius, took the young man and fervently prayed to God for him.

After a day or two, the demon ceased tormenting him. Then Saint Macarius said to the young man’s mother: “How much do you want your son to eat?”

She replied: “I beg you, order him to eat only ten pounds of bread.”

Reproving her for saying too much, he said: “Woman, why did you say this?”

After praying and fasting for seven days, he drove out the destructive demon of gluttony and established for him a diet of up to three pounds of bread, which he himself was to eat if he worked.

Having thus cleansed the boy by the grace of God, he returned him to his mother.

God performed these marvelous and unexpected deeds through Saint Macarius, whose immortal soul is now with the angels.

I did not meet him, for he had died one year before I entered the desert. But I met the man who was his companion in works of faith and who bore the same venerable name as he.

I mean Saint Macarius the Alexandrian, who was presbyter of the place called the Cells. I lived in those Cells for nine years; for three of those years Macarius lived with me in quiet. Some of the works and signs of his excellent way of life I saw myself; others I learned from those who had lived with him.

When he had seen the chosen palm branches that the great man and Father Antony himself had cultivated, he asked Antony for one bundle of palm branches.

Antony said to him: “It is written: ‘You shall not covet your neighbor’s possessions’” (Deuteronomy 7).

When he had said only this, all the branches immediately became as though scorched by fire.

When Antony saw this, he said to Macarius: “Behold, the Holy Spirit has rested upon you, and from now on you will be the heir of my virtues.”

Later, the devil found him in the desert, with his body greatly exhausted, and said to him: “Behold, you have received Antony’s grace. Why do you not use your authority and ask God for food and strength to undertake the journey?”

He replied: “The Lord is my strength and my praise; but you must not tempt God’s servant.”

The devil therefore caused a phantom to appear to him: a camel carrying loads and wandering through the desert, bearing everything necessary for use. When it saw Macarius, it sat down near him.

Macarius suspected that it was a phantom and stood still to pray. At once the phantom was swallowed up by the earth.

At another time Macarius of Alexandria again came to the great Macarius who was in Scetis. As both were about to cross the Nile, it happened that they boarded a very large ferry. Two tribunes also boarded it, with great pomp and display, having inside a complete bronze carriage, horses with golden bridles, and soldiers, attendants, and boys wearing torques and golden belts. When the tribunes saw the two men dressed in old rags and sitting in a corner, they judged that their humble and meager way of life was blessed. One of the tribunes said to them: “Blessed are you who mock the world.”

Macarius, who was urbane, replied: “We have mocked the world, but the world has mocked you.” Know, however, that you did not say this of your own accord, but prophetically: for both of us are called Macarius, that is, “blessed.” The tribune, moved to compunction by his words, returned home, removed his clothing, and chose to lead a solitary life, giving many alms.

Again, when on one occasion he desired to eat fresh and very beautiful grapes that had been sent to him, he demonstrated his self-control by sending them to another brother who was ill and also desired grapes. When that brother received them and was filled with great joy, wishing to conceal his own self-control, he sent them to another brother who was ill and likewise desired that food. When the latter had also received them, he did the same again, although he himself very much desired to eat them. After the grapes had consequently passed through many brothers, and none of them had wished to eat them, the last recipient sent them back to Macarius, as though bestowing a great gift upon him. When he had carefully investigated the matter, he marveled and gave thanks to God for such great self-control on their part; finally, he too did not eat any of them.

This, then, was the discipline of the great Macarius, which I and many others learned accurately from him. Whenever he heard that someone had practiced some form of ascetic discipline, he eagerly practiced it himself without fail.

When he heard from some people that the Tabennesiots ate nothing throughout the whole of Lent that had been exposed to fire, this holy man decided to eat for seven years nothing that had passed through fire. Throughout that entire seven-year period he tasted nothing except raw vegetables or, if he happened to find any, legumes soaked in water. When he had lived correctly in this manner, he rejected that way of life. He then heard from another of the monks, an excellent man, that a certain monk ate a pound of bread. Emulating him, he broke up the piece of bread he had and put it into a jar, deciding to eat only as much as his hand could lift out. Great was this man’s severity in treating his body. He used to tell us humorously:

“I would take hold of more pieces—722—but the narrowness of the opening did not allow me to bring them out. For my tax collector did not permit me to eat at all.”

For three full years he practiced this self-control, eating four or five ounces of bread and an equivalent amount of water; he consumed, however, a sextarius of oil as food over the entire year.

Another discipline of the athlete: this unconquered man decided to overcome sleep. He related this himself for our benefit:

“For twenty full days and nights I did not enter under a roof, so that I might conquer sleep. By day I burned in the heat, but at night I stiffened with cold. If,” he said, “I had not entered under a roof and made use of sleep, my brain would have become so dried up that afterward I would have fallen into ecstasy. As far as I was concerned, I conquered sleep; but I yielded to nature, because it required it.”

[Note: [Col. 1113] This paragraph differs in the Greek. It appears as in Heraclides, chapter 6.]

On one occasion the spirit of fornication troubled him.

[Note: [Col. 1221D] “The spirit of fornication.” Hervetus seems to have used a different Greek text, as did the old translator of Palladius. The Greek gives a fuller account and in another sense. See Heraclides, chapter VI.]

Then he condemned himself to sit naked for six months in the marsh of Scetis, which lies in the vast desert. There the mosquitoes are able to pierce even the hides of wild boars, for they are as large as wasps; so deeply did they fix their stings throughout his body that some people thought he was a leper. After six months he returned to his cell, and by his voice it became known that he was the lord Macarius.

As he himself told us, he once desired, while he was in the gardens, to enter the tomb called the *kepotaphion*—κηποτάφιον—of Janne and Mambre, the magicians who lived in Pharaoh’s time, in order to see it, or even to meet the demons who were there. It was said that many demons, and exceedingly savage ones, had been placed there by them through the excellence of their infamous art.

This tomb had been built by the brothers Janne and Mambre, who on account of their mastery of magic held the first rank at that time with Pharaoh. Since they possessed the greatest power in Egypt during that period of their lives, they constructed the building out of squared stones and made their tomb there. They had deposited much gold there and planted every kind of tree; they had also dug a very large well, for the place is damp.

[Note: [Col. 1221D] “Out of squared stones.” Greek: ἐκ τετροπέδων λίθων. Hervetus had translated “of a size four feet long.” See the *Onomasticon*.]

[Note: [Col. 1221D] “The place is damp.” In Greek, ὕπικμος, according to the manuscript, not ὕπιγμος, “a damp place,” as in the printed Lyon edition. Hervetus translated “a place that easily yields,” as though the word were εἰκτικός, ἐπιεικτικός, or εὔεικτος, from εἴκειν, “to yield.” Heraclides supports our correction: “They also made a well, because the same place appeared to be without any moisture.” Another old translator has, “For the place is moist.” The reason is given why they dug a very large well. FRONTO.]

They did all this in the hope that, after departing from this life, they might enjoy the delights of that paradise. Since the servant of God Macarius did not know the road leading to the garden, he followed the stars by conjecture and, like sailors crossing the sea, traversed the whole desert. After obtaining a number of reeds, he planted one at each mile-marker so that by those signs he might find his way back.

When he had traversed the whole desert in nine days and was near the garden, night came on and he slept a little. But the monstrous demon who always opposes Christ’s athletes gathered up all those reeds while Macarius slept and placed them near his head, about one stone’s throw from the tomb; then he withdrew. When Macarius arose, he found the reeds he himself had fixed as markers tied together.

Perhaps this too was permitted by God for the sake of his greater discipline, so that he would not place his hope in reeds but in God’s grace, which led Israel for forty years through that dreadful desert by means of the pillar of cloud.

Macarius said:

“When I drew nearer to the tomb, about seventy demons came out of it to meet me, appearing in various forms. Some were shouting; others were leaping about; others, with a great roar, gnashed their teeth at me; others flew like ravens. They dared to insult my face, saying: ‘What do you want, Macarius, temptation of the monks? Why have you come to us? Have we not also tormented some of the monks? What belongs to us you have there with your kind: solitude. From there you have driven away our relations. We have nothing in common with you. Why are you invading our places? As a solitary, be content with solitude. Those who built this place assigned it to us; you cannot remain here. Why do you seek to enter this possession, into which no living human being has entered since we performed the funeral rites here for the brothers who founded it?’

“While the demons were still causing much disturbance and insulting me, holy Macarius said to them: ‘I shall merely enter, look around, and depart from here.’

“The demons said: ‘Promise us this in your conscience.’

“The servant of Christ said: ‘I will do so.’

“And the demons vanished.

“When I entered the paradise, the devil came to meet me with a drawn sword, threatening me. Holy Macarius answered him with these words: ‘You come against me with a drawn sword; but I shall enter against you in the name of the Lord Sabaoth, in the battle-line of the God of Israel.’

“After entering, I examined everything. There I found a bronze bucket hanging by an iron chain from the well, already worn away by time, and pomegranates that had nothing inside them—for they had been dried up by the sun—and many golden offerings.”

When the holy man had departed from there without disturbance or any agitation, he returned to his cell over twenty days.

When the bread and water he was carrying had run out, he was in great distress. For, as I suppose, while entering through the desert for twenty days, he tasted nothing at all, as the outcome itself also showed. Perhaps he was also being tested by impatience.

When he was already close to collapsing, there appeared before him, as he himself related, what looked like a girl dressed in a clean linen garment and holding a dripping water jar. Macarius said that she was about one stadium away from him. For three days he proceeded while seeing her as though she were standing there and enticing him, but he was unable to reach her. Yet hope of drinking enabled him to endure the labor of the three days courageously.

After that a herd of buffalo appeared, one of which stood opposite him with a calf. There are many such animals in those regions. Macarius told us that its udder was flowing with milk, and a voice sounded from above, saying to him: “Macarius, approach the buffalo and drink its milk.”

“When,” he said, “I approached it and had drunk, I was satisfied. But to show still greater grace, the Lord, teaching me my littleness, commanded the buffalo to follow me to my cell. She obeyed the command and followed me, giving me milk but not allowing her own calf to nurse.”

At another time, while this man endowed with virtue was digging a well to refresh the monks—he was near leaves and branches that had been placed there—he was bitten by an asp, a poisonous and deadly creature. Holy Macarius seized both jaws of the asp with both hands, tore it apart, and said: “Since my Lord did not send you, how did you dare approach me?”

When the great Macarius again heard that the Tabennesiots had an outstanding rule of life, he changed his clothing, put on the dress of a laborer, and reached the Thebaid after fifteen days, entering through the desert.

When he came to the monastery of the Tabennesiots, he sought their archimandrite, named Pachomius, a most distinguished man who also possessed prophetic grace.

[Note: Concerning him below, chapter 38.]

At that time the great Macarius had not yet been revealed to this holy man. When Macarius met him, he said:

“I beg you, receive me, I pray you, into your monastery, so that I may become a monk.”

The great Pachomius said to him:

“You can no longer become a monk, since you are so advanced in age; you cannot practice the discipline. There are brothers who have trained themselves from youth and endure hardship. But at your age you cannot endure the trials of ascetic practice. You will be offended, leave, and curse us.”

He did not accept him, either on the first day or the second, and continued in this way for seven days. Macarius remained steadfast and fasted.

Afterward the elder Macarius said to him:

“Receive me, abba; and if I do not fast and do what they do, order me to be expelled from the monastery.”

The great Pachomius persuaded the brothers to admit him. The community of this one monastery consists, even to the present day, of 1,400 men.

So he entered. After some time had passed, Lent arrived. The elder Macarius saw each man undertaking a different way of life: one eating in the evening, another after two days, another after five; one standing throughout the entire night and sitting at his work during the day.

Macarius himself moistened some palm branches and stood in a corner. Until the forty days had been completed and Easter had arrived, he took neither bread nor water, did not bend his knee, did not sit, did not recline, and tasted nothing except a few raw cabbage leaves, which he ate on Sunday so that he might appear to be eating and not fall into an arrogant opinion of himself.

Whenever he went out for some necessary purpose, he quickly returned and stood at his work, not opening his mouth, but standing in silence. He did nothing except practice silence in his heart, offer prayer, and work the palm branches that he held in his hands.

When all the ascetics of that monastery saw this, they raised a revolt against their superior:

“Where have you brought us this man without flesh, to our condemnation? Either expel him, or, know this, we shall all leave.”

When the great Pachomius heard this from the brothers, he inquired about him. After learning how he lived, he asked God to reveal who he was. It was revealed to him that he was the monk Macarius.

Then the great Pachomius took him by the hand and led him outside. When he had brought him to the house of the oratory, where the altar was, and had embraced him, he said:

“Come here, venerable elder. You are Macarius, and you concealed this from me. Many years ago I desired to see you when I heard about you. I thank you for subduing my sons, lest they boast and look around proudly because of their ascetic practice. I ask you, therefore, return to your own place. You have sufficiently edified us, and pray for us.”

Then, having been asked by Pachomius, while all the brothers prayed with him, he departed in this manner.

This impassible man related to us again:

“When I had properly fulfilled the whole rule of monastic life, I then came to another spiritual desire. I decided for five days to arrange my mind in such a way that it could not be torn away from God and would think of nothing else at all.

“When I had made this decision, I closed my cell and its outer courtyard so that I would answer no one. I stood there, beginning from the second hour, commanding my mind and saying to it: ‘See that you do not descend from the heavens. You have angels, archangels, all the heavenly powers, cherubim and seraphim, and God, the maker of all these. Remain there; do not descend beneath the heavens, and do not fall into worldly thoughts.’

“When I had persevered for two days and two nights,” he said, “I so enraged the demon that he himself became a flame of fire and burned everything I had in the cell, so that even the mat on which I stood was burning with fire. I thought that I too would be completely consumed.

“Finally, overcome by fear, on the third day I abandoned this purpose, since I could no longer keep my mind undivided, but descended to contemplation of this world—perhaps by God’s permission, so that this would not be counted against me as pride.”

I once approached him and found lying outside his cell a certain presbyter of a village. His head had been so eaten away by the disease called cancer that even the entire bone itself was visible at the crown. He had come to Macarius to be healed, but Macarius would not admit him to conversation.

I asked Macarius, saying: “Have mercy on this wretched man and at least give him an answer.”

He replied to me:

“He is unworthy to be healed, for this discipline has been sent to him by the Lord. If you wish him to be healed, persuade him henceforth to abstain from ministering the holy sacraments.”

I said to him: “Why, I pray you?”

He replied:

“He committed fornication and performed the sacred ministry; therefore he is being punished. Now, if through fear he ceases from what he dared to do contemptuously, God will heal him.”

When I told the afflicted man this, he promised under oath that he would no longer perform the duties of a priest. Then Macarius received him and said to him:

“Do you believe that there is a God from whom nothing is hidden?”

He answered: “I certainly do, I beg you.”

Then Macarius said to him:

“Were you able to mock God?”

He replied: “I was not, my lord.”

Macarius said to him:

“If you acknowledge your sin and God’s discipline, because of which you have suffered these things, correct yourself hereafter.”

He confessed his sin and promised that he would sin no more or minister at the altar, but would embrace the lot of the laity. Then the saint laid his hands upon him, and within a few days he was healed. His hair grew back, and he returned home in good health, glorifying God; he also gave thanks to the great Macarius.

This saint had various cells: one in Scetis, which is farther within the desert; one in Libya; one in the Cells; and one on Mount Nitria. Some of them had no door, and it was said that during Lent he sat in them in darkness. Another was narrower, so narrow that he could not stretch out his foot; another was wider, in which he received those who came to visit him.

He healed such a multitude of people afflicted by demons that it cannot be counted. When we were there, a noble and wealthy virgin was brought to him from Thessalonica, on the borders of Achaea. She had suffered from paralysis for many years. Moved by mercy, he had her laid before his cell, anointed her with holy oil with his own hands for twenty days, and prayed. He sent her back healed to her city. She departed on her own feet and sent a generous offering to the saints.

In my presence a boy afflicted by a spirit was brought to him. Macarius laid one hand on the boy’s head and the left hand over his heart, and prayed until he caused him to hang in the air. The boy swelled up like an inflated wineskin, until he became exceedingly heavy. Then he suddenly cried out and discharged water through all his bodily senses. When he stopped, he returned to the size he had previously been.

Macarius handed him over to his father after anointing him with holy oil. He poured water over him and ordered that for forty days he taste neither meat nor wine. In this way he healed him.

At one time vain-glorious thoughts came upon him. They drove him out of his cell and suggested that, for a worthy purpose and a just cause, he should go to Rome for the benefit of those who were ill, for grace worked powerfully in him against the spirits.

When he had refused obedience for a long time, he was greatly agitated. Falling at the threshold of his cell, he thrust his feet outside and said:

“Drag and pull, demons, if you can. I am not leaving on my own feet. I swear that I shall lie here until evening, and unless you shake me off, I shall not listen.”

After lying there for a long time, he arose. When night came, they again troubled him. He filled a basket holding two *modii* with sand, placed it on his shoulders, and traversed the whole desert.

Theosebius the Cosmetor, an Antiochene by birth, met him and said:

“What are you carrying, abba? Give me the burden, and do not trouble yourself.”

He replied:

“I am troubling the one who troubles me. For, since I am lax and sluggish, he suggests journeys to me.”

After proceeding for a long time, he entered his cell with his body exhausted.

[Note: [Col. 1117D] Heraclides attributes this to Mark.]

[Note: [Col. 1222A] “He told us.” At this point Heraclides inserts Macarius’s narrative concerning Mark, which is also found and follows here in chapter 21. Here there follows the narrative of Paphnutius also concerning Mark. Mark is said to have given Athanasius the skin, and Athanasius to have given it to Melania. Perhaps “Mark” was written for “Macarius,” through abbreviation of the letters. Yet what is related of his age—namely, that he was sixty years after baptism and forty before baptism, as Heraclides has it—fits Mark, whom he says lived one hundred years. Rufinus, however, in book II of the History, chapter 4, attributes to Macarius the story of the lioness, as does the Greek text here. A similar story occurs above, book IV, chapter 8, from Sulpicius Severus’s Dialogue 1, chapter 9, concerning an anonymous anchorite near Memphis and the five blind cubs of a lioness, whose sight he restored.]

Paphnutius, the servant of God and disciple of this distinguished saint, told us that one day, while holy Macarius was sitting in his courtyard and addressing God, a hyena brought her own cub, which was blind, to holy Macarius. After striking the door of the courtyard with her head, she entered while he was still sitting there and threw the cub at his feet.

When holy Macarius had taken the cub and spat into its eyes, he prayed, and immediately it saw. Its mother nursed it, took it, and departed.

On the following day she brought the hide of a large sheep to holy Macarius. When the saint saw the hide, he said to the hyena:

“Where would you have obtained this unless you had devoured someone’s sheep? What proceeds from injustice I will not accept from you.”

With her head bowed to the ground, the hyena knelt at the saint’s feet and set down the hide. He said to her:

“I have said that I will not accept it unless you promise that you will no longer harm the poor by eating their sheep.”

She nodded her head to this also, assenting to holy Macarius. Then he accepted the hide from the hyena.

The blessed servant of Christ Melania told me that she had received that hide from that Macarius, and that it was called “the hyena’s gift.”

What is so surprising, among men crucified to the world, if a hyena, having received a benefit, brought gifts to the glory of God and the honor of his servants, recognizing this? For the one who tamed the lions in the prophet Daniel also granted understanding to this hyena.

It was also said of him that from the time he was baptized he never spat upon the ground, although sixty years had passed since his baptism. He had received baptism at the age of forty.

His appearance was as follows—for I too must report this to you, servant of Christ, since I know it well, having been his contemporary for a time. His appearance was rather small, misshapen, and scant-haired; he had hair only on his lip, and only a few hairs on the top of his head. Indeed, because of the immense labors of his ascetic practice, not even hairs grew upon his chin as a beard.

When I once came to this holy Macarius and was very anxious in spirit, I said to him:

“Abba Macarius, what shall I do? Thoughts afflict me, saying to me: ‘You are doing nothing; leave this place.’”

Holy Father Macarius answered me:

“Say to your thoughts: ‘For Christ’s sake I guard the walls.’”

These things, zealous and most beloved servant of Christ, I have related to you from among the many great signs and struggles of the renowned and virtuous Macarius.

This Macarius told us—for he was a presbyter—that during the distribution of the mysteries of Christ he had observed that he never gave an offering to Mark the ascetic, but that an angel gave one to him from the altar; he saw only the finger of the hand of the one who was giving it.

### Chapter XXI. The Life of Abba Mark

[Note: [Col. 1222B] “Mark.” Sozomen, book VI, chapter 29; and from him Cassiodorus, book VIII, chapter 1; and Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 35.]

When Mark was younger, he could recite the Old and New Testaments from memory, and he was remarkably gentle and supremely temperate.

One day, when I had ample leisure in my cell, I went to him in the extreme old age of his life and sat by the door of his cell. Since I was still inexperienced, I regarded him as something more than human—as indeed he was—and listened to what he might say or do.

Inside, alone, having already passed his hundredth year and lost his teeth, he was fighting with himself and with the devil. He said:

“What do you want now, κακόγηρε (*kakogēre*), that is, ‘evil old man’? Look, you have already drunk wine and touched oil. What do you want now, πολιόφαγε (*polióphage*), that is, ‘gray-haired glutton,’ and κοιλιόδουλε (*koiliódoule*), that is, ‘servant of the belly,’ disgracing and insulting yourself?”

And speaking to the devil, he said:

“Depart from me, devil. You have grown old with me in your quarrels; you have inflicted bodily weakness upon me; you have made me drink wine and take oil, making me pleasure-loving. Do I still owe you anything? You find nothing in me that you wish to plunder. Depart from me now, enemy of mankind.”

And as though challenging and provoking himself, he spoke to himself, saying:

“Come then, trifler, gray-haired glutton and old-age gourmand. How long shall I be with you?”

### Chapter XXII. The Life of Abba Moses, Who Had Been a Robber

[Note: [Col. 1222B] “Moses.” Sozomen, book VI, chapter 29; and from him Cassiodorus, *Tripartite History*, book VIII, chapter 1; Nicephorus, book XI, chapters 36 and 46. Theodoret also treats him in book IV of his *History*, chapter 21.]

There was a certain man named Moses, an Ethiopian by race and black, who was a slave of a man holding public office. Because of his wicked character and the crime of robbery, his master cast him out. He was said even to have progressed to murder. I am compelled to relate his wicked deeds so that I may afterward display the virtue of his repentance.

Some people reported that he had been the leader of a large band of robbers. Among his other acts of robbery, this is also related: he was hostile toward and intent on taking revenge against a shepherd who, as Moses was going to carry out some undertaking, had hindered him with his dogs.

When Moses wanted to kill him, he went around the place where the shepherd’s sheep were stationed, but he was informed that the shepherd himself was across the Nile. At that time the river was in flood and extended a thousand paces in width. Holding a sword in his teeth and placing over his head the tunic he was wearing, he swam across the river.

While he was swimming across, the shepherd was able to hide somewhere by burying himself. Since Moses’s attempt had not succeeded, he killed four excellent rams, tied them together with a rope, and swam across the Nile again. When he came to a small village, he skinned the rams, ate the best of the meat, and sold the skins for wine. After drinking a *saïte* equivalent to approximately eighteen Italian measures—

[Note: [Col. 1222B] “A *saïte* equivalent to approximately eighteen Italian measures.” Greek: σαΐτην ὡς Ἰταλικῶν δεκαοκτώ. See the *Onomasticon*.]

—he went fifty miles from there to the place where his band was staying.

This leader of robbers was at last moved to compunction by some misfortune that befell him and surrendered himself to a monastery. He advanced to such great repentance as his deeds themselves demonstrated.

Among other things, it is said that when four robbers broke into his cell while he was sitting there, not knowing that he was Moses, blessed Moses tied them up like a sack of straw, placed them on his shoulders, and carried them to the church of the brothers, saying:

“Since it is not permitted for me to wrong anyone, and I found these men attacking me, what do you command should be done with them?”

In this way, having been seized by holy Moses, they confessed to God. When they learned that he was Moses, who had once been a distinguished leader of robbers, they glorified Christ on this account, renounced the world themselves because of his repentance, and became excellent monks. They reasoned as follows:

“If this man, who was so powerful in strength and regarded robberies as insignificant, now fears God in this way, why do we still delay our salvation?”

After this, demons attacked blessed Moses—for thus he must be called—and drove him toward the habit of sexual intemperance. As he himself related, he was tested by them to such an extent that they came close to removing him from his purpose.

When he approached the great Isidore, who was sitting in Scetis, he reported the battle of fornication to him for the third time. The saint answered him:

“Do not be troubled, brother. These are beginnings, and for that reason they have attacked you more vehemently, seeking their former habit. Just as a dog, once accustomed to gnawing hams in a butcher’s shop, does not abandon the habit, but if the shop is closed and no one gives it anything, it dies of hunger and no longer approaches, so you too, if you persist in the discipline of your self-control, putting to death your members that are upon the earth (Colossians 3), and shutting out at the entrance gluttony, which produces intemperance, the demon will grow angry and depart from you, since he has no foods with which to kindle the passion.”

The servant of Christ Moses withdrew. From that hour he shut himself in his cell and practiced the greatest endurance in everything, especially abstinence from food, taking nothing except twelve ounces of dry bread, working very hard, and performing fifty prayers every day.

Although he had worn down his little body, he nevertheless remained inflamed, especially in dreams. When he arose, he met another holy and highly distinguished monk and said to him:

“What shall I do, abba? Dreams darken my reason, since by an old habit I take pleasure in them.”

The holy man said to him:

“You have not restrained your mind from the sights that appear in them; that is why you suffer these things. Do what I tell you. Give yourself gradually to wakefulness, and pray soberly; you will soon be freed from them.”

When the distinguished man heard this advice, as from one who was a craftsman through experience, he returned to his cell and told him—as his conscience knew—that he had not slept all night, and had not knelt under the pretext of prayer, in order to escape the tyranny of sleep.

After remaining in his cell for six years, standing in the middle of it all night, praying constantly to God and not closing his eyes, he could not conquer his intemperate desire. For desire truly cannot be chastised in this way. Although he had wasted himself away through labors, he could not subdue that shameful affection.

After this he devised another method of practicing a harsh life. This fighter against Satan—for he fought him in various ways—went out at night to the cells of monks who had grown old in ascetic labors and could no longer carry water for themselves. Without their knowledge he took their jars, filled them with water, and returned them.

In those places water is at a fixed distance: for some, two stones’ throws away; for others, five; for others, half a stone’s throw.

One night, while he was doing this, the demon who had been watching him could no longer endure the athlete’s strength. When Moses bent down into a well to fill a monk’s jar, the demon struck him in the loins with a club and left him lying there as though dead, entirely without sensation and unaware either what he had suffered or from whom.

The next day a certain monk came to draw water and found him lying there unconscious. He reported this to the great Isidore, the presbyter of Scetis. Isidore came with several others, took him, and carried him to the church.

Moses was ill for a whole year, and his body and soul scarcely recovered.

Then the great priest of Christ, Isidore, said to him:

“Cease from now on, brother Moses, to contend with the demons, and do not insult them in this way; there is also a measure of strength in ascetic practice.”

He replied:

“I will not cease fighting them until the phantasms of dreams cease for me.”

Then Isidore the presbyter, the servant of Christ, said to him:

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, from this moment your shameful dreams shall cease. Henceforth communicate in the mysteries with a good and confident spirit.”

[Note: [Col. 1222B] “Communicate in the mysteries.” There was formerly great reverence for holy communion, so that anyone who had been disturbed by pleasurable dreams would abstain from communion on that day. See *Pollution by Night* in the *Onomasticon*.]
