“For, lest you should boast that you had conquered the passion by your own discipline, it exercised its power over you so strongly for your benefit, lest you fall into pride of spirit.”

After hearing this, Moses returned to his cell and thereafter attended quietly to a moderate rule of ascetic practice.

Two or three months later, when blessed Isidore the presbyter asked the ascetic Moses whether the spirit had troubled him any further, he replied:

“From the hour when the servant of Christ prayed for me, nothing of that kind has happened to me.”

This saint had been granted grace against demons to such an extent that, just as we disregard flies in winter, so—and even more—this great Moses disregarded demons.

This is the religious and holy life led by the unconquered athlete Moses the Ethiopian, who himself was also counted among the great. He died in Scetis [the text reads *ante*; perhaps read *autem*], at the age of seventy-five, after he had become a presbyter, leaving seventy-five disciples.

### Chapter XXIII. The Life of Abba Paul

[Note: [Col. 1222B] “Paul.” Concerning him, Sozomen, book VI, chapter 29; and from him Cassiodorus, book VIII, chapter 1; Nicephorus, book XI, chapter 36; and Cassian, *Conferences*, VII, chapter 26, concerning Paul at Panephysis.]

A mountain in Egypt, leading off into the vast solitude of Scetis, is called Pherme. About five hundred men engaged in ascetic discipline dwell on this mountain. Among them was a certain Paul, an excellent monk, who practiced this life throughout his entire time. He never took up a craft or undertook any business, and never accepted anything from anyone except what he could eat that same day. His work and discipline consisted in praying continually. He had three hundred prayers specifically prescribed and appointed, and carried the same number of pebbles in his bosom, casting one pebble away at each prayer.

[Note: “Pebble.” From this the ancient use of rosary beads is also demonstrated, so that the heretics are confuted who denounce it either as a recent invention or as superstition. See the entry “Rosary” in the Onomasticon.]

When he had come to the holy Macarius called “the Political,” in order to meet him and for spiritual benefit, he said to him: “Abba Macarius, I am greatly distressed.” The servant of Christ compelled him to state the cause of his affliction. He then said to him:

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Virgin Who Prayed Seven Hundred Prayers

In a certain village there lives a virgin who has now practiced ascetic discipline for thirty years. Many have told me of her that, except on Saturday and Sunday, she eats on no other day; rather, throughout the entire period she goes on for whole weeks, eating after five days, and performs seven hundred prayers. When I learned this, I reproached myself for being a man endowed with these bodily powers, yet unable to perform more than three hundred prayers.

[Col. 1122D] The holy Macarius replies to her, saying: “It is now the sixtieth year since I began to perform one hundred appointed prayers, while laboring with my hands to obtain what is necessary for food and rendering to the brothers the service owed in fellowship; nor does my own judgment judge me to have been negligent. But if, while performing three hundred prayers, you are judged by your conscience, you plainly show that you are not praying purely, or that you are able to perform more prayers than you do.”

## CHAPTER XXV. On Cronius [Note: “Cronius.” Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 37.] the Presbyter

A certain Cronius, a presbyter of Nitria, told me—Rufinus, Book II, chapter 25, on Cronius, the disciple of Antony:

“When I was young at the beginning, and was fleeing from the monastery of my archimandrite because of anguish and sadness of spirit, wandering about I came to the mountain of Saint Antony. The blessed Antony was sitting between Babylon [Note: “Between Babylon.” Hervetus: between Babylon and Heraclea. Heraclides: between the places that bear the names Babylon and Heracles. Another ancient translator: ‘between Babylon and Heraclea.’ In chapter 72 mention is made, in Rufinus, of Ἡρακλέως Θηβαΐδος, ‘Heracles of the Thebaid,’ in the regions of Heracles.] and Heraclea, in the vast solitude that leads toward the Red Sea, about thirty miles from the river.

“When I had come to his monastery, which is near the river, where his disciples Macarius and Amatas were sitting in the place called Pisper—a place where they also buried him after he had died—I waited five days in order to meet Saint Antony. He was said to come to this monastery sometimes after ten days, sometimes after twenty, and sometimes after five, as was expedient for the benefit of those who came to the monastery.

“Various brothers had therefore assembled for various reasons. Among them was also Eulogius, an Alexandrian monk, together with another man who was maimed in his limbs; they had come for such a reason.”

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Eulogius [Note: “Eulogius.” Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 23, discusses another Eulogius.] the Alexandrian and the Man Who Was Maimed in His Limbs

728 This Eulogius was a scholar of the liberal arts—Paschasius, chapter 19, no. 3—who, wounded by divine love and longing for immortality, renounced the world’s turmoil. After distributing all his possessions, he kept only a few coins for himself, since he was unable to work. When he was inwardly troubled and sad, and neither wished to associate with others nor could persuade himself to remain alone, he found a man who was lame and mutilated, thrown down in the marketplace. He had neither hands nor feet; only his tongue remained intact, so that he could address those who came upon him.

Eulogius stood gazing fixedly at him, prayed to God, and made this covenant with God, saying: “Lord, for your name’s sake I take this mutilated man, and I promise to refresh and nourish him until the hour of his death, so that I too may be saved through him. Grant me, therefore, O Christ, patience, so that I may serve him.”

Approaching him, he said: “Do you wish me to take you into my house and refresh and nourish you?” He replied: “Would that you were willing, but I am unworthy.”

“Then,” he said, “I will go and bring a donkey, and carry you away from here.”

The mutilated man gladly agreed. Eulogius lifted him up, carried him to his lodging, and cared for him in everything he needed. For fifteen uninterrupted years the mutilated man was kindly cared for by him like a father: he was washed, anointed, warmed, and carried in Eulogius’s arms; he was kept above what his condition required, and was suitably nourished in his illness.

After fifteen years, however, a demon attacked the mutilated man, wishing to deprive Eulogius of his charge and purpose, and the mutilated man of sustenance and thanksgiving to God, and to stir up a revolt in Eulogius. The demon began to pursue him with many insults, even assailing him with curses, saying: “Go away from here, wicked fugitive.”

[Note: “Go away from here, wicked fugitive.” In Greek: σχάτα, γλούττων, φυγοκύρι. Meursius, in his Glossary, thinks that σκατογλούττων should be read here in place of σχάτα, γλούττων, meaning the same as Aristophanes’ σκατοφάγος in the *Plutus*, that is, “dung-eater.” In place of φυγοκύρι he found φαγοκύρι, which he explains as “lord glutton,” as though from φάγων κυρίως, and he thinks that it was spoken as an insult. In the *Lives of the Fathers*, Book VII, translated by Paschasius, we read: “Fugitive, who have devoured your own house”; and in the old translator of Palladius: “You have committed many evils, fugitive; perhaps you have stolen your master’s money.” Thus Paschasius, when he translates “who have devoured your own house,” seems to have read φαγοκύρι, as though κυρίων φάγος. Yet he also has the word “fugitive,” as do Hervetus and the old translator of Palladius. Therefore φυγοκύρι is the more accurate reading, as though from φυγὰς κυρίου, “you who flee from your master,” like φυγοδέμνιος, φυγοπόλεμος, and φυγαργός. Thus Plautus writes in the *Pseudolus*: “Thief, fugitive, fraud of the people, fraudulent one.” — FRONTO.]

“You have stolen other people’s money and robbed your master; and under my pretext you wish to hide, as though you had taken me into your lodging under the pretext of doing good and wished to be saved because of me.”

Eulogius, however, softened his anger, saying: “No, master, do not say such things. Instead, tell me in what way I have troubled you, and I will correct it.”

But the lame man said arrogantly: “I cannot bear these flatteries. Take me away from here and throw me into the marketplace; I reject your care.”

Eulogius said: “I beg you, permit me to care for you, and tell me if anything is burdensome to you, my lord.”

The mutilated man, becoming still more inflamed, said to him: “I can no longer endure your deceitful and ironic flattery. I do not like this frugal and sordid life. I want to eat meat.”

Patiently, Eulogius brought him meat. When the impatient man saw it, he said: “It is not enough for me merely to be with you. I want to see crowds.”

Eulogius said to him: “I will now bring a multitude of monks to you.”

But the other, again displeased, said: “Woe to me, miserable man! I cannot bear the sight of you, and you bring me others like yourself, who, though idle, eat.”

With an insolent voice, tearing at himself, he shouted: “I do not want this, I do not want this! I want to be taken to the marketplace. What violence! Throw me back where you found me.”

I say that if he had possessed hands, he would have resolved either to strangle himself or to stab himself with a sword.

When the demon had so inflamed him, Eulogius went to the neighboring monks and said to them: “What shall I do? The mutilated man has driven me to despair.”

They said to him: “Why?”

He replied: “He afflicts me grievously, and I do not know what to do. Shall I cast him away? But I have given my right hand to God, and I am afraid. Shall I not cast him away? Then he mistreats me day and night. I do not know what to do.”

They answered him decisively: “That great man”—for that is what they called Saint Antony—“is still alive. Go up to him, placing the mutilated man in a boat; carry him to the monastery, wait until the great man comes out of his cave, and refer the judgment to him. Whatever he tells you, abide by his decision. God will speak to you through him.”

Eulogius obeyed their words. He soothed the mutilated man, placed him in a small pastoral boat, left the city by night, and carried him to the monastery of the great Antony’s disciples.

It happened that on the following day the great man came late in the evening, as Cronius related, wearing a cloak of animal skin. He entered his monastery. It was his custom to address Macarius and ask him: “Brother Macarius, have any people come here?”

Macarius would answer: “They have.”

The great man would ask: “Are they Egyptians or Jerusalemites?”

The great man had given Macarius this sign: when he saw that those who had come were less occupied with business, he was to say, “They are Egyptians.” When he saw that they were more religious and somewhat more thoughtful, he was to say, “They are Jerusalemites.”

The great man therefore asked Brother Macarius as usual: “Are the brothers Egyptians or Jerusalemites?”

Macarius answered: “There is a mixture.”

Whenever Macarius said, “They are Egyptians,” the great man would say to him: “Prepare lentils for them and give them something to eat.” He would then offer one prayer for them and dismiss them.

But whenever Macarius said, “They are Jerusalemites,” the great man would sit throughout the entire night and tell them what pertained to salvation.

That evening the great man summoned everyone. Since no one had told him the scholar’s name, and it was already late in the evening, he called out: “Eulogius, Eulogius, Eulogius!” When the scholar Eulogius did not answer after he had called three times, thinking that someone else was being called by that name, the great man said to him: “I am speaking to you, Eulogius, who have come from Alexandria.”

Then Eulogius said to him: “What do you command, I pray?”

The great man said: “Why have you come here?”

Eulogius answered: “The one who revealed my name to you has also revealed the reason for which I came.”

Saint Antony said: “I have learned why you came; but tell it in the presence of the brothers, so that they too may hear.”

Commanded by the great man, Eulogius spoke before them all:

[Col. 1125B] “I found this mutilated man thrown down and neglected in the marketplace. Taking pity on him, I prayed God to grant me grace and patience toward him, and I took him in. I also gave my right hand to God that I would care for him in his illness, so that I might be saved through him and he might be refreshed by me. It has now been fifteen years since we have lived together, as everything has also been revealed to your holiness. But I do not know what evil he has suffered from me; after all these years he troubles me exceedingly, and I have resolved to cast him out, since he compels me to do so. For this reason I have come to your holiness, so that you may advise me what I ought to do and pray for me; for he afflicts me grievously.”

The great Antony said to him in a grave and stern voice: “Are you going to cast him away, Eulogius? Yet the one who created him does not cast him away. If you cast him away, God will raise up someone better than you to take him in.”

Eulogius fell silent and was afraid when he heard this.

After leaving Eulogius, the great Antony began to scourge the mutilated man with his tongue and to cry out at him: “Mutilated one, defiled one!”

[Note: “Mutilated one, defiled one.” In Greek, λελωβημένε, πεπηλωμένε. In the passage cited above, Book VII, chapter 19, no. 3, Paschasius has: “Elephantine, horrible with filth and mud.” The old translator of Palladius has: “Leprous one, hardened in days of evil.” Since Paschasius translates it as “horrible with filth and mud,” he appears to have read πεπηλωμένε, from πηλὸς, “mud,” or something similar. Certainly πηλούμενος means “muddy,” “covered with mud.” The Venetian manuscript reads λελωβημένον καὶ πεπηρωμένον, “mutilated and maimed”; at the beginning of this chapter it calls him λελωβημένον, ὅς οὔτε χεῖρας εἶχεν, οὔτε πόδας, “mutilated, who had neither hands nor feet.” Such a person is called Κυλλὸς by Suidas. Suidas: κυλλὸς, ὁ πεπηρωμένος, οὐ μόνον πόδα, ἀλλὰ καὶ χεῖρα, “Cyllus: one who is maimed not only in foot but also in hand.” Fronto says that πεπηρωμένε, as in the epigram, ὁ μὲν γυίοις πηρὸς, means “crippled and mutilated in the limbs.” In Herodotus, a person is said ἑαυτὸν λωβᾶσθαι λώβην ἀνάκεστον, “to mutilate his own face so as to disfigure it.” Thus it is not necessary to suspect elephantiasis here, although Heraclides, chapter 32, translates Λελωβημένοις as “those suffering from elephantiasis.”]

“Unworthy of earth and heaven, do you not cease fighting with God and provoking your brother? Do you not know that it is Christ who ministers to you? How dare you speak such things against Christ? Has he not enslaved himself to your service for Christ’s sake?”

After restraining him with these reproachful words, he dismissed them. Having discussed with the brothers what was necessary for each of them, he again approached Eulogius and the mutilated man and said to them:

“Do not remain anywhere, brothers, but go away in peace. Do not separate from one another, having laid aside all the distress that the demon has inflicted upon you, and return with good affection to the cell in which you have lived for so long. God will now come to you. This temptation has been stirred up against you by Satan because he knows that you have already reached the end and are about to receive crowns from Christ—him through you, and you through him. Therefore think of nothing else. If the angel comes and does not find you in the same place, you will be deprived of your crowns. So hurry quickly.”

They entered at once and returned to their cell in perfect love.

[Note: “In love.” The Latin Fathers call *agapae* certain Christian banquets at which they received the poor, as the translator Hervetus noted here; therefore he had translated the phrase, “and they returned to their cell at the end of the agape.” Heraclides, however, saw that love was rather indicated here, translating in chapter 9, “with peace restored”; Paschasius likewise, in chapter 19. Thus Antony had said shortly before: Καὶ μετὰ καθαρᾶς ἀγάπης ὑποστρέψατε, “and return with good affection,” as in 1 John 4:18: Ἡ τελεία ἀγάπη ἔξω βάλλει τὸν φόβον, “Perfect love casts out fear.” — FRONTO.]

Within forty days the blessed Eulogius died and departed to the Lord. Within three further days the man who was mutilated in body but firm and strong in soul also died; he too commended his spirit into the hands of God.

When Cronius had spent some time in the regions around the Thebaid, he descended to the monastery in Alexandria. It happened that the brotherhood was celebrating the fortieth day after the death of the blessed Eulogius, while it was the third day after the death of the mutilated man. When Cronius learned this, he was astonished. He took the Gospel, placed it in the midst of the brothers so that those who heard might believe, and swore to them as he related the great Antony’s foreknowledge of these events and everything that had happened. He said:

“I was the interpreter of these words, since the blessed Antony did not know Greek, while I knew both languages. By the grace of Christ I interpreted for the blessed Eulogius and the mutilated man in Greek what had been spoken by the great man; and for the holy, blessed, and great Antony I interpreted in Egyptian what had been said by each of them.”

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Vision Seen by Abba Antony

Cronius also related that Antony had told them that night:

“I had prayed for an entire year that the dwelling-place of the righteous and of sinners might be revealed to me—see above, Book I, in the *Life of Saint Antony*, chapter 38; Paschasius, chapter 19, no. 4.

“I saw an exceedingly tall black giant who reached as far as the clouds. His hands were stretched out as far as heaven. Beneath him was a lake equal in size to the sea. I also saw souls flying upward like birds. Those that flew above his hands and head were guarded by angels, but those that were struck by his hands fell into the lake.

“A voice then came to me, saying: ‘The souls you see flying above the giant’s head and his hands are the souls of the righteous, who are guarded by angels in paradise. Those struck by the black one’s hands are plunged into hell. They were drawn by the desire of the flesh and followed hatred and the desire to repay injury.’”

## CHAPTER XXVIII. The Life of Abba Paul the Simple

[Note: “Paul the Simple.” On him, Sozomen, Book I, chapter 13; and from him Cassiodorus, Book I of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 11; Nicephorus, Book VIII, chapter 40.]

The servant of Christ Hierax, Cronius, and many other brothers related what I am about to say—Rufinus, Book II, chapter 31:

A certain Paul, a rustic farmer, remarkably innocent and simple in character, had married a very beautiful woman who was wicked in character. She had sinned for a very long time without his knowledge. One day, returning unexpectedly from the field and entering his house, he found them committing an indecent act; Providence was leading Paul toward what was beneficial for him.

When he saw her with the man with whom she was accustomed to commit adultery, he laughed honorably and decently and shouted to them: “Good, good; truly, I do not care. By Jesus, I will not take her back again. Go, keep her and her children. I am leaving and becoming a monk.”

Without telling anyone anything, he crossed eight stopping-places.

[Note: “He crossed eight stopping-places.” Ὀκτὼ μονάς. This ought to be translated here in this way, not as Hervetus has it, “eight monasteries.” See the *Onomasticon*.]

He went to Saint Antony and knocked at the door. Saint Antony came out and asked him: “What do you want?”

Paul replied: “I want to become a monk.”

Antony answered him: “A sixty-year-old man cannot become a monk here. Rather, go to the village, work, and live a working life, giving thanks to God. You cannot endure the afflictions of solitude.”

The old man replied: “Whatever you teach me, I will do.”

Antony said to him: “I told you that you are old and cannot be a monk. Go away. If you want to be a monk, enter a coenobium where there are many brothers who can bear with your weakness. I sit here alone, eating only after an interval of five days—and then while hungry.”

With these words he drove Paul away. But after he had refused to admit him, Antony closed the door and did not go outside for three days, not even to attend to his necessities, because of him. The old man remained and did not leave.

On the fourth day, when necessity pressed him, Antony opened the door and came out. Seeing Paul again, he said to him: “Go away from here, old man. Why are you troubling me? You cannot remain here.”

Paul said to him: “It is impossible for me to die anywhere but here.”

When Antony looked at him and saw that he had none of the necessities of life—not bread, water, or anything else—and that he had persisted in fasting for four days, he thought to himself: “Perhaps he will die, since he is not accustomed to fasting, and he will stain my soul.”

He therefore admitted him. Then Antony said to him: “You can be saved if you have obedience and do whatever you hear from me.”

Paul replied: “I will do whatever you command.”

Antony then imposed upon him the discipline of the austere life that he himself had practiced in the early days of his youth.

Testing Paul’s mind, Antony said to him: “Stand here and pray until I enter and bring you something to work on.”

He entered the cave and through a window observed him remaining motionless in that place for an entire week, while he was scorched by the heat. After a week he came out, wetted branches of palm, and said to him: “Take these and weave a rope as you see me do.”

The old man wove until the ninth hour, fifteen cubits, with great labor. When Antony saw what he had woven, it did not please him at all, and he said to him: “You have woven it badly. Undo it and weave it again.” He was now in his seventh day of fasting, and was advanced in years. Antony afflicted him so greatly over this matter that the old man, distressed, fled from Antony and from the monastic life.

But Paul undid the same branches and wove them again with great labor, since they had become wrinkled from the first weaving. When the great Antony saw that he had neither complained nor lost heart, that he had not turned his face away at all, and that he had not become even slightly angry, he was moved with compassion for him.

At sunset he said to him: “Little father, would you like us to eat a piece of bread?”

Paul replied: “As you think best, abba.”

This too moved Antony, because Paul had not immediately rushed forward at the mention of food but had left the decision to him.

“Prepare the table, then,” Antony said.

Paul obeyed. Antony brought bread and placed four *paxamates* on the table, of six ounces. He soaked one for himself, since they were dry, and three for Paul. Antony sang a psalm that he knew; after singing it twelve times, he prayed twelve times, in order to test Paul in this matter as well.

The old man prayed at the same time more readily and eagerly than the great Antony. For, as I think, he preferred feeding scorpions to living even one day with an adulterous woman.

After twelve prayers the great Antony said to Paul: “Sit down, and do not eat until evening; attend only to the food.”

When evening came and Paul had not eaten, Antony said to him: “Rise, pray, and sleep.”

Paul left the table and did so. In the middle of the night Antony awakened him for prayer and continued the prayers until the ninth hour. When the table had again been set, and Antony had again sung and prayed, they sat down to eat late in the evening.

The great Antony ate one *paxamas* and did not touch another. The old man, eating slowly, still held the piece he had begun. Antony waited until he had finished, and then said to him: “Eat, little father, one more piece.”

Paul replied: “If you eat, I too will eat; but if you do not eat, neither will I.”

Antony said: “For me it is enough, since I am a monk.”

Paul replied: “For me too it is enough, for I also want to become a monk.”

He rose again, performed twelve prayers, and sang twelve psalms. After the prayers, they slept a little during the first sleep, and again awoke to sing psalms from midnight until daybreak.

Then Antony sent him to go through the solitude, saying: “Come here after three days.”

When this had happened and certain brothers came to him, Paul watched Antony to see what he wanted him to do. Antony said to him: “Serve the brothers in silence, and taste nothing until the brothers have set out on their journey.”

After Paul had gone three full weeks without eating, the brothers asked him: “Why are you silent?”

When he did not answer, Antony said to him: “Why are you silent? Speak with the brothers.”

He then spoke with them.

On one occasion, when a jar of honey had been brought to him, Antony said: “Break the vessel and let the honey spill out.”

Paul did so. Antony then said to him: “Gather the honey again with a shell, taking care not to introduce any dirt.”

Again he ordered him to draw water throughout the entire day. Again, after loosening his clothing, he ordered him to sew it.

This man possessed such great obedience that divine grace was also granted him, namely, the power to cast out demons.

When the great Antony saw that the old man readily followed everything in the practice of the ascetic life, he said to him: “See, brother, if you can continue this way day by day, remain with me.”

Paul replied: “I do not know whether you can show me anything more. For whatever I have seen you do, I also do easily and without labor, with God’s help.”

The next day Antony said to him: “In the name of Jesus, behold, you have become a monk.”

When the great and blessed Antony had sufficiently and abundantly discovered in all things that the servant of Christ was an exceedingly perfect soul, being entirely simple, then, after certain months, with the grace of God assisting through the blessed Antony, he built a cell for him three or four stone-throws from his own cell.

He said to him: “Behold, with the power of Christ assisting you, you have become a monk. Henceforth remain apart, so that you may also test yourself against the demons.”

When Paul the Simple had lived by himself for one year, he was granted grace against demons and every kind of illness, and conducted himself perfectly in the practice of virtue.

One day a young man who was being tormented exceedingly severely by a demon was brought to the blessed Antony. He was possessed by a chief demon, exceedingly savage.

[Note: “Having a chief and exceedingly savage demon.” See our Serrarius on Tobit, part I, question 5, concerning the manner in which some demons are called chief demons.]

This demon even pursued heaven itself with curses and insults. When the great Antony had observed the young man, he said to those who were leading him:

“This is not my work. For against this order of demons, namely, a chief demon, I have not yet been granted grace. This is the grace of Paul the Simple.”

The great Antony therefore went to the proven Paul and led the men to him as well. He said to him: “Abba Paul, cast this demon out of the man, so that he may return home healed and glorify the Lord.”

Paul said to him: “What about you?”

Antony replied: “I have no time; there is something else I must do.”

Leaving the boy there, the great Antony returned to his cell.

The innocent old man rose, poured out an effective prayer, and said, challenging the demoniac: “Abba Antony has said, ‘Come out of the man.’”

The demon cried out with insults and curses, saying: “I will not come out, old glutton, old fool.”

[Note: “Old glutton, old fool.” In the Paris Greek manuscript: φαγόγηρε, “old glutton.” But in my Greek manuscripts: κακόγηρε, “wicked old man.” So also above, chapter 21. See the *Onomasticon*.]

Taking his sheepskin, Paul beat the demon on the back, saying: “Come out, Abba Antony has said.”

The demon pursued Paul and Antony with curses:

“These gluttons in their old age!”

[Note: “These gluttons in their old age.” In Greek: πολιοφάγοι οὗτοι. See the *Onomasticon*.]

“Senile, insatiable men, who are never content with what belongs to them—what have you in common with us? Why do you exercise tyranny against us?”

Finally Paul said to him: “Either you will come out, or I will go and tell Christ, and he will make it woe for you.”

But that savage demon also pursued Jesus with insults and curses, shouting: “I will not come out.”

For this reason Paul became indignant with the demon, left his lodging at the very hour of noon, and went out into the heat; the heat of Egypt is akin to a Babylonian furnace.

Standing like a pillar upon a rock, the holy old man prayed to Christ in this way:

“You see, Jesus Christ, who were crucified under Pontius Pilate, that I will not come down from this rock, nor eat or drink until I die, unless you hear me now, cast this demon out of the man, and free him from the unclean spirit.”

While the simple and humble Paul was still speaking with Jesus, before he had finished his prayer, the demon cried out, saying:

“I am leaving, I am leaving! By force I am coming out; I am being expelled by tyranny. I am leaving the man and will no longer approach him. Paul’s simplicity and humility drive me out, and I do not know where I shall go.”

Immediately the demon came out and changed into a very large dragon, about seventy cubits long. It withdrew, crawling, into the Red Sea, so that what had been spoken through the Holy Spirit might be fulfilled:

“The righteous man will proclaim the faith that is demonstrated” (Proverbs 12).

And again elsewhere:

“Upon whom shall I look,” says the Lord, “except upon the meek and humble and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66).

For lesser demons are usually cast out from human beings by those who have chief faith, while chief demons are in turn driven away by the humble.

These are the miracles of Saint Paul, the Simple and Humble, along with many others, greater than these. He was called “Simple” by the entire brotherhood.

## CHAPTER XXIX. The Life of Abba Pachon

[Note: “Pachon.” On him, Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 29; and from him Cassiodorus, Book VIII of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 1; Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 36; Vincent, *Speculum historiale*, Book XVII, chapter 79; Antonius, part II, title 15, chapter 11. Cassiodorus, Heraclides, Vincent, and Antoninus call him Pachomius, but he should be read as Pachonius, from Pachon. P. Maturius notes this in our edition of Antoninus, where he cites Cassiodorus’s passage concerning Pachomius of Tabennesi; Palladius discusses him below, in chapter 38.]

A certain man named Pachon, when he had reached the age of seventy, was sitting in Scetis. It happened that I was suffering from the affliction of sexual desire, together with thoughts and nocturnal visions, and was finding it difficult to endure. Since I was nearly ready to leave the desert because of this temptation—for this disturbance of mind was driving me with the greatest force—I did not disclose the matter to my neighbors, nor even to my teacher Evagrius [Al.: Eulogius]. Instead, I secretly came into the desert and spent fifteen days with the aging fathers who were in Scetis. Among them I encountered the holy man Pachon.

When I found that he was more candid and more experienced in ascetic discipline, I dared to open my heart to him. The holy man said to me:

“Do not think that this is something strange and foreign. This has not happened to you because of luxury, idleness, or negligence. Your conduct bears witness to that, as does your lack of the necessities of life, and the fact that you have no association here with women [Col. 1130C]. Rather, this has happened to you from the adversary because of your devotion to virtue.

“For there is a threefold enemy who drives us toward fornication. Sometimes the flesh attacks us when it is luxuriant and has been excessively well fed and delicately cared for. Sometimes the movements of the mind rise up against us because of our thoughts. Sometimes the demon himself exercises tyranny over us out of envy. For I too, after making many observations, discovered this.

“Look at me, as you see me, an old man. I have now spent forty years in this cell, caring for my salvation, and have reached this age, yet I am still tempted to this very day. And he swore, saying: ‘For twelve years now, after I had completed my fiftieth year, he has not let a single day or night pass without attacking me.’ [Col. 1130D]

“When, therefore, I suspected that God had withdrawn from me, since the demon was using such power against me, I chose rather to die senselessly than to conduct myself disgracefully through the fault and affection of the body. I left my cell and wandered through the desert, where I found a hyena’s den. I entered that den naked and remained there the whole day, so that when the beasts came out they might devour me.

“When evening came, as it is written, ‘The sun knew its setting. You appointed darkness, and it became night. In it all the beasts of the forest will pass through. The young lions roaring, that they may seize and seek their food from God’ (Psalm 103). The beasts therefore came out at that hour, male and female, and, beginning at my feet and proceeding up to my head, they sniffed me and licked me all around. As I waited to be devoured [Col. 1131A], they withdrew from me.

“After I had lain there the whole night, I had not been devoured. Believing, therefore, that God had altogether spared me, I arose and returned again to my cell.

“When the demon had held back for a few days, he attacked me more violently than before, so that I came very near blaspheming. For he was transformed into an Ethiopian girl whom I had seen in my youth gathering ears of grain in the summer. She appeared to me sitting on my knees, and moved me so greatly that I thought I had intercourse with her. Driven by rage, I struck her with a slap; and she vanished.

“But believe me when I say this: for two years I could not endure the stench of my hand. When, because of this, I had escaped with a small and abject spirit and had abandoned all hope in myself, I went out wandering through the vast desert [Col. 1131B] and found a small asp. When I had picked it up, I brought it to my genitals, intending to die by its bite. I even placed its head against my male members—the very things that had been the cause of my temptation—but, by the gracious providence of God, I was not bitten even then.

“After this I heard a voice saying to me in my thoughts: ‘Go, Pachon, fight! For this is why I allowed such power to be exercised against you: so that your spirit might not become more exalted and arrogant, as though you yourself could overcome this passion; but so that you might recognize your weakness and never place confidence in the discipline of your life, but flee to God’s assistance.’

“Thus admonished and strengthened, I returned to my cell. From then on I sat there confidently, taking no further account of the battle, and spent the rest of my days in peace [Col. 1131C]. When the demon realized that I despised him, he was thereafter put to shame and did not approach me again.”

With these words he had strengthened me for the struggle against Satan, equipped me for battle, and prepared and instructed me against the demon of fornication. He dismissed me, commanding me to conduct myself courageously in all things.

## CHAPTER XXX. The Life of Abbot Stephen

[Note: Stephen. Concerning him, Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 29; and from him Cassiodorus, Book VIII of the Tripartite History, chapter 1; Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 36.]

A certain Stephen, a Libyan by birth, lived for sixty years beside [Note: Beside. Hervetus: “across from.” It should rather be written “beside Marmarica,” or “not far from Marmarica.” Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 22, has περὶ τὸν Μαρεώτην οὐκ ἄποθεν τῆς Μαρμαρικῆς, “around Mareotis, not far from Marmarica” [Col. 1131D]. Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 36, has περὶ τὸν Μαρεώτην οὐ πολλῷ τῆς Μαρμαρικῆς ἄποθεν, “around Mareotis, not far from Marmarica.” Compare Deuteronomy 31:26: Θήσετε αὐτὸ ἐκ πλαγίων τῆς κιβωτοῦ, “Place it beside the ark of the Lord.” And 1 Kings 20:24: Ἐκάθισεν Ἀβεννὴρ ἐκ πλαγίων Σαούλ, “Abner sat beside Saul.” So also below, chapter 35: Ἐκ πλαγίων τοῦ μοναστηρίου, “beside the monastery.” FRONTO.] Marmarica and Mareotis.

Since he had been thoroughly practiced in ascetic discipline and had been endowed with the power of discernment, he received this grace: whoever came to him, no matter what affliction troubled him, departed from him free of that affliction.

He too was known to blessed Antony. He even survived into our own times. I myself, however, did not associate with him because of the length of the journey. But the holy Ammonius and Evagrius, who had visited him, told us that they found him in those very regions fallen into a severe illness of the testicles and penis, where a very serious cancer had ulcerated him—a cancer called φαγέδαινα, “eating ulcer.”

They said: “We found him being treated by a physician. With his hands he was working, weaving palm branches, and speaking with us, while a surgeon was operating on the rest of his body. Yet by the grace of God he possessed such patience that he seemed to be affected as though another person’s body were being cut. When his limbs were cut away, he remained as unmoved as if they were insensible hairs. So remarkably and wonderfully had God equipped him.”

“When we were partly distressed and partly terrified,” they continued, “that the life of so great a man had fallen into such a disease and such operations by physicians, and when blessed Stephen perceived our thoughts, he said to us:

“‘Do not be offended by this, my sons. Nothing that God does is ever done for evil, but for a good end. Perhaps the limbs deserved punishment, and it is better for them to suffer their penalties here than after their departure from this arena.’

“Having thus encouraged us and strengthened us by his words for endurance, he edified us for bearing afflictions courageously.”

I have related this so that it may not seem strange to us when we see some holy people fall into such calamities.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning Valens

[Note: Valens. Nothing concerning him occurs to me at present.]

There was a certain Valens, a Palestinian by birth but a Corinthian in mind; for the holy Paul attributes the vice of conceit to the Corinthians, saying: “And you are puffed up” (1 Corinthians 5).

When he came into the desert, he too lived with us for many years. He advanced so far in pride that he was deceived by demons. As he was gradually deceived, he came to think magnificently and gloriously of himself, as though angels associated with him and served him in every ministry.

One day, as they related, while he was working in the darkness, he dropped the needle with which he used to make a basket. When he himself could not find it, the demon made a lamp for him, and he found the needle. Inflated again by this event, he adopted an exalted opinion of himself and became so uplifted that he even despised communion in the Sacraments.

When Christ the Lord took pity on him, he arranged matters so that his downfall would quickly become evident to the whole brotherhood. Some visitors arrived and brought delicacies into the church for the brotherhood. Our priest, the holy Macarius, received them and sent about a handful to each person in his cell, including Valens.

When Valens received his portion, he insulted and struck the man who had brought it, saying to him: “Go and tell Macarius: ‘I am not inferior to you, so that you should send me blessings.’”

When the holy Macarius realized that he had been deceived, he came to him one day afterward to exhort him. He said to him: “Valens, you have been deceived. Stop and pray to God.”

But when he did not heed his admonitions, Macarius withdrew, greatly distressed and grieving over Valens’s ruin.

When the demon became fully convinced that Valens had placed the greatest confidence in his deception, he departed, assumed the form of the Savior, and came by night in a phantasm, with a thousand angels holding lamps and with a fiery wheel in which the figure of the Savior appeared to be represented.

One angel went before him and said: “Christ has loved your discipline, your freedom of life, and your confidence, and he has come to see you. Come out of your cell, and do nothing else except, when you see him from a distance, fall down and worship him; then enter your cell.”

When Valens came out and saw the display of lamps, he worshiped the Antichrist from about a stadium away.

On another day his mind was so disturbed that he entered the church and, with the brotherhood assembled, said: “I have no need of communion, for today I have seen Christ.”

The Fathers then bound him for a year, put him in iron chains, and treated him—by prayers, contempt, and a harsher way of life—by taking away his delusion. For, as the saying goes, opposite things are cured by opposite remedies.

It is necessary to insert in this book the lives of those who are such, for the security of those who read, just as the tree of paradise—the knowledge of good and evil—was added to the holy plants (Genesis 2). Thus, if at some time they happen to conduct themselves rightly in some matter, they will not become puffed up or boast of their virtue.

For virtue itself often becomes an occasion of falling when it is not performed with the right aim. For it is written: “I saw the righteous man perishing in his righteousness” (Ecclesiastes 7). This too is vanity.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning Heron

[Note: Heron. Cassian, Conference V, chapter 2, mentions an old man named Heron who threw himself into a well; he seems to be different from this Heron.]

There was a certain man named Heron, my neighbor, an Alexandrian by birth, a cultivated young man, of good natural ability and pure life. After great labors and distinguished exertions, he too was seized by arrogance and conceit, fell headlong, and became proud and insolent toward the Fathers. He even insulted blessed Evagrius [Al.: also the priest Macarius], saying:

“Those who obey your teaching are deceived. One ought to pay attention to no teachers other than Christ.”

He also misused a scriptural testimony to support the perverse aim of his folly, saying: “Do not call anyone teacher on earth” (Matthew 23).

His mind was so darkened by the empty persuasion of his own opinion that he was even bound in iron when he refused to come to the Sacraments.

Yet truth is friendly. His way of life had been extremely strict and exact, so that many who had associated with him say that he often ate only after three months, content with communion in the Sacraments and with whatever wild vegetable might appear to him.

I too experienced his way of life with blessed Albinus when I was going to Scetis. Scetis was forty miles from us. During those forty miles we ate twice and drank water three times. But he, although he had tasted nothing and was walking on foot, recited from memory fifteen psalms, then the great psalm, then the Epistle to the Hebrews, then Isaiah, then part of the prophecies of Jeremiah, then Luke the Evangelist, and then Proverbs. We could not keep up with him as he walked.

Finally, seized by the activity of an evil demon, so that he seemed to be driven by an exceedingly fierce fire, he could not remain seated in his cell. He went to Alexandria and, by a certain divine dispensation, drove out one nail with another.

For he fell of his own accord into the promiscuous and indiscriminate use of things, and afterward found salvation involuntarily. He went to the theaters and the horse races and frequented taverns. Since he was devoted to gluttony and drunkenness, he fell into the mire of sexual desire. Having decided to sin, he spoke constantly with a certain actress and exposed his ulcer.

While these things were happening, by a certain divine dispensation a carbuncle arose on his glans. For six months he suffered so severely that his male members rotted and fell off of their own accord.

Afterward, when he recovered, he returned to the perception of divine things and came into the desert, confessing all these matters to the Fathers. But before he had attained the practice of virtue, he fell asleep a few days later.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning Ptolemy, Who Fell Away

Another man, again, named Ptolemy, after having spent a life difficult to relate—or rather impossible to relate—initially lived beyond Scetis in the place called Κλίμαξ, that is, “stairway.”

It is a place so called in which no one can live, because the nearest well of water is eighteen miles away. He therefore carried many earthen vessels, collected dew in December and January—for there is a great deal of dew in those regions—and squeezed it from the stones with a sponge. He continued living there for fifteen years.

Separated from the teaching, association, benefit, and continual communion of holy men, he departed so far from the right path that he too confessed what some impious people say: that everything happens by chance. The demon of error then gained power over him.

For this enemy suggested to the foolish man that he should say that things have no essence, but that everything exists simply because the world moves of its own accord. The enemy of all life implanted these thoughts in his soul, saying:

“If matters are so, why do you uselessly discipline yourself outside? What will help you, Ptolemy, if there is no reward? What reward would be sufficient for you for so many and such great labors, even if there were someone to repay you? What judgment is there in the threats of Scripture if there is no providence?”

Surrounded by these satanic thoughts, the wretched Ptolemy is said to have become deranged and to wander through Egypt to this day. He has surrendered himself to gluttony and drunkenness, associating with no one, but silently going about the marketplace—a pitiable and tearful spectacle to Christian eyes, but a laughingstock to those who do not know our way of life.

This incurable calamity overtook the miserable Ptolemy because of a certain arrogant ignorance of reason. Deceived by the seducing demon, he believed that he possessed knowledge superior to that of all the holy Fathers. Inflated by this belief, he became his own enemy and was hurled headlong into the depths of destruction. He had never visited any of the holy Fathers who had wisely governed their lives, nor had he been grounded in their spiritual teaching. Found without a guide, he fell into the ultimate depth of death. Like a tree covered with green leaves and adorned with fruits that in a single moment was stripped bare of everything and made dry, so was he.

For, as it is written: “Those who have no guidance fall like leaves” (Proverbs 11).

## CHAPTER XXXV. Concerning a Fallen Virgin

I also knew a certain virgin in Jerusalem who wore a hair shirt for six years and was enclosed. She accepted none of the things that lead to pleasure, but practiced the strictest continence among women.

Afterward, however, she was abandoned by divine assistance because of the extreme pride that is the nurse of all evils. She fell, opened the window, admitted the man who served her, and had intercourse with him. She had not practiced discipline with divine purpose and out of charity, but in order to serve the human stage—something that belongs to vainglory and a corrupt way of life.

For while her pious thoughts were occupied in condemning others, and she was stirred to rage by the demon of pride and took great pleasure in it, the holy guardian angel of temperance withdrew from her.

For this reason, most faithful man, we have written both the lives of those who conducted themselves rightly and virtuously and those who, after many labors, fell through idleness and negligence from the highest and most perfect way of life, captured by the devil through every kind of snare. Thus each person, by understanding from their way of life the hidden nets of the enemy of good things, may flee his snares.

Although there are many—and they are great men and women—who conducted themselves rightly from the beginning in an honorable ascetic discipline but were finally overthrown by the adversary of all human beings, I shall pass over most of them in silence after mentioning a few. I do this so that I may neither raise them up nor benefit myself by dwelling at length on them while neglecting the outstanding athletes of Christ and failing to relate the virtues of their divine discipline.

## CHAPTER XXXV. The Life of Abbot Elias

A certain Elias was an excellent ascetic and greatly devoted to virgins, caring for the weaker sex. There are indeed such souls, whose end bears witness that they do this out of virtue.

Because he pitied the order of women who practiced ascetic discipline, and possessed property in the city of Athribis [Al.: Athlebe], he built a large monastery there. He gathered all the wandering virgins into it and thereafter cared for them in every respect, supplying everything necessary for their use: gardens and the tools for cultivating them [Note: Tools for cultivating them. The Greek has Κήπους, καὶ τὰ τούτων χρηστήρια. Hervetus translated this as “gardens and their oracles,” but not only are oracles called μαντεῖα, while τὰ χρηστήρια may mean the places where oracles are given; τὰ χρηστήρια σκεύη also means utensils, in Pollux τὰ ἔπιπλα. Therefore Heraclides here published “little gardens and also the necessary tools of various equipment.” FRONTO.], and, to put it briefly, everything required by the ascetic life.

They had been drawn from different ways of life and private associations, and they were constantly fighting among themselves. Since this holy man had to listen both to them and to bring about peace among them—for he had gathered nearly three hundred, and it was necessary for him to act as their mediator for two years, although he was young in age, being about thirty or forty years old—he was tempted by sexual desire.

Leaving the monastery fasting, he wandered through the desert for two days, praying and saying:

“Either kill me, so that in my distress I may not see them, or remove my passion [the text reads *auter*, evidently corrupt], so that I may care for them as duty requires.”

When evening came, sleep overcame him in the desert. Three angels came to him, as he himself related, and, restraining him, said:

“Why did you leave the monastery of women?”

He told them the matter, saying: “I was afraid that I would harm both them and myself.”

The angels said to him: “If, therefore, we free you from this passion, will you return and care for them?”

He agreed. They required an oath from him; he related the oath:

“Swear this oath to us: ‘By him who cares for me, I will care for them.’”

He swore this to them.

Then the angels restrained him: one held his hands, another his feet, and the third, taking a razor, cut off his testicles as though in an ecstasy—not in reality, but in a certain vision.

Thus, in that ecstasy, he appeared to have been castrated and healed. After this the angels asked him:

“Have you felt any benefit?”

He said to them: “I have received a very great benefit. I have been greatly relieved, and I am convinced that I have been freed from the labor and the passion.”

Then the angels said to him: “Go, therefore, to your monastery.”

He returned after five days, while the whole monastery mourned him, and entered inside. From that time onward he remained in a cell beside the monastery [printed: *ad lactus* (sic)], since, being nearby, he continually corrected them as far as he was able.

After he had lived another forty years, he affirmed to the Fathers that from that time the passion of sexual desire had never risen into his heart.

This is the grace of the holy man Elias, his discipline, and the manner in which he cared for the monastery of virgins.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. The Life of Abbot Dorotheus

Dorotheus, a most approved man, succeeded him. He grew old in the good life and in the practice of virtuous action.

Although he could not care for the monastery in the same way as this blessed man, nor remain in that cell, he enclosed himself in an upper room within the monastery and made a window that looked toward the women’s monastery. He opened and closed it.

He therefore sat constantly at the window, ensuring that quarrels among them ceased. Thus he grew old in the upper room, since no one could ascend separately and he could not descend; for there were no stairs.

This was the religious and virtue-adorned life of blessed Dorotheus. Here was the end of that life.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Concerning Amma Piamun

A certain virgin named Piamun lived out the years of her life with her own mother, the two of them eating supper alone together and spinning flax. She was deemed worthy among human beings of the grace of foretelling the future.

Once in Egypt, when the Nile was rising, it happened that one village attacked another. They were fighting over the division of the water, so that killings and wounding followed.

The more powerful village therefore attacked her village. A multitude of men came with spears and nails to destroy it.

An angel appeared to this blessed woman, revealing their invasion. She summoned the priests of the village and said to them:

“Go out and meet those who are coming against you from this village, lest you too perish together with the village; and beg them to desist from the ambush they have prepared against you.”

The priests were terrified, fell at her feet, and begged her, saying:

“We do not dare to go out to meet them. We know their drunkenness and insolence. But if you will show mercy to us, to the whole village, and to your own household, go out to meet them yourself and turn them away in peace.”

She did not consent. She went into her little house, stood praying all night, and did not bend her knee at all, but prayed, saying:

“Lord who judge the earth, to whom nothing unjust is pleasing, when this prayer has come before you, may your power make them stand motionless like a pillar wherever it finds them.”

When this holy virgin had prayed in this manner, the following thing happened. At about the first hour, the enemies, three miles away, were fixed in place like a pillar and could not be moved.

It was also revealed to them that they had been hindered through the intercessions of Piamun, Christ’s servant. They therefore sent to the village asking for peace, saying:

“Give thanks to God and to the prayers of Piamun, which have hindered us from inflicting great harm upon you.”

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. The Life of Abbot Pachomius and of Those Who Were with Him

[Note: Pachomius. Concerning him, see the authors cited in Book I, in his Life.]

Tabennesis [Note: Tabennesis. In Greek Ταβεννήσιος, from Tabenna. See the Onomasticon.] is a place so called in the Thebaid. Pachomius the monk lived there, a man belonging to those who pursued the highest and most perfect way of life. He was even deemed worthy of predictions of future events and angelic visions.

He was greatly devoted to the poor and possessed great charity toward human beings.

As he was sitting in this cave, an angel of the Lord appeared to him and said:

“Pachomius, you have conducted yourself rightly and virtuously in what concerns you. You are therefore sitting here needlessly. Rise, go out, gather all the younger monks, live with them, and establish laws for them according to the form I will give you.”

He gave him a bronze tablet on which the following had been written:

“Allow each person to eat and drink according to the capacity of those who eat. Assign them also tasks that are proportionate and appropriate to them. Do not forbid them either to fast or to eat.

“Assign difficult tasks to the strong, but weak and light tasks to those who practice more intensely and are weaker.

“Make different cells in the same courtyard, and let three remain in each cell. Let food be prepared for everyone in one house.

“Let them sleep not lying down, but sitting on seats they have built for themselves, somewhat inclined backward, and let them sleep there seated, with their bedding placed upon them.

“At night let them wear linen tunics, girded up. Each of them shall have a worked white sheepskin; without it they shall neither eat nor sleep.

“When they enter for communion with Christ on Saturday and Sunday, let them loosen their belts, remove the sheepskin, and enter wearing only the hood.

“He made hoods for them without wool [Note: Without wool. In Greek, the Paris edition has ἄμαλλα, and so too Heraclides’s translator read it, translating ‘without wool.’ Hervetus translated it as ‘soft,’ as though he had read ἀπαλά, which appears in the Excerpts from the Augustan Codex; Hesychius explains ἀμαλόν as ‘soft.’ The Venetian edition had ἀμαλλαιῶς; but read ἅμαλλα ὡς.], like children’s hoods. On them he also commanded that a purple cross be placed.

“He commanded that there be twenty-four ranks of brothers, corresponding to the number of the twenty-four letters. He ordered each rank to be given the name of a Greek letter, beginning with α and β and proceeding through ω. Thus, when the archimandrite asks about someone among such a great multitude, he may inquire of the man who belongs to the second rank after him how the α-rank is doing, or how the β-rank is doing.

“Again, greet the ρ-rank, following a certain characteristic naming of the letters. Give the simple and sincere the name ι; give the more difficult the name ξ. In this way, according to their discipline, life, and character, assign to each rank the appropriate letter, with only the spiritually discerning understanding what is signified.

“It was also written on the tablet:

“‘If a guest from another monastery comes, one that has a different form of life, he shall neither eat nor drink with them, nor enter the monastery, unless he is found on the road.

“‘If someone enters once but cannot endure the contest with them for three years, do not admit him. Only after he has performed the more difficult tasks may he enter the arena after three years.

“‘When they eat, let them cover their heads with their hoods, so that brother may not see brother chewing. The one who is eating may not speak, nor turn his eyes anywhere outside the square and the table.

“‘Let them make twelve prayers throughout the day; at the evening light [Note: And when they come to the evening light. In Greek it is ἐν τῷ λυχνικῷ, that is, “at the evening light,” as Heraclides’s translator has it. See the Onomasticon.] twelve; at the night vigils twelve; and three at the ninth hour.’”

When it seemed that it was time for the multitude to eat, he arranged that each rank should first sing a psalm at each prayer.

When the great Pachomius objected to the angel that there were too few prayers, the angel said to him:

“I established these so that even the little ones may progress toward fulfilling the rule and not find it burdensome. Those who are perfect do not need laws to be imposed upon them, for when they are by themselves in their cells, they devote their whole life to contemplation.

“I have given this law to those who have little understanding, so that, like disobedient servants who fulfill their entire discipline through fear of their master, they may live securely and freely.”

When the angel had arranged these things and completed his ministry, he departed from the great Pachomius.

These are the monasteries that adopted this form of life, containing about seven thousand men. The first and great monastery is the one in which blessed Pachomius himself lives. It gave birth to the other monasteries and contains about one thousand four hundred men.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. The Life of Abbot Aphthonius

[Note: Aphthonius. The Greek likewise has Ἀφθόνιος. In Heraclides, Antonius formerly appeared in the first edition. I have now restored Aphthonius from various manuscripts.]

Among them is also a servant of God named Aphthonius, my brother and sincere friend, who now holds second place in that monastery.

Because he is powerful in Christ, firm and steadfast, and not easily offended, they send him to Alexandria for their affairs, to sell their products and buy what they need.

There are also other monasteries consisting of two hundred and three hundred persons [Note: The Greek has here a passage that Heraclides includes in chapter 19.].

At Panopolis I entered the city [Note: The city of Panopolis. In Greek, εἰς Πᾶνος τὴν πόλιν. Heraclides’s translator likewise read this in chapter 19. Hervetus had “into Spain.” See above, chapter 16.]. There is a monastery there consisting of three hundred men.

They practice every craft, and from what remains over they distribute [Note: Distribute. Hervetus seems to have read οἰκοδομοῦντες, “building.” But the Augustan, Venetian, and Paris manuscripts have οἰκονομοῦντες, “distributing,” correctly. That is, they distribute among the monasteries and prisons what they have earned through their manual labor. Heraclides, chapter 19: “From what could remain beyond the daily food, they also supplied whatever was necessary to the women’s monasteries and neighboring prisons.”] supplies to the women’s monasteries and the prisons.

In the morning, therefore, those to whom this duty falls by rotation rise. Some are occupied in the kitchen; others prepare the tables, placing upon them loaves, wild vegetables, olives, cheeses, scraps of meat, and chopped vegetables.

Those who are less robust enter at the seventh hour and eat, since they are weaker; others at the ninth hour, others at the tenth, others late in the evening, others after two days, others after three days, others after four days, and others after five days, so that each letter signifies its own hour.

Their occupations were likewise distributed. One worked in cultivating the field, another in the garden, another in the bakery, another in the bronze workshop [Col. 1139B], another in construction, another in the fulling trade, another in preparing hides [Note: In the fulling trade, another in preparing hides. In Greek, ἄλλος γναφεῖον, ἄλλος βυρσεῖον. Hervetus’s Latin text did not contain this, having only “another in sewing shoes.” Perhaps he had it in his Greek text, or perhaps he rendered βυρσεῖον in that way. Heraclides, chapter 19, after discussing the fuller, adds: “Another labored in the preparation of skins, another in the making of leather.” His translator therefore had an expanded Greek exemplar. The Augustan Excerpts have συντοτομεῖον after βυρσεῖον. Read σκυτοτομεῖον; Hervetus perhaps translated this as “in sewing shoes.”], another in sewing shoes, another in beautiful writing, another wove large baskets, and another small baskets and wickerwork.

All of them recite the Scriptures from memory.

There is also a women’s monastery of about four hundred, which has the same way of life and the same discipline, except for the sheepskin. The women are on the far side of the Nile, while the men are opposite them.

If a virgin dies, the remaining virgins prepare her for burial, carry her out, and place her on the bank of the river. The brothers cross over with palm branches, olive branches, and psalmody; they transport her and bury her in their own burial places.

Apart from the priest and the deacon, no one crosses over to the women’s monastery, and then only on Sunday.

## CHAPTER XL. Concerning the Virgin About Whom False Testimony Had Been Given

[Note: Virgin. For the offering made here for one who was in despair but not offered, see a similar example in Cassian, Conference II, chapter 5.]

In this monastery of women the following incident occurred. A secular shoemaker, having crossed over there through ignorance, was looking for work. One woman, younger than propriety required—for the place is deserted—came out and, unwillingly, spoke with him, giving him this answer: “We have our own shoemakers.” Another woman, who had seen her conversation with him, later became involved in a dispute with her and, at the devil’s prompting, out of extreme malice and anger, accused her before the sisterhood because of that conversation. A few others joined her, women who were not regarded as especially malicious.

The first woman, overcome with grief because she had suffered such an accusation—one that had never even entered her mind, and whose consequences she could not endure—secretly threw herself into the river and thus died. When the woman who had accused her realized this, and saw that she had maliciously brought the accusation against her and had caused the sisterhood such distress over the crime she had committed [Note: [Col. 1224C] “And had caused such distress over the crime.” Hervetus had written *et hoc scelus*, “and this crime,” but apparently read ἄλγος (*algos*, “pain” or “distress”) rather than ἄγος (*agos*, “crime” or “pollution”), as the printed text has. Heraclides translated it, “not enduring the horror of so great a crime.” But Palladius’s addition, ἀδελφότητος (*adelphotētos*, “of the sisterhood”), suggests that we should prefer ἄλγος, unless one would rather alter the case so that the text reads εἰργάσατο τὸ ἅλγος τῇ ἀδελφότητι, “she caused distress to the sisterhood.” FRONTO.], she too secretly strangled herself, unable to bear what had happened.

When the presbyter arrived, the remaining virgins reported the matter to him. He therefore ordered that no offering be made for either of them. But the others, as accomplices—those who had not restrained the accuser and who had believed what was said—he excluded for seven years, excommunicating them.

## CHAPTER XLI. Concerning the virgin who pretended to be foolish

[Note: [Col. 1224C] “Virgin.” This Amma was not called by her proper name, as some have thought, but by a title derived from her virtue; for spiritual mothers were called this, as follows here. See the *Onomasticon*.]

[Col. 1140A]

In this monastery there was another virgin who, for Christ’s sake, pretended to be foolish (Pelagius, *Booklet* XVIII, no. 19) and to be possessed by a demon, believing that by these means she was practicing virtue most effectively, comporting herself admirably and making herself despised and humble. The other women despised her so completely that they would not even eat with her; she accepted this with joy.

She therefore ran about in the kitchen and performed every kind of service for the others, never taking even an hour’s rest, but serving like a maidservant. This blessed woman was, as they say, the monastery’s sponge, truly fulfilling what is written in the Gospel: “Whoever wishes to be great among you must be the servant of all, and the minister of all” (Matthew 20; Mark 10). And again elsewhere: “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish so that he may become wise” (1 Corinthians 3).

The other virgins wore a distinctive habit: their heads were shaved and they wore hoods on their heads. She, however, wrapped her head in a cloth and went about serving them all. None of the four hundred women ever saw her chewing throughout all the years of her life. She never sat at table and never ate a piece of bread; instead, she was content to gather up the crumbs from the tables with a sponge and to wash the pots. She never put on shoes, never insulted anyone, never grumbled, and never said anything, whether great or small—even when she was insulted, beaten with fists, attacked with curses, and despised by very many.

## CHAPTER XLII. Concerning the holy Pitirum

[Col. 1140C]

An angel appeared to the holy anchorite Pitirum, who lived in Porphyrite and was a man highly distinguished in ascetic virtue (Pelagius, *Booklet* XVIII, no. 19, where he is called Pyoterius), and said to him:

“Why are you pleased with yourself and look upon yourself as something great because of the things you rightly and virtuously do, as though you were devout and religious and sat here in this place? Do you wish to see a woman more devout and religious than yourself? Go to the monastery of the Tabennesiot women, and there you will find one who has a headband [Note: [Col. 1224C] “Headband.” Τὸ διάδημα (*to diadēma*), “the diadem.” Hervetus rendered this in Latin as *diadema in capite*, “a diadem on her head”; Heraclides, “She had her head wrapped in cloth.” Pelagius, book VI, *Booklet* XVIII, translated it as “crown,” but later wrote, “when he saw her forehead wrapped in cloth.” The Greek here is καὶ τὸ ῥάκος ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς αὐτῆς καὶ τοῦ μετώπου, “and the cloth on her head and forehead.” The other religious virgins evidently had their heads covered with hoods, whereas she had a headband, or a simple ribbon, or a cloth. FRONTO.] on her head. She is better than you. Although she struggles amid such a great crowd and serves everyone without distinction, she has never withdrawn her heart from God, even though all treat her with arrogant contempt. You, however, even if you sit here, wander in thought through the cities, although you have never set foot on the inhabited world.”

The great Pitirum then rose and came to the monastery of the Tabennesiots. He asked the superiors to allow him to cross over to the women’s monastery. Since he was a man of great reputation among the Fathers and had grown old in ascetic practice, they brought him across the river in good confidence and admitted him.

After they had prayed, the great Pitirum asked to see all the virgins face to face. When they had all come forward, she did not appear. At last the holy Pitirum said to them: “Bring them all to me.”

When they replied, “We are all here,” he said: “One is missing—the one the angel showed me.”

They answered: “We have one, Salem [Note: [Col. 1224D] “Salem.” What *Sale* means follows: “For that is what they call there those who are not sound in mind.” See the *Onomasticon*.], [Col. 1141A] who is in the kitchen. For that is what they call there those who are not sound in mind.”

The great man said to them: “Bring her also; let me see her.”

They went to summon her, but she did not obey at all, since she understood what was happening—for perhaps this too had been revealed to her. They therefore dragged her by force, saying to her: “The holy Pitirum wishes to see you,” for he was a man of great renown.

When she had been brought in, the great man saw her face and the cloth on her head and forehead. He fell at her feet and said to her: “Bless me, Amma.”

She too fell at his feet and said: “You bless me, my lord.”

When all the women saw this, they were astonished and said to him: “Do not bring shame and reproach upon yourself; she is a *Sale*.”

The holy Pitirum said to them: “You are the *Sales*. For she is better than both me and you. She is an Amma [Col. 1141B]—for that is what they call spiritual Mothers—and I ask that I may be found worthy of her at the hour of judgment.”

When they heard this, they fell at her feet weeping and all confessed that they had mistreated the blessed woman in various ways. One said: “I was always mocking her.” Another: “I ridiculed her humble clothing.” Another: “I insulted her because she kept silent.” Yet another: “I often poured out the wash-water from a basin over her.” Another: “I struck her.” Another: “I was the one who punched her.” Yet another: “I sprinkled mustard on her nostrils.” In short, they all declared that they had subjected her to various insults.

After the holy Pitirum had heard their confession, prayed with them and with the woman, and consoled the venerable servant of Christ for a long time, he departed.

A few days later, when she was being greatly honored and observed by everyone, the blessed woman could not endure the glory and honor bestowed upon her by the whole sisterhood. Considering the explanations and excuses a burden, she secretly left the monastery. To this day no one knows where she went, what place she entered, or where she died. Such were the noble and humble virgin’s blessed deeds and works.

## CHAPTER XLIII. Concerning Abba John of the city of Lycus

[Note: [Col. 1224D] “John.” See the authors cited above concerning him, at Book II, chapter 1.]

There was a certain John in the city of Lycus who had learned the craft of a carpenter from childhood; his brother was a dyer (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 1). Later, when he was about twenty-five years old, he renounced the world. After spending five years in a monastery, [Col. 1141D] he withdrew alone to the mountain of Lycus. At the summit of the mountain he built three domed chambers for himself and entered, enclosing himself within them. One dome was for the needs of the body, another for his work, and the third for prayer.

After he had completed thirty years in confinement, receiving through a window from the person who served him whatever was necessary for his use, he was deemed worthy of the gift of foretelling the future. His possession of the gift of prophecy was made clear by his deeds. For he first announced to the pious emperor Theodosius all that was coming upon the world from God, and he foretold what was afterward to happen: the uprising of the tyrants against him [Note: [Col. 1224D] “Tyrants.” The Greek codex gives their names, Μαξίμου καὶ Εὐγενίου, “Maximus and Eugenius.” Heraclides does likewise.], [Col. 1142A] their swift destruction, and the annihilation of the peoples who were rushing against him.

Thus, when a certain army commander came to ask him whether he would defeat the Ethiopians who are in Syene—which is the beginning of the Thebaid—for they had then invaded and devastated the neighboring region, John said to him: “If you go up, you will catch them, defeat them, subdue them, and become renowned among the emperors.” This too happened, and the events confirmed his prophecy.

He said that the most Christian emperor Theodosius would die by his own death. This man also possessed an astonishing prophecy, exceeding all ordinary measure, as we heard from the Fathers who lived with him and whose lives were approved by all who were there.

That they did not relate anything about him for the sake of winning favor, but rather said less than he deserved, can easily be understood from the following. A certain tribune came to him and earnestly begged him to permit his wife to come to him. She had suffered much and wished to see him; she was going to Syene so that he might pray for her first and dismiss her after giving her a blessing.

But John, who had not seen a woman for forty years, was ninety years old, had never himself left the cave, and did not allow himself to see a woman, refused to see the man’s wife. No man, either, ever entered to him. He blessed people only through the window and greeted those who approached, conversing with each one about whatever he wished [Note: [Col. 1141] Some Greek texts insert here material found in Heraclides, chapter 22.].

When the tribune persisted and asked whether he should order his wife to come—for she lived five miles from the city in the desert—John did not consent, saying that this could not be done, and dismissed the man sorrowful.

His wife, however, did not cease troubling her husband day and night and swearing that she would go nowhere unless she saw the prophet. When the blessed John was informed by her husband of her oath, he understood her faith and said to him: “Tonight I shall appear to her in a dream; she should not continue trying to see my face in the flesh.”

The husband reported to his wife what the Father had said. The woman saw the prophet coming to her in a dream. He said to her: “What do you want with me, woman? Why did you wish to see my face? Am I a prophet, or do I hold the place of a righteous man? I am a sinful human being, subject to suffering just as you are. Nevertheless, I have prayed for you and for your husband’s household, that it may be done for you according to your faith. Go in peace.”

Having said this, he departed.

When the woman awoke, she reported the prophet’s words to her husband and described his appearance and clothing. Through her husband she sent him thanks.

When the blessed John saw the husband, he anticipated him and said: “See, I have fulfilled what you requested. I saw her and warned her not to see me again, but said, ‘Go in peace.’”

The wife of another official was pregnant while her husband was away. After she had given birth, on the very day her husband visited Father John, she fell into a faint and came close to death. The saint announced this to him, saying:

“If you knew the gift of God” (John 4), and that a son has been born to you today, you would glorify God. But his mother has nearly died. When you arrive, you will find the infant seven days old. Give him the name John. When you have raised him properly and he reaches his seventh year, send him to the monks who are in the desert.”

These things he revealed as miracles to those who came from abroad. To his own townspeople, who came to him continually for their needs, he both knew and foretold future events: what each had secretly done, matters concerning the Nile, and the coming fertility of the year. Likewise, he announced beforehand the threats of God that were coming upon them and rebuked those responsible for them.

The blessed John did not perform healings openly. But by giving oil, he cured many of those who were suffering.

The wife of a certain senator, who had lost her sight and whose pupils were covered with a white film, asked her husband to take her to him. When he said that the man had never met a woman, she asked that her condition simply be reported to him and that he do this on her behalf. He did so, and John sent oil.

After she had applied it to her eyes for only three days, she regained her sight and openly gave thanks to God.

And why should I speak of his other deeds, which we saw with our own eyes? We were seven brothers, all strangers in the desert of Nitria: I, the blessed Evagrius, Albinus, and Ammonius. We wanted to learn precisely what kind of virtue this man possessed.

The great Evagrius said: “I would gladly learn from someone who knows how to examine both a man’s mind and his prayer what sort of person he is. If I cannot see him myself, but can hear an accurate account of his way of life from someone else, I will learn enough to visit him; but if I do not learn this, I will not go as far as the mountain.”

When I heard this, without saying anything to anyone, I rested for one day. On the next, I closed my cell, commended myself and the cell to God, and set out for the Thebaid. I reached him after eighteen days, traveling partly on foot and partly by boat on the river.

It was the season of the Nile’s rise [Note: [Col. 1224D] “Season of the ascent.” In Greek, Καιρὸς ἀναβάσεως (*kairos anabaseōs*), “the season of ascent.” I think the rise of the Nile is meant. So above, chapter 37, when the Nile was rising. See the *Onomasticon*.], when many people fall ill; this happened to me as well.

When I arrived, I found the entrance closed. For the brothers later built a very large vestibule [Col. 1143D] that could accommodate about one hundred men; they locked it with a key and opened it only on Saturday and Sunday.
