After I had learned why it was closed, I kept silence until Saturday. When I came at the second hour, I found him sitting in the window where he used to console those who approached.

After greeting me, he said through an interpreter: “From what region are you? Why have you come? I suspect that you are from Evagrius’s community.”

I said that I was a visitor from Galatia and acknowledged that I belonged to Evagrius’s circle.

While we were speaking, the governor of the region entered, named Alypius. When he hurried in, John ceased speaking with me. I withdrew a short distance and gave them space.

After they had spoken for some time, I became sad and murmured against the venerable old man [Note: [Col. 1224D] “Venerable old man.” In Greek, καλόγηρον (*kalogēron*).], thinking that he had despised me but honored the other man. Troubled by this, I intended to leave, disregarding him.

But he summoned his interpreter, named Theodore, and said to him: “Go and tell that brother not to take it badly. I am dismissing the governor now and will speak with him.”

It seemed to me that I should bear it patiently, since I had recognized that he was a spiritual man.

When the governor had left, John summoned me and said: “Why were you angry with me? What did you find in my conduct that justly offended you, so that you considered those things which are neither present in me nor fitting for you? Do you not know that it is written: ‘Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick’” (Matthew 9; Mark 2; Luke 5)?

“When I wish, I can find you, and you can find me. If I have not consoled you, other brothers console you, and other Fathers do so as well. But this man, who was devoted to worldly affairs and had been given over to the devil, came to gain some benefit after having briefly drawn breath like a slave who has escaped from a harsh master. It would therefore have been absurd for me to leave him and spend time with you, since you are continually devoted to salvation.”

When I asked him to pray for me, I became convinced that he was a spiritual man.

Then, joking with me courteously, he gently tapped my left cheek and said: “Many afflictions await you. You have suffered severe battles in order to leave the desert; you were afraid and delayed. The demon harasses you by presenting pious and reasonable pretexts. He suggested to you the longing for your father and for your brother and sister’s adoption of the monastic life.

“Here, then, is good news for you: both are safe, for they have renounced the world, and your father will live another seven years. Be strong and steadfast in the desert, and do not wish to return to your homeland because of them. For it is written: ‘No one who has put his hand to the plough and then turned back is fit for the kingdom of God’” (Luke 9).

Strengthened and sufficiently encouraged by these words, I gave thanks to God when I understood that the pretexts which had been troubling me had been dealt with.

Then he again joked with me courteously: “Do you wish to become a bishop?”

I replied: “Not at all; I already am one.”

He said to me: “Where?”

I answered: “In the kitchens, in the storeroom, at the tables, and among the jars. I inspect them carefully, and if the wine has turned sour, I set it aside; but I drink the good wine. Likewise, I carefully inspect the pot, and if it lacks salt or some seasoning, I season it, and then I eat from it. This is my episcopate—my inspection, I mean. My appetite chose me for it.”

He said, smiling: “Stop joking. You are going to be chosen as a bishop, and you will labor and suffer greatly. If you flee from afflictions, do not leave the desert, for in the desert no one can ordain you bishop.”

I forgot his words. Three years later I suffered from my spleen and stomach. From there the brothers sent me to Alexandria, for the illness [Note: [Col. 1224D] “For the illness.” Hervetus, fearing that I might become dropsical, translated it as “was tending toward dropsy.” Heraclides likewise, “and there considering dropsy.” Μελετᾷν (*meletan*) here has the sense of “to practice,” “to contemplate,” or “to tend toward”: one who contemplates desertion tends toward it. So Jonah 1:4: “The ship thought—or tended—to be broken,” according to Vatablus’s Hebrew-based interpretation; the Vulgate has “was in danger of being broken.” FRONTO.], was tending toward dropsy. From Alexandria the physicians advised me to go to Palestine for the sake of the air, since it has a finer atmosphere suitable to my constitution.

From Palestine I went to Bithynia. There, I do not know whether through human effort or divine will [Note: [Col. 1225A] “Or divine will.” The translator had printed “or by a more powerful will.” Heraclides more correctly has, “whether through human effort or through the will of God,” ἐξ εὐδοκίας τοῦ Κρείττονος (*ex eudokias tou Kreittonos*), a phrase that signifies the divine Power even among pagan authors. Plutarch, in *Pyrrhus*: Ὥς τινα τῶν κρειττόνων θαυμάσαντες (*hōs tina tōn kreittonōn thaumasantēs*), “as though admiring one of the gods.” Socrates, Book I, chapter 4 of the *History*: Ὁμολογῆσαι χάριν τῷ Κρείττονι, τοῦ Κρείττονος ἐπινεύοντος (*homologēsai charin tō Kreittoni, tou Kreittonos epineuontos*), “to acknowledge gratitude to the Higher Power, with the Higher Power granting assent.” Nicephorus, Book XVI, chapter 29: “with God’s assistance.” Likewise in chapter 52 of this *Lausiac History*, Τὴν εὐδοκίμησιν οὕτω σχοίη παρὰ τῷ κρείττονι (*tēn eudokimēsin houtō schoie para tō kreittoni*), which the translator wrongly rendered, “may he attain what is worthy of his labors from the more powerful one.” FRONTO.], God knows, I was deemed worthy of an ordination beyond my strength, falling into the situation which John had foretold. For eleven months I remained hidden in a dark cell, and I remembered that blessed man who had foretold what I would suffer.

He also told me the following, intending by this account to help lead me toward patiently enduring solitude:

“For forty years I have lived in this cell. I have not seen a woman’s face, not a single coin, and I have not seen anyone chewing. No one has seen me eating or drinking.”

After leaving him, I returned to the desert [Col. 1145B] at the customary place, recounting all this to the blessed Fathers who came two months later and conversed with him. They reported these things to us.

When we came to him, he received and greeted us with a joyful face, showing himself cheerful toward each of us. We asked him to pray for us immediately, for this is the custom of the Fathers in Egypt.

He asked us whether any cleric was among us. After we had all said that there was not, he looked around at us all and recognized the one who was concealed. One of us had been deemed worthy of the diaconate; one brother knew the matter, and the deacon had instructed him to tell no one. Out of humility, and in comparison with such Fathers, he scarcely considered himself worthy to be called a Christian, much less to possess any rank.

Pointing him out with his hand, John said to everyone: “This man is a deacon.”

When the man repeatedly denied it and tried to remain hidden, John reached through the window, took his hand, and kissed it. He admonished and exhorted him, saying: “Do not render God’s grace void, my son. Do not lie by denying God’s gift. Falsehood is alien to Christians; whether the matter is great or small, it is not praiseworthy, since the Savior says: ‘Falsehood is from the evil one’” (John 8).

The man, thus proved wrong, fell silent and accepted the Father’s paternal rebuke.

After we had completed our prayers, one of our brothers, who was already suffering from a severe tertian fever, asked to be healed. John said that the brother’s affliction was due to the little faith he possessed, but nevertheless gave him oil and ordered him to anoint himself.

After he had anointed himself, he expelled through his mouth whatever was inside him, was completely freed from the fever, and returned to the guesthouse on his own feet.

It was possible to see a ninety-year-old man so afflicted throughout his body by ascetic practice that not even a beard had grown on his face. He ate nothing except the fruits of trees, and that only after sunset, despite his extreme old age and his previous severe asceticism. He had never eaten bread or anything prepared by fire.

When he ordered us to sit, we gave thanks to God that we had been granted his company. After receiving us for a long time as beloved sons, he spoke to us with a smiling face:

“From where, my sons, and from what region, have you come to a worthless and humble man? When we had told him our homeland and added, ‘We have come to you from Jerusalem for the benefit of our souls, so that we might see with our eyes what we had received by hearing—for ears are less trustworthy than eyes. What is heard is often followed by forgetfulness, but the memory of what is seen is not erased; rather, the account is somehow stamped upon the mind’—the blessed John said to us:

“‘What wondrous thing did you expect to see, dearly beloved sons, that you have endured so much travel and labor to come here, wishing to see worthless and humble men who have nothing worthy of being looked at or admired? Everywhere there are God’s prophets and apostles, worthy of admiration and praise, who are read in the churches and whom you ought to imitate.

“‘I am greatly amazed at your zeal: how, having disregarded so many dangers, you came to us for your benefit, while we, through sluggishness, are unwilling even to leave the cave.

“‘But come now: even if your undertaking is worthy of praise, do not think that it is enough for you merely to have accomplished something admirable. Rather, imitate the virtues which your fathers pursue. And even if you possess them all—which is rare—even then do not trust yourselves. Some who trusted in this way and reached the very summit of virtue eventually fell from the heights.

“‘See whether your prayers are in proper order; whether the purity of your hearts has been disturbed; whether your minds are occupied with other affairs while you pray; whether some thought entering your mind turns it toward something else; whether the memory of any thought causes distress in your soul.

“‘See whether you have truly renounced the world; whether you entered as observers of our freedom; whether you pursue your virtues for vain glory, so that you may appear to people to imitate our works for display.

“‘See that disturbance of soul does not trouble you; that honor, glory, and human praise do not trouble you; that the pretense of concern for sacred things or self-love does not trouble you. Do not think yourselves righteous, and do not glory in your righteousness. Do not become elated because of your virtues. Do not let the memory of your relatives take root in your mind while you pray; nor the memory of compassion, or of anything else, or even of the whole world itself, come to your aid.

“‘Otherwise the matter becomes vanity, when someone addressing the Lord is thrust downward by thoughts that pull in the opposite direction [Col. 1146D]. This collapse of the mind happens to anyone who has not wholly renounced this world but venerates it in order to please it. For because of the many things he undertakes, bodily and earthly cares divide his mind; and while he continues struggling with the disturbances of his soul, he cannot see God.

“‘Nor ought he to contemplate knowledge itself accurately and exactly, lest, if he should prove unworthy of possessing such knowledge and should attain some part of it, he imagine that he has grasped the whole and fall utterly into ruin. Rather, one must always approach God moderately and piously, advancing in mind as far as each person can and attaining as much as human beings are capable of attaining.

“‘The minds of those who seek God must therefore be free from all other things. “Be still and know that I am God,” he says (Psalm 45).

“‘Whoever has attained a partial knowledge of God—for no one can receive the whole—also attains knowledge of all other things. He sees the mysteries of God, who reveals them to him; he foresees the future; he contemplates revelations like those of the saints; he performs miracles; and he receives from God every request.’”

He said many other things about ascetic practice: that one ought to await death as a passage into the good life and not regard bodily weakness; and that one should not fill one’s stomach with whatever happens to be available.

“For whoever,” he said, “has been filled has the same thoughts in his head as those who live in luxury. Rather, through ascetic practice one must strive to render even one’s appetites incapable of suffering.

“No one should seek what is prepared for him or relaxation of soul. Instead, let him now be weak, afflicted, and oppressed, so that he may inherit the breadth of the kingdom of God. For we must enter the kingdom of God through many afflictions” (Acts 14).

“For,” he said, “the gate is narrow and the way is constricted that leads to life, and few are those who find it. And: ‘Broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter by it’” (Matthew 7).

“We must,” he said, “be despised here, since shortly afterward we shall go to eternal life. No one should become elated over what he has rightly accomplished. He should always be humble and seek more remote solitudes whenever he senses himself becoming elated. Dwelling near villages has often caused even those who were perfect to stumble.

“David also sings of this, since something of the kind happened to him: ‘Behold, I have fled far away and dwelt in the desert. I awaited him who saves me from faintheartedness and storm’” (Psalm 54).

This has happened to many of our brothers as well, and through arrogance they have fallen away from their goal.

## CHAPTER XLIV. The account of Abba John concerning one who fell

He said:

“There was a certain monk who lived in a nearby desert in a cave. He had displayed every form of ascetic practice and obtained bread for himself by the work of his own hands” (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 1).

After he had persevered in prayers and advanced in virtue, he eventually became confident in himself, relying upon the excellence of his way of life.

The tempter sought him out for temptation, as he had sought Job, and in the evening presented him with the apparition of a beautiful woman wandering through the desert. When she found the door open, she entered the cave, fell at the man’s knees, and asked permission to rest there, since night had overtaken her.

He pitied her—which he ought not to have done—admitted her into the cave, and questioned her about her wandering. She told him her story, but also mixed in flattering and deceitful words and prolonged the conversation with him.

Little by little, somehow, she enticed him toward love. They exchanged many words, then laughed and smiled at one another. By much conversation she deceived him, and afterward by touching his hand, beard, and neck [Col. 1148A]. Finally she reduced the ascetic to slavery.

While he was turning these thoughts over within himself, and reasoning that he now had the opportunity and security to satisfy his pleasure, he assented to the thought and attempted to have intercourse with her, having already become foolish and crazed with desire for women.

But when she suddenly cried out in a loud voice, she escaped from his hands and vanished like a shadow. The laughter of many demons was heard in the air. They rebuked him, led him into the trap, and cried out to him in a loud voice: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11).

“You were exalted as far as the heavens, but you have been humbled as far as the abyss.”

From then on he rose in the morning, drawing night-long mourning after him. After spending the entire day in lamentation and despairing of his salvation—which he ought not to have done—he returned to the world.

For this is the devil’s aim: when he has mocked someone, to reduce him to folly so that he cannot afterward rise again.

“Therefore, my sons, living near villages is not beneficial for us, nor is conversation with women, since from these things arises a memory that cannot be erased, which we draw from sight [Col. 1148B] and conversation.

“Yet neither should we lose heart or drive ourselves into despair. For even those who did not abandon hope were not deprived of the merciful compassion of God.”

## CHAPTER XLV. The account of the same Abba John concerning the brother who was led to repentance
[Col. 1148C] “There was,” he says, “another young man in the city who had committed many evil deeds and grievously sinned” (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 1). Moved by God’s will on account of his many sins, he came to the tombs and mourned his former life. Falling prone upon his face, he did not dare to utter a sound, name God, or even make supplication, considering himself unworthy of life itself. He had shut himself up in the tombs of the dead and, as he recounted his life, groaned from the depths of his heart.

When a week had passed from that time, demons appeared to him by night—the same demons who had previously brought ruin upon his life. They shouted, saying: “Where is that wicked and profane man who, sated with lusts and wantonness, has now suddenly appeared to us as an untimely, temperate, and respectable person? And when he can no longer do anything, then he wants to be a Christian and live by virtuous and orderly conduct? What further good do you expect to come to you, when you have been filled with our evils? Will you not rise quickly from here? Will you not come to the things customary among us? Prostitutes and taverns await you. Will you not come and enjoy your desires, since every other hope for you has been extinguished? Judgment will swiftly come upon you, since you are destroying yourself in this way. Why, wretched man, are you hastening toward punishment? Why are you striving to inflict penalties upon yourself sooner?

“Moreover,” they said many other things, “you are ours; you have been enrolled in our order; you have practiced every iniquity. You are liable to us all, and you dare to flee? Will you not consent? Will you not answer? Will you not go out with us?”

But while he remained steadfast in his weeping and did not even lend them his ears, nor answer a word when the demons pressed him for a long time—when, I say, they had accomplished nothing, repeatedly saying the same things to him—the evil and shameful demons seized him and maltreated his entire body, beating him severely with whips. After torturing him harshly, they departed, leaving him half dead.

He nevertheless lay motionless where they had left him, groaning again after he had recovered his composure. When his relatives searched for him, found him, and learned what had happened to his body, they begged him to return home; but although they often tried to force him, he resisted.

Again, on the following night, the demons afflicted him for the same reasons, worse than before. Even then his relatives [Col. 1149B] could not persuade him to leave, for he said that it was better to die than to live amid such stains upon his life.

The third night almost drove him from among human beings, when the cruel demons attacked him with tortures and tormented him to his final breath. When they saw that he had not yielded, they withdrew, leaving the man lifeless. As they departed, they cried out: “You have conquered, you have conquered, you have conquered.”

After that no further evil befell him. He lived purely in a most pure tomb for the rest of his life, practicing pure virtue. He became precious to God and was renowned for his virtues and the working of miracles, so that he brought many to wonder, stirred them to zeal, and led them to emulate honorable practices. Thus it came about that many even of those who had utterly despaired of themselves began good works and conducted themselves rightly. What happened to them was what Scripture says: “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV).

Therefore, my children, let us especially practice humility, which is the first foundation of all the virtues. A longer and more remote solitude also greatly benefits us.

## CHAPTER XLVI. Another narrative of Abba John, concerning one who fell and was led to repentance

There was also another monk who had taken possession of a more remote solitude and had conducted himself rightly and virtuously for many years (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 1). When he was afterward worn down by old age, he was tested by the demons’ snares.

He was a practitioner who greatly embraced silence. He spent the day in prayers, hymns, and many contemplations, and clearly saw certain divine visions, sometimes while awake and sometimes in dreams. He was kept by the incorporeal life almost free from sleep, neither cultivating the earth nor taking any care for food, nor seeking among the plants anything to provide for his needy body. He did not hunt birds or pursue any animal. Full of confidence, from the time he had migrated there from the inhabited region, he gave no thought to keeping his body nourished. Forgetful of everything, he sustained himself by perfect longing for God, awaiting his call and his departure from this world.

For the most part he was nourished by delight in things unseen and hoped for. His body was not emaciated by the passage of time, nor was his soul troubled or sad; rather, he possessed a good disposition in a certain honorable and venerable state.

In truth, God honored him by placing upon his table, after a predetermined interval, bread sufficient for two or three days, so that it could be seen, exist, and be used by him. When he entered the cave and felt his body in need, he found nourishment there. After worshiping and eating, he again devoted himself to hymns, persevering in prayer and contemplation, growing daily, giving himself over to present virtue and future hope, and continually advancing further. He was already almost confident of his better lot, as though he held it in his hands. This also became the cause of his fall, [Col. 1150B] when he nearly fell away through the temptation that later attacked him.

What should we call the fall that came near to him? After he had advanced to this way of thinking, he gradually and unknowingly reached the point of believing that he was worth more than others and already possessed something greater than other people. Being in this condition, he thereafter placed his confidence in himself.

Not long afterward, a small slackening of spirit arose in him—so slight that it did not even seem to be slackness. Then greater negligence appeared, which eventually advanced so far that it became perceptible. He rose more slowly from sleep for the hymns; his prayers became somewhat more sluggish; the hymn was no longer so lengthy; his soul said that it wished to rest, and his mind agreed. His thoughts fluctuated and wandered, and he was already secretly meditating something absurd.

Yet his former habit still drew him onward to some extent, like a kind of movement arising from his earlier zeal, and preserved him for the time being. Once, after his customary prayers, he entered the cave in the evening and found upon the table the bread divinely supplied to him, and refreshed himself.

At that time he neither cast away those detestable thoughts nor reckoned that his soul was being harmed by contempt. He did not turn to seek a cure for the evil; rather, he thought little of how close he was to falling away from what ought to be done.

The love of desire therefore carried him away in thought to the inhabited region. Nevertheless, after restraining himself until the following day, he returned to his customary discipline. Having prayed and recited hymns, he entered the cave and found that the bread set before him was not prepared with the same care, nor was it as pure, but dirty and defiled. Although he was astonished and distressed, he took it and refreshed himself.

The third night followed and added a threefold evil. His mind quickly burst into thoughts. His memory was so affected that it seemed as though a woman were present with him and reclining beside him; he kept the matter before his eyes and persisted as though he were actually doing it.

Nevertheless, on the third day he went out again to work, prayer, and hymns, but he no longer had pure thoughts. He repeatedly turned and raised his eyes upward, twisting them here and there, for the memories of his thoughts interrupted his beautiful work.

When he returned in the evening, needing bread, he found it on the table as though gnawed by mice or dogs, with certain dry remnants outside. Then he groaned and wept, but not enough to restrain the wickedness. Having eaten—not as much as he wished—he prepared himself for rest.

But thoughts attacked him in a mass, surrounding him on every side. They assaulted his mind and immediately carried him captive into the world. Rising, he went toward the inhabited region, traveling by night through the wilderness.

When daylight overtook him, while the inhabited region was still far away and the heat oppressed him, he grew exhausted. Looking around in every direction, he searched to see whether a monastery might appear somewhere, so that he could enter it and rest.

This too came to pass. Some pious and faithful brothers received him; when they saw him as though he were their own father, they washed his face and feet. After praying, they set a table before him and asked him to partake lovingly of what had been prepared.

When he had refreshed himself, the brothers requested from him a word of salvation: how they might be saved from the devil’s snares and how they might overcome shameful thoughts. He, admonishing them as a father admonishes his children, urged them to be brave and steadfast in their labors, since they would shortly be placed in the highest rest. Discussing many other matters of discipline with them, he greatly benefited them.

When he had finished admonishing them and had gathered himself for a little while, he considered how, while admonishing others, he was not admonishing or correcting himself. Recognizing that he had been defeated, he returned at a run to the solitude, mourning himself and saying: “Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell” (Psalm XCIX). “I have almost been reduced to every evil; they have almost destroyed me upon the earth.”

In him was fulfilled what is said: “A brother helped by his brother is like a fortified and lofty city, and like a wall that cannot fall” (Proverbs XVIII).

Nevertheless, from that point onward he mourned continually for the rest of his life, deprived of the table divinely provided for him and seeking his bread through labor. For when he had shut himself in the cave and spread a sack and ashes beneath himself, he neither rose from the ground nor ceased weeping until he heard an angelic voice saying to him in a dream:

“The Lord has accepted your repentance [Col. 1151D] and has had mercy on you. From now on, take care lest you be deceived. For the brothers whom you admonished will come to you and bring you eulogiae (blessed gifts); when you have received them, you will eat with them and give perpetual thanks to God.”

I have told you these things, my children, so that you may practice humility, whether you appear to be among the lowly or among the great. For this is the first commandment of the Savior, who says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew VI).

And do not be deceived by demons who raise up visions and fantasies for you. If anyone comes to you—a brother, a friend, a woman, a father, a teacher, a mother, or a sister—first extend your hands in prayer; and if it is a phantom, it will flee from you.

If demons or human beings deceive you by agreeing with and praising you, do not obey them or become elated in mind. For demons often deceived me in this way at night. They would neither allow me to pray nor let me rest, presenting me with various fantasies throughout the night. In the morning they would throw themselves upon the ground in mockery, saying: “Forgive us, abba, for giving you such trouble throughout the night.”

But I would say to them: “Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Psalm VI); do not tempt the servant of the Lord.

Therefore, my children, pursue quietness as well, always training yourselves for contemplation, so that you may possess a pure mind while praying to God.

That practitioner too is good who is constantly active in the world and occupied with honorable deeds: one who shows humanity, mercy, hospitality, and charity; gives alms; treats those who arrive well; helps those who labor; and remains without giving offense. Such a person is indeed very good: he is engaged in action and carries out the commandments. Yet he is occupied with earthly matters.

Certainly superior and greater than this person is the one engaged in contemplation, who turns from active affairs to understanding, leaving those matters for others to manage, while he, having denied himself and forgotten himself, examines heavenly things. Released and unencumbered from everything, he stands before God, drawn back by no other concern. Whoever is such a person lives with God, conducts himself with God, and continually glorifies God in hymns.

I know a man in the wilderness who tasted no earthly food for ten years. Every third day an angel brought him heavenly food and placed it in his mouth; it served him as both food and drink.

I also know that demons came to this man in a vision, displaying angelic armies, chariots of fire, and many attendants, as though belonging to some approaching king. They said to him: “In everything you have conducted yourself rightly and virtuously, man. From now on worship me, and I will take you up like Elijah.”

But the monk said to himself: “Every day I worship my King and Savior. If this were he, he would not ask this of me.”

After he had stated what was in his mind—“I have God as my Lord and King, whom I always worship; you are not my king”—the demon immediately vanished.

He wished to conceal these things by discussing them as though they concerned someone else, speaking of the practices of his life and his deeds. But the fathers who were with him said that he himself had seen these things.

The blessed John told us these and many other things, speaking for three days until the ninth hour, and cared for our souls. When he had given us his blessings, he ordered us to depart in peace, also uttering this prophecy to us:

“Today,” he said, “the victory of the most devout Theodosius has been announced in Alexandria, because the tyrant Eugenius has been removed from the midst; and the emperor must die his own death”—which indeed happened.

[Note: [Col. 1225A] “It has been announced.” The translator retained the Greek expression: “Today,” he said, “the *epinicia* [victory celebrations] of the most devout Theodosius have arrived in Alexandria.” Prosper, in his *Chronicon*, under the year of Christ 395, mentions this prophecy of John: “John the anchorite is held in high esteem. Adorned with the gift of prophecy, he foretold to Theodosius, who consulted him about the outcome of the war he was waging against Eugenius, that he would be victorious.” FRONTO.]

It was possible to see the multitude of monks who were with him in the church, like choirs of the righteous clothed in radiant garments and glorifying God with continual hymns.

[Col. 1153A] After we had also seen many other Fathers, brothers came to announce to us that the blessed John had reached his end in a wondrous manner. For after he had ordered that no one be allowed to come to him for three days, he knelt in prayer and was brought to completion, going to God, to whom be glory forever.

## CHAPTER XLVII. Concerning Poemenia

He did not converse with Christ’s handmaid Poemenia, who had come to see him, but he did reveal certain secrets to her. He instructed her, saying: “When you descend from the Thebaid, do not turn aside to Alexandria, since you are destined to fall into temptations.”

But she either disregarded the prediction of the great John [Col. 1153B] or forgot it, and turned aside to Alexandria in order to see the city.

On the journey, near the city of Nicia, her ships put in to shore so that she might rest. Her servants, acting with some insolence, came to blows with the inhabitants of that place, men who were mad and dissolute. They cut off one eunuch’s finger, killed another, and, without recognizing him, threw the most holy bishop Dionysius into the river. They also assailed Poemenia herself with insults and abuse, and wounded all the remaining servants.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. The Life of Abba Ammonas [Note: [Col. 1225B] “Ammonas.” Concerning him, see what is said above regarding Rufinus, Book II, chapter 3.], and of those who were with him

We also saw another man in the Thebaid, named [Col. 1153C] Ammonas (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 3), the Father of three thousand monks. He called them Tabennesiotes. They had a strict rule of life: they wore little sheepskins, ate with their faces covered, and bent downward so that no one might see his neighbor eating. They practiced such profound silence that they seemed to be in solitude, each secretly carrying out his own way of life. They sat together at table only in outward appearance, striving to remain hidden from one another.

Some of them brought their hand to their mouth only once or twice, touching bread, oil, or something else that had been set before them. After tasting each dish once, they were satisfied with that nourishment. Others slowly chewed bread while taking other foods without concealment and continued in this manner. Others tasted the broth only three times and abstained from the rest.

Although, as was natural, I admired these practices, I did not neglect the benefit that could be drawn from them.

## CHAPTER XLIX. Concerning Abba Be [Note: [Col. 1225B] “Be.” This man is called Benus in Rufinus, Book II, chapter 4. See him there.]

We also saw another old man who surpassed all human beings in gentleness, named Abba Be (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 4). The brothers who lived with him asserted that he had never sworn an oath, never lied about anyone, never rebuked anyone with a word, and never become angry. His life was exceedingly tranquil and his manner gentle, as one who possessed an angelic state. He was also extremely humble [Col. 1154A] and despised himself.

When we repeatedly begged him to give us an exhortatory discourse, he scarcely persuaded himself to speak a few words to us about gentleness.

Once, when a hippopotamus was devastating the neighboring region, he stood near the river. At the farmers’ request, and after seeing the enormous beast, he commanded it, saying: “I charge you in the name of Jesus Christ: do not devastate this region any longer.”

The beast immediately vanished, as though driven from the place by an angel. He likewise once drove away a crocodile.

## CHAPTER L. Concerning Abba Theonas [Note: [Col. 1225B] “Theonas.” This man is called Theon by Rufinus, Book II, chapter 6; consult him there.]

We also saw another man not far from the city, in the wilderness, named Theonas, a holy man enclosed by himself in a small dwelling, who had practiced silence for thirty years [Col. 1154B] (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 6).

Since he performed very many virtues, they regarded him as a prophet. Every day a multitude of sick people came to him. He laid hands upon them through the window and let them depart healed. It was possible to see that his face had an angelic appearance, his eyes were cheerful, and his whole person was filled with the greatest grace.

Not long before, thieves had attacked him by night, expecting to find a great amount of gold with him and intending to kill him. He prayed, and they remained motionless at his doors until morning.

When the crowds approached him in the morning and intended to consign the thieves to the fire, he spoke only one word to them: “Let them go unharmed; otherwise the grace of healing will depart from me.”

They obeyed him. They did not dare contradict him, and the thieves immediately went away to the monasteries in the surrounding region, changed in their manner of life and led to repentance by what they had done.

He was a learned man, endowed with a threefold grace of speech—in Roman, Greek, and Egyptian letters—as we heard from many people and from the man himself. When he learned that we were guests, he wrote upon a tablet and gave thanks to God on our behalf.

He ate uncooked seeds. At night, they say, he would leave his cell and associate with wild animals, giving them water from the supply he possessed. It was possible to see the tracks of buffaloes, wild asses, and certain goats around his monastery; he was always delighted by them.

## CHAPTER LI. Concerning Abba Elias [Note: [Col. 1225B] “Elias.” See the authors cited concerning him above, in Rufinus, Book II, chapter 12.]

[Col. 1154D]

We also saw another old man in the wilderness of Antinoe, which is the metropolis of the Thebaid, named Elias, who was one hundred and ten years old (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 12).

They said that the spirit of the prophet Elijah had rested upon him. He was highly celebrated, having spent seventy years in that dreadful wilderness. No prayer can adequately describe that harsh wilderness on the mountain where he sat, never descending to the inhabited region.

The path used by those who approached him was such that they could scarcely stand upon its tracks; it was enclosed on either side by rough stones. He sat beneath a certain rock [Col. 1155A] in a cave, so that even seeing him was terrifying.

He now trembled all over, being oppressed by old age. Yet he performed many signs every day and never ceased healing the sick. The Fathers who lived with him said that no one remembered his having ever climbed the mountain.

In his old age he ate three ounces of bread and three olives in the evening. In his youth he ate only once a week.

## CHAPTER LII. The Life of Abba Apollo [Note: [Col. 1225B] “Apollo.” See the authors cited concerning him in the aforementioned book of Rufinus, chapter 7.]

We also saw another holy man in the Thebaid, in the territory of Hermopolis (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 7). The Savior came there with holy Mary and Joseph, fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy, which says: “Behold, the Lord sits upon a light cloud and will come into Egypt; and the handmade things of Egypt will be shaken before him and fall to the ground” (Isaiah XIX).

For there too we saw a temple in which, when the Savior entered the city, all the idols fell face down upon the ground at once.

In the wilderness there we saw a man named Apollo, who had monasteries upon the mountain. He was the father of approximately five hundred monks and was very famous and renowned throughout the Thebaid. His deeds were great; through him the Lord performed mighty works, and through him very many signs and wonders were accomplished.

From childhood he had displayed great discipline, and in mature age he attained such grace. When he was eighty years old, he gathered for himself a large monastery of perfect men, almost all of whom were able to perform signs.

When he had withdrawn from the world at the age of fifteen, spent forty years in the wilderness, and practiced every virtue there, he later seemed to hear the voice of God saying to him:

“Apollo, Apollo, through you I will abolish the wise men in Egypt and the prudence of prudent nations. With them you will destroy for me the wise men of Babylon and remove all demonic worship from the midst. Now go to the inhabited region, for you will generate for me a chosen people, zealous for good works.”

He replied: “Take arrogance away from me, Lord, lest I become exalted above the brotherhood and be deprived of every good work” (Titus II).

The divine voice said to him again: “Put your hand upon your neck; then seize and bury in the sand.”

As soon as he placed his hand upon his neck, he seized a little Ethiopian and buried him in the sand while he cried out: “I am the demon of pride.”

Again a voice came to him, saying: “Go, for whatever you ask from God, you will receive.”

When he first heard this, he went to the inhabited region in the time of the tyrant Julian, and then came to a nearby wilderness.

After taking possession of a small cave, he remained beneath the mountain. His practice was to recite prayers throughout the entire day: a hundred times at night and as many times by day, on his knees.

Even then, as before, his food was supplied by God in an extraordinary and unexpected manner. An angel brought him nourishment in the wilderness.

His clothing was a *lebiton*, which some call a *colobium*, and a small linen cloth upon his head. These were all that remained with him in the wilderness, and they did not grow old.

His wilderness was near the inhabited land. There he performed astonishing signs and virtues through the power of the Spirit. Because of the extraordinary greatness of the miracle, no one can recount them all, as we heard from the elders who lived with him. They too were perfect men and presided over many brothers.

He therefore quickly became famous and renowned, like some new prophet or apostle who had come to our age. When great fame about him had spread, all the monks living scattered throughout the surrounding region continually came to him, and, as to their own father, offered him their souls as gifts.

He urged some toward contemplation; others he trained to pursue the virtue expressed in action, first showing by his deeds what he admonished them to do in words. Often he displayed discipline to them. He spent Sundays with them, taking nothing himself beyond vegetables that grew spontaneously from the earth. Meanwhile he ate neither bread nor legume, nor anything from the fruit of trees, nor any food that is prepared by applying it to fire and used by human beings.

Once, in the time of Julian, he heard that a brother in the army had been captured and was being held bound in custody. He went to him with the brotherhood, asking and exhorting him to be brave and steadfast in his labors and to despise the dangers threatening him. He said that it was a time of contests, so that even then his soul might be tested by the assault of temptations.

After strengthening the man’s spirit with these words, the tribune arrived. Driven by some criminal impulse, and after someone had reported the matter to him, he closed the doors of the prison and shut inside both Apollo and all the monks who were with him, as though they would be suitable for military service. He stationed as many guards as seemed sufficient and returned home, refusing even to listen to their pleas.

In the middle of the night an angel appeared to the guards carrying a lamp and illuminating all who were in the prison, so brightly that the guards stood gaping in astonishment. When they rose, they begged the monks to depart, opening the doors for them. They declared that it was better for them to die than to despise the freedom that had come to those unjustly detained by divine intervention.

Therefore, when the tribune came in the morning with the magistrates to the prison, he insisted that the men leave the city. He said that his house had fallen in an earthquake and that the best of his servants had been crushed.

When the monks heard this, they gave thanks to God and went into the wilderness. They were all together, as the Apostle says, having “one heart and one soul” (Acts IV).

Every day Apollo taught them to adorn themselves with virtues and immediately to repel the devil’s devices in their thoughts at the outset. When the serpent’s head has been crushed, the whole body is dead.

The Lord commands us to guard the serpent’s head. This means that at the beginning we must not admit evil and shameful thoughts, not merely so that we may destroy the obscene fantasies of our mind, but so that we may strive to surpass one another in virtues, so that no one may appear inferior to another in these praises.

“This,” he said, “should be your sign of progress in virtue: when you have become empty of affections and desires. For these are the beginning of Christ’s gifts.

“When someone has received from God a manifestation of miracles, let him not swell up excessively, as though he had progressed sufficiently, or become elated in thought, as though he were already more honored than others. Nor should he display the fact that he has received such grace. Otherwise he deceives himself, having lost his reason, and will be deprived of grace.”

Thus he possessed this great teaching in his discourses, which we too often afterward heard from him. In his deeds he accomplished even greater things, for every request was immediately granted to him by God.

He also saw certain revelations. He saw his eldest brother, who had likewise reached completion in the wilderness and surpassed him in that beautiful way of life. Apollo had lived with him for a long time in the wilderness.

He seemed to see his brother seated upon the same throne as the apostles, having left him the inheritance of his virtues. Apollo therefore interceded on his own behalf, asking God that his translation might be swift and that he might grant him rest in heaven together with his brother.

The Savior seemed to say to him that he still had to remain for a short time on earth for the perfection of many, until many became imitators of his virtue. For a great multitude of monks would be credited to his faith, and a devout army would arise, so that he might obtain from God a glory worthy of his labors.

He saw these things, and they came to pass. For when many monks from every direction had gathered to him after hearing of him, and very many had renounced the world altogether through his teaching and manner of life, a common brotherhood was established. About five hundred brothers lived a common life with him, sharing one table and wearing entirely white garments.

In them Scripture was fulfilled, which says: “Rejoice, thirsty desert; burst forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, for the children of the desolate woman are many, more than those of her who has a husband” (Isaiah LIV).

This prophetic utterance was indeed fulfilled through the Church gathered from the nations. It was also completed in this Egyptian wilderness, which offers more children to God than the inhabited land.

Where are there in the cities as many flocks of those who are being saved as the Egyptian wildernesses offer to God? As many peoples as there are here, so many monks are there in the deserts.

It seems to me that the Apostle’s saying was fulfilled in them as well: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Romans V).

For formerly abundant and impious worship of idols prevailed in Egypt, more than among any other people. Some worshiped dogs and monkeys; others garlic and onions; and many regarded worthless vegetables as gods. We heard the holy Father himself recount these things and explain the reason for the former ignorance.

“The pagans who formerly lived among us,” he said, “regarded the ox as a god, because by means of it they practiced agriculture and procured food for themselves. They worshiped the water of the Nile, because it irrigates all the fields. They also worshiped the earth, because it was more fertile than all other regions.

“As for the remaining abominations—the dogs and monkeys, and the whole disgraceful worship of animals and vegetables—they worshiped them because their use had been an occasion of salvation for them. In the time of Pharaoh, these things occupied the people, while Pharaoh himself pursued Israel and was drowned.

“For each person attributed to the gods whatever had occupied him, since he had not followed Pharaoh, saying: ‘This was my god today, through which it came about that I did not perish together with Pharaoh.’”

These were the matters the holy Apollo discussed in his discourses.

Before the discourses, however, we should record what he accomplished in deeds.

At that time pagans still lived nearby throughout all the surrounding places, and the ten villages closest to him especially worshiped demons. In one village there was a very large temple and a particularly notable idol. The statue was wooden.

Impious priests led it in procession, carrying it around the villages. They raved together with the multitude, celebrating their rites as though they were honoring river water.

It happened that Apollo was there at that time with a few brothers. When he saw the multitude suddenly raging demonically throughout the region, he knelt before the Savior and caused all the pagans suddenly to become motionless.

Since they could not move from that place, pushing one another and being scorched by the heat throughout the day, and since they did not know why this had happened to them, their priests said that a Christian lived within their territory beneath the wilderness who was doing these things. They spoke of Apollo and said that they ought to supplicate him; otherwise they would come into danger.

When those who lived farther away heard the cries and lamentations, they approached and asked them: “What has suddenly happened to you? How did this come about?”

They replied that they did not know, except that they suspected a certain man and that they ought to appease him. Others testified that they had seen him passing by. Thus they begged that help be given them quickly.

They brought oxen and tried to move the idol, but it remained immovable together with the priests. Since they could find no means of escape, they sent a delegation through the neighboring inhabitants to Apollo, asking to be released from that error and allowed to depart.

When Apollo was informed of this, the man of God descended very quickly. After he had prayed, he released them all from the bond.

They all approached him with one mind, believing in the Savior of all and in God who performs wonders. They immediately committed the idol to the fire. After instructing them all in catechesis, he added them to the churches.

Many of them still live in the monasteries to this day. The fame of this event spread everywhere, and many believed in the Lord [Col. 1159A], so that no pagan was henceforth named within his territory.

Not long afterward, two villages began waging war against each other, disputing over fields. When Apollo was informed, he immediately went down to them to reconcile peace between them. Those who were on the opposing side did not obey but contradicted him, relying upon one of the leaders of the robbers, a man outstanding in warfare. When Apollo saw him contradicting him, he said to him: “If you obey, my friend, I shall ask my Lord that your sins be forgiven.” When the man heard this, he did not hesitate but cast down his weapons, fell at Apollo’s knees, and entreated him. When peace had been made through Apollo’s intercession, he sent his own men back home.

When they had made peace and departed, their distinguished champion followed Apollo thereafter, openly demanding the promise that had been made. The blessed Apollo took him into the nearby desert and admonished and urged him to be patient and steadfast in spirit, for God could indeed forgive him. When night came, both men saw in a dream that they were standing before Christ’s tribunal. Each of them saw angels worshiping God together with the righteous. When they themselves had fallen down with them, they worshiped the Father, and God’s voice came to them, saying: “What fellowship is there between light and darkness? Or what share has the faithful with the unbeliever?” (II Cor. II). “What connection, moreover, has a murderer with the righteous, since he is unworthy of such a vision? But you, depart, man; for this late-born fugitive has been granted to you.”

After they had seen and heard many other wondrous things—things which speech neither dares to utter nor the ear to hear—they awoke and announced them to those who lived with them. Great amazement seized everyone, since both men reported the same vision. The man who was no longer a murderer remained with the ascetics until death, correcting his life and being changed from a wolf into a simple and innocent lamb. In him also Isaiah’s prophecy was fulfilled, which says: “Wolves and lambs shall feed together, and the lion and the ox shall eat straw together” (Isaiah 65:25). There too one could see Ethiopians practicing asceticism with monks and surpassing many in virtue, and Scripture fulfilled in them, which says: “Ethiopia shall hasten to stretch out her hand to God” (Ps. 67:31).

At another time the pagans were fighting against Christian peasants over their boundaries. There was a multitude of armed men on both sides, and Apollo stood among them, reconciling peace between them. The pagan army’s standard-bearer resisted him in the battle. He was a grave and savage man, and he insisted and declared that he would not grant peace until death. Apollo said to him: “Then let what you have chosen happen to you; for no one except you will be killed. When you are dead, the earth will not be your tomb, but the bellies of beasts and vultures will be filled with you.”

His word immediately took effect: no one on either side was killed except the standard-bearer. Although they buried him in the sand, they found his limbs in the morning torn apart by hyenas and vultures. When the pagans saw the miracle and the fulfillment of what he had said, they all believed in the Savior and proclaimed Apollo a prophet.

Previously the holy Apollo had still been in a cave in the mountain with five other brothers, who were his first disciples when he had recently come from the desert. When the feast of Easter arrived and they had completed the worship of God, they were hungry for whatever could be found. There were a few dry loaves and some stored vegetables. Apollo said to them: “If we are faithful, my children, and truly sons of Christ, let each of you ask God for whatever food is pleasing to his heart.”

But they left everything to him, believing themselves unworthy of such grace. When he had prayed with a joyful countenance and they had all said “Amen,” certain completely unknown men came into the cave during the night. They said that they had come from a distant region, and they carried almost everything, including things of which they had not even heard and which do not grow in Egypt: garden produce of every kind, grapes, pomegranates, figs, and nuts—all out of season. They even brought some honeycombs that had been found, a vessel of fresh milk, enormous nicolauses, and clean, hot loaves from a foreign region.

[Note: [Col. 1225B] “And enormous nicolauses, and clean and hot loaves.” The Greek Venetian manuscript reads: Καὶ νικολάους παμμεγέθεις, ἄρτους δὲ καθαροὺς καὶ θερμούς (“and enormous nicolauses, but clean and hot loaves”). The Paris Greek edition has δέκα (“ten”) instead of δὲ (“but”). Hervetus was deceived and translated: “And enormous nicolauses, and pure lupins.” Evidently he read θέρμους, meaning “lupins,” instead of θερμοὺς, “hot.” See the notes on Book II of Rufinus, 7, II. 21.]

Those who had brought these things, having merely handed them over as though sent by a great and wealthy man, immediately withdrew in haste. When the monks had received the food, it was sufficient for them until Pentecost, so that they themselves marveled and said that it had truly been sent by God.

One of the monks asked the Father to pray to God immediately on his behalf, so that he might obtain some grace. When Apollo had prayed, the monk was given the grace of humility and gentleness, to such an extent that everyone marveled that he was so meek. The brothers who had been with Apollo told us about these virtues of his, and many other brothers also bore witness to them.

Indeed, not long before, when there had once been a famine in the Thebaid, the people who lived in those regions heard that the monks who were with Apollo were being fed every day beyond all hope and expectation. With one accord they came to him with their wives and children, asking together for a blessing and for food. Apollo, fearing nothing—not even that food might someday fail him—gave to everyone who came whatever would suffice for that day.

Only three large baskets of loaves remained. As the famine grew more severe, he ordered the baskets to be brought into the middle, since the monks were hungry that day. With all the brothers and the multitude of the people listening, he said in a loud voice: “Is the hand of the Lord not powerful enough to fill these?” The Holy Spirit says: “Bread shall not fail from these baskets until we have been satisfied with new grain.”

All who were present then affirmed that the loaves were sufficient for four months. The same happened with oil and grain, so that Satan came and said to him: “Are you Elijah, or one of the other prophets and apostles, that you do these things?”

Apollo said to him: “What then? Were not the apostles and prophets holy men who handed these things down to us? Or was God present then but has now gone abroad? God can always do these things, and there is nothing he cannot do. If God is good, why are you evil? Why should we not also tell what we have seen—namely, that brothers would enter carrying baskets and bring loaves to the tables, and, after five hundred brothers had eaten their fill, would receive the baskets back full again?”

Another miracle, which we saw and were astonished by, ought also to be related. When we had come within three days’ journey of them, we were recognized from a distance by the brothers, who had heard of our coming to Apollo. They hurried out to meet us, singing psalms—for this is the custom among all monks. After prostrating themselves and worshiping on the ground, they kissed us, pointed us out to one another, and said: “Look, the brothers have come of whom our father spoke three days ago, saying: ‘After three days three brothers will come to us from Jerusalem.’”

Some of them led us, while others followed behind us, singing psalms, until we came near Apollo himself. When Father Apollo heard the voice of those singing psalms, he came to meet us, as was his custom toward all the brothers. When he saw us, he was the first to worship, stretching himself out on the ground. When he had risen, he kissed us; and after he had brought us inside, he prayed and washed our feet with his own hands, urging us to take refreshment. He did this for all the brothers who came to him.

The brothers who were with him did not receive food before they had shared in the Eucharist of Christ. They did this at the ninth hour of the day. Then, after eating in this manner, they sat listening to him teach all the commandments until the first sleep. From there some of them withdrew into the desert, reciting the Scriptures from memory throughout the night; others remained there, praising God with unceasing hymns until daybreak. I saw them with my own eyes: having begun their hymns in the evening, they did not cease singing until morning.

Many of them descended from the mountain only at the ninth hour, received the Eucharist, and then climbed back up, content with spiritual nourishment until the next ninth hour. Some did this for many days. One could see them rejoicing in the desert, to such an extent that no other such rejoicing, nor any bodily happiness, could be seen on earth. No one among them was dejected or sad. If anyone appeared to be displaying sadness, Father Apollo immediately asked him the reason and revealed what was hidden in each person’s heart.

He used to say: “We ought not to be sad on account of salvation, since we are going to be heirs of the kingdom of heaven. The pagans will be sad, the Jews will weep, and sinners will mourn; but the righteous will rejoice. Those who occupy their minds with earthly things rejoice in earthly matters; but we, who have been deemed worthy of so great a hope—how could we not rejoice forever, since the Apostle urges us always to rejoice and to give thanks in all things?” (1 Thess. 5:16–18).

Who could describe the grace of his speech and his other virtues, which, because of their extraordinary greatness, we have passed over in silence, although we heard of them from him himself and from others?

When he had often discussed privately with us ascetic discipline and the ordering of life, he also frequently spoke about receiving monks. He said that one ought to worship the brothers who arrive: “For,” he said, “you have not worshiped them, but God. For you have seen your brother? You have seen the Lord your God. We received this from Abraham” (Gen. 18). He also said that one ought sometimes to compel brothers to take refreshment; “we received this from Lot, who compelled the angels” (Gen. 19). He said that monks ought, if possible, to share daily in the sacraments. “For whoever keeps himself far from them, God also withdraws far from him. But whoever does this continually continually receives the Savior. For there is a saving word: ‘Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him’” (John 6:56).

This remembrance of the saving Passion benefits monks who practice it continually and prepare themselves daily, so that at all times they may be worthy to receive the heavenly sacraments, since by this means also they obtain forgiveness of sins.

The Catholic and universal fasts may not be broken without great necessity. On Wednesday the Savior was betrayed, and on Friday he was crucified. Whoever therefore breaks it at the same time betrays and crucifies the Savior. But if a brother who needs to be refreshed comes to you while it is a fast, set a table for him alone. If he does not wish to eat, do not compel him, for we have a common tradition.”

He strongly reproved those who carried iron and grew their hair long. “They display themselves,” he said, “and seek to please human beings, when they ought rather to mortify the body with fasts and do what is good in secret. They do not act in this way, but expose themselves to everyone.”

And why say more? His entire teaching resembled the ordering of his life, which no one could adequately write or describe. After discussing many things privately with us, often for a whole week, he finally dismissed us, saying: “Have peace among yourselves, and do not separate from one another on the road.”

When he had asked the brothers who were with him which of them wished to lead us to visit the other Fathers, the holy Apollo chose three men who were capable both in speech and in their manner of life and who were skilled in the Greek, Roman, and Egyptian languages. Dismissing us with them, he ordered them not to leave us before our desire to see the Fathers had been satisfied. If anyone wished to see them all, an entire lifetime would not suffice to visit them.

After blessing us, he sent us away, saying: “May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of your life” (Ps. 127:5).

As we were walking at midday through the desert, we saw the track of a great dragon, stretched across the sand like a beam. When we saw it, great fear seized us. But the brothers who were leading us urged us not to be afraid, but to be courageous and follow the dragon’s track.

“You will see,” they said, “our faith, when we ourselves overcome it with our hands. We have killed many dragons and horned serpents with our hands, as it is written. For in us was fulfilled the saying: ‘I have given you authority to walk upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy’” (Luke 10:19).

But we, overcome by unbelief and seized by even greater fear, begged them not to go by the dragon’s tracks but by the straight road. One of the brothers, with great eagerness, left us there and went into the desert in search of the beast. When he found it not far from its cave, he shouted loudly that the dragon was in the cavern and called the others to come and see what would happen. While the other brothers urged us not to be afraid, we went with great fear to see the beast.

Suddenly one of the brothers came toward us, seized us by the hand, and dragged us to his monastery. He said that we could not withstand the beast’s attack, especially since we had not yet seen one like it, whereas he himself had often seen that beast, which was so immense that it was more than fifteen cubits long.

After ordering us to remain where we were, he went to the brother and told him to withdraw from the cavern, for that man was trying not to leave the place before killing the dragon. When he had persuaded him, he led him to us, rebuking our weak faith. We rested with that brother, whose monastery was about one mile away, and were sufficiently refreshed.

## CHAPTER LIII. The Life of Abbot Amun

He told us that in the place where he himself lived there had been a holy man, whose disciple he had been, named Amun (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 8, calls him Ammon). Amun performed many miracles in that place. Robbers often came to him and took his bread and provisions.

Taking this badly, Amun one day went out into the desert and brought back with him two great dragons. He ordered them to remain in that place and guard the gate. When the murderers came, as was their custom, and saw the miracle, they fell on their faces, gaping with astonishment.

Amun went out and found them mute and almost half dead. When he had roused them, he rebuked them, saying: “See how much more savage than wild beasts you are. These creatures, for God’s sake, obey our will; but you have neither feared God nor respected the religion of the Christians.”

After bringing them into his cell, he set a table before them and urged them to change their ways. When they rose, they immediately appeared to be much better men; and not long afterward they too were seen performing the same signs.

“On another occasion,” he said, “when a great dragon was devastating the neighboring region and killing many animals, all who lived near the desert came together to the Father, asking that the beast be removed from their territory. He dismissed them as though he could do nothing for them in their distress.

“But when he rose in the morning, he went to the place through which the beast was to pass. After bending his knees three times in prayer, the beast came toward him, emitting a heavy breath with a great hiss, swelling and whistling, and producing a foul vapor.

“Without being frightened, he turned toward the dragon and said: ‘Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, who is to overcome the great sea-monster, will conquer you.’ When he had said this, the dragon immediately burst open, vomiting all its poison together with blood through its mouth.

“When the peasants came the next day and saw that great miracle, and could not endure the stench, they heaped a great quantity of sand upon the animal. The Father stood there with them, for although the dragon was dead, they did not dare approach it.”

[Col. 1164B] “But when a boy who was pasturing suddenly saw that the dragon was still alive, he immediately lost his reason and became lifeless. The boy lay there in the desert all day, breathing nothing. When his relatives found him in the evening, barely breathing and completely swollen from his ecstasy, they brought him to the Father, not knowing the cause of what had happened.

“When the Father had prayed and anointed him with oil, the boy rose and recounted what he had seen. At this the man was deeply moved and turned to kill the dragon.”

## CHAPTER LIV. The Life of Abbot Copres the Presbyter

[Note: [Col. 1225C] Copres. Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 28; Cassiodorus, Book VIII, chapter 50; Nicephorus, Book II, chapter 34.]

There was there a certain presbyter who had a monastery in the desert nearby, named Copres (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 9). He was a holy man, nearly ninety years old, superior of fifty brothers. He too performed many miracles: healing diseases, effecting many cures, driving out demons, and accomplishing many other things—indeed, some of them before our own eyes.

When he saw us, he greeted us and prayed for us. After washing our feet, he asked us what was happening in the world. We, however, asked him instead to explain to us the virtues of his manner of life, how God had bestowed gifts upon him, and by what means he had become a participant in God’s grace.

He was not at all lifted up by pride on this account, but told us about his own life and about his predecessors who had surpassed him, whose manner of life he had imitated. “My children,” he said, “what is done by me is not remarkable when compared with what was accomplished in the lives of our Fathers.”

As the presbyter Copres was telling us what the Fathers had rightly and virtuously accomplished, one of our brothers, who was dozing and did not at all believe what was being said, saw in Copres’s hands a marvelous book written in golden letters, and an old man standing beside him, threatening him and saying: “Are you not listening attentively to the reading, but sleeping?”

The brother was shaken. While we listened, he immediately explained in Latin what he had heard and seen. While he was still telling us these things, a certain peasant arrived carrying a basket of sand. He waited until the brother had finished his account. We asked the presbyter: “What does the peasant with the sand mean?”

The Father answered us, saying: “My little children, I ought not to have gloried before you, nor to have related what was accomplished by the Fathers, lest, becoming proud in mind, we lose our reward. But because of your zeal and benefit—for you have come to us from so far away—I shall not deprive you of the benefit. I shall tell the brothers who are present what the Savior has accomplished through us.”

A field near us was barren. The peasants who owned it, when they sowed, scarcely harvested twice the amount of seed, because a worm that developed in the ear ruined the entire crop. The farmers, having been instructed by us in the catechism and become Christians, asked us to pray for the harvest.

I said to them: “If you have faith in God, even the sand of the desert will bring you fruit.” Without hesitation they filled their laps with this sand, which we tread upon, and brought it to us, asking us to bless it.

After I had prayed that it might be done for them according to their faith, they sowed it together with grain in their fields. Suddenly their field multiplied its produce so greatly that it surpassed all Egypt. They have made a practice of doing this, and each year they cause us considerable trouble.

“God also granted me a great miracle in the presence of many people. When I once went down into the city, I found a Manichaean who had led the people astray. Since I could not persuade him publicly, I turned to the crowd and said: ‘Light a great pyre in the square, and let us enter the flames. Whoever among us remains unharmed by the fire has the true faith.’

“When this had been done and the crowd quickly lit the pyre, they were dragging him with me into the fire. He said: ‘Let each of us enter separately, and you, who gave the order, must enter first.’

“After I had made the sign of Christ and entered, the flame divided to this side and that and caused me no harm, although I remained in it for half an hour. When the crowd saw the miracle, they shouted and compelled him to pass through the fire. He refused, overcome by fear. The people seized him and pushed him into the middle; completely burned by the flame, he was expelled from the city while the people shouted: ‘Burn the living deceiver!’

“But the crowd took me and, praising me, led me to the church.”

When I was once passing by a certain temple, some pagans were sacrificing to their idols. I said to them: “Why, although you possess reason, do you sacrifice to things without reason? And why are you henceforth more devoid of reason than they are?”

Since I had spoken rightly, they immediately followed me, believing in the Savior.

On another occasion I had a garden in a nearby field for the sake of the brotherhood that came to us, and a poor man worked it. A certain pagan entered to steal vegetables. When he had stolen them and departed, he could not cook them for three hours; they remained in the pot just as he had taken them, since the water would not heat at all.

The man came to himself, brought the vegetables to us, and asked that his error be forgiven and that he might become a Christian. This was done. At that very hour there were brothers visiting us as guests, and the vegetables were brought to us at exactly the right time. When we had eaten them, we gave thanks to the Lord, receiving a double joy: both at the man’s salvation and at the refreshment of the brothers.

## CHAPTER LV. The Life of Abbot Surus

“Abbot Surus,” he said, “and Isaiah (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 10), and Paul suddenly met one another at the river. They were devout and outstanding ascetics, going to visit the great Abbot Anuph. They were separated by a distance of three stages. They said to one another: ‘Let each of us display his manner of life and how he has been honored by God in this life.’

“Abbot Surus said to them: ‘I ask God for the gift that, by the power of the tireless Spirit, we may reach the place.’ When he had prayed only once, a boat was immediately found ready, with a favorable wind, and in a moment they were at the place, although they had sailed against the current.”

## CHAPTER LVI. The Life of Abbot Isaiah

Isaiah said to them: “And what is surprising, my friends, if a man should meet us who will recount the life of each one?” (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 10.)

## CHAPTER LVII. The Life of Abbot Paul

Paul said to them: “If God has revealed to us that he is taking a man away after three days…”

When they had gone a little farther, a man met them and greeted them. Paul said to him: “Tell us what you have done rightly, for the day after tomorrow you will depart to God” (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 10).

## CHAPTER LVIII. The Life of Abbot Anuph

[Note: [Col. 1225C] Anuph. Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 14.]

Anuph said to them: “Blessed be God, who has also revealed these things to me: both your manner of life and your arrival” (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 10).

After he had stated what each of them had done rightly, he then explained what he himself had done, saying:

“From the time when I professed the Savior’s name on earth, no lie has come out of my mouth. I have taken no human food, since an angel feeds me daily with heavenly nourishment. No desire for anything else has entered my heart except desire for God. God has concealed nothing from me among earthly things without signifying and showing it to me.

“I have not slept by day, nor rested by night, while seeking God. One angel was always present with me, showing me the powers of the world. The light of my thought was never extinguished. I received every petition from God immediately.

“I have often seen myriads of angels standing before God. I have seen choirs of the righteous, a multitude of martyrs, and the manner of life of monks. I have seen the work of all those who praise God. I have seen Satan handed over to fire, his angels punished, and the righteous rejoicing forever.”

After recounting these and many other things, he gave up his soul on the third day. The angels and choirs of martyrs immediately received it and carried it up into the heavens, while those present saw and heard their hymns.

## CHAPTER LIX. The Life of Abbot Hellen

[Note: [Col. 1225C] Hellen. Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 28; Cassiodorus, Book VIII, chapter 50; Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 34.]

Another Father, named Abbot Hellen (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 11), had practiced asceticism vigorously from an early age. He often carried fire in his bosom, inciting the brothers nearby to display signs of power. He said to them: “If you truly practice asceticism, display signs of virtue from now on.”

On one occasion, while he was alone in the desert, a desire for honey came over him. When he immediately found honeycombs beneath a rock, he said: “Depart from me, intemperate desire; for it is written: ‘Walk by the Spirit, and you shall not fulfill the desire of the flesh’” (Gal. 5:16). Leaving the honeycombs, he went away.

After he had fasted in the desert for three weeks, he found scattered fruits and said: “I shall not eat or touch any of these, lest I scandalize my brother—that is, my soul. For it is written: ‘Man does not live by bread alone’” (Matt. 4:4; Luke 4:4).

After he had fasted another week, he later fell asleep. An angel came to him in a dream and said: “Rise, take what is to be found, and eat.”

He rose and, looking around, saw a spring surrounded by a circular growth of delicate herbs. When he had taken the drink and eaten the vegetables, he declared that nothing had ever been more pleasant to him.

When he found a small cave in that place, he remained there fasting for a few days. Whenever he needed food, he prayed on bent knees, and every kind of food was immediately set before him, together with hot bread, olives, and various fruits.

On another occasion he visited his brothers. After giving them much instruction, he set out for the desert, carrying certain things necessary for their use. When he saw some wild asses grazing, he said to them: “In the name of Jesus Christ, let one of you come and carry my burden.”

One of them immediately approached him. After he had placed his belongings upon it and mounted it, he reached the cave in a single day. When he had put the bread and fruit down in the sun, wild beasts came to them, as they are accustomed to come to a spring. As soon as they touched only the bread, they died.

On another occasion he came to some monks on the Lord’s Day and said to them: “Why have you not held the synaxis today?”

When they openly said, “Because the presbyter has not come,” he said to them: “I shall go and call him.”

They said that no one could cross the channel because of its depth. They also said that a huge beast was in that place—a crocodile that had devoured many people.

Without hesitation he immediately rose and went to the ford. The beast received him on its back and carried him to the farther bank. When he found the presbyter in the field, he asked him not to disregard the brotherhood.

Seeing Hellen dressed in many patched garments, the presbyter asked him where he had obtained the cloth, saying: “You have a most beautiful garment for the soul, brother.” Admiring his humility and frugality, he followed him as he returned to the river.

When they could not find a boat in which they might cross, Abbot Hellen called out to the crocodile. It immediately obeyed him and presented its back. He asked the presbyter to climb on with him, but the presbyter, overcome with fear at the sight of the beast, drew back.

While he was still filled with astonishment, the brothers who lived on the opposite bank saw Hellen crossing the channel with the beast. When he had climbed ashore, he drew the beast along with him, saying that it was better for it to die than to incur punishment for the souls it had destroyed. When it fell, it immediately died.

He remained with the brothers for three days, sitting and teaching them the commandments and openly revealing each one’s hidden thoughts. He said that one man was troubled by fornication, another by vainglory, another by pleasures, and another by anger; one, he declared, was meek, and another peaceable.
