He rebuked the vices of the former and praised the virtues of the latter.

When they heard these things, they marveled, saying that they were truly so. He said to them: “Prepare vegetables for us, for many brothers will come to us today.” While they were still preparing them, the arriving brothers greeted one another.

One of the brothers asked Hellen if he might live with him in the desert. When Hellen said that he could not endure the demons’ temptations, the man insisted that he would endure everything. Hellen received him and ordered him to live in another cave.

The demons came to him at night and began to strangle him, after first disturbing him with shameful thoughts. He ran out and reported to Abbot Hellen what had happened. Hellen impressed the sign of the cross upon the place and then ordered him to remain there safely.

On another occasion, when the bread in his cave had run out, an angel came in the form of a brother and brought him food.

Again, ten brothers were once looking for Hellen. They wandered through the desert, having already remained fasting for seven days. When he found them, he ordered them to rest in the cave. They, however, reminded him that they needed food.

Since he had nothing to set before them, he said: “God is able to prepare a table in the desert.” Immediately, while they were praying, a certain young man from the ferryboat knocked at the door. When Hellen opened it, they saw a young man carrying a large basket of bread and olives. After receiving these things, they ate and gave thanks to God, while the young man immediately disappeared.

After Father Copres had told us these and many other miracles, and had treated us kindly and humanely, he led us into his garden and showed us palm trees and other fruit-bearing trees that he himself had planted in the desert. He had been encouraged by the faith of the peasants, to whom he had said: “Can the desert produce fruit for those who have faith in God?”

“After I saw,” he said, “that those who had sown sand had harvested a crop from their field, I too attempted the same thing and obtained the same result.”

## CHAPTER LX. The Life of Abbot Apelles

[Note: [Col. 1225C] Apelles. Sozomen, Cassiodorus, and Nicephorus, in the same places.]

[Col. 1169A]

We also saw another presbyter in the upper region, named Apelles (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 15), a righteous man who had first practiced the craft of copper-working and afterward turned to asceticism.

When the devil came to him in the form of a woman, at a time when he was working on certain metal objects for the monks’ use, Apelles snatched an iron plate from the fire and, taking it in his hand because of the urgency of the moment, burned the devil’s entire face and body. The brothers heard her howling in the cell.

From that time onward the man always held burning iron in his hand, and he was not harmed. When he received us kindly and humanely, he told us about the renowned and God-worthy men who had been with him and were still alive.

## CHAPTER LXI. The Life of Another John

[Note: [Col. 1225C] John. Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 30.]

“There is,” he said, “in this desert our brother named John (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 15), a man of another generation who surpasses all the monks in virtue. No one can find him quickly, because he continually moves from place to place in the deserts.

“At first he stood for three years beneath a certain cliff, praying continually. He never sat down and never slept except insofar as, while standing, he stole a little sleep. He ate nothing except the Eucharist, which the presbyter brought to him on the Lord’s Day.

“Indeed, one day Satan transformed himself into a presbyter and went to him quickly, pretending that he wished to give him the Eucharist. When the blessed John recognized him, he said: ‘O father of every fraud and wickedness, enemy of all righteousness, will you not cease deceiving Christian souls? Do you dare insult the holy Sacraments?’

“The devil answered him: ‘I came very near gaining you by casting you down. For in this way also I deceived one of your brothers and drove him out of his mind into madness. Many righteous men pleaded earnestly for him, and they could scarcely bring it about that he should recover his sanity.’

“When the demon had said this, he departed from him.”

When his feet had become ulcerated because he had stood motionless for so long, and pus was issuing from them, an angel came, touched his body, and said: “Christ will be your true food, and the Holy Spirit your true drink; for the present, however, spiritual nourishment is sufficient for you, lest, being filled, you vomit it up.” And when he had healed him, he removed him from that place.

Afterward he lived in solitude, wandering about and eating herbs; but on the Lord’s Day he was found in the same place receiving Communion. When he had asked a presbyter for a few palm branches, he made belts for animals. When a certain lame man wished to come to him to be healed and had mounted only a donkey, as soon as the animal’s feet touched the belt made by the holy man, he was immediately cured. At other times he sent blessings to the sick [Note: [Col. 1225C] “He sent blessings.” Hervetus, the translator, rendered this “he dispatched blessings.” See the *Onomasticon*.], and they were at once freed from their illnesses.

Moreover, it was revealed concerning his monasteries that some of those living in them were not ordering their lives rightly. Through a presbyter he wrote letters to them all, saying that some were devoted to idleness, while others were striving toward virtue; and the truth was found to be as he had said. He also wrote to their Fathers that some of them were insufficiently concerned for the salvation of the brothers, while others exhorted them as much as was necessary; and he announced the honors and punishments of both groups.

Again, urging others toward a more perfect condition, he admonished them to transfer themselves from sensible things to those perceived by the intellect. “It is time,” he said, “to display henceforth such a way of life. We ought not always to remain children and infants, but already to apply ourselves to more mature thoughts, to attain the virtue of a great and lofty spirit, and to undertake the other highest virtues.”

These and many other things our Father told us about this Father. We have not written down everything, because they exceed the bounds of ordinary miracle—not because they are untrue, but because of the unbelief of certain people. We ourselves, however, were sufficiently assured of these matters, since many eminent men related them to us, men who had seen them with their own eyes.

## CHAPTER LXII. On Abbot Paphnutius [Note: [Col. 1225C] “Paphnutius.” Concerning the various Paphnutiuses, see what was said above in Book II of Rufinus, chapter 16.]

We also saw the place of Paphnutius the anchorite, a great man endowed with virtue, who was brought to completion not long before in the region around the Heracleotic district of the Thebaid. Many people related many things about him (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 16).

## CHAPTER LXIII. On the Piper

After much ascetic discipline, he asked God to reveal to him which of the saints who had conducted themselves rightly he resembled (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 16). An angel appeared to him and said: “You resemble the piper who lives in this city.”

He went eagerly to the man, asked him about his manner of life, and carefully investigated all his deeds. The man told him what was in fact true: that he was a sinner, a drunkard, and a fornicator; and that, not long before, he had come there from the profession of brigandage.

When he was carefully questioned about anything he had ever done rightly, he said that he knew of no honorable deed of his, except that once, when he was living the life of a robber, he had rescued a Christian virgin whom the robbers intended to violate and had escorted her by night as far as her village.

“Again,” he said, “I once found a beautiful woman wandering in the wilderness, driven away by the bailiffs and officials of the governor and the senators because of her husband’s public debt, and lamenting her misfortune. I asked her the reason for her weeping. She said:

‘Do not question me, my lord, nor examine me, unhappy woman that I am; but take me away as your slave wherever you wish. For since my husband was repeatedly flogged and imprisoned for two years because of a public debt of three hundred gold pieces, and my three beloved sons were sold, I have fled, changing from place to place. Now, wandering through the wilderness, repeatedly discovered and constantly beaten, I have remained fasting in the wilderness for three days.’

“Having pitied her,” the robber continued, “I led her into a cave, gave her three hundred gold pieces, escorted her to the city, and secured the release of her husband and children, without any disgrace or insult.”

Paphnutius replied: “I am conscious of no deed such as this; but in ascetic discipline you have certainly heard that I am renowned, for I have not passed my life in idleness. God has revealed to me that in your deeds you are in no way inferior to me. Therefore, brother, if you are not regarded as insignificant by the Godhead, do not carelessly neglect your soul.”

Immediately he threw down the pipes he held in his hands, and the musical harmony of the lyre was transformed into a spiritual melody. He followed the man into the desert. After disciplining himself with all his strength for three years and spending the time of his life in hymns and prayers, he set out on the journey to heaven. He was numbered among the choirs of angels and the ranks of the righteous, and entered into rest.

## CHAPTER LXIV. On the Chief Magistrate

After he had first sent to God the man who had practiced virtue, imposing upon himself a way of life more demanding and exacting than before, he asked God to reveal to him which saint he resembled. Again a divine voice came to him, saying: “You resemble the chief magistrate of the neighboring village” (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 16).

He went to him with great speed. When he knocked at the door, the man came out, as was his custom, to receive a guest. He washed his feet, set a table before him, and urged him to eat.

When Paphnutius asked about his deeds and said to him, “Tell me, man, the ordering of your life; for, as God has shown me, you have surpassed many monks,” the man replied that he was a sinner and unworthy of the name of monk.

When Paphnutius persisted in questioning him, the man answered:

“I have no need to relate the things I have done; but since you say that you have come from God, I will tell you what concerns me. It is now thirty years since I separated from my wife, after having lived with her for only three years and having had three sons by her; they now also serve me in my affairs. I have never ceased practicing hospitality up to this very day. Let none of my companions boast that he received a guest before I did. No poor man or traveler has left my courtyard empty-handed without first being supplied with suitable provisions.

“I have not passed by a poor man afflicted by misfortune without supplying him with whatever consolation was sufficient. I have not favored my son in judgment. No one else’s produce has entered my house. There has been no dispute that I did not settle and reconcile. No one has rebuked my sons for behaving dishonorably. My herds have not touched another’s crops. I was not the first to sow my fields; rather, after making them common to all, I gathered whatever remained.

“I have not allowed a poor man to be oppressed by the power of a rich man. I have not caused anyone distress during my life. I have never pronounced an evil judgment against anyone. With God’s will, I am conscious of having done these things.”

When Paphnutius had heard of the man’s virtues, he kissed his head and said: “May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see the good of Jerusalem all the days of your life” (Psalm 127). “In these matters you have conducted yourself rightly. One thing remains for you, the chief of virtues: the all-wise knowledge of God, which you will not be able to attain without labor unless you renounce yourself from the world, take up the cross, and follow the Savior.”

When the man heard this, he immediately followed him to the mountain, without even bidding farewell to his household. When they came to a river and no boat was found, Paphnutius ordered him to cross the river on foot, although because of its depth no one had crossed it on foot at that time. When they had crossed and the water had reached their waists, he settled him in a certain place.

After separating from him, Paphnutius asked God that he might appear superior to such men. Not long afterward, he saw the man’s soul being taken up by angels, who praised God and said: “Blessed is the one whom you chose and took up; he shall dwell in your courts” (Psalm 64). Again, the righteous answered, saying: “Great peace belongs to those who love your law, and there is no stumbling-block for them” (Psalm 118). Then he understood that the man had died.

## CHAPTER LXV. On the Merchant [Note: [Col. 1225C] “Merchant.” Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 31; Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 38.]

While Abbot Paphnutius continued to worship God with prayers and to multiply his fasts, he again asked that it be shown to him whom he resembled (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 6). Again a divine voice said to him:

“You resemble a merchant seeking good pearls. But rise henceforth and do not delay, for a man resembling you will meet you.”

When he had gone down, he saw a merchant from Alexandria, devout and devoted to Christ, who traded in twenty thousand gold pieces and was coming down from Upper Thebaid with one hundred ships. He had distributed all his possessions and merchandise among the poor. This man was bringing him, together with his sons, ten sacks of vegetables.

“And what is this, my friend?” Paphnutius asked him.

The man replied: “These are the fruits of my trade, which are offered to God for a proper meal.”

“But what are these things,” Paphnutius asked him, “and you yourself do not share in our calling?”

He confessed that he was eagerly striving toward it.

Paphnutius replied: “How long, then, will you conduct an earthly business and not attain the heavenly merchandise? You will leave these things to others; but attach yourself to what is most fitting and follow the Savior, for you will soon go to him.”

Without delay, the man ordered his sons to distribute the remaining goods to the poor. He himself went up into the mountain and shut himself in at the place where the two earlier men had been brought to completion. He persevered in prayers. After a short time, leaving the body, he became a citizen of heaven.

After he too had sent him ahead into heaven, Paphnutius himself lost heart, since he could no longer continue his ascetic discipline. An angel stood beside him and said: “Come here henceforth; come, blessed one, into the eternal tabernacles of God. The prophets have come to receive you into their choirs. I did not reveal this to you earlier, lest, if you became elated, something should be taken away from your merits.”

After he had lived only one further day, certain presbyters came to him through a revelation. After relating all these things to them, he surrendered his soul. The presbyters clearly saw him being taken up among the choirs of the righteous and the angels, and they praised God.

## CHAPTER LXVI. The Life of Abbot Apollonius [Note: [Col. 1225C] “Apollonius.” I am uncertain whether this is the Apollonius mentioned by Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 29, and by Cassiodorus on the basis of him, Book VIII of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 3; Nicephorus, Book IX, chapter 14. See the notes on Rufinus above, Book II, chapter 19.]

There was in the Thebaid a certain monk named Apollonius (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 19). He displayed very many virtues and excellent deeds, and he was also considered worthy of the gift of teaching beyond many who were then distinguished for their virtues. During the persecution, he encouraged Christ’s confessors and made many martyrs. He himself, moreover, was arrested and kept in prison. The more wicked among the pagans came to him, disputed with him, assailed him with curses, and mocked him.

## CHAPTER LXVI. On Philemon [Note: [Col. 1225D] “Philemon.” See what was said concerning Rufinus in the same book and chapter.] the Martyr and Those Who Were Martyred with Him

One of them was a flute-player accompanying a chorus, a man notorious for his wickedness. He approached Apollonius and attacked him with insults, calling him impious, an impostor, a deceiver, hated by everyone, and one who ought to die as soon as possible (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 19).

Apollonius said to him: “The Lord will have mercy on you, man, and none of what you have said will be counted against you as sin.”

When the chorus-singer, whose name was Philemon, heard this, he was stung in his heart and pierced by Apollonius’s words. He immediately went to the tribunal, presented himself before the judge, and said in the presence of the people:

“You are acting unjustly, judge, in punishing pious men who are guilty of no offense; for Christians neither do nor say anything evil.”

At first, while he was saying these things, the judge thought that he was speaking ironically and making sport of him. But when he saw that Philemon persisted, he said: “You are mad, man; your mind has suddenly been deranged.”

Philemon replied: “I am not mad, most unjust judge; I am a Christian.”

The judge, together with the crowd, tried by many flatteries to persuade him. When he saw that Philemon remained unmoved, he subjected him to every kind of torture. After seizing Apollonius and treating him with many insults, he tortured him as a deceiver.

Apollonius said to him: “I would wish, judge, that you and all who are present would follow me in this error of mine.”

While he was saying this, the judge ordered that both men be handed over to the fire, with the entire people watching. When they were in the flames in the presence of the judge, blessed Apollonius raised his voice to God, and the entire people and the judge heard him:

“Do not deliver, Lord, to the beasts the soul that confesses you, but openly reveal yourself to us” (Psalm 73).

A dewy and radiant cloud came and covered the men, extinguishing the fire. The crowds and the judge marveled and cried out: “There is one God, the God of the Christians!”

But some sorcerer reported these events to the prefect of Alexandria. The prefect selected certain cruel and savage guards and officials and sent them to bring the judge and Philemon in chains. Apollonius, together with certain other confessors, was led along with them.

As they all set out on the journey, grace came upon Apollonius, and he began to teach the soldiers. When they too were pierced in their hearts and believed in the Savior, they were all bound together in one mind.

When the prefect saw that none of them could be moved from the faith, he ordered them to be thrown into the depths of the sea. This became for them a sign of baptism. When their own people found them scattered along the shore, they built one shrine for them all, where many miracles are now performed.

Such was the man’s grace that whatever he prayed for was immediately granted, so greatly did the Savior honor him. We too, having invoked him in the martyr-shrine [Note: [Col. 1225D] “In the martyr-shrine,” that is, in the church of the martyrs. See the *Onomasticon*.], saw him, together with those who had suffered martyrdom with him, worshiping God; and we greeted their tabernacles [Note: [Col. 1225D] “Tabernacles.” In Greek, σκηνώματα. Our Fronto substitutes *corpora*, “bodies.” For either word, σκήνωμα is used, as also for “tabernacle.”] [Col. 1174B] in the Thebaid.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. The Life of Abbot Dioscorus [Note: [Col. 1225D] “Dioscorus.” He is called a presbyter here. Therefore he seems distinct from Dioscorus the bishop, mentioned above in chapter 10—unless he was first a presbyter and later became a bishop. See what was said above concerning our Dioscorus in Rufinus, Book II, chapter 20, where we cited other authors concerning him.] the Presbyter

We also saw another presbyter in the Thebaid, named Dioscorus, the Father of one hundred monks (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 20). When they were about to approach the grace of God, he would say to them:

“See to it that no one who has had a nocturnal fantasy of a woman dares approach the holy Sacraments. Let none of you who has dreamed under the influence of visions and fantasies come forward. For emissions of semen that occur without fantasies happen by accident; they are not present through the free choice of each person’s mind, but without the will. They proceed from nature and are expelled from an excess of matter; therefore they are not liable to sin. Visions and fantasies, however, proceed from the free will of choice and are evidence of an evil mind.

“A monk ought,” he said, “to leap beyond even the law of nature: he must liquefy the body and not be found in any defilement of the flesh, but mortify the flesh and not allow matter to accumulate in it. Strive, therefore, to drain it by frequent and prolonged fasts; otherwise it incites us to appetites and desires. A monk ought not to touch the appetites of the mind. For in what would he differ from worldly people, whom we often see abstaining from pleasures for the sake of bodily health or for some other reason not at all contrary to reason? How much more, he said, must a monk care for the health of the soul and spirit!”

## CHAPTER LXIX. The Nitrian Anchorites [Note: [Col. 1225D] “Nitrian.” See the notes above on Rufinus, Book II, chapter 21.]

We also came to the Nitrian region, where we saw many great anchorites, some natives and some visitors. They surpassed one another in virtue, practiced with great zeal, and competed with one another in the conduct of their lives (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 21).

Some of them devoted themselves to contemplation, others to active works. When some of them saw us approaching from a distance, some came out to meet us with water; others washed our feet; others cleaned our garments; others invited us to eat; and others invited us to contemplation and the knowledge of God. Each one endeavored to help us in whatever he was able.

And who could recount all their virtues, when no one could describe them worthily? They inhabit a deserted place and have cells widely separated from one another, so that no one can recognize another at a distance, nor quickly see him, nor hear his voice. They live in profound quiet, each one shut in by himself.

They gather only on Saturday and Sunday in the churches and receive one another. Many of them are often found remaining in their cells for four days, since they do not see one another except at the assembly. Some of them came to the assembly from the third or fourth milestone, so far are they separated from one another.

Yet they possess such love for one another—even beyond their love for the rest of the brotherhood—that, for the sake of many who wish to be saved together with them, each strives to give his own cell to them for refreshment.

## CHAPTER LXX. On Abbot Ammonius [Note: [Col. 1225D] “Ammonius.” I do not remember reading anything about him except what is found above in Rufinus, Book II, chapter 23.] and Those Who Were with Him

[Col. 1175B]

We also saw the Father of those who lived there, named Ammonius. He possessed excellent cells, a courtyard, a well, and the other necessities. When a brother who wished to be saved came to him and asked him to find a cell in which he could live, Ammonius immediately went out and ordered him not to leave the cells until he had found him a suitable dwelling. After leaving him everything he possessed, together with the cells, he shut himself up in a small cell.

If several people came together wishing to be saved, he gathered the entire brotherhood. While one supplied bricks and another water, the cells were completed in a single day. They invited those who were to live in the cells to the church for banquets. While the newcomers refreshed and enjoyed themselves, each monk filled his own sheepskin or basket with bread and other necessities from his cell and carried it to the new cells, so that no one would know what each person had offered.

At night, when the new inhabitants came to their cells, they suddenly found everything necessary. Many of them ate neither bread nor fruit, but only wild chicory. Some of them did not sleep throughout the entire night; sitting or standing, they persevered in prayer until morning.

## CHAPTER LXXI. The Life of Abbot Isidore [Note: [Col. 1226A] “Isidore.” See the note on Rufinus, Book II, chapter 17.] and Those Who Were with Him

We saw in the Thebaid the monastery of a certain great Isidore, which contained one thousand monks inside (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 17). It had wells and gardens and everything necessary for use, and no one left the monastery. A presbyter served as doorkeeper and permitted no one to go out or anyone else to enter, unless someone wished to remain there until death, never going elsewhere.

He received those who entered through the gate as guests in a small dwelling. In the morning, after giving them blessings, he sent them away in peace. Only two of the presbyters went out, administering the affairs of the brothers, and brought back what they needed for their use.

The presbyter who guarded the gate told me that those inside were holy men of such a kind that all of them could perform miracles, and that no one fell ill before his death. Rather, when each person’s departure had come, he first announced it to everyone and, reclining, went to sleep—

## CHAPTER LXXII. The Life of Abbot Ammonas [Note: [Col. 1226A] “Ammonas.” He is called Piammon above by Rufinus, Book II, chapter 32; see the note there.] the Presbyter

There is another solitude in Egypt, lying by the sea but extremely difficult, in which many great anchorites live. It is near the city of Diolcos (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 32, where he is called Piammon).

There we saw a holy and very humble presbyter who continually saw visions, named Ammonas. Once, while offering sacrifice to God [Note: [Col. 1226A] “Sacrifice.” Προσφέρων λατρείας. Although this expression properly means “offering worship” or “service,” it is also used for sacrifice. Rufinus supports us here: in chapter 32 we find that Piammon saw these things while offering sacrifice to the Lord—for this is how he names the man whom Palladius here calls Ammonas—and that the angel was σημειούμενον—“marking,” as Hervetus rendered it, or more clearly “marking down,” namely writing their names on a tablet—as Rufinus likewise explains: the angel was writing the names of those approaching the altar. Sozomen gives a fuller account in Book VI, chapter 29: Τὸν Πιάμμονα ἱερωμένον θεάσασθαι περὶ τὴν ἱερὰν τράπεζαν θεῖον ἄγγελον ἑστῶτα, καὶ τῶν μοναχῶν τοὺς παρόντας ἐγγράφειν βίβλῳ, τοὺς δὲ ἀπόντας ἀπαλείφειν. “Piammon, while performing the sacred rite, saw an angel of God standing beside the holy table, writing the monks who were present in a book and erasing those who were absent.” Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 35. FRONTO.], he saw an angel standing on the right side of the altar, marking the brothers who were approaching the grace and writing their names in a book.

When certain people were absent from the assembly, he saw their names erased; those people died three days later. Demons often tormented him and brought him to such weakness that he could neither stand at the altar nor offer sacrifice. But an angel came, took him by the hand, immediately strengthened him, and set him upright and healthy at the altar. When the brothers saw his sufferings, they were astonished.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. On Abbot John [Note: [Col. 1226B] “John.” Consult the notes above on Rufinus, Book II, chapter 33.]

We also saw another man in Diolcos, named John (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 33), the father of monasteries. He too possessed abundant grace, the appearance of Abraham, and the beard of Aaron. He performed miracles and healings, having cured many who were paralyzed or afflicted with gout.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. The Life of Abbot Pityrion and [Note: [Col. 1226B] “Pityrion.” Nicephorus mentions Pithyrion, who had an ascetic establishment near Athens, in Book IX, chapter 14.] Those Who Were with Him

[Col. 1176C]

In the Thebaid we saw a high mountain overhanging a river, exceedingly terrifying and precipitous, with monks living there in caves (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 31). Their father was named Pityrion. He had been one of Antony’s disciples and was the third to occupy that place. He performed many miracles and drove out spirits effectively.

Since he had succeeded Antony and his disciple Ammonas, he rightly also succeeded to the inheritance of their gifts. He held many other conversations with us, and especially discussed the discernment of spirits carefully. He said that there are certain demons who follow the movements of the mind and often turn our affections toward evil.

“Therefore,” he said to us, “my children, whoever wishes to drive out demons must first bring the affections of the mind into subjection. For whatever affection a person conquers, its demon also does he expel. You must gradually overcome the affections, so that you may expel their demons.

“The demon of gluttony follows. Therefore, if someone conquers gluttony, he expels its demon.”

He ate twice a week, on Sunday and Thursday, a small porridge made from flour [Note: [Col. 1226B] “A small porridge made from flour.” In Greek, ζωμὸν ἀλεύρου. Hervetus translated it “a small broth of flour.” I believe the reference is to what are elsewhere called *sippulae*. See the *Onomasticon*.]. He could not take anything else, because he had so fashioned his way of life.

## CHAPTER LXXV. The Life of Eulogius [Note: [Col. 1226B] “Eulogius.” See the authors cited in the notes on Rufinus, Book II, chapter 14.] the Presbyter

We also saw another presbyter, named Eulogius, who had received such a great gift of knowledge in offering gifts to God that he recognized the mind of each monk who approached (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 14).

When he often saw certain monks about to approach the altar, he held them back, saying:

“How do you dare approach the holy Sacraments when you have evil thoughts? You, during this very night, entertained in your mind an impure thought of fornication. Another considered in his mind, saying that it made no difference whether a sinner or a righteous person approached the grace of God. Another doubted the gift, saying: ‘Will it sanctify me as I approach?’

“Therefore, withdraw for a little from the holy Sacraments, and repent from your heart, so that you may receive forgiveness of sins and be worthy of communion with Christ. Unless you first cleanse your thoughts, you will not be able to approach the grace of Christ.”

## CHAPTER LXXVI. The Life of Serapion [Note: [Col. 1226B] “Serapion.” See what was noted concerning the two Serapions in Rufinus, Book II, chapter 18.] the Presbyter

[Col. 1177B]

We also saw in the Arsinoite region a certain presbyter named Serapion (Rufinus, Book II, chapter 18), the Father of many monasteries and the head of a very large brotherhood, numbering ten thousand men. He administered a great stewardship through the brothers.

At harvest time, all of them brought him all the produce they had received as the payment for their harvest, each one contributing twelve Egyptian *artabas* of grain [Note: [Col. 1226B] “Artabas.” This is an Egyptian measure, equivalent to three and one-third *modii*. See the *Onomasticon*.], which amount to approximately forty of the *modii* used among us. He himself distributed it for the service of the poor, so that thereafter there was no poor person in the surrounding region; he even sent provisions to the poor who were in Alexandria.

The Fathers mentioned above also never neglected this administration throughout Egypt. From the labor of the brotherhood they sent ships full of grain and clothing to the poor in Alexandria, because there were few needy people among themselves.

## CHAPTER LXXVII. The Life of Abbot Posidonius

There are many things to relate about Posidonius of the Thebaid, and they are difficult to tell: how gentle he was, how fiercely he disciplined himself, and how great was his innocence. I do not know whether I ever met anyone like him.

For I lived with him for one year in Bethlehem, when he was residing beyond Poemenium [Note: [Col. 1226B] “Poemenium.” A place in Palestine, so called by the shepherds: Ποιμένιον. See the *Onomasticon*.], and I saw many of his virtues. Among other things, he himself told me one day:

“When I lived in the Porphyrite region for one year, I met no human being throughout the entire year, heard no conversation, and tasted no bread, except when I used a few dates or found wild herbs somewhere.

“During that time, when my bread had occasionally run out, I left the cave to come to the inhabited world. After walking all day, I was scarcely two miles from the cave. When I looked around, I saw a horseman wearing the dress of a soldier and a turbaned helmet on his head. Concluding that he was a soldier, I went as far as the cave and found a basket of recently picked grapes and figs. When I took it, I returned happily to the cave, possessing food for my refreshment for two months.”

[Col. 1178A]

The blessed Posidonius performed this miracle in Bethlehem. A certain pregnant woman had an unclean spirit, and at the very time when she was about to give birth she was suffering in labor, the spirit tormenting her.

When the woman was being afflicted by the demon, her husband came and asked the holy man to be present. When we entered to pray, Posidonius stood and prayed; after the second genuflection, he expelled the spirit.

Then he rose and said to us: “Pray, for the unclean spirit is now being expelled. There ought to be some sign by which we may become certain of it.”

As the demon departed, it demolished the entire wall of the courtyard from its foundations. The woman had not spoken for six years; but after the demon had departed, she gave birth and spoke.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. On Jerome [Note: [Col. 1226B] “Jerome.” Here the master of the Sacred Palace, in the book cited above, comments on Posidonius’s words concerning Jerome: either this Posidonius, prophesying against the holy Jerome, was an impostor, or Palladius, out of hatred for the holy Jerome—which is more likely—is openly lying and raving madly against him. But do not believe, reader, the shameless Origenist and Pelagian Palladius when he gives free rein to abuse against the most holy man, worthy of veneration by the angels.]

[Col. 1178B]

I have learned this further prophecy concerning that holy man. A certain presbyter named Jerome lived in those regions. He was endowed with great eloquence in the Roman language and with remarkable intelligence; but his envy was so great that it overwhelmed the virtue of his learning.

After the holy Posidonius had spent many days with him, he said to me in my ear:

## CHAPTER LXXIX. On Paula [Note: [Col. 1226C] “Paula.” A most famous and noble woman, whose Life you have in Saint Jerome.]

“Paula, the freeborn woman who cares for him, will die before him, liberated from his envy. As I believe, because of this man the holy man will not remain in these regions; rather, his envy will extend even to his own brother.”

And so it happened.

## CHAPTER LXXX. On Oxyperentius

For this man expelled the blessed Oxyperentius, an Italian, from there.

## CHAPTER LXXXI. On Peter

[Page 761]

And another Peter, an Egyptian.

## CHAPTER LXXXII. On Simeon

And Simeon—remarkable men whom I recorded.

This most continent Posidonius, devoted above all to virtue, told me that for forty years he had not tasted bread and had not remembered an injury he had received beyond midday.

[Col. 1178D]

These are the contests and illustrious signs of the outstanding athlete of Christ, Posidonius, which were accomplished by his providence, the greatest of all virtues. In these things is the distinguished end of the life of this blessed man.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII. The Life of Serapion the Sindonite [Note: [Col. 1226C] “Serapion the Sindonite.” In the *Menaea*, 21 May, he is called ὁ ἀπὸ Σειδόνος. If he is the same as our man, it should be read ὁ ἀπὸ Σίνδονος. For Palladius clearly says that he was called Sindonite because he used only a sindon.]

There was another Serapion the Sindonite—for he never wore anything except a sindon, a linen cloth—who practiced great freedom from possessions and property. For this reason he was also called “the passionless.”

Although he was uneducated in letters, he recited all the Scriptures from memory. Neither his lack of possessions nor his meditation on the Scriptures enabled him to remain at rest in a cell—not because he was drawn by earthly matter, but because he followed the apostolic life. He traveled throughout the inhabited world, displaying the most exacting poverty, and thus attained complete freedom from passion here.

He had been born with this nature; for there are differences of natures, not of substances [Note: “Read with caution.”].

The Fathers therefore related that, when he had acquired a fellow ascetic to play with him, he sold himself in a certain city to pagan actors for twenty solidi [Note: [Col. 1226C] “Twenty solidi.” The interpreter rendered this “twenty coins.” See the *Onomasticon*.]. He hid the solidi under a seal and kept them with him.

He remained for a long time and served the actors who had bought him, until he made them Christians and drew them away from the theater. He took nothing except bread and water, and, because of his meditation on the Scriptures, never ceased speaking.

After a long time, the male actor was the first to be pierced in heart, then the female actor, and then their entire household. It was said that, while they were unaware of him, he washed the feet of both of them.

After they had both been baptized, they withdrew from the theater. When they had entered upon an honorable and pious life, they held the man in great reverence. They said to him:

“Come, brother; we will set you free, since you yourself have freed us from disgraceful slavery.”

He replied to them:

“Since my God has acted, and you have cooperated with him, and your souls have been saved, I will tell you the mystery of the deed.”

I pitied your souls, which were wandering in great error. Since I was a free trainer, an Egyptian by birth, I sold myself for this reason: to save you. Since God accomplished this, and through my humility your souls escaped unharmed, take your gold, [Col. 1179C] so that I may also help others.

But after they had pleaded with him at length and insisted, saying, “We shall regard you as our father and master; only remain with us,” they could not persuade him. Then they said to him, “Give the gold to the poor, for it was the cause of our salvation.” He said to them, “Give it yourselves, since it is yours; for I do not give other people’s money to the poor.” Then they urged him, saying, “At least visit us after a year.” And so he departed from them.

Through frequent journeys he reached Greece. After staying three days at Athens, he found no one to provide him with bread; for he carried neither money nor a bag, neither a sheepskin nor a staff—nothing of the kind—but was clothed only in a linen garment. When the fourth day came, he became very hungry, for he had tasted nothing during that time. Involuntary hunger is indeed a grievous matter, especially when unbelief is its companion.

Standing on the city’s burial mound, where those who held civic rank gathered [Note: [Col. 1226C] “Those who held civic rank.” Hervetus seems to have read οἱ εὐτελεῖς rather than οἱ ἐν τέλει, for he translates “those who were worthless and contemptible.” The translator of Heraclides, however, agrees with the reading of the Royal Manuscript and the printed edition: “He stood upon a certain hillock of the city, where the leading men of that town were accustomed to hold their council.” FRONTO.], he began to lament vehemently and tearfully, crying out, “Men of Athens, help!”

Everyone wearing a cloak and a rough garment [Note: [Col. 1226D] “Wearing a cloak and a rough garment.” In Greek, τριβωνοφόροι τε καὶ βυρροφορόι, “wearers of the rough cloak and the coarse garment.” See the *Onomasticon*.] ran up to him and said, “What is wrong with you? Where are you from, and what are you suffering?”

He answered them: “By birth I am an Egyptian, and by profession a monk. Since I am absent from my true homeland, I have fallen among three moneylenders. Two have withdrawn from me, because I paid them what I owed and they had no further claim against me; but one does not leave me.”

They therefore eagerly asked about the moneylenders, wishing to satisfy them, and questioned him: “Where are they? Who is troubling you? Show him to us, so that we may bring you help.”

Then he said to them: “Avarice, gluttony, and fornication have troubled me. I have been freed from two of them, namely avarice and fornication; for I possess neither gold nor anything else, and I do not enjoy the delicacies that nourish this disease. Therefore they no longer trouble me at all. But I cannot escape gluttony. For four days now I have eaten nothing, and my belly continues to trouble me, demanding its accustomed debt, without which I cannot live.”

Then certain philosophers, suspecting that he was telling some contrived and fictitious story, gave him a solidus. He took it, put it in a baker’s shop, and, having received bread, departed; [Col. 1180B] he immediately left the city and never returned to it. Then the philosophers recognized that he truly possessed virtue. After paying the baker the price of the bread, they recovered the solidus.

When he reached the region near Lacedaemon, he heard that one of the city’s leading men, 762 together with his entire household, was a Manichaean, although otherwise a good man. This excellent monk once again sold himself to him, as in the earlier episode. Within two years he had drawn him away from the heresy, together with his wife and entire household, and brought them into the Church.

Then, loving him, they no longer regarded him as a servant, but as more than a blood brother and father. They treated him with great honor and praised God with him.

Shortly afterward, after exhorting them at length, this spiritual diamond, Serapion, left them. After he had paid his price to these masters, he put himself aboard a ship as though he were sailing to Rome. The sailors, assuming that he had either brought provisions or possessed gold with which to pay his expenses, received him without asking anything further, each supposing that another had received his belongings.

When they had set sail and were five hundred stades from Alexandria, the passengers began to eat around sunset, after the sailors had already eaten. On the first day they saw that he did not eat, and they thought that the voyage was the reason. They thought the same on the second, third, and fourth days. But on the fifth day they saw him sitting quietly while everyone else ate, and they said to him, “Man, why are you not eating?”

He answered them, “Because I have nothing to eat.”

When they had therefore asked among themselves who had taken responsibility for his provisions or expenses, and discovered that no one had done so—for he had nothing—they began to argue with him: “How did you come aboard without provisions? How will you pay us the fare? What will you live on?”

He answered them, “I have nothing. Put me ashore and throw me out wherever you found me.”

But they said, “Why are you angry? Even if you gave us a hundred gold pieces, we would gladly do this, since the wind is so favorable. Let us therefore pursue our course and complete what we have undertaken.”

Thus he remained on the ship, and they fed him all the way to Rome. When he reached Rome, he carefully inquired who in the city was a great male or female trainer.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV  
### The Life of Abbot Domnion

[Col. 1181A]

Among these he came upon a certain Domnion, a very strong and exceedingly abstemious man, a disciple of Origen, who was reported to have performed many miracles, and whose bed healed the sick after his death.

## CHAPTER LXXXV  
### On the Silent Virgin

When he had encountered him and received benefit from him—for he was a man adorned with character, learning, speech, and life—and had learned from him who else in that place was a male or female trainer, he discovered that there was a certain virgin who practiced silence and lived in quiet. She had already been shut up in a cell for twenty-five years and had never spoken with anyone. [Col. 1181B]

When he had learned where she lived, he came there and said to the old woman who served her, “Tell the virgin that I must meet her.”

The old woman replied that she had not met anyone for many years. Then he said to her, “Tell her that I am going to meet her, for God has sent me.”

But even then she did not consent. After waiting two or three days, he went to her. He said to her, “Why are you sitting?”

She answered him, “I am not sitting; I am walking.”

He said, “Where are you walking?”

She answered, “To God.”

He said, “Are you alive or dead?”

She replied, “I believe that I am dead to the world. For whoever lives according to the flesh cannot walk toward God.”

He said to her, “Then, to convince me that you are dead to the world, do what I do.”

She replied, “Command me to do things that can be done, and I will do them.”

He said to her, “There is nothing a dead person cannot do, except be ungodly.”

Then he said to her, “Come down and walk forward.”

She answered, “It is now the twenty-fifth year since I have walked forward, so why should I walk forward now?”

He said to her, “Ah! Did you not say, ‘I am dead to this world’? It is therefore clear both that you are dead to the world and that the world is dead to you. If this is true, and a dead person feels nothing, then walking forward and not walking forward are the same for you. So walk forward.”

She then walked forward. After she had gone as far as a certain church, he said to her in the church, “If you wish to convince me that you truly are dead, and that you no longer live to please human beings, do what I do, and I will know that you are dead.”

He said to her, “Take off, as I do, all your clothes; put them on your shoulders and cross through the middle of the city, with me going before in this attire.” [Note: [Col. 1181D] This is astonishing, not to be imitated.]

She answered him, “This is wholly improper. I would offend many people, and they might say that I am deranged and possessed by a demon.”

He said to her, “What concern is it of yours if they say that you are deranged and possessed by a demon? You are dead to them. A dead person does not care if someone insults or mocks him, for he can feel nothing.”

Then she said to him, “Tell me if you want anything else; I do not boast that I have come as far as this.”

Then Serapion, who was impassible, said to her, “There you have it: no longer boast or take pleasure in yourself as though you were more devout than everyone else and dead to the world. For I am more dead than you, and I show in reality that I am dead to the world, since I do this without any disturbance of soul or shame.”

After he had trained her in humility and broken her arrogance, he departed.

There are also many other great and illustrious deeds of this teacher of Christ, a man endowed with virtue, which concern impassibility. We have selected and written down a few of the many, so that the purity of his life might become evident from them. He died at the age of sixty and was buried in the desert regions.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI  
### On Evagrius [Note: [Col. 1182D] He was an Origenist.] the celebrated deacon

[Note: [Col. 1226D] “Evagrius.” A lid worthy of its pot. Palladius, himself an Origenist, celebrates his teacher Evagrius, who was likewise a heretical Origenist and was repeatedly condemned by the Church. But what kind of man Evagrius was, see above, Book II, note 45, on chapter 27, so that from this you may discern what confidence should be placed in a heretic speaking about a heretic and an initiate of the same heresy. Thus writes the often-cited master of the sacred palace.]

It is not right to remain silent about Evagrius, the renowned deacon of Christ, who lived like the apostles. Rather, it is right to commit these matters to writing for the edification of those who will read them and for the glory of the goodness of our Savior. I shall relate from the beginning how he came to the monastic way of life and how, after practicing himself worthily, he died in the desert at the age of fifty-four. As it is written: “Having been perfected in a short time, he fulfilled long years” (Wisdom 4).

His soul was indeed pleasing to the Lord. By birth he was from the Pontic city of the Iberians [Note: [Col. 1226D] “The city of the Iberians.” Heraclides: “of the Hiberians.” The Greek Venetian edition has Ἰβόρων; the Parisian, Ἰβήρων. Hervetus printed *Liberorum*. There is elsewhere a city of the Liberians, Ἐλευθερίων; but since Evagrius is called Pontic, the city of the Iberians in Pontus must be investigated. Saint Jerome, in his letter to Ctesiphon against Pelagius, calls him *Hyperborita*, where Gravius restored *Iberita*. In the Council of Constantinople I, which was the Second Ecumenical Council, the subscriptions of the bishops mention two Pontuses: that of Amasia, where Pantophilus is listed as bishop of the Iberians, and that of Polemoniacus, where Atarbius is listed as bishop. Therefore I understand Evagrius as Pontic and Iberian to mean that he came from the Pontus of Amasia, which was called Helenopontus, as distinct from Polemoniacus. In the *Authentics*, Collation IV, title 7, Novel 28, in the work of Porphyrogenitus on Cappadocia, there is Ἰβωρά, the city of Ibora in Helenopontus. Hence in Jerome I read *Iborita*. Sozomen, Socrates, and Nicephorus, in the passages soon to be cited, make Evagrius a native of the Iberians who inhabit the Euxine Pontus.]

He was the son of a presbyter and was promoted to the office of reader by Saint Basil, bishop of the Church of Caesarea at Argeus [Note: [Col. 1227A] “Bishop of the Church of Caesarea at Argeus.” The words following this—“After the death of Saint Basil the bishop”—are absent from the Venetian Greek text but present in the Parisian edition.].

After the death of Saint Basil the bishop, Gregory, the most wise bishop of Nyssa, brother of the bishop to whom honor is given among the apostles, [Note: [Col. 1227A] “Nyssaean.” Thus the Parisian Greek, Heraclides, and the Venetian Greek text. In the text, “Nazianzen,” and “the brother of the bishop, to whom honor is given among the apostles,” are absent. One may rightly doubt whether Nyssaean or Nazianzen is intended here. The case for Nyssaean is strengthened by the statement that this Gregory, coming to the council, left Evagrius with Nectarius. For it is established that Gregory of Nyssa came to the Council of Constantinople, whereas Gregory of Nazianzus had already lived in Constantinople for several years. If Nicephorus’ catalogue is reliable, he is said to have lived in Constantinople for twelve years. Nazianzen himself, in his farewell speech, which he entitles *Syntaktērion Logos*, says in the name of the 150 bishops: “So long a time, they say, has passed since you have governed the Church, relying upon the influence and assistance of the time.” In favor of Nazianzen it could be argued that his testament mentions the deacon Evagrius, to whom he leaves certain bequests. Baronius understands our Evagrius here, in volume IV, under the year of Christ 389; and he also asserts, under the years 379 and 381, that this Evagrius was ordained deacon by Nazianzen. Certainly Socrates too, Book IV, chapter 23 of the Greek edition, but chapter 18 of the Latin edition, writes that Evagrius was ordained deacon by Nazianzen; Suidas copies him under “Makarios.” Thus Socrates writes about Evagrius: “Evagrius became the disciple of these two men and acquired philosophy through works, although formerly he had been a philosopher in words alone. In Constantinople he was first appointed to the order of deacon by Gregory of Nazianzus; then he went down with him to Egypt, and, after meeting the men mentioned above, he became zealous to imitate their way of life. And as many miracles occurred through his hands as through those of his teachers.” Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 30, and Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 42, say similar things. I have suggested reasons for doubt on both sides. The matter could be decided more certainly if more Greek manuscripts agreed with one side or the other.]

observing his aptitude, his wisdom, his freedom from the passions, and his distinction in every kind of learning, ordained him deacon. From there, when Saint Gregory the bishop came to the great synod at Constantinople, he left him with the blessed bishop Nectarius, since he was the most skilled of all in the art of disputation.

He therefore flourished in the great city, exulting in youthful vigor in debates against every heresy. But it happened that he, who was honored by the whole city because of his outstanding goodness of character, was pierced by the image of a woman’s desire. He later told us this himself, when his mind was free. The little woman, for her part, also loved him. She was one of the city’s leading women.

Evagrius, fearing God, revering his own conscience, keeping before his eyes the disgrace of such shame, and remembering the joy that heresies derive from the misfortunes of others, earnestly begged God to prevent the woman’s intended purpose. She was pressing him with desire and was held by an insane passion for him. When he wanted to withdraw from her, he could not, for he was held by the persuasive bonds of her service.

Not long afterward, before he had experienced the outcome of the prayer just mentioned, an angelic vision appeared to him in the guise of soldiers belonging to a prefect. The vision seized him and led him away as though to judgment, then threw him into what is called the prison, placing an iron collar around his neck and binding his hands with an iron chain. Those who had come against him gave him no explanation of the charge.

Because his conscience tormented him, he supposed that he was undergoing these things because of her, imagining that the woman’s husband had brought a legal action against him on this matter. [Col. 1183A] Evagrius therefore stood in great anxiety while another case was being heard and other men were being questioned for such a crime.

After that great fear and extreme anguish of soul, the angel who had presented the vision at the beginning changed his form and appeared to be Evagrius’ genuine and trusted friend. He was greatly astonished and grieved at the disgrace of so many chains, and he said to Evagrius, who was bound among forty prisoners, “Why are you being detained with criminals in such disgrace, my lord deacon?”

He answered him, “In truth I do not know. But I suspect that N., one of the prefects, has accused me, moved by jealousy without any reason. I fear that he has bribed the magistrate and will subject me to the severest punishment.”

The one who had assumed the form of his friend said to him, [Col. 1183B] “If you will listen to a friend, I advise you: it is not good for you to remain in this city.”

Evagrius said to him, “If God delivers me from this calamity and you see me in Constantinople, know that I deservedly undergo this punishment and am worthy of an even greater one.”

His friend said, “If that is so, I shall bring you the holy Gospel. Swear to me upon it that you will leave this city and care for your soul, and I will free you from this necessity.”

Evagrius replied, “I beg you; I will swear whatever you wish. Only free me from this dark cloud.”

Meanwhile he brought him the holy Gospel and demanded an oath. Evagrius swore upon the Gospel in these words: “I will not remain here beyond one day, and that only so that I may put my clothes aboard a ship.”

When he had completed the oath, he returned to himself from the ecstasy that had come upon him during the night. When he arose, he thought: “Even if the oath was given to me in an ecstasy, I nevertheless swore it.”

After putting all that he possessed aboard a ship, he came to Jerusalem, where he was received by the blessed Roman Melania.

Again, when the devil had hardened his heart like Pharaoh’s—since he was a young man and luxuriant in age—doubt attacked him once more, and his mind was divided, although he had said nothing to anyone. As a result he again changed his clothes, and in delaying he was afflicted by the lethargy of vainglory.

But God, who prevents the destruction of us all, again brought calamity upon him, casting him once more into a fever and then into a prolonged illness. For six months he wasted his flesh, which had been an impediment to virtue, while the physicians were uncertain and unable to find a means of curing him.

The blessed Melania said to him, “My son, I do not approve of your prolonged illness. Tell me, then, what is in your mind, for this is not your true illness.”

He confessed to her what had happened to him in Constantinople.

The blessed woman said to him, “Promise me, with the Lord as your witness, that you will pursue the purpose of the monastic life. Then I, although a sinner, will pray to God that you may be granted time for recovery and a continuation of life.”

He agreed. When she had prayed, he recovered within a few days. When he rose, she herself clothed him in the monastic habit, and he set out as a pilgrim for Mount Nitria, which is in Egypt. After living there for two years, he entered the desert in the third.

After living fourteen years in the place called the Cells, he ate a pound of bread each day and a sextarius of oil over three months—he who had been raised in a soft, luxurious, and refined life. He performed one hundred prayers and each year copied texts worth only the cost of what he ate; for he wrote elegantly in a rapid hand.

After purifying his mind over a period of fifteen years, he was deemed worthy of the gift of knowledge, wisdom, and discernment of spirits. He composed three sacred books for monks, called Ἀντιῤῥήτικα, that is, *Contradictions*, supplying methods to be used against demons.

On one occasion the demon of fornication caused him severe distress, as he himself told us. Throughout an entire winter night he stood in a well, until his flesh was congealed by the frost. On another occasion the spirit of blasphemy again troubled him, and he did not enter a roofed building for forty days, as he himself told us. His body swarmed with ticks (*ricini*), like the body of wild animals. [Note: [Col. 1227D] “Swarmed with ticks.” The Greek reads: Ὡς καὶ τὸ σῶμα κρότωνας εὐβρᾶσαι, “so that his body swarmed with ticks,” which Heraclides translates, “so that various eruptions appeared over his whole body.” See the notes on the old *Lausiac History* of Palladius and the *Onomasticon*.]

Three demons appeared to him in the dress of clerics, questioning him about the faith. One said that he was an Arian, another an Eunomian, and the third an Apollinarian. He overcame them in a few words through the spirit of wisdom.

Again, when one day the key to the church had been lost, after making the sign of the cross over the lock, he pushed it open with his hand, invoking Christ. He was scourged by demons to such an extent and acquired such extensive experience of various demons that they cannot easily be counted.

He told one of his disciples what would happen after eighteen years, predicting everything to him in detail.

This blessed man used to say: “Since I came into the desert, I have not touched lettuce, a small vegetable, anything green, fruit, grapes, a bath, meat, bread, wine, or anything at all that passes through fire, except certain raw vegetables and a little water.”

Later, in the sixteenth year of his way of life without cooking by fire, when his body and stomach had become so weak that his flesh needed him to take something that had passed through fire, he touched bread, but did not eat cooked vegetables. For two years he took either gruel or legumes.

In these things this blessed man wasted away his body, giving life to his soul through the Holy Spirit, and he received Communion in the church on Epiphany.

This noble athlete of Christ told us around the time of his death: “It is now three years since I have been troubled by carnal desire.”

If, after a life so virtuously lived and such immense labor in ascetic practice—practice that was especially unbending—and perpetual, sober prayer, this immortal man was so violently attacked by a demon hostile and destructive to good, what do we suppose those who are more careless suffer from the accursed demon because of their negligence?

At one time the death of his father was announced to this holy man. He said to the one who told him, “Cease blaspheming; my Father is immortal.” [Note: [Col. 1183D] A similar saying appears above, in the *Pelagianus*, Book I, no. 5.] He meant God.

Thus far extends the most exact and complete account of the way of life of the distinguished Evagrius. [Col. 1185A]

## CHAPTER LXXXVII  
### The Life of Abbot Pior [Note: [Col. 1227D] Pior. He is mentioned above, chapter 11. Sozomen also speaks of him in Book VI, chapter 29; Cassiodorus, Book VIII, chapter 1; and Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 37.]

A certain man named Pior (Rufinus, Book III, no. 31; Pelagius, Book IV, no. 34), an Egyptian by birth and still young in age, renounced the world and left his father’s house. Because of his outstanding spiritual love, he professed to God that he would never again see any of his family.

Fifty years later, his sister, who had grown old and had learned from someone that her brother was still alive, was in danger of losing her mind unless she saw him. Since she could not come into the immense desert, she asked the bishop of that region to write to the holy Fathers who were in the desert and ask them to send him, so that she might see him.

When strong pressure was brought to bear upon him, he obeyed the Fathers and decided to leave after taking one other man with him. He informed his sister’s household that her brother Pior was arriving and standing outside.

When he sensed the sound of the door and that his sister was coming to meet him, Pior, keeping his eyes closed, cried out to her: “O sister N., I am Pior, your brother; I am here. Look—see as much as you wish.”

When she had thus been assured, she glorified God. Although she did much to persuade him to enter the house, she could not do so. After praying at the threshold, he returned to the desert, acquiring for himself there, through virtue, his true homeland.

This is reported as his miracle: when he dug in the place he had built, he found extremely bitter water, and he remained there until his death, content with the bitterness of the water that he had found. [Note: [Col. 1227D] “Content with the bitterness of the water that he had found.” Heraclides translated it thus. Hervetus: “shutting himself up in the bitterness of the water,” as though he had read τειχίσας ἑαυτόν instead of στοιχήσας. Rufinus, Book III, chapter 31, says that this same Pior thought to himself: “Whatever water I find, I must be content with it.” FRONTO.] [Col. 1185C]

Thus the endurance of this noble man might become known. Many monks after his death attempted to remain in his cell, but could not do so for a whole year. The place is terrifying and deprived of every consolation.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII  
### The Life of Abbot Moses [Note: [Col. 1228A] Moses. Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 37.] of Libya

765 Moses of Libya was a very gentle man and endowed with the greatest charity. He was deemed worthy of the gift of healing.

He related the following: “I was in the monastery when I was very young, and I was digging a very large well, twenty feet wide. Eighty men had dug in it for three days, and, after passing through the usual vein, which was visible about a cubit deep, we did not find water.

“Greatly distressed, we were deliberating about abandoning the work. While we were deliberating, Pior came to us from the vast desert at the very sixth hour of the heat. He was an old man dressed in his sheepskin. After greeting us, he said to us, ‘Why have you lost heart, men of little faith? I saw that you had already lost heart yesterday.’

“After saying this, he immediately lowered ladders into the excavation of the well, prayed with us, took a mattock, and struck the ground three times. Then he said, ‘God of the holy patriarchs, do not make the labor of your servants fruitless and useless, but send them a supply of water.’

“Immediately water flowed out, so that we were all sprinkled with it. After praying again, he departed, saying, ‘For this reason I was sent.’ And it was opened.

“When they pressed him to eat there, he could not bring himself to do so, saying, ‘For the sake of which I was sent.’ [Note: [Col. 1228A] “For the sake of which I was sent,” δι’ ὃ ἀπεστάλην. The translator Hervetus contracted the sense in this way: “I was not sent for that purpose.” But the fuller meaning is supported by the Greek witnesses. Heraclides, chapter 27: “This was done, he said, for the sake of which I was sent; for no one sent me to take food.” Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 29: Οὐκ ἠνέσχετο, φήσας, μὴ ἐπὶ τούτῳ ἀπεστάλθαι, ἠνύσθαι δὲ ἐφ’ ᾧ ἦλθεν, “He would not consent, saying that he had not been sent to them for this purpose, but that the task for which he had come had already been completed.” Nicephorus, Book XI, chapter 32: Οὐκ ἠνέσχετο, εἰπὼν, μὴ ἐπὶ τούτῳ ἥκειν, ἠνύσθαι δὲ αὐτῷ, δι’ ὃ παραγέγονε, “He would not comply with them, saying that he had not come for this purpose, but that what he had come to accomplish had been completed.” FRONTO.]

“This is the deed of the admirable Pior, that noble pillar of endurance. And this is the end of that virtue: he who for the sake of a bitter spring endured it enjoys an everlasting stream of sweetness with great spiritual joy.”

## CHAPTER LXXXIX  
### The Life of Abbot Chronius [Note: [Col. 1228A] Chronius. Another Cronius is mentioned above, chapter 25.]

A certain man called Chronius, from the village called Phoenix, measured fifteen thousand paces from his village—which lay near the desert—by counting with his right foot. There, after praying, he dug a well. When he found excellent water, which lay seven cubits below the surface, he also built himself a small lodging there.

From the day on which he settled in the monastery, he asked God never to return to an inhabited place. After a few years had passed, he was deemed worthy of the priesthood, and a brotherhood of about two hundred men gathered around him.

This is reported as the virtue of his ascetic practice: although he had sat beside the altar for sixty years while carrying out his priestly ministry, he never left the desert and never ate bread except as the fruit of the labor of his hands.

## CHAPTER XC  
### The Life of Abbot Jacob

A certain Jacob from the neighboring region lived with him. He was surnamed “the Lame,” and was a man endowed with the highest knowledge. Both men were known to the blessed Antony.

## CHAPTER XCI  
### The Life of Abbot Paphnutius Cephala [Note: [Col. 1228A] Paphnutius Cephala. See what is said about the various Paphnutiuses in Book II, chapter 16, no. 32.]

[Col. 1186C]

One day we also met Paphnutius, the remarkable man called Cephala. He possessed the gift of understanding the divine Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, interpreting all of them although he had not read the Scriptures. He was so modest that he concealed his prophetic gift.

It is said of him that for eighty years he never possessed two tunics at the same time. When I and the blessed deacons Evagrius and Albinus met with him, we sought to learn the causes of the brothers who fell or slipped into a dishonorable life.

## CHAPTER XCII  
### On Cheremon

It happened in those days that Cheremon, an ascetic, died while sitting. He was found dead, still seated in his chair and holding work in his hands.

## CHAPTER XCIII  
### On Another

[Col. 1186D]

It also happened that another brother, while digging a well, was buried by the well.

## CHAPTER XCIV  
### On Another

It also happened that another man, coming from Scetis, died of thirst for water.

## CHAPTER XCV  
### On Stephen Who Fell [Note: [Col. 1228A] Stephen. This is another Stephen, distinct from the one mentioned above, chapter 30.]

Among these we also mentioned Stephen, who fell into disgraceful intemperance, and Eucarpus, and Heron of Alexandria, and Valens of Palestine, [Col. 1187A] and Ptolemy of Egypt, who was in Scetis [Note: [Col. 1187] Concerning Heron, above, chap. 32. Concerning Valens, above, chap. 31. Concerning Ptolemy, above, chap. 33.]. Accordingly, we asked together what the reason might be that, although such men live in solitude, some of them are deluded in mind while others break out into intemperance.

The following answer was given us by them, together with the holy Paphnutius, a man endowed with the greatest knowledge:

“Whatever happens is divided into two categories: what is pleasing to God, and what God permits. Whatever happens through virtue for the glory of God happens by God’s good pleasure; but whatever is harmful or dangerous, and whatever brings misfortunes and accidents, happens by God’s permission. Permission arises either from poverty of understanding or from the unbelief of those who are abandoned.

“For it is impossible that someone who lives piously and thinks rightly should fall into disgrace or into the deception of demons. Those who appear to undertake virtue with a wicked aim and purpose—namely, in order to please human beings—and with arrogant thinking fall into calamities when God abandons them [Col. 1187B] for their benefit, so that, when they perceive a change through their abandonment, they may correct either their purpose or their action.

“Sometimes, indeed, the purpose is sinful, when it is undertaken with an evil aim. Thus it often happens that an intemperate person gives alms to young women for a shameful purpose, while the action itself is in agreement with reason if one gives assistance to orphans and to a nun engaged in ascetic practice. It also happens that someone gives alms with a right purpose—to the sick, to those whose possessions have been ruined, or to the aged—but sparingly and with grumbling. In that case the purpose is right, but the action is unworthy of the purpose. For the merciful person ought to show mercy cheerfully and generously.

“He also said this: In many souls there are certain particular gifts. In some there is natural goodness; in others, aptitude for ascetic practice. But when this is not done for the sake of goodness itself and from a divine purpose, and neither the action, nor natural goodness, nor those who possess exceptional gifts ascribe these things to God, the giver of good things, but to their own free will, talent, and sufficiency, Such people, abandoned by providence, fall into shameful deeds, shameful sufferings, insults, and dishonor.

“Thus abandoned, through the humility and shame that come upon them, they gradually—I do not know how—drive out the arrogance they had acquired from what was regarded as virtue. No longer trusting in themselves but in God, who bestows everything, they attribute the benefit to him by their confession.

“For when a person is puffed up—when, I mean, he is elated by the goodness of his natural ability and does not attribute that goodness, nor the knowledge supplied to him, to God, but either to his own practice or to his nature—God removes from him the angel of providence, who has been appointed over this grace. When that angel has departed, the man who is elated by his natural ability is overcome by the power of the adversary and falls into intemperance because of his insolence. Once the witness of self-control has been taken away, what such people say no longer appears credible; the pious flee from the teaching that proceeds from such a mouth as though from a spring teeming with leeches. Thus what is written is fulfilled: ‘But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my justifications and take my covenant upon your lips?’ [Col. 1188A] (Psalm 49).

“For the souls of those who labor under vices are truly like different kinds of springs. Those who are devoted to gluttony and wine are like muddy springs; those possessed by avarice and the desire to possess more are like springs containing frogs; and the envious, who have an aptitude for knowledge, are like springs that nourish serpents, in which reason is always in turmoil. No one draws from such springs, either because of the harshness of their character or because of the stench of their unjust actions.

“Therefore David asks God to teach him three things: goodness, discipline, and knowledge (Psalm 118). For knowledge without goodness is useless. But if such a person is corrected—if he lays aside the cause of his abandonment, namely, arrogance, and takes up humility, recognizes his own measure, no longer exalts himself against anyone, and gives thanks to God—then the knowledge that is supported by testimony returns to him.

“For spiritual utterances that do not have an honorable and self-controlled life accompanying them are ears of grain destroyed by the wind. They have the appearance of ears of grain, but their nourishment has been taken away.

“Every fall, whether it occurs through the tongue, through the senses, through actions, or through the whole body, occurs in proportion to a person’s arrogance through God’s abandonment, as he spares those who are abandoned. For if, along with intemperance, the Lord were also to bear witness to their natural ability by supplying them with eloquence, pride would make them demons themselves, exalting themselves amid uncleanness.”

These holy men and excellent Fathers also said to us:

“When you see someone whose life is corrupt but whose speech is persuasive, remember the demon who speaks with Christ in sacred Scripture, and the testimony that says: ‘Now the serpent was more prudent than all the beasts that were upon the earth’ (Genesis 2). His prudence became a detriment to him because no other virtue accompanied it.

“For the faithful and good person ought to think in his soul what God gives, to speak what he thinks, and to do what he says. If affinity of life does not accompany the truth of his words, he is bread without salt, as Job says (Job 6); and such bread is not to be eaten at all. But if it is eaten, it throws the one who eats it into a bad condition. For, he says, ‘If bread without salt is eaten, and if there is taste in empty words’—that is, words not directed toward usefulness [Note: [Col. 1228B] That is, not directed toward usefulness.] The passage has been restored here; the translator had presented it mutilated as follows: ‘In empty words, not completed by the testimony of words. Therefore, one of the abandonments is …’ Job’s passage is first at 6:6, and the second at 40:3, though it differs somewhat. Ἦ ἀποποιῇ μου τὸ κρίμα; οἴει δέ με ἄλλως σοὶ κεχρηματικέναι ἢ ἵνα ἀναφανῆς δίκαιος; ‘Will you reject my judgment? Do you suppose that I have answered you in any other way than so that you might appear just?’ In some printed books, however, the reading found here, as Palladius cites it, is μὴ ἀποποιοῦ, ‘Do not reject.’ FRONTO.], completed by the testimony of good works.”

There are therefore several causes of abandonment. One is that virtue may be brought to light when it has been hidden, as with Job, when God answered and said (Job 40): “Do not reject my judgment, nor suppose that I answered you in any other way than so that you might appear just; for you are known to me, who know hidden things and behold the depths of human thoughts. But since you are unknown to human beings—for they sometimes suspect that I am worshiped by you because of your riches—I therefore caused you to fall into such a calamity. I cut away your riches so that I might show them your thanksgiving and your philosophical way of life.”

Another cause is the removal of arrogance, as in the case of Paul. Paul was abandoned to calamities, blows, and various afflictions, and he said: “There was given to me a thorn in the flesh, to strike me with blows, lest I should be exalted” (2 Corinthians 11)—lest, when miracles, peace, success, and honor were added to him, he should be cast into diabolical arrogance and be lifted up by pride.

The paralytic was also abandoned because of sin. The Lord said to him: “Behold, you have been made well; sin no more” (John 5).

Judas was also abandoned because he valued money more highly than the word of life; therefore he was also suffocated (Acts 1).

Esau was also abandoned and fell into intemperance, since he preferred the filth of his entrails to his father’s blessing (Genesis 27).

Thus, when the blessed Apostle Paul had understood all these things, he said concerning certain people: “Because they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is not fitting” (Romans 1). Concerning others who seemed to possess knowledge of God while having a corrupted mind and empty conceit, he says: “Because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, God handed them over to dishonorable passions.”

From this we learn that no one can fall into intemperance unless he has been abandoned by God’s providence, because of the negligence and sluggishness of those who are abandoned and forsaken so that these things may happen to them.

## CHAPTER XCVI. The Life of Abbot Solomon

Having spent forty years in the city of Antinoe in the region of Thebaid, during that time I also learned about all the monasteries that are there. Around the city live about two thousand men, supporting themselves by their hands and practicing asceticism with the utmost rigor. Among them are also anchorites who have shut themselves up in caves in the rocks.

Among these is Solomon, a most gentle and self-controlled man, endowed with the gift of endurance. He has spent fifty years in a cave, providing himself with food by the work of his hands, and has learned all sacred Scripture.

## CHAPTER XCVII. The Life of Abbot Dorotheus

There was also a certain presbyter named Dorotheus who lived in another cave. He too lived an irreproachable life in the highest goodness, was considered worthy of the presbyterate, and ministered to the brothers who lived in the caves.

At one time the younger Melania, the niece of the elder Melania, about whom I shall speak later, sent him five hundred solidi, asking him to minister to the brothers. But after accepting only three, he sent the rest to the anchorite Diocles, a man endowed with the highest knowledge, saying: “Brother Diocles is wiser than I and can distribute them completely and blamelessly, since he knows better than I do to whom assistance ought properly to be given. These are sufficient for me.”

## CHAPTER XCVIII. The Life of Abbot Diocles

This Diocles was first instructed in grammar.
