Later, after devoting himself to philosophy, and finally after grace drew him toward heavenly philosophy, when he was twenty-eight years old he renounced the liberal disciplines and joined himself to Christ. He has now spent thirty-five years in a cave.

He said to us that a mind which has withdrawn in thought from the contemplation of God becomes either a demon or a beast.

When we asked him, “How so?” he replied:

“A mind that has withdrawn from the contemplation of God necessarily [Note: [Col. 1228B] Necessarily.] Here the mutilated translation of Hervetus has been restored from the author’s words and those of the old translator. As Cicero interprets Plato’s ψυχῆς κίνησιν, ‘motion of the soul,’ as animi commotionem, ‘movement of the mind,’ so in Tusculan Disputations 4 he defines anger: Πάθος ἐστὶν ἄλογος καὶ παρὰ φύσιν ψυχῆς κίνησις, ‘A disturbance turned away from right reason, a movement of the mind contrary to nature.’ Ὀργὴ ἐπιθυμία τιμωρίας τοῦ δοκοῦντος ἠδικηκέναι οὐ προσηκόντως. ‘Anger is the desire to punish one who seems to have inflicted an injury unjustly.’ Aristotle, Rhetoric, chap. 2: Ὀργὴ, ὄρεξις μετὰ λύπης τιμωρίας φαινομένης διὰ φαινομένην ὀλιγωρίαν μὴ προσηκόντως. ‘Anger is an appetite, accompanied by pain, for an apparent retaliation because of an apparent slight that was not deserved.’ FRONTO.] falls either into the demon of desire, which drives him into lust, or into the evil spirit of anger, from which irrational appetites arise. He called lustful desire bestial, but anger a demonic movement.”

When I objected, “How can the human mind be with God without interruption?” he replied:

“Whenever the soul is engaged in any thought or action that is pious and divine, it is with God.”

## CHAPTER XCIX. The Life of Abbot Capito

Near him lived a certain Capito, who had been a robber. After spending fifty years in caves four miles from the city of Antinoe, he did not leave his cave even to go to the river Nile, saying that he could not meet crowds because the common adversary still resisted him.

## CHAPTER C. The Life of an Anchorite Who Was Mocked

With these men we also saw another anchorite who likewise lived in a cave. In dreams he had been mocked by the gadfly of vainglory; in turn he mocked those who were deceived, “feeding the winds” [Note: [Col. 1228C] Feeding the winds.] The translator had omitted this, as had Heraclides: “and seemed somehow to be a foolish shepherd of the winds and a pursuer of shadows,” chap. 47. The passage is Ecclesiasticus 34:2: Ὡς δρασσόμενος σκίας, καὶ διώκων ἄνεμον, οὕτως ὁ ἐπέχων ἐν ὕπνοις. “Like one who grasps at shadows and pursues the wind, so is the one who attends to dreams.” In the Latin Vulgate we indeed read at Hosea 12:1, “Ephraim feeds on wind,” but the Greek is: ὁ δὲ Ἐφραῒμ πονηρὸν πνεῦμα, “But Ephraim is an evil spirit.” There is also Proverbs 10:4 in the Latin Vulgate, whose Greek does not correspond at all: “He who relies on lies feeds the winds; he himself also pursues flying birds.” FRONTO.], and pursuing shadows (Ecclesiasticus 34).

His body did possess self-control, partly because of his old age, partly because of the time, and perhaps also because of vainglory. But his mind had been corrupted by the intemperance of vainglory and alienated from religious conduct.

## CHAPTER CI. The Life of Saint Ephraem the Deacon [Note: [Col. 1228D] Ephraem.] See what was said above, book I, under his Life.]

You have certainly heard of Ephraem, deacon of the church of the Edessenes [Note: [Col. 1189] His Life appears above in book I.]. He was one of those worthy to be mentioned by the holy servants of Christ. After he had worthily completed the way of the Spirit and had not deviated from what was right, he was considered worthy of the grace of natural knowledge, which theology follows, and finally of blessedness.

After he had lived an ascetic life of quiet and had for many years edified those who came to him, he later left his cell for the following reason. When a great famine had overtaken the city of the Edessenes, he pitied all the country people who were perishing. He went to the wealthy men of the city and said to them:

“Why do you not pity human nature, which is perishing, but allow your riches to rot for the condemnation of your souls?”

They made a respectable excuse, saying:

“We have no one whom we can trust to supply bread to the hungry, for everyone is making merchandise of everything” [Note: [Col. 1228D] “Everyone is making merchandise of everything.” Καπηλεύουσι τὰ πράγματα, as the ancient poet said in Cicero, On Duties: “Not huckstering war, but waging war.” Ignatius, Letter to the Trallians: Περιφέροντες τὸ ὄνομα Χριστοῦ, καὶ καπηλεύοντες τὸν λόγον τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου. “Carrying about the name of Christ and huckstering the word of the Gospel.” Basil of Seleucia, Oration 8: Οἱ μὲν οὖν τὴν φύσιν καπηλεύοντες νενοθευμένον δουλείᾳ τὸν παῖδα καταδικάζουσι. “Those who make merchandise of nature condemn the bastard child to slavery.” The Apostle himself, 2 Corinthians 2:17: Καπηλεύοντες τὸν λόγον τοῦ Θεοῦ. “Adulterating the word of God.” In Herodotus, καπηλεύειν πάντα τὰ πράγματα means “to treat all things as a source of profit”; likewise in Philostratus, τὴν σοφίαν καπηλεύειν means, according to Budaeus, “to prefer profit to philosophy.” [Col. 1229A] Sozomen, concerning this same Ephraem, book III, chap. 15: Σχεδὸν πάντων πρὸς κέρδος κεχηνότων, καὶ καπηλίαν τὸ πρᾶγμα ποιουμένων. “Since almost all are burning with desire for profit and make this matter a commercial undertaking for gain.” Nicephorus, book IX, chap. 16: Πάντες γὰρ πρὸς κέρδος κεχηνότες εἰσὶ τὰ τοιαῦτα αἰσχρῶς καπηλεύοντες. “For all gape after profit and disgracefully turn such things to their own gain.” FRONTO.].

He then said to them:

“What do you think of me?”

He was held in great esteem by everyone, and not falsely but truly.

They replied:

“We know you to be a man of God.”

“If you have formed that opinion of me,” said the servant of Christ, “believe me from now on. Behold, for your sake I appoint myself to receive guests.”

After receiving money, he built an enclosure surrounded by stakes and set up beds for three hundred people. He cared for those who were weaker and supplied food to those who were being consumed by hunger. He buried those who were dying, cared for those who still had hope of life, and, in short, provided lodging and daily service during the famine from whatever supplies were available.

When the year was completed, prosperity returned and everything went well. Since he had nothing more to do, he entered his cell, and died a month later, when God had granted him this opportunity to gain a crown in his final days. He also left writings worthy of study, which testify to the man’s great virtue.

## CHAPTER CII. The Life of Abbot Julian

I heard that a man named Julian lived in those regions, a man of the greatest ascetic practice. After he had afflicted his flesh beyond measure, he carried about nothing but bones covered with skin. In the final days of his life he was considered worthy of the gift of healings.

## CHAPTER CIII. The Life of Blessed Innocent

You have heard from many people, and from great ones, about blessed Innocent, the presbyter of the Mount of Olives. Nevertheless, you shall hear about him from us as well, for we lived with him for three years. Matters that had often escaped their notice became known to us; and not merely one or two, but not even ten people could recount the virtues of this man.

He was exceedingly simple. Although he had been distinguished in the palace under the emperor Constantius [Note: [Col. 1229A] “Under the emperor Constantius.” Heraclides the translator: “Under the emperor Constantius, at the beginning of his reign, he had served among the ranks of great men.” Another old translator, Palladius: “At the beginning of Constantine’s reign he renounced the world.” Hervetus translated it “among the magistrates.” Τὰς ἀρχὰς therefore should not be understood here as “magistracies,” but as “the beginnings of the reign,” as in the Spiritual Meadow, chap. 112: Ἐν ταῖς ἀρχαῖς Τιβερίου τοῦ βασιλέως, “At the beginning of the reign of the emperor Tiberius”; and chap. 155: Εἰς τὰς ἀρχὰς τοῦ πιστοτάτου ἡμῶν βασιλέως Μαυρικίου, “At the beginning of the reign of our most faithful emperor Maurice.” 1 Esdras 4:6: Ἐν ἀρχῇ βασιλείας αὐτοῦ, “At the beginning of his reign.” FRONTO.], at the beginning of his reign, he renounced the world and departed from marriage. In that marriage he had a son named Paul, who served among the domestics [Note: [Col. 1229B] “Who served among the domestics.” Δομεστικὸν στρατευόμενον. Hervetus translated it “a domestic who served.” The domestics were called by this special designation those who served in the emperor’s court, both cavalry and infantry—whom others also call οἰκείους—assigned to the emperor’s guard. Meursius discusses them at length in his Glossary. FRONTO.].

When Paul sinned against the daughter of a presbyter, Innocent pronounced a curse upon his own son, praying to God and saying:

“Lord, give him a spirit so that his flesh may no longer find time to sin.”

He considered it better for him to fight against a demon than against intemperance. And so it happened. He is still on the Mount of Olives, carrying iron and chastised by the spirit. What is remarkable is that this man’s father, who heals others, did not take pity on him, though he was tormented by the demon for so long.

This Innocent was so merciful—though perhaps I shall seem to be joking while telling the truth—that he often secretly took things from the brothers and gave them to the needy. He was exceedingly simple and innocent.

He was considered worthy of a gift against demons. Once a young man was brought to him in our presence, having been seized by a spirit and paralysis. When I saw him, I wanted to drive away openly the mother and those who had brought him, despairing of any possibility of his cure.

Meanwhile an old man arrived and saw the mother standing there, weeping and wailing because of her son’s indescribable calamity. The illustrious old man wept and, moved with compassion, took the young man and entered his martyrium, which he himself had built and in which the relics of John the Baptist were kept. After praying for him from the third hour until the ninth, he returned the young man healed to his mother. On that same day he expelled both the paralysis and the demon.

His paralysis was of such a kind that, when the boy spat, he spat upon his own back; so inverted was his body.

Another sign of his power was the following. An old woman who tended sheep near the places around the Lazarium had lost a sheep. She came to him weeping. He followed her and said:

“Show me the place where you lost it.”

She led him to the places around the Lazarium. He stood and prayed. The young men who had stolen the sheep had first killed it.

While he was praying, with no one confessing and the flesh hidden in the vineyard, a crow came from somewhere and stood over the stolen object. It seized a piece of it and flew away again. When the blessed man noticed this, he saw that the victim had been slaughtered.

The young men then fell at his feet and confessed that they had killed it. The just price was exacted from them, and they were punished so that they would not dare to do anything of the kind again.

## CHAPTER CIV. The Life of Abbot Adolius

Again, at Jerusalem I came to know a certain man named Adolius, a native of Tarsus. When he came to Jerusalem, he entered a path that was little trodden [Note: [Col. 1229B] “A path that was little trodden.” The translator rendered it “very unchangeable,” as though he had read ἄτρεπτον rather than ἄτριπτον. Heraclides translated it “he entered a path scarcely worn by anyone.” Thus Lucretius, book IV:

“I traverse the pathless places of the Pierides,
untrodden before by anyone’s foot.”

Ambrose, Sermon 74, On the Birthday of a Martyr: “The path of life, where the Lord rose again, became known and was worn smooth by the feet of many.” FRONTO.], not one on which many had traveled, but one in which he had chosen for himself a certain new discipline of life.

He practiced asceticism beyond human measure, so that even the wicked demons, terrified by his austerity, did not dare approach him. Because of the extreme severity of his ascetic practice and his vigils, he was thought to be an apparition.

During Lent he ate after five days; throughout the rest of the year, he ate every other day. This was also a great achievement of his virtue. From evening until the time when the brotherhood gathered in the oratories on the Mount of Olives, on the hill of the Ascension from which Jesus ascended, he stood continually singing psalms, praying, and fasting. Whether it rained or hailed, he remained motionless.

When the appointed time was complete, he struck the cells of everyone with a mallet used to awaken them, gathering them to the oratories. In each oratory he sang one or two antiphons together with them and prayed with them. Then, as day approached, he went to his cell. In fact, the brothers would strip him and wring out his clothing, which dripped as though it had been washed, and then dress him in other garments.

After resting until the third hour, he was awakened by the singing of psalms and remained intent upon it until evening.

Such was the virtue of Adolius of Tarsus, who completed his course at Jerusalem, fell asleep there in eternal sleep, and was buried there.

## CHAPTER CV. Concerning Abramius [Note: [Col. 1229C] Abramius.] Cassian, Conferences XV, chapters 4 and 5, concerning another abbot Abraham.]

There was a certain Abramius, an Egyptian by birth, who led an extremely harsh and very primitive life in the desert. Wounded in mind by an untimely delusion, he came into a church and contended with the presbyters, saying:

“By night I was ordained presbyter by Christ. Receive me as a priest.”

The Fathers took him away from the desert and led him into a more ordinary and less extreme way of life [Col. 1193A]. They cured him of his pride by leading him to recognize his weakness, since he had been deceived by the demon of pride, and by their holy prayers restored him to his former holiness of life.

## CHAPTER CVI. The Life of Abbot Elpidius

In the caves of the Amorites near Jericho—which had once been built by those who fled from Jesus son of Nun, who at that time was devastating foreign peoples—there was on Mount Luca a certain Elpidius, a Cappadocian by birth. Later he was deemed worthy of the presbyterate of the monastery there and was appointed by Timothy, chorepiscopus of Cappadocia, a man of great ability.

He lived in a certain cave and displayed such self-control in ascetic practice that he surpassed everyone. For twenty-five years he has lived, eating only on Saturdays and Sundays; and standing throughout the whole night, he sang psalms.

An innumerable multitude of brothers followed him as bees follow their king and built up that mountain. There one could see in each person different forms of ascetic discipline.

Once, when this Elpidius—truly Elpidius, since he genuinely rejoiced in hope and endured affliction for Christ—was singing psalms at night, while we were singing with him, a scorpion stung him. Although he crushed it while standing, he did not change the posture of his body. Such was his endurance that he paid no attention to the pain inflicted by the scorpion.

On another occasion a brother was holding a piece of vine-shoot [Note: [Col. 1229C] “A piece of vine-shoot.” Κόμμα κλήματος. Hervetus wrote “a piece of a ladder,” as though he had read κλίμακος. Heraclides: “While he held a small piece of vine-shoot from a dry vine.”]. While Elpidius was sitting at the edge of the mountain, the saint took it from him and planted it as though he were planting it, although it was not the season. It grew to such an extent, and the vine became so large, that it covered the entire church.

## CHAPTER CVII. The Life of Abbot Aenesius

With this holy athlete of God there was also perfected the illustrious servant of God Aenesius, a man of great reputation and distinguished in ascetic practice.

## CHAPTER CVIII. The Life of Abbot Eustathius [Note: [Col. 1229C] Eustathius.] Sozomen, book III, chap. 13, concerning another Eustathius, bishop of Sebaste.]

His brother Eustathius was equal to him in honor and pursued the contests of the ascetic life with a ready and eager spirit.

Blessed Elpidius carried his mortification of the body so far that the whole structure of his bones was plainly visible [Note: [Col. 1229C] “So that the whole of his …” This corrupt reading produced an absurd translation, as though the sun clearly displayed the framework of his bones. Thus the Lyon edition, p. 131: Ὡς ἥλιον διαφαίνειν αὐτοῦ τῶν ὀστέων τὸ πῆγμα, “So that the framework of his bones shone through like the sun.” Nor did Heraclides find a more accurate manuscript; in him I read, chap. 37: “So that the joining of his bones shone like the sun.” But the royal manuscript has ὡς ὅλον διαφαίνεσθαι αὐτοῦ, “so that his whole [body] appeared through.” FRONTO.].

His devoted disciples also report the following among the accounts of his virtue: for twenty-five full years he never turned toward the west, although the entrance to his cave was situated at the summit of the mountain. Even after the sixth hour he never saw the sun, which hung over his head, decline toward the west; nor did he see the stars that rise in the west for twenty years.

This great athlete of endurance, from the time he entered the cave, did not descend from the mountain until he was buried.

These are the heavenly achievements of the crowned and unconquered athlete Elpidius, who now dwells with those like him in paradise.

## CHAPTER CIX. The Life of Abbot Sisinnius

His disciple, named Sisinnius, had come from a servile condition but was free in faith, and was a Cappadocian by birth. We ought also to mention such origins for the glory of Christ, who makes us illustrious by birth and leads us to blessed and true nobility, namely, the kingdom of heaven.

After Sisinnius had for a long time been with blessed Elpidius as a vigorous athlete in the practice of virtue, having learned the man’s virtues and the strength of his labors in ascetic practice over six or seven years, he later shut himself up in a tomb.

After remaining there for three years, he persevered in prayers, neither sitting by night nor by day, nor reclining, nor going outside. He attained grace against demons.

Now he has returned to his homeland and has been deemed worthy of the presbyterate. After gathering a brotherhood of men and women around him, and giving testimony to freedom from passion through an honorable way of life—his masculine desire having been expelled and the softness of women restrained by self-control—the saying written in Scripture was fulfilled: “In Christ Jesus there is neither male nor female; there is neither slave nor free” (Galatians 3).

He is also remarkably hospitable, although he lacks possessions, to the reproach of the rich, who share nothing.

## CHAPTER CX. The Life of Abbot Gaddanas [Note: [Col. 1229C] Gaddanas.] Sozomen, book VI, chap. 34.]

I knew a certain old man, a Palestinian by birth, named Gaddanas, who lived without a roof throughout his entire life. He lived near the Jordan.

When Jewish men, stirred by rivalry, attacked this blessed hermit in the regions around the Dead Sea and invaded him with drawn swords, the following miracle occurred. As one of them raised his sword and wished to bring death upon Gaddanas, the hand of the man holding the sword dried up, and the sword fell from him in such a way that he did not feel it.

This aid was brought by God to blessed Gaddanas, and such was the way of life of the blessed man until the end of his life.

## CHAPTER CXI. The Life of Abbot Elias

Again, a certain highly approved monk named Elias lived in a cave in the same region. Since his life was most honorable and especially religious, he devoted himself to self-control and prayer, receiving everyone who came with kindness.

One day several brothers came to him, since they had to pass that way, and he ran out of bread. He solemnly affirmed to us:

“I was nearly dead from lack of food. I then entered my cell, overcome with grief because I did not know how I could fulfill, as far as possible, the measure of charity toward those who had arrived. There I found three fresh loaves. I joyfully took them and set them out.”

When twenty men had eaten to satiety, one loaf remained. After I had taken it up, I used it for twenty-five days.

This was accomplished by the Lord’s grace with the hospitable Elias, whose rewards for his labors are prepared with the gracious Lord.

## CHAPTER CXII. Concerning Sabbatius

A certain layman named Sabbatius, a native of Jericho, had a wife. Out of fear of God he loved the monks so greatly that by night he himself visited the cells and the whole desert. At each monastery he placed outside one measure of dates and a sufficient quantity of vegetables, since those who practice asceticism in the Jordan do not eat bread.

He was an “innkeeper for the monks” [Note: [Col. 1229C] “An innkeeper for the monks.” Τούτῳ δὲ τῷ δεξιωτῇ τῶν μοναχῶν. Sabbatius performed a twofold service for the monks: he received them as they passed by into his lodging, and he carried the necessities to their cells. Hervetus translated it “a right-hand servant arranging the table,” a task for which the single word εὐτράπεζος, which follows, is sufficient.].

When one day he had brought the saints what was necessary for their ascetic practice and for a well-furnished table, a lion, moved by the malice of the enemy, came upon him. The adversary of the monks had stirred up the savage beast against their servant, intending both to deprive them of nourishment and to frustrate this man in his purpose.

When the beast seized him by the stone of one of the monks, it dragged him out and overturned him with its claws. But the one who taught lions to fast in Daniel prevented the lion from devouring the man who kept the commandments, even though it was very hungry.

As a result, after taking the old man’s donkey, it withdrew. He who had given the man his life also satisfied the beast’s hunger.

## CHAPTER CXIII. Concerning the Presbyter Philoromus [Note: [Col. 1229D] Philoromus.] Another Philoromus was a martyr with Philaea under Diocletian; Eusebius mentions him in book VIII, chap. 10, and Nicephorus in book VII, chap. 9. Our Philoromus suffered under Julian. Meursius is wrong to confuse him with the other man.]

The most devout priest and greatest lover of God, Philoromus, we met in Galatia and spent a long time with him. He was a man of exceptionally rigorous discipline. He was born of a slave mother but of a free father. Yet he displayed such nobility of virtue in the formation of Christian life that even those unsurpassed by birth revered his life as equal to that of the angels, as well as the effective power of his discipline.

He renounced the world during the days of the execrable emperor Julian. Freely he spoke with that impious man: the noble athlete of Christ, Philoromus, whom Julian ordered to be shaved and beaten most severely by boys.

[Note: **Beaten most severely.** We have followed the translator of Heraclides, chapter 32 of the *Paradise*: “After he had first been made bald, he ordered him to be beaten by boys; and he endured the punishment of the blows most patiently.” Hervetus’s translation can nevertheless be defended: “and for boys to slap him while he was standing,” which in Greek is κοσσισθῆναι. Suidas: Κόσσος, τὸ ῥάπισμα, “a slap or blow.” Thus above, chapter 29: Ἀπομανεὶς οὖν ἐγὼ ἔδωκα κόσσον, “Therefore, overcome by fury, I struck him a blow.” Heraclides, chapter 40: “I struck him with my right hand.” Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, chapter 30: “He is battered with blows.” Martyrs were sometimes beaten in this way with blows and slaps. FRONTO.]

He bore the matter bravely and patiently, and thanked him for it, as he himself told us. At the beginning, this distinguished man was attacked by the warfare of fornication and gluttony. He said that he overcame the disease that exercised tyranny over him as though he were extinguishing an immense conflagration with abundant water.

[Note: **The disease exercising tyranny.** We have written Τυραννῆσαν τὸ πάθος from the manuscript. The translator seems to have read πλῆθος rather than πάθος, for he translates: “which, exercising tyranny, afflicts the multitude.” Heraclides said: “He overcame the diseases of soul and body in such a way as if someone were extinguishing an immense fire with the strongest waters.” FRONTO.]

He did so by practicing the strictest continence: carrying an iron weight, shutting himself in, abstaining from food and from wheat bread, and, in a word, from everything cooked. In all these practices he conducted himself bravely and endured them for eighteen years.

[Col. 1195D] When he had conquered it, he was able to sing the hymn of victory, saying:

“I will exalt you, Lord, because you have received me, and have not made my enemies rejoice over me” (Psalm 29).

Attacked in various ways by the spirit of fornication, he persevered for forty years in the monastery. He himself told us:

“For thirty-two years I touched no fruit. But when,” he said, “timidity had attacked me with the greatest force, so that I was afraid even during the day, I shut myself up for six years in a tomb; and in that way I prevailed, waging war through endurance against the spirit that imposed this slavery upon me.”

The blessed Bishop Basil took great care of this distinguished man. He delighted in his austerity, steadfastness, and diligence in work. Even to the present day he has not withdrawn from pen and paper, although he is eighty years old.

This blessed man said:

“From the time I was initiated and reborn through Spirit and water until the present day, I have not eaten another person’s bread for nothing, but only bread prepared through my own labors.” And, speaking before God—

[Note: **Speaking before God.** The Greek is Ὡς ἐπὶ Θεοῦ ἡμᾶς ἔπεισεν. The translator of Heraclides renders it obscurely: “as he used to persuade us before God.” Hervetus is still more obscure: “but the one who came to us from his own means, divinely.” Ὡς ἐπὶ Θεοῦ has the same force as “I speak before God,” as above, chapter 16: ὡς ἐπὶ Θεοῦ ἀμφοτέρους εἶδον, which Heraclides renders, “I speak before God to you both.” And chapter 30, concerning Adolius: “For I speak truly under God.” And chapter 2 of this *Lausiac History*: ἐπὶ Θεοῦ μάρτυρος οὐκ ἔγνων τοῦτον, “I call God as witness that I never knew him.” FRONTO.]

—he assured us that he had given two hundred and fifty solidi from the work of his hands to those who were crippled and maimed, and that he had never wronged anyone.

He came on foot as far as Rome to pray at the shrine of the holy martyrs Peter and Paul. He also reached Alexandria, after vowing to visit the shrine of the venerable athlete Mark. “I was considered worthy,” he said, “to come twice on my own feet to Jerusalem for the sake of my vow, to honor the holy places; and I myself supplied the expenses.”

He told us this so that we might derive benefit from it:

“I do not remember ever having withdrawn in spirit from my God.”

Such were the contests of this blessed Philoromus, and in them lies his unconquered victory. The end of his blessed labors is rewarded him: an unfading crown of glory.

## CHAPTER CXIV. The Life of the Blessed Severian [Note: **Severian.** What is here given as “in Ancyra of Galatia” is, in the Greek Venetian manuscript, τῇ Καισαρείᾳ τῆς Καππαδοκίας, “in Caesarea of Cappadocia.”] and His Wife

In Ancyra of Galatia, in that very place, I happened to speak with a certain Severian, one of the *comites*, together with his wife Bosphoria; I did not, however, have extensive personal knowledge of them. They were filled with great good hope and deprived their children of their possessions, truly looking toward the future.

For they spent the income from their estates on the needy. They had four sons and two daughters, to whom they gave no property—

[Note: **No property.** He said Οὐδὲν κτῆμα, not οὐδὲ κλῆμα, as was misprinted in the Lyon edition. The translator extracted from a manuscript an even less suitable version: “to whom they did not give even a vine-shoot”; but the Royal manuscript has κτῆμα, “property,” just as shortly afterward Palladius says: τοὺς καρποὺς κτημάτων ἡμεῖς κομισόμεθα, “we shall gather the fruits of our possessions.” Heraclides, chapter 54 of the *Paradise*: “to whom they did not hand over even a single ounce.” FRONTO.]

—except to the daughters who had married. To their remaining children they said:

“After our death, everything will be yours. But as long as we remain alive, we shall gather the fruits of our possessions, distributing them to churches, monasteries, hostels, and all the needy. Their prayers will obtain eternal life for both you and us and for our children in exchange for this temporary and laborious life” (Ecclesiasticus 21:6).

Their outstanding virtue was also evident in this. When there was a great famine, which penetrated the entrails of all people, they then converted the heretics who were present to right belief. For when they had opened their granaries on many estates, they provided food for the poor. Thus, through their indescribable goodness, those who held heretical opinions were brought into one harmony of right faith, giving thanks to God for their simple faith and boundless benevolence.

Their other discipline was admirable. Their clothing was most respectable and frugal; their manner of life was exceedingly spare, indeed beyond description. Their expenses were very small, and they were content with the modest provision that life required. They practiced devotion to God in a wondrous manner. They spent much time in the countryside, always avoiding cities and the vices that arise from them, lest they draw civil disturbances upon themselves through pleasant intercourse with the crowds and fall away from God’s purpose.

Because of all these deeds of right living performed by these blessed people, they now behold with enlightened eyes the eternal blessings prepared by the glory of God.

## CHAPTER CXV. The Life of the Monk Eleemon

In this city we saw a monk who refused to accept the rank of priest. He had adopted this purpose after a short period of military service. At the age of twenty, he entered upon his discipline of life and adopted this way of living: he remained with the city’s most holy bishop.

He is so kind and merciful that he even goes around the cities and shows compassion to those in need. He neglects neither the prison, nor the hospital, nor the poorhouse, nor rich nor poor, but brings assistance to everyone. Among the rich, whom he regards as harsh and merciless, he speaks of mercy; for each of the needy he provides what is necessary; he makes peace between those who are quarrelling; he supplies clothing to the naked and brings medicines to the sick for their treatment.

What ordinarily occurs in all great cities also occurs there. In the church portico lies a multitude of crippled and maimed people begging their daily food; some have not married, while others have married.

One day it happened that the wife of one of them gave birth in the portico, in the middle of winter. As she cried out when she was pierced by unbearable pain, this blessed man, who was praying in the church, heard her howling. Leaving his customary prayers, he went out and looked around. When he found no one to assist her in this necessity, he himself acted as midwife, not shrinking from the unpleasantness associated with women giving birth; the woman’s insensibility was granted to him by this deepest act of charity.

The value of the clothing in which he is dressed is not even one obol; his food competes with his clothing in poverty. He does not allow himself to devote time to a book, compassion drawing him away from reading. If one of the brothers gives him a book, he immediately sells it and distributes the proceeds to the poor.

To those who asked him, “Why do you sell these things?” he would say:

“How can I persuade my teacher that I have learned his art accurately unless I use the very means by which to practice that art properly?”

[Note: A similar saying occurs in the following chapter and above, in Pelagius, book 6, number 5, and Rufinus, book 3, number 70, under the name of Serapion.]

This immortal man, having continued in this activity to the present, left his name as a perpetual source of remembrance to the whole surrounding region. He himself, enjoying eternal joy in the kingdom of heaven and receiving rewards worthy of his blessed labors, now rejoices with every kind of delight in the presence of the rewarder of good works—he who here fed the hungry and gave clothing to the naked.

## CHAPTER CXVI. The Life of Abba Bisarion [Note: **Bisarion.** Various sayings of Bisarion occur throughout the *Lives of the Fathers*. What follows here concerning the book that was sold is related by Nicephorus, book 11, chapter 43, from Evagrius, with the name suppressed.]

There was an old man named Bisarion, without possessions and merciful. When he came to a certain village, he saw a naked beggar lying dead in the marketplace. He himself wore one tunic, in accordance with the evangelical tradition, and a small shoulder-cloth; for he possessed nothing apart from this necessary covering.

He also always carried a small Gospel under his armpit, either to test himself—to see whether he continually obeyed the Lord’s voice—or rather because he carried the word that he had put into practice.

This man lived such an admirable life, and without any disgrace, that he legitimately completed a heavenly journey as though he were an earthly angel.

When he saw the corpse, he immediately removed his shoulder-cloth and clothed the dead man with it. After he had gone a short distance, he met a naked man in need. He stopped, arguing with himself and reasoning as follows:

“How am I, who have renounced the world, clothed, while my brother is stiffening with cold? If I allow him to die, I shall certainly be responsible for my neighbor’s death. What then? Shall I remove my garment, tear it, and distribute part of it, or shall I give the whole of it to him who was made in the image of God? But what use will the torn portion be to him or to me?”

After debating with himself, he said:

“Will we suffer any harm if we do more than has been commanded?”

Thus this noble athlete, with a ready and cheerful spirit, called the poor man into the vestibule. After sending him away clothed, he stood naked, covering himself with his hands, kneeling and sitting down, possessing under his armpit only the word that makes the rich rich.

A passing *irenarch*—

[Note: **Irenarch.** That is, a man concerned with public peace and security, a suppressor of banditry. See the *Onomasticon*.]

—recognized the old man. He said to his companion nearby:

“Look over there. Is that not the old man Abba Bisarion?”

When the other replied, “Indeed it is,” the irenarch dismounted from his horse and asked the saint:

“Who stripped you?”

He, extending the Gospel with his right hand, said:

“This stripped me.”

Immediately the irenarch removed his own clothing and clothed the perfect soldier. Then, carrying what was in effect a small monastic garment, he withdrew, hiding himself from the world. He avoided the praise of the man who had seen his manner of life, concealing the honor that comes from secrecy and awaiting it from the One who is hidden.

After this man had rightly fulfilled every evangelical command, and had nothing of this world remaining in his mind, he advanced toward the more perfect fulfillment of the divine sayings. When he saw a poor man while passing by, he hurried to the marketplace. After standing there for a short time, he sold the Gospel.

A few days later, the disciple of the abba who was with him, named Dulas, asked the old man:

“What happened to the little book, Abba?”

The old man gently spoke to him a very beautiful and wise word, saying:

“Do not be sad, brother. In order that we may have confidence there, I sold the very word that was always saying to me: ‘Sell what you have and give to the poor’” (Mark 10; Luke 18).

There are also very many other deeds accomplished through the virtue of this great Father. May we too be considered worthy, through the grace of Christ, to have a share with him. Amen.

## CHAPTER CXVII. The Life of the Blessed Melania [Note: **Melania.** See the preliminary material to book 2, where her life and pilgrimage are discussed according to the account of Rufinus, as Baronius believes.]

I considered it necessary in this book also to remember manly and honorable women, to whom God granted rewards equal to those of men who lived virtuously, and returned to them the crown of those who pleased him. This was so that the soft and delicate might not become more negligent and seek a pretext and excuse, as though they were weaker for the contests of virtue and for living honorably.

I saw many devout and religious women, and met very many virgins and widows distinguished for virtue. Among them was the most blessed Melania the Roman—

[Note: **Roman.** In Greek: Σπάνη ἦν τὸ γένος ἤγουν Ῥωμαίη, “she was Spanish by race, that is, Roman.” The translator of Heraclides seems to have intended: “the blessed Melania, descended from Spanish or urban stock.” For in Paul we read, Romans 15:24: ἐὰν πορεύσωμαι εἰς τὴν Σπανίαν, “when I begin to depart for Spain”; and in Gellius, book 9, chapter 13, for “Spanish sword” they restore *spanico gladio*; and in Jerome, on Isaiah 64, “of Spain and Lusitania.” Likewise above, chapter 16, Σπανόδρομος, in Heraclides: “a Spanish merchant.” FRONTO.]

—who was the daughter of Marcellus the consul—

[Note: **Marcellus the consul.** Μαρκελλίνου τοῦ ἀπὸ ὑπάτων, “of Marcellinus, from the consuls.” The translator of Heraclides renders it: “daughter of a certain Marcellinus, an ex-consul,” more suitably than Hervetus, “daughter of Marcellus the consul.” See the *Onomasticon*.]

—and the wife of a man who held great authority, whose name I do not remember correctly.

When she was a widow, at the age of twenty-two—

[Note: **Twenty-two.** So both Heraclides and the Greek text. Hervetus had “she was only twenty.”]

—she was considered worthy of divine love. Without saying anything to anyone—for at that time, while Valens held the empire, such things were forbidden—she arranged for her son to be named her guardian. Then, taking her movable goods and loading them onto a ship with several male and female servants, she sailed swiftly to Alexandria.

After selling her possessions there and converting them into coined gold, she entered the mountain of Nitria and met the holy Fathers Pambo, Arsisius—

[Note: **Arsisius.** In Greek, Ἀρσίσιον. Hervetus had “Orsisius.”]

—and the great Serapion, Paphnutius of Scetis, Isidore the Confessor, bishop of Hermopolis, and Dioscorus. She spent about half a year among them, traversing the desert and seeing all the saints.

After this, when the Augustal of Alexandria had exiled Isidore, Pissimus, Adelphius—

[Note: **Pissimus and Adelphius.** In Greek, Πισσίμιον and Ἀδέλφιον. Hervetus had “Pitimium and Adelus.”]

—and Paphnutius, Pambo, and among them also Ammonius Parotes, or “the One-Eared,” together with twelve bishops, priests and clerics, and anchorites—in all, one hundred and twenty-six persons—to Palestine, around Diocaesarea, she herself followed them, supplying from her own funds the expenses of their needs and providing everything.

When the ministers were forbidden to serve them, as they related—for I had met the holy Pissimus, Isidore, Paphnutius, and Ammonius—this courageous woman, dressed in a slave’s *caracalla*—

[Note: **A slave’s *caracalla*.** The Greek Augustan and Parisian manuscripts have παιδαρίου καρακάλλιον, “a little caracalla of a boy”; the Venetian has καρακάλλιον δούλου, “a slave’s caracalla”; Beractides has “a child’s tunic.” See the *Onomasticon*.]

—brought them in the evening what was necessary for their use.

When the governor of Palestine learned of this and wanted to fill his purse, he hoped that he could frighten her—

[Note: **That he could frighten her.** Προσεδόκησε ταύτην καπνίσαι. One manuscript gave ταύτην καταπονήσαι, “to wear her down with labor, to exhaust her.” But elsewhere the same codex had καπνίσαι, and the translator of Heraclides seems to have read no differently: “believing that he could fill his purse with some smoke and terror from her money.” And afterward: “Therefore you are unable to frighten me in any way.” Hervetus: “he hoped that he might sting her eyes with smoke”; but metaphorically καπνίζειν here has the same meaning as “to exhaust” or “to terrify.” You have a similar attempt by another provincial governor in Acts 24:27, “hoping that money would be given to him by Paul.” FRONTO.]

—and, detaining her, threw her into prison, not knowing her freedom.

She said to him:

“I was the daughter of the one man and the wife of another, who was illustrious by birth on earth; but now I am Christ’s slave. Do not despise my humble clothing. If I wish, I can raise myself up. Nor can you frighten me, nor take anything from my possessions. Therefore, lest through ignorance you fall into some offense, I have explained to you who I am.

“For dealing with the foolish one must use pride of spirit, as with a dog or a hawk, and at the proper moment set it against their arrogance.”

When the judge had heard this, he excused himself, bowed before her, and ordered that she associate with the holy men without any hindrance.

## CHAPTER CXVIII. The Life of the Priest Ruffinus [Note: **Ruffinus.** Palladius the Origenist, and Gennadius and Cassian, who favored the Pelagians, exalted Ruffinus with many praises. But Saint Jerome continually attacked Ruffinus as a heretic, and it is proper that we too approve the judgment of the Roman Church itself. For Saint Gelasius I said in the Roman council of seventy bishops: “But since blessed Jerome censured Ruffinus in certain matters concerning free choice, we hold those opinions which we know blessed Jerome to have held. And not only concerning Ruffinus, but also concerning all those whom the man so often mentioned reproved with zeal for God and reverence for the faith.” Thus Saint Gelasius. Volumes 4 and 5 of the *Ecclesiastical Annals* present Ruffinus’s affairs most faithfully, excerpted from approved authors. Thus far the frequently cited master of the sacred palace.]

After the exiles had been recalled, she built a monastery in Jerusalem and lived there for twenty-seven years, with a community of fifty virgins.

With her lived the most noble, most similar in character, and most steadfast Ruffinus from Aquileia, a city of Italy. He was later considered worthy of the priesthood; among men there was found no one more learned or gentler.

For twenty-seven years they received those who came to Jerusalem because of a vow—bishops, monks, virgins, married people, persons of distinction, people of private status, and everyone who arrived—and supported them at their own expense.

They also assisted the schism—

[Note: **Schism.** This passage, which has been badly corrupted, should be restored in a remarkable way. The translator seems to have read σχῆμα rather than σχίσμα, for he translates: “They also assisted the way of life that follows Paulinus.” See also Sozomen, book 4, chapter 26.]

—that followed Paulinus, comprising the monastic life of about four hundred men. They persuaded and brought into the Church every heretic among the Pneumatomachi—that is, those who wage war against the Holy Spirit. Honoring the clergy who were in that place with gifts and food, they passed their lives without offending anyone, but helping almost the whole world.

I have already spoken briefly above of the admirable and holy woman Melania. Nevertheless, I shall append the rest—or rather, what I remember—of her virtues: namely, the indescribable benevolence of this most religious woman. Having woven for herself through her labors the blessed garment of incorruption, and having fashioned and put on her own head, from her own funds, the unfading crown of glory, she departed from this life to the Lord with great confidence.

If I wished to recount what I know as I begin to narrate the remarkable deeds of this blessed woman, time would fail me. I do not think that even a flame of fire, if it fell upon abundant fuel, could consume as much wealth as she spent on the needy, seized by heavenly desire.

This is not something I alone can report, but also those who inhabit Persia, Britain, and all the islands. No part of the world—neither West, nor East, nor North, nor South—was without the benefactions and gifts of this immortal woman.

For thirty-seven years she received guests and supplied from her own resources what they needed: to churches, monasteries, hostels, prisons, and, in a word, no one who came to her failed to receive some portion of her wealth. Her relatives, her own son, and her stewards supplied her every year with money, providing oil like that of a bright lamp, so that, kindling a flame with the radiant light of almsgiving, she might illuminate everyone.

Although she persevered so greatly in hospitality, she did not possess even a palm’s breadth of land. Nor was she drawn away from her love of solitude by longing for her son; nor did the desire for her only-begotten son—

[Note: **Only-begotten.** The Greek is μονογενοῦς. Yet it should be said and translated “only.” This is correctly rendered by the old translator of Heraclides, for she had two other children as well.]

—separate her from charity toward Christ.

Nevertheless, through her prayers the young man attained the highest learning, was most distinguished in character, entered an honorable and illustrious marriage, and obtained worldly honors. He also had two sons—

[Note: **He also had two sons.** Meursius’s edition has ἔσχε δὲ τέκνων δύο δικαίωμα. Hence the notes state that one should read τέκνων τριῶν δικαίωμα, since the Roman law of three children was well known and the error arose from confusion between β and γ. But the Royal manuscript gives the true reading, τέκνων δυάδα, “a pair of children,” supported by Heraclides: “a marriage from which he also had two sons.” Hervetus’s book, which the translator used, agrees. FRONTO.]

—who testified that the marriage was legitimate.

[Col. 1201A] Many years later, when she heard about the condition of her granddaughter—that she had married and wished to renounce the world—she feared that they might be drawn into some evil doctrine, heresy, or wicked life. At the age of sixty, the old woman boarded a ship and sailed from Caesarea to Rome, a journey of twenty days.

While there, she instructed in the catechesis and made Christian the most blessed and highly esteemed Apronianus, who was a pagan—

[Note: **Apronianus.** The Greek Augustan, Venetian, and Parisian manuscripts have Ἀπρονιανόν. Hervetus printed “Aprianus.”]

—and persuaded him to practice continence even with his wife, who was his sister’s daughter, named Avita.

After Melania had also confirmed her granddaughter, Melania, together with her husband Pinianus—

[Note: **Pinianus.** Πιννιανῷ. Hervetus incorrectly had “Aprianus.”]

—and had instructed her daughter-in-law Albina, the wife of her son—

[Note: **Son.** The Venetian Greek has ἀδελφοῦ, “of her brother.”]

—and persuaded all of them to sell what they possessed, she led them out of Rome and brought them to the honorable and tranquil harbor of life.

Thus she fought against beasts—namely, the members of the senatorial order and their wives—who prevented her from renouncing the rest of her houses. Christ’s slave said to them:

“Children, more than four hundred years ago it was written: ‘It is the last hour’ (1 John 2). Why, then, do you willingly and deliberately linger in the vanity of life? Perhaps the days of the Antichrist will come, and you will not be able to enjoy your wealth and the possessions of your ancestors.”

When she had liberated them all by these words—

[Note: **Had liberated them.** I have supplied certain words here from the Greek. In the Venetian codex was: Ἤγαγεν ἐπὶ τὸν μονήρη βίον καὶ τὸν Πουπλίου δὲ υἱὸν τὸν νεώτερον κατήχησε, “She led him to the solitary life and instructed Publicus’s younger son in the catechesis.” Heraclides likewise has this, though the name Publicus is absent. The Greek Augustan codex has Ποπληκόλα; the Parisian, Ποπλίκολα, in place of Πουπλίου.]

—she brought them over to monastic life. After instructing the younger son, Publicola, she took him to Sicily. Having sold all her remaining possessions and received the proceeds, she brought them to Jerusalem. After distributing her wealth, she died within forty days in a good old age and with the greatest gentleness, overflowing with alms and leaving behind a monastery and its expenses in Jerusalem.

After all those who had been instructed in the catechesis by the blessed Melania had departed from Rome, a barbarian storm—one that had long ago been foretold even in the prophets—burst upon Rome. It left not even bronze statues in the forum, but ruined everything by barbarian insolence and plunder, so that Rome, which for twelve hundred years had been most beautiful and most populous, was destroyed and became deserted. As the Sibyl says, it became ῥύμη, that is, “a village,” rather than Rome.

Then those who had been instructed in the catechesis and had not opposed her praised God, who through the transformation of circumstances had convinced the unbelieving that, while all the others had been reduced to slavery, those families alone had been saved who, through the zeal of the blessed Melania, had become holocausts to the Lord. The others, who had opposed their salvation, were held fast by a useless repentance.

## CHAPTER CXIX. The Life of the Younger Melania [Note: **The younger Melania.** See the account of her pilgrimage in the preliminary material to book 8.]

Since I promised that I would report also on Melania’s daughter, it is necessary now to fulfill my obligation. It would not be right to disregard the life of the younger Melania in the flesh, or to pass over in silence the great virtue of the granddaughter of the elder Melania, which perhaps far surpasses that of prudent and diligent old women.

Though young in age, she was old in her disposition toward piety. Her parents gave her unwillingly in marriage, joining her to the leading man of the city of Rome. Always stirred by the stories of her grandmother, she was so deeply wounded that she could not devote herself to marriage.

When two male children were born to her and then died, she began to hate marriage so greatly that she said to her husband Pinianus—

[Note: **Pinianus.** The Augustan Greek has Πιννιανῷ; the Parisian, Πινιανῷ; the Venetian, Ἀπρινιανῷ or Ἀσπρινιανῷ. Hervetus had “Pipianus.”]

—the son of Severus—

[Note: **Son of Severus.** In the life of Saint Melania preserved by Metaphrastes, 31 December, “the brother of Severus.”]

—who had been one of the prefects:

“If you wish to live with me according to the rule of continence, I acknowledge you as my master and confess that my life is in your power. But if this seems burdensome to you, as you are young, keep all my possessions for yourself and leave me alone, free in body, so that I may satisfy the desire that comes from God—having become the heir of my grandmother’s virtue, which comes from God and whose name I also bear.

“For if God had wished us to remain in this world and enjoy worldly things, he would not have taken away from me the children born to me while they were still immature.”

After they had long disputed with one another, God later took pity on the young man and instilled in him also a zeal for religion, so that he too renounced the world’s earthly substance. Thus what the Apostle wrote was fulfilled:

“What do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband?” (1 Corinthians 7).

She had married the man at the age of thirteen and had lived with him for seven years. In the twentieth year of her life she renounced the world.

First, she gave all her silk shoulder-cloths—

[Note: **Shoulder-cloths.** The Greek has ἡμιφόρια. See the *Onomasticon*.]

—and coverings to the altars, as Olympias also did. After cutting up her remaining silk garments, she made various ecclesiastical furnishings.

She entrusted her silver and gold to a certain Paul, a priest and Dalmatian monk—

[Note: **Priest.** The Venetian Greek adds καὶ μοναχῷ Δερματησίῳ, “and to the Dalmatian monk”; the Parisian has Δαλματησίῳ. The translator of Heraclides has “to the Dalmatian monk.” I have accordingly added it to the text.]

—and sent it by sea to the East. To Egypt and the Thebaid she distributed ten thousand solidi; to Antioch and the regions around it, ten thousand solidi; and to Palestine, fifteen thousand solidi.

She herself supplied churches in the West, monasteries, hostels, and all the needy, and she supplies them still with four times as much, as God knows, rescuing them through her faith from the mouth of the lion—

[Note: **From the mouth of the lion.** Fronto says that, speaking of Alaric, she alludes to the Apostle’s words, 2 Timothy 4:17: Ἐρρύσθην ἐκ στόματος λέοντος, “I was delivered from the mouth of the lion.” Eusebius, in the *Chronicle*, year 2427 of Abraham, approximately A.D. 413: “Rome, once the conqueror of the world, was captured by the Goths under their leader Alaric.”]

—Alaric, through her faith (2 Timothy 4:17).

She freed eight thousand slaves who wished to be freed. The others refused and preferred to remain with her brother—

[Note: **Brother.** That is, her husband Pinianus. Elsewhere, “brother” is now used in the ordinary sense, unless she also had a true brother to whom this could refer.]

—of their own accord.

After selling all the possessions she had in Spain, Aquitania, Tarraconensis, Gaul, and other cities, she distributed them, down to as little as three solidi. But what she possessed in Sicily, Campania, and Africa she retained for herself, so that she could support monasteries and the needy.

This is the wisdom concerning money of Melania the younger, who was supremely religious and had acquired an old woman’s understanding.

Her discipline was as follows: she ate every other day, and at first every fifth day, serving her maidservants in various ways; she also made them disciplined practitioners together with herself.

She herself led many of her relatives to divine zeal and caused them likewise to worship God religiously.

This is the life of the younger Melania, through our Lord Jesus Christ.

## CHAPTER CXX. Concerning Albina [Note: **Albina.** The holy Jerome discusses her in various letters.]

[Col. 1203A]

She also had with her her mother Albina, who practiced the same discipline and likewise distributed her money separately. They lived in the countryside, sometimes in Sicily and sometimes in Campania, with fifteen eunuchs, virgins, and maidservants.

## CHAPTER CXXI. Concerning Pinianus [Note: **Pinianus.** The Venetian Greek manuscript has Ἀπρινιανός, Aprinianus; the Augustan, Πιννιανός, Pinnianus; the Parisian, Πινιανός.]

Likewise Pinianus, formerly her husband and now her like-minded helper in the work of virtue, practiced the discipline with thirty monks. He read the divine Scriptures and devoted himself to cultivating a garden and to discussions.

When we came to Rome because of the blessed Bishop John, they showed us no small honor: they refreshed us, received us with the most abundant provisions for our journey, and summoned us to the eternal life of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the formation of an excellent life.

## CHAPTER CXXII. Concerning Pammachius [Note: **Pammachius.** The Venetian Greek manuscript has Μάλχιος or Μάλαχιος, Malchius or Malachius.]

A man from the former proconsuls, named Pammachius, was related to these people. After renouncing the world, he lived an excellent life. While alive he distributed part of his wealth; at his death he left the rest to the poor.

## CHAPTER CXXIII. Concerning Macarius [Note: **Macarius.** The Venetian Greek manuscript has Ἀγάθων, Agathon.]

Similarly, there was also a certain Macarius, from the vicariate [Note: [Col. 1232A] “From the vicariate.” The Venetian Greek manuscript has ἀπὸ βρικίων; the Paris manuscript, ἀπὸ βικαρίας; Heraclides, “from the vicars.” See the *Onomasticon*.].

## CHAPTER CXXIV. Concerning Constantius [Note: [Col. 1232A] “Constantius.” Here he is called an assessor, which in Greek is συγκάθεδρος, “one who sits with another; an assessor.” Heraclides’ translator has “counselor.” See our Jacobus Sirmondus, on Sidonius, book I, letter 3.].

[Col. 1203C]

Constantius also was an assessor of the prefects of Italy, a distinguished and highly learned man, who attained the summit of piety and religion. I believe that he is even now still in the flesh, practicing an excellent rule of life and awaiting the blessed life that is subject to no destruction.

## CHAPTER CXXV. Concerning Paula [Note: [Col. 1232A] “Paula.” What nonsense the raging Origenist Palladius babbles against the holy Jerome and holy Paula! Their holiness is all the more illustrious because Palladius’ wickedness is all the more detestable. John Maria, master of the sacred palace, advises that this be written here.] the Roman woman.

Among them was also Paula the Roman, mother of Toxotius and wife of N., exceedingly well suited to the spiritual ordering of life. A certain Dalmatian, Jerome [Note: [Col. 1203D] Palladius slanders the most holy Jerome.], proved an impediment to her. For although she could have surpassed many—not to say all—since she was endowed with an excellent disposition for living a virtuous life, he hindered her through his envy, drawing her toward his own objective.

## CHAPTER CXXVI. Concerning Eustochium

Her daughter, named Eustochium, is still practicing the ascetic life at Bethlehem. I did not meet her. She is said to be exceedingly chaste and to have a community of fifty virgins.

## CHAPTER CXXVII. Concerning Venerea

I also met Venerea, daughter of the count Ballomecius, who properly scattered the burden of the camel and was freed from the wounds that arise from matter.

## CHAPTER CXXVIII. Concerning Theodora [Note: [Col. 1232A] “Theodora.” Nicephorus, book XVII, chapter 5, speaks of another Theodora who embraced monastic life under male attire.]

[Col. 1204A]

And the blessed Theodora, daughter of a tribune, who advanced to such poverty of possessions that she died herself receiving alms.

## CHAPTER CXXIX. Concerning Usia [Note: [Col. 1232A] “Usia.” See Heraclides here, who translates differently.]

In the monastery of Hesycha, near the sea, I knew a woman named Usia, far the most honorable in every respect.

## CHAPTER CXXX. Concerning Adolia

And her sister Adolia, who likewise lived virtuously and, not according to her dignity but according to the capacity of her strength, lived in zeal for God.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning Basianilla

[Col. 1204B]

I also knew Basianilla, daughter of Candianus, master of the soldiers. She practiced virtue with a pious and eager spirit and continues vigorously to pursue her contests even to the present day.

## CHAPTER CXXXII. Concerning Photina

And Photina, a most honorable virgin, daughter of Theoctistus, the presbyter in Laodicea.

## CHAPTER CXXXIII. Concerning Asella

I also saw at Rome Asella, an honorable virgin of God, who grew old honorably in a monastery—a woman exceedingly gentle, who presided over gatherings in which I saw both men and women recently instructed in catechesis.

## CHAPTER CXXXIV. Concerning Avita [Note: [Col. 1232A] “Avita.” Here her husband is said to have been Apronianus; this has been restored from the Greek text. Hervetus had printed “Primianus.”]

[Col. 1204C]

I also saw the blessed and God-worthy Avita, together with her husband Apronianus and their daughter Eunomia, all pleasing God in every respect. They had plainly been transferred from a dissolute and pleasure-loving life to an honorable and continent ordering of life. They were also deemed worthy to sleep in Christ, free from every sin, contending perfectly in the honorable contest and leaving their life behind in good remembrance.

## CHAPTER CXXXV. Concerning Magna [Note: [Col. 1232B] “Magna.” Here she is said to have lived in the city of Ancyra, but in the Venetian Greek manuscript it reads “in Caesarea of Cappadocia.”]

In the city of Ancyra there are many other virgins, indeed as many as ten thousand, and two or more who practice the ascetic life and serve in every discipline of virtue. All the women are renowned and distinguished for the laws of temperance and pursue the divine contest with zeal.

Among them, Magna, a most honorable and excellent woman, holds the first place in piety. I do not know what I should call her: a virgin or a widow. For, forcibly joined to a husband by her mother, she nevertheless kept herself undefiled and untouched by corruption, ensnaring him with various delays and alleging illnesses of the body, according to what her relatives say. Not long afterward her husband died, and she became the sole heir of all his property. Thereafter exchanging temporal things for eternal, she offered her whole self to God, taking the greatest care for the life that always endures.

She gave honorable commands to her servants and led a most laborious life, full of temperance. In public meetings she was so severe that even the most eminent bishops revered her very appearance because of her distinguished piety and religion. She consumed in the fire of poverty the excessive and superfluous mass of her wealth. What remained she assigned for the support of monasteries, poorhouses, guesthouses, churches, the poor, travelers, bishops, orphans, widows, and all who were in need. She never ceased cheerfully to practice piety in secret, both personally and through her most faithful servants, never withdrawing from the church, especially at night, practicing virtue in everything because of her hope in the life that truly is life.

## CHAPTER CXXXVI. Concerning the Virgin [Note: [Col. 1232B] “The Virgin.” The entire account of the virgin who concealed Athanasius for six years is shown to rest on doubtful evidence by strong arguments in volume III of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, under the year of Christ 356. Thus John Maria, master of the sacred palace, notes here.] who received Bishop Athanasius.

[Col. 1205B]

I knew in Alexandria a virgin whom I encountered when she was approximately seventy years old. The entire clergy testified about her that, when she was young—about twenty years old and exceedingly beautiful—those devoted to virtue avoided her because of her beauty, lest it bring upon them some stain through suspicion.

When it happened that the Arians, through Eusebius, who at that time was chief officer under the emperor Constantius, laid snares for the blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, accusing and slandering him with wicked crimes, he avoided being judged by a corrupt tribunal. He did not dare to hide with anyone—not with a relative, a friend, a cleric, or any other acquaintance. But suddenly, when the prefect’s officials had entered the episcopal residence and were searching for him, taking his sticharion, or tunic, and his cloak [Note: [Col. 1232B] “Sticharion and cloak.” Heraclides: “tunic and cloak.” Metaphrastes, in the *Life of Saint Athanasius*, has τὸ στιχάριον καὶ τὸ βίῤῥιν, “the sticharion and cloak.” Hervetus read κηρόν instead of βίῤῥον or βίῤῥιν, and therefore had “wax-cloth” here. See the *Onomasticon*.], at midnight he fled to this virgin.

She was stunned by the novelty of the event and seized with fear. The bishop therefore said to her:

“Since I am being sought by the Arians and accused by them of wicked crimes, I have decided to flee, lest I too fall into ill repute and cast into sin those who wish to punish me. For this reason God revealed to me this night that I could be safe with no one except you.”

Then, in great joy and having cast out all hesitation, since she belonged wholly to the Lord, she concealed the most holy bishop with a ready and eager spirit for six years, as long as the emperor Constantius lived. She washed his feet, removed his excrement, served him in other matters that were useful to him, and lent and supplied him with books.

For six years no one in Alexandria knew where the blessed Bishop Athanasius was living. When the emperor Constantius’ death was announced and the news reached his ears, Athanasius, dressed in an honorable and venerable manner, was again found in the church at night. When everyone saw him, they were filled with immense astonishment, as though they had received him alive from the dead. At the same time, his friends asked him about the hiding place that they had been unable to discover because of their ignorance.

The blessed Athanasius replied to his true friends:

“I did not flee to you for this reason: so that you could swear truthfully that you did not know where I was. Moreover, because of the search, I fled to the woman whom no one could suspect, since she was beautiful and young. In this way I secured two benefits: her safety and mine. I benefited her, and I safeguarded my reputation and security.”

## CHAPTER CXXXVII. The Life of Amma Talida

In the city of Antinoe there are twelve monasteries of women. There I also met Amma Talida, who had been practicing the ascetic life for eighty years, as she herself and her neighbors related. Sixty young women lived with her. They loved her so greatly that, unlike in other monasteries, there was not even a key to the monastery hall: they were all held there by their love for her.

The old woman had advanced to such freedom from passion that, when I entered and sat down, she too entered, sat down beside me, and with great freedom and confidence in Christ placed her hand upon my shoulders.

## CHAPTER CXXXVIII. The Life of Amma Taor

[Col. 1206B]

In this monastery there was a virgin, her disciple, named Taor, who had spent thirty years in the monastery, as those who knew her related. She refused to accept a new garment, a cloak, or shoes, saying:

“I have no need of them, lest I also be compelled to go out.”

All the others went out to church on Sunday for communion, but she remained in the monastery, covered in rags and constantly devoted to her work. She was so elegant in appearance that even men of great steadfastness would almost have been deceived by her beauty, had she not possessed temperance as a notable defense, which brought impudent eyes to fear and modesty through her dignity.

## CHAPTER CXXXIX. Concerning the Virgin Who Had Renounced the World

There was another virgin who devoted herself manfully to the works of the religious life and lived near me. I never saw her face, for, as they say, she had never gone out since she renounced the world. After she had completed sixty years of ascetic practice with her own mother, she was soon to depart this life.

A martyr named Colluthus [Note: [Col. 1232B] “Colluthus.” In former times Saint Basil the Martyr appeared to Saint John Chrysostom and foretold his death.]—who was venerated in those places—appeared to her in a vision and said:

“Today you are going to the Lord and will see all the saints. Come, therefore, and dine with us at the martyr shrine.”

When she rose in the morning and dressed herself, she took bread, olives, and small vegetables in a basket and, after so many years, went outside. When she reached the martyr shrine, she prayed. Having watched throughout the day for a time when no one was inside, and the ninth hour having already arrived, she sat down and said to the martyr:

“Bless my food, holy Colluthus, and accompany me on the road by your prayers.”

After she had eaten and prayed again, she returned home around sunset. Having given her mother Clement’s work, the *Stromata*, on the prophet Amos, she said to her:

“Give this to the exiled bishop.”

And she said to her:

“Pray for me, for I am going to my Lord.”

She died that very night. Although she had suffered neither fever nor headache, but had prepared herself for burial, she commended her spirit into the hands of God.

## CHAPTER CXL. Concerning the Virgin Who Fell and Practiced Repentance

[Col. 1207A]

A certain ascetic virgin lived with two other virgins and practiced the ascetic life for nine or ten years. A certain singer seduced her, and she had sexual relations with him; after conceiving, she gave birth.

When she came to hate intensely the man who had deceived her, she was deeply pierced in spirit and reached such a measure of repentance that, persevering in it, she wished to kill herself by starvation. She prayed about this with tears, entreating God and saying:

“Great God, who bears the sins of us all and the immeasurable wickedness of the whole world; who do not desire the death of sinners or the destruction of those who fall, but have mercy on every creature—for it is your will that all should be saved (Ezekiel 33)—if you also wish me, who am perishing, to be saved, show me your goodness in this matter, and let your wonders now reach me. Command that the fruit of my iniquity, conceived in wantonness and begotten in sin, be taken away and gathered up [Note: [Col. 1232B] “Taken away and gathered up.” In Greek, συνάγεσθαι, “to be gathered.” Thus in Numbers 31, “you shall be gathered to your people.”]. For unless this happens, I will either strangle myself with a noose or throw myself over a precipice.”

As she prayed in this way, she was heard. For the infant who had been born died not long afterward. From that day she no longer met the man who had reduced her to slavery. Instead, devoting herself entirely and conspicuously to continence, she served the sick, the maimed, and the mutilated for thirty years. Thus she appeased God and made him gracious to her, so that it was revealed to a certain holy presbyter that she had pleased God more in repentance than in virginity.

I write this so that we may not despise those who commit many sins but repent wholeheartedly and sincerely. This blessed woman crushed her heart and dissolved her life in humility; she was not despised by the Lord of those who are led to repentance.

## CHAPTER CXLI. Concerning the Presby­ter’s Daughter Who Falsely Accused a Lector, and Concerning Eustathius the Lector

A certain presbyter’s virgin daughter fell in Caesarea of Palestine. The man who had violated her had taught her to accuse a certain lector of the city falsely and to place the blame for her corruption upon him. When she began to show pregnancy, her father examined her, and she named the lector.

When the presbyter heard this, he was troubled and reported it to the bishop. When the bishop heard it, he convened a council of priests, summoned the lector, questioned him about the matter, and investigated the case. Asked by the bishop, the lector did not confess the deed. For how could something not done by him be said to have been done by him?

The bishop, therefore, took this very badly and said to him in a most severe voice:

“You will not confess your fall and perform penance, you wretched man, entirely polluted?”

The lector replied:

“I beg you: I have stated what is true—that this matter has nothing to do with me. I am entirely free of guilt, since I never even thought about it. But if you wish to hear what is not true, I will say: ‘I did it.’”

When he had said this, the bishop removed him from the office of lector.

After this had happened, he fell at the bishop’s feet [Col. 1208A] and begged, saying:

“If this seems good to you, lord bishop—since I have said, ‘Yes, I fell,’ let me be expelled from the ecclesiastical rank and no longer be deemed worthy to be a cleric of your holiness—command that from this time she be given to me in marriage. For I am no longer a cleric, nor is she any longer a virgin.”

When the bishop and the presbyter heard this, her father handed her over to the lector, hoping that the young man would be well disposed toward her and also believing that he could not be drawn away from the relationship.

But when the young man had received her from the bishop and her father and had consoled her, he took her away and placed her in a women’s monastery. He asked the woman who was chief administrator there to tolerate her until she gave birth.

After leaving her in the monastery, the lector [Col. 1208B] withdrew and shut himself in a filthy cell. Undertaking the utmost severity of life, he approached Christ with a contrite heart, amid many tears and groans, saying:

“You, Lord, know my deeds. You know all things; nothing is hidden from you, nor is there any secret place in which anyone can hide from your power, which sees everything. You see all things before they happen. You alone see the depths of thoughts, and every conception of the mind is perceived by you as though it were seen with the eyes. Since you are a keen examiner of thoughts, you judge perfectly.

“You who offer help to those who suffer injustice, who cannot be deceived when you avenge those who are attacked by slanders; you who approve of nothing unjust, while every moment of the balance of justice is always from you. For light, inaccessible, stands perpetually before you, and every human deed is in your sight.

“It is therefore the work of your just and immutable judgment to pronounce my right also.”

As the young man prayed fervently and persevered diligently in fasting, the pains of childbirth came upon her within a short time. When the hour arrived, God’s just judgment also appeared, bringing vehement and intolerable pain upon the woman who had been the false accuser. An immense multitude of groans, indescribable labor pains, and terrifying visions of the punishments of hell besieged the wretched woman violently; and, because of its size, the infant did not emerge from the womb.

The first and second days passed, and the pains became more intolerable. The third and fourth days arrived, and a pain more severe than that of many births followed. The fifth, sixth, and seventh days were dark, and the wretched woman, because of the great pain, was as though in hell. Throughout all these days she remained without taking any food at all and without seeing even the slightest sleep. Amid successive griefs and the most severe torments of pain, after all this, the inflexible heart of the corrupted and false accuser, overcome by God’s power, which is beyond human sight, added confession to her intolerable pains. She cried out in a mournful voice:

“Alas for me, wretched woman! I am coming into danger lest I perish, for I have fallen into two evils: slander and fornication. Having lost my virginity, I have been delivered over to disgrace; and although another inflicted the violation upon me, I accused the lector.”

When the virgins of the monastery heard this, they reported everything to her father. Her father, fearing that he would be condemned as a slanderer if he did not believe her words, remained silent for two days.

Again the wretched woman was afflicted with bitter pains following one another, since she could neither continue to live nor die. When this had passed, the eighth day arose, and again the ninth, darkening her with the most severe and continual dizziness. Since the community could not endure her loud lamentations, they hurriedly reported to the bishop that it was already the ninth day since she had confessed that she had accused the lector and that she could not give birth because she had slandered him.

When the bishop heard this from the virgins, he sent two deacons to the lector, informing him of everything and asking him to pray for her so that the wretched woman might be freed from her distress.

But the excellent young man gave them no answer and did not open [Col. 1209B] the door. From the day he entered the cell, he had not left it, fulfilling his customary rule of fasting and pouring out prayers to God.

His father, however, was moved and took pity on his daughter. He went to the bishop and earnestly begged that prayers be offered for her in the church. When everyone had poured out prayers to the Lord for her, the wretched woman was still not freed from her distress. For the prayers of the man who had been accused through slander, reminding the Lord of his case, prevented him from admitting their prayers.

After these things had happened, the bishop rose and went to the cell in which the lector was staying. When he knocked on the door, the man did not wish to open it. After the bishop had remained outside for a long time, he ordered the door to be removed. They entered and found the young man persevering in prayer [Col. 1209C] and prostrate on the ground.

The bishop begged him earnestly and said:

“Brother Eustathius the lector, since the slander has been brought into the open by God’s providence and your prayers have been heard, have mercy on the woman who sinned against you and who has been tortured by the scourges of suffering. Have mercy now on the wretched woman, and, rising, release what you have bound. She is suffering these things because of your prayers. Ask the Lord to free her from the labor of childbirth.”

When the renowned lector prayed fervently together with the bishop, the wretched woman was immediately freed from her distress and gave birth to the infant. She begged everyone to forgive her iniquity through the intercession of that just man. From then on they all regarded that excellent man as a martyr.

For after he had freed himself from every worldly concern, he attained the highest degree of the life lived in virtue, so that he was deemed worthy of spiritual grace.

We have written these things so that no one may be ensnared by slander in the nets of the enemy and fall into intolerable pains of the flesh, as this false accuser first did. After being freed from the body, she would otherwise have been handed over to eternal and intolerable punishments that would never end.

For the slanderer provokes God to anger. But the one who is accused through slander, bears it with a pious and equitable spirit, and entrusts the exposure of the matter to prayers while awaiting God’s just judgment—as this man, crowned by Christ, did—is both praised, insofar as his case can be told, and held in honor, and receives an eternal crown.

Let us therefore learn carefully how unconquerable are the powers of prayer: prayer strengthens the faithful, takes pity on sinners, bends and moves the Creator of all things, crowns those who conduct themselves rightly in virtue, and grants the kingdom of heaven to those who persevere in it.

## CHAPTER CXLII. The Life of Saint Silvania [Note: [Col. 1232C] “Silvania.” George of Alexandria, in the *Life of Saint Chrysostom*, discusses her. In Greek she is called Σάλβια, “Salvia.”]

At that time it happened that we sailed together from Aelia to Egypt, escorting the blessed virgin Silvania, sister of Rufinus, who had been one of the prefects.

## CHAPTER CXLIII. Concerning Jubinus [Note: [Col. 1232C] “Jubinus.” Heraclides has “Jovinus.”]

Among us was also Jubinus, then a deacon but now bishop of the church of Ascalon, a pious and learned man.

When an exceedingly intense heat had seized us and we had reached Pelusium, it happened that Jubinus took a basin, washed his feet and hands with very cold water, and, after washing, rested on a small hide spread on the ground.
