When she noticed this, like a wise mother concerned for her own son, she reproved his softness, saying:

“Do you, at your age, while your blood is still vigorous, set your mind on pampering your little body to such an extent, without perceiving the harms that result from it? Take courage, take courage. I am sixty years old this year; apart from the extremities of my hands [Note: [Col. 1232C] “Apart from the extremities of my hands.” The reason is added why she washed the extremities of her hands: namely, because the most holy body of Christ was given to be received by those hands. See the *Onomasticon*.], and this because of communion, no foot of mine has touched water, nor my face, nor any of my limbs, even when various illnesses have attacked me. When physicians compelled me to use a bath, I did not resolve to give the flesh its due, neither resting in a bed nor entering anywhere carried in a litter.”

Although she was most learned, she embraced learning with love. She transformed nights illuminated by abundant oil into days, reading through all the works of the ancients who had published commentaries: three million lines of Origen; and two hundred and fifty thousand of Gregory, Stephen, Pierius [Note: [Col. 1232C] “Pierius.” The Venetian Greek manuscript has Πέτρου, “of Peter.”], Basil, and certain other men of outstanding virtue.

She did not read these works superficially or casually, but carefully, reading each book seven or eight times, so that through the words of these authors she might be lifted on high, making herself a spiritual bird through good hope and flying toward Christ, from whom she was to receive immortal rewards.

## CHAPTER CXLIV. Concerning Olympias [Note: [Col. 1232C] “Olympias.” Concerning her, see Sozomenus, book VIII, chapter 24; Nicephorus, book XIII, chapter 24; and George of Alexandria, in the *Life of Saint Chrysostom*. Olympias’ celebrated memory appears in the Greek *Menologion* on July 28:

“Of Saint Olympias, who lived under the emperor Theodosius and his sons Arcadius and Honorius; daughter of Anysius the Second, count; granddaughter of Ablavius the prefect; for a short time bride of Nebridius, who had been one of the prefects. While she was still a virgin, her husband was taken away before consummation, and she remained both virgin and widow, spending all her time in fasts and prayers and benefactions to the poor. Accordingly, she exhausted all her wealth in caring for the priests of Christ, especially Saint John Chrysostom, whom she honored above all.”

The Roman Martyrology, December 17: “At Constantinople, Saint Olympias, widow.”

That she remained a virgin is also attested by Nicephorus, book XIII, chapter 24:

“Although she had been placed in marriage with a husband, she was not entirely deprived of the celibacy of virginity. For after spending twenty months in marriage with him, when death had taken him away, although she was of an age that would not have dishonored a second marriage, she preferred to embrace chastity and remain in it throughout her life.”

Palladius likewise testifies that she remained a virgin in this chapter, chapter 144, and Heraclides, chapter 43. George, *Life of Chrysostom*, chapter 50:

“Having been orphaned of her parents, she was indeed joined to a husband, but the celebrated report about her taught that she did not thereby corrupt the honor of virginal sanctity. After living with her husband for about twenty months, he was summoned away, and, when the debt owed to nature had been paid, he brought his life to an end in so short a time.”

These words are taken from Palladius’ dialogue on the affairs of Chrysostom. Therefore συνουσία ἀνδρός, “association with a man,” in Chrysostom’s second letter to Olympias should be understood as familiar companionship with a husband, not sexual intercourse.] 

[Col. 1210D]

The most venerable and honorable Olympias followed in her footsteps and every virtue of the divine spiritual life. She was devoted with the greatest zeal to the path that leads to heaven and followed the teaching of the divine Scriptures in everything.

According to the flesh she was the daughter of Seleucus [Note: [Col. 1233A] “Daughter of Seleucus.” The *Menologion* just cited has “of Anysius the Second.”], one of the counts; according to the spirit, she was truly a daughter of God. She was the granddaughter of Ablavius, who had been one of the prefects, and for several days the bride [Note: [Col. 1233A] “Bride.” Heraclides’ translator has “daughter-in-law.” The Greek word is νύμφη, which signifies both. Baronius, volume IV, under the year of Christ 388, writes: “The fact that the Greeks in the *Menologion* have her given in marriage to Nebridius, while Palladius—or rather Heraclides, whom Baronius always cites under the name of Palladius, as I said in the fourth section of the general prologue, paragraph 3, since Palladius here calls her a bride—says that she was Nebridius’ daughter-in-law, can be reconciled in this way: she may have been married to the son of that Nebridius, a most illustrious man who under the emperor Constantius was distinguished by the prefecture of the praetorium and whom Ammianus mentions in book XXVII; he too was called Nebridius, and Olympias, of whom we are speaking, may have been joined to him in marriage.” Thus far Baronius. I believe that the discrepancy among the authors arose from differing interpretations, since one translated νύμφη as “daughter-in-law” and another as “bride.” Above, in chapter 118, Albina is called the daughter-in-law of the elder Melania, where the Greek is νύμφη.] of Nebridius, who had been one of the prefects of the city of Constantinople. In reality, however, she was the wife of no one.

She is said to have died a virgin, undefiled, having become a conqueror through the divine Word, and the spouse of every true humility, sharing with and ministering to all who were in need. After she had scattered all those infinite and immeasurable riches, she offered help to everyone without exception or distinction.

No city, countryside, or wilderness remained without the benefactions of this renowned virgin. She supplied churches with gifts assigned for sacrifice, as well as monasteries, coenobitic houses, hospices, prisons, and exiles. In short, she scattered alms throughout the whole world.

This blessed woman advanced to the furthest limit of humility, beyond which nothing more could be found: a life without any empty glory; an appearance entirely without pretense; sincere conduct; a face without cosmetics; a flourishing body; a mind without self-glory; a spirit alien to arrogance; a heart entirely free from agitation; sleepless vigilance; a spirit without curiosity; immeasurable love; a sharing that cannot be comprehended; cheap and despised clothing; boundless continence; right thinking; eternal hope in God; almsgiving that cannot be recounted; the adornment of all the humble.

Many temptations were kindled against her through the activity of him who is evil of his own will and devoid of every good—that is, the devil. For the sake of truth she entered into no small contests and lived long and abundantly amid immense tears, subject to all human beings for the Lord’s sake.

With all piety she submitted to holy bishops, reverenced the presbyterate, honored the clergy, respected ascetic practice, embraced virginity, assisted widowhood, cared for orphans, protected old age, visited the sick, pitied sinners, led the erring back to the way, and showed mercy to everyone. She was especially generous toward the poor. She also provided food for the wives of many unbelievers who were receiving catechetical instruction, and throughout her life she left a name of kindness worthy of perpetual remembrance.

Restoring innumerable crowds of slaves from servitude to freedom, she made them equal in honor to her own nobility—or rather, if the truth must be told, they became nobler through the conduct of this holy woman. For nothing more wretched could be found than her garments; even those who were heavily covered in rags would have considered this holy woman’s clothing unsuitable for themselves.

Her gentleness was so great that it far surpassed even the simplicity of little children. No one living near her ever found in her anything worthy of blame. Her entire non-worldly life was spent in compunction and the frequent outpouring of tears. One could more readily see a spring in summer fail in its streams than see tears fail from the eyes of this woman—eyes that were not lifted toward worldly things but always beheld Christ.

Why should I linger over these matters? The more my mind dwells, as upon a soul hard as stone, on recounting her contests and virtues, the more words will be found to fall short of her deeds. Let no one suppose that I have collected these things about this exceedingly patient woman in a brilliant and grandiloquent manner, seeking out the remains of the most chaste Olympias, who was wholly a precious vessel of the Holy Spirit. I saw the life and angelic discipline of this blessed woman with these very eyes. I was her intimate spiritual friend and extremely close to her relatives, so much so that many of her funds were distributed by me according to her direction.

Therefore, no longer setting my mind on the things of the flesh, she was subject to principalities, obedient to authorities, reverent toward the presbyterate, and honoring the entire clergy. She was also deemed worthy of confession because of the truth, after undergoing many storms caused by persistent refusals.

All the pious people living in Constantinople reckon her life among the confessors, since in the contests concerning divine things she nearly shared the danger of her mother. Having died amid these struggles, she received blessed glory; and, crowned in the endless age, she celebrates her triumph, dwelling forever with the saints and those like herself in mansions subject to no destruction, and confidently receiving from Christ the Lord the rewards of her good works.

## CHAPTER CXLV. Concerning Candida

[Col. 1212B]

After her, the blessed Candida likewise lived in the Lord with equal devotion. She was the wife of Trajan, master of the soldiers. She attained the highest honor, adorned the churches in a manner consistent with reason, revered the bishops in accordance with the dignity of Christ’s sacraments, openly honored all the clergy of Christ, and instructed her daughter in the lot of virginity. She sent her daughter ahead to Christ, the gift of her own womb; afterward she herself also followed her daughter through temperance, chastity, and the distribution of money.

I saw this outstanding woman laboring and grinding throughout the entire night, making the bread of offering with her own hands, to weaken the strength of her body. She said:

“Since fasting is not sufficient, I give it this laborious companion, vigilant wakefulness, so that I may dissolve and enervate Esau-like wantonness.”

She entirely abstained from things possessed of blood and life, except that she consumed fish, oil, and vegetables, and even these only on a feast day. At every other time she was content with oxycrate [Note: [Col. 1233B] “Oxycrate.” In Greek, ὀξυκράματι. Heraclides, chapter 44, has *posca*, “vinegar-water,” as I restored there. See the *Onomasticon*.] and dry bread.

In this severity of life, when this renowned woman had fallen asleep in blessed repose, she now enjoys the eternal goods prepared for those who have loved the life lived in virtue.

## CHAPTER CXLVI. Concerning Gelasia [Note: [Col. 1233B] “Gelasia.” A letter of the divine Jerome to her exists, says the Parisian marginal annotator of Palladius. But I fear that he is mistaken and that he remembered Algasia, to whom Jerome’s letter 151 is addressed.]

Following the zeal of this good woman, the most venerable Gelasia, daughter of a certain tribune, entered the way of truth, piously taking upon herself the yoke of virginity.

Her outstanding virtue is said to have been this: the sun never set upon her anger—against a male slave, a female slave, or anyone else. This blessed woman escaped the way of those who remember injuries received, a way that leads to eternal death. She avoided this evil goad of the devil, namely hatred and ill will. And because she desired the eternal forgiveness of sins, she forgave small offenses, so that she too might find forgiveness for greater ones.

## CHAPTER CXLVII. On Juliana

[Note: [Col. 1234A] Juliana. After Baronius, in volume II, under the year of Christ 205, had recounted from Eusebius, book VI, chapter 3, how Origen, harassed at Alexandria, was compelled repeatedly to change his residence—and how Origen himself mentions these hiding places in Palladius—he adds: “These events must certainly be referred to no other period than the persecution under Severus; for Symmachus’s books had been discovered long before the persecution of Maximinus or Decius. But concerning the interpretation received by Origen from Juliana, Eusebius likewise reports the testimony of Origen himself, in book VI, chapter 12.” Thus far Baronius.]

A certain woman named Juliana, a virgin in Caesarea of Cappadocia, was said to be both exceptionally learned and exceptionally faithful. She received Origen, the writer, when he was fleeing a pagan uprising, concealing him for two years and supporting the man at her own expense and by her own service.

“I found these things in a very ancient book written in verse, which had in fact been written in Origen’s own hand. I myself found this book with Juliana the virgin in Caesarea, and I too—” [Note: [Col. 1234A] “And I too.” The sense is now clear from the Greek manuscript: Origen was concealed, not the book, as Hervetus translated it. Heraclides is correct: “since I was hiding with her.”] “—was concealed with her. She said that she had received it from Symmachus, the Jewish translator.”

It was not foreign to the purpose of this work to record the virtues of these women, so that we may know that, if we wish, gain may be drawn from various circumstances.

## CHAPTER CXLVIII. On a Woman

[Note: [Col. 1234A] “Woman.” Nicephorus, book VII, chapters 12 and 13, concerning virgins who defended their chastity with remarkable skill.]

who was always a virgin and of the highest nobility.

In another very ancient book, written by Hippolytus, who was a companion of the apostles, I found the following account:

[Col. 1213B] There was a most noble and exceedingly beautiful virgin who was practicing at Corinth the life that must be lived according to virtue. At that time she was brought before a judge who was a pagan during the period of the persecutions, because she was said to have attacked the times, the emperors, and the images with insults.

The traffickers in such matters displayed her beauty before the impious judge, a man consumed by mad love for women. He, with the ears of a horse and thoughts of insane love for women, accepted the accusation; and when she had been brought before the wicked man, he was seized by an even more insane passion.

After he had employed every device against her and could not persuade this woman of God [sic], he subjected the brave woman to various tortures. But when he had not achieved what he wanted even by these means—that is, since he could not turn her away from confessing Christ—he raged against her with cruelty. He did not hand her over to the torments of execution; instead, he placed the chaste and temperate woman in a brothel and ordered the man who owned them, saying: “Take this woman for me and bring me three solidi from her every day.”

The man, seeking gold through a shameful business, handed her over to those who wished to use her in the workshop of abominable vice. When those who were held by an insane love of women learned of this, they sat around the workshop of criminal destruction, paying the price of dishonorable activity.

But that most honorable and especially venerable virgin, turning her words toward deception, humbly said to them in supplication:

“I have an ulcer in a hidden place which emits an astonishingly foul odor, and I fear that, because of this repulsive ulcer, you may come to hate me. Therefore grant me a few days, and then you may have me even without payment.”

By these words the blessed woman sent the intemperate men away, having persuaded them. Meanwhile, by constant prayers she sought to appease God, and by contrite supplications moved him to mercy. Therefore God, who knows the thoughts of the heart, observing how earnestly she cared for her chastity, devised something for the salvation of all during those days.

## CHAPTER CXLIX. On Magistrianus

[Note: [Col. 1234A] Magistrianus. I discussed this name above, in book V of Pelagius, booklet VI, no. 2. See the *Onomasticon*.]

A certain young man, Magistrianus, handsome in appearance and devout in mind, was one in whom God had kindled so ardent a spiritual zeal that he even despised death. Under the pretext of sexual indulgence, he went there late in the evening, entered the house of the man who supported those women, and gave him five solidi. He said to him: “Allow me to remain here tonight with this girl.”

After entering a secluded place with her, he said to her: “Rise and save yourself.” Having dressed her in his own garments—a tunic, a shirt [Note: [Col. 1234B] Shirt. In Greek: τοῖς τε καμισίοις, καὶ τῇ χλαμύδι, “both the shirts and the cloak.” Hervetus has: “a tunic, a shirt, and a cloak.” He seems to have had a fuller exemplar; unless, because καμισίοις is plural in Greek, he rendered it by “tunic and shirt.” See the *Onomasticon*.] and a cloak, together with all the other clothing of a man—he said to her: “Go out, covering yourself with the upper part of the cloak.”

When she had done this and fortified herself entirely with the sign of the cross, she went out from that place wholly unviolated and undefiled. She was preserved by the grace of Christ and because of the young man who had freed her from shameful vice at the cost of his own blood.

The next day the matter became known, and Magistrianus was brought before the most savage judge. When the impious man had examined the vigorous athlete of Christ and learned everything, he ordered him to be thrown to the beasts, so that the demon, hostile to evils, might also be put to shame in him.

For when he had intended to subject the brave man to a wicked punishment, he made him a double [F. “in a double manner”] martyr of Christ: he had fought nobly for his own soul and had persevered valiantly in hardships for the sake of that blessed woman. Therefore, by Christ’s kindness, he was judged worthy of double honor and two distinguished crowns.

## CHAPTER CL. On the Wife

[Note: [Col. 1234B] Wife. Concerning the fact that she is said here to have killed herself after taking up a sword, see Augustine, *The City of God*, book I, chapters 17–28, and the opinions of other Fathers in our Leonard Lessius, *On Justice and Right*, book II, chapter 9, doubt 6.]

of a Senatorial Man.

I also remember another story, and it is good not to pass it over. It is said of the rebel Magnentius that he had made a practice of sexual debauchery with many pagan women and had resolved to do the same with Christian women; but they preferred to die rather than betray their chastity.

When he had come into a certain city, he fell in love with the wife of a senator who had been among the prefects. Her husband, seized with fear, said to him: “Send for her; take her.” When the soldiers came to her, the woman said to them: “Wait a little until I arrange my toilette, to which I am accustomed.”

Entering her own bedchamber, she took up a sword and drove it into her own entrails.

Let virgins hear this and blush—those who profess to have Christ as their bridegroom, yet betray him through wicked lust. But may God grant each of us to preserve virginity and, rejoicing, to cry out with the psalmist:

“Fix my flesh in your fear, for I have feared your judgments” (Psalm 118).

And:

“I live, yet it is no longer I who live; Christ, however, lives in me” (Galatians 2).

Let it also be granted that you may say, in chastity:

“I belong to my cousin, and my cousin belongs to me”—

at one time bridegroom, at another brother—so that nothing carnal may be imagined (Song of Songs 6). For if you hear “bridegroom” and “bride,” it signifies a spiritual union with the Father.

We also saw other Fathers and monks throughout Egypt performing many virtues and signs. We do not mention them because of their number, but have narrated a few in place of many (Rufinus, book II, in the epilogue).

What could anyone say about the upper Thebaid, extending toward Syene, where there are exceedingly admirable men and an innumerable multitude of monks, whose way of life no one would believe, since it surpasses human life? They still raise the dead even to this day and walk upon the waters, like Peter; and whatever the Savior accomplished through the holy apostles, he accomplishes now as well.

But because great danger threatened if we went beyond the Lycus, on account of the incursion of brigands, we did not dare to see those holy men. Indeed, we did not see the Fathers mentioned above without danger, nor did we behold these holy women without labor. We first endured many hardships and nearly perished before scarcely managing to see them.

Seven times we fell into mortal danger; but on the eighth occasion evil did not touch us, since God had preserved us completely.

First, for five days and nights we walked through the desert and were nearly exhausted by hunger and thirst. At another time, falling into sharp and rugged marshes that pierced our feet so that the pain became intolerable, we were nearly killed by the cold.

Third, we became stuck in mud up to our waists, and there was no one to rescue us. We cried out these words of blessed David:

“Save me, O God, for the waters have come in even to my soul. I am stuck in the mire of the deep, and there is no firm ground” (Psalm 68);

and:

“Rescue me from the mire, so that I may not become stuck.”

Fourth was the great quantity of water that poured in from the rise of the Nile, when we walked through the waters for four days and were nearly overwhelmed at the mouths of the river. Then we cried out, saying:

“Let not the storm of water engulf me, nor let the deep swallow me” (Psalm 68).

Fifth, we encountered brigands on the seashore as we were traveling toward Diolcos. They pursued us even that far, wishing to seize us, until scarcely a breath remained to us, since they had chased us for ten thousand paces.

Sixth, while sailing on the Nile, we were nearly capsized and drowned.

Seventh was when, in the Mareotic marsh where papyrus grows, we were cast onto a small deserted island. We remained in the open air for three nights and days, with intense cold and rains threatening us; for it was the season of Epiphany.

It is unnecessary to recount the eighth event, yet it is useful. When we had come through a certain place near Nitrea, there was in that region a great hollow in which many crocodiles had remained after the water had withdrawn from the fields. Three crocodiles were stretched out along the edge of the ditch. We approached to look at the beasts, thinking that they were dead, but they immediately rushed upon us.

When we called upon the Lord in a loud voice—“Christ, help us!”—the beasts at once, as though turned away by an angel, hurled themselves into the water.

We hastened at full speed to Nitrea, meditating upon the words of Job, where he says:

“Seven times he will deliver you from troubles, and on the eighth no evil will touch you” (Job 5).

Therefore we give thanks to God, who delivered us from so many dangers and showed us such great spectacles.

## CHAPTER CLI. The Life of the Brother

[Note: [Col. 1234B] Brother. It is nowhere stated who this man was. Was he Heraclides, who published another work under the title *Paradise*?]

who lived with him.

Since I have said only a little about the brother who has lived with me from youth until the present day, I shall now bring this discourse to an end.

I knew him for a long time. When he ate, he was free from every appetite of gluttony; likewise, when he fasted, he was not distressed, since, as I think, he had overcome desire. He was far removed from avarice, always content with what was present, not adorning himself with clothing, despised yet giving thanks, and willing to face dangers for his close friends.

He encountered demons more than a thousand times, so much so that one day a demon made a pact with him and said:

“Make a pact with me that you will sin even once, and whatever woman you name to me in this life—whether noble or rich—I will bring her to you.”

Again, when he had fought with the demon for fourteen nights, as he told me, and the demon had dragged him by the foot during the night, it addressed him, saying:

“Do not worship Christ, and I will not come near you.”

He replied:

“That is precisely why I worship him, and I will glorify him countless times more and pray more often, because his worship afflicts you.”

He visited 106 cities and spent some time in many of them. He had no experience with a woman, not even in dreams, unless he dreamed that he was being attacked by the demon of fornication.

Three times I knew him to receive food from an angel when he was in need. One day, when he did not have even a crumb in the uttermost desert, he found three hot *paxamidia*—twice-baked loaves—in a sheep’s skin. At another time, wine and bread appeared. At yet another time a voice came to him, saying:

“I know that you lack food. Go and receive grain and oil from that man N.”

When he came to the man to whom he had been sent, the man said to him:

“Are you that monk?”

He replied:

“Yes, I am the one you mean.”

The other continued:

“The master of the household has indeed ordered me to give you thirty *modii* of grain and twelve *sextarii* of oil.”

I could boast and proclaim what sort of man he was. I knew him often to weep on behalf of those who were suffering from necessary poverty. He provided whatever he had, except his own body. I also knew him to weep for one who had fallen into sins, and by his tears to lead that person to repentance.

He once told me this:

“I asked God not to prick anyone to compunction—especially among the rich and the wicked—so that they might give me something necessary for my use.”

For me it is enough that I have been judged worthy to remember all these things which I have committed to writing. This did not happen without God’s providence: your mind was moved to order me to write this book—to commit to writing, I say, the life of these holy and blessed Fathers.

But you, most faithful servant of Christ and venerable Lause, my dearest and most truly brotherly head, by reading this book willingly will provide great benefit to your immortal soul, as you embrace in your mind, at the resurrection of the just, the practices, labors, great endurance, and patience in a harshly lived life of these illustrious athletes of upright conduct.

Therefore follow these examples with a ready and joyful spirit, nourished by a good and incorruptible hope, always looking back upon the days that have preceded you as shorter. And pray for me, preserving yourself free from blame and keeping yourself whole—such as I have known and possessed you from the consulship of Tatianus until the present day—and such as I now know you again: improved in character and chosen as prefect of the most devout chamber.

For although you possess such great dignity, such vast sums of money, and such power, you have not acted in a manner worse than the fear of God required. He is dedicated to Christ who heard the devil say:

“I will give you all these things if you will fall down and worship me” (Matthew 4).

But the Lord put him to shame, saying:

“Go behind me.”

Imitating him, you too drove away riches upon the winds and rejected the shadowy glory of the present life. You desired the heavenly and immortal life, the eternal kingdom, enduring glory, and those hidden good things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor entered into the human heart” (Isaiah 64; 1 Corinthians 2).

May the Lord make you an heir of these things with his holy patriarchs and prophets, apostles and martyrs, and with those whom we have mentioned in this book, through the grace of our Savior Jesus Christ, with whom be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.
